## The following are the contents of the first book <note>original: "σύγγραμμα," meaning a written work or treatise</note> of the Preparation for the Gospel. <note>original: "Εὐαγγελικῆς προπαρασκευῆς"</note>

What the promise of the Gospel's subject matter <note>original: "ὑποθέσεως"</note> is.
What the Saving Word <note>The "Saving Word" refers to the Christian message or the Logos.</note> says to us in response to those who attempt to slander our way of life.
That we have not chosen to follow the Saving Word without careful examination.
That our faith concerning the most beneficial matters is not adopted by us without due consideration at the appropriate time.
That it was not by any irrational reasoning of the mind that we withdrew from the error of our ancestral superstition.
The things recorded among the Greeks, and what they say concerning the first creation of the world <note>original: "κοσμοποιΐας," or cosmogony</note>, and why we reasonably withdrew from them.
That the natural philosophers have disagreed concerning first principles, and how we have departed from them with sound judgment.
That the ancients did not develop a theology for anything more than the stars appearing in the heaven.
That they originally had no mythology about gods, nor the setting up of wooden cult images. <note>original: "ξοάνων," referring to "xoana," the primitive wooden statues believed by the ancients to have fallen from heaven.</note>
That the things later rumored and added to the beliefs of the ancients concerning the gods were not a more recent invention.
A summary of the ancient Phoenician theology, and concerning those who wrote it down, and why we have rightly rejected <note>original: "κατεπτύσαμεν," literally meaning to "spat upon" or "treated with contempt."</note> it.

# THE FIRST OF THE FIFTEEN BOOKS OF THE **PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL** BY EUSEBIUS OF PAMPHILUS.
### What the promise of the Gospel's subject matter is.

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap 'T' within a square frame decorated with dense floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>

THINKING it necessary to present what Christianity really is to those who are unaware of it, I promise that the present treatise will encompass the **Evangelical Demonstration** <note>original: "εὐαγγελικὴν ἀπόδειξιν" – This refers to Eusebius's companion work, the *Demonstratio Evangelica*, which followed this "Preparation."</note>. This work I address to you, Theodotus <note>Theodotus was the Bishop of Laodicea and a friend of Eusebius to whom the work is dedicated.</note>, a man beloved of God and a sacred leader among bishops, with my prayers. I do so in the hope that I might obtain assistance from your god-loving service, which will greatly contribute to the subject I have set forth concerning the teaching of the Gospel. 

However, it is first good to clarify what this "radiant Gospel" <note>original: "φαιδρὸν εὐαγγέλιον"</note> intends to reveal. To all people, it brings good news of the highest and greatest blessings—blessings that were proclaimed long ago but have recently shone forth upon all. It does not concern itself with "blind" wealth <note>original: "οὐ τὸν οὐ βλέποντα πλοῦτον" – A reference to the Greek god of wealth, Plutus, who was traditionally depicted as blind.</note>, nor with this brief and suffering-filled life, nor with things belonging to the body and its decay. Instead, it offers what is dear and fitting to souls that possess a rational nature <note>original: "νοεράν οὐσίαν" – literally "intellectual essence."</note>, things to which the affairs of this world are attached like a following shadow. 

The essence of these blessings is Piety <term>eusebeia: a Greek term for religious devotion, godliness, or the proper way to honor the divine</term>—not the kind that is falsely named and full of error, but the kind that inscribes true contemplation into the soul. This is the turning of the mind toward the one and only truly acknowledged God, and a life lived according to His will. From this arises a friendship with Him, followed by a truly god-beloved and thrice-blessed end, which hangs down from the highest power above, is guided toward it, and finally comes to rest within it. 

What could be more blessed than this virtuous and prosperous friendship with God? Is He not Himself the steward and provider of life, light, truth, and all good things to all? Does He not encompass the cause of the existence and life of all things? What could still be lacking for the person who has sought friendship with Him? What could the person lack who is made at home with the Creator of all good things? What could such a person not achieve, who claims the Great Protector and King of All as both a father and a guardian? 

Indeed, one cannot say otherwise: the person who draws near to the King of All through the Divine Word, and who has been deemed worthy of this all-blessed friendship through a knowledgeable piety, will find that all things—soul, body, and external circumstances—are well. This good and saving friendship between God and men was sent down from the all-good God by the **Divine Word** <term>Logos: "The Word" or "Divine Reason," referring here to the second person of the Trinity through whom Christians believe God communicates with humanity</term>, like a boundless...

### The following are contained in the first book of the Evangelical Preparation. <note>original: "Τάδε περιέχει τὸ πρῶτον σύγγραμμα τῆς Εὐαγγελικῆς προπαρασκευῆς."</note>

What the promise of the evangelical <term>subject</term> <note>original: "ὑποθέσεως"; referring to the overall thesis or purpose of the Gospel message.</note> is.
What our custom is to say to those who attempt to slander our affairs.
That we have not chosen to hold the opinions of the <term>saving word</term> <note>original: "σωτηρίου λόγου"; a reference to the Christian message or Logos.</note> without examination.
That our faith concerning the most beneficial things is not taken up at an opportune time without critical judgment.
That it was not with an irrational state of mind that we withdrew from our <term>ancestral, superstitious error</term> <note>original: "πατρίου δεισιδαίμονος πλάνης"; Eusebius is referring to the Greek and Roman paganism of his ancestors.</note>.
How much they previously believed, and what sort of things they record concerning the first <term>creation of the world</term> <note>original: "κοσμοποιΐας"</note>, and how reasonably we withdrew from them.
How much the natural philosophers have disagreed concerning first principles, and how we have departed from these after careful judgment.
That the ancients did nothing more than <term>theologize</term> <note>original: "ἐθεολόγουν"; here meaning "to treat as gods" or "worship as divine."</note> about the stars appearing in the sky.
That they originally had no mythology about gods, nor any setting up of <term>wooden images</term> <note>original: "ξοάνων"; primitive statues carved from wood.</note>.
That the opinions and legends of the ancients regarding gods were introduced later into life.
A summary of the ancient theology of the <term>Phoenicians</term> <note>Eusebius famously uses Phoenician sources, such as Sanchuniathon, to argue that pagan gods were originally just famous mortals.</note>, and for what reasons we have written about it, and that we have justly looked down upon it.

# THE FIRST OF THE FIFTEEN BOOKS OF THE EVAN-
# gelical Preparation by Eusebius of Pamphilus. <note>Eusebius added "of Pamphilus" to his name to honor his mentor and teacher, Pamphilus of Caesarea.</note>

### What the promise of the evangelical subject is.

Thinking it right to present to those who do not know what Christianity actually is, through the present work, the **Evangelical Demonstration** <note>original: "Εὐαγγελικὴν Ἀπόδειξιν"; this refers to Eusebius's companion work, *Demonstratio Evangelica*, which provides proofs for Christian claims after this "Preparation" clears the way.</note> which it promises, I address this to you, O Theodotus <note>Theodotus was the Bishop of Laodicea and a friend to Eusebius.</note>, dear to God and a sacred head of divine bishops. With my prayers, I call upon your name, hoping that I might obtain the help of your God-loving ministry, co-operating greatly with me in the proposed subject of the evangelical teaching. However, it is good to first articulate exactly what this bright **Gospel** <note>original: "Εὐαγγέλιον"; literally "Good News."</note> intends to reveal. To all men, it brings the "good news" of a gift of the highest and greatest goods—blessings that were foretold long ago, but have recently shone forth upon all. It does not provide "blind" wealth <note>A reference to the Greek god Plutus, often depicted as blind; Eusebius is contrasting material riches with spiritual ones.</note>, nor this brief and suffering life, nor anything belonging to the body and its decay. Rather, it offers those things which are dear and familiar to rational souls whose essence is in motion, things to which our physical bodies are attached like a following shadow.

The summary of these things is **piety** <term>eusebeia</term> <note>original: "εὐσέβεια"; a central term for Eusebius meaning correct worship and a godly lifestyle.</note>—not the falsely named and wandering kind, but that which is inscribed with the name of truth. This consists in the soul’s looking upward to the one and only truly acknowledged Being, God, and the life lived according to Him. From this arises friendship with Him, which is followed by the truly God-beloved and thrice-blessed end—an end suspended from above from the Highest Power, steered back toward Him again, and finally resting in Him. 

What, then, could be more blessed than this good and abundant love of God? Is He not Himself the steward and provider of life, light, truth, and all good things to everyone? Does He not encompass the cause of all things and of life itself? To the man who has secured friendship with Him, what could still be lacking? What could he possibly lack who has been made a member of the household of the Creator of all good things? Or what could he reach for that is higher, who claims the great Protector and Universal King of all as his father and guardian? 

Indeed, one cannot deny that he who approaches the Universal King through God <note>Eusebius here refers to approaching the Father through the Son or the Word (Logos).</note>, and who is deemed worthy of this most blessed friendship through a **disciplined piety** <note>original: "ἐπιστημονικῆς εὐσεβείας"; literally "scientific" or "knowledge-based" piety, implying a faith grounded in reason and study.</note>, would find that all is well with his soul, his body, and all his external affairs. This good and saving friendship between God and men was sent down from the all-good God by the **Word of God** <term>Logos</term> <note>original: "θεὸς λόγος"; the Divine Reason or Word, identified in Christianity as the second person of the Trinity.</note>, who, like a skilled...

<summary>Eusebius begins his work by dedicating it to Bishop Theodotus and defining Christianity not as a pursuit of material wealth, but as the pursuit of "true piety" and friendship with God through the Logos.</summary>
<keywords>Eusebius of Caesarea, Theodotus of Laodicea, Gospel, Piety, Logos, Evangelical Preparation, Friendship with God</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s introduction to the Gospel, transitioning from a description of its spiritual nature to its universal reach and the prophetic proofs that support it. He begins to address critics who claim Christianity is based on "blind faith" without reason.</meta>

-># EUSEBIUS<-

the brightness of its great light is sent out to all people. Not from one place or another, but spontaneously from among all nations, it urges people to come, to hasten, and with all readiness of soul to receive the gift—Greeks and barbarians <note>In the ancient world, "Barbarian" simply referred to anyone who did not speak Greek or follow Greek customs.</note> alike, men together with women and infants, the poor and the rich, the wise and the unlearned. Nor does it exclude any family of those who belong to it from the calling. For since their Father established a single holy nature for all, he rightly deemed all worthy of one and the same great gift, bestowing the knowledge of himself and friendship with him upon all who are willing to obey, and who welcome his grace even dimly. This word of Christ has come, announcing this friendship with his own Father to the whole world. "For God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their <margin>»</margin> trespasses against them," <note>A quotation from the New Testament, 2 Corinthians 5:19.</note> or as the divine words teach. And he says to those who listen, "he announced <margin>»</margin> peace to those far off, and peace to those near." <note>A quotation from Ephesians 2:17, echoing Isaiah 57:19.</note> These things the <margin>»</margin> children of the Hebrews <note>Eusebius uses "Hebrews" to refer to the ancient prophets and patriarchs of the Old Testament.</note> of old, being moved by God, prophesied to the whole world. One of them <margin>»</margin> cries out: "All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the <margin>»</margin> families of the nations shall worship before him." <note>Psalm 22:27.</note> And again: "Say among the nations <margin>»</margin> that the Lord reigned; for he established the world, which shall not be moved." <note>Psalm 96:10.</note> <margin>»</margin> Another says: "The Lord will appear among them, and will utterly destroy all the <margin>»</margin> gods of the nations of the earth, and they shall worship him, every man from his own <margin>»</margin> place." <note>Zephaniah (Sophonias) 2:11.</note> These things, which were laid up of old in divine oracles, have now appeared in our own time through the teaching of our Savior Jesus Christ. Thus, the knowledge of God among all the nations—which was once proclaimed but not then infinitely expected—is now rightly announced to us by the Word who recently came from heaven, showing that the voices of the ancients have met their results through his deeds.

But why must I hasten forward, outstripping the readiness of those who wish to hear the middle of my discourse? I must begin from the start and dissolve all the obstacles in our way. For some have supposed that Christianity brings no reason to bear, but that those who desire the name do so with an irrational faith and an unexamined agreement. Others have assumed that we can provide no clear evidence of the truth in what we promise, but that we require those who approach us to attend with faith alone; for this reason, they say we are called "the faithful" because of an uncritical grace and an untested faith. It is for this very reason that I call this work the **Evangelical Demonstration**. <note>original: "εὐαγγελικῆς ἀποδείξεως"; the *Demonstratio Evangelica* is Eusebius's massive work of proofs, to which this current book, the *Praeparatio*, serves as the introduction.</note> As a preparation for the whole subject, I think it necessary to first briefly address the questions that might be irrationally asked of us by the Hebrews and those of the circumcision <note>The "circumcision" refers to Jewish people or those following Jewish law.</note>; and we shall conclude after investigating our own affairs with an accurate examination. In this way, I believe the discourse will proceed in order to the more complete instruction of the *Evangelical Demonstration*, and to the understanding of the deeper doctrines, if our progress follows a preparatory path, holding the place of elements and an introduction, and fitting for those from the nations <note>original: "ἐκ ἐθνῶν"; the Gentiles, or non-Jewish converts.</note> who are just now approaching. The things after these will be handed over to those who have already passed through these stages and are prepared in their habit of mind for the reception of higher things—the accurate knowledge of the most cohesive mystic economy <note>original: "μυστικῆς οἰκονομίας"; "Economy" here refers to God's plan or administration of human salvation through Christ.</note> according to our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ, the God. Let us begin the preparation with the things irrationally asked of us by the Hebrews and all those of the circumcision with accuracy...

<summary>Eusebius argues that the Gospel is a universal gift for all humanity, fulfilling ancient Hebrew prophecies. He also defines the purpose of his work: to provide a rational "preparation" for the Christian faith against critics who claim it is based on blind, unproven belief.</summary>
<keywords>universality of the Gospel, Hebrew prophecy, Psalms, Zephaniah, irrational faith, Evangelical Demonstration, Gentile converts, mystic economy</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the general universal calling of the Gospel to the specific intellectual and legal challenges Christians faced in the 4th century. Eusebius begins a "cross-examination" of the Christian identity, addressing the common accusation that Christians are "atheists" for abandoning traditional Greek religion and "thieves" for claiming Jewish scriptures without following Jewish law.</meta>

-># PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 1<-

...bringing forward what will be said after investigating our own affairs through examination.

First, one might reasonably ask: who are we who have come to this writing? Are we Greeks or barbarians, or is there some middle ground between these? And who do we claim to be—not just in name, for that is clear to everyone, but in our manner and purpose of life? For we are seen neither thinking like the Greeks, nor practicing the customs of the barbarians. What then could be this strange thing of ours? What is this "innovation" in our way of life? How could they not be considered impious and <term>atheists</term> <note>original: ἄθεοι (atheoi). In the ancient world, "atheist" was a legal and social charge against those who refused to worship the traditional gods of the city or state.</note> from every side—those who have deserted their ancestral customs, through which every nation and city is held together? 

What good can those expect who have become enemies and combatants against their "saviors," <note>Referring to the traditional Greco-Roman gods who were believed to protect and preserve society.</note> and have made war on their benefactors? For what else is this but "fighting against God"? What kind of forgiveness will they be deemed worthy of, who have turned away from things theologized from age to age by all Greeks and barbarians—in every city and countryside, with all kinds of temples, rites, and <term>mysteries</term> <note>Secret religious rituals, such as the Eleusinian Mysteries, which were central to Greek spiritual life.</note>—by all kings, lawmakers, and philosophers alike? Instead, they have chosen the impious and godless things found among men. To what punishments might they not be justly subjected—those who are fugitives from their fathers' ways, becoming zealots for foreign <term>Jewish mythologies</term> <note>The Greeks often viewed the Old Testament stories as "myths" comparable to their own, but less sophisticated.</note> that are slandered by everyone? 

How could it not be the height of wickedness and recklessness to easily trade away one’s own traditions and, with an irrational and unexamined faith, choose the ways of those who are impious and enemies to all nations? Unless, through the very things honored by God among the Jews and the laws commanded among them, they have aimed at a certain "community" and "solitude" that dissolves their ties, keeping neither the ways of the Greeks nor the Jews?

These are the questions a Greek might reasonably ask us, knowing nothing of the truth of their own traditions or ours. But the <margin>»</margin> children of the Hebrews <note>Eusebius refers to the Jewish community of his own time.</note> might also blame us: if we are of another race and lineage, why do we use their books which do not belong to us? They might say we shamelessly and audaciously claim these books for ourselves, while trying to push aside the rightful and noble heirs of their own ancestral heritage. For if there is some "Good One" being prophesied, it was the prophets of the Jews who proclaimed his arrival. They announced that a redeemer and king would come for the *Jews*, not for the foreign nations. 

Even if the scriptures hint at more glorious things, they say these were spoken for the Jews, and it is not right for us to overhear them. It is quite absurd, they say, that we do not readily accept the rebukes directed at their nation for the sins they committed, but instead we silence the promises of good things prophesied for them—or rather, we "force" the text and transfer it to ourselves. This is outright greed, and nothing more than deceiving ourselves. This is the most illogical thing of all: that we do not even follow the laws in a manner similar to them, but openly break the law, yet we snatch for ourselves the rewards promised to those who keep the law.

Since these questions have been reasonably raised against us at the start, let us—calling upon the God of all through our Savior, his Word, as through a high priest—clear away these charges. We shall prove that our detractors are slanderers when they claim we have nothing to show by way of proof and assert that we hold to an "irrational faith." I will begin the explanation immediately, not by telling a long story, but by using the—

### EUSEBIUS

We employ proofs for those approaching for instruction in our teachings, as well as solutions for those who oppose us in more logical inquiries. Through these, we strive to provide both unwritten and written discourses, individually to each person who asks, and collectively to the masses. Furthermore, through the writings at hand, we encompass the general treatise of dialectical proof. In this, the present discourse—announcing the good news of God’s grace and heavenly benevolence to all people—confirms the <term>dispensation</term> <note>original: οἰκονομία (oikonomia). In early Christian writing, this refers to God's "management" or "plan" for the world, specifically through the incarnation of Christ.</note> of our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, in a more logical manner through numerous and vivid proofs. We have therefore been diligent, for there has been much effort by many before us—sometimes composing refutations and rebuttals against those who oppose our words; at other times, explaining the divine and sacred Scriptures through interpretive commentaries and translating specific portions in homilies; and at other times, approaching our doctrines in a more combative style. For us, however, our purpose is uniquely distinct from theirs. First of all, the holy Apostle Paul, rejecting unpersuasive and natural "persuasive words," and using undeniable proofs,

> „ says somewhere: "And our word and our preaching were not in the persuasive words of human wisdom,
> „ but in the demonstration of Spirit and power." To which he adds: "But we speak wisdom
> „ among the mature; yet a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age who are
> „ passing away, but we speak the hidden wisdom of God in a mystery." <note>original: 1 Corinthians 2:4-7</note> And again, "Our sufficiency,"
> „ he says, "is from God, who also made us sufficient as ministers of a new covenant." <note>original: 2 Corinthians 3:5-6</note>

Reasonably then, in all things that have gone before, we should be ready to give a defense to everyone who asks us for a reason for the hope that is in us. From this, we can discern the numerous works of recent writers—which, as has been said, are fulfilling and clear proofs involving syllogisms written by our elders—as well as not a few commentaries painstakingly produced on the sacred and divine Scriptures. These leave behind for us a true and unerring account of the <term>godliness</term> <note>original: θεοσέβεια (theosebeia). Specifically meaning the proper worship of the true God as opposed to pagan "superstition."</note> that has been demonstrated, presenting it with "geometrical proofs." <note>original: γραμμικαῖς ἀποδείξεσιν. Eusebius uses this mathematical metaphor to suggest his arguments are as logically certain as a geometric proof.</note> However, the words of these accounts are many, and their works are most vivid and clear. These works the divine and heavenly power of our Savior, announcing the good news to all people through Himself and through His disciples, explicitly demonstrates even now. For instance, having prophesied that His teaching would be proclaimed throughout the whole inhabited world as a testimony to all nations, He also foretold the Church that was later established by His power from among all nations—at a time when it was not yet seen, nor yet established—declaring by foresight that it would be unconquerable and invincible, and never to be overcome by death. He declared that it would exist even unto infinity, as if it had stepped upon and been rooted in an "unshakable and unbreakable rock" <note>An allusion to Matthew 16:18, where Christ promises that the gates of Hades will not prevail against His church.</note> by His power. This fulfillment of the prophecy, being beyond all reason, would reasonably stop every wide-open mouth of those prepared to be shamelessly insolent. For who would not admit that the prophecy of these events is true, when the facts themselves clearly speak out—almost as if they had a voice—that it is the power of God, and not human nature, that dared to prophesy these things in such a manner and to fulfill them with deeds?

...most perfectly, and he has filled the whole world, as much as the sun looks upon, with the fame of the Gospel concerning him. It has run through all the nations. <margin>"</margin> **shall not prevail against it."**

By remembering the things said and predicted by our Savior, and by gathering them into a proper arrangement, we demonstrate the truth for which we are glorified as indisputable—showing that the fulfillment of the prophets' words harmonizes with the foreknowledge shown in his works. In these, thousands of years ago, the prophets among the Hebrews proclaimed the promise of good things for mortal life. I speak of the final siege of their **Royal Metropolis** <note>Jerusalem. These things were foretold and clearly appear to have been suffered by them following the arrival of our Savior.

For long before he was to come, they announced the falling away of the Jews and the calling of the nations in bright and clear voices. This very thing has now clearly come to pass according to the prophecy, following the teaching of our Savior. Through him, from every place under the sun, countless thousands of men have turned away from the error of idols and have accepted the true knowledge and piety of the God over all. They are almost literally fulfilling the ancient oracles and the sayings of the people, as spoken through the prophet **Jeremiah**:

<margin>"</margin> **"O Lord my God, the nations shall come to you from the end of the earth,**

Furthermore, they were set before all men from God through our Savior. Again, it is not without God that this work is empowered and held together; though it has been breathed upon for so many years by invisible spirits and opposed by various powers throughout time, it shines much brighter, and every day it excels and grows. It increases much more as the things from above...

# EUSEBIUS

We employ these proofs as we proceed toward the instruction of our own doctrines, as well as for the solutions required in more logical inquiries <note>The "logical inquiry" refers to formal debates with Greek philosophers and skeptics who demanded rational proof rather than simple faith.</note> against those who oppose us. Through these means, we take care to produce both unwritten and written discourses, both privately for each person who asks a question and publicly for the crowds. Indeed, this is the purpose of the work now in hand, which contains the general treatment of the **Evangelical Demonstration**. In this work, the present discourse proclaims the whole grace of God and his heavenly benevolence to all people, confirming—more logically through numerous and clear proofs—the divine plan <note>original: οἰκονομίαν (oikonomian) — the "economy" or management of the world through the incarnation of Christ.</note> concerning our Savior and Lord, Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

Many before our time have indeed applied themselves to various other treatises—at times composing refutations and replies to arguments directed against us, at other times interpreting the divine and sacred Scriptures through explanatory commentaries and specific sermons, and at still other times approaching our doctrines in a more competitive or athletic spirit <note>original: ἀγωνιστικώτερον (agōnistisκōteron) — referring to "polemical" writing, like an athlete in a contest.</note>. However, this treatise now in our hands shall be labored upon in its own distinct way. For the holy apostle Paul first writes that he rejected threatening and sophisticated persuasive words, instead using undeniable proofs when he says:

» **"And our word and our preaching were not with persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the Spirit and of power."** <note>original: 1 Corinthians 2:4</note>

To which he adds:

» **"But we speak wisdom among the perfect; yet a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age who are coming to nothing. But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom."** <note>original: 1 Corinthians 2:6–7</note>

And again he says:

» **"Our sufficiency is from God, who also made us sufficient as ministers of a new covenant."** <note>original: 2 Corinthians 3:5–6</note>

Reasonably then, we have been commanded in all things to be <margin>ready</margin> to give a defense <note>original: ἀπολογίαν (apologian) — a formal legal defense or justification.</note> to everyone who asks us for an account concerning the hope that is in us. For this reason, even among the newer writers, there are records—as has been said—of clear and present proofs using syllogisms, through which the logic of our doctrines is made manifest to all. Not a few commentaries have also been labored over regarding the sacred and divinely inspired Scriptures, which establish—with geometric precision—the truth and the infallible nature of the doctrines of godly worship that were initially laid down for us. 

Yet, above all these many words, there are the works themselves, which are most vivid and clear. These works the divine and heavenly power of our Savior expressly displays even now, proclaiming the saving and heavenly life to all people. For instance, his teaching was prophesied to be preached throughout the whole inhabited world as a testimony to all nations; and later, the Church—consisting of countless nations—stood firm by his power. This was not yet visible during the times when it was first spoken, nor had it yet been established; yet by divine foreknowledge, he declared it would be invincible and unconquerable, never to be defeated even by death. He declared that the Church would stand unshaken, as if rooted and founded upon an immovable and unbreakable rock by his own power. This outcome of the prophecy, being beyond all reason, would naturally shut every gap in the mouths of those who are prepared to act with easy impudence. For who would not confess the truth of the aforementioned prophecy? The events themselves almost let out a voice, crying that it was the power of God, and not human nature, which grasped that these things would happen in this manner concerning the Savior—prophesying them and bringing them to completion through deeds.

It multiplies immediately by the power from above...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument regarding the divine power of Christ, moving from the growth of the Church to the global peace established during the reign of Augustus Caesar. # EUSEBIUS

If the invincible and undefeated nature of the cooperation of the God of the universe, and the victory over enemies, are contained within the teaching and the name of our Savior... and if this was immediately directed toward a good life for all people—not only through His famous words but also through a secret power put forward—how could this not be a demonstration of His divine power? 

For how was it a matter of secret power? It was because, at the same time as His word and His teaching concerning the **monarchy** <term>Monarchy <note>original: μοναρχίας (monarchias) — meaning the "rule of one." Eusebius argues that the belief in one God (monotheism) naturally aligns with the political rule of one Emperor.</note></term> of the one God over all was put forward, the widespread error of demonic activity and the **polyarchy** <term>Polyarchy <note>original: πολυαρχία (polyarchia) — the "rule of many." This refers to the era when many different kings, tyrants, and local gods ruled over small, warring territories.</note></term> of the nations were extinguished from human life just yesterday and the day before. 

In ancient times, there were countless kings and local rulers in every nation, and local powers dominated cities and lands. Some were governed by democracies, others by tyrants, and others by many rulers. Naturally, all kinds of wars broke out from this; nations clashed with nations, constantly attacking their neighbors, ravaging and being ravaged, and plotting against one another with sieges. As a result, the entire population—both those living in cities and farmers in the fields—were taught the arts of war from childhood; they carried swords at all times on the highways, in the villages, and in the fields. But this changed because of Christ, concerning whom it was spoken long ago through the prophets:

> **"In his days justice shall arise, and an abundance of peace. And they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, and they shall no longer learn to fight."** <note>A synthesis of Psalm 72:7 and Isaiah 2:4.</note>

The deeds followed directly in accordance with this prophecy. Immediately, the "polyarchy" of the Romans was abolished when **Augustus** <note>The first Roman Emperor (ruled 27 BC – 14 AD). Eusebius sees his reign as a divinely timed preparation for Christianity.</note> became the sole ruler at the time of our Savior’s appearance. From then until now, you will not see—as you did before—cities at war with cities, nor nations going to battle with nations. Nor is life worn down by the total confusion of the past.

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 1. 9

...to persist in their choice, and to pursue unnatural pleasures; nor to expose their own dead to dogs and birds as those of old did, nor to subject the elderly to hanging, as was the custom before; nor to feast on the flesh of their dearest dead according to ancient habit. # EUSEBIUS EVANGELICAL PREPARATION
<meta>catchword: truly</meta>

...to believe. According to our perspective on the Gospel’s purpose, it is held by all that <term>Christianity</term>—as it might be properly called—is neither <term>Hellenism</term><note>The culture, language, and religion of the Greeks, often used by early Christian writers to mean 'paganism.'</note> nor <term>Judaism</term>, but a certain new and true **divine wisdom**, carrying its very innovation in its name. 

Come then, let us first examine their most ancient traditions, which they themselves celebrate as their "complete theologies," still talked about in every city even now. Let us look at the evidence provided by their noble Philosophers regarding the constitution of the world and their assumptions about the gods, so that we may know whether we have rightly departed from them or not. I come to this task not by proclaiming my own words, but by using the voices of those who have most especially trusted in the piety concerning those they call gods. In this way, the argument will be placed beyond all suspicion of us fabricating the evidence.

### On the first theology of the Phoenicians and Egyptians.

A tradition holds that the Phoenicians and Egyptians were the first of all people to declare the sun, moon, and stars to be gods—identifying them as the sole rulers of the earth and the causes of all generation and decay. Later, they introduced many "god-making" and "god-begetting" systems that were harmful to human life. Before these developments, no one knew anything more than the visible phenomena in the heavens, with the exception of a few men mentioned among the **Hebrews**. These men, looking up with the clearest eyes of the mind beyond the visible world, worshipped the Maker and Creator of the whole universe. They were struck with wonder at His vast wisdom and power, which they perceived through His works. Convinced of God alone, they logically developed a theology for Him alone, having received the true and primary piety as a heritage passed from father to son. 

The rest of humanity, however, fell away from this sole and true piety. Dazzled by the light-bearing heavenly bodies with the eyes of their flesh—being like infants in their souls—they assumed these objects were gods. They honored them with sacrifices and prostrations, though at that time they did not yet build temples or fashion images and wooden statues in the likeness of mortals. Instead, they gazed directly at the sky, their souls reaching only as far as the visible things they saw there. 

But the error of "many gods" did not stop with them. Later generations, sinking into a depth of evils, practiced a form of impiety even greater than <term>atheism</term><note>original: "atheotētos". Here, Eusebius suggests that worshipping many false gods is in some ways worse than believing in none at all.</note>. The Phoenicians and then the Egyptians initiated this error. From them, it is said that Orpheus, the son of Oeagrus, first brought the Egyptian mysteries to the Greeks. Similarly, the Phoenicians brought their traditions to the Greeks along with the teaching of the alphabet, for at that time the Greeks did not yet know how to use letters. 

Therefore, we will first examine the written accounts of the "first cosmogony" <note>An account of the origins of the universe.</note> as these people understood it. Second, we will look at the first and oldest superstitions in human life. Third, the Phoenician traditions. Fourth, the Egyptian traditions. After these, as a fifth point, we will go through the Greek traditions—first observing their old and more mythical errors, then their more dignified and "natural" philosophy concerning the gods. After that, we will investigate the accounts of their wondrous oracles. Following these, we will examine the dignity of our own noble philosophy. Once these matters have been clarified by us, we shall move on to the history of the Hebrews, who were the first and the truly...

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 1
<sig>b.i.</sig>

...truly <note>original: "ἀληθῶς" (alēthōs) — the text begins mid-word</note> of the **Hebrews**, and after these, those who obtained the name of **Jews**. In addition to all these, as a seal of the whole work, we have established our own position. We will necessarily mention the history of all these groups, so that by setting the admired traditions of each side by side, the proof of the truth might be demonstrated. What our own position is compared to all others, or what has been said of it, will become clear to those who read this work. 

But let us proceed to the subject at hand. How shall we verify our proofs? We shall not do so from our own writings, lest we seem to be framing the argument in our own favor. Instead, let external witnesses stand by us—men who boast of their <term>philosophy</term><note>In this context, it refers to the systematic study of nature and the divine by Greek and Roman intellectuals.</note> and who have thoroughly investigated the history of other nations. 

For instance, **Diodorus Siculus** <note>A 1st-century BC Greek historian famous for his "Bibliotheca historica," a massive universal history.</note>, a man most well-known to the most learned scholars for bringing together an entire historical library into a single treatise, writes of the ancient theology of the **Egyptians**. From his work, we will set forth at the very start of our discussion what he has gathered concerning the <term>cosmogony</term><note>A story or theory regarding the origin and evolution of the universe.</note> of the universe and the opinions of ancient histories, in the following manner:

---

### The nature of the cosmogony under examination.

<margin>»</margin> Regarding what notions about the gods those who first pointed out the divine to us might have had, and 
<margin>»</margin> concerning the myths told about each of the immortals, we will try to arrange most of them 
<margin>»</margin> separately, because this subject requires much discussion. 
<margin>»</margin> But whatever things seem to be similar to the history now before us, we will set forth 
<margin>»</margin> in summary, so that nothing worthy of being heard is left wanting. Concerning the origin of all 
<margin>»</margin> mankind, and the things done in the known parts of the inhabited world, 
<margin>»</margin> as far as is possible regarding such ancient matters, we will accurately record them, 
<margin>»</margin> starting from the most ancient times. 

<margin>»</margin> Concerning the **first generation of men**, 
<margin>»</margin> two opinions have arisen among the most authoritative <term>natural philosophers</term><note>Early thinkers (physiologoi) who sought natural, rather than purely mythical, explanations for the world.</note> and 
<margin>»</margin> historians. Some of them, assuming the world to be uncreated and indestructible, declared 
<margin>»</margin> that the race of men also existed from eternity, their procreation 
<margin>»</margin> never having had a beginning. Others, considering the world to be created and destructible, said 
<margin>»</margin> that like the world, men also obtained their first birth at fixed times. 

<margin>»</margin> For during the initial constitution of the universe, **heaven and earth had a single form**, 
<margin>»</margin> their natures being mixed together. After this, as the bodies separated from each other, 
<margin>»</margin> the world embraced the entire arrangement seen within it. The air 
<margin>»</margin> attained continuous motion. Its fiery part ran together toward the highest places, 
<margin>»</margin> such a nature being upward-tending because of its lightness. 
<margin>»</margin> For this reason, the sun and the rest of the multitude of stars were caught in the universal 
<margin>»</margin> rotation. The muddy and turbulent part, combined with the fluids, settled in the same place 
<margin>»</margin> because of its weight. Being turned within itself and rolled together continuously, 
<margin>»</margin> from the fluids it created the sea; and from the more solid parts it made the earth, 
<margin>»</margin> which was muddy and entirely soft. 

<margin>»</margin> This earth, at first, when the fire of the sun shone upon it, began to grow firm. 
<margin>»</margin> Then, because the surface was boiling due to the heat, some of the fluids swelled 
<margin>»</margin> in many places, and <term>fermentations</term><note>Original: "σηπεδόνας" (sēpedonas). This refers to a theory of "spontaneous generation" where life bubbles up from rotting or fermenting organic slime.</note> occurred around them...

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 1
### Chapter 7 (continued)

...ignorance. Regarding the first generation of humans and the most ancient way of life, we shall be satisfied with what has been said, aiming for a balanced account. This is the account of the aforementioned writer <note>referring to Diodorus Siculus, whose work Eusebius has been quoting</note>, who did not mention even the name of God in his account of the world's origin (*cosmogony*), but instead introduced a certain coincidental and automatic arrangement of the universe. In agreement with him, one might find the majority of the Greek philosophers, whose opinions on the first principles—along with their mutual disagreements and contradictions—we shall now set forth from **Plutarch’s** *Miscellanies*. These opinions were driven by conjecture rather than by certain understanding. You should examine these not casually, but with careful reasoning, precisely because of the great distance between their various claims.

## Opinions of the philosophers on the constitution of the universe.

<margin>Thales</margin> They say that **Thales** <note>Thales of Miletus (c. 624–546 BC), often called the first philosopher.</note> was the first of all to suggest that water is the origin of the whole; for he claimed that all things come from it and into it all things return. After him, **Anaximander**, who was a companion of Thales, said that the "Infinite" <note>original: "ἄπειρον" (apeiron) — the boundless or indefinite source.</note> contains the entire cause for the birth and destruction of the universe. From this, he says, the heavens were separated, and in general, all the worlds, which are infinite in number. He declared that destruction occurs, and much earlier, birth, with all these things cycling back from an infinite age. He says the earth is cylindrical in shape, and its depth is one-third of its width. He also says that at the birth of this world, a productive seed of heat and cold was separated from the eternal, and from this a certain sphere of flame grew around the air surrounding the earth, like bark around a tree. When this sphere was broken off and enclosed into certain circles, the sun, the moon, and the stars were formed. Furthermore, he says that in the beginning, humans were born from animals of a different kind, because while other animals quickly find food for themselves, humans alone require long-term nursing. Therefore, if a human had been such as they are now in the beginning, they could never have survived. These, then, are the views of Anaximander.

They say **Anaximenes** claimed air is the principle of all things, and that it is infinite in quantity but defined by the qualities associated with it. He said all things are created through a certain thickening of this air (*condensation*) or a thinning of it (*rarefaction*). He claimed that motion has existed from eternity. When the air was compressed, he says the earth was formed first, being very flat; therefore, it reasonably floats upon the air. The sun, the moon, and the rest of the stars have the origin of their birth from the earth. He declares, at any rate, that the sun is earth, but because of its swift motion, it acquired a very great amount of heat.

**Xenophanes of Colophon**, having traveled a path of his own that diverged from all those previously mentioned, allows for neither birth 

> nor destruction. Instead, he says that the "All" is always the same. For if it were to come into being, he says, it is necessary that it did not exist before. But that which does not exist cannot come to be, nor could that which does not exist do anything, nor could anything be created by that which does not exist. He also declares that the senses are deceptive, and along with them, he generally attacks reason itself. 

He declares that as time passes, the earth is continuously sliding down and, little by little, is moving into the sea. He also says the sun is gathered together from many small sparks of fire. Concerning the gods, he declares that there is no hierarchy among them; for it is not holy for any of the gods to be ruled by another.

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 1

...acuteness of mind. Regarding the first nature of human beings and the most ancient way of life, we shall be satisfied with what has been said, aiming for a balanced account. For the rest, he <note>Diodorus Siculus, whose text preceded this section</note> wrote his history without mentioning the name of God even once in his account of the world's origin <note>original: "κοσμογονίᾳ" (cosmogony)</note>, instead introducing a sort of accidental and spontaneous arrangement of the universe. You would find that most of the Greek philosophers agree with him; we shall now set forth their opinions regarding first principles <note>original: "ἀρχῶν" (archai) — the fundamental "stuff" or origins of the universe</note> and their mutual disagreements and contradictions—which arose from conjecture rather than firm comprehension—drawing from the *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Στρωματέων" (Stromateis) — a title used for collections of varied topics</note> of **Plutarch**. Do not look upon this lightly, but consider with leisure and reason the internal contradictions of these claims.

->Opinions of the philosophers concerning the constitution of the universe.<-

They say that **Thales** was the first of all to posit water as the first principle of the whole; for from it all things exist, and into it they return. After him, **Anaximander**, who was a companion of **Thales**, said that the Infinite <note>original: "τὸ ἄπειρον" (to apeiron) — a boundless, indeterminate substance</note> contains the entire cause for the generation and destruction of the universe. From this, he says, the heavens were separated, and generally all the worlds, which are infinite in number. He declared that destruction occurs, and much earlier generation, as all these worlds cycle through an infinite age. He says that in shape the earth is cylindrical, and it has a depth equal to one-third of its width. He further says that the "generative principle" of hot and cold was separated from the eternal at the generation of this world, and from this a certain sphere of flame grew around the air surrounding the earth, like bark around a tree. When this was broken off and enclosed in certain circles, the sun, moon, and stars were formed. Furthermore, he says that in the beginning, humans were born from animals of a different kind, because while other animals quickly find food for themselves, man alone requires a long period of nursing. For this reason, in the beginning, humans could never have survived being as they are now. These then are the views of **Anaximander**.

They say **Anaximenes** declared air to be the principle of the whole; that it is infinite in its nature but defined by the qualities surrounding it. All things are produced by a certain condensation of this air, and again by rarefaction. However, motion has existed from eternity. He says that as the air was "felted" <note>original: "πιλουμένου" — a technical term comparing the thickening of air to the process of making felt fabric</note>, the earth was the first to be produced, and it is very flat; for this reason, it logically floats upon the air. The sun, the moon, and the other stars have the origin of their generation from the earth. He declares, at any rate, that the sun is "earth," but because of its swift and quite sufficient motion, it has acquired extreme heat.

**Xenophanes of Colophon**, having traveled a path of his own that diverged from all those mentioned before, allows for neither generation nor destruction. Instead, he says that the All is always the same <note>original: "ὅμοιον" — uniform or unchanging</note>.
<margin>»</margin> For if something were to come into being, he says, it must necessarily not have existed before;
<margin>»</margin> but that which "is not" cannot come to be, nor could that which "is not"
<margin>»</margin> create anything, nor could anything be created by that which "is not."
He also declares the senses to be false, and along with them, he generally attacks reason itself. He further declares that over time the earth is continuously sinking and gradually passing into the sea. He also says that the sun is gathered together from a multitude of small fiery particles. He also makes declarations about the gods, stating that there is no "rule" or hierarchy among them; for it is not holy for any of the gods to be mastered by another.

For he declares that the All <note>original: "τὸ πᾶν" (to pan) — the totality of existence</note> is eternal and motionless, according to the actual truth of things.

He says that the earth was formed from dense air sinking down. **Zeno** the Eleatic set forth nothing peculiar of his own, but examined these same problems at greater length. **Democritus** of Abdera supposed the All to be infinite, because it was in no way fashioned by anyone. Furthermore, he says it is unchangeable. And regarding the nature of the whole, he explicitly sets forth that the causes of what is happening now have no beginning <note>original: "ἀρχήν" (archen)</note>, but that from above, throughout infinite time, all things that have been, are, and will be, are held fast simply by necessity. He says the sun and moon are in the process of becoming. He claims these move individually, not yet possessing a hot nature at all, nor indeed a very bright one, but on the contrary, having a nature similar to that of the earth. For each of these was produced earlier as a sort of separate foundation for a world. Later, as the circle around the sun increased in size, fire was trapped within it.

**Epicurus**, son of **Neocles**, an Athenian, attempts to suppress the "first principles" <note>original: "ἀρχάς" (archas)</note> of beings. But even he says that things are produced from what does not exist, <gloss>nor again into that which does not exist</gloss> because it was always such as it is, and will always be such. He claims that nothing strange is completed in the universe compared to the infinite time that has already passed; that the All is body, and not only unchangeable, but also infinite. He teaches that the "end of all goods" is pleasure. **Aristippus** of Cyrene also calls pleasure the end of goods, and pain the end of evils. He dismisses other studies of nature <note>original: "φυσιολογίαν" (physiologian)</note> as being only moderately useful, saying one should seek:

**Empedocles** of Agrigentum posits four elements: fire, water, air <note>original: "αἰθέρα" (aithera)</note>, and earth; and as the cause of these, Love and Strife. He says that from the first mixing of the elements, the air was separated and poured around in a circle. After the air, the fire broke out, and having no other place, it ran upward beneath the thickness around the air.

He believes the beginning of movement happened by chance during the accumulation, when the fire pressed down. The sun, in its nature, is not fire, but a reflection of fire, similar to the reflection produced by water. He says the moon was composed on its own from the air that was cut off by the fire. For this air became frozen, just like hail; and she <note>the moon</note> has her light from the sun. The "ruling part" <note>original: "ἡγεμονικόν" (hegemonikon) — the seat of the soul or consciousness</note> is neither in the head nor in the chest, but in the blood. Hence, in whatever part of the body the ruling part is more widely distributed, he thinks that in that respect humans excel. **Metrodorus** of Chios says the All is eternal, because if it were created, it would have come from "not-being"; and it is infinite, because it is eternal. # EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 1
<header>EVANG. PREPAR. Book 1</header>

...nor in the same way; but the All <note>original: "τὸ πᾶν" (to pan) — the totality of the universe</note> does not even participate in motion. For it is impossible to move without changing. And change must necessarily be either into a state of fullness or into a void. When the ether thickens, it creates clouds, then water, which, when it falls upon the sun, extinguishes it; and again, when it thins, it ignites. In time, the dry things are solidified by the sun, and from the bright water stars are produced; night and day result from the extinguishing and the ignition. And in general, he explains eclipses in this way. **Diogenes of Apollonia** posits air as the primary element; and that all things are in motion, and that there are infinite worlds. He explains the creation of the world as follows: since the All is in motion, and becomes thin in one place and thick in another, where the thick part happened to meet, it created a cluster, and so the rest, by the same logic, with the lightest parts taking the upper rank and forming the sun.

Such is the explanation of the constitution of the All and the primary origin of the world <term>cosmogony: the branch of science or philosophy dealing with the origin of the universe</term> by these "multi-wise" men of ours, who are indeed called natural philosophers. They did not posit any craftsman or creator of the whole, nor did they make any mention of God at all; instead, they declared the arrangement of all things to be driven only by irrational impulse and spontaneous motion.

So great is their opposition to one another; they have agreed with each other in nothing, but have filled everything with strife and discord. Hence the marvelous **Socrates** exposed them all as being mad, and thought they differed in no way from the insane—if indeed **Xenophon** testifies truly in the *Memorabilia*, saying the following:

> No one ever saw Socrates do anything impious or unholy, nor heard him say any such thing. For he did not discuss the nature of all things, as most others did, looking into how the "cosmos" <note>original: "κόσμος" — meaning order or world-system</note> (as the sophists call it) is structured, and by what necessities each of the heavenly things happens. Rather, he showed that those who worry about such things are foolish. 

And he adds next: 

> He marveled if it was not clear to them that it is impossible for humans to find these things out. Since even those who pride themselves most on speaking about these matters do not hold the same opinions as one another, but are disposed toward each other like madmen. For among the mad, some do not fear even the terrible, while others fear things that are not frightening. Among those who worry about the nature of all things, some think that "Being" is only one, while others think it is infinite in number. Some think all things are always moving; others that nothing ever moves. Some think all things are born and perish; others that nothing could ever be born or perish. 

These are the words of Socrates, as Xenophon testifies. **Plato** also walks alongside these views in his work *On the Soul* <note>The *Phaedo*</note>, recording him saying: 

> "For I," he said, "O Cebes, when I was young, desired this wisdom wonderfully, which they call the investigation of nature; for it seemed to me a magnificent thing to know the causes of each thing, why each thing comes to be, and why it perishes, and why it exists. And many times I turned myself upside down, looking first at things like this: Is it when the cold and the hot undergo a kind of fermentation <note>original: "σηπεδόνα" (sepedona) — literally rot or decay, but used here for a biological 'simmering' or process</note>, as some used to say, that living creatures are then nurtured? And is it the blood by which we think, or air, or fire? Or is it none of these, but the brain that provides the senses of hearing, seeing, and smelling; and from these memory and opinion might arise, and from memory and opinion reaching a state of rest, knowledge comes to be according to these? Again, looking at the destructions of these things, and the things concerning the heavens..."

<sig>b. iii.</sig>

Through Xenophon and Plato, Socrates is shown rejecting these materialist inquiries as contradictory and "mad," preferring instead to focus on ethics and piety.</summary>

Having just finished discussing the theories of Anaximenes and Diogenes of Apollonia, he now transitions to the testimony of Socrates and then moves into a historical account of "astrolatry" (star-worship) among the Egyptians and Phoenicians, citing the historian Diodorus Siculus.</meta>

# 18 EUSEBIUS
<header>18 EUSEBIUS</header>

» "...or [judging by] my own experiences, finally, I seemed to myself so naturally unsuited for this investigation <note>Socrates is referring to 'natural philosophy'—the study of the physical origins of the universe.</note> that I did not need to state any strong proof. For the things I previously understood clearly—or so I thought and so it seemed to others—I was then so blinded by this investigation itself that I unlearned even those things I thought I knew before." These are the words of Socrates himself, that man famous among all Greeks. Since such a great philosopher felt this way regarding the physical theories mentioned, I believe I am justified in rejecting their absolute godlessness. For even their errors concerning polytheism <note>original: "πολυθέου πλάνης" (polytheou planes) — literally 'polytheistic wandering' or error</note> do not seem foreign to what has been said. We shall examine this in due time as promised, when we demonstrate that a thousand years ago, **Anaxagoras** was the only one recorded to have set a "Mind" <term>Nous: the intellect or divine reason that Anaxagoras argued was the primary cause of the universe</term> over the cause of the whole. But now, turn with me to **Diodorus**, and observe what he relates concerning the first theology of men.

### That the ancient people worshipped only the lights in the heavens, knowing nothing of the God of the universe, nor about the setting up of statues, nor about demons.

The ancient people of Egypt, looking up at the cosmos and being struck with awe and wonder at the nature of the universe, supposed that there were two eternal and primary gods: the sun and the moon. Of these, they named the sun **Osiris** and the moon **Isis**, each name being given for a specific etymological reason. For when these names are translated into the Greek language, "Osiris" signifies "holy and many-eyed" <note>original: "ὅσιον πολυόφθαλμον" (hosion polyophthalmon). This is an ancient folk etymology; the 'eyes' refer to the sun's rays.</note>. This is fitting, for by casting his rays everywhere, he sees the entire land and sea as if with many eyes. The poet <note>Homer, Odyssey 12.323</note> speaks in agreement with this: "The sun, who sees all and hears all." Some of the ancient mythologists among the Greeks say that Osiris is the same as **Dionysus**, and also use the name **Sirius** as a derivative. Of these, Eumolpus says in his Bacchic verses: "Dionysus, shining like a star, fiery in his rays." Orpheus also says: "For this reason they call him both Phaethon and Dionysus." Some even say that the deerskin <term>nebris: a fawn skin worn by followers of Dionysus</term> was draped around him to represent the variety and speckling of the stars. They say that "Isis," when translated, means "ancient," a name given to the moon because of her eternal and ancient origin. They place horns on her because of the appearance she presents when she is crescent-shaped, and also because of the cow, which is sacred to her among the Egyptians. These gods, they maintain, govern the entire cosmos.

Such is their account. Next, in the **Phoenician theology**, it is held that the first naturalists among the Phoenicians recognized only the sun, the moon, the other wandering stars <term>planets: from the Greek 'planētai', meaning 'wanderers'</term>, the elements, and things connected to them as gods. The most ancient people dedicated the fruits of the earth to these and considered them gods; they worshipped the very things upon which they themselves, their descendants, and all their ancestors depended for survival, and they performed drink-offerings and libations to them. They felt pity and lamented when the vegetation of the earth withered and died, and they marveled at the first birth of animals from the earth, their reproduction with one another, and their death when they departed from life. These were their concepts of worship, matching their own human weakness and the lack of courage <note>original: "ἀτολμίᾳ" (atolmia) — literally 'timidity' or 'lack of daring'</note> of their souls. These things are also found in the writings of the Phoenicians, as will be shown hereafter.

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument regarding the history of religious error. He moves from discussing the physical theories of the Greeks to the historical development of worship, specifically citing how early humans transitioned from "pure" offerings of vegetation to the "cruel" practice of animal sacrifice. He uses the testimony of Porphyry—an opponent of Christianity—to support his claim that the oldest forms of worship were focused solely on the celestial bodies (the sun, moon, and stars) and lacked the elaborate mythology of the later Greek gods.</meta>

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 1

But even that very man who lived in our own times, who gained fame through his slanderous writings against us <note>original: "δυσφημίαις" (dysphemiis). Eusebius is referring to the philosopher **Porphyry**, a famous critic of Christianity.</note>, in the work he titled *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, records the memory of ancient history in almost these exact words, using **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus was a student of Aristotle and his successor as head of the Peripatetic school.</note> as his witness:

„ An unmeasurable amount of time has passed (as it seems) since the most learned race of all—as Theophrastus says—those who began to inhabit the most sacred land created by the Nile <note>The Egyptians</note>, first began to offer sacrifices from their hearths to the heavenly gods. These were not offerings of myrrh, nor of cassia and frankincense mixed with saffron; for such things were introduced many generations later. Man, becoming a seeker and a searcher of the wanderings <note>original: "πλάνης" (planes) — referring to the wandering paths of the stars</note>, offered the first fruits of his necessary sustenance to the gods with much labor and many drops of tears. They did not sacrifice animals in the beginning, but rather **grasses**, picking the downy bloom of fertile nature with their hands. For the earth brought forth trees before animals. From these trees, they plucked the grass that grows annually—harvesting its leaves, roots, and all its shoots—and burned them, welcoming the visible heavenly gods with this sacrifice, and making their honors immortal through fire. For they kept fire immortal in their temples, because it was most similar to the gods. From this "fuming" <term>thumiasis: the act of burning incense or herbs</term> of the products of the earth, they derived the names for "incense-burners," "to sacrifice," and "sacrificing" <note>original: "θυμιατήριά," "θύειν," "θυσιάζειν." Theophrastus is arguing that the Greek word for sacrifice (*thuein*) originally meant simply "to cause smoke."</note>. We, however, do not understand this correctly, as we use these words to signify the later error, calling the supposed service through animals a "sacrifice." The ancients cared so much about not transgressing this custom that they would place curses upon anyone who abandoned the old way and introduced another; thus, they called these offerings "fumes."

Having said this, he adds further remarks:

„ For when the lawlessness regarding sacrifices had advanced far among men, the adoption of the most terrible sacrifices, full of cruelty, was introduced. It seemed as if the curses previously mentioned against us had now reached their fulfillment, with men slaughtering animals and staining the altars with blood.

Such are the words of Porphyry, or rather, of Theophrastus. And **Plato** might serve as a seal on our argument in his *Cratylus*, saying these words exactly concerning our predecessors:

„ It seems to me that the first of the men in Greece held only these to be gods—the same ones many barbarians <note>In this context, "barbarian" simply means anyone who was not Greek.</note> believe in now: the sun, the moon, the earth, the stars, and the sky. Since they saw all these things always moving in a course and **running**, from this nature of **running** <term>thein: the Greek verb 'to run'</term>, they gave them the name **gods** <term>theous: the Greek word for 'gods'</term>.

But it is clear, I think, to anyone who considers it, that the first and most ancient of men did not concern themselves with the building of temples, nor with the setting up of wooden images <note>original: "ξοάνων" (xoanon) — ancient, primitive wooden cult images</note>. The arts of painting, modeling, carving, or statue-making had not yet been invented, nor had the crafts of building or architecture been established. Furthermore, no memory of those who were later named "gods" and "heroes" existed among the people of that time. They had no Zeus, no Cronus, no Poseidon, no Apollo, no Hera, no Athena, no Dionysus, nor any other male or female god, such as the thousands who appeared later among both barbarians and Greeks. Nor was any demon, whether good or bad, held in wonder among men. Only the visible stars of heaven, because of their "running" (which is to say, their movement), received the title of "gods," as they themselves say. And even these they did not worship with animal sacrifices or with the rituals devised later.

# EUSEBIUS

The word is not ours, but the testimony comes from within their own house and from themselves. Let us establish the proof through their own much-celebrated voices and the passages that will follow. Our own sacred scriptures also teach this, commanding all nations in the beginning to praise the visible luminaries <note>original: "φωστήρων" (phosteron) — the sun, moon, and stars</note> assigned to them, but entrusting only the Hebrew race with the contemplation and vision of the Maker and Creator of the universe, and true piety toward Him. Therefore, among the most ancient of men, there was no talk of a Greek or barbarian "birth of the gods" <term>theogony: an account of the origins and genealogies of a group of gods</term>, nor the setting up of wooden statues, nor the much-talked-about nonsense of naming gods as male and female. These titles and names, invented later by men, were not yet known among people then. Nor were there invocations of demons or invisible spirits, nor strange myths about gods and heroes, nor the mysteries of secret rites; nor, in short, any of the massive and unexpected superstition of men of later times. These were, therefore, human inventions, fabrications of a mortal nature, or rather, the shameful and undisciplined devices of those about whom a divine oracle <note>referring to the Wisdom of Solomon 14:12 from the Septuagint</note> says: "The invention of idols was the beginning of fornication." If, then, the immense and complex error of the nations arose many ages later—beginning with the Phoenicians and Egyptians, and passing from them to the rest of the nations, even to the Greeks—let us examine this history and art of the ancients, through the eyes of those from Phoenicia.

**Sanchuniathon**, an ancient man, who they say lived before the time of the Trojan War, records these things. The Phoenician history is testified to have been accepted for its accuracy. **Philo of Byblos** <note>A scholar and grammarian of the 1st–2nd century AD</note> (not the Hebrew Philo) is the witness; he translated Sanchuniathon’s entire work from the Phoenician tongue into the Greek language and published it. Our contemporary <note>Eusebius refers to **Porphyry**, the Neo-Platonist philosopher and critic of Christianity</note>, who organized the conspiracy against us, mentions these things in the fourth book of his work against us, testifying to Sanchuniathon in these exact words:

<margin>»</margin> "Sanchuniathon of Beirut <note>modern-day Beirut, Lebanon</note> relates the most truthful things about the Jews, as his accounts are most
<margin>»</margin> consistent with their places and names. He received these memoirs from **Hierombalus**, the priest of the god 
<margin>»</margin> **Ieuo** <note>Likely a Greek rendering of the Hebrew name Yahweh</note>. He dedicated his history to **Abibalus**, the king of the Beirutians, and it was accepted by 
<margin>»</margin> him and by those investigating the truth in his time. The dates of these men fall even before the Trojan 
<margin>»</margin> times, and they are nearly contemporary with **Moses**, as shown by the successions of the kings of Phoenicia. 
<margin>»</margin> Sanchuniathon, writing in the Phoenician dialect with a love for truth, gathered the ancient history from the 
<margin>»</margin> city records and the inscriptions in the temples. He lived during the time of **Semiramis**, the 
<margin>»</margin> queen of the Assyrians, who is recorded to have lived before or during the Trojan times. The 
<margin>»</margin> works of Sanchuniathon were translated into the Greek tongue by Philo of Byblos."

So spoke the aforementioned man, testifying both to the truth and the antiquity of this "theologian." But as Sanchuniathon proceeds, he does not speak of the God over all, nor even of the gods in heaven, but of mortal men and women—and not even of a decent character, such as would be worth accepting for their virtue or imitating for their philosophy. Instead, he treats as gods those wrapped in every kind of vice, wickedness, and corruption. He claims these very people are the ones considered gods to this day in all cities and regions.

### EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 1

Receive then the proofs of these things from the written records. Philo, having divided the entire work of Sanchuniathon into nine books, says the following about Sanchuniathon in the preface of his first volume, using these very words:

> >> Since these things are so, Sanchuniathon—who was a man of great learning and an active researcher—desired to know everything from the beginning, ever since the universe was first composed. He searched out these matters with great diligence, knowing that among all those who have lived under the sun, the oldest was Taautos <note>original: "Τάαυτος"</note>, the inventor of letters and the one who began the practice of keeping records. He made Taautos the foundation of his account—the one whom the Egyptians call Thoyth, the Alexandrians call Thoth, and the Greeks have translated as Hermes. 
> >> Having said this, he blames the more recent writers who followed them for having forcibly and falsely reduced the myths about the gods into allegories and physical explanations <term>allegory: a story where characters or events symbolize deeper moral or natural truths</term> and theories. He says concerning them: "But the most recent of the theologians rejected the actual events that happened from the beginning, inventing instead allegories and myths, and fabricating a connection with cosmic events. They established mysteries and surrounded them with much vanity <note>original: "τῦφον" (tuphon) — literally 'smoke,' referring to delusion or intellectual arrogance</note>, so that no one could easily perceive the things that actually occurred in truth." 
> >> But Sanchuniathon, by consulting the secret writings of the Ammuneans <note>hidden writings found in the *adyta* or inner sanctuaries of temples, likely belonging to the god Amun</note> which he discovered—writings which were certainly not known to everyone—mastered the learning of all things himself. Having finished his work, he put away the original myths and allegories and completed his purpose, until later priests again wanted to hide the truth and restore the mythical character. From this emerged the 'mystic' element which had not yet reached the Greeks. 
> >> Following this, he says (and we have found these things): "Those desiring to know the affairs of the Phoenicians accurately have searched through much material, not that of the Greeks. For the Greek accounts are discordant, and composed by some for the sake of rivalry rather than for the truth." And after other things: "Convinced that the writing is just as he [Sanchuniathon] wrote it, they see the discordance among the Greeks, about which I have written in the books entitled *History of Paradoxes* <note>original: "παραδόξου ἱστορίας"</note>." 
> >> And again, after further remarks, he adds: "Having gained confidence that these things are sufficient to clarify matters for later times, and from reading the parts in detail, I see that the most ancient of the barbarians <note>a term used by Greeks for all non-Greek peoples, including Phoenicians and Egyptians</note>, and especially the Phoenicians and Egyptians—from whom the rest of humanity received their traditions—regarded as the greatest gods those who had discovered things necessary for life, or who had in some way done good for the nations. Regarding these men as benefactors and causes of many blessings, they worshipped them as gods. 
> >> When these men passed away, they established temples, dedicated pillars and rods in their names, and held them in great honor; the Phoenicians assigned the greatest festivals to them. Specifically, they gave the names of their own kings to the cosmic elements and to some of those considered to be gods. They recognized only the natural elements <note>original: "φυσικούς" (physikous)</note>—the sun, the moon, the other planets, and the elements, and things related to these—as gods. Thus, for them, some were mortal gods and others were immortal gods."

Philo, having made these distinctions in his preface, then begins his translation of Sanchuniathon, setting forth the Phoenician theology in this manner.
