Having introduced the historian and his sources in the previous page, the text now details the specific Phoenician creation myth (cosmogony) and the early stages of human civilization.</meta>

->EUSEBIUS<-

## Theology of the Phoenicians.

He supposes the beginning of all things to be a dark and windy air, or a breath of dark air, and a turbid, gloomy chaos <term>chaos: a state of total disorder or the void existing before the creation of the universe</term>. These things were supposedly infinite and for a long age had no limit. But when, he says, the "breath" became enamored with its own origins and a mixture occurred, that connection was called *Pothos* <note>original: "πόθος" — meaning 'Desire' or 'Longing'</note>. This was the beginning of the creation of all things. 

But the breath itself did not know its own creation; and from its own embrace, the breath produced *Mot* <note>original: "μώτ"</note>. Some say this is mud; others say it is a rotting of a watery mixture. From this came all the seed of creation and the birth of the universe. There were certain animals that had no sensation, from which came intelligent animals, and they were called *Zophasemin* <note>original: "Ζωφασημὶν" — interpreted as "watchers of heaven"</note>, that is, "the observers of heaven." They were formed in the shape of an egg. Then *Mot* shone forth, as did the sun, the moon, and the great stars. Such was their "cosmogony" <term>cosmogony: a theory or story regarding the origin of the universe</term>, which directly introduces atheism. 

Let us see next how he says the "zoogony" <term>zoogony: the origin or evolution of living beings</term> came to be. He says: 

"Therefore, as the air became luminous, through the fiery heat of both the sea and the land, winds were produced, and clouds, and great downpours and floods of celestial waters. And when these were separated and displaced from their proper home due to the sun's heat, and all met again in the air, clashing together, thunders and lightnings were produced. At the crash of the thunder, the aforementioned intelligent animals were awakened, startled by the sound; and male and female began to move on the land and in the sea." 

Such is their account of the generation of life. Following this, the same author adds: 

"These things were found written in the cosmogony of Taautos <note>The Egyptian god Thoth, whom the Greeks identified with Hermes</note> and in his memoirs, based on the conjectures and evidence which his mind saw and discovered, and which he enlightened for us." 

Next, after giving the names of the winds—the South wind, the North wind, and the rest—he adds: "But these first people consecrated the plants of the earth, and considered them gods, and they worshiped the things upon which they themselves lived, as did their followers and all those before them; they even made libations <term>libation: a drink poured out as an offering to a deity</term> and sacrifices to them." And he adds: "These were their ideas of worship, corresponding to their own weakness and the timidity of their souls." 

Then he says that from the wind *Kolpia* <note>possibly meaning 'the voice of the breath'</note> and his wife *Baau* <note>translated here as 'Night'</note> were born *Aion* <note>meaning 'Age' or 'Eternity'</note> and *Protogonos* <note>meaning 'First-born'</note>, who were mortal men. *Aion* discovered the way to get food from trees. From these two were born children called *Genos* and *Genea*, who inhabited Phoenicia. When droughts occurred, they stretched their hands toward the heavens to the sun. For this, he says, they considered the sun to be the only god, the lord of heaven, calling him *Beelsamen* <note>original: "βεελσάμην" — the Phoenician 'Baal Shamin'</note>, which among the Phoenicians means 'Lord of Heaven,' and among the Greeks is 'Zeus.' 

After this, he blames the Greeks for their error, saying: "For it is not without reason that we have distinguished these things in many ways, but rather to counter the later misinterpretations of the names given to these events. The Greeks, being ignorant of the facts, received them differently, having been led astray by the ambiguity of the translation." 

Next he says that from the race of *Aion* and *Protogonos* were born, in turn, mortal children whose names were Light, Fire, and Flame. These, he says, discovered fire from the rubbing of sticks and taught its use. These men fathered sons who surpassed others in size and excellence, and whose names were given to the mountains they occupied. Thus, from them were named Mount Cassius, Lebanon, Anti-Lebanon, and Brathu. From these, he says, were born *Mesourumos* and *Hypsouranios*. They took their names from their mothers...

->PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book I.<-

...the women of that time cohabited freely with whomever they happened to meet. Then he says that Hypsuranius <note>original: "Ὑψουράνιος" — meaning 'High-Heavenly'</note> inhabited Tyre, and he devised huts made of reeds, rushes, and papyrus. He fell into a quarrel with his brother Usous <note>original: "Οὔσωος"</note>, who discovered a covering for the body made from the skins of wild beasts that he managed to catch. When violent rains and winds occurred, the trees in Tyre rubbed against one another and kindled a fire, which burned down the forest there. Taking a tree and lopping off its branches, Usous was the first to venture into the sea on a log. He consecrated two pillars to fire and wind and worshiped them, pouring out libations to them from the blood of the animals he caught in the hunt. 

When these men died, he says those who remained consecrated staves to them, worshiped the pillars, and held annual festivals in their honor. Many years later, from the line of Hypsuranius came Agreus <note>original: "Ἀγρεύς" — 'the Hunter'</note> and Halieus <note>original: "Ἁλιεύς" — 'the Fisherman'</note>, the inventors of hunting and fishing, from whom hunters and fishermen take their names. From these were born two brothers who discovered iron and how to work it. One of them, Chousor <note>original: "Χουσὼρ"</note>, practiced discourse, incantations, and divinations; he is identified as Hephaestus <note>the Greek god of fire and blacksmithing</note>. He also invented the fishhook, bait, fishing line, and the raft, and was the first of all men to sail. For this reason, they revered him as a god after his death. He is also called Zeus Meilichios <note>original: "Δία μειλίχιον" — 'the Gentle' or 'Propitiatory' Zeus</note>. Others say his brothers invented the construction of walls from bricks. 

After this, from that same race, there were born two youths, one called Technites <note>original: "Τεχνίτην" — 'the Craftsman'</note> and the other Geinos Autochthon <note>original: "Γήϊνον Αὐτόχθονα" — 'the Earthly Native'</note>. These men discovered how to mix straw with the clay of bricks and dry them in the sun; they also invented roofs. From them came others, one called Agros <note>original: "Ἀγρὸς" — 'Field'</note> and the other Agroueros <note>original: "Ἀγρούηρος"</note> or Agrotes <note>original: "Ἀγρότης" — 'Countryman'</note>. The latter has a wooden statue that is still greatly revered and a shrine drawn by a yoke of oxen in Phoenicia; among the people of Byblos, he is preeminently called the greatest of the gods. These men devised the addition of courtyards, enclosures, and caves to houses. From them came husbandmen and hunters. These are also called "Wanderers" and "Titans." 

From these were born Amynus <note>original: "Ἄμυνον"</note> and Magus <note>original: "Μάγον"</note>, who established villages and flocks. From them were born Misor <note>original: "Μισὼρ"</note> and Sydyk <note>original: "Συδύκ"</note>, which is to say "Well-freed" and "Just." These discovered the use of salt. From Misor came Taautus <note>original: "Τάαυτος"</note>, who invented the writing of the first elements; the Egyptians called him Thoor <note>original: "Θωὼρ"</note>, the Alexandrians Thoth, and the Romans Mercury <note>the text notes the Greek equivalent as Hermes</note>. From Sydyk came the Dioscuri <note>original: "Διόσκουροι" — the divine twins</note>, or Cabiri <note>original: "Καβειροί"</note>, or Corybantes, or Samothracians. These, he says, were the first to invent a ship. From them were born others who discovered herbs, the healing of venomous bites, and incantations. 

In their time lived a certain Elioun <note>original: "Ἐλιοῦν"</note>, called "Most High" <note>original: "Ὕψιστος"</note>, and a female called Beruth <note>original: "Βηροὺθ"</note>, who lived near Byblos. From them was born Epigeios or Autochthon, whom they later called Ouranos <note>original: "Οὐρανόν" — 'the Sky'</note>. Thus, because of his extraordinary beauty, they named the element above us "heaven" after him. He had a sister born of the same parents, who was called Ge <note>original: "Γῆ" — 'the Earth'</note>, and because of her beauty, they called the earth by the same name. Their father, the Most High, died in an encounter with wild beasts and was consecrated as a god, to whom his children offered libations and sacrifices. Ouranos, succeeding to his father's dominion, took his sister Ge in marriage and had four sons by her: Ilos <note>original: "ᾞλον"</note>, also known as Cronus, Betylus <note>original: "Βέτυλον"</note>, Dagon <note>original: "Δαγὼν"</note>—who is Siton <note>original: "Σίτων" — 'the god of grain'</note>—and Atlas. Ouranos also had many children by other wives. Because of this, Ge grew bitter; out of jealousy she reproached Ouranos, such that they were separated. But Ouranos, though he had left her, would return with force whenever...

<meta>This page continues the "zoogony" or the history of living beings within the Phoenician mythos, as recorded by Sanchuniathon and translated by Philo of Byblos. It provides the foundational cosmogony that precedes the cultural developments described in the previous page.</meta>

### Phoenician Theology.

He supposes the principle of the universe to be a dark and windy air, or a breath of dark air, and a turbid, gloomy chaos. These things were infinite and for a long age had no limit. But when, he says, the spirit became enamored of its own principles, and a mixing occurred, that entanglement was called Desire <note>original: "πόθος" (Pothos) — a personification of longing or sexual desire as a creative force</note>. This was the beginning of the creation of all things. Yet the spirit itself did not know its own creation; and from its entanglement, *Mot* was produced. Some say this is "mud," others a "putrefaction of a watery mixture." From this came all the seeds of creation and the generation of the universe. 

There were certain living beings that possessed no sensation, from which came intelligent beings called *Zophasemin* <note>original: "ζωφασημὶν" — likely derived from the Hebrew/Phoenician for "beholders of heaven"</note>. It was shaped like an egg, and *Mot* shone forth, as did the sun, the moon, the stars, and the great constellations. Such was their cosmogony, which introduces outright atheism <note>Eusebius, as a Christian historian, is critiquing the lack of a divine creator in this Phoenician system</note>. Let us see next how he says the generation of life took place. He says then:

<margin>„</margin> When the air became transparent through fire, both the sea and the land produced winds,
<margin>„</margin> clouds, and great downpours and floods of heavenly waters. And when these were 
<margin>„</margin> separated and moved from their own place due to the heat of the sun, and everything 
<margin>„</margin> met again in the air and collided, thunders and lightnings were produced. At the
<margin>„</margin> crash of the thunders, the previously mentioned intelligent beings were 
<margin>„</margin> awakened, startled by the sound; and male and female began to move on the land 
<margin>„</margin> and in the sea. Such was their generation of life. 

Following these things, the same author adds: 

<margin>„</margin> These things were found written in the *Cosmogony* of Sanchuniathon and in his 
<margin>„</margin> records, based on the observations and evidence which his mind perceived and 
<margin>„</margin> discovered, and which he has enlightened for us. 

Next, explaining the names of the South and North winds and the rest, he adds: 

<margin>„</margin> But these people were the first to consecrate the fruits of the earth; they 
<margin>„</margin> considered them gods and worshiped the things upon which they themselves, 
<margin>„</margin> their descendants, and all those before them had lived, performing libations 
<margin>„</margin> and sacrifices to them. 

And he adds: 

<margin>„</margin> These were the inventions of worship, matching their own weakness and the 
<margin>„</margin> timidity of their souls. Then he says there were born from the wind *Kolpia* 
<margin>„</margin> and his wife *Baau* <note>which he interprets as "Night"</note>, *Aeon* <note>Age</note> 
<margin>„</margin> and *Protogonos* <note>First-born</note>, mortal men so named. *Aeon* discovered 
<margin>„</margin> the food obtained from trees. Their offspring were called *Genos* <note>Race</note> 
<margin>„</margin> and *Genea* <note>Generation</note>, and they inhabited Phoenicia. When droughts 
<margin>„</margin> occurred, they stretched their hands toward the heavens and the sun. For this 
<margin>„</margin> being, he says, they considered the only god and lord of heaven, calling him 
<margin>„</margin> *Beelsamen* <note>original: "βεελσάμην" — Phoenician for 'Lord of Heaven'</note>, 
<margin>„</margin> which is Zeus among the Greeks. 

After this, he blames the Greeks for error, saying: 

<margin>„</margin> For it was not in vain that we distinguished these things in many ways, but in 
<margin>„</margin> view of the later interpretations of the names of things, which the Greeks, being 
<margin>„</margin> ignorant, took differently, having been led astray by the ambiguity of the translation. 

Next he says that from the race of *Aeon* and *Protogonos* were born again mortal children, whose names were Light, Fire, and Flame. These, he says, discovered fire by rubbing pieces of wood together and taught its use. They fathered sons who surpassed them in size and excellence, whose names were given to the mountains they occupied: Casius, Libanus, Antilibanus, and Brathy. From these, he says, were born *Mesouramos* and *Hypsuranius* <note>original: "Ὑψουράνιος" — 'High-Heavenly'</note>. He says they were named after their mothers...

At that time, women mingled shamelessly with anyone they happened to meet. Next, he says that Hypsouranios <note>original: "Ὑψουράνιον" — meaning "High in the Heavens"</note> inhabited Tyre, and he devised huts made of reeds, rushes, and papyrus. He quarreled with his brother Ousoos <note>original: "Οὐσωον"</note>, who was the first to find a covering for the body made from the skins of wild beasts he was able to catch. When heavy rains and winds occurred, the trees in Tyre rubbed against one another and caught fire, burning down the forest there. Ousoos then took a tree, lopped off its branches, and was the first to venture out into the sea. He consecrated two pillars to Fire and Wind and worshipped them, pouring libations to them from the blood of the wild beasts he hunted. 

When these men died, those who remained consecrated rods to them, continued to worship the pillars, and held annual festivals in their honor. Many years later, from the line of Hypsouranios were born Agreus <note>original: "Ἀγρέα" — meaning "The Hunter"</note> and Halieus <note>original: "Ἁλιέα" — meaning "The Fisherman"</note>, the inventors of hunting and fishing, from whom hunters and fishermen take their names. From them were born two brothers who discovered iron and the way to work it. One of them, Chrysor <note>original: "Χρυσὼρ"</note>, practiced speech, incantations, and prophecies; he is the same as Hephaestus <note>The Greek god of fire and smithing</note>. He also invented the fishhook, bait, fishing line, and the raft, and was the first of all men to sail. Therefore, they worshipped him as a god after his death. He was also called Zeus Meilichios <note>original: "Δία Μείλιχιον" — meaning "The Gentle" or "Gracious" Zeus</note>. His brothers, it is said, devised the building of walls from bricks. 

After these things, from this race were born two youths, one called Technites <note>original: "Τεχνίτην" — "The Craftsman"</note> and the other Geinos Autochthon <note>original: "Γήϊνον Αὐτόχθονα" — "Earth-born of the Soil"</note>. They devised the method of mixing straw with the clay of the brick and drying them in the sun; they also invented roofing. From them came others, one of whom was called Agros <note>original: "Ἀγρὸς" — "Field"</note> and the other Agroueros or Agrotes <note>original: "Ἀγρότης" — "Countryman" or "Farmer"</note>. Of the latter, there is still a highly revered statue and a shrine drawn by a yoke of oxen in Phoenicia; among the people of Byblos, he is specifically named as the greatest of the gods. These men devised the addition of courtyards to houses, as well as enclosures and caves. From them come farmers and those who hunt with dogs. They are also called Aletae <note>original: "Ἀλῆται" — "Wanderers"</note> and Titans. 

From these were born Amynos and Magos, who established villages and flocks of sheep. From them came Misor and Sydyk <note>original: "Μισὼρ καὶ Συδύκ"</note>, which means "Easy-to-Release" and "Righteous." These men discovered the use of salt. From Misor came Taautos <note>original: "Τάαυτος"</note>, who discovered the writing of the first letters; the Egyptians call him Thoor, the Alexandrians Thoth, and the Greeks Hermes. From Sydyk came the Dioscuri, or Cabeiri, or Corybantes, or Samothracians <note>Various groups of "helper" deities or mystery-cult figures in the ancient world</note>. These, he says, were the first to invent a ship. From them were born others who discovered herbs, the healing of venomous bites, and incantations. 

In their time, there lived a certain Elioun <note>original: "Ἐλιοῦν" — corresponding to the Semitic "El," meaning God</note> called "The Most High," and a female called Berouth; they lived near Byblos. From them was born Epigeios or Autochthon, whom they later called Ouranos <note>original: "Οὐρανόν" — "Sky" or "Heaven"</note>; so that from him, they named the element above us "heaven" because of its supreme beauty. He had a sister born of the same parents who was called Ge <note>original: "Γῆ" — "Earth"</note>, and because of her beauty, they say the earth was named after her. Their father, the Most High, died in an encounter with wild beasts and was consecrated as a god; his children offered libations and sacrifices to him. When Ouranos took over his father’s dominion, he married his sister Ge and had four children by her: Ilos (who is also called Kronos), Betylus, Dagon (which means "Grain"), and Atlas. Ouranos also had many children by other wives. Therefore, Ge became angry and, out of jealousy, reproached Ouranos so much that they separated from one another. But Ouranos, though he had departed from her, would return by force whenever...

And he <note>Ouranos/Heaven</note> desired to approach her <note>Ge/Earth</note>; but after drawing near to her, he withdrew again. He also attempted to destroy the children born from her. Earth, however, repeatedly defended herself, gathering allies to her side. When Time <note>original: "ὁ χρόνος" — here referring to the god Kronos</note> reached manhood, using Hermes the Thrice-Great <note>original: "ἑρμῇ τῷ τριςμεγίστῳ" — Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage</note> as his counselor and helper (for he was his scribe), he defended himself against his father Heaven, taking vengeance for his mother. To Kronos were born children: Persephone and Athena. The former died a virgin. By the advice of Athena and Hermes, Kronos fashioned a sickle <note>original: "ἅρπην"</note> and a spear out of iron. Then Hermes, having enchanted the allies of Kronos with magical words, instilled in those in the heavens a desire for battle on behalf of the Earth. And thus Kronos, engaging Heaven in war, drove him from power and succeeded to the kingdom.

In the battle, the lovely concubine of Heaven, who was then pregnant, was also captured. Kronos gave her in marriage to Dagon <note>A Semitic deity associated with grain and agriculture</note>. While with him, she gave birth to the child she carried from Heaven, whom she named Demarous <note>A name associated with Zeus or Adad</note>. Following these events, Kronos built a wall around his own dwelling and founded the first city, Byblos <note>original: "Βύβλον"</note> in Phoenicia. Afterward, Kronos became suspicious of his own brother Atlas <note>original: "Ἄτλαντα"</note> and, on the advice of Hermes, threw him into a deep pit in the earth and buried him. At that time, the descendants of the Dioscuri <note>The "sons of Zeus," here viewed as early maritime inventors</note> constructed rafts and ships and set sail. Having been cast ashore at Mount Casius, they dedicated a temple there. 

The allies of Ilos <note>The Phoenician name for Kronos, equivalent to the Semitic 'El'</note> (who is Kronos) were called *Elohim* <note>original: "ἐλωεὶμ" — the Hebrew word for God/gods</note>, signifying they were the people of Kronos. These were the ones so named by Kronos. Kronos had a son named Sadidus, whom he slew with his own iron sword because he had become suspicious of him; he thus deprived the boy of life with his own hand. Likewise, he cut off the head of his own daughter, so that all the gods were struck with terror at the mind of Kronos. 

As time passed, Heaven, while in exile, sent his virgin daughter Astarte with two of her sisters, Rhea and Dione, to kill Kronos by treachery. But Kronos captured them and, though they were his sisters, made them his legal wives. When Heaven learned of this, he sent Destiny <note>original: "εἱμαρμένην"</note> and Hour <note>original: "ὥραν"</note> with other allies to war against Kronos. But Kronos won these over as well and kept them with him. Furthermore, he says the god Heaven devised *baetylia* <note>original: "βαιτύλια" — meteorites or "thunderstones" worshipped as sacred</note>, having engineered "living stones." 

To Kronos were born by Astarte seven daughters, the Artemides or Titanides. And again, to the same [Kronos] were born seven sons by Rhea, the youngest of whom was consecrated at his birth. And by Dione, daughters were born; and by Astarte again, two males, Desire <note>original: "πόθος"</note> and Love <note>original: "ἔρως"</note>. Dagon, since he discovered grain and the plow, was called *Zeus of the Plow*. And one of the Titanides united with the one called the Just and gave birth to Asclepius <note>The god of healing</note>. To Kronos there were also born in the region across the river three sons: Kronos, named after his father, Zeus Belus <note>A fusion of the Greek Zeus and the Semitic Baal</note>, and Apollo. 

Contemporary with these were Sea <note>original: "πόντος"</note>, Typhon, and Nereus, the father of Sea. From Sea was born Sidon <note>The personification of the city Sidon</note>, who, because of her exceedingly beautiful voice, was the first to invent the singing of hymns. Poseidon was also born. To Demarous was born Melqart <note>original: "μήλκαρτος" — the patron god of Tyre</note>, who is also called Hercules. Then Heaven again made war against Sea, but having withdrawn, he joined himself with Demarous. Demarous then attacked Sea, but Sea put him to flight; Demarous then vowed a sacrifice for his escape. In the thirty-second year of his rule and reign, Ilos—that is, Kronos—having ambushed his father Heaven in an inland place and having him at his mercy, cut off his genitals near certain springs and rivers. <meta>catchword: Heaven</meta>

...and he [Heaven] desired to approach and draw near to her [Earth], but then he would withdraw again. He also attempted to destroy the children born from her. But Earth defended herself many times, gathering an alliance to her side. When Kronos <note>Original: "Χρόνος" (Chronos/Time). In this Phoenician context, he is identified with the god El</note> reached manhood, utilizing Hermes the Thrice-Great <note>original: "Ἑρμῇ τῷ τρισμεγίστῳ" — Hermes Trismegistus, here acting as a divine scribe</note> as his counselor and helper (for he was his scribe), he defended against his father Heaven <note>original: "Οὐρανὸν" (Uranus)</note>, taking vengeance for his mother.

By the counsel of Athena and Hermes, Kronos fashioned a sickle <note>original: "ἅρπην" (harpe) — a curved ritual blade</note> and a spear out of iron. Then Hermes, having charmed Kronos’s allies with magical words, instilled in those in heaven a desire for battle on behalf of the earth. And so Kronos, engaging Heaven in war, drove him from power and succeeded to the kingship. 

In the battle, Heaven's favorite concubine, who was pregnant, was captured. Kronos gave her in marriage to Dagon. In his house, she gave birth to the child she carried from Heaven, whom he named Demarous. After these events, Kronos built a wall around his own dwelling and founded the first city, Byblos in Phoenicia. 

Later, Kronos became suspicious of his own brother Atlas and, with the advice of Hermes, threw him into a deep pit in the earth and buried him. At this time, the descendants of the Dioscuri <note>The "sons of Zeus" or twin deities, often associated with the protection of sailors</note>, having constructed rafts and ships, took to the sea. Being cast ashore at Mount Casius, they dedicated a temple there. The allies of Ilos <note>A Semitic name for Kronos/El</note> (who is Kronos) were called *Elohim* <note>original: "Ἐλωεὶμ" — a Hebrew term for gods, here linked to the followers of El</note>, as if they were the "Kronian" party. These were the ones so named in the time of Kronos. 

Kronos had a son named Sadidos, whom he killed with his own iron blade because he suspected him; he became his own child's murderer and deprived him of life. Likewise, he cut off his own daughter's head, so that all the gods were stunned by Kronos’s state of mind. 

As time went on, Heaven, while in exile, sent his virgin daughter Astarte with two of her sisters, Rhea and Dione, to kill Kronos by treachery. But when they arrived, Kronos made them his lawful wives, even though they were his sisters. When Heaven learned this, he sent Fate <note>original: "εἱμαρμένην" (Heimarmene)</note> and Hour <note>original: "ὥραν" (Hora)</note> with other allies against Kronos. But Kronos won them over and kept them with him. Furthermore, the author says the god Heaven invented *Baetylia* <note>original: "Βαιτύλια" — sacred stones, often meteorites, believed to be "living" or animated by divinity</note>, crafting "living stones." 

In time, seven daughters called Titanides or Artemides were born to Kronos from Astarte. Again, seven children were born to him from Rhea, the youngest of whom was consecrated at birth. From Dione, female children were born. From Astarte again, two males were born, Longing <note>original: "Πόθος" (Pothos)</note> and Desire <note>original: "Ἔρως" (Eros)</note>. Dagon, since he discovered grain and the plow, was called Zeus of the Plow. 

To Sydyk <note>A name meaning "The Just"</note>, one of the Titanides bore Asclepius <note>The god of medicine and healing</note>. In Peraea, three children were also born to Kronos: a second Kronos named after his father, Zeus Belos <note>Associated with the Semitic Lord, Baal</note>, and Apollo. Contemporary with these were Pontos (the Sea), Typhon, and Nereus, the father of Pontos. From Pontos came Sidon, who by the extraordinary sweetness of her voice first invented the singing of hymns; and Poseidon. To Demarous was born Melqart <note>The patron deity of the city of Tyre</note>, who is also called Heracles. 

Then Heaven once again fought against Pontos. Breaking away, he joined Demarous. Demarous attacked Pontos, but Pontos routed him, and Demarous vowed a sacrifice for his escape. In the thirty-second year of his reign and kingship, Ilos (that is, Kronos), having ambushed his father Heaven in an inland place and taken him captive, castrated him near springs and rivers. There his blood was consecrated...

## Preparation for the Gospel, Book 1

...and he <note>Referring to Ouranos (Heaven)</note> desired, by coming upon her and drawing near to her, to return again. He also attempted to destroy the children born from her. But Earth <note>original: "γῆν" (Ge/Earth)</note> defended herself many times, and they say she gathered an alliance for herself. When Time <note>original: "ὁ χρόνος" (Kronos), here identified with the god Kronos/El</note> reached manhood, using Hermes the Thrice-Great <note>original: "ἑρμῇ τῷ τρισμεγίστῳ" (Hermes Trismegistus), the Greek identification for the Egyptian/Phoenician scribe-god Taautus</note> as his counselor and helper (for he was his scribe), he avenged himself on his father Heaven, acting on behalf of his mother.

Of Time <note>Kronos</note>, children were born: Persephone and Athena. The first, indeed, died a virgin. By the advice of Athena and Hermes, Kronos fashioned a sickle <term>harpē: a curved sword or scythe, famously used in myth to castrate Ouranos</term> and a spear out of iron. Then Hermes, having charmed the allies of Kronos with magical words, instilled in them a longing for battle against Heaven on behalf of Earth. And thus Kronos, engaging Heaven in war, drove him from his rule and succeeded to the kingdom.

Also captured in the battle was the favorite concubine of Heaven, who was pregnant. Kronos gave her in marriage to Dagon <note>A Semitic deity associated with grain and fertility</note>. While she was with him, she gave birth to the child she carried from Heaven, whom she named Demarous.

Following these events, Kronos built a wall around his own dwelling and founded the first city in Phoenicia, Byblos. After this, Kronos, becoming suspicious of his own brother Atlas, acting on the advice of Hermes, threw him into a deep pit of the earth and buried him.

During this time, the descendants of the Dioscuri <note>The "sons of Zeus," often associated with sailors; in the Phoenician context, they are the Cabeiri</note>, having constructed rafts and ships, put to sea. Being cast ashore at Mount Casius, they consecrated a temple there. The allies of Ilus <note>original: "ἴλου" — the Phoenician name for Kronos/El</note>, who is Kronos, were called "Elohim" <note>original: "ἐλωεὶμ" — a Greek transcription of the Hebrew/Phoenician word for gods, 'Elohim'</note>, as they were the "Kronians." These were the ones so named by Kronos.

Kronos also had a son named Sadidos, whom he dispatched with his own iron sword because he held him in suspicion; thus, becoming the slayer of his own child, he deprived him of life. Likewise, he cut off his own daughter's head, so that all the gods were struck with terror at the mind of Kronos.

As time went on, Heaven, being in exile, sent his virgin daughter Astarte, along with two of her sisters, Rhea and Dione, to kill Kronos by treachery. But Kronos took them and made them his lawful wives, though they were his sisters. When Heaven learned of this, he sent "Fate" and "Hour" <note>original: "εἱμαρμένην καὶ ὥραν" (Heimarmene and Hora)</note> with other allies against Kronos, but Kronos won these over as well and kept them with him.

Furthermore, he says that the god Heaven devised "Baetylia" <term>Baetylia: sacred stones believed to be animate or "soul-possessing" (lithoi empsychoi), often meteorites</term>, by engineering "living stones."

To Kronos, from Astarte, were born seven daughters, the Titanides or Artemides. And again, to the same, seven sons were born from Rhea, the youngest of whom was consecrated at his birth. From Dione, female children were born. From Astarte again, two males were born: Desire <note>original: "πόθος" (Pothos)</note> and Love <note>original: "ἔρως" (Eros)</note>.

Dagon, since he discovered grain and the plow, was called "Zeus of the Plow" <note>original: "ζεὺς ἀρότριος" (Zeus Arotrios)</note>. One of the Titanides joined with the one called "The Just" <note>The god Sydyk</note> and gave birth to Asclepius.

There were also born to Kronos in Peraea <note>The region "beyond" the river</note> three sons: Kronos, who shared his father’s name, Zeus Belus, and Apollo. Contemporary with these were Sea <note>original: "πόντος" (Pontos)</note>, Typhon, and Nereus, the father of Sea. From Sea was born Sidon, who by the extraordinary beauty of her voice first invented the hymns of song; and also Poseidon. To Demarous was born Melkarth, who is also called Hercules.

Then again, Heaven made war against Sea, but retreating, he joined himself to Demarous. Demarous then attacked Sea, but Sea put him to flight; Demarous then vowed a sacrifice for his escape.

In the thirty-second year of his rule and kingship, Ilus (that is, Kronos), having ambushed his father Heaven in an inland place, and having gotten him into his power, castrated him near certain springs and rivers. There, Heaven was consecrated...

Heaven <note>original: οὐρανὸς (Ouranos)</note>, and his spirit was exhausted, and the blood from his genitals <note>Continuing the story of the castration of Ouranos by his son Kronos</note> dripped away into the springs and the waters of the rivers; and even to this day the location is still pointed out. These then are the deeds of Kronos, and such were the prestigious lives of those among the heroes in that age. For these people, they say, there first existed the **golden race** of mortal men, partaking in that celebrated happiness of the ancients.

Again the author <note>Sanchuniathon</note> adds to these things, saying after other matters: 
» "**Astarte** the greatest, and **Zeus Demarous**, and **Adodos** <note>A Semitic name for Hadad, the storm god</note> the king of the gods, reigned over the land by the will of Kronos. And Astarte placed upon her own head a bull’s head as a sign of royalty. While wandering through the inhabited world, she found a star fallen from the sky, which she gathered up and consecrated in the holy island of Tyre. The Phoenicians say that Astarte is **Aphrodite**." 

And Kronos, as he went about the inhabited world, gave the kingdom of Attica to his own daughter, **Athena**. But when a plague and a deadly destruction occurred, Kronos offered up his only-begotten son as a whole burnt offering <note>original: ὁλοκαρποῖ</note> to his father Heaven, and he circumcised his own genitals, forcing his allies who were with him to do the same. And not long after, he consecrated another of his sons by Rhea, named **Mouth**, who had died. The Phoenicians name this figure **Death** and **Pluto**. 

And after these things, Kronos gave the city of **Byblos** to the goddess **Baaltis** (who is also called Dione), and **Berytus** <note>Modern Beirut</note> to **Poseidon** and the **Cabeiri** <term>Cabeiri: mysterious chthonic deities often associated with metalworking and seafaring</term>, who were farmers and fishermen. It was they who consecrated the remains of the Sea <note>original: Πόντου (Pontus)</note> at Berytus. 

But before these events, the god **Taautus** <note>The Phoenician Thoth or Hermes</note>, having imitated the appearance of Heaven, drew the faces of the gods—such as Kronos and Dagon—and the sacred characters of the elements <note>This refers to the invention of writing or sacred symbols</note>. He also devised symbols of royalty for Kronos: four eyes, two in front and two behind; two of them were quietly closed, and upon his shoulders were four wings—two as if flying, and two as if folded. 

The symbol meant that Kronos saw while he was sleeping, and slept while he was awake. And likewise with the wings: that while resting he was flying, and while flying he was resting. For the other gods, he gave two wings each upon their shoulders, to signify that they flew along with Kronos. And on Kronos’s head, he again placed two wings: one for the supreme mind, and one for the senses. 

When Kronos came into the southern land, he gave all of **Egypt** to the god Taautus, so that it might be his kingdom. These things, he says, were first recorded by the seven sons of Sydek, the Cabeiri, and their eighth brother **Asclepius**, as the god Taautus had commanded them. 

All these things the son of Thabion—who was the very first <term>hierophant: a priest who interprets sacred mysteries</term> of the Phoenicians from the beginning of time—turned into allegories, mixing them with the physical and cosmic forces of nature, and handed them down to those who celebrate the secret rites and to the prophets who lead the initiations. These men, seeking to increase the sense of awe <note>original: τύφον (typhon) – pride or smoke, implying a clouding of the truth with mysticism</note> by every means, passed them on to their successors and to those who were introduced to them. One of these was **Isiris**, the inventor of the three letters, the brother of **Chna** <note>Canaan</note>, the first to be renamed "Phoenician." 

» Then he <note>Sanchuniathon</note> follows this by saying: "But the **Greeks**, surpassing all others in natural cleverness, at first claimed most of these stories as their own. They then dramatized them with various embellishments, intending to charm by the pleasures of myths, and adorned them in every way. From this came **Hesiod** and the Cyclic poets, who echoed stories of 'Theogonies' <note>The origins of the gods</note>, and 'Gigantomachies' <note>The war of the giants</note>, and 'Castration-battles,' and by fashioning their own versions, they overwhelmed the truth. Having been nurtured on these fictions, our ears have become accustomed to them and are preoccupied by them for ages..."

### PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 1

<page-num>27</page-num>

> As for Ethallyn <note>A name likely derived from an Egyptian or Phoenician epithet for a creator deity; some scholars link it to the Agathodaemon or "Good Spirit"</note>, he is a serpent having the form of a hawk, delightful with splendor. If he should look up, he filled the whole world with light in his first-born region; but if he should blink, darkness followed. He who spoke of this gave the impression that the deity shines through light because of his fiery nature.

For it is the nature of light to shine through. Pherecydes <note>Pherecydes of Syros, a 6th-century BCE philosopher known for his mytho-cosmological writings</note> also took his starting points from the Phoenicians and theologized about the god he calls Ophioneus <term>Ophioneus: A serpent-god in Greek mythology who ruled the cosmos before being overthrown by Kronos</term>, and about the "Ophionidae" [the serpent-descendants], of whom we shall speak again later. Furthermore, the Egyptians, following the same concept when drawing the world, sketch a circular, airy, and fiery circle, and a hawk-shaped serpent stretched through the middle. (The whole shape is like our letter **Theta** [Θ]). By the circle, they signify the world; and by the serpent in the middle, they signify the unifying "Good Spirit" <note>original: ἀγαθὸν δαίμονα (agathon daimona)</note> who holds it together. Zoroaster the Mage also says word-for-word in the *Sacred Collection of Persian Lore*:

> But God is he who has the head of a hawk. He is the first, incorruptible, eternal, unbegotten, indivisible, most unlike any other, the driver of every good thing, one who cannot be bribed, the best of the good, the wisest of the wise. He is also the father of good order and justice, self-taught, natural, and perfect, and wise, and the only discoverer of the sacred natural world.

Ostanes <note>A legendary Persian magus and sage often cited in ancient alchemical and occult texts</note> says the same things about him in the work titled *The Eightfold Book*. For all of them, taking their starting points from him [Taautos], studied nature as described above. They set up the first elements of worship using serpents in temples, dedicated them, and performed sacrifices, festivals, and mysteries <term>mysteries: Sacred, secret rituals intended for initiates that often involved symbolic reenactments of divine stories</term> for them, believing them to be the greatest gods and the leaders of the universe.

So much for the serpents. Indeed, the Phoenician theology is of this character. The word of salvation [the Gospel] proclaims that we must flee from these things without turning back and seek a cure for the mental blindness of the ancients. It is clear that these are not mere myths or the inventions of poets containing some hidden allegorical theory, but are the true testimonies of wise and ancient theologians—as they themselves would say. These accounts contain things older than the fictional poets and historians; they derive their credibility from the names and histories of the gods that still prevail today in the cities and villages of Phoenicia, and from the mysteries celebrated among each of them. It should be obvious, then, that there is no longer a need to seek forced physical explanations for these things, as the evidence presented carries its own clear refutation. Such, then, is the theology of the Phoenicians. It is time to move on and examine that of the Egyptians.

Eusebius argues that these pagan traditions are ancient and widespread, yet ultimately something to be rejected in favor of the Christian Gospel.</summary>

The following are contained in the second book of the *Preparation for the Gospel*:
A summary of Egyptian theology, and how it was transmitted to the Greeks.
That we do not act irrationally in turning away from all these things.
Concerning the fact that the theology held by the Greeks was introduced to them recently.
A summary of the myths told by the Greeks regarding the gods and their shrines.
A summary of the secret rites and hidden mysteries of the error of polytheism <note>The worship of many gods.</note>.
By what reasoning we departed from holding views about the gods similar to the Greeks.
A recapitulation of what was said previously.
Concerning the so-called "holy things" of the gods found at the tombs of the dead.
What sort of opinion the ancients held regarding the gods.
Concerning the more dignified and "natural" theology of the Greeks.
How Plato thought regarding the theology of the ancients.
Concerning the theology of the Romans.

->Introduction<-

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring ornate foliate and scrollwork designs within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>
**T**he matters of Phoenician theology were indeed discussed by us in the preceding discourse, which the saving word <note>original: ὁ σωτήριος λόγος (ho sōtērios logos) — referring here to the Christian Gospel or the "Reason" of Christ</note> proclaims as an inescapable flight and a healing from the mental madness of the ancients. It so happens that these are not mere myths and poetic fictions containing some hidden theory within their underlying meanings <note>Eusebius is arguing against "allegory," where philosophers claimed myths were just symbols for nature</note>. For they are true testimonies from their own ancient theologians, as they themselves would say, containing things older than all poets and historians. They bring credibility to their accounts from the names and histories of the gods still prevailing to this day in the cities and villages of Phoenicia, and from the mysteries performed among each of them. This will be clear when we see the agreement of the other writers, and even of those considered "theologians," through which they testified that the ancients and those who came before them had mythologized about the gods. These stories do not pertain to natural explanations <note>original: φυσικὰς ἐκτολογίας (physikas ektologias)</note>, nor are the myths about the gods to be allegorized; rather, the histories must be preserved in their literal sense. This was shown by the voices of those already quoted, suggesting that one should no longer try to violently track down "natural philosophy" <note>original: φυσιολογίας (physiologias)</note> in these tales, as the aforementioned accounts bring a clear refutation of that idea from within themselves. Such, then, was the theology of the Phoenicians. It is now time, having moved on, to also examine the affairs of the Egyptians, so that we may understand and examine their animal-worship <term>original: ζωιδίων (zōidiōn) — the practice of treating animals as divine beings or zodiacal symbols</term>, and see if our departure from them was not established for sound and rational reasons. This was achieved not otherwise than through the Gospel proof, first of all for the Egyptians themselves, and then for those who think like them. Now, Manetho the Egyptian <note>An Egyptian priest and historian (3rd century BCE) who wrote in Greek</note> translated the whole of Egyptian history into our language <note>i.e., Greek, which Eusebius assumes his readers know</note> at great length, specifically the parts concerning their theology, both in the *Sacred Book* he wrote and in his other works. Diodorus, too, whom we mentioned earlier <note>Diodorus Siculus, a 1st-century BCE Greek historian</note>, has tracked these histories from many sources and has accurately detailed the traditions of each nation as much as possible,

<meta>catchword: accurately,</meta>

<header>GOSPEL PREPARATION Book 2. 4.</header>

...having precisely investigated, a distinguished man <note>referring to the historian Diodorus Siculus</note>, who has acquired no small reputation for learning among all scholars. This man, having collected all ancient history and connected the earliest events with those that followed, began his entire treatise with the theology of the Egyptians. It seemed better for me to present my evidence from his work, as his writing is more familiar to the Greeks. He records these things word-for-word:

->Egyptian Theology.<-

> The Egyptians say that at the original birth of the universe, the first humans were born in Egypt, both because of the mild climate <note>original: εὐκρασία (eukrasia) — a "well-mixed" or temperate environment</note> of the country and the nature of the Nile. For since this river is very fruitful and provides natural food, it easily sustained the living creatures it produced. They say that the gods were originally mortal humans, but because of their wisdom and their common service to mankind, they achieved immortality. Some of these even became kings. When their names are translated, some are found to have the same names as the celestial bodies, while others have their own distinct titles: the Sun <note>original: ἥλιος (helios)</note>, Cronus <note>original: κρόνος (kronos)</note>, and Rhea; and also Zeus, who is called Ammon by some; and in addition to these, Hera and Hephaestus; then Hestia, and finally Hermes. They say the Sun was the first to rule over Egypt, being named after the star in the sky. However, some of the priests say that Hephaestus ruled first, having been the inventor of fire. After this, Cronus reigned, and having married his sister Rhea, he fathered—according to some—Osiris and Isis, but according to the majority, he fathered Zeus and Hera, who ruled over the entire world because of their virtue. From these were born five gods: Osiris, Isis, Typhon, Apollo, and Aphrodite. They say that Osiris is Dionysus, and Isis is Demeter. She married Osiris, and when he succeeded to the kingdom, he performed many deeds for the common benefit. He founded a "hundred-gated" city in the territory of Thebes, which some call the "City of Zeus" <note>original: Διὸς πόλιν (Dios polin) — Diospolis</note> and others call Thebes. He also established a temple for his parents, Zeus and Hera, and golden shrines for the other gods, assigning honors to each and appointing priests to care for them. Osiris was also the discoverer of the vine; he was the first to use it and taught other men the art of agriculture. He honored Hermes most of all, as he was gifted with an extraordinary nature for inventing things capable of benefiting common life. For they say he was the inventor of writing and organized the sacrifices to the gods; he invented the lyre and taught the Greeks the art of interpretation <note>original: ἑρμηνείαν (hermēneian) — the word for "interpretation" or "translation," from which the name "Hermes" was derived by the Greeks</note>, which is why he was named Hermes. He also discovered the olive tree. When Osiris traveled throughout the inhabited world, he appointed Busiris over Phoenicia and Antaeus over Ethiopia and Libya. He himself set out on his campaign with his brother Apollo, who they say was the discoverer of the laurel tree. Osiris also took along his two sons, Anubis and Macedon. They also encountered Pan, who is exceptionally honored by the Egyptians and after whom the "City of Pan" <note>Panopolis</note> is named. While staying with Pan in the region of Taposiris, he brought along a group of Satyrs. Since Osiris was a lover of music, he led about a great number of musicians, among whom were also young women...

->Introduction.<-

<image-desc>An ornamental drop cap "T" inside a square frame decorated with stylized foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

The preceding sections encompassed the Phoenician theology, so that the word of salvation might announce a cure for ancient madness and a flight without turning back. It turns out that these are not myths and varied fabrications containing some hidden theory within their underlying meanings <note>original: ὑπονοίαις (hyponoiais) — often referring to "hidden meanings" or allegories used by philosophers to defend offensive myths</note>. For there are true testimonies from their own ancient theologians, as they themselves would say, and the poetic works contain the oldest records of all the prose writers. These accounts gain credibility from the names and histories of the gods still prevailing to this day in the cities and villages of Phoenicia, and from the mysteries performed in each place. 

It would be clear, from the agreement of other writers and even those considered theologians, through which they testified that the ancient and earlier myths about the gods do not differ into natural explanations <note>original: φυσικὰς ἐτυμολογίας (physikas etymologias) — the practice of explaining gods as symbols for physical forces like wind or fire</note>, nor are the myths about the gods allegorical, but they preserve the histories based on the literal wording alone. For the voices of those already quoted showed that one should no longer seek forced physical explanations for these things, as the subjects themselves carry a clear refutation of themselves. Such then was the Phoenician theology. 

It is time to move on and examine the Egyptian accounts, to understand and see clearly those who were driven out <note>meaning the ancient gods or those who followed them</note>, unless our departure from them was unexamined and irrational. This is established not otherwise than through the evangelical demonstration alone, first of all for the Egyptians themselves, and then for those who hold the same views as they do. Now, the whole of Egyptian history has been translated into our own language <note>Greek</note> at great length, and specifically the parts concerning their theology by Manetho the Egyptian, both in the *Sacred Book* he wrote and in his other works. However, Diodorus, who was previously mentioned and put forward by us, having collected the histories from many sources and having accurately recorded the customs of each nation as much as possible...

# EUSEBIUS
## EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, BOOK II

...they say the **ichneumon** <note>The Egyptian mongoose (*Herpestes ichneumon*), famous in antiquity for its supposed enmity with the crocodile</note> is honored because it crushes the eggs of crocodiles, being beneficial to humans. It is even said to kill the crocodiles themselves by rolling in mud, jumping into their open mouths, and eating through their internal organs. Among the birds, the **hawk** is considered useful for its hunting of snakes, locusts, and caterpillars. Another kind of **hawk** <note>original: *hierax* (the term was used broadly for various birds of prey)</note> is honored for its protection against scorpions and horned vipers, and for its role in the small biting beasts, and because it is utilized in the practice of divination. The **eagle** is honored because it is of a royal nature. 

They say the **goat** was deified—much like **Priapus** <note>A Greek god of fertility, usually depicted with a permanent and oversized erection</note> among the Greeks—because of its reproductive organ; for this animal is exceptionally prone to mating. They believe this part of the body, being the cause of generation, should be honored accordingly, as it is the "first cause" of the nature of all living things. Generally speaking, the phallus is consecrated during the sacred rites not only by the Egyptians but by many others, as the source of animal life. The priests in Egypt who inherit their ancestral offices are initiated into the mysteries of this god. 

Furthermore, they say the **Satyrs** <note>In Greek myth, goat-like spirits of the wild</note> were honored by men in ancient times for the same reason. This is why most people dedicate statues of them in temples with their members erect, resembling the nature of the goat. For this animal is handed down as being the most active in sexual union. 

The sacred bulls, **Apis** and **Mnevis**, are honored similarly to the gods. This is partly for their use in agriculture, and partly to attribute the discovery of fruits and grains to them. **Wolves** are honored due to their natural similarity to dogs. Moreover, they say that in ancient times, when **Isis** and her son **Horus** were about to do battle against **Typhon** <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian chaos-god Set</note>, **Osiris** came from the underworld to help his child and wife, appearing in the form of a wolf. Others say that when the Ethiopians campaigned against Egypt, they were driven away by a great pack of wolves; because of this, the region was named **Lycopolis** <note>literally "City of the Wolf," known in Egyptian as Zawty or Asyut</note>. 

The **crocodile** is said to be worshipped because its presence prevents bandits from Arabia and Libya from daring to swim across the Nile. There is also a story that one of the ancient kings, being pursued by his own dogs, fled into the lake; then, having been miraculously picked up by a crocodile, he was carried to the opposite shore. 

Some suggest other reasons for the honor given to these irrational animals. They say that in ancient times, when the masses were rebelling against the kings and uniting to end the monarchy, a clever person devised various objects of worship for different groups. He did this so that each group, by honoring its own sacred animal and looking down upon those consecrated by others, would never be able to reach a common agreement throughout all of Egypt. 

When any of the aforementioned animals dies, they cover it with a linen cloth and, after striking their chests with lamentation, bury it in sacred tombs. Anyone who willfully kills one of these animals is put to death—except in the case of a **cat** or an **ibis**. If anyone kills one of these, whether intentionally or unintentionally, they are inevitably put to death. It is clear that in whatever house a dog is found dead, everyone shaves their entire body and enters into mourning. If wine, grain, or any of the necessities of life happen to be stored in that house, they can no longer bring themselves to use them. 

They raise **Apis** in **Memphis**, **Mnevis** in **Heliopolis**, the **Goat** in **Mendes**, and the **Crocodile** in **Lake Moeris**. Other wild beasts are kept in sacred enclosures, where the keepers provide fine flour...

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, BOOK II

...offering them food, or providing thick gruel in milk, as well as all kinds of pastries shaped [into various forms], and raw meats—some boiled and others roasted. They also throw many birds to those animals that eat raw meat, and for each of the sacred animals, they maintain female mates for their pleasure, which they call "concubines." 

When the **Apis** <note>The sacred bull of Memphis, considered an incarnation of the god Ptah or Osiris</note> dies and has been buried with great magnificence, they seek another like it. When a new one is found, the crowds are released from their dread and mourning. The calf is first led to **Nilopolis** <note>A city in Egypt, likely "City of the Nile"</note>. At that time only, women are permitted to see him face to face, standing before him; they show themselves to the bull by pulling up their skirts and exposing their private parts. At any other time, it is forbidden and strictly prohibited for women to come into the sight of this god. They say that the soul of **Osiris** <note>The god of the afterlife and rebirth</note> migrates into this bull after his death. 

Such is the shameful "atheism"—or rather, the "theology"—of the Egyptians, which it is shameful even to understand. Having rightly spat upon these things, we have withdrawn from them, finding no worse filth among such great evils than that which is cured only through divine and logical teaching, which brings the "recovery of sight to the blind" <note>A reference to the Gospel of Luke 4:18</note> in their understanding. We shall examine their more "solemn" theories and natural philosophies a little later, after we have discussed the Greek traditions. 

Thus, since the Egyptian and Phoenician mythologies have converged with such power, the superstitions of ancient error have understandably prevailed among most nations. However, we must also speak of the Greek traditions. While the "solemn" parts of Egyptian mythology were left behind in the manner previously described, it has often been said—and can be seen through the reading of the aforementioned authors—that the Greek traditions are merely fragments and echoes of these very things. Indeed, it will immediately become clear from Greek theology itself that, when recording their own accounts of the gods, they produced nothing of their own but filled their accounts with foreign mythologies. They utilize similar guest-rites and the same mysteries, as can be learned from the history of these matters written by the man who "collected the libraries into one" <note>Diodorus Siculus, author of the *Bibliotheca historica* (Historical Library)</note>, whom I mentioned before. He records this in the third and fourth books of his work, beginning his history from the time of **Cadmus**. 

The accurate successions of the chronographers will demonstrate that Cadmus lived after **Moses**, as we shall show in due time. Thus, even the Greek goddess is proven to be later than Moses. But if the account concerns Cadmus, then the gods appear to have been born later than the age of Cadmus. Listen, then, to the words of the author.

# EUSEBIUS: PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL

...the **ichneumon** <note>A mongoose-like animal, the *Herpestes ichneumon*</note>, they say, crushes the eggs of crocodiles. It even kills the crocodiles themselves by rolling in mud and, when they are gaping with their mouths open, jumping into their throats; it then tears away their internal organs and leaves them dead. Among the birds, the **ibis** <note>A wading bird with a long, curved beak</note> is honored because it is useful against snakes, locusts, and caterpillars. The **hawk** is honored for its use against scorpions and horned vipers, as well as other small venomous creatures, and also because it is employed in **divination** <note>The practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means</note>. The eagle is honored because it is a royal bird. 

They say the **goat** was deified—much like **Priapus** <note>A Greek god of fertility, often depicted with a permanent and oversized phallus</note> among the Greeks—because of its reproductive organ. For this animal is said to be most inclined toward sexual intercourse. They believe that the part of the body which is the cause of generation should be honored appropriately, as it is the very source of the nature of all living things. Generally, the **phallus** <note>original: "αἰδοῖον" (aidoion), referring here to the male generative organ</note> is consecrated during religious rites not only by the Egyptians but also by many other peoples, as it is seen as the cause of the birth of animals. They claim that the priests in Egypt who inherit their fathers' offices are initiated into the mysteries of this god. 

They also say that the **Pans** and the **Satyrs** <note>Mythological woodland deities associated with lust and nature</note> are honored by men for the same reason. This is why most people set up statues of them in temples with their organs erect, mimicking the nature of the goat; for this animal is handed down as being most active in sexual union. The sacred bulls, both **Apis** and **Mnevis** <note>The Mnevis bull was the sacred bull of Heliopolis, associated with the sun god Ra</note>, are honored similarly to the gods—partly for their role in agriculture, and partly because the discovery of cultivated fruits is attributed to them. 

**Wolves** are honored because of their natural similarity to dogs. Some say that long ago, when **Isis** and her son **Horus** were fighting against **Typhon** <note>Also known as Set, the god of chaos and storms</note>, **Osiris** returned from the underworld to help his wife and child, taking on the appearance of a wolf. Others say that when the Ethiopians marched against Egypt, they were driven away by a great pack of wolves; because of this, the region was named **Lycopolis** <note>Meaning "City of the Wolf"</note>.

They say the **crocodile** is worshipped so that robbers from Arabia and Libya might not dare to swim across the Nile for fear of the crocodiles. There is also a story that one of their ancient kings, while being pursued by his own dogs, fled into the lake; he was miraculously picked up by a crocodile and carried to the opposite shore. 

Some suggest other reasons for the honor given to these irrational animals. They say that in ancient times, the common people were revolting against the kings and conspiring to no longer be ruled by them; so, a clever person devised various objects of worship for them in the form of animals. This was done so that each group would worship their own honored animal while looking down upon the animal consecrated by others, ensuring that the people of Egypt could never act in one accord. 

Whenever any of the aforementioned animals dies, they wrap it in a linen cloth and, with loud wailing and beating of their breasts, bury it in sacred tombs. Anyone who willfully kills one of these animals is put to death, except in the case of a cat or an ibis. For if someone kills one of these—whether on purpose or by accident—he must certainly be put to death. Indeed, in whatever house a dog is found dead, all the inhabitants shave their entire bodies and enter into mourning. If there happens to be wine, grain, or any of the necessities of life stored in the house, they can no longer bring themselves to use them. They feed the **Apis** bull in **Memphis**, the **Mnevis** in **Heliopolis** <note>The City of the Sun</note>, the goat in **Mendes**, and the crocodile in **Lake Moeris**, keeping other wild beasts in sacred enclosures while

But we must also speak of the Greek accounts. The "solemn" parts of Egyptian mythology have already taken up their place in our discussion. As for the Greek accounts—that they are actually fragments and mishearings of these very Egyptian rites—this has been stated many times, as can be seen through an examination of the aforementioned authors. Furthermore, it would become clear from the Greek theology itself, if one were to recount their own records about the gods; they have nothing of their own, but have stumbled upon the mythologies of foreigners. Thus, even the Greek theology is shown to be more recent than Moses. If the story is about Cadmus, then those who came after Cadmus clearly appear to be of a later age.

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 2

...[it is said that she] married her brother Hyperion and gave birth to two children, whom she named Helios <note>original: "ἥλιον" (helion), the Sun</note> and Selene <note>original: "σελήνην" (selenen), the Moon</note>. But the brothers, fearing Hyperion, conspired to slaughter him, and they drowned Helios in the Eridanus river <note>Historically identified with the Po River in Italy</note>. When Selene learned of this, she threw herself from the roof. Their mother, driven mad by grief, wandered throughout the land with her hair disheveled, making a great noise with drums and cymbals, until she eventually disappeared entirely. The crowds, marvelling at this tragic turn of events, transformed Helios and Selene into the stars of the heavens. They also came to regard their mother as a goddess, establishing altars and honoring her with the same beating of drums and clashing of cymbals used in her madness. 

The Phrygians say that Meion, while reigning over Phrygia, had a daughter named Cybele. She was the first to invent the shepherd's pipe <note>original: "σύριγγα" (syrigna), the panpipes</note> and was called the "Mountain Mother." Because she loved a certain Phrygian man, they say her family was formed. She remained a virgin until her death <note>This detail varies significantly in different mythological traditions</note>. Cybele lived with Attis and became pregnant. When this was discovered, her father put Attis and his nurses to death. Cybele, driven mad, fled into the countryside. From that time on, she continued to wail aloud and beat upon a drum. 

She was joined by Marsyas, who later entered into a musical contest with Apollo; having been defeated, he was flayed alive by Apollo. But Apollo, having fallen in love with Cybele, accompanied her as far as the land of the Hyperboreans <note>A mythical land of perpetual sunshine in the far North</note>. He cared for and buried the body of Attis, and honored Cybele as a goddess. Because of this, even to this day, the Phrygians perform these rites, mourning the death of the youth. Having established altars, they offer sacrifices and honor Cybele. Later, in Pessinus in Phrygia <note>The ancient capital of the Galatians and a major cult center</note>, they constructed a lavish temple and established the most magnificent honors and sacrifices. 

After these events, following the death of Hyperion, the sons of Uranus divided the kingdom among themselves. The most illustrious among them were Atlas and Cronus <note>Identified with the Roman Saturn</note>. This Atlas took the regions near the Ocean, and became an excellent astrologer. He had seven daughters, called the Atlantides. These daughters mated with the most illustrious gods and became the ancestors of most of the human race, giving birth to gods and heroes through their virtue. The eldest of them, Maia, mated with Zeus and gave birth to Hermes. 

But Cronus, who was distinguished by greed and impiety, married his sister Rhea. From her, he fathered Zeus. There had also been another Zeus, the brother of Uranus and king of Crete, but he was far inferior in reputation to the later one. This [later] Zeus ruled over the entire world. The Zeus of Crete fathered ten children, who were named the Curetes <note>Young spearmen who protected the infant Zeus</note>. They say his tomb is still pointed out in Crete to this day. Cronus held power over Sicily, Libya, and Italy. 

Regarding him, they agree that Zeus sought a life opposite to that of his father. Some say he succeeded to the kingdom when his father voluntarily stepped down; others say he was chosen by the crowds because of the hatred they felt toward his father. When Cronus and the Titans made war against him, Zeus prevailed in battle and went on to visit the entire inhabited world. He excelled in physical strength and all other virtues. He took great care to punish the impious and reward the good, for which reason, after his departure from among men, he was named "Zena" <note>original: "Ζῆνα" (Zena) - a play on the Greek word "zen," meaning "to live," implying he provided the means of life</note>.

# EUSEBIUS

» ...And the appearance of being the cause of "living well" for mankind <note>Diodorus is concluding a section on how these ancient figures were credited with inventing the arts of civilization</note>. These, then, are the main points of what is theologized concerning the fixed stars. They say that people also made use of the sun in these matters. These things Diodorus says in the third book of his *Histories*. But the same author, in his sixth book, drawing from the writings of Euhemerus of Messene, confirms the same theology, stating his words somewhat as follows:

» "Concerning the gods, the ancients have handed down two different notions to later generations. For they say that some are eternal and imperishable, such as the Sun and the Moon, and the other stars in the heavens; and in addition to these, the winds and others who have attained a similar nature. For they say each of these has an eternal origin and permanence. But they say others were earthly gods <note>original: 'ἐπιγείους' (epigeious), meaning those who live upon the earth</note> who, because of their benefactions to mankind, attained honor and glory, such as Heracles, Dionysus, Aristaeus, and others like them. 

» "Concerning these earthly gods, many and varied accounts have been handed down by both historians and myth-writers. Among the historians, Euhemerus, who composed the *Sacred Record* <note>original: 'ἱερὰν ἀναγραφὴν' (hieran anagraphēn)</note>, wrote a specific account; but among the mythologists, Homer, Hesiod, Orpheus, and others like them have fashioned more monstrous myths about the gods. We shall attempt to run through the records of both briefly, aiming for a balanced summary.

» "Now Euhemerus, having been a friend of King Cassander <note>A successor of Alexander the Great who ruled Macedon (c. 305–297 BC)</note> and having been compelled by him to perform certain royal duties and undertake great journeys abroad, says that he was driven out into the ocean toward the south. After sailing out from Arabia Eudaemon <note>original: 'εὐδαίμονος ἀραβίας' (eudaimonos arabias), "Happy Arabia," roughly modern Yemen</note>, he made a voyage through the ocean for many days and was carried to islands in the open sea. One of these was outstanding, called Panchaea. 

» "On this island, he observed that the inhabitants, the Panchaeans, were distinguished by their piety, honoring the gods with most magnificent sacrifices and notable offerings of silver and gold. There was also on the island a temple of the gods, and many other things admired for both their antiquity and the costliness of their construction. Concerning these, we have recorded the details in the books preceding this one. 

» "He says there is a hill on the island that is exceedingly high, where a temple of Zeus Triphylius <note>meaning "Zeus of the Three Tribes"</note> stands, established by Zeus himself during the time when he ruled over the entire inhabited world, while he was still living among men. In this temple stands a golden pillar, on which are recorded in summary the deeds of Uranus, Cronus, and Zeus, written in Panchaean characters. 

» "After this, he says that Uranus <note>The name means "Heaven"</note> was the first to become king, an equitable man and a benefactor, knowledgeable in the science of the movement of the stars. He was also the first to honor the heavenly gods with sacrifices, for which reason he was himself addressed as Uranus. He had sons by his wife Hestia, namely Pan and Cronus, and daughters, Rhea and Demeter. 

» "Cronus reigned after Uranus, and marrying Rhea, he begat Zeus, Hera, and Poseidon. Then Zeus, succeeding to the kingship of Cronus, married Hera, Demeter, and Themis; from whom he had children: the Curetes <note>Armed dancers who protected the infant Zeus</note> from the first, Persephone from the second, and Athena from the third. 

» "And going to Babylon, he was hosted by Belus <note>The Greek form of the Babylonian god/king Bel or Marduk</note>. After this, arriving at the island of Panchaea located in the ocean, he established an altar to Uranus, his own forefather. From there he went through Syria to the ruler of that time, Casius, from whom Mount Casius <note>A mountain on the border of Syria and Turkey, famous for its cult of Zeus</note> takes its name. Going then into Cilicia..."

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 2

» ...conquering Cilicia in war and letting Cilix <note>The mythical founder of Cilicia</note> rule it. Most of these nations, having been visited, were honored by all and proclaimed as gods. 

Having recounted these things and similar matters as if they were about mortal men, while describing the gods, he adds, saying: "And regarding Euhemerus, who compiled the *Sacred Record* <note>original: 'ἱερὰν ἀναγραφήν' (hieran anagraphēn)</note>, we shall be satisfied with what has been said." But the myths told among the nations concerning the gods, following Hesiod, Homer, and Orpheus, we shall attempt to run through briefly. Next, we shall attach the mythologies of the poets. But enough has been said regarding those matters derived from "natural theology" <note>original: 'φυσικῆς θεολογίας' (physikēs theologias) — a term for interpreting gods as physical elements like fire or water</note>. It would be irrational to join to these the rites of their gods performed in the inner sanctuaries <note>original: 'ἀδύτοις' (adytois)</note> and their secret mysteries. 

We must consider whether these mysteries, which supposedly hold a truly divine theology, carry some god-befitting sign, or whether they originate from somewhere below, from a long and demonic error. This error is even more worthy of shame—or rather, it is worthy of pity for those who are blind to it. 

The wonderful Clement, in his *Exhortation to the Greeks* <note>The 'Protrepticus' by Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Christian theologian</note>, reveals these things with boldness. He was a man who indeed had experience in all these things, but quickly looked up from the error, as if by the saving Word, and was ransomed from evils through the Gospel teaching. Hear, then, a few things from his writings:

---

->Concerning the secret rites and hidden mysteries of polytheistic error.<-

---

<margin>A</margin> 
Do not, therefore, meddle with the forbidden inner sanctuaries <note>original: 'Αδυτα' (Adyta) — the 'un-enterable' most sacred parts of temples</note>, nor the mouths of pits full of wonders, nor the Thesprotian cauldron, nor the Cirrhean tripod, nor the Dodonian bronze. And as for the Garamantian oracle honored in the desert sands, and the oracle there withered along with its oak—leave them all behind to aging myths. At least the Castalian spring has fallen silent, and another spring of Colophon, and the other prophetic waters have died in the same way. And indeed, though late, they have been proven empty of vanity, flowing away along with their own myths. 

Describe for us the useless oracles of the rest of divination—or rather, of "madness" <note>original: 'μανικῆς' (manikēs), a pun on 'mantikēs' (prophecy/divination)</note>: the Clarian, the Pythian, the Didymaean, the Amphiaraus, the Apollo, the Amphilochus. And if you wish, consider the wonder-watchers, the bird-diviners, and the interpreters of dreams. Crawl through with them, and set the "belly-prophets" <note>original: 'ἐγγαστριμάντεις' (engastrimanteis) — ventriloquists or spirit-mediums</note> and barley-diviners alongside the Pythian, and those "belly-talkers" still honored by the masses. 

Truly, let the inner sanctuaries of the Egyptians and the necromancies of the Tuscans be consigned to darkness. These are truly mad sophistries of faithless men, and the gambling dens of unmixed error. Partners in this sorcery are goats trained for divination, and crows taught by men to give "prophecies" to men. 

What are these mysteries? I shall list them, though I will not "dance them out" <note>original: 'ἐξορχήσομαι' (exorchēsomai) — a reference to revealing secret rituals through dance, famously associated with the scandal of Alcibiades in 415 BCE</note> as they say Alcibiades did. But I will thoroughly strip bare the sorcery hidden in them, following the Word of truth, and your so-called gods themselves, whose rites are "mystic." Let those who celebrate the "mad" Dionysus <note>original: 'μαινόλιν' (mainolin)</note> with frenzied Bacchic rites be summoned as spectators to the stage of the life of truth, leading their holy madness through the eating of raw flesh. They perform the distributions of meat from the murders, crowned with snakes, shouting out that name "Eva" <note>Clement puns the Bacchic cry 'Euoi' with 'Eva' (Eve), suggesting the rites honor the source of the Fall of Man</note>—the one through whom error followed, and death followed after. And the sign of the Bacchic rites is a consecrated snake. For instance, according to the precise meaning of the Hebrews...
