# EUSEBIUS

...voice, a name which, when pronounced with a rough breathing, is interpreted as "snake" <note>original: 'ὄφις' (ophis). Clement is likely punning on the Hebrew name 'Eve' (Hawah) and the Bacchic cry 'Euai,' connecting the fall of man to the serpent in the garden</note>. Deo <note>Another name for Demeter, the goddess of agriculture</note> and Kore <note>The "Maiden," Persephone</note> have already become the subject of a mystic drama; Deo carries torches to commemorate their wandering, the abduction, and their grief. 

It seems to me that we should look into the etymologies of the words "orgies" <note>original: 'ὄργια' (orgia)</note> and "mysteries." The former, "orgies," comes from the "anger" <note>original: 'ὀργή' (orgē)</note> of Deo directed against Zeus. The latter, "mysteries," comes from the "defilement" <note>original: 'μύσος' (mysos)</note> that happened regarding Dionysus. Or perhaps it comes from a certain Myous of Attica, whom Apollodorus says was killed while hunting. You would not begrudge your mysteries being received with the voice and honor of a funeral monument! There is also another way to look at it: by rearranging the letters, "mysteries" <note>original: 'μυστήρια' (mystēria)</note> becomes "myth-eries" <note>original: 'μυθέρια' (mytheria) — Clement is making a pun here to suggest mysteries are merely "fables"</note>. For even if only a few are caught by them, such myths as these—originating from some most barbaric Thracian or most foolish Phrygians—expose the superstitious. 

May the man who first introduced this absurdity to humanity perish! Whether it was Dardanus <note>Mythical founder of Troy</note>, who taught the mysteries of the gods, or Eetion, who established the orgies and initiations of the Samothracians. Or perhaps that Phrygian, Midas, who, after learning from the Odrysian <note>A Thracian tribe</note>, then passed on this crafty deception to his subjects. Never shall Cinyras, the islander from Cyprus, deceive me, he who dared to hand over the lewd orgies of Aphrodite from the darkness of night into the light of day, in his ambition to deify a local harlot. Others say that Melampus, the son of Amythaon, brought the festivals of Deo from Egypt to Greece—a grief expressed in song. 

I would call these men the "original authors of evil" <note>original: 'ἀρχεκάκους' (archekakous)</note>, the fathers of atheistic myths and destructive superstition, who planted the seed of wickedness and corruption in human life by establishing the mysteries. Now—for it is time—I will expose your orgies themselves as being full of deception and charlatanry. If you have been initiated, you will laugh all the more at these myths you once honored. I speak openly of things kept hidden, not feeling shame to say what you are not ashamed to worship.

Aphrodite, the "Cyprus-born" who was dear to Cinyras—I mean the "genital-loving" Aphrodite <note>original: 'φιλομηδέα' (philomēdea) — Clement puns on the myth that she was born from the severed genitals (medea) of the god Uranus</note>—is so named because she appeared from the genitals, those lustful genitals of Uranus which were cut off and then forced the waves into a foam. In your initiations, this "fruit" of sea-born pleasure is honored; as a token of her birth, a handful of salt and a phallus are given to those being initiated into the adulterous craft. Those initiated pay a coin to her, as lovers do to a harlot.

Then there are the mysteries of Deo: the embrace of Zeus with his mother Demeter, and her wrath. I do not know what to call her hereafter—mother or wife of Zeus? Because of this, she is said to have been addressed as "Brimo" <note>The "Terrifying One"</note>, and there is the supplication of Zeus, the "drink of gall," the tearing out of hearts, and unmentionable deeds. These things the Phrygians perform in honor of Attis, Cybele, and the Corybantes. They have spread the story that Zeus, having torn the testicles from a ram, brought them and threw them into the lap of Deo, paying a fake penalty for his violent embrace, as if he had castrated himself. It is worth setting out the symbols of this initiation, for they will provoke laughter and certainly not leave you indifferent due to the passage of time: 

**"I have eaten from the drum; I have drunk from the cymbal. I have carried the sacred vessel; I have slipped under the bridal curtain."**

Are these symbols not an insult? Are the mysteries not a mockery? Why should I add the rest? Demeter becomes pregnant, the Maiden <note>Persephone</note> is reared, and this same Zeus who fathered her then couples with his own daughter, Persephone, after her mother Deo—forgetting his former defilement. He couples with her having become a dragon <note>original: 'δράκων' (drakōn)</note>, which was proven by...

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 2

...of evil mysteries, the "god through the lap" <note>original: 'ὁ διὰ κόλπου θεός' (ho dia kolpou theos). This refers to a ritual where a snake was passed through the initiate's clothing to symbolize a union with the god.</note> is a symbol for the initiates. This is a serpent drawn through the lap of those being initiated—a proof of Zeus's lack of self-control. Pherephatta <note>A common variant of the name Persephone</note> also conceives a child in the form of a bull; indeed, as a certain poet says:

<margin>"</margin> *A phantom bull, the father of a serpent,*
<margin>"</margin> *And the serpent, father of a bull;*
*On the mountain, the hidden cowherd, the goad.*

I believe he calls the <term>narthex</term> <note>A giant fennel stalk used as a ritual wand</note> a "cowherd's goad," which the Bacchic worshippers brandish. I will also describe to you the flower-gathering of Pherephatta, and the basket, and the abduction by Aidoneus <note>Another name for Hades, god of the underworld</note>, and the chasm in the earth, and the swine of Eubouleus that were swallowed up along with the goddesses. This is the reason why, at the <term>Thesmophoria</term> <note>A festival held by women in honor of Demeter and Persephone</note>, they throw pigs into "megara" <note>Sacred caverns or pits</note> while performing their rites. Women celebrate this mythology in various ways throughout different cities, calling them the Thesmophoria, Scirophoria, or Arretophoria, dramatizing the abduction of Pherephatta in many ways.

For the mysteries of Dionysus are utterly inhuman. While he was still a child, and while the <term>Curetes</term> <note>Armed youths who performed a rhythmic, clashing dance</note> performed their armored dance around him, the Titans craftily slipped in. Having deceived him with childish toys, these Titans tore him to pieces while he was still a mere babe, as the poet of the rite, the Thracian Orpheus, says:

<margin>"</margin> *The top, and the bullroarer, and jointed dolls,*
<margin>"</margin> *And fair golden apples from the clear-voiced Hesperides.*

It is not useless to list the useless symbols of this rite for the sake of condemning them: the knucklebone, the ball, the top, apples, the bullroarer, the mirror, and the fleece. Now, Athena, having stolen away the heart of Dionysus, was called **Pallas** from the "palpitating" <note>original: 'πάλλειν' (pallein). A pun connecting the name Pallas to the throbbing or quivering of the heart.</note> of the heart. But the Titans, who had torn him apart, placed a cauldron on a tripod, threw the limbs of Dionysus into it, and first boiled them; then, piercing them with spits, they held them over the fire of Hephaestus <note>A poetic way of saying "over the fire."</note>. 

Later, Zeus appeared—if he was a god, perhaps he was attracted by the steam of the roasting meat, which your gods confess is their chosen portion—and he struck the Titans with lightning. He entrusted the limbs of Dionysus to his son Apollo to bury. Apollo did not disobey Zeus; he carried the dismembered corpse to Parnassus and laid it to rest.

Shall I also tell you about the secret rites of the **Corybantes**? These men, after murdering their third brother, covered the head of the corpse with a purple cloth, crowned it, and buried it, carrying it on a bronze shield to the foothills of Mount Olympus. These are their "mysteries," to put it briefly: murders and burials! 

The priests of these rites, whom those involved call the "Lords of the Rite," add further misery to the tragedy by forbidding people to place **celery** <note>original: 'σέλινον' (selinon)</note> on the table, roots and all; for they believe that celery sprang from the blood that flowed from the slain Corybant. Similarly, the women celebrating the Thesmophoria are careful not to eat the seeds of the **pomegranate** <note>original: 'ῥοιάς' (rhoias)</note>, believing that pomegranates sprouted from the drops of blood that fell from Dionysus. 

Calling the Corybantes by the name "Cabeiri," they proclaim the **Cabeiric Rite**. For these two brother-slayers, having taken up the chest in which the genitals of Dionysus were placed, carried it into Tyrrhenia <note>The land of the Etruscans in Italy</note>, being traders of "glorious" cargo. There they lived as exiles, passing on their highly prized teaching of "piety"—worshipping genitals and a chest—to the Tyrrhenians. For this reason, some people quite naturally want to call Dionysus **Attis**, because he was deprived of his genitals. And what is there to wonder at, if the barbarians of Tyrrhenia are initiated into such shameful passions, when among the Athenians and...

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s (quoted by Eusebius) denunciation of Greek mystery religions. The previous page ended mid-word while discussing the "Pherephattian" (Persephone) myths and the rituals of the Thesmophoria. # EUSEBIUS

...with the goat-staff, singing and saying, the mythology concerning Deo <note>Deo is another name for Demeter, the goddess of agriculture.</note> is full of shame. For while Deo was wandering in search of her daughter, the Maiden <note>original: 'κόρη' (Kore), the title for Persephone.</note>, around Eleusis—this is a district in Attica—she grew weary and sat down by a well, grieving. Even now, those being initiated are forbidden to sit there, so that the initiates do not appear to be imitating the mourning woman. At that time, the inhabitants of Eleusis were "earth-born." Their names were Baubo, Dysaules, Triptolemus, and also Eumolpus and Eubuleus. Triptolemus was a cowherd, Eumolpus a shepherd, and Eubuleus a swineherd. From these come the families of the <term>Eumolpidae</term> <note>The hereditary priests of the Eleusinian Mysteries.</note> and the Heralds, the <term>hierophantic</term> <note>Priests who "showed the sacred things."</note> race at Athens.

And indeed—for I will not fail to mention it—Baubo, having welcomed Deo as a guest, offered her a <term>kykeon</term> <note>A ritual drink made of water, barley, and herbs.</note>. When the goddess refused to take it and was unwilling to drink because she was in mourning, Baubo became deeply distressed, feeling slighted. She then lifted up her robes and exposed her private parts to the goddess. Deo was delighted by the sight and finally accepted the drink, having been pleased by the spectacle. These are the secret mysteries of the Athenians. These are the things that Orpheus <note>The legendary poet and mythical founder of Orphic mysteries.</note> records. I will set before you the very verses of Orpheus, so that you may have the teacher of mysteries himself as a witness to this shamelessness:

> Having spoken thus, she drew up her robes, and showed
> All the unseemly parts of her body. And the boy Iacchus was there,
> And laughing, he kept waving his hand under Baubo’s breasts.
> Then the goddess, when she smiled, smiled in her heart,
> And she accepted the variegated vessel in which the *kykeon* lay.

And this is the password of the Eleusinian mysteries: "I fasted, I drank the *kykeon*. I took from the chest. Having worked, I placed it into the basket; and from the basket into the chest." Truly beautiful sights, and worthy of a goddess! These rites are indeed worthy of the night, and of fire, and of the great-hearted—or rather, the vain-minded—people of the Erechtheidae <note>A poetic name for the Athenians.</note>.

Moreover, there are the rites of other nations, about which certain "lords of the ritual" do not even speak. To whom does Heraclitus of Ephesus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for his cryptic sayings.</note> prophesy? "To night-walkers, magi, priests of Bacchus, maenads, and initiates." To these he threatens what comes after death; for them he prophesies the fire. For they are initiated into the mysteries recognized among men in an unholy manner. Therefore, the common custom and opinion, and the mysteries of the serpent, are a kind of deception practiced in worship, leading to truly uninitiated "initiations" and rituals devoid of true religious frenzy, turning people away with a bastardized form of piety.

For what kind of things are in the mystic chests! For I must strip bare their "holy" things and speak out the unutterable. Are these not pomegranates? Are they not pyramids, and <term>elytai</term> <note>Small cakes or ritual objects.</note>, and cakes with many navels, and grains of salt, and a serpent—the ritual object of Dionysus Bassareus? And are there not also woollen balls? And in addition, hearts? And fennel stalks and ivy? And also round cakes and poppies? These are their "holy" things. And furthermore, the unutterable symbols of Themis: oregano, a lamp, a sword, and a "woman’s comb"—which is a euphemism for the female genitals.

Oh, the open shamelessness! In the past, the silent night was a veil for the pleasure of self-controlled men; but now, for those being initiated, the night is a time for talking about their lack of restraint. And the fire, carried in torches, exposes the passions. Put out the fire, O Hierophant! Be ashamed of the torches, O Torch-bearer! The light exposes your Iacchus. Permit the night to hide the mysteries; let the rituals be honored by darkness. The fire does not act a part; it is commanded to expose and to punish. These are the mysteries of the atheists. And I rightly call those "atheists" who have remained ignorant of the truly existing God, but worship a child torn apart by Titans, and a mourning woman, and...

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 2, Page 43

...truth is removed, as truly, by incorporeality, they worship inharmoniously, being held by a double **atheism** <note>In the early Christian context, "atheism" was a reciprocal accusation: Pagans called Christians "atheists" for rejecting the state gods, while Christians called Pagans "atheists" for not knowing the one true God.</note>. For on one hand, they are ignorant of God, not recognizing the one who truly exists as God; and on the other hand, in a second error, they suppose those who do not exist to be real, and give the name of "gods" to those who have no real existence, or rather do not exist at all, having only obtained the name. And so forth.

---

### By what reasonings we departed from these views and ceased to think the same things about the gods.

Rightly, then, we confess that we have become free from all these things, having been redeemed from a long and ancient error, like some terrible and most difficult disease. And first, we credit this to the grace and beneficence of **Almighty God**; second, to the ineffable power of our **Savior’s** evangelical teaching; and third, to sober reasoning. We have judged it to be unholy and impious to honor with the venerable title <note>i.e., the name of "God."</note> those mortal men who long ago lay among the dead, and who did not even leave behind a sober memory of themselves among men. Instead, they handed down to their successors demonstrations of extreme lack of self-control, licentiousness, cruelty, and madness.

For how is it not the most foolish thing of all for sober lovers of virtue to offer the initial sacrifices to the shameful and licentious? Or for the intelligent and wise to provide venerable honor to those who have lost their minds? Or for those who practice justice and **philanthropy** <note>original: 'φιλανθρωπία' (philanthropia), meaning love for humanity or kindness.</note> to honor those held in the stains of excessive cruelty and inhumanity, such as the murder of children and infanticide?

What excess of impiety has not been surpassed by enslaving the majestic and all-holy name of God to the private parts of men and women, and to the irrational and beast-like nature? To **theologize** <note>To speak or write about the nature of the divine.</note> such shameful and inhuman things—things which, if proved against criminals among men, would subject them to the unsparing punishments of the laws!

If it were necessary to go on at length, having gone through all people, both barbarian and Greek, we would show that our freedom from the aforementioned evils and our departure from the falsely-named gods is entirely reasonable. This is especially true now that even many of the most superstitious people, as if awakened from a deep sleep and opening the eye of the soul from the ancient mist, have perceived the deep nonsense of their ancestral error.

Standing upon reflection, they chose the other path, departing from the old one. Some of these, facing the issue directly, laughed at the whole mythology of their ancestors, ridiculing it broadly. Others, however, wishing to avoid the reputation of **atheism**, neither stayed with the former beliefs nor entirely departed from them. Instead, seeking to flatter and serve their own reputation, they claimed that the histories regarding the gods celebrated among them were <insert>yet</insert> true myths fashioned by poets, hiding within them certain **natural theories** <note>The practice of "allegoresis," where myths were re-interpreted as scientific or physical metaphors (e.g., Hera as the air, Zeus as fire) to make them more acceptable to philosophers.</note>. 

Even if these allegories bear no evidence of truth, it is nevertheless necessary for us to set them forth, to examine what is considered "venerable" even among these people. We do this so that the reason for our departure from these things may be shown to be rational, and so that the logic of our Savior’s evangelical teaching may be presented. Come then, let us take up the account of these matters from the beginning and examine them.

In truth, because of Iambe—who joked and spoke—the mythology concerning Deo <note>Deo is a common poetic name for Demeter, the goddess of agriculture and the harvest.</note> is full of shame. For while Deo was wandering in search of her daughter, the Maiden <note>Kore, also known as Persephone, who had been abducted by Hades.</note>, she arrived at Eleusis in Attica (this is a specific place), grew weary, and sat down by a well in her grief. To this day, this act is forbidden to those being initiated, so that the "perfected" <note>Initiates who have completed the ritual.</note> do not seem to be imitating the mourning goddess. At that time, Eleusis was inhabited by "earth-born" people. Their names were Baubo, Dysaules, Triptolemus, and also Eumolpus and Eubuleus. Triptolemus was a cowherd, Eumolpus a shepherd, and Eubuleus a swineherd. From these come the families of the Eumolpidae and the Heralds, the priestly class of the Athenians.

And indeed—for I will not refrain from speaking of it—Baubo, having welcomed Deo as a guest, offered her a *kykeon* <note>original: "κυκεῶνα" — a ritual drink typically made of barley, water, and mint.</note>. When the goddess refused to take it and would not drink because she was in mourning, Baubo became deeply distressed as if she had been slighted. She then lifted her robes, exposing her private parts and displaying them to the goddess. Deo was delighted by the sight, and at last she accepted the drink, pleased by the spectacle. These are the secret mysteries of the Athenians. Orpheus also records these things. I will provide you with the very verses of Orpheus, so that you may have the teacher of the mysteries himself as a witness to this shame:

> So saying, she drew up her robes and showed all
> the parts of her body that were not even fit to be seen.
> And there was the boy Iacchus, who laughed and
> waved his hand under Baubo's breasts.
> Then the goddess smiled, she smiled in her heart,
> and she accepted the dappled vessel in which the drink lay.

And this is the password <note>term: "synthema" — a secret sign or spoken phrase used to identify fellow initiates.</note> of the Eleusinian mysteries: "I fasted; I drank the *kykeon*; I took from the chest; having worked, I placed it in the basket, and from the basket back into the chest." Truly beautiful sights, and worthy of a goddess! These rites are indeed worthy of the night, and of fire, and of the great-hearted—or rather, the vain-minded—people of the Erechtheidae <note>A poetic name for the Athenians.</note>. And also of the other Greeks, for whom there remain things that follow after death. To whom does Heraclitus of Ephesus prophesy? To "night-walkers, magi, priests of Bacchus, maenads, and initiates." To these he threatens what comes after death; to these he prophesies the fire. For they are initiated into the mysteries held among men in an unholy fashion.

Therefore, the common custom and opinion, and the mysteries of the dragon, are a religious deception, involving "uninitiated initiations" and "unholy rites" that encourage a corrupted piety. And what are those "mystic chests"? For it is necessary to strip bare their "holy" things and speak out their "unspeakable" secrets. Are they not sesame cakes, and pyramid-shaped cakes, and balls of wool, and cakes with many navels, and grains of salt, and a dragon—the rite of Dionysus Bassarus? And also pomegranates, as well as hearts? And fennel-stalks and ivy? And also round cakes and poppy seeds? These are their "holy" things! And furthermore, the "unspeakable" symbols of Themis: marjoram, a lamp, a sword, and a "woman’s comb"—which is a euphemism for the female genitals.

What a display of manifest shame! Once, for sober-minded people, the silent night was a cover for pleasure; but now, for those being initiated, the "sacred" night of excess is spoken of aloud, and the fire exposes their passions by torchlight. Extinguish the fire, O Hierophant! <note>The high priest who "reveals the sacred things" in the mysteries.</note> Be ashamed of your torches, O Torch-bearer! The light exposes your Iacchus. Permit the night to hide the mysteries; let the rites be honored by darkness. The fire does not play a part; it is commanded to expose and punish. These are the mysteries of the atheists. And we rightly call those "atheists" who have ignored the God who truly exists, but worship a child being torn apart by Titans <note>Dionysus-Zagreus, who in myth was dismembered by the Titans.</note>, and a mourning woman, and...

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 2

...the truly unspeakable things, they shamelessly worship out of a sense of shame, held fast by a double form of atheism. First, in that they are ignorant of God, not knowing the One who Truly Exists <note>original: "τὸν ὄντως ὄντα" — a philosophical term for the eternal, unchanging God, contrasted with the "becoming" and decaying nature of mortals.</note> as God; and second, through this very error, by considering those who do not exist as if they did exist, and naming those who are not truly gods—or rather, who do not exist at all and have only attained a name—with the titles of divine pride. And so forth.

-> By what reasonings we have moved away from holding such views about the gods. <-

<margin>EI</margin> Justly, then, we confess that we have been redeemed from all these things through our Savior, having been delivered from a long-standing and ancient error, as if from some terrible and most difficult disease. We have done this, first, by the grace and benevolence of Almighty God; second, by the unspeakable power of our Savior’s Gospel teaching; and third, by judging with sober reasoning that it is unholy and impious to honor with the venerable title of God those mortal men who have long since lain among the dead—men who were not even sober in their lives, but were shut up in the tombs of men, and who handed down to those after them clear examples of extreme lack of restraint, licentiousness, cruelty, and madness. 

For how is it not the height of stupidity for those who love self-control to concede their own honors to the shameful and the unrestrained? Or for the intelligent and sensible to offer venerable honor to those who have lost their minds? Or for practitioners of justice and philanthropy to honor those held fast by the stains of infanticide and parricide <note>Greek mythology is full of stories of gods killing their own children (like Cronus) or fathers (like Zeus overthrowing Cronus).</note> through an excess of cruelty and inhumanity? What excess of impiety would it be to cast the solemn and all-blessed name of God upon the "unspeakable parts" <note>A reference to the ritual display of reproductive organs in the mysteries of Eleusis and Dionysus.</note> of men and women, and upon irrational and beast-like natures? To theologize such shameful and inhuman things, which, if they were proven against criminals among men, would subject them to the Pitiless punishments of the laws!

If it were necessary to speak at length in refutation of everyone, both Barbarian and Greek, we should bring to light the reason for our salvation from the aforementioned evils—which comes from the abandonment of these falsely named gods. For even the majority of those who were once intensely superstitious <note>original: "δεισιδαιμόνων" — often translated as "religious," but used here by Eusebius in the pejorative sense of "superstitious."</note>, as if awakened from a deep stupor and opening the eye of the soul to remove the ancient mist, have recognized the profound nonsense of their ancestral error. By reflection, they have all chosen the other path, departing from the old one. 

Among these, some, moving together, condemned the whole mythology and laughed heartily at their ancestors; others, seeking to avoid the reputation of atheism, neither stood by their former beliefs nor entirely withdrew from them. Instead, aiming to flatter and preserve their own reputation, they claimed that the stories told among them about the gods were not true, but were myths fashioned by poets, hiding within them certain "natural theories" <note>This refers to the practice of "allegorization," where philosophers argued that myths about the gods’ adultery or violence were actually metaphors for natural forces like fire, water, or the stars.</note>. Even if these people bring no evidence of truth, it is nevertheless necessary for us to set forth an exposition of the things held as solemn among them. We do this so it may be seen that our withdrawal from them was not irrational, and so the reasonableness of our position may be established through the Gospel teaching of our Savior. Come then, let us take up the account of these matters from the beginning and examine them.

### Recapitulation of what has been said before.

The character of Greek theology, then—I mean the popular and more mythical kind, as well as the much earlier versions among the Phoenicians and Egyptians, and those other nations whose history is contained in the discourses on this subject—has been demonstrated to be of this sort. This has been shown through the previously cited words of the Greek writers themselves. We have reasonably placed this at the beginning of the present *Preparation for the Gospel* <note>original: "εὐαγγελικῆς παρασκευῆς" (Evangelike Paraskeue) — the title of this work, which argues that Greek philosophy and history were a "preparation" for Christian truth.</note> for the diagnosis and judgment of those who will read it, so that we might learn from it. 

We ourselves, and those here in our community who until now were inexperienced—having been born of such ancestors, and having been bound by such great evils of theirs, and having had our souls buried in a stupor of impiety and ignorance of God—we were deemed worthy of release, looking upward and finding freedom. This was achieved through the teaching of the Gospel alone, which did not come to us by any other means than through the appearance of our Savior, Jesus Christ, the Son of God. He did not appear in just one part of the earth, nor in a corner of one nation’s land, but throughout the whole inhabited world of men, over which the error of superstitious fear <note>original: "δεισιδαίμονος πλάνης" — often translated as "superstition," but literally a "fear of demons" or "fear of the divine."</note> had especially been poured. Like a sun for the intellectual and rational soul, spreading the rays of His own light, He simultaneously moved the entire race of men—both barbarians and Greeks—as if out of a terrible darkness and a most gloomy and sunless night of superstitious error, into the bright and most clear day of true piety toward God, the King of all. 

Indeed, the prophetic voices explicitly taught that all those who were caught up in the error of polytheism throughout cities and villages were terrified to worship and revere idols of the dead and images of men long departed. This was because the men of old, through exceeding savagery, took no account of God the Creator of all, nor did they fear the punishment of the avenging Justice for their crimes, but plunged into every kind of wickedness. For no law had yet been introduced to guide their lives, nor had a civilized constitution been established among men. Living like a herd in a nomadic life, and being beast-like, they cared for nothing more than filling their bellies like irrational animals. To these, the first form of atheism was a support. 

But for those who were stirred by a small degree of natural intuition, they considered that God and the power of God must be something salvific and good. Wanting to find this, they stretched their souls upward to heaven. Standing there in their minds, and being struck by the beauty of the lights appearing in heaven, they declared *these*—the stars—to be gods. 

Then a third group, casting themselves down to earth, venerated those thought to excel in intelligence, or those who through bodily strength and the power of sovereignty ruled over many—certain giants, or tyrants, or even sorcerers and magicians. Through a kind of human deification, these men accumulated malicious enchantments, or by their words initiated some common and life-benefiting service. These they proclaimed as gods while they were still living and even after their death. Hence their "houses of the gods" are recorded as being the tombs of the dead, as Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 AD), a Christian theologian who argued that pagan gods were merely divinized humans.</note> records in his *Exhortation* to us, bringing in the Greeks themselves as witnesses to his argument. If...

If it please you, hear again the manner of this superstition from the same author <note>Eusebius is continuing his lengthy excerpt from Clement of Alexandria's "Protrepticus" (Exhortation to the Greeks), written around 190 AD.</note> as he writes of it.

### Concerning the dead, and that <gloss>a)</gloss> their so-called temples of the gods are actually tombs.

> It was with good reason, then, that superstition <note>original: "δεισιδαιμονία" (deisidaimonia) — literally "fear of spirits/demons," used here by Clement as a pejorative for pagan religion.</note>, having taken its start from some beginning, became a fountain of similar vice. Then, not being checked, but pouring forth in full flood, it became a great stream, the creator of many and evil demons, offering hecatombs <note>A "hecatomb" was a great public sacrifice of a hundred oxen.</note>, performing festivals, erecting statues, and building temples. These temples—for <gloss>b)</gloss> even this shall not be kept silent—have themselves been given the honorable name of "temples," but they were actually graves; that is to say, the graves have been called "temples." But you, at least even now, should forget your superstition and feel ashamed of honoring tombs. In the temple of Athena at Larissa, in the acropolis, is the tomb of Acrisius. And in the acropolis of Athens is the tomb of Cecrops, <gloss>c)</gloss> as Antiochus says in the ninth book of his *Histories*. And what of Erichthonius? Is he not buried in the temple of Athena Polias <note>Athena "Polias" is Athena as the Protector of the City.</note>? <gloss>d)</gloss> And Ismarus the son of Eumolpus, and Daeira, are they not buried in the precinct <gloss>e)</gloss> of the Eleusinion beneath the acropolis? And were the daughters of Celeus not buried in Eleusis? Why should I go through the list and the Hyperborean women? Hyperoche and Laodice are buried in the Artemisium <note>The temple of Artemis.</note> in Delos. There is also a shrine in the temple of the Delian Apollo. Leander says that Cleomachus is buried in Miletus, in the Didymaeum. Here, the monument of Leukophryne is not worth passing over; it has been seized by the living Midius <note>Clement implies a local ruler or priest took over the site.</note>, and she is buried in the temple of Artemis in Magnesia. Furthermore, they record that the altar in Telmissus of Apollo is also the monument of Telmissus the seer. Ptolemy the son of Agasarchus, in the first book of his *History of Philopator*, says that in Paphos, in the temple of Aphrodite, Cinyras and the descendants of Cinyras are buried. But truly, if I were to go over all the tombs you worship, even all of time would not suffice for me; and as for you, if some shame for your daring deeds does not steal over you, then you wander about as dead men who have put your trust entirely in the dead, O wretched ones! And do you suffer this evil? And after a few words he says: A fitting time has come to mention the god whom the Emperor of the Romans <note>The Emperor Hadrian (reigned 117–138 AD).</note> deified, his most beautiful favorite, Antinous <note>Antinous was a youth who drowned in the Nile; Hadrian, overcome with grief, established a cult in his honor across the empire.</note>, just as Zeus did Ganymede. For desire is not easily restrained when it lacks fear; and men now worship his "sacred nights," which the lover who kept watch by night knew to be shameful. He adds: <gloss>f)</gloss> And now the tomb of the favorite is the temple and city of Antinous. For just as temples are admired, so too are tombs—pyramids, mausoleums, and labyrinths are just other "temples" of the dead, as those others were "tombs" of the gods. Then again after a few words: Come then, let us also briefly survey the athletic games, and let us put an end to these funeral festivals: the Isthmian, the Nemean, the Pythian, and alongside these, the Olympic. <gloss>g)</gloss> At Pytho, the Pythian dragon is worshipped, and the festival of the snake is proclaimed as the Pythian games. At the Isthmus, it happened that the sea cast up a corpse, and the Isthmian games lament Melicertes. At Nemea, another child, Archemorus, is buried, and the funeral games for the child are called the Nemean. And Pisa <note>The region near Olympia.</note> is a tomb among you, where the festival belongs to a Phrygian charioteer <note>Pelops, for whom the Peloponnese is named.</note>, and the Olympic games are simply the libations offered to Pelops, which the Zeus of Phidias <note>The famous gold and ivory statue of Zeus by the sculptor Phidias.</note> has usurped. So says this writer.

But you, taking up from the beginning the account of the error of superstition <note>original: "δεισιδαιμονίας πλάνης" (deisidaimonias planes) — the wandering or delusion of superstitious fear.</note>, examine its downfall.

### A Recapitulation of what was said before.

Now, a certain outline has been demonstrated regarding Greek theology—I mean that which is widely popular and more mythical, and which existed long before the Phoenicians and Egyptians, and those people whose memory the accounts concerning this subject contain. This outline has been revealed through the previously set forth voices of the Greek writers themselves. We have reasonably placed this at the beginning of the present **Gospel Preparation** <note>This is the title of the work: *Praeparatio Evangelica*. Eusebius wrote it to prove that Christians were right to reject Greek religion in favor of Hebrew scripture.</note> for the diagnosis and judgment of those who will read it, so that they might learn for themselves. We ourselves—and those here with us who were until recently inexperienced—were once such people long ago. We were men born of such fathers, and we were bound by the nourishment of such great evils, our souls buried in a drunken stupor of impiety and ignorance of God. We were deemed worthy of release and freedom from all these things through the one and only Gospel teaching, which was provided to us in no other way than through the appearance of our Savior, Jesus Christ, who is God. He did not appear in just one part of the earth, nor in a corner of a country belonging to a single nation, but throughout the entire inhabited world of men. In this world, where the error of superstition <note>original: "δεισιδαίμονος πλάνης" (deisidaimonos planēs). In this context, "superstition" implies a fearful or misplaced religious awe.</note> had especially taken hold, He—like a sun for the intellectual and rational soul—spread out the rays of His own light. He moved our whole race of men, both barbarians and Greeks, as if out of a terrible mist and a most gloomy and relentless night of superstitious error, into the bright and most transparent day of true piety toward God, the King of all.

Certainly, the voices of the prophets expressly taught that the idols of the dead and the images of men long deceased were being feared and worshipped by all the people throughout the cities and villages who were startled by this polytheistic error. This was the ancient "nonsense" <note>original: "λύδραν" (lydran), likely a scribal error for "φλυαρίαν" (phlyarian) meaning nonsense or humbug.</note> that characterized this beast-like life among men of old, who took no account of God the Creator of all things, nor were they sobered by the punishments for their transgressions, but instead cast themselves into every kind of unholy deed. For at that time, laws by which one ought to live were not yet established, nor was a civilized way of life organized among men. Instead, they led a wandering and nomadic life, established in a beast-like manner; like irrational cattle, they cared for nothing more than the filling of their bellies. One would not be speaking out of turn to call this a state of "godlessness." Yet, even in these people, some small part of their natural intuition was stirred, and they realized that God and the power of God was something saving and good. But having utterly forgotten Him, they stretched their souls upward toward heaven. There, they were all struck with awe by the beauty of the lights in heaven—the luminaries that appear and shine—and they declared these to be gods. 

A third group, clearly casting themselves down to the earth, took those who were considered to excel among them in intelligence, or in physical strength and the power of sovereignty (those who had dominated many, such as certain giants, or tyrants, or even sorcerers and magicians), and because of some distraction of ours, these people kept their evil-working charms secret. Or, perhaps these leaders had initiated some common and life-benefiting service for others. Consequently, while they were still living and even after their deaths, the people proclaimed them to be gods. To these people, the "houses of the gods" are actually the tombs of the dead that are held in memory, just as **Clement** <note>Clement of Alexandria, a prominent Christian teacher and philosopher (c. 150 – 215 AD).</note> records in his *Exhortation* <note>original: "Προτρεπτικῷ" (Protrepticus), Clement's famous appeal to the Greeks to abandon paganism.</note> addressed to us, bringing forward the Greeks themselves as witnesses to his argument. If indeed...

### Concerning the fact that the so-called temples of their gods are actually the tombs of the dead.

> It is quite likely, then, that superstition <note>original: "δεισιδαιμονία" (deisidaimonia). In early Christian writing, this term shifted from meaning "piety" to "irrational fear of gods" or "superstition."</note>, having taken its origin from some point, became a fountain of foolish vice. Then, because it was not checked, but poured out in abundance and flowed as a great stream, it became the architect of many demons—offering hecatombs <note>A "hecatomb" was a high-stakes sacrifice of 100 oxen.</note>, performing festivals, erecting statues, and building temples. Nor indeed shall I be silent about this, but I shall even make a point of it: those structures which are honorably named "temples" are actually graves; that is to say, graves that have been renamed "temples." But you, at least even now, must forget your superstition and feel ashamed to honor tombs. In the temple of Athena in Larissa, in the acropolis, there is the tomb of Acrisius <note>The mythical King of Argos and grandfather of Perseus.</note>. At Athens, in the acropolis, is the tomb of Cecrops <note>The legendary first king of Athens, often depicted as half-man, half-serpent.</note>, as Antiochus says in the ninth book of his *Histories*. And what of Erichthonius? Is he not buried in the temple of Athena Polias? And were Ismarus, the son of Eumolpus, and Daeira not buried in the enclosure of the Prytaneion <note>A public building containing the holy hearth of the city.</note> beneath the acropolis? Are not the daughters of Celeus buried in Eleusis? Why should I list for you the women from the Hyperboreans? Let them be called Hyperoche and Laodice; they are buried in the Artemisium in Delos, which is in the temple of the Delian Apollo. Leandros says that Cleomachus is buried in Miletus, in the Didymaion <note>The great temple of Apollo at Didyma.</note>. Here, the monument of Leucophryne is not worth passing over; she is said to be buried in the temple of Artemis in Magnesia. Furthermore, regarding the altar of Apollo in Telmessus, they say this is the monument of Telmesses the seer. Ptolemy, the son of Agasarchus, in the first book of his work *On Philopator*, says that in Paphos, in the temple of Aphrodite, Cinyras and the descendants of Cinyras are buried. "O you who suffer evil things," <note>Clement is quoting a line of poetry, likely from a tragedy or Homeric hymn.</note>

after a few words he says:

> The Roman Emperor <note>Referring to Hadrian, who reigned 117–138 AD.</note> has perfected a new and strange god in Egypt, and has almost done so among the Greeks: Antinous, his extremely beautiful young favorite, whom he consecrated just as Zeus consecrated Ganymede. For desire is not easily restrained when it lacks fear. And men now observe "sacred nights" in his honor—nights which the lover, who stayed awake for him, knew were actually shameful.

He continues:

> Already, the tomb of the beloved is the temple and city of Antinous. And just as temples are admired, so too are the tombs—pyramids, mausoleums, and labyrinths are other temples of the dead, just as those others were tombs of the gods.

At Pytho <note>Another name for Delphi.</note>, the Pythian dragon is worshipped, and the festival of the serpent is announced as the "Pythian Games." At the Isthmus, the sea cast up a miserable corpse, and the Isthmian Games mourn for Melicertes. At Nemea, another child, Archemorus, is buried, and the funeral games for the child are called the "Nemean Games." ### A Recapitulation of the Previous Arguments.

**S**uch is the character of Greek theology—by which I mean the popular and more mythical sort—which has been shown to be much preceded by the identical traditions of the Phoenicians and Egyptians, as well as others mentioned in my earlier accounts. These matters have been demonstrated through the very words of the Greek authors themselves, which I have already set forth. In the beginning of this present dialectical work, I reasonably placed these matters before my readers for their examination and judgment, so that they might learn for themselves.

<margin>11</margin>As for us, and those who until now were as ignorant as people of old—born of such ancestors and bound by such great evils, our souls buried in the deep "drunkenness" of impiety and ignorance of God—we have been deemed worthy of a recovery and a liberation from all these things. This was achieved through the one and only teaching of the Gospel, provided to us through the appearing of our Savior, the Word of God, Jesus Christ <note>Eusebius often uses the term "appearing" (epiphaneia) to refer to the Incarnation of Christ as a historical intervention.</note>. He did not appear in just one part of the earth, nor in a corner of the land belonging to a single nation, but throughout the whole inhabited world of men—over which the error of superstitious delusion had been poured out. Like an intellectual and rational sun of souls, he spread the rays of his own light, and at once relocated all of us—the whole race of mankind, both barbarians and Greeks—from a terrible mist and a most gloomy, unseen night of superstitious error into the bright and most transparent day of the true worship of God, the King of All.

Indeed, the words I previously laid down explicitly taught us that the images of the dead and the statues formerly stained with gore <note>original: "λύθρων" (lythron), referring to the defilement of blood from animal or human sacrifices.</note> were the objects of devotion for all those who, in their various nations, were terrified by the prevailing evil of polytheistic error. In former times, due to the excessive "bestiality" of this life <note>Eusebius uses the term "θηριωδία" (theriodia) to describe a state of primitive lawlessness where humans lived like wild animals.</note>, people took no account of God the Creator of all things, nor did they heed the punishments of a vengeful justice for their sins, but instead threw themselves into every kind of shameful practice. 

For in those times, there were no laws to live by, nor was a civilized way of life established among men. Living in lawlessness and a nomadic, bestial state, they cared for nothing more than the satisfaction of their bellies, just like irrational cattle. Their first form of "atheism" <note>Eusebius paradoxically calls early paganism "atheism" because it failed to recognize the one true Creator.</note> occurred when, stirred by a small spark of natural intuition, they realized that "God" and "the power of God" must be something saving and good. However, in their attempt to find this, they stretched their souls upward to the sky. Stopping there in their thoughts and being struck by the beauty of the luminaries appearing in the heavens, they declared these to be gods. 

A third group of people cast themselves down to the earth and declared those who excelled in intelligence, physical strength, or the power of sovereignty to be "gods." These were certain giants, or tyrants, or even magicians and sorcerers <note>original: "γόητας, καὶ φαρμακέας" (goētas kai pharmakeas). The latter refers to those who used drugs or poisons for magic.</note> who, due to a later fall into wickedness, devised deceitful sorceries, or those who had been the first to provide some common and useful benefit to the public. These they proclaimed to be gods while they were still living and even after their death. This is why the houses of their gods are recorded as being the tombs of the dead. As Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 AD), a Christian theologian who argued that pagan gods were merely divinized humans.</note> records in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*, he brings forward the Greeks themselves as witnesses to this argument. ## PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL

<page-num>46</page-num>
<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

By nature and through self-taught—or rather, God-taught—conceptions, mankind discovered a noble and useful truth that points toward the name and essence of God. For everyone was from the very start predisposed by common reason, since the Creator of the universe sowed a pattern within every rational and intelligent soul through natural conceptions. Yet they did not employ their will according to reason. For perhaps one or two, or a very few—whose memory the <term>Hebrew oracles</term> <note>original: "ta Hebraiōn logia." This refers to the Old Testament scriptures, which Eusebius views as the preserved record of those who kept the true faith.</note> preserve—did not apply their conception of the divine to anything visible. Instead, with undistorted reasoning, they rose from visible things to the Creator of the whole world and the great Maker of all. With the "eyes of the mind" purified, they understood Him alone to be God, the Savior of all, and the sole giver of good things.

But the rest, stumbling in the darkness of the soul's error, sank into the depths of impiety. In the manner of wild beasts, they limited what is "noble," "advantageous," and "good" to what their eyes could see and the pleasure of the flesh. In this way, as I said before, they took the virtues of things considered beautiful or useful for the body and elevated them. They raised up powerful tyrants, or sorcerers and magicians—men who were mortal by nature and subject to human misfortunes—and proclaimed them providers of good, "saviors," and gods. They transferred the venerable conception of God that naturally existed within them to those they considered benefactors. 

Such a madness of the mind seized them that they did not even account for the crimes committed by those they treated as gods. Nor did they blush at the shameful things rumored about them. Instead, they marveled at everything about these men because of the benefits they provided, or because of the power and tyranny they held at that time. Since laws, as I mentioned, were not yet established among men, and shame was not yet attached to sins, they celebrated adultery, the corruption of males, unlawful and illegal marriages, murders, parricides, and the slaughter of children and siblings. These were the very acts performed by their own protectors, whom they regarded and addressed as gods. Thus, alongside their achievements and brave deeds, they left behind the memory of these acts as something solemn and manly for future generations.

Such was the nature of the ancient theology. However, some "moderns," who cropped up just yesterday or the day before, boasting of a more rational philosophy, introduced what they call a more <term>physical interpretation</term> <note>original: "physikiōteran." In ancient philosophy, "physics" referred to the study of the natural world. Here, it refers to "allegorizing" myths as symbols for natural forces.</note> of the history of the gods. They invented more "solemn" explanations for the myths. They neither fully escaped the impiety of their ancestors, nor could they endure the blatant wickedness of those they called gods. Desiring to heal the ancestral error, they transformed the myths into physical explanations and theories. They boasted quite mystically that these myths actually signified the nourishing and growth-promoting qualities of nature's food. From this starting point, they too proclaimed the elements of the world to be gods. They did not stop at the sun, moon, and stars, but included the earth and water, air and fire, and the combinations and results arising from them. Indeed, they even deified the seasonal fruits of the earth and other growths from dry and wet nourishment—the very things that sustain our bodily life—naming them <term>Demeter, Kore, and Dionysus</term> <note>Demeter was the goddess of grain/agriculture; Kore (Persephone) her daughter; Dionysus the god of wine and vegetation.</note>, and...

Whatever things similar to these they have added and published, they have introduced a forced and untrue "beautification" of the myths. Yet these later writers never claimed to be speaking on behalf of the ancestral theologies; instead, each one, out of a personal desire for solemnity <note>original: "semnologias" — a term Eusebius uses to describe the act of dressing up crude myths in grand, "solemn" language to make them sound more respectable</note>, added their own interpretations to the stories about the gods. They did not dare to change the traditional customs, for they held antiquity in high regard and cherished the habits they were raised with from childhood.

Indeed, those even older than these writers decreed the deification of irrational animals alongside the deification of men. They did this because animals were useful to them, as explained in the reasons given previously. They dedicated the same religious rites to irrational beasts—libations, sacrifices, and mystical ceremonies—as well as hymns and songs. As they elevated men to gods and heaped honors upon them, they eventually drove themselves into such a peak of wickedness that, through an excess of uncontrolled self-indulgence, they even took the urinary parts of the body <note>This refers to the "Phallophoria" or fertility rites involving the public display and worship of reproductive organs</note>—things used by humans for shameful acts—and honored them with god-like status in their religious processions. They did not seek any solemn use for these things, but openly declared them part of their theology.

It must be observed that the most ancient people knew nothing more than the literal history of these stories; they clung only to the myths and were "thunderstruck" <note>original: "embrontēthēsan" — literally "struck by lightning," here meaning stunned or blinded by tradition</note> by them. But since we have set out to examine even the solemn and secret thoughts of the noble philosophers, come, let us inspect these as well, so that we do not seem ignorant of their "admirable" philosophies.

Before we set out their views, I think it is important to point out how even these admirable philosophers contradict one another on these matters. Some tell the stories one way, and each presents his own private opinion as fact; they do not agree with one another when studying the laws of nature <term>physiologia</term> <note>original: "physiologousin" — here meaning the attempt to explain the gods as symbols for natural elements like fire, water, or the stars</note>. The more decent among them do not entirely reject the unseemly stories about the gods according to the laws of their own city, but they do cast away the interpretations of those stories. Sometimes, out of fear of the punishment prescribed by the laws, they use "euphemisms" <note>original: "hypokorizon" — to use a sweet or mild word to cover up something harsh or ugly</note> for the myths. 

Listen, then, to those very men through one who was the best of all the <unclear>Greeks</unclear>. At one moment, he speaks with holy reverence; at another, he refuses to accept the myths entirely. This "admirable" Plato, when he is stripping away pretense to show his own true choice, quite boldly forbids and tears down all this nonsense and the way it was told by the ancients—whether they intended the stories to be <term>allegories</term> <note>original: "allēgoreien" — interpreting the myths as symbols for deeper truths rather than literal events</note> or whether they were told without any hidden meaning. Yet, when he "sugar-coats" his words for the sake of the laws, he says that one must believe the myths about the gods, even if they have no hidden meaning revealed within them. Indeed, having at one time defined his own theology regarding the ancient myths—studying the nature of the heaven, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the whole universe and its parts separately—he then speaks specifically and separately about the gods who were deified in the old days. He discusses them in the *Timaeus* using these very words:

By nature, and through self-taught concepts—or rather, God-taught <note>original: "theodidaktois" — implying that the knowledge of God is not just discovered by humans, but implanted by the Divine</note> ones—the term that signifies the name and essence of God is both beautiful and beneficial. For all people have a shared, preconceived understanding that the Creator of the universe <note>original: "demiurgon"</note> has sown this idea into every rational and intellectual soul through natural concepts. However, they did not use their power of choice in accordance with reason. For perhaps one or two, or a very few others whose memory is preserved in the Oracles of the Hebrews, did not apply this concept of God to anything visible. Instead, with undistorted reasoning, they rose above the creator of the entire world and the great Maker of all things. With the eyes of their minds purified, they recognized Him alone as the one God, the Savior of all and the sole Giver of good things.

But the rest of humanity, their whole households overcome by a darkening of the soul, were cast into the depths of impiety. Like wild beasts, they limited their definition of "the beautiful," "the useful," and "the good" to mere impulse and the pleasure of the flesh. Consequently, following what was said before, they took those who were chosen for their physical beauty or usefulness—or even tyrants, sorcerers, or magicians—and proclaimed these men, who were mortal by nature and had suffered extraordinary misfortunes, as "saviors" and "gods" and "givers of good." They transferred the venerable concept of God, which exists naturally within them, onto those they considered their benefactors.

Such a mental paralysis seized them that they took no account of the transgressions of those they called gods, nor did they blush at the shameful stories told about them. They admired these men entirely for the benefits they provided, or for the powers and tyrannies they established at that time. Since there was no law yet established for human society—as I have said before—and no punishment hanging over their sins, they committed adulteries, the corruption of males, unlawful and illicit marriages, murders, parricides, and the slaughter of children and siblings. These deeds, actually committed by their own leaders whom they called gods, were commemorated by later generations as achievements of virtue and courage. They left behind the memory of these acts as something noble and brave for posterity.

Such was the nature of the ancient theology. But certain more recent thinkers, appearing only yesterday or the day before, boasted of a more "logical" way of philosophizing and introduced a more "scientific" <note>original: "physikoteran" — literally "more physical," meaning an interpretation based on the laws of nature</note> view of the history of the gods. They devised more solemn allegories for the myths. They neither completely escaped the errors and impiety of their ancestors, nor could they stomach the obvious wickedness of the stories told about the gods. Eager to heal the ancestral error, they transformed the myths into physical descriptions and theories. They boasted that the stories actually revealed the things that nourish and grow physical nature, speaking with a more "mystical" tone. Then, these thinkers also proclaimed the elements of the world to be gods—not just the sun, moon, and stars, but also earth, water, air, and fire, as well as the compounds and results formed from them. Furthermore, they deified the seasonal fruits of the earth and the other growths used for dry and liquid food. Considering these to be the causes of physical life, they called them Demeter <note>The goddess of the harvest and grain</note>, Kore <note>The "Maiden" or Persephone, associated with the cycle of growth</note>, and Dionysus <note>The god of wine and fertility</note>, and...

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 2. 47
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

...that they stood by and were amazed by similar things, introducing a forced and untrue beautification of the myths. But these people, appearing later as if ashamed of the theologies of their ancestors, invented for themselves various stately interpretations to add to the myths about the gods, crafting an empty recantation <note>original: "palinōdian" — a formal retraction or "singing back" of a previous statement</note> that amounts to nothing. They have blamed antiquity and the solemn and sober upbringing they received from childhood. Indeed, those even older than these, in the same way as they practiced wretched deification, also arranged for the deification of irrational animals, because of some useful benefits or services attributed to them. 

They offered equal worship to irrational beasts, with libations and sacrifices, mystic rites, and similarly with hymns and songs. To these deified men, they also assigned honors, and they were driven to such a degree of wickedness that, through an excess of unmixed indulgence, they consecrated the parts of the body used for shameful acts and the unrestrained passions within them, giving all honor to the gods. They claimed that nothing absurd should be excluded from such stately talk, as the theologians themselves declared. We should note that the most ancient people, knowing nothing more than the historical narrative, were testified to have relied solely on the myths. 

But since we have once set out to look into the solemn and secret matters of the noble philosophers, come, let us also examine these, lest we seem to be ignorant of their admirable philosophies. But before making an exposition of these, it seems to me necessary to point out that even these "admirable" philosophers contradict themselves in these matters. For some have interpreted things in one way, and each one declares his own view individually; for they do not agree with each other in their natural philosophy. 

But the more fair-minded among them completely reject the myths and banish from their own state not only the unseemly stories about the gods but also the interpretations of them. Yet there are times when, out of fear of the service of the laws, they use flattering language for the myths. Hear then their own words through one who is the best of many, who at one time pushes them away, and at another time adopts the myths. The marvelous Plato, when he lays bare his own preference, more freely forbids thinking or saying such things about the gods as was said by the ancients, whether they contain a hidden meaning signified through an "under-thought" <note>original: "hyponoia" — the ancient term for allegory or deep meaning</note> or are spoken without any such meaning. But when he fawns upon the laws, he says one must believe the myths about the gods, as if they have nothing hidden in their "under-thoughts." Having already at some point distinguished his own theology of the ancient myths—concerning the heaven, the sun, the moon, the stars, and even the whole world and its parts separately—he then speaks separately and distinctly about the gods who were celebrated in song of old, as he proceeds in the *Timaeus* with these very words.

<meta>This page transitions from Eusebius’s general argument about the origins of religion to a specific critique of how the Greeks attempted to sanitize their scandalous myths. He moves from discussing the "God-taught" instinct to the "physical" or "natural" (allegorical) interpretations used by later philosophers to justify the deification of the elements.</meta>

-># EUSEBIUS<-

By nature, then, and through self-taught—or rather, God-taught—conceptions, people have identified the name and essence of God as something beautiful and beneficial. For all humans have understood this through common reasoning, since the Creator of the universe sowed this into every rational and intelligent soul through natural conceptions. Yet they did not make use of this reason in their choices. For perhaps one or two, or a very few others whose memory the Hebrew oracles preserve <note>original: "logia" — divine utterances or scriptures</note>, did not apply the concept of God to any visible thing. Instead, with undistorted reasoning, they were led from visible things to the Creator of the entire world and the great Maker of all things. With purified eyes of the mind, they saw Him alone as God, the Savior of all, and recognized Him alone as the Giver of good things. 

But the rest, overturned by a total darkening of the soul, were cast into the depth of impiety. In the manner of wild beasts, they limited what is "beautiful," "beneficial," and "good" to the level of their eyes and the pleasure of the flesh. Thus, they considered only what was pleasant and useful for the body to be desirable. They even proclaimed certain rulers and tyrants, or even sorcerers and poisoners <note>original: "pharmakeas" — those who use drugs or spells; in this context, "charlatans"</note>, as gods and "saviors." Although they were mortals subject to human misfortunes, people hailed them as the providers of good things, transferring the venerable concept of God that existed naturally within them onto those they considered their benefactors. 

Such a mental paralysis <note>original: "apoplēxia" — a striking away of the senses or intellect</note> seized them that they did not even consider the crimes committed by those they treated as gods. They did not even blush at the shameful stories told about them. Instead, they marveled at everything regarding these men because of the benefits they provided, or because of the dynasties and tyrannies they were then first establishing. Since no laws were yet governing human behavior and no punishment was yet hanging over their sins, they attributed to their gods acts of adultery, the corruption of males, unlawful marriages, murder, parricide, and the slaughter of children and brothers. They even recorded these wars and rebellions as deeds of courage, leaving the memory of these acts to posterity as if they were solemn and brave achievements.

Such was the nature of the old theology. But certain newer writers, who appeared just yesterday or the day before, boasting of a more rational philosophy, introduced a "physical" interpretation <note>This refers to "Physical Theology," where gods are interpreted as natural forces like wind or fire</note> of the history of the gods. They devised more dignified explanations for the myths. They neither completely escaped the error of their ancestors’ impiety, nor could they endure the obvious wickedness of the mythological subjects. Eager to "heal" the ancestral mistake, they transformed the myths into physical descriptions and theories. They claimed that the nourishing and growth-promoting elements of nature were what was really being revealed through the myths. 

Boasting of this more "natural" approach, they deified the elements <term>stoicheia (the fundamental components of the universe)</term> of the world. They did not stop at the sun, moon, and stars, but included the earth, water, air, and fire, as well as the compounds and results formed from them. Indeed, they even deified the seasonal fruits of the earth and the other growths that provide dry and liquid nourishment, naming them Demeter, Kore, and Dionysus...

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 2, Page 47

...adding whatever similar details they could to these stories, introducing a forced and untrue **embellishment** to the myths. But these later writers were the only ones who—long after the fact and as if fulfilling a promise—invented grandiloquent explanations <note>original: "semnologias" — literally "solemn speech," referring here to high-sounding allegorical interpretations</note> for the theologies of their ancestors, adding these to the myths about the gods. Yet, no one dared to actually change the ancestral traditions, for they held antiquity in high regard and honored the customs and upbringing they had shared since childhood.

Indeed, those even older than these writers arranged for the deification <note>original: "ektheōseis"</note> of irrational animals <note>original: "alogōn zōōn" — animals lacking the power of reason</note> alongside the deification of men, for the same reasons previously given. They dedicated equal forms of worship to these unreasoning beasts—including libations, sacrifices, secret rites, and similar hymns and songs. They looked upon these with the same honors given to the men who had been turned into gods. 

They were driven to such an extent of evil that, through an excess of uncontrolled indulgence in pleasure, they even assigned divine honors to the parts of the body used for shameful acts <note>Eusebius is likely referring to the cult of the phallus in the mysteries of Dionysus</note>, as well as to undisciplined and destructive passions. They felt no need to speak solemnly about these secret shames, as their own theologians had already made them public.

It must be observed that the most ancient people, knowing nothing more than the literal history, were shaped by the myths alone. But since we have once set out to examine the "solemn" and "secret" views of the philosophers with a naked eye, let us also look into these matters, so that we do not appear ignorant of their "admirable" philosophies. 

Before we set out this exposition, I think it is necessary to point out that even among these "admirable" philosophers, there is a great deal of disagreement. Some offer a physical <note>original: "physiologia" — an interpretation where gods represent natural elements like fire or water</note> explanation for the myths, but they do not agree with one another's natural theories. Others, being more sensible, do not entirely do away with the myths but argue that a well-ordered state should banish not only the indecent stories about the gods but also the allegorical interpretations of them. 

Sometimes, out of fear of legal punishment, they try to reconcile themselves to the myths. Listen, then, to how the best of them all—who sometimes pushes the myths away and at other times invites them back in—speaks on our behalf. Their wonderful **Plato**, when he is revealing his own true intent, quite boldly forbids one to think or say such things about the gods as the ancients did, whether they are meant as **allegories** <note>original: "allēgoriōn" — speaking one thing to mean another</note> or as hints of some hidden meaning, or even if they are said without any hidden meaning at all. 

Yet, when he is flattering the laws, he says that one must believe the myths about the gods, even if they show no clear hidden meaning. Having already defined his own theology regarding the heavens, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the entire universe—explaining its parts through natural philosophy <note>original: "physiologēsas"</note>—he then speaks separately and specifically about the gods who were praised in hymns of old. In the *Timaeus*, he discusses them in these very words:

It is impossible to disbelieve the children of gods, even if they speak without probable or necessary proofs; rather, as they claim to be reporting their own family matters, we must follow the law and believe them. Thus, then, according to them, the origin of these..."

# EUSEBIUS

> » ...let the origin of the other gods be described and accepted as follows: Ocean and Tethys were the children of Earth and Heaven. From them were born Phorcys, Cronus, and Rhea, and all those who accompanied them. From Cronus and Rhea came Zeus, Hera, and all those whom we know are called their siblings, and still other descendants from these. 

Plato says these things <note>This quote is from Plato's *Timaeus* (40d-e)</note> because he felt bound to follow the law and the tradition that had been believed. He admits that these accounts were spoken without the usual likely or necessary proofs. Yet, he speaks cautiously, as if he has nothing secret to hide, revealing the names and genealogies of the gods as they are declared in natural philosophy <note>original: "physiologiais" — the study of the nature of the gods through physical allegory</note>. Elsewhere, however, the same author strips away his disguise and reveals his own true preference, using these words:

> » First of all, I said, the person who told the greatest lie about the most important matters did not lie well—I mean how Uranus <note>The personification of the Sky</note> did what Hesiod says he did, and how Cronus took his revenge on him. Even if the deeds of Cronus and the suffering he endured at the hands of his son [Zeus] were true, I would not think they should be told so lightly to the foolish and the young. It would be best to keep silent about them. But if there were some necessity to speak, they should be heard in secret, and those listening should have first offered a sacrifice—not just a common pig, but some great and unrepeatable sacrifice <note>original: "aporrhēton thyma"</note>—so that as few as possible would happen to hear them. For indeed, these stories are harmful. They must not be told in our city, O Adimantus, nor should a young listener be told that if he commits the worst crimes, he is doing nothing extraordinary—nor even if he punishes a father who has done wrong in every possible way. For in doing so, he would only be doing what the first and greatest of the gods did. 
> 
> » In my opinion, it is not suitable to say these things. Nor should we say at all that gods wage war against gods, or plot against one another, or fight. For these things are not true—at least not if those who are going to guard our city are to consider it the most shameful thing to be easily set at odds with one another. Far be it from us to tell them myths of the War of the Giants <note>original: "gigantomachias"</note> or describe the various enmities of gods and heroes against their own kin and relatives. Rather, if we are to persuade them that no citizen was ever an enemy to another, and that such a thing is unholy, these are the kinds of things that should be told to children from the start. Both the old men and the old women, as the children grow older, should compel the poets to compose stories close to these. But we must not admit into our city the stories of Hera being bound by her son, or Hephaestus being hurled down by his father when he was about to defend his mother from a beating, or any of the "Battles of the Gods" that Homer composed—whether they were composed with hidden allegories <note>original: "hyponoiais" — literally "under-meanings"</note> or without them.

Through these words, the philosopher clearly teaches that the ancient myths about the gods—and even the "hidden meanings" or natural allegories people try to find in those myths—are far from the truth. This shows that our own withdrawal from such traditions and our turning toward the teaching of the Savior’s Gospel is not irrational. Since these myths have been rejected even by the Greeks' own thinkers, I am moved to admire the ancient Romans. They perceived that all the Greek allegories regarding the gods were absurd, useless, and essentially forced or inconsistent, and so they excluded these myths from their own state theology. You can see evidence of this in the *Roman Antiquities* by Dionysius of Halicarnassus. In his second book, while recording the history of Romulus, the first founder of Rome, he describes his various achievements and how he established the law concerning the gods.
