# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 2.
e.i.
<meta>catchword: menon</meta>

" ...and they practice justice and military skills, they build a good city. Regarding these things, he [Romulus, the founder of Rome] had great foresight, beginning with the reverence shown toward divine and spiritual matters <note>original: "theia kai daimonia" — the realm of gods and lesser spirits</note>. He established temples, sacred precincts, altars, the setting up of ancient wooden statues <note>term: xoana — primitive wooden cult images believed to have fallen from heaven</note>, their forms and symbols, their powers and the gifts with which they have benefited our race, as well as festivals and the kind of assemblies that should belong to the gods or spirits. He also established the sacrifices in which they delight to be honored by men, the seasonal truces and public gatherings, the rest from labors, and all such things, following the best of our ancestral laws.

" As for the myths handed down about the gods—those containing blasphemies, accusations, or wicked, useless, and indecent behavior—he considered them unworthy not only of gods but even of good men. He rejected and cast them out, and he prepared the people to speak and think only the most beautiful things about the gods, attributing nothing to them that was unworthy of a blessed nature. 

" Among the Romans, for instance, there is no story of Uranus <note>The personification of the Sky</note> being castrated by his own children, nor of Cronus <note>Saturn</note> devouring his own offspring out of fear of being overthrown. Nor do they tell of Zeus <note>Jupiter</note> overthrowing the reign of Cronus and locking his own father in the prison of Tartarus. One does not hear of wars, wounds, bonds, or the enslavement of gods among men. No festival among them is celebrated by wearing black or with mournful rites involving the beating of breasts and the wailing of women over "vanishing gods"—rites which are performed among the Greeks regarding the abduction of Persephone <note>Proserpina</note>, the sufferings of Dionysius <note>Bacchus</note>, and all other such stories. 

" One would see no signs of religious madness among them, nor the 'god-possessed' frenzies, nor the Corybantic <note>term: Corybantic — wild, rhythmic dancing used in the cult of Cybele</note> ravings, nor Bacchic revelries and secret mysteries, nor men and women spending the night together in temples. Instead, everything regarding the gods is done and said with piety, unlike anything found among either the Greeks or the foreigners <note>original: "barbarois"</note>. 

" And what I have wondered at most of all is this: although countless nations have come to the city [Rome] and are under great necessity to worship their ancestral gods according to their own domestic laws, the city has never publicly adopted any foreign practice—a thing which has happened to many others. Even if any foreign rites were introduced because of oracles, the city adapted them to its own laws, casting out all mythical nonsense—as in the case of the rites of the Idaean Goddess <note>term: Idaean Goddess — Cybele, the Great Mother, brought to Rome from Phrygia during the Punic Wars</note>. For the Roman magistrates lead sacrifices and games in her honor every year according to Roman law, but the priest is a Phrygian man and the priestess a Phrygian woman. They carry her image through the city, begging for alms <note>original: "metragyrto" — collecting money for the Mother goddess</note> as is their custom, wearing symbols on their chests and playing the flute while their followers strike drums to the 'Mother's songs.' Yet, no native-born Roman goes through the city begging for alms, or playing the flute, or wearing colorful robes, or celebrating the goddess with wild orgies or Phrygian oaths, neither by law nor by decree of the Senate. Such is the piety the city maintains toward customs regarding the gods that are not indigenous. 

" It rejects every myth that contains nothing decent. And let no one suppose that I am unaware that some Greek myths are useful to men—some demonstrating the works of nature through symbols, others composed for the sake of comforting human misfortunes, others to remove disturbances and fears from the soul and to clear away unhealthy opinions, and still others fashioned for some other kind of benefit. But although I understand these things as well as anyone, I nevertheless remain piously disposed toward them and find the theology of the Romans much more acceptable, considering—"

### EUSEBIUS

...offspring, because the benefits found in Greek myths are small and can only help those few who have examined the deeper reasons for which these stories were told; however, those who have partaken of this philosophy are few. The large and unphilosophical crowd, taking the stories about the gods in the worst sense, suffers one of two consequences: either they despise the gods as being tossed about in great misery, or they do not hold back from any of the most shameful and lawless acts, seeing such behaviors attributed to the gods. But regarding these matters, let the consideration be left to those who practice only the theoretical part of philosophy. As for the state established by Romulus <note>The legendary founder and first king of Rome</note>, he considered the following things worthy of history. The views handed down by the best of the philosophers, and by the ancient and primary leaders of the Roman empire regarding Greek theology, were such that they in no way accepted "natural explanations" <note>term: physiologia — the practice of explaining away embarrassing myths by claiming they represent natural forces like wind or fire</note> within the myths about gods. Nor did they accept those paraphrases that try to appear solemn. However, since we have once set out to refute these things, come, let us look at their interpretations and theories to see what solemn and god-befitting qualities they actually bring forward. Let us use nothing of our own, but use their own voices throughout, so that we may learn their own domestic affairs from them directly.

# GOSPEL PREPARATION, Book 3

->Preface.<-

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial letter 'T', decorated with intricate foliage and floral scrollwork within a square frame.</image-desc>

Such then were the views held by the most excellent of the philosophers and the ancient and primary leaders of the Roman empire regarding "heroic theology"; they in no way accepted "Naturalistic Explanations" <note>original: "Physiologia" — the practice of explaining myths as allegories for natural forces</note> within the myths about the gods, nor those sophisticated and solemn-looking tricks of speech. However, since we have set out to refute these things, come, let us examine their own interpretations and theories to see if they ever bring forward anything truly grand and worthy of God. We shall use nothing of our own, but rather employ their own voices throughout, so that we may learn about their own "solemn and secret" matters from their own mouths. Though countless other philosophers have made such promises, and much labor has been spent on these things by those who have created various systems of classification—each insisting that their own view is the correct one—it is enough for me to present proofs from the most famous authors, those well-known to all philosophers, who have won no small fame for their wisdom among the Greeks.

Taking from these first, read the words of Plutarch of Chaeronea <note>A famous Greek historian and Platonist philosopher, c. 46–120 AD</note> concerning the matters at hand. In these, while speaking solemnly, he interprets the myths—which he claims contain a "mysterious theology"—in a different way. While uncovering these meanings, he says that Dionysus is "drunkenness," rather than the mortal man described by history in his writings on the subject. He says Hera represents "marriage," the union of man and woman. Then, as if forgetting this explanation, he piles on another story immediately after, calling Hera "the Earth" instead of her previous definition. He calls Leto "oblivion" and "night," and then again says that Hera is the same as Leto. Furthermore, he introduces Zeus as being an allegory for "ethereal power." Why should I summarize these things before you hear the text itself? In his work entitled *On the Daidala at Plataea* <note>A lost work by Plutarch describing a wooden-image festival in the city of Plataea</note>, he reveals to the masses the hidden secrets of the "Naturalistic Explanations" of the gods.

->Concerning the Natural Theology of the Greeks.<-

<margin>»</margin> That ancient "Natural Science" <note>original: "Physiologia"</note>, among both Greeks and foreigners, was a discourse on
<margin>»</margin> nature veiled in myths, concealed for the most part through riddles and deeper meanings, 
<margin>»</margin> and was a "mysterious theology." In this system, things spoken are clearer to the masses 
<margin>»</margin> than the things left silent, while the things left silent are more profound than those 
<margin>»</margin> spoken. This is evident in the Orphic poems <note>Ancient poems attributed to the mythical singer Orpheus</note> and in the Egyptian and Phrygian discourses. 
<margin>»</margin> Above all, the ecstatic rites <note>original: "orgasmoi" — referring to the intense religious fervor of the mysteries</note> associated with the initiations, and the symbolic actions 
<margin>»</margin> performed in the sacred ceremonies, reveal the mindset of the ancients. But we are 
<margin>»</margin> wandering far from the present discourse. They do not believe, nor do they think it 
<margin>»</margin> right, that Hera should have any fellowship with Dionysus. They take care to keep 
<margin>»</margin> their sacred rites from mixing, and it is said that the priestesses at Athens, when 
<margin>»</margin> meeting one another, do not even offer a greeting. They do not allow ivy to be brought 
<margin>»</margin> into the sanctuary of Hera at all—not because of the mythological and nonsensical 
<margin>»</margin> stories of "jealousy" <note>referring to Hera's mythological jealousy of Dionysus's mother, Semele</note>, but because the goddess is the patron of marriage and the 
<margin>»</margin> conductor of brides. Drunkenness is unseemly for newlyweds, and most unsuitable for 
<margin>»</margin> weddings, as says the...

<meta>This page continues the excerpt from Plutarch’s lost work "On Using the Oracles," quoted by Eusebius to illustrate how the Greeks attempted to explain away their scandalous myths by turning them into allegories for nature.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

"...Plato’s view. For he says that drinking unmixed wine <note>original: "akratoposia"</note> causes a disturbance in both souls and bodies. From this, unformed and wandering thoughts take root, much like those who are unrefined and crowned with ivy <note>A reference to followers of Dionysus, symbolizing wild or uncultured behavior</note>. Again, those who sacrifice to Hera do not dedicate the gall <note>The bile or gallbladder, associated with bitterness</note> at the altar, but instead bury it nearby. This is done to signify that the marriage union of a man and a woman ought to be free from anger and bile, purified of all rage and bitterness. This symbolic style is found even more prominently in their stories and myths."

"For example, they tell a story that while Hera was being raised in Euboea, she was stolen away by Zeus while still a maiden. Having been carried off, she was hidden there, for Mount Kithairon provided them with a shadowed nook and a natural bridal chamber. When Makris <note>A nymph of Euboea who acted as Hera's nurse</note> came searching for her, Kithairon would not allow her to be meddlesome or to approach the place, claiming that Zeus was resting and spending time there with Leto. Thus, Makris went away, and Hera remained hidden for a time. Later, remembering her debt to Leto for providing this 'cover,' Hera shared her altar and temple with her, so that people would pray to 'Leto of the Nook' <note>original: "Letoi Mychiai"</note>. Some, however, call her 'Leto of the Night' <note>original: "Nychian"</note>. In both names, the meaning is something 'hidden' or 'unseen' <note>original: "kriphion kai aphanigedon"</note>."

"Others say that Hera herself represents the life-giving force of the air, which is often hidden. In this way, they say Leto is called 'Night-like' because the air can be dark. When the marriage was finally acknowledged openly near Kithairon and the news of their union spread, Hera was then addressed as 'Hera the Perfect' and 'Hera of Marriage.' Those who understand the myth in a more natural and fitting way bring Hera and Leto together into the same identity. Hera is the Earth, as has been said. Leto is the Night—a kind of 'forgetfulness' <note>A Greek pun: "Leto" sounds like "Lethe," the river of forgetfulness</note> for those who turn toward sleep. And Night is nothing other than the shadow of the Earth. For when the Earth approaches the sunset and hides the sun, she stretches out and darkens the air. This is the 'eclipsing house' that encompasses us when the moon moves through it and the shadow of the earth touches and cuts off the light."

"You can learn from the following that Leto is no different from Hera: we call Artemis the daughter of Leto, yet we also call her 'Hera Eileithyia' <note>The goddess who assists in childbirth</note>. Therefore, Hera and Leto are two names for a single goddess. Again, from Leto comes Apollo; from Hera comes Ares. Yet there is but one power for both. Ares is so named as he 'aids' <note>original: "aregon"</note> in incidents of violence and battle. Apollo is named as he 'delivers' <note>original: "apallatton"</note> and 'releases' <note>original: "apolyon"</note> humans from the bodily sufferings of disease. Therefore, among the most fiery and burning stars, the Sun is called Apollo, while the 'fiery one' <note>The planet Mars</note> is named Ares. It is not unfitting for the same goddess to be called 'Goddess of Marriage' and to be considered the mother of both Childbirth and the Sun. For the end goal of marriage is birth, and birth is the journey from darkness into the sun and the light. The Poet <note>Homer</note> spoke well of this:"

> "But when the goddess of painful labor, Eileithyia, had brought him forth to the light and he saw the rays of the sun."

"Here the Poet emphasized salvation through the goddess, showing the forceful nature of birth pangs. He made the 'seeing of the sun' the completion of the birth process. Thus, the same goddess brought about the union of marriage in order to prepare for birth. Perhaps I should also tell the later myth. It is said that when Hera quarreled with Zeus and no longer wished to associate with him but hid herself, Zeus was at a loss. He wandered through Alalkomeneus <note>A town in Boeotia</note> and met with a man of that same land, and was taught by him that..."

<meta>This page continues the excerpt from Plutarch’s lost work "On the Festivals of the Daedala," as quoted by Eusebius. On the previous page, Plutarch began explaining the mythical origins of the reconciliation between Zeus and Hera as an allegory for nature.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS’S PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 3

» ...how Hera had to be deceived by Zeus, who devised a plan to pretend he was marrying another. With the help of Alalcomeneus <note>A legendary figure in Boeotia, often said to be the first man or a tutor to Athena</note>, they secretly cut down a sturdy and beautiful oak tree, shaped it, and dressed it in bridal attire, calling it "Daedale." Then, in this manner, they began to sing the wedding hymn.

### The Wedding Hymn

» The Tritonian nymphs <note>Nymphs associated with Lake Tritonis or local Boeotian springs</note> were said to bring the ceremonial bath-water, and flutes and revelry were provided throughout Boeotia. As these celebrations moved forward, Hera could no longer restrain herself. She descended from Mount Cithairon followed by the women of Plataea; driven by anger and jealousy, she ran to Zeus. But when the deception became clear—the "bride" being merely a wooden statue—she was reconciled with him. With joy and laughter, she herself led the bridal procession. Although she granted honors to the wooden image <note>original: "xoanon" (a primitive wooden cult image)</note> and named the festival "Daedala" after it, she nonetheless burned the statue—even though it was lifeless—out of a lingering sense of jealousy. This, then, is the myth.

» The explanation <note>original: "logos" (here meaning the underlying rational or allegorical meaning)</note> of the myth is as follows: The disagreement and strife between Hera and Zeus is nothing other than a disharmony and disturbance of the elements, occurring when they are no longer balanced with one another in a cosmic order. When irregularity and harshness take over, they break their partnership with great difficulty and work the destruction of the whole universe. If Zeus—that is, the hot and fiery power—becomes the cause of the dispute, drought overtakes the earth. But if the dispute concerns Hera—that is, the moist and airy nature <note>The Stoics often associated Hera (Aer) with the air and Zeus with the fiery ether</note>—and some excess or surplus occurs, a great flood comes, raining down and covering everything.

» Since such a thing occurred in those ancient times, and Boeotia especially was submerged, when the plain first re-emerged and the flood subsided, the restoration of the environment's order was described as the "concord and reconciliation of the gods." The oak was the first of the earth's plants to rise up from the ground, and humans cherished it because it provided a lasting source of food and survival. For the oak bears fruit not only for the "wicked," as Hesiod says, but also for those who survived the destruction: "The top bears acorns, and the middle bears bees." <note>A quote from Hesiod’s "Works and Days," describing a golden age of nature’s bounty</note>

These are the words of Plutarch. We, however, recognize from his quoted words that even this much-admired and secret "natural philosophy" <note>original: "physiologia"</note> of Greek theology contains nothing divine, nor anything great and worthy of God, nor anything worthy of the resurrection. For you have heard that Hera is sometimes called the "Goddess of Marriage," representing the cohabitation of man and woman; and at other times, the earth itself is named Hera; and at other times, she is the moist essence. Dionysus is reduced to drunkenness; Leto to night; and the sun to Apollo. Even Zeus himself is reduced to the hot and fiery power.

Therefore, in addition to the indecency of the myths themselves, even this supposedly more dignified narration and "natural philosophy" did not lead the mind toward any heavenly, intellectual, and divine powers, nor to rational and incorporeal essences. Instead, it sank back down into drunkenness, marriages, and human passions. It collapsed the world into fire, earth, the sun, and the other material elements, deifying nothing more than physical matter.

Even Plato knows this. He certainly admits explicitly in his dialogue *Cratylus* that the first humans in Greece knew nothing more of the gods than the visible parts of the universe. They thought only the lights in the heavens were gods, along with the rest of the visible world. He says, word for word, as follows: "It seems to me that the first..."

# EUSEBIUS

» ...that those men before our time considered these only to be gods—the same ones whom many of the barbarians still worship today: the sun, the moon, the stars, and the heaven. Such are the Greek accounts. But let us also look at the most ancient traditions of these people. For some of the Egyptians say that Osiris is the sun and [Isis] is the moon <note>The text here attributes both to Osiris, but the following Diodorus quote clarifies the pair</note>. They say that the spirit pervading all things is through the air; that fire is called Hephaestus; and that the earth is named Demeter. Among the Egyptians, moisture is thought to be the "Ocean," and they identify the Nile as their own river, to which they also attribute the births of the gods. They say that they address the air as Athena.

These five gods—I mean the air and the water, the fire and the earth, and the spirit—travel throughout the whole inhabited world, at different times taking on different shapes and appearances, assuming the forms of men and all kinds of animals. They say that mortal men were born among these same Egyptians who shared the same names as the gods: being called Sun, Cronus, and Rhea, and also Zeus, Hera, Hephaestus, and Hestia. Manetho <note>An Egyptian priest and historian (3rd century BCE) who wrote a history of Egypt in Greek</note> writes about these matters more extensively, but Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> records them more concisely in his previously mentioned work, writing word-for-word as follows:

->On the Natural Philosophy of the Egyptians<-

" Some say that these are the gods—the sun and the moon—being Osiris and Isis according to the Egyptians, and that they govern the entire universe, nourishing and increasing all things by means of three seasonal periods <note>original: "horais" (seasons)</note> which complete the cycle through invisible motion: the spring, the summer, and the winter. These seasons, although having natures most contrary to one another, complete the year in perfect harmony. They say that these gods contribute the greatest amount of nature toward the <term>zoogonia</term> <note>the generation of living beings</note> of all things: the male [Osiris] contributing the fiery and the spiritual elements, while the female [Isis] contributes the moist and the dry, and both share the air in common. Through these elements, all things are born and nourished. Therefore, the entire body of the nature of the universe is completed by the sun and the moon.

" As for the parts of these, they are the five aforementioned elements: the spirit, the fire, the dry, the moist, and finally the airy. Just as we count the head, hands, feet, and other parts of a human being, they said the body of the world is likewise composed of these aforementioned parts. They considered each of these to be a god, and the first people among the Egyptians to use articulate speech assigned a unique name to each according to its nature. Thus, they addressed the spirit as 'Zeus' <note>original: "Dia"</note>, when the word is translated; since he is the cause of the vital spirit <note>original: "psychikou" (pertaining to the soul or breath of life)</note> in living creatures, they considered him to be the father, as it were, of all things. They say that even the most famous of the Greek poets <note>Homer</note> agrees with this when he says of this god:

" *Father of men and of gods.*

" They named the fire, when translated, 'Hephaestus,' believing him to be a great god who contributes much to the birth and perfect growth of all things. Regarding the earth, as they perceived it to be a kind of vessel for all things that grow, they addressed it as 'Mother'; and the Greeks likewise call her 'Demeter,' the word having been slightly altered over time. For in ancient times she was called <term>Ge Meter</term> <note>Earth Mother</note>, just as Orpheus <note>The legendary mythical poet and musician</note> testifies when he says:

" *Earth, mother of all, Demeter giver of wealth.*

" They say the ancients named the moist element 'Ocean,' which when translated means 'Mother of Nourishment,' though among some of the Greeks it is understood as Ocean..."

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page, where Eusebius quoted Diodorus Siculus. Having discussed the identification of gods with elements like the Nile or the air, he now moves to demonstrate that these "gods" were originally mortal men, citing the historian Plutarch to show they even had human physical descriptions like skin color.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

...to the universal elements, that they were certain mortal men who had lived, and that these were the ones proclaimed
as gods. If this is so, it would be reasonable to say that their shapes and images—those
carvings in lifeless wooden statues—represent either the universal elements, or, as clear
sight demonstrates, those mortals who now lie among the dead? But even if they themselves should stop speaking,
Truth itself cries out and shouts, almost letting out a voice, that the ones being described
were ten thousand mortal men. Indeed, Plutarch, in his surplus of evidence, even
sketches what sort of physical character their bodies had in his writings *On Isis and the 
Egyptian Gods*, saying something like this: "For the Egyptians relate that the one <note>Plutarch likely refers to the bull-god Apis here, though the name is missing in this specific transcription</note> was
copper-colored in body; that Typhon was fiery-red in complexion; Horus was white; and
Osiris was black-skinned, as if they were men who had been born by nature." These are the words of Plutarch.
It is established, then, that their entire process of making gods was based on the dead. Their 
natural philosophy <note>original: "φυσιολογίας" (physiologia) — in this context, it refers to the practice of explaining myths as allegories for natural phenomena</note> is a fiction. Or does it come to this: that from stony and naked figures one should 
fashion life, and first and separately from these, worship the sun and moon and the remaining elements of the world? 
Which of these, then, and from what source were they dependent when they bestowed such 
titles upon them? I mean Hephaestus <note>The god of fire and craftsmanship</note> and
Athena <note>The goddess of wisdom and war</note>, on account of some great power or strength. For is it proper 
that these names, being specific to the elements, were secondly applied to mortals as synonyms for the heavenly 
bodies? Or, conversely, from the invocation of deifying these men, have they made a metaphor 
to apply to the physical substances? And why is it necessary to bestow the names of mortals upon 
universal natures? And what of the mysteries belonging to each god, the hymns and the songs, 
and the secrets of the initiations—do they belong to the universal elements, or to those 
men who died long ago, whose symbols are brought forward under the same names as 
the gods? But indeed, the wanderings, the bouts of drunkenness, the loves, 
the corruption of women, the plots of men, and ten thousand other things truly mortal and 
shameful and undignified—how could anyone attribute these to the universal elements, since the mortal and 
human-suffering mask is obvious? So, from all these things, their 
wonderful and noble natural philosophy is caught, having touched upon no truth, nor 
proclaiming anything divine in a clear way, but possessing an outward appearance of 
solemnity that is forced and deceptive. Hear now what Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher often quoted by Eusebius</note> 
records about these same things in his *Letter to Anebo the Egyptian*.

<meta>The previous page discussed Plutarch’s physical descriptions of Egyptian gods to prove they were originally mortal men. This page continues the argument by quoting a letter (likely from the philosopher Porphyry to Anebo) and Porphyry's work "On Abstinence," further arguing that Egyptian "theology" is merely a worship of physical elements, stars, and animals rather than spiritual truths.</meta>

### PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 3

» ...the daily [sun], or the river [Nile], and generally interpreting everything as physical phenomena, and nothing as
» incorporeal and living essences. Most of these people attached "that which is in our power" <note>original: "τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν" (to eph' hemin) — a philosophical term for free will or moral agency</note> to the
» movement of the stars, binding everything with the unbreakable bonds of necessity, which they call Fate,
» tying all things to these stars as gods. Furthermore, they claim these gods are the only
» releasers of Fate, and they serve no others through their priests, images, and other rituals.

Let these points from the aforementioned letter be established, clearly declaring that even the notorious theology of the Egyptians did not theologize about any others except the stars in the heaven—both the so-called "fixed" stars and those named "planets"—and it identified the Creator <note>original: "δημιουργόν" (demiourgon) — the Demiurge or craftsman of the universe</note> of the whole as not being some incorporeal being, nor a creative Reason <note>original: "λόγον" (logon) — the Logos</note>, nor indeed a God, nor gods, nor any intellectual and invisible powers. Instead, they recognized only the visible sun, and they attributed the cause of the whole to the stars alone, attaching all things to the movement and course of the stars. This is indeed the very opinion that has prevailed among them even until now. 

If, therefore, Egyptian theology is interpreted as referring only to the visible elements of the world, and nothing to incorporeal and living essences; and since the elements and all visible bodies are, by their own nature, soulless and irrational, and established as fluid and perishable; then see into what depths their theology has fallen: it treats soulless things as divine and buries its worship in dead and soulless bodies. This is especially true since they referred nothing to incorporeal and intellectual essences, nor to a Mind <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun) — the divine Intellect</note> and creative Reason of the whole. Since it was previously agreed that Egyptian theology was translated into other languages, it is as if these elements themselves were given languages, yet they continue to theologize in the same way as the Egyptians. They are thus exposed as deifying nothing more than soulless matter. 

These, then, are the "venerable" traditions of the Egyptians, according to the writing of the aforementioned author. This same author, in his work entitled *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, discusses these same matters as follows:

» "Starting from this training and this familiarity with the divine, they recognized that the divine
» did not pass through man alone. Nor did the soul dwell in man alone on earth, but almost the
» same soul passed through all living beings. Therefore, they included every animal in their process of
» making gods, and they mixed together wild beasts and humans, and again the bodies of birds and
» humans. For they have certain images that are human as far as the neck, but possess the face of
» a bird, or a lion, or some other animal. And again, they show a human head with the parts
» of other animals, sometimes placed below and sometimes above. By these, they demonstrate
» that according to the will of the gods, these creatures also share a common nature with one another, and the
» wild beasts of the field are our foster-siblings and are tamed to us, not without some divine purpose.
» Hence the lion is worshipped as a god, and a part of Egypt, which they call a Nome <note>A "Nome" was a territorial administrative division in ancient Egypt</note>, has the name 
» 'Leontopolite' [City of Lions]; another 'Busirite'; and another 'Cynopolite' [City of Dogs]. For they 
» worshipped the power that extends over everything through the related animals which each of the 
» gods provided. They worship water and fire, the most beautiful of elements, as being most responsible 
» for our salvation. And they display these things in the temples, as indeed even now in the opening 
» of the holy Sarapis <note>Sarapis was a Graeco-Egyptian deity whose cult was prominent in Alexandria</note>, 
» the service is performed through fire and water, while the singer pours the water and displays 
» the fire, and standing upon the threshold, awakens the god in the ancestral language of the Egyptians."

These things, then, they worship as participants. And they revered even more than these...

### EUSEBIUS

» ...sharing even more in the sacred rites. All such animals [are worshipped], since they even worship a
» human in the village of Anasis, where one is treated as such, and they burn sacrifices on the altars

-> That these things also were subject to full condemnation. <-

Such are the things set forth by the aforementioned author concerning the physical study of nature by the Egyptian sages, [revealing] to us the secrets of Egyptian <gloss>philosophy</gloss>: that they worship water and fire, and that for them, one essence—both rational and irrational—is mixed, not only of bodies but also of the soul. As a result, it seems to him that wild beasts have been irrationally proclaimed as gods. And how is it not the height of irrationality to take the irrational and beastly nature for the creation of gods? If, as they say, [animals] share an equal soul with humans, then if indeed they were equal to humans, one ought to lead them and share with them human reputation and honor. But those who did not do this named them "irrational beasts" by their very nature, and having received this title, they were not even deemed worthy of human address, nor were they deemed worthy to be received like humans. Yet, taking the supreme title of the "King of All" and of the "God who is the Creator of all things," they have cast it down into the nature of beasts and nicknamed them gods—titles which they did not even deem worthy to give to humans. In these things, you have heard also of the "mystic theosophy," for the sake of which the "admirable" Egyptians worshipped wolves, dogs, and lions. You have also learned the wonder of the beetle and the virtue of the hawk. Do not laugh at the gods hereafter; see the wretched race of men in much folly and blindness. And indeed, look around at everything: what blessings have come to us from Christ our God, the Giver, who has redeemed us from such a disease, and from a long and ancient blindness—and who has redeemed even the souls of the Egyptians through his Gospel teaching, so that most of those in Egypt are now set free from this disease.

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 3, 59

You have seen how the Greeks and Egyptians together established their superstition of many gods. You have learned that among them, nothing was known of the truly divine, nor of those non-physical and intellectual beings. Nevertheless, let us grant and concede to these "star-gazers" <note>original: "μετεωρολέσχαις" (meteōroleschais) — a mocking term for those who talk endlessly about the heavens</note> that they speak the truth, and that they succeed in their "natural science" <note>original: "φυσιολογίᾳ" (physiologia) — in antiquity, this referred to the study of the physical nature of the universe rather than biology</note> through allegories. Let the sun be, for them, sometimes Apollo, and again, let it be the Seasons, or let the sun itself have ten thousand names and be many suns. Let it be the same for the moon, whether she is Isis or Artemis, or whatever else one might wish to list. For let these names not refer to mortal men, but let them be titles and indicators of the heavenly luminaries themselves. 

Should we then worship the sun, the moon, the stars, and the other parts of the cosmos as gods? In this way, the noble philosophy of the Greeks—as if by some theatrical machine—elevates the promise of its argument to a great height, but then brings the mind of the "wise" back down to the perceptible and visible creation of God. It achieves nothing more than focusing on fire and "hot substance," or the parts of the world seen through the heavenly lights. Let it even include the "wet" and the "dry" <note>referring to the classical elements of water and earth</note> and the things that complete the mixture of bodies. 

How, then, is the Gospel of our Savior Jesus Christ not great and wonderful? It instructs all races of men to worship—with the proper understanding—the God and Master of the sun and moon, the Creator of the whole universe, who is himself the highest and beyond all things. It teaches us to praise not the elements of physical bodies, but the Steward of life itself and the provider of all good things. It teaches us never to be struck with awe by the visible parts of the world, nor by anything that can be grasped by the senses of the flesh—as these are of a perishable nature. Instead, we should marvel only at the invisible Mind <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun)</note> within all these things, the great and universal Creator. We should recognize as divine not only the power that permeates and organizes everything—being a certain non-physical and intellectual nature—but something even more inexpressible and incomprehensible. This power moves through the visible world in a non-physical way, interacting with all things without becoming entangled by them, showing the enduring greatness of its divinity not only in the heavens, but also upon the earth, both in the elements as a whole and in their individual parts. This power presides over all things invisibly and beyond our perception, governing the entire cosmos with the unutterable logic of wisdom.

Since we have demonstrated so many things to expose this inconsistent "wisdom" or "theology"—both the so-called "mythical" kind and the "higher" natural kind, which the ancient Greeks and Egyptians were shown to pride themselves on—it is now time to look at the embellishments of the "moderns" who claim to be philosophers. For these men have attempted to weave the theology of the ancients together with the ideas of Plato's circle—discovered much later—concerning the Creative Mind of the universe, non-physical forms, and intellectual and rational powers. Having devised these through sound reasoning, they have elevated the promise of these myths with even greater arrogance. Listen to the sort of "natural science" they have produced, and with what "purple" <note>a pun on the name of the philosopher Porphyry and the royal color "purple," implying his pompous or arrogant style</note> arrogance it has been delivered.

->The types of explanations that the more recent philosophers have woven into the myths about the gods.<-

# EUSEBIUS

"...participating more in sacred things. Such are all the animals, since they even worship a human being in the village of Aneisis <note>A village in Egypt, sometimes associated with the city of Heracleopolis</note>, where such a thing takes place; he burns the offerings upon the altars, and a little later he might eat his own portions, as if they had not yet been consecrated. Just as one must abstain from eating humans, so too should one abstain from animals. Furthermore, from this same wisdom and piety toward the divine, they grasped that certain animals are more beloved to the gods than humans are—such as the hawk is to the Sun—and that they all possess a nature of blood and breath. They do not think of it as merely human, and they even weep over a dead animal." After some mocking remarks, he says a little later: "A beetle <note>original: "Κάνθαρον" (kantharon) — the dung beetle or scarab, sacred to the sun-god Khepri</note> might be loathed by someone ignorant of divine matters; but the Egyptians worshipped it as a living image of the Sun. For every beetle is male, and discharging its seed in marshes, and having made it into a sphere, it rolls it backward with its hind feet, just as the sun moves the heavens, following a cycle of days—an image also of the moon." Likewise, they philosophize about the ram, and he explains things concerning crocodiles. Again, he speaks of the vulture and the ibis, and generally how they arrived at the worship of each animal through a kind of prudence and excessive "divine wisdom" <note>original: "θεοσοφίας" (theosophias)</note>.

->Were these things not full of every reason for condemnation?<-

Such are the details concerning the "naked natural science" <note>original: "φυσιολογίας" (physiologias) — here referring to the physical explanation of myths</note> of the wise Egyptians set forth by the aforementioned author <note>Porphyry, the Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, who has revealed to us the Egyptian secrets: that they worship water and fire, and that among them a single rational and irrational essence is mixed, not only of bodies but of the soul, so that they irrationally think the beasts should be proclaimed as gods. And how is it not the height of irrationality to admit the irrational and beastly nature into "god-making" <note>original: "θεοποιΐαν" (theopoiian) — the process of deifying something</note>, on the grounds that it shares—as they say—an equal soul with humans? For if indeed it were equal to humans, they ought to have regarded the animals as leaders and shared with them human reputation and honor. 

But those who did not do this instead treated the naturally irrational beasts as heroes, bestowing this title upon them without even deeming them worthy of the name "human." They did not think it right to give them human status, yet they brought down the highest title of the King of All—the name of the God who is the Creator of all things—and cast it upon the nature of beasts, calling them gods. These are creatures that have not even been granted the human title by God. In these matters, you have heard the "divine wisdom" of the mystery, for which the "admirable" Egyptians worshipped wolves, dogs, and lions. You have learned of the "wonder" of the beetle and the "virtue" of the hawk. Do not laugh at these gods hereafter. Rather, pity the wretched race of men for such great senselessness and blindness. And indeed, look around at everything and see what kind of blessings Christ our God, the Giver of good, has provided for us, redeeming the souls of the Egyptians through His Gospel teaching from such a disease—a long and ancient blindness—so that the majority of those in Egypt are now set free from this sickness.

->Therefore, it was not without reason that we withdrew from their "physical" theory about the gods, preferring instead the only true theology.<-

## PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOKS 3 & 4

...of the sun, and likewise of the ancient Egyptians who established this polytheistic superstition. Among them, as you have learned, nothing was recognized of the truly divine—that is, an incorporeal and intellectual essence <note>original: "ἀσωμάτῳ τε καὶ νοερᾷ οὐσίᾳ" (asōmatō te kai noera ousia) — the idea of a god without a physical body who exists as pure mind</note>. Nevertheless, let it be granted and conceded to these **chatterers about the heavens** <note>original: "μετεωρολέσχαις" (meteoroleschais) — a derisive term for those who speculate idly about celestial phenomena</note> that they speak the truth regarding the results found in their "natural science" <term>Physiologia: here meaning the allegorical interpretation of nature as a divine system</term> of allegories. For them, let the sun be at one time Apollo, and again Horus or Osiris, and then again the sun itself or whatever else they might wish. So too with the moon: let it be Isis or Artemis, or whatever names one might wish to enumerate. For let these names not refer to mortal men, but let them be titles signifying the heavenly luminaries themselves. 

It follows, then, that the sun, the moon, the stars, and the remaining parts of the world must be worshipped as gods. In this way, the noble philosophy of the Greeks—as if by a theatrical machine <note>A "mechane" was a crane used in Greek theater to lower gods onto the stage; Eusebius suggests their philosophy uses a trick to appear profound</note>—naturally raises the promise of its argument to a great height; yet it turns back downward, revolving around the perceptible and visible creation of God. It treats the intellect of the "wise" as nothing more than fire and hot essence, or the parts of the world seen through the heavenly luminaries. Let it also be the "wet" and the "dry" essences, warming the whole mixture of the universe. 

How, then, is it not a great and wondrous thing that the Gospel of our Savior Jesus Christ is proclaimed? It teaches every race of men to worship the God and Master of the sun and moon, the Creator of the entire universe—the one who is supreme and beyond all things—with the appropriate thoughts of piety. It teaches us to hymn not the elements made of bodies, but the very Giver of Life, the Wise One, and the Steward of all good things. We are taught not to be struck with awe by the visible parts of the world or anything grasped by the senses of the flesh—as these are of a perishable nature—but to wonder only at the invisible Mind within them all, the Creator of the whole and of every part. We are to speak of God not merely as one who pervades and arranges all things by divine power—an incorporeal essence and an intellectual nature—but rather, to speak of Him inexpressibly. He is incomprehensible through all things, yet He acts through what is visible, pervading all things incorporeally and moving through all without becoming entangled in them. This lasting majesty of the Godhead is displayed not only through the riches of the heavens, but also through the things upon the earth, both the universal elements and the individual parts. It presides over all things invisibly and imperceptibly to us, governing the entire world by the unutterable principles of wisdom. 

Since so much has been demonstrated by us to refute this inconsistent wisdom or "theology"—both the so-called "mythical" kind and the "higher" or "natural" kind, which the ancient Greeks and Egyptians were shown to take pride in—it is now time to look upon the "ornaments" of the more recent thinkers who claim to philosophize among us today. For these men know the teachings regarding the Creator Mind of all things, and those concerning incorporeal "ideas" <note>Platonic "Forms" or archetypes</note> and intellectual and rational powers—concepts discovered long afterward by the followers of **Plato** and conceived through correct reasoning. Attempting to weave these ideas into the theology of the ancients, they have sought to elevate the promise of their myths with even greater vanity. 

Listen, then, to their "natural science" and the manner in which it has been brought forth by the arrogance of **Porphyry**.

## PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 3

By showing these things, men who depicted invisible things through visible forms have indicated both God and the powers of God through images akin to our senses. To those who have learned to read the statues like the letters in a book, this provides a reading of the matters concerning the gods. There is nothing wonderful in the fact that the most ignorant people consider these cult images <term>Xoana: ancient, often wooden, cult images believed to have fallen from heaven or been made by legendary figures</term> to be merely wood and stone. In the same way, those who are mindless regarding letters see monuments as mere stones, and tablets as mere wood, or books as nothing but woven papyrus. Having boasted such things in his introduction, listen to what he <note>Eusebius is referring to the philosopher Porphyry</note> writes next, word for word:

> Since the divine is of the nature of light, and is established in the surrounding area of ethereal fire, and happens to be invisible to the senses preoccupied with mortal life, he <note>the worshipper/craftsman</note> leads the mind toward the concept of this light through translucent matter—such as crystal, or Parian marble, or even ivory. Through gold, he leads the mind to the thought of fire, and to its purity, because gold does not tarnish. Many, again, have indicated the invisibility of His essence by using a black stone. They have depicted the gods in human form because the divine is rational; and beautiful, because beauty in them is uncorrupted. They use different shapes and ages, sittings, stances, and garments—some male, some female, some virgins, some youths, or those who have experienced marriage—to represent their various differences. Hence they assigned everything white to the celestial gods. They assigned the sphere and all spherical things specifically to the universe, the sun, and the moon, and sometimes even to Fortune and Hope. They assigned the circle to eternity <note>original: "αἰῶνι" (aiōni) — meaning an age, eternity, or a specific divine being representing time</note>, to the motion of heaven, and to the zones and circles within it. They used segments of circles for the phases of the moon; pyramids and obelisks for the essence of fire, and for this reason also for the Olympian gods; just as they used the cone for the sun, and the cylinder for the earth. For sowing and generation, they used phalluses <note>original: "φάλητα" (phalēta)</note> and the triangular shape, because of the female part.

These are the words of that "admirable" philosopher. What could be more unseemly than this? They speak solemnly of shameful things! What if one were to forcefully claim that soulless materials—gold and stones and such—could bear images of the light of the gods and serve as indicators of the heavenly and ethereal nature? You can see that these clever arguments are modern inventions, which never even entered the dreams of the ancients, by learning that the ancients actually rejected cult images made of gold or the materials now considered more precious. Plutarch speaks on this somewhere, word for word:

### On the ancient construction and dedication of statues.

The making of cult images <term>Xoana</term> seems to be something ancient and of old, if indeed the wooden image of Apollo was brought by Erysichthon to Delos for the sacred embassies, and the wooden image of Athena Polias <note>Athena "of the City," the ancient wooden protector of Athens</note> was established by the "autochthones" <note>the "original" people born from the earth itself</note>, which the Athenians preserve to this day. The people of Samos also had a wooden form of Hera, as Callimachus says:

> “Not yet was it the work of Skelmis <note>a legendary sculptor</note>, but by ancient law, a piece of uncarved wood was the goddess whom Samos ruled. For thus they used to establish the gods.”

Thus also Pelops dedicated a stone seat to Danaus in Lindos. And Peiras, who first established the temple of Hera in Argolis, having appointed his own daughter Kallithyia as priestess, cut a trunk from the wild pear trees around Tiryns to fashion an image of Hera. For they did not want a stone for the god’s form, because they thought such an image was hard, difficult to work, and soulless. They considered gold and silver to be the "sickly colors" of a barren and corrupted earth, and stains that break out like bruises caused by

## From the Allegorized Theology of the Greeks and Egyptians.

Those who investigate the wisdom of the Greeks in this way consider Zeus to be the Mind <note>original: νοῦς (nous)</note> of the world, who created all things within it, possessing the world as his soul. In this theology concerning him, those following Orpheus said:

> „ Zeus was first, Zeus of the bright lightning is last,
> „ Zeus is the head, Zeus is the middle, from Zeus all things are made.
> „ Zeus became male, Zeus became an immortal nymph.
> „ Zeus is the foundation of the earth and the starry heaven.
> „ Zeus is king, Zeus himself is the original progenitor of all.
> „ One power, one divine spirit <note>original: δαίμων (daimon)</note> exists, the great ruler of all.
> „ One royal body, in which all these things revolve:
> „ Fire and water, and earth, and ether, night and day,
> „ And Wisdom <note>original: μῆτις (metis)</note>, the first creator, and delightful Love.
> „ For all these things lie within the great body of Zeus.
> „ His head and beautiful face are the bright Sky, 
> „ Around which his golden hair, the sparkling stars, hang beautifully.
> „ Two golden bull's horns rise on either side:
> „ The East and the West, the paths of the heavenly gods.
> „ His eyes are the Sun and the reflecting Moon.
> „ His mind is the unerring, royal, immortal Ether,
> „ By which he hears and considers all things; and there is no sound,
> „ No cry, nor noise, nor voice,
> „ That escapes the ears of Zeus, the almighty son of Kronos.
> „ In this way he has an immortal head and thought.
> „ His body is vast, boundless, unshakable,
> „ Strong and mighty-limbed, fashioned thus:
> „ The shoulders, chest, and broad back of the god
> „ Are the wide-stretching Air; wings grew upon him,
> „ By which he flies over all things. His holy belly
> „ Is the Earth, mother of all, and the high peaks of the mountains.
> „ His waist is the swelling of the deep-sounding sea
> „ And the ocean; his feet are the lowest roots of the earth,
> „ The misty Tartarus <note>the deep abyss used as a dungeon for the Titans</note>, and the furthest ends of the world.
> „ Having hidden all things, he brings them back again into the joyful light,
> „ Planning to bring forth many-staged wonders from his heart.

Zeus, therefore, is the whole world, a living being made of living beings, and a god made of gods. Zeus, insofar as he is Mind, is the source from which he brings forth all things and creates them through his thoughts. When those who explained the matters of this god in a theological way wished to create an image, they did so in the manner that the discourse indicated—as far as was possible. Just as someone might represent the vital, intellectual, and providential power through a sphere, they have made the image of Zeus in human form because he is Mind and the one according to whom he created, completing all things with "seminal reasons" <term>Logoi spermatikoi: the Stoic and Neoplatonic concept of rational "seeds" or formative principles that organize matter</term>. He is shown seated to symbolize the stability of his power. His upper parts are naked, because he is manifest in the intellectual and heavenly parts of the world; but his lower parts are covered, because he is hidden from those below.

» ...hidden below. He holds the scepter in his left hand, because that side, near the shoulder, is where the governing and intellectual power <note>original: ἡγεμονικώτατόν τε καὶ νοερώτατον; referring to the Stoic concept of the "commanding faculty" of the soul</note> resides; for that is where the heart is located. For he is the king of the world, the creator mind <term>Demiurgos Nous: the intellectual craftsman who shapes the universe</term>. In his right hand, he holds out either an eagle—signifying that he rules over the gods who travel through the air, just as the eagle rules over high-flying birds—or a Victory, because he himself has conquered all things.

These are the words of Porphyry. Now that we have provided the passage mentioned, it is good to consider calmly and at leisure who exactly they claim Zeus to be. Based on the verses, I believe he is nothing other than the visible world <note>original: κόσμον (kosmon)</note>, composed of all various parts: those in the heavens and the ether <term>Aither: the pure, upper air or "fifth element" where the stars reside</term>, and the stars that appear within them, which are set in the front like the head of a great body; and the things in the air, the earth, the sea, and similar regions. Indeed, the parts of the world are the earth, the mountains, and the hills. The sea has been placed in the middle of these, like a belt. Fire, water, night, and day would also be parts of the same nature of the world.

We believe these things clearly point to the visible world. Indeed, the text teaches quite strongly that the whole is composed of these parts. It says:

» "And the Earth lies here in this great living body."

And so that all things are clearly defined:

» "Fire, water, earth, and ether, night and day."

And in the head, we may see:

» "Beautiful faces, the radiant Heaven, around which the golden hair
» "Of the shimmering stars hangs beautifully."

And other things following these. In these lines, the author implies that Zeus is the intellectual ether. To such people, God is nothing more than a fiery and warm substance which they claim is the governing part of the world. For them, God is a body <note>a physical entity</note>, and the Creator himself is not distinct from the power of fire. I believe the same is said in the verses:

» "The kingly Mind that speaks no lies is the imperishable ether,
» "By which he encircles and perceives all things."

Through these words, the author openly assumes the world is a "great living being" and calls it Zeus; he defines the ether as its mind and declares the remaining parts of the world to be its body. Such is the Zeus described through these verses. But the interpreter of the verses <note>Porphyry</note>, starting from the poems, says accordingly:

» "Zeus, therefore, is the whole world, a living being made of living beings, a god made of gods."

Thus, he clearly interpreted the Zeus of their theology to be nothing other than the visible and sensible world. This is the teaching of the Egyptians, from whom Orpheus received his theology, saying that God is a single world made up of many various parts. This is because it was demonstrated previously that they divinize the parts of the world as they consist together. The quoted words of the verses make this and nothing more clear.

However, after this first interpretation, the author devises a second one based on it, suggesting we should understand God as the maker of all things, the Creator. He claims this is the one described in theology. But how could they have divinized him in this way, when the author of the verses did not even know him in the first place? Whether it was Orpheus or someone else, if the theological traditions concerning him came from the Egyptians or the early Greeks, it has been shown that they understood nothing intellectual or incorporeal <note>non-physical</note>.

Indeed, such a being is not contained in a hidden or bodiless essence. This is why Plato is worthy of belief when he admits in the *Cratylus* that the first men in Greece considered only those to be gods whom many of the barbarians still do today: the sun, the moon, the earth, the stars, and the heaven. Even Chaeremon <note>a Stoic philosopher and Egyptian priest</note>, a short while ago, testified that the Egyptians considered nothing else to be God except the visible world...

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 3
f.ii.

...gods, except for the planets and the other stars. And they interpret everything into the visible parts of the world, and nothing into incorporeal and living essences.

---

->Refutation of the forced interpretation derived from these descriptions.<-

**T**he poet who is perceived through these descriptions—from where, or how, or from whom did he receive in his verses the idea of a God beyond the world, the creator <term>Demiurgos: a craftsman-creator who shapes the universe</term> of the sun and moon, the stars, heaven itself, and the entire universe? From where did the knowledge of an incorporeal being come to him? But you happen to know nothing of these things, for the creative mind that produced the whole could not be composed of many parts. Heaven could not be its head, nor could fire, water, and earth be its body; neither would the sun and moon be its eyes. How could the fiery air, the earth, and the steep peaks of mountains be the shoulders, chest, back, and belly of the God who is the creator of all things? Or how could the ether <note>original: αἰθὴρ; the "fifth element" or pure upper air</note> ever be conceived of as the mind of the creator of the whole, or as the creative intellect? 

For all these things have been cleverly devised by the interpreter of the verses; one should add nothing to them. I, however, claim it is the height of impiety to say that the parts of the world are the parts of God. And even more so to declare that the world itself is God. Furthermore, it is impious to believe that the mind of the world is the creator of the whole. For it is a pious act to declare Him the poet and savior of the world, being distinct from that which was made; but to say that He is merely the mind of the world—like the soul of some living animal—wrapped in many things, would no longer be holy. 

Yet our sacred oracles <note>A common term Eusebius uses for the Bible</note> teach us that He is present to the creator and present to the world, theologizing in a way that is worthy of God and fitting for the divine. Through these, He says: 
<margin>,,</margin> “Do I not fill heaven and the earth? says the Lord.” 
<margin>,,</margin> And again: “Is not God in heaven above, and on the earth 
<margin>,,</margin> below?” And again: “For in Him we move, and live, and exist.” <note>Quotes from Jeremiah 23:24, Deuteronomy 4:39, and Acts 17:28</note> 
But He is not in them as a part of the world, nor as a mind within its soul. But if one must use a more god-befitting and truer example, the sacred word has appropriately proclaimed: “Heaven is my throne,” He said, “and the earth is my footstool.” 

For if one must use human language to describe divine things, the various aspects of theology are clear. For the one who called heaven a “throne” defined the Great King, God, as being beyond the throne and highest of all, yet without separating the earth from His presence; for he teaches that His providential powers incline even toward the things of this world. This is why He says: “And the earth is my footstool.” But neither the footstool nor the throne are the body of the one sitting upon them, nor could they ever be called his parts. 

But the one who claimed heaven is the head of God (and the things within it), and that the ether is His mind, and that the remaining parts of the world are His parts and body—this person does not truly know a creator or a God. For God would not create Himself, nor could He still be called “Mind.” The ether does not “think” in any way. And what kind of God would he be whose parts are the earth and the mountains beneath the earth—mere irrational masses of matter? How is it even reasonable to proclaim a God who is the brother and kinsman of fire, air, and water—the offspring of irrational and perishable matter? For even if the “Mind of Zeus” is nothing other than the aforementioned ether, ether is simply the highest and most fiery air—taking its name from *aithein*, which means “to burn” or “to kindle,” as they say. Both are bodies: both the air and the ether. Look at where your God has gone...

<summary>Eusebius critiques the pagan view that the physical universe is the body of God, arguing instead that God is a separate, incorporeal creator who transcends his creation as a king transcends his throne.</summary>

# EUSEBIUS

> ...hidden below. In his left hand he holds the scepter, near that part of the body where the heart—the most commanding and intellectual organ—dwells. For the Mind that fashions the world is King. In his right hand he extends the eagle, because he rules over the gods who traverse the air, just as the eagle rules the soaring birds. He holds Victory <note>Nike</note> because he himself has conquered all things.

This is what Porphyry tells you. Having presented the aforementioned opinion, it is good to examine it quietly and at leisure, to see who this "Zeus" mentioned in the verses actually is. For my part, I believe he is nothing other than the visible world <term>Cosmos: the universe understood as an ordered, physical system</term>, composed of all sorts of parts: those in heaven and the ether, and the stars appearing in them, arranged like the head of a great body; and those in the air, earth, sea, and similar regions. Certainly, the parts of the world include the earth, mountains, and hills. For they are within the zones, as is the sea. And fire and water, night and day, would be parts of the same nature of the world. I believe these things clearly represent the visible world. Unless I am mistaken, the poet teaches that the whole is composed of these parts. He says, at any rate:

> For these things lie here in the great body of Zeus.

And so that all things are Zeus: 

> His eyes are Fire, water, and earth, and ether, night and day. To see his head and beautiful face is the radiant Heaven, around which the golden hairs of the shimmering Stars hang most beautifully.

And so on with the lines following these. In them, he introduces the "mind" of Zeus, saying it is the ether. According to the poets, this is nothing other than a fiery and hot substance, which they claim is the commanding part <note>original: ἡγεμονικὸν (hegemonikon); in Stoic philosophy, the "ruling part" of the soul or world-soul</note> of the world. Thus, they claim God is a body, and that the Creator himself is not distinct from the power of fire. I believe the same things are also said in these verses:

> Royal unerring Mind, immortal Ether, by which he circles and considers all things.

Through these lines, he openly assumes the world is a "great living being" <note>original: ζῶον (zoon); a term implying the universe itself is an animal with a soul</note>, and having called this "Zeus," he declared that its mind is the ether, while its body consists of the remaining parts of the world. Now, the Zeus described through the verses is the one found in the poems <note>specifically the Orphic hymns</note>. But the interpreter of the verses, beginning with the poems, consistently says: "Zeus, then, is the whole world, a living being made of living beings, a god..."

> ...made of gods.

He clearly shows that the Zeus of their theology is nothing other than the visible and sensible world. This is also evident in the interpretations. This was the doctrine of the Egyptians, from whom Orpheus <note>The mythical poet to whom these hymns were traditionally attributed</note> received his theology and came to believe the world was God, composed of many gods who are its parts. For it was shown previously that by treating the constituent parts of the world as gods, they constructed their theology. The quoted verses make this no clearer than that. 

But after this first interpretation, the author adds a second of his own, suggesting we should understand the Maker of all things—the Creator <term>Demiurge: a craftsman-god</term>—as this theological figure. But how could he have described Him as such, when the poet of the verses did not even know Him from the beginning? Whether the poet was Orpheus the Thracian or someone else. If it came from the Egyptians, or even those who lived a thousand and twenty years before him, they were shown to have no understanding of anything purely intellectual, nor anything contained in an invisible and incorporeal essence. 

Plato is a sufficient witness of this, admitting in the *Cratylus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the origins of names and language</note> that the first men in Greece believed only those to be gods whom many barbarians still worship today: the sun, moon, earth, stars, and heaven. And Chaeremon <note>A Stoic philosopher and Egyptian priest</note>, as was testified a little earlier, stated that the Egyptians believe in no other god than the visible world. It is clear...

gods, and more of the planets than of the other stars. All these things they interpret as referring to the visible parts of the world, and nothing as referring to immaterial and living essences.

### Refutation of the forced interpretation based on these claims.

From where, then, or how, or from whom did this poet—who is seen here—receive the idea in his verses of a God "beyond the world," yet then list the sun, the moon, the stars, heaven itself, and the creator of the whole world as part of him? From where did he get the knowledge of an immaterial being? In truth, he happens to know nothing of these things. For the creative Mind <term>Nous: the divine intellect or reason</term> of the universe is not composed of many parts, nor would heaven grow upon him as a head, nor fire, water, and earth as a body. Nor indeed would the sun and moon be his eyes. How could the "mighty air," the earth, and the "steep peaks of the mountains" be the shoulders, chest, back, and belly of the God who is the creator <term>demiurge: the craftsman or maker of the world</term> of all things? Or how could the ether <note>original: "αἰθήρ"</note> ever be conceived of as the creative power of the whole, or as the creative Mind? 

When an interpreter has devised these clever sophistries through verses, it is unnecessary to add anything further; for my part, I say it is the height of impiety to claim that the parts of the world are the parts of God. It is even more so for one to declare that God is the same as the world. At times, these people say the Mind that governs the world is the creator of all. Now, it is a pious thing to declare him the creator and savior of the world, being something different from what he has made. But it is not holy to think that the world is like the soul of some living animal, or that the "all" is his clothing. To say that the winds are his breath, or like the "tail of the world," is utterly wicked. For our sacred oracles <note>referring to the Hebrew Scriptures</note> speak of God in a way that is worthy and fitting of His divinity. 

<margin>»</margin> Through these, He says: "Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord." <note>Jeremiah 23:24</note> 
<margin>»</margin> And again: "Is not God in heaven above, and upon the earth below?" <note>cf. Deuteronomy 4:39 or Joshua 2:11</note> 
<margin>»</margin> And again: "For in Him we move, and live, and have our being." <note>Acts 17:28</note> 

He is in them not as a part of the world, nor as the Mind is in a soul. But if one must use a more god-befitting and truer example, the sacred word has appropriately cried out: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet." <note>Isaiah 66:1</note> If it were necessary at all to use personification <term>prosopopeia: a rhetorical device where an abstract thing is given a human face or voice</term> in a more sensory way, this view is indifferent to theology <note>meaning it does not harm the true concept of God</note>. For he who called heaven a "throne" set apart the Great King, God, as being beyond the throne and highest of all things, yet without separating his tongue from his providence. For he teaches that the providential powers of his divinity descend even to the things here below. 

This is why he says: "And the earth is the footstool of my feet." But neither the footstool nor the throne is the body of the one sitting upon it, nor could they ever be called parts of him. But he who said that heaven is the "head of God" and described the things within it—calling the ether his "mind" and the other parts of the world his "limbs and body"—is caught knowing neither a creator nor a God. For God would not be his own creator, nor could he still be called "Mind" if the ether is what is meant by that mind. And what kind of God would he be whose parts—the earth and the mountains upon the earth—are merely irrational masses of matter? How is it reasonable to proclaim him as God when he is a brother and kinsman of fire, air, and water, the offspring of irrational and perishable matter? And even if the "Mind" is assigned to the "divine" <note>original: "τῷ δίῳ" - referring to Zeus</note>, it would be nothing more than the aforementioned vapors of the ether. For "ether" is the highest and most fiery air, having received this name, as they say, from the word "to burn" <note>original: "αἴθειν," which means to kindle or burn</note>. Both air and ether are bodies; however much of the divine you...

# EUSEBIUS

> "...mind has fallen away. And who could exist before these man-slaying gods, this one in whom you imagine [the mind] resided, homeless and irrational? If indeed such is the nature of every body, it seems to us that in matters of theology, we must assume the exact opposite of everything just mentioned. He is not the heaven, nor the ether, nor the sun, nor the moon, nor the whole choir of the stars, nor even the entire atmosphere of the world. These are but the works of His hands, small and brief, or else assigned to mortal and intellectual powers. For every body is corruptible and irrational, and such is the nature of things seen. But the things beyond, which are invisibly rational and immortal, contending alongside the blessed life of God the King of All, would be far better than all things seen. Reasonably, then, the divine oracles <note>A common term for the Holy Scriptures.</note> teach us about the visible parts of the world in this way: <term>I will behold the heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars which you established.</term> <note>original: Psalm 8:3</note> And again: <term>You, Lord, in the beginning established the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.</term> <note>original: Psalm 102:25</note> And once more: <term>Look up on high with your eyes, and see who revealed all these things.</term> <note>original: Isaiah 40:26</note> Let these things be said regarding the first interpretation of the verses. But come, let us also examine what follows. 
> 
> Since it was not possible, he says, to create such an image as Reason revealed, for this reason they have made the <term>image</term> <note>original: "δείκηλον" (deikelon) – a representation or cult image.</note> human-shaped in its form. This is because you conceive of the one according to whom He created, and through "seminal reasons" <note>A Stoic term for the creative principles that organize matter.</note> He completed all things. And how was it not possible to make such an image as Reason revealed? For Reason revealed the parts of the visible and seen world: heaven, and the things in heaven, the air, and the earth, and the things in them. If, therefore, it was not possible to construct an image of the visible parts of the world, in the way that God conceives of them, how could one create an image of God Himself? Or do you have a human body that resembles the mind of God? 
> 
> For my part, I do not think it even resembles a human mind; for the mind is incorporeal, uncomposed, and without parts. But this [statue], the work of men’s hands, has been imitated from a mortal body, and a deaf and speechless image has been sketched out of living flesh in soulless and dead matter. Now, the rational and immortal soul—which is the impassive mind in the nature of man—is that according to which it is said to preserve the "image and likeness" of God, insofar as it is immaterial and incorporeal, intellectual and rational; it is not even "composed," being receptive to virtue and wisdom. If anyone were able to craft a statue and form of the soul in an image, he might also be able to do so for the greater powers. But if the human mind is formless, invisible, and without shape—neither visible to the eye nor graspable in its essence by speech or hearing—who could imitate it so much as to declare that a man-like <term>wooden image</term> <note>original: "ξόανον" (xoanon) – an archaic wooden cult statue believed to have fallen from heaven.</note> bears the form and image of the highest God? 
> 
> The nature of God is envisioned far beyond all mortal matter, perceived by a clear mind and in silence by purified souls. But that which is in the visible form of Zeus—that "image"—would be an image of the nature of a mortal man. And not even of a whole man, but an imitation of his worse part, because it carries no trace of life or soul. How then could the God over all, the Mind which is the creator <term>demiurgic: from 'demiurge,' the craftsman of the universe</term> of all things, be the same as the "Zas" <note>original: "Ζάς" – an alternative name for Zeus used in ancient theological poetry.</note> living in bronze or dead ivory? And how, indeed, could the creative Mind of the universe ever be that very Zas, the father of Heracles by Alcmene? And the rest of the men mythologized as coming from Zeus, who ended their lives as all men do, by the law of their own nature...

He critiques the use of human-shaped statues to represent the divine, noting that even the human soul is too formless to be captured in stone or wood.</summary>

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 3

> "...they have left memorials to those who came after them. The first theologians of the Phoenicians, as I indicated in my first book, recorded that Zeus was the son of Cronus, a mortal born from a mortal, and a Phoenician by race. The Egyptians, claiming the man as their own, likewise admitted he was a mortal—even though they speak the same language as the Phoenicians on this point. Furthermore, the Cretans, by pointing out the tomb of Zeus in their own land, would be third witnesses to the same fact. The Atalantians, and all those who have been mentioned regarding this subject, claim Zeus according to their own local history, and all alike declared him to be mortal. They recorded his actions as mortal and human—and not particularly holy ones at that—but rather full of every kind of obscenity and licentiousness. 
> 
> But for those who claim that a 'holier' meaning is appropriate for these myths, at one moment Zeus is a kind of 'heat' or 'fiery power'; at another, he is 'spirit' <note>The Greek 'pneuma' can mean spirit, breath, or wind.</note>. Now, somehow, the 'creative mind' <term>demiurgic nous</term> of the universe has been revealed to them in him. We must ask them, therefore: who would they say is his father, if indeed a father existed before him? For according to all the theologians, Zeus is acknowledged to be the son of Cronus. Having read through the verses of Orpheus set before us, he mentioned that Zeus was the son of Cronus, and Cronus the son of Uranus <note>Uranus represents the Heavens.</note>. It is granted by them, then, that Zeus is the 'God over all' and the 'Mind that created all things.' Who then is his father? Cronus. And who is the grandfather? Uranus. 
> 
> If Zeus is truly the first as the creator of all, he should surely be listed first, followed by those made by him. For if Cronus is 'Time' <term>Chronos</term>, born of Uranus, because time came into existence along with the heavens; and if Cronus's father is Uranus himself, with Time following after him—well, regarding these things, God is the cause of the whole, the creator of both heaven and time. If this is true, Zeus could not be a son born from Uranus. How then is he mythologized by all the Egyptians, Phoenicians, Greeks, and philosophers as the son of Uranus, this 'creative mind' of the universe? The fictions of the philosopher have been caught, and they will be caught even more." 
> 
> After these points, he adds the following:

> "Regarding Hera, they have made her a kind of life-giver, calling the ethereal and aerial power 'Hera.' For ether is the most refined form of air. Earlier, the verses showed that the ether was the 'Mind of Zeus.' But now the argument disputes what ether actually is, saying it is the most refined air. But air is a body <note>By 'body,' the author means physical matter.</note>, and ether even more so. Therefore, the 'Mind of Zeus' is admitted to be a physical body, even if it is the most refined of all. And how could body and mind be thought of as the same thing, since they are so vastly different in their natures? Then, I know not how he could have forgotten the verses that explicitly state:
>
