> *Nor sound, nor any noise, nor any rumor...*
> 
> But then he says again that Hera is the ethereal and aerial power. Then, making a distinction, he adds: 'And the power of all the air is called Hera, named after the air <term>aer</term>.' But the symbol of the air below the moon, which is lit and shaded, is Leto. For they say she is Leto because of the lack of sensation during sleep <note>A wordplay linking 'Leto' to 'Lethe' (forgetfulness).</note>, or because souls..."

# EUSEBIUS

» ...to those born of the moon, she symbolizes "oblivion" <note>original: "lethe," a pun on the name Leto</note> for the sun. And for this reason, she is also the mother of Apollo and Artemis, who are the causes of light during the night. Among these figures, he <note>Porphyry</note> says that the air beneath the moon is the mother of the sun and moon; for this air, he claims, is Leto. Yet how could the air become the mother of the causes of light, when it is itself more a product of their action than a creator? For it is evident that the sun and moon clearly transform the air. But proceeding further, he says:

» "And the ruling power of the earthly force is called **Hestia** <note>Goddess of the hearth and home</note>. Her statue is a female figure established upon a hearth of fire. Insofar as she represents a fertile power, they signify her with the form of a woman with breasts. They called **Rhea** the power of the rocky and mountainous earth, and **Demeter** the power of the flat and fertile earth. Demeter is either the same as Rhea or holds the same qualities as Rhea. They differ only in that Demeter is said to conceive by the 'Lord from Zeus'—that is, she produces the 'fullness' <term>koron</term> <note>A pun on 'Kore,' the name of Demeter’s daughter, and 'koros,' meaning satiety or the abundance of the harvest.</note> from the stalky seeds. This is why her cult image is fashioned with ears of grain, and poppies are placed around her as a symbol of high fertility."

» And here again, consider whom they called Rhea, the so-called 'mother of the gods'; they have cast her down as if she were the mountain itself, or something to do with rocks and grass. He says she is the same as Demeter in all respects, except for the distinction that Demeter is said to conceive the 'fullness' <term>koron</term> from Zeus. Just as the plains produce 'fullness' from the stalky seeds, you see how Zeus has once again been transformed into the 'stalky seeds.' He joins to these points the following:

» "Since there is also a specific power belonging to the seeds cast into the earth, which the sun draws up as it travels through the lower hemisphere during the winter solstice, **Kore** <note>The Maiden, also known as Persephone</note> is that seminal power. **Pluto** is the sun traveling beneath the earth, wandering through the invisible world and the winter solstice. He is said to 'snatch' Kore, whom Demeter longs for while she is hidden beneath the earth. The power of fruit-bearing trees, and generally of all leaf-covered plants, is named **Dionysus**. 

» Look also at the images of these gods. For Kore bears symbols of the sprouting of fruits that break forth from beneath the earth. Dionysus has horns in common with the 'fullness' <term>koros</term>, but he is 'female-formed' <note>androgynous</note>, indicating the male-female power involved in the generation of tree fruits. Pluto, the snatcher of Kore, has a dog <note>Cerberus</note> as a symbol of the invisible pole. He carries a scepter, but a broken one, a sign of the kingdom below. His dog signifies the 'gestation' <note>original: "kyesin," a pun on "kyon" (dog)</note> of the fruits, divided into three parts: the sowing, the reception, and the sprouting. For the dog was not named because of any 'cries of death'—as if it signified souls—but because of 'gestation' <note>kyein</note>, of which Pluto is the provider when he snatches Kore. 

» **Attis** and **Adonis** are also related to the analogy of fruits. Attis represents the flowers that appear in the spring and perish before they can reach maturity; this is why the myth of his castration was invented, because the fruits did not manage to reach seminal perfection. Adonis, on the other hand, is the symbol of the cutting of the mature fruits. **Silenus** is a symbol of the movement of the spirit <note>original: "pneumatikes kineseos," referring to wind or breath</note>, which contributes not a little to the whole universe. His symbols are the bright and shining crown of his head, representing the heavenly revolution, while the hair surrounding his lower parts is an image of the density of the air near the earth. Since this power also partook of prophetic ability, the power was called **Themis**, because she speaks of things 'firmly established' <note>original: "tethemeliomena"</note> and laid down for each person." It is clear, then, that all of these represent the power concerning the earth...

<meta>This page continues the extensive quotation from Porphyry’s "On Images" within Eusebius’ "Preparation for the Gospel." Having previously discussed Zeus as the cosmic spirit, Porphyry now details how various Greek gods represent specific terrestrial and elemental forces. Eusebius then interjects to critique these allegories, arguing that reducing gods to physical phenomena like grain or fire makes their worship absurd.</meta>

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 3

» ...having received an interpretation, she is worshipped. For insofar as she represents hospitality and the hearth, she is the "center-bearer" <note>This refers to the Earth as the center of the universe in ancient cosmology</note>. Insofar as she is strong, she is **Hera**. As **Rhea**, she is the maker of plains and mountains. As **Demeter**, she is the "bringer of green grass." As **Themis**, she is the giver of oracles. Because the "seminal principle" <term>spermatikos logos</term> <note>A Stoic term for the creative force that shapes matter</note> descending into her is fashioned into the seasonal cycle, the part of it concerned with dry fruits is called **Kore**, while that concerned with moist fruits and orchard crops is called **Dionysus**. 

» **Kore** is said to be "snatched by Pluto" <note>The Roman name for Hades</note>, which refers to the sun going beneath the earth at a certain constellation. **Dionysus**, meanwhile, represents the "passions" or transformations of this power: he begins to sprout beneath the earth while young and "fair-birthing." **Attis** is the symbol of the power that is contested as the growing season comes to an end. **Adonis** represents the "cutting away" during the completion of the harvest, where the spiritual power is shaped through all things as if into a state of decay. The "extension" or ecstasy derived from this process is represented by the **Bacchante** <note>A female follower of Dionysus</note>; just as the impulse that incites sexual desire is represented by the **Satyrs**. Through these symbols, the various powers of the earth are revealed."

So many and such things are these—which I have briefly abridged and set forth—so that we might not be ignorant of the "solemn" secrets of the philosophers. For indeed, this is how they assign them: Kore is the power of seeds; Dionysus the power of orchard fruits; Attis is the symbol of spring flowers; and Adonis is the symbol of the ripe fruits. 

Why then is it necessary to deify these things, which are merely the varied nourishment of animals on earth brought forth from the ground? And why is it fitting for us to worship earthly power—we who possess a soul of a heavenly nature, rational and immortal, granted by the King of all, God—a soul capable of contemplation with the purified eyes of the mind? Why should I listen to talk of "decays" when I am seeking that spiritual movement and the power that pervades all things? 

At one moment they show the rotation of the heavens through a "head"; at another, the thickness of the air through the "shaggy hair" of the sun. How could anyone think it reasonable that the Creator is later deemed worthy of no reverent honor—He who ought to be deified before all—while Adonis and Dionysus (which is to say, the fruits and orchard crops) are deified? And who could endure hearing Satyrs and Bacchantes spoken of with such solemnity, when they represent shameful and unbridled human passions? For if the Satyrs signify the impulses that incite sexual acts, and the Bacchantes represent the "extension" or loss of control that occurs during them, what is there to worship? And why must I refute every single point, when I should instead run through them so that none of their secrets escape us, and abridge the following "natural philosophy" <note>original: "physiologia"</note>? The stated author <note>Porphyry</note> sets it out, proceeding in this manner:

» "The whole water-making power they called **Ocean**, naming it with a word that symbolizes 'nursing' <note>original: 'tithon', likely an etymological pun on the goddess Tethys or 'tithene', a nurse</note>. Of this whole element, the part that produces fresh, drinkable water is called **Achelous** by them. The power of the seas is **Poseidon**. Again, they call the sea-making power **Amphitrite** insofar as it is generative. The specific powers of sweet waters are called **Nymphs**, while those of the seas are called **Nereids**. 

» Furthermore, assigning the power of fire to **Hephaestus**, they have fashioned his cult image in a human-like form. They placed a dark blue cap <note>original: 'pilos'</note> on him as a symbol of the rotation of the heavens. For there is a part of fire that is ethereal and most pure. But the fire brought down to earth from heaven is weaker, requiring a support and a base upon matter. Therefore he limps, as he needs matter..."

# EUSEBIUS

...ted into a breath of air. And having understood this same power in the Sun, they called him **Apollo**, a name derived from the "vibration" <note>original: *palsis*</note> of his rays. There are Muses who sing with him: the sublunary sphere, the seven spheres of the planets, and one for the fixed stars. They crowned him with the laurel because the plant is full of fire, and for this reason, it is hateful to demons. Furthermore, the plant is "chattering" <note>referring to the rustling or crackling of laurel leaves in fire</note> and celebrated in song, used to honor all who prophesy in the name of God. And insofar as the Sun is the "averter of evil" <term>alexikakos</term> <note>a title for a protective deity</note> among things on earth, they called him **Heracles**, because he "breaks" his path through the air as he travels from east to west. Mythology invented his twelve labors to serve as a symbol for the division of the signs of the zodiac in the heavens. They adorned him with a club and a lion’s skin: the club signifies the unevenness of the year, and the skin reveals his strength within the sign of Leo.

**Asclepius** is the symbol of the Sun's healing power. They have given him a staff to represent the support and "raising up" of the sick. The snake coiled around it is a sign of the salvation of both body and soul; for the animal is most "spirited" <note>Greek *pneumatikotaton*, meaning full of *pneuma* or life-breath</note> and sloughs off the weakness of the body through shedding its skin. It is also thought to be highly skilled in medicine, having discovered the remedy for sharp vision, and it is rumored in myth to know a certain herb for resurrection. 

On the other hand, the power of fire that governs choral and circular motion, and by which fruits are ripened, is called **Dionysus**—otherwise known as the power of juicy fruits. Because of the "whirling" or the Sun "completing" <note>a pun on *Dionysus* and the Greek word *dianyein*, "to complete"</note> its course, he generates the motion of the heavens. The Sun’s patrol around the seasons of the world makes him the creator of time and opportunity, and for this reason, he is called **Horus**. 

In his agricultural power and as the source of wealth, he is symbolized by **Pluto**. Similarly, in myth, he possesses a destructive power, which is why they wed **Persephone** <note>OCR reads *Pheraphe*, a common variant or corruption in manuscript traditions for Persephone</note> to Pluto. This is a symbol of the light having sunk beneath the earth, or the Sun donning a "purple robe" <note>the color of the sunset</note>. The scepter hidden below signifies the power of the underworld and the shape of the earth <note>OCR reads *chthoros*, likely *chthonos* (earth)</note>, representing the transition into the invisible realm. **Cerberus** is three-headed because there are three regions of the Sun: the rising, the midday, and the setting. 

Regarding the Moon: having perceived her through the lens of religious awe, they called her **Artemis**, meaning "air-cutter" <note>original: *aerotomos*</note>. Artemis is a midwife and yet remains a virgin, because the power of the new moon is effective for childbirth. What Apollo is in the Sun, **Athena** is in the Moon; for she is a symbol of wisdom, being "Athena" <note>the text implies a pun on *a-the-na*, meaning "never suckled" or "eternal mind"</note>. Furthermore, the Moon is called **Hecate** because of her changes in form and her power according to those phases. This is why her power is "three-formed": the new moon wears white robes and golden sandals and carries lit torches. The basket <term>kalathos</term> that she carries above the earth is the symbol of the cultivation of fruits, which she nourishes as her light increases. The bronze sandal is a symbol of the Moon, or perhaps one might take the laurel branch as a symbol of its fiery nature. The poppy represents fertility and the multitude of souls who make their home in her as if in a city—for the poppy is a symbol of a city. Artemis carries a bow because of the "sharpness" of labor pains. Again, the **Fates** <note>original: *moirai*</note> are referred back to her powers: **Clotho** represents the power of generation, **Lachesis** the power of nutrition, and **Atropos** the inexorable will of God. They wed her to...

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 3

...of her and the power that sweetens fruits. This power is **Demeter**, who bestows this strength upon the earth. The **Moon** is also the sustainer of the **Maiden** <note>Kore, also known as Persephone</note>. They also represent **Dionysus** in a similar way, both because of the growth of his horns <note>a reference to the crescent moon or the bull-like nature of the god</note> and because of the substance of the clouds which lie beneath the lower regions of the atmosphere.

The power of **Time** <note>original: *Chronos*, often identified with the god Saturn</note>, they perceived as sluggish, slow, and cold; therefore, they assigned the power of time to him. They depict him standing and grey-haired, to emphasize that time itself grows old. The **Kouretes** <note>mythical armed youths</note> are symbols of the **Seasons**, who are said to "herd" Time because time proceeds forward through the cycle of the seasons. 

Regarding the **Hours** <note>the *Horae*, goddesses of the seasons</note>, the "Olympian" ones belong to the Sun, while the "Dionysian" ones belong to the gates of the air. The terrestrial seasons are governed by **Demeter** and the **Maiden** [Kore]: the season of flowers is the symbol of Spring, while the season of the ears of grain belongs to the Maiden. 

Having observed that the power of **Ares** <note>Mars</note> is capable of causing harm and is the source of wars and bloodshed—yet also capable of both hurting and helping—they fashioned his image accordingly. When they looked upon the star of **Aphrodite** <note>Venus</note>, they saw it as the generator of life and the cause of desire and procreation. They modeled her as a woman because of birth, and made her beautiful because she is the "Evening Star," which stands as the fairest star in the heavens. They placed **Eros** <note>Cupid</note> beside her to represent desire. She is shown covering her breasts and private parts because her power arises from procreation and nourishment. She is born from the sea, a moist and hot element that is in constant motion and foams due to its agitation—which is a riddle for the **seminal nature** <term>spermatikon</term> <note>the life-giving "seed" or creative principle of nature</note>.

**Hermes** represents **Reason** <note>original: *Logos*</note>, as the creator and interpreter of all things, appearing in an active role. A "vigorous" Hermes signifies muscular strength and health. He also demonstrates the **Seminal Reason** <term>spermatikos logos</term> <note>a Stoic term for the rational principle that organizes and gives life to matter</note> which pervades all things. 

Furthermore, there are composite "Reasons": 
*   **Hermes** is the reason within the Sun.
*   **Hecate** is the reason within the Moon.
*   **Hermopan** is the reason within the All <note>Pan, whose name means "All"</note>. 

For the seminal and creative principle is over all things. These composite forms occur through the mixing of powers, such as **Hermanubis** among the Egyptians. Since Reason [Logos] is also the power of desire, **Eros** is its active expression. Therefore, Eros is called the son of Hermes, yet he is depicted as an infant because of the sudden and unexpected onset of the desires he causes.

They made **Pan** the symbol of the **Universe** <note>the All</note>. They gave him horns as symbols of the Sun and Moon, and a fawn-skin <note>original: *nebris*</note> to represent the stars in the sky or the manifold variety of the universe. 

So much for the psychic <note>pertaining to the soul or mind</note> interpretations. Regarding the symbols of the Egyptians, the text says they have the following: The **Creator**, whom the Egyptians call **Kneph**, is human-shaped; his skin is a dark blue approaching black, and he holds a belt and a scepter. On his head, he wears a royal feather, because Reason [Logos] is hard to discover and hidden—it is not obvious, yet it is life-giving, royal, and moves intellectually. This is why the nature of the feather is placed on the head. They say this god emits an **Egg** from his mouth, from which is born a god they call **Phtha** [Ptah], whom the Greeks call **Hephaestus**. They interpret this Egg as the **Cosmos** <note>the Universe</note>.

A sheep is also dedicated to this god, because the ancients lived on its milk. As for the image of the **Cosmos** itself, they modeled it like this: it is a human-shaped statue with its feet joined together, draped from head to toe in a multicolored robe. On its head, it has a golden sphere, representing its lack of local movement <note>meaning the universe as a whole does not move from place to place</note>, the diverse nature of the stars, and the fact that the universe is spherical. 

They represent the **Sun** sometimes as a man embarked on a ship, with the ship resting on a crocodile. The ship signifies movement in moisture; the crocodile signifies fresh water, in which the Sun is carried. Thus, the Sun signifies that his circuit is made through moist and sweet air...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of how ancient peoples, particularly the Greeks and Egyptians, used physical statues and myths as allegories for natural forces. Having previously discussed the seasons and the nature of time, the text now focuses on the "heavenly" and "earthly" powers manifested in the Moon, the Nile, and specific cult images in Egypt.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

...of her. They spoke of the power of the "heavenly earth" <note>the Moon</note> and the "earthly earth" as being equal because of their equality, which is the source of justice. They say the Moon is the heavenly earth, while the fruit-bearing earth on which we live is the terrestrial one. This same power is called **Demeter** by the Greeks and **Isis** by the Egyptians. Again, she is called the **Maiden** <note>Kore/Persephone</note> among the Greeks, while among the Egyptians she is identified as **Dionysus**, **Isis**, and **Osiris**. She is the one who nourishes and grows all things upon the earth.

**Osiris**, among the Egyptians, represents the fertile power. They attempt to appease this power with lamentations when it disappears into the earth during the sowing of seeds, and when it is consumed by us as food. He is also understood to represent the power of the river **Nile**. When they mean the terrestrial earth, Osiris is understood as the fertile power; but when they mean the heavenly realm, Osiris is the Nile, which they believe is brought down from heaven. They also offer prayers to appease this power when it wanes and is spent. **Isis**, who in the myths is joined with Osiris, is the land of Egypt. Through this union, the land is made equal <note>referring to the annual flood</note>, conceives, and produces fruits. For this reason, Osiris is traditionally described as the husband, brother, and son of Isis.

### Regarding the statue at Elephantine.

In the city of **Elephantine**, a statue is honored that is fashioned in a human likeness and shown sitting. Its skin is blue in color, and it has the head of a ram with a royal crown and goat horns. Above these is a disk-shaped circle. He sits near a potter’s vessel, upon which he is molding a human being. The ram’s face and the goat’s horns signify the conjunction of the **Sun** and **Moon** in the constellation of Aries <note>the Ram</note>. The blue color of the skin indicates that the Moon is a "water-bringer" during this conjunction.

The "second light" of the Moon is consecrated in the **City of Apollo** <note>Edfu/Apollinopolis Magna</note>. Its symbolic form is a hawk-headed man taming **Typhon**, who is depicted as a hippopotamus. The statue is white in color. The whiteness represents the Moon when it is shining brightly. The hawk's face signifies that the Moon is illuminated by the Sun and receives its spirit from it, for the hawk is dedicated to the Sun. To them, the hawk is a symbol of light and spirit because of its swift movement and its habit of flying to great heights where the light is. The hippopotamus represents the western pole, because it appears to "swallow" the stars as they set. The god honored in this city is **Horus**.

The city of **Eileithyia** <note>Nekheb/El Kab</note> worships the "third light." Its cult image is shaped like a flying vulture, whose plumage is made of precious stones. The vulture-like form signifies the "generative spirit" <note>original: *gonimikon pneuma*</note> in the Moon. They believe that vultures conceive through the wind alone, claiming that all vultures are female.

In the **Mysteries at Eleusis**, the **Hierophant** <note>the "revealer of sacred things"</note> is dressed in the likeness of the **Creator** <note>the Demiurge</note>. The **Torch-bearer** represents the Sun, and the one at the altar represents the Moon. The **Sacred Herald** represents **Hermes**. A human element is also included in the Egyptian rites. There is a village in Egypt <note>likely Lycopolis or a related district</note> where a man is worshipped and sacrificed to, and the sacred offerings are burned upon the altars. A little while later, he would eat the things prepared for him as if he were a man. The fact that they do not actually consider animals to be gods—but rather made these things as images and symbols of gods—is shown by the fact that in many places they bring oxen to the gods during the sacred festivals and sacrifice them in their religious worship.

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s critique of allegorical interpretations of pagan religion. Having previously discussed the Nile and the land as Osiris and Isis, he now examines the sacred bulls of Egypt—Mnevis and Apis—and uses them to argue that such worship is fundamentally materialistic, despite the attempts of philosophers like Porphyry to find spiritual meaning in them.</meta>

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 3

### Concerning the ox dedicated to the Sun in the City of the Sun.

> <margin>»</margin> For they dedicated oxen to both the Sun and the Moon. But the one dedicated to the Sun in the City of the Sun <note>original: "Heliopolis"</note>,
> <margin>»</margin> called **Mnevis**, is the greatest of oxen and is exceptionally black. This is primarily because the intense
> <margin>»</margin> sun darkens human bodies. He has a tail different from other oxen, and the
> <margin>»</margin> hair on his entire body grows in the opposite direction <note>literally "against the pole"</note>, just as the sun makes its path contrary to the heavens.
> <margin>»</margin> His testicles are very large, because the desire for sexual union is spurred by heat, 
> <margin>»</margin> and the sun is said to "seed" nature. To the Moon, they dedicated a bull which they 
> <margin>»</margin> name **Apis**. He is also blacker than other bulls, and bears the symbols of the sun and 
> <margin>»</margin> the moon. This is because the light of the moon comes from the sun; and the sun’s symbol 
> <margin>»</margin> is the blackness of the body, as well as the beetle <note>original: "kantharos," referring to a mark like a scarab</note> under its tongue. 
> <margin>»</margin> The symbol of the Moon is the bull’s divided <note>half-moon</note> and 
> <margin>»</margin> curved <note>crescent</note> shapes.

Let these excerpts from the writings of the aforementioned man <note>likely the philosopher Porphyry</note> be summarized here, so that none of the secrets of Egyptian and Greek theology may escape us. We confess that we have distanced ourselves and become fugitives from this theology by our own judgment and reasoning. 

Consider this as well: I will not be struck with awe by that arrogant voice <note>a reference to the Orphic mysteries</note> which cries out to those for whom it is lawful, saying, "*Close the doors, you profane ones!*" For it is not we who are profane, but those who declare that these shameful and indecent myths about beetles and irrational beasts are actually the insights of "theological wisdom." They are the ones of whom the wonderful Apostle spoke, saying that "*claiming to be wise, they became fools*," because "*they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for an image resembling a corruptible human being, and birds, and four-footed animals, and reptiles.*" <note>quoting Romans 1:22–23</note>

But since they have allegorically led all these "secrets" into a more mystical explanation involving **incorporeal powers** <note>spiritual forces without physical bodies</note>, so that their deification no longer seems to apply to the visible parts of the world but to certain invisible powers, let us consider whether an even greater blasphemy against the Divine does not arise from this. For even though many shapes, parts, and limbs are created within a single body, we are not required to believe that just as many souls live within it, nor should we assume there are as many poets and creators of the body as there are parts. Rather, one soul moves the whole body, and one creative power fashioned the entire living being. 

In the same way, regarding the entire universe—which is one, consisting of one material substance, though divided into many parts—it displays a single natural sympathy throughout the whole. It shows a blending and mixing of the elements within it, and their alterations and changes into one another. Since the whole and the "all" demonstrate one world and one harmony, we must not assume there are many creative powers. We should recognize only one: the power of God and the wisdom of God. 

The man <note>Porphyry</note> who tries to transfer Egyptian myths back to "incorporeal powers" has, despite his great wisdom, failed to notice his own contradiction. For you heard in the previous sections how he admitted that **Chaeremon** <note>an Egyptian priest and historian</note> and many others believed the Egyptians did not recognize anything beyond the visible worlds, and placed these at the very beginning of their reasoning. For these writers interpret everything as natural forces and nothing as incorporeal or living essences. If, therefore, by their own admission, the Egyptians do not trace anything back to incorporeal or living essences, but instead transfer all their myths about the gods to the physical parts of the world, why do these modern thinkers start a new school of thought and attribute to the Egyptians things that do not belong to them, claiming their myths refer to incorporeal powers?

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Egyptian and Greek theological allegories. # EUSEBIUS

...to be considered. They called the power of the celestial earth <note>the Moon</note> and the terrestrial earth equal, because of the "equality" from which justice arises. They say the Moon is the "celestial earth," while the "terrestrial earth" is the fruit-bearing land in which we dwell. This same power is called **Demeter** <note>the Greek goddess of agriculture</note> among the Greeks, and **Isis** among the Egyptians. Again, she is called **Kore** <note>the "Maiden" or Persephone</note> among the Greeks, and **Dionysus**, **Isis**, and **Osiris** among the Egyptians. This power is what nourishes and increases all things upon the earth.

Among the Egyptians, **Osiris** represents the fruit-bearing power. They appease this power with laments when it "disappears" into the earth during the sowing of seeds, and when it is consumed by us as food. Osiris is also understood as the power of the river Nile. However, when they use the name to signify the terrestrial earth, Osiris is taken as the fruit-bearing power of the soil; but when they mean the celestial realm, Osiris is the Nile, which they believe is brought down from heaven. They also convince people that this power must be appeased as it wanes and is consumed. **Isis**, who is joined with Osiris in the myths, is the Egyptian land itself. For this reason, she is "made equal" <note>likely referring to the Nile flood leveling the land</note>, becomes pregnant, and produces fruits. Thus, Osiris is traditionally handed down as the husband, brother, and son of Isis.

->About the statue at Elephantine.<-

In the city of **Elephantine** <note>an island in the Nile near Aswan</note>, a statue is honored. It is fashioned in a human-like form and is seated; its complexion is blue, and it has the head of a ram wearing a royal crown with goat's horns, topped by a disk-shaped circle. He sits near a potter’s vessel, upon which he is modeling a human being. The ram’s face and goat’s horns signify the "conjunction" <note>alignment</note> of the sun and moon in the zodiac sign of Aries <note>the Ram</note>. The blue color indicates that the moon is a "water-bearer" during this conjunction.

The "second light" of the moon is consecrated in the City of Apollo <note>Edfu</note>. The symbol for this is a hawk-faced man subduing **Typhon** <note>the chaotic god Set</note>, who is depicted as a hippopotamus. This statue is white in color; the whiteness represents the moon being illuminated. The hawk’s face indicates that it is lit by the sun and receives "spirit" <note>original: "pneuma," meaning breath or life-force</note>, for they dedicate the hawk to the sun. To them, the hawk is a symbol of light and spirit because of its swift movement and its habit of flying toward the heights where the light is. The hippopotamus signifies the western pole, which "swallows up" the heavenly bodies as they travel around it. The god **Horus** is honored in this city.

The City of **Eileithyia** <note>El Kab</note> worships the "third light." Their cult image <note>term: "xoanon," a primitive wooden cult image</note> is shaped like a vulture in flight, whose wings are made of precious stones. The vulture signifies the moon's light as the generator of spirit. They believe this because they think vultures conceive from the wind, claiming that all vultures are female.

In the **mysteries** of Isis, the **Hierophant** <note>the head priest who reveals sacred secrets</note> is dressed to represent the Creator; the **Torch-bearer** represents the Sun; the priest at the altar represents the Moon; and the **Sacred Herald** represents Hermes. Even a human being is included in the Egyptian temples; for Egypt is considered a power of the world, in which man is served, and sacrifices are made to him, and sacred offerings are burned upon the altars. A little later, he might eat food prepared in a most human fashion. The fact that they do not actually consider animals to be gods, but rather made them as images and symbols of gods, is shown by how often they dedicate oxen to the gods in their sacred rites and sacrifice bulls in their worship of the gods.

<summary>This page explains the allegorical identities of Isis and Osiris as the land and the Nile, and details the symbolic iconography of Egyptian statues (such as the ram-headed Khnum and the hawk-headed Horus) as representations of celestial movements.</summary>
<keywords>Isis, Osiris, Elephantine, Khnum, Horus, Nile allegory, Greek-Egyptian syncretism, animal symbolism, religious mysteries</keywords>

### EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 3.

### Concerning the bull dedicated to the Sun in the solar region.

> For a bull is consecrated to both the Sun and the Moon. The one dedicated to the Sun in the place called the solar region is named **Pan** <note>This likely refers to the Mnevis bull of Heliopolis, which was sacred to the sun god Ra; Pan was often identified by Greeks with Egyptian pastoral or solar deities</note>; he is the greatest of bulls and is exceedingly black. This is chiefly because the great heat of the sun blackens human bodies. He has the tail and the ears of a bull, but his whole body is otherwise like a human's, just as the Sun moves in a direction opposite to the pole. His testicles are very large, because the desire for sexual union is stirred by heat, and it is at this time that the Sun is said to "seed" nature. To the Moon, they have dedicated a bull which they call **Apis**. He too is blacker than others, but he bears the marks of the Sun and the Moon. This is because the light of the Moon comes from the Sun; the Sun's mark is the blackness of the body and the <term>beetle</term> <note>original: "kántharos" — the scarab beetle was a symbol of the sun and regeneration</note> under his tongue. The symbols of the Moon are the half-moon and the crescent shapes. Let these excerpts suffice as a summary from the writings of the aforementioned man <note>Porphyry, the philosopher whose work Eusebius is quoting</note>.

I have shared these things so that nothing regarding the secret theology of the Greeks and Egyptians together might escape us. We admit that we have abandoned these beliefs and consider ourselves fugitives from them, having taken our stand against them with a sober mind and sound judgment. I will not be struck with awe by that boastful voice which says: "Close the doors, you uninitiated!" <note>original: "θύρας δ’ ἐπίθεσθε βέβηλοι" — a standard warning used in Greek mystery religions to keep the "profane" or uninitiated away from sacred rites</note>. For we are not the "profane" ones; rather, they are the ones who, under the guise of "theological wisdom," attempt to honor such shameful and indecent myths about beetles and irrational beasts. 

These are the ones of whom the wonderful apostle <note>St. Paul</note> said: *Claiming to be wise, they became fools. For they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed animals, and of reptiles.* <note>A quotation from the New Testament, Romans 1:22-23</note>

But they claim that all these things are metaphors—that they are leading the mind away from physical objects toward certain "secret" and "mystical" meanings regarding **incorporeal powers** <note>spiritual or non-physical forces</note>. They suggest their deification does not apply to the visible parts of the world, but to invisible forces. Let us consider, then, whether it is not better to wonder at the single Divine Power instead of assuming there are many. For even though many shapes, parts, and limbs are created within a single body, we do not say we have many souls. Nor do we believe there are many different creators of our body. Instead, we believe one soul moves the whole body, and one creative power fashions the whole living being. 

In the same way, regarding the entire universe—which is one, consists of a single material substance, and displays a single natural "sympathy" or connection through the blending of its elements and their changes into one another—we should not assume there are many creative powers. We should only recognize one "theology": the truly divine power and wisdom of God. 

The philosopher who tries to turn Egyptian myths back into "incorporeal powers" has, in his cleverness, forgotten himself. You heard earlier how he admitted that **Chaeremon** <note>A Stoic philosopher and Egyptian priest</note> and many others believed the Egyptians at the start of their history recognized nothing other than the visible worlds. For these men interpreted everything as physical phenomena and nothing as incorporeal or living essences. If, then, by their own admission, the Egyptians did not trace anything back to incorporeal souls, but instead applied all their myths about gods to the physical parts of the world, why do these modern thinkers now invent new arguments and attribute to the Egyptians things that were never theirs, claiming they refer to "incorporeal powers"?

<summary>Eusebius concludes a passage from Porphyry describing the solar and lunar bulls of Egypt, then critiques these allegories by citing the Apostle Paul and arguing that the universe reflects one Creator rather than many "incorporeal powers."</summary>

# EUSEBIUS

...to make of their theology. Generally, therefore, these things must be blamed. Even regarding the specific details, we now declare that the refutation of their forced interpretations does not require a lengthy lesson. To avoid Egyptian vanity <note>original: "typhon" — referring here to the arrogance or "smoke" of complex, prideful Egyptian myth</note> and their abundant, babbling nonsense, the author has turned to the natural philosophies of the wise Greeks. Yet how could any right-thinking person fail to immediately find fault with those attempting to explain such things? 

Suppose Zeus is no longer the fiery and ethereal substance, as the ancients used to believe—according to Plutarch himself—but is instead the supreme Mind, the creator of all things, who gives life to all. How then can **Cronus** <note>original: "Kronos"</note> be his father, whom they say is **Time**? <note>original: "chronon" — a common pun in Greek philosophy between the names of the Titan and the word for time</note> And how could his mother be **Rhea**, whom the interpreter claimed was the stony and mountainous power of the earth? What kinship did they have with the air? For the author says that **Hera** <note>original: "Hera" / "aera" (air)</note>—nurtured in the upper ether—is both his sister and his wife. This is an insult to the creator and life-giving Mind! 

Furthermore, let **Leto** again be called "forgetfulness" <note>original: "lethe" — another etymological wordplay</note> because of the lack of sensation that occurs during sleep, as they say; and because forgetfulness rains down upon the souls that exist under the moon. How, then, could Forgetfulness be the mother of the Sun and the Moon—that is, **Apollo** and **Artemis**? For they claim the children of Leto were transformed into the Sun and Moon. 

And why should one worship Rhea or **Demeter** as a goddess, if the former is said to carry the symbols of the stony and mountainous earth, and the latter the symbols of the plains? Why do they introduce the **Maiden** <note>original: "Kore" — referring to Persephone</note>? Do they think they must honor her with a venerable title through some logic? If she is instead the power of seeds and the nature of fruit-trees, or if they name **Dionysus** and **Adonis** as gods to be worshiped because they are symbols of the spring blossoms—which appear and then fall away before reaching maturity—or symbols of the harvest of ripe fruits, why are they called gods? Should not the beneficial Sun be preferred over all these things? For the God who is the creator of the universe established these things from the beginning for the Sun's use. 

Moving on from these points, one could find a similar method of defense through natural philosophy for the remaining myths, but one would rightly blame such "dignified" explanations as irrational. Take, for instance, those who declare the Sun itself is Apollo, and also **Heracles**, and again Dionysus, and likewise **Asclepius**. How could the same person be both father and son—Asclepius and Apollo together? How could the Sun be transformed into Heracles, if they admit that Heracles was born of a mortal woman, **Alcmene**? How could the Sun go mad and slaughter his own children? For they also invent these stories about Heracles. 

But they say that Heracles, in completing his twelve labors, is a symbol of the division of the zodiac circle in the heavens, which they say the Sun travels through. If that is so, then who would **Eurystheus** be—the one who commanded the Sun (as Heracles) to perform these labors? And how could the fifty daughters of **Thestius**, and the multitude of other captives with whom the story says Heracles slept, be traced back to the Sun? From these unions, mortal children were born to him, extending a very long succession of heroes. And how could there be a **Centaur** <note>Nessus</note>, with whose blood **Deianeira** stained the robe, thereby wrapping the Sun—as Heracles—in that famous disaster? 

But perhaps let the Sun no longer be Heracles to them. Let him be Dionysus. One might reasonably say the same things regarding Dionysus. How could the Sun be born of him? Whether he is said to be born of the Moon or of **Persephone**. How could Dionysus be simultaneously the Sun, and the spirit within moist fruits, and the tree-fruits...

<summary>Eusebius critiques the allegorical interpretations of Greek myths, arguing that turning gods like Zeus and Heracles into natural forces like "Mind" or "the Sun" creates logical contradictions and fails to explain their mythical biographies.</summary>

### EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 3

...the power causing fruit-trees to sprout, but what could be said of the multitude of women listed alongside him? And who is the **Ariadne** of **Dionysus** <note>original: "Dionysou Ariadne"</note>, just as there is one for the sun? 

If he is more about wine and not the "pulse" <note>original: "osparian" — refers to legumes or beans</note> or grain, and the solar provider of all the earth's fruits is Dionysus transferred to the sun? And if **Asclepius** <note>original: "Asklepios"</note> were again the sun for them, how is he struck by the thunderbolt of **Zeus** <note>original: "Dios"</note> on account of filthy greed? 

According to the Boeotian song-maker **Pindar** <note>original: "Pindaron"</note> who says something like this: 
<margin>"</margin> "But even wisdom is led astray by gain. Gold appearing in the hands turned him 
<margin>"</margin> with a grand reward; but with his hands the Son of Cronus <note>original: "Kronion" — referring to Zeus</note>, snatching the breath 
<margin>"</margin> from the chests of both, brought them down quickly, and the flashing thunderbolt dealt their doom." 

Some say the **Asclepiads** <note>original: "Asklepiadai" — the followers or mythical descendants of the healing god</note> come from the sun, to guard the long life of the mortal race of men, having been crafted like all other humans? 

But again, as if by some stage-machine <note>original: "mechanes" — referring to the *deus ex machina* of Greek theater</note>, they would escape the shameful and mythical stories about the gods, and their argument would run back to the sun, the moon, and the other parts of the world. For them, **Hephaestus** <note>original: "Hephaistos"</note> would be fire and the power of heat; **Poseidon** the moist substance; **Hera** the air. And again, the mountainous and rocky power would be **Rhea**; the level and fertile land, **Demeter**; and **Kore** <note>original: "Kore" — The Maiden, Persephone</note> the receiver of seeds. **Dionysus** is the nurturing power of fruit-trees, and **Apollo** is the sun along with the attributes already mentioned. The moon is sometimes **Artemis**, sometimes **Athena**, or again **Hecate** and **Eileithyia**. 

Therefore, they are again convicted of theologizing about the creation <note>original: "ktisin"</note> instead of the Creator <note>original: "ktisten"</note>, and the workmanship of the universe rather than the Workman—an extremely unstable and dangerous path, and to the harm of their own heads. 

If they say they do not deify the visible bodies of the sun, moon, and stars, nor the sensible parts of the world, but rather the invisible powers within them—even the one God over all, who fills all things with various powers, and reaches through all, and presides over all things incorporeally and invisibly—and that they reasonably worship Him through these things we have mentioned: why then do they not stop these shameful and unseemly mythologies as lawless and impious? 

Why not hide those books that contain such impious and licentious things, and instead praise the one and only invisible God plainly and purely, without any shameful entanglement? For this is what those who have known the truth ought to do: they should not bring down and degrade the venerable name of God into shameful and passionate stories. 

Nor should they shut themselves up in small houses and dark recesses, or in the buildings of men, as if they will find God inside. Nor should they think they honor divine powers in wooden statues <note>original: "xoanois"</note> made of lifeless matter, nor think it proper to approach God by polluting themselves with earthly vapors of blood and the gore of dead animals. 

Having been released from the bonds of error, the wise and "high-talking" <note>original: "meteôroleschas" — a term for those who discuss heavenly matters, sometimes used disparagingly for star-gazers</note> men ought to share their natural theory <note>original: "physikes theorias"</note> freely with all people, almost nakedly proclaiming to all that they should not admire visible things, but only the invisible Creator of visible things. They should worship His invisible and incorporeal powers invisibly and incorporeally—not by lighting fires, nor by sacrificing rams and bulls, nor by imagining the Divine in enclosures, statues, or temple buildings, but with purified thoughts.

He calls for a pure, non-materialistic worship of the one invisible God through reason and thought rather than blood sacrifice or idols.</summary>

### EUSEBIUS

...and with right and true doctrines, they do this in the dispassion of the soul, and by the imitation of virtue toward Him as much as is possible. But no one ever, neither barbarian nor Greek, initiated all of humanity into this truth, except only our Savior. He, having proclaimed to all nations an escape from ancient error, generously extended to all the turning back toward and piety for the true and only God. But the "wise men" of old, though they claimed to have attained the highest philosophy in life, were—as the divine Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> says—"knowing God, they did not glorify Him as God, or give thanks, but became futile in their thinking, and their senseless heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever" <note>original: Romans 1:21-25</note>.

->They do not refute mythical stories about gods by their actions.<-

<margin>M</margin> After all their long and extensive philosophy, and after their solemn "meteorologies" <note>Discussions of celestial phenomena</note> and "physiologies" <note>In this context, the study of the nature of the divine and the universe</note> from above, they fall as if from the highest peak and are dragged down along with the masses. They were carried away by the polytheistic error of the ancients, doing the same things as the common people. Out of fear, they even approach the <term>xoana</term> <note>Ancient, primitive wooden cult statues</note> pretending to give glory, thus increasing and further strengthening the popular and mythical narrative about the gods. How then could they not be obvious to everyone? They speak solemnly in their studies of nature, and through their words they dress up shameful things with a pretense of truth; yet by their very deeds, they uphold the mythical error and the widespread superstition. For it is not yet a thing of wonder when they themselves record that these same gods agree with the myths told about them. 

Hear, for example, how **Apollo** himself teaches a hymn about himself, which he issued concerning himself, confessing that he was born on the island of **Delos** by **Leto**. And again, **Asclepius** within a wall; just as **Hermes** is placed, confessing he is from **Maia**. **Porphyry** <note>A famous Neoplatonist philosopher and critic of Christianity</note> also writes these things in the work he titled *On the Philosophy from Oracles*, and then he recalled the oracles which go something like this:

> <margin>,,</margin> "O great joy to all mortals from your holy ones,
> <margin>,,</margin> looking upon the holy mother of the suppliants." To which he adds: "But when all the holy labor of Leto brought forth 
> <margin>,,</margin> the birth of the twins within the sanctuary, the earth stood still, the air stood still, the island was fixed, 
> <margin>,,</margin> the wave was fixed. Rise up from the steep-peaked mountain, three-headed **Phoebus** <note>A name for Apollo</note>, king who speaks oracles 
> <margin>,,</margin> from beneath the ground." And Asclepius again says of himself: "From holy **Trikke** I have come, a god whom 
> <margin>,,</margin> once a mother, having lain with Phoebus, conceived—the King of Wisdom, the Knower of healing, 
> <margin>,,</margin> Asclepius." But why do you ask? This Hermes says: "Since I, whom you call, was alive and the son of Maia, 
> <margin>,,</margin> Hermes went forth, leaving the starry lord." And they even describe the appearance of his 
> <margin>,,</margin> form, just as he himself once said of himself in oracles, teaching these things: "I 
> <margin>,,</margin> pray to a god born as a mortal, joined in many parts, two-headed, two-footed, shining-clothed, bellowing."

The aforementioned man <note>Porphyry</note> placed these things among the secrets of the "philosophy from oracles." It was no longer through symbols, then, that the evil demon existed—whatever such a thing might be—as he is described and as he was presented in the oracle. For it was not the ancient world or the whole universe that uttered the things set before us. Therefore, men did not model the image of this demon, but rather they imitated the shape previously described.

### PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 3

75

41. And as for Hermes, how could he be understood as the <term>Logos</term> <note>original: λόγος; here meaning the power of speech and interpretation</note> which is creative and interpretive for mankind, while he is admitted—at least according to their own recorded mythology, if one does not include their natural philosophy—to have been born of Maia, the daughter of Atlas? In the same way, how could Asclepius be transformed into the Sun, when he is recorded as having Tricca <note>A city in Thessaly famous as the birthplace of Asclepius</note> as his father, and is admitted to have been born of a mortal mother? And how, if he is the Sun, could he be shown to be the son of the Sun once again? For you are well aware that his father Phoebus is also identified in their natural philosophy as the Sun. Is it not the most ridiculous thing of all for him to be born from the Sun and a mortal woman? Furthermore, if his father is the Sun himself—whom they say is Apollo—how is it reasonable for him to have been born on the island of Delos, once again from a mortal mother, Leto? These points I have theologized for examination against all those gods supposedly born of women, should they ever attempt to silence the appearance of our Savior.

---

-> *That they also confirmed the theories of philosophers through oracles,* <-
-> *allegorizing in a manner contrary to the myths about them.* <-

---

<margin>T</margin> These are not the voices of poets, but the very proclamations of the gods themselves set before us. The poets, as they say, fashion myths about the gods, while the philosophers provide "physiologies" <note>Explanations of gods as natural phenomena</note>. One should, reasonably, flee from the former and admire the latter as philosophers. It would be better to accept the poetic nonsense through the persuasive arguments of the higher powers; yet, when gods and philosophers enter into a contest of beauty, the gods teach more accurately about themselves in their oracles as those who know best, while the philosophers turn toward inconsistent and unproven allegories—mere suspicions about things they do not know. To which side does reason demand we yield? Or is this not even worth asking? If the gods speak the truth when they confirm these allegorical interpretations of themselves, then those who deny the myths would be liars. But if the natural philosophies of the philosophers are true, then the testimonies of the gods must be false. Yet, as one might say, Apollo himself, when asked in an oracle who he was, said:

> "Sun, Horus, Osiris, King, Dionysus, Apollo,
> Steward of the hours and seasons, of winds and rains,
> The Charioteer wielding the reins of fire-bright rays,
> King of the burning stars and immortal fire."

Therefore, the gods agree both with the myths of the poets and the theories of the philosophers. For if they claim mortal mothers or admit to earthly birthplaces, how could they be interpreted as natural forces? For if Apollo is the Sun—and here the argument will be caught running in circles around the same dry ground—how could Delos, the island visible in the sea even now, be the Sun’s birthplace, and Leto his mother? For his own oracles just now confirmed these things as being true. And how could the Sun be the father of Asclepius, a man mortal by nature, if he had not fathered him by a mortal woman? But let these things be spared further comment.

It is not impossible by nature for the parts of the world, by the necessary forces of their own particular powers, to be drawn down and to be observed by those who inquire through oracles.

But the falsehood of the oracle must be refuted once again. For the Sun did not come from heaven...

# EUSEBIUS P.

...to these men, descending and filling the **vessel** <term>dochaeus</term> <note>original: δοχέα; a term for a human medium or "receiver" who was supposedly possessed by a deity to deliver an oracle</note> with the prophecy he breathed into them. For it is neither possible nor lawful for such a great **luminary** <note>Referring to the Sun as a cosmic light</note> to be subjected to the compulsions of men. But surely they would not claim that the divine and intellectual power within these celestial bodies is what descends; for a human soul could never be capable of receiving such a thing.

The same logic would apply to the **Moon**. For if they claim that she is Hecate herself, and that she is somehow "drawn down" by the compulsions of men to give prophecies through a medium—even being recruited for shameful and erotic services—then it would be logical for Hecate to do these things, since she is the ruler of evil powers, that is, of demons. Even their own author <note>Likely referring to Porphyry, whom Eusebius quotes extensively in this work</note> admits this, as we shall also demonstrate regarding her. 

And how is it possible for **Pluto** and **Sarapis** <note>Sarapis was a Graeco-Egyptian deity who combined traits of Osiris and Apis with those of Zeus and Pluto</note> to be interpreted through <term>physiology</term> <note>original: φυσιολογεῖσθαι; the practice of explaining gods as allegories for natural forces</note> as being one and the same as the Sun? When the same author again declares that Sarapis is the ruler of evil demons—being the same as Pluto—in oracles that were actually inscribed with the name of Sarapis, how is it possible for him to say that Sarapis is the Sun? Indeed, from all these contradictions, one must admit that the aforementioned natural interpretations contain nothing of the truth. They are merely the **inventions of sophists** and the products of sectarian reasoning.

---

### That all such things are the result of demonic activity.

To the attendants of these oracles, one might say with a word of truth that these are **wicked demons**, playing both sides of the game to deceive mankind. One demon supports the more mythical ideas about the gods to maintain the popular delusions, while another confirms the views of the philosophers through oracles, validating the "natural" interpretations of these myths. Thus, they are undermined from every side, and there is nothing "healthy" or sound in them. 

Since we have said this much, it is now time to move on and examine the **third species of Greek theology**, which they call "political and legal." This is particularly influential among the masses because of the celebrated oracles and the healings and cures for physical ailments granted through these prophecies, as well as the divine warnings sent against certain people. Claiming to have experienced these things firsthand, they have convinced themselves that by being "pious" toward these gods, they are acting justly. They charge us with the greatest **impiety** because we do not honor such manifest and helpful powers with the appropriate worship. Regarding these matters, then, let us take up a new starting point for our argument.

He then introduces the next topic: "political theology," which concerns the public oracles and healings that the common people used to justify their paganism.</summary>

Here, Eusebius shifts his focus to the "political" or civic religion of the Greeks, specifically targeting the prestigious oracles and the practice of animal sacrifice.</meta>

# The following are the contents of the fourth book of the **Preparation for the Gospel**.

Preface regarding the oracles in the various cities, and those prophetic sites most famous for the miraculous appearances of **demons** <note>original: δαιμόνων; in this context, Eusebius views these spirits not as neutral entities but as deceptive, malevolent beings masquerading as gods</note>, and for what reason we have come to despise them.

That for those who wish to see it, it is not difficult to show that the promises of the oracles are closely related to the trickery of **sorcerers** <term>goētōn</term> <note>original: γοήτων; refers to low-level magicians or charlatans who used sleight of hand and psychological tricks to mimic divine acts</note>.

That their **divination** <term>mantikē</term> <note>original: μαντική; the traditional Greek art of foretelling the future through divine inspiration or signs</note> is inconsistent and full of lies, and that their foretelling is both useless and harmful.

That the Gospel teaching of our Savior has liberated us from these greatest of evils.

What the division of Greek theology is.

That we do not use our own arguments, but provide the evidence for our refutations from their own domestic writings.

Concerning the secrets of the oracles, taken from their own domestic writings.

An **oath** <note>A common feature in "mystery" religions or occult texts, where the reader is sworn to secrecy before certain "truths" are revealed</note> regarding what is about to be said.

That one must not disclose what will be said to everyone.

How Apollo commands the people to serve the gods through sacrifices.

That those who take pleasure in the sacrifice of animals could not be gods.

That nothing from the earth should be sacrificed to the **God over all** <note>original: τῷ ἐπὶ πάντων θεῷ; a recurring title in Eusebius's work for the supreme, transcendent Creator</note>, neither by burning incense nor by slaughter.

That it is not appropriate to sacrifice or burn anything from the earth even to the divine powers.

Further concerning why one should not offer things from the earth to the God over all.

That the sacrifice of animals to gods is illegal, harmful, unjust, and unholy, and that it is subject to curses.

That the things sacrificed to all of them are sacrificed to demons and not to gods.

Concerning the ancient practice of human sacrifice, and that it was abolished after the Gospel teaching.

That the entire theology of the **Gentiles** <note>original: ἐθνῶν; referring to the non-Christian, polytheistic nations, particularly the Greeks and Romans</note> was dedicated to evil demons.

That one must not sacrifice to evil demons.

How one ought to pray to the God over all.

How Apollo commands people to sacrifice to an evil demon.

That no one else from the beginning of ages, except for our Savior and Lord alone, has liberated the whole human race from demonic error.

The manner of demonic activity.

Concerning the evil demons, and who their rulers happen to be.

# EUSEBIUS

->Preface.<-

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut drop-cap initial letter 'T' (Tau) featuring intricate classical scrollwork of vines and leaves within a square frame.</image-desc>

THE third form of the error of many gods—from which we were set free by the power and benevolence of our Redeemer and Savior **Jesus Christ** <note>original: Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ; Eusebius consistently attributes the intellectual and spiritual "liberation" of the world to Christ’s intervention</note>—is now at a favorable time to be refuted in this fourth book of the **Preparation for the Gospel**. For their entire system of **theology** <term>theologia</term> <note>original: θεολογία; here referring to the pagan system of gods and religious study</note> is divided into three primary categories: the **mythical** <note>original: μυθικόν; referring to the dramatic and often scandalous stories found in epic and tragic poetry</note>, which is dramatized by the poets; the **physical** <note>original: φυσικόν; the "natural" theology where philosophers interpreted gods as elements like fire, water, or stars</note>, which was devised by the philosophers; and the **political** <note>original: πολιτικόν; the "civic" religion actually practiced and enforced by the laws of cities</note>, which is upheld by the laws and maintained in every city and country. Two of these parts have already been explained by us in the preceding books: the historical part, which they call "mythical" or "theoretical" (or whatever else they may enjoy naming it). It is now time to filter through the third part in the present work. This is the religion established throughout cities and countries, which they call "political," and which is defended most strongly by the laws. They claim it is both ancient and ancestral, and that it demonstrates its own virtue through the power of those who are worshiped as gods. 

Indeed, they boast of their celebrated **oracles** <note>original: μαντείαι; the various sites, such as Delphi, where gods were believed to speak to humans</note> and divine responses, the cures and healings of all kinds of diseases, and the punishment of the impious. Claiming to have experienced these things firsthand, they have thoroughly convinced themselves to honor divine things and to act justly. They accuse us, however, of the greatest impiety, because we hold such visible and benevolent powers in no regard. They claim we are outright lawbreakers, arguing that every person ought to worship their ancestral traditions and "not move that which is fixed" <note>This was a common Greek idiom (μὴ κινεῖν τὰ ἀκίνητα) meaning that one should not disturb ancient, settled traditions or laws</note>, but rather follow and walk in the piety of their forefathers, and not meddle through a love of innovation. For this reason, they say that the laws have justly appointed the penalty of death for those who commit such an offense. 

Now, the first form of theology—the historical and mythical—was left to the poets to arrange as they pleased. Likewise, the second form—the philosophical—was refuted by showing it was merely a more "natural" allegory for the myths. But this third form, which has been legislated by rulers as something both ancient and political, they say should be honored and guarded; neither poet nor philosopher, they claim, should disturb it. Let the ancient customs prevail in both the countryside and the cities, with everyone remaining obedient to the laws of their fathers.

It is time, therefore, to provide our own response to these claims, and to make a **defense** <term>apologismos</term> <note>original: ἀπολογισμόν; a formal legal or logical defense of one's position</note> for our Savior’s **Gospel** <note>original: εὐαγγελικῆς πραγματείας; literally "Gospel business" or "the matter of the Gospel"</note> which proclaims the opposite of these things and sets its own laws against the laws of the nations. It has already been made clear to them that lifeless statues are not gods. It was shown in the first book that the contents of their mythical theology carry nothing dignified or worthy of God. Similarly, in the second and third books, it was shown that the philosophical and "natural" interpretations of the myths do not provide a logical or unforced explanation. Come then, let us consider this third point: what exactly we should think about the "powers" that lurk within the statues. Are they truly good, as if they were actually gods, or is the reality the exact opposite of this? It is clear that as I proceed with the argument regarding these matters...

### PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 6

->PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 6<-

...[he] <note>Likely referring to Oenomaus of Gadara, a Cynic philosopher whose critique of oracles Eusebius is citing</note> assumed that these things were the schemes and frauds of sorcerers <note>original: γοήτων; here meaning charlatans or magicians who deceive for profit</note>, altogether stripping away their reputation. He argued that one should not believe the rumors about them as being from a god, nor even from a wicked spirit <note>original: δαίμονος</note>. For he claimed that the poems and the compositions of the oracles were not the work of unskillful men, but were fabrications carefully contrived to deceive. They were composed in a middle-ground and ambiguous <note>original: ἀμφιβόλῳ; double-meaning</note> manner so as to fit either of the expected outcomes of an event, and they were quite cleverly adapted. Furthermore, the "miracles" that deceive the masses were actually dependent on natural causes. 

For there are many kinds of roots, herbs, plants, fruits, and stones—both dry and liquid powers of all sorts of matter found in the nature of the universe. Some are repellent and drive things away, while others are naturally inclined to attract and bind. Some have the power to separate and scatter, and others to thicken or dissolve. Others can loosen, moisten, and provide dew, or again cool and release; still others can kill or turn a crowd, and alter the present state of things. Sometimes they change things in one way, sometimes in another. Some do this for a long time, others for a short duration. Again, some are powerful enough for a large number of people, while others affect only a few. Some of these lead the way, followed by others, running together with one another, coming to life or decaying together. 

Indeed, there are even certain productive seasons, not far removed from the science of medicine <note>original: ἰατρικής</note>. Other things are found to be sickly or poisonous. Furthermore, certain natural necessities occur, waxing and waning with the moon. There are a thousand antipathies among animals, plants, and roots, and many types of fumigations <note>incense used in rituals</note> that are generally sleep-inducing, while others produce varied visions. 

The locations and the places in which these events are performed contribute not a least bit to the effect. Mechanical tools and hollow vessels <note>original: σκάφη; could also refer to basins or types of acoustic devices used to throw voices</note> are prepared long in advance, suited to their craft. Many accomplices in this sorcery are brought in from the outside, who pry into the business of those who arrive and find out the specific needs for which someone has come to ask. Many secret sanctuaries <note>original: ἄδυτα; "the unenterable" inner rooms of temples</note> and corners inaccessible to the public are hidden within the temples, and the darkness itself provides no small assistance to their underlying plot. Not least of all is the staged hypocrisy itself, the superstition <note>original: δεισιδαιμονίαν; literally "fear of spirits"</note> of those who approach them as if they were gods, and the opinion handed down to them by their ancestors. 

To this, let us add the stupidity of the minds of the many, the weakness of reasoning, and the lack of critical examination among the masses. On the other hand, consider the cleverness and malicious ingenuity of those who spend their lives in this evil-minded practice—the deceptive and villainous nature of the sorcerers, who promise each person what they want to hear and treat the present moment with fair hopes. They guess at the future and play the prophet concerning the unknown. They obscure the meaning of the oracles with ambiguities of speech and unclear language so that no one can understand what was prophesied, and by the obscurity of what was said, the oracle escapes being proven wrong. 

Many things also occur through certain deceptions and wonders, with incantations <note>original: ἐπωδῶν</note> being included in the proceedings along with some unintelligible and barbaric <note>original: βαρβαρικῆς; meaning non-Greek, often used in magic to sound more ancient or mystical</note> pronunciation. By these means, things that are not at all brought about by them seem to be done with great effort. Most of all, the masses, starting from their education, are struck by the poetry of the oracles, which is beautifully adorned by the arrangement of the words and the grandeur—

# EUSEBIUS

->PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 6<-

...[of gran]diloquence <note>original: λοφωνίας; likely a continuation of a word meaning high-crested or grand speech</note>, puffed up with a weight of arrogance and a great deal of boastful pride. These fabrications of so-called "divine inspiration" were signaled through ambiguous speech <note>original: ἀμφιβόλου φωνῆς; a technical term for 'amphiboly' or double-meaning sentences like 'I know that you the Romans shall conquer'</note>, which almost always deceived the common people with a display of wealth. Indeed, whenever they managed to escape the trap of ambiguity in their oracles, it was not because they had any foreknowledge of the future, but rather because they had hit upon the truth through a kind of "guesswork." 

One could find thousands—or rather, almost all—of these prophecies frequently failing and falling short. The outcome would turn out either the opposite of what was predicted, or would take a turn that required a complete re-interpretation <note>original: παραμυθίας; here meaning a comforting explanation or 'spinning' of a failed prediction</note>. It was only on those rare occasions where, out of ten thousand instances in a city, a prediction happened to coincide with reality by some accidental stroke of luck <note>original: συντυχικήν</note> or through a shrewd guess about what might happen, that everyone then considered the oracle to be true. This is what they chatter about most of all in private, delighting in rumors and shouting it to the ends of the earth. 

They choose to never mention the countless times they were mistaken; but because once in ten thousand times some prediction happened to come true, they carry that success up and down as if it were a great marvel. It is as if someone were to play with two copper tokens <note>original: χαλκίουσιν; likely referring to a game of chance similar to dice or 'heads or tails'</note> out of ten thousand, and if once, by some coincidence, he happened to get the same result, he should marvel at it as if he had predicted the number through prophecy and foreknowledge! This is exactly how it is: when ten thousand things are predicted ten thousand times, one of them will eventually happen to come true by sheer chance. 

Anyone who looks into this and possesses even a little depth of soul would be stunned by the oracle—for it would have been much better if he had not behaved so foolishly as to ignore how these oracles have been the causes of death, civil unrest <note>original: στάσεώς</note>, and wars. If one examines the histories of the ancients, they will see that the oracles never demonstrated any act of virtue, even when the art of divination was at its peak and things were going as they wished. 

But now these oracles no longer exist, even though they were once deemed worthy of every care and diligence by the locals—those who worshiped and served them according to ancestral laws and mysteries. Their powerlessness was utterly exposed, especially during the calamities of war. In those times, when the "noble" prophets <note>original: θεοπρόποι; a sarcastic use of the term for those who speak for the gods</note> were unable to help, they were caught playing word-games <note>original: σοφιζάμενοι</note> with those who fled to them for refuge by using the ambiguity of their oracles. 

As we have shown at the appropriate time, the oracles actually pushed those who consulted them into wars against one another. They did not provide answers that offered any real comfort to virtuous people; instead, they played games through their prophecies, mocking those who asked questions. In the darkness of their obscurity, they hid their own ignorance. 

Consider also those who consulted them about illness: the priests often promised health, life, and safety to the sick. Having been believed as if they were gods, and having charged high fees for this "divine" expertise, it was not long before they were caught. They were exposed as charlatans <note>original: γόητες; often used to describe street-magicians or fraudulent sorcerers</note> and men, not gods, when no favorable outcome reached those they had deceived. Why even mention that these wonderful "seers" provided no help even to their own neighbors—those living in the very same city? They themselves lived in houses with people who were sick, suffering, and whose entire bodies were maimed in countless ways. If they ever offered "fair hopes" to those arriving from abroad or from far away, they certainly did not do so for their own neighbors. To these neighbors, above all others, they should have provided the "good" from the gods' providence, as they were their own friends and fellow citizens. But they knew they could deceive strangers who were ignorant of their trickery <note>original: ῥᾳδιουργίας; literally 'easy-working' or sleight of hand</note>, whereas they could not deceive their daily companions, who were familiar with their...

<meta>catchword: ...art/craft (τέχνης)</meta>

<summary>Eusebius (quoting Oenomaus) argues that oracles are not divine but are based on linguistic ambiguity and the law of averages. He points out that priests often failed to help their own neighbors, proving they were merely charlatans profiting from strangers.</summary>
