# EUSEBIUS

->PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 4<-

...not inexperienced in the art, being accomplices in the play being performed. Thus, the fire was not divine, nor superior to human invention. So that even in the greatest calamities—those brought directly by God, the King of All, against the impious—their very offerings and wooden statues <note>original: ξοάνοις; ancient wooden cult images believed to have fallen from heaven</note> underwent ultimate destruction, and their temples suffered a sudden collapse. 

For where is the temple in Delphi, sung of by all and famous from of old? Where is the Pythian? The Clarian? Where is the one at Dodona? Report has it that the Delphic oracle was completely burned by the Thracians; the oracle was unable to contribute anything toward knowing the future, or even to protect its own property. History records that the Capitol in Rome <note>The religious center of Rome, home to the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus</note> suffered the same fate during the times of the Ptolemies. During those years, it is said that the temple of Vesta in Rome also endured being burned. 

Around the time of Julius Caesar, the great Olympian statue of the Eleans—which was in Olympia itself <note>The Statue of Zeus at Olympia, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World</note>—was struck by lightning by God and shattered. And they say again that the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol was burned; and long before that, it was destroyed by lightning. Similarly, the Serapeum in Alexandria was consumed by fire. 

One must seek the reasons for these things in the myths. It would be a long story if one tried to enumerate everything in detail to show that these wonderful oracle-givers were caught being unable to defend even their own temples. Those who are useless to themselves when calamities strike would hardly be able to help others. 

Beyond what has been said, a most important point would be observed: that even those who were excessively "god-possessed"—the most high-ranking hierophants <note>original: ἱεροφαντῶν; those who "show the sacred things," the high priests</note>, theologians, and prophets—not only long ago, but recently in our own time, being brought to trial for this "divine wisdom," confessed the whole error of men, the deceptions of the race, and the contrived sorcery, after being subjected to the torture of the rack in Roman courts. They gave a full confession. They even recorded all the details of the construction and the methods of their evil-craft in their own unsparing accounts. Having paid the penalty for their destructive error, they uncovered the whole story, confirming the proof of what was revealed by their very deeds. 

Do not think these were some outcasts or obscure people; they were those who started from this "wonderful" and "naked" philosophy, wearing the philosopher’s cloak <note>original: τρίβωνα; a coarse garment worn by Cynics and Stoics to show their rejection of luxury</note> and raising an unusual eyebrow <note>A common Greek idiom for intellectual arrogance or "looking down one's nose" at others</note>. Some were caught from among the leading men of the city of Antioch. These were the ones who distinguished themselves by insulting us during the persecutions. We also know of the philosopher and prophet who suffered similar things in Miletus. 

Anyone gathering more evidence than this would say they are not gods, nor even demons, who are the causes of the oracles in the cities, but rather the error and deception of sorcerous men. And even among them, there were already distinguished philosophical sects supporting this view: the followers of Aristotle and all the Peripatetics in succession, the Cynics, and the Epicureans. I especially marveled at these men—how, having been raised in their own customs from their very cradles, and having understood that everything said to be "gods" among them was nothing else but robbers. But even that man, and the famous oracles, and the divinations sought after by all...

# EUSEBIUS

<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

<margin>
Preparation,
Book 4,
Chapter 10
</margin>
...they proved that these oracles bring nothing of the truth, and declared them to be useless—even rather harmful. Since they are merely a memory of things past, and have caused many people to fall into the deception of oracles, I think it suffices for me to mention what has been said for the present. I shall meet the arguments of one of these men against the constructions of Chrysippus <note>Chrysippus (c. 279–206 BC) was a leader of the Stoic school who famously argued that because oracles could predict the future, a fixed "Fate" must exist.</note> regarding fate <note>original: εἱμαρμένη / heimarmene; the Stoic concept of a pre-determined, causal chain of events</note> based on the predictions of oracles. The author writes against him, proving that he wrongly uses oracles as evidence for fate, that the oracles of the heroes lie in most cases, that it is impossible for them to be anything more than a coincidence, and that their predictions are useless and harmful. Listen to his exact words:

---

->From the writings of Diogenianus: that their divination <note>original: μαντική / mantike</note> is for the most part false and inconsistent, and that their predictions are useless and harmful.<-

---

<margin>F</margin> Come now, let us look at another proof in the aforementioned book. For they <note>The Stoics</note> do not say that the predictions of the seers are true unless all things were contained within the scope of fate. This claim itself is full of much absurdity. It is as if it were self-evident that all the predictions of the so-called seers turn out true, or as if anyone would grant this—that everything happens according to fate—and not rather say that the claim is equally false. This is clear—I mean the fact that not all predictions come to pass. Rather, actual experience demonstrates that most of them fail. 

This is the proof Chrysippus has brought us, establishing each point by the other <note>This is a critique of circular reasoning: Chrysippus uses Oracles to prove Fate, but then uses Fate to explain why Oracles work.</note>. If he wants to show that everything happens according to fate because divination exists, he would not be able to demonstrate that divination exists unless he first assumed that everything happens according to fate. What more wretched method of proof could there be than this? 

For the fact that some things predicted by seers turn out true in practice is not a sign of the science <note>original: ἐπιστήμη / episteme; a systematic body of knowledge</note> of divination, but of outcomes coinciding by chance with the predictions. This indicates no "science" to us. For we would not call an archer "skilled" <note>original: ἐπιστήμονα / epistēmona</note> who hits the target once by luck but misses many times. Nor would we call a man a doctor who kills most of those treated by him but happens to save one person once. In general, we do not call anything a "science" that does not succeed in all, or at least most, of its own proper works. 

That the so-called seers fail most of the time is witnessed by the whole life of men, and even by those who profess the art of divination themselves. They do not help themselves through this art in the needs of daily life; instead, they use their own judgment, or seek the advice and cooperation of those considered to have experience in each matter. But concerning the inconsistency of this thing which we have called "the noble art of divination," we will provide a fuller account elsewhere, quoting the views of Epicurus <note>Epicurus (341–270 BC) was a philosopher who rejected divination and fate, teaching that the gods do not involve themselves in human affairs.</note> on this subject. For now, we add this much: if the so-called seers ever speak truly in their predictions, it is the result of chance, not of science. For success is not a matter of "never hitting the mark," but rather it is not "science" when one hits it only occasionally by luck, rather than always or for the most part.

<summary>Eusebius quotes the philosopher Diogenianus to attack the Stoic belief in fate, arguing that oracles are not a "science" because they fail more often than they succeed, making their occasional hits mere coincidences.</summary>
<keywords>Chrysippus, Fate, Divination, logic, circular reasoning, Diogenianus, Epicurus, science vs. chance</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical critique of Stoic logic. Having established that the Stoics use the existence of oracles to prove the existence of Fate, Eusebius (via the writer Diogenianus) now argues that even if oracles were true, they would be completely useless and psychologically harmful to humanity.</meta>

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 6

<header>EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 6</header>

> „ It is a fine thing to seize upon the work at hand, especially for those who have accurately defined the clear concepts assigned to every name. Next, even if we grant for the sake of argument that the art of divination <note>original: μαντική / mantike</note> regarding the human future is indeed both a theoretical and a predictive science, and if all things were to happen according to Fate <note>original: εἱμαρμένη / heimarmene</note>, we must still investigate it in this way. If, however, there is something useful or beneficial for life in it, that has never yet been shown. This is the very reason why Chrysippus <note>A famous leader of the Stoic school who argued that since gods can predict the future, the future must be fixed by Fate.</note> seems to champion divination so strongly.
> „ For what benefit would it be to us to learn beforehand of those hardships that are absolutely going to happen, which it would be impossible to even guard against? For how could anyone guard against things that happen according to Fate? Therefore, divination is of no benefit to us; rather, it would even result in some evil, providing people with a reason to grieve in advance <note>original: προλυπεῖσθαι / prolypeisthai</note> for no purpose over the difficulties that have been predicted and will necessarily occur.
> „ For no one can say that the prediction of future good things provides an equal amount of joy. This is because a human being is not naturally inclined to rejoice over expected goods as much as they are inclined to grieve over expected evils. Furthermore, we do not even fully expect that these good things will actually happen to us until they are delivered. But we expect good things even when they are absent, so to speak, because of our natural affinity <note>original: οἰκείωσιν / oikeiosin</note> toward them.
> „ Indeed, the masses even hope for things greater than what is possible to happen. From this, it follows that the prediction of good things does not increase our joy very much at all. This is because, even without a prediction, everyone expects the better outcome for themselves, or they only increase their expectation slightly due to the perceived certainty of the oracle. Often, it even diminishes the joy, whenever someone hears that the reality will be worse than what they had hoped for.
> „ But the prediction of evils—because of their naturally repulsive character and because they are sometimes expected against one's hopes—would cause great disturbance. Nevertheless, even if one does not perceive this happening, the prediction will still be useless, for a reason that should be clear. For if someone says that the utility of divination is preserved because a predicted hardship (which will certainly happen) can be avoided if we guard against it, then he no longer shows that all things happen according to Fate, since it would be 'up to us' <note>original: ἐφ’ ἡμῖν / eph’ hemin; a technical term in Greek philosophy for free will or agency</note> whether to guard against it or not.
> „ But if someone considers this, saying that Fate extends to all things that exist, then once again the utility of divination is destroyed. For we will guard against it if it has been predicted, and we will not guard against it if it has not been predicted; clearly, we will not guard against it even if all the seers predict the future to us.
> „ At any rate, Chrysippus himself says that Oedipus <note>The mythical King of Thebes who unknowingly killed his father and married his mother despite prophecies.</note> and Alexander the son of Priam <note>Also known as Paris; it was prophesied he would cause the destruction of Troy, so his parents exposed him as an infant, but he survived.</note> were the subjects of many schemes by their parents to kill them, so that they might guard against the evil predicted through them—yet they were unable to do so. Thus, he says there is no benefit even to them from the prediction of evils, because of the cause stemming from Fate. Let this be said, then, as a surplus of argument, to show that divination is not only groundless but also useless.

And indeed, given how much truly "wonderful" things are rumored about the miracle-working of the oracles, it was likely that even these people would have been struck with awe, being foolish and accurately knowing their ancestral traditions, and placing nothing worthy of knowledge in a secondary position. # EUSEBIUS
<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

...preparation of the argument concerning the oracles, there was a very great abundance of material. But it does not seem to me right to proceed with the argument in this way now, but rather to begin from the things they themselves have set forth and start by speaking the truth. Granting to those who stand as their champions that—based on what is admitted among them—there are true oracles, and that the things revealed are divinely-inspired prophecies <note>original: θεοπρόπια / theopropia</note> given by Pythian Apollo <note>The "Pythian" refers to the oracle at Delphi, the most famous prophetic site in the Greek world.</note>, we might learn to understand the exact nature of the things revealed by their manifestation.

## That the Gospel teaching of our Savior has freed us from the greatest of these very evils.

I think it is clear to everyone that the refutation of the matters before us occupies not a small, but a very great and most necessary part of the Gospel purpose. For consider those before the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ: all Greeks and barbarians everywhere supposedly knew the true God, yet they either glorified things that do not exist as if they did, or they were dragged here and there like blind men by the subjection to wicked and god-fighting spirits—evil and impure demons—and were dragged down into a depth of evil. Indeed, what were they but demon-possessed? 

How could the great mystery of the Gospel dispensation <note>original: οἰκονομίας / oikonomias — referring to God's organized plan for human salvation</note> not be seen as even greater, when all people from everywhere have been called back from their ancient, ancestral error and the tyranny of demons through the voice of our Savior? And how could it not be seen as great that the people dwelling even to the ends of the earth have been ransomed from the deception that has cursed their entire lives from ages past? 

Consequently, from that time until now, the ancient foundations of the nations' fruitless error, along with their very temples and wooden idols <note>original: ξοάνοις / xoanois — ancient, often wooden, cult images</note>, have been dissolved and torn down. Instead, truly venerable shrines and schools of piety have been raised up throughout the whole world, in the midst of cities and villages, by the power and virtue of our Savior, dedicated to the King of all and Creator of the universe. Divine sacrifices have been purified of all wickedness through holy prayers, practiced in the tranquility of the soul and the attainment of every virtue. These divine and saving teachings are carried out daily and continually from the secret places of the nations—teachings which are the only true virtues and are sacrifices pleasing to the God over all. 

Since these things are so, how could we not have given a good account of ourselves? For we have become "apostates" from ancestral superstition with self-control and order, and not by yielding ourselves to irrationality. Rather, by a just and true judgment, we have loved what is better and become lovers of God and true piety. But enough of these matters; we must now touch upon the subjects at hand.

## What is the division of theology according to the Greeks.

Those who have precisely examined Greek theology, and who divide the whole discourse into four parts—doing so in ways other than those we have previously mentioned—set apart the "First God." They say they know him to be the one who is first over all, the supreme God, both Father and King. After him, they say the Sun exists as a second god, followed by the order of demons <note>original: δαιμόνων / daimonōn</note>, and fourthly, that of the heroes <note>In Greek religion, "heroes" were divinized mortals who received cult worship.</note>. All these participate in the "Form of the Better"; in one way they are led, and in another they lead, and they are called "light" because of their participation in Light. However, they also speak of an essence of a worse kind, which they say should be considered "evil."

<summary>Eusebius argues that the triumph of Christian teaching over demonic pagan oracles is proof of the Gospel's divine power, and he begins a systematic classification of Greek theology into four ranks: the First God, the Sun, demons, and heroes.</summary>

# GOSPEL PREPARATION, BOOK 4

<margin>And this would be</margin>
And this would be a vile race of demons, in no way maintaining friendship with the Good, yet possessing a surplus of power within the nature of opposites, for according to those who are superior, so is God. But from where is such darkness named? Having thus partitioned the universe by location, they say that the heaven and the **ether** <note>The "ether" was considered the pure, upper atmosphere where the gods lived, distinct from the denser air near Earth.</note> as far as the moon are assigned to the gods; the regions around the moon and the air to the **demons** <note>original: δαίμοσι / daimones — In Greek thought, these were intermediate spirits, not necessarily evil, but Eusebius is refuting this neutral view.</note>; and the regions around the earth and the underworld to **souls**. 

Using such a definition, they say that first of all, one must worship the celestial and etheric gods. Second, the good demons. Third, the souls of the **heroes**. Fourth, they say one must appease the base and wicked demons. While they divide these by theory, in practice they throw everything into confusion, worshiping only the wicked powers among all those mentioned—or rather, they are enslaved to them—as the proceeding argument will prove. Indeed, you have before you the powers operating through the **images** <note>original: ξοάνων / xoanon — specifically referring to ancient wooden cult statues believed to have fallen from heaven or possess divine power.</note>; you must consider from what is said here what kind they should be declared to be—whether gods or demons, and whether base or good. 

For our divine oracles <note>A common term Eusebius uses for the Holy Scriptures.</note> do not know how to call a demon "good" at all. They hold that all who have shared in this word and title are wicked, just as they hold there is no other truly and properly God except the One who is the Cause of all. As for the invisible and good powers—since they are kind by nature and perform many services for the unbegotten God who is their creator, and because they are distinguished by nature from the vile nature of demons—the Scripture does not deign to call them either gods or demons. Being intermediate between God and demons, it is accustomed to name them by a favorable and middle-ground title: **angels of God** <note>The word "angel" (angelos) literally means "messenger."</note> and **ministering spirits**, divine powers and archangels, and other titles named according to their duties. 

As for these "demons": if we must examine their etymology, it is not as it seems to the Greeks—deriving from being "knowing" <note>original: δαήμονας / daemones — meaning wise or skilled</note>—but rather from "fearing" <note>original: δειμαίνειν / deimainein</note>, which means to be terrified and to strike fear; thus they are appropriately named "demons." For this reason, the good powers, as they belong to God, do not share in this demonic title. Indeed, it would be the most irrational thing of all to deem those who are alike neither in their purpose nor in their nature from God worthy of one and the same name.

Though there are countless writers and philosophers among the Greeks, I judge that one above all is suitable for the task: that "friend of demons" himself, who lived in our own time and testified against us with false speeches. For he is considered a most significant philosopher among our opponents, even by the demons and those he calls gods, with whom he claims to have conversed; they say he was their ambassador and has articulated the facts about them with great accuracy. # EUSEBIUS

<page-num>84</page-num>

...a convoluted path <note>original: σκόλιον / skolion — this can mean a "crooked" path or a complex song; here it refers to the confusing nature of pagan arguments about oracles.</note> regarding the subject of oracles, where there was much idle talk. But I do not think I should conduct the current argument in this way. Instead, I shall start from the very things they believe to be true. By granting the claims of their own ambassadors—as if agreeing with their own admissions—that prophecy is real and that the declarations revealed by the **Pythian** <note>Referring to the Oracle of Delphi, associated with Apollo the "Pythian."</note> are divine, we may then learn the exact nature of what is being revealed.

## How the Gospel teaching of our Savior has freed us from these very greatest of evils.

I think it is clear to everyone that the refutation of the matters before us is no small part, but rather a very great and necessary part of the Gospel's purpose. For if those who lived before the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ—both Greeks and barbarians alike—were proven to have known the true God but instead honored things that do not exist as if they did, they were like blind men tossed here and there by the influence of winged, wicked, and god-fighting spirits, and by evil and unclean **demons** <note>original: δαιμόνων / daimones — In this context, Eusebius views these not just as "spirits" but as malicious entities.</note>, rolling themselves in a depth of malice. And what was this but a form of demonic possession? 

How then could the great mystery of the Gospel **dispensation** <note>original: οἰκονομίας / oikonomia — the divine "plan" or "management" of human history by God.</note> not be seen as a greater thing? It has called everyone from every direction away from ancient, ancestral error and the tyranny of demons through the voice of our Savior. It has ransomed people living even at the ends of the earth from the deception that has held all of life captive since time began. 

Consequently, from that time until now, the ancient foundations of the vast error of the nations have been dissolved and torn down, along with their temples and **wooden cult images** <note>original: ξοάνοις / xoanois — ancient, often primitive wooden statues believed to have divine power.</note>. In their place, truly sacred schools of piety dedicated to the King and Creator of all things have been raised in the midst of cities and villages throughout the entire world by the power and virtue of our Savior. Daily, from among all nations, sacrifices worthy of God—purified of all malice through the prayers of holy people, in a state of soul free from passion and full of every virtue, according to divine and saving teachings—are continually performed. These are the only sacrifices that are truly pleasing and acceptable to the God who is over all.

Since these things are so, how can it not be reasonably concluded that we have not abandoned our ancestral superstition through some mindless impulse or irrationality? Rather, we have become apostates from that error by a just and true judgment, having loved what is better and become lovers of a divine and true piety. But enough on these matters; let us proceed to the rest of the subjects before us.

## What is the division of theology according to the Greeks.

Those who have precisely examined Greek theology divide their entire discourse into four types, differing from the methods we mentioned previously. First, they set apart the "First of the First" as God; they say he is the one who is first over all, the God of all, both Father and King. After him, they say there is a second race: that of the gods. Following this is the race of **demons**. The fourth is that of **heroes**. 

They claim that all these participate in a superior form—partly angelic, partly ruling—and are simply called "light" due to their participation in Light. But they also speak of a substance of a worse kind, which they say is evil.

# GOSPEL PREPARATION BOOK IV 85

This malicious race of demons, being in no way a friend to what is good, has been allotted a primary power in the nature of opposites—just as God is primary among superior beings. Again, this sort of power is referred to as **darkness**. Let these things define their place: they say that the heavens and the **aether** <note>original: αἰθέρα / aithera — the "upper air" or "fifth element" thought to be the substance of the stars and the home of the gods.</note> reaching down to the moon are assigned to the gods; the regions around the moon and the air to the demons; and the regions around the earth and the underworld to souls.

Having made such a distinction, they say that first of all, one must worship the heavenly, divine, and ethereal gods. Second, the good demons. Third, the souls of heroes. Fourth, they say one must **propitiate** <note>original: ἀπομειλιώσασθαι / apomeiliosasthai — to appease or soothe the anger of a spirit through sacrifice.</note> the base and wicked demons. But while they divide these things in theory, in practice they throw everything into confusion, worshipping only those wicked powers mentioned, or becoming entirely enslaved to them, as the following argument will prove. Indeed, you may now consider the powers operating through the **cult statues** <note>original: ξοάνων / xoanon — specifically ancient, often wooden, carved images of deities.</note>, and what sort they ought to be declared—whether gods or demons, and whether base or good—based on what has been said before.

For our own **divine oracles** <note>Referring here to the Christian Scriptures.</note> do not know how to name a "demon" as something good at all. They hold that all who bear this title are wicked, even if they have somehow shared in the name, so that the term now properly signifies nothing else. Instead, they recognize only the one Cause of all things. As for the starry and good powers—being limited in nature and falling far short of the God who is the maker of both them and us—the scriptures do not see fit to call them either gods or demons, as they are distinct from the malicious race of demons. Rather, being intermediate between God and demons, the scriptures usually name them with a well-advised and middle-ground title: **messengers of God** <note>original: ἀγγέλους θεοῦ / angelous theou — the word "angel" literally means messenger.</note> and **ministering spirits** <note>original: πνεύματα λειτουργικά / pneumata leitourgika.</note>, as well as divine powers and **archangels**, and other titles named after their specific duties.

As for the **demons** <note>original: δαίμονας / daimones</note>—if it is appropriate for us to examine the etymology of this word—it is not as the Greeks believe (derived from being "knowledgeable" or "skilled"), but rather from the word meaning **to terrify** <note>original: δεμαίνειν / demainein — Eusebius is proposing a Christian folk-etymology here to link demons with fear rather than wisdom.</note>, which is to be afraid and to cause fear; thus they are fittingly called "demons." For why should the good powers, like God himself, receive a title associated with demonic absurdity? Indeed, it would be the most irrational thing of all to grant one and the same name to beings who are similar neither in their purpose nor in their God-given nature.

# EUSEBIUS

...he wrote concerning the *philosophy derived from oracles* <note>original: ἐκ λογίων φιλοσοφίας / ek logion philosophias — This refers to a famous (and now mostly lost) work by the Neoplatonist Porphyry where he tried to find a consistent theology in traditional oracles.</note>, making a collection of the responses given by Apollo and the other gods and "good spirits." He selected these specifically because he believed they were sufficient both to demonstrate the excellence of their theology and to encourage what he personally likes to call **theosophy** <note>original: θεοσοφίας / theosophias — literally "divine wisdom," a term Porphyry used to describe a spiritual path through pagan ritual and philosophy.</note>. From these oracles that were approved and deemed worthy of record, it is perhaps good to distinguish and examine what kind of power they actually possess. First, let us observe how the man mentioned above, at the beginning of his writing, swears that he is indeed telling the truth, speaking as follows:

->Concerning the secrets revealed by oracles from the ethical tradition.<-
->And the oath concerning the oracles, from the writings of Porphyry.<-

> The one who hopes is certain and steady, being attached to the hope of gaining knowledge from the only steady source; to such a person, you shall grant a share, though you must reveal these things to no one else. For I myself call the gods to witness that I have neither added nor taken away anything from the meaning of what was prophesied—unless perhaps I corrected a mistaken word, or changed a phrase for the sake of clarity, or filled in a missing foot in the poetic meter, or deleted something that did not contribute to the main purpose. In this way, I have preserved the pure mind of what was said, fearing the **impiety** <note>original: ἀσέβειαν / asebeian — "unholiness" or "irreverence" toward the divine.</note> of doing otherwise more than the punishment that Justice exacts for **sacrilege** <note>original: ἱεροσυλίας / hierosylias — literally "temple-robbing" or the theft/violation of sacred things.</note>.
> 
> What follows in this collection will seem to contain a great deal of philosophical teaching, according as the gods have decreed it useful to possess. We shall also touch briefly upon the practice of oracle-giving, which will be of benefit both for contemplation and for the purification of life. The benefit of this collection will be best known by those who, being in the "birth-pangs" of seeking the truth, have prayed that they might obtain a manifestation from the gods to find rest from their doubt through the reliable teaching of those who speak.

Having used these introductions, he calls upon witnesses and gives a warning that no one should reveal what is about to be said to the masses, speaking as follows:

->That one must not reveal what is said to everyone.<-

> And you, if you ever make use of these things, try not to make them public, nor cast them even before the **profane** <note>original: βεβήλων / bebelon — the uninitiated or those who have not been purified for religious secrets.</note> for the sake of reputation, or profit, or any other ignoble flattery. For there is a danger—not only to you if you transgress these commands, but also to me for easily trusting one who could not keep these secrets within himself. These things must be given only to those who have set their lives toward the salvation of the soul.

And after other things he adds:

> Keep these things hidden for me, as the "most secret of secrets." For even the gods did not prophesy concerning them openly, but through riddles.

Since the discourse has made such lofty claims, come now, let us finally examine through these "divine" and "Python-given" <note>original: πυθοχρήστων / pythochreston — referring to the Pythia, the priestess of Apollo at Delphi.</note> oracles what kind of invisible powers these "theologized" beings ought to be considered. For a man may be judged by his own words and practices. Now, this man mentioned above, in the very works he titled *On the Philosophy Derived from Oracles*, includes oracles of Apollo that command the performance of **animal sacrifices**. And he commands to sacrifice animals not only to spirits or to the earthly powers, but also to the **ethereal** and **heavenly** ones.

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Eusebius introduced Porphyry’s work "On the Philosophy to be Derived from Oracles," noting that Porphyry claimed to be recording these divine responses faithfully. # PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 8

In other passages, this same author—while admitting that all those to whom the Greeks performed sacrifices involving blood and the slaughter of irrational animals are **daemons** <note>original: δαίμονας / daimonas — In Greek thought, these were intermediary spirits, but Eusebius uses this admission to argue they are not true gods.</note> and not gods—asserts that it is neither necessary nor holy to sacrifice living creatures to the gods. Listen, then, to his own excellent words, through which he collected the teachings of the *Philosophy from Oracles*, and see how Apollo teaches the proper way to serve the gods. Porphyry writes as follows:

### How Apollo commands the worship of the gods through sacrifices.

<margin>A</margin>
Following what has been said concerning piety, we shall now record what he prophesied regarding their worship, parts of which we have already cited in the section on piety. The oracle of Apollo contains a classification of the orders of the gods:

> "Work, my friend, upon this god-given hymn unto the end,
> and do not forget the sacrifices for the blessed ones, by slaughtering them.
> To the terrestrial, to the celestial, and then to the kings
> of the ether itself and of the moist-pathed air,
> and to the marine and the subterranean ones as well.
> For the nature of these beings receives a sweet appeasement,
> from as many animals as it is lawful to kill for purifications.
> I shall sing it; carve my oracle upon your tablets:
> Triple sacrifices for the terrestrial, and six for the celestial gods.
> Bright things for the celestial, but for the terrestrial, things of a different color.
> For the subterranean ones, again performing triple sacrifices,
> bury them deep, and pour the blood into a pit.
> Pour honey for the nymphs, and the gifts of Dionysus <note>Dionysus’s "gifts" refers to wine.</note>.
> For all those who are forever wandering around the earth,
> fill the altar with a pyre and satiate it with fire.
> Throw the body into the fire after sacrificing a winged creature,
> and having mixed it with divine barley meal,
> add the fragrance of incense and sacrificial grains.
> And when you go to the sands by the gray sea, 
> sacrifice from the head, and into the deep wave of the sea
> cast the whole animal; having finished all these things,
> go to the wide aerial dance of the heavenly ones.
> Then for the star-gods and all the inhabitants of the ether,
> let the blood from the throats flow in streams around the sacrificial offerings,
> but let the limbs be prepared for the gods for a feast.
> Let the extremities be shaken with fats, and let the rest
> be tasted, filling the surging air with savory vapors. 
> And then send up your prayers to these."

And after a few words, he explains the oracle, interpreting it thus: "The sacrifices have this form, being assigned according to the aforementioned division of the gods. For there are subterranean and terrestrial gods; the former are called the 'nether ones' <note>original: νερτερίων / nerteriōn</note>, and the latter are named the 'earthly' gods. He commands that black, four-footed animals be sacrificed to both of these in common, but he differentiates the method of sacrifice. For the terrestrial, he commands slaughtering upon altars; for the subterranean, over a pit. Furthermore, he commands that the victims sacrificed to these latter ones be buried. That the four-footed animals are common to both was confirmed by the god when he was asked, adding:

> "These things are common to the subterranean and the terrestrial:
> four-footed animals, and the newly-fashioned earth of lambs <note>This likely refers to young lambs or specific earth-rituals involving them.</note>."

To the aerial gods, he commands the sacrifice of birds as whole burnt offerings, encircling the altars with the blood. To the sea gods, he likewise commands birds, but these are to be released alive into the waves, and they must be black in color. For he says:

> "To the gods, birds; but to the sea-gods, black ones."

By saying "to all the gods" he means birds are for all except the terrestrial; but only for the sea gods are they black. Therefore, for those that are manifest <note>Likely referring to the visible celestial bodies.</note>, they should be white. For the celestial and etheric gods, he commands that the extremities of the victims—which must be white—be consecrated.

86 EUSEBIUS

He wrote concerning the philosophy derived from oracles, making a collection of the responses of Apollo and the other gods and good spirits <note>original: δαιμόνων / daimonon — while often translated as "demons" in a Christian context, here it refers to the intermediary spirits of Neoplatonic thought.</note>. Having selected these especially, he considered them sufficient both for a demonstration of the virtue of theology and for the refutation of "theosophy"—as he likes to call it. It is perhaps good to distinguish right away from these selected and noteworthy oracles, as they deliver their prophecies, and to examine what kind of power they happen to possess. But first, let us see how the man mentioned above, at the beginning of his writing, actually swears to tell the truth, saying as follows:

### On the secrets to be kept concerning the oracles, from the ethical collection. And the oath concerning the oracles, from the works of Porphyry.

> Firm and stable is he who hopes, being fortified in his hopes for help from the only Stable One <note>original: μόνου βεβαίου / monou bebaiou — referring to the unchanging nature of the Divine.</note>. To such people you shall impart these things, revealing them to no one else. For I call the gods to witness that I have neither added nor taken away anything from the meanings of the oracles, except where I corrected a mistaken word, or changed it for the sake of greater clarity, or filled in a deficient meter, or deleted something that did not contribute to the purpose. 
> 
> Thus, I have preserved the pure sense of the words, fearing the impiety resulting from such things more than the justice following the punishment for temple-robbery <note>original: ἱεροσυλίας / hierosylias — sacrilege or the stealing of sacred objects.</note>. This present collection contains a record of many philosophical doctrines, as the gods decreed the truth to be. We shall also touch briefly on the practice of oracles, which will be of benefit both for contemplation and for the purification of life. Those whom this collection has benefitted in practice will especially know—those who, being in labor for the truth, once prayed that by obtaining a divine manifestation from the gods, they might find rest from their perplexity through the trustworthy teaching of the speakers. 

Using such introductions, he calls the gods to witness and issues a warning that no one should reveal what is to be said to the many, saying as follows:

### That one must not reveal what is to be said to everyone.

> You, then, if anyone else, try not to make these things public, nor to throw them even to the uninitiated <note>original: βεβήλων / bebelon — the "profane" or those outside the sacred mysteries.</note> for the sake of reputation, or profit, or any other shameful flattery. For there is danger, not only for you who violate these commands, but also for me who easily trusted one who could not keep these emanations as a private delight. They must be given to those who have established their lives toward the salvation of the soul. 

And after other things, he adds: 

> Hide these things from me, as the most secret of secrets. For not even the gods decreed clearly concerning them, but through riddles. 

Since the discourse has made such claims, come now, let us examine through his own oracles given by the Pythian <note>The Pythian Apollo, the voice of the Oracle at Delphi.</note> what kind of things those invisible powers spoken of in theology should be considered. For a man’s refutation can come from his own words and practices. Now, the man mentioned above, in the very works he titled *On the Philosophy from Oracles*, includes oracles of Apollo commanding that sacrifices of animals be performed. And he commands to sacrifice animals not only to spirits, nor only to the earthly powers, but also to the ethereal and heavenly ones.

## How Apollo commanded that the gods should be served through sacrifices.

<margin>A</margin>
> Following what has been said concerning impiety, we should record what he prophesied regarding their service—parts of which we have already set forth for those who philosophize on piety. This is the oracle of Apollo, which also contains a division of the gods according to their rank: "Labor, O friend, entering upon this god-given path, and do not forget the sacrifices of the blessed ones, slaying them—for some, the terrestrial <note>literally "those upon the earth"</note>, for others, the celestial, and sometimes for the kings of the air and the moist-pathed atmosphere, and for all those submerged in the sea. For all things are contained within the fullness of nature. For the animals, it is the law to die as purifications. I shall sing, and you must carve my oracle upon tablets: Three for the terrestrial gods, and three for the celestial. Bright offerings for the heavenly ones, but for the gods of the earth, offerings of a different color. From the gods of the earth, remove the sacrificial victims as you slay them; bury those of the underworld, and pour the blood into a pit. Pour libations for the nymphs, and gifts for Dionysus. For all those who forever haunt the earth, fill the altar with the blood of a final fiery sacrifice, cast the body well into the fire after sacrificing a winged animal, and having sprinkled honey with thirsty barley-meal, add the fumes of frankincense and sacrificial grains. And when you are upon the shining shores or pouring into the grey sea, sacrifice from the head, and cast the whole animal into the deep wave of the sea. Having completed all these things, go to the broad requirement of the airy dwellers in heaven. Then, for all the starry and ethereal ones, let the blood from the throats stream around the sacrificial offerings in containers. The earth <gloss>is not</gloss> burdened by the feast for the gods; give the extremities of the holy offerings <gloss>as a gift</gloss>, and taste the rest yourselves, filling all the rushing air with the sweet-smelling vapors. Send these to the gods upon the sacrificial embers." And after a few words, he explains the oracle, interpreting it as follows: "The sacrifices have this form, issued according to the aforementioned division of the gods. For there are gods of the underworld and gods of the earth; those of the underworld are called 'subterranean,' while those on the earth are called 'terrestrial.' To both of these, he commands the common sacrifice of black four-footed animals. But he changes the style of the sacrifice: for the terrestrial gods, he commands slaughtering upon altars; for the subterranean, he commands a pit. Indeed, he also commands the burying of the bodies of those sacrificed to the latter. That the four-footed animals are common to both, he himself added when questioned: 'Common to the subterranean and terrestrial are these things alone: four-footed animals, and the newly-planted earth of the oaks.' For the gods of the air, he commands the sacrifice of birds as whole burnt offerings, leading the blood around the altars. For the sea gods, he commands birds, but to let them go alive into the waves, being black in color. For he says: 'To the gods, the winged things, but to those of the sea, the black ones.' By saying 'to all the gods' he means the winged things, except for the gods of the earth. But only for the sea gods does he specify the black ones. Therefore, for the gods of the air, the white ones. For the celestial and ethereal gods, one should dedicate the extremities of the sacrificial victims, provided they are white."

### That they cannot be gods who rejoice in sacrifices of animals.

Come now, compare his own contradictory voices, which he set down in his writings concerning the *Abstinence from Animal Food*. There, moved by right reasoning, he confesses first of all that one should not offer anything at all—not even incense—to the God over all. Furthermore, he says this applies even to the divine and celestial powers that come after Him. Then, proceeding further, he pulls down the common assumptions of the many, claiming that one must not suppose those who rejoice in sacrifices of animals to be gods. 

For he says, first, that the slaughter of animals <term>zoothutein: the ritual killing of living beings</term> is most unjust, unholy, defiled, and harmful; and for this reason, it is not pleasing even to the gods. In saying this, he would clearly be refuting his own god. For he just recently attached a prophecy—as he said—commanding that animals be sacrificed not only to the gods beneath the earth and upon the earth, but also to those of the air, the heavens, and the aether. 

And while Apollo says such things, Porphyry, calling Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle who wrote on piety</note> as a witness, says that animal sacrifice is not appropriate for gods, but only for spirits <note>original: δαίμοσι / daimones — intermediary spirits, often viewed as lower or malevolent in Christian thought</note>. Thus, according to the reasoning of both himself and Theophrastus, Apollo is a spirit, but not a god. Furthermore, this applies to all those who are considered gods among all the nations, to whom all leaders and subjects alike, throughout cities and countrysides, perform animal sacrifices in public. For one must not think these beings are anything other than the aforementioned spirits. 

If they say these spirits are "good," how could they be good if the sacrifice of blood is unholy, defiled, and harmful? And if they say they do not only rejoice in such sacrifices, but also—through an excess of cruelty and inhumanity—take pleasure in the slaughter of men and human sacrifices, how could they not be bitter and murderous, characterized by every kind of cruelty and inhumanity, and nothing other than evil spirits? Having obtained proof of these things, I believe a reasonable explanation has been given for our withdrawal from these practices. For it is neither holy, nor pious, nor right to cast down the title of "Venerable God" and the highest honor upon evil spirits—nor to assign the royal dignity that belongs to all mankind to robbers and tomb-robbers. Hence, we alone have been taught to worship the God over all, and to honor as is fitting both the...

h.iii.

...around Him are God-loving and blessed powers. We bring nothing earthy or dead, neither gore nor blood, nor anything derived from corruptible and material substance. Instead, with a mind purified of all wickedness, and a body clothed in the ornament of purity and self-control—which is more radiant than any garment—and with right and God-befitting doctrines, and above all these, with sincere truth, we pray to preserve that piety handed down by our Savior <note>original: Σωτῆρος / Soteros — referring here to Jesus Christ</note> even unto death. But since we have already distinguished these matters, it is time to proceed to the proofs of what has been said. First of all, let us go through the discourse which Porphyry wrote in his work titled *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, where he says that one ought not to offer anything earthy, nor burn incense, nor sacrifice, either to the God over all or to the divine powers that come after Him. For such things are foreign to the piety that is fitting.

### That nothing from the earth should be used for the God over all, neither incense nor sacrifice.

To the God who is over all, as a certain wise man said <note>Eusebius likely refers here to Apollonius of Tyana, whom Porphyry quotes</note>, we should offer nothing perceptible by the senses, neither burning incense nor calling Him by names. For there is nothing material that is not immediately impure to the Immaterial. For this reason, even the spoken word <note>original: λόγος / logos — here meaning the physical "sound" or "speech"</note> is not appropriate for Him, nor even the internal word when it is defiled by the passion of the soul. Rather, let us worship Him through pure silence and pure thoughts about Him. It is necessary, therefore, that having been joined to and made like Him, we should offer our own "ascent" <note>original: ἀναγωγήν / anagogen — a philosophical lifting up of the soul</note> as a holy sacrifice to God; this same act being both a hymn and our salvation. In the passionless state of the soul and the contemplation of God, this sacrifice is perfected.

### That it is not fitting to offer incense or sacrifice anything of the earth even to the divine powers.

To His offspring, the intelligible gods <note>original: νοητοῖς θεοῖς / noetois theois — the "intellectual" or "spiritual" deities in the Neoplatonic hierarchy</note>, one must now add the hymnody of reason. For sacrifice is the first-fruits <note>original: ἀπαρχὴ / aparche</note> of each thing He has given, through which He nourishes us and holds our substance together in being. Just as a farmer offers first-fruits of the sheaves and the fruit of the trees, so let us offer to them the first-fruits of our thoughts, giving thanks for the beautiful things they have given us the ability to contemplate. And because they truly nourish us through the vision of them, being present with that which is manifest and shining upon our salvation. These are his words. And kindred and related to these things concerning the Great God are the following, which that same Pythian Apollo—so celebrated by the many—is said to have written in his responses concerning sacrifices.

### From the [writing] concerning the fact that one must not offer anything of the earth to the God over all.

In this way, therefore, I think one might best provide the proper care for the Divine, and would immediately find Him gracious and favorable: if to the God who is One—whom we said was the First and separate from all, after whom the others must be recognized—one should not sacrifice anything at all, nor light a fire, nor name Him by any sensible thing. For He is in need of nothing, not even from those who are better than we are. Nor is there anything which the earth produces as a plant, or nourishes as a living creature, or even the air itself, which is not a defilement <note>original: μίασμα / miasma</note> to Him. Rather, let one always use the better reason <note>original: λόγῳ / logo</note> toward Him—I mean the one that does not pass through the mouth. And from the most beautiful of beings, through the beauti—

<margin>3</margin>
> As the practice of human offerings <note>original: ἀπαρχῶν / aparchon — literally 'first-fruits' or initial offerings</note> moved far away from their original purpose, a lawlessness involving the most terrible rages was introduced, full of cruelty. It seems that the curses I mentioned earlier have now reached their fulfillment, with men slaughtering animals and staining the altars with blood. This began when, having experienced famines and wars, they first laid hands on blood. Therefore, as Theophrastus says, the **Divinity** <note>original: τὸ δαιμόνιον / to daimonion — a general term for the divine power or providence</note>, being indignant at both of these things, seems to have imposed a fitting punishment. Consequently, some men have become **godless** <note>original: ἄθεοι / atheoi</note>; others might more justly be called "evil-minded" or even **"evil-godded"** <note>original: κακόθεοι / kakotheoi</note>, because they believe the nature of the gods is base and no better than ourselves. Thus, some appeared to be "non-sacrificers," while others were "evil-sacrificers," laying hands on offerings in an unlawful manner.

> Again, after some other remarks, the same author says: Since these things are so, Theophrastus rightly forbids those who wish to be **pious** <note>original: εὐσεβεῖν / eusebein — to show proper religious devotion</note> from sacrificing **living beings** <note>original: τὰ ἔμψυχα / ta empsycha — literally 'ensouled things'</note>, using such reasons as these. He adds: "Furthermore, one ought to sacrifice those things which, when sacrificed, will harm no one. For a sacrifice, above all else, must be harmless to everyone." But if someone should say that God gave us the animals for our use no less than the fruits of the earth, it does not follow that we should desire to bring harm to the animals by depriving them of their **soul** <note>original: ψυχῆς / psyches</note>. Therefore, these should not be sacrificed. For a sacrifice is, according to its very name, something **holy** <note>original: ὁσία / hosia</note>. But no one is holy who pays back favors using things that belong to others—even if he takes fruits or plants against the owner's will. For how can it be holy when those who are deprived are treated unjustly? If a person who takes the property of others is not sacrificing holily even when using fruits, then it is certainly not holy to sacrifice by taking away the most precious thing an animal possesses <note>its life</note>. Indeed, the dreadfulness of the act is greater. The soul is much more precious than the things that grow from the earth, and it is not proper to take it away by sacrificing animals.

> And he adds: "One must therefore abstain from animals in sacrifices." And again he says: "That which is neither holy nor inexpensive should not be sacrificed." And following this: "So, if it is necessary to kill animals for the gods, for what purpose should they be sacrificed?" For if we sacrifice them for some reason, would the gods—or we—consider it an **honor** <note>original: τιμῆς / times</note> when we are shown to be acting unjustly toward the animals through our offering? Or would they rather consider such an act a dishonor? In these cases where we admit to doing wrong by killing animals that have done no harm, we should not sacrifice any of the other living beings for the sake of honor. Nor, indeed, should we do so as a way of returning thanks for benefits received. For one who gives a just return for a benefit or a kindness ought not to provide this by doing evil to someone else. He will no more be seen to be making a return than if he were to rob his neighbor and then crown someone as a way of returning thanks and honor. Neither should we sacrifice for the sake of some future good. For he who hunts for a future favor through an unjust deed is suspected of not being truly grateful for what he has already received. Thus, one must not sacrifice animals to the gods even in the hope of a benefit. For even if the lot of humanity—

### EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 4

...just as someone might perhaps act toward you. But it is impossible to escape the notice of God. If, therefore, one must not sacrifice for any of these reasons <note>referring to the previous arguments that God lacks nothing and cannot be bribed</note>, and if it should not be done for the sake of any of these things, it is clear that the sacrifice of animals is not something pleasing to the gods. And again he adds: "For nature and the entire human sense of the soul were in agreement with the things being done. **The altar was not wetted with the pure slaughter of bulls, but it was still the greatest pollution among men to eat the sturdy limbs after tearing out the life.**" <note>original: Ταύρων δ' ἀκηράτοισι φόνοις... — Eusebius is quoting the philosopher-poet Empedocles, who believed that the Golden Age involved only bloodless offerings</note> 

And after other remarks: "When a young man learns that the gods rejoice in lavish expenses and, as they say, in the feasts of oxen and other animals, when would he ever choose to be temperate? And how could he not believe it is permissible to act unjustly, thinking that he can sacrifice these things to the gods as a favor and at least buy his way out of his sin through the sacrifice?" 

But if he is persuaded that the gods have no need of these things, and instead look toward the character of those who approach them—receiving as the greatest sacrifice a correct understanding about themselves and their affairs—how could he not be temperate, just, and holy? To the gods, the "first-fruit" <note>original: ἀπαρχὴ / aparche — the traditional first portion of a harvest or sacrifice</note> should be a **pure mind** <note>original: νοῦς καθαρὸς / nous katharos</note> and a **soul free from passion** <note>original: ψυχὴ ἀπαθής / psyche apathes</note>. It is also appropriate to offer "first-fruits" of other modest things, not in an over-elaborate way, but with all readiness of heart. For these honors should resemble the marks of respect shown to good men—such as giving up a seat or standing up—rather than the payment of a tax.

Clearly, through these arguments, it has been admitted both by the Greeks and by their philosophers that no living creature should be sacrificed to the gods without reason. For the practice is ill-omened, unjust, and harmful; it is an unholy pollution. 

Therefore, it was not a god, nor any truthful and good spirit <note>original: δαίμων / daimon — a supernatural being, not necessarily evil in a Greek context, but here Eusebius is distinguishing them from the true God</note>, who was the "giver of oracles" who a little while ago was demanding libations of blood and the smell of roasting meat. Nor were those entities gods, for whom the oracle commanded the sacrifice of animals. It must be said, then, that the falsehood belongs to wandering, deceitful, and outright wicked spirits, who have insulted both gods and spirits by commanding the sacrifice of animals not only to the gods of the earth, but even to the heavenly and astral gods. 

Who then are these beings, if it is not appropriate to consider them all as the aforementioned gods? The author himself will explain this through the following words:

---

-> **That the sacrifices offered among them are made to demons and not to gods.** <-

---

If anyone cares for piety, they would recognize that no living creature is sacrificed to the gods, but rather to spirits—whether to good ones or even to base ones. They would also recognize who it is that performs these sacrifices, and that they are those who stand in need of some useless thing. And again, he says in sequence: "That they offered the sacrifices of blood not to gods, but to demons, was understood by those who studied the powers in the universe; this is confirmed by the **theologians** <note>original: θεολόγων / theologōn — here referring to ancient poets and philosophers like Orpheus or Hesiod who wrote about the origins of the gods</note> themselves." 

Furthermore, he states that some of these spirits are malevolent and others are good, and that they will not trouble us. This is what the aforementioned author said. But since he claimed that some demons are good and others are base, come now, let us see how it can be proven that not even those considered "good" are such, but that all their acknowledged gods are caught being base. You may find the proof of this in the following way: 

That which is good provides benefit, while its opposite causes harm. But if those who are proclaimed as gods or spirits in every place are talking nonsense—even those who are shouted about by everyone and worshipped by the nations of men, such as **Kronos** and **Zeus**, **Hera** and **Athena**, and those like them—as well as the unseen powers and the spirits that work through animals, who rejoice not only in the slaughter and sacrifice of irrational animals, but even in the slaying of men and **human sacrifice** <note>original: ἀνθρωποθυσίαις / anthropothysiais</note>, and in this way they [harm] the souls...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument in the *Evangelical Preparation*. Having used the pagan philosopher Porphyry to argue that animal sacrifice is unnecessary and even harmful, Eusebius now transitions to his most shocking evidence of "demonic" influence in the pre-Christian world: the widespread practice of human sacrifice. He argues that if philosophers find animal blood offensive to true divinity, then human blood must be the ultimate "pollution," proving that the ancient gods were actually malevolent spirits.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

...harming those wretched men. Could one conceive of a worse harm than this? For if the sacrifice of irrational animals has been proved by the philosophers to be accursed and ill-omened—foul, unjust, and unholy, and not even harmless to the sacrificers, but in every way unworthy of the gods—what must we think of the slaughter of human beings? How could such a thing ever be considered most pious or holy? Is it not reasonable to say that such a practice is dear not to good spirits, but to all-polluted and wicked spirits?

Come then, let us examine and demonstrate how much the ruinous error of evil spirits dominated human life before the Gospel teaching of our Savior. This error was seen to cease and be wiped out once and for all around the time of Hadrian <note>Hadrian ruled from 117–138 AD; Eusebius marks this as the era when Christian influence began to noticeably end ancient "barbaric" rituals</note>, when the teaching of Christ was already shining like a light upon the whole world. 

To prove this, we will not use our own words, but the voices of those who do not share our faith. They will testify explicitly, accusing the times before that of such great wickedness that the human condition surpassed even the bounds of superstition. Men were driven mad and possessed by destructive spirits, believing they could appease bloodthirsty powers through the blood of their dearest ones and countless other human sacrifices. A father would sacrifice his only-begotten son, or a mother her beloved daughter, to the demon. Those dearest to them would slaughter their own kin as if they were nothing more than cattle or foreign livestock. Indeed, cities and whole countries sacrificed their fellow citizens and neighbors, sharpening their compassionate human nature into something cruel and inhuman, displaying a truly insane and demonic character.

I shall pass over the general history of how some sacrificed their sons, some their daughters, and others even themselves to these demons. Instead, I will bring forward a witness from among those very authors who, in the same works where he forbade the sacrifice of irrational animals as unholy and most unjust, spoke these words verbatim:

---

### Concerning ancient human sacrifice, from the writings of Porphyry and others.

And we say this not simply, but because history is full of such accounts; these examples should suffice to prove the point. 
> In **Rhodes**, in the month of Metageitnion <note>An Attic month corresponding roughly to August/September</note>, on the sixth day, a human being used to be sacrificed to **Kronos**. This custom, which prevailed for a long time, was later changed: they would keep one of those who had been publicly condemned to death until the festival of the *Cronia*. When the festival arrived, they led the man outside the gates, across from the shrine of Aristoboule <note>original: "the seat of Aristoboule," referring to a temple of Artemis "of the Good Counsel"</note>, and after giving him wine to drink, they slaughtered him. 

> In what is now **Salamis** (but was formerly called Coroneia), in the Cypriot month of Aphrodisios, a human was sacrificed to **Agraulos**, the daughter of Cecrops and the nymph Agraulis. This custom continued until the times of Diomedes; then it changed so that the human was sacrificed to **Diomedes** himself. The temple of Athena, the temple of Agraulos, and that of Diomedes are all within a single enclosure. The victim, led by young men, would run three times around the altar. Then the priest would strike him in the stomach with a spear, and in this manner, they would burn him whole <term>holocaust</term><note>meaning "burnt whole" (Greek: holokautizon)</note> upon a prepared pyre. 

> This law was abolished by **Diphilus**, the King of Cyprus, who lived during the times of Seleucus the Theologian. He changed the custom to the sacrifice of an ox, and the spirit <term>daemon</term><note>The Greeks used "daemon" for any spirit; Christians like Eusebius used it to mean "demon" or evil spirit</note> accepted the ox in place of the human.

<summary>Eusebius argues that human sacrifice was a widespread demonic practice before Christ, citing Porphyry's accounts of rituals in Rhodes and Cyprus to prove that ancient religions were bloodthirsty.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s compilation of evidence regarding human sacrifice in the ancient world. Following the introduction, he cites various historical authorities—including Manetho, Philo of Byblos, and Porphyry—to document specific instances where humans were slaughtered to appease ancient deities, arguing that these practices only ceased with the rise of Christianity and the reign of Hadrian.</meta>

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION
## Book 4

...willingly; such is the weight of this widespread report. Furthermore, Amosis <note>Amosis I, founder of the 18th Dynasty of Egypt</note> abolished the law of human sacrifice in the Egyptian city of Heliopolis, as witnessed by Manetho in his work *On Antiquity and Piety*. Previously, these victims were sacrificed to Hera and were examined for purity, just as the special calves used for sacrifice are inspected and marked with a seal. Three people were sacrificed each day. In their place, Amosis ordered that three wax figures of equal size be offered.

Human sacrifices were also performed on the island of Chios to "Raw-eating" Dionysus <note>original: "Διονύσῳ ὠμαδίῳ" (Dionysō omadiō), a title for Dionysus reflecting a primitive and wild nature</note>, where the victim was torn limb from limb. The same occurred in Tenedos, according to Anticleides of Carystus. Apollodorus records that even the Spartans sacrificed a man to Ares. 

The Phoenicians, in times of great calamity—whether war, plague, or drought—would sacrifice one of their dearest loved ones to Cronus <note>The Greek equivalent of the Phoenician god El or Baal</note>, chosen by a public vote. Phoenician history is full of such sacrifices. Sanchuniathon wrote about this in the Phoenician language, and Philo of Byblos translated his work into Greek in eight books. Likewise, Istros, in his *Collection of Cretan Sacrifices*, states that the Curetes <note>Mythological guardians of the infant Zeus on Crete</note> anciently sacrificed children to Cronus. 

Pallas, who compiled the best account of the mysteries of Mithras, states that human sacrifices were abolished almost everywhere during the reign of the Emperor Hadrian. Before that time, in Laodicea in Syria, a virgin was sacrificed to Athena every year; now, however, a deer is sacrificed instead. Furthermore, the Carthaginians in Libya performed this sacrifice until Iphicrates and Doumates put an end to it. 

The inhabitants of Arabia used to sacrifice a child every year and bury him beneath an altar, which they treated as a sacred cult image. Phylarchus records that it was a common custom among all Greeks to commit manslaughter [human sacrifice] before going out to face an enemy. He mentions this was done recently by the Thracians and Scythians, and recounts how the Athenians put the daughter of Erechtheus and Praxithea to death. 

Even now, who is unaware that in the "Great City" <note>likely referring to Rome, or a major center of the cult of Zeus Laphystius</note> a man is slaughtered at the festival of Zeus Laphystius? And again he says: 

"From then until now, not only in Arcadia at the Lycaean festivals, nor in Carthage for Cronus, do they all publicly perform human sacrifice, but periodically, for the sake of preserving the legal memory of the rite, they continue to sprinkle the blood of their own kind upon the altars."

Let these accounts from the previously mentioned writings suffice. However, I will also provide the following from the first book of Philo’s *Phoenician History*: 

"It was a custom among the ancients, during great and dangerous calamities, for the rulers of a city or nation to give up their most beloved child for slaughter as a ransom to the avenging spirits <note>original: "τιμωροῖς δαίμοσι" (timōrois daimosi)</note>, so that the entire population might avoid destruction. Those given up were slaughtered in a mystical rite. Thus Cronus—whom the Phoenicians call Israel <note>A controversial identification in the text linking the mythological Cronus/El with the biblical patriarch Israel</note>—who was king of the land and was later consecrated as the star of Saturn after his death, had a unique son by a local nymph named Anobret. They called this son Ieoud <note>A Phoenician term related to the Hebrew 'Yachid', meaning 'only-begotten'</note>, a name still used by the Phoenicians for an only-begotten son. When the greatest dangers from war had overtaken the land, Cronus dressed his son in royal robes, prepared an altar, and sacrificed him."

This, then, was the nature of those ancient practices. It is with good reason that the wonderful Clement, in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*, laments this multitude of human sacrifices and rebukes these very things, saying: 

"Come then, let us add this: how inhuman and misanthropic your gods are! Not only do they rejoice in the mental delusions of men, but they even take pleasure in human slaughter. Now they find occasions for their own pleasure in the armed rivalries of the stadiums, and now in the calculated ambitions of wars, ensuring that as much as possible..."

These are the very sacrifices that Euripides dramatizes on the stage <note>A reference to the play *Iphigenia in Tauris*</note>. Anticleides, in his *Returns*, reveals that the Lyctians—a nation of Cretans—slaughter humans to Zeus. And Dosidas says that the Lesbians offer a similar sacrifice to Dionysus. 

» Nor should we pass over the Phocaeans; Pythocles, in his fourth book *On Harmony*, records that they offer a human as a burnt sacrifice to Artemis Tauropolos <note>original: "τῇ ταυροπόλῳ ἀρτέμιδι"; an epithet of Artemis associated with bulls or foreign lands</note>. Erechtheus the Athenian and Marius the Roman both sacrificed their own daughters. Erechtheus offered his to Pherrephatta <note>A variant name for Persephone, queen of the underworld</note>, as Demaratus records in his first book of *Tragedies*. Marius sacrificed his to the "Averting Gods" <note>original: "τοῖς ἀποτροπαίοις" (tois apotropaiois); deities invoked to turn away evil</note>, as Dorotheus records in the fourth book of his *Italian History*. 

» How "loving of humanity" these demons must be! And how can you not, by the same logic, blame the superstitious? Those who praise these beings as "saviors," yet ask for "salvation" from those who plot against them through sorcery. They think they are performing "fair offerings" by handing themselves over to these "bandits" and slaughtering fellow humans. This was not a "sacrifice" in the way a horse might be slaughtered. Even if someone slaughters a human for Artemis or Zeus in what is supposedly a "sacred" place, it is no different than doing so out of anger or greed; they are being slaughtered for equally savage demons on altars or in the streets, even if the act has been given a "sacred" name. Such a sacrifice is nothing but murder and manslaughter. 

» Why is it then, O humans—who are supposed to be the wisest of all unreasoning animals—that we flee from wild beasts? If we ever encounter a bear or a lion, we avoid it. 
*As when a man sees a snake in a mountain glen and shrinks back, and trembling seizes his limbs, and he withdraws.* <note>A famous simile from Homer's *Iliad* (3.33-35)</note> 
Yet, when it comes to destructive and accursed demons—who are plotters, haters of humanity, and bringers of ruin—you do not avoid them or turn away, but instead rush toward them and sing their praises. 

» These are the words of Clement. 

One may also cite another testimony regarding the bloodthirstiness of these godless and inhuman demons: Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a man who wrote an accurate account of Roman history. He writes, word for word, about those who were once commanded by Apollo to perform human sacrifices. When they were asked, they sacrificed a tenth of all their crops and livestock to the gods; but because they did not also sacrifice humans, they fell into many great disasters. It is best to hear the historian himself describing it in this way: 

» "Only a small portion of the Aborigines <note>The earliest inhabitants of central Italy</note> remained in Italy through providence. The earth, afflicted by drought, seemed to suggest the ruin of their households, so that no seasonal fruit remained on the trees, but fell off while still green. Whatever seeds sent up shoots and began to bloom failed to complete their natural cycles of growth. No lush, well-watered grass grew for the cattle, and of the springs, some were no longer fit to drink, others failed during the summer, and others were completely extinguished. Similar things happened regarding the offspring of sheep and women. Either the embryo was miscarried, or it perished during birth..."

» ...carrying life-destroying pollution. If any child managed to escape the danger of the birth-pains, it was born crippled or incomplete, or damaged by some ill-fortune; it was not considered profitable to rear them. Furthermore, the rest of the population, especially those in the prime of life, were afflicted by diseases and deaths that were frequent beyond all expectation. When they consulted the oracle <note>original: "μαντευομένοις" (manteuomenois); seeking divine guidance from a prophet or shrine</note> to ask which of the gods or spirits they had offended to suffer such things, or what they might do to hope for a relief from these terrors, the god replied that although they had obtained what they desired, they had not paid what they had vowed, but were holding back their most valuable possessions. 

» For the Pelasgians <note>An ancient group of people who inhabited the Aegean region before the Classical Greeks</note>, during a time of total barrenness of the land and all its resources, had vowed to Zeus, Apollo, and the Cabiri <note>original: "καϐείροις" (Kabeirois); mysterious underworld deities worshipped in Samothrace and elsewhere</note> that they would sacrifice a tenth part <term>tithe: a "decate" or ten-percent offering given to a deity</term> of all their future increase. Once their prayer was fulfilled, they set aside a portion of all their crops and livestock and sacrificed them to the gods, as if they had only made their vow concerning these things. 

» Myrsilus of Lesbos <note>An early Greek historian and chronicler</note> has recorded these events, writing in almost the exact same words as I am now using, except that he says these things were done not by the Pelasgians, but by the Tyrrhenians <note>The Greeks' name for the Etruscans of Italy</note>. I will explain the reason for this a little later. 

» When the oracle was brought back and they learned its meaning, they were unable to understand what was being said. In their helplessness, one of the elders spoke up, having grasped the meaning: he said they had entirely missed the point if they thought the gods were making an unjust accusation against them. For while the first-fruits of their goods had been paid correctly and justly, the "portion of humans"—the most precious of all things to the gods—was still owed. If they would give the gods their rightful share of these as well, the prophecy would be fulfilled. To some, this seemed to be the correct interpretation; to others, the argument seemed like a conspiracy. 

» When someone suggested they should ask the god if it was his pleasure to receive a tithe of human beings, they sent messengers <term>theopropoi: official legates sent to consult an oracle</term> a second time, and the god replied that they should do so. During this time, a civil conflict <note>original: "στάσις" (stasis)</note> broke out among them regarding the method of selecting those for the tithe. Those who governed the cities were the first to be thrown into turmoil with one another. Then the rest of the multitude began to suspect those in power. 

» The uprisings occurred without any order; as was likely, people were driven by frenzy and divine madness. Many entire households were wiped out as a portion of them migrated away. The relatives did not think it right to be abandoned by their loved ones, while some remained behind with their worst enemies. First, those who moved away wandered through much of Italy and both Greek and barbarian lands. After the first group, others suffered the same fate, and this continued to happen for years. For the rulers in the cities did not cease selecting the first-fruits from the youth as they reached manhood, claiming they were performing what was just for the gods, but also fearing the spasms of civil discord. 

» Meanwhile, many were driven out by their rivals under a fair-sounding pretext due to long-standing hatreds. Thus, many uprisings occurred, and the Pelasgian race was scattered over the greatest part of the earth. And a little later [Myrsilus] says: they say that these sacrifices were performed to Cronus <note>Identified by the Romans as Saturn</note> and the ancients, just as the practice persisted in Carthage as long as that city remained, and as it remains among the Celts to this day. And among certain nations of the West, they still commit human slaughter. 

» They say that Heracles <note>The hero Hercules</note> ended this law of sacrifice, wishing to establish an altar upon the Saturnian hill and to begin sacrifices of holy offerings consumed by purifying fire. In order that the people might have no fear in their hearts for having ignored their ancestral sacrifices, he taught the locals to appease the wrath of the god by using [effigies] instead of humans...
