Binding their feet and rendering them useless for the land, they used to cast them into the stream of the Tiber. They made man-like effigies <note>original: "εἴδωλα... ἀνδρείκελα" (eidōla andreikela); life-sized puppets or figures made of straw</note>, decorated in the same manner as those victims had been. They threw these into the river so that the intended benefit—the same kind performed for the "averting" spirits <note>Deities or spirits invoked to turn away evil or bad luck</note> of the demons—might be achieved, while still preserving the memory of the ancient suffering through these images. The Romans continued to do this even until my time, shortly after the spring equinox in the month of May, on the day called the Ides, choosing the day of the <margin>if</margin> full moon. On this day, after offering sacrifices according to the laws, those called the Pontiffs <note>original: "ποντίφικες" (pontiphikes); the most high-ranking priests in ancient Rome</note>—who are the most distinguished of the priests—along with the virgins who guard the immortal fire [the Vestal Virgins], as well as the generals and other citizens permitted by sacred law to attend, take thirty effigies shaped like humans and throw them from the Sacred Bridge <note>The Pons Sublicius, the oldest bridge in Rome</note> into the current of the Tiber, calling them "Argives" <note>original: "Ἀργείους" (Argeious); likely referring to the *Argei* ritual</note>. Diodorus also records similar things in the twentieth book of his *Library of History*. He writes about the Carthaginians <note>Ancient inhabitants of Carthage in modern-day Tunisia</note> being besieged by Agathocles, the tyrant of Sicily, after the death of Alexander the Macedonian, writing the following word-for-word:

> They also blamed Kronos <note>The Greek name for the Phoenician god Ba'al Hammon, often identified with the Roman Saturn</note> for being against them. Whereas in former times they used to sacrifice the best of their sons to this god, they had later begun secretly buying children and raising them to be sent for sacrifice. When an investigation was held, it was discovered that some of those who had been sacrificed were substitutes <note>original: "ὑποβολιμαῖοι" (upobolimaioi); "supposititious" children, or those secretly swapped to spare the noble families' own offspring</note>. Realizing this, and seeing the enemy camped at their walls, they were filled with superstitious dread, believing they had abolished the traditional honors of the gods. Eager to correct their errors, they selected two hundred of the most distinguished children and sacrificed them publicly. Others, who were under suspicion, gave themselves up voluntarily, numbering no less than three hundred. There was among them a bronze statue of Kronos, with its hands extended palms-up and sloping toward the ground, so that the child placed upon them would roll off and fall into a certain chasm full of fire.

Such are the things he handed down through his own history. Appropriately, then, the Hebrew Scripture also rebukes those of the Circumcision <note>The Jewish people</note> who imitated such things, saying: *And they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons, and the land was defiled with blood. And the land was polluted by their works.* [Psalm 106:37-38]. Indeed, I believe it has been clearly proven through these accounts that the most ancient and primary establishment of the "gods," and all the idol-worship of the nations, was demonic—originating not from good spirits, but from those who are utterly wretched and wicked. This confirms the truth of the prophetic word: *All the gods of the nations are demons.* [Psalm 96:5]. And the Apostolic word says: 

> *What they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God.* [1 Corinthians 10:20].

For if there were any goodness in them—such that they deserved to share in the name of the "Good"—if they were beneficial, kindly, and a savior of all, a friend of justice and a protector of mankind; if they were such, how could they rejoice in the slaughter of humans? Why did they not use their oracles to forbid the human race from doing such things? Truly, they were worse and more base than humans, who, through the care of laws, established themselves as free from these blood-stained pollutions. For it was not a god, but a human, who over time dissolved the long-standing disease of human sacrifice. That these practices belonged to base and evil demons would be even more evident if one considers the...

### EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 4

...of their unspeakable and unbridled prostitution; that which is still performed today in Heliopolis <note>original: "ἡλίου πόλει" (Heliou polei); the 'City of the Sun,' likely Baalbek in modern Lebanon</note> of Phoenicia, and among many other nations. Indeed, they say that they are required to fulfill acts of adultery, seduction, and other unlawful unions in honor of the gods, as if it were a debt owed to them. They offer the first fruits of this adulterous and prostituted labor to the gods, dedicating the profits of this inglorious and unholy commerce as if it were some kind of good thank-offering for their crops. For these things are similar to human sacrifices. If, therefore, it is not characteristic of even a self-controlled man to delight in murders, foul language, and the unlawful unions of women who sell their beauty for a price, I would say it is far from being the nature of gods—or even of good demons—to accept such things. 

But if someone were to say that these are admittedly the works of wicked demons, yet there are others who are good, whom one ought especially to worship as saviors, then where—I ask—where were their good saviors? If they also ate from the sacrifices, why did they not keep the wicked ones from committing such acts against those who sought refuge in them? Where are the good demons to drive away the harmful ones and to fight alongside those who serve them? Or did they overlook the rational and god-beloved race of men while they were being worn down by the cruelty of wicked demons? Did they not openly proclaim to everyone to flee without turning back, and to turn away from the so-called "vile god," as if he were not a god at all, but a wicked demon who happens to love cruel, unspeakable, unlawful, and shameful things? 

If there was a god formerly presiding in Rhodes <note>A major Greek island and center of culture</note> who delighted in human sacrifices, the True God would have proclaimed to all that this was not a god, but a wicked demon, had anyone then been able to restrain such a practice. Or likewise in Salamis—the city formerly called Coroneia—where a man was sacrificed during the month of Aphrodisius <note>The month dedicated to Aphrodite, roughly equivalent to April</note> according to the Cypriot calendar. The True God would have revealed that this, too, was an accursed demon, putting an end to what was being done as something impious and unholy. 

And if, in the Heliopolis of Egypt, Amosis <note>Ahmose I, the pharaoh who founded the 18th Dynasty and expelled the Hyksos</note> abolished the law of human-slaying, the True God would have taught that the man [Amosis] had become much better than that "god." For that being who presided over human-slaying was not a god, but once again a demon. For the True God would not have legislated that the demon of Tyras <note>original: "Τυρᾶς" (Tyras); possibly referring to a Thracian deity or a specific regional spirit</note> should be considered anything other than a vile being—the one to whom history records that three men were sacrificed every single day. 

Truly, what could be more demonic than the one called Dionysus Omadios <note>original: "ὠμαδίου διονύσου" (ōmadiou dionysou); 'Dionysus the Raw-Eater,' a primitive and violent aspect of the wine god</note>? They say that in Chios <note>An island in the Aegean Sea</note> they used to sacrifice a man to him by tearing him to pieces. It was the same in Tenedos, where they also used to appease him through human sacrifice. The True God would also have forbidden the sacrifice of a man to Ares among the Bruttians <note>original: "βρεττοῖς" (brettois); an ancient people of Southern Italy, though sometimes used for Britons</note>, that war-loving demon. He would have legislated that they should not slaughter their dearest ones, whether kin or strangers. For if a maiden was sacrificed annually to Athena in Laodicea of Syria, as they say, the True God would not have hesitated to call her a wicked demon. The same applies to the one in Libya who delighted in similar things, and the one in Arabia, to whom they also sacrificed a child each year and buried him beneath the altar.

### Evangelical Preparation, Book 4

...or if only the one celebrated among the Hebrews remembers, since he is the only true God who has acted. For he alone, through the prophet and theologian Moses <note>Eusebius considers Moses a "theologian" because he provided the first systematic account of God and the creation of the world</note>, proclaimed to all people that they should not worship the wicked as if they were good spirits <term>demons: from the Greek "daimones," which in paganism meant spirits or minor deities, but in Eusebius's context refers to malevolent fallen entities</term>. On the contrary, he taught them to turn away from them and drive them out, as they are in fact evil spirits. Furthermore, he commanded them to cleanse their temples, their dedications, and their unholy rites, seeking to completely erase the memory of them as gods from among humanity, as well as the honors attributed to their names. For it is never holy to appease the wicked—those who are hated by the good.

Whether it is Phylarchus <note>A 3rd-century BCE Greek historian known for his vivid descriptions of customs and wars</note> or anyone else who records the history, they tell how all the Greeks would commit human sacrifice <term>anthropoktonia: literally "human-slaying," referring here to ritual murder or sacrifice</term> before marching out to war. Do not hesitate to accept this witness to the demonic madness that was once so highly regarded. One should not overlook those in Africa, nor the Thracians and the Scythians who did the same; it is clear they were driven by these same demonic manias. Even the Athenians, the inhabitants of that great city, were known to slaughter humans during the festivals of the "Great Zeus."

If you were to gather together the list of all those mentioned, you would find that, almost without exception, among every nation, the practice of making gods was dedicated to these very human-slaying spirits and evil demons. Whether in Rhodes, or in Salamis, or the other islands; whether in Heliopolis <note>the "City of the Sun" in Egypt</note>, or in Chios, Tenedos, Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>, and Arcadia; in Phoenicia and Libya; and similarly throughout Syria and Arabia. In every city, and even among the most prominent, such as Carthage and across Africa, as well as among the Thracians and Scythians, the rites of demonic human sacrifice were accepted, performed with blood in ancient times and continuing right up until the time of our Savior.

How could you not reasonably say that everyone was enslaved to evil demons back then? There was no pause to such evils in life until the teaching of our Savior shone forth. History records that these practices persisted until the time of Hadrian <note>Roman Emperor from 117–138 CE; Eusebius argues that human sacrifice was finally abolished throughout the Empire during this period due to Christian influence</note>, but ceased from that point on. This was precisely the time when the saving teaching reached its peak among all people.

It is not even possible for the pagans to claim they were only sacrificing to "evil" demons. History reveals that these human sacrifices were performed for the greatest of their gods! They say they sacrificed to Hera, and Athena, to Cronus and Ares, and Dionysus, and even to the father of all, Zeus himself—and to Phoebus, that most venerable and wise Apollo. These are the ones they proclaim as the greatest and "good" savior gods. Yet, they themselves must be the evil spirits! For if they delight in such human sacrifices and murders, how could you not rightly number them among the bloodthirsty evil spirits? Whether they are said to delight in such things themselves, or to permit and overlook them when done by others. Why should men be permitted to appease evil spirits at all? Or why should they be so deluded as to serve and flatter the wicked? If these gods were truly good, they would be far removed from the deception of men. How could a good and divine power not drive away the wicked and evil? Surely a good father would not stand by and watch his own child be corrupted by wicked men, nor would a sensible master permit it for his servants...

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION
### Book 4

...will [a general] look on while his people are led away by enemies? Nor will a general, when war is present, betray his own people by leaving them as captives to the foe. Nor will a shepherd abandon his flock to the wolves. Will gods, then, and good spirits <term>demons: from the Greek *daimones*, which in paganism meant spirits or minor deities, but in Eusebius's context refers to malevolent fallen entities</term> abandon the human race to the wretched and the base? And will those appointed as guardians of mortal men—who are indeed shepherds and saviors, kings and fathers and lords—surrender their dearest possessions to enemies and foes, and to wild beasts, to be led away and plundered so mercilessly and cruelly? 

Will they not rather fight as shields for their refugees, and keep the enemies and wicked spirits away from humans, driving them far off like bloodthirsty dogs and wild beasts? They would teach every person to be initiated into the fellowship of the multitude of gods and good spirits, taking courage because they are consecrated not only to superior beings, but to the most numerous and greatest gods, turning very little—or rather not at all—to the threats of the wicked spirits. 

But since they did not do this, but on the contrary cooperated with the wicked themselves, releasing <note>original: ἀνιέντες, implying a loosening of moral or protective restraint</note> through their oracles the instructions for human sacrifices, and rejoicing in all shameful deeds and the actions that follow them, they show by their work (as the saying goes) that they themselves do not differ at all in nature from the base spirits. Rather, they belong to one and the same purpose and mind. 

And to speak even more plainly: there was no god at all, nor any good spirit, who was worshiped of old among the nations throughout every city and land. For how could the base ever become a friend to the good? That would be like saying there is a mixture of light and darkness during the day. 

How much better, then, is the reason found among men than these supposed gods, since reason commands that one should not even sacrifice to base spirits? At any rate, the aforementioned author <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who, despite being an opponent of Christianity, is quoted here by Eusebius because Porphyry also criticized traditional animal sacrifice</note>, in the section where he said one must not sacrifice living animals, says that one must not sacrifice to base spirits either, in this manner:

## That one must not sacrifice to wicked spirits.

> Therefore, a sensible and prudent man will be wary of using such sacrifices, through which he will draw such beings to himself; instead, he will strive to purify his soul in every way. For they do not attack a pure soul because it is unlike them. But if it is necessary for cities to appease even these beings, that is nothing to us. For in cities, wealth, external things, and bodily goods are considered to be blessings, and their opposites to be evils. But the city cares little for the soul. To these things he adds the following, saying:

## How one must be dedicated to the God over all.

> We, however, as far as we are able, will not need what these beings provide, but from the soul and from manifest things we make every effort to become like God and those around Him. This happens through freedom from passion <term>apatheia: a state of being unmoved by emotional distress or worldly desires, highly valued by ancient philosophers</term>, and through a well-articulated understanding of those things which truly exist, and a life toward them and according to them. But we must become unlike wicked men and spirits, and generally everything that rejoices in the mortal and material. Hence we also, when describing a philosopher as one who stands apart from external things, reasonably say that he will not trouble the spirits, nor will he need diviners, nor the entrails of animals. For the sake of these things, divinations exist...

<summary>Eusebius argues that the pagan gods are identical to evil spirits because they permit human sacrifice, whereas true divinity would protect humanity. He uses Porphyry’s philosophical arguments to demonstrate that a pure soul seeks God through reason and detachment, not through bloody rituals.</summary>
<keywords>Eusebius, Porphyry, demons, human sacrifice, purification of the soul, apatheia, Neoplatonism, paganism vs Christianity</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s polemic against pagan oracles and sacrifices. Following his argument that "gods" should protect rather than exploit humans, he now uses the writings of the Neoplatonist philosopher Porphyry to show that even the "highest" pagan gods, like Apollo, acknowledge and demand appeasement for evil spirits. He transitions into a specific quote from Porphyry's "Philosophy from Oracles."</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

"...he has resolved to abstain. For he will not stoop to marriage in order to receive some oracle about it, nor to trade, nor concerning a servant, nor concerning theft or any other such vanity <term>vanity: *doxokopia*, the seeking of mere opinion or reputation, here referring to trivial worldly concerns</term> common among men. No true diviner seeks after these things, nor will the entrails of animals reveal them. But the wise man, on his own—as we say—approaches God, who is established within his own true 'inwards' <note>original: *splangchnois*, meaning both the physical organs used in divination and the metaphorical inner heart/conscience</note>. As for eternal life, such seekers receive no useful advice at all from these sources."

Through these words, the discourse has clearly revealed which entities are responsible for the oracles and the inquiries made through animal sacrifice <term>sacrifice: *thutike*, the technical art of animal sacrifice and divination from organs</term>, as well as the predictions of hidden things so admired by the masses. For all these are merely titles for vanity, as they are driven by the work of evil demons. In discussing the nature of base demons, the account claims that a prudent and sober man should never surrender himself to them, nor draw such things to himself through sacrifice.

He follows this by saying: "The philosopher will have no need of oracles, nor of the entrails of animals, and such like," seeing them as the products of demonic trickery <term>trickery: *kakotechnia*, literally 'evil craft' or 'fraudulent art'</term>. If, therefore, the prudent and sober man must guard against using such sacrifices—through which he would draw demons to himself—it is clear that these were the rituals involving the shedding of blood and the slaughter of irrational animals. No one would call those who of old sacrificed animals to demons "sober" or "prudent," and much less so those who performed human sacrifices. Yet such customs were almost universal in nearly every city until our Christ was received among men; these cities were led by base demons to perform human sacrifices in every form. None of these people, then, were truly prudent or sober.

Common and human reasoning, following right logic, explicitly proclaims to every prudent and sober person that one must not court evil demons through sacrifices, but rather strive to purify the soul in every way. For that which is unlike them does not settle upon a pure soul. But their own god, Apollo—and here we must show how far right reasoning is lacking, so that men may be on their guard—commands sacrifice to be made to the evil demon, not secretly, but clearly as his friend. For like is friend to like. Of this, again, the initiate Porphyry writes in his work entitled *The Philosophy from Oracles*, recording it word for word as follows:

### How Apollo Commanded Sacrifice to the Evil Demon

"When the prophet was eager to meet the Divine, and was pressing for it, Apollo said such a thing was impossible before giving ransoms <note>original: *lutra*, meaning a price for release or atonement</note> to the evil demon; he speaks thus:

> 'Give ransoms to the venerable dweller of the father-land.
> First libations, then fire, and black blood,
> Of jet-black wine, and white streams from sheep.'

"And he spoke even more clearly about these same matters:

> 'Cast in wine and milk, and the bright form of water,
> And wood bearing the fruit of translucent oaks,
> And having laid down the entrails, pour a libation with oily streams.'

"When asked with what prayer he should begin, he did not complete it, but said this:
'O demon, having obtained by lot the realm of sin-minded souls...'"

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 4
i.iii.

...beneath the recesses of the air, and above the subterranean regions <note>original: "Ἠρείων ὑπένερθε μυχῶν, χθονίων τ’ ἐφύπερθεν"</note>. These things says that "wonderful god"—or rather, that wandering demon. Reason, by its nature, advises the opposite: to purify the soul. It commands us not to offer sacrifices that delight evil demons, for they do not attack a pure soul because it is unlike them. Indeed, if a man is "sober" and is rightly judged to be "harmless" <term>harmless: *ablabes*, a term used here to mean one who does not participate in the harmful or "bloody" rites of paganism</term> by not sacrificing to demons, while another man—persuaded by an oracle—sacrifices to evil spirits, I leave it to you to consider which one should reasonably be thought of as godly.

Upon reflection, it will become obvious what kind of nature those beings possessed who delighted in the "rule of many" <term>polyarchy: *polyarchia*, the pagan system of many gods/rulers as opposed to one God</term> in ancient times, and who had enslaved the human race long ago. If someone were to say that the practice of **human sacrifice** was not a foul thing, it would be the height of correctness—following the logic of those ancient rites—for everyone living now to be blamed for not being as "pious" as their fathers were!

---

->How no one else through the ages, but only our Savior and Lord,<-
->has liberated the whole human race from demonic delusion.<-

---

If we today have wisely turned away from that "savage and wild cruelty" <note>referring back to the human sacrifices mentioned previously</note>, then none of the ancients could truly be called "wise" while they were appeasing evil demons through **human-slaughter**. Indeed, it is clear even to a blind man that these were neither gods nor "good demons," though they were absolutely treated as gods by the ancient nations. They were, in fact, exiled as far as possible from the Good. Therefore, they might justly be called "fighters against God" <term>theomachoi: those who wage war against the divine will</term> and impious, for they corrupted the entirety of human life. 

No one throughout history—except our Savior and Lord alone, Jesus Christ the Son of God—has proclaimed to all men a way to escape them. As a healer of all, he cured the "ancestral disease" <note>original: *patrikes nosou*, referring to the hereditary habit of paganism and demonic worship</note> that had corrupted even the barbarians. The logic of our **Gospel Demonstration** <note>the title of Eusebius's companion work, *Demonstratio Evangelica*</note> now hastens toward that bitter and ancient slavery, crying out with a great voice for all to hear: 

<margin>„</margin> "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news 
<margin>„</margin> to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind; 
<margin>„</margin> to heal the brokenhearted." <note>A quotation of Isaiah 61:1 and Luke 4:18</note> And again: "To bring out the prisoners from 
<margin>„</margin> their chains, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison house." 

Truly, by dissolving these things from of old, the divine oracles among the Hebrews prophesied the truth, announcing redemption for our souls—we who were formerly blind and bound by the complex chains of evil demons. Therefore, it is right that the eyes of our intellect have been enlightened to worship the Word <term>Word: *Logos*, referring to Christ as the Divine Reason</term>. Having become sober, harmless, and in harmony, we shall no longer sacrifice to, nor serve, the supposed "gods" of the nations who previously tyrannized us. 

Led forward by the teaching of our Savior, we acknowledge only the one true God—our Master, Nourisher, Savior, and Benefactor; the Maker, Creator, and King of all. We believe Him alone to be the true God, and to Him alone we render the honor that is due, worshipping Him alone and being pious toward Him alone—not in a way pleasing to demons, but in the way handed down by the Savior of all men, who was sent from Him through His Gospel teaching. By practicing this godliness, we shall drive these evil demons away from ourselves; we are far from fearing them through ignorance...

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 4
### Chapter 23

» ...Porphyry has reminded us. For [the wise man] does not stoop to marriage [queries], so as to trouble the oracle about marriage, nor about trade, nor about a servant, nor about theft, nor other such vanities <term>vanities: *doxokopia*, literally "glory-seeking" or empty reputation</term> found among men. Concerning these matters, no one [who is wise] seeks advice. Nor will the wise man reveal things through the entrails of animals. But he himself, through his own self, as we say, approaches God, who is established within his own true "entrails" <note>original: "σπλάγχνοις" (splangchnois) - Porphyry uses the term for physical guts metaphorically to describe the inner seat of the soul or conscience</note>. Concerning eternal life, he receives no beneficial instructions at all from these [sources] that flow together.

Most clearly, then, through these words, the argument has revealed what one should think of the oracles, and the inquiries made through the art of sacrifice <term>sacrifice: *thutike*, the technical practice of interpreting omens from animal slaughter</term>, and the prognostications about hidden things that are so admired by the masses. For all these are merely names for vanity, being the discharge of activities driven by evil demons. 

At any rate, in explaining the account of the low-level demons, [Porphyry] claims that the prudent and temperate man should never happen to give himself over to them, nor draw them toward himself through sacrifice and such things. Next, he adds the following: "The philosopher will not need oracles, nor the entrails of animals, and similar things, since they belong to the demonic craft of evil." 

If, therefore, according to these statements, the prudent and temperate man must guard against using such sacrifices—through which he would draw the demons to himself—and since these were the rites involving the pouring of blood and the slaughter of irrational animals, then no one could be called just, temperate, or prudent among those of old who sacrificed animals to demons. This applies even more so to those who performed **human sacrifices**. 

Indeed, such was the state of affairs in ancient times among almost everyone for many years, until our own time [the era of Christ] was distributed among men: they led the evil demons [by] human sacrifices performed everywhere in secret. Therefore, none of those people was truly prudent or temperate. Thus, common human reasoning, following right logic, explicitly proclaims to the prudent and temperate man everywhere not to use sacrifices for the service of evil demons, but to strive to purify the soul in every way. For they [the demons] do not attack a pure soul because it is unlike them. 

But their very god, Apollo—and again, men must be on guard and shown how far he falls short of right reason—ordered men to sacrifice to the evil demon, no differently than if he were a friend to him. For "like is friend to like." Witness to this is [Porphyry] himself, in his work titled *The Philosophy from Oracles*, recording the history word for word as follows:

->**How Apollo commanded them to sacrifice to the evil demon.**<-

When the prophet was eager to resist the divine power and was pressing on, Apollo said such a thing was impossible until he gave a ransom to the evil demon. He speaks thus:

» "Give ransom to the holy inhabitant of the fatherland's earth.
» First, drink-offerings; then with grain <note>original: "πυρῷ" (pyro) - can mean wheat or fire-offering</note>, and dark blood, 
» of jet-black wine, and with them white streams of sheep." 

And he spoke more clearly about these same things:

» "Cast in wine and milk, and the bright form of water, 
» and wood bearing the fruit of opened acorns, 
» and pour the entrails upon the fatty streams in the air."

When asked with what kind of prayer [the ritual] should begin, he did not complete it, but spoke thus:

» "Demon, crown of the sin-thinking souls, fiery-eyed..."

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 4

...below the depths of the sanctuaries, and above the earthly realms. These are the words of the "wonderful god" <note>Eusebius is likely referring to Apollo with heavy irony</note>, or rather, of a deceptive demon. Natural reasoning, however, dictates that the soul should be purified, rather than fumigated with sacrifices to evil demons. Indeed, they themselves admit that a pure soul is not a suitable target for their influence. If a man is truly prudent and is rightly judged as harmless for *not* sacrificing to demons, while he who sacrifices to evil spirits is acting insanely according to the oracle's own logic—then I leave it to you to consider how such a person should reasonably be regarded.

For once we look back at the facts, it will be clear what kind of beings they were—those who rejoice in the abundance of flesh <term>abundance of flesh: *polysarkia*, referring to the heavy smoke and fat of animal sacrifices</term> and those who, through blind wandering, enslaved the human race long ago. If anyone should claim that human sacrifice is not a foul thing, they would be most rightly condemned by the ancient rites themselves; for everyone today blames the ancients because no one now practices such impiety as their fathers once did.

---

->That no word since time began, except alone our Savior and Lord, has liberated the human race from demonic delusion.<-

---

If we have wisely turned away from such cruel and savage brutality, we are not enemies of the ancients by refusing to appease evil demons with human slaughter. Even to a blind man it is clear and manifest that these could neither be gods nor "good demons"—those who were once considered gods among the nations. They are, in fact, as far removed from the "Good" as possible. Therefore, they might rightly be called "fighters against God" and impious, for they ruined the whole of human life.

Throughout all ages, no one except alone our Savior and Lord, Jesus Christ the Son of God, has proclaimed healing for the souls of all men. He has embraced both Greeks and barbarians alike, offering a cure for the "paternal disease" <note>The "paternal disease" refers to the inherited pagan customs and idolatry of one's ancestors</note> and liberating them from a bitter and ancient slavery. Toward this goal, the argument of our *Evangelical Demonstration* proceeds, shouting with a great voice for all to hear:

<margin>,,</margin> "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me;
<margin>,,</margin> he has sent me to preach the gospel to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;
<margin>,,</margin> to heal the brokenhearted." <note>This is a quotation from the Prophet Isaiah (61:1), which Jesus famously read in the synagogue to announce his mission (Luke 4:18).</note> And again: "To lead forth those who are bound
<margin>,,</margin> from their chains, and those sitting in darkness from the prison house." For these divine words among the Hebrews truly predicted from of old the dissolution of these bonds, announcing a ransom for our souls—once blind and bound by the complex chains of evil demons. 

Therefore, it is only right that the eyes of our minds have been illuminated by the light of the Word. Having become prudent and harmless, and having been liberated from all these things, we shall neither sacrifice to nor serve those who were once considered the "gods" of the nations, who formerly tyrannized us. For having been led and brought forward by the teaching of our Savior to the only true God—who is also Lord and Overseer, Savior and Benefactor, and furthermore the Creator and King of all—we shall regard Him alone as the true God. We render to Him alone the honor that is His due, worshipping Him alone and being pious toward Him alone—not in a way pleasing to demons, but as has been handed down through His evangelical teaching for the salvation of all men. By this way of worshipping God, we shall pursue and drive away from ourselves the evil demons, for we no longer fear them through ignorance.

# EUSEBIUS

...somewhere, of a temperate and all-virtuous life, which brings us into a close relationship with the Divine. For it is not possible for anything to approach the Pure <note>i.e., God</note> unless it has first achieved a likeness to Him. Furthermore, we shall have no need of divination or oracles, nor shall we scrutinize the entrails of animals, nor busily meditate on anything produced through demonic movement. The Word of Christ has commanded us to distance ourselves from those things which the masses zealously pursue. He has instructed us to desire only those things which no diviner and no animal entrails can reveal, but which are made clear only by the Word of God Himself. This Word dwells in the "true entrails" <note>original: σπλάγχνοις (*splanchnois*). Eusebius is making a pun: pagans look at animal organs (entrails) for truth, but God dwells in the "inner organs" or heart of a pure person.</note> of those who, through extreme purity of soul, are able to contain Him within themselves. Concerning these, it says somewhere 
<margin>,,</margin> in the Sacred Scriptures: *I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will 
<margin>,,</margin> be their God, and they shall be my people.* <note>Quoting 2 Corinthians 6:16 or Leviticus 26:12</note> These arguments, then, drawn from the topic of sacrifices, serve to expose the wickedness of the demons. But hear again what the author of the treatise *On Abstinence from Animal Food* <note>The Neoplatonist philosopher Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), whom Eusebius frequently quotes to turn pagan philosophy against itself</note> records about these same beings. He explicitly confesses that evil demons, imprinting themselves in many shapes and characterizing themselves with various forms, hide themselves and deceive the majority of men. 
<margin>,,</margin> "For," he says, "by putting on the masks of good beings, they 
<margin>,,</margin> draw the crowds toward them, because they kindle the desires of 
<margin>,,</margin> men. They wish to be thought of as gods by them." He says they have 
<margin>,,</margin> such power as to deceive even the wisest of poets and philosophers. 
<margin>,,</margin> To these he admits that the common people have become the cause of 
<margin>,,</margin> distortion—because from these demons all sorcery <term>sorcery: *goēteia*, often implying fraudulent or "low" magic compared to high philosophy</term> is established, 
<margin>,,</margin> and everything aimed at human pleasure is prepared through them. He 
<margin>,,</margin> explains how they wish to be gods despite being foul demons, and how 
<margin>,,</margin> their presiding power appears to be the "Greatest God." Porphyry records all these things in this manner.

### The Manner of Demonic Activity.

"All souls that do not control the vital spirit <term>vital spirit: *pneuma*, here meaning a semi-material substance that connects the soul to the body</term> but are for 
<margin>,,</margin> the most part controlled by it, are led and carried away excessively 
<margin>,,</margin> whenever the angers and desires of the spirit take hold of their impulse. 
<margin>,,</margin> These souls are themselves demons, and they might reasonably be 
<margin>,,</margin> called 'evil-doers.' All these, along with those of the opposing power, 
<margin>,,</margin> are invisible and completely imperceptible to human senses. For they 
<margin>,,</margin> are not clothed in a solid body, nor do they all have a single form. 
<margin>,,</margin> Instead, their forms—imprinting and characterizing their spirit in

<margin>T</margin> ,, It is not without reason that we place the evil demons under the authority of **Sarapis**, nor were we convinced only by the symbols. ,, Consequently, among the **Egyptians** and **Phoenicians**, and generally among those wise in divine matters or prophets, these spirits are "burst forth" in the temples <note>referring to a ritual manifestation or the breaking of a demonic presence</note>, and the deity receives animals for the worship of the gods. ,, Since every house is full of them, they purify and cast them out whenever they call upon a god. Even our bodies are full of them, for they especially delight in certain kinds of foods. These rituals are not primarily for the sake of the gods, but so that these demons might stay away. They especially delight in blood and impurities, and they enjoy these by slipping into those who partake in them. Human nature dares to discover the snares set around itself up to this point. But if a god should enter in this way, the spirit is multiplied.

,, These things, then, concern the evil demons, of whom he says **Sarapis** is the ruler. **E**nough <note>The Greek text begins with the word "ΙΚανὰ" (Ikana), meaning "Enough" or "Sufficient."</note> has been set forth in the preceding sections to establish that those honored as gods among the nations—both in cities and rural areas—were not gods, nor even good spirits <note>original: "δαίμονες" (daimones). In ancient Greek, this term could refer to any supernatural being or spirit, but Eusebius uses it here to mean "demons" or malevolent entities.</note>, but quite the opposite. Yet it is not burdensome to further confirm this same premise out of an abundance of evidence, using more and clearer proofs. This demonstration will reveal to all people the benefit brought by the evangelical teaching of our Savior, which exposed the evils of old. 

Listen, then, to those very spirits confessing that their oracles have failed. This never happened before in history, but only after the times of the saving and evangelical teaching—when the message of the one God and Savior Christ was spread across the earth, rising like light for all mankind. Indeed, we shall very soon demonstrate that after His appearance, the deaths of these spirits were recorded, and the wondrous oracles so famous of old have ceased. 

It has also been previously shown that the cruel and merciless practice of human sacrifice <term>human sacrifice: the ritual killing of humans to appease deities, common in various ancient Mediterranean cultures before the spread of Christianity</term> among all nations came to an end—never before, but only after the evangelical teaching. At the present moment, it is good to add that since then, not only has the superstition of demonic worship been extinguished, but also the "polyarchy" <note>original: "πολυαρχίας" (rule by many)</note> of the nations. 

For almost every city and village had its own kings, tyrants, and rulers. Thus, in ancient times, one could see diverse types of rule and many local governments. Because of these, people were constantly rushing into wars against each other, always and through everything [carrying out] the plundering of lands, the sieges of cities, and the enslavement and capture of their neighbors...

...they acted, being driven to a frenzy by their own demons <note>The author uses the term 'daimones' not just as 'demons' in the modern sense, but as the spiritual entities the Greeks worshipped.</note> into war against one another. Given that things were in such a state, you can observe for yourself in what a confusion of evils and successive misfortunes the whole of life was submerged. When all these things vanished at once, along with the error of polytheism, it happened at no other time than after the arrival of our Savior among men. How can one not marvel at the great mystery of this truly saving and evangelical proof? Through this, suddenly throughout the whole inhabited world, houses of prayer and temples dedicated to the King of all, the Creator and only God, were established everywhere on earth—whether in cities and villages, or among barbarian nations in the wilderness. Books and readings, all kinds of learning and teachings containing instructions for the highest virtue and the true worship of God, are delivered to the hearing of men, women, and children alike.

All the oracles and divinations of the demons are now dead. Nor is any man defiled to such an extent now—since the divine and angelic power of our Savior shone forth upon all like light—whereas previously, those driven to a literal demonic frenzy delighted in the murder of their dearest ones and the slaughter of victims for spirits that craved blood and hated humanity. Since these foul demons can no longer exert any power after the passage of our Savior among men, even the advocate of the demons himself, in his plot against us, shall be a witness where he says:

» "But now they wonder why the disease has gripped the city for so many years, while the presence <note>original: 'ἐπιδημίας' (epidemias), referring to a god's visitation or residence in a temple.</note> of Asclepius <note>The Greek god of healing and medicine.</note> and the other gods no longer exists. For since Jesus is honored, no one has perceived any public benefit from the gods."

These are the very words of Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and one of the most famous intellectual critics of early Christianity.</note>. If, then, by his own admission, while Jesus is honored, no one has perceived any public benefit from the gods—neither the presence of Asclepius nor that of the other gods being any longer felt—where then does this child <note>Referring to the source of Porphyry's oracles or perhaps a rhetorical flourish regarding his logic.</note> get his doctrines about gods and heroes? Why have they turned their backs and yielded all their ground to a mortal—one who is no longer even present, as they themselves would say?

Yet even after death, he is seen to be served every day among all nations, demonstrating a life after death that is clear and divine to those capable of sober thought. Though he is but one, he does not, as one might suppose, merely drive away the multitude of gods throughout the whole world, but he prevails by setting aside their honors. Thus, the gods no longer exist, nor act, nor appear anywhere, nor do they visit the cities as was their custom. This is because they were not gods, but evil demons. Conversely, if those gods were truly the guardians of the earth, they should have utterly removed the "error" (if that is what it was) and should have continued to provide their own cures and benefits abundantly to everyone. # EUSEBIUS

...divine power among us, which overthrows all the uprisings of evil demons against his teaching and drives them away. These are truly base spirits, yet they have been falsely thought of as gods or "good spirits" <note>original: "agathous daimones"</note>.

### The Nature of Demonic Activity

These beings, being of the air and the underworld, wander through the heavy and murky air near the earth. They are condemned to inhabit a crooked and earthy dwelling place for reasons we will explain later. They frequent the tombs and monuments of the dead and all kinds of foul and impure matter. They delight in blood and gore, in the bodies of all sorts of animals, and in the steam and vapors rising from sacrifices and from the earth. 

Their rulers—aerial or subterranean powers—noticed that the human race was maddened by a dismal practice of deifying the dead <note>Eusebius is describing "Euhemerism," the theory that the gods were originally historical human beings who were posthumously deified.</note>, working with great zeal to offer sacrifices and steam, which are the very things most pleasing to these spirits. Lurking nearby, they acted as accomplices in this error, fortifying themselves against human misfortunes. They ruthlessly deceived the souls of the foolish through the movements of wooden statues <term>xoana: ancient, often primitive, wooden cult images believed by some to have fallen from heaven</term> which had been dedicated by the ancients to honor the departed. 

They also deceived through the illusions of oracles and the healing of bodies. These were ailments that they themselves had secretly inflicted through their own demonic activity; then, by ceasing their influence or "releasing" the person, they appeared to be the ones providing the cure. Through these tricks, they drove the superstitious even further down the precipice, leading them to believe that these spirits were either heavenly powers and true gods, or the souls of deified heroes. 

From this point, a greater and more solemn reputation for the error of polytheism grew among the masses. Their minds shifted from the visible objects to the invisible powers hidden within the statues, which gave the error a stronger hold. Thus, these aerial demons—the "world-rulers" <note>original: "kosmokratores," a term used in the New Testament (Ephesians 6:12) to describe spiritual forces of evil</note> of the atmosphere and the "spiritual forces of wickedness"—and the highest of them, the masters of evil, were regarded by everyone as the greatest gods. 

The memory of the long-dead was honored with even greater service. Their physical appearance was represented by the shapes of the images dedicated to them, but the base demons impersonated their souls and incorporeal powers. Through many wonders, they led the priests and worshippers into an ever-increasing vanity of imagination, often using the deceptive arts of sorcery. These base demons themselves first taught these practices to their priests, making them the cause of the original evil of sorcery in human life, as my previous argument has shown.

### The Multifaceted and Diverse Superstition of the Greeks Concerning the Gods

Therefore, these wretched and earthly demons, these spirits of the air and the underworld—whom the Divine Word <note>A common way for Eusebius to refer to Holy Scripture.</note> calls "world-rulers," "spiritual forces of evil," "principalities," and "powers"—sometimes masquerade as good spirits, and sometimes present themselves as heavenly gods, and at other times as heroes...

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 6, Page 109
### Iz.i.

...transforming themselves. In some cases, a kind of grief expressed through their rituals, or a display of the wickedness of those appearing, naturally caused even more error to be raised up among men, who did not acknowledge the Spirit of God but rather spoke of heroes and demons as gods. Regarding these demons, they designated some as "good," while calling others "most base." They claimed it was necessary to appease even the base ones because of the harm they might cause. Consequently, their entire system of deification <note>original: "theopoïia," the process of making or inventing gods</note> fell into several distinct types.

First is the type arising from the luminaries appearing in heaven. These, they say, were the first to be addressed as "gods" <note>original: "theoi"</note>, either because of the word "to run" <note>original: "thein"</note> or because they are the cause of "beholding" <note>original: "theorein"</note> the things that are seen. Second is the type based on deeds of benefit to common life, as they claim. Even the pagans admit these gods were born from men, long ago bringing forward the so-called "heroes"—Heracles, the Dioscuri <note>the twin brothers Castor and Pollux</note>, Dionysus, and similar figures among the barbarians. 

From these, they set apart and fashioned even more shameful myths, proposing a third type of deification which they called "mythic." Marvelling at this—whether it happened to be a new truth or something very ancient—they transformed it into a more "natural" explanation, as they say, using foreign allegories and suggesting certain theoretical interpretations. 

But their practice of error was not satisfied even with this; they eventually cast down the venerable and worshipful name of God to the level of their own human passions. They devised a fourth type of deification—which I say is not even worthy of a refutation, for their own feelings suggest its nature. They spoke of "gods" such as Love <note>original: "Eros"</note>, Aphrodite, and Desire <note>original: "Pothos"</note>, which are simply their own shameful and unrestrained lusts. They named Speech "Hermes" and Reason "Athena." This, they claim, is a theology based on the internal soul. 

They also fashioned a fifth type from the power shown in practical affairs. Personifying military and technical activities, they attributed them to gods: Ares and Athena for military matters, Hephaestus and others for technical ones. 

Beyond all these, a sixth and seventh type for them is the entire demonic nature, which is evidently versatile and many-formed. Sometimes it acts the part of gods, and at other times the souls of the dead. It contributes nothing to the virtue of the soul; instead, it always leads the superstitious man toward the precipice through deceptive error. This whole category is base, yet they divided it into two—the harmful and the beneficial—giving them the names of "good" and "base" spirits. 

Since these things are so, it seems necessary to me to pass over those points that do not even require a refutation and to examine the following logical account concerning demonic activity. We have already viewed part of this in the treatise on this subject; let us now complete what remains. Come then, let us proceed to the proofs themselves. I will first present those from the writing of Plutarch <note>a famous Greek historian and Middle Platonist philosopher</note> which he composed *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*. He writes in the following manner to show that the prophecies and oracles found among the nations are the work of evil demons.

---

### That the prophecies and oracles among the nations are the work of evil demons.

### Page 110

>> ...a difficulty concerning philosophers. It seems to me that those who placed the race of **demons** <note>original: "daimones," here referring to intermediary spirits, not necessarily "evil" in the modern sense</note> in the middle between gods and men have solved more and greater difficulties, having discovered the way our community is brought together and joined into one. Whether this doctrine comes from the Magi <note>the priestly caste of ancient Persia</note> associated with **Zoroaster**, or is Thracian from **Orpheus**, or Egyptian, or Phrygian—as we may judge from the rituals in both places, seeing many mortal and mournful elements mixed into the celebrations and the sacred rites performed.

**Xenocrates the Illustrious**, using names common to both, sometimes even addressed the gods as demons. **Hesiod**, however, was the first to set forth clearly and distinctly the four classes of rational beings: first **gods**, then **demons**, then **heroes**, and finally, **humans**. From these, he seems to create a transformation, where those of the "Golden Race" become many good demons, and those called demigods are separated into heroes.

Continuing, he says: "But concerning these matters, it is not necessary for us to argue before the public. For whether the time in which a demon's soul or a hero's life changes is long, short, or fixed, it will nonetheless be shown by wise and ancient witnesses to be exactly as he wishes: that there are certain natures, as if in a borderland between gods and men, which experience mortal passions and necessary changes. It is right to worship and name these as 'demons' according to the law of our fathers."

To these points, he adds others: "Therefore, the idea that the oracles are presided over not by gods—from whom it is fitting to be removed from earthly affairs—but by demons who are servants of the gods, does not seem to me to be a bad claim. But to take from the verses of **Empedocles** the sins, calamities, and god-driven wanderings of these demons, and to impose them almost like a lash—even going so far as to suggest they suffer deaths like humans—I consider this to be rather bold and barbaric."

And again, he adds this to what has been said: "For just as among humans, there are differences of virtue among demons, as well as differences in the passionate and irrational parts of their nature. In some, there is a weak and dim remnant of this, like a waste product; in others, much of it remains, and it is hard to extinguish. Traces and symbols of these things are preserved and kept scattered in many places by sacrifices, rituals, and mythologies. 

Regarding the **mysteries** <note>secret religious rites, like the Eleusinian Mysteries</note>, in which one can find the greatest manifestations and revelations of the truth about demons, 'let a seal be placed on my lips' as **Herodotus** says. But as for festivals and sacrifices—which are like 'unlucky' and gloomy days <note>original: "apophrades," days on which temples were closed and no official business was conducted</note>, involving the eating of raw flesh, the tearing apart of victims, fasts, and breast-beating, and in many places again, obscenities at the temples, and these manias stirred up with a 'neck-tossing' turmoil—I would say these are performed not for any god, but for the sake of warding off **evil demons**. 

And as for the ancient myths concerning **human sacrifices**, it is not plausible that the gods demanded or accepted them. Nor would kings and generals have sacrificed their own children in vain, performing the initial rites and the slaughter, unless they were trying to appease the anger and gloom of harsh and hopeless spirits, or satisfying the 'manic loves' of **avenging spirits** <note>original: "alastores," spirits of vengeance or "unforgettable" ones who punish crime</note> in these matters. These spirits are neither able nor willing to have intercourse with bodies or through bodies. But just as **Heracles** besieged Oechalia for the sake of a maiden, so often do powerful and violent demons, demanding a human soul enclosed in a body, bring plagues to cities and infertility to the land, and stir up wars and civil strife, until they obtain what they love."

Clearly through these things the aforementioned philo... <note>catchword: "sophos" (philosopher)</note>

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 5

...it is wise to note that the things mentioned previously were performed throughout all the cities for **evil demons**. If there were indeed some among these who were, as they say, good by nature or gods, why was it necessary to worship the base ones, when they ought to have been driven away by the good? If, on the other hand, the good ones had the base as companions, then surely—being superior in both word and deed—they should have testified that nothing regarding the lesser ones should be a concern. One should not have to turn away opposing powers through **foul language** <note>original: "aischron-rhemosyne," referring to ritual obscenity used in certain mystery cults to ward off evil</note>. 

Yet, when nothing of the sort was seen, but instead a life both shameful and licentious—marked by unholy words, the **eating of raw flesh** <note>original: "omophagia," a ritual practice in the cults of Dionysus</note>, dismemberments, and sacrifices performed for evil demons—how is it not reasonable to conclude that those who do such things and perform what is pleasing to the base are far from being reconciled to God, or to the divine powers beside Him, or to anything good at all? Indeed, it is clear to everyone that he who performs what is dear to the base could never be a friend to the good. Therefore, these rites were not for gods, nor for good demons, but for the base alone. 

This is further confirmed by **Plutarch** where he says that the mythical stories told as if they were about gods are actually accounts concerning demons. He suggests that the Greek tales of **Giants** and **Titans** are stories of demons, offered as a more modern interpretation. Could it be that these are the same as the ones mentioned in Holy Scripture concerning the **Giants** before the Flood, and those who fathered them? As it is written:

> The angels of God, seeing the daughters of men, that they were beautiful, took for themselves wives from all whom they chose. From these were born the giants, the famous men of old. <note>A reference to Genesis 6:2–4</note>

For one might say that these are those very beings, and that their spirits were deified by later generations of men; their battles, their internal strife, and their wars are the very things told in myths as if they concerned the gods. Plutarch, in the work he composed concerning **Isis** and the **Egyptian gods**, says these things in these very words:

---

->Concerning the fact that the mythical stories told about the gods contain<-
->hidden histories of demons.<-

<margin>B</margin>
> Those stories told about **Typhon**, **Osiris**, and **Isis** are not the experiences of gods, nor of men, but are considered to be the deeds of **Great Demons**. In this, **Plato**, **Pythagoras**, **Xenocrates**, and **Chrysippus**—following the ancient theologians—say that these beings were stronger than men and far surpassed our nature in power, yet they did not possess the divine element in a pure or unmixed state. Rather, they shared in the nature of the soul and the physical senses of the body, which admit pleasure and pain and all the passions resulting from these changes, which disturb some more and others less. 

> For among demons, as among men, there are differences of virtue and vice. The stories of the **Giants** and **Titans** sung by the Greeks, and many lawless deeds—the opposition of **Python** against **Apollo**, the flights of **Dionysus**, and the wanderings of **Demeter**—differ in no way from the stories of Osiris and Typhon. One can hear these things told in myths by everyone; they are preserved as secret initiations, veiled in mystic rites, and though kept from sight, they bear the same meaning in relation to the gods. And further...

### EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 5

...wise, <note>Eusebius is likely speaking ironically here about the founders of pagan religious laws.</note> in that these offerings were performed in every city to **evil demons** as if they were ambassadors. <meta>catchword: to the</meta>

"Consider," he says, continuing the argument, "Empedocles <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that the universe is made of four elements moved by Love and Strife.</note> says that the demons also pay a penalty to the gods for the sins and errors they have committed:

> 'For the force of the high air drives them into the sea,
> And the sea spits them out onto the floor of the earth, and the earth into the rays 
> Of the tireless Sun, who then casts them back into the swirls of the high air.
> One receives them from another, and all of them loathe them.'

This continues until, having been punished, they eventually recover their natural place and rank. They say that the stories told about **Typhon** <note>A monstrous giant in Greek myth who attempted to overthrow Zeus; often associated with chaos and storms.</note> are brothers to these accounts: how he committed terrible deeds out of envy and harsh resentment, throwing all things into confusion and filling both the entire land and sea with evils, before finally paying the penalty. 

Plutarch, having set these things down in the aforementioned treatise <note>Plutarch’s 'On Isis and Osiris'.</note> and having worked out the argument at greater length, records similar things in his work *On the Obsolescence of Oracles* in this manner: 

He, at least, attributed the power of prophecy to the demons, and his argument carried great weight at **Delphi**. <note>The site of the most famous oracle of Apollo in the ancient world.</note> He was not unacquainted with any of the sacred rites performed and spoken there concerning **Dionysus**; rather, he claimed that those events—as well as the stories about the **Pythian** <note>Apollo, so named after the dragon Python he slew at Delphi.</note>—were the great sufferings of demons. He said that the one who killed [the Python] did not flee for only nine years, nor just to the **Vale of Tempe**, but was cast out and sought refuge in another world. 

Later, after nine cycles of 'great years,' <note>original: "eniautōn megalōn." A technical term for a long cosmic period, far longer than a standard year.</note> having become pure and truly becoming **Phoebus** <note>Meaning 'the Bright' or 'Pure,' an epithet of Apollo.</note>, he returned to take over the oracle, which in the meantime had been guarded by **Themis**. <note>The goddess of divine law and order.</note> He explains that the stories of Typhon and the **Titans** <note>The generation of gods preceding the Olympians, who were defeated and imprisoned in Tartarus.</note> are of the same nature: they were battles of demons against demons. 

Then followed the exile of those who were defeated, or the punishments by God for those who had sinned—such as the sins Typhon is said to have committed against holiness, and **Cronus** <note>The leader of the Titans who castrated his father Uranus.</note> against Uranus. The honors given to these figures among us have become obscured or have vanished entirely since they migrated to another world. Indeed, I learn that among the Solymi <note>An ancient people of Lycia in Asia Minor.</note>, the Lycian leaders honor Cronus above all others. But after he killed their leaders, Artalus and Dryas, he fled and moved elsewhere. They cannot say where he went, only that he was neglected. However, Artalus and his followers are addressed as 'harsh gods,' and the Lycians perform curses upon them both publicly and privately."

Many such examples can be taken from the myths. "If we call certain demons by the names of the gods," the stranger said, "it is not surprising. For each demon is ranked under a specific god whose power it shares, and it is customary for the demon to be called by that god's name. Even among us, one man is named **Dios** <note>Derived from Zeus.</note>, another **Athenaios** <note>Derived from Athena.</note>, and others **Apollonios**, **Dionysios**, or **Hermes**. While some were named correctly by chance, many others acquired the titles of gods that do not belong to them at all." So far Plutarch.

In these passages, he took pains—among other things in his work *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*—to persuade his readers that the demons are mortal, a point which I will also set forth at the proper time. For now, let us collect the evidence concerning the power and activity of the so-called "good" demons. Once again, the same author <note>Eusebius is likely referring to Porphyry here, whose work 'Philosophy from Oracles' he quotes extensively to critique paganism from within.</note>—who has since drawn back from us—sets this out in the work he titled *On the Philosophy from Oracles*. We shall use these as witnesses most frequently now, to expose the error regarding those whom they suppose to be gods. Thus, forced by their own writings to confess the truth, they may be put to shame. For in this way, from their own words...

### EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 5 113

Among those dear to the gods, and even those considered impious, who have precisely articulated the accounts regarding their own kin, you will find proofs of the riddles and deceptions in what lies before us. The aforementioned author <note>original: "ὁ δεδηλωμένος" — referring to Porphyry, a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> has set these things down in writing in the work he entitled *On the Philosophy from Oracles*, where he testifies that he does not reveal the secret things of the gods, swearing by them and commanding to keep them hidden, and not to bring what is to be said before the many. To understand such things, he says that **Pan** <note>The god of the wild, shepherds, and flocks, often depicted with goat-like features.</note> is a servant of **Dionysus**. He says that it is the nature of this "good" spirit <note>original: "ἀγαθόν δαίμονα" (agathon daimona). While "demon" now implies evil, the Greek word "daemon" originally meant a spirit or lesser deity.</note> to sometimes appear to those working in the fields, either to provide some good necessity or to end the expectation of some good for those deemed worthy of the god’s appearance. From these encounters, did something good come to the spectators of this good spirit, or shall he be called an evil spirit by those who have felt the experience in practice? At any rate, this wonderful initiate says that those deemed worthy of this "good" sight suffered sudden death, speaking thus:

<margin>»</margin> > Golden-horned Pan, servant of grim Dionysus,

You have heard what kind of spirit—one he calls "good"—the Apollo at Branchidae has described, both in form and in actions. See also the rest of their "civilized" achievements. It is for the sake of these things, having abandoned their heavenly dwelling, they exchanged it for a life among men. Surely it was necessary for them to lead the way in self-control and to suggest what is profitable and useful to humanity. But they do none of these things. Listen to what he reveals—he who has articulated the most secret of secrets and was deemed worthy of secret knowledge. He says that some of these "good" spirits serve erotic pleasures; others rejoice in the flutes of drums and the clashing of women. Still others, again, delight in battles and wars, and Artemis in huntings, and **Deo** <note>Another name for Demeter, the goddess of agriculture and the harvest.</note> in the fruits of the earth. He says that even now the holy **Isis** <note>An Egyptian goddess whose mystery cult was widespread in the Greco-Roman world.</note> and Apollo practice divination for heroes. Such are the things they say of "good" spirits, claiming they are for the benefit of men. Accept also the proofs of these things.

One part of it is **spirited** <note>original: "θυμοειδές" (thymoeides) — the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and pride.</note>; another is **desiring** <note>original: "ἐπιθυμητικόν" (epithymetikon) — the part associated with physical appetites.</note>; from which it is also called toward erotic things. ### GOSPEL PREPARATION, Book 4

...and even to those released from the earth, whether they are charmed by raw, unintelligible, and barbaric sounds and voices, while using certain chance men as their instruments, and being enslaved to them as if by chains. This would mean they do not even possess the self-governing <note>original: "αὐτεξούσιον" (autexousion). This refers to the power of free will or self-determination.</note> and elective power of life within themselves. And how could they be called "good spirits" <note>original: "δαίμονες" (daimones). In this period, "daemon" refers to an intermediate spirit, not necessarily an evil "demon."</note> if they are dragged down by force and necessity? For what is the reason for them to give themselves over to those who need help—not of their own free will, but as if they were unwilling? For if they make their approach for the sake of good because they are good, or if there is some benefit to the soul from them, they ought to embrace the good by their own choice, anticipating the needs of those in distress, rather than waiting for compulsion. But if the act being performed was not honorable, nor through any benefit, nor even according to their own judgment, then how could they be good, when they do what is neither honorable nor profitable? How would they be worthy of admiration or receive any religious service? For it would be absurd, as he says, if they were enslaved to total destruction, and forced to do what is neither honorable nor profitable against their will, being distressed and held down by force because of a human's lack of self-control—and not for the sake of virtue or any part of philosophy, but by the captured methods of sorcerers <note>original: "γοήτων" (goēton). This term usually implies a fraudulent magician or a charlatan.</note>. The same author, writing again in his letter to the aforementioned Egyptian <note>Porphyry’s "Letter to Anebo," a famous critical inquiry into Egyptian religion.</note>—as if perhaps to a prophet—risked putting these secret matters into words; and the means by which they accomplish these things are not worthy to be taught by him. At any rate, he inquires as follows, being at a loss and saying:

->By what methods are their marvelous gods dragged down by sorcerers?<-

> » "It greatly disturbs me how they are invoked as superiors but commanded as inferiors; and while they demand that their servant be just, they themselves endure doing unjust things when ordered. They would not listen to a caller who is not pure from sexual relations, yet they themselves do not hesitate to lead any person at all into unlawful sexual acts. They also command that 'god-seekers' <note>original: "θεοσόφους" (theosophous).</note> must abstain from animal food so they are not defiled by the vapors from bodies, yet they themselves are mostly lured by the vapors of sacrifices from animals. And while they say the observer <note>original: "ἐπόπτην" (epoptēn). A term for a witness to high-level religious mysteries.</note> must not touch a corpse, most 'god-summoning' rituals <note>original: "θεαγωγίαι" (theagōgiai). Theurgy or the art of compelling a god to appear.</note> are carried out using the carcasses of animals. But much more irrational than these things is the fact that a man—not even to a spirit, perhaps, or the soul of a dead man, but to the King Sun <note>The sun god Helios or Ra.</note> himself, or the Moon, or some other celestial body—threatens and terrifies them with lies in order to make them tell the truth! For to say that he will 'shatter the heavens,' or 'reveal the secrets of Isis,' or 'show the hidden thing in Abydos,' or 'stop the sacred boat,' or 'scatter the limbs of Osiris for Typhon' <note>In Egyptian myth, Typhon (Set) murdered Osiris and scattered his limbs. Threatening to repeat this was a standard "compulsion" in magical papyri.</note>—what excess of madness does this leave to the one who threatens what he neither knows nor is able to do? And what depth of degradation for those who fear such empty terror and fictions, like children being frightened? And yet Chaeremon, the sacred scribe <note>original: "ἱερογραμματεὺς" (hierogrammateus). Chaeremon was a Stoic philosopher and Egyptian priest.</note>, records these things as being talked about among the Egyptians. And they say these and such things are the most forceful methods of compulsion. And the prayers themselves—what sense do they make when they speak of one 'appearing as filth from the mud,' or 'sitting on a lotus,' or 'sailing on a boat,' or 'changing forms according to the hour' and 'transforming according to the sign of the zodiac'? For they say he is seen in this way, being ignorant that they are attaching the specific suffering of their own imagination to him. But if these things are said symbolically, being symbols of his powers, let them tell us the interpretation of the symbols. For it is clear that if it were a physical condition of the sun..."

<summary>Porphyry questions the logic of Egyptian "theurgy," asking why supposedly divine beings are subject to the threats and commands of human sorcerers. He highlights the contradictions in rituals that demand purity from humans but involve the gods in "impure" acts or animal sacrifices.</summary>

# EUSEBIUS

...[similar to the way things appear] in eclipses, it would be seen by everyone, the same to those gazing upon it.

> What is the meaning of those meaningless names, and why are foreign <note>original: "βάρβαρα" (barbara). To a Greek speaker, this meant any non-Greek language, particularly Egyptian or Babylonian in the context of magic.</note> terms preferred over those native to each person? For if the focus is on the meaning, the thought itself remains sufficient to demonstrate the intent, no matter what the name might be. For surely a person called an "Egyptian," if he is indeed Egyptian, or whoever uses the Egyptian tongue, would not use [Greek] in his religious service at all. Either these are all the tricks of sorcerers <note>original: "γοήτων" (goētōn). A "goēs" was a lower-class magician or "howler," often contrasted with the more "divine" theurgist.</note> and veils for our own human passions which are attributed to the divine, or we hold false conceptions about the divine, or it truly is as it appears. Having said these things, he again expresses his doubt to the Egyptian [priest], saying:

> For if some are beyond passion <note>original: "ἀπαθεῖς" (apatheis). In Greek philosophy, the gods were often thought to be "apathetic," meaning they could not be moved or changed by human emotion or suffering.</note> and others are subject to passion <note>original: "ἐμπαθεῖς" (empatheis).</note>—those whom they say are stirred up by phallic symbols and obscene language—then the invocations of the gods will be in vain, as they promise protection and soothing propitiations through sacrifice, and even more so the so-called "necessities of the gods" <note>This refers to the magical concept that a deity could be "forced" or "necessitated" (ananke) to appear through the correct ritual.</note>. For that which is without violence is unmovable, and that which is beyond passion cannot be coerced.

And again, he adds the following:

> Their wisdom has been practiced in vain regarding the choice of religious service, or our prayers, or marriage, or trade, if they have troubled the divine mind with such things. For there are some who do not speak clearly, while others, being solemn, say the truest things about the universe but nothing certain or reliable regarding spirits <note>original: "δαιμονίας" (daimonias). "Daemons" in this context are intermediate spirits between gods and humans.</note>. You should not be ashamed, then, of the gods or the good spirits, but only of that one called "the deceiver" <note>original: "πλάνος" (planos). A reference to a wandering or misleading spirit.</note>.

So much for these matters; let the writings of Porphyry be set aside for now. Furthermore, it was the "gods" themselves who first taught the arts of wicked sorcery. For how else would men know these things, unless the spirits themselves revealed the details about their own natures and explained the "bindings" <note>original: "καταδέσμους" (katadesmous). These are "binding spells" or curse tablets intended to restrain or compel a person or spirit.</note> used against one another? Do not think this is merely our own argument; we do not admit to knowing or desiring any of these things, except to expose their folly. Our witness for this, and for our withdrawal from these things, will be the very man who provided them to us—one who is highly esteemed among their famous scholars and who knew and researched all their private matters accurately. He himself, in his aforementioned *Collection of Oracles*, says these things word for word:

-> That the spirits, whom they have presumed to be gods, taught men their own <-
-> meddlesome arts. <-

Not only have they revealed their own way of life and the things already mentioned, but

> they also suggested the things in which they take pleasure and which give them strength. And indeed, they also showed what things they are compelled by, what one ought to sacrifice, and which days to avoid. They taught the form of their statues, how they should be made, and in what shapes they themselves appear, as well as the places in which they dwell. In short, there is absolutely nothing that men did not learn from them before honoring them in such a way. Since there are many things that demonstrate this, we will present a few out of the many, so as not to leave our argument without a witness.

-> That they themselves taught how to magically construct the statues. <-

To show that they themselves suggested how the statues should be made and from what material, the matters concerning Hecate <note>Hecate was the goddess of magic, crossroads, and spirits, central to later "theurgical" practices.</note> will make clear, being in this manner:

-> "But you shall complete a purified wooden image <note>original: "ξόανον" (xoanon). A primitive, often wooden, cult image believed to have fallen from heaven or been divinely inspired.</note> as I shall teach you..." <-
