<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s critique of Porphyry’s work "Philosophy from Oracles." Eusebius is arguing that the "gods" of the Greeks are actually lowly, material-minded spirits (daemons) because they demand physical statues, specific colors of wax, and magical symbols to appear.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

The same author <note>referring to Porphyry</note> also presents the following. These are the symbols of Hecate <note>Hecate was the goddess of magic, crossroads, and the night</note>: a three-colored wax consisting of white, black, and red, formed into a figure of Hecate carrying a whip, a torch, and a sword, with a serpent coiled around her. Furthermore, starfish <note>original: "ἀστέρες οἱ θαλάττιοι" (asteres hoi thalattioi)</note> are to be nailed around the door. For the gods themselves have initiated men into these secrets through these means. And the Pythian <note>The Pythian Apollo, speaking through his oracle at Delphi</note> says:

> "And for these things again, place wax of varied hue in the cast of fire. 
> Let it be white and black, and the light-bearing fire of burning coal;
> A terror to the hounds of the underworld <note>original: "νερτέρων κυνῶν" (nerterōn kynōn), the ghostly dogs that accompanied Hecate</note>.
> Let there be a terrible growl of Hecate, a torch in her hand,
> And a sword that brings punishment, and a serpent coiled
> With powerful eyes <note>original: "ἄμμ'ασι κύριον" (ammasi kyrion). The text is slightly corrupt here but implies a commanding or powerful gaze</note>, placed about her head,
> Along with a varied key, and the power of the daemons,
> And the loud crack of a whip."

Through these instructions, and others like them, that "noble" philosopher of the Sun <image-desc>solar symbol: circle with central dot</image-desc>, that "wonderful" theologian and initiate of secrets, reveals his "Philosophy from Oracles." He displays the secrets contained in these oracles as though they were powers capable of loosening the pull of evil and demonic forces, while in reality, he is merely proclaiming the snares set against mankind. What possible benefit to the gods could come from such malicious sorcery? Why should anything "beloved of God" be found in the meddling with lifeless statues? What kind of divine power is represented by the formation of Egyptian shapes <note>original: "ἰσιακῶν σχημάτων" (isiakōn schēmatōn), literally 'Isiac shapes' referring to the iconography of the goddess Isis</note>? Does he encourage men to pursue true philosophy, or rather to follow the forbidden deeds of magical counselors, while the life lived according to virtue and philosophy is supposedly sufficient on its own to reach a blessed state of happiness? To sharpen his own self-refutation, he adds the following to what has already been said:

### That they also love lifeless materials.

They also love the symbols of the magical characters <term>charaktēres: specific sigils or celestial signs believed to hold the power of a deity</term>. Hecate, having received [these things] for the sake of modesty <note>original: "ἀφιλοδοξίαν" (aphilodoxian), suggesting a lack of worldly ambition or perhaps a ritual requirement</note>, has initiated men through these symbols.

> "What mortal has not yearned to possess the characters?
> Of gold, of bronze, and of gleaming silver?
> And who does not love those things upon the earth,
> Collected into one, where I weave the many-formed [thread] of men?"

He has shown not only that these characters are "dear" to them, but that they even circumscribe themselves <note>i.e., they are bound or localized</note> within them, and are present in the sacred place within the underlying image. Is it the earthly union, or rather that they were able to grasp the sacred things, that causes the image to carry these unspeakable receptions? This is what allows the divine to hold sway upon the earth. Through these points, I believe it has been clearly proved that these "gods" are actually certain earth-bound and passion-driven daemons <note>original: "δαίμονες" (daimones). In this context, Eusebius uses the term to mean lower, often deceptive spirits, as opposed to true divinity</note>. Therefore, I think I have made a prudent assessment of their love for material things. You see how they claim to rule in various places on earth through magical forms and characters. 

If there were truly anything divine here, it ought not to tread upon the earth at all, but should dwell only in the mind of the soul—a soul purified of every stain and blemish, adorned with temperance, justice, and the other virtues. For when these qualities are present in a human soul, as if in a truly sacred place, the presence of the divine spirit follows naturally. There is no longer any need for malicious sorcery to receive the divine for those who have prepared themselves through a virtuous and god-loving soul. Thus, it is explicitly captured from all these points that these beings we were just discussing are merely certain earth-bound, passion-loving, and body-loving spirits. But hear next what the same author says about their famous oracles having failed.

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 5

### Concerning the failed oracles, Apollo himself gave an oracle.

<margin>He said that it is necessary to conquer.</margin>
> Concerning Pytho <note>The ancient name for Delphi, the most famous oracle in Greece</note> and the Clarian <note>Claros was a major oracle of Apollo in Ionia (modern Turkey)</note> cares of Phoebus [Apollo],
> Our prophetic voice speaks in whispering utterances.
> Countless divine mysteries once gushed forth from the back of the earth,
> Both springs and the swirling leaps of water,
> But the earth herself, opening her mouth, took them back again
> Into the depths of the underworld; and a vast eternity destroyed them.
> Only for the Sun, who brings light to mortals, do there still remain
> The Myceleian <note>Likely referring to the oracle at Didyma near Mount Mycale</note> divine waters in the hollows of Didyma,
> And along the foot of Pytho beneath the Parnassian height,
> And the noisy springs of the fountain of prophetic speech.
> But is it not impossible for Pytho to raise its talkative voice?
> For already, obscured by the long passage of time,
> It has been bound by the keys of an unshakeable silence.

---

<margin>At this point, it is fitting to place alongside these words the things said by Plutarch concerning the failed oracles.</margin>
Perform, as is the custom, god-pleasing sacrifices to Phoebus.

> "As for Panthoides the son of Ammonius," I said, "tell us more about the oracle there, O Cleombrotus. For the glory of the divinity there was great in the old days, but now it seems to be fading away." While Cleombrotus remained silent and looked downward, Demetrius said there was no need to ask about things there or to be perplexed by the darkening of the oracles here—or rather, seeing their total failure except for one or two. "Instead," he said, "we should consider together the reason why they have withered so. For why should I speak of other places, when the oracles of Boeotia <note>A region in central Greece</note>, which were many-voiced in former times, have now completely failed like dried-up streams? A great drought of prophecy has taken hold of the land. For nowhere else now in Boeotia, except around Lebadeia, is there an opportunity for those who wish to draw from the spring of prophecy. As for the others, some are silent, and others are held by total desolation."

### In addition to these, the same author <note>Plutarch</note> says the same regarding the mortal nature of those they call daemons.

<margin>Concerning certain mortal daemons, whom they honor as gods.</margin>
"To suggest that it is not gods who oversee the oracles—for it is fitting for gods to be free from earthly matters—but <term>daemons</term> <note>In Greek thought, *daemons* were intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil spirits</note> who are servants of the gods, does not seem to me to be a bad claim. But for someone to almost take the rods from the verses of Empedocles <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher who wrote about the cycle of souls</note> and apply to these daemons the 'sins' and 'follies' and 'divinely-driven wanderings,' and finally to assume they end in death just like human beings—this I consider to be a rather bold and barbaric claim." Cleombrotus then asked Philip who the young man was and where he came from. Learning his name and city, Philip said, "O Heracleon, it has not escaped my notice what kind of difficult arguments we have entered into. For it is impossible to approach the probability of a truth regarding great matters without using great principles. But you yourself are unaware that you are taking away what you give; for you admit that daemons exist, yet by demanding they be neither flawed nor mortal, you are no longer preserving them as daemons. For in what do they differ from gods, if they do not possess immortality in their essence and passionless sinlessness in their virtue?" While Heracleon was considering this in silence, Philip said to him, "But as for flawed dae—"

# EUSEBIUS: EVANGELICAL PREPARATION

,, ...not only did Empedocles leave behind <term>monads</term> <note>original: μονας; here referring to singular spiritual units or entities</note>, but so did Plato, Xenocrates, and Chrysippus; even Democritus left behind remnants of "irrational images" <note>original: ἀλόγων εἰδώλων; Democritus believed these were spiritual films or "idols" that could influence human thoughts</note>. It is clear that he [Plutarch] recognizes other spirits that are difficult to manage and malicious, possessing certain intentions and impulses.

,, Regarding the death of such beings, I have heard a story from a man who was neither foolish nor a boaster—Aemilianus the rhetorician, whom some of you have also heard. His father was Epitherses, my fellow-citizen and a teacher of grammar. He said that once, while sailing to Italy, he boarded a ship carrying merchandise and many passengers. In the evening, near the Echinades Islands, the wind died down, and the ship drifted close to Paxi. Most of those on board were awake and drinking, as they had already finished dinner. Suddenly, a voice was heard from the island of Paxi, calling "Thamus!" with such a loud cry that it caused wonder. This Thamus was an Egyptian pilot, and he was not known by name even to many of those sailing with him.

,, Though called twice, he remained silent. But the third time, he answered the caller, who then raised his voice even louder and said: "When you arrive at Palodes, announce that Great Pan <note>The Greek god of the wild, shepherds, and nature</note> is dead." Upon hearing this, Epitherses said everyone was struck with amazement and began to debate whether it was better to do as commanded or not to meddle. Thamus decided that if there was a breeze, he would sail past in silence, but if there was a dead calm and stillness near the place, he would report what he had heard. When they reached Palodes, with neither wind nor waves, Thamus, looking from the stern toward the land, spoke the words as he had heard them: "Great Pan is dead."

,, As soon as he finished, there was heard a great groaning, not of one person but of many, mingled with cries of wonder. Since many people were present, the story quickly spread through Rome, and Thamus was summoned by Tiberius Caesar. Tiberius put such faith in the story that he made inquiries and sought information about Pan. The <term>scholars</term> <note>original: φιλολόγους; literally 'lovers of words,' referring to the emperor's circle of researchers and intellectuals</note> around him conjectured that he was the son of Hermes and Penelope. Philip [one of the speakers in Plutarch's dialogue] had some of those present as witnesses who had heard the story from the aged Aemilianus.

,, Then Demetrius said that among the islands around Britain, there are many scattered and deserted ones, some of which are named after <term>daemons</term> <note>original: δαιμόνων; in Greek thought, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil</note> and heroes. He said he himself had sailed there for the sake of history and sightseeing, by the king’s commission, to the nearest of the desert islands. It had few inhabitants, all of whom were considered sacred and inviolable by the Britons. Shortly after his arrival, a great disturbance occurred in the air, and many celestial portents appeared; winds broke out and fiery bolts <note>original: πρηστῆρας; fire-storms or lightning-flashes</note> fell. When the storm subsided, the islanders said that one of the "superior beings" had passed away. For just as a lamp, they said, while burning, causes no harm, but when extinguished is offensive to many, so great souls have a benign and painless radiance; but their extinction and destruction often, as now, breed winds and hail, and often infect the air with pestilential diseases.

,, He added that there is one island there where Cronus <note>The father of Zeus in Greek mythology, often associated with time</note> is imprisoned, guarded by Briareus <note>A hundred-handed giant from the Titan wars</note> while he sleeps; for sleep has been devised as a bond for him. Around him are many daemons as his followers and servants.

These are the words of Plutarch. It is worth observing the time at which he says the death of the daemon occurred: it was in the time of Tiberius...

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 5

...at the time when our Savior, during His stay among men, is recorded to have driven every kind of <term>daemon</term> <note>original: δαιμόνων; in this context, Eusebius refers to malevolent spirits or fallen deities rather than the neutral "daimons" of earlier Greek philosophy</note> out of humanity. It is even recorded that some of these spirits fell at His knees and begged not to be delivered yet to the <term>Tartarus</term> <note>original: ταρτάρῳ; the deepest abyss of the underworld used as a place of punishment</note> that awaited them. You have, therefore, the specific time of the daemons' downfall, a thing not recorded from earlier ages. Just as the practice of human sacrifice among the pagans met its end at no other time than after the preaching of the Gospel's teaching had reached all mankind.

Let these things, then, be said by us from more recent history. But since these accounts are perhaps not known to everyone, it seems best to me to move briefly toward things that are plain to all lovers of learning. I shall examine the most ancient oracles, which are sung on the lips of all Greeks and are handed down to students in the schools of every city. Taking up these ancient histories from the beginning, consider what the Pythian god <note>Apollo at Delphi</note> proclaimed to the Athenians when they were oppressed by a plague because of the death of Androgeos <note>Son of King Minos of Crete, killed in Attica, which led to a war and a subsequent cruel tribute</note>. All the Athenians were suffering because of the death of a single man, and they thought it right to seek help from the gods. What, then, did their "savior" and "god" advise them?

Perhaps someone might think he would urge them to practice justice and philanthropy from then on, or some other virtue, or to show <term>repentance</term> <note>original: μετάνοιαν; a change of mind or heart</note> for their transgressions and perform holy and pious acts, so that the gods might be appeased by these things. But it was none of these. For what do these "wonderful gods"—or rather, these utterly wicked daemons—care for such things? Again, they demanded things akin to their own nature: cruel, harsh, and inhumane acts. They brought "plague upon plague," as the saying goes, and "death upon death." Apollo commanded them to send every year seven young boys and an equal number of seven maidens to Crete—fourteen innocent and unblemished children in exchange for one man. This was not a one-time event, but is recorded as happening many times under Minos in Crete. Thus, until the time of Socrates, more than five hundred years later, this dreadful and most inhumane <term>tribute</term> <note>original: δασμός; a forced payment or tax, in this case of human lives</note> was preserved in the memory of the Athenians.

Is it not this very thing that brought the accusation of death upon Socrates? Even then, a certain writer among the youth, possessing a manly reason, exposed the oracle as a collection of sorcerers' tricks in his own work. Listen to his words—not mine—as he addresses the one who delivered the oracle in this manner:

->To whom Apollo gave an oracle to send twice-seven boys and girls<-
->to be slaughtered by the Cretans at the hands of the Athenians.<-

Why then did the Athenians, having killed Androgeos and suffered a plague for it, not speak of repentance? Even if they did not speak of it, was it not fitting for the god to speak of repentance rather than saying, "There will be an end to the plague and famine if you choose by lot from your own bodies a male and a female and give them to Minos, sending them at once to <term>Hades</term> <note>The realm of the dead</note> as a repayment for unjust deeds"? Only then, he claimed, would the god be appeased. I pass over the fact that you [the god] were indignant over the death of one Androgeos at the hands of the Athenians, yet so many others have been falsely accused everywhere and at all times. And yet, the god knew that Minos then held the "mastery of the sea" <note>original: ἐθαλασσοκράτει; referring to the Minoan thalassocracy or naval empire</note> and was very powerful, and all our people served him. For this reason, Minos was considered "most just" and a "good lawgiver," and according to Homer, he was the "confidant of great Zeus," and after death, a judge in Hades. Or perhaps it was for this reason that you entrusted the...

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 5

## EUSEBIUS

...exacted these penalties, yet I will nonetheless pass over these things for you. And because you <note>Oenomaus is addressing Apollo directly</note> used sophistry regarding the murder, you ordered that innocent people be sent to their deaths, and this for a man whom you did not even accept as a common judge of men. For he [Minos] knew how to judge this man himself. And yet, how is it that you gods, in exchange for these things, sent a common punishment upon the Athenians, whom you unjustly killed on account of Androgeos? The same writer, showing how many deaths Apollo caused through the ambiguity of his oracles, takes up the history of the Heracleidae <note>The "Descendants of Hercules," who sought to reclaim their ancestral kingdom in the Peloponnese</note>, speaking again as follows:

---

->How Apollo became the cause of many deaths through the ambiguity of his oracles.<-

---

"Since I have somehow been reminded of this account, come, I shall go through the details concerning the story of the Heracleidae. For these men once set out by way of the Isthmus <note>The narrow strip of land connecting central Greece to the Peloponnese</note>, but failed in their invasion of the Peloponnese. For Aristomachus <note>A great-grandson of Hercules</note> died there. His son <note>Temenus</note> comes to hear from you about the 'way'—the same oracle under which Aristomachus had died—seeking to hear about the route for the invasion. For he desired it just as his father did. And you say to him: 'The gods show you victory through the narrow-way' <term>stenychron</term> <note>original: στενύχρων; this word can mean a "narrow place" or refers to the pass at Stenyclarus. Apollo uses the term to trick the listener into thinking of the land route (the Isthmus)</note>. Because he set out attempting it by way of the Isthmus, he died in battle. 

"His son was Temenus, an unfortunate man, who came to you in his misery. You gave him the same advice you gave to his father Aristomachus, and it seemed clear. And he, being persuaded by you, saw his people die in the invasion. You then said: 'I do not mean the narrow-way by land, but by the broad-bellied one' <term>eurygastora</term> <note>original: εὐρυγάστωρα; a poetic and highly ambiguous term meaning "wide-bellied," which the oracle later claimed referred to the sea</note>. How difficult it was to simply say 'by the sea'! So he went by the sea, creating the impression that he would enter by land, and he occupies the space between Nauplia and Typaeum. There, Hippotes the Aetolian pierces with a javelin Carnus <note>A seer or priest of Apollo</note>. In doing this, it seems to me, a plague happened to break out nearby, and Aristodemus died. 

"They retreated again, and Temenus came to complain of the misfortune. He heard that he was suffering a penalty for the murder of the divine agent, and that the Apollo of the event <note>Apollo Carneus</note> was reciting a poem about the oracle, saying: 'By killing our Achaean, you have brought a penalty upon yourself.' Oh, what things the far-shooter says! What must I do? And how might I heal you? 'Pray to Apollo.' 

"O most cruel one! Did you not know that he who heard 'the narrow-way' would not understand it as anything other than a land passage? But you, knowing better, gave the oracle anyway, and then later blamed him for the error. The 'narrow-way' was made ambiguous so that if we should win, you are seen as the cause <margin>if</margin> of the victory. But if we are defeated, you are not the cause of the defeat. You have a way to escape by pointing to the <margin>if</margin> 'broad-bellied' one. If a man went by the 'broad-bellied' way and failed, it would still have been said that he failed for some other reason. <margin>if</margin> Again, you have the death of the unholy Carnus as an excuse. And yet, O 'mighty one,' you who supposedly care so much for Carnus: you clearly ordered him to be possessed by a god, but you did not protect him. And though it was necessary to save Carnus, who was but one man, you let him die, and when he was dead, you inflicted a Homeric plague <note>A reference to the plague Apollo sends in the beginning of the *Iliad*</note> upon the multitude, and then you prescribed prayers for the plague. 

"If you were truly pained, you would have found a cure by your own wisdom, and you would never have ceased your sophistry—they, asking the questions, and you, playing the sophist—so that whether they win or lose, you remain undetected in your villainy. For the suffering and the desire of men are enough to deceive their minds, so that even if they were slaughtered a thousand times, they would not cease to believe in you. To these things it is worth joining the story of Proetus, who ruled over Lydia <note>A slip in the text or transcription; Proetus is traditionally the King of Argos</note>, and the ancient traditions he received..."

<meta>This page continues the critique by the Cynic philosopher Oenomaus of Gadara, as quoted by Eusebius. Having previously discussed the Heracleidae, the author now turns to the famous story of King Croesus of Lydia to illustrate the deceptive and useless nature of the Delphic Oracle.</meta>

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 6

### EUSEBIUS

...Then, what more did he hope to achieve by his desire to know the future? He intended to revere the gods, and after putting them all to the test, he chose Apollo at Delphi above the rest. Afterward, he adorned the temple with mixing bowls, golden bricks, and a multitude of countless offerings, making it in a short time the wealthiest place on earth. Nor did he, in his magnanimity, overlook anything required for sacrifices. Consequently, believing he had received a pledge from the gods, the Lydian <note>Croesus, King of Lydia (r. 560–546 BCE), famous for his immense wealth</note>, naturally emboldened by these great works of piety, intended to march against the Persians. He planned to expand his empire greatly, looking forward to the god’s alliance. 

What then did that "wonderful" oracle-giver himself do—the one at Delphi, the Pythian, the "Friend"—for his suppliant, his pious follower, his refugee? Did he help him obtain a foreign empire? No—he predicted he would even lose his own! He did this, it seems to me, out of a willful ignorance rather than a hidden treasury of wisdom. For the god did not know—since he is not a god at all, nor any power superior to a human—and so he framed an oracle that could fit either of two natural outcomes, saying almost exactly this:

> "Croesus, having crossed the Halys <note>The Halys River was the border between the Lydian and Persian empires</note>, shall destroy a great empire."

By this, he overthrew the Lydian empire—that great and long-lasting succession which had come down from his ancestors to this pious man—as the "god-beloved" fruit of his excessive zeal for the oracle. Hear now how the writer <note>Oenomaus of Gadara</note> expresses his quite reasonable indignation at these events.

<margin>D</margin>
> "How he also became the cause of Croesus losing his own empire through an ambiguous oracle."

> "You seem truly to know things 'worth a grain of sand' <note>A mocking reference to the Pythia’s claim: 'I know the number of the sand and the measure of the sea'</note>, but to know nothing that is actually good. For that which we know has entered your mind—such as the boiling of the tortoise <note>According to Herodotus, Croesus tested the oracles by asking what he was doing at a specific moment; Delphi correctly identified him boiling a tortoise and lamb in a bronze pot</note>—is a token 'worth a grain of sand,' for it was not even true in itself. Rather, it was a likeness suited to a boaster and a charlatan who raises his eyebrows at empty swellings of pride. You are the one who persuaded the Lydian Croesus—to his own ruin—to do things not to his advantage. A man who, after a short time, intended to ask you based on his experience whether he should march against the Persians, and to take a sign from you in exchange for his folly and greed. You did not hesitate to tell him that 'by crossing the Halys, he would destroy a great empire.' 

> Yet you did not care that by your ambiguous oracle you would lead him into an impossible situation, resulting in his attack on a foreign empire. Even if certain bitter and malicious men were to say that they ought to praise you for ruining a madman—and might further accuse you of not even uttering a balanced word that might make the Lydian hesitate and deliberate—you instead caused him to think only of destruction toward the continent. You did not even care that he would fall from his own rule, provided he attempted to acquire another's. 

> For as for the 'half-ass' <note>The oracle later claimed Cyrus was the 'mule' because he was of mixed parentage: a noble Mede mother and a lower-class Persian father</note>, or 'half-Persian' Cyrus, or the one whose mother was of royal blood but father was a commoner—being a 'mule' in your riddle—you merely displayed the image of a middle-ground after the fact. This was but a prophetic display of ignorance. For if the prophet did not already know that the king would not understand the riddle—or if he played with him not out of ignorance but out of decadence and wickedness—then oh, what divine games these are! But if he did not even know this much, and yet we must consult you so, then you are the most unholy of sophists. Why then, you wretched thing, do you sit in Delphi singing vain and empty songs? Of what use are you?"

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION

### EUSEBIUS

Why are we so mad as to pursue you from every corner of the earth? And why are you such a drone <note>Original: κηφιάς (*kephias*), a drone bee; Oenomaus insults the god Apollo as a lazy creature who lives off the labor of others</note>? Such were the bold names he gave to the activities of these charlatans, characterized by an equal measure of **Cynic bitterness**. He argues that these are not the works of a spirit—let alone a god—but are instead the errors and sophistries of sorcerers, manufactured to deceive the masses. Since we have mentioned these things once, nothing prevents us from hearing further proofs. He describes how he himself was deceived by the Clarian Apollo <note>The Oracle of Apollo at Claros was a major prophetic center in Ionia, modern-day Turkey</note>, writing as follows:

->*How he mocks those who ask questions by dissolving their concerns through oracles.*<-

> But indeed, it was necessary for us to take part in this comedy ourselves, rather than putting on airs as if we hadn't fallen into this common madness. I must speak of the "merchandise" that we ourselves traded for wisdom out of Asia, O Clarian god! You told me: *"In a walled place, there is a garden of Heracles, where all things flourish; it is harvested by thinning, and from this they live. It is made firm by ever-flowing waters."* Then I, being a simpleton <note>Original: βάκηλος (*bakelos*), often referring to a priest of Cybele, but here used by Oenomaus to mean a gullible fool</note>, was puffed up by this mention of Heracles. Regarding that "flourishing garden of Heracles," I perceived some sort of "dream-sweat" <note>An expression for a fleeting or illusory vision</note> because of the wall and the "easy life" promised by those flourishing gardens. 
> 
> Later, as I was praying—asking if the gods were witnesses to my journey—someone from the crowd spoke up, swearing by those very same gods. He said he had personally heard that this same oracle had been given to **Callistratus**, a merchant from Pontus <note>A region on the southern coast of the Black Sea</note>. When I heard this, you can imagine how I raged! I felt as if I were being robbed of my virtue by this merchant. Nevertheless, in my frustration, I began to observe the merchant to see if he, too, was "puffed up" by Heracles. It turned out that he, too, was performing some labor, seeking profit, and expecting to enjoy a certain lifestyle from that profit. 
> 
> Once it became clear that the merchant was exactly like me, I no longer accepted the oracle, nor Heracles. I refused to share the same lot with them, looking at their present labors and their "hopes for the manger" <note>A cynical metaphor for basic, animalistic rewards</note>. But it appeared you oracles are not without your share of small change: whether it is a soldier, a man in love, a woman in love, a flatterer, a lawyer, or a con artist—the god leads each one according to their desire through various "labors," so they might expect the fruits of their efforts.

After turning these matters around and examining them directly, asking a second and third time, he realized that this "wonderful god" knew nothing at all. He concluded that they hide their own ignorance only within the darkness of ambiguity. Thus, he says:

---

->*Those who hide their own ignorance in the darkness of ambiguity.*<-

Since I was already on my way regarding this "merchandise," and I needed a guide to lead me toward wisdom, but it seemed impossible to leave it alone, I begged you <note>Apollo</note> to become a model of instruction—to tell me in what places, or among which Greeks, I should place my trust. Your answer was neither small nor insignificant! What do you say? If I desired to be a sculptor or a painter and sought out teachers, would it be enough for me to hear "in what places" I might find them? Would I not call the person saying such a thing mad? 
 
But perhaps you are not capable of knowing even this. For matters of "remedial service" <note>Referring to the practical advice oracles often gave for health or success</note> already contain much obscurity. But as to where it is better for me to travel from Colophon <note>The city near the Oracle of Claros</note>, surely that is not so hidden from a god? Yet you replied: *"From a stone-feeding, plunder-nurturing sling, a man let fly and slaughtered geese by his infinite, grass-eating plans."* To those...

Having previously mocked the oracle he received personally at Claros, Oenomaus now turns his razor-sharp wit toward the most famous prophecies in Greek history, specifically those given to the Athenians during the Persian Wars.</meta>

<page-num>127</page-num>

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 5

### EUSEBIUS

Since I have mocked these obscure riddles, who could blame me, or what might they say? Who is it—the one at Amphilochus, or the one at Dodona, or you at Delphi—who speaks of "the tight-spun sling" <note>Original: τανύστροφον σφενδόνην (*tanustrophon sphendonen*); Oenomaus is mocking a specific, overly poetic phrase used in an oracle</note>? If it is not a means of ransom, why don't you go away and hang yourself with that "tight-spun sling," rather than composing unintelligible poems?

But since these matters have been so exposed, it is time to look again at their case, so that the same man might refute the oldest oracles at Delphi—those most admired in the **heroic histories**. A great armed host <note>This refers to the massive Persian army under King Xerxes in 480 BCE</note> was advancing against the Athenians. No other hope of safety remained for them except God alone. Knowing this "ancestral helper," as they called him, they invoked him. This was the Delphic Apollo. And what did this "wonderful" god do? Did he fight on behalf of his own people? Did he remember the libations or the fat of the sacrifices, or the hecatombs <note>A "hecatomb" was a high-status sacrifice of one hundred oxen</note> of others who had joined him? Not at all. What does he say instead?

He tells them to flee and keep fleeing, and to look for a "wooden wall" after the city is lost—meaning the navy, by which alone he says they would be saved after the city was burned. **What "great divine help" indeed!** Then, the destruction not only of the city built of timber and brick, but even of the very temples dedicated to the gods, was predicted as if it were a great revelation. But even without an oracle, anyone could have expected this from the enemy's invasion. The author, acting quite reasonably, mocks them again, exposing this "heroic deception" in the following words:

-> Since the god was unable to help in the misfortunes of war, they used ambiguous oracles to play the sophist and deceive those seeking refuge. <-

**But** perhaps such things come from someone who is willfully malicious; however, we must rather bring the case of the Athenians to judgment. Let the words spoken to the Athenians be told:

> "O wretched ones, why do you sit? Flee to the ends of the earth, leaving your homes and the high peaks of your circular city.
> For neither the head remains firm, nor the body,
> Nor the hands, nor the feet below. For it is being razed 
> By fire and sharp Ares <note>In Greek poetry, "Ares" is often used as a synonym for war or the attacking army</note>, driving a Syrian chariot.
> Many other strongholds shall he destroy, not yours alone.
> And many temples of the immortals shall he give to ravening fire;
> They who even now stand dripping with sweat,
> Shaking with fear."

Behold the oracle given to the Athenians! Is there anything truly prophetic in it? You might say someone would marvel at it, by Zeus! But if you add what was said to them when they begged for help, the truth will be known. Behold, let this be added:

> "Pallas Athena cannot appease Olympian Zeus,
> Though she prays with many words and deep wisdom.
> But to you I speak this word again, making it firm as adamant:
> Though all else be taken,
> Wide-seeing Zeus grants a **wooden wall** to the Trito-born <note>Original: Τριτογενὲς (*Tritogenes*); a traditional title for the goddess Athena, possibly meaning "thrice-born" or born from the river Triton</note>,
> To be alone uncaptured, which shall protect you and your children.
> Do not wait for the cavalry or the great host of infantry
> Coming from the continent; turn your back and withdraw. 
> You shall yet live to stand against them another day.
> O divine **Salamis**, you shall destroy the children of women,
> Whether Demeter <note>The goddess of the harvest; here the oracle refers to the season when grain is either scattered (sown) or gathered (harvested)</note> is being scattered or gathered."

<summary>Oenomaus mocks the Delphic Oracle's famous "wooden wall" prophecy given to the Athenians during the Persian invasion, arguing that the god's advice to flee was obvious and his "divine" help was merely a riddle about ships.</summary>

He now continues his biting satire of the relationship between Zeus, Athena, and the Delphic Apollo (the "son of Zeus").</meta>

<page-num>128</page-num>

# EUSEBIUS

### THE PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL

Zeus certainly seemed worthy to you, O son of Zeus <note>Apollo</note>. But so did Athena—or at least the things of Athena—O brother of Athena. This great zeal and this excessive domesticity—to leave it to the father and the daughter, or rather to the gods, to decide that the "Olympian" is the one who will destroy this single city of Athens, unless he brings that infinite army <note>The Persian army under Xerxes</note> against it because of you. He must be someone great, then, possessing the power to stir up evil and being persuasive at the same time, because he moves so many nations from Asia into Europe. Yet, once in Europe, he is unable to overturn a single city. 

And you, you babbler, who are at the same time reckless regarding things that mean nothing—will you not lament? Would men not have said this, from whom Pallas <note>Athena</note> is unable to appease the Olympian Zeus? Did Zeus smile upon the humans, but not upon the stones and wood? And then, while you were "saving" the humans, he was setting the buildings on fire. For he did not allow his thunderbolt to burn around it. Or perhaps we are even more babbling and reckless for not permitting you to babble in this way.

How is it, O prophet, that you knew "divine Salamis" <note>Original: Σαλαμὶς ἡ θείη (*Salamis he theie*); a reference to the famous line in the Delphic oracle before the Battle of Salamis</note> would destroy the children of women? Whether Demeter was being scattered or gathered <note>Original: σκιδναμένης δήμητερος ἢ συνιούσης (*skidnamenēs dēmēteros ē suniousēs*); "Demeter" here is a poetic metaphor for grain, referring to the seasons of sowing or harvest</note>, did you no longer know? How did you not even know this: that one might say "children of women" refers to one's own people, but one might also say it refers to the enemy, depending on who benefits from the trickery? This ambiguity is necessary for what is to be put away. For it will indeed be "put away" in one of these ways. 

Tell us then: "Divine Salamis" will destroy you—speaking of the Persians—for two days as if calling them home? Especially in that sea-battle, whether grain was being scattered or gathered, you have plastered it over with poetic grandiloquence so that the lack of enlightenment might be hidden by the sophistry, and so it would not be immediately obvious that a naval battle does not take place in winter. 

Even now, the tragedy is not hidden, nor are the gods who have been struck. One is a suppliant, the other is unbending—useful roles for the future and for the unexpected "festival" of war; the one for the victors, the other for the perishing. For if they were saved, look: the prayers of Pallas were already offered, sufficient to bend the wrath of Zeus. But if not, even this was not unprepared by the prophet: for "Pallas is unable to appease Zeus." 

The craftsman <note>The oracle-writer</note> mixed his speech to suit these half-bad fortunes. As if Zeus would, on the one hand, carry out his own purpose, but on the other hand, would not utterly despise his daughter's prayer. And that "many towers will fall"—unless he attacked with a stalk of fennel rather than with iron and fire—would quickly have been proven a lie. Since even those many men did not detect a mere fennel-stalk against her. 

"But I," he says, "discovered the wooden wall <note>Original: ξύλινον τεῖχος (*xylinon teichos*); the famous riddle that Themistocles interpreted as the Athenian navy</note>, which alone you should conclude is unassailable," so that the prophecy might not be a lie. It is not unlikely, then, to flee, nor to loose oneself, nor to fear that it is an evil thing. That deep riddle, therefore, was no worse than yours to see through: that the city of the Athenians was the pretext for the journey into Persia, and the whole expedition was directed against it and became the most prominent goal. Since even I, though no prophet, would recognize this; and that the Athenian—and not just that Lydian <note>Croesus of Lydia</note>—would turn to his ships to flee. For there will still be war. Great cavalry and infantry are coming. He says "by ships," but not "by land." For since they had a naval fleet and lived by the sea, they could not be saved all at once, and they could save only as much as they could throw into the ships, handing over the land to those who wanted it.

These prophecies to the Athenians, then, are extremely weak and laughable; but those given to the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> are even more so. For he says either the whole city will be besieged, or they will mourn a fallen king...

Having mocked the oracle given to the Athenians, Oenomaus now turns his sharp wit toward the prophecies given to the Spartans (Lacedaemonians) and the Cnidians during the Persian Wars.</meta>

<page-num>129</page-num>

-> EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 6 <-

...this. One might say that it is not at all likely, considering the ways of this sophist <note>Oenomaus mocks the Delphic Apollo by calling him a "sophist," implying he is a clever deceiver rather than a god</note>, that "either this or that" would happen. But surely, it was the duty of a god to help the prophet with these ambiguous matters and his ignorance of the future. He should have appeared as a savior of our people in their time of need, providing the Greeks, as if they were his own friends, with a victory over their enemies and the barbarians. Or, if he were not capable of that, he should at least have provided a way for them to avoid suffering or being captured. For he did not even know enough to tell them—not that much!—even how to recognize the signs of their own defeat. Therefore, listen to what the critique says regarding these matters.

## Regarding the Lacedaemonians.

"But you shouldn't," you will say, "put the Lacedaemonians to the test in this way." Don't say that! For you did not know, O sophist, whether things in Sparta would turn out as they did in Attica. You were afraid that if you ordered them to flee, they might flee while the enemy never even arrived. So, since you had to say something, you spoke to the Lacedaemonians thus:

*For you, O inhabitants of wide-wayed Sparta,*
*Either your great and glorious city will be sacked by the sons of Perseus* <note>Original: ἀνδράσι περσείδῃσι (*andrasi perseidēsi*); a reference to the Persians, whom the Greeks mythically linked to the hero Perseus</note>,
*Or, if not that, then the borders of Lacedaemon will mourn*
*A dead king from the race of Heracles.* <note>Original: ἀφ' ἡρακλέος δὲ γενέθλης (*aph' herakleos de genethlēs*); the Spartan kings claimed direct descent from the hero Heracles. This refers to King Leonidas, who died at Thermopylae</note>

Again, we see that "most ignorant conjunction" <note>Oenomaus refers to the word "Either/Or" (ἢ). He argues that by giving two options, the oracle is never wrong, but also never useful</note>. If their affairs had been stale, so that no one would stumble upon them, you, acting like a slave and seeming at a loss, would not have examined the rest. Everyone looked to you in such great danger, yet you remained a counselor only of the future and of what must be done. They believed you were faithful, but you had convinced yourself they were fools. The present crisis was not enough to lead you to stop tripping up these witless people—not only with Delphic and Dodonian sophistries, but already with bird-divination, flour-divination <note>Original: ἀλευρομαντεῖα (*aleuromanteia*); a form of fortune-telling using meal or flour</note>, and the inspection of entrails. Not only are the gods trusted in these matters, but by now even weasels, crows, and the phantoms of dreams are too!

Is it not clear that they would not have preferred both outcomes over one, nor the greater over the lesser? It would be a "lesser" evil for one king to fall instead of many. Therefore, they will not sack the city, nor will there be any escape for them. If the king himself were to be caught somewhere, perhaps something paradoxical might happen to you. It remains for those who calculate these things either not to send the king to war—staying at home themselves out of danger and appearing wise—or to face the obvious destruction of the infinite crowd. Yet Sparta held onto its fear and its hopes for a successor. Nevertheless, the trick remains unbearable, whether the city escapes or is captured. Why on earth was it not simply said: "By Zeus, if the king dies, the city will be saved"? It is clear whether he alone will perish, or the entire city. In either case, it is "safe" <note>Meaning the prophecy is "safe" from being proven wrong because it covers all bases</note>, whether he dies alone or not. This is the fruit of vanity and folly. But enough of these matters. It is also worth mentioning what you prophesied to the Cnidians when they, too, were in trouble and seeking an alliance from the god.

## The same regarding the Cnidians.

The Cnidians suffered something similar to this when Harpagus <note>A Median general serving the Persian King Cyrus the Great</note> campaigned against them. For they attempted to cut through the isthmus there to make their city an island. At first, they took up the work; but when the labor became difficult, and they were already giving up...

...they were using. But you <note>Oenomaus continues to address the god Apollo directly</note> said to them: *Do not fortify the Isthmus, nor dig it through. For Zeus would have made it an island had he so willed.* And the fools were persuaded, and by ceasing their work, they delivered themselves over to the "Snatcher" <note>original: ἁρπάγῳ (*harpagō*); a pun on the name of Harpagus, the Persian general, which also means "robber" or "predator"</note>. This was a piece of trickery; since your prediction was not certain to be a way of escape for those who dug, you stopped them from doing it. But since you did not command them to stick to the work, you simply returned them to the choice of either staying or fleeing. In this, you were no better to them, by speaking to those who did not dig. Rather, it seems you did not think they would be able to succeed. Yet your discouragement was not helpful, as it left both options equally balanced; but in your encouragement, it was proper to be on guard. Surely it was not safe, for one who claims to be wise, to overturn their plans. Thus, having said nothing of the reasons for which they had come, you sent them away thinking they had heard something useful. I believe these things sufficiently expose the weakness of both those who give the oracles and those who consult them, and show that nothing straight or true can be found in these declarations. But what is even worse regarding these beings—whether they be wicked demons or men acting the part of the oracles—is to see how they provoked those who consulted them into war against one another, when they ought to have been the arbiters of peace and friendship. At one time, as if they were his own kin and friends, the one at Delphi <note>Apollo</note> acts as a patron for the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> against the Messenians. At another time, he gives oracles to the Messenians against the Lacedaemonians—if only they would appease the demons through counter-sacrifices. Listen now to the accounts of these matters.

### How he drove those who consulted him into frenzy for war against one another.

Wisdom will judge such things more than the art of divination, and will not allow it to speak at random. First, the persuasions were ignorant, and the embassies were unfulfilled. For he says one should not provide oracles for a vain desire—neither to these people, nor to the Lacedaemonians regarding the Messenians and the land which the Messenians held after defeating the Lacedaemonians by deceit.

<margin>»</margin> By the same arts it shall be captured as it was held before.

I do not accept these "preliminary sacrifices," because the sanctuary was not pure from a soul untouched by fire, which is why the Messenians’ efforts were unfulfilled. For this is the very definition of chaos. Such are the stories of ancient history; but it is also possible for us to see similar things in our own day, from ancient times down to our own, regarding the rulers of various periods—how they are sometimes driven into unshielded wars through the counsel of oracles, and at other times they are brought to ruin by...

...the obscurity of the oracles. But perhaps, lest they be led astray by the foolish deception of these utterances, why is it necessary to prove how, in the greatest calamities—either in battle-lines against enemies or in the dangers of bodily illnesses—they gained nothing from the help or healing of those believed to be gods? For such things always and throughout come to them from the oracles, just as the things kept silent in ancient histories. But since one of the most frequently mentioned oracles among the living was the one given to Lycurgus, whom the Pythia <note>the priestess of Apollo at Delphi</note> addressed as he approached with that well-known greeting:

> » Give it to you.

» They are beyond; whom you then order to lead the peoples.

<margin>Those arriving.</margin>
» That which is through the silence of strife and destructive ruin...

The oracle commands that one must especially be courageous in guarding against this ruin. This we have heard many times, even from the simple-minded, but also concerning harmony. This comes not only from the wise, but even now from the factionalists <term>original: phasiadzontes; those who stir up political parties or strife</term> themselves. So, I will grant you this as a matter of your own eagerness. And yet, though you are a fault-finder, you did not realize that we have received this many times and from many people, without even eating the laurel or drinking the water of Castalia <note>The sacred spring at Delphi where the Pythia and pilgrims purified themselves</note>, nor ever having raised our eyebrows too high in a display of wisdom. Speak then about courage, speak about temperance, speak about harmony, so that many might say: "These things have been said before." And do not command us, who do not know how, to lead the peoples, nor command us in this way, but lead them yourself! For the task is noble, but for us, it is impossible and terrifying. To these things he adds, saying:

->They did not deliver oracles concerning serious matters.<-

But you are ready to speak even concerning marriage.

<margin>Concerning children.</margin>
» Take the dark-maned foal of horse-pasturing Argos.

» The suns would not shine on you being in the place of many prayers...

<margin>Concerning colonies.</margin>
» Labda <note>The mother of Cypselus, future tyrant of Corinth</note> is pregnant; she will bring forth a rolling boulder.

» Send men to the flowery land for the sake of gold.

<margin>Concerning empty glory.</margin>
» Displaying fine bronze on the shoulders, iron in the hands.

» Of all the earth, the Pelasgian soil <note>Refers to the land of the Pelasgians, the ancient inhabitants of Greece</note> is best.

» Thracian mares are the best, but Lacedaemonian women <note>The Spartans were famously praised for the strength and beauty of their women</note>.

» And the men who drink the water of beautiful Arethusa <note>A famous spring in Syracuse, Sicily</note>.

And you seem to me to be no better than those called omen-readers <term>original: teratoskopoi; diviners who interpret monstrous births or signs</term>, nor even better than the wandering beggars and sophists. Indeed, I would not wonder at them if they perform wonders for a fee. But of you, a god, I would wonder if you trade in truth for a price. Consider how that famous Socrates answered neither way to the man asking whether he should marry, except to say that he would regret both choices. To the one desiring children, he did not say he would provide them, as if to leave it written how, if children were born, he might best treat them. He made no account of this. He only considered how they might be born to him. And when another had decided to travel abroad because things were going poorly at home, Socrates said he was not deliberating correctly. For he would go away leaving his fatherland there, but bringing his ignorance with him—which would make things difficult for him there, just as it did here. And he did this not only when asked, but even going uninvited to such gatherings.

->They did not advise what must be done with common and human reasoning.<-

Twenty days before the Dog Star <note>Sirius, the brightest star, associated with the hottest part of summer</note>, and twenty after,
Use Dionysus <note>A poetic reference to wine</note> as a physician in a shaded house.
This was medical advice for the Athenians troubled by the heat, but it was not prophetic.
Erginus, son of the famous Presbon,
You have come late seeking offspring, but even so...

» For an aged man, to make a young crow his equal in cry.

For an old man to live with a young woman—if he desires children—this is not the work of a prophet, nor is it even a mystery; it is simply the nature of a bull-like man <term>original: epitaurodou; acting with raw, animalistic vigor</term>, where desire drives the foolish into a frenzy.

### That they often offered praise in a manner that was not unphilosophical.

Therefore, you should have a fennel-stalk <note>A narthex, or fennel-stalk, was a staff carried by worshippers of Dionysus, but here it implies a schoolmaster’s rod used for discipline</note> ready to use on him, unless you can persuade him to learn from those loathsome questions of yours, which are supposedly worthy of a divine visit. Or you might say to the Pythian flute-player—who lost his inheritance in city-life nonsense and came to you in grief:
» "Antiochus has come to the land, and dwells on an inglorious island; he who once lived among twenty Cretans... I command you, the Pythian, to perform a radiant Phoebian purification, so that you might re-establish Crete. Do not trample on wealth through the laws, but revere the living."
To those who must hear that Cretan nonsense: "Inhabitant of wealth and madness, I will destroy many things. I command those who are radiant to perform a purification of oblivion, so that you might re-establish wisdom. Do not trample on wealth through the laws, but revere the divine things."
In this way, you might not find yourself in more need of a Cretan purification than of some Orphic or Epilynician rituals, while you are busy chasing phantoms.

### That they even sided with those who committed injustice.

And why, O wisest one, was there an oracle for Archelaus <note>likely referring to King Archidamus of Sparta</note>, the king of the Lacedaemonians? "Apollo takes half the share of the allotted spoils; it will be much better for them." And to what kind of "Apollo" are you speaking? Surely not the one residing in the earth! Do not mock the prophet, lest someone rebuke him for being a partner who divides the ill-gotten gains with the robbers. Let these matters stand as they are.

But come, let us add to these things the way in which Apollo, in turn, admires Archilochus <note>A famous Greek poet (7th century BCE) known for his biting satire and obscene verses</note>—a man who used all kinds of shameful language regarding women and unspeakable words which no temperate man could endure to hear, filling his own poems with them. And you would also benefit my friend Euripides, who fell away from philosophy and is even now still being performed as a tragedy upon the stage. Or consider Homer after these, whom the noble Plato cast out of his own Republic as being of no use, but rather someone who corrupted the youth to the extreme with his poetic nakedness. Regarding these men, the aforementioned author mocks the oracle-giving god in this way:

### That they indiscriminately praised poets who had demonstrated nothing worthy of a philosophical life, even to the common people.

"Your son shall be immortal and celebrated in song, O Telesicles <note>The father of the poet Archilochus</note>; he shall exist among men." This was said concerning the son, Archilochus. And to Euripides: "There shall be for you a child... whom all men shall honor, and he shall rush toward noble fame, and receive the holy, sweet grace of crowns." And for Homer: "You have obtained a share of life from Zeus, equal to the immortal suns; you are of equal portion with the immortals, both in life and in death." And because of these things, he heard: "O blessed and ill-fated one, for you were born for both."

But a man might say to you: "One must not cross-examine him, for he is a god of rulers, not of men." Come then, O god, do not be invisible to us. For I desire—if we are not being wronged—that those who...

...for some, the glory of the noble; for others, sacred crowns; for others, fellowship with the gods; and for others, immortality itself. Why, then, was there such a fire <note>referring to poetic inspiration or passion</note> that Archilochus seemed to you to be worthy of possessing a mind? Do not be envious, O most philanthropic of gods—lest you show the way to other gods. Does it lead us to the head? Or is it clearly through Archilochus, if we are to appear worthy of your hearth <note>The "hearth" or *hestia* refers to the sacred center of the temple or divine favor</note>? Should we bitterly abuse those women who are unwilling to marry us? 

<margin>4</margin>
Or others among the effeminate men <term>original: kinaidōn; a derogatory term for men perceived as passive or flamboyant</term>, insofar as they are far more wicked than other villains? And let it not be without meter <note>Greek poetry was written in strict rhythmic meters</note>, for this is the dialect of the gods, just as it is of divine men like Archilochus. There is nothing surprising in this. For because of their excellence in these matters—by which one man manages a household, another a private life, a city lives in harmony, and nations stand by their power—it was not unreasonable, then, that he seemed to be a servant of the Muses. 

And his killer was deemed unworthy of approaching you gods, nor of receiving your voice, because he was a murderer who had killed a man. Therefore, was the threat against Archias <note>Archias of Naxos, who killed Archilochus in battle</note> unjust? Was the Pythia <note>the priestess of Apollo</note> not untimely in avenging Archilochus, who was long since dead, when she ordered the "polluted man" to leave the temple because he "killed a servant of the Muses"? 

To me, at least, while defending the poet, this seemed unpleasant. For I still remembered another poet and the sacred crowns given to Euripides. Yet I am at a loss, and eager to hear: not merely that he was crowned, but how these things were considered "sacred." It is not because his glory echoed in the mountains <note>original: oreusin</note>, but how that was "noble." I know he was applauded among the crowds, and I know he pleased tyrants. He pursued a craft for which not only was he, the admirer, esteemed, but the city of Athens was as well—at a time when she alone followed the tragic poets. 

If applause is a sufficient judge, and the table on the Acropolis <note>Refers to the *prytaneion*, where distinguished citizens were given the honor of public meals</note>, then I have nothing more to say while seeing Euripides dining on the Acropolis, with the people of Athens and the people of Macedonia <note>Euripides spent his final years at the court of King Archelaus of Macedon</note> dancing in accompaniment. But if, apart from these things, there is some judgment of the gods—or even a human one, no less than that of tyrants or crowds—come, tell us: for what noble quality did you gods grant a favorable vote for the life of Euripides? 

We ask so that we might find it and pursue heaven with our feet, following your praises. For surely there are people even now ready to be mocked, like the Sabians and the family of Lycambes <note>Lycambes was the target of Archilochus’s famously lethal poetic insults</note>. As for tragedy, nothing would stand in the way. Neither Thyestes, nor Oedipus, nor that Phineus <note>All legendary figures associated with great suffering or crime in Greek tragedy</note>—nor, I think, would they envy anyone desiring the friendship of the divine. 

Indeed, it seems to me that even those tragic figures, if they realized that a man like Euripides would become "beloved by the gods" for embracing them, they would forget their own evils. They would not focus on higher things but turn toward moderation. They would use their names—even if those names were full of weight and sorrow—to journey toward heaven, so that they might be held in Olympus after their stay in the court of Zeus. 

For these are the things the poet in Delphi says. Come, let us also look at the question asked by the "blessed one" before Homer <note>Likely referring to Hesiod or a legendary figure in competition with Homer</note>. He asks the god—for surely some heavenly power called the god forth. For the god would not have so easily pronounced him "blessed" unless he had assigned it to him. He said:

> » "You seek a fatherland; but your mother-land is not your fatherland.
> » From the land of Minos <note>Crete</note>, neither near nor far,
> » it is your fate to end your life’s journey."

> When from the tongue you know how to live away from children — a thing said in many words. <note>original: "Εὖτ' ἂν ἀπὸ γλώσσης γνῶς παίδων ἀζωεύειν — πολλοῖσι λόγοις εἰρημένον." This appears to be a fragment of a cryptic oracular response.</note>

For it is a terrible thing, O wisest of men—or rather, of gods—if the common crowd knows neither where on earth they sprang from their mother, nor where they shall lie with eyes closed. I used to think it was just as much a matter of "playing the hostage" <note>Oenomaus is likely playing on the name "Homer" (*Homeros*), which means "hostage."</note> for the god to twitter on about these things as it is for a comic actor; and that the god should no more use Homer to explain such ignorance than he would use a comedian. 

If some comic actor were born and did not spend his life or grow old in that state of "dumbness," <note>The word *kophia* refers to being deaf, mute, or simply dull/silent. Oenomaus is mocking the "silence" or lack of clarity in oracles.</note> but rather by an enemy's outrage, a pitiable fate, and a harsh divine storm, he was lifted up by force and carried off to some hostile land and a hostile silence. From there, seeking a way to Delphi, he asked what his father’s "dumbness" was doing to him, and what land would receive him when he died. These things, then, concern the poets.

> It is not for boxers and athletes to provide a ball for you young men.

<margin>E</margin> Since the "wonderful" god has deified through his own oracles not only poets but even boxers and athletes, it seems reasonable to me to refute these things as well, using these very words: "O you who know the number of the sand and the measures of the sea, and who understand the mute and hear the one who does not speak." <note>This is a famous quote from the Pythian Oracle's response to King Croesus, used here sarcastically to contrast the god's supposed omniscience with his poor choice of heroes.</note> If only you were ignorant of all such things, but knew this: that boxing is no different from kicking! Then you might have encountered donkeys, or you might not have spoken such "invincible" things about the boxer Kleomedes, saying:

> The last of the heroes is Kleomedes of Astypalaea.
> Honor him with sacrifices as one who is no longer mortal. <note>original: "Ὕστατος ἡρώων Κλεομήδης Ἀστυπαλαιεύς. / Ὃν θυσίαις τιμᾶσθ' ὡς οὐκέτι θνητὸν ἐόντα."</note>

Why indeed, O interpreter of all things forgotten—to use a Platonic phrase—did you deify this man? Was it because at the Olympic games, having wrestled his opponent with a single blow, he broke open the man's side, thrust in his hand, and seized his lung? Is that an act worthy of a god, Apollo? Or was it not only that, but also because when he was fined four talents for these actions, he could not endure it, and out of spite and heavy-heartedness, he vented his rage on the children in the schoolhouse by pulling out the pillar that held up the roof? 

Is it for these reasons, O god-maker, that Kleomedes must be honored by you? Or will you add that other proof of his "manliness" and "divine favor"—that he climbed into a sacred chest, pulled down the lid, and became impossible to catch for those pursuing him who tried to drag him out? O Kleomedes! Is a hero then not a mortal? What sort of "immortal" mechanisms did you invent, or what god—or gods—took you up for your "good deeds," just as Homer’s gods took up Ganymede? <note>In Greek myth, Ganymede was a beautiful youth snatched up by Zeus to be the cupbearer of the gods.</note> But they took him for his beauty; they took you for your strength—and what a fine use of strength that was! 

If then, O "Future-Teller" as I called you, you had left aside the sand and the salt water and learned instead how much boxing is worth, you would have considered the kicking donkeys to be gods, and the wild asses the best of the gods. A fitting oracle comes to mind, more suited to a dead wild ass than to your boxer:

> The donkey is the most excellent of the immortals, not Kleomedes,
> Whom you honor with sacrifices as one who is no longer mortal.

Do not be surprised if a wild ass sues for immortality, having sufficiently prepared the divine things by number. And having heard this, do not be indignant, but threaten to strike Kleomedes himself and cast him into the pit. For they would not both linger in heaven equally.

<sig>m.ii.</sig>

<summary>Oenomaus of Gadara ridicules the Delphic Oracle for deifying Kleomedes of Astypalaea, a violent boxer who murdered an opponent and a schoolroom full of children. He sarcastically suggests that if such violence is divine, then donkeys—famed for their kicks—are more deserving of worship than athletes.</summary>

...to return to life. For he considers himself more worthy of the halls of divine gifts, inasmuch as he was ready to fight not only by himself—even if he used those iron-studded leather straps <term>himantes</term> <note>original: "ἱμᾶσιν" — These were leather thongs wrapped around a boxer's knuckles, which in later periods were often weighted with lead or iron to increase the lethality of the blow.</note>—but also to take on the Thasian boxer <note>Theagenes of Thasos, a famous champion in boxing and the pancration in the 5th century BCE.</note> both at once. It was because of this athlete that the gods were angered on account of a statue, for which they made the Thasian land barren. 

We are expected to believe this story, not on human authority, but from the god himself. From these accounts, I have fully realized that boxing must be something "divine." To the many who consider themselves wise, the god showed mercy; so that, abandoning the pursuit of being "good and noble" <term>kalos kagathos</term> <note>A central Greek concept of aristocratic virtue combining physical beauty and moral goodness.</note>, they themselves practiced the ways of the Thasian boxer. While the gods did not grant him immortality, as they did for Kleomedes, they loved him greatly. This was demonstrated by his bronze statue: when it was pulled down by the images of foolish men, it fell flat upon the enemy who was scourging it—by some divine providence, it seems. 

But the foolish Thasians, ignorant of divine matters, "enslaved" the heavy bronze; they brought a legal charge against the statue and dared to sink it into the sea. Yet the Thasians did not escape justice; the gods taught them what an evil they had dared by sending a famine, the servant of retribution. This famine barely taught them the plans of the gods, until you, Apollo—the most "loving of humanity" among the gods—sent them help through your own oracle, saying:

->“By bringing the exiles back to their fatherland, you shall reap the harvest of Demeter.”<-

But the fools again misunderstood, thinking they should recall the men fleeing for murder, knowing no better. For why should the most "un-philanthropic" gods care about men being recalled, as much as they care for statues? No benefit came to the land to stop its sickness, until someone understood that the "exile" commanded by the divine mind was the statue that had been cast into the sea, and they set it back up. As soon as it was raised, the land flourished once more. 

How, then, are these clear proofs of "god-befitting" athletics—that it is a state of divine possession? For the gods were also enraged over the dishonored statue of a pentathlete, and the Locrians went hungry. Nor did these people find relief until you healed them with a word that went like this: 

> "While you keep the dishonored one among you, only then shall you plow the earth." 

For the Locrians did not perceive the meaning before, or before you became their patron <term>proxenos</term> in this matter. Because of Euthykles the pentathlete, whom they had cast into prison—accusing him of taking bribes against his country—and not only this, but even after his death, they continued to insult his images. This continued until the gods, unable to tolerate what was happening, unleashed a mighty famine upon them. They would have perished by hunger if help had not come from you, saying that they must honor "shining" men, whom the gods love no less than those whom the statue-makers "fatten" with their craft. <note>The Greek "πιάνοισι βοᾶς" is likely a corrupted reference to "fattening" like oxen, or making the statues physically imposing.</note> 

Through these men, people sometimes persuade you by sacrificing; though they have no less sweat, these "fattened" men delight you much more than fat oxen. Indeed, you are delighted to the point that sometimes an entire city or an entire nation faces your anger because one or two people wronged these "livestock." How I wish, O Witness <note>original: "μάρτυ" — martyr or witness.</note> Aristes, that you had become a prophet for us instead of a witness—or perhaps both witness and Aristes at once—so that just as there is a Delphic oracle, there might also be a "gymnastic-oracle." For it is not foreign to the Pythian games <note>The Pythian Games at Delphi included both athletic and musical contests in honor of Apollo.</note> for the gymnasium to be "Pythian" as well. I believed these things which he says while refuting them. But see how they are accustomed to flatter tyrants...

”But also for the inhabitants of Methymna it will be much better,

For the cities offer sacrifices and perform rites, not only for the "Dionysus-Phallens" of the fruit-harvest, but even for those made of stone, bronze, and gold. Not only for the "Phallen" ones, but for the Dionysoi themselves, and for many other Hesiodic gods. If there were any man keeping watch over such insolence and lawlessness, he would not be so blind as to let the evil proceed even until now, reaching as far as you. They even attempt to reach Olympus, because they say it is the "ever-secure seat of the gods." <note>A traditional Homeric description of Mount Olympus.</note> And yet, if it is as "secure" as the nonsense of these worshippers suggests, not one of the Olympians would have come to such a state of mind as to honor a log of olive wood <note>original: "ὕαινον κορμὸν" — Likely referring to wood from the wild olive tree.</note>, which the people of Methymna hauled up when it got tangled in the linen of their fishing nets.

For, by Dionysus, the log would not have stayed tangled in their nets any longer, but it would have vanished from the surface of the water, a ruined piece of craftsmanship.

<header>OF EUSEBIUS</header>

## The following is contained in the sixth book of the Preparation for the Gospel.

That even what the demons seem to prophesy in the oracles, they merely conjecture from the motion of the stars, in the same way that humans do.

That they also abolish "that which is in our power" <note>original: "τὸ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν" — a technical philosophical term referring to free will or moral agency.</note>, claiming that even our choices are moved by fate.

That they were not even able to assist their own consecrated images when they were struck by lightning.

That they say the matters of fate are dissolved through magic.

That they also tell lies when prophesying.

A refutation of the discourse concerning fate.

How their own philosophers refuted the opinions of their gods concerning fate using more correct reasoning—from the works of Oenomaus.

Further concerning these matters, from the works of Diogenianus.

Further concerning this, from the works of Alexander <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle who wrote "On Fate."</note>.

How the discourse concerning fate is refuted by mathematical <term>mathematical theory</term> <note>In the ancient world, "mathematics" often referred specifically to astrology and the calculation of horoscopes.</note>—from the works of Bardesanes.

How [it is also refuted] from the interpretation and testimony of the Divine Scriptures—from the works of Origen.

---

### Preface to the entire subject.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial letter 'T' (Tau), decorated with scrolls and foliage within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

Since the topic concerning oracles has been sufficiently refuted by us in the preceding sections, and since the divine power of our Savior through his Gospel teaching has been demonstrated—which we have shown to be both worthy of God and beneficial for life—it is clear that through Him alone, freedom has become available to all men from the demonic phantasms that have darkened and ruined our whole life from ages past. 

Come then, let us also direct our discourse against the false opinions held by them concerning fate, so that the demons believed to move the oracles may be exposed as base and powerless, not only because of the wickedness of the places they inhabit, but also because of their incorrect and untruthful doctrines. Consider, then, if the discourse concerning them will not reveal to you their lack of power, both from the traditional arguments that overturn their views on fate, and directly from the very method by which they are said to produce their prophecies. 

For they do not claim to have grasped the knowledge of the future by some superior power, but rather they conjecture what is to come from observing the movement of the stars, just as humans do. Consequently, they can do nothing, nor help, nor effect anything at all, except—as they say—those things determined by fate. The refutation of these things is provided by that very advocate of the demons <note>Eusebius is referring to the Neoplatonist philosopher Porphyry, who frequently defended traditional religion while attempting to systematize it.</note>, in the work he titled *Philosophy from Oracles*, where he says literally the following:

<meta>catchword: Not un-</meta>

Eusebius argues that demons have no divine foresight, but merely guess the future by looking at the stars, thereby stripping humanity of free will.</summary>

-> That even what they seem to prophesy, they guess from the motion of the stars, <-
-> just like humans do. <-

That even the things the gods seem to speak, whether they say them because they know what has been fated, they reveal through the motion of the stars. And almost all of those who are called the "truth-telling" gods have made this clear. Furthermore, a little later, he <note>Eusebius is likely quoting Porphyry’s "Philosophy from Oracles" here.</note> says: Apollo, having been asked what a woman would give birth to, said from the stars that it would be a female, based on the knowledge of the <term>aporeimos</term> <note>original: "ἀπορείμου" — an astrological term referring to the "separation" or "detachment" of a planet from another, used in calculating horoscopes.</note> time. He speaks thus:
> "From the natural paths of the earth, meadows of rain,
> Thirst mixed the entire draught of her mother
> While she moved within for a sufficient time. Not a girl,
> But a boy. For bright Cypris, aiming well, pleased
> Phoebus as he hastened; oh friend, save the female offspring."

Look, from the "departure" of the planet—because the moon was moving toward Venus—he said she would give birth to a female. And if they also predict diseases from there:
<margin>For listen.</margin>
> "Truly a very evil poison subdues the limbs,
> Whispering the painful wickedness of the indicator."
<margin>and next, to which he adds:</margin>
> "These things the mind of the Fates brought about, and into the dark
> Strife it entered, to subdue with evil trials,
> While high-walking time moves along a bad path."
<margin>and after other things:</margin>
> "But for you to fulfill the fated day of life,
> The man-destroying pain hastening the portion in time
> Has destroyed the foundation from your mind with lies.
> Therefore also the god-fearing holy heart of the father
> Threatened with mournful garments and bitter gifts."

These things, then, they do not prophesy from their own divine power, but from the observation of the stars according to <term>mathematical</term> <note>In this context, "mathematical" (μαθηματικῶν) specifically refers to the calculations of astrologers.</note> ratios, so that in this they differ in no way from humans, nor do they display any work that is superior or of a more divine nature. Observe also how they abolish "that which is in our power" <note>original: "τὸ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν" — the philosophical concept of free will or moral agency.</note>, attributing to the motion of the stars not only external things and things not in our power, but even our own choices.

-> That they also abolish "that which is in our power," claiming that even <-
-> our choices are moved by fate. <-

Thus also Apollo, speaking about someone and at the same time taking away their zeal regarding a failure, said (knowing from where it came to him):
> "He has swift Ares as his birth-sign who stirs him,
> Nor will you bury him. For the counsel of Zeus attacked,
> Which reached out to offer him glory from Ares at once."
<margin>and again of another:</margin>
> "The time of prayer lay upon him, but the serpent holds
> The valiant, hard-to-attack form of the son of Talaus."

The "noble gods" have yielded so much to the matters of fate that they even confess they are unable to help their own temples when they are struck by lightning. There would be great hope, then, for humans praying to obtain help from those who cannot even help themselves!
