...for the explanation of things that are possible. What need is there, then, to practice piety, and to worship, revere, and serve the gods, if they are completely powerless and cannot even help themselves? Listen, then, to what the oracle says.

<margin>That they were unable to protect even their own dedicated temples when they were struck by lightning.</margin>
Thus, even the portions of temples and sacred places—even the one that Apollo himself was allotted as his sanctuary—were fated to be struck by lightning, as he says:

> "O children born of the divine race of Erichthonius, <note>original: "ἐριχθονίοιο γενέθλης" — This refers to the Athenians, as Erichthonius was a legendary early king of Athens and a son of the earth.</note>
> "You have endured to see the destruction of the shelter of my voice. <note>original: "ἐρεφνέμεν ὀμφήν" — literally 'the roofing of the oracle,' referring to the temple building that housed the prophetic voice.</note>
> "Where the seats of the most beautiful shrine are being ravaged.
> "Hear the divinely spoken voice from the laurel-covered depths.
> "Whenever the spirits of the air, breathing and howling,
> "Are fulfilled with crashes, fighting against soulless things.
> "A cruel chill will then surround the infinite world,
> "Lest the damaged air should burst forth.
> "Once, a glowing fire fell wherever it happened upon the earth.
> "Beasts in the mountains, fearing it,
> "Flee into the deepest hiding places, nor do they stay
> "To look with their eyes upon the descending spear of Zeus. <note>original: "Διὸς ἔγχος" — a poetic metaphor for a lightning bolt.</note>
> "By this, even the temples of the blessed ones, and tall trees,
> "And the peaks of high mountains, and ships on the sea,
> "Are overcome, struck by the fiery flights.
> "And you yourself, the companion of Poseidon, <note>Likely referring to a coastal city or a specific nymph/deity associated with the sea and the temple's location.</note>
> "Often driven back, are struck by the sounding sea.
> "Therefore, though you have unbearable pain in your hearts,
> "Endure in your souls the unchangeable gifts of the Fates.
> "For the head of heavenly Zeus has nodded assent to these things,
> "That they should spin the unshakable thread on their spindles.
> "For it was Destiny <term>Aisa</term> <note>original: "Αἶσα" — a personification of Fate or the 'lot' assigned to someone.</note> that in the long reaches of time, the beautiful shrine
> "Should be overcome by the fire-bolts falling from the sky."

If, therefore, by the spindles of Fate, the temples of the revered gods and their sacred dwellings are overcome by "fiery flights," what hope is left for us mortal men to escape what has been decreed? If no help exists from the gods, and one must absolutely "endure in the soul the unchangeable gifts of the Fates," why this vain zeal concerning the gods? One might ask: why the need for libations and the smell of burnt offerings? Why offer reverence to those who are not even worthy of it, if they can help us in nothing? 

Furthermore, we should not even consider them givers of good things; rather, they have confessed to being the cause of the opposite. For if something good or something contrary is fated for men, it will happen by necessity, whether the gods wish it or not. Therefore, only Necessity <note>original: "ἀνάγκην" — the personified force of *Ananke*, often seen as a power even the gods must obey.</note> should be served—or rather, we should pay no mind at all to the gods, who are unable to either cause us grief or do us good. If indeed only the one who is above the...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s systematic dismantling of pagan theology in Book 6 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*. Having previously shown that the gods’ own temples are subject to "Fate" (specifically lightning and natural decay), he now uses the writings of the philosopher Porphyry to show that these gods are not only subservient to the stars but also admit to using magic and telling lies when the astrological conditions are unfavorable.</meta>

<page-num>141</page-num>
<header>PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 6</header>

God presides over all things, and He alone is their Lord. Regarding these matters, he <note>Eusebius is referring to the philosopher Porphyry, whom he is quoting.</note> says that He "nodded his head," <note>original: "κατένευσε κάρινον" — an allusion to Zeus’s nod in Homer, signifying an irrevocable decree.</note> for they [the Fates] shall move even the unshakeable with their spindles. Why then, having subjected all things to the King of all, do you also confess that only God is the Master of Fate, and the only giver of good things and Savior? For you say that it is easy for Him alone to turn and change even those things which you claim are the unalterable decrees of the Fates. Thus, one who is dedicated to the King of all, God, and who piously serves Him alone, should serve neither Necessity nor Fate. Like one who is pulled away from a harsh and evil bond, he follows the divine and religious dispensations without hindrance. But while that was the discourse addressed to mortals, look again at what he says elsewhere regarding the "dissolving" of the things of Fate.

### That they claim to dissolve the bonds of Fate through magic.

For after something was stated, and a god was asked to receive someone, the god replied that the person was "unsuitable" because he was bound by nature <note>original: "ὑπὸ φύσεως καταδεδέσθαι" — this refers to being under the deterministic influence of the stars at birth.</note>; and because of this, after prescribing certain "drawings-away," <note>original: "ὑποσπασμοῖς" — likely referring to magical rites or "evocations" intended to pull a soul away from its astrological destiny.</note> he adds:

> "For a divine rush, a snake-like trail, has run over,
> "To save the offspring, which you must flee by such magic."

Through these words, it is clearly shown that magic was given by the gods as a "dissolution" of the things of Fate, in order to change it in some way. These are Porphyry’s words, not mine! If, therefore, he attempts to dissolve the things of Fate with magic, how is it that he, being a god himself, did not dissolve the things decreed for his own temple when it was struck by lightning? And if he overlooks magic but not philosophy, how is it not clear what kind of character he happens to possess? For in all these things, the same author confesses that the gods also tell lies.

### That they also lie when giving oracles.

But he now says that an accurate knowledge of the "course" <note>original: "φορᾶς" — referring to the movement of the stars.</note> and the events resulting from them is incomprehensible to men—and not only to them, but even to the demons. This is why they lie when questioned about many things. To this he further adds: "And the environment <note>original: "τὸ περιέχον" — the 'surrounding' atmosphere or astral condition.</note> forces the oracles to become false, and it is not the prophets who voluntarily add the falsehood." Often, at least, they did not lie when they intended to. But the seekers of oracles compel them to speak through their own ignorance. Indeed, Apollo once said—when the state of the "environment" was as we have shown, in a bad condition:

> "Close the gates of life, the fruit of words; I shall speak lies."

And the oracles will show that these things we have said are true. For one of the gods, when summoned, said:

> "Today it is not fitting to speak the path of the stars, or the peace
> "Of the throne. For the power of prophecy is now fettered among the stars." <note>original: "ἀμαντοσύνη" — a rare word meaning the lack or binding of prophetic power.</note>

And he adds: "It is natural, then, from where the falsehood is often composed."

### A review of the things concerning Fate.

Is your doubt finally at an end? That there is nothing divine in the oracles of the gods? For how could the Divine ever lie, being by nature the most truthful? If the Divine is indeed without falsehood, how could a "good spirit" <note>term: <gloss>Agathos Daimon</gloss> — a benevolent deity or spirit in Greek religion.</note> ever deceive with false speeches?

<vocab>Eusebius, Porphyry, Fate (Heimarmene), Magic, Oracles, Demon (Daimon), Lack of Prophecy (Amantosyne)</vocab>

...[a narrative] of those who are powerful. What reason remains, then, to be pious, or to worship, honor, and serve the gods, if they are entirely incapable of anything and cannot even help themselves? Listen, then, to what the oracle says.

### That they were unable to help even their own dedicated temples when they were struck by lightning.

In this way, there are fates for those gods and for their temples; even Apollo's own temple was fated to be struck by lightning, as he himself says:

> "O you who are born of the most divine, earth-born race,
> Endure these tidings, and let my voice be shrouded in gloom.
> Wherever the foundations of a most beautiful sanctuary are built,
> Hear the divinely spoken voice from the laurel-wrapped inner chambers.
> Whenever the roaring winds from above, sounding through the air,
> Are stretched out and contend against each other with crashes,
> Then a snowy frost shall surround the infinite world,
> Lest the afflicted upper air have any outlet.
> A smoky fire once fell upon the earth wherever it chanced;
> The wild beasts on the mountains, dreading it,
> Fled into fiery hiding places, nor did they remain
> Once the swift-descending weapon of Zeus <note>original: "Διὸς ἔγχος" — Zeus's "spear" or "bolt," referring to lightning.</note> came within.
> By this, the temples of the blessed ones, and tall trees,
> And the peaks of steep mountains, and ships on the sea,
> Are subdued when they encounter its fiery blasts.
> And indeed, even the companion of Poseidon <note>original: "ποσειδάωνος ἑταίρη" — a poetic reference to the sea goddess Amphitrite.</note> is struck,
> And often the shore-fretting sea retreats.
> You, therefore, though you have unbearable pain in your hearts,
> Endure in your soul the unalterable gifts of the Fates.
> For the head of heavenly Zeus has nodded <note>original: "κατένευσε κάρηνον" — Zeus’s nod in Greek epic poetry signifies an irrevocable decree.</note> his assent to these things,
> To whatever the unshakeable haven <note>original: "λιμὴν ἀσάλευτον" — here referring to the fixed nature of Fate.</note> spins with its <term>spindles</term> <note>The "spindles" refer to the tools of the three Fates (Moirai), who spin, measure, and cut the thread of human and divine destiny.</note>.
> For it is Destiny that in the fullness of time the most beautiful sanctuary 
> Be subdued by the fires falling from heaven."

If, then, by the spindles of the Fates even the temples of the venerable gods and their sacred houses are subdued by fiery blasts, so that no hope remains for mortal men to escape what is fated—and if no help comes from the gods, but one must endure at all costs "the unchangeable gifts of the Fates" in one's soul—what, someone might ask, is the point of this vain devotion to the gods? Why is there need of drink-offerings and the steam of sacrifice, and why pay honor to those who are not even worthy of it, if they can help us in no way? Indeed, we should not even think of them as the givers of good things; rather, they themselves admit they are the cause of the opposites. For if it is fated for humans that something good or something contrary happens, it will happen by necessity, whether the gods wish it or not. Therefore, one should worship only Necessity—or rather, pay no mind to the gods at all, since they can neither cause pain nor grant benefits. If, indeed, only He who is above the Fates...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s systematic dismantling of pagan theology in Book 6 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*. Having established on the previous page that the pagan gods are helpless against Fate (Heimarmene)—even failing to protect their own temples from lightning—Eusebius now turns to the contradictions found in the writings of Porphyry. He highlights how these oracles alternate between claiming Fate is unchangeable and suggesting that magic can provide a loophole, ultimately concluding that these "gods" are self-admitted liars.</meta>

<page-num>141</page-num>
<header>EVANGELICAL PREPARATION BOOK 6</header>

God presides over all things, and He alone exists as their Lord. For "to all those who are well-disposed," he says, "He has brought an end to the joy of prayer, because they [the Fates] move an unshakeable destiny with their spindles." <note>original: "ἀσάλευτον ἀτράκτοις" — referring to the spindles of the Moirai (the Fates) which spin the thread of human life.</note> Why then, having subjected all things to the All-King, do you also confess that God alone is the Master of Fate, and the only giver of good things and Savior? For you say that it is easy for Him alone to turn and change even those things which you call the unalterable decrees of the Fates. Thus, one who is consecrated to God the All-King, and who serves Him alone with piety, is subject to neither necessity nor Fate. But like a prisoner being dragged from a bond by someone more powerful and wicked, he follows without hindrance the dispensations found in sacrifices and religious rites. Such is the argument put forward by those who seem reasonable. On the other hand, look at the means by which he says the bonds of Fate are loosed.

### That they claim the bonds of Fate are loosed through magic.

<margin>D</margin> For when someone had offered a prayer, the god, after saying that he was "unfit" because he was bound by nature, and for this reason having suggested certain hypotheses, adds:
> "For a divine glance is a rushing vision that has run over
> your lineage, which you must flee through such magic."

By these words it is clearly shown that magic was given by the gods as a release from the bonds of Fate, in order to transform Fate in whatever way possible. These are your words, Porphyry, not mine. Therefore, how can one who attempts to loose the bonds of Fate through magic be a god himself, if he did not loose the fated destruction of his own temple when it was struck by the fated lightning? And as for the one who practices magic rather than a pure philosophy, is it not clear what kind of character he happens to possess? Especially since this same author confesses that these gods even tell lies.

### That they also tell lies when giving oracles.

<margin>A</margin> But now he admits that the accurate knowledge of the celestial rotation, and the events resulting from them, is incomprehensible to men—and not only to men, but even to the spirits <note>original: "δαιμονίων" — daemons or lesser spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note>. For this reason, they tell lies when asked about many things. Regarding this, he adds: "And the surrounding atmosphere, by forcing the oracles to become false, does not mean the prophets lie willingly," because it is a lie. For often, though they choose not to, they will lie. But the diviners force them to speak through their own ignorance. At any rate, Apollo once said, when the state of the surroundings was poor (as we have shown):
> "Hear my life, and the strength of my words: I shall speak falsehoods." <note>original: "ψευδήγορα λέξω"</note>

And the oracles themselves will show that these things are true of them. For one of the gods, when summoned, said:
> "Today it is not fitting to speak of the path of the stars,
> or of the seat of peace. For the power of prophecy is now fettered among the stars."
And he adds: "It is natural, therefore, that from this source falsehood is often composed."

### Recapitulation of the arguments concerning Fate.

<margin>A</margin> Has the matter of this doubtful opinion finally reached its end? That there is nothing divine in the oracles of these gods? For how could something divine ever lie, since its nature is the most truthful of all? If the divine is without falsehood, how could a "good spirit" ever deceive anyone with false words?

Here, Eusebius argues that if human actions were truly dictated by the stars, virtue and philosophy would be meaningless.</meta>

<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

...to those who use them? How could that which is shackled by the movement of the stars be superior to a human being? A mortal man, having brought forth even a brief zeal for virtue, would never lie once he has chosen to honor the truth; he would not blame a necessity of fate or the movement of the stars for a lie. Even if one were to bring fire or iron against his body, forcing him to destroy his truthful word, he would stand against it and cry out in opposition:

<margin>$\triangle$</margin>
->Let the fire come, let the sword come. Cut,<-
> Burn my flesh, be filled drinking the black, 
> Dark blood. For sooner shall the stars go 
> Beneath the earth, and the earth rise into the height of heaven, 
> Before you hear a word of flattery from me.
<note>This is a quote from the lost play *Bellerophon* by the Greek dramatist Euripides. It serves as a classic expression of human integrity in the face of physical coercion.</note>

But the "brilliant" and deceptive demon <note>original: "δαιμόνιον" — Eusebius uses this to refer to the pagan spirits or gods behind the oracles.</note> puts on a pretense, playing the sage to those who are foolish. This is so that in instances where one might fail to predict the future, the soul’s lack of reason might lead it to credit Fate. Yet, by suspending your affairs upon Fate through these oracles, the demon destroys that which is within our power <term>the power of free choice; original: ἐφ' ἡμῖν (eph’ hēmin)</term> arising from our self-determined movement. He enslaves even this to necessity, so that he may cast those who believe him into the same pit of evils into which he has fallen. 

For if we must attribute not only external circumstances but also the inclinations of our reasoning to the stars and Fate—and if an inexorable necessity forces our dispositions and judgments—then philosophy is gone, and piety is gone. There would be no praise of virtue for the diligent, no love of God, nor any worthy fruit of the labors spent in spiritual discipline <note>original: "ἀσκήσει" — ascetic or philosophical training</note>, since Fate and Necessity would have taken on the cause of everything. 

Therefore, it would not be right to find fault with those who commit offenses in this life, nor even with the impious and the most infamous; nor should we admire those who are diligent. In this way, as I said, the great glory of philosophy will vanish, being suspended not from self-determined practice and discipline, but from the necessity of the stars. 

See, then, into what a pit of evils these "wonderful gods" have clearly cast themselves, when this doctrine encourages and incites a seed, as it were, toward licentiousness, injustice, and a myriad of evils. It altogether works the overthrow of a virtuous life. For if someone were to believe these wonderful oracles of the gods—assuming they speak the truth and do not lie—that it is not our own work, but the inexorable power of Fate that determines the desire to go to war, or to set out upon any other action, or even the lack of desire for such things, how could he not choose to be negligent and sluggish in all matters that cannot be set right without our own toil, labor, and zeal? 

For if one believes that a certain thing will happen by Fate, whether we toil and are diligent about it or not, how could one not choose the easier path and be negligent, as the deed to be done is being brought to pass by Fate and Necessity? Hence, one may hear many people saying: "This will surely happen if it is fated for me; why then must I exert myself?" For if the man setting out for war did not do so from his own choice, but was clearly led by an external necessity, the same would apply to robbery, grave-robbing, and other unholy acts and licentiousness, or to decent and self-controlled pursuits. This would be the logical consequence of the argument concerning Fate. How then could the man who does not even believe these things himself have written...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s philosophical refutation of Fate. On the previous page, he argued that if humans were merely subjects of the stars, the moral integrity shown by figures like Bellerophon would be impossible. Here, he moves into a practical "reductio ad absurdum," arguing that if Fate were real, all human social structures—from parenting to the legal system—would be nonsensical.</meta>

<page-num>143</page-num>
<header>PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL BOOK 6. 143</header>

If a person were driven by an external necessity, would they ever accept a warning? Or could they be taught not to surrender themselves to the impulses I mentioned before? Such a person would say to their counselor—or to anyone who speaks about our lives as if they were ruled by Fate <note>original: "ὥς φησιν εἱμαρμένη" (as Fate says)</note>—"Why do you admonish me, friend? For these actions are no longer up to me <term>within our own power; original: ἐπ᾿ ἐμοὶ (ep’ emoi)</term>, which is the very thing that normally allows a person to change their choice. Fate has already seized control. Why then must I be ordered toward goals that I do not even have the power to desire? (Unless, of course, even my 'desire' is fated for me? And if it is fated, why then do you trouble yourself in vain with your teaching, while I am merely being led along by Fate?)"

But even if you, the teacher, claim that you are now compelled by necessity to perform this task of advising and persuading me, what is the point of being earnest about it? Such advice is idle and useless. For if it is fated for me to be industrious, I shall be so. But if it is not fated, you only make our efforts a waste for both of us. 

How much more likely is it that a person holding this opinion would say to themselves: "Come now, do not be industrious at all, nor trouble yourself in vain." For you will claim that Fate is an external necessity. 

Yet, consider the person who strives to be helpful, or who teaches, or who urges themselves or another to obey or not to obey, to reward or not. Consider the one who rebukes those who sin and praises those who do right. Do they not clearly refute this error? One person, through their actions, abandons the idea of Fate in favor of what is 'up to us' <note>original: "τὸ παρ’ ἡμῖν" (to par' hēmin)</note> and our self-governing nature <term>free will or self-determination; original: τὸ αὐτεξούσιον (to autexousion)</term>. 

The fatalist, however, merely hangs the name of "Fate" upon human action. It is as if someone took the nature of "the Good"—by whose presence a living being is best governed—and addressed it by the name of "the Evil." We clearly perceive ourselves acting without being forced by any external cause—whether we are disciplining our children, whipping servants for their faults, or simply choosing to want or not want something. We arrive at these movements independently from our own power. Therefore, anyone who claims these things happen according to Fate is in error.

Such a doctrine destroys our own eagerness and the encouragement or advice we give to others—the very tools through which we see human affairs most successfully managed. Indeed, this reasoning would even overturn the laws that are established for the benefit of humanity. For why is it necessary to command or forbid those who are held fast by a different kind of necessity? There would be no need to punish those who do wrong, since they did not sin through their own fault. Nor would we need to award honors to those who perform the most beautiful deeds. Yet both punishment and honor are the primary means of overturning injustice and encouraging a readiness for holiness.

Furthermore, this opinion would overturn piety toward the Divine. If we are shackled by the necessities of Fate, God would contribute nothing to us—nor would the oracles themselves—no matter how much we pray or act with piety. To claim that we move like inanimate objects, pulled here and there by some external power like puppets <note>original: "νευροσπαστουμένους" (literally 'pulled by strings')</note>, forced to "will" this or "choose" that by a necessity, rather than by our own choice... how could this not be the most shameless and impudent claim? 

For we clearly perceive that it is by our own impulse and movement that we are eager for certain things. We catch ourselves hesitating, and we succeed or fail because of this internal cause, not because we are forced by anything else. We choose things with a willing mind and flee from others, acting out of our own free choice <term>deliberate choice; original: προαιρέσεως (proaireseōs)</term>. This principle of self-determination is so clear that it is like feeling pain or pleasure, or seeing and hearing; it is not understood through logical deduction, but through direct experience.

<summary>Eusebius argues that fatalism is logically and practically impossible because it renders education, law, morality, and religion meaningless. He asserts that free will is a self-evident fact of human experience, as undeniable as physical sensations like pain or sight.</summary>
<keywords>Fate, Free Will, Self-Determination, Law and Punishment, Piety, Puppetry, Determinism, Eusebius of Caesarea</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument from the previous page, shifting from the practical absurdities of believing in Fate to a deeper psychological and ontological analysis of human nature. He is establishing that because humans possess a rational soul, they cannot be entirely subject to the mechanical necessity of the stars.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

[...things are] prepared for ourselves from our very selves, originating from our own will, and choosing certain things while turning away from others, so that in every way "what is in our power" <term>what is in our power; original: τὸ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν (to eph’ hemin), a standard philosophical term for agency</term> and the free will of the rational and intellectual nature within us may be justly acknowledged. If the myriad things that happen to us because of our choice <term>choice; original: προαίρεσις (proairesis)</term> trouble the majority of people, we must distinguish here between the nature of things outside of us, and we must contemplate the principle by which things not in our power occur. For in this way, the cause of these things—the irrational "Fate"—will be exposed as a meaningless concept <note>original: ἄλογος εἱμαρμένη (alogos heimarmene); a play on words meaning both "irrational Fate" and "a Fate without a rational principle"</note>. It is a "word" without reason, detached from the providence of the whole.

Come then, let us carefully examine the problem. The laws of true piety declare that all things truly exist and are governed by God’s providence. However, each thing that happens does so according to its own specific form: some by necessity; some by nature; some by impulse and imagination; and some moved by reasoning, private judgment, and choice. Some things happen according to a primary principle, while others happen as accidents <note>original: ἐπισυμβεβηκότα (episymbebekota); things that "fall upon" or occur as side-effects of primary actions</note> to those things that occurred primarily. He who established the decoration of the universe made the whole thing varied and complex, assigning to each being its own distinct and defined natural constitution as the Cause of all things. 

There will be time elsewhere to discuss other matters; but the matter concerning free will <term>free will; original: αὐτεξούσιον (autexousion)</term> can be more easily understood in this way: Since man is not a single-form thing, nor does he happen to consist of a single nature, but has received a union from two opposites—body and soul—the one, the body, is an instrument enslaved to the soul by circumstance; the other, the soul, is the rational essence that constitutes the primary reality. The one is irrational, while the other is rational. Again, the one is corruptible, the other incorruptible; the one mortal, the other immortal. We might say that we carry the body as a brother to the irrational animals, but the soul is kin to the rational and immortal nature. 

For this reason, it is likely that as a dual-natured creature, sharing in a double nature, man then enjoys a double and different kind of life. Sometimes he is enslaved to the nature of the body; at other times, he embraces his own freedom through his more divine part. Thus, the same person is both slave and free, having been allotted such a mixture of soul and body by God for reasons known to Him alone. 

If, therefore, someone should use the name of "Fate" to describe the natural properties of either the body or the soul, and should attribute them to a cause of necessity, they would be using an incorrect title. For if Fate were an unhindered necessity, but many of the natural properties of the body and soul are often blocked—and myriad other things happen from the outside contrary to nature, following both soul and body by accident—how could these things be "Fate" and "Nature"? For if they say that Fate is unchangeable and that nothing can happen contrary to it, but it is necessary that many things remain unaccomplished—as I said, occurring contrary to the nature of both soul and body—one would not be speaking correctly by calling these things Fate and Nature. 

Therefore, of the things that exist within us, some happen according to reasoning and choice and are done by us, such as the natural activities of the soul. Others are according to the nature of the body. Still others are accidents of these—I mean of the soul and the body—which are brought to completion by other external factors according to nature. But one could not justly blame the Cause for "what is in our power" regarding the soul, nor for what is natural regarding the body, nor indeed for what happens by accident from outside. For God Himself has been revealed as the Creator of the whole: of the things in our power, of the things according to nature, and of the things according to accident.

<meta>catchword: In general (καθόλου)</meta>

<summary>Eusebius argues that human beings possess a dual nature of body and soul, granting them a "free will" that operates independently of the mechanical "Fate" proposed by astrologers. He categorizes events into those caused by choice, nature, or accident, all of which fall under God's overarching providence rather than an irrational necessity.</summary>

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 6

» For regarding all things, one must listen to the Scripture concerning God, which says: *He spoke, and they were brought into being; He commanded, and they were created.* <note>original: Αὐτὸς εἶπεν, καὶ ἐγεννήθη· αὐτὸς ἐνετείλατο, καὶ ἐκτίσθησαν; a reference to Psalm 33:9 or 148:5</note> Let us declare this. If, then, things should ever happen to those who wish for something else, contrary to our own judgment, we must remind them that there is a double and diverse nature in our composite makeup—I mean, of course, the **soul** and the **body**. 

» On the one hand, the essence of the soul is by nature intellectual and rational; yet, in a body that is infantile by nature, it has taken up a place that is, in a sense, contrary to its nature—the place of the irrational. And while intellectual wisdom is its proper state, the soul's distinctive qualities are often hidden by the accidents <note>In ancient philosophy, an "accident" is a property that isn't essential to the thing's nature, like being sick or old.</note> of life—for instance, by the illnesses of the body. Often, too, the onset of old age has deprived the mind of its naturally upright peak, dulling the rational part of the intellectual soul against its nature. Again, physical torments, bodily pains, and disabilities that occur against nature have at times overcome the **self-governing** <term>self-governing; original: αὐτεξούσιον (autexousion), the power to act on one's own authority</term> power of the soul through these circumstances. The soul gives in to the pain because of its entwinement with the body, as if an inescapable bond had been thrown in the way of the soul's dispositions—sometimes by the body's own nature, and sometimes by external events. 

» Yet, the "power within us" <term>power within us; original: τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν (to eph' hemin), the core of human agency</term> belonging to our **choice** <term>choice; original: προαίρεσις (proairesis), a deliberate moral decision</term> has reached such a height of virtue and strength that in many cases it dares to act independently, speaking against both the nature of the body and external circumstances. For the nature of the body calls a man toward sexual impulse; but the soul, placing a bridle on the passions with a temperate reason, proves itself stronger than the body's nature. And again, while the body calls out with hunger, thirst, cold, and such sensations, urging toward their natural remedies and fulfillments, the power of choice—persuaded by temperate reasons and embracing certain ascetic goals of self-sufficiency—prevails over the nature of the body through many days of fasting and endurance, having judged and chosen this as the virtue of reason. 

» And again, while the body by nature delights in all pleasures and the smooth movement of physical things, the power of choice, through a desire for virtue, welcomes a life of toil and hardship. There are some who, having turned toward the worse, have even "exchanged the natural use for that which is against nature," <note>original: μετήλλαξαν τὴν φυσικὴν χρῆσιν εἰς τὴν παρὰ φύσιν; a reference to the Apostle Paul in Romans 1:26-27</note> men working shame with men. Thus, reason sometimes yields to nature in name only, but in most cases it prevails, just as it is sometimes prevailed upon. Sometimes reason itself rules; at other times it is led, as when it might even command the departure from the body with its own hands <note>A reference to the philosophical debate on suicide as an ultimate act of agency or "rational departure."</note> whenever it judges that living is no longer profitable. 

» If, then, its entire struggle were only against the body’s own nature, this struggle would be moderate. But since God has cast its citizenship and human life into the midst of many things—as if among wild beasts and venomous reptiles, in the midst of fire and water, and the surrounding air—and has made its dwelling place among all these varied and different natures, it is reasonable that its conflict and resistance is not only against the soul's own joined and self-governing nature of the body, but also against ten thousand external accidents in the midst of which anyone who leads a mortal life must live. Thus, one must also endure these things with fortitude. Indeed, there are many such kinds of nourishment, and such mixtures of the surrounding atmosphere, the onset of frosts, and the scorching of heat, and many other things moving naturally according to their own principles, which fall upon us by chance, providing our **self-governing powers** with no ordinary [struggle]...

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 145, where Eusebius explores the relationship between the rational soul and its physical container. # EUSEBIUS

The soul has taken on an entanglement with the body through our natural impulses; as a result, it does not always withstand external pressures but is sometimes mastered and conquered by things outside itself that occur according to their own nature. Furthermore, we live our lives among a great many other men; they also share the same essence as us, and they exercise their own **self-governing** <term>self-governing; original: αὐτεξούσιος (autexousios), referring to the human capacity for free choice independent of cosmic necessity</term> power through their own choices. For this reason, we will reasonably be subject at times to the wills of others, as they use their own freedom of choice against our body or concerning our soul. 

For just as our physical nature is often conquered by external circumstances, so too is our **purpose** <term>purpose; original: προαίρεσις (proairesis), a technical term in Stoic and Platonic philosophy for the moral will or choice</term> occasionally troubled by a myriad of other choices; though it is a self-governing judgment, it sometimes yields itself to external influences. At one time it results in something better, and at another, something worse. For we know that bad company can corrupt, just as, conversely, the company of the good makes us better. *Bad company corrupts good character.* <note>original: Φθείρουσι γὰρ ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί. This is a famous line from the playwright Menander, also quoted by the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:33.</note> 

Just as in animals the influence of the herd can extinguish good traits, so too the rational power of the soul is carried this way and that by external occurrences and arguments. Yet, there is a strength proper to the virtue of the rational essence, and it demonstrates a power that is truly divine and godlike when it holds out against all external things. Having conquered everything through a sacred mindset, it yields nothing of its own virtue and remains prepared for the pursuit of wisdom. However, to the extent that it is negligent, it is influenced for the worse by worse things—just as it receives external care when it acts with faith. 

What must be said regarding these things? All the fortunes and misfortunes of every soul and body occur according to certain circumstances, in harmony with the management of the whole universe. These events are rightly ordered for the whole and for each individual part. Whether they are caused by our own movements toward wickedness or happen to us from the outside as a result of our own actions—even those things that occur naturally—one multifaceted and all-powerful force presides over them all: the **Providence** <term>Providence; original: πρόνοια (pronoia), the proactive care and forward-thinking governance of God</term> of God that pervades everything. 

This Providence manages most things by laws that are unutterable to us, continually steering the whole. In various seasons, it reshapes even natural events for the better, cooperating and working with our own choices and assigning the necessary order to external events. These things are divided into three modes: 
1. The things in our power (our choices).
2. The things that happen according to nature.
3. The things that happen by accident.

Since all these are summed up in a single Reason proceeding from the will of God, the doctrine of **Fate** <note>original: εἱμαρμένη (heimarmene), the idea of an inescapable, pre-determined destiny often linked to the stars.</note> shall have no place anywhere. 

This may help us answer the question many struggle with: the source of evil. Evil has no place in the things of nature, neither in bodies nor in essences; much less does it exist in external accidents. Rather, it is found only in the self-governing movement of the soul. This occurs not when the soul walks the straight path according to nature, but when it turns aside from the **royal road** <note>The "royal road" (βασιλική) is a common philosophical and biblical metaphor for the path of virtue and moderation.</note> by its own judgment, acting as its own master. This was an exceptional gift the soul received from God—to be fresh and independent, having taken upon itself the criterion of its own impulse. For a divine law is bound to it by nature, like a lamp or a light, sounding from within and saying:

<summary>Eusebius argues that human actions are governed by free will and Divine Providence rather than Fate. He identifies the source of evil not in nature or God, but in the soul's freedom to turn away from the "royal road" of virtue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on human agency. On the previous page, Eusebius noted that the rational power of the soul can be carried away by external influences and the company of others. Here, he pivots to the moral responsibility of the individual, arguing that despite external pressures, the "royal road" of reason and free will remains the God-given standard for human conduct, countering the deterministic views of the astrologers.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL Book 6 147</header>
<page-num>147</page-num>

"You shall travel by the royal road; you shall not turn to the right nor to the left." <note>original: ὁδῷ βασιλικῇ πορεύσῃ...; a reference to Numbers 20:17, frequently used by early Christian writers to symbolize the moderate path of virtue.</note> By "royal road," he is teaching that the path of **right reason** <term>right reason; original: ὀρθὸς λόγος (orthos logos), a central concept in Greek philosophy meaning reason that is in harmony with nature and truth</term> is the one to follow. For the Creator of the universe established this **natural law** in every soul as its helper and ally in determining what must be done.

Through this law, He showed the soul its proper path; and through the gift of **self-governing freedom** <term>self-governing freedom; original: αὐτεξουσίου ἐλευθερίας (autexousiou eleutherias), the capacity to choose one's own actions</term>, He demonstrated that the choice of better things is worthy of praise and acceptance. He also established rewards and prizes greater than rewards for those who succeed, because they achieve success not by compulsion, but by their own self-governing will, even though it was possible for them to choose the opposite. Conversely, the soul that chooses worse things is worthy of blame and punishment because it acts by its own movement—thereby transgressing the **natural law** <term>natural law; original: κατὰ φύσιν νόμον (kata physin nomon), the inherent moral order of the world</term>. Such a soul gives birth to the very beginning and fountain of vice, having used itself poorly, not out of some external necessity, but from its own free will and judgment. 

->The fault lies with the one who chooses; God is blameless.<- <note>original: αἰτία δὴ τοῦ ἑλομένου, θεὸς ἀναίτιος. This is a famous quote from Plato's Republic (617e), which Eusebius uses here to defend God's goodness against the idea that He created evil.</note>

For God did not create a wicked nature, nor did He create the essence of the soul to be such. It is not permitted for the Good to create anything except good things. And everything according to nature is good. Every rational soul possesses by nature the good of **self-governance**, and this was created for the purpose of choosing good things. When a soul acts poorly, one must not blame its nature. For evil does not happen to it according to its nature, but contrary to its nature; it is a result of **choice** <term>choice; original: προαίρεσις (proairesis), the moral will</term>, not a product of nature. For when someone possesses the power to choose the good, but fails to choose it and deliberately turns away from what is better to claim what is worse, what excuse remains for them? They have become the cause of their own sickness, disregarding the innate law that acts like a healing physician.

But those who take no account of these things, and instead attribute everything to necessity and the movement of the stars, claim that the causes of human failings do not come from us, but from the power that moves everything. How can they not be introducing a lawless and impious way of thinking? For if they claim the movement of the universe is spontaneous and without **providence** <term>providence; original: πρόνοια (pronoia), the belief that God actively cares for and governs the world</term>, they are exposed as foolish atheists, blind to the radiant harmony and the arrangement of the whole—the movement that cycles through the world for all eternity. 

On the other hand, if they acknowledge that God's providence leads and carries everything, overseeing all things and governing them with radiant reason, they still do not escape the charge of impiety. Regarding the sins committed by men, they offer an escape to the wrongdoers, as if they had done nothing strange by their own will. Instead, they refer the cause of evils back to universal providence, calling it "Necessity" or "Fate." They claim this is the cause of all human shame, unspeakable acts, cruelty, and bloodshed. What could be more impious than this argument? It introduces the God of all—the very Maker and Creator of this world—as one who forces these things by necessity. It suggests He makes a man act impiously against his will, making him an atheist by necessity and a blasphemer against God himself. It suggests that because God Himself established the male nature, He forces it to suffer things contrary to nature, like the actions of women, driven toward it by necessity. And it suggests that a murderer becomes such not by his own judgment, but is driven by the necessity of God. Thus, we should not pointlessly blame those who do wrong! In this view, either these things are not sins at all, or God is declared the creator of all evils. For if He Himself oversees all, sees all, and hears all, yet makes these things happen by necessity...

<sig>n.ii.</sig>

<summary>Eusebius argues that God granted humans free will (self-governance) and a natural moral law, making individuals responsible for their own virtues and vices. He vehemently rejects astrological determinism (fate), arguing that blaming the stars or God's providence for human sin is both illogical and impious.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument against celestial determinism. On the previous page, Eusebius established that God gave every soul a "royal road" of reason and the gift of free will. Here, he argues that if we were forced to act by the stars, God—as the creator of the stars—would be the ultimate source of evil, a conclusion he finds blasphemous. He concludes by pointing to the historical reality of the Christian martyrs as living proof that the human will can overcome any physical necessity or external "fate."</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>148</page-num>
<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

...whether the movement of the stars and their particular course was established by Him as something productive of results and necessitating actions, then He who constructed such an instrument <note>original: ὄργανον (organon); here referring to the cosmos or the celestial spheres as a machine</note> would Himself be the one who produced these effects. And if He is the one who devised the trap for those being hunted, He would also be the cause of those who are caught in it. Whether, then, He acts by Himself, or whether He wraps the unwilling in evils through some other necessity engineered for that purpose, He and no other would be the maker of all evils. In that case, man could no longer be justly called blameworthy, but rather God, his maker. This, in turn, would be the most impious of all arguments. For such a person does not merely introduce nothingness, but directly equates God and **Fate** <term>Fate; original: εἱμαρμένη (heimarmene), the idea that all events are predetermined by a chain of causes, often linked to the stars</term>. It is as if one who sets God over all things were to turn back and make Him the very principle of Fate.

For either God and Fate are the same thing, or one is distinct from the other. Certainly, they cannot be the same. For if they say that Fate is a "chain of causes" <note>original: εἱρμόν τινα αἰτιῶν (heirmon tina aition); a standard Stoic definition of fate</note> descending from eternity in an unalterable and immovable way from the motion of the heavenly stars, how are the physical **elements** <term>elements; original: στοιχεῖα (stoicheia), the basic building blocks of the universe</term> from which the heavens are composed not always prior to Fate? One might reasonably call Fate a "contingent accident" <note>original: συμβεβηκός τι σύμπτωμα (symbebekos ti symptoma); a technical term for something that is not essential but happens as a result of other things</term> of these elements. And how could a mere accident of the elements be the same as the God over all? If, indeed, the elements are soulless and irrational, carried along according to their own nature, while God is outside their impulse and happens to be Wisdom itself—granting the enjoyment of His craftsmanship to both the individual elements and the arrangement of the whole—then God and Fate are not the same.

But if Fate is something different, which of the two is superior? Nothing is more beautiful than God, nor anything more powerful. Therefore, He should master and prevail over the lesser thing. Otherwise, by permitting Fate to be a doer of evil, He would draw the blame upon Himself—He who, being able to restrain or check the necessity of doing evil, failed to do so. He would be looking on without sparing a thought for the ruin and destruction of all things; or rather, He Himself would have worked this destruction, if He is introduced as the maker and creator of all things, including Fate itself.

But if they say He has no concern for the arrangement of the whole, then once again an atheistic voice will cry out. Let such a voice be shut out from our ears, for His **Providence** <term>Providence; original: προνοία (pronoia), God's proactive care and guidance for the world</term> and power clearly reveal themselves both through the universal, multi-formed, and masterful results of His work, and through the power of the rational soul—which is undeniably demonstrated among us through experience and its own **self-governing power** <term>self-governing power; original: αὐτεξούσιον (autexousion), the capacity for free choice and moral agency</term>. 

Despite ten thousand external obstacles—the nature of the body and the impulses that fall upon us by chance—the choice of what is good remains something within our power, demonstrated as a supernatural struggle, unconquered and undefeated, through the virtue of the soul. This has been most clearly established by the very deeds of the present time through the Gospel teaching of our Savior. These are not just sounds and empty words; one may look upon the struggle of the godly and see those who, by their own self-governing choice, have taken up the labors of the contests for the sake of **piety** <term>piety; original: εὐσεβεία (eusebeia), right conduct and devotion toward God</term>. Throughout the whole inhabited world, a vast multitude of our own people and foreigners have shown this, eagerly enduring every physical outrage and every kind of torture with a radiant face. Finally, after many such trials, they have welcomed the release of the soul from the body with joy. No argument will allow anyone here to blame Fate. For where in the long ages of the past were such champions...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s refutation of fatalism. Having previously argued that attributing human actions to the stars makes God the author of evil, he now pivots to an empirical argument: the universal spread of Christianity. He contends that if human life were governed by the mechanical "cycles" of the stars, such a unique, global transformation of the human will—unseen in all previous history—would be impossible.</meta>

<page-num>149</page-num>

-> # THE PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 7 <-

Is it the motion of the stars that governs our piety, or was the life of men once led by earthly concerns until a teaching descended to all mankind, a teaching that has surpassed the struggles of the entire inhabited world? For where in all of time has there been a school of thought <note>original: διδασκάλιον (didaskalion); a place of instruction or a system of teaching</note>, capable of removing the delusion of demons and teaching the knowledge of the one God over all to all people—Greeks and barbarians alike? Which of the famous sages of old, whether barbarian or Greek, was ever granted such a destiny <term>Destiny; original: εἱμαρμένη (heimarmene), often used interchangeably with "Fate" in this context</term> as to make the **Word** <note>original: λόγον (logon); referring here to the Christian message or the Divine Reason</note> he put forward manifest to the whole world, known even to its furthest reaches, and to gain the glory of God among those dedicated to him? 

If these things never existed in the past, nor happened, nor were even heard of, then this phenomenon cannot be part of a "chain of causes" or a physical necessity. For if it were, then long ago, through the same repeating cycles and revolutions of the stars, others would surely have met with the same birth and fate, and such a thing would have happened before. By what kind of **Fate**, then, did our **Savior God** appear? His appearance brought a light to the whole world that abolished the gods formerly recognized by both Greeks and barbarians. What "Fate" could possibly have announced God the Creator of all to all mankind? 

If one were to claim this is not Fate but "Necessity," I would ask: how could Necessity teach a person to think and speak for themselves? And what of those who have struggled through countless trials for the sake of our Savior’s pious teaching? Those who gathered in the past and those who still assemble today—did they all just happen upon the same "portion" or luck? How is it they were all brought under one Word and teaching, displaying a single mind, a single purpose, and a single virtue of soul? How did they all come to embrace the same life, love the same Word, and lovingly endure all hardships to maintain their stand for piety? 

What right reason would concede that young and old, the elderly and small children, men and women, barbarians, slaves and rustics, the learned and the uneducated—not just in one corner of the earth, nor governed by one specific set of stars—were all "forced" by the voice of Fate’s necessity to prefer the one **Word of the Father of all**? Who would believe they were "forced" to lovingly choose death for the sake of piety toward the one God, to be trained in the doctrines of the soul's immortality, and to value a philosophy not of mere words, but of deeds? 

These things would be clear even to a blind man: they do not happen by any necessity, but are the result of learning and teaching. They are the visible examples of a mind and purpose acting with **free will** <note>original: αὐτεξουσίου (autexousiou); "self-ruling" or "acting by one's own power"</note>. I could provide a myriad of other proofs for this, but I will leave most aside and be satisfied with what I have said. 

However, I will leave you to consider your own reading of your own philosophers. Through this, you may learn how much wiser and better a human being is than your oracular gods. I speak of a man who, using these very "wonderful oracles," proves them false and rebukes the Pythian god <note>Apollo, the god of the Oracle at Delphi</note> himself for what he prophesied regarding Fate. 

Listen then to this man, who titled his work *The Detection of Impostors* <note>original: Φωρὰν γοήτων (Phoran goeton); a work by the Cynic philosopher Oenomaus of Gadara, who mocked oracles as frauds</note>. With a very vigorous spirit, he exposes the error of the masses and even of Apollo himself. He writes word for word as follows:

Just as our own philosophers have refuted the opinions concerning **Fate** <term>Fate; original: εἱμαρμένη (heimarmene), the idea that all events are predetermined by a chain of causes</term> held by the gods themselves through more sound reasoning—specifically from the writings of **Oenomaus**. <note>Oenomaus of Gadara (2nd century AD) was a Cynic philosopher famous for his aggressive attacks on the reliability of oracular shrines like Delphi.</note>

<margin>Section</margin> It is impossible to sit in Delphi, even if you wished to remain silent. But does **Apollo**, the son of Zeus, truly "will" to speak to you now? It is not because he wills it, but because he has been appointed by **Necessity** <note>original: ἀνάγκης (anankes)</note> to be cast into this role. I think I shall set aside all other matters—though I do not know how they all originated in this discourse—and seek out a matter that is both personal and worthy of inquiry. For "that which is in our power" <term>In our power; original: τὸ ἐπὶ τοῖς σφοῖς (to epi tois sphois), a variant of the technical term 'eph' hemin' referring to human free will</term> has perished from human life; it has perished! Whether one calls it the "helm," the "ballast," or the "foundation" of our life, our **authority** <note>original: ἐξουσία (exousia); our power to choose</note> is gone. 

Alas! We have submitted to something far more "manly" than the most necessary things. **Democritus**, unless I am mistaken, and **Chrysippus** <note>Democritus was an atomist who believed in physical necessity; Chrysippus was a Stoic who attempted to reconcile fate with human responsibility.</note>—the former called our will a "slave," while the latter called it a "half-slave"—yet they thought it the most beautiful thing to demonstrate its freedom. But the words of such men are only worth as much as a free man would grant to other men. Yet if the **Divine** itself takes up arms against us, oh, what things we shall suffer! But this is neither likely nor just, at least to those of us judging by these [oracles]:

> Hearing hateful things, yet dear to the immortal gods, 
> Against which you should remain on guard, holding yourself back.

For what does the messenger say? "If I wished, it is possible for me; but I could not, if it seemed [fated] to me, or if everything were already guarded against." You say it is possible to both "wish" and "be able." Otherwise, how could I then have commanded you:

> Dear son of **Chiron**, glorious one, to arrive quickly,
> Leaving behind **Pelion**, to reach the heights of **Euboea**.
> There, to found a sacred land, as much as is divinely ordained.

But come now, stop stalling! Is there truly anything "up to man," O Apollo? Am I the master of my own will to leave Pelion? I have heard from many wise men that if it is "fated" <note>original: πέπρωται (peprotai); 'it is woven' or 'destined'</note> for me to reach the heights of Euboea and found a sacred land, I shall arrive and I shall found it, whether you say so or not, and whether I wish it or not. If I "must" also wish it because it is necessary for me—even if I did not want to wish it—then you, O Apollo, seem more worthy of being believed than those who stand before you.

> Splendid for the Pythians, achieving glory, as I command you
> To found a visible city in the misty island.

"Splendid," by Zeus, he says! For there is still some conceited person, or someone refuting you, even if you do not command it. For it is fated, and the "misty island" is **Thasos**. And the "Pythians" will come to it, led by my friend **Archilochus** <note>Archilochus was a famous Greek lyric poet; his father, Telesicles, supposedly received this oracle about colonizing Thasos.</note>. For they say this island was called "Misty" in ancient times. 

You, then, since a terrible [fate] has overtaken you, did not live it out, I think—being so ungrateful and bold—for if you had not willed to remain with him, he would never have come, nor would his son Archilochus have guided the Pythians, nor would the Pythians have inhabited Thasos. I do not know, then, if you are saying these things, or if I even know what you are saying. But since we seem like a "lame man" engaging in a long-winded discussion, and this argument is no mere side-issue, I hesitate to speak. Perhaps a few points out of many are enough. 

What, then, would you say that you and I are? And from where do we know this? When did we decide to know this? Or is it not that our self-consciousness and perception of ourselves are so ignorant? And why is it that we are "living beings"—how did we ever find that out? And how do we know that among living beings, as I would say, we are "men"? But if we are men, let us not be "sorcerers." For the sorcerer is one who is refuted. But according to you, one is a man, and the other is a god. And the one is a proph—

» Like a slanderer, even if he were a sophist, I am grieved to show how we have come to know what was said between us in the present moment. What are you saying? Have we not rightly judged our **absolute authority** <note>original: αὐλίαν αὐτήκρημνον (aulian autēkrēmnon); Oenomaus uses this phrase to mock the idea of a self-determined life that is supposedly rendered "precipitous" or impossible by fate.</note> by that most distinctive of all things? For let it be clear that it is neither more dissoluble, nor older, nor more trustworthy. For if this is not the case, then let no one ever again summon you, someone named **Alcmaeon**, to **Delphi** <note>Alcmaeon was a mythological hero who killed his mother, Eriphyle, to avenge his father. He sought purification from the Oracle at Delphi.</note> after you have killed your mother, as you wander from there, yearning for home. For such a man knows neither if he himself is a human being, nor if he is wandering from home, nor if he yearns for home; rather, if even Alcmaeon is mad, and kills those who do not even exist, then when the **Pythian** <note>The "Pythian" refers to Apollo, the god of the Oracle at Delphi.</note> is also mad, do not speak in such a manner.

-> Thirst for the island, tread to reach the land — **Amphidryadie**. <-
<note>This is a mocking imitation of a cryptic oracular response. Amphidryadie was an ancient name for the island of Delos, Apollo's birthplace.</note>

» For it is not possible, if someone asks you about **Amphidryadie**, that you—being the one questioned—can speak with knowledge about the things the person asks. Nor let **Chrysippus** <note>Chrysippus (c. 279–206 BC) was a leader of the Stoic school who famously tried to reconcile the idea of Fate with human moral responsibility.</note>, who introduces that "semi-slavery," escape to the **Stoas** <term>Stoas; original: στοὰς, the "porches" or colonnades where Stoic philosophers taught</term> regarding what this does to him. Let no one think that you will be defended by those viewpoints, as if they were listening to a "nobody." Nor should anyone persist in affirming anything, whether **Arcesilaus** <note>Arcesilaus (c. 316–241 BC) was a Skeptic philosopher who argued that nothing could be known with certainty.</note> is present, or **Epicurus** is present. 

» For what is Arcesilaus, or the Epicureans, or what are the wise, or the young, or who is "whoever"? He neither knows, nor is he capable of knowing. For it is much worse if he does not even know what he himself is. But neither you nor **Democritus** <note>Democritus (c. 460–370 BC) was the father of the atomic theory, which Oenomaus views as a mechanical form of fate.</note> would tolerate it if someone said these things—for I have never yet spoken to that extent. Nor would you tolerate it if someone there thought they were "something." (To this, at least, add or subtract the "loosening," for the virgins are not loosened). Therefore, he might say again: "O Democritus, and you, O Chrysippus, and you, **Manes** <note>Likely a reference to a common slave name, used here to mock philosophers as slaves to their own theories of fate.</note>, you are all indignant if someone wishes to somehow shatter your absolute authority. For you are not found in those many books of yours.") 

» Come now, let us be indignant! Why then, if it should ever seem so to you, will this be both most trustworthy and most ancient? And then again, if it does not seem so, will what was said be cross-examined as to whether it has not grown old? These are the things each of you is fated to carry: some from God, and others from the impulse of those small things—those atoms—that are carried downward, and bounce back again, and entwine with one another and dissolve <note>This is a satirical description of the "atomic swerve" and collision theory of Democritus and Epicurus.</note>, showing and setting themselves aside by necessity. 

» For look how your absolute authority stands! This belongs to the things within us that are both voluntary and forced. You should not tell us how great is the distance between "walking" and "being led," nor between "choosing" and "being compelled." For what reason did I bring these things into the discourse? Because it has escaped you, O Manes—things of which we are the masters, and He who knows all things. You could not know these things, whose ropes are tied to our own will. This will appeared to be, among you, a beginning of no small importance; but as for where the beginning is, or whatever cause follows these things, it has escaped you. Here, he moves from the tragedy of Oedipus to the general absurdity of gods praising or blaming humans if all actions are predetermined by an unbreakable "chain" of causality.</meta>

For which reason, I would not be deceived, O Apollo—or if they are united, they do not even deceive, because of your Necessity. And what of that famous **Lycurgus** <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note>? Why, Apollo, do you praise him? He was not good by his own will—whether it was a famine or whatever—but by necessity; if indeed anyone ever becomes good against his will. What you are doing now is like someone who praises and paints those with beautiful bodies, but blames and punishes the ugly. And as for the good, who have been well-sharpened and tended, no one will permit them [to take credit], but will say: "O **Chrysippus** and **Cleanthes** <note>Chrysippus and Cleanthes were the second and third heads of the Stoic school, famous for their rigorous defense of determinism.</note>, and all of you from that chorus, for you have made them to be good; I myself, along with the praise, do not praise you for the virtuous." ->From the same work, from the writings of Diogenianus the Peripatetic.<-

» Against Chrysippus, who wants to simultaneously preserve the causes that depend on us <note>This refers to the concept of "free will" or moral responsibility.</note> while also claiming that everything happens according to fate; and [arguing] that he did not even understand what is said in Homer concerning fate. In addition to all this, it is worth laughing at the views Chrysippus expresses in the second book of his treatise *On Reason*, and again in the first book of his work *On Fate*. Wishing to demonstrate that everything is seized by Necessity and Fate, he employs various testimonies, and particularly the verses spoken by the poet Homer:
» “But as for me, a hateful doom
» Seized me, which was allotted to me at my very birth.” <note>Homer, *Iliad* 23.78-79. The word "doom" translates *kēr*, a personification of violent death.</note> And:
» “Afterward he shall suffer whatever Fate
» Spun for him with her thread at his birth, when his mother bore him.” <note>Homer, *Iliad* 20.127-128. "Fate" here is *Aisa*, the "allotment" of one's life.</note>
» “No man, I say, has ever escaped his destiny.” <note>Homer, *Iliad* 6.488. "Destiny" translates *Moira*.</note>
» He does not observe that what the poet says elsewhere, conversely, directly contradicts these; verses which he himself even uses in his second book, wanting to establish that many things also happen because of us, such as:
» “For they perished by their own recklessness.” <note>Homer, *Odyssey* 1.7. Referring to the companions of Odysseus.</note> And:
» “Look you now, how mortals blame the gods!
» For they say that evils come from us, but they themselves,
» Through their own recklessness, have sorrows beyond what is fated.” <note>Homer, *Odyssey* 1.32-34. "Beyond what is fated" translates *hyper moron*.</note>
» For these and similar lines contradict the idea that everything happens according to fate. Furthermore, he was not even able to see this: that Homer by no means fails to testify to his doctrine in those very verses. For it will be shown from the very propositions that it is not that *everything* happens according to fate, but rather that *certain* things happen according to it.
» For the line, “But as for me, a hateful doom seized me, which was allotted to me at my very birth,” would not suggest that *everything* happens according to one's doom, but specifically the act of dying itself. For indeed, as is the case for all, it would appear to be according to fate for every created living thing. Moreover, the line, “Afterward he shall suffer whatever Fate spun for him with her thread at his birth, when his mother bore him,” intends the same thing. For he does not say that *everything* that happens to him thereafter will be according to fate, but that *some* certain things will happen to him by necessity. For either the word “whatever” refers to one thing or to another, or it signifies this: many things are imposed on us by necessity, even if not all things. And the line, “No man, I say, has ever escaped his destiny,” is spoken without fear [of contradiction]. For who could escape the things that happen by necessity to every living creature? Thus, not only would Chrysippus not have Homer’s vote in his belief that *everything* happens according to fate, but he would even have him as an opponent, since the poet has clearly and frequently said that many things depend on us. Certainly, he could nowhere be found explicitly saying that *everything* happens according to necessity. And for the poet—since he does not promise us the absolute truth of the nature of things, but is mixed with passions and customs and all sorts of human opinions—it would be fitting to say contradictory things often. But for a philosopher, it is not fitting to say contradictory things, nor to use a poet as a witness for that very reason, who says neither one thing nor the other [consistently].
» And we have clear evidence in the way Chrysippus thinks fate exists in all things: his definition of such names. For he says that “destiny” <term>destiny: πεπρωμένη (pepromenē)</term> is that which is “limited” <term>limited: πεπερασμένη (peperasmenē)</term> and...

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 6

> ...a completed administration. He defines Fate as a certain chain <note>Greek: *heirmos*, meaning a string or sequence of causes.</note>, whether arising from the will of God or from whatever other cause. Moreover, he claims the Fates <note>The *Moirai*.</note> are so named from the act of being "apportioned" <note>original: *memeristhai*</note> and distributed to each of us. Likewise, he says "necessity" <note>original: *to chreon*</note> is so called because it is that which falls upon us and is fitting according to Fate. He says the number of the Fates is three because of the progression of time, in which all things revolve and through which they are fulfilled. He claims Lachesis is named from the "allotting" <note>original: *lagchanein*</note> of destiny to each person; Atropos from the "unchangeable" <note>original: *atrepton*</note> and unalterable nature of the distribution; and Clotho from the "spinning together" <note>original: *synkeklōsthai*</note> and linking of all things, such that there is a single ordered path for them. By babbling these and similar points, he tries to prove that one should believe in a certain Necessity in all things.

But I wonder what came over him, that in saying such things he did not perceive his own empty-headedness. For even if we grant that men used these concepts when they established the names—just as he etymologizes from existing terms—thinking that a certain Fate had seized all things, and that causes were unalterably fixed from eternity in everything that exists or happens; why then, O Chrysippus, do you follow all the opinions of men? Does it seem to you that no one is ever deceived about anything,

> but that we have all perceived the truth equally? How then can you say that no one is free except the one who is not mad? <note>This refers to the famous Stoic paradox that "every non-wise person is insane."</note> If it seems that men desire and neglect things in equal measure—and sometimes more than is right—and yet you say only one or two people have ever been truly wise, while all others, through their folly, are just as "mad" as those previously mentioned? How is it right to dismiss those opinions as mistaken which the majority hold regarding wealth, glory, power, and pleasure in general as being "good"? And how, looking at established laws—which you say are absurd, as are the political constitutions—could you have written such a massive number of books against them if men did not have mistaken opinions? For surely we will not say that when they disagree with you they are thinking correctly, but when they differ from you they are mad. First of all, you do not even say that you yourself are wise, nor are we, so that we might use that as a criterion for when those people were thinking well and not being "sober" according to your own opinion. Furthermore, even if this were true, why was it necessary to say that everyone is equally mad? Why not say that, insofar as they seemed to hold these opinions, it appeared to them they were rightly convinced; but insofar as they disagreed, you assume they were in error? Certainly, one should not consider common opinion as a strong proof of truth. Even then, it would not be a natural necessity, and they would not be "mad" in the way you think, though everyone would admit they were far from wisdom. Therefore, you are acting ridiculously by using these people as witnesses through their assignment of names—people who, by your own admission, cannot differ from you in understanding—unless it turns happened that those who originally assigned these names were wise. But you will never be able to prove that. But let it be granted to you that this is so, and that those names were established as you wish, possessing those meanings, and that this did not happen based on false opinions. Where, then, is it signaled through them that absolutely everything happens according to Fate? What if only those things that have a "fate" are included? For the number of the Fates, and their names, and the spindle of Clotho, and the thread wound upon it, and the spinning of it, and all such other things said among them, indicate the unalterable and eternal sequence of causes through which things are forced to happen in this way, and all that they are prevented from having otherwise. For many...

<meta>Catchword: πολ- (many/much)</meta>

Diogenianus argues that if the Stoics believe most people are "mad" and unwise, they cannot use common language and names created by those same people as evidence for philosophical truth.</summary>
