<meta>This page continues the critique by the Peripatetic philosopher Diogenianus against the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, as preserved in Eusebius’s *Preparation for the Gospel*. The previous page discussed how Chrysippus used etymologies of the names of the Fates to argue that all things are governed by an unalterable Necessity. Here, Diogenianus examines how Chrysippus attempts to reconcile this total determinism with human effort and free will.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

,, ...and even if such things were not the case. But regarding those things that do not happen in this way, there are some who have attributed them to gods as administrators and creators. Others have supposed ourselves to be the causes of some things. Others, again, attribute things to Nature, and others to Fortune <note>original: *tyche*</note>. Wanting to demonstrate the unstable and fickle nature of Fortune—now being one way, now another—they personified <note>original: *eidōlopoiēsantes*</note> this accidental quality of events, depicting Fortune standing upon a slippery base. For have these ideas not also been held in high regard among men? For if the causes were always confusing the cities, people would think that whatever happens by Fate or by Fortune happens by a divine power. But whatever is up to us, they think happens by Fate.

,, But it is quite clear that they hold these causes to be very much among existing things. Consequently, it has not come to pass that human opinions, nor the assignment of such names, bear witness to the doctrine of Chrysippus. To these points he adds the following: If, therefore, in the first book *On Fate*, he used such proofs, in the second he attempts to resolve the absurdities that seem to follow from the argument that says all things are governed by necessity. These are the same points we touched upon at the beginning: that because of these arguments, our own zeal <note>original: *prothymia*</note> is destroyed, along with blame and praise, and exhortations, and everything that clearly happens through our own cause.

,, He says, then, in his second book, that while it is clear that many things happen through us, these things are nonetheless "co-fated" <note>original: *synkatheimarthai*; the Stoic idea that an outcome and the means to it are bound together in the same destiny</note> with the administration of the whole. He uses examples such as these: He says that for a cloak not to be destroyed is not simply fated, but fated along with its being cared for. And being saved from enemies is fated along with fleeing from those enemies. And the birth of children is fated along with the desire to be with a woman.

,, Just as, he says, if someone were to say it is not necessary for a boxer <note>original: *pyktēs*</note> to defend himself in a match to remain entirely un-struck, it would be absurd; for he would be expecting the man to fight in the match with his hands down just because it was fated for him to leave un-struck—since the person who made the declaration said this because of the man’s extraordinary defense against being hit. So it is with other things as well. For many things can happen without our will, but the fact that our zeal and effort are applied to them is not excluded; he says these things are fated to happen with this effort.

,, Again, one might wonder at this man for his unreflective and inconsistent claims, and the lack of logic in his own arguments. For I think that just as what is called "sweet" happens to be the opposite of what is called "bitter," and just as "hot" is to "cold," so too—as they themselves say—is "what is up to us" <note>original: *to par' hēmas*; human agency</note> to "what is according to Fate." For he previously defined as "according to Fate" those things which happen regardless of whether we are willing or unwilling. But "up to us" are those things which come to a conclusion through our striving and acting, or which are not completed through our neglect and laziness.

,, If, therefore, I do not strive to look after my cloak, and it is not saved; and if a man does not wish to approach a woman, and children are not born; and if one does not wish to flee the enemy, or is killed by them; and if one does not strive bravely against an opponent and guard against the blows of his hands, he does not depart the match un-struck—how then will "according to Fate" be preserved here? For if these things happen according to Fate, they could not be said to happen "because of us." And if they happen "because of us," they clearly would not happen according to Fate, because these two things cannot coincide with one another.

<summary>This page records the critique of Chrysippus's theory of "co-fated" events, where the Stoic philosopher attempts to argue that human effort is part of a fated sequence. The critic, Diogenianus, argues that Fate and Human Agency are mutually exclusive opposites that cannot logically coexist in the same action.</summary>

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 6

» ...to each other. But "that which is up to us" <term>original: *to eph' hēmas* — a technical term referring to actions within human control</term> will exist, he says, though it is already encompassed by 
» fate. And how could we say it is already encompassed, if indeed both the guarding of the cloak <note>original: *thoimation* — a standard Greek outer garment</note> and 
» the not guarding it happened from my own power? For in this way, I would clearly be the master of 
» its being saved; and from the very assignment <note>original: *apostolēs*</note> that Chrysippus <note>A leader of the Stoic school who argued that fate and free will could coexist through "compatibilism"</note> makes, 
» it is clear that fate is set apart from the cause that comes from us. For he says: "You will not 
» save the cloak unless you guard it; and you will have children only if you wish to." 
» Clearly, then, none of these things would happen [without our effort]. But regarding those things 
» already encompassed by fate, we would never suppose that such conditions would apply. 
» Therefore, it would become clear that everything would be said to happen in this way—either 
» that you will not die if such-and-hers does not happen, or that you will 
» simply die, even if every possible way of not dying were to occur. Or that 
» a certain human would not be receptive to pain, even if he were to suffer an injury. But every 
» human is receptive to pain, whether he wishes it or not. And the things in the world 
» would not be and happen in this way. So even this particular thing "of ours" is necessary if we 
» should wish it; but clearly it is not so, for it is evident that our wishing and not 
» wishing has been encompassed by no other cause, but lies within 
» our own free will <term>original: *autexousiō* — the power of self-determination</term>. But if this were un-
» coerced, and this "of ours" was also such, then it is clear that it was not encompassed from 
» eternity—unless, of course, the very act of wishing to guard the cloak, or not 
» wishing to, was destined to happen by an external cause of necessity, contrary to 
» fate. But in this way, our own power of choice <note>original: *exousiastikē dynamis*</note> is completely 
» destroyed, and the cloak would no longer be saved or

» construct an argument concerning these efficient causes. For in this way it will become clear whether one must blame Fate for *everything* that happens, or if we must allow that some things happen apart from Fate, as if there were other specific efficient causes. 

» Aristotle, when raising problems and making a division of things that happen, says that some of them occur "for the sake of something," meaning they have a target <note>original: *skopos*</note> and an end proposed by the one who does them. 
» Others, he says, happen for the sake of nothing; these do not occur according to any choice of the maker, 
» nor do they have a reference to a defined end. Such things 
» include, for example, the clutching of certain bits of straw, or twirling them, or the touching and

» Things that happen in this way—aimlessly and 
» simply—do not admit of any further logical division. 

» But of those things that have a reference to an end and happen for the sake of something, some occur by **nature** and some occur by **reason**. 
» For those things that have a cause of their creation in nature proceed toward an end according to certain numbers and a defined order—and once they reach that end, they cease to be "in process"—unless 
» something stands in their way and hinders 
» their natural path toward the proposed goal. 
» But things that happen by reason also have an end. For nothing that happens by reason happens by chance; rather, their differences all have some specific target. » the manner in which they might be brought about. Such are all things that happen according to the **arts** <note>original: *technas* — specialized skills or crafts like medicine or carpentry</note> and according to 
» **choice**. 

» These differ from things that happen by nature in that natural things

» the things happening before the end occur for the sake of something clear, but when they result in something unintended, 
» that result is called "spontaneous" or "by chance."

# EUSEBIUS

->160<-

...actions seem to be of necessity. But it clearly appears that among all other living creatures, **man** alone has this advantage from nature: that he does not follow his impressions <term>original: *phantasiai* — the way things appear to the senses or the mind</term> in the same way they do, but possesses **Reason** <term>original: *logos* — the rational or judging faculty</term> as a judge of the things that encounter him. 

Using this Reason, if the things perceived through the senses are examined and found to be truly as they appear, he gives his assent to the impression and pursues them. But if they appear otherwise, he no longer persists in accepting them, as Reason has refuted them after deliberating on the matter. We certainly deliberate only about those things which we have the power to do. If we ever act without deliberating, we often repent and blame ourselves for our **thoughtlessness** <note>original: *aboulia* — a lack of counsel or deliberation</note>. 

Furthermore, if we see others acting thoughtlessly, we accuse them of having done wrong, and we deem it right to use advisors for these matters, since such things are within our power. That their doctrine concerning **Fate** <term>original: *heimarmenē*</term> is false is sufficiently evidenced by the fact that those who advocate for it are unable to be persuaded by their own words. For they promise both to exhort and to teach, and they advise people to learn and be educated. They also hate and rebuke those who do not do what is fitting, as if they were sinning by their own **choice** <term>original: *proairesis* — deliberate moral choice</term>. 

Moreover, they leave behind many writings through which they expect the young to be educated. We might have ceased this verbal rivalry if they had noticed that they themselves grant pardon to those who sin involuntarily, while they say those who offend **voluntarily** are worthy of punishment—since it is clearly within their power both to sin and not to sin. Thus, even by their own standards, the necessity of Fate is abolished. 

Our inherent power of **Free Will** <term>original: *autexousios* — being one's own master or having self-governing power</term> is thus established, alongside which many things exist—including those not within our power, such as natural events and matters of chance—which are distinct from the doctrine of Fate, as was shown previously. These points have been summarized by us from a great many sources as a preface to the discourse on Free Will within our own doctrines. In this, the voices of the philosophers have converged with our own, bearing witness to our **Divine Scriptures**. They refute the false opinions concerning Fate held not only by the common people but even by the "wonderful" oracles of the gods. 

Some of these critics have addressed the naked oracles in a rather "Cynic" fashion <note>The Cynic philosophers were known for their biting, blunt criticism of social and religious norms</note>, while others have addressed the esteemed philosophers. Now that their views are well known, it is time to examine the arguments against those who "Chaldeanize" <note>The Chaldeans were famous in antiquity as astrologers; "Chaldeanizing" refers to the practice of casting horoscopes and believing in astral determinism</note>, who profess this "evil-arted sorcery" as if it were a branch of science. I will set before you the proofs of these matters from a man who was **Syrian** by race, but who reached the very peak of Chaldean science. **Bardesanes** is the man's name, who is remembered to have said the following in his *Dialogues with his Companions*:

» ...guarded by those who protect them). The same can be said of every species of scorpion: they strike with their tongue, and they harm even the three who have done no wrong, striking with a poisonous sting. This same wickedness is ingrained in all scorpions. The ant, by its nature, knows the coming of winter; it toils throughout the whole of summer and sets aside food for itself, and all ants work in the same way. The bee especially "farms" honey, from which it is also nourished; and this same farming is common to all bees. There are many species of animals to behold; since they are unable to depart from their nature, they create a sense of wonder in the observer.

» I could have given you many more examples, but I considered the evidence already presented sufficient to prove that while other animals are driven by necessity to follow the common traits and differences given to each by nature, human beings alone possess an exceptional gift: the ability to think and to understand the reason <term>original: *logos* — here meaning the rational principle or discourse</term> offered by this faculty. According to their common nature, they follow nature as I said before; but according to their exceptional gift, they no longer conduct their lives in such a uniform way.

» For there is not just one kind of food for everyone. Some feed like lions <note>referring to heavy meat-eaters</note>, while a few others are like sheep, not having a constitution that allows for such a diet. There is no single custom or single law of citizenship among them, nor a single movement of desire that dictates their choice; rather, each human being chooses a life for himself according to his own private will, not mimicking his neighbor, except for those things he wishes to imitate. For that which is within his own power <term>original: *autexousion* — the power of self-determination or free will</term> is not subject to slavery. Even if he should ever choose to serve as a slave, even this is an exercise of his freedom. Who can force a man to serve against his will?

» Consider how many men—and especially those from the countryside—eat meat like wild animals, possessing nothing of the irrational beasts themselves, for it is not because they lack the ability to choose, but because they do not wish to do otherwise. Others do not taste meat at all, like domesticated animals. Some eat only fish; others never taste fish, nor do they touch wine. Some are water-drinkers, others are wine-drinkers, and others drink fermented liquor <note>original: *sikera* — a strong alcoholic drink often made from grain or fruit other than grapes</note>. Quite simply, there is a vast difference in food and drink among humanity, extending even to the variety of vegetables and fruits they consume.

» Furthermore, some people, like scorpions or asps, commit wrongs without having been wronged themselves. Others, like irrational animals, only defend themselves when they are wronged. Others, like wolves, snatch and take joy in thievery. Still others, like lambs or ewes, are seen by all their peers to be gentle, not returning wrong for wrong. Some are called good, others bad, and others just. From this, one can understand that man is not entirely good by nature. For what kind of nature was assigned to him? Rather, in one way he is moved by nature, and in another by choice <term>original: *proairesis* — purposeful choice or moral disposition</term>. Therefore, he receives praise, blame, and condemnation in those things he does by choice. In those things done by nature, he is blameless—not according to his character, but according to reason.

» And next he says: "Human beings have established different laws in every region, some written and some unwritten. I will recount these as I know them and as I remember them, starting from the beginning of the world. Among the **Seres** <note>The Seres were the ancient Greek and Roman name for the people of North China</note>, it is the law that no one may murder, or commit fornication, or steal, or worship idols. In that vast country, you cannot see a temple, nor a woman known as a prostitute or an adulteress, nor a thief brought to trial, nor a murderer, nor a victim of murder. For the star of **Ares** <note>Mars</note>, even when in the mid-heaven and fierce in its influence, has never forced the free will <term>original: *autexousion*</term> of any man there to use the sword to kill. Nor has **Kypris** <note>Venus</note>, when joining with Mars in the mid-heaven at any hour or day, ever forced a man among the Seres to have intercourse with a woman in public, even though such astrological configurations occur every day.

» Among the **Indians** and **Bactrians**, there are many thousands of those called **Brahmans**. According to the tradition of their ancestors and their laws, they neither commit murder nor worship idols..."

<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

...necessity governs all that is done. But it is clearly evident that among all other living creatures, man alone possesses an extra gift from nature: he does not follow his mental impressions <note>original: *phantasiai* — the way things appear to the senses</note> in the same way they do, nor is he without reason <term>original: *logos* — here meaning the faculty of rational judgment</term> as a judge of the things that befall him. By using this reason, if the things he imagines are examined and found to be true to reality, he gives his internal assent to the impression and pursues them. But if they appear otherwise, he does not remain fixed in his initial assumption once reason has tested them, which is why we deliberate about them. 

We certainly do not deliberate only about things we are able to do. Indeed, if we ever act without deliberating, we often regret it and blame ourselves for our lack of counsel. Furthermore, if we see others acting without counsel, we accuse them of having erred, and we consider it right to use advisors, as if such matters were within our own power. That their theory regarding Fate <term>original: *heimarmene* — the Stoic or astrological concept of a pre-determined life</term> is false is sufficiently proven by the fact that not even those who champion it can be persuaded by their own words. For they profess to both encourage and teach, and they advise people to learn and be educated; moreover, they hate and rebuke those who do not do what is fitting, as if they were erring by their own free choice. They even leave behind many writings through which they expect the young to be educated. 

I would have ceased this verbal rivalry if they also rightly acknowledged that those who err unintentionally deserve forgiveness. Yet they say that those who do wrong voluntarily deserve punishment—clearly implying that both sinning and not sinning lie within their own power. Thus, even by their own standards, the necessity of Fate is dismantled. I will pass over the fact that we possess a self-determining nature <term>original: *autexousion* — the power of free will or self-governance</term>, which accounts for most things, and that there are other factors not within our power—such as things governed by nature or by chance—which are distinct from the logic of Fate, as was demonstrated previously. 

Since these points concerning the doctrine of free will in our own teachings have been summarized from many sources, and since the most respected voices of the philosophers have agreed with them, bearing witness to our own Divine Scriptures, I shall now refute the opinions concerning Fate. These opinions belong not only to common men but also to those admired oracles of the "gods," which are proved false. Some of these are refuted by those who speak more sharply <note>literally "in a more Cynic-like manner," referring to the critical style of the Cynic philosophers</note> against vulgar oracles. Others are refuted by the admirable philosophers who have dismantled what was familiar to them. It is now time to examine the arguments against those who follow the "Chaldean" ways <note>referring to practitioners of Babylonian astrology</note> and those who profess this treacherous sorcery as if it were a branch of learning. I will set before you proofs on this matter from a man who was Syrian by birth and had reached the very pinnacle of Chaldean science. Bardaisan is the man's name, and in his *Dialogues* with his companions, he is recorded to have said something like this:

A lion eats meat and defends itself if it is harmed; for this reason, all lions eat meat and defend themselves. Camels eat grass and do not touch meat, and when they are wronged...

<margin>»</margin>not imitating his neighbor in the things he wishes to do. For that which
<margin>»</margin>concerns his own self is not subject to slavery. And if he ever chooses to serve, even this is part of his
<margin>»</margin>freedom: the ability to submit himself to service. How many people, especially
<margin>»</margin>out of necessity, eat raw meat like wild animals without any preparation? Yet others,
<margin>»</margin>having no such need but through their own choice, never taste meat at all, like domesticated animals. Some eat only
<margin>»</margin>fish. Others never taste fish, nor even chew on salt. Some
<margin>»</margin>drink only water; others drink wine. Others drink fermented liquor <note>original: *sikera* — a strong alcoholic drink, often made from grain or dates</note>, and in short, there is a great variety of
<margin>»</margin>foods and drinks among humanity, even differing down to the
<margin>»</margin>eating of vegetables and fruits. Furthermore, some—like scorpions and asps—do wrong without being wronged.
<margin>»</margin>Others, like irrational animals, only defend themselves when wronged. Others, like wolves,
<margin>»</margin>snatch things away, and others steal like foxes. Others, like sheep and bleating goats, appear among those who
<margin>»</margin>suffer similar fates, yet they do not wrong those who wrong them. Some are called good, some
<margin>»</margin>evil, and some just. From this, one can perceive that man is not led entirely by nature. For
<margin>»</margin>what kind of nature could he be following? Rather, in some ways he is moved by nature, and in others by choice <term>original: *proairesis* — deliberate moral choice or free will</term>.
<margin>»</margin>Therefore, he receives praise, blame, and condemnation in those things done by choice. In
<margin>»</margin>those things done by nature, he is blameless—not according to custom, but according to reason. And he says
<margin>»</margin>next: Humans have established diverse laws in every region, some written,
<margin>»</margin>and some unwritten. I will recount these as I know them and as I remember them, beginning from
<margin>»</margin>the edge of the world. Among the Seres <note>original: *Seres* — the ancient Greek and Roman name for the people of China, the "Silk People"</note>, the law is that no one may murder,
<margin>»</margin>commit adultery, steal, or worship idols. And in that vast country, you cannot
<margin>»</margin>see a temple, nor a harlot, nor a woman called an adulteress, nor a thief
<margin>»</margin>being led to trial, nor a murderer, nor a victim of murder. For no one’s free will was
<margin>»</margin>forced by the star of fire-bright Mars <note>original: *Ares*</note> being at the meridian <note>original: *mesouranon* — an astrological term for a planet at its highest point in the sky</note> to strike a man with a sword. Nor did
<margin>»</margin>Venus <note>original: *Kypris*</note>, whether rising or being present, force any man among them to have intercourse with a woman in public, even though she is at the meridian in the sign of Mars
<margin>»</margin>every day, and the Seres are being born at every hour and every day.
<margin>»</margin>Among the Indians and the Bactrians, there are many thousands of those called Brahmans,
<margin>»</margin>who, according to the tradition of their ancestors and laws, neither murder nor worship idols...

<summary>This page contains a portion of Bardaisan's "Book of the Laws of Countries," arguing that human diversity in diet, morality, and law proves the existence of free will. It specifically challenges astrological determinism by noting that the Seres (Chinese) and Brahmans follow their own virtuous laws regardless of the position of the stars.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the text of the philosopher Bardaisan, as quoted in Eusebius’s "Preparation for the Gospel." The previous page established the argument that human behavior is not dictated by nature or instinct like that of animals, but by free will and reason. On this page, Bardaisan provides ethnographic evidence to prove that different nations follow different laws and customs, even when they live under the same astrological conditions or geographical climates, thereby refuting the idea of fatalistic astrology.</meta>

### EUSEBIUS.

...revere <note>referring to the Brahmins mentioned on the previous page</note>. They do not eat of anything that has a soul <note>original: "ἐμψύχου" (empsychou) — meaning meat or living creatures</note>. They never get drunk on wine or strong drink <note>original: "σίκερος" (sikeros) — likely a fermented grain or palm liquor</note>. By doing so, they share in no evil, devoting themselves to God; meanwhile, other Indians commit murder, practice harlotry, get drunk, worship carved images <note>original: "ξόανα" (xoana) — primitive wooden idols</note>, and are carried along almost entirely by fate <term>original: *heimarmene* — the philosophical concept of inevitable destiny or astral fatalism</term>. Yet in this very same climate of India, there is a certain tribe of Indians who hunt any strangers who fall into their hands, sacrifice them, and eat them. Neither have the "good-doing" stars <note>benefic planets like Jupiter or Venus</note> prevented these men from being blood-guilty and marrying unlawfully, nor have the "evil-doing" stars <note>malefic planets like Saturn or Mars</note> forced the Brahmins to commit crimes. 

Among the Persians, there is a law to marry their own daughters, sisters, and mothers. And the Persians did not practice these unholy marriages only in that country and in that climate; rather, as many of them as traveled away from Persia—who are called Magusaeans <note>a priestly caste or sect of Zoroastrian origin</note>—maintain the same lawlessness, handing it down to their laws and their children in succession. Many of these people exist to this day in Media, Egypt, Phrygia, and Galatia. And surely Aphrodite <note>original: "Cypris"</note>—sitting in the houses of Saturn <note>original: "Cronus"</note> alongside Saturn as he changes the nature of Mars <note>original: "Ares"</note>—did not produce this behavior just during the shedding of beards <note>This astrological passage is highly technical, suggesting that specific planetary alignments do not dictate these cultural habits</note>. 

Among the Geli <note>a people from the shores of the Caspian Sea</note>, it is the law for women to farm, build, and perform all manual labor, and to consort with whomever they wish without being accused by their husbands. Nor is the name "adulteress" used for them; they are all laborers and consort with everyone, especially with strangers. Furthermore, the Gelian women do not use perfume or wear dyed clothes, and they all go barefoot; yet the Gelian men are adorned in soft garments of diverse colors, wearing gold and perfumes—and not because of any feminine weakness. For they are brave, very warlike, and fond of hunting. Not all the women of the Geli happened to have the sign of Capricorn or Aquarius, nor was Aphrodite in a state of misfortune <note>original: "κακοδαιμονοῦσαν" (kakodaimonousan) — a technical term for a planet in a bad "house" or "aspect"</note> for all of them. Nor do all their men have the Paphian <note>Another name for Aphrodite</note> in Aries together with Mars—a configuration that those who follow the Chaldaeans <note>astrologers</note> say produces men who are both brave and luxurious. 

Among the Bactrians, the women differ from the men in every kind of adornment and use every perfume; they are served by young boys and youths more than the men are. They go forth with great display on horses, decorating their horses with much gold and precious stones. They do not fear, but indifferently consort with slaves and strangers, acting thus without fear and without being accused by their husbands; indeed, they almost rule over them. It is certainly not the case that on every single day among the Bactrian women, the laughter-loving Aphrodite culminates in mid-heaven <note>original: "μεσουρανεῖ" (mesouranei)</note> with Jupiter <note>original: "Zeus"</note> and Mars in their own terms <note>specific degrees of the zodiac</note>. 

In Arabia and Osrhoene, not only are adulteresses killed, but even those merely suspected are not left unpunished. Among the Parthians and Armenians, murderers are executed, sometimes by judges and sometimes by the relatives of the victims. Yet if a man kills his own wife, or a childless brother, or an unmarried sister, or a son, or a daughter, he is not accused by anyone—such laws exist in those regions. Among the Greeks and Romans, however, those who murder their own family and relatives are subject to the greatest punishments. In Gaul, one who steals even a single obol <note>a small coin</note> is disgraced. Among the Bactrians, one who steals a little is spat upon. Among the Romans, such a person is tortured with beatings. These are the laws from the Euphrates river to the Ocean. Just as in the case of adultery, a man who is insulted <note>original: "λοιδορούμενος" (loidoroumenos)</note> as a murderer or a thief is greatly indignant; but the man who is insulted as a sodomite <note>original: "ἀρσενοκοίτης" (arsenokoites)</note>— 

insulted- <meta>catchword: λοιδορού- (loidorou-)</meta>

<summary>Bardaisan argues against astrological fatalism by listing the diverse and often contradictory laws and customs of various nations (Indians, Persians, Geli, Bactrians, Romans), noting that these behaviors persist across different climates and locations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Bardaisan, a 2nd-century Syriac philosopher, preserved by Eusebius. Bardaisan is arguing against the idea that the stars (astrological fate) control human behavior. He uses "the laws of countries" to show that people in the same geographic or astrological region behave differently based on their local traditions and their own free will.</meta>

### PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 6
->o.iiii.<-

...[a man] who is insulted avenges himself even unto murder. Among the Hyrcanians <note>A region southeast of the Caspian Sea</note>, the wise men are not blamed for having male lovers. In that same East, those who are dishonored <note>likely referring to women or men involved in illicit sexual acts</note>, if they are discovered, are killed by their brothers or fathers and relatives, and they are not even granted a public burial. 

Among the Gauls <note>original: "γάλλοις" — likely referring here to the Galatians or Celts</note>, the young men marry one another openly, not considering this a cause for blame, because of the law among them. And it is not possible that all those in Gaul who are so godlessly insulted could have had in their horoscopes <note>original: "γενέσεσι" (genesesi) — literally "births" or "nativities"</note> Venus <note>original: "φωσφόρον" (phosphoron) — "the bringer of light," a common name for Venus</note> with Mercury, in the houses of Saturn, and in the decans of Mars <note>This is a technical astrological configuration meant to explain "unnatural" behavior</note>. 

In Britain, many men share one wife. In Parthia, many women have one husband, and all remain chaste, obeying him according to the law. The Amazons have no husbands, but like irrational animals, once a year around the spring equinox, they cross their own borders and join with their neighbors, treating this as a festival. From this they conceive and return, and of necessity they give birth in due time according to the law of nature. And the males who are born they cast away, but the females they rear. They are warlike and care for physical training. 

Mercury with Venus, in the houses of Mercury, makes sculptors and painters and bankers. In the houses of Venus, it produces perfumers, or singers, and actors of poems, and those who are bold in such things. And yet in Upper Libya, and among the Moors, and among the nomads near the mouth of the Ocean, and in Outer Germany, and in Upper Sarmatia <note>Regions in modern-day Russia/Poland</note>, and in Scythia, and in all the nations of the northern regions or the Pole, and all Gaul, or Britain, and Oceania, and Spain, and in the Golden Land <note>original: "χρυσῇ" (chryse) — possibly referring to the Malay Peninsula or a mythical land of gold</note>, one cannot see a banker, or a sculptor, or a painter, nor an architect or a geometrician, or a singer, nor an actor. Rather, the influence <term>original: *energeia* — the active power or operation of a planet</term> of Mercury and Venus is absent in the whole circuit of these inhabited lands. 

The Medes all throw their dead, while still breathing, to dogs that are carefully bred for this purpose; and surely not all the Medes have Mars with the Moon in the sign of Cancer below the earth in their horoscopes. Indians burn their dead, and with them they burn their wives who do so voluntarily <note>This refers to the practice of Sati</note>. And surely not all the Indian women who are burned alive have Mars and the Sun in Leo below the earth in a nighttime birth, in the houses of Mars. 

Most Romans die by hanging, and a multitude of Romans are subject to such fortunes, or have the Moon intercepted by Saturn and Mars at their hour. Yet in every nation, and on every day, and in every place of birth, men are born. But in each group of men, law and custom <term>original: *nomos kai ethos* — the pillars of social order</term> prevail because of the free will <note>original: "αὐτεξούσιον" (autexousion) — the power of self-determination</note> of man. 

The horoscope does not force the Seres <note>The "Silk-people," or Chinese</note> to kill against their will, or the Brahmans to eat meat, or the Persians to refrain from unlawful marriages, or the Indians not to be burned, or the Medes not to be eaten by dogs, or the Parthians not to practice polygamy, or the women in Mesopotamia not to be chaste, or the Geli <note>A tribe from the shores of the Caspian Sea</note> not to exercise with naked bodies, or the Romans not to rule, or the Gauls not to be married [to men]. Nor does it force the other barbarian nations to participate in the "muses" <note>likely meaning the cultural laws or arts</note> established by their ancestors. 

As I have said, this shows that each nation and each man uses his own freedom as he wishes and when he wishes, and is only a slave to birth <note>astrological fate</note> and nature in those things where works are found sometimes as he wishes and sometimes as he does not wish. For everywhere and in every nation there are rich and poor, rulers and subjects, and the healthy and the sick—each according to the conditions of his birth.

<summary>Bardaisan refutes astrological fatalism by listing the wildly different laws and customs of various nations (Gauls, Indians, Medes, etc.), arguing that if the stars controlled behavior, people in the same region would not have such distinct moral codes. He concludes that while physical circumstances (like wealth or health) might be fated, human conduct is governed by free will and local law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Bardaisan, the 2nd-century philosopher, as quoted by Eusebius. Having previously listed the diverse sexual and social customs of various nations, he now addresses the counter-argument that these customs are dictated by astrological "climates" or geographic zones rather than human choice.</meta>

### EUSEBIUS
->of the teacher<-

...to the lots. "These things, O Bardaisan, have strongly persuaded us," I said to him. But the astronomers say that this earth is divided into seven zones <note>original: "κλίματα" (klimata) — geographic latitudes that were believed to be ruled by specific planets</note>; and that at the head of each zone is one of the seven stars <note>the seven classical planets: Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>. They claim that the various laws were not established by men for themselves, but rather that the will [of the ruling star] prevails in its own region over time. This law is what those who are ruled there have come to accept. 

But the "True One" <note>likely referring to Bardaisan himself as the speaker of truth in this dialogue</note> replied with this answer: "O Philip. For even if the inhabited world is divided into seven parts, nevertheless in one single part we find many differences of laws. For there are not only seven laws according to the seven stars, nor twelve according to the signs of the zodiac, nor thirty-six according to the decans <note>sub-divisions of the zodiac signs into ten-degree segments</note>, but there are ten thousand. 

You ought to remember what I stated before: that even in one zone and in one country—the land of the Indians—there are cannibal Indians, and there are those who abstain from eating living creatures. And remember that the Magians <note>original: "μαγουσταῖοι" (magoustaioi) — Zoroastrian priests of Persia</note> do not only marry their daughters among themselves, but they do so in every nation where they might dwell, keeping the laws of their ancestors and the rites of their own mysteries. 

But we have also observed many barbarian nations—those in the south and west, and east and north, that is, in different zones—who do not participate in the Hermetic science <note>astrology and alchemy attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note>. How many wise men, do you think, have abolished laws that were badly laid down? How many laws have been dissolved by necessity? How many kings, having conquered nations, abolished the local laws and established their own? And yet none of the stars lost its own zone. Just yesterday, when the Romans conquered Arabia, they changed the laws of the barbarians. It follows, then, that it is not our astrological fate that rules us, but our free will. 

We will set forth for you something that can persuade even the unbelieving. All the Jews who received the law through Moses circumcise their newborn male children with blood on the eighth day—not because they are following the command of a star, nor because they are avoiding the power of a zone, nor because they are being led by the local law of a country. But whether they happen to be in Syria, or in Gaul, or in Italy, or in Greece, or in Parthia, or wherever they may be, they do this. This is not according to <unclear>nativity</unclear> <note>original: "γένεσιν" (genesin) — the astrological configuration at the moment of birth</note>; for if it were, all Jews could not have the same nativity. 

Furthermore, every seven days, wherever they are, they rest from all work; they neither travel nor use fire. Even when the 'nativity' <note>fate</note> might compel a Jew either to build a house or to tear one down, he will not work; he will not sell or buy on the day of the Sabbath. Yet on that same day, Jews are being born and giving birth, falling ill, and dying. For these things <note>birth, illness, and death</note> do not belong to the realm of free will. 

In Syria and in Osroene <note>A kingdom in Mesopotamia</note>, many men used to castrate themselves in honor of Rhea <note>a mother-goddess often associated with Cybele whose priests practiced self-castration</note>; but in a single moment, King Abgar <note>Abgar IX of Edessa, a contemporary of Bardaisan</note> commanded that whoever was castrated should also have his hands cut off. From that time on, no one castrated himself in Osroene. 

And what shall we say about the sect <note>original: "αἱρέσεως" (haireseos) — a school of thought or group</note> of the Christians? We, the believers, being many in number, have arisen in various zones, in every nation and climate. Though we are many, we are called by one name. The Christians in Parthia do not practice polygamy, even though they are among the Parthians. Nor do those in Media throw their dead to the dogs. Nor do those in Persia marry their daughters, even though they are Persians. Among the Bactrians and others, they are not corrupted by illicit marriages. Those in Egypt do not worship Apis <note>the sacred bull</note>, or the dog, or the goat, or the cat. But wherever they are, they are not conquered by badly laid laws and customs. The nativity <note>astrological fate</note> decreed by the stars does not compel them to those forbidden evils, which are prohibited by...

<summary>Bardaisan argues that human behavior is governed by free will and cultural law rather than astrology, citing the consistent practices of Jews and Christians regardless of their geographic location or "astrological climate." He highlights King Abgar's ban on self-castration as proof that human laws can override supposed celestial influences.</summary>

<header>GOSPEL PREPARATION Book 6</header>

> ...to use [the laws of] their teacher. But they are subject to disease, poverty, passions, and what are regarded as misfortunes. For just as a free man among us is not forced to be a slave even if he is unfortunate, but withstands necessities; likewise, a man who appears to be a slave among us could not easily escape his subjection. For if [Fate] gave everything <note>The Greek here is somewhat elliptical; the speaker is arguing that if Fate controlled every aspect of life, humans would be mere tools</note>, we would be the instruments of others, and not our own. But when God has devised a plan, all things are possible and unhindered, for nothing can resist His will. Even the things that seem to grieve Him—since He is good and allows each nature to have its own character and **free will** <term>original: "αὐτεξούσιον" (autexousion) — the power of self-determination or "that which is in our own power"</term>—He permits, rather than His will being truly grieved.

Such things said the Syrian <note>Bardaisan of Edessa, a 2nd-century Christian philosopher often cited for his views on free will</note>. Since no one has yet recorded this discourse [in this context], I will set it down. For although the evidence from external <note>i.e., non-Christian or "secular" Greek and Syrian</note> writings has been sufficiently presented, there remains the evidence from the **Sacred Scriptures**. These are what we especially need, O friends, to provide a demonstration of the truth. What then will be the result of these things if they are considered on equal terms, so that the argument lacks nothing regarding the problem at hand? Therefore, I shall make these things clear to you. It would be no less valuable to bring forward the many things from the **Sacred Oracles** <note>The Bible</note> that have been passed over in silence. Accept, then, the interpretation I shall provide. If you are not put to the test by better men because of this man <note>referring to Origen</note>, you would still be bound to serve Christ through the labors he underwent, not being diminished by those who act out of ignorance, through which he has shown his love for learning regarding these teachings. Consider then how much and what kind of things the wonderful **Origen** has discussed in his commentaries on Genesis concerning the proposed hypothesis, and how he approached the discourse concerning **Fate**.

---

->How the doctrine concerning **Fate** is refuted from the explanation<-
->and testimony of the **Divine Scriptures**. From the works of **Origen**.<-

> Concerning the fact that the **luminaries** <note>The sun, moon, and stars</note> were made "for signs" <note>A reference to Genesis 1:14: "Let them be for signs and seasons..."</note>, it is not only a matter for the Sun, the Moon, and the stars. It is extremely necessary to take this up, not only because of the pagans who have fallen away from the faith of Christ and gone astray into the topic of Fate by their reckoning of the so-called **wandering stars** <note>The planets</note>—thinking that everything on earth happens to each man (and perhaps even to irrational animals) according to the planets' relationship to the signs of the **Zodiac**. Indeed, many who are considered believers are falling into the idea that human affairs are governed by necessity, and that it is impossible for things to happen otherwise than as the stars "decree" through their various configurations. It follows for those who dogmatize these things that they utterly destroy **"that which is in our power"** <note>original: "τὸ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν" (to eph' hemin) — a technical term in Greek philosophy for human agency or free will</note>. Because of this, praise and blame, and deeds worthy of acceptance or rejection, are done away with. For if this were the case, the proclaimed **Judgment of God** vanishes, as do the threats against sinners that they shall be punished, and the honors and blessedness for those who have given themselves over to better things. For if nothing happens reasonably, and if one looks at the logical consequences of what he dogmatizes, then faith will be in vain. The advent of **Christ** would achieve nothing, nor would the whole **economy** <term>original: "οἰκονομία" (oikonomia) — God's plan or management of human salvation</term> through the Law and the Prophets, nor the labors of the Apostles for the establishment of the Church of God through Christ. Unless, of course, Christ Himself were subject to such things, falling under the necessity of the stars...

<summary>Eusebius concludes the arguments of Bardaisan and introduces a lengthy excerpt from Origen's commentary on Genesis. Origen argues that if astrology and Fate were true, it would negate human free will, the justice of God's judgment, and the entire purpose of Christ's mission.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the excerpt from Origen’s commentary on Genesis, preserved by Eusebius. Having previously discussed how human laws vary by region—proving that the stars do not dictate human behavior—the text now turns to a moral and theological critique of astrology. Origen argues that if the stars caused human actions, it would make God the author of evil and render prayer useless.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS
## GOSPEL PREPARATION Book 6

<page-num>166</page-num>

» [of their] movement, to have taken their position by agreement, having done and suffered all things, not because of God and Father—who bestowed these wondrous powers upon Him—but because of the stars. Certain godless men follow these impious arguments, even those who say that believers are led by the stars while also claiming to believe in God. For how can we think that God Himself, if He so willed it, made such a world in which there are men who suffer the passions of women, having in no way become the causes of their own **wantonness** <note>original: "ἀσελγείας" (aselgeias) — referring here to sexual immorality or licentiousness attributed to celestial influence</note>? 

» And others, having taken on the state of wild animals, as if the rotation of the universe made them such; and because God so ordered the whole, they give themselves over to the most cruel and utterly inhuman deeds, such as murders and acts of piracy. And what need is there for us to speak of the things that happen among men—the myriad sins committed by them—for which those who promote these arguments regarding the stars acquit many of their crimes, and instead attribute the cause of all evils and shameful deeds to God? 

» But if some of them, as if defending God, say that the "Good One" is someone else <note>This refers to Gnostic or Marcionite dualism, which distinguished between a "Good God" of the New Testament and a "Justice-oriented" or "Evil" Creator of the Old Testament</note> who has no part in the beginning of these things, and they attach such matters to the **Creator** <term>original: "δημιουργῷ" (demiourgo) — the Demiurge, the figure who crafts the physical world</term> of all things, let us first see how they will be able to demonstrate that He is just, according to their own wishes. For how can the father of so many evils, according to them, be irrationally called "just"? 

» Second, we must examine what they will say about themselves. Do they themselves fall under the influence of the rotation of the stars, or are they not carried along by it? Even while existing in this life, do they have nothing acting upon them from that source? For if they say they are subject to the stars, it is clear that the stars will produce in them whatever they think. And the Creator will have subjected them, through the movement of the universe, to the argument concerning that far-off "fabricated god," as much as they might wish otherwise. 

» But if some should answer that they stand outside the laws of the Creator regarding the stars—so that their statement does not remain a mere unproven assertion—let them try to provide us with a more compelling distinction, defining one **origin** <note>original: "γένεσις" (genesis) — here meaning the birth-chart or astrological beginning</note> and **fate** <term>original: "εἱμαρμένη" (heimarmene) — the fixed destiny determined by the stars</term> that is subject to law, and another that is free from these. For it is clear that if such people were required to give an account, they would in no way be able to do so. 

» In addition to what has been said, **prayers** are included in vain and are superfluous. For if these things are necessitated by the days, and the stars bring them about, and nothing can happen except through their entanglement with one another, then we are irrationally asking God to grant us certain things. And why is there a need to lengthen the argument further, having demonstrated the impiety of this system of "Fate" which is so unthinkingly accepted by the masses? For the things already said are sufficient for a description. 

» But from what source do we investigate the phrase: **"Let the luminaries be for signs"** <note>A reference to Genesis 1:14. Origen is reinterpreting the "signs" not as causes of events, but as a language of God that can be read, like a book, without being the cause of the actions it describes</note>? Since we proclaim these things, let us remind ourselves: those who learn the truth about certain things, or who have been eyewitnesses to the facts, declare that such things exist. They have either beheld the suffering and the activity of those who suffered or acted, or they have heard from those reporting, who are in no way the cause of what happened; thus they come to know these things. 

» Let the argument now set aside the possibility that those who have done or suffered things, by narrating what they did or suffered, provide clear voices of what was done to someone who was not present. If, therefore, a person is taught by one who is in no way the cause of the events that such and such things have happened or will happen to these people, he should not conclude that the teacher is responsible...

For if they say they are subject to the stars, it is clear that the stars would be the ones performing this work in them. And the Creator <note>original: *demiurgos*</note> would have placed them under the motion of the whole universe—a theory concerning a "higher God" that is entirely fabricated, which is why they do not want to follow this logic. 

But if they respond by saying that the law governs the Creator's relationship to the stars—so that their claims do not appear unproven—let them try to bring us a more compelling distinction, defining the laws that are subject to nature and fate <term>heimarmene: the Greek concept of destiny or predetermined fate</term>, and those that are free from them. It is clear that when such people are asked to give an account, they will be unable to do so.

For if these things are necessitated for us, and the stars cause them, and nothing can happen except through their entanglement with one another, why do we irrationally ask that certain things be granted to us? And why should we lengthen the argument further, having already pointed out the impiety of this conviction regarding the common view of fate? What has been said is sufficient for a sketch of the matter. 

From what source, then, do we proclaim these things when we examine the statement "let the luminaries <note>original: *phosteres*. They see either the suffering or the activity of those who have been affected or who have acted; or they hear from those who were in no way the cause of what happened, and thus they come to know these things.

And from one of them came forth one strong horn, and it grew exceedingly great toward the south and the west. <note>Quoting Daniel 8:5-9, describing the rise of Alexander the Great and the subsequent division of his empire.</note>

What need is there to mention the prophecies concerning **Christ**? Such as his birthplace, **Bethlehem**, and the place of his upbringing, **Nazareth**, and his flight into **Egypt**, and the miracles he performed, and the manner in which he was betrayed by **Judas**, who had been called to the apostleship. For all these are signs of God’s foreknowledge. Even the Savior himself says:

> When you see **Jerusalem surrounded by armies**, then you will know that its desolation is near. <note>Quoting Luke 21:20.</note>

These things later happened at the final destruction <note>original: "κατασκαφῆς" — literally 'razing' or 'digging down'.</note> of Jerusalem. Since it has been demonstrated by us that God is the one who foreknows—not without purpose, but so that we might explain how the stars serve as "signs"—it must be understood that the stars are arranged in this way. Through the circular movement of the so-called **planets** <note>original: "πλανωμένων" — literally 'wanderers'.</note> relative to the **fixed stars** <note>original: "τοῖς ἀπλανέσιν" — stars that do not appear to move relative to each other.</note>, signs are produced by the configurations of all the stars around each individual. Those who "receive the whole" <note>likely referring to angelic powers or spiritual beings</note> know these signs, but humans do not. For the ability to truly grasp from the movement of the stars the facts about each person—what they will do or what they will suffer—is a power far greater than any human possesses. For there are powers that must know these many things, as we will show to the best of our ability in the following sections. Men, however, having grasped certain things through observation, or even from the teachings of **angels who transgressed their own order** <note>A reference to the "Fallen Angels" who, in ancient traditions (like the Book of Enoch), were said to have taught forbidden arts like astrology to humans.</note> and taught these things to the detriment of our race, claim that the stars from which they think they receive signs are the *causes* of these events. But the Word says...

<summary>Eusebius uses prophecies from Isaiah, Daniel, and the Gospels to demonstrate that God foreknows historical events without causing them. He then applies this to the stars, arguing they are "signs" of future events for higher powers, though humans mistakenly view them as causal agents in astrology.</summary>

# GOSPEL PREPARATION
## Book 6

<page-num>169</page-num>
<header>EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 6</header>
<sig>p. i.</sig>

Now we must immediately proceed to a concise treatment of the matters at hand. Let these problems be set forth first: how, if the actions to be performed by each person are foreknown from eternity—or even forever—can <term>what is up to us</term> <note>original: "τὸ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν" — a technical term in Greek philosophy referring to human agency or free will.</note> be preserved? Next, I stated that the stars are not the causes of human affairs, but are only **indicators**. Furthermore, humans cannot have an accurate knowledge of these things; rather, these signs are set forth for powers greater than human ones. Fourthly, we shall examine the reason why God created these signs for the knowledge of these powers.

Regarding the general movement of the spheres, many who have lived have been led to believe that things are governed by fate, and that <term>what is up to us</term> is in no way preserved. They argue that if God has foreknown the things to come, it is better to accept a lengthy, even impious doctrine rather than God’s providence—as they call it—if such providence makes life unlivable by destroying our free will. For if free will is removed, neither is there any place for "the good," nor for praise or blame, nor for the acceptance of virtues, nor for the avoidance of vices.

They say: "If God knew from eternity that a certain man would act unjustly and commit specific crimes, and if God's knowledge is unfailing, then that man will certainly be unjust and commit those crimes. If such a person is foreknown, it is impossible for him not to act unjustly; he is compelled to do so, and it will be impossible for him to do anything other than what God knew." If it is impossible for him not to do these things, we should not say he is more unjust for doing them, nor should we blame those who act unjustly. From the case of the unjust man, they extend this to all other sins, and then, by contrast, to those things considered right actions. They claim it follows that either God does not foreknow the future, or <term>what is up to us</term> cannot be preserved.

To these people we must say: when God applied Himself to the beginning of the creation of the world—no other cause having yet existed—He traversed in His mind each of the things that would be. He saw that because "this" happened, "this" would follow; and if the soul pursues "this," then "that" follows. This is how it will be, with no possibility of it being otherwise. Having thus traversed through the end of all things, He knows what will be, though He is not at all the **cause** for the occurrence of each thing known.

For just as if someone sees a person who, through ignorance, is reckless, and because of that recklessness is mindlessly embarking on a **slippery path**, and realizes that the person will slip and fall—that observer is not the cause of the other's slip. In this way, we must understand that God has foreseen what kind of person each individual will be and perceives the causes why he will be such a person, and that he will commit these sins or achieve these right actions. And if one must say so, **foreknowledge is not the cause of what happens.** For God does not touch the person foreknown to sin at the moment he sins. 

Rather—and we shall say something paradoxical but true—the future event is the **cause** <note>original: "αἴτιον"</note> of the foreknowledge being what it is. For it is not because it is known that it happens; rather, it is because it was going to happen that it is known. But a distinction is needed here: if someone interprets "it will certainly be" in a way that suggests a **necessity** <note>original: "ἀνάγκην"</note> for the foreknown event to occur, we will not grant that. For we will not say that because it was foreknown that **Judas** would become a traitor, it was an absolute necessity for Judas to become a traitor. In the prophecies concerning Judas, there are reproaches and accusations recorded against him, demonstrating that he possessed <term>what is up to us</term>. Blame would not have been attached to him if he were a traitor by necessity and if it had not been possible for him to become like the rest of the apostles. 

See if these points are not made clear through the scriptural passages we shall cite, which read as follows: "Let there be none to extend mercy to him, nor any to have pity on his fatherless children, because he did not remember to show mercy, but persecuted the poor and needy man, and the brokenhearted, to put them to death..." <note>A quotation from Psalm 108:12, 16 (Septuagint numbering), traditionally applied to Judas Iscariot.</note>

<summary>This page addresses the conflict between divine foreknowledge and human free will, arguing that God's knowledge of the future is not the cause of human actions. Using the analogy of a spectator watching a reckless person on a slippery path, the text posits that things happen not because they are known, but are known because they will happen.</summary>

# EUSEBIUS
## Book 6

<page-num>170</page-num>
<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

...he loved cursing, and it came to him; he did not desire <term>blessing</term> <note>original: "εὐλογία" (eulogia) — literally "good words" or divine favor.</note>, and it shall be far from him. If, however, as the story will relate, what must surely happen according to what He signifies to him—stating that such things will be, while it was also possible for them to happen otherwise—we concede this to be true. For it is impossible for God to lie. Yet it is possible for things that are capable of both happening and not happening to be perceived as they are. 

Let us state this more clearly in this way: If it is possible for Judas to be an apostle just like Peter, it is possible for God to think concerning Judas that he will remain an apostle just like Peter. But if it was possible for Judas to become a traitor, it is possible for God to foreknow concerning him that he will be a traitor. If, therefore, Judas will be a traitor, God—in His foreknowledge of the two aforementioned possibilities—knowing truly which one will happen, will foreknow that Judas will become a traitor. 

However, the matter about which there is knowledge was still capable of happening otherwise. God’s knowledge would not say, "It is possible for this man to do this, but also the opposite," for while both are possible, He knows which one he *will* do. For God would not say, "It is not possible for this certain man to stumble," when He gives an oracle about someone; He does not grant a prophecy where the outcome is impossible. 

For the primary power to stumble is not inherently fixed in a man, but there is a power to act and a power of <term>licentiousness</term> <note>original: "ἀκολασίας" (akolasias) — a lack of self-control or moral discipline.</note>. When both powers exist, the one who does not pay attention to encouraging and educational words gives himself over to the worse path. But the one who seeks the truth and desires to live according to it gives himself to the better path. One person does not seek the final goal because he inclines more toward pleasure. Another examines these things, chosen by <term>common notions</term> <note>original: "κοινῶν ἐννοιῶν" (koinon ennoion) — a Stoic term for innate or universal moral principles.</note> and encouraging reason. Again, one chooses pleasure, not because he is unable to look it in the face, but because he does not struggle against it. Another despises it, seeing the ugliness that is often found within it.

That God’s foreknowledge does not impose <term>necessity</term> <note>original: "ἀνάγκην" (ananken) — the idea that things must happen and cannot be otherwise.</note> on the things He has perceived is clear from what has been said; and this is also stated in many places in the Scriptures, where God commands the prophets to preach <term>repentance</term> <note>original: "μετάνοιαν" (metanoian) — a change of mind or heart.</note>. He does this not because He is unsure of whether those who hear will turn back or remain in their sins. As He says in <term>Jeremiah</term>: "Perhaps they will hear and repent." 

God does not say "Perhaps they will hear" because He is ignorant of whether they will or not. Rather, He is showing, as it were, the equal balance of their powers through His words. He does this so that His foreknowledge, if announced beforehand, does not cause the listeners to despair by wrapping them in an appearance of necessity—as if turning back was not "up to them," and as if this very foreknowledge became the cause of their sins. 

Or again, for those who might have lived in virtue because they were ignorant of some foreknown good, but who could still have struggled and resisted wickedness—foreknowledge might become a cause of <term>sloth</term> <note>original: "ἐκλύσεως" (eklyseos) — a loosening, or a loss of moral vigor.</note> if they no longer stood in the struggle against sin, thinking that the predicted outcome would happen anyway. In this way, foreknowledge of a future good would actually become an obstacle. 

Therefore, God, wisely administering all things in the world, reasonably "blinded" us toward the future. For the knowledge of it would have caused us to relax our struggle against evil; it would have allowed us—thinking the outcome was already seized—to stop wrestling against sin and quickly become its subjects. It was better for someone to become good by fighting for what is noble...

<meta>catchword: ὃ τὴν (the one which...)</meta>

<summary>Eusebius argues that God's foreknowledge of an event (like Judas's betrayal) does not cause the event or remove human choice. He explains that God uses conditional language like "perhaps" in Scripture to preserve human motivation and prevent the despair that comes from a belief in fatalism.</summary>

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL
## Book 6

<page-num>171</page-num>
<header>PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL. Book 6.</header>
<sig>p.ii.</sig>

...to have received foreknowledge regarding a specific person, that he will certainly be good. For in addition to what we already possess, we have need of intensity and greater exertion to become noble and good. But if the knowledge that we would certainly be noble and good were grasped in advance, it would loosen our <term>discipline</term> <note>original: "ἄσκησιν" (askēsin) — referring to the rigorous training or practice of virtue.</note>. For this reason, it is to our advantage that we do not know whether we will be good or whether we will be wicked. 

Since we have said that God has "blinded" us toward future things, and since a specific saying from Exodus is being sought, see if we can clarify it in this way: "Who made the mute and the deaf, and the seeing and the blind? Was it not I, the Lord God?" <note>Exodus 4:11.</note> This was so that He might make the same person both blind and seeing: seeing toward present things, but blind toward the future. For the reason why there was a need for the "hard of hearing" and the "deaf" will not be recounted at the present time. 

However, we will also admit that many of the things <term>within our power</term> <note>original: "ἐφ’ ἡμῖν" (eph’ hēmin) — a technical Stoic and Christian term for free will or moral agency.</note> are caused by things *not* within our power. If these things—I mean those not within our power—did not occur, then certain things within our power would not be enacted. But once certain things within our power are performed in accordance with these foreknown events, it is not possible for us to do something other than what was foreknown based on those same circumstances. 

But if someone should say that what is "within our power" is entirely detached, so that we do not choose these things because of certain events that happen to us, [they ignore] that one is part of the world, and entangled in human society and with those who gather together. Thus, I believe it has been moderately demonstrated, as in a summary, that God's foreknowledge is not a compelling force over the things foreknown.

<margin>,,</margin> ...certainly. Come now, let us also contend against the idea that the stars are in any way the <term>causes</term> <note>original: "ποιητικοὺς" (poiētikous) — literally "makers" or "productive causes."</note> of human affairs, but are signs only. It is clear that if this specific <term>configuration</term> <note>original: "σχηματισμὸς" (schēmatismos) — the relative positions or "aspects" of the planets in an astrological chart.</note> of the stars were thought to be the cause of certain things moving around a person—let this be the question we investigate—today's configuration (let's say) for a person being born could not be conceived to have caused past events through another person, or about another. 

<margin>,,</margin> For the cause is much older than the effect. But as far as the theories of those who profess such things go, the configuration is said to be "older" than the humans [it affects]. For they profess to take the hour of a specific man and grasp how each of the <term>planets</term> <note>original: "πλανωμένων" (planōmenōn) — literally "the wanderers."</note> stands, whether in this degree of a zodiac sign or in its minutes, and what kind of star was "painting" the chart at the <term>ascendant</term> <note>original: "ἀνατολικὸν" (anatolikon) — the eastern horizon or rising sign.</note> as it appeared to the eye. 

<margin>,,</margin> They also look at which star is at the setting horizon, and which at the <term>midheaven</term> <note>original: "μεσουρανήματος" (mesouranēmatos) — the highest point of the sun's path.</note>, and which at the <term>anti-midheaven</term> <note>original: "ἀντιμεσουρανήματος" (antimesouranēmatos) — the lowest point, or Imum Coeli.</note>. And whenever they see the stars—which they believe they have charted for themselves—configured in such a way at the time of someone's birth, they examine not only future things but also past ones, and things regarding the birth or the conception of the person in question: 

<margin>,,</margin> what sort of father he happens to have—whether rich or poor; whether he is physically sound or maimed; whether his character is better or worse; whether he is propertyless or wealthy; whether he has much activity or rest. They claim the same things regarding the mother and older brothers, if they happen to exist. Let us for the moment allow that they grasp the truths of the situation. Regarding this very point, we shall show later that it is not so. Therefore, we ask those who suppose human affairs are compelled by the stars: in what way can today's configuration, being such as it is, [cause things]?

<summary>Eusebius argues that God's foreknowledge of the future does not force human actions, and that God intentionally keeps the future hidden to maintain moral effort. He then begins a logical critique of astrology, questioning how the positions of stars at a child's birth could possibly "cause" the pre-existing status of their parents.</summary>

"He loved a curse, and it shall come to him; and he did not desire a blessing, and it shall be far from him." <note>original: Psalm 108:17 (LXX) / 109:17 (KJV). This quote is used to show that consequences follow from human choices.</note> If someone explains that a thing will definitely happen according to what was signaled to him, saying "this specific thing will be," even though it was possible for it to happen otherwise, we allow this as a true concession. For it is not possible for God to lie. It is possible, however, for Him to think concerning things that *might* happen and *might not* happen, that they indeed might happen and might not happen. We shall express this more clearly in this way: If it is possible for Judas to be an apostle just like Peter, it is possible for God to think concerning Judas that he remains an apostle just like Peter. If it is possible for Judas to become a traitor, it is possible for God to think concerning him that he will be a traitor. 

But if Judas will be a traitor, God, by His <term>foreknowledge</term> <note>original: "προγνώσει" (prognōsei) — knowledge of events before they happen.</note> of the two aforementioned possibilities, knowing that which is true in advance, will foreknow that Judas will become a traitor. Yet the thing about which He has knowledge is still capable of happening otherwise. Even if the knowledge of God says that it is possible for a certain person to do this thing, it also knows the opposite is possible. For when both are possible, I know that he will do *this*. It is not as if God would say, "It is impossible for this particular man to drink"; rather, if He were giving an oracle about someone, He would say it is not impossible for this man to be <term>temperate</term> <note>original: "σωφρονῆσαι" (sōphronēsai) — to be of sound mind, self-controlled, or virtuous.</note>. 

For the power to be completely disobedient does not exist in man at all; rather, there is a power both to be temperate and to be self-indulgent. Since both powers exist, the one who does not pay attention to encouraging and educational words gives himself over to the worst path. But the better man is he who seeks the truth and lives according to it by his own will. One man does not seek the worse because pleasure "flows over" him more; rather, the other man examines these things, having been chosen by common sense and encouraging reason. Again, one man chooses pleasure, not because he is unable to look it in the eye, but because he does not struggle against it; whereas the other man despises it, seeing the uselessness that is often found within it.

Rather, He is showing, as it were, the equal balance of their powers through His words, so that His foreknowledge—by being grasped in advance—might not cause the listeners to fall into despair by presenting an appearance of necessity, as if it were not within their power to turn back, and as if this foreknowledge itself were the cause of the sin.

They might no longer stand firmly against sin, thinking that the predicted outcome will happen regardless. In this way, the foreknowledge of the coming good would become a hindrance. Therefore, God, who administers all things in the world for our benefit, has reasonably "blinded" us toward future events. For the knowledge of them would have relaxed us from the struggle against wickedness; it would have allowed us, thinking the outcome was already caught, to fall more quickly under the hand of sin rather than wrestling against it. Indeed, it would have been a battle against the "good" for a person to become good who...

### EUSEBIUS
<page-num>172</page-num>

...to have produced the things that came before. For if this is impossible—inasmuch as it is found that what is sought concerning things older in time makes it clear that no stars, however they are arranged in heaven, could have "made" the things that previously occurred and are now occurring, simply by being in such a state. But if perhaps the aforementioned point is what they should seek, by paying attention to what is said about those who speak of these matters, I would be ashamed for them; for some claim the stars do not "act" <note>original: "ποιεῖν" — to do, make, or cause.</note> but only "signify." But if someone were to claim that the stars do not cause past events, but that at one time certain divine communications were the causes of knowledge of those things, while the current communication has only signaled them—yet the things revealed are shown by the present communication of a particular person's birth—how could I not perceive the distinction? It would have to be shown from the stars that some things are produced by them as "causes," while other things are merely "signs." But since they are unable to provide this distinction, they must stubbornly concede that nothing concerning human affairs happens because of the stars, as we said before. If indeed anything is signified, it is as if one receives knowledge of the past and future not from the stars themselves, but from the Mind of God through some prophetic word. 

For just as we demonstrated before that it does nothing to harm the argument concerning what is <term>within our power</term> <note>original: "ἐφ' ἡμῖν" (eph' hēmin) — human agency or free will.</note> for God to know the things pre-allotted to each person, so too the signs which God appointed for signifying do not hinder what is within our power. Rather, just as a book contains future events in a prophetic manner, the whole heaven—being, as it were, a Book of God—is able to contain the future. This is why in the *Prayer of Joseph* <note>An ancient Jewish apocryphal text, now mostly lost, which Origen frequently cites to explain how the cosmos functions as a repository of divine information.</note> what is said by Jacob can be understood in this way: "For I read in the tablets of heaven all that will happen to you and your sons." And perhaps the heaven will be "rolled up like a scroll," revealed by the words contained within it, which signify things to come as they are restored and, so to speak, fulfilled—just as prophecies are said to be "fulfilled" and to have come to pass. Thus the stars will have been created "for signs," according to the voice that says, "Let them be for signs." <note>A reference to Genesis 1:14.</note> But Jeremiah turns us away from this, [warning against] the lowly fear toward things thought to be signs. Perhaps he says we should not fear what is thought to come from there: "Do not be afraid of the signs of heaven." <note>Jeremiah 10:2.</note>

Let us also look at a second argument for how the stars cannot be "causes," even if they are "signs." Consider, from the vast number of births, that someone takes a reading for a single man. We say this by way of hypothesis, granting for the sake of argument that such knowledge can be grasped by humans. Suppose it is said of this man that he will suffer such-and-such and will die by falling among robbers or being murdered; this could be grasped from his own birth chart, but also (if he happens to have many brothers) from the chart of each of them. For each person’s birth chart would contain the fact that a brother will die by robbers. Likewise, it would be found in the chart of his father and mother, and that of his wife, and his sons, and his household servants, and his dearest friends. Perhaps even in the charts of the murderers themselves. How then is it possible for a single event, contained within so many different birth charts, to be "caused" by the communication of the stars in this man's birth rather than in that one's? It is improbable to claim that the communication in a particular person’s birth "caused" these things, while in another’s birth it did not "cause" them but only "signified" them. For it is better to say that the knowledge of all things has encompassed every person in a complex way...
