argument has been condensed into two greatest points: either that those 
considered gods by various cities are not gods, or that they are not even 
good spirits. For it happens that they are some kind of impoverished sorcerers, 
vagabonds, and deceivers, existing for the destruction and perversion of true 
piety; or [they lead] humans into some crooked opinion. And so, having first 
put forward what has been said—from which no one throughout the ages, except 
Jesus our Savior, has separated the grace of our Father from humans—it 
is reasonable that at the beginning of this *Preparation for the Gospel*, we 
have treated all these present matters with diligence. This is so that we might 
learn by deed from what ancestors we have sprung, and by what sort of 
deception we were previously held, and how great a [Savior] has 
restored us—both ourselves and the whole life of humanity—from blindness 
and godlessness. We have received the healing from that long and ancient 
demonic activity through the teaching of the Saving Gospel alone.

->Concerning the life of the ancient Hebrews, and why we reasonably preferred their divine scriptures over our ancestral traditions.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter "Ε" featuring floral and leafy scrollwork inside a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

**I**t is now time to describe the way of life of the Hebrews—their philosophy and their piety—whose scriptures we have preferred above all our ancestral traditions. Since we have stood firm in making our departure from the deceptive theology of all nations and barbarians <note>original: "βαρβάρων" — In this context, "barbarian" is a technical term for any non-Greek culture, such as the Egyptians, Phoenicians, or Hebrews, and is not necessarily a slur.</note> alike—not without reason, but with a judged and sober logic—it is time to resolve the second point by providing the reason for our adoption of the Hebrew teachings. 

Lest anyone bring a charge against us for taking what is beneficial from "barbarians," we shall demonstrate at the proper time that all the philosophical teachings—and even other common knowledge useful for political needs—were plundered from barbarians by the Greeks, and even by their own most famous philosophers. But that which has never yet been found among any of the nations—namely, the spiritual good provided to us by the Hebrews—will be made clear as follows.

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument from the beginning of Book 7. Having established the "Hebrew" way of life as the ideal, he now critiques the alternative: the various forms of Greek and "barbarian" polytheism, which he argues are all rooted in the pursuit of physical pleasure rather than spiritual truth.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

In the time that followed, relying solely on physical sensation, as if they had perceived no benefit of the soul within themselves, and having assumed nothing more exists among beings than what is seen, they took the beautiful, the profitable, and the only good to be the immeasurable pleasure <note>original: "ἡδονήν" (hedone) — In Greek philosophy, especially Epicureanism, *hedone* was a central topic of debate regarding the "highest good."</note> of the impulses. This alone they proposed as the most desirable thing—being the only good, agreeable, and sweet—and sufficient for the enjoyment of a happy life; they considered and established it as the greatest of the gods. They did not even desire life itself unless it shared in the pleasure of bodies, embracing not merely "to live," but "to live pleasantly" as the only life worth living. This they even prayed for their own children to possess as the only good. 

From this, some—judging the sun, moon, and stars to be the providers of life in the flesh, and being struck by the sight of the light—proclaimed them gods, declaring them to be the sole causes of the universe. Others honored with the title of gods the fruits of the earth, the wet, dry, and hot substances <note>The four traditional elements: water, earth, fire, and air.</note>, and the remaining parts of the world, through which their bodies were nourished and fattened, charming their life in the flesh and their pleasure at once. Others, much worse than these, with "naked and uncovered head" <note>An idiom meaning "shamelessly" or "openly."</note> deified their own passions and their mistress, Pleasure—calling them Love (Eros), Longing (Pothos), and Aphrodite—and even claimed they ruled over the gods themselves. 

Others deified certain tyrants and rulers who had been the providers and inventors of pleasures for them, because of the enjoyments they happened to receive from them, both while they were still living and after their death. Others, becoming the playthings of wretched spirits and demons, introduced an even greater and more passionate cause for the soul's condition, providing pleasures and the things obtained through them because of their customary worship of these spirits. Still others, touching upon none of these, introduced atheism as something much better than such a "theology." Finally, others, led away by all these things, declared that the philosophical and thrice-blessed life was nothing else but the pleasant life, defining pleasure as the "end of goods" <note>original: "τέλος ἀγαθῶν" — A technical philosophical term for the ultimate goal of human life.</note>. 

In this way, therefore, from the first humans onward, being enslaved to Pleasure as a god—or rather as a bitter, most harsh mistress and a shameful, licentious demon—they were entangled in the misery of myth-making.

> For their females, according to the Holy Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul in Romans 1:26–27.</note>, exchanged natural relations for those that are contrary to nature. Likewise, the males, giving up natural relations with females, were consumed with passion for one another, males committing shameless acts with males and receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error.

Rooted in this, both barbarians and Greeks, the wise and the unlearned alike, falling to the ground on their bellies, worshipped Pleasure as a god. Casting themselves down like reptiles, they considered and cherished this goddess as invincible and inexorable. In songs and hymns, in the festivals of the gods, and in the public spectacles of the crowds, they were initiated into and performed the secret rites of shameful and licentious pleasure. As someone might say—and this is well-fitted to our argument—"the invention of idols was the beginning of fornication" <note>A quote from the Wisdom of Solomon 14:12.</note>. And the theology of the nations' common people reached such a point that, to speak briefly, it was a multi-branched flame kindled from one beginning—that of impure and defiled pleasure—like a many-necked and many-headed hydra, branching out into many various divisions and segments. In this way, they happened to put forward such great...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s critique of pagan lifestyles, transitioning from a description of the moral decay found in ancient polytheistic cultures to the contrasting intellectual and spiritual foundations of the Hebrew tradition.</meta>

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION BOOK 7

...wealth, as is likely for those who treat pleasure as a god and an evil demon, leading to their own continuous lusts for women, and the corruption of males, and both mixed marriages and incest with daughters. They fled from a life of many troubles, yet they were overcome by an excess of wickedness in their wild and beastly nature. Such was the manner of the ancient nations and their false theology, as has been demonstrated in what preceded this through the silent testimony <note>original: "σιωπηλῶν" (siopelon) — Eusebius suggests that even when Greek writers are "silent" or not intentionally supporting his cause, their own histories and philosophies prove his point about the corruption of paganism.</note> of Greek chroniclers and philosophers.

### Comparison of the Hebrew way of life and how they thought about the Maker and Creator of all.

If then the life of the ancients stands thus, consider now in your mind the children of the Hebrews alone among these, moving in the opposite direction. For these were the first and only ones among all people who, right from the first foundation of life, raised their minds with rational contemplation and piously applied themselves to the study of nature <note>original: "φυσιολογίᾳ" (physiologia) — Here meaning the philosophical study of the natural world and its origins.</note> regarding all things. First, they understood that the elements of bodies—earth, water, air, and fire, from which this universe is composed—and the sun, moon, and stars, were not gods, but works of God being administered. They concluded that the nature of bodily substance is not only irrational but also soulless, insofar as it is fluid and corruptible. 

Furthermore, they reasoned that it is impossible for the arrangement of the whole world—so wisely harmonized and full of living beings, both rational and irrational—to be attributed to a soulless cause. Nor should one suppose the creative principle of living things to be soulless, nor that the creator of rational beings is himself irrational. For a building would never be composed of wood and stones by itself, nor could a cloak be completed without a weaver, nor a city’s government exist without laws and the arrangement of a ruler. Nor could a ship exist without a pilot, nor the smallest tool of art come into being except through a craftsman. Nor, again, could a ship ever reach a harbor's mooring if not for a good pilot. 

In the same way, the nature of the universal elements—being always soulless and irrational in itself—could never participate in reason and life without the supreme wisdom of God. Having considered these and similar things, the fathers of the Hebrew piety, reasoning from the magnitude and beauty of created things and using the clear-sighted eyes of the soul, sought out the God who is the Creator of all.

### How they thought about the immortality of the soul, and about the substance of bodies.

And then, perceiving themselves to be no small part of the whole, they considered what was most precious within them. This they found to be the "true man," understood to be the soul; while that which holds the place of an outer covering, they understood to be the body. And indeed, having distinguished them in this way, they devoted all their care and diligence toward the life of the inner man. For they reasoned that this inner self is dear to the God who is the Creator of all, who granted that the nature of humans should rule over all things on earth—not by strength of body, but by the virtue of the soul. For some things are soulless, such as stones and wood; others participate in a life-giving power, such as plants from the earth; and others are allotted sensation and the impulse of imagination, such as irrational animals.

<summary>Eusebius contrasts the "beastly" and pleasure-seeking lifestyle of pagan nations with the rational, monotheistic philosophy of the Hebrews, who recognized God as the Creator through the logical design of the universe. He argues that the Hebrews prioritized the "inner man" (the soul) over the physical body, viewing the soul as the seat of human dominion over nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument in Book 7 of the *Evangelical Preparation*. Having previously dismissed the myths of the Phoenicians and Egyptians as irrational, he now describes the intellectual and spiritual superiority of the ancient Hebrews, specifically their focus on the soul and their direct relationship with the Divine.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

...and all these things serve the human race alone for its use, constrained not by bodily force or strength, but by reason and the virtue of the soul, which they understood had been granted from above by the Cause of all things as a ruling and royal privilege among those on earth. Starting from this point, they decided not to value the body or bodily pleasures any more than the other creatures on earth. But whatever in them was ruling—as it was akin to the Ruler of all—namely the rational and intellectual part of the soul, both divine and capable of knowledge—as it bore the likeness of the God over all—this alone they held in high esteem. 

Then, thinking no other thing to be a "good" but God, the provider of all good things, they declared that the goal of all happiness was the knowledge and friendship of Him. Because He alone was the cause for them of life itself, and of soul and body, and of external necessities. Thus they dedicated themselves entirely, body and soul, hanging their whole life upon Him, attending to Him alone, and deigning to care for nothing else among visible things. Thus appearing both lovers of God and beloved by God, they were revealed as certain servants and priests of the Most High God, or even a sacred and royal race, and were deemed worthy to be called a "priesthood of God" and a "holy nation" <note>original: "ἔθνος ἅγιον" (ethnos hagion) — A reference to Exodus 19:6, describing a people set apart for divine service.</note>, leaving a seed proclaimed to those of the same piety and their descendants. Should we then, by such sober reasoning, prefer our own heritage, and rather than the Phoenician and Egyptian gods and the shameful deception regarding those gods, accept the Hebrew accounts of pious men?

### How, as lovers of God, they were deemed worthy of recorded divine appearances and oracles.

As they say, the men described proceeded so far in God-beloved virtue that the Divine, accepting their piety and philosophy <note>original: "φιλοσοφίας" (philosophias) — Here Eusebius uses 'philosophy' to describe a way of life dedicated to truth and God, rather than just academic study.</note> in the rest of life, as well as their service to Him, now deemed them worthy of saving oracles and divine appearances <note>term: "theophanies" (θεοφανειῶν) — Visible manifestations of God or the divine to human beings.</note> and angelic visitations, correcting the deficiencies of mortal nature with instructions on what must be done, and revealing to them doctrines and teachings of the knowledge of things befitting God. So that their minds were no longer illuminated by syllogisms or conjectures, but by the flash of truth itself, so that already being God-inspired, they could contemplate and grasp future events as if they were present, and announce beforehand what would generally happen to the human race. Such are the celebrated and truly God-beloved words concerning Hebrew virtue, which we have preferred over our own ancestral myths and nonsense; for while some cultures told the most shameful things about gods, these provided pious teachings about men beloved by God.

### How they shone in piety before "Judaism" existed or before Moses was born.

These things were recognized long ago, before Moses and the Jewish nation arose, from a long age past among the forefathers of the Jews. Indeed, it is good to clarify this point: that "Judaism" <note>original: "ἰουδαϊσμός" (Ioudaismos) — Eusebius makes a historical distinction between the later religion of the Jews and the earlier "Hebrew" way of life.</note> did not yet exist then, but the people described were called Hebrews...

<summary>Eusebius argues that the ancient Hebrews reached the height of human happiness through the knowledge of God and intellectual virtue, receiving divine revelations long before the formal establishment of Judaism or the laws of Moses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument in Book 7 of the *Evangelical Preparation*. Having established that the ancient Hebrews focused on the rational soul and direct friendship with God, he now distinguishes them from the later "Jews" who were defined by the Mosaic Law, emphasizing that the Patriarchs lived by a "natural" and "free" piety before the Law was even written.</meta>

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 7

...alone, they were [Hebrews] both in name and in their way of life. But "Jews" did not yet exist, nor were they so called. You might understand the difference between Hebrews and Jews in this way: the name of the latter comes from Judah <note>original: "Ἰούδα" (Iouda)</note>, from whose tribe the kingdom of the Jews was established long ages later. The others, however, take their name from Eber <note>original: "Ἔβερ" (Eber) — In Genesis 10:24, Eber is an ancestor of Abraham; Eusebius uses this etymology to show the antiquity of the "Hebrew" identity compared to the later "Jewish" identity.</note>, who was the forefather of Abraham. Sacred history teaches us that the Hebrews existed before the Jews. 

As for their manner of piety, the Jews were bound by the entire legislation of Moses. This included the tradition of the Sabbath day and its very strict observance as a reminder to devote leisure to the sacred words. It also included the distinction between animals that may or may not be eaten, annual festivals, and certain bodily purifications—symbolic rites performed after a long period of time. 

But the Hebrews, who were older than Moses in time, and had heard nothing of the legislation given through Moses, achieved a free and untouched way of piety. They were adorned with a life lived according to nature, so that they had no need of those later laws because of the supreme detachment <note>original: "ἀπάθειαν" (apatheian) — A Stoic term meaning freedom from suffering or irrational passion, which Eusebius applies to the spiritual discipline of the patriarchs.</note> of their souls, having received the true knowledge of doctrines concerning God. Since these things have been stated in this manner, it is time to seek further evidence through the texts themselves.

### How Moses himself, being a Hebrew, recorded the lives of his own people in writing according to their ages.

Therefore, the great theologian <note>original: "θεολόγος" (theologos) — Here meaning a divinely inspired author or one who speaks of divine things.</note> Moses, being a Hebrew born of Hebrews—if anyone else ever did—understood his ancestral traditions. In the introductions to his sacred laws, he handed down the lives of the Hebrew forefathers in indelible memory, recording the good things they were deemed worthy of by God. 

Conversely, he recorded what sort of godless and impious people existed, along with their deeds and punishments. He considered it a necessary lesson for those who were to be instructed in his laws, both to avoid imitating the wicked and to be encouraged toward the life of the pious. Indeed, one must not be ignorant of the fact that even before his written laws, many of the forefathers were already adorned with the virtue of godliness through right reasoning. Having been called "friends of God" and "prophets," they obtained eternal memory with Him. 

The account of these men should not miss its mark with those for whom the laws were ordained. For this reason, it was all the more necessary for their descendants—born of men so beloved by God and so righteous—to be revealed as zealous imitators of their forefathers' piety, and to strive to obtain the same rewards from God as their ancestors did. They should not grow weary or shrink back, despairing of the hope of good things as if they were impossible. For these things were entirely possible and successfully achieved by their own forefathers. Moses handed down these examples to those being educated in divine matters, recounting their lives in ancient times and sketching the unique virtue of each individual, as if portraying them in a painted image.

### How with reasonable judgment and sober reasoning we accepted the history concerning these matters. And a survey of the men beloved of God before the flood and up to Moses.

Nothing prevents us from running through this history briefly. Regarding the flood, as the writing of Moses itself contains, it is necessary somewhere...

# EUSEBIUS

As I see it, one should examine the ancestral traditions of the Hebrews from no other source than from within their own house. Just as we learn of Egyptian matters from the Egyptians, and those of the Phoenicians from their own people, and again those of the Greeks from their own illustrious men—and the doctrines of philosophers from the philosophers, rather than from those ignorant of philosophy—for how else would it be proper to learn of medical matters than from those who possess the science? In this same way, I consider it followable and necessary to accept the matters of the Hebrews from the oracles <note>original: "λογίων" (logion) — sacred utterances or scriptures</note> found among the Hebrews, and not from any other source.

Now, as the account held among them goes, from the beginning before the flood—from the very first generation of mankind and into the subsequent successions—there have been certain men beloved by God, and many who were righteous. One of these "hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God." <note>This is a reference to Genesis 4:26. In the Septuagint version Eusebius used, the text says Enosh "hoped" to call on God, whereas modern translations often say he "began" to call on Him.</note> This signifies that he acknowledged no one as the master and God of all things except the Creator of the universe. He was convinced that the entire world was established not only by a creative power, but also that God governs, manages, and acts as the head of the household, just like a ruler of a great city or the whole world, being simultaneously Lord, King, and God. This man, beloved by God, did not direct the concept and title of "Lord" and "God" toward different types of beings <note>original: "ἑτερογενῆ" (heterogene) — i.e., he did not fall into polytheism by worshiping various gods.</note>, but setting aside every other existence and title, or rather instead of every other good, he hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God. He made this name for himself a treasure of blessings for both soul and body. Because of this, he is recorded among the Hebrews as the first to be called a "true man." 

<margin><image-desc>A small circle is drawn in ink in the right margin.</image-desc></margin>

He was called **Enosh** <note>original: "Ἐνὼς" (Enos)</note>, which signifies a "true man," a name chosen with great accuracy. For they say that it is not fitting to consider or name someone a "man" unless they have attained a degree of knowledge and piety—one who is both mortally wise <note>original: "γνωστικὸν" (gnostikon) — possessing spiritual knowledge</note> and pious. Those who are raised in folly are no different from irrational cattle; they are cast down prone beneath the belly and pleasure. The Hebrew Scripture teaches us to call such beings something other than "men," for it is accustomed to using titles in their literal sense. Among such people, it sometimes calls them "wolves" and "dogs," and at other times "swine" who delight in and use filth. And again, it is accustomed to call those who resemble the various forms of wickedness "creeping things" and "serpents." 

Even when the Scripture refers to the common and general "man" <note>original: "ἄνθρωπον" (anthropon)</note>—the term we must use for ourselves—it uses a proper and fitting title: it signifies the first man by the name **Adam** <note>original: "ἀδάμης" (adames)</note>. Among the Hebrews, this is the title for all humanity, a proper and fitting name which, when translated into the Greek tongue, indicates one who is "earthly" <note>original: "γηϊνὸν" (geinon)</note>. 

However, **Enosh** is recorded as the first of the God-beloved among the Hebrews, since he was the first who "hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God." He was the one who truly educated the rational part of the soul to be knowledgeable, and scientific in matters of piety toward the Divine. Of these two things, the first would be a demonstration of true knowledge of God, and the second a demonstration of hope in the God who has been recognized. For to not treat the knowledge of God as something unheard of or secondary, but always and through all things to "hope to call upon the name of the Lord God"—sometimes as servants to a Master, and sometimes as to a merciful and good Father—this would be the perfect and blessed end of all things. 

Such a person, then, is introduced among the Hebrews as the first and "true man"—not the one nicknamed "earthly" (**Adam**), who through the transgression of God's commandment fell away from the lot of better things, but the first of the God-beloved, who "hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God." Judging for ourselves with a sober mind, we too have sought to emulate such a man...

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION BOOK 7

### PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK VII

->TEXT<-

We have cherished and accepted as a profitable and most clear account for us this narrative of the Word—not according to a myth equal to the image already revealed—which calls upon the name of the Creator and Master of all things with firm and good hope. But also after the one previously mentioned <note>Enosh, mentioned on the previous page</note>, another man—Enoch—was well-pleasing to the Lord. And "he was not found," as Moses says, "because God translated him" <note>original: "μετέθηκεν" (metetheken) — to transfer or transport. In Genesis 5:24, this refers to Enoch being taken to heaven without dying.</note> on account of his extreme perfection in virtue. For the wise man is indeed hard for mortals to find, since for his own sake his end is in God, having been removed from the distractions of the many. 

For those who are not like him are swallowed up in the depth of vice in the midst of marketplaces and law courts, shops and centers of trade, where they pursue the great crowd, being pushed and pushing others. But the man who has been taken up by God, and who has "translated" his departure from here <note>transformed his way of leaving this life</note>, remains invisible and unfindable by men, but having become a friend to God, he is found by God. The Hebrews name this man Enoch, which signifies "Friend" <note>The name Enoch (Chanokh) is often interpreted in this tradition as "dedicated" or "initiated." Eusebius notes it signifies "Grace of God" or "Friendship."</note>. Therefore, we consider it a blessed thing to emulate the life of this man as a beautiful image.

After these, there was yet another man who was righteous by nature, Noah, who was testified to in his generation. The proofs of his righteousness are as follows: once, a drought and destruction of deadly vice overtook the whole race of mankind. The "Giants," who are talked about by everyone, were committing god-fighting acts of buffoonery against God through their godless and impious crimes. Indeed, they are said to have been the causes of this unrestrained behavior—whether because they possessed some superior lot or surpassed the nature of mortals, or however else they were pleased to be called—and having initiated the many-creeping teachings among men, they are said to have handed down to this life the inventions of sorcery <note>original: "γοητείας" (goēteias) — witchcraft or jugglery</note> and other ill-reputed magic. 

Consequently, the entire human race came under a single sentence of judgment before God. And while all were about to be destroyed by a single deluge <note>original: "κλύσματι" (klysmati) — a washing or flood</note>, Noah alone is shown to us as having been found righteous in his generation along with his household. While everyone else on earth was being utterly destroyed by the flood, and the earth itself was being cleansed of its former evils by a sudden surge of waters, this God-beloved man, together with his sons and wives, was preserved by God to be kept as a "living spark" <note>original: "ζώπυρον σπέρμα" (zōpyron sperma) — a spark of seed or life-germ</note> for the life that would come after. In him, a living and ensouled image of the archetype was preserved as a model of a God-beloved man for those born from him.

Such were those around the time of the flood. But after the flood, there were again friends of God who were distinguished for their piety, whose memory the sacred oracles preserve. One of these is recorded as a priest of the Most High God, having been designated a "Righteous King" <note>This refers to Melchizedek, whose name in Hebrew (Melchi-zedek) literally translates to "King of Righteousness."</note> in the Hebrew language. For all these men, there was no mention of a law of circumcision, nor of the Jewish commands given through Moses. 

Therefore, it is not just to call them "Jews," nor indeed "Greeks," because they did not acknowledge many gods as the Greeks or other nations did. They should more properly be called Hebrews, either after Eber <note>an ancestor of Abraham</note> or rather according to the etymological meaning of the name. For they are interpreted as "Passers-over" <note>original: "περατικοὶ" (peratikoi). Eusebius connects the name 'Hebrew' to the root 'avar,' meaning to cross over.</note>, as those who set out to cross over from the things of this world to the contemplation of the God of the universe. For having completed the straight path of virtue through natural reasoning and unwritten laws, they are recorded as having "crossed over" beyond the pleasures of the flesh to a life that is all-wise and God-fearing. 

Among all these men, let Abraham also be counted—the patriarch of the entire nation—to whose righteousness the oracles bear witness, which was not based on the law of Moses, for that did not yet exist. Certainly, after Abraham...

### PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK VII

->TEXT<-

In the seventh generation Moses appeared; however, he too is said to have been a righteous and godly man, even if he appeared later, in a manner similar to those already described. At any rate, 
<margin>»</margin> the Scripture says, *And Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness* <note>original: "ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην" — a central verse from Genesis 15:6, cited here to show that Abraham was justified by faith before the Law was given.</note>. 
The divine oracle proclaims that this man would be the father of many nations, and it was said that in him all the nations of the earth and all the tribes would be blessed. This explicitly prophesies the things now being fulfilled among us <note>Eusebius sees the spread of Christianity to all nations as the fulfillment of this promise to Abraham.</note>. But when that famous Abraham—after his perfection in righteousness, which was achieved not through the Law of Moses but through faith—was about to father a legitimate child in his old age after the prescribed sacrifices, he performed a certain secret oracle, which is to circumcise the body. He passed this on to be performed by his descendants, either as a visible sign of the great multitude of his children, or so that his children might have a paternal mark of recognition, whether they lived according to the zeal of their ancestors or fell short of their virtue. Or it may have been for any other reason, which we do not have time to investigate now. 

Such a man was he, following the example of those before him. After him, Isaac is again shown as the successor of his father’s knowledge of God and his love for God, having inherited from his father this most beautiful and thrice-blessed heritage. The divine oracles say that he lived with only one wife and practiced the procreation of children only once <note>referring to the birth of his twin sons, Esau and Jacob</note>. Having been shown to be the father of twin offspring, he limited his intimacy with his wife due to an excess of self-control. 

From him, Jacob—who is also called Israel—was introduced. He was a man with two names, shining through his own virtues. When he was being trained in practical ethics and testing the labors of a godly life, his name was Jacob—a name which, when translated into the Greek language, means <term>Practitioner</term> <note>original: "ἀσκητὴν" (asketen) — Jacob's name was traditionally interpreted by Greek-speaking Jews like Philo as the "one who exercises" or "struggles" toward virtue.</note> or <term>Athlete</term>. But later, when he received the crown of victory over his opponents and already enjoyed the rewards of contemplation, then the God who gives oracles changed his name, granting him at once a divine dignity and a more heavenly prize by the gift of this new name. 
<margin>»</margin> For the oracle says to him: *Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name, because you have been strong with God, and powerful with men* <note>Genesis 32:28</note>. 
This suggests that Israel is a man of vision and contemplation, since the name, when translated, means "a man seeing God." Such a man was he, from whom the twelve tribes of the Jewish nation arose. 

One could say ten thousand things about the lives of these men, and their philosophical endurance and discipline—some things observed according to the literal text, and others through allegorical meanings. We have spoken about these briefly, and also in our works concerning the large families of the ancient men <note>likely referring to Eusebius’s lost work "On the Numerous Offspring of the Ancients."</note>. Such were these men. 

In addition to these, I can also tell you of a famous man named Job. The sacred oracles witness that he was a man blameless, true, righteous, and god-fearing, abstaining from every evil deed. Furthermore, it is witnessed that he achieved all these successes in godliness despite not belonging at all to the race of the Jews. 

The children of Jacob, having loved the ancestral knowledge of God and the godliness of old, advanced the fame of the Hebrews to a great height of glory, so that their leadership eventually appeared throughout all of Egypt. For Joseph, having been adorned with the prizes of self-control...

### PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK VII

<header>EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 7</header>

And then, after he received the governorship of the Egyptians, he <note>Eusebius is referring to Joseph, son of Jacob.</note> demonstrated the God-beloved character of the Hebrews. We have made it our prayer to emulate this very man, who became a slave through the plotting of his own kin, and a slave to an Egyptian man. I pass over those other things in which he was fortunate, such as his youthful vigor, bodily strength, and physical beauty, even if the scriptures record that he surpassed all others in the beauty of his prime. But as for the qualities of his soul, how could anyone worthily report them according to the merit of the man's virtue, if one were to undertake a full narration of his praise? By nature, he possessed a rational and free character, and the truth of his disposition was verified by his outward appearance. He was exceptionally disciplined in the most excellent ornaments of piety, so that his soul shone with temperance, justice, wisdom, and courage; but much earlier still, he excelled in the knowledge and piety directed toward the absolute God. We say this in parallel for those who would train themselves: he had firmly established these things in his soul.

The wife of his master, then, became maddened with passion for him, attempting to drag him into licentious and erotic intercourse since he was young in body. First, she tried to deceive him with words; then, she flattered him with entreaties; and finally, she laid hands on him more violently, using shameless and unambiguous embraces in her attempt to ensnare him. But the hero, calling to mind the pious teaching of his fathers and proving himself a God-fearing and true Hebrew in both deeds and words, rejected the shameful and licentious woman, escaping from her hand even when she became more daring. Like one escaping from some terrible and predatory beast, he sought safety in flight. And then, he is said to have reasoned within himself and said: "If my master—"

<margin>»</margin>
> —because of me, knows nothing of what is in his house, and has put all that he has into my hands, how then shall I do this great wicked thing, and sin against God? <note>original: "καὶ ἁμαρτήσομαι ἐναντίον τοῦ θεοῦ;" — This is a direct quote from the Septuagint version of Genesis 39:8-9.</note>

For these things, God, the ruler of all, crowned him with the prizes of victory for his virtue, and delivered to him the kingdom and governorship, not only over his master but over all Egypt. Yet he too was a "Hebrew of Hebrews," and not a "Jew," because the customs of the Jews did not yet exist; he is included among those who were most God-beloved and thrice-blessed. 

After these aforementioned Hebrews, the race of their descendants rapidly increased into a great multitude. Once the nation of the Jews was established from them, it increased and multiplied daily. However, the practice of the pious way of life, which had been laid down for them by the God-beloved men of old, gradually became weak and dulled among them. The influence of their stay among the Egyptians took such a hold of the multitude that they forgot their ancestral virtue and were carried away into a similarity of lifestyle with the Egyptians, so that they seemed to differ in character from the Egyptians in no way at all. At this point, when these things had come to pass, the God of their forefathers sent forth Moses as a leader and lawgiver, confirming through him the promises made by oracles to their ancestors. Then, having performed through him the recorded wonders and miraculous divine signs, he imposed the Law that was suited to the character of his listeners. Since they were unable, due to their lack of training in character, to emulate their ancestral virtue—inasmuch as their souls were passionate and diseased—they received a constitution that was appropriate for them. Some things Moses ordained clearly and openly; other things he hinted at through deeper meanings, using symbols and shadows, but not the naked truth...

and laying down the foundation for them and for those who came after. And indeed, the Jewish commonwealth <note>original: πολίτευμα (politeuma), referring to their political and religious constitution</note>, beginning from some point with Moses and lasting until the presence of our Savior Jesus Christ, continues in accordance with the voices of its own prophets. For this too was a decree of Moses himself and the later prophets: that the laws and ordinances of Moses should not fail until the things of Christ appeared—namely, those of the New Covenant <note>original: καινῆς διαθήκης (kainēs diathēkēs)</note>, which has been proclaimed to all nations through our Savior. These things have indeed reached their fulfillment, or have been publicly proclaimed. But since we have already examined the life of the Hebrews before Moses in brief, or at least set forth the character of their piety, it is time to inspect their doctrinal form, both from the writing of Moses and the prophets after him.

### ->Concerning the doctrinal teachings among the Hebrews.<-

First of all, then, that wonderful theologian and lawgiver himself <note>Eusebius refers to Moses here.</note>, in establishing a commonwealth through his own writing for the Jewish nation—one fitting for piety—did not think it necessary to use the common and well-trodden preambles of speech. Before taking up any practical law concerning what must be done, or any prohibitions of what must not be done, or the public and civil ordinances regarding contracts with one another, he thought it necessary to begin with ancestral theology. He made this the starting point of his instruction, considering no other learning to be as fitting for the laws of piety as the theology that had come down to him from his forefathers. He begins, therefore, with God and the ancestral theology of the Hebrew ancestors. He does not follow the path dear to the Egyptians and Phoenicians, nor does he address the "venerable" by casting it into a multitude <note>A critique of polytheism, where the divine is split into many gods.</note>, as do those who think they should attend to visible gods—the luminaries in the sky. Nor does he attend to the unseen and invisible ones who have passed away among men, or the earthly and aerial spirits <note>original: δαίμονας (daimonas), meaning lesser spirits or deities</note>, according to the things we have recently examined. Rather, he makes the starting point of his entire discourse the First Cause, the invisible and incorporeal Creator <note>original: δημιουργοῦ (demiourgou)</note>. He teaches that the Lawgiver of the constitution of the universe is also the King, having established Him as the King over the world, as if over one great city. He teaches by proceeding to show that this Being is the cause and master, not only of the laws to be ordained for men shortly thereafter, but also of the laws within the nature of all things. For he presents Him as the King and Lawgiver of the entire cosmos.

### ->Concerning universal providence, and the constitution and creation of the world.<-

For by His nod and power, the bringing into being of all things occurred; and by His divine laws, in a path and order, the entire age is governed. For by the Word <note>original: λόγῳ (logō), meaning the divine Reason or Word of God</note> and Law of God, first of all, the heaven was made firm. The heavy and earth-bound nature of the land, contrary to its own nature, is suspended by elements finer than itself. By the divine Word and Law, the alternating course of night and day cycles round; and by the Word and Law, the sun itself, the moon, and the dance of the other stars,

### GOSPEL PREPARATION BOOK 7.
#### q.iii.

...journey in an unseemly fashion or complete a course that is out of harmony. For by the law of the King of All, who persuades all things, the changes of the seasons, the cycles of the year, and the annual periods are fulfilled in the all-harmonious symphony of the universe. By the law of God, winter is permitted to withdraw and give way to those seasons following closely behind. The depths of the sea, though they surge with their own waves, are—by divine law—shut within their proper oceans, so that they do not dare to overstep the sacred boundaries of the laws by flooding the dry land. By divine law again, the earth is watered in due measure by the supply of rain or snow, bringing forth a myriad of species of both plants and animals. In a word, nature—the mother of all things—having been enslaved to the command of God, yields to divine laws and the will of the Leading God. For this great and most beautiful masterpiece did not come together by chance, nor by accident, nor by some automatic and irrational force <note>original: ἀλόγῳ φορᾷ (alogō phora) — a common philosophical argument against the Epicurean view that the world formed by random chance</note>, nor is it the work of a disordered nature. Rather, it is the creation of the All-Wise Architect of the universe. It was necessary, then, for it to be governed by sacred reasons and laws.

Starting from this point, the prophet <note>Eusebius refers to Moses as "the prophet."</note>, before setting down legislation for men, first set forth laws concerning the nature of the universe. Placing God as the Great King at the "forecourt" of all things, he proclaimed the Law based on His utterances. He showed that even the sun, the sky, the cosmos, the earth, and everything upon it—all those things considered "works of nature"—serve His sacred laws and reasons, as they are not outside of His arrangement. Therefore, it is even more necessary for human beings, who are no small part of the whole, to naturally attend to the divine decrees and not fall short <margin>»</margin> of the individual elements. For in the beginning, when the Creator gave the law, the earth brought forth <margin>»</margin> "the grass of the field, the seed-bearing herb according to its kind, and the fruit-bearing tree yielding <margin>»</margin> fruit." <note>A quotation from Genesis 1:11.</note> This obedience to the law, shown by the inanimate world alongside the Word <note>original: λόγῳ (logō) — referring here both to God's command and the rational order</note>, has remained constant <margin>»</margin> within the arrangements of the divine command until now. In the same way, when God spoke concerning the <margin>»</margin> liquid essence, "Let the waters bring forth the creeping things of living souls, and the winged birds flying <margin>»</margin> across the firmament of heaven," <note>A quotation from Genesis 1:20.</note> the work was performed alongside the word. This is still visible today <margin>»</margin> as nature obeys the divine persuasion. And if indeed the sun, the moon, and the stars, having been assigned to their own proper courses by the divine law, are "for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years," <note>A quotation from Genesis 1:14.</note> and do not transgress that legislation, what excuse could possibly remain for those who neglect the divine laws?

Having provided this preliminary training, that wonderful man [Moses] won us over and rightly made us zealots for true knowledge of God and piety. We have been unable to find anything similar to these things among the "theologians" of the previously mentioned nations. After this "first theology," he moves to a second doctrine, which is both physical and philosophical. For after the knowledge concerning God and the arrangement of the whole universe, he added in order the "second nature." This is the study of human nature. For after the knowledge of God, it is necessary to know oneself, so that one may then be taught what a human being is, and what leads him toward the knowledge and piety of God, and what the "primary life" of a human being ought to be. Discussing the relationship between the soul and the body, he defines the true human being as the soul, which participates in an intellectual, incorporeal, and rational essence, created "according to the image" [of God].

<summary>Eusebius argues that Moses began the Bible with the creation story to prove that the entire universe obeys God's laws, leaving humans with no excuse for disobedience. He defines the "true human" as the rational soul made in God's image.</summary>

# EUSEBIUS

...to enjoy them, establishing for them an endless foundation. And indeed, the Jewish way of life <note>original: πολίτευμα (politeuma) — referring here to their religious and civil constitution</note>, beginning from Moses and lasting until the presence of our Savior Jesus Christ, endured in accordance with the voices of their own prophets. For both Moses and the later prophets decreed that the customs and ordinances of Moses would not fail until the appearance of Christ—that is, the New Covenant <note>original: καινῆς διαθήκης (kainēs diathēkēs) — also translated as the New Testament</note> announced through our Savior to all the nations. These things have reached their fulfillment or have been proclaimed. But since we have briefly narrated the life of the Hebrews according to Moses—marking the character of their piety—it is time to examine their doctrinal framework from the writings of Moses and the prophets who followed him.

### Concerning the Doctrinal Teachings Among the Hebrews.

First of all, that wonderful theologian and lawgiver himself, after establishing a way of life most fitting for piety for the Jewish nation through his own writing, did not think it necessary to use common or well-trodden introductions. Before any practical law of things to be done or forbidden, and before the public and civil regulations regarding contracts with one another, he thought it necessary to begin from "complete theology" <note>original: παντελοῦς θεολογίας (pantelous theologias) — a full account of the nature of God</note>. He made this the starting point of his teaching, believing no other learning was more fitting for the laws of piety than the knowledge of God that reached him through his ancestors. He begins, then, with God and the theology of the Hebrew forefathers. This does not descend into a multitude of objects of worship, as was the custom for Egyptians and Phoenicians among the other nations, nor did they consider the visible lights in heaven to be gods. Nor did they worship the unseen and invisible forces that dwell among men, or the earthly and airy demons, as we have previously refuted. Instead, starting from the Cause of all things—the invisible and incorporeal Creator—he teaches that the very nature of the Lawgiver is the one who established the constitution of the whole, setting Him up as the King of the world, as if it were one great City <note>original: μεγαλοπόλεως (megalopoleōs) — a "Great City" or Cosmopolis, a Stoic-influenced term for the universe governed by divine reason</note>. In the beginning, he teaches his followers to consider Him the author and Lord not only of the human laws to be ordained shortly thereafter, but also of the laws within the nature of all things. For he presents Him as the King and Lawgiver of the entire universe.

### On Universal Providence, and on the Constitution and Creation of the World.

For by His command <note>original: νεύματι (neumati) — literally a "nod," signifying God's effortless will</note> and power, the essence of all things came into being. By His laws and customs, the entire age is steered in a path and order. By the Word and Law of God, first of all, the heaven was made firm, and the heavy and earth-bound nature of the land was—contrary to its own nature—suspended by the more subtle of the elements <note>Eusebius reflects the ancient view that the heavy earth is miraculously suspended in space or held up by lighter air/fire by divine decree</note>. By the divine Word and Law, the mutual course of night and day cycles around. By Word and Law, both the sun and moon, and the dance of the remaining stars...

...service <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion of the orderly movement of the cosmos.</note> in an unseemly world or to proceed in an unsuitable course. For by the law of the King of All, the successions and changes of the seasons, the cycles of the year, and the annual periods are fulfilled in the all-harmonious symphony of the universe. By the law of God, winter yields and gives way; and this, in turn, is followed by the closest of the seasons. And the depths of the sea, surging with their destined tides, are shut up within their proper oceans by divine law, so that they do not dare to overstep the boundaries of the sacred laws onto the dry land; while the earth is watered by showers of rain and snow, supplied again in due measure by divine law. A myriad of plants and animals are brought forth by the earth. In a single word, the nature of all things, the mother of all, being enslaved to the command of God, yields to divine laws and the will of the presiding God. For it was not by chance, nor as it happened, nor by a spontaneous and irrational force that such a vast world-order <note>original: διάκοσμον (diakosmon) — the orderly arrangement of the universe</note> was established; nor is this great and most beautiful masterpiece <note>original: τεχνούργημα (technourgēma) — a work of artistic skill</note> the work of a disordered nature. Rather, it is the creation of the all-wise Architect of all things, and it is well-governed by sacred reasons <note>original: λόγοις (logois) — can also mean "principles" or "divine words"</note> and laws. Beginning from this point, the prophet <note>referring to Moses</note>, before setting forth the laws for human legislation, placed first the laws concerning the nature of the universe. By setting the King of All, God, at the threshold of all things, he proclaimed beforehand that no one should neglect His law. For if the sun itself, and the heaven, and the cosmos, and the earth, and all things upon the earth—everything considered to be the work of nature—serves Him in order and by His decrees, and by sacred laws and reasons, then it is all the more necessary for human beings, who are no small part of the whole, to follow and attend to the divine decrees. They should not prove weaker than the individual elements. For when God first gave the law at the beginning, saying:

<margin>»</margin> **Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed according to its kind, and the fruit tree yielding fruit.** <note>Genesis 1:11</note>

The earth, showing its obedience to the law simultaneously with the word, has continued even until now to be obedient to the divine decrees. So also the liquid substance, at the command of God:

<margin>»</margin> **Let the waters bring forth the creeping things of living souls, and winged creatures flying above the firmament of heaven.** <note>Genesis 1:20</note>

It rendered the work simultaneously with the word. And even until now, it is seen to be obedient to the law through persuasion. And if the sun, moon, and stars, by the divine law appointed for them, fulfill their proper courses to serve for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years, and do not transgress their legislation—what excuse for forgiveness would remain for those who would treat the divine laws with neglect? Having pre-instructed us with these things, that wonderful man <note>Moses</note> won us over and rightly established us as zealots for the knowledge of God and true piety. For we have been able to find nothing similar to these things among the theologians of the previously mentioned nations. For after the first theology <note>the study of God</note>, he passes on to the second doctrine, which is both physical and philosophical. Indeed, after the knowledge concerning God, he brings forward the arrangement of the whole in its order, which is second in nature. And this is the doctrine concerning the nature of man. For after the knowledge of God, it is necessary for one to know himself. Therefore, he teaches next what man is, and what it is that leads him toward the knowledge and piety of God, and what the primary life of man consists of. Going through the discourse concerning the soul and the body, he defines the true man as being found in the soul, a participant in an intellectual, incorporeal, and rational substance, as if according to the image...

...fashioned by God. He possesses an earthy body, a dwelling place for the soul. To these elements, [Moses] adds that a certain "breath of life" came to dwell within, a connecting power between that which was taken from the earth and that which was made according to the image of God <term>Imago Dei: the theological concept that humans are created in the likeness of God</term>. He records that the first dwelling of man was in a "thrice-blessed" paradise of God, filled with immortal and eternal blessings. Yet, like the other things clearly subject to the laws of God from the beginning of the universe, man—through negligence and the transgression of the divine command—was deprived of that most delightful life. 

These are the things Moses philosophizes upon in the introductions to his sacred laws. He does so almost as a public proclamation, warning us not to forget our own proper dignity, in which we obtained a likeness to the Divine, and from which the immortality of the soul was allotted to us. For it is surely not lawful for the image of the King to be destroyed—at least not the original and true image of the God of all, which is His Word <note>original: λόγον (Logon) — referring to the second person of the Trinity as the "Reason" or "Word" of God</note>, being Wisdom itself, Life itself, Light, and Truth, and whatever else is beautiful and good that one might conceive. 

Understand man, then, to be the "image of an image" <note>Eusebius explains that if the Word/Logos is the direct image of God, then man is a secondary image modeled after the Word</note>, which is why it is confessed that he was made "according to the image of God." Moses believed it was necessary to provide this preliminary instruction to those who were going to devote themselves to the sacred laws: that they should remember both the part of them taken from the earth (which will again be dissolved into earth) and the part in us that is better and resembles God. He taught how to treat each of these parts accordingly—not to insult or act impiously toward the human being made in God's image, nor to defile it with shameful and unlawful deeds, but to constantly carry a longing for that first and thrice-blessed dwelling and life, and to hasten to run back, making the journey "immaterial" <note>living a life focused on spiritual rather than physical concerns</note> so as to obtain that thrice-blessed life and dignity once more. 

Furthermore, they say we must guard ourselves regarding the departure and exit from this life; for it is not otherwise possible for the unholy and unpurified to attain that sacred radiance, from which even the first man fell through negligence, having looked down upon the divine command. In addition to these things, the "hierophant" <note>original: ἱεροφάντης (hierophantēs) — a priest or teacher of sacred mysteries, here referring to Moses</note> adds a most essential doctrine, teaching us not to be ignorant of the fact that there is a certain evil demon <note>original: πονηρὸς δαίμων (ponēros daimōn)</note> lying in wait for each person—envious, a hater of the good, and a slanderer who plots against humanity through deceptions. 

He names this creature a "dragon" and a "serpent," one who is black and belongs to the darkness, full of poison and wickedness. He says that even now, this being attempts to undermine us out of envy for our God-given life, and tries to drag down each of those who have anchored themselves with God. It was by his deception that our ancestors fell from that sweet allotment. Therefore, there is a constant need to be awake against the crafty villainies of this aforementioned worker of evil. 

But why should we add these summaries when it is time to go through each of the decrees from the written records themselves? We shall begin first with God, calling upon Him as our helper in the first place, through our Savior.

And again, God said, “Let the earth bring forth the grass of the field, sowing seed according to its kind and according to its likeness, and the fruit-bearing tree producing fruit, whose seed is in itself according to its kind upon the earth,” and it was so. And further, God said, “Let there be luminaries in the firmament of heaven, so as to shine upon the earth, and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years,” and it was so. And again, God said, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls according to their kind, and all the winged birds of heaven according to their kind,” and it was so. And again, “Let the earth bring forth four-footed beasts and creeping things and wild animals of the earth according to their kind,” and it was so.

In saying these things, when Scripture says, “God said,” it presents the divine will <note>original: θεῖον νεύμα (theion neuma) — literally a "divine nod" or "commanding gesture"</note> and the fact that God willed the things that exist to be thus; it is certainly not necessary to suppose that He spoke with a physical voice or syllables. Rather, summarizing the account of the primary things, it says, “This is the book of the generation of heaven and earth, on the day that God made the heaven and the earth, and all things within them.” Such is the theology of the Hebrews, teaching that all things consist by the creative Word of God <note>original: λόγῳ θεοῦ (Logō theou)</note>. Furthermore, it does not teach that the entire world was left desolate like an orphan by its Father after being established, but that it is forever governed by the providence of God <term>Providence: the concept of "pronoia," or God's ongoing care and active intervention in the world</term>. Thus, God is not only the Creator and Maker of all things, but also the Savior, the Administrator, the King, and the Leader—presiding forever over the sun itself, the moon, the stars, and the entire heaven and world. With a "great eye" and divine power, He oversees everything, being present to all things celestial and terrestrial, arranging and administering all things in the world. Just so, the prophets who came after Moses spoke in accordance with this:

> Speaking sometimes as if in the person of the Divine itself, they say: “I am a God at hand,” says the Lord, “and not a God from afar. If a man does anything in secret, shall I not know it? Do I not fill the heaven and the earth?” says the Lord. And at other times, theologizing in this manner: “Who has measured the water in his hand, and the heaven with a span, and all the earth in his palm? Who has set the mountains in a scale, and the glens in a balance? Who has known the mind of the Lord, and who has been His counselor?” And again, He who spoke of the heaven as a "vaulted chamber" <note>original: καμάραν (kamaran) — often translated as "curtain" or "canopy"</note> and stretched it out like a tent to dwell in. And further: “Lift up your eyes to the heights and see: who revealed all these things?” And following this: “The Lord God who made the heaven and fixed it, who established the earth and the things in it, and gives breath to the people upon it, and spirit to those who tread upon it, I am the Lord God.” And further: “I alone stretched out the heaven, and I established the earth, I am the Lord God, there is none besides me.” And again: “Thus shall you say to them: The gods who did not make the heaven and the earth, let them perish from the face of the earth and from under the heaven. The Lord is He who made the earth by His strength, who set the world right by His wisdom, and by His understanding stretched out the heaven, and brought up clouds from the end of the earth; He made lightnings for the rain, and brought forth winds from His treasures; every man has become foolish for want of knowledge.” And again: “Where shall I go from your spirit, and from your face, where shall I be hidden? If I go up to heaven, you are there. If I go down to Hades, you are present. If I should take up my wings at dawn and settle in the farthest parts of the sea, even there...”

I do not mean those who talk sheer nonsense about the divine, but those who claim the stars are "fiery masses" <note>original: μύδροι (mydroi) — red-hot metal masses; a theory attributed to Anaxagoras</note> fixed in the sky like nails or plates; or those who call God a "craftsman-like fire" following a path. <note>A reference to the Stoic definition of God</note> Others claim the world is not governed by the providence of God, but by irrational nature; others say that only heavenly things are governed by God, and certainly not things on earth. And again, some say the world is ungenerated and was not made by God at all, but exists automatically and by chance. Others say the composition of the universe came about from atoms and certain thin, soulless, and irrational bodies. These, in brief, are the oracles from the Hebrews concerning the God of the universe. One can also perceive what they have philosophized regarding the "Second Cause" after the God of the universe, concerning the beginning of created things.

### Concerning the theology of the Second Cause.

Thales the Milesian declared that water was the beginning of all things. Anaximenes said it was air; Heraclitus, fire; Pythagoras, numbers; Epicurus, together with Democritus, said it was atomic bodies; and Empedocles, the four elements. Let us therefore look at the Hebrew oracles. After the beginningless and ungenerated essence of the God of the universe—which is unmixed and beyond all comprehension—they introduce a second essence and divine power, the beginning of all created things, which was the first to subsist and was generated from the First Cause. They call this "the Word," "Wisdom," and "the Power of God." <note>original: λόγον, καὶ σοφίαν, καὶ θεοῦ δύναμιν (logon, sophian, theou dynamin) — logos, sophia, and dynamis</note>

Job teaches this when he says:

<margin>»</margin>Mortal man does not know its way, nor has it been found among men. 
<margin>»</margin>But we have heard of its fame. The Lord established its way, and He 
<margin>»</margin>knows its place.” <note>Job 28:12-23</note> And in David, somewhere in the Psalms, he names 
<margin>»</margin>Wisdom through another person, saying: “By the Word of the Lord the 
<margin>»</margin>heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit...

For she is a breath of the power of God, and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty; therefore nothing defiled gains entrance into her. For she is a reflection of eternal light, a spotless mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness. She reaches mightily from one end of the earth to the other, and she orders all things well." <note>Quoting the Book of Wisdom 7:22–8:1</note> And indeed, divine Scripture introduces this divine Word as having been sent to all nations for the salvation of humanity. The history records that he revealed himself in this way to Abraham, to Moses, and to the holy and God-beloved prophets, and that he taught many things through oracles and foretold things to come, at times appearing as God and Lord, and at other times appearing through prophetic words. He was to come into the knowledge of all people as a savior of the sick and a physician of souls, sent by the Greater One <note>meaning God the Father</note>, as he prophesies:
> "He sent his word and healed them, and delivered them from their destructions." <note>Psalm 107:20</note>
> And again, it says more clearly: "His word runs with speed." <note>Psalm 147:15</note>

From this, the Gospel teaching, renewing the prophetic and ancestral doctrine, clarifies the theology in this way:
> "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
> He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him 
> nothing was made that has been made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men." <note>John 1:1–4</note>
Fittingly then, the all-wise Moses himself, beginning his account of the creation of the world, says that "in the beginning" <note>original: ἐν ἀρχῇ — the same phrase used in Genesis and John</note> God made the heaven and the earth. And he introduces God as communicating with his own proper and fitting Word regarding the creation of man, where he writes:
> "And God said, 'Let us make man according to our image and likeness.'" <note>Genesis 1:26</note>
This was also hinted at by the Psalmist, when discussing the First Cause, he says:
> "He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created." <note>Psalm 33:9</note>
This directly implies the instruction and command given by the First Cause to the Second Cause <note>term: Second Cause (δεύτερον αἴτιον) — a common philosophical term in early Christianity to describe the Son/Logos as the agent of the Father's will</note>, as if from a father to a son.

<summary>Eusebius identifies the "Wisdom" of Solomon and the "Word" (Logos) of the Psalms as the same divine figure described in the Gospel of John, acting as the bridge between God the Father and the created world. He argues that this "Second Cause" was the agent through whom God spoke during the creation of humanity in Genesis.</summary>

<header>EUSEBIUS</header>
<meta>catchword: creative</meta>

"...your hand shall guide me." <note>A reference to Psalm 139:10</note> These statements, and others like them, belong to the "theologians" who followed Moses; they were themselves Hebrews whose views harmonize with those of the most ancient fathers. But let us first inquire of those men—beloved by God and thrice-blessed—who lived before Moses and were the very first of the Hebrews. Let us listen to Abraham himself, who has been called the forefather of the entire Jewish nation. Abraham said to the King of Sodom:
> "I will lift up my hand to God the Most High, who created the heaven and the earth." <note>Genesis 14:22</note>
And concerning Abraham, Melchizedek <note>A mysterious figure from Genesis 14, described as a priest-king who blesses Abraham</note>, the priest of God the Most High, is introduced blessing Abraham with these words:
> "Blessed be Abraham by God the Most High, who delivered your enemies into your power. And blessed be God, who created the heaven and the earth." <note>Genesis 14:19–20</note>
In addition to these, the account introduces Abraham instructing his own servant to pray, saying:
> "Put your hand under my thigh, and I will make you swear by the Lord, the God of heaven and the God of earth." <note>Genesis 24:2–3</note>
And he adds:
> "The Lord, the God of heaven and the God of earth, who took me from my father’s house and from the land of my birth." <note>Genesis 24:7</note>
Finally, in the divine manifestation to Moses, when Moses asked how one should conceive of God, the oracle replied:
> "I am HE WHO IS." <note>original: Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν — the famous 'I Am' from Exodus 3:14</note>
"Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS has sent me to you."

Let these examples, out of countless thousands, suffice for the theology of the Hebrews. Is it not then worthwhile to compare them with the "theologies" of the wise Greeks? Among the Greeks, some did not believe in God at all. Others claimed the stars were gods. Some said the stars were "red-hot masses" <note>Anaxagoras' theory that the sun was a molten rock, which led to his exile</note> in the heavens, or fixed to the sky like metal plates or petals. Others said God was an "artistic fire" <note>original: πῦρ... τεχνικὸν — a Stoic term for a rational, creative fire that forms the universe</note> moving along its path. Some claimed the world is not governed by God’s providence, but by a contradictory nature; others said only heavenly things are governed by God, but certainly not those on earth. Again, some said the world is uncreated, or not made by God at all, but exists by chance and coincidence. Still others held that the composition of the universe resulted from atoms and tiny, soulless, irrational bodies.

Such is the Hebrew scripture's brief account regarding the God of the universe. But it is also necessary to observe what the Hebrews philosophized regarding what follows after the God of all: the principle of created things.

---

### Regarding the theology of the Second Cause.

Thales of Miletus declared that water was the beginning of all things. Anaximenes said it was air. Heraclitus said fire. Pythagoras, numbers. Epicurus, along with Democritus, proposed atoms. Empedocles proposed the four elements.

Let us see, therefore, the Hebrew scriptures. After the essence of the God of all—which is without beginning, uncreated, unmixed, and beyond all comprehension—they introduce a **Second Essence and Divine Power**. This is the beginning <note>original: ἀρχὴν — the 'archē' or first principle</note> of all created things, which first took substance and was generated from the First Cause. They call this power "Word" <note>term: Logos (reasoned speech/divine principle)</note>, "Wisdom," and the "Power of God."

Job teaches this clearly, saying:
> "But where has Wisdom been found? And what is the place of understanding? Mortal man does not know her way, nor has she been found among men. But we have heard her fame. The Lord established her way, and He Himself knows her place." <note>Job 28:12, 13, 22, 23</note>
And David somewhere in the Psalms names Wisdom as a distinct Person <note>original: προσώπῳ — literally 'face' or 'mask,' used here in a theological sense for a distinct entity or persona</note>, saying:
> "By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath..." <note>Psalm 33:6</note>

He introduces the "Second Cause" (the Logos or Wisdom) as a divine being generated from the Father to act as the architect of creation.</summary>

For it is surely clear that everyone who says something, says it to another. And he who gives a command, gives that command to another person rather than to himself. Moses himself explicitly mentions two Lords—namely, the Father and the Son—when he records the punishment of the ungodly in this way, saying: **"And the Lord rained brimstone and fire from the Lord upon Sodom and Gomorrah."** <note>original: *kai ebrexe kyrios para kyriou*. This verse from Genesis 19:24 was a primary proof-text for early Christian writers to argue for the existence of two divine persons: the Father and the Son (the Logos).</note> In harmony with this, David also said in the Psalms: **"The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet."** <note>Psalm 110:1 (Psalm 109 in the Septuagint).</note> And before these words, David hinted at the Word's hidden and ineffable <term>creation|original: demiourgian. Refers to the act of bringing the world into being.</term> of all things, saying: **"From the womb, before the morning star, I begat you."** <note>Psalm 110:3.</note>

Now, so that you do not think I am merely being clever with these interpretations, I will present to you a Hebrew man as an interpreter of the meaning within the Scripture. He was a man who accurately studied the traditions of his fathers and learned the doctrine from his teachers—if, indeed, Philo seems like such a man to you. Listen, then, to how he interprets these divine voices.

## Philo on the Second Cause.

> Why is it that he says, as if speaking about another god, **"In the image of God I made man,"** rather than "in his own image"? <note>Philo is commenting on Genesis 1:27 and 9:6.</note> This was spoken with supreme beauty and wisdom. For nothing mortal could be formed in the likeness of the Most High and Father of all, but only in the likeness of the **second god**, who is that Father’s **Word** <term>Word|original: Logos. In Greek philosophy and Jewish-Hellenistic thought, the Logos is the divine Reason or "blueprint" through which God organizes the universe.</term>. For it was necessary that the rational type in the human soul be stamped by the divine Word, since the God who exists *before* the Word is superior to every rational nature. It would be unlawful for anything created to be made like Him who exists above the Word in the most excellent and unique form of being.

These things I have set down from the first book of Philo’s *Questions and Solutions*. And the same author, in his earlier book *On Husbandry*, names the Son of God—his first-born Word—the "Evening Star." He writes:
> "God, as Shepherd and King, leads all these things according to justice, having set over them His right Word and first-born Son, who, like the lieutenant of a great king, shall take over the care of this sacred flock."

And in his second book, the same author again writes these words exactly:
> "If anyone, then, wishes to escape difficulties even in matters of doubt, let him say with confidence that nothing material is strong enough to bear the weight of the world; but the eternal Word of the everlasting God is the strongest and firmest support of the whole universe. This Word, extending from the center to the edges and from the extremities to the center, runs the undefeated course of nature, bringing all the parts together and binding them fast. For the Father who begat him made him the unbreakable bond of the universe. Naturally, then, the whole earth will not be dissolved by the water that has moved into its hollows, nor will fire be quenched by air, nor, conversely, will air be set ablaze by fire, because the divine Word sets himself as a boundary between them, like a mediator in the midst of speechless elements. He does this so that the whole world, like music written on a scale, might not fall into silence, but might harmonize by his mediation and arbitration, quieting the threats of opposing forces with persuasion."

These are the words of Philo. And Aristobulus, another wise man of the Hebrews who flourished during the reign of the Ptolemies, confirms this doctrine as ancestral. Addressing King Ptolemy himself on the interpretation of the sacred laws, he says the following:

> ...they have said that those who follow this choice <note>original: *hairesis*, meaning a school of thought or a chosen way of life.</note> possess it in the rank of a lamp. For by following it continuously, they will be established in a state of tranquility throughout their whole life. These things, then, and others like them, the children of the Hebrews have philosophized about this matter. Would it not, then, be most worthy of God to attribute the origin of the constitution of the universe to a rational and all-wise power of God—or rather to Wisdom itself and the very Word of God—rather than to lifeless and irrational elements? But such are the views among the Hebrews concerning the beginning of all things. Let us now examine what they teach about the constitution of rational beings following the first principle.

->On the Constitution of Rational Beings.<-

**A**fter the beginningless and unbegotten <term>essence|original: ousia. The fundamental nature or being of God.</term> of God, the King of all, they teach a beginning produced from the Father—not from within, but begotten. This is the Firstborn and the fellow-worker of the Father’s will, formed in His image. This being, who stands before all subsequent created things, they are accustomed to call the Image of God, the Power of God, the Wisdom of God, the Word of God, and indeed the <term>Commander-in-Chief|original: archistratēgos. Eusebius uses the Apostle Paul to support the idea of a spiritual hierarchy.</note> In this way, he compared the world of incorporeal and intellectual essences. All things enjoy the inexpressible and infinitely great power of the God of all, while the creative and illuminating power of the Divine Word holds the second place after the Father. For this reason, it is dear to the Hebrews to call Him the **True Light** and the **Sun of Righteousness**. The Holy Spirit is placed in the third rank, in the position of the moon, following the second essence; they number the Spirit among the first and royal rank of the principle of all things, being appointed by the Maker of all for the rule of things created afterward—I mean those of lower rank that stand in need of the help the Spirit provides. Therefore, holding the third rank, the Spirit supplies those of lower rank with the better powers within itself, yet also receiving from another—that is, from the Word, whom we said holds the second place after the supreme and unbegotten nature of God the King of all. From Him, indeed, the God-Word Himself is supplied, as if from an ever-flowing fountain welling up with divinity, and He shares and imparts His own light to all together—including the Holy Spirit itself, who is nearer and closer to Him than all others—and to the intellectual and divine powers that follow, doing so abundantly and without stint. For the unbegotten Principle of all things is the fountain of all good, the cause of divinity, life, light, and every virtue, and is never surpassed...

...the beginning of first things and origins—or rather, a state even beyond any "origin" or "first thing," and beyond every expressible or conceivable notion. This source first shared with His own offspring <note>Referring to the Son/Logos.</note> alone those unutterable powers that he might receive and contain what is unreachable and uncontainable to others, for He is a never-failing source of all good.
