The highest and most holy of these gifts was granted to the "Third," who rules and leads those who come after, and through whom we receive the things concerning the Father. 

Hence, all the Hebrew theologians, after the God who is over all and after His firstborn Wisdom, recognize and deify a third and holy power, which they call the Holy Spirit. By this Spirit, they themselves were enlightened while being carried along by God. Next, they say that just as in the heavens the sun and moon differ, so "star differs from star in glory." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 15:41.</note> It is impossible for a mortal nature to find the exact number of these beings, except that the Hebrew scriptures say that the King of All, God, is not ignorant of the vast numbers and names of the heavenly host.

The fundamental nature of a being.</term>, speaks of the Creator in this majestic way:

Do not suppose that these "spirits" and "fire" refer to the mortal and earthy substances we know, nor the air breathed by irrational animals. Rather, just as God himself is named after such things, He is a nature that is bodiless, immaterial, and never-sleeping—or rather, a nature above all mind and reason. Yet, in a more condescending way, He is named "Spirit," "Fire," and "Light," and other such titles suitable for mortal ears.

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 7

> ...in the highest! Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers. Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light. Praise him, you heavens of heavens, and let the waters above the heavens praise the name of the Lord. For he spoke, and they were brought into being; he commanded, and they were created. He established them forever, even forever and ever; he set down ordinances, and they shall not pass away. <note>This is a continuation of Psalm 148:1–6.</note>

Such are the doctrines found among the Hebrews. We have preferred these over our former polytheistic and demonic errors, recognizing the divine powers as servants of God—the King of All—and as liturgical <note>In this context, "liturgical" means performing a public service or sacred duty on behalf of the Creator.</note> beings. We honor them as they deserve, but we confess only one God and worship Him alone, whom the heaven itself and all things in heaven, and even those beyond heaven, have been taught to worship, hymn, and speak of as God. For even the Only-begotten of God <note>The Logos or Word of God, often identified with Jesus Christ in Eusebius's theology.</note>, who existed before all things and is the beginning of all, was taught to consider His Father alone as God, and He commands us to worship Him alone.

## Concerning the Subordinate Powers.

It follows that we should also examine what the Hebrew oracles hand down concerning the "opposite power." While they describe the divine powers—the holy angels and archangels of God—standing over the whole world by the Father’s will as "ministering spirits" sent out for service to those who will inherit the kingdom <note>A reference to Hebrews 1:14.</note>, and every intellectual essence that serves goodness as being full of light, acting as servants of the gifts bestowed by God upon humans, they describe these beings as a bodyguard for God, the King of All. After these, they speak of the "Sun of Righteousness" <note>original: ἥλιον τῆς δικαιοσύνης. A title for Christ drawn from Malachi 4:2.</note>—the heavenly judge of the stars—and His companion <note>original: σύζυγον. A term implying a close, paired relationship, here referring to the Holy Spirit.</note> and Holy Spirit, as enjoying the vast supply of light from these sources. For this reason, they are rightly compared to the luminaries in heaven.

But for that power which fell away from these and was deprived of the company of the better beings due to its own inherent depravity—exchanging light for darkness—the scripture conversely uses disgraceful names based on the wickedness of its character. Indeed, for the one who began the fall and became the cause of the rebellion of others against the better beings—having fallen completely to the ground from our state of piety, and having become a craftsman of the poison of malice and impiety for himself, a maker of the darkness of irrationality by his own free choice to depart from the light—the scripture is accustomed to calling him a "dragon," a "serpent," black and crawling, full of deadly poison, a "wild beast," a "gluttonous lion," and again, the "basilisk" <note>The basilisk was considered the "king of serpents" in antiquity, capable of killing with a glance.</note> among reptiles.

The theologians say that the cause of his fall was a madness of mind and a delirium of the intellect, describing the fall and the mental illness together in this way: "How has Lucifer <note>original: ἑωσφόρος, literally "the Day-bringer" or "Morning Star."</note>, who rose in the morning, fallen from heaven? He who sends to all the nations was crushed to the ground. But you said in your heart, 'I will ascend into heaven, I will set my throne above the stars of heaven, I shall be like the Most High.'" <note>Isaiah 14:12–14.</note> And again, the Lord says these things: "Because your heart was lifted up, and you said, 'I am a god, I have dwelt in the habitation of God.'" <note>Ezekiel 28:2.</note> And once more: "You are the seal of likeness and a crown of beauty; you were born in the luxury of the paradise of God. You were clothed in every precious stone..." and so forth. To which he adds: "You were born on the holy mountain of God, you were born in the midst of fiery stones; you were blameless in your days, from the day you were created until..." <note>Ezekiel 28:12–15.</note>

They try to lure the innocent with prophecies and oracles, as if with some alluring baits, to tear them away from looking toward the God of All, and to drag them down into the bitter-deadly depth of impious and godless superstition. Long ago, while their deceptions were a common evil for all, only the Hebrews were diligent in teaching from of old that "all the gods of the nations are demons." But now, as we may say with God's help, through the Gospel teaching of our Savior, all the nations throughout the world have been freed from these demonic chains. We have learned to know the true God—the only one who is Savior, King, and God of All.

->**On the Nature of Human Beings.**<-

**H**ere again, the "origin of life" <term>zoogonia: the study or myth of how living beings were first generated</term> accounts of the Phoenicians and Egyptians introduced a spontaneous generation of all animals and humans upon the earth. They described one and the same nature for all, emerging from the earth by chance, assuming that the rational soul and essence differ in no way from the irrational animals. This was clearly shown by the words of their writers which were previously cited. 

However, we have rightly preferred the children of the Hebrews, who have understood the facts regarding the first constitution of humans in a truly beautiful and wise manner. They say that there is something within us that is divine and immortal, incorporeal and bodiless in its nature. This, they say, is the "true human," created according to the image and likeness of God. It is the work of God, not of chance or a purposeless nature. By the divine judgment of the Cause of All, it was willed that even the things of the earth should not be without a share of an intellectual and rational essence, so that through all...

### Philo, *On the Soul*.

<margin>A</margin> "While others, claiming our mind is a part of the ethereal nature, have linked man to the ether through a shared weaving; the great Moses, however, did not liken the form of the rational soul to any created thing. These are his words.

Reasonably then, in the Divine Scripture, it does not say that man came into being in the same way as the other animals. For it says some were called forth from the earth by a single command of God, the King of All; and others were molded from the watery substance, again by His nod. But we ourselves—the most "God-beloved" of the animals on earth—were made so that the soul exists "according to the image and likeness of God." To this soul is given a nature that is ruling and kingly, and it alone of the things on earth possesses reason, creativity, judgment, and the power of law-giving, craftsmanship, and the capacity for scientific knowledge. For only the soul in man is an intellectual and rational essence, in which the other animals on earth have no share. Therefore, He provided the wild beasts to inhabit the lands as servants; but he made them subject and enslaved to men as to a master and leader—animals which are much stronger in body, but by nature inferior in their intellectual essence.

For this reason, they say man was established "according to the image and likeness of God" by God Himself, with a certain distinguishing excellence. Because of this, he is able to form conceptions of God, and he attains a perception of wisdom, justice, and every virtue. He is also able to calculate the paths of the sun, the moon, and the stars, and the cycles of days and hours—a kinship with the divine which man alone among mortals displays.

That which is fashioned on the outside <note>i.e., the physical body.</note> was of a different nature, though it too was carved as God's work, taken from the earth and returning to it. Therefore, this part has needs such as a master must provide for an unreasoning beast, and it requires good things and nourishment like a servant prepared for the ministry of human life. But the "master" within <note>the soul</note>, being of a high nature and kin to God, is what proves our relationship to the Cause of all things...

**The** Oracles <note>original: "τὰ λόγια" — referring to the Holy Scriptures.</note> therefore tell us that the Universal King, having adorned the primary nature of man with divine powers and the likeness of God, granted him a fitting gift and assigned him his first dwelling-place in a paradise of good things, numbering him among the divine companies. These were the things granted to him in the beginning by God, as if from a father. 

But when, by a free choice of the will, he fell away from that higher state and exchanged his divine command for the debt of mortality through a disregard for the commandment—it is for this reason especially fitting that we should first reclaim our piety. We must correct that first transgression with secondary successes and hasten toward our proper return and restoration. For the end of human nature is not found here on earth, where it sinks into corruption and destruction, but begins from that place from which the first man fell away. 

Therefore, it is necessary once again to regain the god-like quality of the intellectual essence within us. For this purpose, we must strive to ascend to the Creator, as is required of all men who care for piety and virtue. Such were the philosophical views held by the Hebrews regarding human nature from the earliest times, long before they even reached the Greeks. For certain people, quite young and recently "risen from the earth" <note>A metaphorical jab at the Greeks as being a "young" civilization compared to the ancient Hebrews.</note>, intended to plunder the ideas of the foreigners <note>original: "βαρβάρων" (barbaron) — non-Greeks.</note>, and they did not hold back from the ideas of the Hebrews, as the forthcoming discourse will demonstrate very shortly. 

But since the Hebrew view is unique in considering the God over all to be the one Creator of everything—including the very substance that underlies all bodies, which the Greeks call matter <term>hyle</term> <note>original: *hyle* (ὕλη) — the raw material of the universe.</note>—behold, ten thousand Greeks and foreigners alike have stood in opposition. Some declared matter to be the source of evil and to be unbegotten <note>original: *agennēton* (ἀγέννητον) — meaning uncreated, eternal, or having no beginning.</note>; others said that while it is by its own nature without quality or shape, it received the world's qualities through the power of God. It must be said that the Hebrew view was far superior, presenting itself with logical proof and setting aside opposing arguments through correct reasoning. Listen to the voices of those who have accurately defined this doctrine for us—and first of all to Dionysius, who, in the first book of his exercises addressed to Sabellius <note>Dionysius was a 3rd-century Bishop of Alexandria; Sabellius was a teacher often accused of blurring the distinctions between the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note>, writes the following regarding the subject at hand:

### Concerning the fact that matter is not unbegotten.

> "For they are not holy who offer matter to God as something unbegotten and subject to His hand for the arrangement of the world. For they claim that while it is passive and changeable, it yields to the divine-wrought alterations. But let them explain: from where did God and matter get their similarity and their difference? For one would have to imagine something superior to both, which is not even lawful to think concerning God. For if the quality of being 'unbegotten' is said to be the same in both, yet is understood as something else alongside each of them, where did it come from in them? For if God is the 'unbegotten' itself, and unbegotten-ness is His very essence, as one might say, then matter could not be unbegotten. For matter is one thing and God is another. 

> But if each is what it is—both matter and God—and the quality of being 'unbegotten' is present in both, it is clear that this quality is something different from either of them, and is older and higher than both. And the difference in their opposite states completely destroys the idea that these things could coexist—or rather, it destroys the idea that one of them, matter, could exist by itself. For they must assign the cause for why, if both are unbegotten, God is impassive, unchangeable, immovable, and active, while matter is the opposite: passive, [changeable]..."

He cites Dionysius of Alexandria to argue that matter cannot be "unbegotten" or eternal, as that would imply a principle higher than God.</summary>

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 7
r.iii.

> » ...mortal, changeable, unstable, and ever-transforming. And how were these things harmonized and brought together? Was it that God, having made the nature of matter His own, crafted it? But that is truly absurd—it is absurd to think that God works with His hands <note>original: "χειροκμητεῖν" — to perform manual labor or handicraft.</note> like a goldsmith or a stonemason, or according to any of the other arts where materials are molded and shaped. But if He made matter such as He Himself willed according to His own wisdom—stamping upon it that multiform and richly-varied shape and pattern of His craftsmanship—then the account is both pious and true. Furthermore, it praises God as the one who established the very substance of all things; for He joined together both the "how" of their existence and the reason for those things which lack reason. There is much more to be said on these matters, but that is not our current purpose. Compared to those who hold the more impious views of polytheism, these men <note>likely referring to those who believe in a single Creator but struggle with the origin of matter.</note> speak with greater reverence. These words are from Dionysius. Now, listen also to those of Origen.

### From the works of Origen on Genesis.

> If anyone is offended by the comparison to human arts and cannot accept that God could create existing things without unbegotten <note>original: "ἀγεννήτου" — uncreated or eternal, having no beginning.</note> matter already lying at hand—since a builder of stones cannot do his specific work without bronze, nor a carpenter without wood, nor a builder without stones—we must question him regarding the power of God. If God willed to bring into existence whatever He wished, and His will neither fails nor grows weak, is He not able to bring into existence that which He wills? For by the same logic that He introduces qualities and all the spheres <note>original: "σφαιρίους" — likely referring to the celestial spheres or the perfect forms within the cosmos.</note> into His own Word <note>original: "λόγῳ" — here meaning the divine Reason or plan.</note>—which did not exist as He willed them for the decoration of the whole—and establishes them by His ineffable power and wisdom; by this same logic, His will is strong enough to create the very substance <note>original: "οὐσίαν"</note> as much as He requires. 
>
> We shall ask those who wish things to be this way: is it not absurd to encounter a God who, having found substance to be unbegotten, would have been unable to perform any work if He had not received it as unbegotten? In that case, He would merely be a craftsman <note>term: <term>demiurge</term> (δημιουργὸς) — a craftsman-god who shapes pre-existing matter rather than creating it from nothing.</note>, and not a Father, nor a Benefactor, nor Good, nor any of the other things irrationally said about God. From where did this substance, which is so vast as to suffice for the existence of such a great world, come to be present? It would be as if some Providence <note>original: "πρόνοια"</note> older than God had laid out the matter and presented it to Him, looking ahead so that the "golden art" within Him might not be practiced in vain for lack of a substance which He could handle to decorate the beauty of such a world. 
>
> And how did matter become capable of receiving every quality that God wills, if God Himself did not make it of such a size and such a kind as He wished it to be? Even if we were to accept the hypothesis that matter is unbegotten, we would say this to those who believe it: if this substance became such as it is by the side of God without a Providence providing it, would a present Providence have made it the same measure, or more? And if He Himself had willed to construct matter when it did not exist, what more would His wisdom and divinity have accomplished than what was established from the unbegotten? For if He finds the same thing being produced by Providence that also existed without Providence, the Creator and the Craftsman will appear to us to be redundant. For just as it is absurd to say that the world was constructed with such skill by some accidental cause without a craftsman, so too is it with matter.

" ...of such a kind and quality, and thus pure, as to have been established by the crafting Word of God <note>original: "τεχνίτῃ λόγῳ θεοῦ" — the Logos (Word) acting as a divine artisan.</note>. To say that matter is equally unbegotten <note>original: "ἀγέννητος" — uncreated, having no beginning; eternal.</note> is irrational. However, to those who dare to claim that no creator can work without material, it must be said that they are making an unequal comparison. For providence <note>original: "πρόνοια" — divine foresight and care for the universe.</note> provides the material to every human craftsman, whether it comes from a previous craft, from human effort, or from the natural world. These points will suffice for the present against those who—because it is written, 'And the earth was invisible and unformed' <note>A quote from the Septuagint version of Genesis 1:2.</note>—imagine that physical nature is unbegotten. Behold, even Philo the Hebrew, in his treatise *On Providence*, discussed these matters regarding material substance."

## Philo on the same subject.

"Regarding the quantity of substance—if indeed it truly came into being—two things must be said. God calculated a perfectly self-sufficient amount of matter <note>original: "ὕλης" — hyle; the raw material of the universe.</note> for the birth of the world, so that there would be neither a deficiency nor an excess. For it would be absurd if local craftsmen, when they create something—especially something costly—had self-sufficient storehouses where their numbers and measures are always consistent, and yet the Mighty One did not take such care. I will say with boldness that the world required neither a lack nor a surplus of substance for its construction. Otherwise, the result would not have been perfect, nor would it be complete in all its parts; nor would it have been crafted from a perfect substance. For it is the mark of an all-wise art to see the 'moisture' <note>original: "ἰκμάδα" — literally 'moisture' or 'essence'; here referring to the fluid, malleable potential of raw matter.</note> of the material before beginning any construction. Now, a man—even if he excels in knowledge—cannot escape the inherent errors of mortals regarding costly things, and might perhaps be deceived about the quantity of material when he practices his craft. Sometimes he might add more as if there were too little, and sometimes he might remove what is in excess. But He, being the very fountain of the sciences, was not going to provide anything deficient or superfluous, as He uses measures that are wonderfully worked out to precision and are praiseworthy in every respect. Anyone who wishes to think otherwise would be suggesting that the works of human craftsmen are better than the divine construction by implying a need for addition or reduction of the materials. But indeed, it is the work of sophistry to overturn the truth, and the work of wisdom to investigate each thing in nature. Let Philo’s words stand in this manner."

Now, by Maximus, a man of no small repute from the school of Christ, a specialized treatise has been written *On Matter*. From this, I think I shall usefully set forth a moderate portion for an accurate examination of the problem.

## That matter is not unbegotten, nor the cause of evils.

"That it is impossible for two unbegotten things to exist together, I think you are not ignorant, even if you seem to have added this to the argument beforehand: that of necessity one must say either that God is separate from matter, or again, that He happens to be inseparable from it. If, then, someone wishes to say He is united with it, he will be speaking of only one unbegotten thing. For each of these would be a part of the other. But if they are parts of one another, they will not be two unbegotten things. In the same way, we do not call the different parts that make up many generated things 'many'—as the logic requires—but we say that one generated thing, such as one man, was made by God with many parts. Thus, it is necessary to say there is only one unbegotten thing, if God is not separate from matter."

» ...[qualities], it is necessary to examine the definition of <term>substance: "ousia" (οὐσία) — the underlying reality or "being" of a thing</term>. Does it seem to you that substance is a kind of bodily composition? It does. And does this bodily composition exist by itself, or does it require something else, through which it receives its existence? It is so. And does it seem to you that evil things are the <term>activities: "energeiai" (ἐνέργειαι) — the actions or operations produced by a substance</term> of something? So it appears to me. And do activities receive their existence only when the one acting is present? That is how it stands. And when the actor is not there, and when he is not acting, will the activity still exist? It will not.
» Therefore, if substance is a bodily composition, does it not require something else in which it must come to be in order to receive its existence? Since evil things are the activities of something, and activities require something else in which they receive their existence, then evil things are not substances. But if you claim evil things are substances, and murder is an evil, and murder is an activity of someone, then murder is not a substance. If you wish to say that the ones acting are substances, I agree. For example, a murderer is a substance according to the definition of being a human being; but the thing he does—murder—is not a substance, but a "work" of the substance. 
» We call a human being "evil" at one time because of murdering, and then again "good" because of doing a kindness. These names are woven around the substance based on its <term>accidents: "symbebekota" (συμβεβηκότα) — non-essential properties or attributes that can change without changing what the thing is</term>. These attributes are not the substance itself. For the substance is not "murder," nor is it "adultery," nor any similar evil. 
» Rather, just as a "grammarian" is named from the study of grammar, and a "rhetorician" from rhetoric, and a "doctor" from medicine—though the substance itself is not medicine, nor rhetoric, nor grammar—the substance receives its name from these attributes. It is named based on what it seems to be, without actually being either one of those attributes. In the same way, it seems to me that the substance takes its name from what are considered evil things, without being either one of them.
» Consider this as well, if you are imagining some "Other" in your mind as the source of evil: <note>The "Other" likely refers to a personified Principle of Evil or a Devil-figure in dualistic thought.</note> Who is this person? Just as a good person acts and suggests doing evil, is he himself evil because of what he does? For he is called "evil" for this reason: because he is a maker of evil things. But what a person does is not the person himself; rather, these are his activities, from which he receives the title of being called "evil." For if we were to say he *is* the very things he does—and he does murders and adulteries and thefts and such things—then he himself is these acts. But if he is these acts, then when these acts cease to be (since they do not have a permanent composition, but stop existing once they are done), then if these acts were the person, the people would be the "makers" of themselves, being the cause of their own existence and their own ceasing to exist.
» But if you say these are his activities, it is because of what he *does* that he is evil, not because of what his substance *is*. We would say he is called evil from the attributes of his substance, which are not the substance itself—just as a doctor is named from medicine. If he becomes "lame" from the way he acts, then that "evil" has a beginning, and these evil things also have a beginning. If this is the case, he is not "evil without a beginning" <note>original: "ἀνάρχως" (anarchōs) — without a source or beginning; unoriginated.</note>, nor are evil things uncreated; rather, it is foolish to say they are co-eternal with him. 
» My friend, you seem to have made your argument well against that other person. From the premises you took for your argument, you seemed to conclude correctly. For truly, if Matter happened to be <term>without quality: "apoios" (ἄποιος) — lacking any distinguishing characteristics or properties</term>, and God is the creator of qualities, and evil things are qualities, then God would be the maker of evil things. 
» While that argument was well-spoken against him, it seems false to me to say that Matter is "without quality." For it is not possible to say of any cause that it is without quality. Even in saying it is "without quality," one reveals its quality—describing what kind of thing Matter is by saying it is "unformed," which is itself a type of quality. Therefore, if it pleases you, let us take up the argument again...

### PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 7

» ...and He began to mix Matter. For if He did not mix them entirely with Matter, He would not be the cause of what He permitted. But since He crafted one part of it and left another part as it was—even though He was capable of turning those parts also toward what is better—He seems to me to deserve blame. He left a portion of Matter in a state of wickedness and destruction, while crafting another part; I remain convinced that the greatest injustice has occurred regarding this part. For why did He construct a part of Matter that is susceptible to evils? 

» Indeed, if one were to examine the facts precisely, they would find that Matter has suffered more severely now than during its previous state of <term>disorder: *akosmia* (ἀκοσμίας) — a state of chaos without arrangement or beauty</term>. For before it was distinguished—which involved no sensation of evils—it felt nothing; but now each of its parts receives a sensation of evils. 

» Take this example as a true illustration: before a living creature is formed by the craftsman’s art, it exists in a state where it perceives none of the evils it had before its nature was formed. But once it reaches its completion, it acquires the sensation of approaching evil. Thus, what you call a "benefit" to Matter—namely, its creation by God—is found to be something that actually results in its worsening. 

» If you say that it is not because God is unable to dissolve evils—which you say has not stopped—you will be claiming that God is weak. This <term>weakness: *adynaton* (ἀδύνατον) — lack of power</term> must either be because He is naturally feeble, or because He is enslaved by fear, being overcome by something more powerful. Now, if you dare to say that God is naturally weak, I think you are risking your very salvation <note>original: "sōtērias" (σωτηρίας) — the speaker warns that diminishing God's power has theological consequences for the soul</note>. But if He is overcome by fear of a greater power, then evils will be greater than God, overcoming the impulse of His will. This seems to me an absurd thing to say about God. 

» But why should these things not rather be gods themselves, if they overcome your reasoning and have power over God? For we call "God" that which possesses absolute authority. Now, I wish to ask you briefly about Matter itself: tell me, was Matter <term>simple: *haplē* (ἁπλῆ) — consisting of one single, uniform element</term> or <term>composite: *synthetos* (σύνθετος) — made of multiple parts or substances</term>? The variety of created things leads me to this investigation. 

» For if Matter happened to be simple and uniform, yet the world is composite and has its consistency from various substances and mixtures—for that which is composite is remembered as a mixture of simple things—then if you wish to say Matter is composite, you must say it is composed of simple elements. But if it was composed of simple elements, there must have been a time when those simple elements (from which Matter was composed) did not yet exist together, and thus Matter is shown to be <term>created: *gennētē* (γεννητή) — brought into being, rather than eternal</term>. 

» For if Matter is composite, and composite things have their consistency from simple things, there was once a time when Matter did not exist—that is, before the simple things came together. And if there was a time when Matter did not exist, and there was a time when the "uncreated" did not exist, then Matter will not be "uncreated." 

» Therefore, it would follow that there are many <term>uncreated things: *agennēta* (ἀγέννητα) — things without a beginning or creator</term>. For if God is uncreated, and the simple elements from which Matter was composed are also uncreated, there will no longer be only two uncreated things <note>referring to the previous premise that only God and Matter are eternal</note>. 

» Now, does it seem to you that any existing thing is contrary to itself? [Answer:] It does not. Is water contrary to fire? It seems so to me. Likewise darkness to light, cold to heat, and dry to wet? It seems to be so. Therefore, if nothing that exists is contrary to itself, they cannot be one single Matter, nor even come from one single Matter. I wish to ask you again about the reasoning behind their similarity. Does it seem to you that parts do not destroy one another? It seems so. You said that fire and water are parts of Matter, and likewise the rest? That is how it is. What then? Does it not seem to you that...

<summary>The speaker argues that if God formed Matter into a sensitive being, He effectively caused it more suffering than its original disordered state. Furthermore, if Matter is made of different elements (like fire and water), it must be a composite creation rather than an eternal, uncreated substance.</summary>

# EUSEBIUS

>> ...just as water seems to be the opposite of fire, and light the opposite of darkness, and all other things similar to these.
>> Therefore, if the parts are not mutually destructive, they will not be parts of each other. But if they are not parts of each other, they will not be of a single <term>matter: *hyle* (ὕλης) — the raw, formless substance from which the world is made</term>. Furthermore, they themselves will not be matter, because nothing that exists is inherently destructive to itself, according to the principle of opposites.
>> For nothing is opposed to itself. Opposites are, by nature, opposed to *other* things. For example, the color white is not opposed to itself, but is said to be the opposite of black. Similarly, light is shown not to be opposed to itself, but appears to be so in relation to darkness. This is clearly the case with many other things as well.
>> If, then, matter were a single thing, it would not be opposed to itself. Since opposites behave in this way, it is demonstrated that matter is not a single substance. 

Such are the words of the aforementioned author <note>Eusebius has been quoting from a dialogue on free will, likely by the 3rd-century writer Methodius of Olympus or Maximus</note>. Since this argument has reached a sufficient conclusion, let us move on to the eighth book of the *Preparation for the Gospel*. With God as our helper, let us complete what is missing from our current investigation.

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 8

### Introduction, and concerning the god-fearing way of life according to Moses.

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap 'Τ' set within a square decorative woodcut frame. The background within the frame depicts a landscape with a building on a hill, trees, and a lone figure with a walking stick. The border of the frame features intricate floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>

Having gone through, in the previous books, the lives of the ancient Hebrews—those men beloved by God who truly lived up to their name, and who were crowned with the prizes of every virtue before Moses even appeared—and having discussed their god-fearing doctrines, their teachings, and their relationship to the pious <term>theologies: *theologias* (θεολογίας) — here referring to their early understandings and descriptions of the Divine</term> of the past (which we confessed we would seek out with love and longing), I now pass, following the proper order, to the <term>way of life: *politeian* (πολιτείαν) — meaning a system of government, citizenship, or a social order</term> according to Moses. This represents the second stage of piety after that first degree I mentioned, and it was a law established specifically for the Jewish nation alone.

I will demonstrate in due time that the laws given through Moses were suited only for the Jews, and not for the other nations throughout the inhabited world, nor were they even possible for everyone to carry out—I mean those Greeks and barbarians living far from the land of Judea. For now, however, I wish to present the character of this Mosaic way of life, once again not using my own words, but the voices of those men who are highly esteemed for their learning among the Jews themselves. 

I believe this approach is proper for me, just as I began: providing the evidence for my proofs through the writings belonging to each group. Just as I called upon the famous figures of the Phoenicians, Egyptians, and Greeks as witnesses of the traditions in their own lands, it seems to me that the present moment is also an appropriate time for this, so that I am not thought to be inventing falsehoods about their traditions. 

For this reason, they say we should investigate how their ancestral oracles came to be known among the Greeks, and the manner in which the translation of the <term>Divine Scriptures: *theiōn graphōn* (θείων γραφῶν)</term> entrusted to them was organized. I believe I should briefly explain to my readers through which men, and what kind of men, and through what royal diligence this change into the Greek language was achieved. This account is not irrelevant to my purpose of demonstrating the <term>Preparation for the Gospel: *hellēnikēs proparaskeuēs* (ἑλληνικῆς προπαρασκευῆς)</term> to the Greeks. 

The saving proclamation of our Savior <note>A reference to the spread of Christianity</note> was soon to shine forth upon all humanity during the time of the Roman Empire. At that time, a remarkable prophecy began to unfold: the life of the ancient God-fearing Hebrews and the lessons of their pious teaching—which had been hidden for long ages in their ancestral tongue—were finally to be brought forward to all the nations to whom God intended to grant the knowledge of Himself. 

God Himself, the author of these blessings, foresaw this as only God can through His foreknowledge. He arranged for the prophecies concerning the Savior of all mankind (who was soon to appear) and the teachings of the one God over all (which were to be established for every nation under the sun) to be revealed to everyone. He brought them into the light by having them accurately translated and placed in public libraries. He accomplished this by putting it into the mind of King Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus (r. 285–246 BCE), who according to tradition commissioned the translation of the Hebrew Bible into Greek, known as the Septuagint</note> to do this, as a preparation, so it seems, for the future participation in these scriptures by the nations who were about to receive them. For we have the good fortune of not being dependent on hearing these things from Jews, who might have hidden their oracles because of their... <note>The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of the page.</note>

## Letter of Eleazar the High Priest to King Ptolemy.

"Eleazar the High Priest to King Ptolemy, his true friend, greetings. If you yourself are well, and Queen Arsinoe <note>Arsinoe II, the sister and wife of Ptolemy II Philadelphus. » ...[he] said he had heard from **Theopompus** <note>Theopompus of Chios (c. 380–315 BC) was a famous Greek historian known for his highly critical style.</note> that because he intended to translate some of the previously mentioned laws rather recklessly <note>original: "episphalesteron" (ἐπισφαλέστερον), meaning dangerously or insecurely</note> from the Law, his mind was thrown into confusion for more than thirty days. During a period of relief, he propitiated God, and it became clear to him for what reason this was happening. Having learned through a dream that he had been meddling by wishing to bring divine things out to common men, he desisted and was thus restored to health. 

» And I myself received this account; but I personally took the story concerning **Theodectes** <note>Theodectes of Phaselis (c. 380–334 BC), a Greek rhetorician and tragic poet.</note> the writer of tragedies. It is said that when he was about to include something from the records in the Book in one of his plays, his eyes were clouded with cataracts. Suspecting that this had happened to him for this reason, he propitiated God and was restored after many days. 

» When the King <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus</note> had received these reports as previously mentioned, and had heard Demetrius's <note>Demetrius of Phalerum, the librarian at Alexandria.</note> thoughts on these matters, he ordered that great care be taken of the books and that they be preserved in holiness.

Let these things be summarized for us from the aforementioned writing <note>The "Letter of Aristeas," the source Eusebius has been quoting.</note>. Come now, let us also observe the constitution of the legislation according to **Moses** from the works of the most distinguished men among them. First, let there be the words of **Philo** <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC – 50 AD), a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Jewish scripture.</note> concerning the journey of the Jews out of Egypt, which was made under the leadership of Moses, taken from the first book of the work he entitled *Hypothetica* <note>original: "Hypothetika" (ὑποθετικῶς). This was a lost work of Philo's, preserved mainly through these quotes in Eusebius.</note>. There, addressing his words as if against their accusers, he says these things:

->Philo concerning the journey of the Jews out of Egypt.<-

» Their ancient ancestor was from the **Chaldeans**, but this people arose as migrants from Egypt, having formerly come from Syria. They multiplied into untold myriads, and as the land was not sufficient for them, and being moreover of high spirit and greatly nurtured in youth, and at the same time God having manifested to them their departure through visions and dreams, they were seized—no less than by a divine passion—with a longing for their rightful ancestral land. 

» For this reason, that ancestor himself migrated to Egypt, whether it seemed good to God or by some providence to make them the most blessed of all, so that from then until now, they have both become and remained a nation. And they reached such an extreme in their great numbers. 

» And after a short while he says: A man was their leader <note>referring to Moses</note> for the exit and the journey, who was in no way different from the common crowd—unless you prefer to believe those who slander him as a sorcerer <note>original: "goēta" (γόητα)</note> and a trickster <note>original: "kerkoppa" (κέρκωπα), literally a long-tailed monkey or a deceitful rogue</note> with words. And yet, though he was considered a sorcerer or a rogue, <margin>A</margin> he led the entire people through waterless regions and famine, through ignorance of the roads and lack of resources for those things that befell them. He not only brought them through to safety, as if on a straight path with safe passage through the intervening nations, but he also preserved them from internal strife among themselves and kept them especially obedient to himself. 

» And this was not for a short time, but for as long as it is likely that not even a single household would remain in harmony despite every abundance. Yet neither thirst, nor famine, nor bodily decay, nor fear of the future, nor ignorance of what would happen, stirred up those deceived and wandering peoples against that "sorcerer." 

» And yet, what shall we say he possessed—whether such great skill or power of words or intelligence—that he could prevail over so many and such strange difficulties that were leading everyone to destruction? Either the natures of the men under him were not ignorant or difficult, but were yielding to the future and not without foresight; or, if these men were indeed most wicked, God Himself smoothed over the difficulties...

» He [Demetrius] said he had heard from **Theopompus** <note>Theopompus of Chios (c. 380–311 BC) was a famous Greek historian known for his biting style and his work *Philippica*.</note> that because he intended to incorporate some of the previously mentioned laws into his history somewhat precariously <note>original: "ἐπισφαλέςερον" (episphalesteron); implying he approached the sacred text with insufficient reverence or as mere secular history.</note>, he suffered a disturbance of the mind for more than thirty days. During a period of relief, he propitiated God, and it became clear to him for what reason this was happening. Having learned through a dream that he had been meddling with divine things and wished to publish them to common men, he desisted and was thus restored to health. I also learned from **Theodectes** <note>Theodectes of Phaselis (c. 380–334 BC) was a renowned rhetorician and tragic poet.</note>, the tragic poet, that when he was about to introduce something from the records in the Book [the Torah] into one of his dramas, his vision became clouded with cataracts. Sensing that this had happened to him for this reason, he propitiated God and was restored after many days. When the King heard these things from **Demetrius** <note>Demetrius of Phalerum, the overseer of the library at Alexandria.</note>, as previously stated, he did obeisance [to the books] and ordered that great care be taken of the volumes and that they be preserved in holiness. Let these things be summarized for us from the writing of the aforementioned author [Aristeas]. Now then, let us also behold the constitution of the legislation according to **Moses** from the works of distinguished men. First, I will set forth the account of **Philo** regarding the journey of the Jews from Egypt, which took place under the leadership of Moses; this is from his first book, which he entitled *Hypothetica* <note>The *Hypothetica* (or *Apology for the Jews*) is a lost work of Philo of Alexandria; these fragments are preserved primarily here in Eusebius.</note>. There, writing a defense of the Jews as if against their accusers, he says the following:

->**Philo on the Journey of the Jews from Egypt.**<-

» Their ancient ancestor was of the **Chaldaeans** <note>A reference to Abraham, who migrated from Ur of the Chaldees.</note>, and this people arose as migrants from Egypt, having moved from **Syene** <note>A city on the southern border of Egypt, modern Aswan.</note> long ago. They were a multitude of countless thousands, and since the land was not sufficient for them, and moreover, being of a youthful spirit and remaining great in number—and at the same time, because God was revealing their departure to them through visions and dreams—they set out (none the less than if driven by some divine power) toward their fatherland and ancient ground. It was from there that that ancestor of theirs had moved into Egypt, whether it seemed good to God or because of some mission, he was most blessed of all; so that from him until the present, their nation has both existed and remained, surpassing others so greatly in its large population. And he says it was no small matter: a leader guided them in their departure and journey, one man from among the many, who was—if you will—extraordinary. Thus, [his accusers] might revile him as a **sorcerer and a juggler of words** <note>original: "γόητα καὶ κέρκωπα λόγων" (goēta kai kerkōpa logōn); "Kerkops" refers to a mythical thievish forest creature, used here to mean a deceptive trickster.</note>. Yet he possessed a noble sorcery and a great capacity for work, by which he preserved the entire people through waterless places and famine, and through ignorance of the roads and of the things that befell them. Not only did he bring them safely into a state of abundance, as if in total cheerfulness, and through the midst of the nations lying between them, but he also kept them free from rebellion toward one another, and especially toward himself. And this was surely for no short time, but for a period such as one would not expect even a single household to remain together in harmony with total cheerfulness. Neither thirst, nor famine, nor the wasting of bodies, nor fear of the future, nor ignorance of what was to come, turned those deceived and wandering peoples against that "sorcerer." And yet his counsel possessed such great art, or power of words, or intelligence, as to prevail over so many and such great absurdities that lead all men to destruction. For either he understood the natures of the men under him not ignorantly nor with difficulty, but found them obedient and not lacking foresight for the future; or, though they were extremely troubled, God smoothed away their difficulties.

„ ...and to preside, as it were, over both the present and the future. For whichever [law] appears to be most true from these things, it will clearly show its power toward their praise, honor, and zeal. As for the matters regarding their **Exodus**: since they came into this land, how they themselves were established and held the territory is shown in the **sacred records**. I myself deem it more right to go through the probabilities concerning them by means of history rather than by mere reasoning. For was it by a plan of war and a multitude of bodies that they extended themselves, and though shut in at the end, they nevertheless broke through with weapons in their hands, and then took the country by force, defeating both **Syrians** and **Phoenicians** <note>original: "σύρους τε ὁμοῦ καὶ φοίνικας" (syrous te homou kai phoinikas); referring to the inhabitants of Canaan encountered by the Israelites.</note> who were fighting in their own land? Or should we suppose that they were un-warlike and unmanly and few in number, lacking the preparation for war, yet they met with respect among these people or received the land from willing hands? Then, after a short time and not long after, they built the whole temple and established all other things pertaining to piety and purification? For these things, as it seems, clearly show that they were acknowledged to be **most beloved of God** <note>original: "θεοφιλεστάτους" (theophilestatous); a common term in Hellenistic Jewish literature to denote divine favor.</note> even among their enemies. For they ought to have been held under accusation by those whose land they had suddenly entered as if by seizure. Since they met with such respect and honor among these people, how do they not appear to show an excess of good fortune in their choice? But whether we speak of the second or third things in order after these: was it due to their lawlessness and disobedience, or to their holiness, justice, and piety? Indeed, they had a man—whoever he was who gave them their laws—whom they admired so greatly that whatever seemed good to him, seemed good to them as well. Whether he devised them himself or heard them from a **divine spirit** <note>original: "δαίμονος" (daimonos); in this context, Philo uses the term to mean a divine or supernatural being, referring to the revelation to Moses.</note> and declared them, they refer it all to God. Although more than **two thousand years** <note>Philo argues for the extreme antiquity of the Jewish Law to prove its superiority over Greek philosophy and legislation.</note> have passed—I cannot say exactly how many, but certainly more than two thousand years—they have not moved even a single word of what was written by him, but would rather undergo death ten thousand times than be persuaded to act contrary to his laws and customs.“ Having said these things, he summarizes the **constitution** <note>original: "πολιτείαν" (politeian); referring to the social and legal structure of the nation.</note> established for the Jewish nation by the laws of **Moses**, writing as follows:

### On the God-fearing Constitution according to Moses.

„Is there anything among other nations that is like or similar to these things? Does it seem to be humble, or involving legal inducements, pretenses, delays, whispers, and again suspicions? Not at all; everything is simple and clear. If you commit **pederasty**, if you commit **adultery**, if you violate a male child—do not even speak of it—but if you do the same to a female, if you prostitute yourself, if you suffer any shameful thing contrary to your age, or even if it is only suspected, **death is the penalty**. If you treat a slave’s body with insolence, or a free man’s, if you keep someone in bonds, if you kidnap and sell them, if you steal profane things or sacred things, if you are impious—not in deed alone, but even in a chance word—against God himself (may God be merciful to us even for our good intentions in these matters, it is not even worthy to speak of it), but against a father or mother, or your own benefactor, **death is likewise the penalty**. And this is not common or accidental, but it is necessary that the one who has merely spoken be condemned, as having committed no less an impiety than if he had transgressed the law. But then again, consider how **wives are to serve their husbands**, not for any insolence, but for obedience in all things; and that **parents are to rule their children** for the sake of the safety and great care of their own possessions...

„ [He ordained] that each individual should be the master of his own property, provided that he does not falsely claim God's name for it, nor pretend to dedicate things to God that he wishes to keep. But if he should happen to make a promise by word alone, it is not permitted for him to touch his possessions with unclean hands; <note>original: "ψαῦσαί γε ἁγνὴν αὐτῶν οὐκ ἔστιν" — likely a scribal error in the transcription for "ἁγνοῖς" or "ἁγναῖς"; the sense is that once a vow is made, the property becomes sacred and the owner's ordinary use of it is restricted.</note> rather, he is immediately excluded from all of them. Let no one invoke God’s name for personal gain, nor plunder the offerings of others, nor even his own dedicated goods. As I said, to choose and to take even a single word for oneself [is forbidden]. Such were their insights. If all things belong to the priests of all, whether they repent or desire, <note>This sentence appears slightly fragmented or corrupted in the transcription.</note> we deliberate on the things spoken, and the soul is made clear. And so the same logic applies to the people. If a husband declares his wife’s food to be sacred, <term>Corban</term> <note>original: "ἱερὰν εἶναι" (to be sacred); this refers to the practice of 'Corban' where an object is declared a gift to God, thus prohibiting its use by others.</note> he must abstain from that food; and likewise if a father does so to a son, or a ruler to a subject. The same applies to the surrender of things so dedicated; the most perfect and greatest release is the decision of the priest. For through God, he is the master of receiving it. And after this, the piety shown by those who are always more in authority makes God merciful, so that there is no necessity to accept any annulment.

„ There are indeed certain reminders regarding these matters, such as those found in unwritten customs and laws, and even in the written laws themselves: that which a person hates to suffer, he should not do himself. <note>An early expression of the 'Golden Rule,' common in both Jewish and Greek ethics.</note> What you did not lay down, you must not take up—not even from a storehouse, nor from a garden, nor from a threshing floor. Furthermore, one should not steal anything, whether large or small. Do not begrudge fire to one who needs it; do not block springs of water. But also, to beggars and the disabled, provide food as a sacred duty before God. Do not prevent the burial of the dead, but even cast upon them as much earth as is required for piety. Do not move the graves or monuments of the departed at all. Do not inflict more chains or any greater evil than is necessary. Do not castrate the race of men, nor cause abortion in women by drugs or other devices. Again, do not mistreat animals, whether those shown to be in the mountains or those established by a lawgiver. Do not destroy seed, do not enslave the offspring. Do not offer an unjust yoke, nor an unmeasured <term>choinix</term> <note>original: "χοίνικα ἄμετρον"; a choinix was a Greek dry measure, roughly a quart. The law forbids using deceptive containers in trade.</note>, nor unjust currency. Do not reveal the secrets of friends during a time of enmity.

„ Where indeed, by God, are those <term>Bouzygia</term> <note>original: "βουζύγια" (bouzygia); these were ancient Athenian ritual curses against those who violated basic social taboos, such as refusing water or failing to bury a body. Philo argues that Jewish law covers all these and more.</note> of ours? But look at these other things: do not separate parents from children, even if you hold them as captives; do not separate a wife from her husband, even if a master has bought her legally. These are surely more solemn and greater matters. But also consider small or common things: it says do not empty a domestic bird's nest, and do not kill animals that come as suppliants for protection. If such a thing is evident, would you say these are worth nothing? But the law concerning them is great, and the cause of all diligence, in which the proclamations are great, as are the curses and the threats of utter destruction; and God is the overseer of such things and the punisher everywhere.

„ And after a short while he says: [The lawgiver required] not just a single day, if it should happen, or rather not even one, but many—and these not immediately following one another, but at intervals—to stand by and be strengthened, as is always reasonable. This was not the custom among the profane, where such things were not established. For by Zeus, this was not introduced among them for the sake of exercise alone, so that they might be equally strong to act or to refrain from works if necessary? Not at all. But if a lawgiver thought it necessary for some great and wonderful work, he wanted them not only to be capable of acting or not acting, but also to be experienced in the laws and customs of their fathers. What then did he do on these **seventh days**? He required them to assemble in the same place, and sitting with one another in modesty and order, to listen to the laws, so that no one would be ignorant of them. And indeed, they always come together and sit with one another; the many in silence, unless [the leader speaks]...

>> it is customary to offer further commentary to those who are reading. One of the priests who is present, or one of the elders, reads the sacred laws to them and explains each point individually until nearly late evening. From this experience, they depart with an expert knowledge of the sacred laws and having made great progress in piety. Does it not seem to you that these practices are more necessary for them than any other serious pursuit? Consequently, they do not need to go to legal experts <note>original: "θεσμωιδεῖς" — literally "law-singers" or those who proclaim the laws; Philo is emphasizing that the average person is so well-educated in the Law they do not need professional legal counsel for daily life.</note> regarding what they ought to do, nor do they ask questions of others. Nor do they act recklessly on their own through ignorance of the laws. Instead, if you should stir any one of them and inquire about the laws of their ancestors, he is ready and able to speak easily; a husband is capable of passing on the laws to his wife, a father to his child, and a master to his slaves. Indeed, regarding the seventh year, <term>the Sabbatical Year</term> <note>original: "ἔτους τοῦ ἑβδόμου"; known in Hebrew as Shmita, this was the year of "release" where the land was left fallow.</note> it is likewise easy to speak, though the practice is perhaps not the same. For they do not themselves abstain from all work as they do on those seventh days [the weekly Sabbaths]. Instead, they let the land lie fallow for the sake of future abundance. For the land differs greatly when it has received a rest, being farmed again the following year, rather than being worn out by the continuity of labor. This is the same thing that happens to bodies, where rest leads to strength. For doctors do not apply ointments and prescribe certain rests from labor for the sake of health alone. For constant and unchanging activity, especially in labor, always seems to be harmful. There is a sign of this: for they would never accept that the land itself should be worked by messengers <note>original: "ἐπ’ ἀγγέλλοις αὐτοῖς" — this suggests that the law is not merely a human convenience but a divine ordinance that even spiritual beings or deputies cannot bypass.</note> so as to spare themselves in this seventh year and then surrender all the fruits [to the owner]. For they did not believe that they alone should abstain from labors—and even if they did this, it would be nothing to wonder at—but rather that the land should receive a certain relaxation and ease for the beginning of another cycle of care and farming. For what, by God, prevented them from leasing out the land during that year and collecting the tribute from the workers for that year? But as I said, it seems to me they do not allow the land to rest in such a way out of any [purely economic] foresight. Their humanity <note>original: "φιλανθρωπίας" — philanthropy or love of mankind.</note> is truly a great sign of this. For since they themselves abstain from work during that year, they do not think it right to gather or store up the crops that grow, as these did not proceed from their own labors. Instead, because God has provided for them and the earth produces of its own accord, they allow those who wish or those in need—whether travelers or others—to use the produce without fear. Let this be enough for you regarding these matters. As for the fact that he [Moses] established the law for them regarding the number seven <note>original: "ταῖς ἑβδομὰς"; the Heptad.</note>, you would not ask this of me, as you have perhaps often heard from many doctors, naturalists, and philosophers about the seventh [number], and what power it has both over the universe and especially over human nature. This is the discourse on the seventh.

” ...to the rule of a few <note>original: "ὀλίγων δυναστείαις" — referring to an oligarchy.</note>, while others entrusted the authority of their governments to the masses <note>original: "πλήθεσιν" — referring to a democracy.</note>. But our lawgiver, Moses, did not look toward any of these forms. Instead, to use a term that might seem forced, he designated the government a **theocracy** <note>original: "θεοκρατίαν" — this is the first recorded use of the word "theocracy" in history, meaning "rule by God."</note>, attributing all authority and power to God. He persuaded everyone to look to Him, as He is the cause of all good things—those that are common to all people and those that they themselves obtained when they prayed in desperate times. He taught that it is impossible to escape God's notice, neither in His mind nor in any of our actions, nor even in our private thoughts. 

” Furthermore, he revealed God to be **unbegotten** <note>original: "ἀγένητον" — existing without a beginning.</note> and unchangeable throughout eternal time, surpassing all mortal beauty. Known to us by His power, yet unknown in His essential nature. I will put aside for now the fact that the wisest among the Greeks were taught to think these things about God, having been provided with these principles by him <insert>Moses</insert>. However, they have borne strong witness that these ideas are beautiful and fitting to the nature and majesty of God. For indeed **Pythagoras**, **Anaxagoras**, and **Plato**, as well as the philosophers of the **Stoic** school <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς στοᾶς" — the Stoics, who taught that virtue is based on knowledge and living in harmony with divine reason.</note> after him, and nearly everyone else, appear to have held these views regarding the nature of God. 

” Yet, while these philosophers spoke to only a few people, they did not dare to bring the truth of their doctrine to the masses who were already gripped by common opinions. Our lawgiver, however, by making his actions harmonize with his laws, not only persuaded his contemporaries, but also planted this unshakeable faith in God in all those who would come after them. The reason for this is that he excelled greatly in the way he crafted his legislation for the benefit of all. 

” He did not make **piety** <term>eusebeia</term> <note>religious devotion and respect for the divine.</note> just one part of virtue, but rather he made the other virtues parts of piety, encompassing them and establishing them as such. I refer to **justice**, **temperance**, **fortitude**, and the mutual **harmony** of citizens in all matters. For all actions, occupations, and words are referred back to our piety toward God. 

” He left none of these things unexamined or undefined. The **Spartans** <note>original: "λακεδαιμόνιοι"</note> and the **Cretans** educated through habits, not through words. The **Athenians** and almost all other Greeks commanded what one should or should not do through laws, but they neglected to make those actions habitual through actual practice. 

” But our lawgiver combined both of these with great care. He neither left the practice of habits "mute," nor did he allow the instruction of the law to go unpracticed. Instead, beginning immediately from the earliest upbringing and the way of life in each person’s home, he left nothing—not even the smallest detail—to the individual's whim. ” He did this so that, living under the law as if under a father or a master, we might not commit any sin, whether intentionally or through ignorance. " ...it is customary to add a blessing to the readings; and let one of the priests present, or one of the elders, read the sacred laws to them, and explain them point by point until almost late evening. » ...legislators to fail, and most people are so far from living according to their own laws that they almost do not even know them. Instead, when they commit an offense, they only then learn from others that they have transgressed the law. Even those who hold the highest and most authoritative offices among them admit their ignorance; for they must seat experts <note>literally "overseers" or "assessors"</note> beside them in the administration of public affairs—men who promise to have experience in the laws. 

» But should anyone ask any one of us, he could recite the laws more easily than his own name. Because we learn them thoroughly from our very first perceptions, we have them engraved in our souls, as it were. Consequently, a transgressor is rare, and escaping punishment is impossible. 

» This, first of all, has produced a wonderful harmony among us. For having one and the same opinion about God, and differing in no way from one another in our manner of life and customs, results in the most beautiful "symphony" in human character. Only among us will you not hear contradictory accounts about God—the kind that are so frequent among others. 

» Among other nations, it is not only common people who say whatever strikes them at the moment; even among their philosophers, some have dared to use their arguments to completely do away with the nature of God, while others try to strip away His <term>providence</term> <note>original: "πρόνοια" (*pronoia*), the concept that God actively cares for and governs the world.</note> over humanity. Nor will you see any difference in our daily practices; instead, our actions are common to all. 

» We have one single doctrine that agrees with the Law regarding God: we say that He watches over all things. Furthermore, regarding the practices of life, you could hear even our women and our servants saying that all things must have <term>piety</term> <note>original: "εὐσέβειαν" (*eusebeian*), meaning religious devotion or godliness.</note> as their goal. 

» This is why some people bring a charge against us: that we have not produced men famous for "new" virtues in our deeds or words. This is a logical result. For while other people think it is noble to remain faithful to none of their ancestral traditions, and they give the highest testimony of wisdom to those who most daringly transgress them, we, on the contrary, have assumed that there is only one form of wisdom and virtue: to neither do nor even *think* anything at all contrary to what was originally established by our laws.

» This might reasonably be seen as proof that our Law was most excellently established. For when laws are not made in this way, experience proves they need correction. But for us, who are convinced that the Law was established from the beginning according to the will of God, it is no longer even a matter of <term>piety</term> to fail to guard it. 

» For what part of it could one move? What better thing could one discover? Or what could one borrow from others as an improvement? Could one change the whole structure of the government? And what could be more beautiful or more just than a system that has made God the leader of all things? 

» It entrusts the administration of the greatest matters to the priests collectively, and then again, it has entrusted the leadership over the other priests to the High Priest. Our first Lawgiver <note>Moses</note> did not appoint these men to such honor because of wealth or any other accidental advantages; rather, he handed over the service of God to those who surpassed others in their power of persuasion and their <term>self-control</term> <note>original: "σωφροσύνῃ" (*sophrosyne*), a classical virtue implying moderation and soundness of mind.</note>. 

» These men were appointed as overseers of all things, judges of disputes, and punishers of those who are condemned. What form of government, then, could be holier than this? What honor more fitting for God? The entire multitude is prepared for piety, and the special care of it is entrusted to the priests. The whole state is organized like a sacred mystery rite <note>original: "τελετή" (*telete*), referring to religious initiations or ceremonies.</note>. # PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 8

### PAGE 215

-> **PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 8** <-

...practicing for only a few days <note>Josephus is likely contrasting Jewish life with Greek "mysteries" or festivals that lasted only a short time</note> (the sort of people who are unable to keep it up), calling them "mysteries" and "rites." We, however, observe these things with great pleasure and an unchangeable purpose throughout all time. 

What then are these simple and well-known announcements and proclamations? The first is that which speaks concerning God: God possesses all things; He is perfectly complete and blessed in Himself, and self-sufficient for all. He is the beginning, the middle, and the end of all things. He is manifest through His works and His graces, and more visible than any other thing whatever, yet in His form and His greatness, He is most invisible to us. All matter is unworthy to be His image, even if it be most precious, and every art is unskillful in its attempt to represent Him. We have never seen anything like Him, nor can we conceive of it, nor is it holy to try to imagine it. 

We see His works: the light, the heaven, the earth, the sun and moon, the waters, the generations of living creatures, and the budding of fruits. These things God made—not with hands, not with labor, and without needing any workers to assist Him—but because He willed them to be good, they were immediately created. Him all must follow, and Him they must serve by practicing <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "ἀρετή" (*arete*), meaning moral excellence or "acting as one's best self."</note>. For this is the most holy way to serve God.

There is one temple for the one God <note>A reference to the Second Temple in Jerusalem, emphasizing the unity of the Jewish faith</note>, for "like is always friendly to like." This temple is common to all, just as God is common to all. The priests serve there continually, and the one who is always first in his lineage leads them. He, along with his fellow priests, shall sacrifice to God, guard the laws, judge disputed matters, and punish those who are convicted. Anyone who does not obey him will suffer punishment as if he were acting impiously toward God Himself.

We offer sacrifices not for our own drunkenness—for such a thing is displeasing to God and would provide an excuse for insolence and luxury—but in a sober, orderly, and holy manner, so that the worshipers may be at their most self-controlled. At the sacrifice, one must first pray for the common safety <note>or "welfare of the community"</note>, and only then for oneself. For we were born for fellowship, and he who prefers this fellowship over his own private interest would be most pleasing to God. 

Let the petition and prayer to God not be that He might give us good things—for He has already given them of His own accord and laid them out in the open for all—but that we might be able to receive them, and having received them, that we might keep them. The law has prescribed purifications for the sacrifice: from mourning, from the bed of childbirth, from sexual relations, and from many other things which would be too long to write now.

Such is our account concerning God and His worship—which is the law itself. And what are the laws concerning marriage? The law recognizes only the natural union with a woman, and that only if it is for the sake of children. It detests the union of males with males, and death is the penalty if anyone attempts it. 

The law commands one to marry, not looking for a dowry, nor by violent abduction, nor again by persuading through trickery and deceit, but by seeking the hand of the woman from the one who has the authority to give her <note>In ancient contexts, this usually referred to the father or male guardian</note>, choosing one who is suitable by kinship. "A woman," it says, "is inferior to a man in all things." <note>This reflects the 1st-century patriarchal legal framework of the Roman and Jewish world; Josephus is presenting this as an argument for social order</note>. Therefore, let her obey, not for the sake of being insulted, but so that she may be directed, for God gave authority to the man. 

The husband must live with this woman alone; but to attempt another man’s wife is unholy. If anyone should do this, there is no escape from the death penalty, whether he rapes a virgin betrothed to another, or persuades a married woman. The law commands us to bring up all our children. It forbids women either to abort what is sown or to destroy it; if a woman is found doing so, she would be a child-slayer for destroying a soul and diminishing the race. 

Therefore, if anyone approaches the bed for the purpose of corruption, he is unclean at the time it is proper. And after the lawful intercourse of man and woman, the law requires them to bathe, for it considers that the soul has undergone a transition into another state. For that which is implanted in bodies suffers, and when it is again separated by death... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence, discussing the spiritual nature of procreation and the body</note>

He ordered for all Jews—indeed, he did not even permit the performance of a sacrifice upon the birth of children, nor for them to make such occasions an excuse for drunkenness. Instead, he ordained that the very beginning of their upbringing should be temperate; he commanded them to be educated in letters and the matters concerning the laws, and to understand the deeds of their ancestors, so that they might imitate them. This was so that, being raised with these laws, they might neither transgress them nor have any excuse of ignorance. —— He also provided for the sacred duty toward the deceased, not by means of expensive burial shrouds or the construction of conspicuous monuments. Instead, he ordered that the funeral rites be performed by the closest relatives, and that all passersby should join and mourn with a funeral procession. He also commanded the cleansing of the house and its inhabitants after a death, so that one who has committed murder might be as far as possible from appearing pure. He ranked the honor of parents second only to the honor toward God. And for the one who does not return the favors received from them, but fails in any way, he delivers him to be beaten to death. <note>original: "ἀποτύμπανον" (*apotumpanon*). This refers to a severe form of corporal punishment or execution, often involving being beaten with clubs or fastened to a wooden plank.</note> He also ordered all to honor their elders, because he says "God is the most ancient." He allows nothing to be hidden from friends; for that would not be friendship which does not trust in all things. And if an enmity should occur, he has forbidden the revealing of secrets. If anyone should take a bribe while acting as a judge, the penalty is death. One who overlooks a suppliant when it is in their power to help is held accountable. That which a person did not deposit, they shall not take away. And one shall not touch anything belonging to another. One who lends shall not take interest. These things, and many others like them, maintain our community with one another.

It is also worth seeing how the lawgiver took thought for <term>fairness</term> <note>original: "ἐπιεικείας" (*epieikeias*)—a Greek term for equity, mercy, or the spirit of the law rather than just the letter.</note> toward foreigners. For he will be seen to have made the best provision of all, so that we neither destroy our own customs nor envy those who choose to share in ours. For all those who wish to live under the same laws as us, having come over to them, he receives kindly; for he considers that kinship is not based on birth alone, but also on the choice of life. But those who approach us only incidentally he did not wish to be mixed into our daily life. For the rest, however, he has commanded that we provide those things which are necessary to share: to provide fire, water, and food to all who need them, and to show the way, and not to leave the unburied to be overlooked. He also deems it right to judge with fairness even toward enemies. For he does not allow their land to be burned, nor has he permitted the cutting down of cultivated trees. Furthermore, he has forbidden the stripping of those who have fallen in battle. And he took thought for captives, that they should be free from outrage—especially the women. He thus educated us in gentleness and humanity, so that we should not even neglect the irrational animals. For he allowed only the lawful use of them and forbade every other. Those animals which flee to our houses as if seeking refuge, he forbade us to kill. Nor did he permit the taking of parent birds together with their young. He commanded us to spare even the working animals of an enemy, and not to kill them. Thus, from every side, he prepared the way for fairness, using the aforementioned laws for instruction. On the other hand, he appointed punishments against those who transgress, not without a stated cause. For the penalty for most transgressions is death—if one commits adultery, if one rapes a maiden, if one dares to make a sexual attempt on a male, or if the one being tried submits to such an act. The law is equally unyielding regarding slaves. Furthermore, there are punishments if anyone should commit a crime regarding measures or weights, or concerning an unjust sale made with deceit. And if anyone steals another’s property, or takes what they did not deposit, there are punishments for all—not like those among other nations, but much more severe. For regarding the mistreatment of parents or impiety toward God, even if a person only intends to do it, they are immediately put to death. To the...
