...indeed, for those who do everything according to the laws. The prize is not silver, nor gold, nor a crown of wild olive <note>original: *kotinos*—the traditional prize for winners at the Olympic Games</note> or parsley <note>original: *selinon*—the prize at the Nemean and Isthmian Games</note>, nor any such public proclamation. Instead, each person, having their own conscience as witness, has believed—the legislator <note>Referring to Moses.</note> having prophesied and God having provided strong faith—that for those who keep the laws, and if it should be necessary to die for them, die willingly, God has granted that they come into being again and receive a better life in turn <note>original: *ek peritropēs*. This refers to Josephus’s description of the Jewish belief in the resurrection or the renewal of life as a cycle or "return."</note>.

<margin>A</margin> I would hesitate to write these things now if it were not clear to everyone through our deeds that many of our people, and many times already, have chosen to suffer everything nobly rather than speak even a single word against the Law. And yet, if it did not happen that our nation was well-known to all men, and if our voluntary adherence to the laws were not manifest, then if someone—either by writing a book or speaking on his own—claimed to know such a group among the Greeks, or said he had found people somewhere outside the known world who held such a solemn opinion about God, and who had for a long age remained firm in their laws, I think everyone would marvel at them because of the constant changes among themselves <note>Josephus is contrasting the stability of Jewish law with the frequent political revolutions and legal changes in Greek city-states.</note>. 

Even those who have attempted to write about similar matters of constitution and laws are accused of composing wonders, as if they were taking up impossible themes. Indeed, we should bid farewell to those philosophers who treated such subjects in their writings. Even Plato—who is admired by the Greeks for the dignity of his life and the power of his words, and for surpassing all who have been in philosophy in persuasion—is almost mocked and ridiculed by those who claim to be experts in politics. And yet, if one examines his work, one would frequently find it easier to follow the customs of the masses. Plato himself admitted that it was not safe to bring the true opinion about God to the ignorance of the crowds. 

But Plato’s words are considered empty, though beautifully written with great authority. Most of all, people admire Lycurgus among the legislators, and everyone sings the praises of Sparta because they endured for so long under his laws. Therefore, let this be admitted as a proof of virtue: to obey the laws. But let those who admire the Lacedaemonians <note>Lacedaemonians is another name for the Spartans.</note> compare the length of their time to the more than two thousand years of our constitution. Furthermore, let them consider that the Lacedaemonians appeared to observe their laws strictly only as long as they had their freedom; but when changes of fortune happened to them, they forgot almost all their laws. We, however, having been in countless circumstances because of the changes of the kings who ruled over Asia, have not betrayed our laws even in the most extreme loss of our power.

Josephus,

Republic*,

[...of the] comprehensive idea, he has constructed the teaching of his discourse in such a manner.

### Eleazar the High Priest’s outline of the <term>allegorical</term> <note>finding a deeper, symbolic meaning beneath the literal surface of the text</note> meaning within the sacred laws.

It is worth mentioning briefly the points demonstrated by him in response to the questions we asked. For many people believe that there is a certain excessive curiosity in our legislation regarding the matters of food, drink, and the animals considered to be "unclean."
<margin>A</margin> "When we asked why—since there is only one creation—some things are considered unclean for eating and others even for touching, since most people view the legislation as <note>original: *deisidaimonos*—meaning "superstitious" or "excessively fearful of the divine."</note> superstitious. In response to this, he began by considering how human interactions and associations work. He said that people, by associating with the wicked, catch their corruptions and become miserable throughout their lives; but if they live with the wise and prudent, they find a way to correct their lives from ignorance.

"Our legislator <note>Referring to Moses.</note> first distinguished the matters of piety and justice, teaching each point about them not merely through prohibitions, but by demonstration, making the harms evident as well as the punishments sent by God upon the guilty. For he demonstrated first of all that God is one, and that His power is made manifest through all things—for every place is filled with His sovereignty—and nothing done secretly by men on earth escapes His notice. Rather, whatever one does is manifest to Him, as are the things yet to happen.

"Elaborating on these points accurately and preparing the mind in advance, he showed that even if one merely thinks of committing an evil act, it would not be hidden, let alone if they performed it—demonstrating the power of God through the whole of the legislation. Having made this beginning, he showed that all other men besides us think there are many gods, although they themselves are far more powerful than the things they vainly worship. For they make images out of stone or wood and claim they are icons of those who discovered something useful for their lives; they worship these, though they have the evidence of the statues’ lack of sensation right at their feet. It would be utterly foolish to think someone is a god because of an invention. For they took things already existing in creation, combined them, and demonstrated their construction to be useful, but they did not create the materials themselves. Therefore, it is empty and vain to bestow divine honors on equals. Even now, there are many men more inventive and more learned than those of old, yet we would not go so far as to worship them—even if those who craft these myths and fables claim they were the wisest of men.

"What need is there to speak of other vanities, such as those of the Egyptians and those near them, who have placed their reliance on wild beasts and most kinds of creeping things and monsters? They worship these, and sacrifice to them while they are living and when they are dead. Therefore, the wise legislator, having considered each of these things and being equipped by God for the knowledge of all things, fenced us in with unbreakable barriers and iron walls, so that we should not mingle with any of the other nations in any way, remaining pure in body and in soul, liberated from vain opinions, worshipping the only God and the Power that is over the whole of creation. This is why the leading priests of the Egyptians, having looked deeply into many things and participated in affairs, call us 'men of God'..."

<margin>»</margin> ...us. We are not different from the rest in our intellects—unless one fails to worship the true God—but [others] are 
<margin>»</margin> "murderers" <note>This likely refers to those who live only for the consumption of living things without regard for the soul.</note> regarding food, drink, and shelter. For their entire disposition is

<margin>»</margin> And so, concerning these matters, I think enough has been said in our conversation 
<margin>»</margin> worthy of note, because of the majesty of the Law, which I have chosen to explain 
<margin>»</margin> to you, Philocrates <note>Philocrates is the recipient of the Letter of Aristeas, a legendary account of the translation of the Hebrew Bible into Greek.</note>, through the love of learning which you possess. These things 
<margin>»</margin> the High Priest went through as his appeal to him, distinguishing the forms of what was 
<margin>»</margin> proclaimed in the sacred laws, so that one might best be persuaded by the interpretations 
of the scriptures that were to be published.

Now, it is time to listen to Aristobulus <note>Aristobulus of Paneas (c. 2nd century BC) was a Jewish philosopher who lived in Alexandria and sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note>, who partook of the Aristotelian philosophy alongside his 
ancestral traditions, and what he said regarding the passages found in the sacred books 
that speak of the "limbs" of God. He is that same Aristobulus whom the second book 
of Maccabees mentions at the beginning <note>Referencing 2 Maccabees 1:10.</note>, in which it says that he addressed 
his writings to King Ptolemy to explain the Law.

### From Aristobulus, concerning the things named as the limbs of God.

<margin>»</margin> Besides the things already sufficiently stated regarding the questions at hand, you also 
<margin>»</margin> remarked, O King <note>Referring to King Ptolemy VI Philometor.</note>: "What is signified by our Law when it mentions hands, an arm, 
<margin>»</margin> a face, feet, and a path in relation to the divine power?" These things require a 
<margin>»</margin> proper explanation, and you will not find our explanations to be at all unacceptable. 
<margin>»</margin> I want to urge you first to take the interpretations in a natural <note>original: *physikos*—meaning a philosophical or allegorical interpretation based on the nature of things, rather than a literal one.</note> sense, 
<margin>»</margin> and to hold the fitting conception of God, and not to fall into a mythical or 
<margin>»</margin> human-like state of mind. For Moses, naming things in many ways when he wishes 
<margin>»</margin> to speak of other matters, makes his arguments regarding <term>natural dispositions</term> 
<margin>»</margin> <note>original: *physikas diatheseis*—the underlying reality or power behind physical descriptions.</note> by describing the arrangements of great affairs. Those who possess 
<margin>»</margin> the ability to think well wonder at the wisdom surrounding him and the divine spirit 
<margin>»</margin> by which he has been proclaimed a prophet. Among these are the aforementioned 
<margin>»</margin> philosophers, and many other poets who have taken great inspiration from him, for 
<margin>»</margin> which they are admired. But to those who do not share in this power and 
<margin>»</margin> understanding, but cling only to the written letter <note>original: *gegraptē*—the literal text.</note>, he does not appear 
<margin>»</margin> to be explaining anything magnificent. I will begin to take up each of the 
<margin>»</margin> meanings as far as I am able. But if I do not seem to hit upon the truth or 
<margin>»</margin> fail to persuade you, do not attach any irrationality to the Lawgiver, but 
<margin>»</margin> rather to me, for being unable to clearly explain the things he intended. 
<margin>»</margin> Now, "hands" are obviously understood among us in a common sense. For 
<margin>»</margin> whenever you, being King, send out your forces wishing to accomplish 
<margin>»</margin> something, we say: "The King has a great hand," with the listeners' minds 
<margin>»</margin> being directed toward the power <note>original: *dynamin*</note> that you possess. This is also 
<margin>»</margin> hinted at by Moses when he says in our Law: "With a mighty hand God 
<margin>»</margin> brought you out of Egypt" <note>Exodus 13:9.</note>. And again God says, "I will send out 
<margin>»</margin> my hand and strike the Egyptians" <note>Exodus 3:20.</note>. And regarding the death of the 
<margin>»</margin> livestock, Moses says to Pharaoh: "Behold, the hand of the Lord will be 
<margin>»</margin> upon your livestock, and upon all those in the fields—a great death" <note>Exodus 9:3.</note>. 
<margin>»</margin> Therefore, the "hands" are understood as the power of God. For it is also 
<margin>»</margin> possible to understand that our entire human life and its activities are 
<margin>»</margin> contained within our hands.

iiii.3
<meta>catchword: [treatises]</meta>

...through which the lawgiver <note>Referring to Moses</note> beautifully indicated majesty, saying that the fulfillments <note>original: συντελείας—Aristobulus is interpreting the completion or outcomes of God's will as His "hands."</note> are the **hands of God**. And "divine standing" <note>original: στάσις—referring to the stability of the natural order</note> might be well-spoken of, in accordance with majesty, as the **arrangement of the world**. By these things, God is over all, and all things are subordinate and have received their "standing," so that humans perceive them as immovable. I say this because never has heaven become earth, nor earth heaven; nor the sun a shining moon, nor the moon again a sun. Nor rivers become seas, nor sea become rivers. And the same logic applies to living creatures: for a man shall not be a wild beast, nor a beast a man. And the same holds for the rest. Regarding plants and other things, they are unchangeable, yet they undergo the same cycles of growth <note>original: ἐλπὶς—literally "hopes," but here suggesting the potential or stages of development</note> and decay within themselves. "Divine standing" might therefore be spoken of in this way, with all things being subject to God. 

And the "divine descent" <note>original: κατάβασις</note> upon the mountain is said to have occurred through the writing of the Law, at the time he was legislating, so that everyone might behold the active power of God. This "descent" is clear. And he <note>Aristobulus</note> himself explained these things thus, wishing to preserve the proper doctrine concerning God. For it is shown that the mountain burned greatly, as the lawgiver says, because God had descended, and there were voices of trumpets and the fire was burning uncontainably. For the multitude of the people—being no less than a million <note>original: ἑκατὸν μυριάδων—literally 100 myriads</note>, besides the minors assembled around the mountain, its circumference being no less than five days' journey—in every place of the vision, for all of them all around as they were encircling it, the burning fire was seen; so that the descent was not local. For God is everywhere. 

But he showed the power of fire, being more marvelous than all things and likely to dissolve everything, burning uncontainably yet consuming nothing, unless the dynamic power of God were present in it. For while the things growing on that mountain were being consumed violently <note>by the natural heat</note>, nothing [in the miracle] was harmed; instead, the grass of all stayed untouched by the fire, and the voices of trumpets sounded more vehemently along with the lightning-like discharge of the fire, though no such instruments were present, nor any one sounding them, but all things happening by divine arrangement. So it is clear because of these things that the divine descent occurred, because those beholding it clearly perceived each thing—neither the fire having burned anything, as was said before, nor the trumpet voices occurring through human action or the construction of instruments; but God, without any tools, was showing His own majesty through all things.

These are the words of Aristobulus. Since we have gone through the commands of the sacred laws and the pattern of the idea manifested in them, it would be next to note this: that the whole nation of the Jews is divided into two sections. One, the multitude, he brought under the instructions commanded according to the literal <note>original: ῥητὴν</note> meaning of the laws. The other, the order of those in a state of habit <note>original: ἐν ἕξει τάγμα—referring to those who have achieved a steady state of virtue or intellectual discipline</note>, he deemed worthy to attend to a philosophy more exalted and elevated above the many, and to the contemplation <note>original: θεωρίᾳ</note> of the things signified in the laws according to their meaning. This was the race of the Jewish philosophers, at whose life and discipline myriads <note>countless thousands</note> were amazed. Of their own people, the most distinguished—deemed worthy of memory—are Josephus and Philo, and many others. Passing over most of these, for the sake of a sample alone, I shall be satisfied for the present with the testimony of Philo, regarding what is shown in many of his own treatises...

Eusebius then classifies Jewish society into those who follow the Law literally and a "philosophical" class represented by Philo and Josephus.</summary>

### On the life of virtue among those of the Jews who anciently lived as philosophers.

> Our lawgiver <note>Referring to Moses</note> trained thousands of his disciples for communal living. These people are called **Essenes**, having been deemed worthy of such a title, I believe, because of their **holiness**. <note>original: Ἐσσαῖοι... ὁσιότητά — Philo is making a wordplay between the name "Essene" and the Greek word for "holiness," *hosiotēs*.</note> They inhabit many cities of Judea and many villages, living in large and populous groups. Their way of life is not defined by birth—for birth is not a matter of choice—but by a zeal for virtue and a longing for the love of mankind.

> Indeed, among the Essenes there are no mere infants, nor even adolescents or youths; for the characters of such ages are unstable and prone to change due to their lack of maturity. Instead, they are mature men, already leaning toward old age, who are no longer flooded by the physical impulses of the body nor led by their passions, but rather enjoy the only true and genuine freedom. 

> Their life is a witness to this freedom. No one among them dares to acquire any private property at all—not a house, not a slave, not a plot of land, not livestock, nor any other of the things that provide and maintain wealth. Instead, they place everything into a common fund for the group, and they all enjoy the benefit of it together. 

> They live in the same place, organizing themselves into "associations" <term>thiassous: communal or religious clubs</term> and shared meals, and they spend their lives constantly working for the common good. They undertake various labors, to which they devote themselves with tireless energy. They never use the cold, the heat, or any changes in the weather as an excuse; instead, they go to their accustomed tasks before the sun rises and only return with difficulty at sunset, rejoicing no less than those who have competed in athletic games. 

> For they believe that whatever work they practice is a form of exercise more beneficial to life, more pleasant to the soul and body, and more lasting than mere athletics, because their work does not cease when the body’s prime has passed. Some of them are tillers of the soil, skilled in sowing and farming. Others are shepherds, leading all kinds of livestock. Some look after beehives, while others are craftsmen in various trades, so that they lack nothing that necessity requires. They never delay anything that might be useful for providing supplies. 

> From these diverse labors, each man receives his wage and gives it to a single **steward** <term>tamia: a treasurer or manager</term> chosen by a show of hands. This steward takes the money and immediately buys the necessities, providing abundant food and the other things required for human life. 

> They live and eat together every day, being satisfied with the same things; they are lovers of frugality and avoid luxury as if it were a disease of the soul and body. Not only is their table shared, but so is their clothing. For there are thick cloaks laid out for winter and inexpensive tunics for summer, so that anyone who wishes may easily take whichever garment they want. For what belongs to one is considered to belong to all, and conversely, what belongs to all belongs to each individual. 

> Furthermore, if any of them should fall ill, he is not neglected because he cannot contribute, but is nursed using the common funds, receiving the care and attention of the whole group. As for the elderly, even if they happen to be childless, they end their lives in a most happy and prosperous old age, as if they were not just the fathers of many children, but fathers of a most excellent family. They are deemed worthy of such high privilege among their community, who choose to care for them by their own free will rather than out of natural necessity. From where else then, or on what [grounds]...

» ...and especially because they saw more keenly that marriage dissolves communal life; thus, they rejected it while practicing self-discipline to an exceptional degree. For none of the companions takes a wife, since a woman is a selfish creature, excessively jealous, and terrible at unsettling a man's character and leading him astray with constant charms. For having practiced the arts of persuasion—just as a spectacle on a stage tricks the eyes and ears—she deceives the **ruling mind** <note>original: τὸν ἡγεμόνα νοῦν — a Stoic term for the "rational faculty" or the part of the soul that makes decisions.</note> as if it were a deluded subject. 

» If children should be born, she is filled with pride and a boldness of speech; whatever she previously hinted at subtly with irony, she now calls out with a crude audacity. Acting shamelessly, she forces him to do things, each of which is an enemy to the community. For he who is bound by the charms of a wife or children, being concerned by natural necessity, is no longer the same toward others. Instead, he has secretly become a slave instead of a free man. 

» Because of this, their life is always celebrated. Thus, not only private citizens, but even great kings, admiring these men, are struck with awe and honor their dignity with even greater acceptance and honors. 

Let these things be set down from the aforementioned writing. <note>Philo's *Apology for the Jews*.</note> Now, from the treatise *On the Fact that Every Good Man is Free*, I will present the following:

->Regarding all of them.<-

» Moreover, Palestinian Syria is not barren of **excellence**, <note>original: καλοκαγαθίας (*kalokagathia*) — a Greek ideal of "gentlemanly virtue" or "noble character."</note> which is inhabited by a significant portion of the very populous nation of the Jews. There are some among them called **Essenes**, numbering over four thousand. In my opinion, they are named—though not in a precise Greek form—after **holiness**; <note>original: παρώνυμοι ὁσιότητος — Philo is again connecting the name "Essene" with the Greek word *hosios* (holy).</note> for they have become, above all, worshippers of God. They do not sacrifice animals, but rather deem it worthy to prepare their own minds in a holy manner. 

» These people live first in villages, avoiding the cities because of the lawlessness of those who live there. They know from experience that from the company of such people a soul-destroying disease arises, which is incurable for impious souls. Some among them till the soil, while others practice crafts that work for peace, benefiting both themselves and those nearby. They do not hoard silver or gold, nor do they acquire large tracts of land out of a desire for income, but rather provide only what is necessary for the requirements of life. 

» For alone among almost all men, they are without money and property by choice rather than by a lack of good fortune, yet they are considered the wealthiest, judging **frugality** <note>original: τὴν ὀλιγοδέειαν — literally "needing little."</note> and contentment to be true abundance. You would find no maker of arrows, spears, daggers, helmets, armor, or shields among them; nor any maker of weapons or machines, or anyone practicing anything related to war. Furthermore, they do not even dream of things that lead to vice in times of peace. They reject commerce, peddling, or seafaring, casting away every opportunity for greed. 

» There is not a single slave among them; instead, all are free, serving one another. They condemn masters not only as unjust for violating equality, but also as impious for overturning the law of nature. Nature, like a mother, gave birth to and nourished all people alike, making them true brothers—not just in name, but in reality. Yet, this kinship has been confused and destroyed by treacherous greed, creating estrangement instead of intimacy and hostility instead of friendship...

...of friendship, instead producing enmity. As for philosophy, they abandon the **logical** part to those who word-smith about the heavens <note>original: μετεωρολέσχαις — literally "heaven-chatterers," a derogatory term for those who study abstract logic or astronomy without practical benefit</note>, seeing it as unnecessary for the acquisition of virtue. They also set aside the **physical** part, regarding it as being beyond human nature—except for the parts of it concerning the existence of God and the creation of the universe. Instead, they work very hard at the **ethical** part <note>Philo is describing the three traditional branches of Greek philosophy: Logic, Physics, and Ethics, noting the Essenes focus almost exclusively on the latter.</note>, using as their guides their ancestral laws, which it would be impossible for a human soul to devise without divine inspiration.

These laws they are taught at all times, but especially on the **seventh days**. For the seventh day is considered sacred, during which they abstain from all other works and go to sacred places called **synagogues**. There, they sit in rows according to their age—the younger men below the elders—arranged with proper decorum, listening attentively. Then one of them takes the books and reads, while another of those most experienced comes forward and explains whatever is not well-known. For most of their philosophy is pursued through **symbols** <note>original: διὰ συμϐόλων — referring to the allegorical method of interpreting scripture</note> in accordance with ancient fashion.

They are instructed in piety, holiness, justice, domestic management, citizenship, the knowledge of what is truly good, evil, or indifferent, and how to choose what is right. In all of this, they use three rules and definitions: **love of God**, **love of virtue**, and **love of humanity**.

Of the **love of God**, they provide a thousand examples: a constant and continuous purity throughout their whole life, the refusal to take oaths, the refusal to lie, and the belief that the Divine is the cause of all good things but of no evil.

Of the **love of virtue**, they show: freedom from the love of money, of glory, and of pleasure; self-control, endurance, and furthermore, having few needs, simplicity, good nature, lack of conceit, law-abidingness, stability, and everything similar to these.

Of the **love of humanity**, they show: goodwill, equality, and a fellowship that is beyond all description, about which it is not out of place to speak briefly.

First, then, no one’s house is his own in such a way that it does not also belong to everyone. For besides living together in communities <note>original: θιάσους — groups or associations</note>, their homes are open to those of the same sect who arrive from elsewhere. Furthermore, there is one treasury for everyone and shared expenses; they have shared clothes and shared food, having established communal meals. One could not find elsewhere the practice of sharing the same roof, the same way of life, or the same table more firmly established in reality—and for good reason. For whatever they earn by working during the day for wages, they do not keep as their own, but bring it into the middle for the common use of those who wish to use it.

Those who are sick are not neglected because they are unable to work; they have at their disposal what is needed for their treatment from the common funds, so that they may spend from a more than sufficient supply with total peace of mind. There is respect and care for the elders, just as parents are cared for by their own legitimate children, being supported in their old age by a thousand hands and minds in the most abundant generosity.

Such are the holy **athletes of virtue** produced by a philosophy free from unnecessary meddling, setting forth praiseworthy deeds as their exercises. From these practices, an unconquerable freedom is established. This is evidenced by the many powerful rulers who have risen up against their land at various times, men differing in their natural characters and their intentions. Some of these rulers, striving to surpass the untamed cruelty of wild beasts, left nothing undone in the way of savagery, slaughtering their subjects in herds, or even butchering them limb by limb while still alive like meat-cutters, until they themselves suffered the same calamities by the Justice that oversees human affairs. Others, however, shifted their turbulent and frenzied nature into another form of wickedness...

<summary>Philo describes the Essenes' rejection of abstract philosophy in favor of practical Ethics, their Sabbath synagogue practices, and their total communal lifestyle, including shared wealth and care for the elderly. He contrasts their "unconquerable freedom" with the cruelty of historical tyrants.</summary>

...practicing out of bitterness, speaking quietly, and assuming a grave-tempered character through the hypocrisy of a calmer voice—injecting the venom of poisonous dogs—they were themselves the causes of the evils that occurred. They left behind many monuments of their own impiety and hatred of humanity in the incurable disasters of those who suffered. But in truth, no one, whether of a cruel spirit or of a long-standing deceitful and treacherous nature, was able to find grounds to accuse the aforementioned gathering of the holy ones <note>original: ἐναγῶν ἢ ὁσίων — here used to contrast the "cursed" or "polluted" with the "holy."</note>. Instead, being overcome by the noble character <term>kalokagathia (nobility of character and virtue)</term> of these men, everyone spoke of them as being naturally independent and free. They celebrated their communal meals <note>original: συσσίτια — a term often used for the shared meals of Spartan citizens, here applied to the Essene community</note> and their fellowship, which is superior to any description—a most clear proof of a perfect and exceedingly happy life.

Such then are the matters concerning the philosophical discipline and way of life among the Jews, according to what has been set forth. As for the rest of their life, which the divine laws prescribed for the multitude of the entire nation, the discourse shall proceed to take these up in order. If it remains, after these things, to present the theological harmony of their views on the gods with the piety of their ancestors, so that the discourse may be rendered complete for us regarding this second proposition: since the oracles of the Scripture are set forth through the contents of this work, come then, let us return to the providence found in the thought of the wise men among the Jews. In this way, we may learn what sort of people the children of the Hebrews have been in theology and in the virtue of their reasoning. Once again, then, we must bring forward Philo, beginning from the first of his writings on the Law.

->Philo on God, and on the world being created.<-

For some, having admired the world more than the world-maker, declared it to be uncreated <term>agennēton (without a beginning or birth)</term> and eternal, ignorantly and falsely ascribing a great deal of inactivity to God. On the contrary, it was necessary to be struck with amazement at His powers as a Creator and Father, and not to glorify the object more than is proper. But Moses, having reached the very summit of philosophy, and having been taught the many and most essential truths of nature through divine oracles, knew that it is most necessary that among existing things there be an **active** cause and a **passive** cause. The active cause is the Mind <note>original: νοῦς — "Nous," the intellect or governing reason of the universe</note> of the universe, which is most pure and unmixed, better than knowledge, and better than Goodness itself and Beauty itself. The passive cause is soulless and motionless of itself, but having been moved, reshaped, and animated by the Mind, it changed into the most perfect work: this world. 

Those who claim the world is uncreated fail to realize that they are cutting away providence—the most useful and necessary element for piety. For reason dictates that a father and creator should take care of what has been brought into being. Indeed, a father aims for the survival of his offspring, and a craftsman for his creations; they use every device to ward off whatever is harmful, while longing to provide in every way whatever is useful and profitable. But toward that which was never "brought into being," there is no such kinship felt by one who did not make it. It is a contentious and useless doctrine, establishing a state of anarchy in this world—as if in a city—leaving it without a presiding officer, or an arbiter, or a judge, by whom it is proper that all things be administered and governed. 

But the great Moses, thinking that the "uncreated" was entirely foreign to the visible world—for everything perceptible to the senses is in a state of becoming and change, never remaining the same—assigned eternity <note>original: ἀϊδιότητα</note> to the invisible and intellectual realities as their brother and kinsman. To the things of the senses, however, he gave the appropriate name of "created." Since, therefore, this world is visible and perceptible to the senses...

<summary>Eusebius concludes his report on the Essenes' communal virtue and introduces Philo’s philosophical defense of the biblical creation story. Philo argues that the world must have been created by a divine Mind to ensure that God's providence and care for the universe remain logically consistent.</summary>

...this very world itself must necessarily be mortal; for this reason, [Moses] did not miss the mark when he recorded its genesis, theologizing with great solemnity. So much, then, concerning the fact that the world is created. This same man <note>Referring to Philo of Alexandria</note> discusses how the world is governed by providence in his treatise *On Providence*, where he most vigorously sets forth the arguments, dissolving the objections of the atheists and responding to them in order. Even if these excerpts seem somewhat long, I will not hide them, but will abridge most of them as they are necessary. He constructs the argument in this manner:

### On the world being governed by the providence of God.

"Do you say there is Providence in such great turmoil and confusion of affairs? For what 
<margin>„</margin> part of human life is truly ordered? Is it not rather full of unworthiness and 
<margin>„</margin> corruption? Or are you the only one who does not know that the most wicked and 
<margin>„</margin> evil of men are visited by an abundance of good things—wealth, reputation, and honors 
<margin>„</margin> from the masses? Or again, leadership, health, keenness of the senses, beauty, 
<margin>„</margin> strength, and the unhindered enjoyment of pleasures, both through the preparation of 
<margin>„</margin> fine foods and through a most robust physical constitution? Meanwhile, those who are 
<margin>„</margin> lovers of wisdom <term>phronēsis (practical wisdom)</term> and all virtue are, as 
<margin>„</margin> disciplined men, often most poor, and not a few are obscure, insignificant, 
<margin>„</margin> without reputation, and humble." After saying more than this for consideration and 
<margin>„</margin> memory, he next resolves these grievances through the following: "God is no tyrant 
<margin>„</margin> who has cast out cruelty—though he has performed all the works of such a raw 
<margin>„</margin> rule—but rather like a king who has received a gentle and lawful leadership, he 
<margin>„</margin> presides over the whole heaven and the world with justice. To a king, nothing is 
<margin>„</margin> more fitting or familiar than a child. For what a parent is to children in 
<margin>„</margin> family relations, a king is to a city, and God is to the world. He has joined two

<margin>„</margin> divine world. Receive this one argument, O soul, as a temporary deposit, and

<margin>„</margin> mean his own mind—into a slave of a thousand masters, such as love, desire, 
<margin>„</margin> pleasure, fear, grief, folly, intemperance, cowardice, and injustice, could never 
<margin>„</margin> be happy, even if the masses, who are fickle in judgment, consider them so—being 
<margin>„</margin> bribed by the twin evils of pride and empty opinion, which sweep away and lead off 
<margin>„</margin> unstable souls like a current..."

...they possessed the bitterness of those who practiced such things, whispering quietly, acting out a character burdened with hypocrisy in a subdued voice, showing the venomous tooth of dogs. They were the causes of their own confessed evils, and they left cities full of their own impiety and hatred of humanity, revealing the misfortunes of those who suffered. But indeed, no one—neither the most cruel-hearted, nor those of old who were deceitful and treacherous—was able to accuse the aforementioned company of lovers of holiness <note>original: "hosion," referring to the Essenes or the virtuous Jews described previously</note>. 

Instead, everyone, being weaker than the noble virtue <term>kalokagathia (the Greek ideal of being both "beautiful and good")</term> of these men, and according to the amount of natural freedom they possessed, were drawn to them. They sang the praises of their earnest pursuits and their superior fellowship in reason, which is the clearest sign of a perfect and exceedingly happy life. 

The things related by the philosopher [Philo] concerning the Jewish practice and way of life have been set forth through what preceded. But the remaining matters of life, which the divine laws prescribed among the multitude of the whole nation, the discourse will now take up and unfold. What, then, remains after this, but to present the harmony of the new theology <note>Eusebius refers to the "new" Christian teachings which he argues are in harmony with "old" Jewish wisdom</note> with the piety of the forefathers, so that the argument of our thesis may be proven complete? 

Since, therefore, the oracles of the scriptures are set before us in this present work, come then, let us look into the thoughts and mind of the wise men among the Jews, so that we may learn what kind of people the "children of the Hebrews" have become in theology and in the virtue of words. Again, therefore, Philo must be brought forward from the first [book] of his [writings] on the Law.

->### Philo on God, and on the world being created.<-

For some, admiring the world more than the Maker of the world, declared it to be uncreated and eternal, falsely and impiously charging God with total inactivity. On the contrary, they ought to have been struck with awe at His powers as Father and Creator, and not to have revered the world beyond measure. 

But Moses, having reached the very summit of philosophy, and having been taught many and most essential things regarding nature through divine oracles, knew that it is most necessary among existing things that there be an active cause and a passive cause. The active cause is the most pure and unmixed Mind of the whole, superior to knowledge, and superior even to the Good itself and the Beautiful itself. The passive part is soulless and motionless of itself, but having been moved and reshaped by the Mind, it changed into the most perfect work—this world. 

Those who say it is uncreated do not realize they are cutting away Providence, the most useful and necessary thing for piety. For reason dictates that the Father and Maker should care for what has been created. Indeed, a father aims for the preservation of his offspring, and a craftsman for his handiwork; he pushes away by every means everything that is harmful, while he longs to provide in every way everything that is useful and profitable. But toward that which is uncreated, there is no kinship for the one who did not make it. 

It is a hopeless and useless doctrine to establish anarchy in this world—as if in a city—having no overseer, or umpire, or judge, by whom it is lawful for all things to be managed and governed. But the great Moses, considering the "uncreated" state to be most alien to the visible world—for everything sensible is in a state of becoming and change, never remaining the same—assigned eternity to the invisible and intelligible as to a brother and kinsman. But to the sensible world, he gave the appropriate name [of "created"]. Since, therefore, the visible and sen— <meta>catchword: himself</meta>

Since this world is mortal, it must necessarily also be created; hence, it was not without purpose that he [Moses] recorded its origin, theologizing with great dignity. These things, then, concern uncreated things and the world. But the same man [Philo] also discusses **Providence** <note>original: "Pronoia"</note>, by which the whole is governed—not a one-time act of providence, but a most vigorous account—setting forth the objections of the atheists first, and answering them in order. Even if these points seem somewhat long, we have abridged most of them as necessary and have not strayed far from the point. He constructs the argument in this manner:

->**On the world being governed by the providence of God.**<-

<meta>This page continues Philo of Alexandria’s defense of Divine Providence, as quoted by Eusebius. On the previous page, Philo began addressing the "atheist" objection that the wicked prosper while the righteous suffer. He now transitions into a philosophical critique of material wealth, beauty, and physical strength, arguing that these "goods" are illusory compared to the true good of the soul.</meta>

### EUSEBIUS, EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, BOOK 8
<page-num>228</page-num>

The sun shines upon the greatest part of humanity. If, however, you were willing to stretch the **eye of the soul** <note>A Platonic metaphor: the "eye of the soul" refers to the capacity for intellectual and spiritual perception as opposed to physical sight.</note> to contemplate God's providence, insofar as it is possible for human reasoning, you would gain a clearer mental image of the true good and laugh at those things among us which you previously admired. For the lesser things are always honored in the absence of the better, inheriting their rank; but when the superior things appear, they withdraw, hidden by the excellence of the immaterial. Having been struck with awe by that god-like good and beauty, you will surely realize that none of the things spoken of by God <note>Or perhaps "spoken of as divine gifts" by the masses.</note> are, in themselves, worthy of a portion of the true Good. 

<margin>p</margin>
For consider that silver and gold mines are actually the most worthless part of the earth, falling entirely below those natures that produce useful fruits. For there is no comparison with food, without which wealth is merely helplessness and poverty. There is one most vivid test of this: **famine**, by which that which is truly necessary and useful is put to proof. At such times, those who have treasures everywhere would immediately and gladly exchange them for a small amount of food. But when there is an abundance of necessities, flowing and pouring through cities in a countless, unrestrained tide of ruin, men indulge in the goods of nature and fail to appreciate them, making **insolent satiety** <note>original: "koron hybristen"—a classic Greek concept where "satiety" (having too much) leads to "hubris" (outrageous arrogance).</note> the leader of their lives, stripping themselves for the acquisition of silver and gold. Having acquired these for the sake of profit, they wander like the blind along with the "beautiful" people, no longer seeing with their intellect because of **love of money** <note>original: "philargyria"</note>. They do not see that these are merely piles of earth, and that from them come the constraints of peace and the violence of war.

As for clothing, it is merely, as the poets say somewhere, the "flower of sheep" <note>A poetic way of describing wool.</note>. And the skill of the craftsmen is merely the praise of weavers. If someone prides himself on fame, welcoming the approval of the worthless, he is perhaps himself worthless. For "like rejoices in like." But if he receives a cleansing of his character, his ears will be healed—the very channels through which great diseases descend upon the soul. 

Let those who are puffed up by ignorance also learn not to carry their necks high <note>i.e., not to be haughty.</note> by looking at the countless herds of both domestic and wild animals, to whom strength and vigor have been allotted. For it is the height of absurdity to pride oneself on the virtues of beasts, whether comparing them to a tamed animal or to a man himself. 

Therefore, if you pride yourself on your own wisdom, or if you should exult in the beauty of your body, a short season will extinguish it before it reaches its full growth, darkening its deceptive prime. One can see these objects of contention in the lifeless works of molders and sculptors, and in the keen skill of artists in paintings, statues, and various weavings, in which both the refined and the **barbarian** <note>original: "barbaro"—referring to non-Greeks.</note> are esteemed in every city. 

None of these things, as I said, are deemed worthy by God to be a portion of the Good. And why should we wonder if they are not esteemed by God? For they are not even esteemed by those men who are dear to God, in whose eyes the truly good and beautiful are honored. Such men may have been born with a meager share of natural gifts, but they have adorned their nature through study and practice, of which a strict philosophy is the creator. 

But those who have cared for a "bastard" education <note>i.e., a superficial or false education that focuses on external rhetoric rather than internal virtue.</note> do not even imitate the physicians—those who, though they claim to heal the "mistress" (the soul), actually hand the body over to be enslaved by it. For whenever some unfortunate person falls ill, even if he be the **Great King** <note>A common reference to the King of Persia, used as a symbol of the ultimate earthly power and wealth.</note>, he wishes for many things to be present: the men's quarters, the women's quarters, paintings, silver, gold (both uncoined and minted), a multitude of drinking vessels or fabrics, the famous and renowned ornament of kings, and even the crowd of servants and the service of friends, relatives, or officials...

<summary>Philo argues that material wealth, physical beauty, and strength are worthless "shadows" compared to the virtue of the soul. He uses the metaphor of a sick king to show that earthly riches cannot cure physical or spiritual suffering.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 228, where Philo of Alexandria (quoted by Eusebius) argues that material goods like gold and silver are inferior to the needs of the soul. He now shifts to a medical analogy to explain why philosophers should focus on inner virtue rather than outward status.</meta>

### EUSEBIUS, EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, BOOK 8
<page-num>229</page-num>

...even if, having arrived at the same bedside and describing the condition of the body itself, they do not stand in wonder because the beds are **jewel-encrusted** or **solid gold**, nor because the patient is clothed in expensive fabrics <note>original: δραχμοϋφὴς, referring to cloth woven with a value of many drachmae</note> or embroidered tunics. Nor do they depart simply because they have touched the cloaks surrounding him, which come in various styles. Instead, pressing their hand against the veins, they accurately measure the pulses to see if they are healthy. Often, they even pull back the tunics to examine if the abdomen is swollen, if the chest is burning with fever, or if the heart leaps irregularly; only then do they apply the appropriate treatment. 

In the same way, those who profess the "medical art" of philosophy should apply it to the nature of the **royal soul**. They ought to despise everything that empty opinions manufacture with such pride. Instead, they should enter within and grasp the mind <note>original: διανοίας</note> itself, to see if its "pulses" are moved unnaturally and uncontrollably by unyielding anger, or if the tongue is blunt and slanderous, or if it has become debased and dishonorable. They should also examine the "stomach," to see if it is consumed by an insatiable "chimera" of desire, and investigate every part to see if it is strengthened against passions and diseases, or if it seems to be in a state of confusion, so that they do not fail to provide what is necessary for salvation. 

But as it is, people are dazzled by the brilliance of external things. Because they are unable to see the **intelligible light** <note>The "intelligible light" (νοητὸν φῶς) is a Platonic concept referring to truth or divine reason that can only be perceived by the mind, not the eyes.</note>, they spend their whole lives wandering. They are unable to reach the "King," which is Reason. Having barely reached the outer portals, they stand in awe of the "virtues" at the doors—wealth, fame, and health—and they worship them. 

Yet, just as it is the height of madness to show colors to the blind or musical sounds to the deaf, so it is to offer true goods to wicked men. For these men have been blinded in the most sovereign part of themselves: the mind, over which the deep darkness of folly has been poured. Why then do we wonder now if **Socrates**, or this or that virtuous man, lived their lives in poverty? They never practiced anything for the sake of profit, nor did they think it worthy to accept the great gifts offered by wealthy friends or kings. They did this because they considered the possession of **virtue** <note>original: ἀρετή (arete), meaning excellence or moral character</note> to be the only "good and beautiful" thing. While we labor for other things, they considered most of those "goods" to be of no account. For how could they not disregard "bastard" goods for the sake of the abundance of the "genuine" ones? 

If, however, having shared in a mortal body and being full of human frailties, and living among such a multitude of unjust people—whose number is impossible to find—they were plotted against or suffered natural injustice, is it not necessary to blame the cruelty of those who attacked them? For if we were to find ourselves in **pestilential air**, we would certainly be bound to fall ill. Vice <note>original: κακία (kakia)</note> is even more destructive than a plague-ridden environment. Just as when there is rain, a man who stays in the open air must necessarily get soaked; or when a cold north wind blows, he must be gripped by shivering and cold; or another must suffer when the summer sun is at its peak (for it is a law of nature that bodies suffer along with the seasons)—in the same way, for one dwelling in such places where murders, plagues, and "tribes of other calamities" exist, it is inevitable that you will be shaped by the effects of such things. 

<margin>»</margin> For consider **Polycrates** <note>Polycrates was the tyrant of Samos, famous for his incredible good luck, which eventually ended in a gruesome death.</note>: for all the terrible injustices and impieties he committed, his "good fortune" turned out to be a worse curse. Add to this that he was punished by the Great King <note>The King of Persia.</note>, fulfilling a prophecy which he, in his madness, had misunderstood. He thought he had seen a vision that he would be "anointed by the sun and washed by Zeus." 

<margin>»</margin> These things, spoken enigmatically through symbols, [meant his death by crucifixion]. <note>In the story from Herodotus, Polycrates dreamed he was being washed by Zeus (rain) and anointed by Helios (the sun). This was a dark omen: when he was crucified, the rain washed his body and the sun "anointed" him by melting the fat/oils from his skin.</note>

He addresses why the righteous suffer, suggesting that living in a corrupt world is like living in "plague-ridden air" where exposure to harm is inevitable.</summary>

### EUSEBIUS
<page-num>230</page-num>

...phases, formerly obscure, now received their clearest confirmation through deeds. This was evident not only at the end but throughout his entire life, as if the soul were suspended from the body. For always fearing and trembling at the multitude of those attacking him in his labor, he clearly recognized that while men feel goodwill toward mortals, everyone is pitilessly hostile toward an enemy due to his perverse nature.

The historians of Sicilian affairs are witnesses to this most unjust and constant distrust. They say he even suspected the women who served him. As a sign of this, he did not allow the entrance to the bedchamber, through which he was to go to her, to be traversed with razors <note>original: ξυρίσιν; here referring to the fear of sharp instruments being smuggled in or used in his presence</note>, lest a wound ever be accidentally or intentionally inflicted. Instead, the sound and noise of the footsteps announced the arrival. Furthermore, he required her to come to the marriage bed not only without garments, but naked in every part—even those things not lawful for men to see. The floor, moreover, was cut with heights and depths like an agricultural trench, lest some plot be hidden through lack of caution, requiring leaps or long strides to cross. To what extent was he filled with such devices against a woman, whom a proper sense of shame should have protected? 

But he left those sights to the steep cliffs, while beneath the most manifest natures he was closing his eyes, treading on precipices. These people, barely reaching as far as the neck, find no retreat from the house, having failed at the remaining height, nor do they dare the descent, dizzied by the sight of the chasms. For having fallen in love with **tyranny** as if it were a divine and enviable thing, he supposed it was safe neither to stay nor to escape. For to one who stays, unspeakable evils flow one after another; but to one wishing to escape, the danger to his very life hangs over him, with men armed against him, if not in body, then certainly in their minds.

The story they tell of Dionysius and the man who called the tyrant’s life "blessed" <note>This refers to the famous legend of Damocles</note> clearly demonstrates this reality. For having invited him to a most brilliant and costly banquet, he ordered a sharpened **axe** <note>original: πέλεκυν; though traditionally told as the "Sword of Damocles," the text here specifies a double-headed axe or hatchet</note> to be suspended by a very thin cord. When the guest, who had reclined, suddenly saw it, he neither dared to be cautious because of the tyrant, nor was he able to enjoy any of the prepared delicacies. Overcome by fear, ignoring the abundant and rich pleasures, he stretched out his neck and eyes, waiting in suspense for his piteous destruction. 

"Do you see now," Dionysius said to him, "our world-renowned and enviable life? For it is such as this, unless one wishes to deceive himself. It contains a multitude of provisions, but the enjoyment of nothing good. It brings endless and eternal destruction through successive fears, incurable dangers, and diseases like creeping sores or madness."

But the majority of the unexamined, deceived by **brilliant nonsense**, suffer the same fate as those tormented by hideous harlots. These women overshadow their deformity with clothing, gold, and facial makeup; for lack of genuine beauty, they manufacture a counterfeit to ensnare those who look upon them. The utterly unfortunate are full of such misery, the extremes of which they judge and vote upon within themselves. But like those who speak out secrets under necessity, they let out the most truthful voices born of suffering: that their life is a fellowship of punishments and ruin, and they live expecting death, just like cattle being fattened for sacrifice. For these things...

### PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 8
<page-num>231</page-num>

...the care they received, they met with slaughters because of their excessive feasting. There are others who have paid quite public, not hidden, penalties for their impiety regarding money <note>original: χρημάτων; referring here to the plundering of sacred temple funds</note>, the list of whom is vast—an endless task to recount—but a single example from history is sufficient for our purpose.

It is said by the historians of the **Sacred War** <note>The Third Sacred War (c. 356–346 BCE) began when the Phocians seized the Temple of Apollo at Delphi</note> in **Phocis**, that according to the law, a temple-robber must be cast from a cliff, drowned, or burned. The three men who plundered the temple at **Delphi**—**Philomelus**, **Onomarchus**, and **Phayllus**—shared these punishments among themselves. Philomelus was cast down a rough and stony hill when a rock broke away, and he was swallowed up. Onomarchus died when his horse bolted and carried him into the sea; the waves rushed over him, and he sank into the bottomless deep along with the animal. As for Phayllus, he either wasted away from a lingering disease—for there are two accounts of his end—or he perished when he was burned along with the temple at **Abae**.

Now, some people insist on saying that these men died by mere chance. If they had been punished at different times or by different means, it would be reasonable to blame the instability of fortune. But since they were all punished together, at the same time, and not by different penalties but by the very ones prescribed in the laws, it is irrational to deny that they were judged by the decree of God.

If some violent men who remain—those who have raged against the masses and enslaved not only other peoples but their own homelands—continue on unpunished, it is no wonder. First, man does not judge in the same way God does. We examine only what is visible, but He, entering into the deepest recesses of the soul as if in the most brilliant sunlight, sees the mind itself. He gazes upon the naked intentions, seeing clearly even what is hidden, and immediately distinguishes between the worthy and the unworthy.

Let us never, then, prefer our own judgment to the Divine; let us say that His judgment is more truthful and more deliberate. To think otherwise is not holy. In human judgment, there are many things that cause us to stumble: deceptive senses, treacherous passions, and the heavy fortress of our own vices. But in God’s judgment, there is no deception, only justice and truth, by which everything is naturally and praiseworthily set right.

Furthermore, my noble friend, do not think that a timely **tyranny** <term>tyranny: here used not just as "cruel rule" but as an extra-legal seizure of power used by God as a tool for discipline</term> is useless. For punishment itself is not useless; paying the penalty for crimes is either more beneficial to the good or at least a necessary debt. For this reason, punishment is included in all rightly written laws, and the lawgivers are praised by all. What a tyrant is to a populace, punishment is to a law. When a city’s virtue is weakened by powerlessness and an abundance of folly overflows, then God—wishing to block the flood of vice like a mountain torrent so that He may cleanse our race—gives strength and power to those who are by nature suited for rule. For vice cannot be cleansed without a harsh soul.

Sometimes cities are handed over to executioners who are murderers, traitors, and temple-robbers; in doing so, God does not approve of these men’s characters, but rather utilizes the usefulness of their service. In the same way, the **Caretaker of this Great City of the World** <note>A Stoic and Philonic concept of God as the providential administrator of the cosmos</note> sets tyrants over cities as "common executioners" in whichever places He perceives violence, injustice, impiety, and other evils overflowing, so that at last these evils may find relief. At that time, He also judges those responsible who, out of a foul and painful soul, served as His instruments, just like...

### EUSEBIUS: PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL
<page-num>232</page-num>

...the ringleaders <note>original: κορυφαίους (koryphaious); literally "head-men" or "summit-dwellers"</note> deserved to be pursued. For according to the power of fire, whenever it consumes the material thrown upon it, it spreads its own nature to everything else. Those who have seized power over the masses might see this: when they have exhausted cities and made them empty of men, they pay the penalty to all by being destroyed in turn. And why do we wonder if God, when vice has overflowed in cities, regions, and nations, drives it out <note>original: ἀποδιοπομπᾶται (apodiopompatai); a term for ritual purification or the "sending away" of an evil influence</note> through the agency of tyrants? For often, not employing other servants, He does this through His own hand, bringing famine, plague, earthquake, or any other god-sent calamity. By these, great and populous crowds perish every day, and a large portion of the inhabited world is deserted, though it was spoken of as flourishing just a day before. Thus, enough has been said for the present regarding this matter; for I do not think anyone has ever spoken of the "happiness" of the wicked, which would be the most convincing argument for someone. But if there is still doubt in one's mind, or if one is not yet persuaded, why should we hide our hesitation? For either we will both fall into error, or we will both find the truth.

And after some other remarks, he [Philo] says again:

The movements of winds and rains are not for the harm of sailors or farmers, as you used to think, but God works them for the benefit of our whole race. With water He cleanses the earth, and with winds He clears the entire atmosphere; by both, He nourishes, grows, and delights both animals and plants. If at times this harms sailors or farmers because it comes "out of season," it is no wonder. For these people are a small part, while the preservation of the **Whole** <term>the Universe/the All</term> must come before all of them. 

Just as in a **gymnasium** <note>original: γυμνασίῳ (gymnasio); here referring to the complex for physical and intellectual education</note>, the **gymnasiarch** <term>director of a gymnasium</term> provides the oil <note>original: ἄλειμμα (aleimma); the ointment or oil used by athletes</note> for the benefit of the students, yet often, because of civic needs, he does not allow the boys to participate at certain hours, whereby they might miss out on their anointing; so too God, caring for the entire world as if it were a city, is accustomed to making winter-like springs and spring-like winters for the benefit of the Whole, even if ten thousand ship-owners or tillers of the soil suffer loss from these imbalances. 

Thus, knowing that the transformations of the elements into one another—from which the world was forged and consists—are a most necessary work, He allows them to proceed unhindered. Frost and snow, and all such things, follow the cooling of the air. Similarly, the clashing and breaking of clouds produce lightning and thunder. Perhaps none of these are primary intentions, but the rains and winds—which are the causes of life, nourishment, and growth for things on earth—have these other phenomena as "byproducts" <note>original: ἐπακολουθήματα (epakolouthemata); secondary consequences or "follow-on" effects</note>. 

It is like when a gymnasiarch, in his generosity, often provides oil at great expense; some unrefined people, while being dusted with sand instead of water, scatter droplets onto the floor. From this, a most foul mud is immediately created. But no one in their right mind would say that the mud and the mess were created by the foresight of the gymnasiarch; rather, they clearly followed from the abundance of the supplies. 

In the same way, snow and similar things are "byproducts" of the clouds being condensed; they are not the primary works of Nature, but they follow upon natural works. Nevertheless, even these provide some necessary use to those who are wiser. For by these signs, they predict snowstorms and winds, or fair weather and storms. 

Do you not see the **stoas** <term>covered porches or colonnades</term> in the city? Most of them face the south. Those walking in them can be warmed in the winter and cooled in the summer by the arrangements of God. Yet something else follows, which does not come from the intention of the builder. And what is this? The shadows that fall from the feet...

<meta>catchword: ἡμετέρᾳ (our)</meta>

<summary>Philo argues that God uses tyrants and natural disasters as necessary "cleansings" for a corrupt world. He explains that "unpleasant" weather is a secondary byproduct of a system designed for the greater good, using the analogy of mud in a gymnasium to show that God's primary intent is always beneficial.</summary>

### GOSPEL PREPARATION, Book 8
<page-num>233</page-num>
<header>GOSPEL PREPARATION, Book 8</header>
<sig>v.iii.</sig>

...having been refined by your own experience throughout the seasons. If fire is indeed a most necessary work of nature, then smoke is its inevitable consequence; yet even smoke provides some benefit on occasion. For instance, during mid-day fires, when the fire is dimmed by being outshone by the rays of the sun, it is by smoke that the approach of enemies is signaled. Just as the story goes regarding Ilium <note>original: Ἰλίδος (Ilidos); referring to the fall of Troy, where fire signals and smoke played a role in military communication</note>, so too is the logic regarding eclipses. For eclipses follow upon the divine natures of the sun and the moon. These serve as warnings, signaling either the death of kings or the destruction of cities. It was regarding such an event that Pindar offered a prayer during an eclipse, which has been mentioned previously. As for the Milky Way <note>original: ὁ τοῦ γάλακτος κύκλος (ho tou galaktos kyklos); literally "the circle of milk"</note>, it shares the same substance as the other stars; and if it is difficult to explain, let those who are accustomed to researching the things of nature not shrink back from the task. For discovery is most profitable, and the search itself is most pleasant to those who love learning. Just as the sun and moon have come into being through providence, so too have all things in heaven, even if we, being unable to track the individual natures and powers of each, remain silent. 

Earthquakes and plagues, the striking of lightning bolts, and all such things are said to be "god-sent" <note>original: θεήλατα (theēlata); meaning driven or sent by a god</note>, but in truth, they are not. For God is the cause of no evil whatsoever; rather, the changes of the elements produce these things. They are not the primary works of nature, but follow upon necessary processes, appearing as consequences of the primary works. If some of the more disadvantaged people suffer from the harm caused by these events, one must not blame the divine administration. First, because it is not for us to decide who is truly "good" in our own estimation, whereas the criteria of God are more accurate than any human mind. Second, God looks upon the most vital connections in the world as a whole; just as in kingdoms or military commands, the focus is on cities and camps, rather than on some individual offender or obscure person who has been brought forward. 

Some say—just as it is legal in the case of killing a tyrant to also execute their relatives, so that the magnitude of the punishment might deter future crimes—in the same way, during pestilential diseases, some of the innocent perish along with the guilty, so that others may be brought to their senses from a distance. Aside from the necessity of those catching a disease when it is carried in the air, it is just like those caught in a storm at sea, who face danger equally. 

Nor should we remain silent about the creation of wild beasts—as if some clever speaker might forestall our defense and mock it—for they were created for the sake of training for the struggles of war. For exercises and continuous hunting strengthen the body and brace the nerves, and they habituate the soul to endure the sudden attacks of the powerful, ignoring the risk to one's strength. As for those of a peaceful nature, it is possible for them to live not only away from the fish of the sea, but also safely within their homes <note>original: κλησιάδων θαλαμευομένοις (klēsiadōn thalameuomenois); likely referring to being sheltered in chambers or enclosed dwellings</note>, enjoying without fear or plot the most abundant, gentle herds. For lions and other such beasts, following their own voluntary nature, are driven far from the city, so that man, who desires to suffer no harm, may be protected.

If, however, some people through laziness go unarmed and unguarded into the dens of wild beasts, let them blame themselves for what happens, and not nature, because they were negligent when it was possible to be on guard. I have even seen people at the horse races who, through sheer mindlessness, rush out—when they ought to remain seated and watch in an orderly fashion—and standing in the middle of the track, they are knocked down by the force of the four-horse chariots <note>original: τεθρίππων (tethrippōn); the standard ancient racing chariot pulled by four horses</note> and crushed by feet and wheels, paying the price for their folly.

<summary>In this passage, Philo defends divine providence by arguing that natural "evils" like smoke, eclipses, and wild animals are either useful byproducts or necessary for human training, while human suffering often results from individual negligence rather than divine malice.</summary>

# EUSEBIUS
<page-num>234</page-num>
<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

...with multi-cubit woven fabrics. Regarding these matters, then, what has been said is sufficient. As for creeping things, the venomous ones did not come into being according to primary providence, but as a "consequence" <note>original: ἐπακολούθησιν (epakolouthesin); Philo uses this to mean a side-effect or a necessary byproduct of a larger natural law</note>, as I said before. For they are brought to life whenever the moisture within the earth undergoes a change toward a hotter state. Some are even animated by decay, such as worms produced from food, and lice from sweat. Those things which had their origin from their own proper matter according to a seminal and primary nature are rightly attributed to providence.

Indeed, I have heard two different accounts regarding even those venomous creatures, suggesting they were created for the benefit of man—accounts which I would not wish to hide. The first of these is as follows: some have claimed that venomous creatures cooperate with many of the needs of doctors; those who practice the medical art with skill use them as needed to provide a wealth of antidotes <note>original: ἀλεξιφαρμάκων (alexipharmakon); literally "defense-medicines" used to counteract poisons</note>, leading to the unexpected salvation of those in the most life-threatening conditions. Even to this day, one can see that those who do not attempt to heal in a lazy or negligent manner make use of the medicines derived from such wild beasts, applying each one with great care.

The second account is not medical, but rather philosophical in nature. It claims that these creatures were subjected to God for the purpose of punishing sinners, serving as "generals" just as whips or the sword are used by men. For this reason, though they remain quiet at other times, they are provoked to display their strength against those who have been condemned—those whose own nature has already sentenced them to death in its own incorruptible court.

As for the claim that these creatures prefer to lurk in houses, this is a falsehood. For they are seen outside the city, in fields and deserts, fleeing from man as if from a master. Nevertheless, if they do dwell inside, there is a reason for it. They love the twists and turns of hidden corners and the abundance of scraps <note>original: σκυβάλων (skybalon); refers to refuse, dung, or food waste</note> into which they can crawl, not to mention that the smell of roasting meat <note>original: κνίσσαν (knissan); the steam or aroma of a burnt offering or cooking meat</note> has an attractive power.

If swallows live among you, it is no wonder; for we refrain from hunting them. The instinct for hunting is implanted in all souls, not only the rational but also the irrational. None of the animals used for our enjoyment dwell with us, for they avoid your plots—moreover, the use of such animals is forbidden by law.

There is an ancient city in Syria named Ashkelon. When I was there at the time we were traveling to the ancestral temple to pray and offer sacrifice, we beheld an incredible number of doves <note>original: πελειάδων (peleiadon); doves were sacred to the goddess Atargatis in Ashkelon</note> on the walls and in every single house. When I asked the reason, they said it was not permitted to catch them, for the inhabitants had been forbidden from using them for food since ancient times. Thus, the animal has become so tamed by this safety that it not only lives under the same roof but even shares the same table, serving as a symbol of a "truce" <note>original: ἐκεχειρίας (ekecheirias); a cessation of hostilities or a sacred peace</note>.

In Egypt, one can see something even more wonderful. The man-eating and most grievous of beasts, the crocodile, is raised in the marshes of the most sacred Nile; yet, even though it dwells in the depths, it senses the benefit of kindness. Among those people where it is honored, it thrives in great numbers; but among those who harm it, it does not appear even in a dream. Thus, for those sailing in places where the river-dwellers are bold, they do not dare to dip even the tip of a finger; yet in places where they are clearly tame, people even swim out and play with them.

The land of the Cyclopes, wherever that race may be, is a fiction of myth. Civilized fruit does not grow without sowing and the labor of men, just as nothing comes into being out of nothing. As for the Hyades <note>likely referring to a fertile region or the star cluster associated with rain</note>, one must not accuse them of being meager or barren, for much of that land is deep-soiled. If the foreigners <note>original: βάρβαροι (barbaroi); meaning non-Greeks</note> differ in their fruitfulness, it is a claim of greed, yet they take hold of the nourishment for the sake of which...

<meta>catchword: grace/favor</meta>

<summary>Philo argues that venomous creatures are either byproducts of natural processes or instruments of divine justice and medicine. He uses examples from Ashkelon (doves) and Egypt (crocodiles) to show how animals respond to human kindness or hostility, reinforcing the idea of a Providential order.</summary>

### PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 8
<page-num>239</page-num>
<header>PREP. EVANG. Book 8</header>

The author says that nature gives thanks to itself; for it alone truly gives birth to humanity as a "heavenly plant" <note>original: φυτὸν οὐράνιον (phyton ouranion); a Platonic concept suggesting humans are rooted in heaven via the mind rather than in the earth like plants</note> and a divine sprout rooted within, bringing forth a faculty of reason most suited to knowledge. The reason for this is that the intellect is naturally sharpened by the thinness of the air. Therefore Heraclitus says, not without purpose: 
<margin>»</margin> "Where the earth is dry, the soul is wisest and best." <note>original: αὑή ψυχὴ σοφωτάτη καὶ ἀρίστη; Heraclitus believed the "dry soul" was the most virtuous and intelligent, whereas "moisture" or drunkenness dulls the mind.</note> One could also prove this from the fact that those who are sober and have few needs are more intelligent, while those who are always stuffing themselves with drink and food are the least prudent, since their reasoning is "drowned" <note>original: βαπτιζομένου (baptizomenou); literally "being submerged" or "baptized" by excess</note> by the things flowing into them.

Therefore, they have observed that the barbarian lands are a desert of the "stems of wisdom," while they are very fertile in the offspring of irrational animals; but the mind is not born there, or only barely so. This is because the constant and successive vapors of earth and water have overpowered the intellect's ability to be raised up by the air. There are no grounds for blaming Nature for the existence of fish, birds, or land animals as if she were enchanting us with pleasures; rather, it is the cold strength of the lack of self-control surrounding them. For it was necessary for the completion of the whole, so that the world might exist in every part, that various forms of living creatures should spring up throughout. 

But it was not necessary for man—a being most closely related to wisdom—to rush toward the enjoyment of these things, transforming himself into the wildness of beasts. Therefore, even until now, those into whom reason has been instilled abstain from all these <term>flesh-meats</term>, using leafy greens and tree fruits as their side-dishes, finding in them the sweetest enjoyment. 

But for those who do not live according to the divine principles already mentioned as being natural, teachers, monitors, and legislators were appointed in every city, whose concern it was to check the excess of desires, not permitting the fearless use of all things by everyone. And if roses, saffron, and the rest of the variety of flowers exist, they were made for health, not for pleasure. For their powers are immense, and they are beneficial in themselves through their scents, stopping the spread of unpleasantness <note>In antiquity, pleasant scents were believed to "cleanse" the air of disease-carrying miasma</note>, and much more so in the medical compositions of drugs. 

For when mixed, they provide their own powers in a more pungent way, just as the pouring out of life and the mixing of male and female occurs, where neither is naturally able to produce individually what they can when coming together. These things have been necessarily said in response to the rest of the questions you raised, being able to create a strong conviction in those who are not contentious, regarding the fact that God takes care for human affairs as a primary concern. 

These things, then, have been summarized from the man revealed [Philo], showing both what kind of people the children of the Hebrews have been even in recent times, and at the same time their pious understanding concerning God, and making manifest their harmony with their ancestors. And now it is time to move from here to the testimonies of those from the outside <note>original: τῶν ἔξωθεν (ton exothen); referring to non-Jewish or "pagan" Greek authors</note> regarding the same matters.

<meta>catchword: α.</meta>
