# EUSEBIUS
<page-num>234</page-num>
<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

...are mostly harmful. Now, enough has been said regarding these matters. Regarding venomous **reptiles**, they did not come into being by primary **providence**, but as a **consequence** <note>original: ἐπακολούθησιν (epakolouthesis); a Stoic philosophical term meaning a "by-product" or "side-effect" of natural laws rather than the primary intended design.</note>, as I said before. For they are brought to life whenever there is a change toward a warmer state in the moist vapors. Some things are even brought to life by putrefaction: for instance, worms are produced from the internal organs, and lice from sweat. But whatever things had their origin from their own specific matter according to a **seminal nature** <note>original: σπερματικὴν (spermatikēn); referring to creatures that reproduce through seeds or eggs as part of a designed cycle.</note> and as a primary purpose, these are rightly attributed to providence.

I have already heard two-fold arguments concerning those creatures, suggesting they were created for the benefit of humanity, which I would not wish to conceal. One of these arguments is as follows: some claim that venomous creatures assist in many **medicinal cures** <note>original: ἰαμάτων (iamatōn)</note>, and that those who practice the art of medicine, by using them skillfully as they ought, find an abundance of **antidotes** <term>alexipharmics: ancient medicines designed to ward off poisons or venom</term> for the unexpected treatment of those who are in the most precarious health. Even until now, one can see those who attempt to practice medicine—not in a lazy or negligent way—making use of each of these things quite seriously in the composition of drugs.

The other argument is not medical, but rather philosophical, as it seems. It claimed that these things were devised by God as a **punishment** <note>original: κόλασιν (kolasin)</note> against sinners, just as generals and leaders use rods or iron weapons. For this reason, they remain quiet for the greater part of time, but when provoked to bite, they fall upon those who have been condemned—those whose own nature has found them guilty of death in its **unseen tribunal** <note>original: ἀδοκήτῳ δικαστηρίῳ (adokētō dikastēriō)</note>. 

As for the claim that they prefer to lurk in houses, it is a falsehood. For others are observed outside in the fields and deserts, fleeing from man as their master. Nevertheless, even if the claim is true, it has a certain reason. For in the corners of houses, there is rotting rubbish and a multitude of scraps in which they love to crawl, quite apart from the domestic influence of the **scents of the kitchen** <note>original: κνισσῶν (knissōn); specifically the smell of roasting meat or fat from sacrifices/cooking.</note>.

If **swallows** live among you, it is nothing to wonder at, for we refrain from hunting them. For a desire for offspring is implanted in souls, not only in rational beings but also in the irrational. As for the lack of similarity regarding pleasure, let that be set aside. As for the plots against temples, these do not occur except among those for whom the use of such things is forbidden by law.

There is a city as an example of this behavior toward animals, named **Ascalon**. While I was there at the time we were traveling to the temple in Syria for the sake of ancestral customs or perhaps a sacrifice, we beheld an impossible multitude of **pigeons** <note>original: πελειάδων (peliadōn); these were sacred to the goddess Atargatis in Ascalon.</note> on the gateways and in every single house. When I asked the reason, they said it was not permitted to catch them, for their use had been forbidden to the inhabitants from ancient times. Thus, the animal has become so tame through lack of fear that it not only lives under the roof, but also becomes a constant companion at the table, luxuriating in this state of truce.

In **Egypt**, one may see something even more wonderful. For that man-eater and most grievous of beasts, the **crocodile**, fawns like a pet when it is fed in the most sacred Nile, and despite being a creature of the depths, it surfaces for the benefit it receives. Among those by whom it is honored, it thrives most greatly; but among those who do it harm, it does not appear even in a dream. Thus, where the sailors are bold, the crocodile does not dare to let even the tip of a finger down into the water, even when the creatures visit in herds. But where the sailors show they are friendly, the crocodiles leap out to swim with them in play.

The "land of werewolves," and the stories concerning **Lycia**, are a figment of myth. Without sowing and the work of farmers, cultivated fruit does not grow, just as nothing comes from that which does not exist. Nor should one complain of the **Iliad** <note>Here referring to the region of Troy (Ilion) mentioned in Homer's Iliad.</note> as being wretched and barren, for there is much deep-soiled land in that region as well. If the barbarian land excels in fruitfulness, it possesses this advantage in crops, which must be granted to those who will consume them...

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 8
<page-num>239</page-num>
<header>PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 8</header>

...for the sake of nutrition. But only that perception which comes through the ears is truly truthful and "generates" the human being; for man is a **heavenly plant** <note>original: φυτὸν οὐράνιον (phyton ouranion); a concept found in Plato’s Timaeus, suggesting that man’s roots are in heaven (the mind) rather than the earth.</note> and a divine shoot brought to perfection, giving birth to reason as its own specific knowledge. As for drought, it exists for the sake of the thinness of the air, through which the intellect is naturally sharpened. Wherefore **Heraclitus** says—not without good <margin>»</margin> reason—**"A dry light is the wisest and best soul."** <note>original: αὐγὴ ξηρὴ, ψυχὴ σοφωτάτη καὶ ἀρίστη. This famous aphorism suggests that a soul "unmoistened" by the "vapors" of excess food and drink is more capable of clear thought.</note> One could also prove this by the fact that those who are sober and require little for their needs are more intelligent. In contrast, those who are always filled with drink and food are the least wise, as their reasoning is **submerged** <note>original: βαπτιζομένου (baptizomenou); literally "baptized" or "drowned."</note> by the things flowing into them. Therefore, even among the **barbarian nations** <note>likely referring to the Egyptians or those living in lush, humid environments</note>, those who live in prosperity and calm are physically protected, and the most noble of the irrational animals are found there; but mind or intellect is absent, or at least occurs very rarely. This is because the mind, which ought to be raised up by the light of the air, is instead overcome by the successive and continuous exhalations of earth and water.

Furthermore, regarding fish, birds, and land animals, nature does not intend them as an indictment of ourselves for the sake of some biting pleasure; rather, it is a terrible reproach against our own **intemperance**. For it was necessary that those things which complete the whole should exist, so that a world might come into being in every part, producing infinite forms of animals. However, it was not necessary for man to rush toward the enjoyment of these creatures. Wisdom is the thing most closely related to man, yet he changes it into the wildness of beasts. Therefore, even until now, those who have applied themselves to **reason** <note>original: λόγος (logos)</note> abstain once and for all from living creatures. They use leafy greens and the fruits of trees as their sustenance, finding a private pleasure in this. 

To the aforementioned habits, therefore, teachers were appointed—by nature as much as by custom—to ensure wise thinking. These include both lawgivers and cities, who cared to persuade people against the lack of moderation in their desires, not permitting the use of everything to everyone without fear. If even roses, saffron, and the rest of the variety of flowers exist, they were created for **health**, not for mere pleasure. For their powers are immense, and they provide benefit even by themselves through their scents, filling everyone with fragrance—and much more so in the **medical composition** of drugs. For some things, when mixed, provide their own powers more sharply. Just as for the production of life, the mixing of male and female occurs; for neither is naturally capable of doing alone what both can do when coming together.

These things have been said of necessity, to provide sufficient proof for the rest of those matters you questioned—proof capable of convincing those who are not contentious—concerning the fact that **God takes care of human affairs.** These things then we have excerpted from the aforementioned man [Philo], showing at once how the children of the **Hebrews** have been consistent in their views even unto modern times, and also showing the nature of their pious conception regarding God and their harmony with their forefathers. It is now time to transition from here to the testimonies from **outside** <note>original: τῶν ἔξωθεν (tōn exōthen); referring to non-Jewish, Greek, or "pagan" sources.</note> regarding the same matters.

<sig>v. iiii. A</sig>

<summary>This page concludes Philo's argument that the physical environment and even the existence of animals serve to discipline the human mind and soul. Eusebius then concludes the section by noting that Philo represents the historical and pious consistency of Jewish thought before moving to pagan testimonies.</summary>

-> PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 9 <-

### Which of the Greek historians made mention of the Jewish nation.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'K' (Kappa) featuring intricate foliate patterns, vines, and leaves within a square frame.</image-desc>

Since our acceptance of the Hebrew oracles <note>original: λογίων (logiōn); refers to the divinely inspired scriptures</note> was not reached without reasoning, but has been examined with judgment and a prepared mind, it is time to hasten to the point where the proofs connect. I shall show that even the most distinguished of those outside <note>meaning non-Jewish or "pagan" Greek authors</note> were not ignorant of Hebrew affairs. Some of them testified to the truth of the lives of the men recorded in their historical narratives, while others likewise touched upon their dogmatic theology. Following the account of the world's creation, I will list how many Greek writers mentioned the names of the Jews and Hebrews, or the philosophy they practiced in ancient times, and the history of their forefathers from the beginning. My discourse will begin with the life of these men, so that you may learn that we have not preferred our declared philosophy out of irrational judgment. Indeed, consistent with what was set forth previously, not only do their own sacred books attest to their writings and their ethical commitment and discipline, but so do the most distinguished of the Greek philosophers who are celebrated among us.

„ Now take and read the words of Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BC) was a Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note>, as they are found in the writings of Porphyry *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, where they are set down in this manner: “And yet, although the Jews among the Syrians still sacrifice living creatures even now,” says Theophrastus, “because of their original form of sacrifice, if someone were to command us to sacrifice in the same way, we would shrink from the act. For they do not feast upon the victims, but burn them whole as an offering <note>original: ὁλοκαυτοῦντες (holokautountes); the origin of the word 'holocaust,' meaning a burnt sacrifice offered in its entirety to a deity</note> during the night, and by pouring much honey and wine over them, they consume the sacrifice quickly, so that the all-seeing God might not become a spectator of the suffering. And they do this while fasting during the intervening days. During this whole time, being a race of philosophers, they converse with one another about the Divine, and at night they observe the stars, looking toward them and calling upon God through prayers. For these were the first to begin sacrificing both other animals and themselves, doing this out of necessity and not out of desire.” And in the fourth book of the same work, Porphyry records such things concerning the same people: “There are, then, the Essenes <note>a Jewish sect known for asceticism and communal living</note>, who are Jews by race, but more affectionate toward one another than others. These men turn away from pleasures as a vice, but they consider self-control and not falling under the power of the passions to be virtue. They have a disdain for marriage, but adopting the children of others while they are still tender and ready for learning, they regard them as kin and imprint them with their own customs; they do not do away with marriage or the succession resulting from it, but they guard against the wantonness of women. They are despisers of wealth. The communal spirit among them is marvelous, and it is not possible to find anyone among them possessing more than another. For it is a law that those entering the sect must surrender their property to the order, so that in all things there appears neither the humbleness of poverty nor the eminence of wealth. The possessions of each are mixed together into one...”

The text highlights the sacrificial rituals of the Jews and the disciplined, communal lifestyle of the Essenes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse started on page 237, where Eusebius begins quoting external authorities to validate the history and practices of the Hebrew people. This specific passage is a famous description of the Essenes, a Jewish sect, largely excerpted from Josephus’s 'The Jewish War' (Book 2).</meta>

<page-num>238</page-num>
<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

> "...just as if they were all brothers, their property is held in common. They consider oil to be a defilement, and if anyone is accidentally anointed, he wipes his body clean. For they consider it a virtue to keep the skin dry and to always be dressed in white garments. The administrators of their common affairs are elected by the group, and each is chosen by the whole body to attend to their specific needs. 
> 
> They do not occupy a single city, but many of them live in every town. Their homes are thrown open to members of the sect arriving from elsewhere, and even those who have never met before enter as if they were lifelong friends. For this reason, they carry nothing with them when they travel, except for weapons <note>original: χωμάτων, though likely ὅπλων ('weapons') as found in the standard text of Josephus; the Essenes carried weapons only to defend against bandits</note> for protection. They do not change their clothes or shoes until the previous pair is completely torn or worn out by time. They neither buy nor sell anything; instead, each person gives what he has to those in need and receives in return what is useful to him. Even without such a reciprocal exchange, they are permitted to take what they want from any member without hindrance.
> 
> Their piety toward the Divine is quite unique. Before the sun rises, they speak of nothing profane, but recite certain ancestral prayers to it, as if entreating it to rise. After this, they are dismissed by their overseers to the crafts they each know, working diligently until the fifth hour <note>roughly 11:00 AM</note>. Then they gather again in one place, gird themselves with linen loincloths, and wash their bodies in cold water. After this purification, they enter a private room where no one of a different faith is permitted to enter. Being pure themselves, they sit in the dining room as if it were a sacred place. When they have sat in silence, the baker serves loaves of bread in order, and the cook sets down a single dish of one kind of food for each person. 
> 
> The priest says a prayer before the food, which is considered holy and pure, and it is unlawful for anyone to taste anything before the prayer. After the meal, the priest prays again; thus, both at the beginning and the end, they honor God. Then, laying aside their garments as if they were sacred, they return to their work until evening. Upon returning, they dine in the same manner, with any guests who happen to be present sitting with them. Neither shouting nor tumult ever defiles the house. They yield to one another in conversation in an orderly fashion, and to those outside, the silence of those within seems like a fearsome mystery. The reason for this is their constant sobriety and the fact that their food and drink are measured only until they are satisfied.
> 
> For those who seek to join the sect <note>original: αἵρεσιν (hairesin), meaning a school of thought or a chosen way of life</note>, entry is not immediate. For one year, the candidate remains outside the community but follows the same strict way of life. He is given a small hatchet <note>used for sanitary burial, a ritual of cleanliness</note>, a loincloth, and a white garment. During this time, he proves his self-control; he partakes in the waters of purification, which are considered holier, but he is not yet admitted to the communal life. After demonstrating his endurance, his character is tested for two more years. If he is found worthy, he is then admitted into the fellowship. 
> 
> But before he may touch the common food, he must swear fearsome oaths: first, that he will be pious toward the Divine; then, that he will observe justice toward men; that he will harm no one, neither by his own will nor by command; and that he will always hate the wicked and side with the righteous. He swears to show fidelity to all, especially to those in power, for no one obtains the right to rule without God’s will. And if he himself should rule, he swears never to abuse his authority, nor to outshine his subordinates with his dress or excessive finery. He swears to love the truth always and to expose liars. He will keep his hands clean from theft and his soul pure from unholy gain..."

<summary>This page provides a detailed account of the Essenes, highlighting their communal property, ritual purity, daily labor, and the rigorous three-year initiation process required to join their sect. It emphasizes their extreme discipline, sobriety, and the solemn oaths of justice and piety they take upon full admission.</summary>

# EUSEBIUS: PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 9

> "[...to swear] to receive [their teachings], and neither to hide anything from the members of the <term>sect<note>original: αἱρέταις (hairetais); in this period, it refers to a chosen school of thought or group, not necessarily 'heresy' in the later sense</note></term>, nor to disclose any of their secrets to others, even if someone should force them to the point of death. He swears to communicate the doctrines to no one in any way other than how he himself received them, to abstain from robbery, and to likewise preserve the books of their sect and the names of the angels. Such are their oaths.
> 
> Those who are caught in transgressions and expelled often perish by a miserable fate. For being bound by their oaths and customs, they are unable to partake of food from others; instead, eating grass and being destroyed by hunger, they waste away. For this reason, out of pity, the community has taken many back in their final breaths, considering this torment unto death a sufficient punishment for their sins. 
> 
> They maintain a rigorous discipline for those undergoing initiation. They even [dig] a trench a foot deep, covering themselves with a cloak so as not to offend the rays of God <note>This refers to the Essene practice of extreme modesty and ritual purity regarding bodily functions, avoiding 'insulting' the sun/divine light</note>. This is their faith regarding their diet and their self-restraint, such that during the <term>Sabbath<note>original: ἑϐδομάδι (hebdomadi); the seventh day</note></term> they do not even relieve themselves, but occupy themselves with hymns to God and with rest. 
> 
> From this discipline, they have achieved such endurance that even when being racked, twisted, burned, and passed through every instrument of torture to make them either blaspheme the Lawgiver <note>referring to Moses</note> or eat forbidden food, they refuse to do either. They demonstrated this clearly in the war against the Romans. They did not flatter their torturers or even weep, but smiling in their pains and mocking those who applied the tortures, they cheerfully gave up their souls, as if they were going to receive them back. 
> 
> For this opinion is firmly held among them: that while bodies are corruptible and their matter is not permanent, souls remain immortal forever. They believe souls are entwined with the body, having come from the thinnest ether, drawn down by a certain natural force. But when they are released from the bonds of the flesh, as if freed from a long slavery, they then rejoice and are carried upwards. 
> 
> Because of such a way of life, and their discipline toward truth and piety, there are many among them who even foreknow the future, as they are initiated into holy books, various purifications, and the sayings of the prophets. It is rare if they ever miss the mark in their predictions."

These things Porphyry has testified, likely from ancient readings, concerning both the piety and the philosophy of the aforementioned men, in the fourth book of his treatise *On Abstinence from Animal Food*.

Furthermore, Hecataeus of Abdera—a man who was both a philosopher and highly capable in practical affairs—composed a specific book on the history of the Jews. He goes into great detail about them, from which these excerpts will suffice for the present:

> "There are many strongholds and villages belonging to the Jews throughout the country. But there is one strong city, Jerusalem, about fifty <term>stades<note>approximately 5.7 miles or 9.2 kilometers</note></term> in circumference. It is inhabited by about twelve <term>myriads<note>120,000 people</note></term> of people, and they call it Jerusalem. 
> 
> Here, roughly in the center of the city, is a stone enclosure, about five <term>plethra<note>about 500 feet</note></term> long and a hundred cubits wide, having double gates. Within it is a square altar made of unhewn, naturally gathered, unworked stones. It is twenty cubits wide on each side and twelve cubits high. Beside it is a large building, where there is an altar and a lampstand; both are made of gold, weighing two <term>talents<note>a massive unit of weight, roughly 115-150 lbs total here</note></term>. Upon these there is a light that is never quenched, both during the nights and..."

# EUSEBIUS
## PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 9

> » ...in these days, there is absolutely no statue nor any votive offering at all, nor any plantation of a grove, nor any marshy ground, or anything of the sort. And the priests continue in [the Temple] both night and day, performing certain purifications, and drinking absolutely no wine while in the Temple.

Having said these things, he continues further down, testifying that the Jews even campaigned with King Alexander <note>Alexander the Great</note>, and afterwards with his successors. He recounts an event that he says he himself witnessed, involving a Jewish man during the campaign. He writes as follows:

> » For instance, while I was traveling toward the Red Sea, there followed along with the others of the cavalry escorting us a certain Jewish man named Mosollamus. He was a man strong of spirit, robust, and acknowledged by all—both Greeks and barbarians—as the best archer. 

> » This man, while many were traveling along the road and a certain <term>seer<note>original: μάντεως (manteōs); a professional diviner who interpreted signs from nature</note></term> was <term>taking omens from birds<note>original: ὀρνιθευομένου (ornitheuomenou); the practice of augury, or predicting the future by watching bird flight</note></term> and demanding everyone stop, asked why they were waiting. 

> » When the seer showed him the bird and said that if it stayed there, it was beneficial for everyone to wait; but if it flew forward, they should advance; and if backward, they should retreat; [Mosollamus], having kept silent and drawn his bow, shot and killed the bird. 

> » When the seer and some others were indignant and began cursing him, he said, "Why are you raging, you wretched people?" Then, taking the bird in his hands, he said, "How could this bird, who did not even foresee its own safety, report anything sound to us about our journey? For if it were able to foreknow the future, it would not have come to this place, fearing lest Mosollamus the Jew should shoot and kill it." 

So says Hecataeus. 

Now, Clearchus the <term>Peripatetic<note>A follower of Aristotle's philosophy</note></term> philosopher, in his first book *On Sleep*, attributes a certain story about the Jews to Aristotle the philosopher, writing word for word as follows:

> » "But it would be a long story to tell most of it. However, those things of his which possess a certain wonder and philosophy, it is not worse to recount similarly. Know clearly," he said, "that I shall seem to tell you things of marvelous exaggeration and equal to dreams." 

> » And Hyperochides, being cautious, said, "For this very reason we all seek to hear it." 

> » "Listen," said Aristotle, "according to the precept of the rhetoricians; let us first go through his race, so that we do not disobey the teachers of narration." 

> » "Speak," said Hyperochides, "if it seems good." 

> » "Well, that man by race was a Jew, from Coele Syria <note>A region of the Levant; the name means 'Hollow Syria'</note>. These people are descendants of the <term>philosophers of India<note>original: καλανοῦ (kalanou); a reference to Calanus, an Indian sage who met Alexander. Greeks often theorized that Jews were a 'sect' of Indian philosophers</note></term>, and the Syrians call them 'Jews,' taking the name from the place. For the place they inhabit is called Judaea. The name of their city is very difficult to pronounce; for they call it Jerusalem. 

> » This man then, having been a guest to many, and coming down from the upper regions to the coastal ones, was Greek not only in language but also in soul. And at that time while we were spending time in Asia, the man, arriving in the same places, met with us and some others of the scholarly sort, testing their wisdom. Since he had associated with many of those in education, he shared more of his own wisdom than he received." 

These are the words of Clearchus. Our own Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Christian theologian</note> also mentions this in the first book of his *Stromata* <note>original: στρωματὶ (strōmati); literally 'Miscellanies' or 'Tapestries'</note>, where he says: 

> » "Clearchus the Peripatetic says he knew a certain Jew who associated with Aristotle." 

And after other things he adds: 

> » "And Numa, the king of the Romans, being a Pythagorean, was benefited by the teachings of Moses..."

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the original page is διεκώλυσεν (diekōlysen), meaning 'hindered' or 'prevented,' which would begin the first sentence of the following page.</meta>

<summary>This page records Greek perceptions of the Jews, including a story of a Jewish archer mocking pagan augury and a dialogue where Aristotle reportedly praises a Jewish sage as "Greek in soul." It reflects the efforts of early Christian writers like Eusebius and Clement to show that even the greatest Greek philosophers respected Jewish wisdom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the collection of testimonies from non-Jewish authors regarding the antiquity and wisdom of the Jewish people. The previous page concluded an account of the Jewish archer Mosollamus; this page shifts to philosophical and poetic testimonies from Roman, Indian, and Greek sources.</meta>

<page-num>241</page-num>

<header>PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 9</header>

» [Numa] prevented them from recently <note>Likely referring to the early period of the Roman state</note> creating a living-form image for the Romans. Indeed, in the first 170 years, while they were building temples, they made no statue, neither molded nor painted. For Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, known for his religious reforms</note> demonstrated to them through a hidden meaning that it is not possible to reach the Best <note>The Divine</note> through the tongue, but only by the mind.

Furthermore, following this, he says: "Megasthenes the historian, who lived with Seleucus Nicator <note>One of the generals of Alexander the Great and founder of the Seleucid Empire</note>, writes as follows in the third book of his *Indica*: 'All that has been said about nature by the ancients is also said by those philosophizing outside of Greece; some among the Indians by the Brahmans, and others in Syria by those called Jews.'"

In addition to these, Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a Christian theologian</note> mentions Aristobulus the Peripatetic and Numenius the Pythagorean, saying: "Aristobulus, in his first book to Philometor <note>Ptolemy VI Philometor, King of Egypt</note>, writes these exact words: 'Plato followed our legislation, and it is evident that he carefully studied each of the things said in it. It had been translated by others before Demetrius <note>Demetrius of Phalerum</note>, before the supremacy of Alexander and the Persians—both the accounts of the departure of our fellow citizens, the Hebrews, from Egypt, and the manifestation of all that happened to them, their conquest of the land, and the explanation of the entire Law. Thus it is clear that the aforementioned philosopher [Plato] took many things from it. For he was very learned, just as Pythagoras also transferred many of our doctrines into his own system of belief.'"

And Numenius, the Pythagorean philosopher, writes outright: "For what is Plato, but Moses speaking Attic Greek?" <note>original: "τί γάρ ἐστι πλάτων, ἢ μωσῆς ἀττικίζων;" — This famous quote suggests that Plato’s philosophy was simply the wisdom of Moses expressed in the refined Greek dialect of Athens.</note> These are the words of Clement.

And I myself shall set forth these words of the Pythagorean philosopher—I mean Numenius—from his first book *On the Good*: "But regarding this, it will be necessary, after speaking and marking the mysteries of Plato, to retreat and bind them to the teachings of Pythagoras. One must call upon the famous nations, bringing forward their rites and dogmas, and the sanctuaries established in agreement with Plato—as many as the Brahmans, Jews, Magi, and Egyptians have ordained." 

So much for these matters. And in his third book, the same author [Numenius] mentions the things concerning Moses, saying as follows: "Next there were Jannes and Jambres <note>Traditional names for the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses</note>, Egyptian <term>sacred scribes<note>original: ἱερογραμματεῖς (hierogrammateis); high-ranking priests skilled in sacred writing and ritual</note></term>, men judged inferior to none in magic, at the time when the Jews were being driven out of Egypt. To Musaeus <note>A Greek name Numenius uses for Moses</note>, the leader of the Jews, a man who had become most powerful in praying to God, these two were deemed worthy by the Egyptian multitude to be the ones to undo the most violent of the calamities which Moses brought upon Egypt."

Through these words, Numenius bears witness both to the extraordinary miracles performed by Moses and to him being one beloved by God. Even Choerilus, an ancient poet, mentions the Jewish nation and how they campaigned with King Xerxes against Greece. He speaks thus:

> » And behind them passed a race, wondrous to behold,
> » sending forth a Phoenician tongue from their mouths;
> » they dwelt in the Solymian mountains <note>The mountains around Jerusalem, often associated by Greeks with the "Solymoi" people</note>, by a broad lake;
> » their heads were shaggy, shorn in a circle; and above
> » they wore the stripped-off skins of horses’ heads, hardened by smoke.

And Porphyry, in the first book of his *Philosophy from Oracles*, introduces his own god <note>Apollo</note> testifying to the wisdom of the race of the Hebrews, along with other nations who are celebrated for their intelligence. > For the road to the blessed is steep and very rough,
> Opened at first by gates bound in bronze.
> The paths revealed are beyond telling,
> Which the first of mortal men showed for the sake of infinite benefit—
> Those who drink the beautiful water of the land of the Nile.
> Many paths to the blessed were also learned by the Phoenicians,
> The Assyrians, the Lydians, and the race of Hebrew men.

The god testified to the discovery of this path by the Egyptians, the Phoenicians and Chaldeans <note>Ancient Mesopotamian astronomers and sages</note>, the Assyrians, the Lydians, and the Hebrews.

> Only the Chaldeans attained wisdom, and the Hebrews too,

->...appearance. His sons, eleven in number, were shepherds. # PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 9

...to transport across. These and the following matters concerning Joseph may be examined from his own *Polyhistor* <note>Original: "πολυΐστορος γραφῆς" (polyistoros graphēs). This refers to the work of Alexander Polyhistor, a 1st-century BCE scholar who compiled these fragments.</note>. But Artapanus says in his work *On the Jews* that our ancestor was Abraham, and that Jacob—who greatly excelled all others in intelligence and wisdom—was plotted against by his brothers. Foreseeing the plot, he <note>Joseph</note> begged the neighboring Arabs to transport him to Egypt. And they, being well-disposed, did so; for the kings of the Arabs were descendants of Israel, sons of Abraham, and brothers of Isaac. 

When he arrived in Egypt and was introduced to the king, he became the administrator of the whole country. Whereas previously the Egyptians had farmed in a disorderly manner because the land was undivided and the weaker were wronged by the stronger, he was the first to divide the land and mark it with boundaries, and he made much of the wasteland cultivable. He also allotted some of the fields to the priests. He also invented measures, and for these reasons he was greatly beloved by the Egyptians. He married Aseneth, the daughter of the priest of Heliopolis, by whom he fathered children. 

After these things, his family—both his father and his brothers—came to him, bringing many possessions, and they were settled in the city of Cessan; and the Syrians multiplied in Egypt. He says that these people also constructed both the Athos <note>Original: "ἀθῶ" (athō). This likely refers to a specific fortress or perhaps the city of Avaris.</note> and the temple in Heliopolis for those called the "Hermas" <note>Original: "τοῖς ἑρμῆσι" (tois hermēsi). Artapanus often identifies biblical figures with the god Hermes/Thoth to show Jewish influence on Egyptian culture.</note>. After this, Joseph died, as did the king of Egypt. Joseph, therefore, while ruling Egypt, stored up an immense amount of grain which had been produced during the seven-year harvest, and became the lord of Egypt. 

— Philo also bears witness to the sacred books in the tenth book of his *On Jerusalem*, saying thus:

> "To these, a blessed abode the great High Ruler
> Bestowed; for whom, honored from Abraham and Isaac,
> Joseph, the offspring of fertile Jacob, who of dreams
> Was a seer, a scepter-bearer in Egyptian times,
> Whirling the hidden things of time by the flood of fate."

And so on. These things also concerning Joseph.

He was righteous and possessed much property; for he acquired seven thousand sheep, four thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred wandering female asses. He also had sufficient farmlands. This Job was previously called Jobab <note>The tradition of identifying the biblical Job with King Jobab of Edom (Genesis 36:33) was common in Hellenistic Jewish literature.</note>. But God, testing his endurance, surrounded him with great misfortunes. For first, his asses and oxen were led away by raiders. Then his sheep were burned up by fire falling from heaven, along with the shepherds. Not long after, the camels were driven off by raiders. Then his children died when the house collapsed. On that same day, his body broke out in sores. While he was in this wretched state, there came to visit him Eliphaz the king of the Temanites, Bildad the tyrant of the Shuhites, and Zophar the king of the Mannaioi. Elihu the son of Barachel the Zobite also came. When they offered comfort, he said that even without comfort he would remain both in his piety and in his sufferings. God, being pleased...

city, Hamor and Shechem persuaded and exhorted the citizens to be circumcised. went into the city fully armed, and first they killed those they encountered. Then they also slaughtered Hamor and Shechem. He speaks concerning their slaughter in this way:

> And struck his head; he moved from the right hand to the left.
> He caught him as he was gasping, for the labor had quickly arisen.

> Overpowering the unwarrior-like Shechem, who was devising unspeakable things.

...to be transported. Following this, let us also examine the subsequent details concerning Joseph from the same many-storied history. Artapanus says in his work *On the Jews* that Joseph was a descendant of Abraham and a grandson of Jacob. Because he surpassed the others in self-control and wisdom, he was plotted against by his brothers. Foreseeing the attack, he pleaded with the neighboring Arabs to transport him to Egypt; and they did as agreed. For the kings of the Arabs are descendants of Israel, being sons of Abraham and brothers of Isaac. Upon arriving in Egypt, he was introduced to the king and became the administrator of the whole country.

Previously, the Egyptians had farmed their land in a disorganized fashion because the country was undivided, and the weaker were treated unjustly by the stronger. Joseph was the first to divide the land and mark it with boundaries, and he turned much of what was wasteland into arable soil. He also allotted certain fields to the priests. Furthermore, he invented measures <note>Joseph is here credited with the invention of standardized weights and measures, a common theme in Hellenistic Jewish literature which sought to attribute civilizing inventions to biblical figures.</note>, and for these reasons he was greatly loved by the Egyptians. He married Aseneth, the daughter of a priest of Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun."</note>, by whom he fathered children. After these events, his father and his brothers came to him, bringing many possessions, and they were settled in the city of Caesarea. As a result, the "swarming ones" <note>Original: "serphous." This likely refers to the Israelites multiplying rapidly, metaphorically compared to small swarming insects, or it may be a linguistic corruption of a tribal name.</note> multiplied in Egypt. He also says that those called "the interpreters" <note>Probably referring to a class of sacred scribes or priests.</note> built the temples in Athos and Heliopolis. Afterward, Joseph died, as did the king of Egypt. Joseph, while ruling Egypt for seven years, had stored up an immense amount of grain and became the master of Egypt. „ ...and to grant him utility, to release him from his illness, and to make him master of many things. Such are the details provided by the Polyhistor <note>Alexander Polyhistor, a 1st-century BCE scholar who compiled excerpts from various historians.</note> concerning these matters. And concerning Moses, the same author sets forth even more, which is worth hearing. The Polyhistor says that Moses was the first wise man, and that he was the first to hand down letters to the Jews; from the Jews, the Phoenicians received them, and the Greeks from the Phoenicians. He also says Moses was the first to write laws for the Jews. 

Artapanus says in his work *On the Jews* that after Abraham died, and also his son Memphathenoth, and likewise the king of the Egyptians, the king’s son Palmenothes took over the sovereignty. This man behaved badly toward the Jews. First, he built the city of Kestos and consecrated the temple there, and then he constructed the temple in Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun," a major religious center in ancient Egypt.</note>. This king fathered a daughter, Merris, whom he betrothed to a certain Chenephres, who was king over the regions below Memphis—for many people were kings of Egypt at that time. Since Merris was barren, she adopted the child of one of the Jews, and she named him Moses. 

By the Greeks, he was called Musaeus <note>A legendary polymath and poet in Greek myth, often associated with Orpheus.</note> once he reached manhood. This Moses became the teacher of Orpheus. When he grew up, he handed down many useful things to humanity. Indeed, he invented ships and machines for laying stone, as well as Egyptian weapons, and hydraulic and military engines, and even philosophy. Furthermore, he divided the state into thirty <term>Nomes</term> <note>From the Greek 'nomos,' referring to the administrative districts of ancient Egypt.</note> and assigned to each of the districts the god to be worshipped, and gave the sacred writings to the priests. These included cats, dogs, and ibises <note>Artapanus claims Moses established the Egyptian animal cults, likely an attempt to show Moses' civilizing influence even on Egyptian traditions.</note>. He also assigned a special territory to the priests. 

He did all these things for the sake of keeping the monarchy secure for Chenephres. For previously, the unruly crowds would sometimes expel kings and sometimes install them, often the same ones, and sometimes others. For these reasons, then, Moses was loved by the crowds, and having been deemed worthy of godlike honor by the priests, he was addressed as Hermes <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Thoth, the patron of scribes and inventor of writing.</note>, because of his interpretation of the sacred writings. 

When Chenephres saw the excellence of Moses, he became jealous of him and sought to kill him on some plausible pretext. And so, when the Ethiopians invaded Egypt, Chenephres thought he had found a suitable opportunity; he sent Moses against them as a general with a military force. He assembled a "rabble" <note>A weak, untrained force of commoners.</note> for him, assuming that Moses would easily be killed by the enemy because of the weakness of his soldiers. 

But Moses, coming to the district called Hermopolis with about one hundred thousand farmers, made camp there. He sent generals who were leaders of the region, who clearly excelled in the battles. It is said by the people of Heliopolis that this war lasted ten years. Because of the size of the army, those with Moses built a city in that place, and they consecrated Isis <note>The principal Egyptian goddess.</note> within it, because she destroys the animals that harm humans. They named the city Hermopolis. Thus the Ethiopians, even though they were enemies, came to love Moses so much that they even learned the practice of circumcision from him. And not only them, but all the priests as well. 

When the war ended, Chenephres accepted him in word, but in deed he continued to plot against him. Indeed, taking Moses’ troops away from him, he sent some to the borders of Ethiopia to keep guard...

...to tear down the temple near the city that had been constructed of baked brick, and to build another of stone, for which they quarried the stone from a nearby mountain. When the king arrived in Memphis with Moses, he inquired of him whether there was anything else useful for mankind. Then Chenephres, having designated the bull as "Apis," <note>The sacred bull of Memphis, worshipped as a god of fertility and a mediator between humans and the divine.</note> commanded the crowds to establish a sanctuary for it. He also ordered that the animals that had been buried by Moses be brought there and buried again, for he wished to keep Moses's inventions hidden.

Because the Egyptians were becoming alienated from him, the king prepared a conspiracy against Moses, swearing his friends to an oath not to report the plot. He then sought out men to assassinate him. When no one would obey, Chenephres reproached a man named Chanethothes, whom he addressed with great familiarity. Having been reproached, Chanethothes promised to make the attack when the opportunity arose. 

Around this time, Merris <note>Moses’s foster mother.</note> passed away. Chenephres promised the body to both Moses and Chanethothes so that they might transport it to the regions beyond Egypt to be buried, secretly believing that Moses would be murdered by Chanethothes during the journey. However, while they were traveling, someone who was aware of the conspiracy revealed the plot to Moses. Moses, being on his guard, buried Merris, and named the river and the city in that place "Merris." <note>Likely referring to Lake Moeris or a similar geographic feature in the Faiyum region.</note> This Merris is honored by the locals no less than the goddess Isis. 

When Aaron, the brother of Moses, learned of the conspiracy, he advised his brother to flee to Arabia. Moses followed this advice and, crossing the Nile from Memphis, departed for Arabia. When Chanethothes learned of Moses’s flight, he lay in ambush to kill him. Seeing him coming, Chanethothes drew his dagger against him, but Moses, acting first, seized the man's hand, drew his own sword, and slew Chanethothes. 

He then successfully crossed over into Arabia and, meeting the ruler of those regions, lived with him, having married the ruler's daughter. This ruler, Raguel, <note>Identified in the Bible as Jethro or Reuel, the priest of Midian.</note> wished to lead an army against the Egyptians to restore Moses and secure the sovereign power for his daughter and son-in-law. Moses prayed to God that he might finally cause the people’s suffering to cease. Moses was terrified by what had happened and began to flee, but a divine voice spoke to him, telling him to march against Egypt, rescue the Jews, and lead them to their ancient homeland.

When the King of the Egyptians <note>The successor to Chenephres.</note> learned of Moses’s presence, he summoned him and asked why he had come. Demetrius <note>Demetrius the Chronographer was a Jewish historian from the late 3rd century BCE who attempted to calculate biblical dates and reconcile genealogies using Greek scientific methods.</note> writes concerning the removal <note>original: "aphairesis" — referring to the killing</note> of the Egyptian, and the difference regarding Moses; he recorded things not for those yet to be born, but similarly for those who wrote the Holy Book. He notes that Moses fled to Midian and lived there with Zipporah, the daughter of Jethro. As can be inferred from the names, she was among the descendants of Keturah, from the offspring of Abraham—specifically from Jokshan, who was born to Abraham by Keturah. From Jokshan was born Dedan; from Dedan, Raguel; from Raguel, Jethro and Hobab; and from Jethro, Zipporah, whom Moses married. 

He notes that the generations also harmonize: for Moses is the seventh from Abraham, and Zipporah is the sixth. For Isaac (from whom Moses descends) was already living when Abraham married Keturah at the age of 140. She bore him a second son, Jokshan. This Jokshan, at the age of one hundred, fathered a son. Thus, Isaac was not born years later than those from whom Zipporah’s <term>genealogy</term> <note>The study of family lineages</note> is traced. There is, therefore, no inconsistency in Moses and Zipporah living at the same time. They lived in the city of Midian, named after one of Abraham’s sons. For he says that Abraham sent his sons to the East to find a place to dwell. For this reason, Aaron and Miriam said at Hazeroth that Moses had married an <term>Ethiopian woman</term> <note>original: "Aithiopida" — often used in the Greek Bible to refer to Cushites or people from southern lands, here linked to Midian</note>. 

Ezekiel also speaks about these matters in his play *The Exodus* <note>original: "Exagoge"</note>, including the dream seen by Moses and interpreted by his father-in-law. Moses himself speaks in a dialogue with his father-in-law roughly as follows:

> “Beckoned to me, and I stood before the throne.

> “He told me to sit. A royal diadem

Eupolemus also says that Solomon made one thousand golden shields, each of which weighed five hundred gold pieces. He lived fifty-two years, of which he reigned forty years in peace.

However, the region between the city and a distance of forty stadia is waterless, while beyond forty stadia, it is well-watered again.

## How noble teachings passed from barbarians to the Greeks, and concerning the antiquity of the Hebrews.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter "T" (Tau) inside a square frame, embellished with intricate vine and leaf scrollwork.</image-desc>
HAVING already discussed the arguments by which we preferred the philosophy of the Hebrews over that of the Greeks, and the reasoning by which we accepted the sacred books of those men; and having shown that even the Greeks were not ignorant of these men, but mentioned them by name, marveling at their lives and recording much about their royal capital <note>Likely referring to Jerusalem</note> and the rest of their history, let us now consider how they deemed them worthy not only of being recorded in writing, but also of being the source of their own teaching and learning—specifically among those who were zealous for doctrines that lead to the improvement of the soul.

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument that Greek intellectual achievements were borrowed from non-Greek sources, transitioning from a general list of sciences to a specific accusation of plagiarism, supported by the writings of Clement of Alexandria.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

The rest of their studies were undoubtedly set forth by some of those we call "barbarians" <term>barbarians: In this context, a Greek term for non-Greeks, including Hebrews, Egyptians, and Phoenicians, often used by Eusebius to show that "older" civilizations preceded Greek wisdom.</term>—most familiarly, geometry, arithmetic, music, astronomy, medicine, and even the very first elements of grammar, along with countless other technical and life-benefiting pursuits, as I will demonstrate shortly. As for their belief in many gods, their mysteries and rites, and furthermore their histories and mythical narratives about the gods, the allegorical interpretation of these myths, and the rest of their superstitious error, my previous discourse has already shown that they received these from the barbarians. This was evident when we saw how the most ancient Greeks, who had been wandering in a state of primitive simplicity, established their own theology—not without effort, as it appeared—by using what they found among the barbarians. In the same way, their particular views on piety toward the one God who is over all, and those doctrines concerning the things most sought after for the benefit of the soul—which would surely be the most essential parts of philosophical discourse—could have come from no other source than the Hebrews alone; this will be demonstrated before long. 

One might say that they happened upon these ideas by being moved by natural intuition, and this would actually support our argument: if these truths were not only handed down from the beginning of time by the divinely-inspired prophets to the Hebrews, but were also sought out and kindled among some (if not all) of those who achieved great fame in Greece through philosophical debates. Among these thinkers, though they are few in number—for they say that "noble things are difficult"—it is not through the abundance of Greek philosophers that these truths are proven, but rather through the reputation of the many that they attempt to cover up those like themselves. One should not wonder if they say it is possible for the Hebrew doctrines to have been "plundered" <note>original: ἐσκευωρῆσθαι (to be cooked up or plundered)</note> by them, since they have not only pillaged the rest of the studies of the Egyptians and Chaldeans and other barbarian nations, but even now they are caught in their own writings competing with one another and robbing each other. Each of them, having stolen the very words and thoughts of their neighbors, as well as entire compositions of discourse, has boasted of them as their own labors. Let no one suppose that this is merely my own claim; you shall hear it again from their own "all-wise" men, who convict one another of theft in their writings. Since we have once set out on this path, it is necessary to speak of this so that everyone can see the pattern of what is being revealed. Our own Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 AD), a Christian theologian who sought to unite Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note>, in the sixth book of his *Stromateis* <term>Stromateis: Meaning "Miscellanies" or "Tapestries," a major work by Clement discussing the relationship between Christianity and secular knowledge.</term>, directed his entire focus extensively to this subject. Taking his work, read these words of his which are at hand.

### Clement on the theft of the Greek writers.

> Having demonstrated the appearance of Greek invention as truth that was passed to us through the Scriptures but rephrased, we have shown their "theft" of the truth—if it is not too offensive to say so. Come then, let us bring the Greeks themselves as witnesses of their own theft against themselves. For those who so easily take their own ideas from one another confirm that they are indeed thieves; they inadvertently show that the truth among us is being treated as spoils of war among their own people. For if they do not even spare their own kind, how should they refrain from ours? We shall remain silent regarding their philosophical doctrines, as they themselves admit in writing...

### EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 10

» Having distinguished the various schools of thought <term>schools of thought: original: "haireseis" (αἱρέσεις), referring here to philosophical sects rather than religious heresies.</term>, so as not to appear ignorant of them, [it is shown that] they received their most important doctrines from others. By using the testimonies of a few well-known and reputable men among the Greeks, you have exposed their thievish nature <note>The Greek word "klopē" (κλοπή) literally means theft or larceny, used here to describe literary and intellectual plagiarism.</note>, taking advantage of different time periods. We shall now turn to what follows. Having said these things in his introduction, he then brings forward proofs from other writers, using abundant demonstrations. He first convicts the poets for having stolen from those similar to them by placing their respective words side by side. Then he adds the following: "So that we may not spare philosophy, history, or even rhetoric from similar scrutiny, it would be unreasonable not to set forth a few examples of these as well."

» Consequently, he sets forth passages from Orpheus, Linus, Heraclitus <note>The OCR text reads "Linakleitou," likely a scribal contraction or error for Linus and Heraclitus.</note>, Plato, Pythagoras, Metrodorus, Theopompus, Thucydides, Demosthenes, Aeschines, Lysias, Isocrates, and countless others. Choosing their phrases from the vast amount of writing available, he says the following regarding these various authors: "You will perceive the character of the Greek intellectual theft, which stands as a clear example before your eyes of those who have been caught. Now, they have been found out not only stealing and paraphrasing thoughts and expressions, as will be shown, but even stealing the works of others in their entirety and putting them forth as their own." 

» Just as the man from Cyrene <note>Likely referring to a specific scholar from the city of Cyrene in Libya, known for its intellectual schools.</note> did with a whole book *On Proverbs* among the unlearned. Furthermore, after bringing forward many proofs for this argument from other sources, he concludes with these words: "Life would fail me if I tried to go through every instance to prove Greek plagiarism, and how they claim for themselves the discovery of the most beautiful doctrines among them, which they actually received from us <note>Clement speaks as a representative of the "barbarian" or Judeo-Christian tradition here.</note>. For they are convicted not only of stealing doctrines from the barbarians, but also of imitating our ways. Moreover, they use rhetorical mythology to turn into wonders the works of divine power that were miraculously performed through those who lived holily for our conversion."

» And indeed, the events they relate are either true or false. We will not say they are false, for they would not willingly condemn themselves for the greatest deceit—that of writing falsehoods. It is clear, then, that they must necessarily admit they are true. And how can the wonders shown through Moses and the holy prophets still appear incredible to them? For God, the Almighty Ruler, cares for all whom He benefits; He turns some toward salvation through commands, some through threats, some through miraculous signs, and others through gentle promises. 

» Long ago, when a long-lasting drought was devastating Greece and a barrenness of fruit prevailed, the survivors, they say, having become suppliants due to the famine, went to Delphi and asked the Pythia how they might be delivered from the calamity. She gave them one solution for their misfortunes: that they should seek the prayer of Aeacus <note>Aeacus (Αἰακός) was a legendary king of Aegina, famed for his piety and justice; in mythology, he became one of the judges of the Underworld.</note>. Aeacus, yielding to them, ascended the Hellenic mountain and, stretching out pure hands to heaven, called upon God as the common Father. He prayed that He would have pity on him, as Greece was being worn away. As he prayed, a sudden thunder sounded, and all the surrounding air grew cloudy; heavy and continuous rains burst forth and filled the whole land. From this, an abundant and rich harvest was brought to maturity, cultivated by the prayers of Aeacus. 

» But it says [in the Scriptures] that Samuel called upon the Lord, and the Lord gave thunder and rain in the day of the wheat harvest. You see that He who sends rain...

## Porphyry on the Greeks being thieves, from the first book of the *Philological Lecture*.

Longinus invited us to Athens; he had invited many others, including Nicagoras the sophist, Maioras, Apollonius the grammarian, Demetrius the geometer, Prosenius the Peripatetic, and Callietes the Stoic. I myself was the seventh reclining with them. As the dinner progressed, and a certain inquiry concerning the consensus on Ephorus <note>Ephorus of Cyme (c. 400–330 BC) was a prominent Greek historian.</note> was raised among the others, I heard (he said) what the fuss was about Ephorus. Those inquiring were Kaustrios and Maximus. For while the one [Maximus] supported Theopompus <note>Theopompus of Chios, another major 4th-century BC historian and a rival to Ephorus.</note>, Kaustrios called [Ephorus] a thief. "For if," he said, "this were Ephorus’s own specialty, I would not wonder; but have I not seen Callisthenes and Dyaximus transposing four hundred whole lines in the very same words?" To him, Apollonius the grammarian said: "Did you then know that even Theopompus, whom you honor, has been seized by this same passion? Not least in the eleventh book of the *History of Philip*, having transcribed those things from Isocrates’ *Panathenaicus* in the very same words: 'that to men, nothing of the good or the bad comes by itself,' and so on." And yet Isocrates does not say he was "defeated by himself," nor in the contest over the lever <note>The "contest over the lever" is an obscure reference to a rhetorical or physical competition mentioned by Isocrates.</note>, which he made as a teacher of facts in a condensed way, transposing things clear in others so that he might lie, making it his own work. For Andron, in the *Tripod* concerning Pythagoras the philosopher, had recorded the stories about his prophecies, saying that once, while thirsty in Metapontum, Pythagoras asked for water from a well, and after drinking, he predicted that there would be an earthquake on the third day. After bringing forward other such things, he reported that Theopompus stole everything from Andron’s history of Pythagoras. While not speaking about Pythagoras—for perhaps others knew about him and would have said, "I would have said these things myself"—he has now made the theft obvious by changing the names. For he used the same prophecies but transferred them to another name. He made Pherecydes the Syrian the one who predicted these things. He hides the theft not only by this name, but also by transposing the locations. For the prophecy of the earthquake which Andron said took place in Metapontum, Theopompus says was spoken in Syria. And as for the matter concerning the ship, he says it was observed not from Megara in Sicily, but from Samos. And he moved the clear thirst [story] to Messene. So that he might not seem to be speaking of something incomplete, he added a foreign "cheese-tower" <note>original: "tyrriōma" (τυρρίωμα), a rare word perhaps referring to a type of fortification or structured tale.</note>, wrapping it up well. "And I," said Nicagoras, "encountering his rhetorical works and those of Xenophon, have caught him transposing many things from Xenophon. There is one such instance where, on the worse side, he relates the meeting of Pharnabazus with Agesilaus <note>Historical figures from the early 4th century BC; Agesilaus was a Spartan king and Pharnabazus a Persian satrap.</note> through Apollophanes of Cyzicus, and the words of both to 
each other

<header>PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 13</header>

> "...having exposed how they harmonize with one another, which Xenophon recorded in his fourth book. Quite gracefully and fittingly for both, Theopompus transferred this to the eleventh book of his *History of Philip* <note>original: "Philippica"</note>, yet he made the work laborious, sluggish, and ineffective. For in his eagerness to display the power of his prose—as well as his skill in theft, elaboration, and interpolation—he appears slow and stalling, as if constantly hesitating, thereby destroying the liveliness and energy of Xenophon's original work." 
>
> When Niceratus had said this, Apollonius replied: "And why should we wonder if the sickness of theft touched Theopompus and Ephorus, men who were truly quite crude? For even Menander <note>A famous Athenian playwright known as the master of 'New Comedy.'</note> was filled with this ailment. Aristophanes the Grammarian <note>A famous scholar and librarian at Alexandria (c. 257–180 BC).</note> exposed him in his *Parallel Passages*, comparing Menander’s own works to those from which he stole. Furthermore, Latinus, in the six books he titled *On the Things Not Belonging to Menander*, revealed the sheer number of his thefts. Similarly, Philostratus of Alexandria produced a treatise regarding the thefts of Sophocles. That author, as if he had caught a great criminal, says that Menander transcribed an entire play, the *Bird-Diviner* by Antiphanes, from beginning to end, and turned it into his own play, *The Superstitious Man*."
> 
> "And since it did not seem possible for the thieves to hide from you," he continued, "I will bring into the center the beautiful Menander and even Hyperides <note>One of the ten great Attic orators.</note>, who stole many things from Demosthenes, both in the speech *Against Diondas* and in the one *Concerning the Gifts*. It is perfectly clear that one transferred the material from the other. Since they were contemporaries, it would be your job, Apollonius, to track down the thief based on the dates. I myself suspect that Hyperides was the one who pilfered it. But since it is unclear which one it was, I admire Demosthenes if, after taking from Hyperides, he improved it as needed; but I blame Hyperides if, after taking from Demosthenes, he distorted it for the worse."
> 
> And after a few more words, he says: "And why do I tell you how Hellanicus <note>An early Greek historian (5th century BC).</note> compiled his *Barbarian Customs* from the works of Hellodorus and Damastus? Or how Herodotus, in his second book, transferred many things from Hecataeus's *Description of the Earth* word-for-word by imitation, only slightly altering the accounts of the Phoenix bird, the hippopotamus, and the crocodiles? Or how the things said about judicial examinations <term>judicial examinations: original "basanon" (βασάνων), often referring to the interrogation of slaves under torture to gather evidence</term> in Isaeus's speech *On the Estate of Cyron* are the same as those found in Isocrates's *Trapeziticus*, or in Demosthenes's speech *Against Onetor*? They are spoken in almost identical words. Or how Dinarchus, in his first book *On the Assault of Cleomedon*, transferred many things with the very same names from Demosthenes’s speech *Against Conon for Assault*?"
> 
> "Or how Simonides, in his eleventh book, took the thought of Hesiod: 'For a man wins nothing better than a good wife; but again, nothing more chilling than a bad one,' and transferred it thus: 'A man wins no possession better than a noble wife, nor any more chilling than a bad one.' And Euripides, in his *Melanippe the Captive*, wrote: 'Than a bad woman, nothing worse is born; but of the noble, nothing is naturally better in excellence. Yet their natures differ.' And where Euripides says, 'We women are the most wretched plant,' Theodectes says in his *Alcmaeon*: 'A clear word is sung among mortals, that there is no plant more wretched than woman.' This man not only took the inspiration from there, but even used the exact words, either because he deviously wished it to seem more like a proverb than a quotation, or because he wished to appear to have taken it from his own father <note>Theodectes was a student of many, but this may imply he was trying to claim the "ancestry" of the thought.</note>. Even Antimachus, when stealing from Homer, would slightly 'correct' the original. For where Homer said, 'He was the strongest of men upon the earth'..."

It argues that even cultural icons like Herodotus, Menander, and Sophocles built their reputations by copying and slightly altering the works of others.</summary>

# EUSEBIUS, PR[EPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL]

» "Antimachus says: '*The sweat of the earth-born was visible from his head*.' <note>original: "ἰδεώ π' δε κάρητος ἐπιχθονίων εἶν' αἰδρώον"</note> And Lycophron <note>A scholar-poet from the 3rd century BC known for his complex, obscure language.</note> expanded upon this by a transposition, doing so with care for the verse. For the phrase, '*Lord Diomedes replied to him in silence*,' <note>original: "ὃ γὰρ, ἢ σ' ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη κρείων Διομήδης, σιγᾷ"</note> which refers to a line of Homer’s that was mocked by Cratinus <note>An early master of Athenian Old Comedy.</note> because of its excessive repetition—specifically the phrase '*and answering him*'—is why Antimachus did not hesitate to rearrange such a well-worn expression. 

» "Similarly, the line, '*among the people over whom he ruled, he was like a gentle father*,' <note>original: "λαῶν οἶσιν ἀνάσσε, πατήρ σ' ὡς ἤπιος ἦεν"</note> which is a Homeric verse that appears in two different places, was rearranged by Antimachus into a hybrid form: '*they taunted the ranks of the people over whom they ruled*.' <note>original: "λαῶν οἶσιν ἀνάσσον ἐκερτύσαντο φάλαγγας"</note> 

» "But so that I myself might not be caught as a thief while accusing others of theft, let the records I have made regarding these matters stand. There are two books by Lysimachus regarding the plagiarism of Ephorus. Alcetus, the poet of mocking iambics and epigrams, also exposed Ephorus's thefts in relation to songs. There is also a letter from Pollio to Phronides regarding the plagiarism of Ctesias. The same author also has a sixth book concerning the plagiarism of Diodorus. Furthermore, in the work titled *The Fishermen*, he says many things about Theopompus. There is also a treatise by Aretades on *Compositional Synthesis*, <note>original: "synegmatoseos"</note> from which many such things can be learned. 

» "While the others were speaking, the gentle speaker said that while others were caught as thieves, even the divine Plato himself—whose namesake festival we are celebrating today—is someone who made excessive use of those who came before him. I feel a sense of shame <note>original: "αἰδοῦμαι"</note> in using the word 'theft' in his case, but you have all understood it in silence." 

» "What are you saying?" asked Callistratus. "I say only what I can provide an account for. For all the books of those who lived before Plato existed... [for] many have detected these thefts of the philosopher. I myself have encountered them by chance. For coming upon a discourse recently that you were reading against those who introduce 'the Being,' <note>original: "τοὺς ἐν δ' ὃν εἰσάγοντας"</note> I found him using such rejected ideas. I was eager to remember the very words that were spoken." And having said these things, he laid out the proofs. 

» "But as to which writer was a contemporary of which words, and the fact that he did not even spare his own work from scrutiny, I think what has been said is sufficient out of the thousands of examples available. 

Since it serves our preparation to show how the Greeks were benefited by the flowing in of ideas from the Hebrew scriptures, it seems to me both good and necessary to demonstrate that all of their desired education and philosophy—even their primary lessons and the solemn parts of their logical science—were gathered together by them from barbarians <note>In this context, 'barbarians' simply refers to non-Greeks, specifically the Hebrews and other ancient Near Eastern peoples.</note>. This is so that none of them may continue to reproach us with the claim that we have preferred the piety and philosophy found among the barbarians over the solemn traditions of their own people."

## That we have not chosen Hebrew theology over our own philosophy without reason.

That we have not preferred the Hebrew theology by placing our own philosophy second to it out of a lack of sound reason, you may know by learning that even those Greeks who applied themselves most correctly to philosophy—and who thought of something further and greater regarding the gods than what was heard among the common people—did not discover doctrines different from those already established among the Hebrews. For while some of them were led away by various false opinions and wandered into a depth of idle talk, those who utilized a somewhat sounder reasoning reached a grasp of the truth in these matters...

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 16

They [the Greeks] have by nature been participants in the teachings of the Hebrews. It is likely, then, that having become men of great learning—having examined the customs and teachings of the various nations with a rather curious eye—they did not fail to recognize the philosophy of those mentioned. Indeed, these Greeks are quite recent in time, so to speak, arising not only after the Hebrews, Phoenicians, and Egyptians, but even after the most ancient of the Greeks themselves.

Among these, it is acknowledged that Cadmus, the son of Agenor <note>original: "Κάδμος ὁ ἀγνοώρης" - a likely scribal error for 'son of Agenor.' Cadmus was the legendary Phoenician prince who introduced the alphabet to the Greeks.</note>, brought traditions from Phoenicia, while mysteries and rites regarding the gods came from Egypt or elsewhere. These were established either by Orpheus the Thracian—or some other Greek or foreigner acknowledged as a leader of this "error" <note>The author views pagan polytheism as a "wandering" or "error" from the truth.</note>—who set up wooden cult images <note>term: "ξόανον" (xoanon) — an ancient, primitive wooden statue of a deity, often believed to have fallen from heaven.</note> and organized hymns, songs, and incantations. Even the Greeks themselves admit they know of no one older than these figures; they say that Orpheus was the first of all, followed by Linus, and then Musaeus, flourishing around the time of the Trojan War or shortly before.

However, the religious practices of the Greeks were nothing more than the "wandering theology" of the Phoenicians or Egyptians. Indeed, among the other nations, throughout every land and city, in temples and mysteries, these same rites—identical to those of the Greeks—were being performed. Certainly, the previously described account concerning the gods prevailed among all people. Temples were beautifully constructed, adorned with statues and votive offerings, and refined by all. Moreover, cult images of every kind of material, fashioned with great care into every form of female living being, were meticulously crafted. 

For my part, I have always been wary of the great and abundant quantity of oracles found among all people—those celebrated as great and holy gods, especially among the Greeks. At that time, the Pythian oracle <note>The oracle of Apollo at Delphi.</note> was at its absolute peak of power, as were the Clarian <note>Another oracle of Apollo in Ionia.</note> and the Dodonaean <note>The oldest Greek oracle, dedicated to Zeus.</note>, followed by the oracles of Amphiaraus and Amphilochus. Beyond these, there was an overflowing crowd of soothsayers, more numerous than the crowd of poets and reciters. 

Long after these times, philosophy appeared. It did not find anything suitable for itself in the traditions of the ancestors; it bypassed the "solemn" and ancient myths of their paternal theology—those very things that were wondered at and shouted about by all, and those divine oracles that had been tested by experience. Because of this, philosophers put those traditions aside as secondary, seeing them as contributing nothing toward the choice of what is necessary and true. 

The rest of the nations, even the foreigners, being "naked" as it were and lacking their own store of words and teachings, translated what they could. They gathered and collected useful things from everywhere, whatever was ready at hand from each nation. Thus, they did not only learn the missing pieces of the aforementioned theology from the Greeks, but also the other arts and the most useful sciences for life. 

The Greeks themselves agree that after Orpheus, Linus, and Musaeus—who, as the oldest theologians, first led them into the error of polytheism—the "Seven Men" <note>The Seven Sages of Greece, including figures like Thales and Solon.</note> were wondered at for their philosophy and were given the name "Wise Men." These men are said to have lived around the time of King Cyrus <note>Cyrus the Great, founder of the Persian Empire (6th century BC).</note>. But the time in which the first and last of the Hebrew prophets prophesied would be reckoned as more than six hundred years after the Trojan War, and no less than one thousand five hundred years from the age of Moses. This will become clear to you a little later as you go through the chronological records. At about the same time, the Seven Sages were named, at a point when they were recalling the upbringing of an older generation, of whose maxims they remember nothing more. Much later in time...
