Eusebius now transitions from religious practices to the origins of Greek philosophy itself, arguing that the greatest Greek thinkers—Pythagoras, Thales, Solon, Plato, and Democritus—were mere students of "barbarian" (non-Greek) wisdom, often coinciding with the periods of Hebrew exile in Egypt and Babylon.</meta>

### EUSEBIUS

...the first philosophers are remembered to have excelled. Among them, Pythagoras was the first to invent the name "philosophy" <note>term: "Philosophy" — Literally "love of wisdom." Before Pythagoras, thinkers were usually called "Sages" or "Wise Men."</note>. He was a pupil of Pherecydes and, according to the Ionians, was a Samian, though others say he was Tyrrhenian <note>Eusebius is highlighting the debate over whether the "father of philosophy" was even a native Greek.</note>. Some even say he was Syrian or Tyrian, and they admit he was a "barbarian" <note>term: "Barbarian" — In the ancient Greek context, this simply meant anyone who did not speak Greek; here, Eusebius uses it to show that wisdom originated outside of Greece.</note> rather than a Greek. Yet this man's name is on the lips of all Greeks. They also record that Pherecydes was a Syrian, and they say Pythagoras was his student. Pythagoras is said to have associated not only with him, but to have spent time with all the local Magi <note>term: "Magi" — Originally a caste of priests from Persia (Zoroastrians) known for their knowledge of astronomy and the natural world.</note> and to have been a student of the Egyptian prophets at the very time when the Hebrews appear to have made their migration <note>referring to the Babylonian Captivity and the flight to Egypt</note> to Egypt and Babylon. 

Indeed, the man in question, being a meddler in the wisdom of every people, visited Babylon, Egypt, and Chaldea. While studying under the Magi and the priests, he is recorded to have heard the teachings of the Brahmans <note>note: original "βραχμάνων" (brachmanon) — the priestly and scholarly caste of ancient India.</note> in their entirety; these are the philosophers of the Indians. From some he gathered astrology, from others geometry, arithmetic from others and music, and various things from various people. He possessed nothing from the Greeks alone, for they lived in a "poverty of wisdom" and a "distress of resources." On the contrary, he himself became the cause of learning for the Greeks by providing them with the knowledge he had procured from foreigners. 

Such was Pythagoras. From him arose the first succession of the so-called "Italian" philosophy, earning its name from his residence in Italy. After this came the "Ionic" school, named after Thales, one of the Seven Sages. Then followed the "Eleatic" school, which lists Xenophanes of Colophon as its father. But even Thales, as the Ionians record, was a Phoenician; others, however, have supposed him to be a Milesian. He too is said to have consorted with the Egyptian prophets. 

As for Solon, who was also one of the Seven Sages and the one whom the Athenians say gave them their laws, Plato says that he likewise visited the Egyptians at the time when the Hebrews were again inhabiting Egypt. In the *Timaeus* <note>One of Plato's most famous dialogues, dealing with the nature of the physical world and human society.</note>, Plato introduces him conversing with an Egyptian youth <note>likely a reference to an Egyptian priest, though the text says "boy" or "child" to emphasize the priest's view of Greeks as young.</note>, in which the Egyptian says to him:

> "O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children; there is no such thing as an old Greek, nor do you possess any learning that is grey with age." <note>original: "ὦ σόλων, σόλων, ἕλληνες ἀεὶ παῖδές ἐστε... οὐδὲ ἔστι παρ' ὑμῖν χρόνῳ πολιὸν μάθημα." This is a famous critique of Greek cultural superficiality compared to the ancient civilizations of the East.</note>

And Plato himself, though he studied with the Pythagoreans in Italy, was not satisfied with their instruction alone. He is said to have sailed to Egypt and to have devoted a great deal of time to their philosophy. He himself bears witness to this in many places in his own writings regarding the "barbarians," doing so, it seems to me, because he did not ungratefully deny that he had imported the finest parts of his philosophy from them. One can hear him in many places, and particularly in the *Epinomis*, mentioning the Syrians and Egyptians together in this way:

> "The cause of this is the first man to observe these things, who was a barbarian. For an ancient land nurtured those who first conceived these ideas, because of the beauty of the summer season, which Egypt and Syria possess in abundance. From there, these observations have reached everywhere, including here [to Greece], having been tested by time for ten thousand years or even infinity."

And proceeding further, he adds:

> "Let us take it as a rule that whatever the Greeks receive from barbarians, they bring it to a more beautiful conclusion in the end." <note>original: "ὅ,τιπερ ἂν ἕλληνες βαρβάρων παραλάβωσι, κάλλιον τοῦτο εἰς τέλος ἀπεργάζονται."</note>

These are the words of Plato. And even earlier, Democritus is said to have composed his works from the "foreign accounts" of the Babylonians. Somewhere, boasting about himself, he says:

> "Of all the men of my time, I have wandered over the most land, investigating the greatest things; I have seen the most climates and earths, and I have listened to the most learned men..."

### EUSEBIUS: PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 6

» ...to understand the arrangement of letters with logical proof, no one has surpassed me. Not even those among the Egyptians called the **horoscope-watchers** <note>term: "Horoscope-watchers" — These were specialized Egyptian priests (horoscopoi) who tracked the hours and the positions of stars to determine the timing of rituals and the fates of men.</note>, among whom I was enrolled for eighty years in a foreign land. I also traveled through the land of **Babylon** and **Assyria**, and visited the Egyptians, being a student to both the common Egyptians and their priests. 

» If I were to list the sacred sites, or the captives of **Delos** <note>original: "δήλους ἥλων" — likely a reference to those "taken" or captivated by the fame of the Delian oracle</note>, through which your form of government is exposed as having been impoverished for a vast age, and left naked of every branch of learning—it was indeed decorated with the rites of the gods, with statues and shrines, with divinations and oracles, and with the great **humbug** <note>term: "Humbug" (Greek: typhos) — Literally "smoke" or "vapor," used by ancient critics to describe the empty pride or delusion associated with pagan religious displays.</note> of the demons who deceive the people; but it was entirely widowed of true wisdom and life-benefiting learning. Their useless oracles contributed nothing further to their discovery of virtuous words. Not even the "wonderful" **Pythian** <note>The Pythian Apollo, the god of the famous oracle at Delphi.</note> himself would have helped them toward philosophy, nor did the Delian god assist them in the pursuit of any necessary occupation. 

» Instead, wandering here and there, and passing through their whole life, they "brightened themselves with **foreign feathers**" <note>An allusion to Aesop's fable of the Jackdaw who dressed himself in the feathers of other birds to appear more beautiful than he was.</note> according to the myth. Thus, their entire philosophy is now found to be a **potluck** <note>term: "Potluck" (Greek: eranos) — Originally a meal where every guest contributed a dish; here used metaphorically for a philosophy made of borrowed parts rather than original insight.</note>. For it is clear that they modeled their learning after others: they have **geometry** from the Egyptians, **astrology** from the Chaldeans, and other things from other peoples. There is nothing they have that did not come from some other source, and some of them even found what is "good" from the **Hebrews**. 

As for the knowledge of the God of the Universe, and the condemnation of their own local gods, the argument will demonstrate this as it proceeds a little further. For the present, it signals to readers that the ancient Greeks were not only devoid of true theology, but also of the learning that benefits philosophy—and not only these things, but even their common and political practices. 

Let us say that this observation is made to prove our intended goal. For if our purpose is to provide an account showing that we have not irrationally preferred the theology found among the **Hebrews**—which they themselves would call "**barbarian**"—over Greek philosophy; and if they themselves are seen to have plundered everything long ago from the barbarians, and to have been helped in no way at all toward philosophy by their own gods (even justly blaming their own gods, which led some to prefer **atheism** over the service of the gods), then it is no longer for us to be blamed. Rather, we should be accepted and praised, because we have loved the better things rather than those suited only for mortals. Having withdrawn from falsehood, we have neither fallen into the atheistic reasoning of the Greek "wise men," nor have we, like those wonderful philosophers, mixed the polytheistic error into our knowledge of the God over all, nor confused falsehood with truth. 

But before we get to that, let me first show those things by which the Greeks plundered everything from the barbarians. Not only their philosophical studies, but even their common and life-benefiting traditions are exposed as stolen.

---

-> **That the Greeks benefited in all things from the Barbarians.** <-

First, then, regarding common letters—the very first elements of grammar—**Cadmus** <note>In Greek mythology, Cadmus was a Phoenician prince who was credited with bringing the alphabet to the Greeks.</note> was the one who introduced their use; he was the son of a Phoenician, which is why some of the ancients called the letters "Phoenician." There are others who say that the **Syrians** invented letters...

# EUSEBIUS
**Page 278**

...they are the first to say so. Furthermore, there are Syrians and Hebrews who inhabit the neighbor of Phoenicia—a land called **Phoenicia** <note>original: "Φοινίκην"</note> in ancient times, later called **Judea**, and finally named **Palestine**. We claim that the sound of the Greek letters is not at all foreign to these people. Indeed, among them, each of the elements <note>term: "Elements" (stoicheia) — In this context, it refers to the letters of the alphabet.</note> bears its name according to a certain meaningful thought, which is something one cannot find among the Greeks. Therefore, it is widely admitted that these letters are not the Greeks' own property. 

Among the Hebrews, there are twenty-two elements in total. The first of these is **Alph** <note>Aleph</note>, which, when translated into the Greek tongue, is called **learning**. The second is **Beth**, which is interpreted as **of a house**. The third is **Giml** <note>Gimel</note>, which is **fulfillment**. The fourth is **Delth** <note>Daleth</note>, which signifies **of tablets**. The fifth is **He**, which is **this** <note>original: "αὕτη" (this/she)</note>. Taken together, the first letters demonstrate a thought such as: **"Learning of the house, this is the fulfillment of tablets."**

Next, after these, is the sixth element, called **Vau** <note>Waw</note> among them, which means **in her**. Then **Zai** <note>Zayin</note>, which means **live**. After which is **Eth** <note>Heth</note>, which is **the living one**. So that the whole phrase is: **"In her lives the living one."** 

After these is the ninth element, **Teth**, which is **good**. Then **Ioth** <note>Yod</note>, which is interpreted as **beginning**. Together the two mean: **"A good beginning."** 

Upon these is **Chaph** <note>Kaph</note>, which is **nevertheless**. Then **Labd** <note>Lamed</note>, which is **learn**. The whole: **"Nevertheless, learn."** 

After these, the thirteenth element is **Mem**, which is **from them**. Then **Nun**, which is **eternal**. Next **Sumch** <note>Samekh</note>, which is interpreted as **help**. So that the saying is: **"From them, eternal help."** 

Upon these is **Ain** <note>Ayin</note>, which, when translated, signifies a **spring** or an **eye**. Then **Phe**, a **mouth**. Then next, **Zade** <note>Tsadi</note>, **righteousness**. The meaning of these is: **"A spring (or eye) and a mouth of righteousness."** 

After these is the element **Koph**, which is interpreted as a **calling**. Then **Res**, which is a **head**. And after these, **Sen** <note>Shin</note>, which is **teeth**. Finally, the twenty-second element is called **Thau** among them, which indicates **signs**. The thought would be: **"A calling of the head and signs of teeth."**

Such is the translation and interpretation of the elements among the Hebrews, completing a certain domestic discourse <note>The author argues that the alphabet itself forms a coherent set of sentences or a "creed."</note> that is appropriate for both instruction and promise. You would not find the like among the Greeks; from which fact one must necessarily admit that these are not the Greeks' own, but were embroidered by them from a **barbarian** <note>term: "Barbarian" — In the ancient world, this simply meant "non-Greek speaker," though here it carries a tone of reclaiming the title as a source of ancient wisdom.</note> tongue. This is clear even from the choice of the names for each element. For how does **Alpha** differ from **Alph**, or **Beta** from **Beth**, or **Gamma** from **Giml**, or **Delta** from **Delth**, or **E** from **He**, or **Zeta** from **Zai**, or **Eta** from **Teth**, and all such similar cases? Thus, it is indisputable that such sounds are not native to the Greeks. They belong, then, to the Hebrews, among whom each is shown to have a meaning. Having begun with these people first, they proceeded to the Lydians, and indeed even to the Greeks.

Let this much be said by me concerning the first elements. But you, having touched upon the harbor of this very subject, listen to what **Clement** <note>Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Christian theologian who argued that Greek philosophy was "stolen" from the Bible.</note> says.

The **Phrygians** were the first to carefully observe the flights of birds. And the **Tyrrhenians**, neighbors of Italy, perfected the art of sacrificial inspection. The **Isaurians** and the **Arabs** labored over the art of augury <note>divination from bird signs</note>, just as...

### EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 10
aa. ii.

„ ...they detest <note>original: "μισοῦσι"</note> divination through dreams. The **Tyrrhenians** <note>The Etruscans of Italy</note> invented the **trumpet**, and the **Phrygians** the **flute**. For the Phrygians were also the ones who [invented] the arts of the Muses. The **Lydians** likewise invented the beautiful [craft of] baskets, while the **Egyptians** divided the year into twelve months and forbade sexual intercourse within temples; they also legislated that no one should enter a temple without bathing after relations with a woman. 
„ These same people were also the inventors of **geometry**. The **Telmessians** [invented divination], and **Damnameneus**, one of the **Idaean Dactyls** <note>term: "Idaean Dactyls" — Mythical ancient metalworkers and magicians associated with Mount Ida.</note>, was the first to discover **iron** in **Cyprus**. **Delas**, a man clearly a **Jew**, discovered the **mixing of bronze** <note>note: Hesiod, however, attributes this to a Scythian.</note>. Furthermore, the **Thracians** were the first to find the so-called **harpe** <note>term: "Harpe" — A curved sword or sickle-shaped blade.</note>; it is a curved knife. They were also the first to use **light shields** <note>term: "Pelta" — A small, crescent-shaped wicker shield.</note> while on horseback. Similarly, the **Illyrians** invented the aforementioned light shield. Some say the **Carians** <note>original: "Κανοὺς" in OCR, likely "Κᾶρας"</note> invented the **plastic arts** <note>molding or sculpture</note>; while **Itymon**, a Samnite by birth, first constructed the **oblong shield** <note>term: "Thyreos" — A large, door-shaped shield used by heavy infantry.</note>.
„ **Cadmus the Phoenician** <note>The legendary founder of Thebes</note> discovered **stone-cutting**, and he devised the **gold mines** around Mount Pangaeum. Yet another nation, the **Cappadocians**, first invented the instrument called the **nabla** <note>term: "Nabla" — A Phoenician or Hebrew stringed instrument, likely a harp or lyre.</note>, which the citizens say has two strings. The **Carthaginians** were the first to construct the **trireme** <note>term: "Trireme" — A galley with three banks of oars, the primary warship of the ancient Mediterranean.</note>; it was built by **Bosporus**, a native of that land. **Midra** <note>likely "Midas" in the original source</note> of Egypt discovered the **shellfish** <note>term: "Kohlis" — Specifically the murex snail used to produce purple dye.</note> used to dye walls. But even later, a nation called the **Rapanonikai** <note>note: Likely a corruption of "Hyperboreans" or a specific local tribe</note>, who are called the domestic race, first worked **bronze** and purified **iron**.
„ **Amycus**, the king of the Bebrycians, invented **boxing thongs** <note>leather strips wrapped around the hands</note>. Regarding music, **Olympus the Mysian** crafted the **Lydian harmony**. The people called the **Troglodytes** <note>literally "cave-dwellers"</note> invented the **sambuca**, a musical instrument. They also say that **Eutyrus** the Phrygian invented the **transverse flute**; similarly, **Agnon** the Phrygian invented the building of walls and the **dissonant harmony**. **Olympus** the Phrygian likewise invented the **chromatic scale**. Both the **Mixophrygian** and **Mixolydian** modes were invented by **Marsyas**, who belonged to the aforementioned regions; and **Thamyris the Thracian** devised the **Dorian mode**. 
„ We have also heard that the **Persians** were the first to judge the **chariot** <note>original: "ἀπήνην"</note> and to manufacture the **footstool**. The **Sidonians** were the first to construct the walls of temples. The **Sicilians**, the first in Italy, invented the **phorminx** <note>a type of early lyre</note>, which is somewhat inferior to the cithara, and the **clappers** <note>term: "Krotala" — Ancient percussion instruments similar to castanets.</note> were also their invention. It is said that **linen garments** were discovered by the citizens under the reign of Queen **Semiramis**. **Hellanicus** says that she was also the first to compose **letters** <note>epistles</note>, being the first woman to rule.
„ Now, **Scamman** of Mitylene, **Theophrastus** of Ephesus, **Cydippidas** of Mantinea, and further **Antiphanes**, **Aristodemus**, and **Aristotle**, and in addition to these **Philostephanus**, and even **Straton the Peripatetic**, record these things in their works *On Inventions*. I have set forth a few of these examples to establish the useful and life-benefiting nature of the **Barbarians**, from whom the Greeks gained their practical skills. 

„ These are the words of **Clement** in his *Miscellanies*. To what has been said, I think it is necessary to add the writings of **Josephus** the historian of the Hebrews, from the two books he composed regarding the **Antiquity of the Jews**. He wrote against the Greeks who think themselves recent, showing that many things were gained from the Barbarians, and that his own records are consistent with themselves. These points serve for an accurate and firm confirmation of what has been said. Hear, then, exactly what he writes:

->**JOSEPHUS, ON THE SAME SUBJECT.**<-

<meta>This page continues the transition from discussing specific cultural inventions to a broader historical argument. Eusebius is here quoting Josephus (*Against Apion*), who argues for the superior antiquity of Eastern records (Jewish, Egyptian, Phoenician) over the relatively "recent" historical consciousness of the Greeks.</meta>

-> # EUSEBIUS <-

» ...for us or for other men to be skeptical. For how can I see the opposite to be the case, if one is not to follow vain opinions, but rather to grasp the truth of matters from the facts themselves? For everything among the **Greeks** will be found to be modern, dating—so to speak—from yesterday or the day before. I am speaking of the founding of their cities, the inventions of their arts, and the recording of their laws. But nearly the most recent of all their pursuits is the care they give to the writing of **histories**. 

» However, concerning the **Egyptians**, the **Chaldeans**, and the **Phoenicians**—if for the moment we include ourselves <note>original: "ἡμᾶς" — referring to the Jewish people, as Josephus is the original speaker here</note> among them—they themselves certainly admit that they possess a tradition of memory that is most ancient and enduring. For they all inhabit regions that are least subject to the destruction caused by the environment <note>A reference to the belief that Egypt and Mesopotamia were less prone to the Great Floods that supposedly wiped out Greek records periodically</note>, and they took great care to leave nothing that happened among them unrecorded, but rather to have it always consecrated in public registers by their wisest men. 

» In the region of **Greece**, however, ten thousand destructions occurred which wiped out the memory of past events; and as they were always establishing new ways of life, each generation considered their own era to be the very beginning of things. It was only late and with difficulty that they learned the nature of **letters**. For those who wish to claim the most ancient use for them boast that they learned them from the **Phoenicians** and **Cadmus** <note>The mythical prince of Tyre who was credited with bringing the alphabet to Greece</note>. 

» Yet, not even from that time could anyone point to any record preserved either in temples or on public monuments. Indeed, even concerning those who campaigned against **Troy** so many years later, there has been much doubt and inquiry as to whether they used writing; and the truth prevails that they were ignorant of the use of letters as they exist today. Generally speaking, no writing is found among the Greeks that is acknowledged to be older than the poetry of **Homer**. And he clearly lived later than the **Trojan War**. They even say that he did not leave his poetry in writing, but that it was preserved by memory and later compiled from songs, which is why there are so many discrepancies within it. 

» Furthermore, those who undertook to write histories among them—I mean men like **Cadmus of Miletus** and **Acusilaus of Argos**, and any others said to have followed them—lived only a short time before the Persian expedition <note>original: "στρατείας" — likely referring to the Greco-Persian Wars</note> against Greece. Moreover, regarding those who first philosophized about celestial matters or divine things among the Greeks, such as **Pherecydes the Syrian**, **Pythagoras**, and **Thales**, everyone harmoniously agrees that they were students of the Egyptians and Chaldeans and wrote but little. And even these writings seem to the Greeks to be the most ancient of all, and they can scarcely believe they were written by those men. 

» How then is it not irrational for the Greeks to be so conceited, as if they alone knew antiquity and could accurately hand down the truth about it? Or who could not easily learn from the historians themselves that they wrote without any certain knowledge, but rather as each man guessed at the facts? At any rate, through their books they refute one another, and they do not hesitate to say the most contradictory things about the same events. I would be a meddler if I were to teach those who know better than I how much **Hellanicus** <note>A 5th-century BCE Greek logographer and historian</note> disagreed with **Acusilaus** regarding genealogies; or in how many ways Acusilaus corrected **Hesiod**; or how **Ephorus** demonstrates that Hellanicus was lying in most matters; or how **Timaeus** refutes Ephorus, and those who came after Timaeus refute him, while everyone refutes **Herodotus**. Indeed, not even concerning the affairs of **Sicily** did the followers of **Antiochus** and...

<meta>This page continues the argument of Josephus (quoted by Eusebius) regarding the unreliability of Greek historical records compared to those of the Near East. The previous page established that Greek history is relatively "new" and that the Greeks lacked the long-standing tradition of public record-keeping found in Egypt and Babylon.</meta>

-> # GOSPEL PREPARATION, BOOK 10 <-

» ...or Philistus, and he [Hellanicus] even thought it right to disagree with Callias <note>These are early Greek historians whose works often contradicted one another</note>. Nor again have those who wrote the *Atthides* <note>original: "ἀτθίδας" — local histories of the region of Attica and the city of Athens</note> followed one another concerning the history of the **Athenians**, nor have those who record the history of **Argos** followed each other concerning Argive matters. And why should I speak of the histories of specific cities or minor events, when the most reputable authors have disagreed even about the **Persian** expedition and the deeds performed within it? Indeed, **Thucydides** is accused by some of lying, even though he is thought to have written the most accurate history of his own time.

» The causes of such disagreement might appear to others who wish to seek them out; but I blame two major factors which I believe have the greatest influence. First, I will state the one that seems most decisive to me: it is that from the beginning, the **Greeks** did not concern themselves with making public records of events as they happened. This more than anything provided the error and the license to lie for those who later wished to write about antiquity. Not only was the matter of records neglected among other Greeks, but even among the **Athenians** themselves—who claim to be indigenous <term>autochthonous: "sprung from the soil," a claim by the Athenians that they were the original inhabitants of their land</term> and dedicated to education—nothing of the sort is found to have existed. They say the oldest of their public records are the laws concerning homicide written for them by **Draco**, which occurred only a little before the tyranny of **Peisistratus** <note>Draco's laws date to around 621 BCE; Peisistratus became tyrant around 561 BCE. This is "late" compared to Egyptian or Jewish records</note>. As for the **Arcadians**, what need is there to speak? They were only barely and much later educated in letters.

» Since no public record existed to teach those who wished to learn or to refute those who lied, a great disagreement arose among the writers. A second cause must be added to this: those who set out to write did not strive for the truth, even though they always made that profession. Instead, they displayed the power of their eloquence. They adapted themselves to whatever way they thought they would gain a reputation over others—some turning to myth-making, others praising cities or kings to find favor, while others proceeded to accuse the deeds [of others] or previous writers, thinking they would win fame in this way. In short, they continued to do the thing most contrary to history. For the proof of historical truth is if everyone says and writes the same thing about the same events; but they thought they would appear the most truthful of all if they did *not* write the same things as others.

» Thus far **Josephus**. The testimony of **Diodorus** might also serve as a seal upon what has been said, which I shall set forth from the first book of the *Library* he compiled, just as it stands word for word:

» ...philosopher. He says that **Pythagoras** of Samos <note>A famous Greek mathematician and philosopher (c. 570–495 BC)</note> also [visited Egypt], as well as the mathematician **Eudoxus**, and furthermore **Democritus** of Abdera, and **Oenopides** of Chios. Of all these men, the Egyptians show proofs: for some, they display statues; for others, they point to places or buildings that bear the same names. They bring forward evidence from the specific education each man pursued, establishing that they transported from **Egypt** everything for which they were later admired among the **Greeks**.

» For they say that **Orpheus** <note>The legendary poet and musician</note> brought back from the Egyptians most of his mystic rites, the ceremonies involving his own wandering, and his mythology concerning those in the **Underworld** <note>original: "ᾅδου" / Hades</note>. For the rite of **Osiris** is the same as that of **Dionysus**, and the rite of **Isis** is most similar to that of **Demeter**, with only the names being changed. They claim he introduced the punishments of the impious in the Underworld, the meadows of the pious, and the common imagery of spirits <note>original: "εἰδωλοποιΐας" — the shaping of phantom-like images</note> by imitating Egyptian burial customs.

» For according to ancient Egyptian custom, **Hermes**, the "guide of souls" <term>psychopompos: a conductor of souls to the afterworld</term>, would lead the body of **Apis** <note>The sacred bull of Memphis</note> to a certain place and deliver it to someone wearing the mask of **Cerberus** <note>The multi-headed hound of the underworld</note>. After Orpheus had pointed these things out, **Homer** followed him by writing in his poetry: *"Cyllenian Hermes called forth the souls of heroic men, holding a wand in his hands."* <note>A reference to the opening of Book 24 of Homer's Odyssey</note>

» Then again, they say that the descriptions of the streams of **Ocean** and the "White Rock" <note>A mythical landmark at the entrance to the underworld</note> were transferred from **Egypt**, as were the rites of **Dionysus** practiced among the Greeks, the myths about **Cronus**, the Battle of the **Titans**, and indeed the entire history of the sufferings of the gods.

» They also say that **Daedalus** <note>The legendary craftsman and inventor</note> imitated the maze of the **Labyrinth**, which still remains to this day; it was built, as some say, by **Mendes**, or as others say, by King **Menes**, many years before the reign of **Minos**. They also claim the style <note>original: "ῥυθμὸν"</note> of the ancient statues in Egypt is the same as those crafted by Daedalus among the Greeks. Furthermore, they say Daedalus designed the most beautiful gateway <note>original: "προπύλαιον"</note> of the temple of **Hephaestus** in **Memphis**. Being greatly admired, he was granted a wooden statue of himself in that temple, which he had fashioned with his own hands. Finally, because of his genius, he was held in great glory and, having invented many more things, attained divine honors. Indeed, on one of the islands near Memphis, there is still even now a temple of Daedalus, honored by the local people.

» Regarding **Homer’s** presence in Egypt, they bring clear proofs, especially the fact that **Helen** obtained a "drug of forgetfulness" <note>original: "φαρμακείαν, καὶ λήθην"</note> from **Polydamna**. For the poet says Helen received the "nepenthe" <term>nepenthe: literally "no-sorrow," a medicine described in the Odyssey that chases away grief</term> from the Egyptian woman Polydamna, the wife of **Thon**. Homer seems to have investigated this accurately, for even now they say the women in this region use this power, and that among the women of **Diospolis** <note>The "City of Zeus," the Greek name for Egyptian Thebes</note>, a drug for anger and grief has been found since ancient times. 

» They say the goddess in **Thebes** (or Diospolis) is the same as **Aphrodite**, and is called "Golden" by the locals according to ancient tradition; there is even a "Plain of Golden Aphrodite" near Memphis. They claim that the myths about **Zeus** and **Hera**—their intimacy and their journey to **Ethiopia**—were also brought from Egypt. For every year, the Egyptians carry the shrine of Zeus across the river into **Libya**, and after some days it returns again, as if the god were arriving from Ethiopia. # GOSPEL PREPARATION, BOOK 10

» ...at the festivals of the temples, both [images] are carried up to a mountain with lengthy chants by the priests. They also claim that **Lycurgus** <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note>, **Plato**, and **Solon** visited and incorporated many Egyptian customs into their own legislation. **Pythagoras** likewise learned from the Egyptians the principles of his "Sacred Word," his geometric theorems, his theories on numbers, and even the transmigration <note>original: "μεταϐολὴν" / metabolen</note> of the soul into every living creature. They believe that **Democritus** also spent five years among them and was taught much concerning astrology. Similarly, **Oenopides** spent time with the priests and astrologers and learned particularly about the solar cycle—how it has an oblique path and moves in a direction opposite to the other stars. Likewise, **Eudoxus** studied astrology among them and, by publishing many useful things for the Greeks, achieved notable fame. Of all the ancient sculptors, those most renowned are said to have spent time there: **Telecles** and **Theodorus**, the sons of Rhoecus, who crafted for the people of Samos the wooden statue <term>xoanon: an ancient cult image carved from wood</term> of **Pythian Apollo**. 

Such are the claims of Diodorus. But since the argument has been demonstrated in this way, let this point reach its conclusion here. It is no longer necessary to accuse us of irrationality if, out of a desire for true piety, we have turned to the teachers of the wise Greeks—or rather, to the teachers of their own philosophers—I mean the "Barbarians" <note>A term used by Greeks for all non-Greek speaking peoples</note>, even if these are the **Hebrew** "Barbarians." It would be well to carefully examine the times in which **Moses** and the prophets after Moses flourished. For this is one of the most essential matters for our present undertaking: that those who intend to grasp the words of these divine men should first understand their antiquity. If it should appear that those among the Greeks who hold the same opinions on theology as the Hebrew prophets lived later, then it should no longer be a matter of doubt for us to see what is likely: whether the elders took from the young, and Hebrews from Greeks, and "Barbarians" from philosophers (whose faces they likely never even saw); or on the contrary and more likely, that the young took from the elders, and that the Greeks, who are celebrated as the most eloquent of nations, were not ignorant of the Hebrew writings, which had been translated into the Greek language from the very beginning.

Concerning the antiquity of **Moses** and the prophets who followed him, many have diligently set forth the proof in their own writings, from which we will immediately present a few brief excerpts. For the second year of Darius fell in the first year of the 65th **Olympiad** <note>A four-year period used in Greek dating; the 65th Olympiad began in 520 BC</note>. <margin>27</margin> The 203rd Olympiad <note>A four-year period used by the Greeks for dating; the 203rd corresponds roughly to 33–37 AD</note> coincides with this time. Therefore, from **Darius the Persian** to **Tiberius**, the Roman Emperor, there are 137 Olympiads, which total 548 years, calculating from the 40th Olympiad. Since the second year of **Darius** was the 70th year of the desolation of the Temple in Jerusalem—as the history of the Hebrews establishes—and calculating back again from the second year of **Darius** to the first Olympiad, the total would be 256 years, or 64 Olympiads. Within these, you would find the period from the final year of the aforementioned Temple’s desolation back to the 50th year of **Uzziah** <note>original: "ὀζίου" / Ozias</note>, King of the Jews, during whose reign **Isaiah** and **Hosea** were prophesying, showing they were contemporaries. Thus, the first Olympiad according to the Greeks was contemporary with the prophet **Isaiah** and those of his time.

Again, from the first Olympiad back to earlier ages, up to the **Capture of Troy** <note>original: "ἰλίου ἁλώσεως" / the fall of Ilium</note>, you will find a total of 408 years, as the Greek chronological records contain. And according to the Hebrews, from the 50th year of **Uzziah**, our King of the Jews, back to the third year of **Abdon** <note>original: "λαβδὼν" / Labdon</note>, who was a judge among the Hebrews, you will calculate the same number of 408 years. Therefore, the Capture of Troy occurred during the time of **Abdon** the Judge.

Furthermore, **Samson** is considered older by some years among the Hebrews; they say he was irresistible in his physical strength, resembling the Greek figure of **Heracles** <note>The hero known in Latin as Hercules</note>. Walking back even further from that point and totaling 400 years, you would find **Moses** according to the Hebrews, and **Cecrops the Earth-born** <note>original: "γηγενῆ" / gegenē; a mythical king of Athens said to have been born from the soil</note> according to the Greeks.

Indeed, those things most admired by the Greeks occurred after **Cecrops**: the flood in the time of **Deucalion**, the great fire of **Phaethon**, the birth of **Erichthonius**, the kidnapping of the Maiden <note>Persephone</note>, the mysteries of **Demeter**, the founding of the **Eleusinian mysteries**, the agriculture of **Triptolemus**, the kidnapping of **Europa** by **Zeus**, the birth of **Apollo**, and the founding of **Thebes** by **Cadmus** <note>original: "μούνιτις" / likely a reference to the founding of the Cadmeia</note>. Even younger than these are **Dionysus**, **Minos**, **Perseus**, **Asclepius**, the **Dioscuri** <note>Castor and Pollux</note>, and **Heracles**. It is established that **Moses** was older than all of these, having reached his prime during the time of **Cecrops**.

Going back from **Moses** yet another age to the first year of the life of **Abraham**, you will find 505 years. If you count back three years from the aforementioned year of **Cecrops'** reign or even earlier, you will reach **Ninus** the Assyrian. They say he was the first to rule over all of Asia except for India; the city of **Ninus** <note>Nineveh</note> is named after him, which the Hebrews call **Nineveh**. During his time, **Zoroaster the Magician** ruled the Bactrians. **Ninus'** wife and successor to the kingdom was **Semiramis**; thus **Abraham** lived during their time. These matters were demonstrably established in the *Chronological Canons* <note>Eusebius's famous reference work on world history</note> which we labored upon.

For the present purpose, in addition to what has been said, I shall use a witness to the antiquity of **Moses** who is the most hostile and warlike toward both the Hebrews and us. I speak of the philosopher of our own time <note>**Porphyry**, a Neoplatonist who wrote a famous critique of Christianity</note>, who, driven by an excess of hatred, produced a work against us. He subjected not only us, but also the Hebrews, **Moses** himself, and the prophets after him, to equal slanders. However, a statement is beyond dispute when it confirms my promise through the testimony of enemies. **Porphyry**, then, writes these very words in the fourth book of his work against us:

"Concerning the Jews, he records the truest history, because both in terms of places and names..."

» Sanchuniathon of Berytus <note>modern-day Beirut</note>, having obtained the records from Hierombalos, the priest of the god Ieuo <note>original: "Ἰευώ"; widely considered a Greek transcription of the Hebrew Yahweh</note>, dedicated his history to Abelo-balos, the king of the Berytians. These are the words of Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century philosopher who, despite being an opponent of Christianity, is cited here by Eusebius as an "expert witness" on ancient dates</note>. We must, therefore, reason through the preceding points as follows: If Sanchuniathon lived in the time of Semiramis, and she is admitted to have lived long before the Trojan War, then Sanchuniathon would also be more ancient than the Trojan War. But since he is said to have received his records from others even older than himself—and they, being older than he, are said to approach closely to the times of Moses—it follows that they did not live exactly at the same time as Moses, but nearly approached his era. This implies that Moses is as much older than Sanchuniathon as those older sources are removed from the one who was admitted to "approach" Moses. Precisely how many years Moses might have preceded the men mentioned is difficult to say. However, I do not think I will let this pass; I intend to show that Moses lived at the same time as Sanchuniathon himself, and not earlier, and I will pursue the proof in this way. If Sanchuniathon was known in the time of Semiramis, Queen of the Assyrians, let it be that Moses was no earlier, but flourished at the same time; thus, he too would have lived under Semiramis. Yet, while our own account <note>meaning the Christian/Hebrew tradition</note> showed that Abraham lived under her, the account of the Philosopher <note>Porphyry</note> establishes Moses as even more ancient. ### EUSEBIUS

This man [Sanchuniathon] is also highly regarded by the most learned theologians among the Greeks. Among the Hebrews at that time, the successors of Joshua <note>original: "Ἰησοῦ"; in Greek, the names Joshua and Jesus are spelled identically</note> were reigning, and the prophets who followed Moses were at their height. Consequently, the total time from Moses until the capture of Troy <note>the traditional end of the Trojan War</note> amounts to more than 827 years, according to the testimony provided by the philosopher <note>Porphyry</note>. 

Furthermore, the lives of Homer, Hesiod, and the rest are remembered as being much more recent than the Trojan events. Only very recently, around the 50th Olympiad <note>approximately 580–577 BCE</note>, did the circles of Pythagoras and Democritus, and the philosophers who followed them, become known—occurring roughly 700 years after the Trojan War. Therefore, Moses and the Hebrew prophets who followed him lived 1,500 years before the Greek philosophers, according to the admission of the man mentioned above <note>Porphyry</note>. 

We have stated these things briefly; now it is time to consider the evidence from our own writers on this same subject. There have been learned men among us who were second to none in their education. They did not study divine matters casually, but precisely calculated the entire timeline based on Hebrew "archaeology" <note>the study of ancient history and origins</note>, using a rich and varied array of evidence. 

Some calculated the dates from agreed-upon histories, while others confirmed their testimony through older readings. Some used Greek records, while others utilized the Phoenician, Chaldean, and Egyptian registers. Together, they gathered Greek and "barbarian" <note>meaning non-Greek</note> records alongside the Hebrew ones. By comparing these various histories and examining events that happened at the same time among all nations, they reached their conclusions. Each used their own methods to build their proof, yet each produced a harmonious and consistent demonstration. Therefore, we should use their own words in this present discourse, so that these "fathers of the discourse" are not deprived of their own fruits, and so that the establishment of the truth may receive an undisputed confirmation through many witnesses rather than just one.

->### From the Third Book of the *Chronographies* of Africanus <note>Sextus Julius Africanus (c. 160 – c. 240 AD) was a Christian traveler and historian who wrote the first major Christian world chronicle</note><-

For this reason, I will briefly go over the most famous and mythical stories up to the first Olympiad. After that, I will link each event according to its time—if they are notable—pairing the Greek histories with the Hebrew ones. I will narrate the Hebrew accounts while touching upon the Greek ones. I will follow this method: I will take one Hebrew action that occurred at the same time as a Greek event, and by holding to this, adding or subtracting as necessary, and noting where Jewish, Persian, or any other events coincided with the Hebrew ones, I might perhaps hit my mark.

Cyrus first began his reign in the year when the 55th Olympiad <note>A four-year period used by the Greeks to measure time; the 55th Olympiad began around 560 BCE</note> was held, as can be found from the "Libraries" of Diodorus and the histories of Thallus and Castor, as well as in the works of Polybius and Phlegon, and others who concerned themselves with the Olympiads. For the chronology is agreed upon by all of them. 

» Cyrus, then, in the first year of his reign—which was the first year of the 55th Olympiad—effected the first return of the people through Zerubbabel. This occurred under Jeshua <note>original: "Ἰησοῦ" (Iesous); here referring to the High Priest Jeshua son of Jozadak, not Jesus of Nazareth</note> the son of Jozadak, when he began the partial restoration of the temple for the people once the seventy years [of exile] were fulfilled, as is recorded in the book of Ezra among the Hebrews. The histories therefore coincide regarding Cyrus, marking both the beginning of his reign and the end of the captivity. By following the Olympiads from that point, the rest of history can be found to agree with us. By following these dates, we shall fit the remaining histories to one another by the same reasoning. 

» The matters concerning these times are calculated in the Attic <note>Relating to Athens and its surrounding territory</note> chronology starting from Ogygus. He was believed by the people there to be an "autochthon" <note>One born from the soil itself; an original inhabitant</note>, in whose time the first great flood occurred in Attica, while Phoroneus was reigning over the Argives, as Acusilaus records. From that time until the first Olympiad—the point from which the Greeks believed they could accurately reckon time—a total of 1,020 years is gathered. 

» This also agrees with the previously mentioned dates, as will be shown in the following. For these events were recorded by Hellanicus and Philochorus, who wrote the *Atthides* <note>Histories of the Attic region</note>, and by the historians of Syria, Castor and Thallus, as well as by Diodorus, who wrote the *Libraries*, and Alexander Polyhistor. Some of our own more accurate writers also mention these Attic events. If, therefore, any notable history occurs within those 1,020 years, it shall be selected for its usefulness. 

» These are the main points: We say that according to the records of this Ogygus—after whom the first flood was named, when many were destroyed by earthquakes—the exodus of the people with Moses from Egypt took place. This is shown in the following way: the aforementioned 1,020 years from Ogygus to the first Olympiad. Then, from the first Olympiad to the first year of the 55th—that is, to the first year of King Cyrus—is 217 years. Thus, it is clear that the end of the captivity is found to be 1,237 years <note>original: "ασλζ"</note> later by calculation. 

» We must ask if the exodus of Israel from Egypt under Moses occurred as long before the 55th Olympiad as Ogygus, who founded Athens. From this, we can grasp certain famous points of Attic chronology. And after other matters, [Africanus] says: "These things concerning Ogygus: at his time, Moses went out from Egypt." And that it is not improbable for these things to have happened is shown thus: From the exodus of Moses to Cyrus, who reigned after the captivity, is 1,237 years. 

» For the remaining years of Moses were 40; Joshua, who led after him, 25 years; the elders after Joshua, 30 years; the period contained in the Book of Judges, 408 years; the priests Eli and Samuel, 60 years; and the following Hebrew kings, 440 years. The last year of these corresponds to the first year of Cyrus’s reign, as we said before. Since there are 1,020 years from Moses to the first Olympiad, and then to the first year of the 55th Olympiad there are 1,237 years, the timing would agree with the Greek records. 

» After Ogygus, because of the great destruction from the flood, the land now called Attica remained without a king for 188 years until Cecrops. As for Actaeus, who is said to follow Ogygus, or other invented names, they are not even...

» Philochorus <note>An Athenian historian (c. 340–261 BCE) known for his work on the history of Athens</note> states that this occurred. Furthermore, some of the residents of Elis record that Moses lived during those same times. Polemon, in the first book of his *Greek Histories* <note>original: "ἡλιακῶν" (Heliakon), likely a scribal error for "Ἑλλαδικῶν" (Helladikon)</note>, says that during the reign of Apis, son of Phoroneus, a portion of the Egyptian army was expelled from Egypt. These people settled in the part of Syria called Palestine, not far from Arabia—clearly referring to those who were with Moses.

» Moreover, Apion the son of Poseidonius, a most learned grammarian, in his book *Against the Jews* and in the fourth book of his *Histories*, says that during the reign of Inachus <note>The first king of Argos</note> at Argos, while Amosis <note>Ahmose I, the pharaoh who founded the 18th Dynasty</note> was ruling Egypt, the Jews revolted under the leadership of Moses. 

» Lysimachus also mentions this revolt and Amosis in his second book. 

» Some even include the Jews among those who practice circumcision, calling them "Assyrians" in Palestine, perhaps because of their descent from Abraham. Polemon of Clyndas, in his investigation into Egyptian history from the earliest times, agrees with all these points. Therefore, the variation in these dates is not significant. 

» It should be noted that whatever is celebrated by the Greeks in myth for its great antiquity is found to have occurred *after* the time of Moses. This includes deluges and great conflagrations, as well as figures such as Io, Europa, Astarbe, the Rape of the Maiden <note>Persephone/Proserpina</note>, the institution of mysteries and legislation, the deeds of Dionysus, the ship Argo and the Argonauts, the Centaurs, the Minotaur, the events at Troy, the labors of Hercules, the return of the Heracleidae <note>The "Dorian Invasion" or return of the descendants of Hercules to the Peloponnesus</note>, the Ionian migration, and the establishment of the Olympiads. 

» It seemed right to me to set forth the required timeline of the Athenian kings, since I intend to compare Greek histories with the Hebrew ones. For anyone who wishes to start from the beginning with me will be able to calculate the numbers just as I have. 

» Therefore, of the 1,020 years which are set forth from Moses and Ogygus until the first Olympiad <note>776 BCE</note>, the first event is the Passover—the Exodus of the Hebrews from Egypt. In the Athenian records, this is the time of the flood of Ogygus, which is logical. For while the Egyptians were being scourged by the wrath of God with hailstorms and tempests, it is likely that parts of the whole earth were affected as well. 

» That the Athenians should share a history with the Egyptians is plausible, as they were thought to be colonists from them, as stated by Theopompus <note>A Greek historian of the 4th century BCE</note> and others. The intervening time has been passed over, as nothing extraordinary is recorded as having lived then. After ninety-four years, Io is mentioned, whom some say <note>The text here is slightly broken in the OCR</note> molded men. For being wise in education, he "re-molded" them from their excessive ignorance. Let these matters be set aside for now. I shall turn again to another topic.

» Now I think it is fitting for me to demonstrate that our philosophy <note>Tatian uses the word "philosophy" to describe the Christian and Hebrew way of life and belief</note> is older than the practices of the Greeks. Let these two be taken by us for comparison. For we shall find that our traditions are not only older than Greek education, but even older than the invention of their letters.

» Relying on the support of your own weapons, having navigated my own course, I finally overtake the Greeks by using your own resources.

» For regarding the poetry of Homer—his lineage and the time in which he flourished—those who investigated this in the earliest times include Theagenes of Rhegium <note>A 6th-century BCE scholar, often considered the first to interpret Homer's works allegorically</note> (who lived during the time of Cambyses), Stesimbrotus of Thasos, Antimachus of Colophon, Herodotus of Halicarnassus, and Dionysius of Olynthus. After them came Ephorus of Cyme, Philochorus of Athens, and the Peripatetic philosophers <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy</note> Megaclides and Chamaeleon. Later, the grammarians <note>Scholars specializing in literary and historical analysis</note> Zenodotus, Aristophanes, Callimachus, Crates, Eratosthenes, Aristarchus, and Apollodorus. 

» Among these, the school of Crates says he flourished before the return of the Heracleidae <note>The legendary "descendants of Hercules" whose return to the Peloponnese was a major marker in Greek traditional history</note>, within eighty years after the Trojan War. The school of Eratosthenes says he lived one hundred years after the fall of Troy. The school of Aristarchus places him during the Ionian migration <note>The movement of Greek settlers to the coast of Asia Minor</note>, which occurred one hundred and forty years after the Trojan War. Philochorus says he lived forty years after the Ionian migration, during the time Acastus was Archon at Athens—one hundred and eighty years after the Trojan War. The school of Apollodorus says he lived one hundred years after the Ionian migration, which would be two hundred and forty years after the Trojan War. 

» Some claim he lived around the time of the Olympiads <note>The first recorded Olympic Games in 776 BCE</note>, which is four hundred years after the fall of Troy. Others brought the date even lower, saying Homer was a contemporary of Archilochus; and Archilochus flourished around the twenty-third Olympiad, during the time of Gyges the Lydian, five hundred years after the Trojan War. 

» Concerning these dates of the aforementioned poets—I mean Homer—let what we have said in summary suffice for those who are able to examine the details accurately, given the complete lack of agreement among those who have spoken about him. For it is possible for all such opinions regarding literature to be shown as false. When the record of dates is inconsistent among them, the historical accounts contained within them cannot be true either. 

» And indeed, even if Homer were not only later than the Trojan War, but were assumed to have lived at the very time of the war itself, or even to have campaigned with Agamemnon’s forces—or even if one wishes to say he lived before the invention of the alphabet—the aforementioned Moses will still appear to be many years older than the fall of Troy itself, and much more ancient than the founding of Troy, or than its kings Tros and Dardanus. 

» For the sake of proof, I shall use witnesses from the Chaldeans, Phoenicians, and Egyptians. And why should I say more? For one who promises to be persuasive must make the narrative of the facts more concise for the listeners. Berossus <note>A Babylonian priest of Bel who wrote a history of Babylonia in Greek for the Seleucid kings</note>, a Babylonian man and a priest of the god Bel in their country, lived during the time of Alexander. He compiled the history of the Chaldeans in three books for the third ruler after Seleucus <note>original: "τῷ μετὰ Σέλευκον τρίτῳ" (the third after Seleucus), likely referring to Antiochus I Soter</note>. In setting out the accounts of their kings, he recounts one of them named Nebuchadnezzar <note>The powerful Babylonian king who conquered Jerusalem in the early 6th century BCE</note>, who campaigned against the Phoenicians and Jews. We know these things were proclaimed by our own prophets, occurring long after the lifetime of Moses, but seventy years before the Persian rule. 

» Berossus is a most capable man. A proof of this is Juba, who, writing about the Assyrians, says he learned the history from Berossus. There are two books of his concerning the Assyrians. After the Chaldeans, the records of the Phoenicians are as follows: there were three men among them, Theodotus, Hypsicrates, and Mochus. Their books were translated into the Greek language by Laitus <note>Also known as Laetus, a scholar of Phoenician history</note>, who also accurately treated the lives of the philosophers...

» ...historian. In the histories of those mentioned above, it is made clear under which of the kings the abduction of Europa took place, and mention is made of the arrival in Phoenicia, as well as the matters concerning Hiram <note>original: "Εἵραμον" (Heiram); the Phoenician King of Tyre</note>, who gave his own daughter in marriage to Solomon, the king of the Jews, and donated timber of all kinds of wood for the construction of the Temple. Menander of Ephesus also made a record concerning these same matters. Now, the time of Hiram nearly approaches the period of the Trojan War <note>original: "Ἰλιακοῖς"</note>. But Solomon, who lived at the same time as Hiram, is much later than the age of Moses. 

» There are, at least, accurate records of the times among the Egyptians. Ptolemy—not the king, but a priest of Mendes <note>An Egyptian priest and historian who wrote in Greek during the Augustan age</note>—is one who sets forth the deeds of the kings; he says that during the reign of Amosis <note>Ahmose I, founder of the 18th Dynasty</note> as king of Egypt, the Jews made their journey out of Egypt to whatever places they desired, under the leadership of Moses. He speaks as follows: "That Amosis lived during the time of King Inachus." 

» After him, Apion the grammarian—a man of high reputation in the fourth book of his *Aegyptiaca* <note>original: "Αἰγυπτιακῶν"; a history of Egypt in five books</note>, which consists of five writings—among many other things, says that Amosis razed Avaris <note>The capital of the Hyksos in the Nile Delta</note> to the ground, living during the time of Inachus of Argos, as Ptolemy of Miletus recorded in his *Chronology*. 

» The time from Inachus until the fall of Troy <note>original: "Ἰλίου ἁλώσεως"</note> fills twenty generations. And the proof of this is found in these famous men who became kings of the Argives: Inachus, Phoroneus, Apis, Argus, Criasus, Phorbas, Triopas, Crotopus, Sthenelus, Danaus, Lynceus, Abas, Proetus, Acrisius, Perseus, Eurystheus, Atreus, Thyestes, and Agamemnon, in the eighteenth year of whose reign Troy was captured. 

» And one must apply one's mind with all possible accuracy to the fact that, according to the tradition of the Greeks, no historical record exists among them. For Cadmus, who handed down the alphabet <note>original: "στοιχεῖα" (elements/letters)</note> to those mentioned above, arrived in Boeotia many generations later. After Inachus, it was only with difficulty under Phoroneus that a record was made of the transition from a wild and nomadic life, and human society was reorganized. 

» Therefore, if Moses is shown to have lived during the time of Inachus, he is older than the Trojan events by four hundred years. This is proved to be so from the succession of the Attic kings, as well as the Macedonian, Ptolemaic, and even the indigenous ones. Hence, if the most famous deeds among the Greeks were performed and are known from the time of Inachus onwards, it is clear they occurred after Moses. 

» For during the time of Phoroneus, who came after Inachus, Ogygus is mentioned among the Athenians, in whose time the first flood occurred. 
» During the time of Phorbas, Actaeus lived, after whom Attica was called Actaea. 
» During the time of Triopas lived Prometheus, Epimetheus, Atlas, the double-formed Cecrops, and Io. 
» During the time of Crotopus occurred the conflagration under Phaethon and the flood under Deucalion.

» During the time of Acrisius occurred the crossing of Pelops from Phrygia, the arrival of Ion at Athens, the second Cecrops, and the deeds of Theseus. 
» During the reign of Agamemnon, Troy was captured.

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 10

» To those who remain devoted to the teachings flowing from the spring of Hermes <note>A reference to the followers of Hermes Trismegistus or the Hermetic tradition</note>, his doctrines were not based on true insight. For many of the <term>sophists</term> <note>professional teachers of rhetoric and philosophy in ancient Greece</note> among them, being quite inexperienced, took what they learned from our Moses and from those who philosophized like him, and attempted to misrepresent it. They did this first so that they might be thought to be saying something original, and second, so that by veiling whatever they did not understand with a kind of artificial rhetoric, they might treat the truth as if it were a mere myth.

» Now, regarding our way of life, our history, and our laws—as well as everything the learned men among the Greeks have said about us, and who the authors were that mentioned us—these things will be made clear in the works written against those who have expressed views about God. But for the present task, I must hasten to clarify with all possible accuracy that Moses is not only older than Homer, but even older than the writers who preceded him: such as Linus, Philammon, Thamyris, Amphion, Orpheus, Musaeus, Demodocus, Phemius, the Sibyl, Epimenides the Cretan (who went to Sparta), Aristeas of Proconnesus (who wrote the *Arimaspeia*), Asbolus the Centaur, Isatides, Drymon, Euclus the Cyprian, Horus of Samos, and Propanides the Athenian.

» For Linus was the teacher of Hercules, and Hercules lived one generation before the Trojan War <note>original: "Ἰλιακῶν" (Ilians/Troy)</note>. This is clear from his son Tlepolemus, who campaigned against Troy. Orpheus lived at the same time as Hercules; indeed, it is said that the works attributed to him were actually composed by Onomacritus of Athens, who lived during the reign of the Peisistratids <note>Tyrants of Athens in the 6th century BCE</note> around the 50th <term>Olympiad</term> <note>a four-year period used for dating; the 50th Olympiad was approx. 580–577 BCE</note>. Musaeus was a student of Orpheus. Amphion, who lived two generations before the Trojan War, is prevented from being considered more ancient than our authors by those who love learning. Demodocus and Phemius lived during the Trojan War itself, for one stayed with the suitors [of Penelope] and the other with the Phaeacians. Thamyris and Philammon are not much older than these.

» Regarding the detailed study of each account and the record of their dates, I believe I have written for you with the greatest possible accuracy. However, to complete what is still missing, let us also provide proof concerning those traditionally called "the Sages." Minos, who was preeminent in all wisdom, insight, and lawgiving, lived during the time of Lynceus, who reigned after Danaus, in the eleventh generation after Inachus. Lycurgus, who was born not long after the fall of Troy, gave laws to the Spartans one hundred years before the start of the Olympiads. Draco is found to have lived around the 39th Olympiad, Solon around the 46th <note>OCR says "μη" (48th), but Solon's archonship was the 46th; Tatian uses "μη" elsewhere</note>, and Pythagoras during the 62nd. We have already demonstrated that the first Olympiad occurred 407 years after the Trojan War.

» Since these things have been proven, I will briefly record the ages of the Seven Sages. Since the oldest of them, Thales, lived around the 50th Olympiad, I have briefly covered the matters concerning those who lived near his time.

» These things, O Greeks, were composed for you by Tatian, a man who philosophizes according to the "barbarian" <note>original: "ϐαρϐάρους" (barbarous); to a Greek, this meant anyone who did not speak Greek, though Tatian uses it as a badge of honor for his Near Eastern heritage</note> way. I was born in the land of the Assyrians, and was educated first in your skills, and secondly in those things which I now profess to proclaim. Knowing henceforth who God is and what His creation is, I present myself to you, ready for the examination of my doctrines, while my way of life according to God remains beyond denial.

...Homer and Hesiod were much later than the Trojan War, and even less ancient were the Greek lawgivers—Lycurgus, Solon, and the Seven Sages—as well as those associated with Pherecydes of Samos and the great Pythagoras, who lived much later, around the time of the Olympiads, as we have demonstrated. These are the words of Clement. But since the current study concerns our own history, it would be well to examine their records as well. I will use the words of Flavius Josephus <note>Josephus was a 1st-century Jewish historian whose works are vital for understanding the Second Temple period</note> in preference to all others.

### From the first book of Flavius Josephus on the antiquity of the Jews.

<margin>»</margin> I will begin with the records of the Egyptians. While it is not possible to present their original writings, Manetho, who was Egyptian by birth but evidently shared in Greek education, wrote a history of his homeland in the Greek language. He says he translated this from sacred records, and he refutes Herodotus for many errors in Egyptian matters caused by ignorance. Thus, in the second book of his *Egyptian History*, Manetho writes the following about us. I will present his own words, bringing him forward as a witness himself: "There was a king named Timaeus. During his reign, for reasons unknown to me, God breathed against us <note>original: ἀντέπνευσε (antepneuse), suggesting a divine "contrary wind" or stroke of ill fortune</note>, and unexpectedly men of obscure birth from the eastern regions grew bold, campaigned against our land, and easily took it by force without a battle." And he adds a little later: "Their entire nation was called <term>Hyksos</term> <note>A term now used by historians to describe the "Shepherd Kings" of the 15th Dynasty of Egypt</note>, which means 'King-Shepherds.' For *Hyk* in the sacred language signifies 'king,' while *sos* is 'shepherd' and 'shepherds' in the common dialect. Thus combined, it becomes *Hyksos*. Some say they were Arabs." But in another copy, it is said that the title *Hyksos* does not signify kings, but on the contrary, denotes "Captive Shepherds." For *Hyk* or *Hak*, when pronounced with a rough breathing <note>A phonetic marker in Greek indicating an 'h' sound at the start of a word</note> in the Egyptian tongue, explicitly means 'captives.' This seems more plausible to me and more in line with ancient history. He says these aforementioned kings, those called shepherds and their descendants, ruled Egypt for 511 years. After this, he says the kings of the <term>Thebaid</term> <note>The region around the ancient city of Thebes in Upper Egypt</note> and the rest of Egypt rose up against the shepherds, and a great and long-lasting war broke out. During the reign of a king named Misphragmouthosis, he says the shepherds were defeated and driven out of the rest of Egypt, but were shut up in a place with a circumference of ten thousand <term>arourae</term> <note>An ancient unit of land area, approximately 2/3 of an acre</note>. The place was named Avaris. Manetho says the shepherds surrounded this entire place with a great, strong wall so they could keep all their property and their plunder in a fortified spot. Then Thmothosis, the son of Misphragmouthosis, attempted to take them by force through a siege, stationing 480,000 soldiers at the walls. When he despaired of the siege, he made a treaty that they should leave Egypt and go wherever they wished, all of them unharmed. <meta>This page continues Eusebius’s chronological synchronization, moving from the legendary antiquity of the Israelites to the historical period of the Kings of Judah and the Babylonian Exile, mapping these events against the rise of the first Greek philosophers and the founding of Rome.</meta>

Hezekiah reigned for 28 years. It was during his time that Romulus founded Rome and became its king. After Hezekiah, Manasseh reigned for 55 years; then Amon for 2 years; then Josiah for 31 years. It was under Josiah that Jeremiah, Baruch, Huldah, and other prophets flourished. Next was Jehoahaz for 3 months; after him Jehoiakim for 11 years; and after him, the very last was Zedekiah for 12 years. Under this king, Jerusalem was besieged by the <term>Assyrians</term> <note>original: ἀσσυρίων (assyriōn). While historical records credit the Babylonians under Nebuchadnezzar with the destruction of the Temple in 586 BCE, ancient authors often used "Assyrian" as a general term for the Mesopotamian powers.</note>, and the Temple was burned. The entire Jewish nation was then led away into captivity in Babylon. Both Daniel and Ezekiel prophesied there. After a certain number of years, Cyrus, King of the Persians, released the Jews from their captivity, allowing those who wished to return to their own land and rebuild the Temple. At that time, Joshua son of Josedech and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel went up and laid the foundations, while Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi—the very last of all the prophets—prophesied. After these men, there were no more prophets among the Jews.

During the time of Cyrus, Solon of Athens was well known, along with those called the **Seven Sages** among the Greeks; before them, no one is remembered as a "philosopher" among the Greeks. Of these seven, **Thales of Miletus**, a <term>natural philosopher</term> <note>original: φυσικὸς (physikos), one who studies the laws of nature</note>, became the first leader of the group. He lectured on the solstices of the sun, eclipses, the illumination of the moon, and the equinoxes. This man became the most distinguished among the Greeks. Anaximander, the son of Praxiades and also a Milesian, was a student of Thales. He was the first to construct <term>gnomons</term> <note>An instrument like a sundial used to measure the sun's shadow</note> to distinguish the solstices, time, hours, and equinoxes. Anaximenes, son of Eurystratus of Miletus, was an associate of Anaximander. Following him was Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, son of Hegesibulus. He was the first to articulate the doctrine of first principles. For he did not merely speak about the <term>substance</term> <note>original: οὐσίας (ousias)</note> of all things as those before him had done, but also about the moving cause behind it. 

<margin>»</margin> For he says: "At the beginning, all things were mixed together; then **Mind** <note>original: νοῦς (nous). This was a revolutionary idea: that an intelligent force ordered the universe.</note> entered and brought them from disorder into order."

Anaxagoras had three famous associates: Pericles, Archelaus, and Euripides. Pericles became the leading man of Athens, surpassing others in wealth and noble birth. Euripides turned to poetry and was called by some the "Philosopher of the Stage." Archelaus succeeded to the school of Anaxagoras in Lampsacus; he later moved to Athens and held classes there, where he had many Athenian students, including **Socrates**. During this same time as Anaxagoras, the natural philosophers Xenophanes and **Pythagoras** also flourished. Pythagoras was succeeded by his wife Theano and his sons, Telauges and Mnesarchus. Empedocles became a student of Telauges, during whose time **Heraclitus** "the Obscure" was also known. It is said that Parmenides succeeded Xenophanes, and Melissus succeeded Parmenides; then Zeno of Elea succeeded Melissus. They say that Zeno, having organized a conspiracy against a certain tyrant, was captured. While being tortured by the tyrant to force him to name his accomplices, he defied the torture; he bit off his own tongue and spat it at the tyrant, and thus died enduring the torments. Leucippus was a student of Zeno, and Democritus a student of Leucippus. Protagoras was a student of Democritus, and during his time Socrates reached his peak. Various other schools of natural philosophy also branched out around the time of Socrates. However, all of these thinkers, beginning with Thales, are shown to have flourished after the time of King Cyrus.

-> **Preface to the Subject** <-

<image-desc>Decorative square woodcut initial letter 'O' containing a seated classical figure, possibly a personification of wisdom, surrounded by ornate floral scrolls and architectural elements.</image-desc>

**THE** preceding volume, being the tenth of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, was composed of the Greeks' own voices and external testimonies. This was fitting for those who, like us, have brought forward nothing of their own, except perhaps for their skill in words and lack of original expression <note>original: ἀγλωττίαν (aglōttian), suggesting that despite their beautiful language, the Greeks lacked the "true language" of divine truth.</note>. They concocted everything from barbarians <note>In the ancient world, "barbarian" simply meant anyone who was not Greek; here it refers specifically to the Hebrews.</note> and did not remain ignorant of the Hebrew oracles. They did not even keep their hands clean of parts of these oracles, despite their competitive pride in their own writings. For it was no ordinary person who revealed them as thieves, as I have said, but one of their own. Furthermore, by comparing the timelines, it was recognized that they were very young in both their wisdom and their age, lagging far behind the antiquity of the Hebrews.

This was the subject of the previous book. The present volume now hastens, as if to pay a debt, to deliver the promised thesis: to reveal the harmony <note>original: συμφωνίαν (symphonian), a "sounding together" or agreement.</note> of the Greek philosophers with the Hebrew oracles in certain—though perhaps not all—doctrinal theories. I have set aside the founders of other sects and chosen to use only the leader of them all as a sacred standard <note>original: γνώμονι (gnōmoni), a tool for measurement or a rule.</note> instead of all the rest. Let Plato be set forward. Since he alone seems to have surpassed all others in reputation, he will be sufficient for us to establish our inquiry. However, if necessary for clarity or to understand the man's thought, I will also use those who have followed his philosophy as witnesses, bringing their supporting voices to bear on the matter at hand.
