<header>PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 11</header>

Let it be noted by me that which might seem to have been remarked not unsuccessfully by another, even if most of his words were spoken in agreement with him <note>Eusebius is likely referring to a previous author or a specific school of thought he has been engaging with.</note>. We shall present this at the proper time, not for the sake of slander, but for our own defense—to explain why we have preferred the "barbarian philosophy" <term>Barbarian philosophy: A term used by Greeks to describe non-Greek wisdom, which Eusebius adopts here to refer to the Hebrew scriptures</term> over the Greek, as is generally acknowledged.

-> **How the philosophy according to Plato followed the Hebrew teachings in the most necessary points.** <-

Plato divided the whole discourse of philosophy into three parts: the Physical, the Ethical, and the Logical. Then, in turn, he divided the Physical into the study of things perceived by the senses and the understanding of incorporeal <note>original: ἀσωμάτων (asōmatōn), meaning things without physical bodies, such as the soul or the divine.</note> beings. You would find this same tripartite form of teaching among the Hebrews as well; indeed, similar philosophical ideas were held by them long before Plato was even born. It is worth hearing first from the followers of Plato, and then examining the records of the Hebrews. Listen to the opinions of Plato as recorded by his elders <note>likely meaning his philosophical predecessors or senior students</note>, of whom a certain man, a clear and true witness among the Platonic philosophers, sets forth the man's views as follows—standing in opposition to those who misinterpreted Plato's teachings according to the views of Aristotle.

-> **Atticus on the tripartite division of philosophy according to Plato.** <-

<margin>»</margin> Philosophy in its complete form is divided into three parts: the so-called Ethical
<margin>»</margin> branch, the Physical, and also the Logical. The first of these makes each of us
<margin>»</margin> noble and good <note>original: καλὸν κἀγαθόν (kalon kagathon), the Greek ideal of "gentlemanly" perfection combining beauty and virtue.</note>, and corrects entire households toward what is best, and
<margin>»</margin> even orders a whole people with a distinguished constitution and the most precise
<margin>»</margin> laws. The second branch gives knowledge of divine things—of the
<margin>»</margin> primary beings and the causes, and of all other things that come from these,
<margin>»</margin> which Plato named the "inquiry into nature." The third branch, Logic, is taken up for
<margin>»</margin> the discernment and discovery of both of these. It is quite clear that Plato was the
<margin>»</margin> first to gather all the parts of philosophy together into one, whereas before they were
<margin>»</margin> scattered and torn apart, like the limbs of Pentheus <note>In Greek mythology, King Pentheus was torn to pieces by his own mother and the Maenads. Atticus uses this as a metaphor for how philosophy was fragmented before Plato.</note>; he revealed philosophy to be
<margin>»</margin> a single, complete body and living being. For it is well known that Thales, 
<margin>»</margin> Anaximenes, and Anaxagoras, and those who lived around the same time,
<margin>»</margin> spent their time solely on the investigation of the nature of existing things. Nor does it 
<margin>»</margin> escape anyone's notice that Pittacus, Periander, Solon, and Lycurgus, and those 
<margin>»</margin> like them, placed that same philosophy into the realm of politics. This group of 
<margin>»</margin> teachers was also quite familiar with the dialectical art <term>Logic and reasoning</term>, 
<margin>»</margin> and was particularly zealous for the skill of arguments. Following these came Plato, 
<margin>»</margin> a man perfected by nature and greatly inspired, as if truly sent down from the 
<margin>»</margin> gods, so that through him philosophy might be seen as a whole. He omitted nothing 
<margin>»</margin> and perfected every detail, neither falling short of what was necessary nor 
<margin>»</margin> being carried away into what was useless. Since we have said that the Platonist 
<margin>»</margin> shares in all these—speaking of nature, of ethics, and of logic—let us 
<margin>»</margin> examine each one individually. These are the words of Atticus. Aristocles the 
<margin>»</margin> Peripatetic also testifies to these same things in the seventh book of his 
<margin>»</margin> composition "On Philosophy," where he writes word for word:

He quotes the Platonist Atticus, who credits Plato with unifying these previously scattered fields into a single body of knowledge.</summary>

<header>OF EUSEBIUS</header>

### From Aristocles: On the Philosophy of Plato.

Plato practiced philosophy, if anyone ever did, in a way that was both genuine and complete. For while the followers of **Thales** <note>Thales of Miletus (c. 624–546 BC) is often called the first Greek philosopher; he focused on the physical origin of the world.</note> spent their time studying nature, those around **Pythagoras** kept all their teachings hidden in secret. **Xenophanes** and his followers, by stirring up "eristic" <term>Eristic: A style of argument aimed at winning a debate rather than finding the truth, often using tricky logic.</term> arguments, caused great dizziness among philosophers but did not actually provide any helpful guidance.

Eventually, **Socrates** arrived and became—as the saying goes—"fire upon fire," <note>original: πῦρ ἐπὶ πυρὶ (pyr epi pyri). An idiom meaning to add intensity to an already heated situation, referring here to Socrates’s provocative method of questioning.</note> as Plato himself remarked. Because Socrates was naturally gifted and remarkably clever at raising doubts about any subject, he introduced the study of ethics and politics, and also the theory of **Ideas** <term>Theory of Ideas (or Forms): Plato's belief that the physical world is just a shadow of a higher, perfect reality of concepts.</term>. Having attempted to demonstrate this theory, and having stirred up every kind of argument and investigated everything, he reached the end of his life.

Others clearly followed him by cutting off specific parts of his teaching and specializing in them: some focused on medicine, others on the mathematical sciences. Some turned to poetry or music. Many, however, were simply amazed by the power of words—these became the rhetoricians—while others called themselves "dialecticians" <note>Those who focus on the logical structure of arguments.</note>.

Yet some of those who succeeded Socrates became quite wicked and held opinions entirely contrary to his. Some praised the life of the "Cynics" <note>The Cynics practiced extreme self-denial and rejected social norms.</note>, seeking a lack of pride and a state of "apathy" <term>Apathy (apatheia): Not "not caring" in the modern sense, but a state of being undisturbed by emotions or external events.</term>. Others, on the contrary, championed pleasure. Some boasted that they knew everything, while others claimed they knew nothing at all. Still others took a middle path and introduced no innovations, making themselves just like the common people. Others appeared as "healers" of sorts, yet they faded away as they lived.

**Plato**, however, realized that there was a single science encompassing both divine and human matters. He was the first to divide it, declaring that one part deals with the nature of the universe (Physics), the second with human affairs (Ethics), and the third with arguments (Logic). He maintained that one cannot arrange human affairs correctly unless one first beholds divine things. Just as doctors, when treating specific parts of the body, first take care of the body as a whole, so too must one first know the nature of the "Whole" before correcting things here on earth—since man is a part of all that exists.

One science belongs to us, the other to the Universe; but the one belonging to the Universe is more authoritative, for through it the other comes to be. **Aristoxenus** the musician says that this was an idea held by the **Indians**. He tells of a certain man from those people who met Socrates in Athens. The Indian asked Socrates what he did in his philosophy. When Socrates replied that he was investigating human life, the Indian laughed and said that no one could understand human things if they were ignorant of divine things.

Whether this story is true, no one can say for certain. Regardless, Plato divided philosophy into the study of the Whole, Politics, and Logic. Since Plato’s philosophy is of this nature, it is time to examine the philosophy of the **Hebrews**, which existed long before Plato was born, and whom I have said practiced philosophy in a similar way. You will find among them a harmony of study: ethics, logic, and physics, arranged in their own manner.

---

### On the Ethical Doctrines among the Hebrews.

Their ethical teachings were the first of all things to be zealously studied by them, and they were expressed in deeds long before they were recorded in idle words, as can be seen by examining the lives of these men. For they considered the "goal of good things" to be a blessed life—the ultimate boundary of piety...

<summary>This page presents a history of Greek philosophy via Aristocles, highlighting Plato's tripartite division of knowledge and the necessity of understanding the divine before the human. It concludes by pivoting to show that the Hebrews practiced this same philosophical structure much earlier.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Book 11 of the "Preparation for the Gospel," shifting from a critique of Greek philosophical schools to an explanation of the Hebrew approach to virtue, ethics, and logic.</meta>

<page-num>301</page-num>
<header>PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 11</header>

§ They embraced and pursued friendship with God—an achievement won through prayer—rather than the pleasure of the body, as **Epicurus** <note>Epicurus (341–270 BC) taught that the greatest good was "ataraxia" or freedom from fear and pain, often simplified by critics as mere "pleasure."</note> taught. Nor did they follow the "three-fold classification" of goods as **Aristotle** did, who valued things of the body and external circumstances as being of equal honor with the goods of the soul. Nor indeed did they embrace that ultimate ignorance and lack of learning which some, using a more dignified name, have called *epoché* <term>Epoché: The "suspension of judgment," a core tenet of Skeptical philosophy where one avoids making definitive claims about reality to maintain peace of mind.</term>. Instead, they focused on virtue within the soul itself. 

How great this virtue is among men, and what kind of release granted by God leads to a life free from pain—a life for which they surrendered everything, hanging as if from a rope of hope upon God—they demonstrated by showing that only the person who is "dear to God" <note>original: θεοφιλῆ (theophile)</note> is truly blessed. For God is the steward of all goods, the provider of life, and the fountain of virtue itself. As the supplier of all things for the body and all external needs, God alone is sufficient for a blessed life for the one who preserves friendship with Him through piety. 

For this reason, the all-wise **Moses** was the first of all to commit to writing the life of the Hebrews who were dear to God, sketching out a life that was both social and practical through historical guidance. From these general examples, he created his teaching, establishing God as the Cause of the universe and describing the creation of the world <note>original: κοσμογονίαν (cosmogony)</note> as its beginning. Then, proceeding in his discourse from general truths to specific details, he used the memory of ancient men to urge his students toward a zeal for their virtue and godliness. In the laws he authoritatively set down as contributing to this goal, it is clear in every way that he followed a "God-loving" path, providing care through the practice of prayer, just as our previous discussions concerning these matters have made clear. It would be a long task to list here the words of the prophets who followed Moses—those who were elders in virtue and who rejected all wickedness. However, they do bring forward the beneficial ethical teachings of **Solomon**, to which he dedicated a book of his own words, calling them "Proverbs"—short, pithy sayings like maxims <note>original: γνώμας ἀποφθέγμασιν (gnomas apophthegmasin)</note>, encompassing a single purpose through an ethical approach. In this way, the children of the Hebrews were deemed worthy from ancient times, even before learning their first letters, to be educated themselves and to share this same education unstintingly with those present.

---

-> Concerning the logical study among the Hebrews. <-

They did not think the "logical" part of Hebrew philosophy should be pursued through cold rivalry or the use of sophisms <term>Sophism: A clever but false argument, often used in ancient Greece to deceive or display intellectual superiority.</term> or through reasonings technically designed for deception. Instead, the philosophers among them reached the highest peak by grasping truth itself, their souls illuminated by light from God. On this basis, they sharpened those being educated in their own studies by delivering sacred words, narrating noble histories, and providing rhythmic compositions of songs and chants. Furthermore, they provided problems, riddles <note>original: αἰνίγματα (ainigmata)</note>, and certain writings interpreted through "allegorical theory" <term>Allegory: A method of interpretation that looks for a hidden spiritual or moral meaning behind the literal words of a text.</term> with beautiful eloquence. These things, expressed with fluency in their own language, were handed down to them from early infancy. Indeed, they even had certain "repeaters" <note>original: δευτερωταί (deuterotai). This likely refers to the "Tannaim" or teachers of the Jewish oral tradition (Mishnah), which Eusebius elsewhere translates as "Deuterosis."</note> for these primary lessons. It is customary to call the interpreters of their scriptures by this name—those who could explain things obscured by riddles, if not to everyone, then at least to those who applied themselves to the precision of these matters...

through interpretation and clarity, they made these things manifest. In this way, the most wise **Solomon**, who belongs to these people, began his book of *Proverbs* from this very starting point, teaching almost as if this were the sole cause for the writing itself. Through these very words, he said it was necessary for every man to know wisdom and instruction,
<margin>»</margin> and to perceive words of prudence, to receive the twists and turns of words <note>original: στροφὰς λόγων (strophas logon). This refers to the complex or veiled meanings found in riddles and parables.</note>, to perceive
<margin>»</margin> true righteousness, and to direct judgment. "So that," he says, "he might give craftiness to the innocent, and to the young child
<margin>»</margin> perception and understanding. For by hearing these, a wise man will become wiser, and a man of understanding will
<margin>»</margin> gain guidance. He will understand a parable and a dark saying, the sayings of the wise and their
<margin>»</margin> riddles." <note>This is a close paraphrase of the opening of the Book of Proverbs (Proverbs 1:1–6).</note> Such are the promises of the aforementioned work.

In addition to the specific commands already mentioned, any who wish to do so may take up the books of their prophetic writings and discover the solutions to these matters, as well as a complete logical system <term>Logic/Logical System: In this context, "logikē" refers to the branch of philosophy dealing with reason, language, and the structure of arguments.</term> suited to the wisdom and voice of these men. If anyone were to apply themselves with a love of beauty to their actual language and experience it firsthand, they would see that among these "barbarians" <note>To the Greeks, "barbarian" simply meant anyone who did not speak Greek; here, Eusebius uses it to refer to the Hebrews.</note> were men of the highest logic, in no way inferior to the **Sophists** or rhetoricians in their own tongue. They also possess poems in meter, such as the Great Song of **Moses** <note>Likely referring to the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15) or the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32).</note> and the instrument of **David**, the *Psalms*, which are composed in what the Greeks call "heroic meter." Indeed, they say these are hexameters <note>Hexameter: A poetic line consisting of six "feet" or beats, the standard meter of Greek epic poetry like the Iliad.</note> composed of sixteen syllables. Their other verses are said to be composed in their own tongue in what are called "tetrameters" and "trimeters." Such is the nature of their logical understanding regarding their mode of expression.

As for the nature of their thought, it is no longer of men but of God. One must receive these same words as oracles, divine utterances, and prophecies. They encompass pious lessons and the doctrines for the knowledge of all things that exist. You may find evidence of the logical precision among these men from the "correctness of the assignment of names." Regarding this, **Plato** is clearly seen to bear witness to the opinion of the Hebrews, being in harmony with the philosophy of these men on this very point, as is easy to discern from what follows.

## Concerning the Correctness of Names among the Hebrews.

Long before the first **Moses**—long before the very name of "philosophy" had even reached the Greeks—he had already dealt with the assignment of names throughout his entire writing. Sometimes he assigned names to all things most naturally, and at other times, he showed that the names of impious men were changed by God's judgment <note>original: μετωνυμίας (metonymias). "Metonymy" here refers to the renaming of biblical figures, such as Abram becoming Abraham.</note> to indicate His approval. He taught that names are assigned to things by nature and not merely by convention <term>Nature vs. Convention: A classic Greek debate (physis vs. thesis) over whether words have a natural, inherent link to the things they describe or are just arbitrary labels agreed upon by humans.</term>. Following him, **Plato** agrees with these same principles, having learned from none other than the "barbarians." In the *Cratylus*, Plato alludes to the Hebrews when he speaks in this manner (since it is not easy to find such a theory preserved among any other barbarian people):
<margin>»</margin> He says in the *Cratylus* that a "name" is not merely whatever some people agree to call something,
<margin>»</margin> pronouncing a portion of their own voice, but that there is a certain correctness of names that exists by nature,
<margin>»</margin> the same for all, both Greeks and barbarians. And proceeding further, he says: "Therefore,
<margin>»</margin> one must recognize that the assignment of names—whether among us or among the barbarians—is valid as long as
<margin>»</margin> the form of the name renders what is appropriate to each thing, in whatever syllables it may be..."

<summary>Eusebius argues that Hebrew scripture contains a sophisticated system of logic and poetic meter (comparable to Greek hexameter) and that Plato's theory of language in the Cratylus was actually derived from much older Hebrew traditions established by Moses and Solomon.</summary>

<margin>»</margin> ...to be a name-giver, whether the one here on earth or clearly the one from heaven. Then, following this, he again calls the expert in the
<margin>»</margin> correctness of names a "dialectician" <term>Dialectician: In Plato’s philosophy, this is a master of logic and reasoning who understands the true nature of things through dialogue.</term> and a "name-giver," saying: "It is the work
<margin>»</margin> of a carpenter to make a rudder, provided a pilot who understands its use supervises him, if the rudder is to be
<margin>»</margin> good. So it appears," he says, "that the work of a name-giver is to provide a name, having as a supervisor
<margin>»</margin> a man who is a dialectician, if the name is to be established well. This is so. It seems then,
<margin>»</margin> O Hermogenes, that the establishment of a name is no small matter, as you think, nor is it the work of small men,
<margin>»</margin> nor of any random person. And Cratylus speaks the truth when he says that names belong to things
<margin>»</margin> by nature, and that not every man is a creator of names, but only that one
<margin>»</margin> who looks toward the name that exists by nature for each thing, and who is able to place that very form
<margin>»</margin> into both letters and syllables." <note>This is a quotation from Plato’s dialogue *Cratylus* (389a–390e), which discusses whether names are arbitrary or natural.</note> Having said these things, after much more, he refers back
<margin>»</margin> to the memory of the barbarians <note>original: βαρβάρων (barbaron). For the Greeks, this meant anyone who did not speak Greek, including the Hebrews.</note>, and then he explicitly confesses that many
<margin>»</margin> names have come to the Greeks from these barbarians, saying in these very words: "I consider that
<margin>»</margin> the Greeks have received many names from the barbarians, especially those Greeks who live among the barbarians.
<margin>»</margin> If, therefore, anyone should seek to find how these names are appropriately placed according to the Greek tongue,
<margin>»</margin> and not according to that language from which the name happens to originate, you know that he would naturally be at a loss."

These are the words of Plato. But observe Moses, who, being at once a wise lawgiver and a dialectician, hear what he says: "And God still formed out of the ground all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the heaven, and he brought them to Adam to see what he would call them. And whatever Adam called every living soul, that was its name." <note>Genesis 2:19</note> Behold what he says: "That was its name," as if he did not use these titles as if they were established by mere custom, for he says that the name which was called out was long ago and previously contained within nature, and that this name remained fixed for each of the things named—that which the man described, being appointed by a higher power, established. And the name **Adam** itself, being a Hebrew name, would become a title for the "earth-born" man in the writings of Moses, since among the Hebrews *Adam* refers to the earth; because of this, the one who stands over the earth is truthfully called Adam by Moses. But the title might have another meaning, being translated as "red," referring to the bloody nature of the body. <note>original: ἐρυϑρὸν (erythron). Eusebius is playing on the Hebrew roots 'Adam' (man), 'Adamah' (earth/ground), and 'Adom' (red).</note> Thus, he marked the earthy, terrestrial, physical, and visible man with the name of Adam.

But the children of the Hebrews also call "man" by another name, calling him **Enos**, which they say refers to the rational part within us, being different in nature from the earthy Adam. They claim that "Enos" contains its own specific meaning, interpreted by the voice of the living. For the rational part in us is natural and unique, though it is joined to the mortal and irrational. For while one part is entirely flowing and decaying, the other is incorporeal, divine, and rational; it alone of those things on earth preserves the memory beloved by God, and it has grasped the knowledge of things to come through the height of the contemplation of virtue. This part, which was made in the beginning, was later entangled with bones and sinews and had the body placed upon it as a great and heavy mass; being full of much forgetfulness and ignorance, the Hebrew tradition has called it by the name of Enos, naming him so because it signifies "the forgetful one." <note>Eusebius derives "Enos" from a Hebrew root meaning "mortal" or "frail," but here interprets it as "one who forgets" his divine origin when trapped in a body.</note> At least, it is written in a certain prophet: "What is man, that you are mindful of him? Or the son of man, that you visit him?" <note>Psalm 8:4</note> Instead of which, the Hebrew text uses the name Enos for the prophet’s "man," using Enos always. And instead of the usual sense, it means: "What is the forgetful one, that you are entirely mindful of him?"

...and truly mindful. He says, “What is man that you are mindful of him, or the son of man <note>original: υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου (huios anthropou)</note> that you visit him?” <note>A reference to Psalm 8:4.</note> or “son of Adam” as it lies among the things revealed. It is as if he is referring to Adam himself and Enosh; the one, “Adam,” represents the "Original" <term>Archikos: Relating to the beginning or the first principle.</term>, and the other, “Enosh,” represents the "Rational." This is how the Hebrew oracles divide their etymology <term>Etymology: The study of the origin of words and how their meanings have changed throughout history.</term>. 

But Plato says that "man" <note>original: ἄνθρωπον (anthropon)</note>, in the Greek tongue <note>The OCR reads 'voice of the sun' (ἡλίου φωνῇ), likely a transcription error for 'Greek tongue' (ἑλλάδι φωνῇ).</note>, was named from "looking up" <note>original: ἀναθρεῖν (anathrein)</note>, saying: “But man has at once seen—and this is what ‘to see’ <note>original: ὄπωπε (opope)</note> means—and he looks up at <note>original: ἀναθρεῖ (anathrei)</note> what he reasons about.” This is based on the word for "having seen," so that he observes what he has seen. 

Again, the Hebrews call a "man" *Ish* <note>original: ἰσ (is)</note>. This name is derived by them from *Esh*, by which "fire" is signified, so that the male is named after the warm and active nature of man. 
But "woman" is appropriately said to have been taken from the man, and she shares in the name of the man. For the woman is called *Isshah* <note>original: ἰσσὰ (issa)</note> among them, just as the man is *Ish*. 

<margin>»</margin> However, Plato says that the "man" <note>original: ἄνδρα (andra)</note> was named from the "upward flow" <note>original: ἄνω ῥοὴν (ano rhoen)</note>. 
<margin>»</margin> And he adds, “But ‘woman’ <note>original: γυνὴ (gyne)</note> seems to me to want to be ‘offspring’ <note>original: γονή (gone)</note>.” 

Again, Moses, in the Hebrew tongue, correctly called the sky a "firmament" <note>original: στερέωμα (stereoma)</note>, based on God’s declaring that after the incorporeal and intellectual substance of this world, there is a solid and sensible body. 
But Plato says that "heaven" <note>original: οὐρανὸν (ouranon)</note> is correctly named because it makes one "look upward" <note>original: ἄνω ὁρᾷν (ano horan)</note>. 

Again, for the Hebrews, the highest God has a name from things unutterable and unspoken, which can only be grasped by the wise through a vision of the mind. But this very one whom we call "God," they call *Elohim* <note>original: ἐλωὶμ (eloim)</note>, apparently from *El*. They interpret this as "strength" and "power." Thus, the name of God among them is calculated as "The Strong One" from the power surrounding Him, through which He is understood to be multi-potent and all-powerful, as the one who established all things. 
But Plato says that "Gods" <note>original: θεοὺς (theous)</note> were named after "running" <note>original: θέειν (theein)</note>, which is to race, referring to the luminaries in the sky.

Such then, to speak in broad terms, are the matters concerning the "correctness of names" <term>Orthotes onomaton: A philosophical concept from Plato’s Cratylus suggesting that names are not arbitrary but reflect the true nature of the object.</term> as refined by the Hebrews and Plato. 

For Plato also says that names among men were established with a certain intention, and he attempts to give a reason for everything. I know not how he explains it, saying that "Hector" was named from "holding" <note>original: ἔχειν (echein)</note> and "ruling" <note>original: κρατεῖν (kratein)</note>, because he was king of the Trojans; and "Agamemnon" because of his "admirable persistence" <note>original: ἄγασαν μένειν (agasan menein)</note>, remaining justly and strongly in his decisions against the Trojans. And "Orestes" from the "mountainous" <note>original: ὀρεινὸν (oreinon)</note> and "wild" <note>original: ἄγριον (agrion)</note> quality of his character. And "Atreus" because of his "stubbornness" <note>original: ἀτειρὲς (ateires)</note>... and "Pelops" because he saw only what was "near" <note>original: πέλας (pelas)</note> and close at hand. And "Tantalus," he says, to signify "most wretched" <note>original: ταλαντατὸν (talantaton)</note> because of the misfortunes surrounding him. 

One could find a thousand such things said by Plato, attempting to teach that names were established by nature, but not that the names were given to things by gods. 
But you would not say that the names in Moses are forced, nor that they were made according to some sophisticated sectarian logic. You will learn that what is "Cain" among the Hebrews is translated as "zeal" <note>original: ζῆλος (zelos)</note> among the Greeks. The one described was deemed worthy of this name because of his zeal (or jealousy) toward his brother Abel. 
And "Abel" is interpreted as "mourning" <note>original: πένθος (penthos)</note>, having himself become a cause of such suffering to his parents. These names were given to those who appeared later as a way of interpreting what happened. 

And why should I bring up Abraham? He was once a student of the heavens <note>original: μετεωρολόγος (meteorologos)</note>, and as I said, he was skilled in the observation of the stars and the science of the celestial bodies when he was involved in Chaldean wisdom; then he was called "Abram." In the Hebrew tongue, this signifies an "exalted father" <note>original: πατέρα μετέωρον (patera meteoron)</note>. But God...

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 11

By moving beyond the visible and manifest world, he <note>Referring to the divine author or Moses.</note> uses a metonymy <term>Metonymy: A figure of speech where a thing or concept is referred to by the name of something closely associated with it.</term> that is not without reason. He says: "No longer shall your name be called Abram, but Abraham shall be your name, for I have made you a father of many nations." <note>Genesis 17:5. original: Ἄϐραμ (Abram), Ἀϐραὰμ (Abraham).</note> It would be a long discourse to explain the full meaning contained in this. It is sufficient to cite Plato as a witness to this argument, who says that the assignment of names was established by a more divine power. For he himself says in the *Cratylus*:

> >> I believe, Socrates, that the most serious account of these matters is this: that a more divine power than that of men established the first names for things. <note>Plato, *Cratylus* 397c.</note>

The sacred Scripture is confirmed by many others, but especially by the Hebrews, in the same way.

Regarding the simplicity of Moses, he taught that by a more divine power, Abraham, his son Isaac, and even Israel were so named. "Isaac" is interpreted as "Laughter," <note>original: Ἰσαὰκ (Yitzhak/Isaac). In Hebrew, the name is derived from the root for "to laugh."</note> which is a promising symbol of virtuous joy, a special gift that God promised to one who is dear to Him. And his son was Israel, to whom the name of Jacob was set aside, and in place of Jacob, God granted him the name of Israel. <note>Genesis 32:28.</note> Thus, he was transformed from one who is "ascetic and practical" to one who is "contemplative." For "Jacob" is interpreted as "Supplanter," <note>original: Ἰακὼϐ (Jacob); πτερνιστὴς (supplanter/heel-catcher). Jacob means "he catches the heel."</note> as one who struggles in the contest of virtue. But "Israel" means "One who sees God," <note>original: Ἰσραὴλ (Israel); ὁρῶν θεὸν (seeing God). A common Hellenistic etymology: 'ish (man) + ra'ah (sees) + el (God).</note> representing the man who is a knower and contemplative among men. Why must I now explain the correctness of the assignment of these proper names from the all-wise Moses or the sacred Hebrew words through initiation? Such an explanation of the type and form would require a longer period of leisure.

Immediately, one could see that the very first elements of the alphabet are not without their own etymologies. Plato himself could not explain the logic or the reason for the vowels or the consonants. But the children of the Hebrews would say that *Alpha* <note>original: ἄλφα</note> represents "strength," which they call *Aleph*, and this signifies "learning." <note>The Hebrew letter Aleph is related to the word 'alaph', meaning to learn or associate with.</note> And *Beta*, which they prefer to call *Beth*, is the name they give to a "house." <note>original: ϐῆτα (Beta), ϐὴθ (Beth).</note> So the meaning revealed is "the learning of the house." Or to say it more clearly, a certain teaching and learning of "stewardship" <term>Economy/Stewardship: From 'oikonomia', the management of a household.</term>. 

And *Gamma* is called *Gimel* among them, which means "earth." Thus they name the "filling of the earth." Next, they call the tablets *Deleth*, which they name as the fourth element <note>original: δέλτος (tablet), δέλθ (Daleth).</note>. They indicate to me through these two elements that written learning is the "filling of the tablets." One would find each of the remaining elements of the alphabet named among them with some specific reason and logic. 

Furthermore, they say that the hexad <term>Hexad: A group or set of six.</term> of vowels, or their combination into one, contains the pronunciation of a certain unutterable name. The children of the Hebrews mark this with four elements <note>The Tetragrammaton: YHWH.</note> and assign it to the highest power of God. They have received this from their fathers as something unspoken and unutterable to the many. But among the wise men of the Greeks, I do not know from where one might have learned this and expressed it through these verses:

> >> Seven vowels praise me, the great immortal God,
> >> The letters that are the tireless father of all.
> >> I am the immortal lyre of the universe, I who have tuned
> >> The melodic songs of the heavenly whirl. <note>A poem often attributed to Gnostic sources or the "Oracles," associating the seven Greek vowels with the seven planets and the divine name.</note>

Until now, I have paused at each of the remaining Hebrew elements to consider their meanings. This has already been spoken of by us previously, when we demonstrated that the Greeks had been benefited in all things by the "barbarians." <note>Eusebius often uses "barbarians" to refer to non-Greeks, particularly the Hebrews, whom he views as the source of true philosophy.</note> One might learn much by observing...

# EUSEBIUS PREP. Book 11
### Page 306

The Hebrew tongue is a diligent study, and the correctness of names is maintained among these men; for even here, the ancestral name <note>The name of the people.</note> has taken its derivative title from Eber. This name signifies "the traverser" or "one who passes over." For in the Hebrew language, a "passage" or a "traverser" is called *Eber*. <note>original: Ἕβερ (Eber). Eusebius connects this name to the Hebrew root ‘abar (עבר), meaning to cross over or pass through.</note> This teaching instructs us to pass over and cross from the things of this world toward divine things, and by no means to remain stuck in those things which our senses perceive while gazing upon visible objects. Instead, from these visible things, one should cross over to the unseen and invisible through the theology <note>In this context, "theology" refers to the study or contemplation of God's nature.</note> of the Maker and Creator of all things. For this reason, those first men—who were dedicated solely to the Author and Cause of the universe and who devoted themselves to pure and constant piety—were called "Hebrews," a name given to those who are "passers-over" and who have "crossed over" in their intellect.

I will not prolong this further by gathering the many instances that prove the correctness and precision of Hebrew names, as such a subject deserves its own dedicated treatise; however, let these brief examples suffice to show the proof of the logical teaching found among the Hebrews. Indeed, even according to Plato—a man of no small or ordinary reputation—it requires a very discerning "legislator of names" <note>A reference to Plato’s *Cratylus*, where he discusses the "Nomothetes" or name-giver who assigns names based on the essence of things.</note> to find names that are naturally suited to the things they represent, just as Moses and the Hebrew oracles have been shown to do for us. 

Now, following this discussion on logic, should we not examine "physics" <term>Physics: In the ancient sense, "physiologia" or the study of the natural world (nature, animals, plants, and the cosmos).</term> to see how the children of the Hebrews fared in this regard?

->On Hebrew Natural Philosophy<-

<margin>K</margin> Indeed, the third part of Hebrew philosophy is the "physical" part. Among them, this is divided into the contemplation of the intelligible and incorporeal, and the natural study <note>original: φυσιολογίαν (physiologian)</note> of sensible objects. Even in this field, the holy prophets knew all things and, whenever the occasion called for it, they revealed them in their own writings. They did not learn these things through guesswork or the mere efforts of mortal intellect, nor did they pride themselves on being taught by men; rather, their knowledge was imprinted upon them by the divine inspiration of a superior power and the Holy Spirit. Thousands of things were prophesied by them regarding the future, and thousands of things were explained regarding the composition of the universe. Furthermore, countless details were grasped regarding the nature of animals, and a great many things concerning plants were set down by each in their respective prophecies. 

Moses, for his part, was deeply knowledgeable about the powers of stones; he did not use them incidentally when considering the design of the High Priest’s robe. <note>Referencing the twelve gemstones on the breastplate of the High Priest described in Exodus 28.</note> And then there is Solomon; if anyone else is recorded as having excelled in this study of nature, it is he, as testified by the Holy Scripture, which contains the following:

> » And Solomon spoke three thousand parables, and his songs were five thou-
> » sand. And he spoke concerning trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hys-
> » sop that grows out of the wall. He spoke also of cattle, and of birds, and of
> » creeping things, and of fish. And all peoples came to hear the wisdom of 
> » Solomon, and he received gifts from all the kings of the earth, as many as 
> » heard of his wisdom. <note>1 Kings 4:32-34 (LXX 3 Kings 5:12-14).</note>

Starting from this same point, the author who attributed "The All-Virtuous Wisdom" to Solomon's person said: "For He Himself gave me unerring knowledge of the things that exist, to know the structure of the world and the activity of the elements; the beginning, the end, and the middle of times; the alternations of the solstices and the changes of seasons; the cycles of years and the positions of stars; the natures of animals and the tempers of wild beasts; the powers of spirits and the thoughts of men; the varieties of plants and the virtues of roots. I learned both what is secret and what is manifest. For..." <note>Wisdom of Solomon 7:17-21. This book was traditionally attributed to Solomon and lists the various branches of ancient science.</note>

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL Book 11
### Page 307

"Wisdom, the fashioner <note>original: τεχνῖτις (technitis). This refers to Wisdom as a master-craftsman or architect of the universe.</note> of all things, taught me." Furthermore, the same Solomon, when explaining the nature of the shifting essence of bodies, says in *Ecclesiastes*: "Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. What profit has a man in all his labor in which he labors under the sun?" He adds: "What is that which has been? The very thing which shall be. And what is that which has been done? The very thing which shall be done. And there is nothing entirely new under the sun." For these and similar things were part of his study of nature <note>original: πεφυσιολόγηται (pephysiologētai). In the ancient world, "physiology" meant the study of nature (physics) rather than just biology.</note> regarding bodily substance. 

You would find, if you went through the records, that the other Hebrews were not without similar profound knowledge. Indeed, as I have said before, they make mention of plants and animals, both those on land and in the water, and furthermore, the nature of birds. Truly, they also spoke of the stars in the heaven. For even of the Bear, and the Pleiades, and Orion, and Arcturus—whom it is common to call the Bear-ward <note>original: ἀρκτοφύλακα (Arktophylax), also known as Boötes.</note> and the Plowman—mention is found in their writings, and not in an ordinary way, by those who understand what is being indicated. 

But they have also excellently and accurately encompassed the composition of the world, the turning and alteration of the universe, the abundance of the soul, and the nature of all rational beings—both the visible creation and the invisible—as well as universal providence. Even before these topics, they grasped the doctrines and theories concerning the First Cause of all things and the theology of the realm beyond the heavens <note>original: ὑπέρου θεολογίας (hyperou theologias). This refers to a study of God that transcends the physical universe.</note>, which can be grasped only by the mind of the holy. These things were so well understood that those who later investigated the nature of these matters could not dispute them, nor could they say that the older teachings followed the newer ones.

So much, then, for their study of the nature of the universe. They divided their discourse on these matters into two parts. Regarding **sensible things** <note>Objects perceived by the senses, like trees or stones.</note>, they did not think it necessary to explain them in extreme detail to the common people, teaching the masses only as much as was worthy: namely, that the universe did not arise by chance, nor does it exist randomly or by a mindless impulse. Rather, it is driven by the Word of God <note>original: θεοῦ λόγῳ (Theou Logō). Eusebius uses the term "Logos" to describe God's organizing principle.</note> as its charioteer, and is governed by the power of unutterable wisdom. 

Regarding **intelligible things** <note>Objects perceived only by the mind, such as souls, angels, or divine truths.</note>—their arrangement, power, and distinctions—these things are indeed spoken of and laid down in the sacred books. They have been handed down to be heard by all, insofar as it is necessary for those who claim piety to know them for the sake of a truthful and temperate life. However, they left the deep and hidden reasoning concerning these matters to be sought in the secret teachings <note>original: ἐν ἀποῤῥήτοις (en apporrhētois). This suggests an "esoteric" or "inner" circle of study for those spiritually prepared.</note> by those capable of being initiated into such things. It would be well to briefly touch upon these explanations in outline, so that Plato may be shown to have held views similar to these recorded truths.

### Concerning the nature of intelligible things.

Furthermore, it is clear through his own words that the wonderful Plato followed the all-wise Moses and the Hebrew prophets in his teaching and contemplation of intelligible and incorporeal things. He may have learned this through reports that reached him, since it is well established that he spent time in Egypt. This was during the time the Hebrews were living among the Egyptians, having moved to that land when their own was under threat. Or, he may have grasped the nature of things for himself, or in some way been deemed worthy of this knowledge by God. For as the Apostle says, "God manifested it to them. For his invisible things, since the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made, even his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse." <note>A quotation from the New Testament, Romans 1:19-20.</note> You may learn what has been said by considering it in this way:

# EUSEBIUS
### On the "Being" of Moses and Plato.

<margin>„</margin> Moses, in the sacred initiations <note>original: ἱεροφαντίαις (hierophantiais). Eusebius uses a term associated with the Greek mysteries to describe the divine revelations given to Moses.</note>, spoke a divine response from the person of God, saying: **I am the One Who Is.** Thus he spoke to the sons of Israel: **He Who Is** <note>original: ὁ ὤν (ho ōn). This is the Greek Septuagint translation of the divine name (YHWH). It implies a Being that is absolute, eternal, and unchanging.</note> **has sent me to you.** First and foremost, I declare that God alone exists in the absolute sense, and is rightly and popularly deemed worthy of this title. Again, Solomon also hints at the generation and corruption <note>original: γενέσεώς τε καὶ φθορᾶς (geneseōs te kai phthoras). These are standard philosophical terms for coming-into-being and passing-away.</note> of sensory things and bodies, saying: *What is that which has been? The very thing which shall be. And what is there lately new under the sun? He shall speak and say, "Behold, this is new," but it has already happened in the ages that were before us.* 

Following these things, the universe is divided into two parts: the **intelligible** <note>original: νοητὸν (noēton). Refers to things grasped by the mind or intellect, usually non-physical and eternal.</note> and the **sensible** <note>original: αἰσθητὸν (aisthēton). Refers to things grasped by the physical senses, which are constantly changing.</note>. The intelligible is shown to be incorporeal and rational in nature, both incorruptible and immortal; the sensible, however, exists in a state of flux and decay, subject to the change and turning of its essence. Since all things are summed up into one first principle, and they dogmatize that there is one "True Being" who is properly and truly the Cause of all things, both incorporeal and corporeal—I might say that Plato, having accepted these doctrines not only in their general thought but in their very words and phrases from the Hebrew Scriptures, made the doctrine his own, explaining it more broadly in this way:

<margin>„</margin> *What is that which always is, and has no beginning? And what is that which is always becoming, but never is? The one is grasped by the mind through reason, always existing in the same way; the other is conjectured by irrational opinion, being born and perishing, but never truly being.*

Does it not clearly appear that this admirable man, having transformed what is said in Moses—**I am the One Who Is**—said: *What is that which always is, and has no beginning?* He clarifies the more general sense by saying that "Being" is nothing other than that which is not seen with the eyes of the flesh, but is apprehended by the mind. At any rate, having asked "What is Being?", he answers himself: *That which is grasped by the mind through reason.* Furthermore, the oracle <note>original: μάντειον (manteion). Referring to the authority of the text as if it were a divine revelation.</note> which Timaeus speaks—"What is that which has been? The very thing which shall be," and "What is that which has been done? The very thing which shall be done"—he clearly interprets in almost these exact words: 

<margin>„</margin> *The other is conjectured by irrational opinion, being born and perishing, but never truly being.*

To which he adds: *All such things as "was" and "shall be" are parts of time. We incorrectly apply these to eternal essence without realizing it. For we say that it "was," "is," and "shall be," but in truth only "is" belongs to it according to true reason. But "was" and "shall be" are appropriate to say regarding that "becoming" which exists in time, for it is a movement. But that which is always the same and unmoved, it is not fitting for it to become older or younger through time; nor to have once been, nor to be now, nor to be hereafter at all, nor any of the things which we attach to things driven by the senses. Rather, these are forms of time which mimic eternity and circle according to number.* 

And in addition to these, he says: *That which has happened is happened, and that which is becoming is becoming, and that which will be is that which will be.* 

And lest anyone think that we are misinterpreting the philosopher's words, we shall use commentaries, so that the thought behind these words may be made clear. Many have applied themselves to the study of these things; but for me, it is sufficient to set forth the words of that man, the illustrious **Numenius the Pythagorean**, which he details in the second book of his work *On the Good*, as follows:

-> From the 2nd book of *On the Good* by Numenius the Pythagorean. <-

"Come then, with all our strength, let us ascend as close as possible to Being, and let us say: That which is...

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 11
### Page 309

> » ...neither was it ever, nor will it ever not be; but it is always in a defined time, which is the present alone. If someone wishes to call the present that exists in the "now" *eternity* <term>Aeon</term> <note>original: αἰῶνα (aiōna). In this philosophical context, Aeon refers to eternal, timeless existence, as opposed to "chronos" or passing time.</note>, I also advise it.
> » But one must think of past time as lakes that have escaped, already fled, and run away into *non-existence* <term>non-being</term> <note>original: μὴ εἶναι (mē einai). Numenius argues that the past and future lack true reality because they are not present.</note>; nor is the future anything yet, though it promises it is capable of arriving into existence. It is not reasonable to think of "Being" in any way as either not existing, or no longer existing, or not yet existing. 
> » So, as this is said, one thing becomes—and Oh!—a great impossibility: to be the same and *not be* <term>non-existence</term> at once. If this is the case, it is unlikely that there is any other power than truly that which is itself by itself; for "Being" is eternal and stable, always according to itself and the same, and it was neither born nor destroyed, nor did it grow, nor was it diminished. 
> » It never became more or less; and indeed, regarding other things, it will never be moved in any way. For it is not lawful for it to be moved, neither backwards nor forwards; neither up at any time, nor down; nor will "Being" ever be shifted to the right or to the left, nor will it ever be moved around its own center, but rather it will stand still, and it will be fixed and stable <note>original: ξηρός (xēros). Literally "dry," but used here to mean firm or unchanging, as opposed to the "fluid" nature of the material world.</note>, holding to the same things always and in the same way. 

And next he adds other points.

» These things then are my thoughts on the path. But again, to speak of it further, I will state the name of the *incorporeal* <term>Asōmatos</term> <note>original: ἀσωμάτου (asōmatou). Something that has no physical body or material substance.</note>. For it is now a risk to speak its name rather than not to speak it. And indeed, I speak its name: for let it be that which has been sought for so long. For it is necessary, if you say so, that there be a name for the *incorporeal*, and that which now belongs to "Being" itself—which has neither been born nor will be destroyed, nor admits any growth or movement, nor any change for better or worse—let it be simple and unalterable, in the same form (idea), and neither willing to depart from its identity, nor being forced to by another. 

And *Plato* also said in the *Cratylus* that names are imitations of things, being themselves applied to them. Let it be, then, and let "incorporeal" be granted to "Being." Then, descending a little further, he adds:

» That which I called "Being" and "incorporeal," this is the *intelligible* <note>original: νοητόν (noēton). In Platonism, this refers to things that can only be grasped by the mind or intellect, not the physical senses.</note>. These things which have been said, as far as I remember them, I shall leave as they are. But I wish to support the argument by further investigation, having suggested this much: that if these things do not agree with the dogmas of Plato, they should at least be thought to belong to another great man of great power, such as Pythagoras. 

At least Plato says—come, let me remember how he says it: 

» *What is that which always is, and has no beginning? And what is that which is always becoming, but never is? The one is grasped by the intellect with reason <note>original: νοήσει μετὰ λόγου (noēsei meta logou). Knowledge gained through pure thought.</note>, being always the same; while the other is the object of opinion with unreasoning sensation, becoming and perishing, but never truly being.* 

For he asked: What is "Being"? asserting it to be undeniably unbegotten. For he said there was no "becoming" for "Being." For it would have to turn (change). And if it turned, it would not be eternal. Then, going further down, he says:

» If "Being" is not entirely eternal by nature and is both unchangeable and unmoving, in no way and in no place departing from itself, but remains according to the same things and stands in the same way, this would surely be that which is grasped by the intellect with reason. But if the body flows and is carried along by subsequent change, it escapes and does not exist. Hence comes the great madness: is "Being" not indefinite, grasped only by opinion, and as Plato says, *becoming and perishing, but never truly being*?

These are the words of *Numenius*, interpreting the teachings of *Plato* and, much earlier, those of *Moses* into clear terms. Rightly then is he led back to that very famous saying, through which he is remembered to have said:

-> **For what is Plato, but Moses speaking Attic Greek?** <-
<note>original: τί γάρ ἐστι πλάτων, ἢ μωσῆς ἀττικίζων; (ti gar esti Platōn, ē Mōsēs attikizōn?). "Atticizing" refers to speaking the dialect of Athens (Attica). ->From the writing of Plutarch entitled<-
->*On the E at Delphi*<-

> Therefore, I do not think the letter <term>E</term> <note>original: "Εἰ" (Ei). The letter Epsilon was inscribed at the temple of Apollo at Delphi. Plutarch argues it is not the number five or the word "if," but the statement "Thou Art."</note> signifies a number, or an order, or a conjunction, or any other of the missing parts of speech; rather, it is a complete address and salutation to God which, by the very word, brings the speaker to a realization of God's power. For God, as it were, greets each of us who approach here with the command "Know Thyself," which is nothing less than "Hail." And we, in turn, answering God, say "Thou Art" <term>You exist</term>, rendering to Him the address "Thou Art" as a true and unerring title which belongs to Him alone. For in truth, we have no part in real "Being." Every mortal nature, being situated in the midst of corruption and birth, presents only a phantom and a dim, unstable appearance of itself. If one tries to grasp it with the mind, it is like the violent squeezing of water: by pressing it and bringing it together, the water flows away and one loses what was held. So too, when the intellect pursues a clear understanding of each of these passive and changeable things, it is led astray—on one hand by its coming-into-being, and on the other by its perishing—since nothing remains to be grasped, nor can it truly exist. For "one cannot step twice into the same river," according to Heraclitus <note>A famous pre-Socratic philosopher known for his doctrine that change is central to the universe.</note>, nor can one touch a mortal substance twice in the same state; rather, by the sharpness and speed of change, it scatters and gathers again—or rather, not even "again" or "later," but at the same time it comes together and leaves, it approaches and departs. Hence, that which is "becoming" never even proceeds into "Being," because the flow never ceases or stands still. Instead, changing from a seed, it forms an embryo, then a babe, then a child, next a youth, a young man, a man, an elder, and an old man, destroying the former births and ages by those that follow. Yet we ridiculously fear a single death, having already died so many times and still dying now. For not only, as Heraclitus said, is "the death of fire the birth of air," but it is clearer in our own lives: the man at his prime is destroyed when he becomes an old man, and the youth was destroyed into the man at his prime, and the child into the youth, and the infant into the child. The man of yesterday has died into the man of today; the man of today dies into the man of tomorrow. No one remains, nor is anyone a single "one," but we become many, driven around a single phantom and a common mold of matter that slips away. For how is it that, if we remain the same, we rejoice in different things now than before? How do we love and hate contrary things, or admire and blame them? How do we use different words and different passions, no longer having the same appearance, form, or even the same mind? For it is not likely that one would have different experiences without change, nor is he who changes the same person. And if he is not the same, he does not even "exist," but by changing from his same self...

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL Book 11
### Page 311

» ...constantly changing, becoming one thing after another. Our perception is deceived by its ignorance of true Being, thinking that the appearance is the reality. That which truly exists, then, is eternal, unbegotten, and incorruptible, upon which no length of time brings change. For matter is something mobile, appearing to move and flow constantly, never holding still, like a vessel of corruption and birth; this is what we call "time." From this time come the terms "after" and "before," "it will be" and "it has been," which are themselves an admission of non-existence. For to say that something "is" when it has not yet come into being, or has already ceased to be, is both mortal and absurd. But where we especially focus our intellect on time—using the words "it is present," "it is here," and "now"—at that very moment, the logic dissolves as it is squeezed out. For "now" is crushed into the future and the past, like a flash of light to those who wish to see it, necessarily splitting apart. If the nature being measured suffers the same fate as these changes, then it does not truly exist itself, but is becoming and perishing according to its coincidence with time. Therefore, it is not possible to say of true Being that "it was" or "it will be." For these are turnings, transitions, and variations of that which has no natural capacity to remain in a state of being. But if God "is"—if one must say so—He "is" not according to any time, but according to the motionless and timeless eternity <note>original: "αἰῶνα" (aion). This refers to a state of existence outside the sequence of past, present, and future.</note>, which is unswerving, in which there is no before nor after, no future nor past, no older nor younger. Rather, being One, He has filled the "always" with a single "now." Only that which exists according to Him truly *is*, having neither been born, nor about to be, nor having a beginning, nor an end. Thus, those who worship Him should salute and address Him in this way, or even, as some of the ancients said, as "Thou Art One." For the Divine is not "many," as each of us is—a confused collection made up of ten thousand different passions and parts—but true Being must be One, just as the One must truly be. If there is "otherness," a difference from Being, it departs into the realm of non-existence.

->That the Divine is Ineffable.<-

Moses and all the prophets among the Hebrews taught that the Divine is ineffable <note>meaning: "unutterable" or "too great to be expressed in words."</note>. They indicated this symbol of the unutterable name through their unpronounceable notation <note>A reference to the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter Hebrew name of God (YHWH) which was not spoken aloud.</note>. Listen to how Plato, in total agreement with them, says the following in his *Great Letter*: "For it is in no way speakable, like other subjects of study; rather, after a long period of living together and being occupied with the subject itself, suddenly—like a light kindled from a leaping spark—it is born in the soul and then begins to nourish itself." And see if he did not take this example of light from the Hebrew prophet who spoke before him, saying: *The light of your countenance was signed upon us, O Lord* <note>original: "ἐσημειώθη ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς τὸ φῶς τοῦ προσώπου σου, κύριε" — Psalm 4:6</note>; and again: *In Your light we shall see light* <note>original: "ἐν τῷ φωτί σου ὀψόμεθα φῶς" — Psalm 36:9</note>.

->That God is Only One.<-

Listen to Moses, who said regarding the God of the universe: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one" <note>original: "κύριος εἷς ἐστι" — Deuteronomy 6:4</note>. Again, Plato concurs with this, teaching that there is one God, just as there is one heaven, saying this in the *Timaeus*: "Have we then rightly called the heaven 'one,' or would it have been more correct to say there are many and infinite heavens? One, if indeed it was crafted according to the Model. For that which contains all intelligible living things could never be a second along with another." It is clear that he knew only one God, even if he used his customary titles in his letters. And from the *Letter to Dionysius*, in which he used symbols—

## Plato on the Second Cause

> And I will teach you that we should not assign a year, nor a month, nor any portion to these [heavenly bodies], nor any span of time in which they traverse their own orbits, completing the order of the cosmos, which the **most divine Word** <note>original: *Logos*</note> has ordained. The happy man first wonders at this, and then feels a longing to learn as much as is possible for a mortal nature. 

And in his *Letter to Hermeias, Erastus, and Coriscus*, his doctrine is set down with a very great deal of caution, where he writes word-for-word as follows:

> All three of you must read this letter, preferably together as a group; if not, then by twos, as often as you can together. Use it as a covenant and a binding law, as is right. Swear an oath with a seriousness that is not without the grace of the Muses, and with that education which is the sister of seriousness. Swear by the God who is the **leader** of all things, both present and future, and swear by the **Lord and Father** of that leader and cause. If we truly practice philosophy, we shall all know Him clearly, as far as is possible for happy men.

Does it not seem to you that Plato, in saying these things, followed the doctrines of the Hebrews? From where else could there have come to him the idea of calling God the "greater cause" of the "cause and leader" of all things—naming Him specifically the **Father** of the Creator? From where did he get the idea to assign the name **Lord** to the Father of the Craftsman <note>original: *demiurge*—the "worker" god who shapes the physical world</note>, when no one before him had ever heard of such things in books, nor had anyone even conceived of them in their mind?

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 11

> » ...of him, the cause of being and the cause of this being many, making this number; but number is not primary. For before the dyad <note>original: *dyados*—the number two, representing the first step away from unity into multiplicity</note> there is the One. The second is the dyad, which is a "one" that has come from the One. And again, proceeding further, he [Plotinus] adds: "How then? And what must we conceive concerning that which remains still? It is a radiation from Him, even while He remains still. Just as the bright light surrounding the sun constantly runs around it, forever generated from it, while the sun itself remains still. And all things, as long as they remain, produce from their own essence a necessary existence around them, directed toward the outside, which is an image of the present power from which it depends—an image that is like the archetype <note>original: *archetypon*—the original model or "blueprint" of a thing</note> from which it sprang. Fire produces the heat within itself. And snow does not only keep its cold within. This is most evident in fragrant things; for as long as they exist, something is poured out from them into the surrounding area, which those nearby enjoy. All things, once they reach perfection, generate. That which is always perfect, therefore, always generates something eternal. And it generates something lesser than itself. What, then, must we say about the most perfect? Does nothing come from it, or only the greatest things after it? The greatest thing after it is the Intellect <note>original: *nous*—often translated as Mind or Divine Intelligence</note>, and it is the second. For the Intellect sees that One and needs only Him, but that One has no need of the Intellect. And that which is generated from a source superior to Intellect must itself be Intellect. Indeed, Intellect is superior to all other things, because the rest come after it." Following these points, he adds: "Where then is that which has been generated? For whenever the producer exists, the generated must necessarily exist alongside it. Thus, they are separated only by their difference <note>original: *heterotēti*—they are distinct in identity but not physically separate</note>. We say that the Intellect is the image of that One. For we must speak more clearly." And again, he adds to this: "And because of this, Plato’s teachings also attempt to say that all things are around the 'King' <note>Plotinus is referencing Plato's *Second Letter*</note>. He says the first things are around the first, the second things around the second, and the third things around the third. He also speaks of the 'Father of the Cause,' calling the Intellect the 'Cause.' For to him, the Intellect is the Craftsman <note>original: *dēmiourgos*—the divine artisan who shapes the physical world</note>. He says this Intellect makes the Soul in that 'mixing bowl' <note>a reference to Plato's *Timaeus*, where the Creator mixes the soul of the world</note>. But of the Cause, which is the Intellect, he calls 'The Good' the Father, that which is beyond Intellect and beyond Essence. In many places, he calls Being and the Intellect the 'Idea.' Thus, Plato knew that the Intellect comes from the Good, and the Soul from the Intellect. These accounts are not new, nor of today, but were spoken of long ago, though not in an unfolded manner. The current accounts have become interpreters of those ancient ones, confirming with testimonies that these doctrines are ancient, found in the writings of Plato himself." Such are the words of Plotinus. And Numenius <note>a 2nd-century philosopher who bridged Pythagoreanism and Platonism</note>, who honored the teachings of Plato, in his works *On the Good*, interpreting these same matters concerning the Second Cause, says:

->Numenius on the same subject.<-

> » The one who intends to understand concerning the first and second God must first distinguish each thing in its proper order and arrangement. Then, when it seems to be well-situated, one should then proceed to speak decorously, lest—if those first things are left behind before they are grasped—the "treasury" <note>an idiomatic way of referring to a wealth of knowledge or divine truth</note> vanishes, as he says. Let us not suffer the same fate. But praying to God to become a guide for our reason, to reveal a treasury of thoughts, let us begin thus: We must proceed now, and we must narrate. The God who is the first, being in himself, is simple, because by being with himself throughout, he is never divisible. However, the God who is the second and third is one. But being brought together with Matter <note>original: *hylē*</note>, which is the Dyad, he unites it, yet is split by it, as Matter has a desiring nature and is in a state of flux. Therefore, because he is not solely focused on the Intelligible—for he would then be with himself—but because he looks toward Matter...

# EUSEBIUS

> ...taking care to see this, having drawn himself away from the earth, he gazes upon the truth; for it is necessary, having reached out toward his own character away from matter. And after other things he [Numenius] says: "For even if it is not necessary for the first to be the creator, yet the one who creates must be considered the son of the Father, who is the First God." If then we must inquire about the creator, asserting that the one who first existed must act in this way, without sparing, this method would be proper to the discourse. But if there is no talk of the creator, and we seek instead concerning the First, I will clear myself of what was said; let those things remain unsaid <note>original: *arrēta*—unspeakable or sacred secrets</note>, and I will proceed to the discourse, attempting it from another side. 
> 
> Regarding the discourse of union, let us agree among ourselves—an agreement not to be disputed—to hear that the First God is the source <note>original: *archē*—beginning or first principle</note> of all works and the King, while the Creative God is the Leader, traveling through the heavens. Through this one the pole exists for us, as the mind is sent down through the passage to all those joined in community. Therefore, when God looks and is turned toward each of us, it happens that we live and are animated, while bodies are cared for by the far-reaching rays <note>original: *akrobolismois*—literally 'skirmishings' or 'darts,' here used metaphorically for the divine emanations or 'glances' of God</note> of God. But when God turns back into his own silence, these things are extinguished. And to perceive is to live, a life enjoying the Blessed One. 
> 
> These are the words of Numenius. Now you, set beside them the words from the Hebrew prophecy, sung of old among the Hebrews in this manner: *How thy works were magnified, O Lord; in wisdom hast thou made them all. The earth was filled with thy creation. All things look to thee, to give them food in due season. When thou givest to them, they shall gather. When thou openest thy hand, all things shall be filled with goodness. But when thou turnest away thy face, they shall be troubled. Thou shalt take away their breath, and they shall fail, and return to their dust. Thou shalt send forth thy spirit, and they shall be created, and thou shalt renew the face of the earth.* <note>This is a quotation of Psalm 104 (Septuagint 103): 24, 27-30</note>
> 
> For do these things differ from the thoughts of the philosopher who says that when God looks and is turned toward each of us, it happens that we live and are animated, and bodies are cared for by God through his rays; but when God turns back into his own silence, these things are extinguished? Again, you might say of the Word of Salvation among us: *I am the vine, my Father is the husbandman, you are the branches.* <note>John 15:1, 5</note> 
> 
> Listen to what Numenius theologizes about the Second Cause: "Just as there is a relation of the husbandman to that which is planted, so again the First God is related to the Creator. For the one, being the seed of every soul, sows into all things that partake of him. But the Lawgiver <note>original: *nomothetēs*—here Numenius uses 'Lawgiver' as a title for the Demiurge/Creator</note> plants, distributes, and transplants into each of us the things previously cast down from there." 
> 
> And next again, concerning how the Second Cause subsisted from the First, he says the following: "Whatever things are given and pass to the receiver, departing from the giver—such as services, goods, or minted money—these are mortal and human. But divine things are such that, though transferred from here to there, they do not depart from the source; and having come to be there, they benefit the one without diminishing the other. They also bring further benefit through the recollection of what was known. This beautiful thing is <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: *epistēmē*—scientific or certain knowledge</note>, of which the receiver benefits, yet the giver is not deprived; just as you might see a lamp kindled from another lamp, having light which it did not take away from the first..."

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, BOOK 11

» ...[knowledge] was not taken away, but kindled from the matter within him by that fire. Such a thing is the nature of knowledge, which, once given and received, remains with the giver while also being preserved by the receiver. The cause of this, O stranger, is nothing human; rather, the state and essence that holds knowledge is the same in the God who gave it and in you and me who received it. Therefore, Plato also said that knowledge was cast among men by Prometheus <note>In Greek mythology, the Titan who stole fire from the gods to give to humanity; here used as a metaphor for the transmission of divine wisdom</note> together with a most brilliant fire. And again, descending a bit in the sequence, he says: "And these are the lives: one belonging to the first God, the other to the second God." Clearly, the first God will be standing still, while the second is, conversely, in motion. The first is concerned with the intelligible things <note>The *noēta*—realities that can only be understood by the mind, like Platonic Forms</note>, and the second with both the intelligible and the sensible things <note>The *aisthēta*—things we perceive with our physical senses</note>. Do not wonder that I said this, for you will hear something even more wonderful. For I say that the movement inherent in the second, which provides a release <note>original: *lytē*</note> for his essence, is an approach to the first, and I call this a natural movement. From this movement, the order of the cosmos, its eternal stability, and salvation are poured out into the whole. In addition to these things, in his sixth book, he adds the following: "Since among men, Plato [is thought to] know only the Creator, whom some call the 'First Mind' <note>original: *nous*</note>, while the one who is truly the first is altogether unknown among them, he [Plato] therefore spoke again as follows: 'O men, the Mind which you suppose is not the first, but there is another Mind before this, older and more divine.'" And after other things he adds: "Like a pilot <note>original: *kybernētēs*—the source of our word 'governor'</note> carried somewhere in the middle of the sea, standing at the high tiller, steering the ship by the rudders. His eyes and mind are strained from the ether toward the heights, from which his path goes upward through the heaven as he sails below on the sea. So too the Creator, binding matter with harmony so that it is neither struck apart nor fully dissolved, is himself established by it as a ship is by the sea. He directs the harmony, steering with the Ideas; his eyes look toward heaven, so that his gaze meets the God above. He receives the power of judgment from contemplation, and the power of impulse from desire." And our Word <note>original: *logos*</note> of salvation says: "This one can do nothing of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it" <note>A direct reference to the Gospel of John 5:19</note>. But let so much be said about these things.

Because these views were clearly not original to Plato but were harmonized with him, there is no need to add anything further to his own words. That Plato was not the first to use these insights, and that the wise men of the Hebrews brought them forward, has been shown through the passages already set forth. Likely then, among the newer philosophers, Amelius <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note> became prominent—himself a zealous follower of Plato’s philosophy if ever there was one—except that he called the theologian of the Hebrews a "barbarian" <note>In the Greek sense, meaning a non-Greek speaker, though often used with a tone of cultural superiority</note>. Even if he did not see fit to mention John the Evangelist by name, he nevertheless bears witness to his words, writing these very things word for word:

### Amelius on the theology of John, our Evangelist.

And this then was the Word <note>original: *logos*</note>, through whom, being eternal, the things coming into being were made, as Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher famous for his doctrine of change and the *Logos*</note> would also maintain; and by Zeus, the barbarian also maintains that, established in the rank and dignity of the Beginning <note>original: *archē*</note>, he was with God and was God. Through him, all things absolutely were made; in him, that which was made has its nature as living, as life, and as being; and falling into bodies and putting on flesh, he appeared as a man, while also at that time showing the grandeur of his nature...
