» ...[he is] a monarch, unpolluted and unharmed, to be deified again and to be God, just as he was before descending into the body, the flesh, and the state of man. These things would be clear as having been translated from "barbarian" <note>In this context, "barbarian" refers to non-Greek, specifically Hebrew or Christian, theology.</note> theology, not in an obscured way, but openly and plainly. And who might this "barbarian" be, if not John, the evangelist of our Savior? He was a Hebrew who, at the very beginning of his own writing, theologizes in this way: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God," <note>original: *en archē ēn ho logos*</note> up until the point where he says, "and we beheld his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father." Hear also what the same Hebrew theologian <note>Eusebius is likely referring here to the Apostle Paul, quoting from the Epistle to the Colossians.</note> recounts concerning him: "who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, for in him all things were created in the heavens and upon the earth; and all things consist through him, and all things were created in him, both the visible and the invisible." Furthermore, concerning the constitution and substantiality of the Second Cause <note>A philosophical term for the Word or Son, acting as the intermediary between the ultimate God and the physical world.</note>, the wise among our people agree with the wisdom of the Hebrews. Let us, then, move on to another point.

### On the Three Primal Hypostases
<term>Hypostasis: A technical term in Greek philosophy and theology referring to the underlying reality or "personhood" of a divine being.</term>

Among the Hebrew oracles, after the discourse concerning the Father and the Son, the Holy Spirit is listed in the third rank. They arrange the holy and blessed Trinity in this manner, as the third power surpasses every created nature; it is the first of the intellectual essences established through the Son, but the third from the First Cause. See how Plato also hinted at such things in his letter to Dionysius, saying: "I must speak to you in riddles, so that if the tablet should suffer anything in the folds of sea or land, the reader may not understand it. For it is thus: all things are around the King of All, and for his sake are all things, and he is the cause of all beautiful things; second things are around the second, and third things around the third. The human soul longs to learn what sort of things these are, looking at things akin to itself." Those who attempt to clarify Plato's meaning refer these to the First God, the Second Cause, and thirdly the Soul of the World, defining the soul itself as a third god. But the divine oracles place the holy and blessed Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in the principle of the "Beginning," according to what has been set forth. It follows from these points to examine the essence of the Good.

### On the Essence of the Good

The divine scripture of the Hebrews teaches in various ways about the essence of the Good, showing that the Good itself is nothing other than God, through passages such as: "The Lord is good to all who wait for him, to the soul that seeks him." And: "Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever." Through these, the Word of the Savior also declared to the one asking about this: "Why do you ask me about the good? No one is good except one, God." Listen also to what Plato says in the *Timaeus*, stating the reason why the Creator composed becoming and this whole universe: "He was good; and in one who is good, no envy ever arises concerning anything. Being free from this, he desired that all things should become as much as possible like himself." And in the *Republic* he says: "Does it not seem that the sun is not sight itself, but being its cause, it is seen by sight itself?" "Yes," he said. "This then," I said, "is what I meant by the offspring of the Good..."

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 11
### Page 319

> » ...offspring, whom the Good begat analogous to itself; what the Good is in the intelligible realm <note>The realm of things understood by the mind, rather than perceived by the senses.</note> in relation to both the mind and the objects of thought, this [offspring] is in the visible realm in relation to both sight and the objects of vision.
> » And following this, he adds: This, then, which provides truth to the things known and gives the power [of knowledge] to the knower, you must say is the **Idea of the Good**.
> » And again he says: The sun, I think you will say, provides to the visible things not only the power of being seen, but also their generation, growth, and nourishment, though the sun is not itself generation. For how could it be?
> » So also, you must say that for the things known, not only is their being known present from the Good, but also their existence and essence <term>Ousia: The inner nature or true being of a thing.</term> come from it, though the Good is not essence, but **beyond essence**, exceeding it in dignity and power.

By these words, Plato most clearly says that for the intelligible things, it is from the Good—that is to say, from God—that they receive not only the quality of being known, but also their very being and essence. He says the Good is not itself essence, but is **beyond essence**, exceeding it in dignity and power. One should therefore not find fault with these things, nor consider these realities unknowable simply because they have received their being and essence from that which is "not essence" but "beyond essence," exceeding it in dignity and power. It is only this [Good], quite reasonably, that the Hebrew oracles <note>The Holy Scriptures of the Jews and Christians.</note> proclaim as God, insofar as He is the Cause of all things. As for other things, which are neither truly "Being" nor have essence from themselves, and do not belong to the nature of the Good, it is not irrational to suggest they are not truly "gods," since their nature does not have the Good as its foundation. For to this one alone, and to no other, must the title be assigned: the **Only Good**, which Plato divinely proclaimed to be "beyond all essence," exceeding it in both dignity and power.

Furthermore, Numenius, in his writings *On the Good*, interpreting the mind of Plato, proceeds in this manner:

-> From Numenius, *On the Good* <-

> » Now, we may grasp bodies through the signs they give, both from similar things and from the images and signs found among visible objects. But the Good is not to be grasped from any of the things lying near it, nor indeed from any similar sensible object <note>Sensible: things perceived by the five senses.</note>; there is no such device. Rather, it is necessary—just as if one were sitting on a lookout and caught sight of a small merchant ship, one of those skiffs, all alone, abandoned in the midst of the waves, and saw the ship with a single sharp-eyed glance—so too must one depart far from the things of the senses to **commune with the Good alone with the alone**. There, there is no man, nor any other living creature, nor any body, great or small, but a certain ineffable and indescribable divine solitude, truly a magnificent desert. There are the "customs" of the Good, its pastimes and its splendors. But the Good itself is in peace, in kindness—the Calm, the Gracious Sovereign riding upon Essence.
> » But if someone, as if obsessed with sensible things, imagines the Good "flying over" him and then thinks he has luxuriated in a meeting with the Good, he is altogether mistaken. For in truth, the methods of approaching it are not easy. It is best, neglecting the things of the senses, to commune vigorously with the branches of learning; by contemplating numbers, one may thus practice the lesson: **What is the One?**
> » These things he says in the first book. And in the fifth book he says the same: If essence and the Idea are intelligible, and if Mind <term>Nous: The higher intellect or divine reason.</term> is admitted to be older than and the cause of essence, then Mind itself is found to be the only thing that is the Good. For if the **Creator God** <note>original: *demiourgos theos*. The "Demiurge" is the divine craftsman who shapes the material world.</note> is the principle of generation <note>The world of change, birth, and decay.</note>, the Good is the principle of Essence. The Creator God is analogous to the Good, being its imitator, while generation is analogous to Essence, being its image and imitation. For if the Creator of generation is good, then surely the Creator of Essence will be the **Good-in-itself**, innate to Essence.

> » ...in essence. For the second [god], being double, himself creates both his own idea and the world, being the **Demiurge** <term>Demiurge: A "craftsman" or creator god who shapes the material world based on spiritual patterns.</term>. Then, being entirely dedicated to contemplation, let these four points be established according to our reasoning on the names of the subjects before us. The first god is the **Good-in-itself** <note>original: "autoagathon" — The absolute essence of goodness.</note>. The one who imitates him is the **good Demiurge**. And as for essence, that of the first is one thing, while that of the second is another. The beautiful world is an imitation of this second essence, having been made beautiful by participation in the Beautiful.
> » And in that work <note>Likely referring to Plato's *Timaeus* or a lost work of Numenius.</note> he adds: "Those things that participate in it do so, and certainly not in any other way, but only by means of thinking." In this way, he might benefit from the union with the Good, even if he does not [always possess it]. Indeed, it happens that this "thinking" belongs properly to the first alone. By whom, then, are visible things manifested and made good? If this belongs only to the one [the first], it would be the mark of a truly searching soul to still dispute it. For if the second is good not from himself, but from the first, how is it possible that the one through whose participation he is good should not be good himself? It is clear that the second might happen to share in the Good. Thus, through reasoning, Plato has granted to the keen-sighted observer what the Good truly is. And again he says: 
> » These things being so, Plato still maintains a division. For specifically regarding the Creator, he appeared in the *Timaeus* saying, "He was good." But in the *Republic*, he called the Good the "Idea of the Good." Thus, the Good is the **Idea of the Creator**, who has appeared to us as good through participation in the first and only [Good]. For just as humans are said to be formed by the "Idea of Man," oxen by the "Idea of the Ox," and horses by the "Idea of the Horse," so it is reasonable that if the Creator is good by participation in the first Good, the **First Intellect** <term>Intellect: "Nous," the divine mind or seat of wisdom.</term> would be the Idea, being the Good-in-itself.

### Concerning the Ideas in Plato.

Clearly, the world having been brought into being in this way, it has been crafted according to what is grasped by reason and wisdom, and according to those same [eternal] principles. These things being so, it is an absolute necessity that this world is an image of something.
> » For that [intelligible realm] contains within itself all intelligible living beings, just as this world contains us. 
These are the words of Plato in the *Timaeus*. Furthermore, I will set forth the mentioned concept from the writings of those who follow Plato <note>Referring to the "Platonists" or "successors" who interpreted his work.</note>. He writes as follows: that the "Ideas" are defined as certain models of the sensible things <term>Sensible things: Objects that can be perceived by the five senses.</term> according to nature, of which knowledge is gained and which are seen [by the mind]. For all things pertaining to humans are conceived of as a certain "Man"; all things pertaining to horses as a "Horse." And generally, beyond all living creatures, there is a "Living Being," unbegotten and imperishable. 
> » As I have said, just as many impressions come from a single seal-ring, and many images from a single man, so from each single Idea of the physical bodies, countless natures arise. From the Idea of Man, all individual men come, and by the same logic, this applies to all other things in nature. If the Idea is an eternal essence, a cause and a principle for each thing being such as it is, then just as a specific archetype precedes the individual physical bodies, so the most beautiful and perfect essence—which contains all things within itself—exists as the **Model of the World**. For it was toward this [model] that the world was crafted by the one who created it, being made according to providence out of all essence. 
These things are also from the man mentioned above.

Indeed, even the all-wise **Moses** says these same things concerning the visible sun and stars, and concerning the visible heaven, which he calls the "firmament"...

### THE PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 11

<margin>38</margin>
38. ...teaching that the dry land we inhabit, our day and night, and a light distinct from that of the physical sun—day and night itself and all the rest—were created by the Great Ruler and Cause of all things, God. Moreover, the descendants of the Hebrews after Moses will show that there is a certain **incorporeal sun** <note>original: "hēlion asōmaton" — A sun without a physical body, existing only in the realm of thought or spirit.</note> that is not visible to everyone, nor subject to mortal eyes. As the prophet says, speaking in the person of God:
> "To those who fear me, the **sun of righteousness** shall rise." <note>A quotation from Malachi 4:2.</note>

And this "righteousness" itself is not merely the kind found among men; rather, another Hebrew prophet—who spoke concerning God—recognized its "Idea," saying:
> "How he brought forth righteousness from the east." <note>Likely referencing Isaiah 41:2 or 62:1.</note>

He also called it His "face" <note>original: "prosōpon" — also translated as "presence" or "person."</note> and says it shall journey before Him. Our shared tradition shows us that these Hebrews signify a **divine Word** <term>Logos: The "Word" or "Reason" of God, viewed here as a conscious, substantial being that exists before the material world.</term> that is incorporeal and essential, as presented in the earlier parts of their scripture. Is it not also said among them concerning this Word:
> "Who became for us **wisdom** from God, and **righteousness**, and **sanctification**, and **redemption**?" <note>A quotation from 1 Corinthians 1:30. Eusebius treats the Apostle Paul as a representative of the Hebrew philosophical tradition.</note>

The Hebrew scriptures further teach that He is called Life, and Wisdom, and Truth, and all things that truly exist in essence and substance. Indeed, the Hebrews and the apostles and disciples of our Savior, after being initiated into the mystery of this incorporeal power, looked beyond the heavens and all material and fleeting substance. They say the "images" <note>original: "eikonas" — symbols or reflections.</note> of these higher realities are imprinted upon the things we perceive with our senses, and from these, they have adopted the name of the "image." They explicitly state that the **first man** was an image of an **intelligible paradigm** <term>Intelligible Paradigm: A "blueprint" or "model" (paradigm) that exists in the mind (intelligible realm) rather than in physical space.</term>, and that the entire life of humanity passes by in an image. Thus Moses says:
> "And God made man; **according to the image of God** He made him." <note>Genesis 1:27.</note>

And again, another Hebrew philosopher <note>Referring to the author of the Psalms.</note> discussing his ancestral traditions says:
> "Truly, man walks about in an image." <note>Psalm 39:6 (Psalm 38 in the Septuagint).</note>

Now, listen to how the interpreters of the sacred laws clarify the meaning found in the writings of Moses. For Philo the Hebrew says, interpreting it in these very words:

-> **Philo on the "Ideas" in the writings of Moses.** <-

<margin>5.</margin>
"If anyone should wish to use words more plainly, he would say that the **Intelligible World** is nothing other than the **Word of God** <note>original: "theou logon" — the Logos.</note> already engaged in the act of world-making. For the "Intelligible City" is nothing else than the reasoning of the architect who is already planning to build the physical city. This doctrine belongs to Moses, not to me. At least, in his account of the creation of man, he explicitly confesses in the following passages that man was shaped 'according to the image of God.' But if the part [man] is an image of an image, it is clear that the whole form—this entire world perceived by the senses—since it is greater than the human form, is an imitation of the divine image. It is also clear that the **Archetypal Seal** <note>original: "archētypos sphragis" — The original "stamp" or "mold" used to make impressions in reality.</note>, which we say is the 'Intelligible World,' would itself be the paradigm, the **Archetypal Idea of Ideas**, the Word of God. 

Moses says that 'In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth,' taking 'the beginning' not as some people suppose in a sense of **time**. For time did not exist before the world; rather, it either began with the world or after it. Since time is the interval of the world’s motion, there could be no motion prior to the thing being moved. Instead, it is necessary that motion was established either later or simultaneously. It is therefore necessary that time also was created either of the same age as the world or younger than it. To declare it older than the world is unphilosophical. If, then, the 'beginning' is not taken here in a chronological sense, it is likely that a numerical order is being indicated, so that 'In the beginning He made' is equivalent to 'First He made the heaven.' Next he says, 'First, therefore, the Creator made...'"

<summary>Eusebius explains that the Hebrew scriptures and the philosopher Philo of Alexandria previously established the concept of an "Intelligible World" or divine "Word" (Logos) as the blueprint for creation, long before or in parallel with Greek philosophy. Philo argues that the "beginning" mentioned in Genesis refers to a logical order of creation rather than the start of time itself.</summary>

[...continuing the previous section] interpreting. For this reason, man was made "according to the image and likeness of God."
» For the "Image of God" is the Divine and Royal Word <term>Logos: In this context, the Word is the intermediary through which God creates and interacts with the world.</term>, while the "impassible man" <note>original: "anthrōpos apathēs" — a human state unaffected by earthly suffering or passions.</note> is the reflection of that Word. ->The Hebrews and Plato on Opposing Powers<-

In addition to these points, Plato—following the accounts of the Hebrews—says that there are not only certain good powers, but also opposing ones. He writes something to this effect in the tenth book of the *Laws*: 
» "Since a soul is that which governs and dwells in all things that move in any way, must we not also say it governs the heavens? Is it one soul, or more? More—I shall answer on your behalf. Let us assume at least two: the one that does good, and the one that is capable of working the opposite." 
» Then, going further down, he says: "For as we have agreed among ourselves, the heaven is full of many good things, but also of things that are not; indeed, it contains more of the latter. We say such a battle is immortal, and it requires a wonderful vigilance. Our allies are the gods and the spirits <note>original: "daimones" — in Greek thought, these are intermediary spirits, not necessarily 'demons' in the modern sense.</note>, and we, in turn, are the possessions of the gods and spirits." 

How Plato came by these ideas, I cannot say. But what I can say is that many thousands of years before Plato lived, this doctrine was established in the laws of the Hebrews. For the Holy Scripture says: 
» "And it happened on that day, the angels of God came to stand before God, and the devil came in the midst of them, having gone around the earth and walked through it." <note>This is a reference to the opening of the Book of Job.</note> 
» It calls the opposing power "the Devil," and the good powers "Angels of God." These good powers are also called "divine spirits" and "ministers of God" in the passage where it says: 
» "Who makes His angels spirits, and His ministers a flame of fire." 
» Moreover, the one who spoke of the struggle between these opposing forces described it this way: 
» "Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the **world-rulers of this darkness** <term>kosmokratoras: A Greek term for powerful spirits or planetary forces thought to govern the material world.</term>, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places." 

Plato seems to be directly paraphrasing the saying of Moses, which states: 
» "When the Most High divided the nations, as He dispersed the sons of Adam, He set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God." 
» It is through these "angels" that Plato defined our status as the "possessions of gods and spirits," as we read just a moment ago.

->On the Immortality of the Soul: The Hebrews and Plato<-

And regarding the immortality of the soul, Plato’s opinion does not differ at all from that of Moses. For Moses was the first to define the soul in man as an immortal essence, saying that it exists as an "image of God"—or rather, that it was made "according to the image of God." For he says: 
» "God said, 'Let us make man according to our image and likeness.' And God made man; according to the image of God He made him." 
» And following this, when he divides the composite human into the visible body and the soul perceived by the mind, he adds: 
» "And God took dust from the earth, and God formed man, and He breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a **living soul**." 
» Furthermore, he says that man was made to be the ruler and king over all things on the earth: 
» "And let them rule over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the sky, and the cattle of all the earth." 
» And so, "God made man; according to the image..."

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument that Plato’s philosophy—specifically his views on the soul—mirrors the teachings of Moses. Having established that man is made in the "image of God," Eusebius now provides specific passages from Plato’s dialogues (the *Alcibiades* and the *Phaedo*) to show how the Greek philosopher described the soul's divine nature and its relationship to the body.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

<page-num>324</page-num>

» ...[God] made him. For how else could the "image and likeness" of God be understood, if not according to the powers within God and the likeness achieved through virtue? For Moses is, in these matters, as if he were a witness for Plato <note>Eusebius frequently argues that Plato "borrowed" his best ideas from the Hebrew prophets.</note>. Plato says specifically in the *Alcibiades*: "Can we then say that there is anything in the soul more divine than that which is concerned with knowing and thinking?" "We cannot." "This part of the soul, then, resembles the divine; and a person looking at this and recognizing all that is divine—both God and wisdom <term>Wisdom: The Greek word is *phronēsis*, referring to practical wisdom or the intelligence of the soul.</term>—would thus also best know himself." We certainly say that just as mirrors are very clear, and the reflection in the eye is even clearer and brighter, so too the divine is found to be better and brighter in our own soul. It seems then, O Cebes <note>The text here mentions Cebes, though the dialogue quoted is the *Alcibiades*; Eusebius is likely moving toward his next citation from the *Phaedo*.</note>, that by looking toward God, we would be using the most beautiful mirror, and also by looking toward the soul’s virtue among human things; and in this way, we would most especially see and know ourselves. 

» These things are in the *Alcibiades*. But in the dialogue *On the Soul* <note>The *Phaedo*.</note> he explains this more broadly. For the man says the following: "Perhaps we should look at it this way. Do you wish," he said, "that we posit two kinds of beings: one visible, the other invisible?" "Let us posit them," he said. "And the invisible is always the same, while the visible is never the same?" "Let us posit these too," he said. "Come then," he said, "is there anything else to us than this: one part is the body, the other is the soul?" "Nothing else," he said. "To which kind, then, do we say the body is more similar and more closely related?" "It is clear to everyone," he said, "that it is to the visible." "And what about the soul? Is it visible or invisible?" "Not visible to humans, at least, Socrates," he said. "But we are speaking of things that are visible or not to the nature of humans, or do you think we mean some other nature?" "To the nature of humans." "What then do we say about the soul? Is it visible or invisible?" "Not visible." "Invisible then?" "Yes." "Therefore, the soul is more similar to the invisible than the body is; and the body is more similar to the visible." "It must be so, Socrates."

» "Did we not also say this: that when the soul uses the body to examine something—either through sight or hearing or some other sense (for to examine something through the senses is to do it through the body)—it is then dragged by the body toward things that are never the same? And the soul itself wanders and is troubled and becomes dizzy, as if it were drunk, because it is touching such things?" "Certainly." "But whenever the soul examines things by itself, it departs to that which is pure, always existing, immortal, and unchanging. And because the soul is kindred to it, it stays with it whenever it is alone and has the power. It ceases from its wandering, and in relation to those things, it is always the same and unchanging, because it is touching such things. And this state of the soul is called wisdom <term>Wisdom: *Phronēsis*. Plato defines it here as the soul's steady state when contemplating eternal truths.</term>." "You speak entirely well and truly, Socrates," he said. 

» "To which kind, then, does the soul seem to you to be more similar and more closely related, based on what was said before and what is being said now?" "I think," he said, "that anyone, even the slowest learner, would agree from this method of inquiry that the soul is in every way more similar to that which is always unchanging than to that which is not." "And the body?" "To the other." "Look at it also in this way: that when soul and body are together, nature commands the one to serve and be ruled, and the other to rule and be master. According to these things, which one seems to you to be like the divine, and which like the mortal? Or does it not seem to you that the divine is naturally suited to rule and lead, while the mortal is suited to be ruled and to serve?" "It seems so to me." "To which one, then, does the soul resemble?" "It is clear, Socrates, that the soul resembles the divine, and the body the mortal." "Consider then, O Cebes," he said, "if from all that has been said, these are our [conclusions]..."

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL BOOK 11
### THE DIVINE NATURE OF THE SOUL

,, ...it follows that: to the divine, immortal, intelligible <term>intelligible: *noēton*, referring to things that can only be understood by the mind, not seen by the eyes</term>, uniform, indissoluble, and always the same and consistent with itself, the soul is most similar; while to the human, mortal, unintelligent, multiform, dissoluble, and never consistent with itself, the body is most similar. Can we say anything else, dear Cebes, to show that this is not the case? We cannot. What then? If these things are so, does it not belong to the body to be quickly dissolved, but to the soul to be altogether indissoluble, or something very close to it? How could it be otherwise?

,, Consider then, he said, that when a person dies, the visible part of him—the body—which exists in the visible world and which we call a corpse, and which is naturally suited to be dissolved, to fall apart, and to be dispersed by the wind, does not immediately suffer any of these things. Instead, it remains for a considerable time; and if someone dies with their body in a graceful state and in the prime of life, it remains very much so. For if the body is collapsed and mummified <note>original: *taricheuthentes* — a reference to the Egyptian practice of embalming</note>, like those who are mummified in Egypt, it remains almost entirely whole for an incredible amount of time. And even if some parts of the body decay—the bones, the sinews, and all such things—they are still, so to speak, immortal. Is that not so? Yes.

,, But the soul—the "unseen" <note>Plato makes a pun here: the word for "invisible" or "unseen" is *aidēs*, which sounds like *Haidēs* (the Underworld)</note>, which goes away to another place that is noble, pure, and invisible—to the "unseen" world in truth, to the presence of the good and wise God, where, if God wills, my own soul must soon go—shall this soul of ours, being of such a nature and so constituted, be blown away and perish as soon as it is released from the body, as many people say? Far from it, dear Cebes and Simmias!

,, Rather, the truth is much more like this: if it is released in a pure state, dragging nothing of the body with it—since it had no voluntary communion with the body during life, but rather fled from it and gathered itself into itself, having made this its constant practice—this is nothing other than practicing philosophy correctly and truly practicing how to die easily. Or would this not be a "meditation on death"? <note>Socrates famously defines philosophy as the practice of dying, meaning the separation of the soul's interests from the body's needs.</note> Certainly. 

,, Being in such a state, then, it departs to that which is like itself—the invisible, the divine, the immortal, and the wise. Arriving there, it attains happiness, having been set free from error, ignorance, fears, wild passions, and all other human evils. As is said of those initiated into the mysteries, it truly spends the rest of time with the gods. Shall we say it is so, Cebes, or otherwise? It is so, by Zeus! said Cebes.

,, But I think if it departs from the body polluted and impure, because it was always with the body, serving it, loving it, and being bewitched by it—by its desires and pleasures—so that nothing seemed true except the "corporeal" <note>body-like or physical</note> which one can touch, see, drink, eat, or use for sexual pleasure; and if it was accustomed to hate, tremble at, and flee from that which is shadowy and invisible to the eyes, but intelligible and graspable by philosophy—do you think a soul in such a state will depart pure and by itself? Not in the least, he said.

These are the words of Plato. But Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who, though often an opponent of Christianity, is used here by Eusebius to support the logic of the soul's immortality.</note> unfolds the meaning in the work he addressed to Boethus concerning the soul, writing in this manner:

->**Porphyry On the Soul.**<-

Immediately, it seems to Plato that there is a powerful argument for establishing the immortality of the soul: that it comes from "likeness." For if the soul is like the divine, the immortal, the invisible, the unscattered, the indissoluble, the holy, and that which consists in incorruption, how could it not by its very nature be a part of that pattern? For when there are two extremes clearly opposite to one another, such as...

# EUSEBIUS
### THE DIVINE NATURE OF THE SOUL

<page-num>326</page-num>

» ...of the rational and the irrational, which is why it is even disputed to which part [the human race] belongs. In this proof, however, it is shown by its likeness to the subjects at hand. For even though the human race was brought down into a lowly state during its first age, and many have grown old while abounding in the sins of irrationality, nevertheless, because it bears many similarities to the purely rational, this race was believed from the beginning to be rational. Since, then, there is a divine form—pure and undefiled—before it appeared, but then falling again into a state of weakness and lying in corruption, the actions of the soul are disputed: to which of the aforementioned parts has it joined itself? Plato thought that one should determine the truth based on likeness. 

» And since the mortal, the dissoluble, the flowing, and that which has no share in life is in no way like that which is impassive <note>original: *apathes* — meaning unaffected by external suffering or change</note>, uniform, and never-perishing, while [the soul] is like the divine, immortal, eternal, and intellectual <term>intellectual: *noerō*, relating to the higher mind or 'nous'</term> living being, a fellow-worker of memory, and all the other things he gathers in his anthology about it, it seemed wrong to concede other similarities to God while taking away and rejecting the likeness of its essence <term>essence: *ousia*, the fundamental nature or 'being' of a thing</term>. It is for this reason that it has been granted these qualities. For just as things that are similar in their main activities are immediately different in the composition of their essence, so it follows that those things which share in the same activities must also share in the likeness of their essence. For by a certain kind of essence, the activities are of a certain kind, as if flowing from it and being the sprouts of the essence itself. To understand the power of this argument, listen to the very beginning of the discourse he made, writing as follows:

> If the soul is immortal, being by nature superior to all destruction, it must be shown through many and primary arguments. However, regarding the idea that nothing is more like God than the soul, one would not need much elaborate effort to believe it, if only because of the continuity and ceaselessness of its movement, which provides life within us. The things pertaining to the mind itself are clear. Looking at this, the physicist of Croton <note>original: *ho Krotōniatēs physikos* — likely referring to Alcmaeon of Croton, a pre-Socratic philosopher who taught that the soul is immortal because it is in constant motion like the sun and moon</note> said that it is immortal and naturally flees from all rest, just like the divine bodies <note>The heavenly bodies, such as stars and planets, which ancient Greeks believed moved eternally</note>. But if one considers the entire form of the soul, and especially the mind that comes to be in us—whenever it is moved by its own wills and impulses—a great likeness to God would appear to the one who succeeds [in understanding it]. And he adds next: "For if the soul is shown to be the most like the divine of all things, then it serves as a preface to the proof of its immortality, needing no further clear arguments..."

» ...counting this as one among many arguments, it is sufficient to show to well-disposed people that it would not share in activities similar to the divine if it did not also possess a divine life in itself. For if, while buried in the mortal, dissoluble, and flowing—which is dead in itself and always perishing and drifting toward the change of destruction—it produces this continuity and reveals its own divine essence (even though it is darkened and hindered by the more sluggish shell <note>original: *plasmata* — literally 'formation' or 'mold', here referring to the physical body</note> placed around it), how much more, if it were separated by reason like gold from the clay molded around it <note>A classic philosophical metaphor: the soul is like pure gold, and the body is the 'mud' or 'clay' that obscures its shine</note>, would it shine forth through its own form? For it is similar not only to God but also through its participation in Him, preserving the likenesses in its activities even in its mortal state. For when it is purified in the mortal, it is no longer hidden that its nature is beyond uninitiated destruction... and descending he says, "Reasonably then, the divine..."

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION BOOK 11

<page-num>327</page-num>

» It is evident from its likeness to higher things; yet it is also mortal in those aspects where it approaches the mortal nature, descends into decline, and exists among mortals, while still being similar to the immortals. For the man who gluttonizes and is eager only to be sated like the beasts is of a doubtful nature. But the man who, through science <term>science: *epistēmē*, certain and systematic knowledge</term>, is able to save a ship in the midst of the sea’s dangers is a different sort of being. So too is the one who brings life in the midst of diseases, finding remedies where none seemed possible, and who has applied himself to the grasp of knowledge, observing through experience, discovery, and foresight, and who, by mimicking the works of the Creator, has himself become a maker. 

» For man has devised ways to save the movements of the seven <note>original: *tōn hepta* — likely referring to the seven "wandering stars" or planets of the ancient geocentric model</note> on the earth, creating a mechanism that mimics the things in heaven. And what has he not devised, proving the divinity within himself by the things he conceives? From these achievements, the offshoots of a heavenly, divine, and in no way mortal nature shine through. Yet, because many people incline toward self-love and the things below, and are unable to see the soul itself apart from outward appearances, they have been persuaded to believe that the soul is mortal just like their bodies. Because of their own wickedness, they seek the comfort of believing that their inner selves are just like their outer appearance—as the outside is, so are all men within. 

» Moses was born to be the teacher who speaks against these views. In recounting the first generation of man according to the words previously set forth, he confirmed the soul’s likeness to the Divine through his teachings on the immortality of the soul. But since the views concerning the incorporeal and invisible essence <term>essence: *ousia*, the fundamental "being" of a thing</term> have been shown to be in harmony and agreement between Moses and Plato, it is time to examine the remaining parts of Plato’s philosophy. We shall show that the man is a friend to the Hebrews in all respects—unless, perhaps, having been led astray, he was moved to speak in a manner more human than according to the true Word. Immediately, whatever has been spoken successfully by the man will be found to run alongside the decrees of Moses; but whatever he supposed that does not please Moses and the Prophets, his argument would not hold together. This we shall demonstrate at the proper time. For now, since a harmony has been detected in the contemplation <term>contemplation: *epopteia*, a term used for the highest level of philosophical vision or initiation</term> of the intelligible world, it is time to return to the natural study of the physical world, and briefly run through the man’s agreement with the Hebrew scriptures.

### Concerning the World Having Been Brought Into Being.

<margin>Evangelical Preparation</margin>

When Moses speaks forth his divine oracle regarding that which was first created by God, he begins his own writing in this way: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." And again, after recounting the details, he adds: "This is the book of the generation of heaven and earth, when the day came that God created the heaven and the earth." Hear now Plato, how he does not fall away from this thought, writing in this manner: "Everything that comes to be must of necessity be brought into being by some cause. For it is impossible for anything to have a beginning without a cause." And he adds: "The whole heaven and cosmos—or whatever other name it might best accept, let it be called that by us—we must first consider regarding it that which is laid down at the beginning to be considered about the whole: whether it always was, having no beginning of its creation, or whether it has been brought into being, starting from some beginning. For it is visible and tangible and possesses a body. All such things are perceptible by the senses; and things perceptible by the senses, being grasped by opinion, appear to be brought into being. And for that which has been brought into being, we say it is a necessity that it was brought into being by some cause."

» ...[guided] and revolved. At one time, God himself guides its motion and helps it roll along, 
» whenever the periods of its appointed measure have reached their full time. But at 
» another time, it is released and revolves in the opposite direction of its own accord—for 
» it is a living creature, having received intelligence from the one who fitted it together 
» in the beginning. This backward motion has become inherent to it by necessity for this 
» reason: to always remain in the same state and in the same way, being identical to 
» oneself, belongs only to the most divine of all things. However, the nature of what we 
» call the body, the heaven, and the **cosmos** <term>cosmos: the universe seen as a well-ordered system</term>, is not of this 
» divine order. Although it has received many blessed gifts from its Father, it has also 
» partaken in a material body. Therefore, it is impossible for it to remain entirely free 
» from change. Yet, as much as possible, it moves with a single motion in the same 
» place and in the same way; for this reason, it has received a reversal—a "back-rolling"—
» which is the smallest possible variation of its own motion. But to turn oneself 
» forever is possible for almost no one except the leader of all things that are moved. 
» And for this leader to move things now in one way and then in the opposite way 
» would be a violation of divine law. From all this, we must say that the world 
» neither turns itself forever, nor is it always turned as a whole by God in two 
» opposite revolutions; nor again is it turned by two certain deities who have 
» opposing purposes. But, as was just said—and this is the only remaining 
» possibility—at one time it is guided by a divine cause, gaining life again and 
» receiving a restored immortality from the **Demiurge** <term>Demiurge: a Platonic term for the "Craftsman" or Creator of the world</term>; but at 
» another time, when it is released, it moves by itself. It is released at such a 
» time that it travels backward for many tens of thousands of periods, because it 
» is of vast size and perfectly balanced, turning upon the smallest possible pivot. 
» It seems, then, that all we have described has been said with the greatest 
» likelihood. Let us reflect on the phenomenon resulting from what has been said, 
» which we called the cause of all those wonders. For it is this very phenomenon: 
» that the motion of the universe is sometimes carried in the direction it now 
» revolves, and sometimes in the opposite direction. One must believe that this 
» change is the greatest and most complete of all the turnings that occur in the 
» heavens. It is likely, then, that the greatest changes happen to us who live 
» within it. And at that time, it is natural for many great and diverse changes 
» to fall upon us. But what we do not realize is how difficult it is for the nature 
» of living beings to endure this; for how could it not be? Therefore, the 
» greatest destructions necessarily happen to the other animals, and only a 
» small part of the human race remains. In addition to these, many other 
» wondrous and strange experiences occur, but the greatest is this one, 
» following the cosmic reversal, when the rotation opposite to the current 
» one begins to take place.

### On the consummation of the world.

» For when the time of all these things was completed, and a change was necessary, and 
» indeed the entire earth-born race had now been exhausted—each soul having given 
» back all its births, as many as were appointed for each, falling as seeds into the 
» earth—then indeed the Helmsman of the universe, letting go of the handle of the 
» rudder, withdrew to his own lookout point. And the world was turned back by 
» destiny and innate desire. All the gods who rule the various places alongside the 
» greatest Spirit <note>original: "daimon," here referring to the supreme guiding divinity</note>, 
» knowing now what was happening, in turn abandoned the parts of the world they 
» cared for. And the world, turning back and clashing together, having been started on 
» a momentum contrary to its beginning and its end, produced a great earthquake 
» within itself, and again brought about another destruction of all kinds of living 
» creatures. But after this, when sufficient time had passed, the world ceased its 
» noise and confusion, and catching hold of a calm following the earthquakes, it was 
» set in order into its accustomed course. It now takes care of and rules itself, 
» possessing the things within it and of itself. 
And after a few short words he says:
» Wherefore, at that very moment, the God who ordered the world, seeing it in 
» distress, and being concerned lest it be shattered by the storm of confusion and 
» sink into the infinite region of unlikeness <note>This is a famous Platonic metaphor for a state of total chaos and lack of divine form</note>, 
» again took his seat at the rudders. Turning the parts that had become diseased 
» and dissolved during the previous period of revolution, he set it in order and, by 
» correcting it, rendered it immortal and ageless. 
This is spoken as the end of all things.

Let us also give credit to this Antyllus. But let us relate the story of Aristella, the daughter of Heracleon.
» For while she was recently ill, she seemed to the doctors to have no life left in her. But having 
» recovered a little from a state of sleep—not a steady unconsciousness—she neither did nor said 
» anything deranged, but she said that she had died and been released again, and that she would

It is for these reasons that the resurrections of the dead are recorded in the Hebrew scriptures. And since they also contain promises that a certain land will be given only to those who are beloved of God, they indeed say: *The meek shall inherit the earth.* <note>Psalm 37:11</note> And the following word clearly explains that this earth is heavenly: *But the Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother.* <note>Galatians 4:26</note> And the prophet also hints at this very land, saying it is composed of precious and costly stones, speaking in the form of an allegory:
» Behold, I prepare for you the carbuncle <note>original: "anthraka," literally 'coal' or 'burning coal', but used for a red gemstone</note> as your stone, 
» and I will make your battlements of jasper, and your foundations of sapphire, and your 
» precinct of choice stones. <note>Isaiah 54:11-12</note>
Observe how Plato also says he was convinced of these very things, or things very similar; for in the dialogue *On the Soul* <note>The *Phaedo*</note> he confesses this, seeking to align the argument in this manner:

->How Plato likewise discusses the things concerning the so-called heavenly earth just as the Hebrews do.<-

» But truly, O Simmias, it does not seem to me to be the "Art of Glaucus" <note>original: "glaukou technē," a proverb for a difficult or elaborate skill</note> 
» to describe what kind of thing it is. However, to prove that it is true seems more difficult 
» to me than even the Art of Glaucus. And at the same time, I might not even be able to 
» learn it. Furthermore, even if I did understand it, my life, Simmias, seems to me 
» insufficient for the length of the argument. Yet nothing prevents me from telling of the 
» appearance of the earth as I am convinced it is, and its regions. And Simmias said, 
» "Even this is enough." "I am convinced then," said he, "firstly that if the earth is in 
» the middle of the heaven and is spherical, it has no need of air to keep it from falling, 
» nor any other such necessity. But the uniformity of the heaven with itself in every 
» direction and the equilibrium of the earth is sufficient to hold it. For a thing in 
» equilibrium, placed in the middle of something uniform, will not be able to incline more

» [they are] pure and are not eaten away or corrupted, as are the things here by rot and brine, which result from the waters flowing together. These things bring ugliness and diseases to stones, the earth, and to other animals and plants. But the "True Earth" itself is adorned with all these things, and even with gold and silver, and other such materials. For these things are naturally manifest, being many and great in number, and found in many places of that earth, so that to look upon it is a sight for happy spectators.

-> That Plato also believes, similarly to the Hebrews, that there will be a judgment after death. <-

The Hebrew Scripture proclaims that there will be a divine tribunal and a judgment of souls after their departure from this life. This is shown through ten thousand other passages, and specifically through the words: "A court sat, and books were opened, and a river of fire was drawn." "A river of fire flowed before him. Ten thousand myriads served him, and a thousand thousands stood before him." <note>original: "κριτήριον ἐκάθισε... ποταμὸς τοῦ πυρὸς εἵλκετο"—this is a quotation from the Book of Daniel 7:10, describing a celestial courtroom.</note> Listen now to what Plato says concerning the divine judgment, and indeed even mentioning a river by name, and describing the many dwellings of the pious and the various punishments of the impious, in agreement with the Hebrew oracles. He says the following in his work *On the Soul* <note>original: "περὶ ψυχῆς"—this refers to the *Phaedo*.</note>:

» This river flows out in the middle of these regions, and near its mouth it falls into a vast place burning with much fire, where it creates a lake larger than our sea, boiling with water and mud. From there it moves in a circle, turbid and muddy, and winding around the earth, it arrives at other places and specifically at the edges of the Acherusian lake, though it does not mix with that water. After winding many times under the earth, it empties into a lower depth of Tartarus <note>The deepest abyss of the underworld.</note>. This is the river they call Pyriphlegethon <note>original: "πυριφλεγέθοντα"—literally "Fire-blazing."</note>. From this river, streams of lava blow up fragments of earth wherever they happen to reach. 

» Opposite this, a fourth river falls first into a place that is terrible and wild, so it is said; its color is entirely like cyanus <note>original: "κυανός"—a dark blue substance, perhaps lapis lazuli or dark metal.</note>, and this they call the Stygian river. The river creates a lake by falling into the Styx. Having fallen there and acquired terrible powers in the water, it sinks under the earth and, winding around, moves opposite to the Pyriphlegethon, meeting it at the Acherusian lake from the opposite side. The water of this river also mixes with no other, but having gone in a circle, it empties into Tartarus opposite the Pyriphlegethon. The name of this river, as the poets say, is Cocytus <note>original: "κωκυτός"—literally "Lamentation."</note>. 

» Since these things are so by nature, whenever the deceased arrive at the place where their guiding spirit <note>original: "δαίμων" (daimon)—a personal protective spirit or fate that leads the soul to judgment.</note> brings each one, they are first judged—both those who lived noble, holy, and just lives, and those who did not. Those who are judged to have lived a middle-of-the-road life journey to the Acheron; they mount the carriages provided for them and arrive at the lake. There they dwell and are purified; by paying the penalty for their wrongdoings, they are released from any injustice they committed, and they receive honors for their good deeds according to each person's merit. 

» But those who are judged to be incurable because of the greatness of their sins—either because they committed many great acts of sacrilege, or many unjust and lawless murders, or other such crimes—these are cast by their fitting fate into Tartarus, from which they never emerge. However, those who are judged to have committed sins that are great but curable—such as those who acted with violence against a father or mother in a fit of anger, but lived the rest of their lives in repentance...

The text describes the geography of the afterlife, including the rivers of fire and lamentation, and the different fates awaiting the holy, the average, and the wicked.</summary>

# The following comprises the twelfth book of the Preparation for the Gospel.

That it was not according to Plato, but correctly, that the children of the Hebrews referred the foundation of belief <note>original: "pistin"—often translated as "faith," but here referring to the initial acceptance of teachings.</note> in their studies to those being introduced to them, for which reason they provided an incomplete version of them.
That even according to Plato, faith happens to be the greatest of virtues.
That one must believe the things said concerning the soul, and the other accounts concerning such matters. From the eleventh book of the *Laws* <note>One of Plato’s last and longest dialogues, focusing on ethics and legislation.</note>.
That it will be necessary to hand down the first introductions to children through the medium of myths.
That one must not enchant children with harmful myths, but only with beneficial ones.
That Plato did not accept faith in word only, but also through that by which he confessed to believe and be persuaded of these things, in which we also believe.
That the sacred doctrines of truth should not be disclosed to everyone.
That Plato says what kind of leaders should be appointed: that they be private citizens and unlettered, provided only that their character is well-ordered.

Concerning the Paradise according to Moses.
How they say that the woman was taken from the man.
Concerning the earlier life of men.
That they also conversed with irrational animals.
How he mentions the flood.
That the matters of teaching, starting correctly for us from divine things, conclude with human things.
That it is good to train children from a very young age in the customs of godliness <term>theosebeia: a specific type of piety or "god-fearing" worship</term>.
That one must consider as education only that which promotes virtue, and not the practice of some livelihood for the purpose of making money.
That similarly to the Hebrews, Plato also held the opinion that the things here are images of other [higher] things.
That young people should be prepared for the attainment of virtue through the learning of correct hymns and songs.
What kind of thoughts these songs ought to contain.
That it is not within the power of everyone to compose correct songs and melodies, but only of God or some divine man.
Concerning those who are able to judge songs composed according to God's will.
That songs should be adopted even in banquets, like certain "banquet laws." — That the drinking of wine should not be permitted to everyone.
That Plato was not unaware that the things he legislated were also practiced among the barbarians <note>In this context, Eusebius uses "barbarians" to refer to non-Greeks, specifically the Hebrews/Jews, whom he argues are the source of Plato's wisdom.</note>.
That our war is against ourselves and the passions within us.
That not the body, but the soul is the cause of the evil things we do.
Concerning the one who philosophizes purely.
Concerning all the wisdom found among men.

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 12

> » ...of our laws, it would be one of the most beautiful regulations: to not allow any of the young people to inquire which of the laws are well-established or not. Instead, with one voice and from one mouth, everyone should agree that all is well-placed, since the gods established them. And if anyone should speak otherwise, they should not be tolerated. But if an old man should perceive something regarding your laws <note>The laws of the community being discussed</note> that he wishes to discuss with an official or a peer of his own age, let him not make such speeches in front of any young person. — You command most correctly, O stranger.</p>

Reasonably then, the Hebrew parabolic scripture <note>referring to the figurative or symbolic nature of the Bible</note> also puts faith before the understanding and contemplation of the divine scriptures, through which it says: "If you do not believe, you shall not understand" <note>original: "ean de me pisteusete, ou me sunete" — a common Septuagint reading of Isaiah 7:9</note>. And again: "I believed, therefore I spoke" <note>Psalm 116:10</note>. 

Hence also among us, to those who are recently introduced and are still imperfect in their spiritual habit—being like infants in their souls—the reading of the divine scriptures is handed down in a simpler fashion, with the instruction that they must believe the contents are the words of God. But to those who have progressed in their habit and are "gray-haired" in their wisdom, it is permitted to delve deep and test the inner meaning of what is said. 

It was the custom of the Hebrews to call such people *deuterotai* <term>deuterotai: literally "repeaters," referring to scholars or teachers of the Jewish oral tradition and deeper scriptural interpretation</term>, as they were the interpreters and explainers of the deeper meaning of the scriptures.

-> That faith happens to be the greatest of virtues according to Plato. <-

Therefore, following these points, we might say: "It seems, O Tyrtaeus <note>A Spartan poet known for his war songs</note>, that you especially praise those who have become famous in regard to external war." Would he not say these things and agree? 

We, on the other hand, say that while these soldiers are indeed good, we say those who become clearly the best in the "greatest war" <note>likely referring to internal/spiritual struggle or civil conflict</note> are far better. And we have as a witness the poet Theognis, a citizen of the Megarians in Sicily, who says:

» A faithful man, worth his weight in gold and silver,
» Is a worthy prize, O Cyrnus, in the midst of harsh civil strife.

We say that such a man in the more difficult war becomes far better than the former, almost as much as justice, temperance, and wisdom—when joined with courage itself—are better than courage alone. For a man who is "faithful" and sound in times of civil strife could never exist without possessing every virtue. But those who are merely aggressive and willing to die fighting in the war of which Tyrtaeus speaks—the mercenaries—are many; most of these become bold, unjust, insolent, and the most foolish of almost everyone, except for some very few. 

Where does this argument of ours lead? And what does it wish to make clear? Clearly this: that more than anyone else, the Lawgiver who comes from God—and indeed anyone of even small benefit—will always establish laws while looking primarily toward the greatest virtue. And this virtue, as Theognis says, is "faithfulness" in the midst of dangers, which one might call "perfect justice." 

And among us, the Saving Word <note>referring to Christ or the Gospel</note>, having joined wisdom together with faith, approves the one who is adorned in both respects by His words, saying: "Who then is the faithful and wise steward?" <note>Luke 12:42</note> and again: "Well done, good and faithful servant; you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many" <note>Matthew 25:21</note>. Clearly, in these instances, it is not fitting to accept an irrational faith, but rather the faith that is yoked with the greatest virtues, such as wisdom and goodness.

-> That one must believe the things said to souls, and the other accounts concerning such matters. From the eleventh book of the Laws. <-

For it seems to me we have not yet had the opportunity in the preceding arguments to explain how...

...the souls of the deceased possess a certain power after death, and they look after human affairs. To mortals, these are long arguments that are difficult to refute. One must believe the various traditions regarding such matters, which are so numerous and very ancient. One should also believe the lawgivers that these things are so, unless they appear to be utterly foolish. And in the Book of Maccabees, it is said that Jeremiah the prophet was seen praying for the people after his departure from life <note>original: "met' allagen tou biou" — literally "change of life" or death. See 2 Maccabees 15:14.</note>, showing that he still cares for the people on earth. Plato also says that one must believe these things.

### That it is necessary to hand down the first introductions to children in the form of myths. From the second book of the *Republic*.

» There are two types of discourse: one true, and the other false. Yes. And children must be educated in both, but first in the false ones <note>original: "pseudesin" — here Plato refers to fictional stories or fables rather than malicious lies</note>. I do not understand, he said, what you mean. Do you not understand, I said, that first we tell myths to little children? This is, generally speaking, a fiction, though there is some truth in it. Do we use myths with children before physical exercises? This is so. — These are the words of Plato. And among the Hebrews, it is the custom to hand down the histories of the Divine Scripture to the souls of infants more simply, like certain myths. But to those whose character is practiced, they provide deeper and more doctrinal contemplations through discourse, using what is called *deuterosis* <term>deuterosis: a term used for the oral tradition or the deeper, secondary interpretation of Jewish Law</term> and the clarification of meanings that remain hidden from the many.

### That one must not use harmful myths for children, but only beneficial ones.

» Do you not know, then, that the beginning of every work is the most important part? Especially for the young and tender. For that is when the character is most easily molded and the impression is taken, which one wishes to stamp upon each person. Precisely so. Shall we then so easily allow children to hear any chance myths composed by anyone, and to receive into their souls opinions that are for the most part contrary to those we think they should have when they are grown? We shall not allow it at all. First then, it seems, we must oversee the myth-makers. If they compose a good myth, it should be accepted. If not, it should be rejected. We shall persuade nurses and mothers to tell the accepted ones to the children, and to mold their souls with myths much more than they mold their bodies with their hands. But most of those they tell now must be thrown out. — This principle of Plato is also observed among the Hebrews. For those possessing a divine spirit, which can distinguish between spirits, tested those things that were spoken and written rightly and by the Holy Spirit. But they rejected those things that were not so, just as they rejected the words of the false prophets. They also used the most beneficial narratives from the Divine Scriptures, like certain mythologies, to enchant <note>original: "katepadein" — to soothe or charm as if by a song</note> infants and children, providing them with understanding and wise habits as a preparation for the godliness they would practice as men.

### That Plato did not accept faith by word alone, but acknowledged that one should believe and be convinced of these things—the same things we believe—by a very inner disposition. From the *Gorgias*.

» Listen then, as they say, to a very beautiful account, which you will think is a myth, as I suppose, but I think is an account...

He also cites the Book of Maccabees to support the idea that the souls of the dead, like the prophet Jeremiah, continue to care for the living.</summary>

» ...[Gorgias] <note>The catchword "gon." from the previous page begins the word "Gorgiou," referencing Plato's dialogue, the *Gorgias*.</note> I will tell you what I am about to say as being true. And a little later: That he who has lived his life justly and piously, when he dies, departs to the **Isles of the Blessed** <note>In Greek mythology, the final resting place for the souls of heroes and the virtuous.</note>, to dwell in all happiness, free from evils. But he who has lived unjustly and godlessly goes to the prison of retribution and justice, which they call **Tartarus** <note>The deep abyss used as a dungeon of torment and suffering for the wicked.</note>. 

» And again, a little later: Then they must be judged naked of all these things. For they must be judged after they have died. And the judge must be naked, deceased, viewing with his soul the soul itself immediately upon the death of each person, stripped of all kin, and leaving behind all that worldly ornament on earth, so that the judgment may be just. 

» And next he adds: These are the things, O Callicles, which I have heard and believe to be true, and from these accounts, I reason that the following occurs. Death, as it seems to me, is nothing else than the separation of two things, the soul and the body, from one another. But when they are separated, each of them retains its own condition, much as when the man was alive; the body retains its nature, and the marks of its treatments and experiences are all visible. 

» For instance, if someone’s body was large by nature or by nourishment, or both, while he lived, his corpse is also large after he dies. And if he was fat, he is fat even when dead. And so it is with other things. Again, if he practiced wearing his hair long, his corpse also has long hair. Or if he was a <term>mastigias</term> <note>original: "mastigias" — a term for a slave or criminal who has been frequently whipped.</note> and had traces of stripes—scars on his body from whips or other wounds while living—the body of the deceased can be seen to have these marks. Or if someone had broken or distorted limbs while living, these remain so when he is dead. In a single word, whatever preparation the body had in life, all these things, or most of them, remain visible for a certain time after death. 

» It seems to me, then, O Callicles, that this is exactly the same regarding the soul. All things are visible in the soul after it is stripped of the body: its natural qualities and the <term>pathemata</term> <note>affections, sufferings, or impressions left upon the soul.</note> which the person's soul acquired through the practice of each deed. 

» Therefore, when they arrive before the judge—those from Asia before **Rhadamanthus** <note>A legendary wise king, son of Zeus, who became a judge of the dead.</note>—Rhadamanthus stands them before him and examines each soul, not knowing whose it is. But often, having laid hold of the **Great King** <note>The King of Persia, considered the most powerful and wealthy man in the Greek world.</note> or some other king or potentate, he perceives that there is nothing healthy in the soul, but that it is thoroughly striped and full of scars from perjuries and injustice, which each man’s own actions have stamped into his soul; and he sees that everything is crooked because of falsehood and arrogance, and nothing is straight because it was nurtured without truth. He sees the soul full of disorder and ugliness due to power, luxury, insolence, and incontinence in actions. 

» And having seen it, he sends it away in disgrace straight to the guardhouse, where it must go to undergo the appropriate sufferings. It is appropriate for everyone who is undergoing punishment, if they are being punished rightly by another, either to become better and be benefited, or to become an example to others, so that others, seeing the things they suffer, may become better through fear. 

» Now, those who are benefited and pay the penalty to gods and men are those who have committed curable sins; nevertheless, the benefit comes to them through pains and sufferings both here and in **Hades** <note>The Greek underworld or the state of the dead.</note>. For it is not possible to be rid of injustice in any other way. But those who have committed the most extreme injustices, and because of such crimes have become incurable, these are the ones from whom the examples are made. And these people themselves are no longer benefited at all, being incurable; but others are benefited who see them suffering for their greatest sins...

<summary>Eusebius quotes Plato's *Gorgias* to describe the "naked" judgment of the soul, where the spiritual "scars" of a person's life—their lies, injustices, and arrogance—are visible to the judges of the afterlife, regardless of their earthly status.</summary>

» ...account <note>Original Greek: "λόγον" (logon). The word began on the previous page.</note>, for I shall tell you what I am about to tell you as being true. And a little later: "He who has lived his life justly and holily, when he dies, departs to the Isles of the Blessed <note>In Greek mythology, the *Makaron Nesoi* were a paradise reserved for those favored by the gods or the exceptionally virtuous.</note> to dwell in all happiness, free from evils. But he who has lived unjustly and godlessly goes to the prison-house of vengeance and justice, which they call Tartarus." And again after a little: "Then they must be judged stripped of all these things; for they must be judged after they have died. And the judge must be naked, and dead, viewing with his soul the soul of each person immediately after they have died, deserted by all their kindred, and leaving behind all that worldly finery on earth, so that the judgment may be just." And following this he adds: "These are the things, O Callicles, which I have heard and believe to be true; and from these accounts I reason that something of this sort happens: death, as it seems to me, is nothing else than the separation of two things, the soul and the body, from one another. But when they are separated, each of them retains its own condition, just as when the man was alive; the body retains its own nature, and the marks of its care and its sufferings are all visible. For instance, if anyone's body was large by nature or by diet, or both, while he was alive, his corpse is also large after he has died. And if he was fat, he is fat when dead. And so with the rest. And if again he made a practice of wearing his hair long, his corpse also has long hair. Or if he was a 'scourge-bearer' <note>Original: *mastigias*—a slave or criminal who has been frequently whipped.</note> and had traces of stripes—scars on his body from whips or other wounds while living—one can see his body having these even when he is dead. Or if any limbs were broken or distorted while he lived, these are also visible when he is dead. In a word, whatever the body was prepared to be while living, all these things, or most of them, are visible for some time after death. The very same thing, Callicles, seems to me to hold true concerning the soul. All things are visible in the soul after it is stripped of the body—both its natural qualities and the experiences which the man’s soul acquired through his pursuit of each particular matter. When, therefore, they arrive before the judge—those from Asia before Rhadamanthus <note>One of the three judges of the dead; in this myth, he judges those coming from the East (Asia).</note>—Rhadamanthus stands them before him and views the soul of each, not knowing whose it is. But often, having laid hold of the Great King <note>A common Greek term for the King of Persia, the pinnacle of earthly power and potential corruption.</note> or some other king or potentate, he perceives nothing healthy in the soul, but finds it thoroughly scourged and full of scars from perjuries and injustice, which each man’s own actions have stamped upon his soul; and he sees everything crooked because of falsehood and vanity, and nothing straight because it has been reared without truth. He sees the soul full of disorder and ugliness because of power, luxury, insolence, and incontinence in its actions. And seeing this, he sends it away in dishonor straight to the prison, where it must go to undergo its fitting sufferings. Now, it is fitting for everyone who is undergoing punishment, if they are being punished rightly by another, either to become better and profit by it, or to become an example to others, so that others, seeing the sufferings they endure, may become better through fear. Those who are benefited and pay the penalty at the hands of gods and men are those who have committed curable sins; nevertheless, their benefit comes to them through pains and agonies, both here and in Hades <note>The Greek underworld or the state of the dead.</note>. For it is not possible to be rid of injustice in any other way. But those who have committed the most extreme injustices, and because of such crimes have become incurable, from these the examples are made. And these themselves no longer profit at all, being incurable; but others profit who see them, because of their great sins..."

” ...pains, and most grievous and fearful sufferings for all time, literally hung up as examples there in the prison-house in Hades <note>In Greek mythology, Hades is the underworld; here Plato uses it as a place of detention and purification for souls.</note>, for all the unjust who arrive to see as warnings and lessons. Among these, I say, Archelaus <note>Archelaus was the King of Macedon (c. 413–399 BCE), known for his ruthless rise to power; Socrates uses him as the archetype of the "successful" but miserable tyrant.</note> will be found—if Polus tells the truth—and any other tyrant who is like him. I believe, in fact, that the majority of these examples are drawn from the ranks of tyrants, kings, potentates, and those who managed the affairs of cities. For these, because they have the power <note>original: "ἐξουσίαν" (exousian)</note>, commit the greatest and most impious crimes. Homer himself bears witness to this; for he has depicted kings and potentates as those being punished in Hades for all time—Tantalus, Sisyphus, and Tityus. But Thersites <note>A low-ranking, loud-mouthed soldier in the *Iliad*, often used as a symbol of the common man.</note>, or any other wicked person who was a private citizen <note>original: "ἰδιώτης" (idiōtēs) - meaning a person not in public office.</note>, no one has depicted as suffering great punishments as if he were incurable. For, I suppose, it was not in his power to do such harm; and for this reason, he was actually more fortunate than those who had the power. 

” Indeed, Callicles, it is from the ranks of the powerful that men become exceedingly wicked. Yet, there is nothing to prevent good men from arising even among them, and those who do are well-deserving of great admiration. For it is difficult, Callicles—and worthy of great praise—to live one's life justly when one has reached a position of great power to do wrong. Few indeed are those who achieve this. Yet there have been such men, both here and elsewhere—and I believe there will be others—who possess the virtue of handling justly whatever is entrusted to them. One in particular has become very famous even among the other Greeks: Aristides, the son of Lysimachus <note>Aristides "the Just" was an Athenian statesman renowned for his integrity.</note>. But the majority of those in power, my good friend, become wicked.

” As I was saying, when the judge Rhadamanthus <note>One of the three judges of the dead in Greek myth, known for his inflexible integrity.</note> receives such a person, he knows nothing else about him—neither who he is nor who his parents were—except that he is wicked. Having perceived this, he sends him away to Tartarus, having first marked him to indicate whether he is considered curable or incurable. When the soul arrives there, it suffers what is fitting. Sometimes, however, the judge looks upon another soul that has lived in holiness and truth—the soul of a private citizen or someone else—especially, as I maintain, Callicles, the soul of a philosopher who has minded his own business and has not been a meddler <note>original: "πολυπραγμονήσαντος" (polypragmonēsantos) - a Greek term for someone who interferes in others' affairs or political intrigue.</note> during his life. He is pleased and sends that soul to the Isles of the Blessed. Aeacus <note>The second judge of the dead, legendary for his piety.</note> does the same; each of these two judges holds a rod while they pass judgment. But Minos <note>The third and final judge, originally a king of Crete.</note> sits looking on, alone holding a golden scepter, just as Homer’s Odysseus says he saw him, 'holding a golden scepter, delivering laws to the dead.'

” I, therefore, Callicles, have been persuaded by these accounts, and I consider how I may present my soul to the judge in its healthiest possible state. So, letting go of the honors sought by the many, and practicing the truth, I shall try in reality to live as well as I am able, and when I die, to die in that same way. I exhort all other men as well, as far as I am able—and I exhort you in return—to take up this life and this contest, which I say is greater than all the contests here on earth. And I reproach you, because you will not be able to help yourself when your own trial and judgment comes—the one I am speaking of now. But when you come before that judge, the son of Aegina <note>A reference to Aeacus.</note>, and when he takes hold of you and brings you forward, you will gape and feel dizzy there, no less than I would here, and you there. Someone will perhaps strike you on the cheek insultingly and treat you with utter contempt.

” Perhaps this seems like an old wives' tale to you, and you despise it. And it would indeed be no wonder to despise such things if, by searching, we could find something better and truer. But now you see that although there are three of you who are the wisest of the Greeks today—you, and Polus, and...

<summary>Socrates concludes his myth of judgment, explaining that while the powerful are more likely to be corrupted and punished in Hades, the philosopher who lives justly will be sent to the Isles of the Blessed. He challenges Callicles to prepare for this ultimate divine trial rather than focusing on worldly power.</summary>

### Concerning justice according to Plato.

Since the oracles among the Hebrews teach that their prophets and righteous men endured the

» own words, which are placed in the second book of the *Republic*. In this passage,
» having described the just man as such, let us again, in our argument, place beside him
