» come to him for seeming to be such. It would then be unclear whether he is such for
» the sake of justice or for the sake of the gifts and honors. He must be stripped of
» everything except justice, and we must make him the opposite of the former man.
» For while doing no wrong, let him have the reputation of the greatest injustice, so
» that he may be tested for justice by not being softened by a bad reputation and the

» should not desire to be just, but to seem so." Plato said these things in words. But

->Concerning the Paradise according to Moses.<-

Since Moses stated, according to certain secret traditions, that in the beginning of the world’s
» constitution a certain "Paradise" of God was made, and that the man was deceived through the
» woman by the serpent, Plato has almost entirely transformed the words into a figurative

» deception that came from it, he speaks of "Poverty" (Penia) plotting against "Plenty" (Poros).

» You seem to refer to the same time [as Moses] by saying it happened when this world was being established, 
» specifically when Aphrodite was born. Thus he allegorized the world because of the beauty 
» within it. Indeed, he says in these very words: "When Aphrodite was born, the gods were 
» feasting, both the others and Plenty (Poros), the son of Counsel (Metis). After they had 
» dined, Poverty (Penia) arrived to beg, as there was a feast, and she was by the doors. 
» Now Plenty, being drunk on nectar—for wine did not yet exist—entered the Garden of 
» Zeus and, being heavy, fell asleep. Then Poverty, plotting because of her own 
» lack of resources to have a child from Plenty, lay down beside him and conceived

## Concerning the life of the first humans.

Moses described the first life of the "earth-born" <note>original: "γηγενῶν" — This term refers to the first humans created directly from the earth, matching the biblical account of Adam.</note> as having taken place in the Paradise of God. He described God as their leader while they lived a life without money or possessions; for them, all things grew without labor or sorrow, and they were naked, lacking the clothing they wore later. Now, listen to the Philosopher [Plato] as he interprets almost these very same things in his own words. He says, for instance:

> God himself was their shepherd and stood over them, just as humans—who are a different and more divine kind of being—now act as shepherds to other, lesser races. While He was their shepherd, there were no states, nor any private possession of wives or children. For they all came back to life out of the earth, having no memory of their previous lives. But all such things were absent; instead, they had fruits in abundance from oaks and many other trees, not produced by farming, but given up spontaneously by the earth. They lived mostly in the open air, naked and without bedding, for the seasons were blended so as to cause them no pain. They had soft beds of grass that grew abundantly from the ground. This life you hear of, my friend, was the life in the time of Cronus <note>In Greek mythology, the reign of the titan Cronus was considered a "Golden Age" of ease and plenty, which Eusebius identifies here with the Garden of Eden.</note>. As for the life that is said to have followed, which is the present one, you have perceived it for yourself.

## That they also conversed with irrational animals.

Again, Moses recorded that the serpent was more clever than all the beasts, and he set out what the serpent said to the woman and the woman to the serpent, as well as their conversations. Listen to what Plato writes on this:

> If, therefore, those nurtured by Cronus—having so much leisure and the power to be able to converse not only with humans but also with beasts through speech—used all these advantages for the sake of philosophy, talking with the beasts and with one another, and inquiring from every creature whether, having some private power, it perceived anything different from the rest to contribute to the gathering of wisdom, then it is clear that those people were infinitely superior to those of the present day in terms of happiness. But if, being filled to satiety with food and drink, they told stories to one another and to the beasts—the kind of myths that are even now told about them—then this too, according to my own opinion, is quite easy to judge. Nevertheless, let us set these matters aside until a sufficient witness appears to show us how those people of old felt about knowledge and the use of speech.

## How he also mentions the Deluge.

Moses, having established a system of laws for humanity, thought it necessary to include "ancient history" <note>original: "ἀρχαιολογίας" — Here meaning the study of origins or primeval history.</note> in his introduction. Having mentioned the Deluge <note>The Great Flood of Noah.</note> and the life that came after it...

...of men. Then he sets forth the ancient history of those among the Hebrews who were beloved by God <note>original: "θεοφιλῶν" — individuals or groups considered dear to the Divine.</note>, whose way of life <note>original: "πολιτείαν" — this term can refer to a political constitution or a general way of living within a community.</note> he describes—having been tested and found not to be in error in other respects—as being suitable for the one who would lead them, providing a history for the laws he was enacting. In the introductions to the *Laws*, listen to what he says, from which your ancient accounts may seem to be true. What kind are they? That many destructions of men have occurred through floods and diseases and many other things, in which only a small portion of the human race is left. This is altogether persuasive. Let us then consider one of these many destructions—specifically the one caused by the Deluge <note>original: "κατακλυσμῷ" — the Greek term for a great flood, specifically the cataclysm.</note>. What should we think about it? That those who then escaped the destruction would likely be some mountain shepherds on the peaks, tiny sparks <note>original: "ζώπυρα" — literally "embers" or "live coals"; a metaphor for the few survivors who keep the flame of humanity from being extinguished.</note> of the human race being saved. It is clear. And such people must necessarily be ignorant of the other arts and the schemes that people in cities devise against one another for the sake of greed and rivalry, and all the other evils they plot against one another. It is likely. Let us then assume that the cities in the plains and those settled by the sea were utterly destroyed at that time. Let us assume it. Therefore, all tools were lost, and if there was any significant invention of art, or politics, or any other wisdom, all these things vanished. This is what we shall say about that time. And after other things, he says: "Let us then say that things were in this state regarding men when the destruction happened: there was a vast and terrifying desolation, but a very great abundance of land."

Having said these and other similar things, he goes through the lives of the men after the Deluge. Then, just as Moses joins the way of life of the ancient God-loving Hebrews to the account after the flood, Plato likewise, after the lives of those following the flood, attempts to provide an ancient history <note>original: "ἀρχαιολογεῖν" — to give an account of origins or "archaeology" in the literal sense of "study of old things."</note> of the Greeks, just as the former did for the Hebrews. He mentions Sparta and the constitution in Crete and Lacedaemon <note>The ancient name for the region around Sparta.</note>, and the lives of those among them, whether they lived rightly or not. Then, following this history, he begins the exposition of the laws, following Moses in this as well.

->Thus, our instruction rightly begins from divine matters and<-

Since Moses anchored his entire system of laws and the constitution he established upon piety <note>original: "εὐσεβείας" — religious devotion or duty.</note> toward the God of all things, having made the beginning of his legislation from the first Creator, he then taught that human goods proceed from divine goods. He traced these divine things back to the Mind that governs all, even the God of the universe. » ...from the divine, O Father; and if a city receives the greater blessings, it also acquires the lesser. But if it does not, it is deprived of both. The lesser blessings are those led by health; beauty is second; the third is strength, both for running and for all other movements of the body. Fourth is wealth—not a "blind" wealth, but one that sees keenly, provided it follows after wisdom. 

» Wisdom <note>original: "φρόνησις" — often translated as practical wisdom or prudence.</note> is the first and leader of the divine goods. Second, following after the mind <note>original: "νοῦ" — the intellect or higher reason.</note>, is the temperate habit of the soul. From these, when mixed with courage, the third would be justice. Fourth is courage. All these are naturally ranked before the human goods, and indeed, a legislator must rank them thus. 

» After this, he should command the citizens that all their other regulations should look toward these goals. Of these, the human concerns look toward the divine, and the divine concerns look altogether toward the leading Mind. This applies to the bonds of marriage, and after that, the birth and upbringing of children—both males and females. It applies to them while they are young and as they grow older, until they reach old age; one must rightly care for them by honoring them, or dishonoring them [when they stray]. 

» In all their social interactions, the legislator should examine and guard their pains, their pleasures, their desires, and the intensity of all their loves, using the laws themselves to rightly distribute praise and blame. Furthermore, the divine [legislator] says that, having looked upon all these things, he will appoint guardians over them: some who walk by wisdom, and others who walk by true opinion, so that the Mind, binding all these things together in the wake of temperance and justice, may declare them as such, rather than as being for the sake of wealth or ambition.

» ...to turn the pleasures and desires of the children toward that goal which they must reach when they arrive at adulthood. We say that the "sum" of education <note>original: "παιδείας" (paideia) — This encompasses both schooling and moral upbringing.</note> is right training, which, while a child plays, leads their soul as much as possible to a love of that thing in which they must be perfect when they become a man: the virtue of the craft itself. And Moses, having received this principle, legislated it by saying: *And these words, which I command you today, shall be in your heart and in your soul, and you shall teach them to your sons.* This is exactly what the children of the Hebrews are accustomed to practicing; from a tender age, they are nurtured in all the divine teachings of godliness. This is still pursued by the Jews even to this day according to an ancestral custom.

->**That education should be considered only that which leads toward virtue, and not that which leads toward money-making or any profession for earning a livelihood.**<-

» Let us not allow what we call "education" to remain undefined. For now, when we criticize or praise the upbringing of various people, we say that one of us is "educated" and another "uneducated," even though the latter might sometimes be highly trained in trade, or shipping, or other such things. However, our current discussion, it seems, does not consider these things to be "education." Rather, it refers to the education from childhood that makes one desire and love to become a "perfect citizen," knowing how both to rule and be ruled with justice. 

» This discussion, as it seems to me, would wish to define this training alone as "education." But the training that aims at money, or at physical strength, or even at some other wisdom lacking intellect <note>original: "νοῦ" (nous) — the higher reasoning faculty.</note> and justice, it considers to be vulgar <note>original: "βάναυσόν" (banauson) — a term used for manual labor or technical trades which were considered inferior to moral and intellectual pursuits.</note>, illiberal, and not worthy to be called education at all. Let us not quarrel with them over a name, but let the argument we just agreed upon stand: that those who are rightly educated generally become good men. 

» And indeed, one must never dishonor education, as it is the first of the most beautiful things that come to the best men. And if it ever goes astray, but is capable of being set right, one must always do so throughout their life to the best of their ability. 

» And in the second book of the *Laws*, he adds: I say that education is the virtue that first comes to children. If pleasure, friendship, pain, and hatred are correctly implanted in souls before they are able to grasp reason—and then, once they have grasped reason, these feelings harmonize with it, declaring it to have been correctly instilled by appropriate habits—this total harmony is virtue. 

» If you take that part of virtue which is trained correctly regarding pleasures and pains, so that one hates what one ought to hate from the very beginning to the end, and loves what one ought to love, and if you separate this part with reason and call it "education," you would, in my view, be naming it correctly. 

» These are the words of Plato. And David, following him in the Psalms, teaching us to hate what we must hate and to love what we must love, says: *Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Who is the man who desires life, loving to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.* And Solomon likewise says: *Hear, children, the instruction of a father. For I give you a good gift; do not forsake my law.* And again: *Acquire wisdom, acquire understanding...*

### That Plato held an opinion similar to the Hebrews, believing that the things of this world are an image of more divine things.

The divine oracle said to Moses: *See that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain.* <note>Exodus 25:40. Eusebius suggests that Plato’s theory of "Forms" or "Ideas" mimics this biblical concept of a divine blueprint.</note> The sacred word states this even more clearly, saying: *Those who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things.* <note>Hebrews 8:5.</note> This teaches us that the symbols used by Moses contain a direct image of the more divine things in the realm of the intellect. Listen now to how Plato interprets similar ideas. Writing in the sixth book of the *Republic*, he says: 
» "Indeed, the philosopher, by communing with the divine and the orderly, becomes as orderly and divine as is possible for a human. But slander is everywhere. If then," I said, "a necessity should arise for him to practice what he sees there <note>original: "ἐκεῖ" — referring to the eternal Forms or the divine realm.</note> and apply it to the characters of men, both in private and in public, and not just to mold himself, do you think he would be a poor craftsman of temperance and justice, and of the whole of civic virtue?" "Not at all," he said. "But if the masses perceive that we are telling the truth about him, will they still be angry with the philosophers? And will they disbelieve us when we say that a city could never be happy unless it were drawn by painters who use the divine pattern?" "They will not be angry," he said, "if they perceive it. But what manner of drawing do you mean?" "Taking the city and the characters of men like a tablet," I said, "they would first make it clean, which is not at all easy. But you know that they would differ from others in this: they would not be willing to touch an individual or a city, nor to write laws, until they either received it clean or made it so themselves." "And rightly so," he said. "After that, do you think they would then sketch the outline of the constitution?" "Of course." "Then, I think, as they work, they would look frequently in both directions: toward what is by nature Just, and Beautiful, and Temperate, and all such things, and again toward that which they are creating in humans, mixing and blending from various practices the 'human-likeness' <note>original: "ἀνδρείκελον" (andreikelon) — a technical term for the color of human flesh in painting, here used metaphorically for a lifelike moral character.</note> based on that pattern. This is what Homer also called the 'god-like' <note>original: "θεοειδές" (theoeides)</note> and 'god-resembling' <note>original: "θεοείκελον" (theoeikelon)</note> quality that arises in men. 'Correct,' he said. 'And they would, I think, erase one thing and paint in another, until they had made human characters, as far as possible, as pleasing to God as they can be.'"

### That it is necessary to prepare the young by learning proper hymns and songs for the attainment of virtue. From the second book of the *Laws*.

» It seems to me that for the third or fourth time the argument has come back to the same point: that education <note>original: "παιδεία" (paideia)</note> is the drawing and leading of children toward the reason <note>original: "λόγον" (logon)</note> declared by the law to be right, and which is agreed to be truly right by the most respectable and oldest men through their experience. So that the soul of the child may not be accustomed to feeling joy or pain in a way contrary to the law and those persuaded by the law, but rather follows along, rejoicing...

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 12

» ...and feels pain at the same things as the law. For the sake of these things, what we previously called "songs" have now truly become "incantations" for the souls, <note>original: "ἐπῳδαὶ" (epōdai) — Plato uses the word for songs to suggest they act like a magic spell to harmonize the soul.</note> having been designed to produce that very thing called "concord." However, because the souls of the young cannot endure serious study, they are called and practiced as "play" and "songs." It is just like those who try to provide healthy nourishment to the sick and physically weak in some sweet food or drink, while providing harmful things in unpleasant ones; this is done so that they might welcome the one and correctly learn to hate the other. In the same way, the upright legislator will persuade the poet—and if he cannot persuade, he will compel him—to express the gestures of the temperate and brave and entirely good men in beautiful and praiseworthy words, and to create them correctly in rhythms and melodies within harmonies. Thus, it is reasonable that among us, too, children are accustomed to practicing the songs composed by the divine prophets, which arise from God’s own manifestation.

->**What kind of thoughts the songs should contain.**<-

» You will compel the poets to say that the good man, being temperate and just, is prosperous and blessed, whether he be great and strong or small and weak, and whether he be wealthy or not. But if he should be wealthier even than Cinyras or Midas, <note>Cinyras and Midas were legendary kings famous in antiquity for their immense, almost supernatural wealth.</note> yet be unjust, he is wretched and lives a life of sorrow. And so on. "I would neither remember," says our poet, if he were to speak correctly, "nor would I place in high regard a man who did not perform and acquire all the things called 'beautiful' with justice; indeed, such a man would even face the enemy by standing close to them. But being unjust, he would neither dare to look upon bloody slaughter, nor would he outrun the Thracian North Wind in a race. <note>These are references to the poet Tyrtaeus, whom Plato is critiquing and "correcting" in the *Laws*.</note> Nor should any other of the things called 'good' ever belong to him. For the things called 'good' by the masses are not spoken of correctly. For it is said that health is the best thing, beauty is second, and wealth is third. And countless other things are called good: such as sharp sight and hearing, and possessing all the senses; and even further, being a tyrant <note>original: "τυραννοῦντα" — here meaning an absolute ruler or dictator.</note> and doing whatever one desires. And indeed, they say the peak of all happiness is to possess all these things and to become immortal as quickly as possible. But you and I surely say this: that all these things are the best possessions for men who are just and holy; but for the unjust, they are all the worst, beginning with health. Indeed, even seeing, hearing, sensing, and living at all is the greatest evil for all time if one were immortal and possessed all the so-called 'goods' but lacked justice and all virtue; the evil would be less if such a person lived for the shortest time possible." I think you will persuade and compel your poets to say these very things that I do, and to teach your youth in this way, by providing rhythms and harmonies that follow these principles. Or do you not see? For I say clearly that the things called 'evil' are good for the unjust, but 'evil' for the just. And 'good' things are truly good for the good, but 'bad' for the bad. Do we then agree, you and I, or how is it? These ideas are not far from the Psalms found in the songs, which [David], having received by the Divine Spirit, composed through songs and hymns, teaching those for whom it is truly blessed and those for whom the opposite is true. This is exactly where his book begins, for we say: "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly," and the like. Having transformed these ideas, Plato says that the poets must say that the good man, being temperate and just, is prosperous and blessed. But if he should be wealth...

### That it is not for everyone to produce correct songs and melodies, but only for God or a divine man.

» While a legislator or a statesman might offer advice, their own inventions are often inferior. This point regarding music is both true and worth considering: it was possible to legislate firmly about such things with confidence, never departing from what is naturally correct. But this task belongs to God or a divine man. It was for this reason, logically, that laws were established among the Hebrews: they were not to accept just any hymns and songs into their divine teachings, but only those produced by the Holy Spirit through divine and prophetic men, along with the appropriate melodies sung among them in a quiet manner.

### Concerning those who judge the songs that have been composed.

» "I agree with you," I say along with the many, "that music should be judged by the pleasure it provides." However, this pleasure should not come from just any random person. Rather, the most beautiful "Muse" <note>original: "μοῦσαν" (mousan) — here referring to music or the arts of the Muses.</note> is the one that delights the best and sufficiently educated people, and especially the one who delights that single person who excels in virtue and education. For this reason, we say that the judges of these things need virtue, because they must possess both wisdom and courage. For the true judge must not form his judgment by learning from the audience, nor should he be intimidated by the noise of the crowd or his own lack of education. Nor, if he knows better, should he—out of cowardice and fear—falsely declare his judgment through laziness from the same mouth with which he called the gods to witness. For the judge sits not as a student but as a teacher of what is right, and he is there to oppose those spectators who do not offer pleasure in a proper or correct way. Similarly, among the Hebrews of old, it was not the task of the crowd to judge the songs brought forward and inspired by the Holy Spirit. Instead, there were a few rare individuals who themselves participated in the Holy Spirit and could distinguish the spoken words; they alone were permitted to select and consecrate the books of the prophets and reject those that were not of such quality.

Let us consider if this has happened. Such a gathering is surely noisy, and as the drinking continues, it necessarily becomes even more so—which is exactly what we assumed would happen at the start regarding the current topic. "Necessarily." Everyone feels lighter, is filled with joy and "free speech" <note>original: "παῤῥησίας" (parrhēsia) — a Greek concept of bold, uninhibited speech.</note> and a refusal to listen during such a...

» ...and a strong ruler <note>Referring to the 'symposiarch' or master of the feast</note> who ensures that order is maintained for himself and others. » This "molder" is the same person who was previously called the good legislator. He must establish laws for drinking parties <term>sympotic laws: rules governing social drinking</term> that are capable of taking a person who is becoming hopeful and bold through wine—perhaps more shameless than is proper, refusing to observe order or the proper turns for silence, speech, drinking, and music—and making them do the exact opposite.

» So it is. And for these laws, there must be "guardians of the law" and "creators of life" <note>original: "ζωοδημιουργοὺς" (zōodēmiourgous) — literally life-crafters</note> over them, men who are undisturbed and sober. This has been handed down to us, with our own guardians taking care of the proper order.

->That the drinking of wine must not be permitted to all.<-

» If a city treats this practice with serious intent, as we have just described, using laws and order as a means of training for self-control, and does not refrain from other pleasures in the same way and for the same reason—namely, to devise ways to master them—then wine may be used in this manner by all. 
» But if it is treated as a mere game, where anyone can drink whenever they want and with whomever they want, alongside any other pursuits, I would never cast my vote in favor of that city or that man using drink.
» Instead, I would go even further than the customs of the Cretans and Lacedaemonians <note>Lacedaemonians: the Spartans</note> and add to them the Carthaginian law: that no one should ever taste this drink while in a military camp, but should stick to water for that entire time; and that in the city, neither a male nor a female slave should ever taste it; nor should magistrates during the year they are in office, nor pilots, nor judges while on duty, taste wine at all. 
» Nor should anyone who is coming to a council to deliberate on matters of importance. Furthermore, no one should drink it at all during the day, except for the sake of physical exercise or illness; nor at night when a man or woman intends to conceive children. 
» One could list many other reasons why wine is not to be drunk by those who possess reason and a correct law. Thus, according to this reasoning, no city would have need of many vineyards. Other agricultural products and the entire way of life would be strictly ordered.

And Moses, having also received the instruction that priests must abstain from wine during the time of their sacred service, legislated by saying: *And the Lord spoke to Aaron, saying, "You and your sons with you shall not drink wine or strong drink <term>sikera: a fermented liquor made from grain or fruit other than grapes</term> whenever you enter the Tabernacle of Testimony, or when you approach the altar, so that you do not die. This is a perpetual law throughout your generations."* <note>Leviticus 10:8–9</note> 
The same legislator also commanded those making a vow, saying: *A man or a woman, whoever makes a great vow of purity to the Lord, shall be purified from wine and strong drink. He shall not drink vinegar made from wine or vinegar made from strong drink.* <note>Numbers 6:2–3</note>
But Solomon also restrains rulers and judges from its use, saying: *Do all things with counsel; drink wine with counsel.* <note>A paraphrase often attributed to Solomon in the tradition, likely drawing on Proverbs 31:4</note> For rulers are prone to anger...

->That there is a war within ourselves against our own passions.<-

"But should we think of a man in relation to himself as an enemy against an enemy, or how should we express it, O Athenian Stranger? For I would not wish to call you 'Attic' in my address, for you seem to me to deserve to be named after the Goddess <note>Athena, the goddess of wisdom</note>. For by leading the argument back to its starting point correctly, you have made it clearer. Thus you will easily find that what we just said was correct: that everyone is an enemy to themselves, both publicly and privately. 

"How can you say this, my wonderful friend? 

"Even here, O Stranger, to conquer oneself is the first and best of all victories; but to be defeated by oneself is the most shameful and worst of all things. For these things signify that a war against ourselves exists within each of us." 

And after other things he adds to these, saying: "Let us consider whether each of us does not suppose himself to be one. Yes. But possessing within himself two counselors, opposing and foolish, which we call pleasure and pain? That is so. And in addition to these two, again, there are opinions about the future, which have the common name of 'expectation'; but specifically, 'fear' is the expectation before pain, and 'confidence' is the expectation before its opposite. And over all these is 'reasoning' <term>logismos: the rational faculty of the soul</term> as to which of them is better or worse, which, when it becomes a common decree of the city, is named 'Law'." 

And next he says: "Look now, let us recognize that these passions within us are like sinews or strings <note>Plato’s famous 'Puppet Allegory' from *Laws* 644d</note> that pull us, and being opposite to each other, they drag us in opposite directions toward opposite actions, where the distinction between virtue and vice lies. For the argument says that one ought always to follow one of these pulls and never abandon it, resisting the other sinews. This is the 'golden and sacred' leading-string of reasoning, called the common law of the city. Others are hard and iron, while this one is soft because it is golden. The others resemble all sorts of forms. It is necessary to always assist the most beautiful leading-string of the law. 

"For since reasoning is beautiful, gentle, and not violent, its leading-string requires assistants so that the 'golden race' within us may conquer the other races. And so, regarding us as puppets <note>original: "θαυμάτων" (thaumatōn) — referring here to marionettes or mechanical dolls</note>, the myth of virtue would be preserved, and the meaning of being 'master of oneself' or 'slave to oneself' would become even more clear. And that both a city and a private individual, having grasped the true word concerning these pulls within themselves, must live following this. A city, receiving it either from some god..."

» “...Theodorus, while looking upward, fell into a well; a certain clever and graceful **Thracian maidservant** <note>The 'Thracian maid' is a stock character in Greek literature representing common sense and domestic wit, contrasting with the 'absent-minded' intellectual.</note> is said to have mocked him, saying that while he was eager to know the things in heaven, those things before him and under his feet escaped his notice. The same mockery suffices for all those who spend their lives in philosophy. For in reality, such a man is unaware of his neighbor; not only of what he does, but almost whether he is even a human being or some other creature. But what a human being actually is, and what is fitting for such a nature to do or to suffer differently from others, is what he seeks and takes pains to investigate. You understand, I suppose, O Theodorus, or do you not?” “I do,” he replied, “and what you say is true.”

» “Therefore, my friend, when such a man associates with someone privately or in public—as I was saying at the beginning—whenever he is forced in a courtroom or anywhere else to speak about the things at his feet and before his eyes, he provides laughter not only to Thracian maids but to the rest of the crowd as well, falling into wells and every kind of impasse through his inexperience. His clumsiness is terrible, giving an impression of stupidity. For when it comes to insults, he has nothing personal to hurl at anyone, since he knows no evil of anyone because he has not practiced such things. Thus, being at a loss, he appears ridiculous.

» “When it comes to praises and the boastings of others, he is seen to be laughing not out of pretense but in reality, and he seems to be a trifler. When a tyrant or a king is praised, he thinks he is hearing one of the herdsmen—such as a swineherd, a shepherd, or some cowherd—being congratulated for getting a large yield. But he considers them to be milking a more difficult and treacherous animal than those others. Such a man, he thinks, must necessarily become no less rustic and uneducated than the herdsmen, due to his lack of leisure, being walled into his mountain-pen.

» “And when he hears that someone possesses ten thousand <term>plethra</term> <note>A plethron was a Greek unit of area, roughly 100 feet or 1/4 of an acre; 'ten thousand plethra' implies a vast estate.</note> of land, or even more, as though they possessed a wonderful amount, it seems to him that he is hearing of something quite small, as he is accustomed to looking at the whole earth. And when they sing the praises of lineages—how someone is noble because he can show seven wealthy ancestors—he considers such praise to be entirely dim-sighted and focused on the small. This is due to a lack of education, being unable to look always at the whole, nor to calculate that every person has had countless myriads of ancestors and progenitors, among whom there have been, many times over, ten thousand rich and poor, kings and slaves, barbarians and Greeks.

» “But when people pride themselves on a list of twenty-five ancestors and trace their descent back to **Heracles** <note>The hero Hercules, a common legendary ancestor for Greek royalty.</note> the son of Amphitryon, the smallness of their logic appears absurd to him. He laughs at the fact that they cannot calculate that the twenty-fifth ancestor back from Amphitryon was simply whatever fortune happened to make him, and the fiftieth ancestor from him likewise, and so they are unable to rid their foolish souls of vanity. In all these matters, such a man is laughed at by the many—appearing, on the one hand, to be arrogant, and on the other, being ignorant of what is at his feet and at a loss in every detail.”

» “You are describing exactly what happens, Socrates.”

» “But whenever he himself, my friend, draws someone upward, and someone is willing to move from the question of ‘How have I wronged you or you me?’ to the investigation of **justice itself and injustice** <note>Plato’s 'Theory of Forms' suggests that 'Justice' exists as a perfect, universal concept beyond individual instances of fair or unfair acts.</note>—what each of them is and how they differ from all other things or from each other—or from the question of whether a king is happy because he possesses much gold, to an investigation concerning kingship and human happiness and misery in general—what kind of things they are and in what way it is fitting for a human nature to acquire the one and flee the other—about all these things, when that man with the small soul and the sharp...”

The text contrasts the philosopher's "upward" gaze with the "small-souled" preoccupation with wealth, status, and local disputes.</summary>

,, ...dignity, and not having to pay a penalty, he in turn pays back the opposite. For being dizzy and hanging from a height, and looking aloft from above <note>The philosopher is depicted as standing on a high intellectual peak, looking down at the petty concerns of the world, which makes him feel light-headed.</note>, due to his lack of habit he is distressed and at a loss; and stammering, he does not provide laughter to Thracian women, nor to any other uneducated person—for they do not even perceive his state—but rather to all those who have been brought up in the opposite way, like slaves. 

,, This is the character of each man, O Theodorus. The one is truly brought up in freedom and leisure, the one you call a philosopher; to him it is not a matter of reproach if he seems simple and is worth nothing when he falls into servile tasks—such as not knowing how to pack a bedroll <note>original: στρωματόδεσμον (stromatodesmon), a bundle containing bedding, often carried by travelers or soldiers.</note>, nor how to season a dish, nor how to use flattering words. 

,, But the other man is able to perform all such tasks sharply and serve quickly, yet he does not know how to throw his cloak over his right shoulder like a free man, nor, having grasped the harmony of words, how to rightly hymn the true life of gods and happy men.

,, **Theodorus:** If, O Socrates, you could persuade all men of what you say as you do me, there would be more peace and fewer evils among mankind.

,, **Socrates:** But it is not possible for evils to be destroyed, O Theodorus; for there must always be something opposite to the good. Nor are they established among the gods, but they necessarily haunt mortal nature and this region. Therefore, one must try to flee from here to there as quickly as possible. Flight is **becoming like God** <note>original: ὁμοίωσις θεῷ (homoiosis theo). This became a central concept in Christian theology, often called "theosis."</note> as far as possible; and becoming like Him is to become just and holy, with wisdom. 

,, But indeed, my excellent friend, it is not at all easy to persuade people that it is not for the reasons the many say—that one should flee wickedness and pursue virtue so that one may not seem bad and may instead seem good. For these arguments are, as it seems to me, what is called **"old wives' tales."** <note>original: γραῶν ὕθλος (graon uthlos); Socrates dismisses the idea that we should be good just for the sake of our reputation.</note>

,, Let us state the truth this way: God is in no way, in no manner, unjust, but is as just as possible. And there is nothing more like Him than whoever among us becomes as just as possible. Regarding this is the true cleverness of a man, or his nothingness and lack of manhood. 

,, For the knowledge of this is true wisdom and virtue, while ignorance of it is manifest stupidity and vice. Other apparent clevernesses and wisdoms, when they occur in political power, are vulgar; and in the arts, they are base. 

,, To the one who does wrong and says or does unholy things, it is by far best not to concede that he is "clever" because of his villainy. For such men exult in this reproach, and they think they hear that they are not "trifles, mere burdens on the earth," <note>A reference to Homer's *Iliad*, describing those who are useless to society.</note> but men such as they ought to be to survive in a city. 

,, We must tell them the truth: they are all the more what they do not think they are, precisely because they do not think it. For they are ignorant of the penalty of injustice, which one should least of all be ignorant of. For it is not what they think—beatings and deaths, which they sometimes suffer even while doing no wrong—but a penalty which it is impossible to escape.

,, **Theodorus:** What penalty do you mean?

,, **Socrates:** Two patterns, my friend, stand in reality: the one divine and most happy, the other godless and most miserable. Not seeing that this is how it is, because of their stupidity and extreme folly, they are unaware that they become like the one through their unjust deeds, and unlike the other. For this they pay the penalty, living the life that resembles the pattern they have become like. 

,, And if we say that unless they rid themselves of their "cleverness," even after they have died, that place pure of evils will not receive them, but they will always have a way of life here similar to themselves—the wicked consorting with the wicked—they will hear these things as "clever" and "villainous" men listening to some fools.

,, **Theodorus:** Indeed, O Socrates.

,, **Socrates:** I know it, my comrade. One thing, however, happens to them: whenever they must give and receive an account in private about the things they find fault with, and they are willing to endure it manfully for a long time, and not flee unmanfully...

<summary>In this excerpt from Plato's Theaetetus, Socrates defines the "flight from the world" as "becoming like God" through justice and wisdom. He contrasts the true philosopher’s heavenly focus with the "clever" man's worldly skill, arguing that the true penalty for injustice is becoming like the miserable, godless pattern of existence.</summary>

### Concerning all the wisdom found among men.

And among us, it has been said concerning all the wisdom found among men: "For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God." For it is written: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent. Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age?" <note>Citing 1 Corinthians 1:19-20.</note> Furthermore, concerning the necessity for those who philosophize for God to hold no petty thoughts, we are taught in the passage where it is said: "While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen; for the things which are seen are temporary, but the things which are not seen are eternal." <note>Citing 2 Corinthians 4:18.</note> 

And concerning the fact that wickedness is coiled around the earth and this mortal life, the Divine Word says somewhere: "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil." <note>Citing Ephesians 5:16.</note> And: "Sufficient for the day is its own trouble." <note>Citing Matthew 6:34.</note> The prophet also says: "Cursing and theft and adultery and murder are poured out upon the land, and they mingle blood with blood." <note>Citing Hosea 4:2.</note> 

Regarding the flight from here toward God, Moses says: "You shall walk after the Lord your God, and to Him you shall hold fast." <note>Citing Deuteronomy 13:4.</note> The same author teaches us to imitate God, saying: "You shall be holy, for the Lord our God is holy." <note>Citing Leviticus 19:2.</note> And David, knowing God to be righteous, urges us to try to imitate Him, saying: "The Lord is righteous, and He loves righteousness." <note>Citing Psalm 11:7.</note> 

The same man instructed us to despise wealth, saying: "If riches increase, set not your heart upon them." <note>Citing Psalm 62:10.</note> And: "Be not afraid when a man is made rich, or when the glory of his house is increased; for when he dies he shall carry nothing away, nor shall his glory descend after him." <note>Citing Psalm 49:16-17.</note> Moreover, he taught us not to marvel at the powers among men in these words: "Put not your trust in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. His spirit shall go forth, and he shall return to his earth; in that very day all his thoughts shall perish." <note>Citing Psalm 146:3-4.</note>

### That it might sometimes be necessary to use a lie as a medicine, for the benefit of those who require such a method.

A lawmaker is of no small benefit, if this were indeed the case as the argument has just stated—even if he dared to lie to the young for their own good. There are times when a lie is more profitable than the truth, being better able to make everyone do what is right, not by force, but willingly. Truth, O stranger, is a beautiful and lasting thing; yet it seems not easy to persuade people of it. <note>This is a paraphrase of Plato’s *Laws* 663d-e regarding the "Noble Lie."</note> 

You would find thousands of such instances even in the Hebrew Scriptures, such as when it speaks of God being "jealous," or "sleeping," or "angry," or being subject to other human passions, which are employed for the benefit of those who require such a method <note>Eusebius argues that Biblical anthropomorphisms—describing God in human terms—are "beneficial lies" or metaphors used by God to educate simple people.</note>.

-> One must not slander the whole nation because of those who live poorly in this way. <-

Let us consider it in this way. Suppose someone raised goats, and praised the animal and the possession as something beautiful. But suppose you had seen goats poorly pastured by a goatherd, doing damage in cultivated fields and destroying them. And seeing every flock without a leader, or with bad leaders, one would find fault. According to such a logic, think whether anyone would ever soundly criticize anything at all. How could they? 

And after a little: what is more praiseworthy than the fellowship of the soul—not that which is a ruler by nature, for with that ruler it is beneficial. But what if one has never seen a soul properly in fellowship with itself under a ruler, but always without a ruler, or living with bad rulers? Do we think such observers of such fellowships would rightly blame or praise? How could they? 

So one should not, if some appear without a protector and ruler, or doing evil things with bad rulers, blame our entire school <note>term: διδασκαλεῖον (didaskaleion). In the early church, Christianity was often presented as a "school" of divine philosophy</note>. Rather, one should admire the godly way of life <note>original: θεοσεβές πολίτευμα (theosebes politeuma); can also be translated as "godly commonwealth"</note> from those who care for it correctly.

» ...praises, but the name of the ungodly is extinguished. <note>original: ὄνομα δὲ ἀσεβῶν σβέννυται (onoma de asebon sbennytai); a quote from Proverbs 10:7</note> And again, it being said: "Call no man blessed before his end," <note>original: μὴ μακαρίσης ἄνδρα πρὸ τελευτῆς (me makarises andra pro teleutes); from Sirach 11:28</note> hear how Plato interprets this thought, saying in the seventh book of the *Laws*: "For those citizens who have reached the end of their lives, and whose bodies or souls have accomplished noble and laborious deeds, having been obedient to the laws, it would be fitting for them to receive praises." How could it not be so? "But to honor those still living with encomiums and hymns is not safe, until someone has run the whole course of life and established a noble end." Let all these things be common to us, for both men and women who have clearly become good and virtuous.

### On Wealth and Poverty.

"Give me neither wealth nor poverty," says Solomon in the *Proverbs* <note>Proverbs 30:8</note>; and Plato says in the third book of the *Republic*: "We have said other things, as it seems, to the guardians, which must be guarded against in every way, so that it may never escape their notice that they <note>wealth and poverty</note> are creeping into the city." What sort of things are these? "Wealth, I believe, and poverty. For the one produces luxury, idleness, and innovation; the other produces meanness and villainy in addition to innovation." Villainy <note>original: κακουργία (kakourgia)</note> is because every such action is dishonorable.

### On Honoring Parents.

Again, Moses says in the *Laws*: "Let each man fear his father and his mother." <note>Leviticus 19:3</note> And: "Honor thy father and thy mother, that it may be well with thee." <note>Exodus 20:12</note> And Plato, similarly to Moses, speaks of honoring and fearing them in the *Laws* in this way: "Every sensible man fears and honors the prayers of parents, knowing that many times and for many people they have been fulfilled." And again in another place he says: "Let everyone among us reverence his elder in both deed and word. And for one who exceeds him in age by twenty years, whether male or female, let him regard them as a father or mother through reverence."

### On the Possession of Servants.

Moses, having forbidden in the *Laws* for Hebrews to be slaves to Hebrews, said: "If you acquire a Hebrew servant, he shall serve you for six years; but in the seventh year you shall send him away free." <note>Exodus 21:2</note> And Plato says similarly in the *Republic*: "Neither should anyone possess a Greek as a slave, nor should they advise other Greeks to do so." "By all means," he said. "Rather, it would be more fitting to behave this way toward the barbarians <note>meaning non-Greeks</note>, but they should abstain from their own kind."

### How he changed: "Do not move eternal boundaries, which your fathers set." <note>Proverbs 22:28</note>

"Let no one move the boundaries of land, neither of a fellow citizen who is a neighbor, nor of another stranger who possesses a neighbor's land on the borders, considering that 'to move the immovable' <note>a Greek proverb for disturbing established laws or sacred things</note> is truly this." And next he says: "Whoever brings his own things into those of his neighbor by overstepping the boundaries, let him pay for the damage; and on account of his combined shamelessness and meanness, let him be healed by paying double the damage to the one who was harmed."

->Similarly: "Repaying the sins of fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation of those who hate me."<- <note>Exodus 20:5</note>

But in his discourse, he says that "the reproaches and dishonors of children should follow no one, unless a man’s father, grandfather, and great-grandfather in succession have been found guilty by the court."

<summary>Eusebius presents a series of thematic parallels between Hebrew Scripture (Proverbs, Exodus, Leviticus) and Plato’s writings (Laws, Republic), arguing that Plato’s views on honoring parents, the dangers of wealth, and land boundaries are derivative of Mosaic law.</summary>

->### On Thieves.<-

Regarding the law of Moses, it says: "If someone steals a calf or a sheep, and slaughters it or sells it, he shall pay five calves for the calf, and four sheep for the sheep. But if the theft is caught and found in his hand, from a calf and a donkey even to a sheep, if they are alive, he shall pay double." <note>original: διπλᾶ ἀποτίσει (dipla apotisei); quoting Exodus 22:1-4</note> Listen to how Plato follows these things when he says: "Whether someone steals something great or small, let one law always be imposed and one penalty of justice for all. For as for the stolen property, it is necessary to pay back double if one is convicted of such a suit, provided he has sufficient other property to pay <unclear>beyond</unclear> his allotted portion. But if not, let him be bound until he pays the amount for which he was condemned." <note>Quoting Plato’s *Laws*, Book 9, 857a-b</note>

->### On a Thief Being Slain.<-

Again, Moses says: "If the thief is found in the act of breaking in <note>literally "in the digging through," referring to the practice of tunneling through mud-brick walls</note> and is struck so that he dies, there is no blood-guilt for him." <note>Exodus 22:2</note> Plato harmonizes with this as well, saying: "If someone catches and kills a thief entering the house at night for the purpose of stealing money, let him be pure <note>original: καθαρός (katharos); meaning legally and religiously blameless of murder</note>; and if one kills a 'cloak-snatcher' <note>a mugger or highwayman</note> while defending himself, let him be pure." <note>Plato, *Laws*, Book 9, 874b-c</note>

->### On Beasts of Burden.<-

"If indeed a beast of burden or any other animal kills someone—except for those that do such a thing while competing in the public games—let the relatives of the deceased prosecute the killer for murder. Let the rural officials, as many as the relative appoints, act as judges. And let the one convicted be killed and cast outside the borders of the territory." These are the words of Plato. <note>Plato, *Laws*, Book 9, 873e</note> But Moses, writing long before, says: "If a bull gores a man or a woman, and they die, the bull shall certainly be stoned, and its meat shall not be eaten; but the owner of the bull shall be innocent." <note>Exodus 21:28</note>

,, [if the child] becomes iron, they should by no means show pity, but assigning the nature that belongs to each, as they are—whether as craftsmen or farmers. ### Further on similar examples.

The Hebrew prophecy says to the leaders of the people: "Woe, shepherds of Israel! Do shepherds feed themselves? Do shepherds not feed the sheep? Behold, you eat the milk, and slaughter the fat ones, and clothe yourselves in the wool, and my sheep you do not feed. And the lost you did not seek, and the broken you did not bind, and the wandering you did not return." <note>Quoting Ezekiel 34:2-4</note> And the saving word also says: "The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. But the hireling, who is not a shepherd and does not own the sheep, leaves them." <note>Quoting the Gospel of John 10:11-12</note> Listen also to Plato, in the first book of the *Republic*, how he once indicated these things: "But now you say, O Thrasymachus <note>Thrasymachus was a Sophist who argued that 'might makes right' and that leaders only look out for themselves</note>, let us look back at what was said before, that the true physician whom we just defined, or the true shepherd, no longer needs to keep watch strictly later, but he shepherds the sheep as a shepherd, not looking toward what is best for the sheep, but like a banquet-guest about to feast, looking toward the festivities, or again toward selling them like a money-maker, but not a shepherd. But the art of shepherding surely cares for nothing else than that for which it is appointed, so as to provide the best for it. For its own affairs are sufficiently provided for, so as to be the best, as long as it lacks nothing of being the art of shepherding. Thus I thought just now that it was necessary for us to agree that every rule, insofar as it is a rule, considers the best for nothing else than for that which it uses and serves, whether in political or private rule. But do you think that the rulers in cities—those who are truly rulers—rule willingly?" <note>Quoting Plato, *Republic*, Book 1, 345c-e. Plato argues that a true leader, like a shepherd, acts for the benefit of those he leads, not for personal gain.</note>

### Further on the same subject.

The Hebrew prophecy says: "From your fear, O Lord, we conceived in the womb and were in labor and brought forth a spirit of salvation." <note>Quoting Isaiah 26:18 from the Septuagint Greek version</note> Plato, in the *Theaetetus*, makes Socrates say these things: "For those who associate with me suffer the same as women in labor. For they are in labor and are filled with perplexity night and day, much more than those women. And my art <note>Socrates famously compared his method of questioning to midwifery (maieutics), helping others 'give birth' to their own ideas</note> is able to rouse and to lay to rest this labor." <note>Quoting Plato, *Theaetetus*, 151a</note>

### Further on the same subject.

The prophet Ezekiel having said: "And the hand of the Lord was upon me, and I saw, and behold a lifting spirit came from the north." And following this he said: "And in the midst, as the likeness of four living creatures. And their appearance was as the likeness of a man upon them, and each had four faces. <meta>This page continues Eusebius’s *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 12. Having previously discussed the "Noble Lie" and the concept of the "Good Shepherd," Eusebius now presents Plato’s famous analogy of the tripartite soul from the *Republic* (Book 9) to illustrate the internal struggle between justice and injustice. He then transitions to comparing Plato's legislative structures in the *Laws* to the tribal organization and geography of the ancient Hebrews.</meta>

-># EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, book 12<-

"Listen then to what he says: 'Now then,' I said, 'let us talk to him, since we have agreed that both doing wrong and acting justly each has its own power.' 'How?' he asked. 'By fashioning an image of the soul in speech, so that the one who says those things <note>The "things" refers to the argument that injustice is more profitable than justice.</note> may know what kind of things he was saying.' 'What kind of image?' he asked. 'One of those natures such as the ancient myths say used to exist, like the Chimaera <note>A fire-breathing hybrid creature with the body of a goat, the head of a lion, and the tail of a snake.</note>, Scylla <note>A sea monster with many heads.</note>, Cerberus <note>The three-headed hound of the underworld.</note>, and many others, where many forms are said to have grown together into one.' 'They are so described,' he said. 'Fashion then one image of a manifold and multi-headed beast, having heads of tame and wild animals in a circle, and able to change and grow all these things from itself.' 'The work of a clever fashioner,' I said. 'Nevertheless, since speech is more easily molded than wax and such materials, let it be fashioned. Now fashion one other image of a lion, and one of a man. Let the first <note>the beast</note> be the largest by far, and the second <note>the lion</note> the second largest.' 'These things,' he said, 'are easy, and they are fashioned.' 'Now join them together into one, being three, so that they somehow grow together with each other.' 'They are joined,' he said. 'Then mold around them from the outside a single image, that of the man, so that to the one not able to see what is inside, but seeing only the outer shell, it appears as one living being—a man.' 'It is molded,' he said. 'Let us then say to the one who says it is profitable for this man to do wrong, and that doing right does not benefit him, that he is saying nothing else than that it is profitable for him to feast the multi-headed beast and make it strong, along with the lion and the things concerning the lion; but to starve the man and make him weak, so that he is dragged wherever either of those leads him, and not to make them live together or be friends; but to let them bite and fight and eat each other.' 'Certainly,' he said, 'the one who praises injustice would say these things.' 'On the other hand, wouldn't the one who says justice is profitable say that one should do and say things by which the inner man <note>original: ὁ ἐντὸς ἄνθρωπος (ho entos anthrōpos); this is Plato’s famous term for the rational part of the soul that distinguishes humans from animals.</note> within the man will be most powerful, and will take care of the multi-headed creature like a farmer, nourishing and taming the gentle parts, while preventing the wild ones from growing, making the nature of the lion his ally, and caring for all in common, making them friends with each other and himself, and thus he will nourish them?' 'Quite so,' he said, 'the one who praises justice speaks this way.'"

---

### That Plato also legislates to divide the citizens into twelve tribes, in imitation of the Hebrew nation.

The law of the nation of the Hebrews was divided from the start into twelve tribes, and Plato similarly legislates that it is necessary to maintain this same number for the citizens, saying thus: "Let the whole land be divided for us into twelve parts, as equal as possible. Let one tribe, assigned by lot to each part, provide five men every year to serve as land-stewards <note>original: ἀγρονόμοις (agronomois); rural police or magistrates tasked with managing the countryside in Plato's ideal city in the *Laws*.</note> and guards." And again he says: "You shall assign to these the twelve generals who have been chosen, a tribal leader for each tribe."

---

### Plato legislates concerning settling the city in a place similar to the description of Jerusalem.

The royal capital of the ancient Hebrews was established long ago far from the sea, situated in the mountains, and possessing a land that produced all things; and Plato says that the city being settled in his *Laws* must be of such a kind. He says thus: "This then is what [needs to be said] about it..."

<summary>In this passage, Plato defines the soul as the "self-moving motion" and argues that because it is the source of all movement, it must exist before the physical body. He concludes that the soul is the primary cause of everything in the universe, including character, morality, and the movement of the heavens.</summary>

> ...those [souls] that order the world, whether it be the best soul or its opposite. O stranger, from what has now been said, it is not even holy to suggest otherwise: that one or more souls, possessing every virtue, lead the heavenly bodies on their rounds. You have followed the argument beautifully, Cleinias. Now listen further to this. What is it? As for the **sun** and the **moon** and the other **stars**, if soul leads all things, does it not also lead each one of them individually? Certainly. Then let us formulate an argument concerning one of them, which will clearly apply to all the stars for us. Which one? Every person sees the body of the sun, but no one sees its soul. Indeed, we cannot see the soul of any other body, whether of a living animal or one that has died. But there is great hope that this kind of being <note>the soul</note> is entirely imperceptible to all the physical senses, and is graspable by the **intellect** <term>nous</term> alone. By the mind and thought, then, let us grasp this point about it. What point? If a soul leads the sun, we would not miss the mark by choosing one of three ways it might act. What are they? Either that it resides within this visible circular body and carries it everywhere, just as the soul within us carries us about; or, having provided itself with a body of **fire** or some kind of **air** from the outside (as some accounts have it), it pushes body with body by force; or thirdly, being itself bare of any body but possessing certain other wondrous powers, it guides the sun. Yes, it must be that by doing one of these things, the soul conducts all things.

These things were stated by the philosopher <note>Plato</note> in the tenth book of the *Laws*. And hear also in the *Philebus* how he establishes the nature of thought. For all the wise agree—truly exalting themselves—that **Intelligence** <term>nous</term> is our king of both heaven and earth. And perhaps they speak well. But let us, if you wish, make a more lengthy inquiry into it through truthful words. Speak as you wish. Do not take the length of the argument into account, Socrates, for we will not be annoyed. You have spoken well. Let us begin then by asking this. What? Whether, O Protarchus, we should say that the universe and this so-called "Whole" is governed by the power of **unreason** <note>original: "alógou," without reason</note> and chance, and by whatever happens to occur; or, on the contrary, as those before us said, that a certain wonderful **Intelligence** <term>nous</term> and **Wisdom** <term>phronēsis</term> coordinates and governs it? 

By no means, O wonderful Socrates! For what you just suggested <note>that the world is governed by chance</note> appears to me to be not even holy. But to say that **Intelligence** orders all things is worthy of the sight of the world, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the whole revolution; I myself would never say or think otherwise about them. Do you wish, then, that we too should agree with what was admitted by those before us, and say that these things are so? And should we not only think it necessary to repeat the words of others without risk, but also share the risk and the blame when a clever man says that these things are not so, but are in disorder? How could I not wish it? Come then, look now at the argument that follows for us. Just speak. Concerning the nature of the bodies of all living beings—**fire**, **water**, **breath** <note>original: "pneuma," often used for air</note>, and **earth**—do we not see these, as those tossed by a storm say, present in our own composition? Certainly. For we are truly "tossed by a storm" of difficulty in our current discussion. 

Come then, take this point regarding each of these elements within us. What point? That each of these in us is small and poor, and nowhere is it pure, nor does it possess power worthy of its nature. Take it in one instance and think the same of all: for example, there is **fire** within us, and there is fire in the universe. Of course. But the fire within us is small, weak, and poor, while the fire in the universe is marvelous in its quantity and beauty, and...

» ...and to hear all things, and that it is impossible for anything to escape his notice? Or is it that he possesses as many senses and forms of knowledge as exist? It is in this way, surely, that he is said to have these things, is it not? It is so. What then? Can he do all things for which there is power among both mortals and immortals? How could they not agree that these things are so? And indeed, have we not agreed that the gods are good and excellent? Certainly. Is it then impossible to admit that they act out of **indifference** <note>original: *rhathymia* — a sense of lazy unconcern or "taking it easy."</note> or luxury in any of their duties, being such as we say they are? For among us, idleness is the parent of laziness, and laziness is the offspring of idleness and luxury. You speak most truly. Therefore, regarding idleness and laziness, no god is negligent. For surely they have no share in cowardice. You speak most rightly.

» It remains then, that if they do neglect the small things among the few details of the whole, they must do so either knowing that it is not necessary to care for any such things, or—what else remains, except knowing the opposite? Nothing. Which then, my most excellent friend, is your position? Do you say they neglect them because they are ignorant and think there is no need to care, or do they know it is necessary, yet act like the basest of men—who are said to know what is better but do not do it because they are overcome by pleasures or pains? How could that be? 

» Human affairs certainly partake of a living nature, and at the same time, man is the most **god-fearing** <note>original: *theosebestaton* — literally "most god-revering."</note> of all living creatures. So it seems. We say that all mortal living things are the **possessions** <note>original: *ktēmata* — property or belongings. Plato suggests humans belong to the gods like livestock to a farmer.</note> of the gods, as is the whole of heaven. How could it be otherwise? Now, whether one says these things are small or great in the eyes of the gods, in neither case would it be fitting for those who own us to be negligent, especially since they are most careful and excellent. 

» Let us consider this further point in addition to these. What is it? Concerning perception and power: are they not naturally opposite to one another in terms of ease and difficulty? How do you mean? It is somehow more difficult to see and hear small things than large ones. But conversely, it is easier for everyone to carry, master, and care for small and few things than their opposites. Much easier. 

» If a doctor is tasked with treating a whole body, being both willing and able, and he cares for the large parts but neglects the small portions and members, will the whole ever be in good condition for him? Not at all. Nor indeed would it be for pilots, nor generals, nor household managers, nor even for statesmen, nor any other such person; for the great many things cannot exist apart from the few and the small. Even the **stonemasons** <note>original: *lithologoi* — those who select and lay stones for building.</note> say that large stones do not lie well without the small ones. How could they? 

» Let us never, then, deem God to be inferior to mortal **craftsmen** <note>term: *demiourgōn* — skilled workers or creators. In this context, it refers to human artisans to contrast with the Divine Creator.</term>, who, the better they are, the more accurately and perfectly they complete their works—both small and great—with a single art. Should we believe that God, who is most wise and both willing and able to care, neglects the very things that are easiest to care for because they are small—acting like a lazy or cowardly man who shrinks from labor—while only caring for the large? By no means let us accept such an opinion about the gods, O stranger. For such a thought would be neither holy nor true. 

» Do we seem now to have argued sufficiently with the one who blames the gods for negligence? Yes, by forcing him through these arguments to agree that he does not speak correctly. Yet it seems to me he still needs some kind of **myth** <note>original: *mython* — here used in the sense of a persuasive story or an overarching explanation of the cosmos.</note>. What kind? My good friend, let us persuade him through words that he does not speak correctly when he says...

» For the one who looks after the universe, with a view toward the salvation and excellence of the whole, all things have been ordered together. Each of these parts, according to its power, experiences and performs what is appropriate to it. Over these parts, rulers have been appointed for even the smallest detail of every action and passion, having worked out the ultimate end to the finest division. One of these parts is yours, O stubborn part <note>original: *schetlie morion* — a phrase Plato uses to address the individual who feels insignificant or resentful of their place in the universe.</note>, which always stretches toward and looks to the whole, even though it is very small. 

» But you have forgotten this very thing: that all creation comes into being for the sake of the universe, so that the life of the whole may possess a blessed existence. It does not come into being for your sake, but you for its sake. For every physician, and every skilled craftsman, performs all his work for the sake of the whole, stretching toward the common best; he produces the part for the sake of the whole, and not the whole for the sake of the part. 

» You, however, are resentful, being ignorant of how your own best interest happens to be best for the whole and for yourself, according to the power of our common origin. And since a soul is always joined with a body—now with one, now with another—and undergoes all sorts of changes through itself or through another soul, no other task remains for the **Draughts-player** <note>original: *petteutē* — a player of a strategy board game similar to checkers or chess. Plato uses this as a metaphor for God moving souls according to their merit.</note> except to move the character that is becoming better into a better place, and the worse into a worse place, according to what is fitting for each, so that each may receive its appropriate portion. 

» In what way do you mean? In the way that I believe I can describe the "ease of care" the god has for all things. For if one were to shape the whole by always looking at it and reshaping everything—for instance, making living water out of fire, rather than many things from one or one from many, partaking in a second or even a third generation of births in great numbers—the arrangement of the shifting order would be infinite. But as it is, there is a wonderful ease for the one who cares for the whole. 

» How so? Like this: Since our King saw that all our actions possess a soul, and that there is much virtue in them and much vice, and that the soul and body are **indestructible** but not **eternal** <note>Plato distinguishes between something that will not be destroyed (indestructible) and something that exists outside of time or has no beginning (eternal), like the "legal gods" or higher deities.</note>—for there would never be a birth of living beings if either of these two were destroyed—and since He recognized that what is always naturally beneficial is the good of the soul, while the evil is harmful; 

» having seen all these things, He devised a position for each of the parts, so that virtue might conquer and vice be defeated in the whole, in the easiest and best way possible. He has devised, then, with a view to this whole, what kind of character, in becoming what it is, must take up which seat and settle in which regions. But He left the causes of *why* a character becomes a certain way to the wills of each of us. For in whatever direction a person’s desires lead, and whatever kind of soul they possess, that is what each of us becomes, for the most part, every time. 

» That seems likely. All things that possess a soul change, having the cause of change within themselves. In changing, they are moved according to the rank and law of destiny. When they change their characters only slightly, they move along the surface of the land <note>This suggests a horizontal change within the same social or moral stratum of life.</note>. But when they change more greatly and more unjustly, they fall into the depths and those places called <term>Hades</term> <note>The Greek underworld; here used by Plato as a state of the soul or a specific lower region for the wicked.</note>, and names like it, which people fear and dream about both while living and when they have been released from their bodies. 

» Whenever a soul changes greatly toward vice or virtue through its own will and through powerful association, if it joins with divine virtue and becomes exceptionally like it, it changes its path and is transported to a holy place, being moved entirely to some other, better location. But when it does the opposite, it moves to the opposite...

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 12
## PAGE 373

> ...[the Creator] established a life within it; this is the very justice of the gods who hold Olympus, O child and young man <note>In Plato's *Laws*, this is addressed to a hypothetical young man who believes the gods do not care about human behavior.</note> who thinks yourself neglected by the gods: that he who becomes worse moves toward the worse souls, and he who becomes better moves toward the better souls, both in life and in every kind of death, to suffer and to do what is fitting for like to experience from like. 

> This is a justice which neither you nor any other unfortunate soul shall ever boast of escaping. It is the justice which those who have appointed it have ranked above all others, and which must be most carefully observed. For you will never be neglected by it. You are not so small that you can hide in the depths of the earth, nor so high that you can fly up into heaven. You shall pay the fitting penalty to these [powers], whether you remain here on earth, or have departed to Hades, or have been transported to an even more savage place than these. 

> The same logic applies to those whom you have seen rising from small beginnings to great power, having committed unholy deeds or some such thing; you thought they had become happy from being wretched, and as if in a mirror <note>original: *en katoptrois* — Plato uses the image of a mirror to describe how we mistakenly perceive the lives of the wicked as successful.</note>, you thought their actions showed the total neglect of the gods, because you did not know how their final end contributes to the whole. You seem to think, O most courageous man, that there is no need to know this; yet he who does not know it could never see the pattern of life, nor be able to contribute an account of life regarding happiness or miserable fortune. If this [Athenian Stranger] and all our council of elders here convince you of these things regarding the gods—namely, that you do not know what you are talking about—God himself would be helping you well. But if you still require an argument from us as we speak, listen to the third point, if you have any sense at all.

The meaning of these things, even if not the exact words, was laid down long ago in the Hebrew oracles <note>original: *hebraion logiois* — referring to the Old Testament scriptures.</note> in the briefest manner, the thought being contained in a few words. For the phrase, *you are not so small that you can hide in the depths of the earth, nor so high that you can fly up into heaven*, is similar to what is found in David <note>referring to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> who expresses the same sentiment: *Where shall I go from your spirit? And from your face, where shall I flee? If I go up into heaven, you are there. If I go down into Hades, you are present. If I should take wings and dwell in the furthest parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me.* <note>Original Greek quotes Psalm 139:7-10 (138 in the Septuagint).</note> 

Moreover, *the heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.* <note>Psalm 19:1.</note> And again in Isaiah: *Lift up your eyes on high and see: who revealed all these things?* <note>Isaiah 40:26.</note> And the passage: *For from the greatness and beauty of created things, the Creator is seen by analogy.* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 13:5.</note> And also: *For his invisible things since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and divinity.* <note>Romans 1:20.</note> 

Furthermore, the sentiment: *I was envious of the lawless, seeing the peace of sinners* <note>Psalm 73:3.</note>, seems to me to have been paraphrased by Plato in the passage: *The same logic applies to those whom you have seen rising from small beginnings to great power, having committed unholy deeds or some such thing; you thought they had become happy from being wretched.* 

As for the rest of what is said similarly to these, Plato took them from the Hebrew oracles and set them out at greater length in his interpretation. You would find each point in detail if you examined them accurately, agreeing with the Hebrew writings. By "Hebrew words," I mean not only the oracles of Moses, but also those of the men beloved of God who came after Moses—whether prophets or even the Apostles of our Savior—whose harmony of doctrines deservedly grants them all the same title.
