» For the one who cares for the universe <note>original: *tou to pan epimeloumenou* — referring to Divine Providence</note> with a view to the preservation and excellence of the whole, all things are ordered together. Each part, according to its power, experiences and does what is fitting for it. Over these parts, rulers have been appointed for even the smallest affections and actions, having worked out the final goal down to the furthest division. 

» One of these parts is yours, O stubborn man <note>original: *o schetlie* — a term of mild rebuke for someone who doubts the gods</note>, which contributes to the whole, always looking toward it, even though it is very tiny. But it has escaped your notice regarding this very thing: that all "becoming" <note>original: *genesis* — the process of birth and physical change</note> occurs for the sake of that whole, so that the existence of the life of the universe may be happy; it does not happen for your sake, but you for its sake. 

» For every physician and every skilled craftsman <note>original: *demiourgos* — here meaning a professional creator</note> works all things for the sake of the whole, aiming at what is best for the common good. He crafts the part for the sake of the whole, and not the whole for the sake of the part. But you are indignant, because you do not know how what is best for you happens to coincide with the whole and with yourself, according to the power of our common origin. 

» Since a soul is always joined to a body—sometimes one, sometimes another—and undergoes all sorts of changes through itself or through another soul, no other task is left to the divine Draught-player <note>original: *petteutē* — a player of a board game similar to checkers or chess. Plato uses this as a metaphor for God moving souls across the 'board' of the universe.</note> except to move the character that is becoming better to a better place, and the worse to a worse place, according to what is fitting for each, so that they may receive their proper lot. 

» In what way do you mean? I think I can explain it in a way that suggests the ease of God's care for all things. If one were to always look at the whole and reshape everything—for example, making living water out of fire, rather than many things out of one or one out of many, which have shared in a second or third generation—the transformation of the cosmic order would be infinite. But now, there is a wonderful ease for the one who cares for the whole. 

» How so? Like this. Since our King <note>original: *ho basileus* — God</note> perceived that all our actions are living, and that there is much virtue in them and much vice, and that the soul and body are indestructible but not eternal (like the gods of traditional law)—for there would never be a "becoming" of living beings if either of these were destroyed—and since He realized that the nature of the soul that is always beneficial is good, while the evil is harmful—seeing all this, He devised where each of the parts should be placed so that virtue might conquer and vice be defeated in the whole, in the easiest and best way possible. 

» He has devised a plan for the whole: what kind of person becomes what, what seat they must occupy, and in what places. But He left the causes of the specific nature of this "becoming" to the wills of each of us. For in whatever way one desires, and whatever kind of soul one has, that is almost always the kind of person each of us becomes. 

» That is likely. Therefore, all things that share in soul change, having the cause of change within themselves. As they change, they are moved according to the order and law of destiny. When the changes of character are minor, they move along the surface of the region. But when they are greater and more unjust, they fall into the depths—those places called "the lower regions" <note>original: *katō legomena*</note>, which men call Hades and other such names, which they fear greatly and dream about while alive. 

» When they are released from their bodies, if the soul has undergone a great change toward vice or virtue through its own will and strong association—when it has associated with divine virtue, it becomes exceptionally like it and is moved to a holy place, being transferred entirely to some other better place. But when the opposite is true, it moves to the opposite...

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 12
### Page 373

» ...established a life within it; this is the judgment of the gods <note>original: *dikē theōn* — divine justice or law</note> who dwell on Olympus, O boy and young man who believes yourself neglected by the gods. As you become worse, you move toward worse souls; and as you become better, you go toward better souls, both in life and through all your deaths, to suffer and to do what is fitting for like to experience from like. 

» Neither you nor any other person who has become unfortunate will ever boast of having escaped this justice, which the ordainers of order have appointed above all others, and which must be followed with total caution. For you will never be overlooked by it. You are not so small that you might sink into the depths of the earth, nor so high that you might fly up into heaven. You will pay the fitting penalty to these [laws], whether you remain here, or pass through into Hades <note>original: *haidou* — the Greek underworld, used here to represent the state of the soul after death</note>, or are even carried away to a place even more savage than these. 

» The same reasoning applies to those whom you have seen becoming great from small beginnings, having committed unholy deeds or performed similar acts, and whom you thought had become happy from being miserable. You imagined that in their actions, as if in mirrors, you had seen the neglect of all the gods—not knowing their final outcome <note>original: *syntéleian* — the ultimate completion or consummation of a purpose</note>, and how it contributes to the whole. 

» But you, O most courageous of men, seem to think that knowing this is of no importance; yet without knowing it, one could never see even a pattern, nor be able to contribute a reason concerning life for the sake of happiness or an unfortunate fate. If this Clinia <note>Plato’s dialogue partner in the *Laws*</note> and all our council of elders here persuade you about the gods—that you do not know what you are saying—it would be well for you to reach an agreement with them. But if you still require more speech from us as we speak, listen to us on the third point, if you have any mind at all.

The sense of these things, even if not the exact words, was laid down long ago in the Hebrew oracles <note>original: *hebraiōn logiois* — the sacred scriptures of the Jews</note> most concisely, containing the meaning in a few words. For the statement: *You are not so small that you might sink into the depths of the earth, nor so high that you might fly up into heaven*, would be similar to what is said in David <note>The King to whom the Psalms are attributed</note> in the passage that goes: *Whither shall I go from your spirit? And from your presence, where shall I flee? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into Hades, you are present. If I should take my wings and settle in the farthest parts of the sea, even there your hand will guide me.* 

But also the saying: *The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the work of his hands.* And again in Isaiah: *Lift up your eyes on high, and see: who has revealed all these things?* And the saying: *For from the greatness and beauty of created things, the creator is seen by analogy.* And also: *For his invisible things since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made, even his eternal power and divinity.* 

Furthermore, the phrase: *I was driven to paths <note>original: *exēlasa epi dromois* — possibly a variant or interpretation of Psalm 73:2-3</note>, seeing the peace of sinners*, seems to me to have been paraphrased by Plato through the words: *The same reasoning applies to those whom you have seen becoming great from small beginnings, having committed unholy deeds... and whom you thought had become happy from being miserable.* 

And as for all other things spoken similarly to these, one would find that Plato's interpretation, laid out at length, was taken from the Hebrew oracles. For if you examine each part accurately, you would find it in agreement with the Hebrew writings. For I say "Hebrew" refers not only to the oracles of Moses, but also to those of the divinely favored men after Moses—whether the Prophets or even the Apostles of our Savior—whose harmony of doctrine would rightly justify them having this single title.

# This thirteenth book of the *Evangelical Preparation* contains the following:

How Plato refuted the absurdity of Greek theology. *From the Timaeus.*

Further, from the discourse *Epinomis*, on the same subjects.

Further, from the second book of the *Republic* on the same subjects, and concerning how God is not the cause of evils.

That the stories about the Greek gods contain nothing more than shameful myths; it was for refusing to believe these that the Athenians executed Socrates. *From the Euthyphro.*

From Numenius, *On the Secret Doctrines in Plato*, on the same subjects. <note>Numenius of Apamea was a 2nd-century philosopher who famously asked, "What is Plato but Moses speaking Attic Greek?"</note>

That one must not heed the opinion of the masses, nor abandon one's own principles <note>original: *proaireseōs* — one's moral choice or settled purpose</note> out of fear of death. *From the Crito.*

That one must not take revenge on those who choose to wrong us. *From the same.*

That one must not reject what has once been rightly decided, even if someone threatens death. This will be applied to those who, in times of persecution, renounce their piety. <note>original: *exomnymenous tēn eusebeian* — literally "swearing away" one's faith; Eusebius is drawing a direct line from Socrates's integrity to the Christian martyrs.</note>

What kind of internal state he will possess who, through fear of death, renounces his own principles.

That one should not flee from a death suffered for the sake of the truth. *From the Apology of Socrates.*

How one should honor the death of those who have departed this life with noble renown. *From Plato.*

How Aristobulus the Peripatetic <note>A Jewish philosopher of the 2nd century BCE who attempted to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note>, a member of the Hebrew nation among our predecessors, confesses that the Greeks drew their inspiration from Hebrew philosophy.

How Clement likewise [shows] that the fine things said by those outside the faith happen to harmonize with the doctrines held by the Hebrews. *From the fifth book of the Stromata (Miscellanies).* <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 AD) was a key Christian theologian who argued that Greek philosophy was a "pedagogue" leading to Christ.</note>

That not everything was said successfully by Plato; that it is not without reason that we reject his errors while we accept the oracles of the Hebrews.

That Plato was not entirely correct in the discourse he pursued regarding the intelligible realm, but the Hebrews were. <note>original: *noētōn* — the world of spiritual or intellectual realities as opposed to the physical world.</note>

That Plato did not hold correct opinions about the soul in all respects, unlike the Hebrews.

That according to Plato, the nature of the soul was not composed of both an impassible and a passible substance. *From the writings of Severus the Platonist, On the Soul.*

Concerning the heavens and the lights within them <note>the sun, moon, and stars</note>, that Plato did not hold entirely correct opinions. *From the Epinomis, the Timaeus, and the tenth book of the Laws.* These are things which Moses forbids us to worship, as Philo the Hebrew also explains.

What sort of things Plato incorrectly ordained concerning women. <note>Likely referring to Plato's views on the communal holding of wives in the *Republic*.</note>

What sort of things the same Plato ordained concerning disorderly love in the *Phaedrus*, against which Moses provides a counter-legislation.

Concerning the laws on homicide in Plato, which are unworthy of his great mind, and which must be compared against the laws of Moses.

<header>EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 13</header>

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'E' featuring intricate vine and leaf patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

Since it is the nature of the writings on this subject that Platonic philosophy, for the most part, interprets the sacred words of Moses and the Hebrews as if they had been translated into the Greek tongue, I come now both to provide what remains of the argument and to sift through what has been said by those among us regarding these topics. At the same time, I wish to clear away a cause for irrational defense, should someone accuse us, saying: "Why, if Moses and Plato philosophized in harmony, do we not follow Plato’s teachings but rather those of Moses?" This is especially relevant since it might be argued that we ought to adhere to the Greek rather than the "barbarian" <note>original: *barbaros* — a term used by Greeks for non-Greeks; here Eusebius uses it to refer to the Hebrew origin of the scriptures</note> when the doctrines are equal or nearly so. However, out of respect for the philosopher [Plato], we shall set aside the argument regarding our hesitation to address this for later. Let us first examine my own statements. Take up and read what opinion Plato held regarding the Greek theologians and poets, how he rejected all ancestral conceptions of the gods and exposed the absurdity within them.

### How Plato refuted the absurdity of Greek theology. *From the Timaeus.*

> Regarding the other divinities <note>original: *daimōn* — here referring to minor gods or spirits</note>, to speak and know their origin is a task greater than we can manage.
> <margin>»</margin> But we must believe those who have spoken before us, being the offspring of gods, as they claimed, and
> <margin>»</margin> who surely knew their own ancestors. It is therefore impossible to disbelieve the children of gods, even
> <margin>»</margin> though they speak without probable or necessary proofs. But as they claim to report
> <margin>»</margin> their own family matters, we must believe them in obedience to the law. Thus, according to them, let the
> <margin>»</margin> generation of these gods be as follows: Of Earth and Heaven were born
> <margin>»</margin> Oceanus and Tethys. From these were born Phorcys, Cronus, and Rhea, and all those with
> <margin>»</margin> them. From Cronus and Rhea were born Zeus, Hera, and all those whom we know are called
> <margin>»</margin> their siblings, and still others who were their offspring. 

By these words, Plato urges belief in the myths about the gods and the poets of the myths themselves, as they are "offspring of gods." First, it seems to me he is mocking the poets by saying they are descendants of the gods, as if the gods were not men and their nature was not similar to that of their descendants. He then immediately slanders the theologians—whom he called offspring of gods—by adding: <margin>»</margin> "even though they speak without probable or necessary proofs." And by adding <margin>»</margin> "as they claimed," he seems to be playing when he says, <margin>»</margin> "who surely knew their own ancestors," and "it is impossible to disbelieve the children of gods." Furthermore, he explicitly shows that saying these things is against his own judgment and solely for the sake of the laws, by admitting that one must believe them <margin>»</margin> "in obedience to the law." To see that this was his meaning, listen to how he slanders all the theologians in a bare and undisguised voice, striking them in the *Epinomis* with these words:

» "In the greater myths we see, we will also see the lesser ones. For there must be the same pattern, and the greater and lesser must have the same power. Or do you not think so?" "I do," he said.
» "But I do not understand which ones you call the greater."
» "Those which Hesiod and Homer told us," I said, "and the other poets. For these surely composed false myths for men, and have told and continue to tell them."
» "What kind," he asked, "and what do you find fault with in them?"
» "That which," I said, "should be blamed first and most of all, especially if someone tells a lie badly."
» "What is that?"
» "When someone portrays badly in speech the nature of gods and heroes, like a painter painting nothing like the objects he wished to resemble."
» "Indeed," he said, "it is right to blame such things. But how do we mean, and what kinds?"
» "First," I said, "the greatest lie about the greatest matters was told by the one who said that Uranus <note>The personification of the Sky and father of the Titans.</note> did what Hesiod says he did, and how Cronus <note>The son of Uranus who castrated his father.</note> in turn took vengeance on him. And the deeds of Cronus and his sufferings at the hands of his son <note>Referring to Zeus overthrowing his father, Cronus.</note>—even if they were true, I should not have thought they ought to be told so lightly to the thoughtless and the young, but rather kept in silence. If there were some necessity to tell them, they should be heard in secret by as few as possible, after sacrificing not a pig, but some great and difficult sacrifice, so that as few as possible might happen to hear."
» "And indeed," he said, "these stories are difficult."
» "And they must not be told, Adeimantus, in our city. Nor should a young listener be told that in committing the worst crimes he would be doing nothing strange, nor again in punishing an unjust father in every way, but that he would be doing what the first and greatest of the gods did."
» "No, by Zeus," he said, "it does not seem to me either that these are fit to be told."
» "Nor," I said, "the general idea that gods wage war against gods and plot and fight. For it is not true; if indeed those who are to guard the city for us are to consider it most shameful to be easily at enmity with one another. Far be it from us to tell them myths of Gigantomachies <note>original: *gigantomachia* — the mythical battle between the Olympian gods and the Giants.</note> or to embroider them, or of many other diverse enmities of gods and heroes toward their kinsmen and relatives. But if we are somehow to persuade them that no citizen was ever at enmity with another, and that this is not holy, such things rather should be told to children immediately, and to the old men and women, and as they grow older, the poets must be forced to compose stories close to these. But the binding of Hera by her son, and the throwing of Hephaestus by his father when he was about to defend his mother who was being beaten, and the battles of the gods <note>original: *theomachia* — conflicts between deities.</note> which Homer has composed, must not be admitted into the city, whether they are composed with allegories <note>original: *hyponoia* — literally 'under-thought,' referring to the hidden or allegorical meanings ancient scholars used to justify scandalous myths.</note> or without them. For the young person is not able to judge what is an allegory and what is not, but whatever opinions he takes in at that age tend to become hard to wash out and unchangeable..."

» ...purified; for which reasons, perhaps, we must make it our highest priority that the first things they <note>The children/citizens of the ideal city.</note> hear are myths most beautifully crafted to lead them toward virtue."
» "That makes sense," he said. "But if someone were to ask us what these myths are, and which stories we mean, what would we say?"
» And I said, "O Adeimantus, you and I are not poets at this present moment, but **founders of a city** <term>oikistai: the leaders responsible for establishing the laws and social structure of a new colony</term>. It is the duty of founders to know the **patterns** <term>typoi: the models or guidelines that must be followed</term> within which the poets must compose their myths, and from which they must not be allowed to deviate. However, the founders themselves do not need to compose the myths."
» "Correct," he said. "But this is the very point: what would these patterns for **theology** <note>literally "speech about the gods"</note> be?"
» "Something like this," I said. "God must always be represented as He truly is. Whether a poet portrays Him in epic verse, in lyric song, or in tragedy, He must be shown in His true nature."
» "He must indeed."
» "Now, is God not truly good, and must He not be described as such?"
» "Certainly."
» "Furthermore, nothing that is good is harmful, is it?"
» "I think not."
» "And does that which is not harmful do any harm?"
» "In no way."
» "And does that which does no harm do any evil?"
» "Neither does it do that."
» "And that which does no evil cannot be the cause of any evil?"
» "How could it be?"
» "What then? Is the good beneficial?"
» "Yes."
» "Then it is the cause of well-being?"
» "Yes."
» "The good, then, is not the cause of all things, but rather it is the cause of those things that are good, while it is **blameless** for things that are evil."
» "Entirely so," he said.
» "Therefore," I said, "since God is good, He cannot be the cause of all things, as the many <note>The common people or traditional poets.</note> say. Rather, He is the cause of only a few things for human beings, and for many things He is blameless. For our good things are far fewer than our evil ones. We must credit no one else as the cause of our blessings, but for our evils, we must seek out other causes, and not God."
» "You seem to me," he said, "to speak the absolute truth."

» *To whomsoever Zeus gives a mixture of both, he meets now with evil, now with good; but to whom he gives the unmixed lot of evils, a foul hunger drives him over the divine earth.*
» Nor should we accept that *Zeus is established as the steward of both our good and our evil.*
» And as for the violation of the oaths and treaties <note>The breaking of the truce in the Trojan War.</note> which **Pandarus** committed—if anyone says this was brought about through **Athena** and **Zeus**, we shall not praise it. » Furthermore, we must not let the young hear what **Aeschylus** says:

» But if someone composes a poem about the sufferings of **Niobe** <note>The queen of Thebes whose children were killed by Apollo and Artemis.</note>—which is the subject of these iambic verses—or the house of **Pelops**, or the **Trojan war**, or any such tale, we must either not let them say these are the works of a god, or if they are of God, they must find an explanation for them similar to the one we are seeking now. They must say that God did what was **just and good**, and that these people were **benefited by being punished**.
» But we must not let a poet say that those who are punished are miserable and that God was the one who made them so. If they say that the wicked were miserable because they required punishment, and that by paying the penalty they were being **helped by God**, then we may allow it.
» But as for saying that God, who is good, becomes the cause of evil to anyone—that we must fight against in every way. No one shall say this in his own city if it is to be well-governed, and no one shall hear it, whether young or old, whether in verse or in prose. For such stories are neither holy to tell, nor profitable for us, nor even consistent with themselves."

» "In the greater myths <term>mythois: traditional stories or legends</term> we shall see the lesser ones also. For the same **pattern** <term>typon: a model or standard</term> must apply, and the greater and the lesser must have the same effect. Or do you not think so?"
» "I do," he said. "But I do not quite understand which ones you call the greater."
» "Those," I said, "that **Hesiod** and **Homer** told us, and the other poets as well. For these men, I suppose, composed false myths and told them to people, and continue to tell them."
» "What kind of myths," he asked, "and what is it you find fault with in them?"
» "The very thing," I said, "that one ought to fault first and foremost, especially if the lie is not told well."
» "And what is that?"
» "Whenever someone poorly represents the nature of gods and heroes in their speech, like a painter who draws a picture that bears no resemblance to the subject he intended to paint."
» "Yes," he said, "it is right to find fault with such things. But how exactly do we mean this, and in what way?"
» "First of all," I said, "the man who told the greatest lie about the greatest of things did not lie well: I mean how **Uranus** <note>The personification of the Sky</note> did what Hesiod says he did, and how **Cronus** <note>The Titan son of Uranus</note> in turn took revenge on him. Even if the deeds of Cronus and the things he suffered at the hands of his son <note>Zeus</note> were true, I do not think they should be told so lightly to the young and the foolish; they should be kept in silence. If there were some necessity to tell them, they should be heard in secret <term>di' aporrhēton: as part of a mystery rite or secret initiation</term> by as few as possible, after they have sacrificed not a mere pig <note>The standard low-cost sacrifice for the Eleusinian Mysteries</note> but some great and rare sacrifice, so that the fewest possible people happen to hear them."
» "Indeed," he said, "these stories are troublesome."
» "And they must not be told, O Adeimantus, in our city. Nor should a young listener be told that by committing the worst crimes he would be doing nothing out of the ordinary, nor even if he were to punish an unjust father in every possible way; for he would only be doing what the first and greatest of the gods did."
» "By Zeus," he said, "it does not seem to me either that these things are fit to be told."
» "Nor," I said, "should it be told at all that gods wage war against gods, or plot against one another, or fight—for these things are not even true. This is especially important if those who are to guard our city must consider it the most shameful thing to hate one another easily. Far be it from us to tell them myths about the **Battles of the Giants** <term>Gigantomachia: the legendary war between the Olympian gods and the Giants</term> or to embroider such stories, or to tell of the many other various enmities of gods and heroes against their own kin and families. Rather, if we are to persuade them that no citizen ever hated another and that such a thing is unholy, these are the kinds of things that should be told to children by old men and women and as they grow older; and the poets must be compelled to compose stories along these lines. But **Hera** being bound by her son, and **Hephaestus** being hurled from heaven by his father for trying to help his mother when she was being beaten, and all the **Battles of the Gods** <term>Theomachia: myths where gods fight one another</term> that Homer composed—these must not be admitted into the city, whether they are composed with **allegorical meanings** <term>hyponoiais: "under-meanings" or hidden philosophical interpretations</term> or without them. For the young person is not able to judge what is allegorical and what is not; and whatever opinions one receives at that age tend to become difficult to wash away and unchangeable..."

» When and for whom is it useful, so as not to be worthy of hatred? Is it not useful against enemies,
» or for those so-called friends who, through madness or some folly, attempt to do something
» evil? In such cases, it becomes a useful medicine <note>original: *pharmakon*</note> for turning them away. And in the
» mythologies we were just discussing—because we do not know the truth of ancient events—
» do we not make the lie as much like the truth as possible, and so make it useful?"
» "We certainly do," he said. "For which of these reasons, then, would a lie be useful to God?
» Would He lie to make things 'like the truth' because He does not know ancient history? That would be
» ridiculous," he said. "Then there is no 'lying poet' in God?" "I think not." "Would He lie because
» He fears His enemies?" "Far from it." "Because of the folly or madness of His own people?" "But
» no one," he said, "who is foolish or mad is a friend of God." "Then there is no reason why God
» would lie?" "None." "Therefore, the demonic <note>The Greek *daimonion* refers to a divine power or spiritual being, rather than a malevolent 'demon.'</note> and the divine is altogether free from falsehood." "Completely,"
» he said. "God is then altogether simple and true in both deed and word; He does not
» change Himself, nor does He deceive others—neither by visions, nor by words, nor
» by the sending of signs, whether one is awake or in a dream." "So it seems
» to me as well," he said, "now that you say it." "Do you agree then," he said, "(that this is our
» second pattern) for speaking and writing about the gods: that they are not sorcerers who transform
» themselves, nor do they mislead us with lies in word or deed?" "I agree." "While we praise many

» her wedding,

> » Dwelt upon my happy offspring,
> » Untouched by sickness, living long lives.
> » Telling of all things, he sang a song of praise
> » For my god-favored lot, gladdening my heart.

> » Brimming with the prophetic art, was free of falsehood.
> » But he, the very one who sang, the one present at the feast,
> » The one who said these things—he is the very one who slew
> » My son."

» Guardians are to be god-fearing and divine, as far as it is possible for a human

<meta>This page continues the comparison between Platonic philosophy and Hebrew Scripture. Eusebius is arguing that Plato’s concept of the Divine—as inherently good, the author only of good, and immutable—aligns perfectly with the books of Moses and the Prophets, in contrast to the "mythologies" of the Greeks.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS #

-> G ii <-

...neither regarding divine angels, nor concerning the god-beloved men, do they [the Hebrew scriptures] contain anything similar to our mythologies. The pattern set out by Plato—that since God is good, all things created by Him are also such—is found there as well. Regarding each of the works of creation, the wonderful Moses adds:

> "And God saw that it was good."
> And concluding the whole account of all things, he says: "And God saw all things that He had made, and behold, they were very good." It is a doctrine of the Hebrews that God is not the cause of evils. Indeed, "God did not make death, nor does He delight in the destruction of the living. For He created all things that they might exist, and the generative powers of the world are wholesome." <note>These quotes are from the Book of Wisdom 1:13–14, which Eusebius attributes to the Hebrew tradition.</note> But "through the envy of the devil, death entered into the world." Therefore, God is introduced by the prophet speaking to one who has stripped himself bare of virtue through his own choice: "I planted you as a fruitful vine, entirely true; how then have you turned into bitterness, O strange vine?" <note>Quoting Jeremiah 2:21.</note> If it should be said anywhere that "evils" happen to the wicked from God, this must be understood equivocally <term>homonymously: where the same word is used for different concepts</term>, as referring to punishments. Since God is good, He is said to bring these not for the harm of those punished, but for their benefit and profit. It is just as medical treatments are thought to bring "evils" for the salvation of the sick, in the form of painful and bitter remedies. Therefore, in the Scripture where it is said that "evils" are brought upon men by God, one must apply Plato's reasoning: that God worked what is just and good, and that these "gloomy" events, though considered "evils" by the senses, come upon those who deserve them. They are benefited by being punished, not only according to the philosopher but also according to the Hebrew Scriptures, which say: "For whom the Lord loves, He disciplines; and He scourges every son whom He receives." <note>Quoting Proverbs 3:12, also cited in the New Testament Hebrews 12:6.</note> Thus, those undergoing punishment are wretched, but God is not the author of these things. We must not allow the poet to say otherwise. But if they say they were wretched because they needed punishment, and that by undergoing it they were benefited by God, that may be allowed. However, we must fight in every way against the claim that God, who is good, is the cause of evil to anyone. Furthermore, regarding the fact that God does not change, the Hebrew prophecy teaches this from the person of God: "For I am the Lord your God, and I have not changed." <note>Quoting Malachi 3:6.</note> And in his divine song <note>original: *theologia*</note>, David cries out: "They all shall grow old like a garment, and like a cloak You shall fold them, and they shall be changed. But You are the same, and Your years shall not fail." <note>Quoting Psalm 102:26–27.</note>

If the Hebrew accounts ever introduce the Word <term>Logos: the Divine Reason or Word of God</term> of God in human form and shape among those to whom He appeared, it must be stated that He does not turn and change after the manner of our [Greek] myths. He does not appear like the gods who come by night in the likeness of many animals and all sorts of phantoms. Rather, as Plato himself says it is sometimes necessary for the benefit of friends—whenever through some madness or folly they attempt to do something evil—then the approach of God to men becomes a useful medicine <note>original: *pharmakon*</note> to turn them away. Since, then, of all living beings on earth, none was more beloved by God than man—being kindred and closely related to the Word of God, by whom the rational nature of his soul was crafted—it is fitting that the Heavenly Word, caring for man as a beloved creature, is said to have come for the healing of our nature. For man had succumbed to a strange disease and madness, such that he no longer knew God as Father, nor the true essence of his own intellectual nature, nor the Providence <term>pronoia: the protective care of God</term> of God which preserves the universe. Rightly, then, as He came to a creature that was, as it were, near to Himself, because...

<summary>Eusebius argues that both Plato and the Hebrew Scriptures agree that God is the source only of good and is immutable. He explains that any "evils" or human-like appearances of the Divine Word are actually medicinal interventions intended to heal humanity's spiritual ignorance.</summary>

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL Book 13 #

They say that the Savior also revealed the things concerning the gods, yet certainly not according to the private nature of each, nor as if he saw people being deceived; rather, he preserved both characters—the invisible and the visible. For in one way it was for the sake of truth, and in another, being the true Word <note>original: *Logos*</note> of God, he was not a deceiver, nor did he mislead through melodies. In this way, it seemed right even to Plato that the Divine is without falsehood. 
» "God, therefore, who is the Word, being entirely simple and true, neither changes himself in deed or word, nor deceives others, neither by visions, nor by words, nor by the sending of signs, neither when they are awake nor in their dreams." <note>Quoting Plato’s *Republic* II, 382e. Eusebius adds the word "Word" (*Logos*) to Plato's text to align it with Christian theology.</note> All such things as men have attempted for the sake of the healing and salvation of rational souls, he truly accomplished through the man he took up <note>Refers to the Incarnation, the human nature of Christ</note>, by means of what appeared, bestowing upon us all friendship and a return to his own Father through the knowledge of God and true piety proclaimed by him. 
» "Such are our teachings. But if they say otherwise, we shall be angry and not grant them permission, nor shall we allow teachers to use such stories for the education of the young, if our guardians are to become god-fearing and divine." This seemed to the philosopher to be the best course.

» ...then he expressed his displeasure with it <note>The city’s traditional mythology</note>, and as an accuser [he cited] their factions against one another, and regarding their children, on the one hand their intermixing <note>A reference to myths involving incestuous relationships among the gods</note> and on the other hand their being eaten <note>A reference to myths like that of Cronus devouring his children</note>, and in return for these, their sufferings: the wedding songs, and brothers singing hymns to brothers, and other such things. Since he would not have preferred to live rather than tell the truth, yet he saw that he who is hard of hearing through arrogance <note>original: *hyperopsian dusēkooton*</note> is deaf to both life and truth, he placed the lack of contemplation <note>original: *atheōrian*</note> in those rumors, being an arrogant man and a fool <note>original: *koalemon* — a blockhead or a simpleton</note>, and whoever else speaks poorly of the gods. ### That one must not pay attention to the opinions of the many, nor change one's own purpose for fear of death. From the *Crito*. ###

» My dear Crito, your zeal is of great value if it is joined with some correctness; but if not, the greater it is, the more troublesome it is. We must therefore consider whether these things should be done or not. For I am not only now, but always, the kind of person who obeys nothing else of mine except the reason <note>original: *logos*</note> which seems best to me upon reflection. The arguments which I used to speak in the past, I cannot now cast away just because this fortune <note>Referring to his imprisonment and death sentence</note> has befallen me. Instead, they appear much the same to me, and I honor and prize the same ones as before. Unless we have better things to say in the present, be well aware that I will not agree with you, not even if the power of the masses frightens us like children with "bugbears" <note>original: *mormoluttētai* — imaginary monsters or ghosts used by nurses to scare children into behaving</note>, threatening us with chains and deaths and the seizure of property. How then might we consider these things most fairly? If we first take up this argument which you mention regarding opinions—whether it was well-said in every case or not—that one should pay attention to some opinions and not to others. Or was it well-said before I had to die, but has now become clear that it was said merely for the sake of talk, but was in truth a game and nonsense? I desire, Crito, to examine in common with you whether the argument appears any different to me, now that I am in this position, or if it remains the same, and whether we shall let it go or obey it. It was said, I believe, in every case by those who think they are saying something—just as I was saying now—that of the opinions which men hold, some should be highly valued and others should not. By the gods, Crito, does this not seem well-said to you? For you, as far as human affairs go, are outside the danger of dying tomorrow, and the present calamity would not lead you astray. Consider then: does it not seem to you to be sufficiently stated that one ought not to honor all the opinions of men, but some and not others? Nor the opinions of everyone, but some and not others? What do you say? Is this not well-said? It is well-said. Therefore, should we honor the good opinions and not the wicked ones? Yes. And are not the good ones those of the wise, and the wicked ones those of the foolish? Certainly. Come then, how were such things stated? When a man is in training <note>original: *gymnazomenos*</note> and practicing this, does he pay attention to the praise and blame and opinion of every man, or only of that one who happens to be a doctor or a trainer <note>original: *paidotribēs* — a physical education instructor</note>? Only that one. Therefore, he should fear the blame and welcome the praise of that one man, and not those of the many? Clearly. In this way, then, he must act...

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 13 #

» "And must he not exercise, and also eat and drink, in whatever way seems right to the one master who possesses knowledge <note>original: *epaionti* — one who 'gets it' or has expertise</note>, rather than to all the others?" "That is so." "Well then, if he disobeys that one man, and dishonors his opinion and his praise, but honors the opinions of the many who have no knowledge, will he not suffer some harm?" "How could he not?" "And what is this harm, where does it lead, and into what part of the disobedient man does it strike?" "Clearly into the body, for it destroys that." "You speak well. Is it not the same then, Crito, with other things—so that we do not have to go through them all—and specifically concerning what is just and unjust, shameful and beautiful, good and bad, about which we are now deliberating? Should we follow the opinion of the many and fear it, or the opinion of the one, if there is someone with knowledge, whom we must respect and fear more than all others? If we do not follow him, we will corrupt and maim that part of us which is made better by justice but is destroyed by injustice. Or is there nothing to this?" "I think so, Socrates." "Come then, if we ruin that which is made better by health but destroyed by disease <note>the body</note>, by not obeying the opinion of those who know, is life worth living for us once it is ruined? This is surely the body, is it not?" "Yes." "So is life worth living for us with a wretched and ruined body?" "In no way." "But is life worth living for us when that part is ruined which injustice maims and justice benefits? Or do we consider that part of us—whatever it is—which is concerned with justice and injustice, to be less valuable than the body?" "In no way." "But more valuable?" "Much more." "Therefore, my best of friends, we must not care at all what the many will say of us, but only what the one who understands justice and injustice says—the one, and Truth itself. So, in the first place, you were not introducing the matter correctly when you suggested we should care about the opinion of the many regarding justice, beauty, goodness, and their opposites."

And the Divine Word also says: "You seek the glory that comes from men, and you do not seek the glory that comes from the only One." <note>A paraphrase of John 5:44</note> Therefore, we also act rightly in our struggles for the sake of piety, not looking at what the many will say to us, but at what the Will is: the one Word of God. Once we have chosen this by judgment, it is fitting to remain in it just as before, and not to change, even if the power of the many tries to frighten us like children with 'bogeymen' <note>original: *mormoluttētai* — to scare with terrifying masks or ghosts; Eusebius likens the threats of persecutors to childhood monsters</note>. Such were those among the Hebrews of old who shone forth in martyrdom.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Crito as preserved by Plato, which Eusebius uses to demonstrate the "preparatory" nature of Greek philosophy for Christian ethics. The previous page discussed the health of the soul versus the body; here, the focus shifts to the refusal to retaliate and the duty to uphold one's agreements with the Law.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS #

» "Since one must never do wrong, it is clearly never right. Nor indeed, Crito, should one do evil <note>original: *kakourgein* — to act wickedly or cause harm</note> in return, or should one? No, indeed, Socrates. Nor is it right to return evil when suffering evil, as the many say—is it right or not? Not at all. For doing evil to people is no different from doing wrong. You speak truly. Therefore, one must neither return a wrong, nor do evil to any human being, no matter what one suffers from them. But look, Crito, in agreeing to these things, take care that you do not agree against your own belief. For I know that only a few people believe these things, or ever will. For those who hold this view and those who do not, there is no common counsel. Instead, they must inevitably look down upon one another when they see each other's deliberations. Consider then, very carefully, whether you share this view and agree with me, and let us begin our deliberation from this point: that it is never right to do wrong, nor to return a wrong, nor to defend oneself against suffering evil by returning evil in kind. Or do you withdraw, and not share in this starting point? For my part, I have long held this view, and I hold it still. But if you have decided otherwise, speak and teach me. If you stand by our previous points, listen to what follows. I stand by them and I agree with you. Then speak. I say then, or rather I ask: should a man do what he has agreed with someone to be just, or should he act with deceit?" "He should do it." "Then it follows that we must not return evil for evil to anyone." And also: "Bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat and persecute you, so that you may become sons of your Father in heaven, who makes his sun rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust" <note>Eusebius here seamlessly weaves Matthew 5:44-45 into the Platonic dialogue to show their "agreement."</note>; and further: "Being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we endure; being slandered, we appeal" <note>1 Corinthians 4:12-13</note>. These things are also found in the Holy Scriptures brought to us. And the prophet among the Hebrews also says: "If I have repaid with evil those who repaid me with evil" <note>Psalm 7:4</note>. And again: "With those who hate peace, I was peaceful" <note>Psalm 120:7</note>.

» "...but you left it even less than the lame, the blind, and the other disabled citizens. So exceptionally did this city and we, the Laws, please you above all other Athenians—for clearly, to whom would a city be pleasing without laws? But now, will you not stand by your agreements? You will if you listen to us, Socrates.

->What kind of character will he possess, who, through the fear of death, swears away his own principles?<-

» Anyone who is a corrupter of the laws would surely be seen as a corrupter of young and foolish men. Will you then flee from well-governed cities and the most orderly men? And if you do this, will life be worth living for you? Or will you approach them and have the face to carry on—saying what, Socrates? The same things you said here: that virtue <note>original: *arete* — moral excellence or "goodness"</note> and justice are of the highest value to mankind, along with customs and the laws? And do you not think the 'affair of Socrates' <note>the Laws are speaking of Socrates' reputation and his life's work as a public spectacle</note> will appear disgraceful? One must certainly think so. 

» But you will depart from these places and go to Thessaly <note>Thessaly was regarded by Athenians as a frontier land of heavy drinking, lawlessness, and "rough" living—the opposite of orderly Athens</note> to Crito’s friends. For there, indeed, is the greatest disorder and licentiousness; and perhaps they would gladly listen to you telling how ridiculously you ran away from prison, wrapping yourself in some disguise—either putting on a peasant's leather skin or some other outfit escapees usually wear—and altering your appearance. 

» Will no one point out that you, an old man with likely very little time left to live, dared to cling so greedily to life by transgressing the highest laws? Perhaps no one will, if you do not annoy anyone. But if you do, Socrates, you will hear many things unworthy of yourself. You will live by fawning upon all men and being a slave—doing what, exactly? Feasting in Thessaly? As if you had traveled all the way to Thessaly just for a dinner party! 

» And those famous arguments of yours about justice and the rest of virtue—where will they be then? But perhaps you wish to live for the sake of your children, so that you may bring them up and educate them? What then? Will you take them to Thessaly and raise them there, making them foreigners so that they may 'benefit' from that as well? Or will they be better reared and educated here while you are alive, even if you are not with them, because your friends will care for them? Will they care for them if you go to Thessaly, but not if you go to Hades? <note>Hades: the Greek Underworld or the realm of the dead</note> If those who claim to be your friends are of any use at all, you must believe they will care for them.

» No, Socrates, be persuaded by us who nurtured you. Do not value children, or life, or anything else more than justice, so that when you arrive in Hades, you may have all these things to say in your defense to the rulers there. For it is clear that doing this is neither better, nor more just, nor more holy for you or any of your friends here, nor will it be better for you when you arrive there. 

» As it stands, if you depart, you depart having been wronged—not by us, the Laws, but by men. But if you escape in such a disgraceful way, returning wrong for wrong and evil for evil, breaking your own covenants and agreements with us, and doing harm to those you should least of all—yourself, your friends, your fatherland, and us—then we shall be angry with you while you live, and there, our brothers, the Laws in Hades, will not receive you kindly, knowing that you attempted to destroy us to the best of your ability."

<summary>In this concluding portion of the Crito dialogue, the Laws warn Socrates that escaping his death sentence would be a hypocritical act of cowardice that would render his philosophical teachings meaningless and anger the divine authorities of the afterlife.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Crito, Laws of Athens, Thessaly, Hades, social contract, justice, virtue, integrity, civil disobedience, afterlife</keywords>

### That one ought not to flee death for the sake of truth; from the *Apology of Socrates*. ###

» I. Perhaps someone might say: “Are you not then ashamed, O Socrates, of having followed such a pursuit <note>original: *epitēdeuma* — a way of life or set of practices</note> from which you now run the risk of dying?” To this man, I would give a just answer: You do not speak well, sir, if you think a man—who is of even the slightest use—ought to calculate the risk of living or dying. Instead, he should consider only this one thing when he acts: whether his actions are just or unjust, and whether they are the deeds of a good man or a bad one.

» For by your logic, all the demigods who died at Troy would be counted as worthless, especially the son of Thetis <note>the hero Achilles</note>. He so despised danger in comparison to enduring disgrace that when his mother (a goddess) spoke to him as he was eager to kill Hector, she said something like this, I believe: “My son, if you avenge the murder of your companion Patroclus and kill Hector, you yourself will die; for immediately,” she said, “after Hector, your own fate is prepared.” But when he heard this, he made light of death and danger, fearing much more to live as a coward and to fail to avenge his friends. He said, “Let me die immediately after I have inflicted justice on the wrongdoer, so that I do not remain here as a laughingstock, beside the curved ships, a useless burden upon the earth.” <note>Socrates is quoting Homer's *Iliad* here to show that even the greatest heroes preferred death to dishonor</note> 

» Do you think he gave a thought to death or danger? For this is how it is in truth, O men of Athens: wherever a man has stationed himself, believing it to be best, or wherever he has been stationed by a commander, there, as it seems to me, he must remain and face danger, calculating neither death nor anything else before disgrace. 

» I would have acted strangely indeed, O men of Athens, if—when the commanders you chose to lead me stationed me at Potidaea, at Amphipolis, and at Delium <note>these were three major battles of the Peloponnesian War in which Socrates served as a heavy infantryman (hoplite)</note>—I remained where they stationed me, just like anyone else, and risked death; but when God stationed me (as I thought and believed) to live as a philosopher, examining myself and others, I were then to abandon my post because I feared death or any other thing. 

» That would be strange indeed, and then truly someone might justly bring me into court for not believing that gods exist, because I would be disobeying the oracle <note>referring to the Delphic Oracle's statement that no one was wiser than Socrates</note>, fearing death, and thinking I was wise when I was not. For to fear death, O men, is nothing other than to think one is wise without being so; for it is to think one knows what one does not know. No one knows whether death might actually be the greatest of all goods for mankind, yet they fear it as if they knew for certain that it is the greatest of evils. 

» And yet, how is this not that most reprehensible ignorance: thinking that one knows what one does not know? In this matter, O men, I perhaps differ from most people; and if I were to say I am wiser than someone in anything, it would be in this: that as I do not know enough about the things in Hades <note>the Greek underworld/afterlife</note>, so I also do not think that I know. But I do know that it is evil and shameful to do wrong and to disobey one's superior, whether god or man. Therefore, compared to the evils that I know to be evil, I will never fear or flee from things that I do not know—which may even turn out to be good. 

» So, even if you were to let me go now, being unconvinced by Anytus <note>one of Socrates' main accusers</note>—who said that either I should not have been brought here in the first place, or that since I have been, it is impossible not to put me to death, telling you that if I escape, your sons will all be utterly corrupted by practicing what Socrates teaches—if you were to say to me: “Socrates, for now we will not listen to Anytus, but we will let you go, on this condition...

<summary>Socrates argues that a man of virtue must prioritize justice over survival, comparing his philosophical mission from God to a soldier's duty and dismissing the fear of death as a form of false wisdom.</summary>

<keywords>Socrates, Plato, Apology, death, duty, Achilles, Athens, philosophy, justice, virtue, divine command</keywords>

## GOSPEL PREPARATION BOOK 13 ##

» [acquit you,] on the condition that you no longer spend time in this investigation, nor practice philosophy. But if you are caught still doing this, you shall die. If you should then acquit me, as I said, on these terms, I would say to you: "I respect and love you, men of Athens, but I shall obey God rather than you. And as long as I draw breath and am able, I shall not cease from practicing philosophy, and from exhorting and showing the way to whichever of you I happen to meet, saying what I usually say." And after a few words, he adds: "Let us consider it in this way also, that there is great hope that death is a good thing. For to die is one of two things: either it is like being nothing, and the dead person has no perception of anything; or, according to what is said, it happens to be a certain change <note>original: *metabolē* — a turning point or transformation</note> and a migration of the soul from this place here to another place. And if there is no perception, but it is like a sleep when one who is sleeping sees not even a dream, death would be a wonderful gain.

» For I think that if someone had to pick out that night in which he slept so soundly that he saw no dream, and compare the other nights and days of his life to that night, and having examined them, had to say how many days and nights he lived better and more pleasantly than that night in his own life—I think that not only a private citizen, but even the Great King <note>The King of Persia, used here as the ultimate standard of worldly wealth and power</note> would find these days easy to count compared to the other days and nights. If, then, death is such a thing, I for one call it a gain. For all time seems to be no more than a single night. 

» But if, on the other hand, death is like a journey <note>original: *apodemēsai* — to go abroad or travel away from home</note> from here to another place, and the things said are true—that all the dead are indeed there—what greater good could there be than this, O judges? For if someone arriving in Hades, having been set free from those who claim to be judges here, will find the true judges, who are said to judge there—Minos, Rhadamanthus, Aeacus, and Triptolemus—and all the other demigods who were righteous in their own lives, would that journey be a paltry thing? Or again, to be with Orpheus and Musaeus and Hesiod and Homer, how much would any of you give for that? 

» For I, indeed, am willing to die many times if these things are true. For to me, my stay there would be wonderful, whenever I happened upon Palamedes and Ajax the son of Telamon, or anyone else of the ancients who died because of an unjust judgment; comparing my own sufferings to theirs, as I think, would not be unpleasant. And indeed, the greatest thing would be to spend time examining and questioning those there, just like those here: who among them is wise, and who thinks he is, but is not." And before these things, it was said: "One must obey God rather than men." <note>Eusebius here quotes Acts 5:29 to show the harmony between Socrates and the Apostles</note> And, "Do not fear those who kill the body, but are unable to kill the soul." <note>A reference to Matthew 10:28</note> And to know that "if our earthly house of this tent be dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens;" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 5:1</note> and that "being away from the body, we are at home with the Lord," <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 5:8</note> who has promised to all those who have hoped in Him that they shall rest in the bosoms of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, along with the other prophets and righteous men beloved by God among the Hebrews, spending a long eternity in a blessed life.

->How we ought to regard the death of those who have departed life with good fame.<-

For of those who die on a campaign, whoever ends his life after having distinguished himself, is he not first—

>> “Shall we say then that they belong to the golden race?” “By all means.” “But shall we not believe Hesiod, that when any of this race die, they become ‘holy spirits <note>original: *daimones* — in Greek thought, these were not "demons" but intermediary divine beings or the souls of the golden age</note> dwelling on earth, noble, averters of evil, and guardians of mortal men’?” “We shall indeed believe him.” “Having then inquired of the god how we ought to rank these godlike and divine men, and with what distinction, shall we not bury them in the way he directs?” “How could we do otherwise?” “And for all time to come, we shall serve and worship <note>original: *proskunēsomen* — to show reverence or prostrate oneself</note> at their tombs, as if they had become spirits. And we shall observe these same customs whenever anyone who has been judged to have lived an exceptionally good life dies of old age or in any other way.” These things are also fitting to say regarding the death of those beloved by God, whom you would not be wrong to call the "soldiers of true piety" <note>Eusebius is drawing a parallel between the Greek "daimones" and the Christian martyrs</note>. Hence it is our custom to visit their tombs and offer our prayers beside them, and to honor their blessed souls, since these things are reasonably done by us. But enough of these matters from the writings of Plato. A lover of the beautiful might find even more than this in his works that agrees with our doctrines, and perhaps in other philosophers as well. But since Clement <note>referring to Clement of Alexandria</note> has also touched upon this same subject with us in a comparative way, it seems good to me to also examine the labors he produced on these things. But first, set forth the words of Aristobulus, the philosopher of Hebrew descent, which run as follows:

### How Aristobulus the Peripatetic, from among us, acknowledged that the Greeks ###
### derived their inspiration from the philosophy found among the Hebrews. ###
### From the writings of Aristobulus addressed to King Ptolemy. ###

“It is evident that Plato followed our system of law, and it is clear that he carefully studied each of the things contained within it. For it had been translated by others before Demetrius of Phalerum <note>Demetrius was the librarian at Alexandria; Aristobulus is claiming an even earlier translation of the Torah existed</note>, before the supremacy of Alexander and the Persians—both the accounts of the departure <note>The Exodus</note> of our fellow citizens, the Hebrews, from Egypt, and the fame of all the things that happened to them, their conquest of the land, and the detailed explanation of the entire Law. Thus, it is quite clear that the aforementioned philosopher took many things from it. For he was a man of great learning <note>original: *polymathēs*</note>, just as Pythagoras also transferred many of our traditions into his own system of doctrines. But the complete translation of all the parts of the Law was made in the time of the king surnamed Philadelphus <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus, 3rd century BCE</note>, your ancestor, who displayed a greater ambition for such things, while Demetrius of Phalerum managed the business.” Then, after saying some intervening things, he adds: “For one must take the ‘divine voice’ not as a spoken word, but as the arrangement of works, just as Moses has spoken of the entire creation of the world in our Law as the ‘words of God.’ For he says continually regarding each part: ‘And God said, and it was done.’ And it seems to me that Pythagoras, Socrates, and Plato, having carefully studied all things, followed him in this, saying that they ‘hear the voice of God’ while they were accurately contemplating the arrangement of the universe as having been made by God and being held together without ceasing. Furthermore, Orpheus, in poems concerning what he called the 'Sacred Account,' sets forth his views on the power that holds all things together—that they are created and that God is over all—in this way:

<margin>»</margin> "From Zeus let us begin, whom we men never leave
<margin>»</margin> Unspoken. Full of Zeus are all the streets,
<margin>»</margin> And all the marketplaces of men; full is the sea
<margin>»</margin> And the harbors; and in every way we all have need of God.
<margin>»</margin> For we are also his offspring <note>original: *tou gar kai genos esmen* — This famous line from Aratus's *Phaenomena* was later quoted by the Apostle Paul in his speech at the Areopagus in Acts 17:28</note>; and he, being kind to men,
<margin>»</margin> Gives favorable signs, and rouses the people to work,
<margin>»</margin> Reminding them of their livelihood. He tells when the soil is best
<margin>»</margin> For oxen and for mattocks. He tells when the seasons are favorable
<margin>»</margin> Both to plant trees and to cast all kinds of seeds."

I think it has been clearly shown that the power of God pervades all things, just as we have indicated by tracing the creative forces through all living things. For the essence of their thought is directed back to God, as we have stated. Therefore, we have introduced these points not without reason regarding the matters under investigation. For it is agreed among all philosophers that one must hold a holy opinion concerning God, which is exactly what our school <note>original: *hairesis* — meaning a choice or a school of thought; here referring to the Judeo-Christian tradition</note> most excellently commands. Indeed, our entire system regarding piety, justice, self-control, and the rest of the true virtues is established in the framework of the Law. Next, let no other things be chosen over these, but following them is the way God constructed the whole world as a single whole, and gave to us for rest, because of the hardships of our life, the Seventh Day <note>The Sabbath</note>. This might naturally be called the "first birth of light," in which all things are contemplated. This same concept might also be transferred to Wisdom; for all light comes from her. Indeed, some of those belonging to the Peripatetic school <note>The followers of Aristotle, who walked while they taught</note> have said that she holds the rank of a beacon. For those who follow her continuously will remain undisturbed throughout their entire life. But more clearly and more beautifully, one of our ancestors, Solomon, said that she <note>Wisdom/Sophia</note> existed before heaven and earth. This is in harmony with what was said before. 

As for what is clarified through the legislation—that God "rested" on this day—this does not mean, as some suppose, that God ceased to do anything; rather, it refers to His having established the order <note>original: *taxin*</note> of things, so as to have ordered them for all time. It signifies that in six days He made the heaven and the earth and all things in them, so that He might reveal the times and state the order of what takes precedence over what. For having ordered them, He thus maintains and transforms them. This day has been clarified for us by the Law for the sake of a sign, concerning the "seventh reason" <note>term: *logou* — here referring to the rational or divine principle inherent in the number seven</note> established within us, through which we have knowledge of human and divine affairs. Indeed, the entire world of living creatures and all growing things revolves in cycles of sevens. The word "Sabbath" is interpreted as "rest." It is clear that even Homer and Hesiod, having taken from our books, say it is a sacred day. Hesiod speaks thus:

-> How Clement likewise shows that what was well said [by the Greeks] is found to agree with the <-
-> doctrines of the Hebrews. From the fifth book of Clement’s Miscellanies <note>original: *Stromateis* — This title literally means "patchwork" or "tapestries," referring to Clement’s wide-ranging collection of thoughts</note>. <-

<margin>The following</margin> We must now add what follows, and more clearly demonstrate the ethical theft <note>original: *klopē* — Clement famously argued that Greek philosophers "stole" their best ideas from the older Hebrew prophets</note> from the barbarian <note>In this context, "barbarian" simply means non-Greek, specifically referring here to the Jewish tradition</note> philosophy. For the Stoics say that God is a body, and spirit in essence, just as they also consider the soul to be. You will find these things directly in the Scriptures. I do not dare to suggest you have fully grasped their allegories as the gnostic tradition <note>original: *gnōstikē paradosis* — Here referring to "true knowledge" or spiritual insight, rather than the Gnostic sect</note> hands them down, even if they show something clearly according to the wise wrestlers; but they remain. However, while some say that God pervades all of essence, we call him the Creator alone, and the Creator by the Word. The saying in the Book of Wisdom was brought before them: "She [Wisdom] reaches and moves through all things because of her purity" <note>A reference to Wisdom of Solomon 7:24</note>, since they did not understand that these things are said concerning the spiritual nature of the wisdom of God. And they speak of it so. But later, the philosophers—the Stoics, Plato, Pythagoras, and even Aristotle the Peripatetic—postulated principles, but not that "nothing" was the beginning. For they knew what is called "matter" <term>hylē: the fundamental substance of the universe</term>, which they called quality-less and formless; this is spoken of in relation to Plato's concept of "that which is not truly being." This was said most harmoniously. For knowing that there is truly one beginning, he says in the *Timaeus* in these very words: "Now then, let it be held by us thus: concerning the principle or principles of all things, or however it seems regarding these matters, we must not speak now, for no other reason than the difficulty of declaring our views according to the present mode of discussion." But that prophetic word declared it: "The earth was invisible and unformed" <note>A reference to the Septuagint translation of Genesis 1:2</note>, which provided them with the starting points for the concept of material essence. Indeed, the intrusion of "chance" and the "spontaneous" found in Epicurus resulted from his failure to follow the scripture which says, "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity" <note>Ecclesiastes 1:2</note>. And Aristotle went so far as to bring Providence down only as far as the moon, perhaps from this Psalm: "Lord, thy mercy is in heaven, and thy truth reaches unto the clouds" <note>Psalm 36:5 (LXX 35:6)</note>. For the revelation of mysteries concerning the presence of the Lord had not yet been revealed to the prophetic word. Furthermore, the punishments after death and the retribution through fire were stolen from the barbarian philosophy, both by the whole poetic Muse and by Greek philosophy. Plato, at least, in the final book of the *Republic*, says in these very words: "At that place, there were fierce men, fiery to look upon, standing by; and hearing the sound, they took some aside and led them away. But Aridaeus and others they bound hand and foot and head, threw them down and flayed them, and dragged them along the road outside, carding them upon thorns <term>asphalathoi: a thorny shrub, similar to gorse or brambles</term>." For these men...

<margin>»</margin> The fiery angels <note>original: *diapyroi aggeloi*</note> signify to him those who receive the unjust and punish them. For he
<margin>»</margin> says, "He who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flaming fire." <note>A reference to Psalm 104:4</note>
<margin>»</margin> It follows from these things that the soul is immortal. For that which is punished or disciplined
<margin>»</margin> must live in a state of sensation and will. See how Plato also knows of fire
<margin>»</margin> and rivers, and the depths of the earth, which is called Gehenna by the barbarians <note>Referring to the Hebrews; "barbarian" was the standard Greek term for any non-Greek culture</note>, 
<margin>»</margin> though he names it poetically as Tartarus, and mentions Cocytus <note>River of Wailing</note>, Acheron <note>River of Woe</note>, and Pyriphlegethon <note>River of Fire</note>,
<margin>»</margin> and such other places of punishment that lead to discipline and self-control. Regarding 
<margin>»</margin> those who are "little" or, according to the Scripture, the "least" <note>A reference to Matthew 18:10</note> among the angels who see God, 
<margin>»</margin> and also concerning the oversight that comes to us through the presiding angels, he 
<margin>»</margin> does not hesitate to write. Indeed, he says that all souls are assigned to their lives as if by lot,
<margin>»</margin> entering into their destiny in order. To each, a guardian spirit <note>original: *daimon* — in the Greek sense of a guiding spirit or destiny, not necessarily an evil demon</note> is sent as a protector 
<margin>»</margin> and companion for their life, and a fulfiller of their choices. Perhaps it was some such thing 
<margin>»</margin> that the divine sign <note>original: *daimonion*</note> hinted at to Socrates. Furthermore, having 
<margin>»</margin> received it from Moses, the philosophers dogmatically taught that the world was created. 
<margin>»</margin> For Plato has spoken of this in two ways: either that the world has a beginning of its generation
<margin>»</margin> as a composite, or that it came into being starting from some first principle, 
<margin>»</margin> being visible to humans and having a body. Again, when he says, "To find the maker 
<margin>»</margin> and father of this universe is a task," <note>A famous quote from Plato’s *Timaeus* 28c</note> he showed not only that the world was created, 
<margin>»</margin> but he also signifies that it came into being from Him, as if from the only-begotten <note>original: *monogenēs*</note> from the only One, 
<margin>»</margin> and from the one who truly exists. The Stoics also posit that the world was created. 
<margin>»</margin> Regarding the "Devil" so often mentioned by the barbarian philosophy—the ruler of 
<margin>»</margin> the demons—Plato says in the tenth book of the *Laws* that he is an "evil soul"
<margin>»</margin> in these very words: "As a soul manages and dwells in all things that move in every way, 
<margin>»</margin> must we not say it also manages the heavens? Only one soul? Or more? More—I shall answer 
<margin>»</margin> for you. Let us posit no fewer than two: one the beneficent, and the other capable 
<margin>»</margin> of working the opposite." Similarly, in the *Phaedrus*, he writes: "There are indeed 
<margin>»</margin> base evils, but some divinity <note>original: *daimon*</note> has mixed a momentary pleasure with most of them." 
<margin>»</margin> Also, in the tenth book of the *Laws*, he clearly shows what the Apostle [Paul] means when he says,

<margin>»</margin> writing something like this: "Since we have agreed among ourselves that the heaven is 
<margin>»</margin> full of many good things, and also of their opposites, and of more that are not good, we say 
<margin>»</margin> such a battle is immortal and requires a wondrous guard." Furthermore, he knows 
<margin>»</margin> both an intelligible world <term>Intelligible world: The *kosmos noētos*, or the realm of perfect abstract Forms that can only be grasped by the mind</term>, which the barbarian philosophy knows, and a sensible world; 
<margin>»</margin> the one being the archetype, the other the image of the beautiful pattern. 
<margin>»</margin> He associated the intelligible world with the Monad <note>The number one, representing unity and the divine</note>, and the

<margin>»</margin> called "marriage," being a generative number. In the Monad, He established an invisible heaven 
<margin>»</margin> and an invisible earth, and an intelligible light. For he says, "In the beginning

<margin>»</margin> leaves the "ideas" of living beings in the intelligible world, and fashions the sensible
