<margin>»</margin> ...earthly [tabernacle], as Plato calls the **body**. <note>original: *skēnos* — literally "tent" or "booth," a metaphor for the physical body used by both Plato and the Apostle Paul in 2 Corinthians 5:1</note> But the **rational soul** was breathed from above by
<margin>»</margin> God into the face. For they say that He established the **mind** as the governing part <note>original: *hēgemonikon* — the Stoic term for the "ruling faculty" of the soul</note>, 
<margin>»</margin> interpreting the entry of the soul into the molded form through the sensory
<margin>»</margin> organs as its "entrance." For this reason, man was made **according to the image and likeness of God.** <note>A reference to Genesis 1:26</note> For the **image of God** is the Divine and Royal **Word** <note>original: *Logos*</note>, the dispassionate man; and the image of the sensory image is the mind.
<margin>»</margin> In another place, taking up the concept of "likeness" by a different name, he called it **following God** <note>original: *hepesis tō theō*</note>, which is named the "middle path of attendance." For he says: *"You shall walk after the Lord your God, and keep His commandments."* <note>Deuteronomy 13:4</note> I believe these "followers" are the **servants of God**, namely all those who are virtuous.
<margin>»</margin> From this source, the **Stoics** have said that the goal of philosophy is **to live in accordance with nature**. **Plato**, however, calls it **likeness to God**, as is stated in the second book of the *Republic*. <note>Clement often attributes the "likeness to God" doctrine to the Republic, though its most famous definition is in the Theaetetus</note> **Zeno the Stoic**, having received this from Plato—who in turn received it from the **barbarian philosophy** <note>A Greek term for the Hebrew Scriptures</note>—says that all things belong to the good, who are friends to one another.
<margin>»</margin> For **Socrates** says in the *Phaedrus* that it is not fated for the evil to be a friend to the evil, nor for the good not to be a friend to the good. He demonstrated this strongly in the *Lysis* as well, showing that **friendship** could never exist in injustice and wickedness. And the **Athenian Stranger** <note>The main speaker in Plato’s *Laws*</note> says similarly that a deed is dear and a "follower" to God, and possesses one ancient principle: that **like is dear to like** when it is moderate, but immoderate things are dear neither to the immoderate nor to the moderate.
<margin>»</margin> **But God should be to us the measure of all things.** <note>Plato, *Laws* 716c; this is a direct rebuttal to the Sophist Protagoras, who said "Man is the measure of all things"</note> Then, moving further down, Plato adds: *"For every good man is like the good [God]. In this respect, being like God, he is entirely a friend both to the good and to God."* In the *Gorgias*, he reminds us of this again. At the end of the *Timaeus*, he says that one must become like the heavenly patterns according to our ancient nature.
<margin>»</margin> This **likeness** is the "goal" <note>original: *telos* — the ultimate aim or end-purpose of life</note> set before men by the gods as the best life, for both the present and the future time.
<margin>»</margin> Furthermore, he adds a few words about us being **brothers**, since we come from one God and one Teacher. Plato also appears to know this well somewhere, when he says: *"For all of you in the city are brothers,"* as we shall say to them in our storytelling. *"But God, in molding you, mixed **gold** into the generation of those among you capable of ruling, which is why they are most honored; and **silver** into the helpers; and **iron and bronze** into the farmers and other craftsmen."* <note>Plato’s "Noble Lie" from *Republic* 414-415</note>
<margin>»</margin> From this, he says, it is necessary to embrace and to love one another. These classes correspond to those characterized by **knowledge** <note>original: *gnōsis*</note> and those by **opinion** <note>original: *doxa*</note>.
<margin>»</margin> Perhaps he is divining this "eclectic" nature that yearns for knowledge—unless someone, assuming three types of natures as some have understood the "polities," describes them as: the **Jews**, to whom the silver belongs; the third [the Greeks]; and the **Christians**, in whom the **royal gold**—the **Holy Spirit**—has been mixed.
<margin>»</margin> Describing the life of Christians, he writes word-for-word in the *Theaetetus*: *"Let us speak of the leaders. For why should anyone speak of those who spend their time poorly in philosophy? These men, surely, do not even know the way to the marketplace, nor where the law court is, or the council chamber, or any other public assembly of the city. They neither see nor hear written laws and decrees. The rivalries of political clubs and meetings, or revelries with flute-girls—they do not even dream of participating in such things. Whether something has happened well or ill in the city, or what evil has come to someone from their ancestors, is more hidden from them than 'the measures of the sea' as the saying goes. And he does not even know that he does not know these things; for in reality, only his body lies in [the city]..."* <note>Plato, *Theaetetus* 173c-d. Clement is using Plato’s description of the "unworldly" philosopher as a template for the ideal Christian life.</note>

<summary>Clement of Alexandria argues that Plato’s concepts of the soul's divine origin, "likeness to God," and the "Noble Lie" regarding metals are borrowed from Hebrew scripture. He interprets Plato’s description of the unworldly philosopher in the Theaetetus as a prophetic description of the Christian life.</summary>

<margin>»</margin> ...on the **Hephaestus-wrought shield**, he describes a **creation of the world** <note>original: *kosmopoiia* — the ordering or making of the universe</note> according to **Moses**:
<margin>»</margin> **"In it he fashioned the earth, in it the heaven, in it the sea,"** he says,
<margin>»</margin> **"And in it all the constellations with which the heaven is crowned."** <note>Homer, *Iliad* 18.483–485</note> For the **Zeus** celebrated through poems and
<margin>»</margin> prose writings refers the concept back to **God**.
<margin>»</margin> Indeed, to speak from the dawn of thought, **Democritus** writes that a few of the men,
<margin>»</margin> stretching out their hands here to what we Greeks now call **"air,"** <note>original: *aër*</note> say that
<margin>»</margin> **Zeus** speaks all things, and knows all things, and gives and takes away, and is King of all.
<margin>»</margin> More musically, the Boeotian **Pindar**, being a **Pythagorean**, hands down that **"one is the 
<margin>»</margin> race of men and gods, and from one mother we both draw breath,"** <note>Pindar, *Nemean Odes* 6.1</note> referring to
<margin>»</margin> matter. And he calls the one **Creator** of these things the **"Master-Craftsman Father,"** who also 
<margin>»</margin> provides the means for progress toward divinity for those who have been judged worthy. 
<margin>»</margin> I pass over **Plato**, who clearly appears in his **Letter to Erastus and Coriscus** <note>original: *pros Eraston kai Kreittona* — though likely referring to the Sixth Letter of Plato</note> to reveal
<margin>»</margin> a **Father** and a **Son**, derived I know not how from **Hebrew voices**, yet expressing them 
<margin>»</margin> most clearly in his own words. Following these with a serious and not uncultured mind, 
<margin>»</margin> and with the education that is sister to such diligence, he swears by the **God who is Cause of all things**, 
<margin>»</margin> and by the **Lord who is Father of the Ruler and Cause**, whom you shall know if you 
<margin>»</margin> philosophize correctly. The speech in the ***Timaeus*** also calls the Creator **"Father,"** 
<margin>»</margin> saying: **"Gods of gods, of whom I am the Father and Creator of works."** <note>Plato, *Timaeus* 41a</note> And 
<margin>»</margin> so he says again: **"Around the King of all are all things, and for His sake are all things, and 
<margin>»</margin> He is the cause of all beautiful things. Second, He is around the second things, and third, 
<margin>»</margin> He is around the third things."** <note>Plato, *Second Letter* 312e</note> I personally understand this as nothing other than 
<margin>»</margin> an indication of the **Holy Trinity**. For the "third" refers to the **Holy Spirit**, and the "second" to the 
<margin>»</margin> **Son**, through whom all things were made according to the will of the Father. 
<margin>»</margin> The same author, in the tenth book of the ***Republic***, mentions the sacred story of **Er the son of Armenius**, 
<margin>»</margin> a Pamphylian by race, who is actually **Zoroaster**. Indeed, **Zoroaster** himself writes: 
<margin>»</margin> **"These things wrote Zoroaster the son of Armenius, a Pamphylian by race, who died in war 
<margin>»</margin> and learned from the gods all that I came to know in Hades."** Plato says this 
<margin>»</margin> **Zoroaster**, after lying on the funeral pyre for twelve days, returned to life. 
<margin>»</margin> Perhaps he is not hinting at the **resurrection**, but rather suggesting that the path for 
<margin>»</margin> souls toward their **ascension** was through the **twelve signs of the zodiac**. He also says the 
<margin>»</margin> same descent occurs back into birth. One must also suppose these things are meant 
<margin>»</margin> by the **Twelve Labors of Heracles**, after which the soul happens to find its guide out of 
<margin>»</margin> this world. We may also include **Empedocles**; this natural philosopher mentions the 
<margin>»</margin> beginning of all things as eventually undergoing a transformation into the **essence of fire**. 
<margin>»</margin> Most clearly **Heraclitus of Ephesus** holds this opinion, judging that while the cosmos 
<margin>»</margin> is eternal, that which is moved and carried along in the cosmic order is not different 
<margin>»</margin> from it in its state. But that it is eternal, being an eternally qualified world made of 
<margin>»</margin> all substance, he now makes plain, saying: **"This world, the same for all, neither god 
<margin>»</margin> nor man has made, but it always was, and is, and shall be: an ever-living fire, kindled 
<margin>»</margin> in measures and extinguished in measures."** <note>Heraclitus, Fragment 30</note> That he also taught it was 
<margin>»</margin> generated and subject to decay is shown by what follows: **"The turnings of fire: 
<margin>»</margin> first sea; and of sea, half is earth, and half is the fire-wind."** <note>Heraclitus, Fragment 31</note> For he means by 
<margin>»</margin> power that the **fire**, by the **Reason** <note>original: *Logos*</note> and **God** who governs all things, is 
<margin>»</margin> turned through air into moisture, which he calls the **sea**, acting as the **seed** of the 
<margin>»</margin> cosmic order. From this, again, arise earth and heaven and all they contain...

<margin>»</margin> ...following. How it [the universe] is again taken up and consumed by fire <note>original: *ekpyroutai* — the Stoic and Heraclitean concept of world-conflagration</note>, he clearly shows through

<margin>»</margin> as "sleep." The **Savior** himself says: **"Pray, and keep watch."** <note>Matthew 26:41</note> By these things you 
<margin>»</margin> practice how to live, and you attempt to separate the soul from the body. **Plato** 
<margin>»</margin> "divines" the **Lord’s Day** <note>The "eighth day" or Sunday, associated with the Resurrection</note> in the tenth book of the ***Republic*** 
<margin>»</margin> through these words: **"When seven days had passed for each of them in the meadow,** 
<margin>»</margin> **those who arise from there must journey on the eighth day, and arrive after four days."** 
<margin>»</margin> By **"meadow"** we must understand the fixed sphere of the stars, as a gentle place and 
<margin>»</margin> a place of rest, and the land of the holy. These "days" will be each movement of the seven 
<margin>»</margin> planets, which hurry toward the end of rest in all their productive craft. The 
<margin>»</margin> journey after the wandering stars leads to heaven, that is, the eighth movement and 
<margin>»</margin> day. He says the souls depart on the **"fourth day,"** showing the journey through the 
<margin>»</margin> four elements. But not only the **Hebrews** know the **seventh day** is holy, but the **Greeks** 
<margin>»</margin> also know it, according to which the whole world revolves, and all things that live and 
<margin>»</margin> grow are brought forth. **Hesiod** says this about it:

<margin>»</margin> ->**"And on the seventh day once more the bright light of the sun."**<- Also **Homer**:
<margin>»</margin> ->**"Then the seventh holy day came down."**<- And,

<margin>>></margin>> Neither touching the laurel-branch nor the lustral water, <note>original: *chernibos* — water used for ritual purification before a sacrifice</note>
<margin>>></margin>> But having the bed of his heart scorched with fire,
<margin>>></margin>> He labored within that crowd of his own thoughts.

Well then, let these matters be left to the favor of the theaters. On the other hand, **Heraclitus** <note>Heraclitus of Ephesus (c. 535–475 BC), a pre-Socratic philosopher known for his doctrine of change and the *Logos*</note> says: **"Of this Word [Logos] which is forever, men always prove to be uncomprehending, both before they have heard it and when they have first heard it."** And the lyric poet **Melanippides**, <note>A 5th-century BC Greek poet famous for his dithyrambs</note> singing, says:

<margin>>></margin>> Hear me, O Father, wonder of mortals,
<margin>>></margin>> Ruler of the ever-living soul.

And the "great melodist," <note>Referring to Parmenides, whom Plato quotes</note> as the philosopher **Plato** calls him, writes something like this concerning the Divine:

<margin>>></margin>> Very many things belong to the Unborn Being and the imperishable;
<margin>>></margin>> It is alone, unique, unshaken, and ungenerated. <note>original: *mounogenes* — unique or "only-begotten," here describing the singularity of the First Cause</note>

And **Hesiod** <note>One of the earliest Greek poets, author of *Theogony*</note> also says:

<margin>>></margin>> For He Himself is King and Lord of all
<margin>>></margin>> The immortals; no other has a power established like Yours.

Indeed, even Tragedy, turning away from idols, teaches us to look up toward heaven. For **Sophocles**, as that author who compiled the histories says—in his work *On Abraham and the Egyptians*—cries out directly upon the stage: <note>Modern scholars generally consider this specific passage to be "Pseudo-Sophocles," a Jewish or Christian composition attributed to the famous playwright to support monotheism</note>

<margin>>></margin>> One in truth, one is God,
<margin>>></margin>> Who fashioned the heaven and the broad earth,
<margin>>></margin>> The blue swell of the sea and the violence of the winds.
<margin>>></margin>> But many of us mortals, wandering in our hearts,
<margin>>></margin>> Have established for ourselves as a consolation for our miseries
<margin>>></margin>> Images of gods made of stone, or bronze,
<margin>>></margin>> Or forms wrought of gold or ivory.
<margin>>></margin>> And by offering sacrifices to these and holding grand festivals,
<margin>>></margin>> We think ourselves to be acting piously.

And **Euripides**, <note>The last of the three great Athenian tragedians (c. 480–406 BC)</note> performing a tragedy upon the same stage, says:

<margin>>></margin>> You see, he says, this infinite Aether <note>The "upper air" or "bright sky" often personified in Greek thought</note> on high,
<margin>>></margin>> Which holds the earth all around in its moist embrace?
<margin>>></margin>> Consider this to be Zeus; this you must deem God.

<margin>>></margin>> To You, the self-born, who in the ethereal 
<margin>>></margin>> Whirl have entwined the nature of all things,
<margin>>></margin>> Around whom light, and around whom the dark-robed
<margin>>></margin>> Night of dappled hue, and the countless
<margin>>></margin>> Multitude of stars dance perpetually.

For here he has spoken of the "self-born" as the "Creator Mind." The following lines refer to the World, in which exist the alternations of light and darkness. And **Aeschylus**, <note>The "Father of Tragedy" (c. 525–456 BC)</note> the son of Euphorion, says most solemnly concerning God:

<margin>>></margin>> Zeus is the aether, Zeus is the earth, Zeus is the heaven;
<margin>>></margin>> Zeus is truly all things, and whatever is higher than these.

I know also that Plato bears witness to **Heraclitus**, who writes that "the Wise is One alone, and is both unwilling and willing to be called by the name of Zeus." And again, "It is law to obey the counsel of the One." Even that saying...

» Some who would release a man from coming evil.

» There is not; but what happens by chance
» As it falls to each person, is called Fortune.

And Sophocles the tragedian says:

» Not even for gods are things of free choice navigable,
» Apart from Zeus. For he holds the end and the beginning.

And Orpheus:

...containing these things, and being inscribed with God as their ultimate author, and confirming their promise through the foretelling of future events and through the results that harmonize with those divine decrees, [the Scripture] is said to be free from every deceptive thought. For the divine oracles are indeed pure, and it has been said they are "silver refined in a furnace of earth, purified seven times." <note>A reference to Psalm 12:6, comparing the truth of the Bible to refined precious metal.</note> But the works of Plato are not of this kind, nor indeed are those of any other of the wise men among humans. For they, possessing mortal minds and relying on perilous conjectures and likenesses—just like a dream, rather than a vision beyond the nature of actual beings—brought a great mixture of falsehood along with the harmful elements of their own nature, so that no teaching among them is pure from the appearance of deceit. 

For instance, if you were willing to set aside self-love for a brief moment and contemplate his light by the power of rational essence, you would recognize that very same "wonderful philosopher" <note>Eusebius uses "wonderful philosopher" sarcastically here to highlight Plato's perceived failure.</note>—the one who alone first touched the rays of the sun at the threshold <note>A metaphor for Plato's "Form of the Good," often compared to the sun in the Republic.</note>—marvelling at corruptible matter and wooden images fashioned by hands into the likeness of a man. You would see him misapplying the title of "gods" to these, even after the heights of his great and lofty speech in which he maintained that he knew the Father and Creator of this universe. He sinks back from the super-cosmic heavens into the lowest depth of god-hated idolatry, identifying himself with the crowd of the uneducated. 

Thus, he does not deny that Socrates spent his life going down to the Piraeus to pray to the goddess <note>The opening of Plato’s *Republic*, where Socrates goes to pray to the Thracian goddess Bendis.</note> and to witness the barbarian festival being celebrated there for the first time by the citizens. He is also found commanding that a sacrifice be made to Asclepius <note>Socrates’ famous last words in the *Phaedo* were "Crito, I owe a cock to Asclepius; will you remember to pay the debt?"</note> on behalf of one who has died, and calling the demon <note>original: "daimona" — in a Greek context, this referred to a divinity or spirit, but Christian writers like Eusebius used it to mean an evil spirit or "demon."</note> residing at Delphi the interpreter for all Greeks. For this reason, one might reasonably attribute the cause of superstitious error among the unphilosophical masses to him.

Indeed, let us take up the argument from a little earlier, and see what the "all-wise" one <note>Plato</note> legislates concerning public opinion after discussing incorporeal and incorruptible Ideas, and after the first and second divine Causes, and after intellectual and 

<margin>Timaeus, p. 40.</margin>
> immortal essences. He says: "But to speak of the other spirits <note>original: "daimonōn"</note> and to know their origin is a task beyond our powers. We must believe those who spoke before us, who were, as they said, offspring of the gods, for they surely knew their own ancestors. It is impossible, then, to disbelieve the children of the gods, even though they speak without probable or necessary proofs. But as they claim to be reporting their own family matters, we must follow the law and believe them. Thus, then, according to them, let the generation of these gods be described and spoken of by us: Oceanus and Tethys were the children of Earth and Heaven. From these were born Phorcys, Cronus, and Rhea, and all those with them. From Cronus and Rhea were born Zeus, Hera, and all those whom we know are called their siblings, and still others who were their offspring." On account of these things, we must reject the philosopher, because, though he is a philosopher, he is not consistent with himself when he hypocritically adopts the mythical genealogies of the poets. 

<margin>Republic, Book 2, p. 377.</margin>
> For you might say that he himself hears these things in the *Republic*: "In the greater myths," I said, "we shall see the smaller ones also. For the same pattern must exist, and the same power must be held by both the greater and the smaller. Or do you not think so?" "I do," he said. "But I do not understand which ones you call the greater." "Those," I said, "which Hesiod and Homer told us, and the other poets. For these men, surely, by composing false myths for mankind, told them and continue to tell them." A little later, he is famous for saying that we should see the same things again, and the things through which he said, "We shall erase, then," I said, "beginning with this verse..."

» There are many such instances, but I would wish now to move on to other matters and ascend further. And in the following passages, from which these selections were taken, we shall again need the help of Homer and the other poets, so as not to make the goddesses’ sons ungraceful—plainly referring to those lying on their sides, and clearly again to Sleep, and the things that follow. To these he adds how, while the other gods and men were sleeping, he <note>Referring to Zeus.</note> alone remained awake to accomplish all that he had planned, which was easily fulfilled through his desire for sexual pleasure; and how he was so struck with wonder at the sight of Hera that he did not even wish to go into the bedchamber, but wanted to unite with her right there on the ground like a lark, saying that he was gripped by a desire greater than when they first visited one another, "hiding from their dear parents." <note>A quote from Homer’s Iliad, Book 14, describing the "Deception of Zeus."</note> Nor should we forget the binding of Ares and Aphrodite by Hephaestus for other such reasons. <note>A reference to the story in the Odyssey where Hephaestus traps his wife and her lover in a golden net.</note> Regarding the way these things are told, does he truly believe them or not? For if an irrational faith is desired, why is it celebrated as an embassy through the laws? For how are Heaven and Earth first, then their offspring Oceanus and Tethys, then Time <note>Chronos, often identified with the titan Cronus.</note> and Rhea and Zeus, and after these all the others—Hera and all those children and brothers mythologized by Homer and Hesiod, and their descendants? Since he says these very things explicitly—for which I ought first and foremost to blame him—he also showed how these lies are not noble. Or this: whenever someone poorly imagines in speech what the gods and heroes are like—just as a painter might paint something not at all resembling the subject he wished to depict. Or again, he says: regarding the gods, he who told the greatest lie about the greatest things did not lie "nobly"—such as how Uranus <note>The personification of the Sky.</note> did what Hesiod says he did, and how Cronus in turn took vengeance upon him. <note>Referring to the myth of Cronus castrating his father Uranus.</note> And what follows these things. How could these same false and untruthful poets again be called "offspring of the gods"? But for the sake of these things, he <note>Plato.</note> must be rejected by us, for he acted out a part before the Athenian people even unto death. <note>Eusebius implies Plato compromised with popular paganism to avoid the fate of Socrates.</note> But Moses is to be celebrated, who set down the oracles of the Hebrews, which are held out as a clear and uniquely true and unerring piety. Behold then and see clearly.

---

-> Plato did not altogether correctly approach the discourse concerning intelligible essences, <-
-> but the Hebrews did. <-

The Hebrews say that the intermediate nature of rational beings is mortal, yet not uncreated. Dividing this nature by reason into intellectual essences, they name them spirits and powers and ministers of God, calling them "angels" <term>angels: from the Greek "angelos," meaning messenger</term> and "archangels." But from the falling away of these beings from their dignity, they introduce to us the concept of "demons" <term>demons: here referring to malevolent fallen spirits</term> and every form of contrary and wicked energy. Therefore, they do not permit them to be considered gods, since beauty and goodness are not inseparable from their nature, but they are beings created by the First Cause. For both their existence and their virtue—even immortality itself—are not possessed in the same way as the God over all, nor through Him by whom all things were established. Plato, indeed, posits incorporeal and intelligible essences and rational natures similar to the Hebrews, but he fails in the logical sequence; first, by claiming they are "uncreated" <note>original: "ἀγεννήτους"</note>, just as he says of every soul. Then, by claiming they are an efflux from the First Cause...

<summary>Eusebius critiques Plato for inconsistently accepting Homeric myths about the gods' scandalous behavior while simultaneously acknowledging they are lies. He then contrasts the Hebrew view of angels as created, fallible beings with Plato's view of souls and spirits as uncreated "effluxes" of the divine.</summary>

...to consist of the divine; for he does not wish to grant that they came into being from non-being <note>original: *ek mē ontos*, referring to the concept of "creation out of nothing."</note>. For this reason, he assumes a race of multiple gods, establishing in his argument certain <term>emanations<note>original: *aporrhoia*, a "streaming off" or "outflow" from a divine source, common in Neoplatonic thought.</note></term> and <term>offshoots<note>original: *probolas*, a technical term for the projection of one divine being from another.</note></term> of the first and second cause. He believes these to be good by nature and in no way capable of departing from their own virtue; hence, he also believes that they exist eternally. But besides these, he considers there to be another race of <term>demons<note>original: *daimones*. In ancient Greek thought, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense of pure evil.</note></term>, one capable of vileness and wickedness, and susceptible to a turn for the worse. Of these, some are good, while others are—and are called—wicked. 

But even though he proposes this as if it were the opinion of the Hebrews, he does not explain from what source it is reasonable to say these demons originated. For no one in their right mind would say they came from incorporeal matter, since such matter is irrational; and rational beings could never be born from the irrational—yet these demons are rational beings. But if they are emanations from the higher powers, how are they themselves not gods equal to those who begat them? And since the source is good, how can that which comes from it not be similar? From where did the malice or harm in these secondary beings arise, if the root of all things proceeds from the good? How could a bitter juice come from the sweet? And if this race of wicked demons contains a corruption and a bitterness more harsh than anything else, how could it be called an emanation from the nature of the higher powers? If they were of that nature, they would not have turned from their own state. If they have been altered, they were not entirely of that nature from the beginning. And if they were not of such a nature, how could they be gods, who you say are capable of sharing in such a fate? 

However, if they are neither emanations from the higher powers nor from incorporeal matter, it is time to say they are unbegotten. Along with the unbegotten matter of bodies, we would have to list another swarm of rational unbegotten causes—whereby we no longer grant that the God of all is the maker and creator of the universe. Or, if we acknowledge Him as such, we must agree with the Hebrew accounts that He made them out of nothing. And what do these accounts teach regarding these matters? They say that the middle nature of rational beings did not originate from the matter of bodies, nor from an emanation of the unbegotten substance that is always the same and unchanging; rather, they say that while it did not exist before, it came into being by the active power of the Cause of all things. In this way, they are not gods, nor are they strictly worthy of this title, because they are not equal in nature to the One who made them, nor are they inseparable from God in the same way that the Good is established. They may even receive the opposite of the beautiful when they neglect the use of the better, because each one has been fashioned to be the master of his own impulse and judgment. So much for these matters; let us move on to others.

->That Plato did not hold correct views about the soul in all respects, unlike<-
->the Hebrews.<-

While assuming the soul to be immortal just like the Hebrews, and saying it is similar to God, Plato does not follow them consistently thereafter. At times, he says its essence is composed as if it were part of the indivisible cause that is always the same and unchanging, and part of the divisible nature that is distributed among bodies. At any rate, he says in these very words in the *Timaeus*:

> "Now the soul, being prior to the body in both birth and virtue, he <note>The Demiurge or Creator.</note> constituted as mistress and ruler of that which was to be ruled, and he fashioned it out of the following elements and in the following way: From the indivisible essence that is always the same and unchanging, and from that which is divisible and comes into being in connection with bodies, he mixed a third form of essence in the middle between both—that is, between the nature of the Same and that of the Other—and he constituted it in the same way in the middle..."

<summary>Eusebius critiques Plato's theory that spirits and souls are "emanations" of the divine, arguing that this fails to account for the existence of evil, whereas the Hebrew doctrine of creation out of nothing explains free will.</summary>

<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

» ...but in the soul, that which is indivisible <note>original: *to ameres*</note>, while the substance of bodies is divisible. And taking these three existing things, he blended them all into one form, the nature of the "Other" <note>In Plato's *Timaeus*, the soul is a mix of "the Same," "the Other," and "Essence."</note>, which was difficult to mix, fitting them together by force into the "Same." From this, quite reasonably, they—and the ancient portion of the soul’s essence—were joined together by the Word <note>original: *logō*</note>.

But while at one time he has understood the holy soul in this way, at another time he speaks worse of them, claiming an absurdity: that this divine and heavenly soul—incorporeal, rational, similar to God, and which through the greatness of virtue traverses the open vaults of the heavens—comes down from somewhere above the super-cosmic realms into asses and wolves and ants or bees. He wishes us to believe this based on his every word, yet without any proof. At any rate, in his dialogue *On the Soul* <note>Referring to the *Phaedo*.</note>, he says the following:

» "They wander until, following the desire of the body, they are bound again into a body. They are bound, as is likely, into such characters as they happened to practice in life. What kind do you mean, Socrates? For instance, those who practiced gluttony, violence, and drunkenness, and did not take precautions, are likely to enter the species of asses and such beasts. Or do you not think so? Certainly, it is very likely. And those who have preferred injustice, tyrannies, and robberies, enter the species of wolves, hawks, and kites. To what other place could we say such souls go? Clearly, said Cebes, to such as these. Is it not then clear, he said, where the others would go, each according to the similarities of its own practice? It is clear, he said, how could it not be? Therefore, he said, the happiest of these, and those going to the best place, are those who have practiced the social and political virtues, which they call self-control <note>original: *sōphrosynēn*</note> and justice, which arise from habit and practice without philosophy and intellect. How then are they the happiest? Because it is likely that these arrive again into a similar social and gentle species, perhaps of bees or wasps or ants, or even back into the same human race."

And in the *Phaedrus*, listen to what he relates: 

» "For the soul does not return to the place from which it came for ten thousand years. For it does not grow wings before such a time, except for the soul of one who has philosophized without guile, or who has practiced 'boy-love' <term>pederasty<note>In the Platonic context, this refers to a mentor-student relationship intended to cultivate virtue and wisdom, though Eusebius likely highlights it here to critique Greek morals.</note></term> alongside philosophy. These, in the third thousand-year period, if they have chosen this life three times in a row, thus grow wings and depart in the three-thousandth year. But the others, when they end their first life, receive judgment. Once judged, some go to the places of correction <note>original: *dikaiōtēria*</note> under the earth and pay the penalty; others, having been lightened by justice, pass their time in heaven in a manner worthy of the life they lived in human form. But in the thousandth year, both groups arrive at the lot and the choice of their second life, and each chooses whichever one it wishes. There, a human soul may arrive at the life of a beast, and from a beast—one who was once human—back into a human again."

These things are in the *Phaedrus*. And in the *Republic*, listen to him writing such things:

» "For he said he saw the soul that was once that of Orpheus choosing the life of a swan, out of hatred for womankind because of his death at their hands, not wishing to be conceived and born of a woman. And he saw the soul of Thamyras choosing that of a nightingale. He also saw a swan changing to the choice of a human life, and other musical animals doing likewise, as was likely. And the twentieth soul chose the life of a lion; it was the soul of Ajax son of Telamon, fleeing from becoming a human because he remembered the judgment concerning the armor. And after him, that of Agamemnon..."

<summary>Eusebius quotes several of Plato's dialogues (Timaeus, Phaedo, Phaedrus, and Republic) to illustrate the Greek philosopher’s theory of transmigration, where souls are reborn as animals based on their past behavior. Eusebius presents these ideas as "absurdities" that contradict the soul's divine nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s critique of Plato’s theory of reincarnation (metempsychosis). Here, he continues with a famous passage from the *Republic* (the Myth of Er) describing souls choosing their next lives before being reborn.</meta>

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 13 #

### PAGE 409 ###

-> PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 13 <-

» ...remembering an enemy, and because of its sufferings, it changed its life to avoid the human race. <note>original: "νοις ἐχθροῦ"; this refers to the soul of the hero Ajax, who, out of hatred for his rival Odysseus, chose to be reborn as a lion rather than a human.</note> In the middle of the lots, the soul of Atalanta <note>A famous huntress and athlete in Greek myth.</note> saw the great honors of an athlete, and she could not pass them by but took them. After her, he saw the soul of Agamemnon <note>The king who led the Greeks at Troy.</note> choosing the nature of an eagle. Far off among the last, he saw the soul of the buffoon Thersites putting on the form of an ape. By chance, the soul of Odysseus happened to have the very last lot of all to choose. Remembering his former labors, he had recovered from his ambition and went around for a long time seeking the life of a private man <term>idiōtou</term> <note>In Greek, this refers to a private citizen who stays out of public affairs, rather than its modern derogatory meaning.</note> who was free from meddling. He found it lying somewhere, neglected by the others, and upon seeing it, he said he would have done the same even if he had the first lot, and he chose it gladly. In the same way, other beasts enter into humans, and into each other—the unjust into the wild ones, and the just into the gentle ones, being transformed and mixed in every possible way.

Plato, having said these things about the soul, is clearly "Egyptianizing" <note>original: "αἰγυπτιάζων"; Eusebius suggests Plato is following the Egyptians, whom many ancients believed invented the idea of reincarnation.</note> in his doctrine. For this is not the teaching of the Hebrews, nor is it a friend to truth. This is not the time to refute it, since he himself did not even attempt to use demonstrations for these assumptions. But let the argument point this out: it is not consistent for him to say that the souls of the impious depart to Hades at the moment of death to pay the penalty for their deeds and be punished there forever, and then again to claim that they choose their lives here according to their own personal will. For he says they are bound to a body by a "corporeal desire." Those who were brought up in insolence and gluttony become asses, and they enter the bodies of such beasts by their own choice, and not according to justice. The unjust and rapacious become wolves and hawks, coming to this as volunteers. Furthermore, he says the soul of Orpheus chose the life of a swan, and Thamyras <note>A mythical singer who challenged the Muses.</note> chose a nightingale, and Thersites chose the life of an ape. Where then would there be a judgment after the departure from here?

<margin>P</margin> <note>Likely standing for "Platon" (Plato), indicating a direct quotation follows.</note>

» For in the writings *On the Soul* <note>Referring to the *Phaedo*.</note> he says: "When the deceased arrive at the place where the spirit <term>daimōn</term> <note>In Greek thought, a *daimon* was a guiding spirit or lesser deity, not necessarily an evil 'demon'.</note> leads each one, those who are judged to have lived a middle life proceed to Acheron. They board the carriages provided for them and arrive at the lake <note>The Acherusian Lake.</note>, where they dwell and are purified. By paying the penalty for their wrongdoings, they are acquitted of any injustice they committed, and they receive honors for their good deeds, each according to their merit. But those who are judged to be incurable because of the greatness of their sins—either many and great acts of sacrilege, or many unjust and illegal murders, or other such things—these are thrown by their fitting fate into Tartarus, from which they never emerge." And while these things concerning the impious are somewhat clear, listen to what he says about the pious: "Those who have sufficiently purified themselves through philosophy live entirely without bodies for the time to come, and they reach even more beautiful dwellings than these, which are neither easy to describe, nor is there sufficient time at present." And in the *Gorgias* <note>Another of Plato's dialogues focused on justice and rhetoric.</note> he speaks first and says: "He who has lived his life justly and holily, when he dies, goes to the Isles of the Blessed and dwells in all happiness, free from evils; but he who has lived unjustly and atheistically goes to the prison of vengeance and justice, which they call Tartarus. Those who have committed the ultimate wrongs, and through such crimes have become incurable, become examples to others. And they themselves no longer benefit from anything, being incurable..."

<summary>Eusebius critiques Plato for contradictions in his view of the afterlife, contrasting the "Egyptian" idea of souls choosing to be reborn as animals with Plato's own descriptions of divine judgment in Hades. He argues that the concept of souls choosing their next lives through desire undermines the idea of a just punishment for sins.</summary>

Here, the argument shifts from the moral "choice" of lives to a more technical, philosophical critique of whether the soul is a mixture of different substances, drawing on the Platonist philosopher Severus.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS’S PREPARATION #

### PAGE 410 ###

-> PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 13 <-

» ...they themselves benefit by seeing others being beaten because of their greatest sins, suffering most painful and terrifying sufferings for all time. They are literally hung up as examples <note>original: "παραδείγματα"; used here in the sense of a 'warning example' or 'deterrent' for others.</note> there in Hades in the prison, serving as spectacles and warnings to the unjust who are always arriving. How could these things harmonize with what was said about the exchange [of lives]? For if someone should claim the soul chooses by a method of choice, by rational arguments: how could the same soul undergo punishments and prisons, and such a great penalty for all time after death here, and then again, like someone released and free from bonds, choose whatever lives it wants? But if it chooses again only according to pleasure, where then is the prison of retribution and penalty? Ten thousand other objections could be raised against this argument if one had the leisure, but it is not the right time to lengthen the thought. And the former bank of Plato's opinion on these matters has ended in this way. But the other [opinion] disagrees in doctrine not only with those who call the rational part of the soul divine, but he also defined some part of it as irrational and passible <term>pathētikōn</term> <note>From the Greek 'pathos'; meaning 'capable of suffering' or 'subject to emotions and external influences.'</note>, and he is condemned by his own acquaintances, as it is possible to learn from these words.

### Not that the nature of the soul, according to Plato, is composed of an impassive and passible substance. From the writings of Severus the Platonist concerning the soul. ###

Regarding the soul according to Plato, which he says was composed by God from an impassive <note>The OCR reads "ἀπαλοῦς" (tender/soft), but the context and subsequent text clearly indicate "ἀπαθοῦς" (impassive/incapable of suffering).</note> and passible substance—just as a middle color comes from white and black—I might say this: it is necessary that when the composition of colors occurs, it [the original state] disappears, like the composition of the middle color, since the private properties of each thing from which it was composed are naturally separated over time. If this is so, I would declare the soul to be perishable, and not immortal. For if this is agreed—that nothing in nature is always material, and that the things in the world were ordered by God from opposite natures by instilling in them friendship and communion—the dry to the moist, the hot to the cold, the heavy to the light, white to black, sweet to bitter, hard to soft, and all such things will accept a mixture and communion of all, [including] the impassive substance with the passible. But things mixed and blended admit a separation from each other in time by nature. And if the soul is assumed to have come into being from impassive and passible substance, it is necessary that, like the middle color, it too should disappear in time by nature, when the opposites from which it was composed hasten back to their own nature. Or do we not see how a thing that is naturally heavy, even if it is carried upward by us or by some lightness surrounding it from the outside, likewise forces itself downward toward its own nature? And similarly, the naturally light thing, being carried downward by similar outside causes, likewise forces itself upward? For it is impossible for things brought together into the same place from two opposites to remain always in the same [state] unless some third thing of the substance of existing things is always in them. But the soul is not some third thing joined from two opposites, but is simple and by its own nature impassive and incorporeal. Hence Plato, and those after him, said it was immortal. But since there is a common argument for everyone that a single human being is composed of soul and body, and the passions <term>pathē</term> <note>In Greek philosophy, 'passions' refers to any emotion or physical sensation that the soul 'undergoes' or 'suffers.'</note> happening in our body—both voluntarily and involuntarily—are said to belong to the soul, the majority, using this as evidence that its substance is passible, say that it is mortal and corporeal, but not incorporeal. But Plato was compelled [to say] its nature is impassive...

<summary>This page critiques Plato's theory of the soul, arguing that if the soul were a mixture of eternal and perishable elements, it would eventually decompose and thus could not be immortal. It highlights the contradiction between the soul as a prisoner in Hades and the soul as a free agent choosing its next life.</summary>

# EUSEBIUS’S PREPARATION #

### PAGE 411 ###

-> PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 16 <-

...or to weave in a passible <term>passible</term> <note>original: "παθητικὴν" (pathētikēn). In ancient philosophy, this refers to a substance that can be acted upon, suffer change, or experience emotion, as opposed to the impassive, eternal divine mind.</note> substance. That it is not otherwise, based on what both sides have said—both Plato and those who are well-known—we shall attempt to approach the argument by handing over the powers acting within us. Let these things be set forth for me from Severus the Platonist <note>Severus was a 2nd-century Platonist philosopher known for his commentaries on Plato's 'Timaeus'.</note> concerning the soul. But consider also this, following what has been said: concerning the origin of the heaven and the luminaries within it.

### Concerning the heaven and the luminaries within it, and that Plato did not hold an entirely correct opinion. From the *Epinomis*, the *Timaeus*, and the tenth book of the *Laws*; Moses forbids worshipping them, as Philo the Hebrew interprets. ###

In harmony with the Hebrews, you <note>Eusebius is likely addressing a hypothetical Greek reader or the philosopher he is critiquing.</note> provide an account concerning the heaven and the phenomena within it, stating that it has a created God—inasmuch as it was made by a Cause—and that it consists of partaking in a bodily and perishable substance. However, Plato does not legislate for their worship in the same way as the Hebrews, but rather commands that they be regarded as gods,

> stating thus in the *Epinomis*: "In order that I may speak with reverence of the god, O Maximus and Clinias, let us sing of the Heaven, which all the famous demons and gods alike [praise], and let us honor it and dedicate ourselves to it with prayers. That it has become the cause of all other goods for us, we all again acknowledge." And further down in the same work he prays for these things: "As for the visible gods, the greatest and most honorable, who see most sharply in every direction—the stars—we must speak of the nature of the stars and all those things that have come to be with them with good names. And after these and under these, in order, the demons. An aerial race, having a third and middle seat, the cause of interpretation <note>original: "ἑρμηνείας" (hermēneias). Plato suggests these beings act as messengers or 'interpreters' between gods and men.</note>, whom we must especially honor with prayers for the sake of a propitious passage." Having said through these words that those mentioned are gods, he goes through the following concerning its sacred composition when discussing nature in the *Timaeus*: "Whatever fire is to air, that air is to water. And whatever air is to water, that water is to the earth; He bound and constructed them, a heaven visible and tangible. And for these reasons and from such things, being four in number, the body of the world was generated through proportion <note>original: "ἀναλογίας" (analogias). Plato believed the universe was held together by mathematical ratios between the four elements.</note>. It gained friendship from these, so that having come together into itself, it became indissoluble by any other except by the one who bound it." Then he adds: "And placing the soul in the middle of it, He stretched it through the whole, and further covered the body with it from the outside; and turning circle upon circle, He established a single, solitary, desert heaven." And again, further down, he adds, saying: "Therefore, from such a reason and thought of God toward the birth of time, in order that time might be generated, the sun, and the moon, and five other stars having the name 'planets,' came to be for the definition and preservation of the numbers of time. And having made each of their bodies, God placed them into the orbits which the circuit of the Other was traveling." And he adds: "And the bodies, being bound with ensouled bonds, became living beings and learned their appointed task." And in the tenth book of the *Laws* he declares universally concerning every soul, saying thus: "Indeed, all things that partake of soul undergo change, possessing within themselves the cause of change; and having changed, they are carried according to the order and law of fate. Those whose characters have changed in smaller ways move down along the surface level of the region; but those that have changed more and more unjustly fall into the depth." If indeed, then, all things that partake of soul undergo change, possessing within themselves the cause of change; and having changed, they are carried according to the order and law of fate; those whose characters have changed in smaller ways move down along the surface level of the region... <note>The final lines repeat the previous sentence, likely a transcription error in the original manuscript or OCR.</note>

mm.ii.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Plato’s cosmology, moving from the physical nature of celestial bodies to a direct quote from the "Timaeus." Eusebius then contrasts Plato’s view (which grants a kind of secondary divinity to the stars) with the strict monotheism of the Hebrew Law, utilizing the commentary of the Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria to argue that the heavenly bodies are merely "servants" or "lieutenants" of the one true Creator.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS #

...shifted into the depths, becoming even more numerous and unjust. If, then, bodies that partake in a soul are subject to change, possessing within themselves the cause of that change—and if the heaven, the sun, and the moon partake in a soul, according to Plato himself—then these things must also be subject to change, possessing within themselves the cause of change by the same reasoning. How, then, can you claim they are eternal? 

And for this reason he says, even regarding those in the *Timaeus* who are perishable: "Do you think they will be dissolved?" For he says again in the *Timaeus*: 

"Now, when all the gods—both those who revolve visibly and those who appear only when they wish—had come into being, the Begetter of this universe addressed them thus: 'Gods of gods, of whose works I am the creator <term>creator</term> <note>original: "δημιουργὸς" (dēmiourgos). While often translated as 'craftsman,' in this context it refers to the divine architect of the physical world.</note> and father, those things brought into being by me shall not be dissolved against my will. Every bond indeed can be dissolved, but to wish to dissolve that which is well-fitted and in good condition is the mark of an evil will. Therefore, since you have been brought into being, you are not immortal, nor are you altogether indissoluble; yet you shall certainly not be dissolved, nor shall you meet the fate of death, for you have obtained in my will a bond even greater and more sovereign than those with which you were bound when you were first created.'"

These are the words of Plato. Rightly, then, does Moses, through the Hebrew law, forbid the worship of these things and refuse to regard them as gods. Instead, he leads us upward to the King of all, God, the very Creator of the sun, moon, stars, and the entire heaven and world. He legislates that we should regard Him alone as God—having awareness of Him through the Divine Word—and that we should offer the honor of worship to Him alone, saying: "Lest, when you see the sun and the moon and all the stars, and all the host of heaven, you be led astray and worship them." <note>This is a reference to Deuteronomy 4:19.</note>

Philo, who was well-educated in the Hebrew traditions, clearly interprets these matters at length, saying word-for-word:

"Some have supposed that the sun, the moon, and the other stars are sovereign gods, to whom they attributed the causes of all things that happen. But to Moses, the world appeared to be both created and like a 'Great City' having rulers and subjects. The rulers are all those in heaven—the planets and the fixed stars. The subjects are the natures below the moon, in the air and the regions near the earth. But these aforementioned 'rulers' are not independent; they are lieutenants <term>lieutenants</term> <note>original: "ὑπάρχους" (hyparchous). This term implies a subordinate official or governor acting on behalf of a higher monarch.</note> of the one Father of all. By imitating His superintendence, they govern each created thing according to justice and law. But those who do not see the Charioteer <note>original: "ἡνίοχον" (hēniochon). Philo uses this famous metaphor to describe God as the driver who controls the 'team' of the universe.</note> mounted above have attached the causes of worldly events to the team of horses as if they were the primary actors. 

The most holy lawgiver transforms their ignorance into knowledge, saying: 'Lest, when you see the sun and the moon and the stars, and all the host of heaven, you be led astray and worship them.' Very accurately and well did he use the word 'straying' <note>original: "πλάνην" (planēn). A clever pun by Philo; the Greek word for 'planets' (planētai) literally means 'wanderers' or 'strayers.'</note> for the acceptance of these things as gods. For those who observed the sun's annual approaches and retreats which establish the seasons—during which the births of animals and the growth of plants and fruits are brought to completion in fixed cycles of time—and the moon as the servant and successor of the sun, taking up the care and presidency of the night while the sun has it by day... and the other stars acting in sympathy with earthly things... they strayed, forgetting the One, and establishing these as gods. 

But if they had walked with diligence along the unerring path, they would have known immediately that, according to perception, the mind has become a subordinate servant—the very mind which I have said, along with all sensible things, is an assistant to the Intelligible." And he continues by saying, "as if..."

<summary>Eusebius uses a quote from Plato’s Timaeus to show that even Plato admitted the stars are naturally perishable and dependent on a higher Will. He then uses Philo of Alexandria to argue that worshipping celestial bodies is a "straying" from the true path of recognizing the one Creator who rules them like a charioteer.</summary>

» ...having ascended by the power of reason <note>original: "λογισμῷ" (logismō) – refers to the rational faculty used to transcend physical perception.</note> beyond all visible substance, we move toward the honor of the unseen and invisible, which is graspable by the mind alone. This is He who is not only the God of things intellectual and sensible, but also the creator <note>original: "δημιουργός" (dēmiourgos)</note> of all things. But if anyone assigns the worship due to the eternal and creating God to another, more recent and created being, let him be recorded as mentally deranged <note>original: "φρενοβλαβὴς" (phrenoblabēs)</note> and guilty of the greatest impiety. Or rather, is it fitting to say these things as an introduction? For I, for my part, greatly admire the man, and I consider him more of a friend than any other Greek. Yet it is necessary to examine my own views alongside his, even if they are not of equal weight. 

» It seems, then, that he chose to emulate Moses and the prophets among the Hebrews—an emulation he displayed in his own thinking. And yet, one might first expect to find ten thousand things to blame or to laugh at, such as his solemn and "wise" arrangements regarding women in his *Republic*, or his admissions regarding love <note>original: "ἔρωτος" (erōtos)</note> based on the laws in the *Phaedrus*. But if you desire to hear these things as well, take and read his own words:

### What things Plato incorrectly ordained concerning women in the *Laws* and the *Republic*, which the doctrine of the Hebrews did not accept. ###

<margin>I</margin> » "It would seem ridiculous," I said, "contrary to what is accustomed, if what we are saying is put into practice." 
» "Very much so," he said. 
» "What then," said I, "is the most ridiculous thing you see? Is it not clearly the sight of women exercising naked in the wrestling grounds <term>palaestras</term> <note>A palaestra was a Greek wrestling school or gym, typically reserved for men.</note> with the men? And not only the young women, but already the older ones, just like the old men in the gymnasia who, even when they are wrinkled and not pleasant to the sight, still love their exercise?" 
» And proceeding further, he says: "The man who laughs at naked women who are exercising for the sake of what is best—harvesting the fruit of 'ridiculous wisdom' as he does—knows nothing, it seems, of what he laughs at." 

» He says also in the seventh book of the *Laws* that it will be necessary for girls and boys to learn to dance and to exercise. For the boys there should be male dance-teachers, and for the girls, female teachers, so that the exertion is not unsuitable for them. He also sets down the following in that same work: 

» "If a girl or a lady among us, having taken pleasure in the education of the dance, did not think it right to play with empty hands, but having been adorned in a complete suit of armor, thus performed the dance—these are things that would be entirely fitting for girls and boys to imitate together." 

» He also legislates that women should go to war in the same way. In all these matters, there must be teachers for each subject, foreign residents <term>metics</term> <note>original: "ξένους" (xenous) – here referring to resident aliens or professional instructors hired by the state.</note> living there and persuaded by wages, to teach those who attend all the lessons pertaining to war and music. It is not to be only if a father wishes his child to attend, or if he wishes to keep them from education; rather, as the saying goes, every man and child must be educated by necessity, so far as is possible, as they belong more to the city than to their own parents. 

» "My law would say the same things concerning females: that the females must practice all the same things as the males. And I would not be afraid to speak this word: that neither horsemanship nor gymnastics are fitting for men while being unfitting for women." 

» And again, following this, he says: "Gymnasia must be established, and all the labors of the body pertaining to war—archery, and every kind of throwing, and light-shield fighting <term>peltastics</term>, and all heavy-armed combat, and tactical maneuvers."

<meta>This page continues Eusebius's critique of Plato. In the preceding section, Eusebius praised Plato's monotheism as being influenced by Moses but began to pivot toward areas where he believes Plato's "ideal state" deviates from the modesty and divine reliance found in Hebrew tradition. Here, he specifically addresses Plato's proposals for the education and social roles of women.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS #

...and every journey, camps and encampments, and all things that pertain to equestrian studies. He suggests there should be common teachers for all these, widely discussed in the middle of the city, and that the students of these should be the boys and men in the city, and the girls and women should be experts in all these things. While they are still girls, they should be practiced in dancing in armor and in fighting; and as women, they should be experienced in maneuvers and formations, and in the putting on and taking off of weapons. 

But the Hebrew word <note>original: "ἑβραίων... λόγος" (hebraiōn... logos) — referring here to the authority of Holy Scripture.</note> will not assent to these things, but speaks against Plato, relying neither on the strength of men, nor at all on the shameless success of women in wars, but attributing everything to God and the alliance that comes from Him. For it says: *Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, the guard keeps watch in vain.* <note>Eusebius is quoting Psalm 127:1.</note> 

Yet the "admirable philosopher" <note>Eusebius uses this title for Plato with a touch of irony here, given his disagreement.</note> introduces women even into the gymnastic games, speaking somewhat like this:

> "For women—girls again—naked, in the stadium, the double-course race, the horse-race, and the long-distance race, competing in the race itself. But for the woman of thirty until she enters the communion of marriage, not for longer than twenty years nor less than eighteen, dressed in fitting attire, she shall go down to the competition of these races. And let these be the rules for the races for both men and women. As for feats of strength, instead of wrestling and such things, which are now considered heavy, let there be fighting in armor, one against one or even more fighting, or two against two." 

And following this, he says: 

> "These things concerning fighting in armor should be legislated by calling upon the experts," and he adds, saying, "let these same things be legislated concerning the females, up until their marriage."

Then again, connecting these in order with the laws concerning the light infantry <note>original: "πελταστικῆς" (peltastikēs) — referring to the peltast, a type of light-armed soldier.</note>, the *pankration* <note>original: "παγκρατίου" (pankratiou) — an ancient Greek martial art combining boxing and wrestling.</note>, and the bow, and the laws for throwing stones by hand and by sling, and concerning the horse-racing competition, he again introduces the females here, saying:

> "As for the females, it is not worth forcing them into the communion of all these things by laws and commands. But if their nature, having been educated from childhood and entering into the habit, accepts it and does not find it difficult, let the maidens share in it with the boys, and do not criticize them."

These are Plato's views concerning women. This "admirable law" also happens to be the same if he leaves females as children; through the successes of brothers and nephews, the males come first, and later the females with one lot. And let the judge, looking on, decide the symmetry or asymmetry of the time for marriages, with the males naked, and the females naked from the navel upwards. <note>original: "ὀμφαλοῦ μέχρι" (omphalou mechri) — Eusebius is highlighting what he considers the indecency of Plato's social regulations.</note> But he also says that in the festivals they must dance naked, in the sixth book of the *Laws*, speaking thus:

> "For the sake of such serious purpose, one must also make the children—both boys and girls—dance, at the same time being spectators and being seen, with reason and at a suitable age having plausible excuses, both boys and girls naked, as far as a modest shame allows each."

In addition to all these, listen also to those things in the *Republic* concerning the law that women should be held in common; for this law follows the previous ones, being of the same kind, as I believe. What is it?

» ...as much as possible of the same nature. But those who lack skill and order, where no one possesses anything of this kind privately, will surely come together. And when they are mixed together both in the gymnasia and in their other upbringing, I believe they will be led toward union with one another by an innate necessity. Or do I not seem to be saying what is necessary? Not by **geometric necessities**, he said, but by **erotic necessities**, which are perhaps sharper than the former in their power to persuade and draw the common people. But perhaps someone will interpret the meaning of this discourse differently, though we say it should not be considered entirely rejected. Nor should it be said without distinction that all women are "common," as if it were permitted for anyone to act with licentiousness; rather, the distribution of women to men lies within the authority of the rulers. For they are "common" in the same way that someone might say **public funds** are common, which it is appropriate for the designated officials to distribute. And let these things be so. But what you might say upon learning how he speaks of not bringing those conceived to light in an orderly fashion: Speaking thus, I said, a woman should begin at twenty years of age and bear children for the city until she is forty. For a man, once he has passed the sharpest peak of his racing speed, he should beget for the city from that point until he is fifty-five. To these things he adds: when, I suppose, both the women and the men pass the age for procreation, we shall let them be free to associate with whomever they wish. And he adds, urging them to be careful, especially not to bring any fetus to light if one should be conceived; but if one should force its way, to dispose of it as though there were no sustenance for such a child. <note>Plato is here discussing infanticide or exposure of children born outside the state's regulated age limits or social planning.</note> Such are the matters concerning the training of women. As for his orderly descriptions of love, listen to what they happen to be.

-> What sorts of things he himself set down concerning love in an orderly fashion in the *Phaedrus*, against which Moses legislates in opposition. <-

» When he spends time doing this and draws near with touch, both in the gymnasia and in other social interactions, then the fountain of that stream—which Zeus, when he was in love with **Ganymede**, named "desire" <note>original: "ἵμερος" (himeros). In Greek mythology, Ganymede was a beautiful Trojan prince abducted by Zeus to serve as cupbearer to the gods.</note>—flows in abundance toward the lover. Some of it sinks into him, but some, when he is filled, flows out. And just as a breath of wind or a sound leaps back from smooth and solid surfaces and returns to where it started, so the stream of beauty goes back into the beautiful one through the eyes. Having arrived there, where it is natural for it to go into the soul, and having fluttered the passages of the wings, it waters them and causes the wings to grow, filling the soul of the beloved in turn with love. He is in love, then, but is at a loss as to what he loves; he does not even know what has happened to him, nor can he explain it. He is like one who has caught an eye infection from another but cannot state the cause. And he adds next: he desires to see, touch, kiss, and lie down with him in a similar way, though more weakly; and naturally, he does these things quickly thereafter. In their lying together, the **undisciplined horse** <note>original: "ὁ ἀκόλαστος ἵππος" (ho akolastos hippos). In Plato’s famous allegory, the soul is a chariot pulled by two horses: one noble and one unruly (representing base desire).</note> of the lover has something to say to the charioteer, and demands to enjoy a small pleasure in return for many labors. But the soul of the beloved has nothing to say, yet it swells with desire; in its confusion, it embraces the lover and kisses him, welcoming him as a very dear friend. And when they lie together, he is not the sort to refuse to grant his share of favor to the lover if he should ask to receive it. If, then, the better parts of the mind prevail by leading them toward a settled life and philosophy, they spend their life here in a blessed and harmonious way, being masters of themselves and orderly...

» ...and of every march, of camps and encampments, and further, as much as pertains to military horsemanship. For there should be common teachers for all these things—certainly not praising those of the city <note>Plato is likely referring to the traditional, less rigorous education found in existing Greek city-states</note>—and the students of these should be the children and men in the city, and the girls and women should be knowledgeable in all these things. This refers to the 'spirited' part of the soul that seeks status and recognition.</note>, perhaps in a moment of drunkenness or some other lapse of attention, the undisciplined beasts of their souls <note>original: "ὑποζύγια," literally "beasts of burden," referring to the lower, irrational parts of the soul in Plato's chariot allegory.</note> might catch them off guard and bring them together. With a powerful voice, he denounces the love of boys <note>original: "παιδεραστίαν" (pederasty).</note> as if he were delivering a judicial sentence. He says, for instance: "Whoever lies with a male as with a woman, both of them have committed an abomination; let them surely be put to death, for they are guilty" <note>A quotation from Leviticus 20:13.</note>. And again: "Cursed is everyone who lies with a male as with a woman." Why should one dare to defend pederasty as a "most wise" practice, when Moses saw fit to establish the death penalty for it in his laws? He even commanded that a servant be punished with death if he failed to report <unclear>something</unclear> attempted by another. And listen further to these points, so that you do not think I am merely slandering him.

### Concerning Plato’s laws on homicide, which are unworthy of his great intelligence, and must be compared with the laws of Moses. ###

<margin>»</margin> He [Plato] says that regarding the killing of property and livestock, the city, serving the oracles, should do the things of God. If a slave is the one who killed [a beast], let him maintain a reputation for virtue, not being stained by vice. » ...should he wish to harvest the so-called "navia" figs <note>original: "νᾶια σῦκα." Such are the regulations regarding these matters, which are hardly worthy of Plato’s greatness of mind. But how venerable and philanthropic are the laws of Moses! You might learn this by hearing him speak in this manner: "If you enter your neighbor’s vineyard, you may eat as many grapes as your soul <note>In this context, 'soul' (ψυχή) refers to one's appetite or desire.</note> desires until you are satisfied, but you shall not put any into a vessel. And again: If you enter your neighbor’s standing grain, you may pluck the ears with your hands, but you shall not put a sickle to your neighbor's standing grain. And again: If you reap your harvest in your field and forget a sheaf there, you shall not turn back to get it; it shall be for the poor, the resident alien <note>original: "προσηλύτῳ." And if you beat your olive trees, you shall not go back to gather what remains behind you; it shall be for the resident alien, the orphan, and the widow." 

These are the laws of Moses. Plato’s laws are clear; and though they contain countless other points that might be beyond reproach—and indeed we especially welcome his most venerable and excellent teachings—we bid a long farewell to those that are not of such a quality. But since these things have been thus examined, we must state the reason why we have decided not to philosophize according to Plato; it is time to bring the rest of the subject to a close and examine the lineage of the various schools of Greek philosophy.

## Preface Concerning the Subject

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'H' within a square frame featuring elaborate floral scrollwork and a stylized human mask or face at the bottom center of the border.</image-desc>

Having discussed and examined, as it were, the matters concerning Platonic philosophy—both its harmony with the Hebrew oracles, for which we admire the man, and again its dissonance with them, for which no right-thinking person would accept him—I explained these things in the preceding book. I shall now move on to the remaining sects <note>original: "αἱρέσεις" (haireseis). In this context, it refers to chosen schools of thought or philosophical parties rather than "heresy" in the modern sense.</note> of those among the Greeks who are celebrated for philosophy. Once again, I will place before the eyes of my readers the evidence from their entire history—not speaking for myself or from my own authority, but through the testimony of the very voices of those who were deemed worthy of honor. In doing so, I do not act out of any personal malice toward these men; indeed, I confess I hold them in great wonder whenever I compare them to the general run of humanity. 

However, when compared to the Hebrew theologians and prophets—and to the God who through them produced both prophecies and wondrous demonstrations, and who established the teaching of the truth through pious doctrines—I believe no one can reasonably find fault if we honor God above men, and Truth herself above mortal reasonings and conjectures. The argument of this present "Preparation" is eager to demonstrate this very point, serving both as an answer and a defense against those famous claims: whether it is truly right for us, having seen the solemn majesty in the "barbarian" <note>The Greeks used "barbarian" to describe anyone who did not speak Greek; here Eusebius uses it to refer to the Hebrew scriptures.</note> writings, to prefer them over our own ancestral and native philosophy. But let the proof now proceed through the actual works.
