->On the disagreement and battle of the philosophers with one another.<-

I believe it is necessary first of all to start from the very beginning, from the first foundation of the philosophers among the Greeks. I intend to examine those who came before Plato—the ones nicknamed <term>natural philosophers</term> <note>original: "φυσικοὺς" (physikoi). These early thinkers, such as Thales and Anaximenes, focused on the physical elements of the universe rather than ethics or logic.</note>—to see who they were and what kind of philosophy they established through their arguments. Then, I shall move to the succession of Plato to see who his followers were and examine their verbal battles <note>original: "λογομαχίας" (logomachias)</note> with one another. I will also observe the objections of the other sects and the opposing stances of their doctrines. I shall display these men to the spectators as if on a stage, like naked wrestlers fighting and ambitiously striking one another. 

For we shall see immediately how Plato mocked those who came before him, and how he in turn was mocked by his own associates and successors. Among these, we will see how Plato's companions refuted the "many-voicedness" <note>original: "πολυφωνίας" (polyphonias). A critique of Aristotle's voluminous and perhaps inconsistent writings.</note> of Aristotle, and how those who followed Aristotle and boasted of the <term>Peripatos</term> <note>original: "περίπατον" (peripaton). The 'Walk' or covered colonnade where Aristotle taught; his followers are thus called Peripatetics.</note> treated the views of their elders as if they were a primary law. We will see the clever and precise hair-splitting <note>original: "λεπτολογίας" (leptologias)</note> of the Stoics laughed at by others, and how everyone from every side empties their lungs against their neighbors, engaging in a most manly battle. They fight with hand and tongue—or rather with pen and ink—fortifying their war against each other, almost hitting and being hit by the spears and missiles of their words. 

In this gymnastic contest, our stadium will also include those who are "naked" of all the aforementioned beliefs and who take up arms against all dogmatic philosophers at once—I mean the followers of Pyrrho. They declare that nothing can be comprehended <note>original: "καταληπτὸν" (katalepton). A technical term in Hellenistic philosophy meaning 'grasped' or 'perceived with certainty.'</note> by humans. We shall also see the followers of Aristippus, who say that only internal feelings <note>original: "πάθη" (pathe), referring to subjective sensory experiences.</note> are comprehensible; and again, those following Epicurus and Protagoras, who claim one should trust only the physical senses. On the opposite side, we encounter the followers of Xenophanes and Parmenides, who think that things as they are perceived are merely conventions and who challenge the reliability of the senses. Nor shall we pass over the champions of pleasure; we shall list the impiety of Epicurus along with the others mentioned. 

I will carry out this refutation against all of them at once, using their own missiles. I will bring to light the varied disagreements of the natural philosophers and the uselessness of their zeal. I do this not because I am a hater of beauty or a "hater of reason" <note>original: "μισόλογος" (misologos). A term used by Plato to describe someone who has lost faith in the power of argument.</note>—far from it—but to clear myself of the accusation that I have preferred the Hebrew oracles over Greek wisdom <note>original: "ἡλικιακῆς... σοφίας" (hēlikianēs sophias). Literally 'wisdom of the age' or 'worldly wisdom.'</note> without good reason.

---

->On the harmony among the Hebrews.<-

The Hebrews, however, from a long age ago—and from the very first creation of man, so to speak—having taken up the true and pious philosophy, have preserved it uncorrupted for those who came after. Receiving and guarding a treasure of words passed from father to son, they dared neither to add to nor take away anything from what had once been decided. Even the all-wise Moses—who was shown previously to be the eldest of all living men <note>original: "πάντων μὲν ζήνων πρεσβύτατος" (OCR reads 'zenon', likely a misspelling of 'zonton'). Eusebius frequently argues that Moses predates the Greek philosophers.</note>, yet was born later in time than the earlier Hebrews—did not move or change anything from what the forefathers had...

<summary>Eusebius introduces Book 14 as a systematic critique of the internal contradictions of Greek philosophical schools, from the early naturalists to the Sceptics and Epicureans. He contrasts this intellectual "warfare" with the ancient, stable, and harmonious tradition of Hebrew philosophy preserved since the dawn of humanity.</summary>

EUSEBIUS PREPARATION [OF THE GOSPEL] Book 14, 421

...those who have expressed their thoughts on dogmatic theology have established, far more than the men before them, a pattern for a suitable way of life and the legislation of a middle-ground <note>original: "μέσης" (mesēs). Eusebius likely means a constitution that balances different social needs or a "mean" between extremes.</note> constitution. Nor did the prophets after him [Moses], who shone forth over countless periods of years later, dare to utter a single discordant word against each other, or against the laws established by Moses and the ancient beloved-of-God <note>original: "θεοφιλέσι" (theophilesi). This refers to the patriarchs and others whom God favored before the formal Law was given.</note> men. But not even our teacher [Christ], starting from that same source and filling all Greece and the barbarian lands through divine power, included anything discordant with those who came before. Unless one were to say that he hands down the same way of life to those Hebrews who were beloved-of-God before Moses, not only in theological doctrines but also in their manner of living. Our traditions are of this sort: through a single mind and a single voice, witnessed by the first, the middle, and the last, they are sealed by the unanimous vote of both piety and philosophy. Our faith fills the whole world, flourishing and blooming daily as if it had just been established in its first prime. Neither the abolition of laws, nor the plots of enemies, nor the frequently sharpened swords of foes have shown themselves more powerful than the reason-guided mind.

Now let us observe what seal confirms your [Greek] philosophy, so that its wealth may finally be displayed. We shall first bring into the contest those nicknamed the <term>Naturalists</term> <note>original: "Φυσικοὺς" (Physikoi). Early Greek thinkers who sought the physical "first principle" (arche) of the universe.</note>. These men, said to have flourished before Plato, were at such odds with one another as we can learn from Plato himself, who exposes the violence and the mutual combat between those around Pherecydes, Heraclitus, and Empedocles. 

For Protagoras, who was a companion of Democritus, acquired a reputation for being an atheist. At any rate, he is said to have used this opening statement:
<margin>On the gods by Protagoras.</margin>
> "Concerning the gods, I am unable to know either that they exist or that they do not exist, nor what they are like in appearance."
<margin>Of Democritus.</margin>
> "Democritus said that the principles of the universe are the <term>void</term> and the <term>full</term> <note>original: "τὸ κενὸν καὶ τὸ πλῆρες". This is the basis of Atomism: atoms (the full) moving in empty space (the void).</note>. He called the 'full' that which *is* and is solid, and the 'void' that which *is not*. Therefore, he says that 'what is' exists no more than 'what is not,' because things exist from eternity, moving continually and swiftly within the void."
<margin>Of Heraclitus.</margin>
> "Heraclitus said that fire is the principle of all things; from it all things come to be, and into it all things are dissolved. For all things are an exchange for fire, and a time is set for the dissolution of all things into fire and for their generation from it. He claimed that all things are in motion."
<margin>Of Parmenides and Melissus.</margin>
> "Parmenides—whom Plato nevertheless admired—dogmatically stated that the All is one, ungenerated and immovable, and that it exists in a spherical shape. Melissus was a companion of Parmenides and held the same opinions as him."

Listen now to what Plato says concerning these matters in his *Theaetetus*.

### How Plato disparaged those before him. From the *Theaetetus*.

"From flow, motion, and mixture with one another, all things come to be, which we say 'exist,' though we address them incorrectly.
<margin>Of Plato.</margin>
> For nothing ever *is*, but is always *becoming* <note>original: "ἔστι μὲν γὰρ οὐδέποτε οὐδὲν, ἀεὶ δὲ γίνεται". This is the core of the Heraclitean doctrine of flux—that the physical world is in a constant state of change.</note>. On this point, let all the wise men in succession agree, except for Parmenides: Protagoras, Heraclitus, and Empedocles, as well as the greatest poets of both kinds of poetry. Epicharmus for Comedy, and for Tragedy, Homer—who, by saying, 'Oceanus, the origin of the gods, and mother Tethys,' implied that all things are the offspring of flow and motion."

Having previously discussed the confusion among the followers of Heraclitus and the "river" philosophers, he now introduces a long quotation from Plato’s *Sophist*. In this passage, Plato critiques the "myths" of earlier philosophers before Eusebius transitions into a historical overview of the succession of the Academy, aiming to show how Plato's successors drifted from his (and by extension, Moses's) truth.</meta>

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 14

> » It seems to me that everyone has told us a kind of myth, as if we were children. One says that there 
> » are three things <note>Referring to early cosmologists like Pherecydes who proposed three fundamental principles of the universe.</note>, and that some of them are sometimes at war with one another, while at other 
> » times they become friends, producing marriages, births, and the rearing of offspring. Another 
> » speaker says there are two—Moist and Dry, or Hot and Cold—and he settles them together 
> » and gives them in marriage. Our own Eleatic tribe <term>Eleatic school</term> <note>A group of philosophers from Elea, including Parmenides and Zeno, who argued that reality is a single, unchanging "One."</note>, starting from Xenophanes and even 
> » earlier, proceeds with their myths on the assumption that what we call "all things" is actually 
> » one. But certain Ionian and Sicilian Muses <note>The "Ionian Muses" refers to Heraclitus (change), and the "Sicilian Muses" refers to Empedocles (the cycle of Love and Strife).</note> later realized it was safer to 
> » weave both views together and say that Being is both many and one, held together by 
> » enmity and friendship. For the more intense Muses say that in its constant "drifting apart," 
> » it is always "drawn together"; but the gentler Muses relaxed the requirement that this be 
> » so forever, saying instead that the Whole is alternately one and friendly under Aphrodite <note>Aphrodite here personifies the force of "Love" or "Union" in Empedocles's system.</note>, 
> » and then many and at war with itself due to a kind of Strife. Whether any of these men spoke 
> » the truth or not is a difficult and serious matter, and it is in poor taste to find such great 
> » fault with famous and ancient men. One thing, however, can be said briefly: regarding 
> » those who have so precisely defined the Whole and the nature of Being, they have all 
> » treated us with neglect. Nevertheless, let that suffice. But we must look again at those who 
> » speak so roughly, so that we may see from the very beginning that "Being" and "Non-Being" 
> » are equally difficult to define. Should we not, then, march against them? It truly looks like 
> » a kind of "Battle of the Giants" <note>The *Gigantomachy*: A mythological war between gods and giants, used here as a metaphor for the violent intellectual clash between Materialists and Idealists.</note> is taking place among them because of their dispute 
> » about the nature of reality. How so? Some of them drag everything down from heaven and 
> » the invisible realm to the earth, literally grasping rocks and oaks in their hands. By 
> » clutching all such things, they insist that only that which offers some resistance and 
> » touch is real; they define "body" and "substance" as the same thing. And if anyone else 
> » says that something exists without having a body, they despise him entirely and refuse 
> » to hear anything else. Truly, you speak of formidable men; I have already encountered 
> » quite a few of them myself. Therefore, those who dispute with them defend themselves 
> » very cautiously from "above," from the invisible realm, insisting that certain 
> » intellectual and incorporeal "Forms" <term>Forms/Ideas</term> <note>Plato’s famous theory that the physical world is just a shadow of a higher, perfect, non-physical reality.</note> constitute true substance. As for 
> » the "bodies" of the others and what they call "truth," these defenders break them into 
> » little pieces in their arguments, calling them a kind of "becoming" or "process" rather than 
> » true "Being." In the middle of this, O Theaetetus, an endless battle between both sides 
> » has always existed.

Thus, Plato has shown the great conflict among the natural philosophers who came before him. We have already explained in our previous sections what his own opinion was regarding these matters, demonstrating that he agrees with the dogmas of the Hebrews and aligns with the teaching of Moses concerning the nature of Being. But come, let us now observe the dialogues of Plato himself in a logical way. They say that Plato, having established his school in the Academy, was the first to be called an "Academic," and from him, the so-called "Academic philosophy" was established. After Plato, Speusippus <note>The OCR reads "Aneusippos," a likely error for Speusippus, Plato's nephew.</note>, the son of Plato’s sister Potone, took over the school. Then Xenocrates, and then Polemon inherited the school. These men, starting from the very hearth of the school, are said to have guarded the Platonic doctrines, though they distorted <note>original: "στρεβλοῦντας" (streblountas) - literally "twisting" or "torturing."</note> the views of their teacher by introducing foreign dogmas. <meta>This page continues Eusebius's critique of the Greek philosophers in Book 14 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*. After quoting Plato's own admission that the earlier philosophers spoke in "myths," Eusebius now turns to the history of the Academy itself. He aims to prove that even Plato’s direct successors could not agree on his teachings, leading to a fragmented and contradictory tradition, which he contrasts with the supposed unity of the Epicureans (paradoxically) and the steadfastness of sacred truth.</meta>

### EUSEBIUS

...at his death, the succession of his doctrines ended in this way: with battle and discord <note>The Greek word is *stasis*, often used for civil war or political factionalism.</note> beginning from that point and never ceasing even to this day among those who zealously embrace the same interests. These followers are effectively no one—unless there is one or perhaps two in a whole lifetime, or some very few and small in number—despite the great multitude of words they produce through their fabricated sophistry. Indeed, even those who succeeded Plato himself have been accused of being such men. 

For they say that Polemon was succeeded by Arcesilaus, who—according to the prevailing account—abandoned Plato’s doctrines and established a certain foreign and "Second Academy," as they call it. For he claimed that one must "suspend judgment" <term>epoche</term> <note>The central practice of the Skeptic Academy: refusing to agree with any philosophical proposition because human reason is seen as fallible.</note> concerning all things. He argued that everything is "incomprehensible" <term>akatalepta</term>, and that the arguments on either side of a question have equal weight; he further claimed that the senses are untrustworthy, as is all reason. He even applied this maxim of Hesiod to the situation: "For the gods have hidden the mind from humans." <note>A quote from Hesiod’s *Works and Days*. In this context, it is used to justify the Skeptical view that truth is inaccessible to mortals.</note> It is said that he took over the succession specifically to "innovate" it. 

After Arcesilaus, they say that those around Carneades and Clitomachus departed from the opinion of their predecessors and became the cause of a "Third Academy." Some even added a fourth, involving Philo and Charmidas; and some list a fifth, centered around Antiochus. In order that you may know what Plato’s own succession was like, and what sort of men those I have mentioned turned out to be, take and read the words of Numenius the Pythagorean <note>Numenius was a highly influential philosopher of the 2nd century AD who believed Plato was essentially a "Moses speaking Greek."</note>, which he set down in the first book of his work entitled *On the Dissension of the Academics from Plato*.

---

->About the first succession according to Plato. From the writings of Numenius the Pythagorean.<-

"During the time of Speusippus—who was Plato’s nephew—and Xenocrates, the successor to Speusippus, and Polemon, who took over the school from Xenocrates, the zeal for nearly the same doctrines always continued. This was because that much-talked-about 'Suspension of Judgment' <term>epoche</term> had not yet appeared, even if some points were being disputed. However, as they began to relax many clear points and twist others, they did not remain faithful to the original succession. Having received the tradition from Plato, they diverged from it—some sooner, some later—either by choice or through ignorance, or for some other cause that perhaps would not be considered honorable. 

"I do not wish to say anything disparaging about Xenocrates; rather, I want to speak in favor of Plato. Indeed, it pains me that they did not endure everything and do everything to preserve a total and complete agreement with Plato in all things. And yet, Plato was worthy of them; he was perhaps not better than the great Pythagoras, but surely he was no less great than he—and the disciples of Pythagoras followed him, were persuaded by him, and held fast to the teachings of the much-celebrated and most worthy Pythagoras. 

"The Epicureans have never been seen to do this <note>i.e., disagreeing with their founder</note>; having learned his teachings, they were never seen to place themselves in opposition to Epicurus in any way. They acknowledge that they are bound together by him, and for this reason, they rightly enjoy the title of his name. Among the later Epicureans, there was no disagreement with Epicurus, nor did they say anything contrary to one another or to Epicurus on any point worth mentioning. Indeed, among them, it is considered a crime—or rather a sacrilege—and any innovation is condemned. For this reason, no one even dares to try. Their doctrines rest in a profound peace because of their perpetual harmony with one another. The school of Epicurus resembles a true republic, entirely free from discord <note>The Greek *astasiastos* suggests a city without civil war.</note>, possessing one common mind and one opinion..."

<summary>Eusebius recounts the history of the Platonic Academy, noting how it fractured into multiple competing "Academies" (Second through Fifth) that abandoned Plato's original teachings for Skepticism. He uses a quote from Numenius to highlight how, unlike the unified Epicureans, the followers of Plato failed to maintain their founder's intellectual legacy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the text from Numenius (quoted by Eusebius), tracing the "civil war" within Greek philosophy. Having previously discussed the initial split of the Academy, the text now focuses on the internal contradictions of the Stoics and the diverse influences that shaped Zeno and Arcesilaus, the two great rivals of the Hellenistic age.</meta>

# PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 14.

> "...holding an opinion. From which they already are and, as it seems, will continue to be followers of factions. The affairs of the **Stoics** have been at variance <note>original: *estasiastai*, suggesting a state of civil war or internal factionalism</note>, beginning from their leaders, and have not yet reached an end even now. They take pleasure in refuting one another under hostile scrutiny. Some of them have remained steadfast, while others have already shifted their positions. Thus, the first leaders yielded to those with more 'oligarchic' <note>In this context, meaning exclusive or authoritative</note> tendencies, who, by being at odds, became the cause of much censure for their predecessors and for one another. Ever more 'Stoic' than one another, they appeared increasingly pedantic <term>mikrologoi</term> <note>Literally "small-speakers," referring to those obsessed with trivial logic and minute details</note> concerning technicalities. For these very men, surpassing others in their meddlesomeness <term>polypragmosyne</term>, were sooner worn out by their own hair-splitting <term>skariphismois</term> <note>Literally "stylus-scratches," a metaphor for overly fine or useless distinctions in logic</note>.

> Much earlier than these, however, the same thing happened to those who drew different doctrines away from **Socrates**. **Aristippus** went his own way, and **Antisthenes** went his own way. And elsewhere, the **Megarians** and the **Eretrians** <note>Two early Socratic schools that focused on logic and ethics</note> took their own paths, along with any others associated with them. The reason was that Socrates knew of three gods <note>This likely refers to the "Three Kings" or principles mentioned in the Platonic *Second Letter*, which Numenius interprets as a Socratic doctrine</note> and philosophized for them in the rhythms appropriate to each; but those who heard this tried to take the reins, yet thought he said everything at random, and from whatever 'Divine Fortune' happened to be blowing, they would offer prayers at any given moment.

> But **Plato**, following Pythagoras <term>pythagorisas</term>, knew that these same things were said by Socrates from no other source than divine inspiration <term>entheou</term>. Thus, Plato bound these matters together, neither in his usual manner nor bringing each thing out into the open as he believed. By hiding his meaning in a middle ground between being clear and unclear, he kept himself safe, yet he himself provided the cause for the factionalism <term>stasis</term> and the 'dual-rule' <term>diarches</term> <note>A state where two conflicting principles or leaders hold power simultaneously</note> of doctrines that followed him. This was not out of malice or ill-will—but I do not wish to speak words that are not auspicious about men of old.

> We who are present should rather form our judgment from this: that just as we initially proposed to separate him from **Aristotle** and **Zeno**, so now, if God assists us, we shall separate him from the Academy and leave him to be a **Pythagorean** in his own right. As it stands now, he is followed in a more frenzied manner than is proper for any five men, through every conflict; yet, taken as a whole, he never truly shifts or reverses his position. Thus, as a man who pursued the way of **Pythagoras** and **Socrates**, he brought in the solemnity <term>semnon</term> of the former while maintaining the humanity <term>philanthropon</term> of the latter. By leading the cleverness and playfulness of Socratic irony into a state of dignity and weight <term>axioma kai ogkon</term>, and by mixing Pythagoras into Socrates, he appeared more popular in some respects and more solemn in others. 

> But I did not come to judge these matters, as they are not the subject of my inquiry. I will return to what we proposed, lest we be knocked off the path that leads there. **Arcesilaus** and **Zeno** became pupils of **Polemon**. We shall imitate them again at the conclusion. I remember saying that Zeno first attended the lectures of **Xenocrates**, then Polemon, and later lived like a Cynic <note>original: *kunisai*, literally "to act like a dog," the root of the word Cynic</note> with **Crates**. Now let it be reckoned that he also shared in the teachings of **Stilpo** and the Heraclitean discourses. For since they were fellow students under Polemon, they became rivals; they brought into their mutual battle other influences: for Zeno, it was **Heraclitus**, Stilpo, and Crates together. From Stilpo, he became a fighter; from Heraclitus, he became austere; and from Crates, a Cynic. 

> But **Arcesilaus** held to **Theophrastus**, **Crantor** the Platonist, **Diodorus**, and then **Pyrrho**. From Crantor, he became a 'maker of persuasions' <term>pithanourgikos</term>; from Diodorus, a sophist; and from Pyrrho, he became all things at once—both bold and nothing at all. This is what has always been sung of him..."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the internal divisions within the philosophical schools. Having just described the hair-splitting of the Stoics, the text now turns to the founder of the 'New Academy,' Arcesilaus, and how his philosophy was a strange hybrid of several conflicting traditions.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

> » ...having brought forward a certain insulting verse: "Plato in front, Pyrrho behind, Diodorus in the middle." <note>original: *Prosthe Platōn, opithen Pyrrhōn, mesos Diodōros*. This famous lampoon by Timon of Phlius parodies Homer’s description of the Chimaera (Iliad 6.181), a mythical beast made of three different animals, to mock Arcesilaus for mixing three distinct philosophies.</note> Timon also says that Arcesilaus was "equipped" by Menedemus <note>A philosopher of the Eretrian school known for his prickly and argumentative nature</note>, if indeed he is speaking of him when he says:
> » "Having the lead of Menedemus beneath his breast,
> » He will place there either Pyrrho, or all-flesh <note>original: *pankreas*, likely a pun or corruption in the text</note>, or Diodorus."
> » Therefore, having entangled the reasonings of **Pyrrho** and his skepticism with the weapons of the "fine-talk" <term>leptologiai</term> <note>Refers to overly subtle or minute logical distinctions</note> of **Diodorus the Dialectician**, Arcesilaus adorned this chattering nonsense with the eloquence of **Plato**. He would say one thing and then contradict himself; he rolled back and forth, shifting from one side to the other, wherever he might happen to land. He was a man who took back his words, hard to deal with, fickle, and at the same time reckless—claiming he "knew nothing," as he himself said, being a wild rogue <note>original: *chlunaios*, a rare Homeric word for a wild boar, used here to describe Arcesilaus as a rough or untamable thinker</note>. In the end, he turned out like a painted figure, colored all over by the "shadow-painting" of his words.

---

### Concerning Arcesilaus, who established the Second Academy. From the same author <note>Numenius of Apamea</note>.

->Just as in that Homeric line about Tydeus, where it was unknown which side he belonged to—whether he was with the Trojans or the Achaeans—so too Arcesilaus remained unknown.<- For he never recognized the one doctrine he once uttered as his own; nor would such a thing ever seem to belong to a "Lycian man." <note>A reference to a character in the Iliad; here it implies Arcesilaus lacked a consistent identity or "homeland" in his thought.</note> He was called a "clever sophist" and a "slaughterer of the unpracticed." For just like the **Empusae** <note>Shape-shifting demons of Greek folklore used to scare children</note>, he enchanted people with the phantoms of his arguments—just as Medea did. He claimed to know nothing, and neither did those who lacked reason. He could overwhelm or throw anyone into confusion. Being the first to carry off the prize for sophistry and the "theft of words," he delighted in insults and took a strange pride in the idea that there is neither anything shameful nor noble, neither good nor evil. But whichever of these might fall into someone's soul, after saying this, he would change again and overturn it many more times than he had built it up.

Thus, like a **Hydra** cutting himself and being cut by himself, he separated both sides of an argument without distinction, showing a necessary lack of foresight. He provided his listeners with more than they could handle at once—just like a man sowing a field—so that he was most pleasant to hear and behold. For men accepted his arguments because they came from a beautiful person and were delivered with a friendly look in his eyes.

One must hear these things not simply, but follow them from the beginning. For after joining with **Theophrastus** <note>The successor of Aristotle</note> in his youth—a man who was not without talent in matters of love, as Arcesilaus was handsome—and while still in his prime, Arcesilaus met the Academic **Crantor** and became his lover. He joined his school, and since his nature was not untalented, he made use of his natural excellence. However, out of a restless love of contention, he meddled with things and took part in the clever tricks of **Diodorus**, making those sophisticated arguments seem persuasive. He also associated with **Pyrrho**.

**Pyrrho**, however, had started from the principles of **Democritus**. Arcesilaus remained a follower of Pyrrho in more than just name, especially in the "total denial" <note>original: *anairesei*, referring to the skeptical denial of the possibility of certain knowledge</note> of all things. At least **Mnaseas**, **Philomelus**, and **Timon** (the Sceptics) call him a **Sceptic**, just as they were themselves, because he also denied the existence of truth, falsehood, and even the "persuasive." Therefore, although he was a Pyrrhonist in everything but name, out of respect for his lover <note>Crantor</note>, he endured being called an Academic. While he was a Pyrrhonist in reality, he was an Academic only in name. I do not believe Diocles of Cnidus <note>A philosopher who wrote a history of the schools</note> when he claims in his work titled...

<meta>catchword: ...entitled [The Refutations]</meta>

It highlights his habit of denying all knowledge and his tendency to overturn his own arguments, suggesting his identity as an "Academic" was merely a mask for his true Pyrrhonist skepticism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Arcesilaus, the head of the Academy, who used a mix of philosophical styles to avoid being pinned down by critics. We now see how his "Skepticism" was used as a defensive weapon against the rising Stoic school led by Zeno.</meta>

# EVANGELICAL PREPARATION, Book 14

» ...of frivolous chatter. **Arcesilaus**, out of fear of the followers of **Theodorus** and **Bion the Sophist** <note>Theodorus 'the Atheist' and Bion of Borysthenes were famous for their biting, aggressive wit and attacks on traditional philosophy</note>, who were constantly attacking the philosophers and shrinking from no kind of refutation, was himself on his guard. To avoid having trouble, he made sure he never appeared to suggest any definite dogma.

» For just as **cuttlefish** discharge their ink <note>original: *melan tas sēpias*. The cuttlefish uses a cloud of ink to escape predators; Arcesilaus used 'Skepticism' to escape logical traps</note>, he put forward "suspension of judgment" <term>epoche</term> <note>The practice of withholding assent to any claim as a way to achieve mental tranquility</note> as a defensive screen in front of himself. This, at least, is what I am told, though I do not believe it. Others, starting from I know not where, say that both **Arcesilaus** and **Zeno**, under the influence of such training—with arguments fighting on both sides—forgot the original starting point they had received from **Polemon**. <note>Polemon was the head of the Academy before it turned toward Skepticism; both Zeno and Arcesilaus studied under him</note> Having drifted apart and equipped themselves for battle:

> » They clashed their ox-hide shields, their spears, and the strength of men
> » clad in bronze breastplates; and the bossed shields
> » pressed against each other, and a great din arose;
> » shield pressed on shield, helmet on helmet, and man
> » jostled against man. <note>These are verses from Homer's *Iliad*, used here to describe the intense intellectual combat between the Stoic and Academic schools</note>

» And there, at once, rose the groans and the boasts of men, as the **Stoics** were both destroying and being destroyed. For the **Academics** were not easily hit by them; they were either ignored or were too clever to be caught. They could only be captured if their very foundation was shaken—that is, if they had neither a starting point nor a basis for battle. Their starting point was to refute the Stoics by showing that what they said was not "Platonic." <note>Arcesilaus claimed he was the true heir to Plato's questioning method, while Zeno claimed to be the heir to Plato's ethics</note> To give themselves a basis for what I have said, they almost completely turned away from the definition concerning the **cognitive impression** <term>katalēptikē phantasia</term> <note>The Stoic 'criterion of truth': a mental image so clear and distinct that it cannot be false</note>. Since there is no greater opportunity for me now, we shall leave this aside for another time, when we come to the part that concerns us most.

It is clear that once they had drifted apart, these members of the same household threw themselves at each other—not just any two, but Arcesilaus against Zeno. For Zeno had a certain dignity and weight in battle, no better than **Cephisodorus** the rhetorician. This Cephisodorus, when he saw his teacher **Isocrates** being assisted by **Aristotle** <note>Numenius seems to be confusing historical figures here; Cephisodorus actually wrote *against* Aristotle to defend Isocrates</note>, was himself ignorant and inexperienced regarding Aristotle. But because he saw the high reputation that **Plato’s** works enjoyed, and thinking that Aristotle followed Plato’s philosophy, he made war on Aristotle but ended up hitting Plato. He began his accusation with the **Ideas** <note>Plato's Theory of Forms</note> and ended with other matters which he himself did not understand, merely suspecting what was commonly thought or said about them.

In short, Cephisodorus was fighting someone who wasn't fighting back, and he was struggling against a person he didn't actually intend to go to war with. Zeno, too, since he had shared in Arcesilaus' circle—if he had not also made war on Plato—would have been, in my judgment, a philosopher of great value, for the reason already mentioned. But if, while perhaps not being ignorant of Arcesilaus’ views, he was ignorant of Plato's—as is proven by what he wrote against him—he acted in a state of distress <insert>internally</insert>, striking one person when he meant another, or striking someone he shouldn't have. He acted most dishonorably and shamefully, behaving much worse than is fitting even for a **Cynic** <note>original: *kuni*, literally 'dog'. The Stoics were heavily influenced by the Cynics, who were known for their 'barking' and aggressive social critiques</note>.

Nevertheless, he displayed a certain high-mindedness, though he was more at a loss than Arcesilaus. Whether through ignorance of the latter's views or because of his own Stoic nature, like a great body, he broke away and separated himself from Plato. But regarding the things Zeno did against Plato—the innovations he made both poorly and ignorantly—I shall speak of them another time, if the needs of philosophy lead me there. Yet I hope I am never led to such a need for their sake, unless perhaps for the sake of a joke. Arcesilaus, seeing what a well-armed and formidable opponent Zeno was, tried to pull him down with the arguments he brought against him, and he did not hesitate. Concerning the public battles he fought against him, I perhaps cannot speak of them; or if I could, there would be no need for it now...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Arcesilaus’s philosophical methods, specifically his battles with the Stoic school, before transitioning into a humorous anecdote about his successor, Lacydes of Cyrene, to illustrate the practical (and absurd) applications of Academic Skepticism.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

» ...to be remembered. They say he put forward a doctrine of his own, even if he appeared to honor the name of the **Academy**. He used every possible device against the **"grasping impression"** <term>original: *katalēptikēn phantasian*; the Stoic concept of a perception so clear it cannot be doubted</term> which was so highly regarded. His opponent, being of a more "Athenian" <note>likely referring to a more traditional or stable temperament</note> character, remained calm and, unable to be provoked, let **Arcesilaus** be, despite having much he could have said. Perhaps he simply hesitated. But Arcesilaus continued to "shadow-box" against **Plato**—who was no longer among the living—and raised a great clamor of **scurrilous abuse** <note>original: *pompēian apo hamaxēs*; literally "procession from a wagon," referring to the insults hurled during Dionysian festivals</note>. He claimed that Plato would not have been better off for it, and that he himself did no more harm to anyone else than to Arcesilaus, whether he realized it or not; at any rate, he thought he had gained the greatest advantage by turning Arcesilaus away from himself. One might even see the trick **Agathocles of Syracuse** <note>A tyrant of Syracuse known for his daring and sometimes deceptive military tactics</note> played on the **Carthaginians** in this. The **Stoics** <term>A rival school that taught that the universe is governed by reason and that certain knowledge is possible</term> listened in astonishment. For their Muse was neither a lover of words <note>original: *philologos*</note> nor a superior craftsman at that time, and so Arcesilaus—now striking them, now cutting them off, now undermining them—constantly defeated them, for he was very persuasive. Therefore, among those who did not catch themselves being defeated, and among those to whom he spoke, a sense of awe prevailed. It was demonstrated to the men of that time that no word, no feeling, and no deed, however small or useless, would ever appear to be anything unless it seemed so to Arcesilaus. Yet, as it turns out, nothing seemed right to him, nor did he declare anything to be more than a mere word, a shadow, or a phantom.

### The lifestyle of those described. About Lacydes, who succeeded Arcesilaus. From the same source.

We wish to relate a pleasant story about **Lacydes**. He was somewhat frugal, and having adopted a certain "economical" style of life, he was well-regarded in some respects but not in many others. He insisted on opening the storehouse himself and locking it himself. Indeed, whatever he needed, he did everything with his own hands—not because he was praising **self-sufficiency** <term>autarkeia</term>, nor because he was suffering from poverty or a lack of slaves (for he had as many slaves as one might expect). I will relate the "pleasant" thing I promised. Because he was his own steward, he kept the key on his person. He didn't think it was enough just to lock up; he would place the key in a hollow writing-case, seal it with his signet ring, and then roll the ring back through the keyhole into the house, so that later, when he returned, he could open the door with the key and easily find the ring inside to break the seal, lock up again, seal it, and toss the ring back inside through the keyhole. The slaves, noticing this "clever" trick, would wait for Lacydes to go out for a walk or wherever he was going, and they would open the storehouse themselves. They would eat and drink to their heart's content, and after taking what they wanted—though they didn't do this every time—they would lock the door, reseal it with the ring, and then toss the ring back into the house through the keyhole. Thus, Lacydes, who had left the jars full, would find them empty. Being at a loss as to what was happening, and having heard from the philosophers at **Arcesilaus’s** school about **inapprehensibility** <term>akatalēpsia; the doctrine that nothing can be truly known or perceived with certainty</term>, he began to think that this very thing was happening to his storehouses. Having accepted this, he began to philosophize under Arcesilaus, claiming that one could see or hear nothing clearly or soundly. And once, when one of his associates was staying at his house, he began to tell him a story about how naturally, as it seemed, a person is carried along...

Lacydes's confusion over his slaves stealing his food leads him to embrace the doctrine of "inapprehensibility," concluding that his senses cannot be trusted.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Academic Skepticism by transitioning from Arcesilaus to his successor, Lacydes of Cyrene. It recounts a famous and humorous anecdote intended to mock the impracticality of the Skeptical doctrine of "incomprehensibility" in everyday life.</meta>

# THE PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 15

» He said, "I can tell you about this disputed matter myself, having learned it from my own experience, not from testing someone else." And then, beginning as if he had encountered some matter regarding his **storehouse** <note>original: *tamieiō*; the household pantry or storage room</note>, he described his own experience. "What then," he said, "could anyone say regarding living creatures to someone who so admittedly talks nonsense through everything, as I do in these matters of **incomprehensibility** <term>original: *akatalēpsia*; the skeptical doctrine that nothing can be known with certainty</term>? For I, who closed the door with my own hands, marked it with a seal myself, and then cast the ring inside through a hole, would return and open the door. I would see the ring inside, but certainly not the goods that were clearly gone. How could I not be right to distrust the facts outside? For I would not dare to say that someone slipped in and stole them while the ring was inside acting as a guard." And the person listening—who was quite a boor, but a great follower of the **Academy** <term>The school of philosophy founded by Plato, which in this period practiced radical skepticism</term>, as one might expect—could barely contain himself at first, but then broke out into a very wide and loud laugh. Cackling as much as he could, he exposed the man's vanity. Consequently, from that time on, Lacydes began no longer to seal the ring inside, and he no longer practiced **incomprehensibility** regarding his storehouse, but rather he began to **grasp** <term>original: *katelambane*; to perceive or understand clearly—a play on the Stoic term for certain knowledge</term> the things he handled, realizing he had been philosophizing in vain. However, his servants were rascals, not at all easy to catch, the sort of characters one sees in comedies or like the Getae <note>A common name for slaves in Greek New Comedy, often depicted as clever and deceptive</note>. Having snatched up bits of Lacydes’ talk, whether hearing some of his **sophisms** <note>original: *psephismata*; here likely referring to logical puzzles or deceptive arguments</note> or clearly learning from him, they went straight for the boldest move and stole his seal itself. At first, they left the impression of the seal behind. Later, they did nothing else but what they thought would lead him to **incomprehensibility**, and so they acted quite freely. He would go in and look. When he saw the writing-tablet or the jar had been tampered with, or sealed but not with his own seal, he would become indignant. When they used **sophisms** <note>clever but fallacious arguments</note> to claim that he could see the seal himself, he would examine it closely and point out the difference. When they were defeated by his demonstration, they would say that if the seal was not there, he had probably forgotten it himself or failed to mark it. He would insist that he had marked it and remembered doing so, and he would show them and push back against their excuses, arguing with them and thinking they were playing a joke, and he would defend his position. But they, taking up his own attacks, thought that they themselves were being played by him. For since Lacydes no longer accepted things "without an opinion," even for someone who forgets, he claimed memory was a good "opinion" <note>original: *doxan*; a technical term for belief or opinion as opposed to certain knowledge</note>. At any rate, after a long time, they said he told these things to his friends. When he brought these attempts to their attention, they said it was not "Academic" of him. They themselves, frequenting the school of a certain Phaedrus, learned the arguments they needed to say, and from that point on they voted for themselves, becoming rival "Academic thieves." He would blame the **Stoics** <term>A rival school that believed in certain knowledge and strict morality</term>, but the servants would dismiss his accusations based on **incomprehensibility**, not without some Stoic-style arguments of their own. Thus, there were constant disputes there—arguments and counter-arguments—and nothing in the house was left alone: not a vessel, nor anything kept in a vessel, nor any of the household furnishings, but everything was treated as fair game. For a while, Lacydes was at a loss, seeing that the help provided by his own doctrine was of no use to him. Then, thinking that everything was being carried out because of his own theories, he fell into a state of confusion. He began shouting to the neighbors and the gods: "Woe! Woe!" and "Alas! Alas!" and "By the gods!" and "By the goddesses!" and all those other artless proofs used by people in the midst of terrible distrust—all these he poured out with shouts and appeals to credibility. In the end, since he had a greater dispute occurring within his house, he himself began to act like a **Stoic** <note>original: *estōikeueto*; i.e., he started demanding certainty and absolute truth</note> toward the servants, while the servants insisted on **Academic** principles so that they would no longer have any trouble...

<summary>This page recounts a humorous anecdote about the philosopher Lacydes, whose commitment to the Skeptical doctrine of "incomprehensibility" allows his clever servants to steal from him and then use his own philosophical arguments to deny their guilt.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the history of the Academic philosophers, specifically focusing on the transition from the "Middle Academy" of Lacydes and Arcesilaus to the "New" or "Third Academy" founded by Carneades. It explains how Carneades modified the radical skepticism of his predecessors to make it more practical for daily life.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

» ...he was publicly proclaimed as the "friend of the storehouse" <note>original: *philos tou tamieiou*; a nickname mocking Lacydes' obsession with his pantry despite his philosophy of "not knowing"</note>. But it was no use to him, for having crept in, those who were clever would come to him and reveal his folly. He would say, "These things are clear, children, in our discussions, but they are altogether a different soup in the living of them." This is what is told regarding Lacydes.

Many people became his students, among whom was also the obscure Aristippus of Cyrene <note>Likely Aristippus the Younger, grandson of the famous founder of the Cyrenaic school</note>. From among his many acquaintances, Evander took over the school, and then those after him. After these, **Carneades** took charge of the school and established the **Third Academy**.

Carneades used the same method of reasoning as Arcesilaus. For he also practiced arguing on both sides of a question, and he would systematically dismantle everything said by others. However, he differed from Arcesilaus on only one point: the doctrine of **suspension of judgment** <term>original: *epochē*; the practice of withholding one's consent or belief from any proposition</term>. He claimed it was impossible for a human being to maintain a suspension of judgment regarding all things. He made a distinction between the "unclear" and the "incomprehensible." He held that while all things are **incomprehensible** <term>original: *akatalēpta*; unable to be grasped with absolute certainty</term>, not all things are **unclear** <term>original: *adēla*; some things are evident enough to act upon even if they aren't "known" in a divine sense</term>. He also participated in **Stoic** <note>The Stoics were the primary rivals of the Academy, believing in absolute certain knowledge</note> arguments, and by standing against them in debate, he increased his own reputation. He appeared **persuasive** <term>original: *pithanos*; providing a "convincing" or "probable" basis for action without claiming it is the absolute truth</term> to the masses, yet he was not aiming at the truth. For this reason, he caused a great deal of annoyance to the Stoics. Numenius <note>A Platonist philosopher who wrote a history of the Academy's "betrayal" of Plato's teachings</note> writes the following about him:

### Concerning Carneades who established the Third Academy. From the same source.

» Carneades, having taken over the leadership, ought to have guarded what was left stable and what was shaken by his predecessor, but he remained quiet on those points. Instead, for the sake of utility—whether for better or for worse—he rekindled the long-standing battle against the Stoics. The following is told of him: how and from where they brought him forth, as he introduced verbal subtleties and refined turns of phrase into the battle. He was skilled at denial and at masking his intentions, a master of arguing from both sides. If ever a topic seemed to hold some wonder, he would rise up fiercely, like a **rushing river** <note>original: *potamos herōdēs*; a metaphor for his overwhelming and turbulent eloquence</note>, flowing violently and flooding everything here and there. He would fall upon his audience and sweep them away in a confused uproar.

» He himself, however, remained undeceived, not following the elders like Arcesilaus. For Arcesilaus, being held fast by the "drugs" <note>original: *pharmakei*; likely a metaphor for the paralyzing effect of total skepticism</note> of his own arguments, failed to notice that he had first deceived himself into believing that one should not feel or be convinced of anything. But Carneades, seeing the evil that Arcesilaus had inflicted on himself by this total "suspension," relaxed it a little. He introduced what he called **persuasive impressions** <term>original: *pithanai phantasiai*; the idea that we can act on what seems "convincing" even if we don't "know" it</term>, which are used for the sake of action and impulse. For example, he would say: "This is a living creature," or "This is not a living creature." 

» He lay in wait like a hunting beast, more violent and more than a match for those who faced his spears. Having yielded everything to his opponents, he then attacked with greater power. Whenever he would establish a position, he would do so from a place they already expected, and then he would mock us and himself. For while he conceded that **truth and falsehood** exist in things, as if he were cooperating with his opponents, he then crept along the old path of inquiry and gained the upper hand. By pouring out the flow of his "persuasive arguments" on both sides, he concluded that neither side could be grasped with certainty. In this, the deceiver was even wiser than the thief. For taking a falsehood that looked like the truth, and a "graspable impression" <note>original: *katalēptikē phantasia*; the Stoic term for a clear, undeniable perception</note> that looked like it could be grasped, he brought them to an equal level. He allowed neither the truth nor the falsehood to prevail—or rather, he held that one was no more likely than the other, except by way of what is **persuasive**. Thus, even a dream could be useful through such a similar impression...

<meta>This page continues the history of the Academic school, focusing on the tactical brilliance of Carneades and his successor Clitomachus, before moving into the shifts in thought under Philo of Larissa and the eventual schism caused by Antiochus of Ascalon.</meta>

->PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 14<-

» ...[he preferred] truth over the false. It was as if comparing a fake egg to a real one. Consequently, troubles followed, and in great number. Carneades used to charm and even enslave me <note>The narrator here is Numenius, a later philosopher whose work Eusebius is quoting</note> with his speech. To some, he was like a thief, unseen; to others, a visible brigand, seizing his prey through both trickery and force, even those who were exceedingly well-prepared. Indeed, the entire mind of Carneades was victorious.

» I heard no one else at all. For even those against whom he waged war were too weak to speak. The time of his opponent <note>Referring to the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, who famously struggled to answer Carneades’ arguments</note> was certainly painful; he spent it in agony and writing. Yet, against the arguments brought daily from the school of Carneades, he never published a public response—not in his lectures, nor in his walks, nor did he ever speak of it or touch upon it. No one, they say, ever heard a single word from him in reply. Instead, he managed his counter-arguments in secret; taking a little corner, he left behind books written for those who would come later. These books were not powerful then, and were even less capable against such a towering figure as Carneades, whose arguments had already dissolved the perceived truths of that time. 

» Nevertheless, even though he was driven into the open by his Stoic competitiveness, he would confess and admit the truth in secret to his own companions, revealing things that any ordinary person might recognize. 

» Then, it is said next: although the first man was master of Carneades' thought, he was not his successor. But while Carneades was still living, he caught an adulterer with his mistress. In that moment, he did not act based on a "persuasive impression" <term>original: *pithanē phantasia*; the Academic skeptic's standard for acting without certain knowledge</term>, nor as if he had not "grasped" the situation. Rather, fully trusting his own sight and having apprehended the truth, he removed the man from the school. The man who was cast out then spent his life in bitterness; being inactive, he did nothing but use his words to argue for **incomprehensibility** <term>original: *akatalēpsia*; the doctrine that nothing can be known for certain</term>. 

» And again, he adds: Carneades, practicing philosophy in a reversed manner, would beautify himself with lies and hide the truth within them. He used lies as a screen and walked a path of deception, rather like a merchant. He suffered the same fate as legumes: the empty ones float on the surface of the water and stand out, while the good ones stay at the bottom and are out of sight. Such things are said of Carneades. His successor and leader of the school was **Clitomachus**. After him came **Philo**, of whom Numenius records the following:

### Concerning Philo, the successor of Clitomachus, who succeeded Carneades. From the same author.

» Philo, as soon as he took over the school, was overwhelmed with joy. Showing gratitude to Fortune as his benefactress, he strengthened the doctrines of Clitomachus and armed himself against the Stoics with "newly-forged bronze" <note>A poetic metaphor for sharpening his rhetorical weapons</note>. 

» As time went on, however, the **suspension of judgment** <term>original: *epochē*</term> that had become habitual to them began to fade. He no longer thought the same things he once did, for the clarity <note>original: *enargeia*; the self-evident nature of certain perceptions</note> and the testimony of his own experiences turned him around. Having already developed a strong intuition, he was eager—I am sure of it—to lay hold of the truth of the matter, provided he did not seem to be turning his back and fleeing the school's traditions by his own choice. 

» **Antiochus** was a student of Philo, and he started a different Academy. Having lost his temper with the Stoic Mnesarchus, he began to hold opinions opposite to those of his teacher Philo, and he introduced countless foreign ideas into the Academy. These things, and thousands more like them, are recorded concerning the succession from Plato. 

» It is time, therefore, to take up the discourse again and examine the false and contradictory opinions of the natural philosophers. These men, having wandered over the wide earth and having placed the highest value on the discovery of truth, have nevertheless fallen into the opinions of the ancients...

<meta>This page continues the critique of Greek philosophical schools. While the previous page focused on the internal conflicts of the Academy and the skepticism of Carneades, this page transitions to Eusebius's broader argument: that pagan philosophy is a collection of human guesses rather than divine truth, using the admissions of the Neoplatonist Porphyry as evidence.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS, PRE[PARATION FOR THE GOSPEL]

...having closely studied, and having accurately examined the theology of all the Phoenicians and Egyptians—which was spoken of long before their own time—so that one might find the fruit of these labors, it is worth hearing from them. Thus, we should not dare to say that they were merely hushed by the elders for fourteen years. For polytheistic superstition had prevailed among the nations since ancient times, and more recent sacred mysteries of the gods had been established and were guarded by everyone in every city and country. Surely, then, there was no need for human philosophy if one had truly received the matters of divine wisdom <term>theosophia: literally 'god-wisdom,' referring here to ancient priestly traditions</term>. Nor was there any necessity for the wise to innovate if the traditions of their ancestors were in good standing. Neither was there any reason for philosophers to be disturbed and to disagree with one another, if indeed the ancestral opinion concerning the gods happened to be harmonious, true, and proven.

But if it were necessary to wage war and fight against one another, or to travel the long road up and down, wandering and plundering the secrets of the barbarians <note>original: "βαρβάρων" - Greeks used this term for anyone who did not speak Greek, including Egyptians and Phoenicians</note>—when they ought to have remained at home and learned from the gods, if indeed there were any gods—or from "theological" men, through words that were truly and unfailingly about the subjects sought in philosophy, why then have they toiled ten thousand times in debate, only to fall far short of finding the truth?

If it were necessary to dare to seek out more recent things concerning the gods, then every inquiry is deceptive among them. If a safe and certain discovery and knowledge of the gods had been piously received in the rites and mysteries, and if that contained the rest of the most ancient theology, was it not possible to keep that very tradition unmoved and harmoniously agreed upon?

On the contrary, there are those who claim they have learned nothing true about God from the elders, but have applied themselves to the study of nature through their own private notions, using conjectures rather than firm comprehension. What remains, then, but to confess that the ancient theology of the nations contains nothing more than the history already delivered in the preceding writings? That the error arose from human conjectures and word-fighting <term>logomachia: a dispute about words or language rather than the underlying reality</term>, and not from any accurate comprehension, you may learn from the letter of Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a major Neoplatonist philosopher and a famous critic of Christianity; Eusebius enjoys quoting him to show that even the "enemies" of the Church admitted philosophy was a mess</note> to Anebo the Egyptian, hearing him confess this very thing in these words:

---

->That conjectures and verbal disputes and much error happen to be among the Greek philosophers; from the letter of Porphyry to Anebo the Egyptian, and from what he himself wrote to Boethus concerning the soul, and from the philosophy derived from oracles.<-

---

<margin>A » » » » » » » »</margin> I shall begin my friendly address to you with the gods and good spirits <term>daemons: in Greek thought, these were intermediate spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil</term>, and with the philosophy that has become confused regarding them—subjects about which a great deal has been said by our own philosophers. But for the most part, they have held their primary convictions based on conjecture. 

And proceeding further, he adds: "For among us, there is a great deal of word-fighting, since the Good is being imagined through human reasonings. But for those who have devised the means of communion with the superior power, if they have practiced their wisdom in vain in this particular area, it has been to no purpose." Moreover, in what he himself wrote to Boethus concerning the soul, the same author confesses word-for-word as follows: "While common sense and the facts of history indisputably establish that the soul is immortal, the proofs brought forward by the philosophers..."

<meta>This page continues the critique of Greek philosophical schools, moving from the internal contradictions of the Academy to a direct confrontation with the "sciences" (the Quadrivium) that Greeks claimed were necessary for truth. It introduces Porphyry's admission that the Greeks were "led astray" while the Hebrews found the true path.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS, PREPARATION [FOR THE GOSPEL], BOOK 9

> » ...arguments that have been set forth seem to be never-ending, because of the "love of pleasing" <note>original: "ἀρεστολογίαν" (arestologian) — a rhetorical style aimed at pleasing the audience rather than finding truth</note> found in all contentious debaters. For what philosophical argument is not disputed by those of different opinions, when even concerning things that seem clear, it seemed best to all of them to withhold judgment?

And in his work entitled *On the Philosophy from Oracles*, he <note>Porphyry, a 3rd-century Neoplatonist and critic of Christianity</note> explicitly confesses that the Greeks have been led astray. He calls as witness his own god, stating that this was also the message issued by Apollo through oracles, which testified that "barbarians" rather than Greeks discovered the truth; he even made mention of the Hebrews among those so witnessed. Indeed, after quoting the oracle, he follows up with these concluding remarks:

> » You have heard how much labor is required,
> » so that one might release the purifications for the sake of the body—never mind finding salvation for the soul?
> » For the path to the gods is bound with bronze, steep and rugged; many of its trails were discovered by the
> » barbarians, but the Greeks went astray. Those who held it already even corrupted it. God testified to the
> » discovery of this path for the Egyptians, the Phoenicians, and the Chaldeans—these are the Assyrians—and for the
> » Lydians and the Hebrews.

Such are the words of the philosopher, or rather, of his own god. Is it not then right, following the critique we have made, that we did not abandon the way of the Hebrews—who are witnessed to have apprehended the truth—for the sake of the Greeks who were led astray? Or what should one expect to learn from philosophers? What benefit is there in them, if their teachings for the most part happen to have the origins of their belief in conjectures and guesswork? For the fruit of their labor is a kind of "word-fighting" <term>logomachia: a battle over words or definitions rather than reality</term>, since all the arguments of the philosophers are shifting and inconsistent because of this "love of pleasing" in everything. You have just heard these things, not from us, but spoken by them. 

It seems clear to me that, having examined the matter with careful judgment and not without reason, we have looked down on the Greek ways and cherished the ways of the Hebrews—not simply because it was witnessed by the demon <note>original: "δαίμονος" — Eusebius uses this term for the pagan gods who spoke through oracles</note>, but because they are proven to participate in divine virtue and power. And so that you may learn not just from their actions but from the "word-battles" of these "wonderful" philosophers—those concerning first principles, gods, and the disagreement regarding the composition of the universe—I will set out their own words a little later. 

But first, let us bring into view how they boast of their subjects of study up and down. They claim that those who intend to experience the apprehension of truth must by all means pursue astronomy, arithmetic, geometry, and music—the very things which they themselves prove came to them from the barbarians. They say that without the mastery of these, it is impossible for a man to become learned or a philosopher, nor can one even touch the truth of existing things unless the knowledge of these is first imprinted in the soul. Then, "fluttered" by the study of these subjects, they almost think they are walking on air, imagining that they carry God himself around in their numbers. As for us, because we do not pursue the same things, they consider us no different from cattle <note>original: "βοσκήμασι" — literally "grazing animals" or "beasts"</note>. They say that in this way we can know neither God nor anything sacred. 

Come then, let us first prove that they are not correct, setting the true Word <term>Logos: here referring to the divine Reason or the Christian Gospel</term> against them like a light. This Word will show that while thousands of Greeks and thousands of barbarian races knew these subjects, they recognized neither God, nor a temperate life, nor anything truly good or beneficial; whereas others, apart from all these studies, have become most pious and most philosophical. At any rate, you may learn what the world-renowned Socrates thought about these things by trusting Xenophon, who records it in his *Memorabilia* in this way:

### On geometry, astronomy, and calculations. From the *Memorabilia* <note>original: "ἀπομνημονευμάτων" (apomnēmoneumatōn) — literally "recollections" or "reminiscences," usually translated as the *Memorabilia* of Xenophon.</note> of Xenophon.

» He <note>Socrates</note> also taught to what extent a properly educated person should be experienced in each subject. 
» For instance, he said that one should learn geometry only so far as to be capable, if the need ever arose, 
» of correctly measuring land to receive or hand it over, or to divide it, or to assign a task. 
» He said this was so easy to learn that anyone who paid attention to the measurement would know 
» at once how large the land was and depart knowing how it is measured. But he disapproved of 
» studying geometry as far as complicated and difficult diagrams. For he said he did not see 
» what benefit there was in these—even though he himself was not ignorant of them. 
» He said that these things were enough to wear out a man’s life and to prevent him from 
» many other useful branches of learning. He also urged them to become experienced in 
» astronomy, but only so far as to be able to know the hour of the night, the month, and 
» the year, for the sake of travel by land and sea and for keeping watch; and for whatever 
» tasks are done by night, month, or year, to have markers to use by distinguishing 
» the seasons of the aforementioned times. He said these things were easy to learn from 
» night-hunters, pilots, and many others whose business it is to know such things. 
» But as for learning astronomy to the point of knowing the stars that are not in the 
» same revolution, such as the planets and the "unsteady stars" <note>original: "ἀσταθμήτους ἀστέρας" (astathmētous asteras) — likely referring to comets or perhaps the irregular motion of planets compared to fixed stars</note>, 
» and seeking their distances from the earth, their periods, and their causes—
» he strongly discouraged wasting time on such things. For he said he saw no benefit 
» in these either, even though he was not unacquainted with them. He said that these too 
» were enough to wear out a man's life and prevent him from many useful things. 
» In general, he discouraged becoming a "thinker" <note>original: "φροντιστήν" (phrontistēn) — a term often used pejoratively for those who speculated on the heavens</note> 
» regarding how God contrives each of the heavenly things. For he did not believe that 
» these things were discoverable by men, nor did he think a person would please the 
» gods by seeking what they did not wish to make clear. He said that the one who 
» worried over these matters would run the risk of losing his mind, no less than 
» Anaxagoras <note>A famous Pre-Socratic philosopher who was the first to suggest that the Sun was a red-hot mass rather than a god.</note> 
» lost his mind, he who took the greatest pride in explaining the mechanisms of the gods. 
» For that man, in saying that fire and the sun are the same thing, ignored the fact 
» that people can easily look at fire, but cannot gaze directly into the sun. 
» And while being shined upon by the sun, their skin becomes darker, but not so 
» by fire. He also ignored that of the things growing from the earth, nothing 
» can grow well without the sun’s rays, but when warmed by fire, they are all destroyed. 
» And when he claimed that the sun was a "red-hot stone," he also ignored that a stone 
» in fire neither shines nor lasts for a long time, whereas the sun remains 
» forever the brightest of all things. He also urged them to learn calculations. 
» But in these, as in the other subjects, he urged them to guard against 
» "vain labor" <note>original: "μάταιον πραγματείαν" (mataion pragmateian)</note>; up to the point of utility, 
» he himself investigated everything and went through it with his associates. 
» These things Xenophon wrote in the *Memorabilia*. And the same author, in his 
» letter to Aeschines, writes the following about Plato and those who boasted of 
» their natural philosophy <term>physiology</term> <note>original: "φυσιολογίαν" (physiologian) — in the ancient sense, the study of the nature of the universe (physics), rather than the modern biological sense.</note>.

### On gymnastics and music. From Plato in the *Republic*. <note>This section translates Plato's *Republic*, Book VII, 521c–531a.</note>

"What then, Glaucon, would be a study that draws the soul away from the realm of 'becoming' toward the realm of 'being'? <note>Plato distinguishes between the physical world of change (becoming) and the eternal world of truth (being).</note> This is 
» what I am considering as I speak. Is it not necessary for these men, being young, to be 
» athletes of war?" "It is necessary," he said. "Then the study we are seeking must have 
» this additional quality." "What quality?" "It must not be useless to men of war." "It must 
» indeed," he said, "if it is possible." "Now, they were previously educated by us in 
» gymnastics and music." "That is so," he said. "And gymnastics, I suppose, is 
» concerned with that which 'becomes' and 'perishes'; for it oversees the 
» growth and decay of the body." "So it appears." "This, then, would not be the study 
» we are seeking." "No." "But what about music, as far as we described it before?" "But that," 
» he said, "was the counterpart to gymnastics, if you remember, educating the guardians 
» through habits, providing a certain harmony through melody—not 'knowledge' <note>original: "ἐπιστήμην" (epistēmēn) — systematic or scientific knowledge</note>—and 
» a certain grace through rhythm; and in its stories it contained other similar habits, 
» both in the mythical ones and those that were truer. But as for a study leading toward 
» such a thing as you now seek, there was nothing of that in it." "You remind me 
» most accurately," I said. "For in reality, it contained nothing of the sort. But, 
» my dear Glaucon, what could such a thing be? For all the arts 
» seemed to be 'mechanical' <note>term: "ϐάναυσοί" (banausoi) — manual or technical crafts, often looked down upon by Greek philosophers as distracting from intellectual virtue.</note>." "How could they not? Yet if you select them in order, 
» let them never label us as 'unlearned' in those things by which we are nourished, and which 
» everyone must pass through, just as we were recently saying about astronomy. Or do 
» you not know that they do something similar regarding harmony? For they measure 
» audible concords and sounds against one another, performing useless labor just like the astronomers." 
» "By the gods," he said, "it is laughable how they name certain 'densities' <note>original: "πυκνώματ'" (pyknōmat') — the smallest intervals in a musical scale.</note> and 
» strain their ears, as if trying to catch a voice from the neighbors; some say they 
» can still hear a small sound in the middle, and that this is the smallest interval 
» by which one must measure; while others dispute..."

Let us then consider, starting from these very points, certain dogmatic statements of the natural philosophers and their contradictions with one another. Plutarch—having collected the opinions of the Platonists and Pythagoreans together, along with those of the even older natural philosophers who have been called upon, and again the later Peripatetics, Stoics, and Epicureans—recorded them in the work he titled *On the Opinions of the Philosophers Regarding Natural Dogmas*; from these, we shall set forth the following.

## Opinions of the Philosophers on First Principles. From the works of Plutarch, in the book *On the Opinions of the Philosophers Regarding Natural Dogmas*.

» Thales of Miletus, one of the Seven Sages, declared the first principle <term>archē</term> <note>The "archē" is the fundamental substance or ultimate underlying principle of all things.</note> of all 
» beings to be water. This man seems to have been the founder of philosophy, 
» and from him the Ionian school <note>One of the earliest traditions of Greek philosophy, centered in Ionia (modern-day Turkey).</note> received its name. There were many 
» successions of followers. Having studied philosophy in Egypt, he came to Miletus 
» as an older man. He says that all things are from water, and all things are 
» dissolved back into water. He guesses this, first, because the seed of all 
» animals is a principle, and it is moist. Thus it is likely that all things 
» have their beginning from moisture. Second, because all plants are 
» nourished by moisture and bear fruit, but when deprived of it, they wither. 
» Third, because even the very fire of the sun and the stars is nourished by 
» the vapors of the waters, as is the world itself. Because of this, even Homer 
» assumes this opinion about water, saying: "Oceanus, who is the progenitor of 
» all." <note>A reference to the Iliad (14.246), where the god of the sea is called the source of all things.</note> These are the views of Thales. 

» But Anaximander of Miletus says that the first principle of beings is the "Infinite" 
» <term>apeiron</term> <note>The Infinite or Boundless; a substance without limits in space or time.</note>. For from this, all things come to be, and into this, all things are 
» destroyed. On account of this, infinite worlds are created, and again 
» destroyed into that from which they were born. He says, therefore, why it is 
» infinite: so that the underlying process of generation might never fail. 
» But he errs in not saying what the Infinite is—whether it is air, or 
» water, or earth, or some other bodies. He errs, therefore, by declaring 
» the matter, but doing away with the making cause <note>Also known as the "efficient cause"—the force or agency that actually creates or moves the matter.</note>. For the Infinite is 
» nothing other than matter. But matter cannot be in actuality unless one 
» assumes the existence of the maker. 

» Anaximenes of Miletus declared the first principle of beings to be air. For 
» from this all things come to be, and into it they are again dissolved. 
» Just as our soul, he says, being air, holds us together, so too a spirit 
» <term>pneuma</term> and air encompass the whole world. Air and spirit are used 
» synonymously. But he also errs in thinking that living beings are 
» composed of a simple and uniform nature of air and spirit. For it is 
» impossible for a single principle...
