» [it is necessary not only for] the matter of existing things to subsist, but one must also posit the efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" refers to the force or agent that brings something into being, as opposed to the "material cause" or the substance it is made of.</note>. For he 
» says a drinking-cup would not come into being unless there were a producer—
» and that is the silversmith. 
» It is the same for bronze, wood, and any other matter. Heraclitus and Hippasus of 
» Metapontum say the principle of all things is fire. For they say that all things come 
» from fire, and all things end in fire. When this fire is extinguished, 
» the universe is formed. 
» For first, the thickest part of it, contracting into itself, becomes earth. 
» Then the earth, being relaxed by the nature of the fire, results in 
» water. Being evaporated, it becomes air. 
» Again, the world and all bodies are consumed by fire in the "conflagration" <note>original: *ekpyrosis* — the Stoic and Heraclitean idea that the universe is periodically destroyed and reborn in fire.</note>. 
» Thus, fire is the principle because all things come from it, and it is the 
<margin>D</margin>» end because all things are dissolved back into it. Democritus—whom Epicurus 
» followed shortly after—posited the principles of existing things to be "atoms" <note>original: *atoma* — literally "uncuttable" particles.</note>, 
» which are bodies perceptible only by reason, having no part of the void, 
» unbegotten, eternal, and indestructible. They cannot even be broken, 
» nor can they take their shape from parts, nor can they be altered, 
» even if they are perceptible only by reason. These, however, move 
» in the void, and because of the void. They say the void itself is infinite, 
» and the bodies are infinite. These three qualities belong to the bodies: 
» shape, size, and weight. 
» Democritus said there were two: size and shape. But Epicurus added 
» a third to these: weight. For he says it is necessary for bodies 
» to move by the impact of weight, otherwise they will not move. 
» He says the shapes of these atoms are limited in variety, not infinite. 
» They are not hook-shaped, nor trident-shaped, nor ring-shaped. These 
» shapes are easily broken, but atoms are "impassive" <note>Incapable of being acted upon or changed by external force.</note> and unbreakable; rather, they have 
» their own specific shapes, perceptible by reason. An atom is called 
» such not because it is the smallest possible thing, but because it cannot 
» be cut, being impassive and without any void within it. So when he says 
» "unbreakable atom," he means it is impassive and contains no void. 
» That the atom exists is clear; for there are elements, and "empty" 
» living things, and the "monad" <note>The monad refers to a single, indivisible unit.</note>. Empedocles, son of Meton, of Akragas, 
» says there are four elements: fire, air, water, and earth. 
» But there are two primary powers: Love and Strife. One of these is 
» unifying, and the other is divisive. He speaks thus:

> Hear first the four roots of all things:
> Gleaming Zeus, life-bringing Hera, and Aidoneus,
> And Nestis, who with her tears wets the mortal spring.

» By [Zeus], he means the heat and 
» the ether. By "life-bringing Hera," he means the air. By "Aidoneus," the earth. 
» And by "Nestis" and the "mortal spring," he means as it were the seed and the water. 
» Such is the great disagreement among the first natural 
» philosophers. Such was their opinion concerning the principles: they hypothesized 
» no God, no maker, no craftsman, no cause of the whole, 
» nor even gods, nor incorporeal 
» powers, nor intellectual natures, nor rational essences—not anything 
» at all outside the senses was placed among their principles. 
» Anaxagoras is the only one remembered as the first among us 
» to declare Mind <note>original: *nous*</note> to be the cause of all things in his discourses on 
» principles. For they say he was greatly admired among the naturalists 
» of his time. Because of his studies, he even allowed his own land 
» to become a sheep-pasture, and he was the first to articulate the discourse 
» on principles from their roots. For he did not only declare 
» concerning the substance of all things, as those before him did, 
» but also concerning the cause that moves it. For "in the beginning," 
» he says, "all things were mixed together," but Mind entered in 
» and led them out of disorder into order.

## On the opinion of Anaxagoras. From the words of Socrates in Plato’s *On the Soul*.

---

> <margin>A</margin> "But having once heard someone reading from a book, as he said, by Anaxagoras, and saying 
> » that it is Mind that arranges and is the cause of all things, I was delighted with this cause, 
> » and it seemed to me in a way to be right that Mind should be the cause of all. And I thought 
> » that if this were so, the Mind, in ordering all things, would order them and place each 
> » thing in the way that would be best for it. If, therefore, anyone wished to find the cause 
> » of each thing—how it comes into being, or perishes, or exists—he must find this 
> » concerning it: in what way it is best for it either to exist, or to act or be acted 
> » upon in any other way. From this reasoning, it was fitting for a man to consider nothing 
> » else, both concerning himself and concerning others, except what is most excellent and 
> » best. And it would be necessary for this same person to also know what is worse; 
> » for the science concerning them both is the same. Considering these things, 
> » I thought I had found, to my own delight, a teacher of the cause of existing 
> » things according to Mind—namely Anaxagoras—and that he would tell me first 
> » whether the earth is flat or round. And after he told me that, he would further 
> » explain the cause and the necessity, speaking of what was 'better,' and that 
> » it was better for it to be of such a kind. And if he said it was in the middle 
> » [of the universe], he would further explain how it was better for it to be in the middle. 
> » And if he could prove these things to me, I was prepared to no longer 
> » desire any other kind of cause. And indeed, I was similarly prepared to ask 
> » about the sun, and the moon, and the other stars, concerning their 
> » relative speeds and their turnings <note>original: *tropōn* — referring to the solstices or the orbital paths of the planets.</note> and their other conditions—how 
> » it is better for each of them to act and to be acted upon as they are. For I never 
> » thought that he, while claiming they were ordered by Mind, would bring in 
> » any other cause for them than that it is best for them to be exactly as they are. 
> » So, by assigning the cause to each thing and to all in common as being what is 
> » best for each, I thought he would also explain the common good for all. 
> » And I would not have sold these hopes for a great price! Rather, taking up 
> » the books with great haste, I read them as quickly as I was able, so that 
> » I might know as quickly as possible what is best and what is worse. 
> » But from this wonderful hope, my friend, I was carried away and disappointed. 
> » For as I went on and read, I saw a man making no use of Mind at all, 
> » nor assigning any causes for the ordering of things, but instead 
> » assigning causes such as airs, and ethers, and waters, and many other 
> » strange things. And he seemed to me to have suffered something very similar 
> » to a person who says that 'Socrates does everything he does by Mind,' 
> » and then, in attempting to state the causes of each of the things I do, 
> » should say first that the reason I am now sitting here is because my 
> » body is composed of bones and sinews; and that the bones are solid 
> » and have joints that kept them apart, while the sinews are such as 
> » to be tightened and relaxed, surrounding the bones along with the 
> » flesh and the skin that holds them together. [The bones being] swung..."

> » ...since the bones are moved in their joints, the sinews <note>original: *neura* — refers to both sinews and tendons, which the Greeks believed controlled movement through tension.</note> by relaxing and contracting 
> » make me able to bend my limbs as I do now. And it is for these physical reasons 
> » that I sit here in this curved position. And again, regarding my conversation with you, 
> » he might name other such causes—voices, air, and hearing—and a thousand other 
> » such things, while neglecting to mention the true causes. The truth is that since the 
> » Athenians thought it better to condemn me, for that reason I have also thought it 
> » better to sit here, and more just to remain and undergo whatever penalty they

> » long ago, carried there by an opinion of what is "best," if I did not think it 
> » more just and honorable to stay and submit to the city’s penalty rather than to 
> » run away and escape. But to call such things "causes" is quite absurd. 
> » If someone were to say that without having such things—bones and sinews 
> » and whatever else I possess—I would not be able to do what I have decided, 
> » he would be speaking the truth. However, to say that I do what I do *because* of 
> » these things, and that I act with Mind <note>original: *nous* — the intellectual principle.</note> in this way, rather 
> » than by the choice of what is best, would be a very great and long-winded 
> » laziness of logic. 
> » He [Anaxagoras] then adds that this is why Leucippus <note>An early philosopher who, with Democritus, founded Atomism.</note> places a "whirl" around the earth, 
> » and claims the earth stays in place because of the heaven. Another supports the 
> » earth like a flat kneading-trough with the air as a base. But as for the power 
> » that arranges things as well as they could possibly be placed, they neither 
> » seek it out nor believe it has any divine strength. Instead, they think they 
> » will eventually discover an Atlas <note>The Titan from Greek myth who held up the sky.</note> stronger, more immortal, and 
> » more capable of holding everything together than this power. They do not 
> » think that the Good and the "Ought" <note>original: *deon* — that which is binding or necessary.</note> truly bind and hold things together at all."

These are the opinions of Socrates regarding other thinkers. Archelaus was the successor of Anaxagoras, both in his school and in his doctrine. It is said that Socrates was a student of this man. Furthermore, other natural philosophers, such as Xenophanes and Pythagoras, who flourished at the same time as Anaxagoras, philosophized concerning the incorruptibility of God and the immortality of the soul. From these men and after them, the various schools of Greek philosophy were established. Some of these followed others, while some devised their own private opinions. Again, Plutarch writes about the conceptions of these same men regarding the gods in this manner:

## The Opinions of the Philosophers Concerning the Gods. From Plutarch.

---

Some of the philosophers, such as Diagoras of Melos, Theodorus of Cyrene, and 
> » Euhemerus of Tegea, say that there are no gods at all. Callimachus of Cyrene 
> » alludes to Euhemerus in his iambic poems. And Euripides the playwright 
> » did not wish to reveal his view openly, fearing the Areopagus, <note>The high court of Athens, which could try cases of impiety.</note> but he 
> » hinted at it in this way: he introduced Sisyphus as the champion of this 
> » opinion and advocated for his view. Following these, he [Plutarch] introduces 
> » Anaxagoras again, claiming that he was the first to think correctly about God. 
> » He says: Anaxagoras says that matter stood still in the 
> » beginning, but the Mind of God <note>original: *nous theos*</note> set it in order and produced 
> » the generations of the universe. Plato, however, did not assume that primary 
> » matter was standing still, but that it was moving in a chaotic way. Therefore, 
> » he says that God, recognizing that order is better than disorder, set it in 
> » order. To which he [Plutarch] adds: commonly, then, both of them are in 
> » error, because they made God concerned with human affairs, 
> » and constructing the world for the sake of these. For the blessed 
> » and incorruptible Living Being <note>Meaning God/the Divine.</note> is filled with all good things and [is free] 
> » from every evil...

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the nature of the divine, transitioning from Socrates’ critique of physical causes to a broader survey of various Greek philosophical schools and their conflicting views on God, providence, and the cosmos.</meta>

<page-num>440</page-num>
<header>EUSEBIUS PREP.</header>

> >> ...accepted, being entirely occupied with the maintenance of its own happiness and incorruptibility, it is unconcerned with human affairs. And it would be a "demon," <note>original: *daimōn* — in this context, a lesser spiritual being or a laboring force rather than a supreme, tranquil God.</note> performing labor like a craftsman or a builder, carrying its own burdens and worrying over the construction of the world. And again, God might be spoken of in terms of the past: either there was an age before when he did not exist, when bodies were motionless, or when they moved in a disordered way; or he was either sleeping or awake, or neither of these. But it is not possible to accept the first, for God is eternal. Nor is the second possible, for if God had been sleeping from eternity, he would have been dead; for eternal sleep is death. Yet God is incapable of sleep. For the immortal and that which is the opposite of death are separated from sleep by a great distance. If, on the other hand, God was awake, he was either lacking in happiness or he was filled with blessedness. If the former, then God was not "blessed," for to live by laboring toward happiness is not a blessed state. If the latter, then his actions would seem like empty phrases to anyone attempting to describe them, as there would be nothing else for him to do. And how, tell me, is God concerned with providence? How are human affairs managed by chance, when one man is clearly unfortunate while another, though wicked <note>original: *asteion* — here meaning "refined" or "clever," but used ironically to mean a person who prospers despite lacking virtue.</note>, suffers the opposite? For Agamemnon—who was both "a good king and a mighty spearman" <note>A famous line from Homer’s *Iliad* (3.179) describing the leader of the Greeks.</note>—was defeated and treacherously murdered by an adulterer and an adulteress. And his kinsman, Hercules, after purging human life of many things that ravaged it, was poisoned by Deianira and treacherously killed. Thales <term>Thales of Miletus: often called the first philosopher, he sought natural explanations for the world.</term> considered the world to be God. Anaximander called the stars "heavenly gods." Democritus said God was a spherical soul of fire within the world. Pythagoras held that of the first principles, the Monad <term>The Monad: the number "One," representing unity and the source of all things.</term> was God and the Good, which is the nature of the One and Mind itself; but the "Indefinite Dyad" <term>The Dyad: representing duality, division, and the material world.</term> was a demon and the Evil, associated with the plurality of matter, since the world is also visible. After these, hear how the more recent thinkers formed their opinions. Socrates and Plato held that the One is of a single nature, self-existent, monadic—that which is Truly Good. All these names point toward the Mind. Therefore, God is Mind, a separate form, being unmixed with any matter and entangled with nothing that can suffer. Aristotle held that the highest God is a separate form, standing upon the sphere of the universe, which is an ethereal body—what he calls the "fifth element." <term>Aether: the "quintessence" or fifth element, which Aristotle believed made up the heavens.</term> While this sphere and God are distinct, they are joined by nature but separate in logic; he thinks each of the spheres is a living being composed of body and soul. Of these, the body is ethereal, moving in a circular path, while the soul is an unmoved principle <note>original: *logos akinitos*</note>, the cause of motion through its activity. The Stoics, speaking more emptily, declare God to be a "creative fire," <term>original: *pyr technikon* — a craftsman-like fire that designs the world.</term> proceeding in a fixed way toward the generation of the world, encompassing all the "seminal reasons" <term>original: *spermatikoi logoi* — the principles or "seeds" that determine how things grow and develop.</term> according to which everything happens by fate. He is a spirit <note>original: *pneuma*</note> pervading the whole world, but receiving different names because of the changes in the matter through which he has passed. They also call the world, the stars, the earth, and the highest mind in the aether "God." Epicurus held that all the gods are human-shaped, but all are perceived only by reason because of the refined nature of their images. He also categorized four other natures as "incorruptible" in name: atoms, the void, the infinite, and the "similar parts" <note>original: *homoiomereias* — a term from Anaxagoras referring to substances that are made of parts like themselves.</note> and the elements. Such are the disagreements and blasphemies of the natural philosophers concerning God, among whom our argument recently established that the followers of Pythagoras and Anaxagoras, and Plato and Socrates, set Mind and God over the world. Yet these men are proved to be mere children in time compared to the eras in which these things were recorded by Hebrew theology. From which, then...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s survey of Greek philosophical history. Having previously discussed the Egyptian and Phoenician origins of polytheism and the transition to natural philosophy, he now focuses on the "Eleatic" school, which rejected sensory perception in favor of pure reason.</meta>

<page-num>441</page-num>
<header>EUSEBIUS: PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 14</header>

The knowledge of the God of all things is considered the most ancient belief among all people, even among those of old who first introduced polytheistic superstition <note>original: *deisidaimonia* — literally "fear of the spirits," often used by early Christian writers to describe pagan religion.</note> among both the Phoenicians and Egyptians. This knowledge was brought forth by those who were leaders among the theologians <note>original: *anagoreas* — speakers or announcers of sacred things.</note> and their followers. Nevertheless, the practice of polytheistic superstition eventually prevailed among all nations. However, it seems this did not contain the true theology; rather, the Egyptians and Phoenicians were the first of all to be recorded as having established it. This system did not involve gods at all, nor any divine powers, but instead deified men who had long been dead, as the true account long ago demonstrated.

Come then, let us resume our discourse. Just as some of the natural philosophers reduced everything to the senses, others in turn spoke against them. These included the followers of Xenophanes of Colophon and Parmenides of Elea, who indeed did away with the senses, claiming that nothing is graspable through sensory perception and that one must trust in reason <note>original: *logos* — here referring to logical deduction or pure intellect.</note> alone. Let us examine what has been said in opposition to these very men.

### Against the followers of Xenophanes and Parmenides, who abolish the senses.
#### From the eighth book of Aristocles <note>Aristocles of Messene was a Peripatetic philosopher who wrote a history of philosophy; Eusebius relies on him as a primary source.</note> on Philosophy.

Others have taken the opposite view, giving voice to a contrary opinion. For they think that one must cast aside the senses and appearances <note>original: *phantasias* — the mental images or impressions formed by the senses.</note>, and trust only in reason itself. Such things were said earlier by Xenophanes, Parmenides, Zeno, and Melissus, and later by the followers of Stilpo and the Megarians. Consequently, these men saw fit to claim that Being is "One," and that "Non-Being" is something else, and that nothing is either born or destroyed, nor is there any motion whatsoever.

While we might have a longer argument against these men when engaging in philosophy, for now, something must be said regarding this specific point. For we would say that while our reason is our most intimate faculty, we certainly have need of the senses as well, just as we have need of the body. It is clear that the senses are naturally "true" <note>Aristocles argues for the reliability of the senses against the Eleatics.</note>. For it is impossible for that which perceives not to be affected in some way. Furthermore, is not the knowledge of what one knows the same as perception? Indeed, if perceiving is being "affected" by something, and this affection comes from what is present, then the "doer" and the "sufferer" <note>The object causing the sensation and the organ receiving it.</note> must be entirely different things. Thus, before perception can exist, there must be that which is called "the other"—namely, color and sound.

Furthermore, if Being is stationary, it will be so, and it will be motionless; but perception is itself a type of motion. In this way, he wishes for the senses to hold their nature, since I believe we trust in those things that exist more than those we merely think about. Reasonably, then, a certain powerful love for them is ingrained in us. No one, unless they have forgotten everything, would cast away even a single sense, even if it meant all clear benefits would come to him.

Those who slander the senses, if they were truly convinced that they possessed them in vain, ought to say what Pindar says in Homer regarding his own bows:

> "Straightway let some stranger cut the head from my shoulders,
> if I do not throw these bows into the blazing fire,
> breaking them with my hands; for they follow me as useless as the wind."
> <note>original: *Odyssey* 21.312-315. Aristocles/Eusebius quotes this to suggest that if the Eleatics really thought senses were useless, they should discard them as useless tools.</note>

After this, they should justly rid themselves of all their senses. For in this way, one might believe them, as they would be teaching by their deeds that they had no need of them. But as it stands, this is the most absurd thing of all: for while they declare the senses useless in their reasoning, they continue to use them as much as possible in their daily actions. Melissus, at least, while wishing to demonstrate that among appearances and the whole of these things, nothing is...

<summary>Eusebius quotes the philosopher Aristocles to critique the Eleatic school (Parmenides, Xenophanes, etc.), arguing that their total rejection of sensory perception is logically flawed and practically hypocritical.</summary>

> >> ...demonstrating them through the things that appear. For he says, if there are earth and water and air, and fire and iron and gold; and if one thing is living and another dead, and black and white, and all the other things that men say truly exist—if we see and hear correctly, each thing ought to remain exactly as it first appeared to us and as it seemed to be, and not change nor become something else, but each should remain just as it is. But now, we claim to see and hear and understand correctly, yet it seems to us that the hot becomes cold, and the cold hot, and the hard becomes soft, and the soft hard. 
> >> When he says these and many other such things, one might quite reasonably be forgotten <note>The text here is slightly corrupt; it likely refers to being "reminded" or "persuaded" by the logic.</note> and ask: "Is it not true that you did not correctly know what is now hot and what is afterwards the cold of the earth?" And likewise concerning other things. For even if sight exists, it would distinguish nothing; rather, by doing away with the senses, one proves he trusts them most of all. These arguments were, so to speak, the moisture <note>original: *ikmas* — a metaphor for the "vital juice" or "essence" of the argument.</note> for which they have since paid the penalty. They have become faded and forgotten, as if they had never been spoken at all. Now, let no one think I speak idly when I say some have practiced philosophy correctly by employing both the senses and reason <note>original: *logos*</note> for the knowledge of things.
> >> Such were those around Xenophanes, whom I mentioned, who flourished at the same time as those around Pythagoras and Anaxagoras. Xenophanes himself was a Colophonian by birth. Then came Melissus, then Zeno, then Leucippus, then Democritus, then Protagoras, and Nausiphanes. 
<margin>4</margin> >> After Nausiphanes came Eudorus <note>The text reads "not Eudorus," possibly a corruption in the manuscript list of names.</note>, then Bryon, then Lazarchus. A pupil of Anaxarchus was Pyrrho, from whom the school of those called Sceptics <note>term: *Skeptikoi* — literally "the seekers" or "the examiners," referring to a school of thought that doubted the possibility of certain knowledge.</note> continues its existence. These men define that absolutely nothing is graspable <note>original: *katalēpton* — a technical term meaning "able to be firmly understood."</note> either by sensation or by reason. We can learn how they suspend judgment in all things—thereby setting themselves apart from those who hold opposing opinions—from the aforementioned treatise, which reads word for word as follows:

---

->**Against the Pyrrhonian Sceptics, or those called "Suspenders of Judgment,"**<-
->**who declare that nothing is graspable. From the same author.**<-

> <margin>A</margin> >> It is necessary, before all else, to examine our own knowledge. For if we are by nature incapable of knowing anything, there is no longer any need to investigate other things. There were indeed some among the ancients who uttered this view, whom Aristotle argued against. Perhaps Pyrrho of Elis said similar things as well. However, he himself left nothing in writing. But his disciple Timon says that the one who intends to be happy must look to these three things: first, what the nature of things is; second, in what way we should be disposed toward them; and finally, what the result will be for those who are so disposed. 
> >> Now, he says that things themselves are equally indifferent, unstable, and undecidable; for this reason, neither our senses nor our opinions tell the truth or lie. Because of this, we must not trust them, but be without opinions, without bias, and unwavering, saying about each thing that it "no more is than is not," or "it both is and is not," or "it neither is nor is not." For those who are so disposed, Timon says the result will be, first, a non-assertion <note>term: *aphasia* — a state of being "without speech" or "refusing to make a claim."</note>, and then tranquility <note>term: *ataraxia* — a state of being "unperturbed" or "free from worry," which was the ultimate goal of many Greek philosophies.</note>. Aenesidemus, however, says the result is pleasure. This, then, is the summary of what they say. Let us then consider whether they speak correctly. Since they say all things are equally indifferent, and for this reason they command us to agree with nothing and to hold no opinions, one might reasonably ask them:

<meta>This page continues the critique of the Sceptical school, shifting from a general history of doubt to a logical refutation of the core Sceptic claim that "all things are unclear." It specifically addresses the paradoxes inherent in the teachings of Pyrrho, Timon, and Aenesidemus.</meta>

<page-num>443</page-num>
<header>PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, Book 14</header>

> » Do those who think things differ believe they actually differ, or not? For certainly, if they believe it of both <note>Likely referring to both the senses and the intellect.</note>, they would not be conceiving things correctly. Thus, it is necessary for them to say that there are some people who hold false opinions about the things that exist. They themselves, then, would be the ones speaking the truth. In this way, there would be such a thing as truth and falsehood. But if the many, who think that existing things differ, do not think so of both, they would meet us with a rebuke; for they themselves would claim that things do not differ in both respects. And indeed, if things were not in some way equally indifferent to them, it is clear that they themselves would not differ from the majority. How then could their wisdom exist? And why do you reproach all others, but praise Pyrrho alone? Furthermore, if all things are equally indifferent, and for this reason one ought to hold no opinions, then even these very things would not differ. I mean "differing" or "not-differing," and "holding an opinion" or "not holding an opinion." For are these things more than they are not, or as Timon says, "Why yes, and why no, and why the 'why' itself?" It is obvious, then, that such a person seeks the impossible. Therefore, let them stop being a nuisance. For now they have closed their eyes <note>original: *memyasi* — a metaphor for shutting one's eyes to reality or being "initiated" into a state of blindness.</note>, far removed from any systematic skill <term>techne</term>, at once exhorting us not to hold opinions, while at the same time commanding us to do this very thing; and saying that one should declare nothing about anything, and then proceeding to make declarations. They claim that one should give <term>assent</term> <note>original: *synkatatithesthai* — a technical term in Greek philosophy for the mind's agreement to a perception.</note> to nothing, yet they command us to be persuaded by them. Then, saying they know nothing, they refute everyone else as if they themselves were not the ones lacking knowledge. It is necessary for those who claim that all things are unclear to do one of two things: either remain silent, or declare something and speak. Now, if they keep silence, it is clear that there can be no argument against such people. But if they make declarations, they must entirely and in every way either say that something is, or that it is not—an affirmation or a negation. If everything were unknown and merely a matter of opinion to everyone, then nothing would be known anywhere. Therefore, the person making a claim must either show what the thing signifies and what its "being" actually is, or it is nothing. But if it signifies nothing, then there is absolutely no one to whom any kind of argument could be addressed. If it does signify something, he would either be speaking of infinite things or finite things. If infinite, there would be no argument with him at all, for there is no knowledge of the infinite. But if the things signified are finite, or even just one thing, then the person speaking defines and judges something; how then could all things be "unknown" and "undecidable"? And if he should say that these things both "are" and "are not," first of all, the same thing will be both true and false. Secondly, he will both speak and not speak, and while using reason <term>logos</term>, he will destroy reason. Furthermore, while admitting that he is lying, he says we must believe him. It is worth asking where they learned that "all things are unclear," as they say. For they must first know what "the clear" is. For only then could they say that things are not of such a kind. First, one must know <term>affirmation</term> <note>original: *kataphasin*</note>, then <term>negation</term> <note>original: *apophasin*</note>. If they are ignorant of what the clear is like, they would not even know what the unclear is. Whenever Aenesidemus <note>The OCR reads "Amnesidemos," a common transcription variant for Aenesidemus of Cnossos.</note> in his *Outline* <note>original: *hypotypōsei* — referring to his work "Pyrrhonian Outlines."</note> goes through the nine modes—for by these he attempts to show that things are unclear—should we say he speaks knowing these things, or being ignorant of them? For he says that animals differ, and we differ from them, and so do cities and lives, and customs and laws. And he says our senses are weak, and many external things ruin our knowledge—such as distances, magnitudes, and motions. Furthermore, he points out that the young and the old are not disposed in the same way, nor are the waking and the sleeping, nor the healthy and the sick; and that we perceive nothing "simple and pure." For everything is confused and spoken of in relation to something else. I say that such clever talk...

It specifically challenges the Sceptics' habit of making assertions while claiming no assertions can be made, referencing the "modes" of Aenesidemus.</summary>

> » ...[if someone spoke] thus, one might pleasantly ask whether he says things are this way because he knows well, or because he is ignorant. For if he does not know, how can we believe him? But if he did know, he would be quite a sun <note>original: *hēlios* — a metaphor for a source of total illumination or enlightenment, used sarcastically here.</note>, simultaneously declaring everything unclear while also claiming to possess knowledge. And indeed, whenever they recount such things, they say nothing other than a sort of inducement, describing what sort of things appearances and individual instances are. And such a thing is a matter of speech and belief. If they assent to it, it is clear they are forming an opinion <term>doxazousin</term>. If they do not believe it, then neither should we pay them any attention. Nor does [Timon] recount for us in the *Pytho* <note>A famous satirical poem by Timon of Phlius, where he describes meeting Pyrrho.</note>, stretching out a long speech about how he met Pyrrho walking toward Pytho [Delphi] to the temple of Amphiaraus, so that they might converse with one another. Should Timon be affected and assent to his words, or pay no attention? For if he was not persuaded, how did he himself become part of that philosophical chorus and spend his life admiring Pyrrho? If he assented to what was said, he would be absurd—philosophizing himself while preventing us from doing so. Quite simply, one might wonder what Timon’s *Silloi* <term>Silloi</term> <note>A series of satirical poems mocking the "dogmatism" of other philosophers.</note>, and the slanders against all men, and the wicked "muddlings" of Aenesidemus <note>A later Sceptic who revived Pyrrho’s ideas.</note>, and all such a crowd of words actually intend. For if they wrote these things thinking they would make us better, and for this reason think they must refute everyone so we stop talking nonsense, they clearly want us to know the truth and to understand that things are as Pyrrho claims. So if we were persuaded by them, we would not <unclear>become</unclear> foolish, but would be making choices by judging what is more beneficial and accepting those who speak better. How then could things be equally "indifferent" <term>adiaphora</term> and "undecidable" <term>anepikrita</term>? And how could we <unclear>be</unclear> "without assent" and "without opinion"? > » "No other mortal could surely contend with Pyrrho." For one would no more admire Pyrrho than a Corybant <note>A dancer of the goddess Cybele, known for frenzied, ecstatic behavior.</note> or a madman, who seem to excel in folly. However, one must also consider these things: what sort of citizen, judge, counselor, or friend—or simply put, what sort of human being—would such a person become? Or what evil would he not dare to do, believing that nothing is truly evil or shameful, or just or unjust? Nor could anyone say that such people have appointed the laws as judges and feared punishments. For how could they, being "impassive" <term>apatheis</term> and "unperturbed" <term>atarachoi</term>, as they themselves claim? For one of you says this about Pyrrho:

> » by passions, and by opinion, and by useless law-giving."
> » Whenever they say this is correct: that one ought to live following nature and customs...

Here, the author (quoting Aristocles) argues that the Sceptic's own logic is self-refuting and that their "ideal" of living without opinions is both impossible and contrary to human nature, illustrated by humorous anecdotes about Pyrrho himself.</meta>

» ...[that] they themselves should assent to nothing. Some are entirely caught up in material concerns. For if they assent to nothing else, they should at least have to assent to this very fact, and suppose that things are indeed this way.
» But should one rather follow nature and custom in matters where one must act, even if one knows nothing and has nothing by which to be moved? For that other argument of theirs is altogether foolish, when they say that **purgative medicines** <term>katarktika pharmaka</term> <note>These are medicines meant to cleanse the body, like laxatives or emetics.</note> expel themselves along with the waste products; in the same way, they say, the argument that destroys everything also destroys itself along with the rest. For if the argument refutes itself, then those who use it are surely talking nonsense. It would be better for them to keep silent and not even open their mouths.
» Furthermore, the purgative medicine and their argument are not at all similar. For the medicine is expelled even if one does not have any particular belief about bodies; however, an argument existing in the soul must be held as something that is both real and constantly believed. For only such an argument could produce a state of non-assent in people. But it is impossible for a human being to be **without opinion** <term>adoxaston</term> <note>To live "without opinion" was the Sceptic goal—to never commit to a belief about the true nature of things.</note>, as one might learn from the following.
» It is impossible for one who perceives not to perceive. And he who perceives knows what he experiences. That he also believes his perception is clear to everyone. For when he wishes to see more accurately, he strains his eyes, comes closer, and touches the object. Indeed, we certainly know when we are feeling pleasure or pain. For it is not possible for someone being burned or cut to be unaware of it.
» And how could anyone say that memories and recollections happen without a formed opinion? For regarding **common notions** <note>Basic self-evident truths that everyone shares.</note>, there is no dispute for anyone; but what can one say about the sciences and arts? For none of these would exist if we were not naturally inclined to form opinions.
» The rest is also clear to me. For what substance is there in arguments? Whether we believe or disbelieve, we must in some way hold an opinion. That it is impossible to be a philosopher in this manner is evident. That it is also against nature and against the laws can be shown as follows. For if the things written in the laws are of no consequence, what is left but to sleep as if in a dream, or to live randomly and erratically? Thus, lawmakers, generals, and educators would all be babbling fools.
» But it seems to me that while all other men live according to nature, these men alone are "puffed up" with pride, or rather, those who talk such nonsense are suffering from a robust madness. One might learn this best from the following stories.
» **Antigonus of Carystus** <note>A 3rd-century BC biographer known for his lives of philosophers.</note>, who lived around the same time and recorded his life, says that **Pyrrho**, when pursued by a dog, fled up a tree. When those present mocked him, he said it was "difficult to strip off the human" <note>original: *anthrōpon ekdunai* — meaning it is hard to rid oneself of basic human instincts and emotions despite one's philosophy.</note>.
» And **Philista**, his sister, was performing a sacrifice; when one of his friends promised to provide the items for the sacrifice but failed to do so, Pyrrho became angry and indignant. When his friend rebuked him for acting in a way that contradicted his words and was unworthy of his **apathy** <term>apatheia</term> <note>Literally "freedom from passion" or "equanimity"—the state of being untroubled by emotions.</note>, Pyrrho replied that one should not display such a demonstration of philosophy upon a "helpless old woman" <note>Referring to his sister.</note>. And yet his friend might have justly said that such philosophy is useless for a woman, a dog, and everyone else.
» If these words are of any use to you, you might rightly learn who his followers were and whom he himself emulated. Pyrrho was said to be a student of a certain **Anaxarchus**, but he was first a painter, and not a very successful one. Then, having come across the books of **Democritus**, he found nothing good and wrote nothing good, but spoke ill of everyone, both gods and men. Later, having wrapped himself in this "puffery" <note>Arrogance or conceit.</note> while calling himself **un-conceited** <term>atuphos</term>, he left nothing in writing. But **Timon** of Phlius became his student...

<summary>This page presents a critique of Pyrrhonian Scepticism, arguing that the Sceptic's attempt to live without opinions is self-refuting and impossible in practice. It includes anecdotes where Pyrrho fails to maintain his own philosophical ideals of "apathy" when faced with a dog or a family matter.</summary>

» [Timon] of Phlius, who was at first a dancer in theaters; then, having encountered them [the Sceptics], he composed bitter parodies and buffooneries, in which he slandered all those who had ever practiced philosophy. He is also the author of the *Silloi* <term>Silloi</term> <note>original: "σίλλους" — these were satirical poems or "lampoons" used to mock the dogmatic beliefs of other philosophers.</note>, in which he says: "Wretched humans, base disgraces, nothing but bellies; from such strifes and groanings are you molded." And again: "Humans, like skins full of empty conceit." Since no one had written in his defense, as if they were not already mad enough in the present, a certain man <note>This refers to Aenesidemus, a famous Sceptic philosopher.</note> began to rekindle this **delusion** <term>typhon</term> <note>original: "τῦφον" — literally meaning 'smoke' or 'mist,' this term was used by ancient philosophers to describe intellectual vanity, pride, or the "fog" of false opinions.</note> in Alexandria, Egypt, which makes people forget their own. These are, perhaps, the most prominent of those who have walked this path. Now, it is clear that no person in their right mind would say that such a sect—or system of discourse, or whatever one wishes to call it—is correct. Indeed, I do not think it deserves the name of "friend of wisdom" [philosophy], since it destroys the very principles of philosophy.

» These remarks, then, are directed at the so-called followers of Pyrrho. But related to them are the arguments against the followers of Aristippus of Cyrene, who claim that only our **internal feelings** <term>pathe</term> <note>original: "πάθη" — in this context, it refers to internal sensations or "affections" (like feeling heat) rather than the external object causing them.</note> are comprehensible. Aristippus was a companion of Socrates and founded the so-called Cyrenaic school, from which Epicurus later took his starting points for his own explanation of the **ultimate goal** <term>telos</term> <note>The "end" or "aim" of human life—what we are all ultimately striving for.</note>. Aristippus was quite "fluid" in his lifestyle and a lover of pleasure; he did not openly discuss the "end" in public, but in effect, he claimed that the basis of happiness lay in pleasures. By constantly speaking about pleasure, he led those who approached him to suspect that he meant the goal was to live pleasantly. His daughter Arete was his student and fellow-servant, and she trained her son, whom she named Aristippus. Because he was led into philosophical discourse by her, he was called **"the Mother-taught"** <term>metrodidaktos</term>. He clearly defined the "end" as living pleasantly, identifying pleasure as "pleasure in motion."

» For he said there are three states in our physical composition: one in which we feel pain, like a storm at sea; another in which we feel pleasure, compared to a smooth wave (for pleasure is a smooth motion, compared to a gentle wind); and the third is an intermediate state in which we feel neither pain nor pleasure, being like a calm sea. He claimed that we have perception only of these internal feelings. Against these views, the following arguments were made:

->Against the philosophers following Aristippus, who say that only internal feelings are comprehensible, while all other things are incomprehensible. From the same author.<-

<margin>Section E</margin> » Next would be those who say that only internal feelings are comprehensible. This was said by some of those from Cyrene. These men demanded, as if they were oppressed by a heavy lethargy, that nothing exists at all unless someone should experience something or be pricked. For when they were being burned or cut, they said they recognized they were suffering something. But whether the thing burning them was fire, or the thing cutting them was iron, they could not say. To those who say such things, one might immediately ask if they recognize *themselves* as the ones who are suffering and perceiving. For if they do not know even this, they could not even say that they know the feeling alone. But if they do recognize themselves, then "feelings alone" would not be the only things comprehensible. For the statement "I am being burned" is a **rational proposition** <term>logos</term> and implies a **subject** <term>hypokeimenon</term> <note>In Greek logic, the *hypokeimenon* is the underlying "thing" or "subject" (in this case, the 'I') that experiences an action.</note>, not just a feeling. It is necessary that these things exist together: the feeling itself, the thing that causes it, and the person suffering it. Therefore, the person who perceives the feeling would certainly perceive the rest. For he surely does not recognize that he is being warmed, if it so happens, but remains ignorant of whether it is himself or his neighbor; or whether it is happening now or last year; or in Alexandria or in Egypt; or whether he is alive or dead; or indeed, whether he is a human or a stone. He will surely know...

<summary>This page critiques the Sceptic Timon of Phlius and the Cyrenaic school of Aristippus, arguing that their focus on internal feelings (pathe) at the expense of external reality is logically self-defeating. It specifically details the Cyrenaic "three states" of being: pain (storm), pleasure (smooth wave), and neutrality (calm).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the critique of Sceptical and Cyrenaic philosophies by Aristocles of Messene, as quoted by Eusebius. The previous page ended with a discussion on the "internal feelings" (pathe). This page argues that if philosophers truly believed they knew nothing, they would be unable to perform basic functions of life or even recognize themselves.</meta>

### EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 16 <note>While the OCR reads "Book 16" (ιϛ), Eusebius’s *Praeparatio Evangelica* traditionally consists of 15 books; this text is found in Book 14.</note>

» ...does not **experience** <term>paschei</term> <note>original: "πάσχει" — in this context, it refers to the sensory experience or the way an object "affects" the observer.</note>. For indeed, they recognize one another, as well as roads and cities, and their food. Furthermore, craftsmen know their own tools. Doctors and sailors note future signs. Among wild animals, dogs find tracks. For everything that experiences something certainly perceives it either as a **familiar** <term>oikeiou</term> or a **foreign** <term>allotriou</term> sensation. From what source, then, is it possible to say that "this is pleasure" and "this is pain"? Or that the act of seeing or hearing is an "experience"? And that one tastes with the tongue, sees with the eyes, and hears with the ears? How do they know that one thing should be chosen and another avoided? If they knew none of these things, they would have neither social interaction nor desire. In such a state, they would not even be living beings. For it is ridiculous when they say that these things happen to them, yet they do not know how or in what manner. In that case, they could not even say they are human beings, seeing as they are alive. Observe, then, what they say and declare. Regarding such people, what can one say? I myself am amazed, it seems, if they are ignorant of whether they are on the earth or in the heaven. It is much more amazing if they do not know—even while claiming to practice philosophy—whether four is more than three, or what the sum of two and two is. They could not even say how many fingers they have on their hand, nor whether each of them is one or many. Consequently, they would not even know their own name, nor their homeland, nor the **architect** <note>original: "ἀρχιτέκτονα" — here likely referring to a creator or the ordering principle of their own lives.</note>. Therefore, they would not know whom they love or hate, nor what they desire. They could not even say if they have a tongue or tears, nor that one thing is sweet and another painful. It is clear, then, that they do not even understand what we are saying right now. Thus, they would differ in no way from gnats or flies. And yet, even those creatures recognize what is according to their nature. Regarding those in such a state, if one must call it "folly," these words should suffice.

It follows from these points, most consistently, to also consider those who walk in the opposite direction and believe that one must trust entirely in the sensations of the body. Among these is **Metrodorus of Chios** <note>A 4th-century BCE philosopher and follower of Democritus.</note>, as well as his predecessor, the man from Abdera [Democritus]. They say this Metrodorus was a student of **Democritus** <note>The famous "laughing philosopher" who proposed that the world is made of atoms and void.</note>. He declared that the primary principles are "the full" and "the empty," of which one is "being" and the other is "non-being." Writing in his book *On Nature*, he used an introduction like this: "None of us knows anything, not even whether we know this very thing, or do not know it." This introduction provided a bad starting point for **Pyrrho** <note>The founder of the Sceptical school mentioned on the previous page.</note>, who came after him. **Protagoras** <note>A famous Sophist known for his relativism.</note> says that all things are whatever anyone perceives them to be. It is said that Protagoras was called an "atheist." Indeed, writing himself *On the Gods*, he used an introduction such as this: "Concerning the gods, I do not know whether they exist or what they are like in form. For there are many things that prevent me from knowing each of these things." Because of this, the Athenians punished him with exile and burned his books publicly in the middle of the marketplace. Since these men, therefore, claimed that one should trust only the senses, let us examine the rebuttals against them.

## Against the followers of Metrodorus and Protagoras, who say one must trust only the senses. From the same author [Aristocles].

There have been some who claim that one must trust only in sensation and "nonsense."
» Some say that even **Homer** <note>The legendary poet of the *Iliad* and *Odyssey*.</note> hints at such a thing when he declares **Oceanus** to be the origin of all things, suggesting that all things are in a state of "flow" <note>This refers to the Heraclitean idea that everything is constantly changing, like a river.</note>. And indeed, Metrodorus of Chios says this very thing, as does Protagoras of Abdera quite openly. For he said that **man is the measure of all things** <note>original: "πάντων χρημάτων τὸν ἄνθρωπον" — Protagoras's most famous dictum, suggesting that truth is relative to the individual perceiver.</note>: of things that are, that they are; and of things that are not, that they are not.

» possess a certain criterion <note>original: "κριτήριον" — a standard or "ruler" by which truth is judged.</note> or steady rule on which they could rely. 
» Or perhaps they concede this, seeing as they would not be quick to declare 
» all opinions to be true. For we are naturally inclined to judge many of the same things,

» When used in one way, they tell the truth; in another, they lie. Furthermore, 
» if every sensation is true, they should not differ so much from one another. 
» For some are from near and some from far; some belong to the sick and some 
» to the healthy, some to craftsmen and some to the unskilled, to the wise and to 
» the foolish. It would be altogether absurd to say that the sensations of drunkards 
» are true, or those of people who see or hear incorrectly. For as the saying 
» goes, the one who sees incorrectly either sees little or sees nothing. Someone 
» might say he sees, but not correctly. However, when they say that sensation, 
» being irrational, adds or subtracts nothing, they seem not to see the obstacles. 
» For in the case of a staff bent in the water, and in paintings and ten thousand 
» other things, it is the sensation that deceives. Therefore, in such cases, we all 
» blame not our mind, but our impression <term>phantasian</term>. For the argument 
» refutes itself by claiming every impression is true. For our own impression, 
» through which we do not believe every..."

### Against those who, following Epicurus, define pleasure as the end. From the same author.

» "Since knowledge is twofold—the first kind concerning external objects, and the 
» second concerning the things we know are to be chosen or avoided—some claim 
» that we have pleasure and pain as the starting point and criterion <note>original: "κριτήριον" — the standard or test by which something is judged to be true or good.</note> for 
» choice and avoidance. Even now, the followers of Epicurus say such things. It is 
» necessary, therefore, to distinguish and consider this point. For my part, I am 
» so far from saying that this passion <note>original: "πάθος" — an experience or feeling that happens to a person, here referring to the sensation of pleasure or pain.</note> is a good, or the only good and 
» the only evil, that it seems to me this very thing requires a criterion. For while it 
» manifests its own existence, another judging power is needed to determine what 
» kind of thing it is. Sensation tells us whether a thing is familiar or alien, but 
» reason <note>original: "λόγος" — the rational faculty.</note> determines whether it is to be chosen or avoided. Indeed, they 
» themselves say that one should not welcome every pleasure, nor turn away from 
» every pain. This is quite logical. For criteria manifest both themselves and the 
» things they judge; but a passion manifests only itself. That this is the case, they 
» testify themselves. For even though they claim every pleasure is a good and 
» every pain an evil, they nevertheless say that one must not always choose the 
» former or avoid the latter. For the quantities change, even if the qualities do 
» not. It is clear, then, that nothing but reason judges the quantity. For it is 
» reason that judges that it is better to endure certain pains so that we may 
» enjoy greater pleasures, and similarly, that it is beneficial to abstain from 
» certain pleasures so that we do not suffer more severe pains; and in all such 
» cases, it is reason that judges. In short, sensations and impressions seem to be 
» like mirrors and images of things. Painful passions and pleasures are like 
» labors <note>original: "πόνοι" — can mean physical pain, labor, or the 'tension' of a feeling.</note>, and they will be likenesses of ourselves. In this way, when we 
» perceive and form impressions, we look toward external things; but when we 
» feel pleasure or pain, we turn back only upon ourselves. For external things 
» produce our sensations; and whatever those things may be, they produce 
» corresponding impressions. But such passions, being what they are because of 
» us and our own state, appear at times pleasant and at other times unpleasant, 
» sometimes more and sometimes less. If we wish to consider the matter, we 
» shall find a way to define it by assuming the principles of knowledge involve 
» both sensation and the mind. Sensation seems..."

» "Let us then judge Mind and Pleasure according to each of these 
» three criteria. For we must see to which of the two we should

» ...speak as much as he likes, for that [atom] is the heaviest of all, and for this reason, imperceptible. But Democritus supposed that there were even some very large atoms. Both say there are atoms, and that they are so named because of their unbreakable <term>hardness</term> <note>original: "στεῤῥότητα" — referring to the solidity and resistance of the particles</note>. Others, while naming them atoms, say they are "partless bodies" <note>original: "ἀμερῆ σώματα"</note>, parts of the whole, from which all things are composed—being indivisible—and into which they are dissolved. They say Epicurus was the creator of the name "partless" for them; but the name which Heracleides <note>Heracleides Ponticus, a 4th-century BCE philosopher and astronomer.</note> called them was "masses" <note>original: "ὄγκους" — meaning bulks, weights, or volumes</note>, a name which Asclepiades the physician also inherited. ->From examples among men. From the same author.<-

How can we tolerate them when they say that wise, and therefore beautiful, works of craftsmanship are merely "lucky accidents"? Each of these things, when it comes into being on its own, is seen to be beautiful by those who arranged it, even if it is collectively destroyed in the same way. For "God saw," it says, "all things that He had made, and behold, they were very good" <note>A reference to Genesis 1:31.</note>. But they do not even learn from the small examples right at their feet, which provide a warning; from these, they could learn that nothing useful or beneficial is produced without design or by mere coincidence. Instead, it is "hand-worked" and prepared for its proper service. When it falls into uselessness and unprofitableness, then it is dissolved wastefully and scattered as chance dictates—since wisdom, by which it was composed into a work, no longer handles or arranges it. For a cloak does not appear by the warp threads composing themselves without a weaver, nor does the woof weave itself in automatically. But if it is worn out, the torn rags are cast aside. A house or a city is built, not by foundations receiving stones that "volunteered" to be there, nor by stones leaping up onto the layers of the wall; rather, the builder <note>original: "οἰκοδόμος" — a house-builder</note> places the suitable ones in the right spot. But if the building is thrown down, the fallen pieces lie wherever they happen to land. When a ship is being constructed, no oar "slips itself" into its place, nor does the mast stand itself upright in the middle; nor does each of the other timbers take its position of its own accord just where it happened to be. Nor do the various pieces of wood for a wagon join themselves together in whatever empty space each one finds. Rather, the carpenter <note>original: "τέκτων"</note> brings the appropriate parts together. But if the ship is broken up at sea, or the wagon while traveling on land, the timbers are scattered wherever they happen to go—some by the waves, some by the violent force of the motion. Thus it would be fitting to say that their atoms, remaining idle, un-hand-made, and useless, are carried along at random. Let those men look upon their "fruitless" ideas and perceive their "mindless" ones—not like that man who confesses this to God: "Your eyes saw my unformed substance" <note>A quotation from Psalm 139:16; original: "ἀκατέργαστόν".</note>. But when they say that even the "woven" structures of atoms become the celestial bodies, and that these are self-wrought by them without wisdom or sensation, who will tolerate hearing that atoms—of which even a spider is wiser—clothe themselves without any rhythm?

The one who established this great house of heaven and earth—called "Cosmos" <note>original: "κόσμον" — this Greek word means both "world" and "order/ornament," implying the beauty of a designed system.</note> because of the magnitude and abundance of the wisdom brought to it—is not by some [lack of] order...

» ...that the universe is adorned by atoms moving in [space], and that a world of order came from disorder. But how was motion » granted to them? Was it given by the atoms themselves, bringing them out of their chaotic tumbling? And how did the all-harmonious » dance of the heavenly bodies arise from unmusical and discordant clashing instruments? Even if we were to say that there is one » and the same substance for all of them, and the same indestructible nature—except for their sizes, » as they claim, and their shapes—are some bodies divine, pure, and eternal, as they themselves might say, » or at least long-enduring according to those who name them so, both visible and invisible? The visible » ones are the sun, the moon, the stars, the earth, and the water; while the invisible ones are the gods, demons, and » souls? For they could not escape these categories even if they wanted to, though it feels strange for them to serve [this logic]. Then there are the long-lived » animals and plants. Among the birds, as they say, are the eagles, ravens, and phoenixes. » Among land animals, there are the deer, turtles, and serpents. Among those in the water, there are the sea-monsters » <note>original: "κήτη" — whales or great sea creatures</note>. Among trees, there are the palms and oaks. For though they share the same nature as other trees, some are [essentially] immortal, » which he enumerated as being nearly fourteen in number; others bloom for a season and » then shed their leaves. Most of the things that grow and turn green are short-lived and soon-fading, » among which is man, as a certain holy scripture said long ago: "Man born » of woman is short-lived" <note>A reference to Job 14:1. The author is contrasting the "eternal" atoms with the fleeting nature of biological life.</note>. But if we dissolve the natural bonds of the atoms, » then this same staying power of destruction becomes eternal. For he says that some atoms are » condensed and tightly bound together, so that they become completely unchangeable » masses <note>original: "πηλήματα" — literally things felted or packed together</note>. Others are softened, and the connection of the atoms is loosened » to a greater or lesser degree, so that they more quickly or slowly depart from their orderly arrangement. And some are made of these [types] and shaped in such a way, while others, consisting of different [types], are mixed together in various ways. Who then is the "Distinguisher" <note>original: "φιλοκρίνων" — a divine intelligence that sorts and judges</note> who gathers them » and pours them out, arranging these in such a way to form the sun, and those in another way so that the moon might come to be, » and bringing each together according to its kinship with the nature of each star? For solar » atoms, united from so many and such types in this specific way, would never have » descended into the production of a moon; nor would the clusters of lunar atoms have ever become a sun. » Not even Arcturus, though he is bright, nor the Morning Star <note>original: "ἑωσφόρου"</note>, despite his great pride, would ever » use those atoms, nor would the Pleiades. For Paul distinguished them well » when he said: "There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star » differs from star in glory" <note>1 Corinthians 15:41. Dionysius uses Christian scripture to reinforce his point about the distinct "kinds" of celestial bodies.</note>. And if their assembly happened without their own perception, as if they were soulless, » then they required a skillful Craftsman. But if their binding was by their own choice or by necessity, as if » they were irrational, then some wise overseer stood over them from the beginning to bring them together. And if they have been summoned » to work together by their own free will, then some marvelous Architect preceded them as a taskmaster. » Or, like a general who did not allow his army to remain in disorder » and everything mixed together, but stationed the cavalry in one part, the heavy infantry <term>hoplites</term> <note>The standard heavily-armed foot soldiers of ancient Greece</note> by themselves, » the javelin-throwers on their own, and separately the light infantry and the slingers where they were needed, » so that those with the same purpose might be allies to one another. If they think this » example is necessary because it compares great bodies to the smallest ones, we shall move » to the very smallest things. Then he adds to these points: "But if neither speech, nor » selection, nor the order of a ruler is set over them, and they direct themselves on their own out of the » massive natural turmoil, and indeed pass through a great din <note>original: "κυδιμόν" — an archaic word for the noise of battle or confusion</note> of collisions, then like [atoms] [moving] toward like [atoms] was not [directed] by God according to the poetic struggle..."

” Let them keep silence, and let them be glorified together, recognizing their kindred. Wondrous indeed is this 'democracy' of the atoms! <note>Dionysius uses "democracy" sarcastically here to mock the idea that atoms govern themselves and cooperate to form the world by mutual agreement.</note> Friends greeting and embracing one another, hurrying to dwell together in a single colony. 

” Through the spontaneous cutting off of myriads <note>original: "χῖ γ' μῖ" — likely a corruption of "μυριάδας" (myriads) in the OCR</note> of atoms into the sun—that great luminary—so that they might create the day. Or perhaps you see from many quarters pyramids of stars set ablaze <note>original: "ἀσέρων" corrected to "ἀστέρων"</note>, so that they might crown the whole heaven? Or perhaps they were set apart so that they might spontaneously solidify <note>original: "σερεώσωσι" corrected to "στερεώσωσι"</note> and vault the ether into a dome, as a platform for the luminaries? Perhaps these 'assemblies' of vulgar atoms interweave themselves into a unity, and then partition the heaven among themselves into homes and stations? 

” Then he says not a word more; but these ignorant men <note>original: "ἀσεγνόητοι" — those who ignore or fail to perceive the divine</note> do not even see the things that are plain to the eyes, let alone perceive that which is hidden. For they seem to ignore the ordered arrangements, even the settings of the sun, and the most conspicuous of its movements. Nor do they make use of the benefits granted to men through these bodies: how the day dismisses us to our labor, while the night covers us for rest. For 'man,' it says, 'shall go forth to his work and to his labor until evening.' <note>A quotation from Psalm 104:23, used to show the providential design of day and night.</note> 

” But they do not even consider the other cycles of the stars, according to which they rise at fixed hours and seasons, completing festivals that never deviate, guided as they are by the atoms from which they are made. But even if they do not wish to believe, those wretched men, yet as the righteous say: 'Great is the Lord who made him [the sun], and at His word it hastened its course.' <note>A quotation from Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 43:5.</note> 

” O blind ones, do the fields bring us winter and rains so that the earth may provide nourishment for you and for all the living creatures upon it through tireless irrigation, and so that you may receive the fruits of the trees for your luxury? And why do you not worship and offer sacrifice to the 'fruit-bearing atoms'? You are ungrateful indeed, not even dedicating a few first-fruits to them from the many gifts you receive from their hands.

” And he says not a few things more: but what of the multiform and multifaceted populace of the stars, which the widely-wandering and ever-tossed atoms have gathered into a cluster? They have marked out a space and a treaty for themselves, like an autonomous colony or settlement <note>original: "αὐχόμοιοι" corrected to "αὐτόνομοι"</note>, with no founder or master of the house standing over them. They keep their neighborly relations with those nearby under oath and in peace, not overstepping the boundaries which they received from the beginning, as if they were being legislated by 'queenly' atoms. 

” But this is not evident to the foolish. For how could you have heard anything of the divine oracles? 'In the judgment of the Lord are His works from the beginning; from their creation, He determined their portions; He garnished His works for ever, and their principles unto their generations.' <note>A quotation from Sirach 16:26-27.</note> 

” And he says not a few things more: or what army <note>original: "φάλαγξ" — phalanx</note> ever crossed a plain with such order, with no one stepping forward, no one turning aside, no one hindering another, and no one falling behind their comrades in arms? Like a wall of shields <note>term: "συνασπιδοῦντες" — the military tactic of locking shields for mutual protection</note>, they always advance—the continuous, unshaken, unhindered, and unobstructed army of the stars. 

” But even if some of them become invisible due to turnings or lateral movements, they <note>meaning the stars or their governors</note> always watch for the right moment and foresee the regions from which each rises. Tell us then, you who speak of atoms—mediators of the indivisible and life-givers of the uncomposed, you who provide for infinite things—whence comes this circular procession and orbit of the heavenly bodies? This is not a single mass of atoms slung out by chance; rather, it is a rhythmic, choral dance, moving with equal steps and revolving together...

” ...disposed without purpose and ignorant of one another, traveling together as a vast multitude. Well did the prophet place this among the impossible and unimaginable things, saying to strangers, ‘Shall even two men walk together at all, unless they have first recognized one another?’ <note>Dionysius is paraphrasing Amos 3:3 to argue that even two people cannot coordinate a journey without mutual intent, let alone trillions of mindless atoms creating a world.</note> Having said these things, and having brought forward countless others like them, he next establishes his thesis through many more examples, starting from the individual elements of the universe, from the diverse animals within them, and indeed, from human nature itself. ## From Human Nature. From the same [Dionysius].

” And they see neither themselves, nor the things concerning themselves. For if any of the leaders of this impious doctrine <note>The "impious doctrine" refers to Epicureanism, which claimed the world was formed by random atomic collisions without divine intervention.</note> had considered who he was and from where he came, he would have cried out as one coming to his senses, and would have said—not to the atoms, but to his father and creator—‘Your hands have fashioned me and made me.’ <note>Dionysius is ironically putting the words of Job 10:8 into the mouth of a hypothetical converted Epicurean.</note> And he would have marveled at the way his own creation was brought about: ‘Did you not milk me like milk, and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews. You granted me life and mercy, and your providence has guarded my spirit.’ <note>A direct quotation of Job 10:10-12, used here to contrast the biblical view of a "knit together" body with the chaotic "clumping" of atoms.</note>

” For how many atoms did the father of Epicurus <note>Epicurus (341–270 BCE) was the founder of the school of philosophy that taught the universe is composed of atoms and void.</note> produce from himself, and of what kind were they, when he begot Epicurus? Or how, within his mother’s enclosed womb, were they fashioned into a living being, smoothed out, shaped, moved, and grown? Or was that tiny drop [of seed] divided, promising many 'Epicurus-atoms,' and did it clothe some of them with skin and flesh as a covering, while for others it stood upright with bony structures, and for others it was sewn together and bound with sinews?

” And so too for the many other members: the internal organs and the entrails, and the sense organs—some fitted within, some without—through which the body was given life. Of these, nothing idle or useless was added, not even the most trivial things like hair or nails; but all things contribute, some to the benefit of the body's structure, others to its beauty and power. For Providence <term>Pronoia: the concept of divine foresight and purposeful design in the universe</term> is careful not only of utility but also of the season of beauty. For the hair is a fence and a covering for the whole head; and the beard is a mark of dignity for the philosopher. 

” He [the Creator] fitted the nature of the entire human body together from all the necessary parts, and established a community between all the limbs, and measured out the supply of the whole. Some of these things are obvious even to common people through experience: the leadership of the head, around which the senses stand like bodyguards to the brain—the ruler in its citadel. <note>The "citadel" (acropolis) of the head was a popular philosophical metaphor for the brain as the seat of the soul or intellect.</note> Vision approaches to see, hearing reports what it finds, taste acts as a tax-collector for food, smell explores and investigates, and touch handles everything that falls under its authority. 

” We shall now run through a few works of this all-wise Providence in summary, but a little later, God willing, we shall work through them more accurately when we address the one who considers himself more learned. <note>Dionysius likely refers to a specific Epicurean opponent or a more detailed section of his own treatise.</note> [Consider] the service of the hands, through which all kinds of work and many-skilled arts are perfected; their individual powers are articulated into a single cooperation, with the joints of the shoulders, the bends of the fingers, and the curves of the elbows—turning inward toward the body and pushing outward, so that they might be able to pull and to push. [Consider] the service of the feet, by which all our...

# EUSEBIUS

” ...a wide incline, the earth is walkable, the sea is navigable, the rivers are beneficial, and there is a blending of all things with all others. The stomach is a storehouse of nourishment for all the coordinated limbs, distributing the food ration from itself in due measure and emptying out the excess. And there are all the other parts through which the administration of the human distribution is shown to be engineered. The "wise" <note>Dionysius uses "wise" ironically here to refer to the Epicurean philosophers.</note> hold the same judgment as the foolish concerning these things, for they do not truly know the knowledge. For some refer this most scientific economy of all things—which is most beneficial to themselves—to their own senseless atheism, even though they are convinced that it is the work of a superior and divine wisdom and power. Others, however, through a clumsy management and the accidental collision of atoms, aimlessly attribute this most wonderful cultivation to chance. 

” Doctors, having accurately investigated the even clearer examination of these things and the arrangement of the internal organs, were struck with wonder and deified Nature. <note>original: "ἐξεθείασαν τὴν φύσιν" — This refers to how ancient physicians like Galen viewed the complexity of anatomy as a "hymn" to the Creator or to Nature itself.</note> But we shall re-examine these things later as we are able, even if only on the surface. In general and in short, who constructed this whole tabernacle <note>term: "tabernacle" (original: σκῆνος, skēnos) — a common philosophical and biblical metaphor for the human body as a temporary dwelling for the soul.</note> to be such as it is: high, upright, rhythmic, sensitive, stable, active, and all-working? Was it the atoms, that "irrational multitude," as they say? But atoms could not even fashion a clay image by some chance coincidence, nor carve a stone statue, nor cast a silver or gold idol. Rather, the arts and the handiwork of these things are clearly established through men. If these imitations and sketches cannot flourish without wisdom, how did the true and prototypical versions of these things happen spontaneously? 

” From where did the soul, the mind, and reason come? How did philosophy arise? Did it collect these things from lifeless, senseless, and irrational atoms? Did each atom inspire it with a specific thought or doctrine? Is it as Hesiod’s myth says of Pandora, who was a "gift from all the gods"? <note>Dionysius is mocking the idea that atoms could collaborate to create human intelligence the way the Greek gods supposedly collaborated to create the first woman, Pandora.</note> No, here wisdom is supposedly "gifted" by the atoms themselves! And will they tell you that all poetry, all music, astronomy, geometry, and the other sciences are no longer the discoveries and teachings of the gods, but that the atoms alone have become the skillful and wise Muses of all? For either the birth of the gods <note>term: "theogony" — the genealogy or origin of a group of gods.</note> described by Epicurus is upright because of infinite worlds, or it has been banished into infinite disorder. <note>Epicurus believed in "intermundia"—spaces between worlds where the gods lived in perfect peace, indifferent to human affairs.</note>
