### That working is not laborious for God. From the same [Dionysius].

” He says that working and administering, and both doing good and exercising providence, and such things, are perhaps burdensome to the rulers and the foolish, the weak and the wicked—among whom Epicurus ranked himself when he thought such things about the gods. But to the serious, the powerful, the intelligent, and the temperate—such as philosophers ought to be, and how much more so the gods—these things are not only not unpleasant or uphill, but are the most delightful and most welcome of all. To such beings, it is a reproach to be pricked or stained by touching what is good. For even the poet <note>The poet mentioned is Hesiod.</note> advises them by way of counsel:

” *Do not put off until tomorrow,* &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; and as a previous trial,
” *For the man who procrastinates always struggles with ruins.* <note>original: "Αἰεὶ δ᾿ ἀμβολιεργὸς ἀνὴρ ἄτῃσι παλαίει" — Dionysius is quoting Hesiod’s *Works and Days*, line 410, to argue against laziness and neglect of duty.</note> 

” And the Prophet <note>The Prophet Jeremiah.</note> instructs us more solemnly, saying that works according to virtue are truly fitting for God, but to neglect them is an abomination. For *Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord negligently.* <note>original: "ἐπικατάρατος γὰρ ὁ ποιῶν τὰ ἔργα κυρίου ἀμελῶς" — A quote from Jeremiah 48:10 (LXX version).</note> Furthermore, labor arises in the attempts of those who are ignorant of an art and who are unaccomplished, due to their lack of experience and the incompleteness of their works. # EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 14
<page-num>457</page-num>

> ” ...more than artisans, who would easily prefer to succeed in their crafts—and would rather choose to practice and perfect their usual tasks—than to possess all the goods available to men. Democritus himself, at least as they say, used to claim that he would **rather find a single causal explanation** <note>original: αἰτιολογίαν (aetiologia) — the study of causes. Democritus famously valued scientific understanding over worldly power.</note> **than gain the kingdom of the Persians.** And yet, he searches for causes in vain and without reason, starting from a void principle and a wandering hypothesis. He fails to see the very root and the common necessity of the nature of existing things. 
> 
> ” Epicurus, on the other hand, unwisely and indiscriminately considers his own understanding of things happening by chance to be of the greatest importance. He sets up **Chance** <note>term: "Chance" (original: Τύχη, Tyche) — often personified as a goddess in Greek thought; here, Dionysius mocks the Epicureans for making her the "ruler" of the universe.</note> as the mistress and queen of all things, even of divine matters. He declares that all our affairs occur according to her, yet he dismisses her role in human life <note>Dionysius is pointing out a logical inconsistency in Epicurean thought regarding how much control chance actually has.</note> and rebukes those who honor her as being senseless. Indeed, in his own writings <insert>citing from Democritus’s storehouses</insert>, he says: *“Men fashioned an image of Chance as an excuse for their own stupidity.”* For he claimed that by nature, wisdom fights against chance, and that wisdom mostly prevails over her. 
> 
> ” Or rather, they utterly destroy and vanish wisdom, and immediately substitute Chance for it. For they do not celebrate wisdom as being produced by chance, but they sing of Chance as being the most "wise." Those who preside over sensible works rejoice in the help they give to their own kind; they reach for praise and glory for the things they have labored at—some as providers of food, some as pilots, some as healers, and others through many other celebrated arts. But these philosophers, who promise to be exceedingly well-educated, are found to be impious. 
> 
> ” Would Epicurus or Democritus dare to say that they are ungrateful while practicing philosophy? Yet they could find no other joy equal to it. For even if they believe that "the Good" is pleasure, they will surely perceive that practicing philosophy is not a matter of hope for them, but a present reality. As for the gods, whom the poets among them sing of as "the givers of good things," these philosophers do not even speak of them with fair words; their gods of the heavens are **without gifts** <gloss>*</gloss> and have no share in anything. <note>The asterisk in the original likely refers to a missing or corrupted textual variant regarding the nature of these "giftless" gods.</note> And what shall I say of those who diminish the status of the gods by saying they possess no providence, nor do they look forward or observe? Like those who marvel at the sun, the moon, and the stars, they are called "gods" through the names of the gods themselves. 
> 
> ” They assign to them no craftsmanship or construction, so that they exist without having *done* anything. For this reason, in truth, the Creator and Maker of all things is the only God. They grant the gods no administration, no judgment, and no favor toward men. Why then should we owe them fear or honor, or worship them? 
> 
> ” Epicurus, peering out from the world and having stepped beyond the heavenly enclosure, passed through some "secret gates" which he alone saw. Having exited, he beheld "gods" in the **Void**, and he blessed their great luxury. From that point on, becoming a lover of pleasure and an admirer of the lifestyle in the Void, he exhorted everyone to join in this "blessedness," urging them to be like those gods. He organized a blessed banquet for them—not in the Heavens or on Olympus as the poets do—but in the **Void**. He set before them an **ambrosia** made of atoms and poured them **nectar** from the same. 
> 
> ” And indeed, regarding those gods who have "nothing to do with us," he wrote in his books with ten thousand oaths and adjurations. He swore constantly, "By Zeus!" and "Yes, by Zeus!", adjuring his readers and those with whom he discussed, by the names of the gods. He did not do this because he feared them or because he was terrified of perjury, but because he was uttering these things as **void, false, idle, and meaningless** sounds to garnish his words...

» ...or even if he were to clear his throat or spit, to nourish his face, or move his hand.
» For such is the unrefined and vain hypocrisy <note>original: ὑπόκρισις (hypokrisis) — originally meaning "acting" or "playing a part" on stage; Dionysius accuses Plato of merely performing a role of piety.</note> toward the divine name on his part. For he did not look up to heaven with the eyes of the mind so as to hear that clear voice from above, which the attentive spectator hears and bears witness to, saying: **The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.** <note>Quoting Psalm 19:1 (18:1 in the Septuagint), a classic text used by early Christians to argue for natural revelation.</note> Nor did he look down with his intellect toward the ground; for he would have learned that **the earth is full of the Lord’s mercy**, and that **the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.** <note>Quoting Psalms 33:5 and 24:1 respectively.</note> And after these things, it says: **the Lord looked upon the earth, and filled it with his good things. He covered its face with the soul of every animal.** <note>Referencing Psalm 104:24–30.</note> If they are not utterly blind, let them observe the immense variety of the multitude of animals—those of the land, the air, and the water—and we shall see how true the testimony of the Master has become regarding the judgment of all things: that **all things are by nature good according to his command.**

These things I have unrolled from the many arguments spoken against Epicurus and those who, in our own time, have conducted such inquiries. <header>EUSEBIUS</header>

### Preface concerning the whole of the subject matter.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial letter 'T' featuring swirling acanthus leaves and floral motifs, contained within a square double-line border.</image-desc>

Having long ago resolved at the beginning of the *Preparation for the Gospel* <note>original: *Evangelica Praeparatio* — Eusebius’s fifteen-volume defense of Christianity written in the early 4th century.</note> to refute the polytheistic error of all the nations, in order to establish and defend our departure from them, I have not done so without rational judgment. In the first three books, I investigated not only the myths which the children of their own theologians and poets have lampooned regarding their respective gods, but also those "venerable" and "secret" physical interpretations <note>original: φυσιολογίας (physiologias) — allegorical explanations used by pagans to argue that their gods were actually symbols for natural forces like the sun or wind.</note> which have been applied to the heavens, the cosmos, and the parts of inanimate nature. Indeed, there is no reason to speak solemnly of these matters, as their own theologians have talked much nonsense about them. It must be noted that the most ancient of their theologians were shown to have known nothing beyond the history <note>original: ἱστορίας (historias) — here referring to the literal, often scandalous, mythological accounts of the gods.</note> and to have paid attention only to the myths. Consequently, in all cities and villages, according to ancient narratives, the rites and mysteries of the gods have been handed down in accordance with the mythical stories of those who came before. Thus, even today, the marriages and child-bearing of the gods, their lamentations and drunkenness, their wanderings and loves, as well as their fits of anger and various other misfortunes and circumstances, are all practiced in accordance with the myths of the most ancient times, through rites, hymns, and the songs composed for these gods. Nevertheless, for good measure, I have also brought to light the monstrous cleverness found in their physical explanations, along with the ingenious inventions <note>original: εὑρεσιλογίας (heuresilogias) — literally "discovery of words," referring to the convoluted arguments philosophers used to justify myths.</note> of their sophists and philosophers.

Furthermore, in the next three books following the first, I exposed the accounts concerning the famous oracles and the false opinion regarding Fate <note>original: εἱμαρμένης (heimarmenes) — the concept of an inescapable, pre-determined destiny.</note> which is so widely talked about. I stripped these bare through refutations, utilizing not only my own arguments but especially the very words of the Greek philosophers to convict them. Moving on from there to the Hebrew oracles, I deemed it worthy to record in an equal number of books the dogmatic theology contained within them, as well as the entire history of the Jews as testified by them. Then, in the following sections, I refuted the Greek way of life, showing how they had benefited in all things from the "barbarians" <note>Eusebius uses the term "barbarians" to refer to non-Greeks, specifically the Hebrews and Egyptians, whom he argues are older and wiser than the Greeks.</note> and that they possess no noble teaching of their own. I also brought to light the comparison of the dates during which their famous men flourished and the Hebrew prophets lived. After this, in the next three books, I demonstrated the agreement of the most esteemed Greek philosophers with the doctrines of the Hebrews, again making use of the men’s own words as witnesses. Furthermore, I exposed those Greek philosophers who differ from us—not only disagreeing with our views but also standing at odds with their own associates and being refuted by their own disciples—in the book dedicated to this subject. Through all these means, I have demonstrated that the criterion of our judgment is impartial <note>original: ἀδέκαστον (adekaston) — literally "unbribed," meaning a fair and objective assessment.</note>...

<meta>catchword: ...demonstrating</meta>

Having previously examined the myths and natural philosophies of the Greeks, he now moves into the final volume of the Preparation for the Gospel, focusing on the contradictions within Greek philosophical schools—specifically Aristotle and the Stoics—compared to the consistency of Hebrew thought.</meta>

<header>EVANGELICAL PREPARATION Book 15</header>

...it reaches those who encounter it, through deeds, so to speak, and by the very facts themselves. We provide these proofs not aimlessly, but with a judged and sober reason, recalling the ancient and true philosophy and piety of our own people, the Hebrews. We have taken this up and established it through the comparison of our own voices. Of this, we are still holding the final discourse—being the fifteenth of the treatise currently in hand—and we shall now grant a conclusion to these detailed discourses. We shall yet again bring to light the venerable aspects of our own philosophy, stripping bare before the eyes of all the useless learning <note>original: ἀχρηστομαθείαν (achrystomatheian) — a term Eusebius uses to describe Greek philosophical debates that offer no practical benefit for the soul.</note> found within them. We stand apart from all who came before, not because we are ignorant of what they admire, but because we hold their internal power in low regard. We have spent very little time on them, preferring the exercise of better things for our own wounded souls.

Since this has been sealed for us with God’s help for the sake of truth, the matters of the *Preparation* will be circumscribed here. Having moved on to the more complete subject of the *Evangelical Demonstration* <note>original: εὐαγγελικῆς ἀποδείξεως (Euangelikes apodeixeos) — this refers to Eusebius’s next major work, which focuses on how Christ fulfilled Hebrew prophecy.</note>, I will mark the beginning of that second treatise by examining the remaining charge against us. This is the charge brought by those who reproach us, claiming that although we have preferred the Hebrew oracles to our ancestral traditions, we have not chosen to emulate the Jewish way of life. After the completion of the present discourse, with God's cooperation, we shall attempt to answer this. For we say that this second part, bound together as if by a single tie to what has already been set forth, will appear as one whole to complete the same argument.

It is the nature of the philosophy according to Plato <note>original: κτ' πλάτωνα φιλοσοφία — Platonism.</note> to be full of such things, as we have received in his writings; sometimes it is in harmony with the Hebrew accounts, and at other times it stands apart from them. In those instances, it was proven to disagree with its own preferred views. Aside from these are the irrational views of those who have been called "natural philosophers," as well as the doctrines of Plato, Xenophanes, Parmenides, and even Pyrrho, who introduced the "suspension of judgment" <note>original: ἐποχὴν (epochen) — the Skeptic practice of withholding belief because nothing can be known for certain.</note>. Through the entire sequence of their absence of truth—whose opinions the preceding discourse refuted—they stood against both the Hebrew and Platonic dogmas. Not only are they refuted by the evidence of truth itself, but they are also convicted by their own customs. 

It is now time to look down from above, as if from a stage, at the remaining vanity of the followers of Aristotle and the Stoic philosophers. We shall observe the rest of their physiology <note>original: φυσιολογίαν — in this context, "physics" or theories about the nature of the universe.</note> and their arrogant pretensions, so that we might learn of the things they speak of so solemnly, and the contradictions raised against them in turn by their own associates. In this way, our departure from these views will be judged as sound, and we may enjoy a defense against every reasonable accusation. It will be clear that we have chosen the pious philosophy of those considered "barbarians" <note>original: βαρβάροις (barbarois) — the Greeks used this term for anyone non-Greek; Eusebius adopts it to describe the Hebrews, emphasizing that "barbarian" wisdom is older and truer than Greek wisdom.</note> not out of ignorance of Greek "venerable" things, but through an examined and tested judgment. 

I shall begin with the followers of Aristotle. Now, some have indeed slandered the man, and these were philosophers of no small reputation. For my part, it is not pleasing to even hear a man spoken of poorly by his own associates. Therefore, I will instead set forth the defenses made on his behalf, taken from the writings of Aristocles the Peripatetic <note>Aristocles of Messene, a 2nd-century philosopher who wrote a history of philosophy.</note>, who in the seventh book of his work *On Philosophy* writes the following concerning him:

# From the works of Aristocles the Peripatetic, concerning Aristotle, and the stories told by others. From the seventh book *On Philosophy*.

> » For how is it possible, as Epicurus says in his letter *On Occupations*, that while he was still a young man, he devoured his paternal inheritance, then rushed off to join the army, and having fared poorly in those affairs, turned to selling drugs <note>original: φαρμακοπωλεῖν (pharmakopolein) — selling medicinal herbs or drugs, often viewed as a low-status or suspicious trade</note>; and then, when Plato’s "walk" <note>original: περιπάτου (peripatou) — referring to the Peripatetic school or a place for walking and talking</note> was open to all, he joined him? Or how could anyone again accept the word of Timon the **Sillograph** <term>Sillograph: A writer of "silli," which were satirical poems or lampoons used to mock the dogmatic beliefs of philosophers.</term>, who says in his *Histories* that he [Aristotle] happened upon a bad reputation and an ordinary one at that, and only late in life was called to his vocation? And how could anyone believe Aristoxenus the "Musician," as he is called, in his *Life of Plato*? For he says that during Plato's travels and his time abroad, certain people—being foreigners—rose up and built rival "walks" against him. Some people think Aristoxenus says these things about Aristotle, ungratefully repaying him. 
> 
> » But perhaps one might reasonably mention the memoirs of Alexinus the **Eristic** <term>Eristic: A philosopher specialized in "eristic" or "wrangling," a style of debate focused on winning arguments through logical tricks rather than seeking truth.</term>. For he depicts Alexander as a child conversing with his father Philip, and while he spits upon the words of Aristotle, he welcomes Eumareas, who was nicknamed "the son of Hermeias." And Eubulides also lies in almost his entire book against him, first bringing forward "cold" <note>original: ψυχρὰ (psychra) — here meaning lifeless, dull, or uninspired</note> poems, claiming he wrote them about marriage and the kinship he had with Hermeias. Next, he claims that Aristotle offended Philip, and that he was not present when Plato died, and that he destroyed Plato's books. 
> 
> » Let Demochares also accuse him—and the philosophers—more than is necessary, for he has spoken shamelessly and poorly not only about Aristotle, but against others as well. If anyone, by looking into these slanders themselves, says he can find the truth, let him look: for Demochares says he intercepted letters from Aristotle written against the city of Athens, and that he was betraying his fatherland’s citadel to the Macedonians. Furthermore, he says that when Olynthus was razed <note>Olynthus was an ancient city destroyed by Philip II of Macedon in 348 BC; Aristotle was often accused of having Macedonian sympathies.</note>, Aristotle informed Philip of the wealthiest Olynthians at the slave auctions. 
> 
> » Cephisodorus, the student of Isocrates, also slandered him in little books, mixing things up and calling him a "builder" <note>likely a slur suggesting Aristotle was a common laborer rather than a thinker</note> and saying other such things about him. Everything said by Lycon, who calls himself a Pythagorean, was full of insolence and foolishness. For he says that Aristotle performed a sacrifice for his deceased wife of the kind the Athenians perform for Demeter, and that he bathed in warm oil and then sold the oil. He also seems to say that when he went to Chalcis, the tax-collectors found seventy-five bronze pots in his boat. 
> 
> » These are almost all the first people who slandered Aristotle. Some of them lived at the same time as him; others came a little later. All of them were sophists, eristics, and rhetoricians, whose names and books have died more than their bodies. As for those who came after them, or those who repeat what those people said, one should let them go entirely—especially those who have not even encountered his books but speak off the top of their heads, such as those who say he had three hundred pots. For no one among those who lived then would be found to have spoken of such a great number, except for Lycon. He, however, as I said, stated that seventy-five pots were found. 
> 
> » One might judge that all these things are false not only from the timing and the character of the slanderers, but also from the fact that they do not all bring the same accusations, but each tells his own specific story. For if there were any truth in any of them, he would surely have been caught not once, but ten thousand times by those who were then...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Aristotle by the Peripatetic philosopher Aristocles, as quoted by Eusebius. Having dismissed the rumors that Aristotle was a failed soldier or a drug-seller, Aristocles now addresses the envy of his contemporaries and the specific scandals surrounding his marriage and his relationship with his teacher, Plato.</meta>

» ...is to be lost. It is nonsense, then, to claim that—as has happened to many others—Aristotle was envied by the sophists of his time because of his friendships with kings and his superiority in discourse. Those who are wise should not look only at the slanderers, but also at those who praise and emulate him. For the latter would be found to be far more numerous and of better character. While the obvious lies have clearly been fabricated, there are two matters that people seem to believe, which are the source of certain reproaches. One is the claim that he married the sister—or as some say, the daughter—of **Hermeias** <note>Hermeias of Atarneus was a ruler in Asia Minor and a friend of Aristotle; he was a former slave who became a philosopher-king.</note>, named Pythias, in order to flatter him. Indeed, Theocritus of Chios wrote an epigram to this effect:

> This empty tomb for Hermeias the eunuch, the slave of Eubulus,
> was set up by the empty-minded Aristotle;
> Who, because of his belly’s uncontrolled nature, chose to dwell
> at the outlets of the filth <note>original: βορβόρου (borborou) — meaning mud or filth, here a pun on the Borborus river and a metaphor for the "muck" of a tyrant's court</note>, instead of in the Academy.

» The second reproach is that he showed no gratitude toward **Plato**. Now, concerning Hermeias and Aristotle’s friendship with him, many others have written, especially **Apellicon** <note>An 1st-century BC book collector and philosopher who famously recovered Aristotle's library.</note>; anyone who reads his books will cease their slanders. As for the marriage to Pythias, Aristotle himself has offered an adequate defense in his letters to **Antipater** <note>Antipater was a powerful Macedonian general and a close friend/executor of Aristotle.</note>. He explains that after Hermeias died, he married her out of goodwill toward his friend; she was a modest and good woman, though she had fallen into misfortune due to the calamities that overtook her brother. He then continues: after the death of Pythias, the sister of Hermeias, Aristotle married **Herpyllis of Stagira** <note>Stagira was Aristotle's birthplace in northern Greece.</note>, who bore him a son named **Nicomachus**. They say this son was raised as an orphan by **Theophrastus** <note>Aristotle's successor as head of the Lyceum.</note> and died in war while still a young man. But let these matters from the writings of Aristocles be set aside; it is now time to examine the dogmatic philosophy of Aristotle.

## Concerning the doctrines of Aristotle. How he differed from the Hebrews and Plato regarding the ultimate good.

Moses and the prophets of the Hebrews posited that the goal of a blessed life is the knowledge and friendship of the God of all things, achieved through piety. (By **piety** <term>original: εὐσέβεια (eusebeia) — a central Greek and Jewish concept of proper reverence and duty toward the divine</term>, I mean that which teaches how to please God through every virtue; for this is the cause of all good things, since everything depends on God alone, and everything is supplied by Him to those who love God.) While Plato accepted views in harmony with these and declared **virtue** <term>original: ἀρετή (arete) — excellence or moral virtue</term> to be the goal of happiness, Aristotle took a different path. He says that no one can be truly happy without the well-being of the body and an abundance of external goods, without which even virtue is of no benefit. How the followers of Plato stood against him, refuting these ideas as false assumptions, may be learned through the following.

## From Atticus the Platonist, regarding the points on which Aristotle differed from Moses and Plato in his discourse on the "Ultimate Good."

While the whole of philosophy, by the common consent of those who have philosophized, promises human happiness, it is divided into three parts: the creative intellect of the universe...

> „ [Atticus] says: So far is he [Aristotle] from appearing as a Peripatetic <note>original: περιπατητικός (peripatētikos) — a member of Aristotle's school, literally 'one who walks about'</note> who teaches anything prior to Plato, that he talks nonsense, being among those who differ most from Plato. And first of all, he created a divergence from Plato regarding the most common, greatest, and most sovereign principle: he did not preserve the measure of **happiness** <note>original: εὐδαιμονία (eudaimonia) — often translated as 'flourishing' or 'well-being'</note>, nor did he concede that **virtue** <note>original: ἀρετή (aretē)</note> is self-sufficient for this purpose. Instead, he fell away from the power of virtue, believing it to be in need of the gifts of **Fortune** <note>original: τύχη (tychē)</note>, lest happiness be left destitute without them. He criticized happiness as something impossible and unattainable if it were taken by itself.
> 
> „ He was, then, ignoble and mistaken in his judgment, both in this and in other matters, as the present occasion bitingly proves. It is, I think, obvious that the goal of happiness is not the same nor does it consist of the same things according to Plato and according to Aristotle. For the one [Plato] is shouting and proclaiming at every turn that ‘the most just man is the happiest.’ But the other [Aristotle] does not permit happiness to follow virtue unless one also possesses a fortunate lot, or beauty, or other such things.
> 
> „ 'And indeed, even if one has gold, he must go to war, like a girl,' <note>A reference to Homer's Iliad 2.872, describing the extravagant but ineffective Nastes</note> for the philosophy had to differ clearly according to the difference in the End <note>The 'Telos' or ultimate goal of life</note> or the guiding star. For when one walks a single path that is naturally inclined toward small and lowly things, it is not possible to behold the greater things that lie on the heights.
> 
> „ Do you see where that high crag stands, rugged and hostile, upon which sits the bird that prides itself? Toward this high crag, that sharp and mischievous fox <note>Atticus uses animal metaphors to contrast the 'heavenly' Platonist with the 'earthbound' Aristotelian</note>—the Aristotelian logic—is unable to lead us. It would be impossible for anyone to reach that place by following the earthly humors of the fox, unless Fortune, dealing poorly with those things, should cause her to fall to the earth when her own resources are destroyed. But if she [Philosophy] breathes into herself what she is not by nature, she might encircle herself with scavenged wings and thus be lifted from the earth to fly toward the high crag. Yet as long as each remains in its own rank, there is no communion between the creatures of the earth and the nurslings of the heavens.
> 
> „ Why then does he add other things? These things being so, and Plato attempting to lead the souls of the young upward toward the Divine—and in this way making them akin to virtue and the Beautiful—what would the Peripatetic say to us? 'O Peripatetic, how will you teach these things? How will you guide those who love Plato toward them?' For where in your sect is there such a height of discourse as to acquire the mindset of the **Heliads** <note>original: Ἡλιάδων — the 'Children of the Sun,' a metaphor for enlightened souls</note> and to seek the way to heaven, which those [Platonists] thought they must be able to see? This path, as Plato says, comes through the withdrawal from human preoccupations.
> 
> „ What help, then, would there be from you for the young regarding these matters? And from where would a discourse come that fights alongside virtue? From which of Aristotle’s writings? From which of those who followed him? From which scriptures? For I would grant it to you even if you wished to lie, provided it was something spirited. But you have nothing to say, nor would any leader of your sect permit you.
> 
> „ Certainly, Aristotle’s treatises on these subjects—the **Eudemian**, the **Nicomachean**, and those titled the **Great Ethics**—hold a small, lowly, and vulgar view of virtue. They treat it as something that any common person, uneducated man, youth, or woman might possess. For Plato says that virtue is, so to speak, the diadem and the royal scepter received from Zeus, which cannot be taken away. Since it is not something that can be taken back, it is placed upon the head.
>

Atticus is arguing that by making happiness dependent on external goods (like health or wealth), Aristotle effectively destroys the inherent value and "dignity" of virtue. The previous page established that Aristotle diverged from Plato by claiming virtue alone is not "self-sufficient" for a happy life.</meta>

» ...[Aristotle's view suggests one cannot] yet be pleased by wealth and glory, or by strength, health, and beauty, and all the other things common to vice. For just as any of these being present without virtue is not self-sufficient to render the possessor **happy** <note>original: εὐδαίμονα (eudaimona) — referring to the state of flourishing or "good spirit."</note>, so too virtue by itself, without these external things, is not enough to make the one who possesses it happy. How, then, is the dignity of virtue not cast down? Yes, they say that virtue far excels the other goods. But what of this? For so does health excel wealth; yet it is common to all these things that without one another they do not suffice for happiness. 

» Whenever, therefore, someone is taught by these dogmas and this sect <note>referring to the Peripatetics/Aristotelians</note> that they must seek the whole of human good in the soul itself, they say he would be shown to be happy by the gods. Yet [they also say] not even one gripped by "thrice-miserable" fortunes could be happy and blessed. But for one possessing virtue, it is not unlikely to fall into such misfortunes. From these premises, it follows that happiness neither follows from wealth for those who have virtue, nor, if it should occur, does it remain forever.

<margin>Flourishing leaves</margin>
» *“As for leaves, the wind scatters some on the ground, while the forest*
» *In bloom puts forth others when the season of spring comes on;*
» *So is the generation of men; one grows, another ceases.”* <note>original: Homer, Iliad 6.146-149. Atticus uses this famous simile to mock the fragility of Aristotelian happiness.</note>
There is yet for you, O poet, a small and wretched example; for the season of spring comes after a long time and where there is no earth. But if piety requires from us an accurate examination and purification, then Aristotle’s happiness is by no means sufficient. This "happiness" grows and falls away more easily than leaves; not month by month, throughout the revolving year, it neither blooms nor grows, but in the selfsame day, the selfsame hour, it is both born and destroyed. Many are the obstacles, and all come from **Fortune** <note>original: τύχη (tychē) — the personified force of luck or chance.</note>.

» For if the plagues of the body—and these are myriad—and poverty and dishonor, and all such things occur, then the qualities of dear virtue are self-sufficient for nothing; they are not enough to provide help. For virtue is too weak to keep away misery or to preserve happiness. If someone were raised on these ideas and took pleasure in these arguments—the very ones Aristotle set against those of **Plato**—how could he ever be strengthened by them? For how is it possible that, starting from these points, one could accept those Herculean and divine dogmas: that **virtue** is a sacred and altogether beautiful thing, and even if it ever lacks external goods for happiness, it is never stripped of happiness itself? 

» But even if poverty, even if disease, even if ill-repute, even if the rack <note>original: πῖνα (pina) — likely referring to the "pinax" or a similar instrument of torture, or possibly a corruption of πείνα (hunger).</note> and the cross, and even if all the tragedies flow together at once, still the **just man** is happy and blessed. Let it be proclaimed to him by the loudest herald, and with the victory-bearing honors of the athletes, that "This man is most happy, for he reaps the fruit of happiness from justice itself." 

» Distinguish then, if you wish, and variegate your definitions of "goods" by fortune and confusion and in many ways. For these things contribute nothing to the matter at hand—the very thing that sets us through them against Plato. For if among goods, as you say, some are **honored** (as are the gods), some **praiseworthy** (as are the virtues), some **powers** (as are wealth and strength), and some **useful** (as are medical treatments); or if, making a distinction without effort, you say that some goods are **ends** and some are **not ends** (naming as "ends" those for whose sake other things exist, and "not ends" those taken for the sake of others); or if one learns that some are **simply good** and others **not for all**; or that some are goods of the **soul**, others of the **body**, and others **external**; or again, that some goods are **powers**, some **dispositions** and **habits**, others **activities**, others **ends**, others **materials**, and others **instruments**? Even if someone learns to divide "the good" ten times over according to the **ten categories** <note>original: κατηγορίας (katēgorias) — a reference to Aristotle’s *Categories*, his foundational work on logic and classification.</note>, what does it matter?

» These teachings stand in opposition to Plato’s judgment. Except for Moses and the prophets among the Hebrews—and indeed Plato, who is in harmony with them—the discourse on the providence over the whole of things has been accurately arranged. Aristotle, however, stopped the divine influence at the **moon** <note>Aristotle famously argued that God's direct influence (Providence) only reached as far as the celestial spheres; the "sublunary" world (Earth) was governed by nature and chance.</note>, and he excludes the remaining parts of the world from God’s administration. On these points, he is refuted by the aforementioned author, who explains it roughly as follows:

» Since the conviction concerning **Providence** is the greatest and most sovereign of the things contributing to happiness—the very thing which most sets the lives of men right—we must not be ignorant of whether a man's character ascends by a holy path or by crooked deceptions. Now, Plato attaches all things to God and derives all things from God. For he says that God is the **beginning, the middle, and the end** of all beings, and that He accomplishes all things by a straight path, traveling according to nature. And again, he says that God is good, and that in one who is good, no envy ever arises concerning anything. Being free from envy, God makes all things as good as possible, bringing them into order out of disorder. 

» Plato teaches that God takes care of us and organizes all things according to His power, and that He is by nature concerned with human affairs. And shortly after, he adds:

» While Plato speaks thus, the other [Aristotle], by putting this divine nature out of the way, cutting off the soul’s hope for the hereafter, and taking away the help from the higher gods in the present, what fellowship could he have with Plato? Or how could he encourage others or confirm Plato’s goals through his own words? Quite the opposite: he would appear to be an assistant and a fellow-combatant for those who wish to do wrong. 

» For any person who is human and gripped by human desires, if he looks down on the gods and believes they have no concern for him—being settled far away from them while living, and ceasing to exist once dead—he will be ready to indulge his desires. For he has gained a guarantee that it is not impossible to escape notice while doing wrong, provided he only needs to hide from men. Indeed, it is not even necessary to seek to hide in every case, provided he is strong enough to overpower those who have caught him. Thus, the despair of **Providence** is a thing that leaves the world a desert, abandoned to injustice. For that man is truly "kind" who, by offering us pleasures as a "good," or claiming the gods are either weak or angry, still thinks he can create a mechanism to prevent wrongdoing. He acts like a doctor who, while the patient is still alive...

» ...it is the mark of one who is suffering to help those present, and not to weave some life-saving machines for a dead man while attempting to save him. The <term>Peripatetic</term><note>The followers of Aristotle, named after the "peripatos" or covered walkway in the Lyceum where they walked while discussing philosophy.</note> view is very similar to this. For their concern is not so much about pleasure as it is an unbelief regarding the divine—namely, that God would care for us—and this unbelief strengthens the hand of injustice. Someone might ask: “So, are you saying that Aristotle and Epicurus say the same thing?” Indeed, they do, at least regarding the matter at hand. For what difference does it make to us whether the divine is banished from the universe <note>The view of Epicurus, who placed gods in the spaces between worlds.</note>, or if we are left with no communion with it, or if the gods are imprisoned in the heavens and kept away from the affairs of the earth? For in both cases, the gods are equally indifferent toward men, and those who do wrong have an equal license to act because there is no fear of the gods. 

» Someone might argue that we enjoy some benefit from the movement of the heavenly bodies and their cycles, but this is a hollow and irrational argument, as if we were speaking of inanimate objects. Indeed, in this sense, one could say there is benefit to humans from the gods even according to Epicurus. For his followers say that the better <term>effluences</term><note>original: ἀπορροίας (aporrhoias) — In Epicurean physics, these are streams of atoms flowing from the gods that can affect the human soul.</note> from the gods become the causes of great blessings for those who partake in them. But it is not right to count either the one view or the other as a theory of <term>Providence</term><note>original: προνοίας (pronoiαs) — The idea that God actively cares for and governs the world and individual human lives.</note>. For if, according to Epicurus, Providence is gone—even though he says the gods bring every care for the preservation of their own particular goods—so too would Providence be gone according to Aristotle, even if the things in the heavens are managed in some order and arrangement. 

» For the providence we seek is one that matters to us, which does not belong to those who believe neither in spirits, nor heroes, nor in any power at all capable of having organized human souls. In my judgment, Epicurus seems to have acted even less impiously. For, as if despairing of the gods' ability to take away the painful things from those who cast the burden of care upon them, he sent the gods away to a far-off land and settled them somewhere outside the universe, excusing the gods from these things by their distance and their lack of communion with all else. 

» But this other man <note>Aristotle</note>, the "discoverer of nature" as we are told, and the one with an "accurate" knowledge of divine things—even though he placed before our eyes the very same divine beings <note>The stars and planets, which Aristotle considered divine.</note>—he left human affairs neglected and unguarded, managed by a sort of "nature" rather than by divine reason. Therefore, he might rightly escape that specific accusation that some bring against Epicurus—that he did not speak his true mind, but only nodded his assent to the gods out of fear, placing them in his own system as if they were characters in a theater. 

» They take as proof of Epicurus's true opinion the fact that he stripped the gods of their activity toward us, which is the only way a person who honors the gods could have a righteous faith. But Aristotle does this very same thing. For by removing this activity, and judging faith in the matter by his limited sight alone, the protection that comes from this is weakened. Perhaps out of shame he says these things are "in the gods." For if he has left the gods outside the world, and does not bring them toward the things on earth, he is forced either to admit he is a total <term>atheist</term>, or to appear to leave some place for the gods so as to seem to live a pious life, having "colonized" the gods in that place. But he who refuses the precision of the higher powers seems, through this lack of connection, to be ungrateful and to lack faith in the gods. 

» These are the things Atticus adds against Aristotle, directing his arguments against him because he refused to believe that the world should be celebrated as a divine work.

## EUSEBIUS, PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL

...through others we shall seek God. Regarding the fact that Plato philosophizes in the same manner as Moses <note>A common claim among Middle Platonists and early Christians like Eusebius, who believed Plato had studied the writings of Moses.</note>, the thought of Aristotle is in these matters by no means refuted. Regarding what has been clearly shown here, writing word for word: "First, then, considering the generation of the world, and this great and much-talked-about doctrine of **Providence**, he thought it necessary to investigate everything, calculating that if the world had not come into being, there would be no need for a Creator, nor for any guardian to make us virtuous. Therefore, so as not to deprive the world of Providence, he [Plato] did not leave it uncreated. 

» We set these points forth now without intending to hinder those 'from our own hearth' <note>Meaning fellow Platonists.</note> who prefer to believe that, according to Plato, the world is uncreated. For it is only fair that they grant us pardon if we believe what Plato seems to say, since he himself—being one of us—has spoken to us more clearly through his own text than through a mere physical presence. 

» 'For taking,' he says, 'all that was visible, which was not at rest but moving discordantly and without order, God brought it from disorder into order, thinking this to be altogether better than the other.' <note>This is a direct quote from Plato’s *Timaeus* 30a, the foundational text for Greek creationism.</note> Furthermore, and even more so because he did not receive this knowledge through riddles, nor did he need it explained where it was already clear, he [Plato] shows through the words spoken by the Father <note>Referring to the Demiurge or Creator God in Plato's dialogue.</note> regarding the creation of the whole. 

» 'Mortal offspring,' he says, speaking to the gods, 'you are not indeed immortal, nor indissoluble in every way. Nevertheless, you shall not be dissolved, having obtained the favor of my will.' <note>Quoting *Timaeus* 41a-b. Plato argues that the "lesser gods" (stars/planets) are not immortal by nature, but are kept alive by the Creator’s will.</note> 

» But as I said, regarding those among us who are fired up with passion, since they are friends, we must examine them through friendly and quiet refutations. For it seems Aristotle also shifted these matters; while they would be unable to provide an adequate defense of the doctrine under accusation, they did not wish to destroy the clear opinion as if it were false, even in Plato's case. 

» According to our own understanding, Plato worthily claims the world came into being as the 'most beautiful work' by the 'most beautiful of creators.' Power was attributed to the Maker of the universe, through which He made the world which did not exist before; and having made it, because He wills it, He shall preserve it safe forever. In this way, the world is both 'generated' <term>genētos</term><note>Meaning it has a beginning in time or a cause for its existence.</note> and 'incorruptible' <term>aphthartos</term><note>Meaning it will never be destroyed.</note> according to him. Our established faith confirms these very things. 

» One must admire the shared struggle in these arguments: it is not necessarily true that if something has come into being, it must perish. Conversely, if something is not going to perish, it is not necessarily uncreated. We should neither grant that the only cause of 'incorruptibility' is being 'uncreated,' nor should we leave a thing that has come into being to a helpless change toward destruction. 

» Why then should we not take Aristotle as a helper in these matters? He is a man who does not seem to speak of these things in an absolute sense, nor based on the facts themselves, but who is arguing directly against Plato. He posits that what is 'generated' is under the necessity of perishing, and that what does not perish is not only—as we say—strengthened into incorruptibility, but he leaves no room for such power in God, as if God could do nothing good by using it. For Aristotle says: 'That which has never happened before could never happen at all.' 

» So far is he from helping Plato’s argument through these points that he has already frightened some of those devoted to Plato; by what he said, he led them away from the doctrine. They were unable to see that Plato conceived of the world’s nature as being produced by a cause, but preserved by the will and power of God. Thus, by its own nature, that which is created is not 'indestructible,' nor is that which is 'uncreated' capable of being 'made.' But when one seeks the highest Cause, which is from God, one must take this as the leader of all things, and not deny Him any of the other causes..."

<meta>catchword: ...deny [neí chei-]</meta>

<summary>Atticus defends the Platonic view that the world was created by God and is kept from destruction by Divine Will, specifically refuting Aristotle's claim that only "uncreated" things can be eternal. He argues that Aristotle's denial of a beginning to the universe is a veiled attack on the concept of Divine Providence.</summary>

Atticus is arguing that God’s providential will is the "bond" that keeps the universe from dissolving, a power far greater than any natural necessity or human craftsmanship. This leads into a specific critique of Aristotle’s physics.</meta>

### PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, BOOK 15
<sig>rr.i.</sig>

...into a worse state. For it is ridiculous to suggest that because something has come into being, it must therefore be destroyed. If God wills that it should not be destroyed, and if that which is **uncreated** <note>original: *agennēton*—meaning something that has no beginning and thus naturally no end</note> has the inherent strength to avoid destruction, then surely that which exists by the will of God does not lack the power to be preserved as something **imperishable** <note>original: *aphtharton*</note> among created things. 

A builder is capable of constructing a house where none existed. Someone else is capable of making a statue that did not exist before. Another, crafting a temple from raw material, provides it to those who have need of it. Each of the other craftsmen, as many as practice the productive arts, possesses this power: to bring into existence things that were not. Shall the King of All and the Supreme Craftsman possess not even as much power as a human artisan? Shall He remain, in our view, without a share in all creation? 

Furthermore, if we consider the cause even briefly, we might be able to grasp it: He is capable of creating and would surely will what is beautiful. For He is good, and in one who is good, there is no envy regarding anything. But is He capable of keeping or guarding what has been created? If other craftsmen are capable of both—for the builder and the shipwright not only construct new ships and houses, but are also capable of assisting those being destroyed by time, replacing worn-out parts with others—then surely we must grant at least this much to God. 

For how could He who is capable of making a whole be partially incapable of maintaining it? What need is there for anything new, especially if the Creator has prepared a beautiful work for all time? For the one who wishes to dissolve what has been created is doing the work of an evil person. 

Conversely, there is no bond for the salvation of created things greater than the **will of God**. If many nations, cities, and works—having received a share of human effort and will—flourish for a long time, shall we laugh when the one who willed them is no longer there? Shall those things which have participated in the mind of God, and which were created by Him and through Him, vanish and not be guarded while their Creator is present? What cause could force the mind of God? Is it some necessity inherent in created things? But necessity itself confessed its defeat by God so that it might be saved and set in order. Is it some external cause competing with God? There is none. Nor, in those things which God said He mastered and ordered, is it worth considering any further dissolution, unless we have completely forgotten that we are speaking about the greatest and most divine power. 

But I seem to be carried away by my enthusiasm into a discussion about the earth. What we proposed is clear: those who do not allow the world a beginning in nature cannot be teachers concerning the world's creation. If we must also discuss what Aristotle introduced regarding the **fifth essence** <note>original: *pemptēs ousias*—also known as the "quintessence" or *aether*, a substance Aristotle proposed for the heavens that is different from the four earthly elements</note>, we should take that up next.

But Aristotle, as it seems, seeking to appear more exceptional in his wisdom, added a **fifth essence** to the four visible bodies, having been previously accustomed to them. In doing so, he treated nature quite brilliantly and generously, but failed to see that he was not...

» to contribute, but would almost be the only thing to stand in opposition. 
» For instance, when we say that every body is either hot or cold, or wet or 
» dry, or soft or hard, or light or heavy, or rare or dense, and when we have 
» distinguished that nothing else could exist that participates in these qualities; 
» it follows that there are four elements. For if it is hot, it is either fire or air; 
» if it is cold, it is water or earth; if it is dry, fire or earth; if it is wet, 
» water or air; if it is soft, air or fire; if it is hard, water or earth; 
» if light and rare and sharp, it is fire or air; but if heavy and dense, water or earth. 
» While we argue from these obvious and universal simple powers 
» that there can be no other body besides these, Aristotle alone finds fault, 
» claiming that a body could exist outside of these and have no share in them. 
» He speaks of a body that is neither heavy nor light, neither soft nor hard, 
» nor wet, nor even dry—calling it "body" in name only, while 
» he has stripped away all the powers through which a body is naturally formed. 
» If, therefore, he convinces us by the facts themselves, he will remove us 
» from Plato's opinion; but if he merely confirms Plato's views, 
» he will depart from his own supposed doctrine. Thus, he is in no way 
» useful for understanding the teachings of Plato. 
» Furthermore, Plato wishes for all bodies—viewed as being made of 
» one similar matter—to turn and change into one another. 
» But Aristotle, in the case of the visible heavens, demands that they be 
» **impassible** <note>original: *apathē*—meaning something that cannot be affected or acted upon by external forces</note>, **incorruptible** <note>original: *aphtharton*</note>, and entirely **unchangeable** <note>original: *atrepton*</note>, 
» so that he might not seem to be troublesome regarding some specific point, 
» though at times he says nothing original at all. 
» He takes the attributes correctly observed by Plato and transfers them 
» to things where they do not belong, just as some followers of Lysimachus 
» do with their charges. For those people, mimicking the head of this Lydian, 
» the chest of that man, and the belt of another, and putting these 
» unrelated things together into one, come forward as if they have created 
» something original. Thus, while the whole thing—which anyone might 
» criticize for being disproportionate—belongs to them, the parts 
» gathered within it that possess beauty do not belong to them. 
» In the same way, Aristotle, hearing from Plato that there is a certain 
» **intelligible substance** <note>original: *ousia noētē*—reality that can only be grasped by the mind, not the senses</note> which exists by itself, 
» incorporeal, colorless, and intangible—neither beginning nor 
» ending, nor turning, nor changing, but always remaining the same

» the heavens, that they are divine, incorruptible, and 
» **impassible** <note>original: *apathē*</note> bodies, he combined and 
» "soldered" together these two incompatible things. 
» For how could he take "being a body" and "being impassible," and 
» construct an "impassible body"? 
» In the case of statues, even if it is not beautiful to make one out of 
» different parts, it is certainly not impossible. Homer teaches us 
» such things when he says:

> » For his eyes and head, he says, were like Zeus who delights in thunder,

» But an **impassible body** could never exist. For a nature that is bound 
» together, subject to affection and in constant flux, is 
» necessarily compelled to suffer along with that to which it is joined. 
» But if it were indeed impassible, it would have to be released and 
» free from that which suffers. Therefore, it would exist apart from 
» matter. If it is separate from matter, it must necessarily be admitted 
» to be **incorporeal**. And regarding these things, the intellect has 
» already shown how Aristotle disagrees with himself and with Plato.

### By the same author against the same person, regarding their disagreement over the immortality of the soul and the Hebrew oracles.

What indeed should we say regarding the soul? For these things are clear not only to philosophers, but surely to almost all common people: that Plato leaves the soul immortal, and he provides many arguments for this, demonstrating in a varied and solemn manner that the soul is immortal. And there has been much ambition among those who are serious about Plato's works as they join the struggle on behalf of both the doctrine and Plato himself. For almost the thing that holds together the entire school of the man is that [doctrine]. For the hypothesis of ethical doctrines followed from the immortality of the soul, as did the great, brilliant, and vigorous nature of virtue, because the soul is able to preserve what is divine. All things in nature are maintained according to the administration of the soul, which is able to be well-governed. For "all soul," he says solemnly, "takes care of the inanimate; it patrols the whole heaven, appearing at different times in different forms" <note>This is a famous quote from Plato's *Phaedrus* (246b), where he describes the soul's cosmic role</note>. But indeed, the matters of science and wisdom are also tied to the immortality of the soul for Plato. For "all learning is recollection" <note>original: *anamnesis*; the Platonic theory that we do not "learn" new things, but "remember" knowledge the soul possessed before birth</note>. And he thinks that inquiry and learning—from which science arises—cannot be carried out in any other way. If the soul is not immortal, there is no recollection; and if not this, then neither is there learning. Since all of Plato's doctrines are absolutely hung and suspended from the divinity and immortality of the soul, he who does not concede this overturns the entire philosophy of Plato. Who is it then who has clearly attempted to work at deceiving us, and to strip the soul of its immortality and all its divine power? It was the other one, Aristotle; for while some others, taking up the views of others, conceded them, or if not this, they at least assigned some power and a certain motion in the body, and works and actions to the soul. But he, as much as Plato...

>> [Plato] dignifies the nature of the soul as the principle of birth and the <note>original: "θεοῦ παίδευμα" (theou paideuma)</note> instruction of God, declaring it to be the priority above all things. But this man [Aristotle] has strove to pull it down and dishonor it, almost declaring the soul to be nothing at all. For in his view, it is neither spirit, nor fire, nor a body at all; yet neither is it incorporeal in such a way as to exist by itself and move itself, but acts only as much as it is unmoving and, so to speak, "soulless" <note>Atticus is being ironic: Aristotle’s unmoving soul is, to him, a soul without a soul.</note> under the body. For by what he has dared—or rather, by what he was forced to do, since the capacity for movement is taken away from the soul by his propositions—how could it deliberate? How could it think, or expect, or remember, or reason? For surely these must be the movements of the soul, as the <note>original: "ὁ τῆς φύσεως γραμματεύς" (ho tēs physeōs grammateus)</note> **Scribe of Nature** says. This man is certainly "trustworthy" in having understood something about real beings, given that he has erred so greatly regarding the soul itself that he does not even follow how it thinks! For he says it is not the soul, but the human being who performs each of these actions, while the soul remains unmoving. Consequently, following him, Dicaearchus <note>A student of Aristotle who famously argued that the soul does not exist as a separate substance.</note>—and quite logically, if one examines it—has abolished the entire <term>hypostasis</term> (underlying substance) of the soul.

>> For it is clear that the soul is something invisible and unseen. Thus, we cannot demonstrate the existence of the soul through the activity of the senses. However, its movements, being invisible, seem to force us to confess that the soul exists. For everyone seems to agree that these things dignify the soul: the act of deliberating, considering, and thinking in whatever way. When we look at the body and its powers, and consider such activities as not belonging to the body, we grant that there is something else within us that deliberates. And this is the soul. For from where else could we have devised the name "soul"? If someone takes away these attributes—from which the soul most clearly appears—and attaches them to something else, the soul would no longer appear to exist, nor would it seem to be of any use. How then can the help of one who wishes the soul to be immortal come from one who destroys the soul’s very essence? How can the teaching of its nature or its movement, by which we say it is <term>self-moving</term>, come from those who do not grant it even a simple movement?

>> "Yes," someone might say, "but regarding the immortality of the **Intellect** <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous)</note>, he [Aristotle] shares Plato's view." For even if he does not grant that the soul is immortal in every respect, he confesses that the Intellect is both divine and incorruptible. Now, as to the essence and nature of this Intellect—where it comes from, how it is inserted into humans, and where it departs again—he alone might know, if indeed he knows anything of what he says about the Intellect. Perhaps he is merely shielding himself from refutation by the obscurity of his speech, like <note>original: "αἱ σηπίαι" (hai sēpiai)</note> **cuttlefish** who retreat into the darkness they create. In any case, even in these matters he differs from Plato. For Plato says it is impossible for Intellect to exist without a soul, but Aristotle separates the Intellect from the soul. And while Plato grants immortality to the Intellect along with the soul itself (since it is not possible otherwise), Aristotle says this immortality belongs only to the Intellect when it is separated from the soul. He did not think it right for the soul to escape the body—because that pleased Plato—but he forced the Intellect to be torn away from the soul, because he realized such a thing was impossible for Plato. These are the words of the Atticus. I shall now join to them the words of Plotinus, which are <note>original: "γυμνὰ ἔχοντα τὸν ἔλαιον" (gymna echonta ton elaion)</note> **naked and oiled** <note>A metaphor for a wrestler prepared for a contest; Plotinus’ arguments are seen as rigorous and ready for intellectual combat.</note>.

» ...the soul, they say, belongs to the second kind of order, holding the "ensouled body" as its matter.
» It is the form not of every body, nor simply in so much as it is a body, but of a natural, organic body, having life in potentiality. <note>This is the famous definition of the soul from Aristotle’s *De Anima*.</note>
» Now, if the soul were cast and shaped like the form of a statue is to bronze, the soul would be partitioned along with the distribution of the body; and if some part were cut off, a portion of the soul would be cut off with it. 
» Furthermore, in sleep, there would be no "withdrawal" <note>The Platonists believed the soul partially withdraws from the body during sleep; if the soul is just the body's function, it cannot "go" anywhere.</note>, if indeed the <term>entelechy<gloss>original: "entelecheia" – the state of being complete or the "actualization" of a body's potential</gloss></term> must be naturally attached—that is, if it exists at all. But the truth is, sleep would not even occur [under this definition]. 
» Moreover, if it were such an actualization, there would be no conflict between reason and the desires. In this whole matter, while they have suffered much [in argument], they do not disagree with themselves. 
» Perhaps physical sensations might occur with difficulty, but thoughts would be impossible. This is why even they [the Aristotelians] introduce the <term>Intellect<gloss>original: "nous"</gloss></term> as an eternal thing, which they claim is immortal. 
» Therefore, either the reasoning soul is clearly an entelechy, or this argument must be necessary—if one must use this name—that even the perceptive faculty is not "with the body," provided it holds the imprints of sensible objects within itself even when those objects are absent. 
» If it were not so, these imprints would exist only as shapes and images. But it is clearly impossible to receive them if they existed in that way. Therefore, the soul is not an inseparable entelechy. 
» Furthermore, even that which desires is not desiring food or drink, but things irrational and apart from the body’s needs; thus, it too is not an inseparable entelechy. 
» What remains is the vegetative faculty, which might seem to provide a counter-argument: perhaps this is indeed an inseparable entelechy in this way, or it only appears to be so. 
» For if the principle of every plant is in the root, and when the body is pulled up by the root—or below in many plants—the soul clearly leaves the other parts and contracts into one. 
» Therefore, it is not in the whole as an inseparable entelechy. For it is also present before the plant has grown, within a small mass. 
» If, then, it goes from a larger plant into a small one, and from a small one to a large one, or if it is prevented from being separated entirely, how could that which is "partless" become a "partitioned" entelechy of a divisible body, even if the soul itself should pass from one animal to another? 
» How then would the soul of the former animal become that of the next, if it is the specific actualization of only one? This is seen in animals that transform into other animals. 
» Therefore, it does not possess its form as being "of" something, but it is a <term>substance<gloss>original: "ousia"</gloss></term>, not receiving its existence from being established in a body, but existing even before this body came to be. 
» The soul is not the movement of the animal's body. Of what, then, is it the substance? 
» If it is neither a body nor an affection of a body, but is activity, and creation, and many things within itself—an essence existing from itself toward bodies—what kind of thing is it? 
» Is it not clear that it belongs to what we call "true being"? For that which is by nature but is not "substance" might be called "corporeal," being born and perishing, never truly existing, but receiving a share of being only in so far as it participates in it. 
» Since we have also gone through the works of Plotinus, let us examine whether it might not be out of place to consider what Porphyry said in his writings *To Boethus* regarding the soul.

» To those who say the soul is an entelechy, and who have assumed it to be a completely unmoving motion, we must ask: from where does the "divine inspiration" <note>original: "enthousiasmoi" – a state of being inhabited by a god.</note> of the living being come?

<margin>»»</margin>one would not," he says, "be ashamed."

### Against the same author [Aristotle] for differing with Plato in the discourse on the Universal Soul. From the same sources.

When Plato says that the soul administers all things and permeates through all 
<margin>»»</margin>things, and that it is from this soul that all individual things are granted governance—and that 
<margin>»»</margin>Nature is nothing other than Soul (evidently a rational soul)—we can conclude 
<margin>»»</margin>from this that all things happen according to Providence, if indeed they also happen according to Nature. 
<margin>»»</margin>Aristotle agrees with us on none of these points. For he does not believe Nature is Soul, nor that things 
<margin>»»</margin>on earth are governed by a single Nature. He assigns different causes to each 
<margin>»»</margin>class of things. For the heavenly realm, which is always the same and in the same state, 
<margin>»»</margin>he posits <term>Fate<gloss>original: "heimarmenē"</gloss></term> as the cause. For the sublunary realm <note>The region below the moon, i.e., the Earthly sphere</note>, he posits 
<margin>»»</margin>Nature. For human affairs, he posits Prudence, <term>Providence<gloss>original: "pronoia"</gloss></term>, and Soul. In these 
<margin>»»</margin>divisions, he goes about with refined distinctions, yet fails to see what is necessary. 
<margin>»»</margin>For if there were not one single ensouled power permeating the 
<margin>»»</margin>whole and giving life and cohesion to everything, the universe could be neither rationally 
<margin>»»</margin>nor beautifully governed. It would be the same sort of blindness to think a city or a 
<margin>»»</margin>household could ever be well-preserved without unity. And wherever it is said that "this 
<margin>»»</margin>whole is preserved beautifully in Reason," how could that be so if things were not harmonized 
<margin>»»</margin>and brought together by a similar communion with a single source? Yet he finds 
<margin>»»</margin>this thing which he says governs each part—as being the source of 
<margin>»»</margin>motion—but he is unwilling to admit that this is "Soul." And this despite Plato himself 
<margin>»»</margin>demonstrating that for all things moved, the soul is the beginning and source of motion. 
<margin>»»</margin>That which is the work of a rational and prudent soul—namely, to do nothing in vain—he 
<margin>»»</margin>attributes to "Nature," but he does not grant it the name of "Soul." It is as if he is 
<margin>»»</margin>dealing in names, rather than the actual powers of the things themselves.

...[leading], he attracted many followers. Crates succeeded him. After Crates came Zeno of Citium, who was established as the founder of the Stoic school of philosophers. Cleanthes succeeded Zeno, and Chrysippus succeeded Cleanthes. After him came another Zeno and those who followed in order; it is said that they all cared exceptionally for a dignified life and for <term>dialectic</term><note>The art of logical argument and investigation into the truth of opinions.</note>. Their philosophical doctrines are roughly as follows.

### Concerning the philosophy of the Stoics, and how they assigned reason to every living being.
#### From the seventh book of Aristocles "On Philosophy."

<margin>»</margin> They say that fire is the element of all existing things, just as Heraclitus did, and that its 
<margin>»</margin> principles are <term>matter</term><note>Hyle: the underlying "stuff" of the universe.</note> and God, just as Plato said. But they say that both are bodies—
<margin>»</margin> both the active and the passive—whereas Plato said that the active cause was 
<margin>»</margin> <term>incorporeal</term><note>Asōmaton: something that does not have a physical body or material substance.</note>. Furthermore, they say that at certain fated and 
<margin>»</margin> determined times, the entire cosmos is consumed by fire. Then, afterward, it is 
<margin>»</margin> organized once again. The primary fire is like a certain "seed," 
<margin>»</margin> possessing the <term>rational principles</term><note>Logoi: the blueprints or "seeds" of reason that govern how things grow and develop.</note> of all things, and the causes of things that 
<margin>»</margin> have been, are, and will be; and the interconnection and sequence of these 
<margin>»</margin> things is <term>Fate</term><note>Heimarmene: the inescapable chain of cause and effect.</note>, Knowledge, Truth, and an inescapable and 
<margin>»</margin> unavoidable Law of all that exists. In this way, all things throughout 
<margin>»</margin> the cosmos are completely administered, as if in a city governed by the very best laws.

### What sort of opinion the Stoics held concerning God and the composition of the whole.
#### From the epitome of Arius Didymus.

<margin>»</margin> They call the whole cosmos, along with its own parts, "God." They say that 
<margin>»</margin> this God is the only one, and is finite, an eternal living being, and God. 
<margin>»</margin> For in this, all bodies are contained, and no <term>void</term><note>Kenos: empty space; the Stoics believed the universe itself was "full" of matter, though a void existed outside it.</note> exists within it. 
<margin>»</margin> For the quality arising from the whole of substance is called "Cosmos." 
<margin>»</margin> Such is its arrangement and order. Some say that the cosmos is eternal 
<margin>»</margin> in its primary sense. But they say the "arrangement" is generated and 
<margin>»</margin> changeable, having occurred and being destined to occur through 
<margin>»</margin> infinite cycles. And while the quality of all substance is the eternal 
<margin>»</margin> Cosmos and God, they say "Cosmos" can also refer to the system composed of 
<margin>»</margin> heaven, air, earth, and sea, and the natures within them. Furthermore, 
<margin>»</margin> they call "Cosmos" the dwelling place of gods and men, and of those things 
<margin>»</margin> created for their sake. For in the same way that a "city" is spoken of in 
<margin>»</margin> two ways—both as the dwelling place and as the system composed of 
<margin>»</margin> the inhabitants together with the citizens—so also the cosmos is like a 
<margin>»</margin> "city" composed of gods and men, with the gods holding the leadership 
<margin>»</margin> and men being subjects. They say a community exists between them 
<margin>»</margin> because they share in <term>reason</term><note>Logos: here meaning the faculty of rational thought.</note>, which is Law by nature. All other 
<margin>»</margin> things were created for their sake. Consequently, one must believe that the 
<margin>»</margin> God who administers the whole provides for humans, being beneficent, 
<margin>»</margin> kind, and a lover of mankind, as well as just and possessing all the virtues. 
<margin>»</margin> For this reason, the cosmos is also called <term>Zeus</term><note>The Stoics often used the name of the king of the gods to represent the rational soul of the universe.</note>, since he is the cause 
<margin>»</margin> of our living. Insofar as he administers all things by the aforementioned 
<margin>»</margin> reason without deviation from eternity, he is named "Fate." He is called 
<margin>»</margin> "Adrasteia" because nothing can escape him. He is called "Providence" 
<margin>»</margin> because he manages each thing toward what is useful. Cleanthes 
<margin>»</margin> preferred the <term>ruling part</term><note>Hēgemonikon: the "command center" or most vital part of a living being.</note> of the cosmos to be the sun, because it is the 
<margin>»</margin> greatest of the stars and contributes the most to the administration of the whole.
