<header>OF EUSEBIUS</header>

## Against the same man who mocked the Ideas found in Plato, which
## the Hebrew accounts had already established even earlier.

-> From the works of <-
-> Atticus. <-

> The core and the authority of Plato’s school of thought is the arrangement concerning the <term>intelligible</term><note>Noēta: objects that can only be grasped by the mind or intellect, as opposed to the physical senses.</note> world. This has been both trampled upon by my opponent and, quite similarly, insulted as much as possible by Aristotle. For Aristotle was unable to conceive that the great and divine aspects of reality are not <term>sensible</term><note>Aisthēta: things perceived through the five senses.</note>, but require a specific nearby power for their recognition. Trusting in his own thin and lowly sharpness, he thought that if one could slip through the fenced-in things of the earth and see clearly what is in them, then one could oversee the things of true reality. Yet, being unable to reach them due to his many deceits, and using his own self as the rule and judge, he denied that there were certain "individual natures" such as Plato recognized. He dared to call the highest of existing things "nonsense" <note>original: lērous</note>, "idle chirping" <note>original: teretismata; literally the twittering of birds, used here to mean empty talk</note>, and "frivolity." This, then, is the peak and the ultimate point of Plato’s philosophy: the doctrine of the intelligible, the divine and eternal essence of the <term>Ideas</term><note>Forms: the perfect, unchanging archetypes of all things in the physical world.</note>. It is toward these that the ultimate labor and struggle of the soul is directed. For the one who participates in and reaches them is entirely happy; but the one who is left behind and is unable to become a spectator of them is left entirely without a share of happiness. For this reason, Plato struggles everywhere to demonstrate the "Idea" of these natures. For he says it is not possible to give a proper cause for anything whatsoever unless one has a "participation" in these, nor is there knowledge of anything true without reference to these. Furthermore, he says that no one will share in <term>reason</term><note>Logos: here meaning rational discourse or the underlying logic of reality.</note> unless they acknowledge the essence of these things. Those who have decided to support Plato's views place the greatest struggle of their arguments in this point, quite advantageously. For nothing is left for the Platonists if someone does not grant them these first and most primary natures established by Plato. These are the things in which he especially excels over all others. For having himself conceived of God as the Father and Maker of all things, and as Master and Guardian—recognizing the Craftsman from his works—he understood more correctly that which He alone created. Then, having brought the intelligible things to bear upon the results in the world, he achieved a greater likeness. Of these things, the names are older than the objects; they are the <term>paradigms</term><note>Models or blueprints upon which the physical world is based.</note> of our world, incorporeal and intelligible, always remaining the same and in the same state. They are primarily the things themselves, and they are the joint-causes for all other things being such as they are, according to their likeness to them. Plato, seeing that these things are not easily seen, nor can they be clearly revealed by speech, again did what he could to speak and think and prepare those who were going to follow him. Having busied himself with these matters and having organized his entire philosophy toward this end, he says that <term>wisdom</term><note>Sophia</note> and <term>science</term><note>Epistēmē: certain, demonstrative knowledge.</note> consist in the <term>intellection</term><note>Noēsis: the act of mental perception.</note> of these things, through which the human end and the blessed life are achieved.

These are the words of Atticus. Before we set forth more from the aforementioned writing of this man, we shall satisfy ourselves with what has been laid out and move on to the school of the <term>Stoics</term><note>A school of philosophy founded by Zeno of Citium, focused on virtue, logic, and a universe governed by divine reason.</note>. Now, Antisthenes became a pupil of Socrates. He was a man who had deafened his own pride; he said that if he had to choose, it would be better to be mad than to experience pleasure. Because of this, he advised his acquaintances never to stretch out a finger for the sake of pleasure. Diogenes "the Dog" <note>The Cynic: 'Cynic' comes from the Greek word for dog, 'kyōn', referring to their unconventional, 'uncivilized' lifestyle.</note> became a pupil of this man, and he in turn was thought to have an even more beast-like mindset...

...having taught <note>original: "ξας", the suffix of "epideixas" (having demonstrated/taught), continuing from the previous page</note>, he attracted many followers. Crates succeeded him. ->Concerning the philosophy of the Stoics, and how Zeno gave an account<-

> They say that fire is the element of all beings, just as Heraclitus did, and that its principles are matter and God, as Plato said. However, they claim that both are <term>bodies</term><note>The Stoics were materialists who believed that even God and the soul were composed of a subtle form of matter.</note>—both the "active" and the "passive"—whereas Plato said the active cause is incorporeal. Furthermore, they say that at certain fated and determined times, the entire universe is consumed by fire <note>original: "ekpyrōsthai", the Stoic doctrine of universal conflagration</note>. Then, afterward, it is ordered once again. They hold that the primary fire is like a seed of all things, containing the <term>rational principles</term><note>Logoi: the formative blueprints or "seeds" that determine how things develop.</note> and the causes of things past, present, and future. The interconnection and sequence of these is Fate, Knowledge, Truth, and a Law of all things that is inescapable and unavoidable. In this way, all things in the universe are governed, looking toward a most well-ordered <term>commonwealth</term><note>Politeia: the Stoic idea of the "Cosmopolis," where the universe is a city shared by gods and humans.</note>.

---

->What sort of opinion the Stoics held concerning God and the constitution of the cosmos.<-
->From the Epitome of Arius Didymus.<-

> They call the whole cosmos, along with its own parts, God. They say He is one alone and finite, a living being, eternal, and God. For in Him all bodies are contained, and no void exists within Him. The "quality" <note>The specific character or identity</note> arising from the whole of substance is called the cosmos, having such an arrangement and disposition. In the first sense, they say the cosmos is eternal. But in terms of its specific arrangement, it is created and changeable, occurring through infinite cycles that have passed and are yet to come. Insofar as it is the quality of the whole of substance, the cosmos is eternal and God. The "cosmos" is also defined as a system of heaven, air, earth, and sea, and the natures within them. Furthermore, "cosmos" is said to be the dwelling place of gods and humans, and the things created for their sake. For just as a "city" is used in two ways—both the dwelling place and the system of inhabitants along with the citizens—so the cosmos is like a city composed of gods and humans, with the gods holding the leadership and humans being subject to them. They have a fellowship with one another because they share in Reason, which is Law by nature. Everything else was made for their sake. Consequently, one must believe that God, who governs the whole, provides for humanity, being a benefactor, kind, a lover of mankind, just, and possessing all virtues. Therefore, the cosmos is also called Zeus, since He is the cause of our living <note>A Greek wordplay: "Zeus" was etymologically linked to "zēn" (to live).</note>. Insofar as He governs everything unchangeably by the aforementioned Reason from eternity, He is named Fate. And He is called Adrasteia <note>A name for Nemesis or Fate</note>, because nothing can run away from Him. He "provides" <note>Pronoia: divine providence</note> in that He arranges each thing for its usefulness. Cleanthes preferred the Sun to be the "ruling part" <note>hēgemonikon: the commanding faculty of the world-soul</note> of the cosmos, because it is the largest of the stars and contributes the most to the governance of the whole.

For some of that school <note>The Stoics.</note> held the opinion that God is the **ruling principle** <note>original: "hēgemonikon"; the governing or "commanding" part of the soul or the universe.</note> of the world. But for Chrysippus <note>A primary architect of Stoic doctrine.</note>, God is the purest and most unmixed **ether** <note>The "upper air" or "fiery" element; the Stoics believed this was the most divine substance.</note>, inasmuch as it is the most stable of all things and yet drives the entire rotation of the cosmos. Let these points from the summary by Didymus suffice for us to set forth. Regarding the Stoic opinion on God, the words of Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist and critic of Christianity and Stoicism.</note> will be sufficient, which he wrote in response to Boethus regarding the soul; they are as follows:

## Porphyry's opinions against those of the Stoics concerning God. From the work "To Boethus on the Soul."

,, For they do not hesitate to say that God is an eternal **intellectual fire**, and they say He consumes and feeds upon all things, as if this God were a fire like the one we are familiar with. They attempt to argue against Aristotle when he says the ether is not composed of this kind of fire. When they are asked how such a fire can endure eternally, they cannot say it is a different kind of fire; yet, having said this, they expect to be believed. They rely on this **unreasoning faith** <note>original: "alogō pistei"; Porphyry is criticizing the Stoics for making assertions without logical proof.</note> to claim that this fire is eternal, even though the etherial fire in our part of the world is extinguished and ignited by turns. But who would dwell any longer on their lack of foresight in these matters, or their laziness and contempt toward the teachings of the ancients?

## That "Being" cannot be a body according to the Stoics. From the first book of Numenius' "On the Good."

,, But what then is "Being"? Is it these four elements—earth, fire, and the other two intermediate natures <note>Air and water.</note>? Are "beings" these four taken together as one, or is it any one of them individually? And if they are subject to birth and being "taken back again," since we can see them being transformed into one another and passing away, they are neither truly elements nor even "syllables" <note>A metaphor for basic building blocks; if elements are like letters, compounds are like syllables.</note> of reality. Therefore, "Being" cannot be a **body** <note>Numenius, a Neopythagorean, argues that physical matter is too unstable to be called "True Being."</note> if it is like this. But if not these, can **matter** itself be "Being"? This is more impossible than anything. For in its constant flux, matter is a **river**, turbid and swift-flowing, indefinite in its depth, width, and length, and yet motionless <note>In the sense of having no purposeful direction or inherent form.</note>. It accomplishes nothing, not even the smallest thing. Thus, the argument was well-stated when it said that if matter is infinite, it must be indefinite; if it is indefinite, it is irrational; and if it is irrational, it is unknown. And being unknown, it must necessarily be disordered. For it would be quite easy for ordered things to be known. But that which is disordered does not stand still; and that which does not stand still cannot be "Being." This is exactly what we agreed upon earlier: it is sacrilegious to associate any of these qualities with "Being." This is the view held by most, or if not all, then certainly by me. Therefore, I say that neither matter itself nor bodies are "Being." What then is it? If we have something else in the nature of the whole besides these, it is perhaps not difficult to say. If so, let us first attempt to discuss it among ourselves. Since bodies are **naturally dead**, corpses, and driven about, never remaining the same, do they not surely require something to hold them together? If they did not have this, would they remain? Not at all. What then is this "holding power"? If this power were a body, it seems to me that it would itself require a "savior" to keep it from dissolving and scattering. If it is to save the body, it must be free from the weaknesses of a body, so that it might ward off the destruction shared by those things it governs.

and holds it fast, it does not seem to me to be anything worthy, except perhaps only the **incorporeal**. For this alone of all natures stands firm, and is intangible, and in no way uniform; for it neither grows nor increases; nor does it move in any way at all, and for these reasons it seemed rightly just to preserve the incorporeal.

### How the Stoics hold opinions concerning the conflagration of the universe.

It is the view of the oldest members of this school <note>The Stoics, founded by Zeno of Citium.</note> that all things are turned into a vapor according to certain vast cycles, all things being dissolved into **ethereal fire**. And it follows, from these things it is clear that Chrysippus <note>The third head of the Stoic school and its most prolific systematizer.</note> did not adopt this "confusion" <note>original: "synchysis"; referring to a total blending of substances where their individual properties are lost.</note> regarding the essence of matter. For that is impossible. Rather, he speaks of it in place of "change." For they do not strictly adopt the term "destruction" regarding the destruction of the world that occurs according to certain vast cycles—those who dogmatize the dissolution of all things into fire, which they indeed call **conflagration** <note>original: "ekpyrōsis"; the Stoic belief that the universe is periodically consumed by fire.</note>—but instead of "natural change" they use the name of "destruction." For it pleases the Stoic philosophers that the entire essence transforms into fire, as if into a kind of **seed**. And then again, from this the world-order <note>original: "diakosmēsis"; the reconstruction or arrangement of the universe.</note> is completed once more, just as it was before. And this doctrine was accepted by the first and oldest of the sect: Zeno, Cleanthes, and Chrysippus. For they say that Zeno, the student of Tycon and successor of the school, attempted to write about the conflagration of the whole.

### How the Stoics hold opinions concerning the regeneration of the universe.

When the universal **reason** <note>original: "logos"; the rational principle governing the universe.</note> and universal nature have progressed to this point and become greater and more abundant— <insert>* having dissolved all things into itself *</insert> for it returns to the first-mentioned reason and to that resurrection, that cycle, the **Great Year**, according to which the **restoration** <note>original: "apokatastasis"; the return of all things to their original state at the end of a cosmic cycle.</note> occurs from it alone back into itself. And being mindful of the order from which it began to organize the world in the same way, it makes the same progression again according to reason, such cycles occurring incessantly from eternity. For there is no cause for the beginning, nor is it possible for all things to come to be without cause, nor the things managed by it. For there must be a substance underlying the things that come to be, naturally disposed to receive all changes, and a creative force working from it. For just as there is a creative nature in us, something of this kind must of necessity exist in the world, being **ungenerated**. For it is not possible for there to be a beginning of generation for this nature. Because it is ungenerated, it is also impossible for it to be destroyed, either by itself or by something external.

### How the Stoics hold opinions concerning the soul.

Zeno says that the **seed** which a man emits is **breath** <note>original: "pneuma"; for the Stoics, a mixture of fire and air that acts as the vital force.</note> mixed with moisture, a part and fragment of the soul, a blend and mixture of the seeds of the ancestors, coming together from the parts of the soul. For having all the same **formative principles** <note>original: "logous"; the "rational seeds" or blueprints that determine the development of an organism.</note> as the whole, when it is released into the womb, it is conceived by another breath—a part of the female's soul—and becomes united with it; having been hidden, it grows and is stirred and fanned into life by that soul, always adding to its matter and increasing from itself. And after a short while...

## Longinus’s Refutation of the Stoic Doctrine of the Soul.

"To speak briefly, they all seem to me to have wandered far from reasoning correctly, as many as have declared the soul to be a **body** <note>Meaning a material or physical substance.</note>. For how is it at all possible for that which is 'according to itself' <note>The soul's essential nature.</note> to be near to any of the elements? Where can one find a place for blendings and mixtures? If these ever occur among many things, they are naturally suited to produce forms of countless types of bodies, in which, if not continuously, then as if from afar, one can see the cause of the elements and the starting point of the primary things for the secondary ones. But no trace or evidence of the soul is found in bodies, even if one were to strive, as **Epicurus** and **Chrysippus** did, to 'move every stone,' searching with all the power of the body for the origin of the soul's actions. For how could the 'fineness of breath' <note>original: "pneuma"; the Stoic material substance of the soul.</note> help us in **imagination** and **reasoning**? Or what <unclear>sort</unclear> of shape of **atoms** has such power and turn compared to others that it produces **wisdom**, whenever it is mixed into the molding of another body? I think not even if one happened upon the tripods and handmaidens of **Hephaestus** <note>The Greek god of the forge; in Homer’s Iliad, he created golden mechanical servants.</note>, of whom **Homer** says the former move automatically into the contest, while the latter work with their master, lacking none of the advantages that the living possess—certainly not by a chance scraping.

,, ...of the psychic spirit <note>original: "ψυχικοῦ πνεύματος" — referring to the refined physical substance Stoics believed carried sensations through the nerves.</note>, passing it on to the next part, and that part again to the next, until it reaches the ruling faculty <note>original: "ἡγεμονικὸν" — the central command center of the soul in Greek philosophy.</note>. It follows that if the first part felt the pain, the sensation would cease in the second part <note>The OCR "εἶ)" likely represents "εἶναι", meaning "to be".</note>, if sensation happened by a chain of transmission. In that case, even a third part would feel it, and there would be many and infinite sensations arising for a single pain. All of these would then reach the ruling faculty, which is the mind <note>original: "νοῦς"</note>, and it would take these sensations as its own. But the truth is that each of those parts would not feel the pain in the finger, but rather the pain located in itself; it would only know its own state and let the rest go, not understanding that the finger is in pain. If, therefore, it is impossible for sensation to occur through such a transmission, then the perceiving subject cannot be a body, which is a physical mass. For in a physical fire, one part is here and another is there; but we must assume the perceiving subject is something that is the same as itself everywhere. This belongs to something other than physical bodies.

,, That it is also impossible to think if the soul were any kind of body must be shown from the following: If perceiving consists of the soul using the body as an instrument to apprehend sensible objects, then thinking cannot be the apprehension of things through a body; otherwise, thinking would be the same as perceiving. If, then, thinking is different from apprehending through the body, it is all the more necessary that the soul itself not be a body while it thinks. For while sensation is directed toward sensible things, thinking is directed toward intelligible things <note>original: "νοητῶν" — abstract realities or forms that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses.</note>. Even if one does not wish to admit this, there will at least be thoughts of intelligible things and apprehensions of things without size. How then can a physical mass, which possesses size, think of that which has no size? Or how can the divisible think of the indivisible? Shall the divisible part think of the indivisible by using its own indivisible part? But if that is the case, the thinking subject will not be a body. For surely one does not need the whole body to see, or even the whole of the part in which the sight resides.

,, If they will grant that the primary thoughts—which is true—must each be pure from the body, then it is necessary that the thinking subject also be pure from the body while it comes to know them. But if someone should say that thoughts are of forms existing in matter <note>original: "τῶν ἐν ὕλῃ εἰδῶν" — the shapes or structures found in physical objects.</note>, nonetheless they are only understood when they are separated from bodies by the power of the one who separates them. For the separation of a circle, a triangle, a line, and a point is not done with flesh or matter in general. Therefore, the soul must also separate itself from the body during such an act. It follows, then, that the soul itself cannot be a body.

,, I also consider beauty <note>original: "τὸ καλὸν"</note> and justice <note>original: "τὸ δίκαιον"</note> to have no physical size; thus, the thought of these things must also lack size. So, as they approach the soul, her parts will receive them, and they will lie within her as indivisible things. But how could temperance <note>original: "σωφροσύνη"</note>, justice, courage <note>original: "ἀνδρεία"</note>, and the other virtues exist if the soul were a body? For then being temperate would be a kind of breath <note>original: "πνεῦμά"</note> or blood. Unless, perhaps, courage were a certain expansion of this breath, and temperance were its good mixture <note>original: "εὐκρασία" — a balanced state of physical elements.</note>. And beauty would be a certain formlessness in patterns, and we would call people "lovely" and "beautiful in body" because of these things. Now, while strength and physical beauty might appropriately be attributed to the breath, why would being temperate be attributed to a breath? On the contrary, would it not be a physical state of being affected in turnings and touches, where the breath takes pleasure in heat, or desires cooling in a balanced way, or touches things that are soft, smooth, and simple? But what of the soul that distributes to each according to their merit, or cares for itself?

,, Are the contemplations of virtue and the other intelligible things eternal, which the soul grasps, or does virtue come into being and then must perish again? But who is the one who creates it, and from where? For it would remain wherever it came from. It must, therefore, be eternal and permanent, like the truths in geometry. But if it is eternal and permanent, it is not part of bodies. Therefore, the subject in which it exists must also be of such a nature. It must, therefore, not be a body—not just one part of it, but the entire nature of the body. For if we see the activities of bodies are heating, cooling, pushing, and weighing...

» ...of the <term>psychic spirit</term> <note>original: "πνεύματος" (pneumatos) — here referring to a subtle physical substance ancient thinkers believed carried sensations through the body.</note>, passing it on to the next part, and that to another, until it reaches the <term>ruling part</term> <note>original: "ἡγεμονικὸν" (hegemonikon) — the central seat of consciousness or "command center" of the soul.</note>. Therefore, if the part that first suffers feels the pain, it is clear that the perception belongs to a second part; and if the perception is also in the transmission, it belongs to a third as well, and there would be many and even infinite perceptions occurring for a single pain. And if the ruling part is the mind, all these perceptions would eventually reach it, and it would perceive all of them as its own. But the truth is that each of those intermediary parts would not perceive the pain in the finger, but rather the pain directly adjacent to itself. If it only knew how to know that, it would ignore everything else, not understanding that the finger is in pain. If, then, it is impossible for perception to occur by this kind of transmission, and since the soul is not a physical mass, then feeling pain must be a form of knowledge. For in every physical <term>magnitude</term> <note>meaning something with physical dimensions or size.</note>, one part is distinct from another; therefore, that which perceives must be positioned such that it is the same as itself everywhere. But this belongs to something other than a body to perform. Nor would <term>intellection</term> <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun) — the faculty of pure thought or understanding.</note> be possible if the soul were any kind of body, as must be shown from the following: if perception consists of the soul using the body as an instrument to grasp sensible objects, then "thinking" cannot also be a grasping through the body, otherwise it would be the same thing as perceiving. If, then, thinking is the grasping of things without the body, it is even more necessary that the thinking principle itself is not a body. For while perception is directed toward sensory objects, thought is directed toward <term>intelligible objects</term> <note>original: "νοητῶν" (noēton) — realities that can only be understood by the mind, like mathematical truths or justice, rather than seen with the eyes.</note>. If they refuse to admit this, they will find that there are no thoughts of intelligible things, nor any "pains" felt for things without physical size. How then can that which has magnitude think of that which has no magnitude? Or how can the divisible think of the indivisible? Perhaps by some indivisible part of itself? But if that is the case, the thing doing the thinking will not be a body. For the whole is not needed for the act of thinking; a single part is sufficient. If they will then concede that thoughts are incorporeal—which is true—then just as the first principle of a body is each thing in its purest state, it is necessary that the thinking principle, being pure of body, must be within us in order to know. But if they say that thoughts are of forms existing in matter, these are grasped by being separated from the body they inhabit, by a specific "separator" <note>the mind's ability to abstract concepts from physical things.</note>. For the separation is not done with physical bulk, nor with matter at all—such as the separation of a circle, a square, a line, or a point. Therefore, the soul itself must also separate itself from the body in such an act. Consequently, it must not be a body itself. And I believe that both Beauty and Justice are <term>magnitudes</term> <note>Plotinus is likely speaking ironically here, or referring to "greatness" in a non-physical sense.</note>; and thought comes from these. Thus, as they approach, the soul’s parts will suggest them, and they will lie within it as indivisible things. And how could the soul, if it were a body, see its own temperance, justice, courage, and the rest? For would temperance, or justice, or courage be a certain "spirit" or a certain kind of blood? Unless, perhaps, courage is that which masters the spirit, or temperance is the lack of excess. But beauty would be a kind of shapeliness in physical forms, and what we say when we see people who are "fair" and "beautiful" in their bodies. Now, strong and beautiful things might be a kind of "spirit" <note>pneuma</note> in physical forms; but it is proper to the temperate person not to be moved by a "spirit," but rather the opposite: not to be well-affected by embraces and touches, where one would enjoy heat or desire a moderate coolness, or approach soft, smooth, and simple things. But for the one who assigns to each what is earned, what would the body care for him? Furthermore, does the soul grasp the objects of virtue and other intelligible forms because they are eternal, or must virtue perish again? But who is the maker, and from where? For in that way, the other would remain. They must, therefore, be eternal and permanent, like the truths in geometry. But if they are eternal and permanent, they are not bodies. And therefore, that in which they exist must be of the same nature. Thus, it must not be a body. For the entire nature of a body does not remain, but is in a state of flux. » ...them, and establishing the soul within them as if in an active <term>instrument</term> <note>original: "ὅπλῳ" (hoplō) — meaning a tool or weapon; here used for the physical organs through which the soul acts.</note>, first indeed [they say] these bodies work by the powers within them. Next, because we do not recognize these powers as the cause, but rather <term>intellection</term> <note>original: "τὸ νοεῖν" (to noein) — the act of pure thought or understanding.</note>, perception, loving, desiring, caring, and acting wisely and well—this seeks another <term>essence</term> <note>original: "οὐσίαν" (ousian).</note>. If one transfers the powers of incorporeal things into bodies, they leave nothing for those bodies. If, on the other hand, you give incorporeal powers to bodies, the result is not clear. For they will admit that quality is one thing and quantity is another, and that every body is a quantity, yet not every quantity is a body—such as <term>matter</term> <note>original: "ὕλην" (hylēn).</note>. By admitting these things, except they will admit that quality is different from quantity, then it is different from body. For how could it be a body if it is not a quantity, if indeed every body is a quantity? Furthermore, as was said above, if a large body being divided from its bulk has any part removed, and if the body is crumbled into bits, the same whole quality remains in each part—just as the sweetness of honey is no less sweetness in each bit—then sweetness would not be a body. Similarly for other qualities. Next, if the powers were bodies, it would be necessary for strong powers to be large masses, and those capable of doing little to be small masses. But if large masses have small powers, and the smallest masses have the greatest powers, the capacity to act must be attributed to something other than size. Therefore, power is without magnitude.

» But regarding the claim that matter itself is a body and an essence, as they say, but that it produces difference by taking on qualities: how is it not clear that these qualities that enter it are themselves <term>rational principles</term> <note>original: "λόγους" (logous) — here meaning formative patterns or blueprints that give matter its shape and function.</note> and are incorporeal? Nor should they say that animals die because the <term>breath</term> <note>original: "πνεύματος" (pneumatos).</note> or the blood departs (for they claim these are the causes of life), because these things themselves are not the soul, but many other things are not the soul either. Either, then, breath and blood are common to all, or just the blood. If the soul, being a body, were the soul because of the blood, it would—if mixed—no longer be [the soul], for <term>mixture</term> <note>original: "κρᾶσις" (krasis) — a technical term for the blending of two substances.</note> is no longer possible in bodies. But if there is a mixture of bodies, then nothing of the things mixed, not even the soul itself, would still exist in <term>actuality</term> in the bodies, but only in <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: "δυνάμει" (dynamei).</note>, having lost what it was to be soul. It is just as if sweet and bitter were mixed: the sweet is no longer sweet. Therefore, we would not have a soul.

» Furthermore, if a body is mixed with another body <term>totally throughout</term> <note>original: "ὅλον δι᾿ ὅλου" (holon di' holou) — referring to the Stoic theory that two physical bodies can occupy the same space simultaneously.</note>, so that wherever one is, there is an equal volume of both, and if they contain fire, and no increase in volume occurs when one is added to the other, nothing remains that is not cut. For the mixture will alternate throughout the large parts. For they say there will also be a relaxation. But if that which is added passes through everything to a smaller degree, this is impossible—or the smaller would have to become equal to the larger. But if it passes through, it cuts everything. It follows, then, that if even any point whatsoever—with no body in between—is not cut, the division of the body must have reached the level of points, which is impossible. And if the cutting is infinite—for whatever body you take is divisible—it will not be so in potentiality only, but there will be infinite parts in actuality. Therefore, it is impossible for a whole body to pass through a whole body. But if the soul passes through the whole, then it must be incorporeal.

» Regarding the claim that by nature, the soul is produced by others, and they call it "breath." And that when it becomes cold and embodied, the soul is formed, becoming finer as it becomes cold—is this not absurd? For many animals live in heat and have a soul that is not made by cold. But they say that the soul is a prior nature and a coincidence of things happening outside. It happens, then, that they make the worse prior to the better, and concerning this, another lesser thing, which they call a <term>habit</term> <note>original: "ἕξιν" (hexin) — a Stoic term for the lowest level of organized existence (like in stones).</note>. But the mind...

» Clearly, the world is the last thing after the soul; or if there is a universal <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous) — the realm of pure thought or divine mind.</note>, one ought to place the soul next, and then <term>nature</term> <note>original: "φύσιν" (physin) — here referring to the lowest level of life that governs physical growth.</note>. And that which comes later is always inferior by nature. If, therefore, God is also later and generated in their view according to the intellect, and possesses a mind that is merely incidental, it might follow that there is neither soul, nor intellect, nor God. If, however, it does not exist potentially, it would first exist in <term>actuality</term> <note>original: "ἐνεργείᾳ" (energeia) — a key Aristotelian term meaning a state of being fully realized or active, as opposed to "potential" (dynamis).</note> within the intellect, and would not even have a path toward actuality. For what would lead it there, if nothing else existed before it to lead it toward actuality through itself, just as a farmer acts—not potentially, but in actuality? Yet that which always remains the same will come into actuality by itself from its potential state, and this will be superior to the potential thing which desires it. Therefore, the intellect and the soul are prior to nature. Thus, the soul is not a "breath" <note>original: "πνεῦμα" (pneuma) — a reference to the Stoic view that the soul is a physical gas or breath.</note>, nor a body. But because it was a body, it might be called both "peace" and other things clearly, and these too as a moisture. But since it is of another nature, one must seek what this is. Is it then something different from the body, yet belonging to the body, such as <term>harmony</term> <note>original: "ἁρμονία" (harmonia)</note>? You know indeed that those around Pythagoras speak of harmony in another way; I have heard that it is something like the harmony found in musical strings. For just as a certain state arises in the stretched strings, which is called harmony, in the same way, according to your view, as dissimilar things in the body are mixed together, this specific mixture produces life, and the soul is merely a state resulting from this mixture. But that this is impossible has already been stated many times against this opinion. For the soul is prior, while harmony is posterior. And while the soul rules and presides over the body, and often struggles against it, harmony, not having its own existence, could not do these things. And while the soul is an <term>essence</term> <note>original: "οὐσία" (ousia)</note>, harmony is not an essence. Furthermore, the mixture of elements from which things are composed in a certain <term>ratio</term> <note>original: "λόγῳ" (logō) — a proportion or rational principle.</note> would be "health." And since every part is clearly mixed, there would be a different soul for each part, so that there would be many souls. And most importantly, it is necessary that before this kind of "soul," there exists another soul that creates this harmony—just as with musical instruments, it is the <term>musician</term> <note>original: "μουσικός" (mousikos)</note> who, possessing the ratio, imposes it upon the strings and knows how to tune them. For neither the strings by themselves, nor bodies, will be able to lead themselves into harmony. In general, these people also make living things out of lifeless ones, and ordered things out of the disordered and unarranged, claiming they have received order and "fall" by chance. But this is possible neither in individual cases nor in others. The soul, therefore, is not a harmony.

These points are from the writings of Plotinus against the opinions of the ancients concerning the soul, those who claimed it was corporeal [physical]. But since I have sufficiently set forth the arguments against Aristotle, and those against Plato, and those against the Stoic sect as if in a summary, it is time to return and examine the marvelous <term>natural philosophies</term> <note>original: "φυσιολογίας" (physiologias) — literally "discourses on nature."</note> of all the ancient philosophers together. For they almost all commonly believed that the visible gods were the Sun, the Moon, and the other stars; and they regarded and worshipped the other parts of the world as such. And they have transferred their mythical and nonsensical narrations about the "many-wandering" ones into more solemn and "Natural" explanations involving the elements and the parts of the whole world. Therefore, it seems necessary to me to also collect the opinions concerning these things, and to look upon their relationships and their vain pride. I will set these things down from the writing of Plutarch, in which he collected the opinions of both the older and newer thinkers concerning these matters, writing in this manner:

### On the Sun.

» **Anaximander** says that the sun is a circle twenty-eight times the size of the earth. It is similar to a **chariot wheel** <note>original: "ἁρματείῳ τροχῷ" (harmateiō trochō)</note> having a hollow rim full of fire, which at a certain point shows the fire through an opening as if through the nozzle of a **bellows** <note>original: "πρηστῆρος αὐλοῦ" (prēstēros aulou) — a technical term for a blowpipe or a meteorological whirlwind-spout.</note>; and this is the sun. **Xenophanes** says it is composed of small fires that have been gathered together from moist exhalations; or that the sun is a concentration of **ignited clouds**. The **Stoics** <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that viewed the universe as a rational, material organism.</note> call it an intellectual ignition from the sea. **Plato** says it is made mostly of fire. **Anaxagoras**, **Democritus**, and **Metrodorus** say it is a <term>mass</term> <note>original: "μύδρον" (mydron) — specifically a red-hot mass of metal or stone.</note> or a red-hot stone. **Aristotle** says it is a sphere made of the **fifth body** <note>original: "πέμπτου σώματος" (pemptou sōmatos) — the aether, distinct from earth, air, fire, and water.</note>. **Philolaus the Pythagorean** says it is a glass-like disk which receives the radiance of the fire in the universe and filters the light through to us, so that in a sense there are **two suns**: the fiery one in the heavens, and the radiance that flows to us from the mirror-like disk by reflection. For if we call the latter the "sun," it is, as it were, an **image of an image**. **Empedocles** says there are two suns: one is the archetypal fire in the other hemisphere of the world, which has filled that hemisphere and always remains opposite its own reflection; the other is the **visible sun**, which is a reflection in the other hemisphere (the one filled with air mixed with heat) produced by the circularity of the earth, reflected into the **crystal-like sun** and carried around by the movement of the fiery sun. To put it briefly, the sun is a reflection of the fire surrounding the earth. **Epicurus** says it is an earthy condensation, sponge-like or perforated like a **pumice stone**, ignited by fire.

### On the Size of the Sun.

» **Anaximander** says the sun itself is equal in size to the earth, but the circle from which it breathes out and by which it is carried is twenty-eight times the size of the earth. **Anaxagoras** says it is many times larger than the **Peloponnese** <note>A large peninsula in southern Greece; this was considered a radical scientific claim in antiquity.</note>. **Heraclitus** says it is the width of a **human foot**. **Epicurus** again says that all the aforementioned views are possible; the sun is either as large as it appears to be, or slightly larger or smaller.

### On the Shape of the Sun.

» **Anaximenes** says the sun is flat, like a **leaf**. **Heraclitus** says it is bowl-shaped and slightly curved. The **Stoics** say it is spherical, like the world and the stars. **Epicurus** says all the aforementioned views are possible. Such is the nature of the sun itself, that great god of the phenomena in the heavens. But **Moses** and the Hebrew oracles do not indulge in such meddling curiosities.

### On the Moon.

» **Anaximander** says the moon is a circle nineteen times the size of the earth, similar to the sun's circle, full of fire; it suffers **eclipses** according to the turnings of the wheel. For it is like a chariot wheel with a hollow rim, full of fire, and having a single breathing-hole. **Xenophanes** says it is a **compressed cloud**. The **Stoics** say it is a mixture of fire and air. **Plato** says it is made mostly of **earthy matter**. **Anaxagoras** and **Democritus** say it is a red-hot solid, containing within itself plains, mountains, and ravines. **Heraclitus** says it is earth surrounded by mist. **Pythagoras** describes it according to its fire-like shape.

### On the Size of the Moon.

» The **Stoics** declare it to be larger than the earth, just like the sun. **Parmenides** says it is equal to the sun, for it is illuminated by it.

### On the shape of the moon.

The **Stoics** say it is spherical, like the sun. **Heraclitus** says it is **bowl-shaped** <note>original: "σκαφοειδῆ" (skaphoeidē) — resembling a hollow boat or trough.</note>. **Empedocles** says it is disk-shaped; others say it is cylindrical.

### On the illumination of the moon.

**Anaximander** says it has its own light, though it is somewhat faint. **Antiphon** says the moon shines with its own light. But another theory suggests that the moon's own light is hidden and is **eclipsed** by the impact of the sun's light, as the stronger fire naturally obscures the weaker; this is also what happens with the other stars. **Thales** and his followers say that the moon is illuminated by the sun. **Heraclitus** says the sun and moon are affected in the same way: since the stars are **bowl-shaped** in their figures, they receive the exhalations from moist vapors and are made bright to our sight—the sun being brighter because it moves in purer air, while the moon moves in air that is more turbid. For this reason, the moon appears fainter.

### What is the substance of the planets and fixed stars.

**Thales** says the stars are earthy but also consist of fire. **Empedocles** says they are fiery, made of the fiery element which the air contained within itself and squeezed out during the primary separation. **Anaxagoras** says the surrounding <term>aether</term> <note>The "upper air" or the fiery substance of the highest heavens.</note> is fiery in its substance, and that by the vigor of its rotation it snatched up **stones from the earth**, set them on fire, and so made them into stars. **Diogenes** thinks the stars are like **pumice** <note>original: "κισσηρώδη" (kissērōdē)</note> and considers them to be the breathing-holes of the cosmos. Again, the same thinker says there are invisible stones which often fall to the earth and are extinguished, just like the **stony star** that fell in a fiery state at **Aegospotami** <note>A famous meteorite fall in 467 BCE near the Hellespont, which was a major scientific event in antiquity.</note>. **Empedocles** says the **fixed stars** <note>original: "ἀπλανεῖς ἀστέρας" (aplaneis asteras) — those that do not "wander" like planets.</note> are fastened to the **crystalline sphere** <note>original: "κρυστάλλῳ" (krystallō)</note>, while the planets are free. **Plato** says they are made mostly of fire, but participate in the other elements as a kind of **glue**. **Xenophanes** says they are made of ignited clouds which are extinguished every day and rekindled at night, like **coals**; for their risings and settings are actually ignitions and extinctions. **Heraclides** and the **Pythagoreans** say that each of the stars is a **world** <note>original: "κόσμον" (kosmon)</note> containing an earth and an aether in the infinite space. These doctrines are also found in the **Orphic writings**, for they make each star into a world. **Epicurus** rejects none of these views, holding to what is possible.

### On the shape of the stars.

The **Stoics** say the stars are spherical, just like the world and the sun. **Anaxaximander** says they are fixed like **nails** <note>original: "ἥλων" (hēlōn)</note> in the crystalline sphere. Some say they are fiery plates, like **paintings**. Such are the inventions of this "wondrous" natural science regarding the gods that appear in nature. What they have also determined regarding the universe as a whole, one may learn from the same voice of **Plutarch**:

### How the world was composed.

The world, then, was formed in a curved shape according to the following concept: Since the **atoms** <note>The indivisible particles theorized by Epicurus and Democritus.</note> were infinite in number and possessed a random motion, moving continuously and very swiftly, many bodies were gathered together into the same place, and for this reason possessed a variety...

» ...their shapes and sizes. As these were gathered together in the same place, those that were larger and the heaviest of all settled toward the bottom. But those that were small, round, smooth, and slippery were squeezed out during the collision of the bodies and were carried up into the heights <note>original: "μετάρσιον" (metarsion) — the upper atmosphere or lofty regions.</note>. When the striking force that tossed them upward failed, and the impact no longer drove them toward the heights, and yet they were hindered from falling downward, they were pressed into the places capable of receiving them. These are the surrounding regions. 

» Whether we must consider the All as one or many, and whether there is one world or several; whether it is ensouled and governed by the **providence** of God, or the opposite; whether it is indestructible or perishable; from where it is carried, and from what point God began his world-making; concerning the order of the world, and the cause of its inclination; concerning the outer circumference of the world, and where its right and left sides are; concerning heaven and its substance; concerning **daemons** <note>In the Greek sense, "daemons" refers to intermediate spirits or divine beings, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense.</note> and heroes; concerning matter, and **Ideas**, and the arrangement of fire. Furthermore, concerning the course and motion of the stars, and from where the stars are illuminated; and concerning those called the **Dioscuri** <note>Castor and Pollux, associated with St. Elmo’s fire or specific constellations.</note>; concerning the eclipse of the sun and moon, and the appearance of the moon—into what form it appears—and its signs, and even concerning the years. 

All these matters have been zealously studied through countless arguments by authors such as **Plutarch**, who gathered the declarations and disagreements of them all in a few words. It would not be useless to set them out in order here to expose their self-contradictions. For if they have held contrary and discordant views among themselves, and have engaged in battles and wars, they have come away with nothing of their own; each, out of a love of strife, merely refuted the arguments of their neighbors. How then should anyone not reasonably agree that our **suspense of judgment** <term>epoche</term> <note>A technical term in Skeptical philosophy meaning the withholding of assent when arguments are equally balanced.</note> regarding these things has become secure? 

Following these things, I will next add what he investigated concerning matters closer to the earth: the shape of the earth, its position, and its inclination; and furthermore concerning the sea. This is so you may know that these babblers have not only differed regarding the high and lofty things, but they have also disagreed even regarding things on the ground. Moreover, so that you may wonder even more at the "wisdom" of these wise men, I will also add their conflicts regarding the **soul** and the **ruling faculty** <term>hegemonikon</term> <note>The commanding part of the soul, thought by various schools to reside in the heart or the brain.</note> within it, for they did not even recognize their own nature. But let us return to the first of the points mentioned.

-> Whether the All is One. <-

The **Stoics** declared that the world is one, which they also said is "the All" and consists of bodies. **Empedocles** said the world is one, yet the world is not "the All," but only a small part of the All; the rest, he says, is idle matter. **Plato** infers that the world is one from the fact that "the All" comes from a single **Idea**. He argues it would not be perfect if it did not contain all things, nor would it be like its paradigm <note>The "Pattern" or "Model" after which the world was created.</note> if it were not unique. He also argues it would not be indestructible if anything existed outside of it. 

Against **Plato**, it must be said that the world is not the "end" <note>original: "τέλος" (telos) — meaning the ultimate goal or completion.</note>. For it does not contain all things; a human being is also a "completion" in a sense, but does not contain all things. There are many paradigms, as in the case of statues, houses, and paintings. How then is it the "end" if something can be understood to exist outside of it? Furthermore, it is not indestructible, nor can it be, being a created thing. **Metrodorus** says it is as absurd for one ear of corn to be produced in a large field as it is for one world to exist in the infinite. That the worlds are infinite in number is clear from the fact that their causes are infinite. For if the world were finite, but the causes were...

„ ...they stretch a tunic and membranes around the world in a circle; the outer limit is porous. There are dense bodies,
„ and of these, some are moving while others are stationary. **Plato** places fire first, then **aether** <note>original: "αἰθέρα" — a refined, upper-atmosphere element distinct from common air.</note>, 
„ after which is air, then water, and finally earth; though sometimes he joins the aether to the fire. **Aristotle** places 
„ aether first as something impassive <note>Meaning it is not subject to change or decay like the other elements.</note>, for it is a kind of **fifth body**; after this are the passive elements: fire, 
„ air, water, and finally earth. To the celestial things among these, he assigns circular motion; but to those 
„ positioned below them, he assigns upward motion to the light elements and downward motion to the 
„ heavy ones. **Empedocles** says the elements are not standing still throughout the whole, nor are they fixed in 
„ their places, but all of them participate in one another.

### What is the cause of the world’s inclination.

<margin>4</margin>
**Diogenes** and **Anaxagoras** say that after the world was composed and had brought forth living creatures 
„ from the earth, the world somehow tilted spontaneously toward its southern part—
<margin>11</margin>
„ perhaps by **providence**, so that some parts of the world might become uninhabitable and others 
„ inhabitable, according to the principles of freezing, burning, and temperate balance <note>original: "εὐκρασίαν" (eukrasian) — a "good mixture" or temperate climate suitable for life.</note>. 
„ **Empedocles** says that as the air gave way to the rush of the sun, the Great Bear <note>The constellation Ursa Major, used here to represent the northern pole.</note> was tilted, and 
„ the northern parts were elevated while the southern parts were lowered, as was the entire world.

### Concerning the outside.

<margin>1</margin>
The followers of **Pythagoras** say there is a **void** <note>original: "κενόν" (kenon) — empty space.</note> outside the world, into which the world breathes, and 
„ out of which it breathes. The **Stoics** say there is an infinite void into which the world is dissolved 
„ during the **conflagration** <note>original: "ἐκπυρώσει" (ekpyrosei) — the Stoic belief that the universe is periodically consumed by fire and then reborn.</note>. **Posidonius** says it is not 
<margin>4</margin>
„ infinite, but only as much as is sufficient for the dissolution. In the first book *On the Void*, **Aristotle** 
„ says there is no void. **Plato** says there is no void either outside or inside the world.

### Which parts of the world are the right, and which are the left.

**Pythagoras**, **Plato**, and **Aristotle** say the eastern parts are the "right" of the world, from which 
„ the beginning of motion occurs; and the western parts are the "left." **Empedocles** says the "right" 
„ parts are those toward the summer solstice, and the "left" are those toward the winter solstice.

### Concerning heaven.

**Anaximander** says the heaven is the revolution of the outermost zone. **Empedocles** says the 
„ heaven is solid, having been composed from air frozen by fire in a crystal-like manner, 
„ containing the fiery and the airy elements in each of the hemispheres. **Aristotle** says it is made 
„ from a **fifth body**, or from a mixture of heat and cold.

### Concerning daemons and heroes.

Next to the discussion concerning the gods, we must record the history concerning **heroes**. 
„ **Thales**, **Pythagoras**, **Plato**, and the **Stoics** say that **daemons** <note>original: "δαίμονας" (daimonas) — in Greek thought, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediate spirits or divine beings between gods and humans.</note> are 
„ substances of the soul. They also say that **heroes** <note>In this context, "heroes" refer to the departed souls of exceptional humans who have attained a semi-divine status.</note> are souls separated 
„ from their bodies; the good souls are good heroes, and the base souls are bad. **Epicurus**, however, 
„ admits none of these things.

### Concerning matter.

**Matter** <note>original: "Ὕλη" (hyle) — the raw "stuff" of the universe.</note> is the substrate for birth, decay, and other changes. The followers of **Thales**, 
„ **Pythagoras**, and the **Stoics** say that matter is changeable, transformable, and fluid throughout its 
„ whole. The followers of **Democritus** say the first principles are impassive: the **atom**, the

### On the Idea.

The **Idea** is an incorporeal substance <note>In ancient philosophy, an "incorporeal substance" refers to a reality that exists without physical bulk or matter.</note>, existing by itself and according to itself. It gives 
,, form to formless matter and becomes the cause for the manifestation of these things. **Socrates** and **Plato**

### On the Order of the Stars.

**Xenocrates** thinks the stars move along a single surface. Other **Stoics** say they move in front of 
,, one another, in height and in depth. **Democritus** places the fixed stars first;

,, Fifth is "The Gleaming One" <note>original: "στίλβοντα" (stilbonta) — Mercury</note>. Sixth is the Sun, and seventh is the Moon. Some of

### On the Carriage and Motion of the Stars.

**Anaxagoras**, **Democritus**, and **Cleanthes** say all the stars move from the east to the

,, for they are carried back from west to east. **Anaximander** says the stars are

### From Where the Stars are Lit.

**Metrodorus** says all the fixed stars are illuminated by the Sun. **Heraclitus**

,, believes the whole cosmos is a single living thing, and the stars are nourished from it.

### On the eclipse of the moon.

**Anaximander** says it is caused by the mouth [of the vessel] around the wheel being blocked. **Berosus** <note>A Babylonian priest and astronomer who introduced Chaldean astrology to the Greeks.</note> says it is

» essence, its composition is not pure.

<page-num>497</page-num>
<header>PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL Book 15. 497</header>

That by these means the wisest Socrates showed that those who boasted greatly about the aforementioned <term>study of nature</term> <note>original: "φυσιολογία" (physiologia) — in this context, it refers to the study of the physical universe and "science" rather than modern biology.</note> were acting foolishly, as they were wasting their time on things useless to life and impossible to comprehend.

<margin>”</margin>No one ever saw Socrates doing anything impious or unholy, nor heard him saying anything of the
<margin>”</margin>sort. For he did not discuss the nature of all things, nor other such matters as most philosophers do,
<margin>”</margin>investigating how the <term>cosmos</term> <note>original: "κόσμος" — the ordered universe.</note>, as the Sophists call it, is arranged, or by what necessary laws
<margin>”</margin>each of the heavenly bodies comes to be. On the contrary, he showed that those who troubled
<margin>”</margin>their minds with such things were acting foolishly. First, he would ask them whether they
<margin>”</margin>thought they already knew enough about human affairs before they moved on to worry
<margin>”</margin>about such things, or whether they thought they were doing the right thing by neglecting
<margin>”</margin>human matters to investigate <term>divine matters</term> <note>original: "δαιμόνια" (daimonia) — here referring to celestial or supernatural phenomena.</note>. He marveled that it was not
<margin>”</margin>obvious to them that it is impossible for humans to find these things out. For even those who
<margin>”</margin>prided themselves most on speaking about these matters did not hold the same opinions as
<margin>”</margin>one another, but were instead disposed toward each other like madmen. For among the
<margin>”</margin>insane, some do not even fear what is truly terrifying, while others fear things that are not
<margin>”</margin>frightening at all. Some think it is not shameful to say or do anything even in a crowd,
<margin>”</margin>while others think they should not even go out among people. Some honor no temple,
<margin>”</margin>altar, nor anything else divine, while others worship even stones, chance pieces of wood,
<margin>”</margin>and wild beasts. So too among those who worry about the nature of all things: to some it seems
<margin>”</margin>that <term>Being</term> <note>original: "τὸ ὂν" (to on) — ultimate reality or existence.</note> is only one thing, while to others it is infinite in number. To some, everything is
<margin>”</margin>always in motion; to others, nothing could ever be moved. To some, everything is constantly
<margin>”</margin>coming into being and perishing; to others, nothing could ever be born or die. He also
<margin>”</margin>considered this regarding them: just as those who learn human crafts think they can
<margin>”</margin>apply what they have learned for themselves and for anyone else they wish, do those who
<margin>”</margin>search for divine things think that, once they know the laws by which everything happens,
<margin>”</margin>they will be able to produce winds, waters, seasons, and whatever else of this sort they might
<margin>”</margin>need whenever they want? Or do they not even hope for such a thing, but are satisfied
<margin>”</margin>simply to know how each of these things comes to be? This is what he used to say about those
<margin>”</margin>who busied themselves with such matters. But he himself always discussed human affairs,
<margin>”</margin>considering: what is pious? what is impious? what is beautiful? what is shameful? what is just? what is
<margin>”</margin>unjust? what is <term>temperance</term>? <note>original: "σωφροσύνη" (sophrosyne) — self-control or soundness of mind.</note> what is madness?

These things, then, were the concerns of Socrates. After him, the followers of **Aristippus of Cyrene** <note>Aristippus was a pupil of Socrates and founder of the Cyrenaic school, which focused on ethics and pleasure.</note> spoke similarly, and later the followers of **Aristo of Chios** <note>A Stoic philosopher who argued that only ethics was worth studying.</note> attempted to say that one should only study <term>ethics</term> <note>original: "ἠθικά" (ethika).</note>. For they argued these matters are possible and useful, whereas arguments about nature are the opposite: they are neither comprehensible, nor—if they could be understood—would they be of any benefit. For we would gain nothing, not even if we were seen to be higher than our own nature, and could see with our own eyes over the "flow of the sea" or the "vault of heaven," observing the entire cosmos and the nature of all things, whatever it may be. For we would not be any wiser, or more just, or more courageous, or more temperate because of it. Furthermore, we would not be strong, or beautiful, or wealthy—things without which it is impossible to be happy. Hence Socrates rightly said that among the things that exist, some are "above us," while others are "nothing to us." For physical things are "above us," and things that fall under death are "nothing to us," and only human affairs "concern us." For this reason, he is said to have "bid farewell" to the natural philosophies of **Anaxagoras** and **Archelaus** <note>Anaxagoras and Archelaus were early scientists; Archelaus was reportedly a teacher of Socrates before Socrates turned to ethics.</note>, because...

<summary>Eusebius uses the testimony of Socrates (via Xenophon) to argue that investigating the physical laws of the universe is futile and leads to madness. Instead, he claims that philosophy should focus exclusively on human ethics and morality, which are within human reach and benefit the soul.</summary>

# EUSEBIUS

good and evil have been fashioned in strife. Indeed, regarding their theories on nature, they are clearly not only difficult and impossible to grasp, but also impious and contrary to the laws. For some claim there are no gods at all, while others say the divine is everything: the <term>Infinite</term>, or <term>Being</term>, or <term>The One</term>. They argue for these concepts more than for the traditional gods. Furthermore, their disagreement is immense. Some declare that the universe is infinite; others, that it is finite. Some claim that everything is in constant motion; others, that nothing moves at all. To me, it seems that <term>Timon of Phlius</term> <note>Timon (c. 320–230 BC) was a Skeptic philosopher known for his "Silloi," or lampoons, which mocked the self-importance and contradictions of other philosophers.</note> spoke best about these very things in his *Silloi* <note>Satirical poems.</note> when he wrote:

> "Who then brought these two together in destructive strife to fight?
> "A crowd of echoing noise; for he, angered by their silence,
> "Sent a foul disease upon the men, and many perished."

Do you see how these noble thinkers already mock one another? Indeed, their rivalry with each other, their battles, and their divisions are described by the aforementioned man in this manner, in addition to what has already been said:

> "Man-destroying Strife wanders about, shouting emptily,
> "The sister of man-slaying Quarrel and Discord;
> "She who is small at first, but then 
> "Fixes her head in the sky and walks upon the earth." <note>This is a parody of Homer’s description of Eris (Strife) in the *Iliad*.</note>

But now, since their self-evident discord and battle has been demonstrated—a conflict that does not concern us—and since the clear and unknowable "education" and "learning" of everyone else (in which the children of the philosophers still take pride) have been refuted not by our arguments but by their own; and since the reason has been made plain why we have turned away from those things and preferred the <term>Hebrew oracles</term> <note>original: "τὰ Ἑβραίων λόγια" (ta Hebraiōn logia) — referring to the Old Testament scriptures.</note>, let our "Preparation for the Gospel" be concluded at this point. 

We must hereafter investigate the more complete treatment concerning the "Proof of the Gospel" <note>Eusebius is referring to his next major work, the *Demonstratio Evangelica*.</note>, beginning from a different starting point in our discourse, as is required by the subject we have set out to teach. It remains, then, to answer those of the <term>Circumcision</term> <note>A common early Christian term for Jewish critics.</note> who complain against us, asking why we—who are foreigners and of another tongue—use their books which (as they would say) do not belong to us, or why we embrace their oracles but do not lead a life consistent with their Law.

->The End.<-

# THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 1.
Aa.iii.
<meta>catchword: resurrection</meta>

> He <note>Referring to Moses as the lawgiver.</note> laid out the laws mentioned above in this manner: "If a soul <note>original: 'ψυχὴ' (psychē); in this context, it refers to a person or individual agent.</note> is overtaken by forgetfulness and sins unintentionally against the holy things of the Lord, they shall bring a ram as their guilt offering to the Lord." And again, he specifies this is to be done through the high priest in the chosen "type" <note>original: 'τύπῳ' (typō). Eusebius often uses 'type' to describe the physical Temple and its rituals as a symbolic foreshadowing of spiritual realities.</note>. And from there he adds a law to these, saying: "If a soul sins and does one thing from all the commandments which ought not to be done, even if he did not know it, and he is guilty and bears his sin, he shall again bring a ram to the high priest; and the priest shall make atonement for him concerning his ignorance which he committed unknowingly, and it shall be forgiven him." And he mentions a seventh case: "If a soul sins and utterly disregards the commandments of the Lord, and lies to his neighbor concerning a deposit, or concerning a partnership, or robbery, or if he has wronged his neighbor in some way, or has found something lost and lies about it, and swears falsely concerning any one of all the things a person might do so as to sin in these—whenever he sins and is guilty, he shall restore the thing he robbed, or the wrong he committed, or the deposit which was entrusted to him, or the lost thing he found, or anything about which he swore falsely; he shall restore the principal and add one-fifth to it."

It was necessary for him, after confessing the sin and holding nothing back, to hasten once more to come from far away to the "type" <note>The Temple in Jerusalem.</note> where God is sought, and to offer an unblemished ram for his guilt. And the priest shall make atonement for him before the Lord, and it shall be forgiven him. These things, and many more, the marvelous Moses defined precisely regarding those who sin unintentionally or through ignorance, showing that even errors of will were not excused without penalty, thereby restraining his own people through these unavoidable punishments. For if he did not grant pardon for unintentional sins until the sin was confessed and then exacted a small penalty through the prescribed sacrifice—enforcing both a diligent journey to the <term>holy place<gloss>The Temple at Jerusalem, the only authorized site for sacrifice under Mosaic Law.</gloss></term> and a commitment to harmlessness for those choosing to live godly lives—how much more would he have restrained the impulses toward willful acts? How then should we conclude these matters, when

> as has been said, Moses summarizes everything by giving a solemn charge, saying: "Cursed is everyone who does not abide in all the things written in the law, to do them." <note>Quoting Deuteronomy 27:26.</note>

Is it then necessary for those from the ends of the earth <note>The Gentiles/non-Jewish nations.</note> who have turned to godliness from idolatry to do all these things in order to escape the curse and obtain the blessing promised to Abraham? Must they travel three times a year to Jerusalem? And must women from all the nations, chosen for their godliness, when they have finished with childbirth and labor pains, undertake such a long journey so that they might offer the sacrifice commanded by Moses for every child born? Or should those who have touched a dead body, or those who have sworn a false oath, or those who have done something unintentionally, come from the ends of the earth, running and hastening to the purification prescribed by the law, so as to escape the curse that was threatened? But it is clear that even for those dwelling around Jerusalem and spending their lives in Judea alone, the life according to Moses was difficult to achieve; how much more impossible would it be for the rest of the nations? Therefore, reasonably, our Savior and Lord, the Son of God, after his resurrection from the

> dead, said to his disciples: "Go and make disciples of all the nations," <note>Quoting the 'Great Commission' from Matthew 28:19.</note>

<summary>Eusebius argues that the Mosaic Law's requirements for sacrifice and purification were geographically restricted to Jerusalem, making them impossible for the global Gentile population to follow. He concludes that Christ's "Great Commission" provides a new, accessible path to godliness for all nations.</summary>

<keywords>Mosaic Law, Jerusalem Temple, Guilt Offering, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Gentiles, Great Commission, Eusebius of Caesarea, Atonement, Universalism</keywords>

# EUSEBIUS

<margin>
Eusebius, 
*Preparation 
for the 
Gospel* 
<note>While the margin reads *Praeparatio Evangelica*, the text itself is from Eusebius's companion work, *Demonstratio Evangelica* (The Proof of the Gospel), Book 1, Chapter 3.</note>
</margin>

,, ...you, and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, and the Levite within your cities, and the
,, proselyte and the orphan, and the widow among you, in the place which
,, the Lord your God shall choose for His name to be called upon there; and the third
,, feast you shall perform in that same place. Listen: you shall keep the Feast of Tabernacles <note>original: 'ἑορτὴν τῶν σκηνῶν' (heortēn tōn skēnōn); also known as Sukkot, a harvest festival.</note> for
,, seven days, when you gather in from your threshing floor and from your winepress, and you
,, shall rejoice in your feast—you, and your son, and your daughter, your male servant, and your female
,, servant, and the widow—in the place which the Lord your God chooses for Himself.

By so many means, then, He marks out the "place," and having said so many times that the whole multitude must meet there, how was it not ill-suited for those living even a short distance from Judea, let alone for the nations across the whole inhabited world? <note>original: 'οἰκουμένης' (oikoumenēs); the Greek term for the civilized or known world.</note> Furthermore, He granted no pardon to those who transgressed what was defined, but brings a curse upon those who do not observe all things, saying in these very words:
,, "Cursed is he who does not abide by all that is
,, written in the book of the Law to do them."

Consider again the things that are impossible for all men through the legislation of Moses. Distinguishing voluntary sins and defining for each a punishment worthy of the greatest penalty, he also sets down laws by which he restores those who have committed unintentional offenses in another manner.
,, One of these laws is as follows: "If a single soul <note>original: 'ψυχὴ μία' (psychē mia); meaning an individual person.</note> sins unintentionally from the people of the land, in
,, doing one of all the commandments of the Lord which ought not to be done, and he commits an offense, and
,, the sin which he committed is made known to him, then he shall bring as his gift a goat, a female kid without
,, blemish, for the sin which he committed, to the place where the
,, burnt offerings are slaughtered; and there the priest shall take some of the blood."

And see how here again, through this judgment, he specifies the "place" where one must meet, where the burnt offerings are slaughtered. These things were already indicated several times before, saying, "the place which the Lord your God shall choose." The lawgiver himself, seeing that this was not possible to be performed by all men upon the earth, noted it accurately, not introducing the law indefinitely for everyone, but saying, "If a soul sins unintentionally *from the people of the land.*" <note>Eusebius argues that "the land" specifically refers to the Land of Israel, not the entire Earth.</note>

Furthermore, he sets down a second law which goes like this: "If a soul hears the voice of an oath, and he is a witness—having either seen it or known of it—if he does not report it, he shall bear the sin." What then must this person do, other than take the sacrificial animal in his hands and hasten to the purifications? Where again? Where else but in the place where they slaughter the burnt offerings?

And again, "A soul," he says, "whoever touches any unclean thing, whether the carcasses of unclean cattle, and it is hidden from him, and he himself is defiled and commits an offense; or from the uncleanness of a man—from any uncleanness of his by which he may be defiled by touching—and it was hidden from him, but afterward he knows it and commits an offense."

What then was it fitting for the defiled person to do, except to meet again in the "place" and offer for the sin which he committed a female from the sheep, either a lamb or a kid of the goats, for the sin? The same law also applies to a soul who swears, distinguishing with his lips to do evil or to do good, according to everything a man might distinguish with an oath, and it is hidden from him, and afterward he recognizes the sin in any of these things and confesses the sin he committed: "It is then required," he says, "that the same man, having taken a sacrificial animal, shall hasten to the place, and the priest shall make atonement for him regarding his sin, and the sin shall be forgiven him." And he makes it clear...
