### THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 1

» He set out the laws mentioned in this manner: “If a person acts unawares, and sins unintentionally against the holy things of the Lord, he shall bring a ram for his trespass to the Lord.” <note>Original: *plemmeleia* (πλημμελείᾳ) – a religious offense or error requiring restitution.</note> And again, this occurs in the presence of the High Priest in the chosen place. And from the types of the Law he adds, saying: “If a person sins, and does one of all the commands which ought not to be done, and did not know it, and yet commits a trespass and bears his sin, he shall again bring a ram to the High Priest, and the priest shall make atonement for him concerning the ignorance which he committed in ignorance while not knowing, and it shall be forgiven him.” And he mentions a seventh case: “If a person sins, and utterly disregards the commands of the Lord, and lies to his neighbor regarding a deposit, or concerning a partnership or robbery, or has wronged his neighbor in some way, or found a lost thing and lies about it, and swears falsely concerning any one of all the things a person might do so as to sin in these matters; then it shall be, if he sins and commits a trespass, he shall restore the robbery which he robbed, or the wrong which he did, or the deposit which was entrusted to him, or the lost thing which he found, from every matter about which he swore falsely, and he shall repay the principal and the fifth part besides.” Furthermore, after confessing the sin and after making restitution, he must hasten from afar to the place which God shall choose, and offer an unblemished ram for his trespass. And the priest shall make atonement for him before the Lord, and it shall be forgiven him.

The marvelous Moses was precise in these matters, both regarding those who sinned unintentionally and those who sinned through ignorance, showing from afar the trespass committed against the choices <note>Original: *hairesin* (αἵρεσιν) – often used for "sects" or "choices," here referring to the legal categories of sin.</note>, in which he distinguishes his own people by inexorable punishments. For if he did not grant forgiveness for unintentional acts until the sin was confessed, and then exacted from the sinner a small penalty through the prescribed sacrifice—increasing both the diligence and the harmlessness of those who chose to live piously by requiring a journey to the holy place—how could he not have much earlier checked the impulses of those acting voluntarily? What, then, must be concluded from this, when, as has been said, Moses sums up everything by enjoining: “Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all the things written in the Law, to do them.” <note>Quoting Deuteronomy 27:26, a pivotal verse in early Christian arguments regarding the limitations of the Law.</note>

For is it truly necessary for those from the ends of the earth who intend to live piously according to Moses <note>The text reads *mousa*, a likely scribal error for *Mosea* (Moses).</note>—so that they might flee the curse and obtain the promised blessing to Abraham—is it necessary for them to prefer all these things and strive to meet in Jerusalem throughout the year? And should women chosen from all the nations to live piously, having just ceased from childbirth and labor pains, 
<margin>4</margin> undertake such a long journey to bring the sacrifice prescribed by Moses for each occurrence? Or should those who have touched a dead body, or those who have sworn a false oath, or those who have done something unintentionally, come from the ends of the earth, running and hastening to the legislated purification, so that they might escape the visitation of the curse? 

But you see how, if the life according to Moses was difficult to achieve even for those living around Jerusalem and spending their lives in Judea alone, it was certainly not possible to be fulfilled by the rest of the nations. For this reason, quite rightly, our Savior and Lord, the Son of God, after his resurrection from the dead said to his disciples: “Go and make disciples of all the nations...”

# EUSEBIUS #

» ...complete, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you. <note>Original: *panta hosa eneteilamēn hymin* (πάντα ὅσα ἐνετειλάμην ὑμῖν) — a reference to the Great Commission in Matthew 28:20.</note> For he did not command them to teach all the nations the legal requirements of Moses, but rather those things which he himself had commanded. These would be the teachings contained in his Gospels. It is with good reason, then, that his disciples and apostles, in their deliberation concerning the Gentiles, confessed that they could not apply the Mosaic customs to the nations, since these laws had proven difficult to fulfill even for themselves and for their fathers. Indeed, Peter says in the *Acts of the Apostles*: "Now therefore, why do you tempt God by putting a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?" <note>Acts 15:10.</note> It is likely that Moses himself, for these very reasons, said that another prophet would arise after him, and he declared that this person would be a lawgiver for all the nations. He was hinting at the Christ, and he made this clear to his own people in these very words, prophesying in this manner: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him in everything he says to you. And it shall be that every soul that does not listen to that prophet shall be utterly destroyed from among her people." <note>Deuteronomy 18:15–19.</note> Regarding this prophet—clearly the Christ—who was to come from the Jews, he proclaims again that he would gain mastery over the nations, saying: "How beautiful are your houses, O Jacob, and your tents, O Israel! Like shaded valleys, and like gardens by the rivers, like tents which the Lord has pitched. A man shall come forth from his seed, and he shall rule over many nations, and his kingdom shall be exalted." <note>Numbers 24:5–7.</note> Furthermore, from which tribe would he come, since there are twelve tribes of the Hebrews? He shows that the Christ, the expected lawgiver of the nations, would come from the tribe of Judah. And at what time? He indicates that it would not be before the eclipse of the ancestral succession of the rulers of the Jewish nation, saying: "A ruler shall not depart from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until the things stored up for him come; and he is the expectation of the nations." <note>Genesis 49:10.</note> And what is this "expectation of the nations" other than the promise made to Abraham, that in him all the nations of the earth would be blessed? It is clear, therefore, that Moses himself accurately understood that the legislation he ordained for his own people was too weak to be applied to all the nations. For the fulfillment of the oracles given to Abraham, there was a need for another prophet, who was foretold to come from the tribe of Judah and to rule over many nations.

-> ΕΥΣΕΒΙΟΥ <-

...lessons and teachings of the covenant? Since some of these things have been demonstrated to be so, it is now time to see the character of the New Covenant, and of the previously heralded "new song" and law.

### What is the nature of Christ’s New Covenant.

The Old Covenant and the law given through Moses have been shown to be appropriate only for the Jewish nation, and specifically for that nation while living in its own land. It was not suitable for the other nations throughout the inhabited world, nor even for those Jews who had settled in foreign lands. However, the character of the New Covenant had to be established as something beneficial for the lives of all nations, so that those intending to live according to its principles would be hindered in no way and from no place—neither by their country, nor their race, nor their location, nor any other bond. Such is the nature of the law and the way of life established by our Savior Jesus Christ; it renews the oldest and most ancient form of piety <note>Original: *eusebeia* (εὐσέβεια) — a term for religious devotion or godliness.</note> from before the time of Moses, the very way of life in which the God-beloved Abraham and his ancestors are shown to have lived. Indeed, if you were to compare the Christian life—which Christ established as a form of godliness for all nations—with the way of life of Abraham and those who were testified to for their piety and righteousness, you would find them to be one and the same. For they too, turning away from the error of many gods and rejecting the superstition surrounding idols, looked beyond the whole visible creation. They did not make gods of the sun, the moon, or any parts of the universe; instead, they raised their minds to the one supreme God, the Most High himself, the creator of heaven and earth. Moses himself confirms this in his ancient histories, recording that Abraham said:

> » "I will stretch out my hand to the Most High God, who created heaven and earth." <note>Genesis 14:22.</note> 
> » And introducing Melchizedek, whom he says was a priest of the Most High God, he shows him 
> » blessing Abraham in this way: "Blessed be Abraham by the Most High God, who created 
> » heaven and earth." <note>Genesis 14:19.</note> Others too, like Enoch and Noah, were justified and 
> » well-pleasing to God in the same manner as Abraham. But also Job, a man who was 
> » righteous, true, blameless, godly, and abstaining from every evil deed, is testified to 
> » before the times of Moses. Having undergone a trial of his piety toward the God of 
> » all through the loss of his possessions, let him be a great example of piety 
> » for those who came after him, having uttered that philosophical word: 
> » "Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall depart. The Lord gave, 
> » the Lord took away. As it seemed good to the Lord, so it happened. Blessed be the 
> » name of the Lord." <note>Job 1:21.</note> And worshipping the Lord of all things, he let out 
> » these cries, which he clarifies further on, saying: "For he is wise in mind, 
> » mighty and great, he who shakes the earth under heaven from its foundations, 
> » and its pillars tremble; who speaks to the sun and it does not rise, and seals 
> » up the stars; who alone stretched out the heaven." <note>Job 9:4-8.</note> If indeed

the word of Christ has likewise commanded all nations to worship only as those men did, it follows that we shall become sharers in their very piety. And by sharing in that piety...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius's argument from the previous page, where he established that the Christian way of life is not a new invention, but a restoration of the ancient piety practiced by the Patriarchs. Here, he focuses on how the "Word of God" (the pre-incarnate Christ) appeared to figures like Jacob and Job.</meta>

-> PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 1 <-

It is clear, then, that we too shall partake in the blessing. We have testified that the Word of God—whom we are pleased to call "Christ"—appeared to them in the same way he does to us. Indeed, they were deemed worthy of his manifest presence and "theophany" <note>original: *theophaneia* (θεοφάνεια) — a visible manifestation of a deity to humankind.</note> in a far more excellent manner. Listen, then, to how Moses again describes the one who appeared to those beloved by God; the one who often spoke to them and who is recorded sometimes as "God" and "Lord," and at other times as the "Angel of God." He is addressed as "God" and "Lord" when speaking to men beloved by God, but as the "Angel" of the Most High Father. He says, in these very words: <margin>"</margin> "Jacob went toward Haran, and he came to a certain place and stayed there for the night, because the sun had set. He took <margin>"</margin> one of the stones of the place and put it under his head and lay down in that place to sleep. <margin>"</margin> And he dreamed, and behold, there was a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to <margin>"</margin> heaven; and behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it. And the Lord <margin>"</margin> stood above it and said, 'I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac; <margin>"</margin> do not be afraid. The land on which you lie I will give to you and to your offspring, and <margin>"</margin> your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth.'" Following these promises, "Jacob rose early in the <margin>"</margin> morning, and he took the stone that he had put under his head and set it up for a pillar." Then, concerning <margin>"</margin> this very God and Lord who appeared to him, he says that he is also named an "Angel." At least, Jacob says: <margin>"</margin> "The angel of God said to me in a dream, 'Jacob,' and I said, 'Here I am!' And he said," <margin>"</margin> and so on, "'I have seen all that Laban is doing to you. I am the God who appeared to you in the <margin>"</margin> place of God <note>original: *topos theou* (τόπος θεοῦ) — translating the Hebrew place-name "Bethel."</note> where you anointed a pillar for me and made a vow to me.'" This is the same one who also appeared to Abraham; he is addressed as God and Lord, initiating those beloved by God into the mysteries <note>original: *mystagogōn* (μυσταγωγῶν) — acting as a guide through sacred mysteries.</note> regarding the Father’s sovereign authority, and teaching some things as if concerning "another God." We shall examine these things in due course.

But also in the book of Job, the one who spoke to him after his sufficient testing is no less called "God." At first, appearing to him through a whirlwind and clouds, he presented himself as being God in his entirety. As he continues, he reveals himself further, so that Job says: <margin>"</margin> "Hear me, O Lord, that I also may speak. I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear <margin>"</margin> before, but now my eye has seen you." If it was not possible for the "God beyond"—the invisible, unbegotten, and universal King of all—to be seen by a mortal nature, who could this manifested one be, except the Word of God, who is rightly called "Lord" by us after the Father? And why is it necessary to gather more evidence on this, when it is possible to take these proofs directly from the sacred books? For we shall immediately select from the subject at hand various passages to prove that it was none other than the Word of God who was seen by the God-beloved forefathers. Therefore, after the concept of the Creator of all things, the teachings concerning Christ have been handed down to us and to them in common. From this, even those God-beloved men before the time of Moses might worthily be called "Christs" <note>original: *christous* (χριστοὺς) — meaning "anointed ones."</note> just as we are called "Christians." Listen to how the Word speaks <margin>"</margin> about them in the Psalms, where they are described as "few in number, very few, and <margin>"</margin> strangers in the land, wandering from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people. <margin>"</margin> He allowed no one to oppress them; he rebuked kings on their account, saying, <margin>"</margin> 'Do not touch my anointed ones <note>original: *christōn* (χριστῶν) — "my Christs."</note>, and do my prophets no harm.'" These words refer to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, as the whole context of the passage demonstrates. Thus, they shared with us even the very name of "Christ."

### What the life proclaimed by Christ to all people according to the New 
### Testament consists of.

But also the life of virtue, and the conduct according to piety—as it has been preached to all the nations through the instruction of Christ, apart from the Mosaic ordinance—was the very same mode of piety successfully practiced by those ancients. They, therefore, did not care for physical circumcision, just as we do not; nor for abstaining from eating certain animals, just as we do not. For instance, Moses introduces Melchizedek <note>A mysterious king and priest mentioned in Genesis 14 who blessed Abraham; Christians view him as a "type" or foreshadowing of Christ.</note> as a "priest of the Most High God," though he was not physically circumcised, nor was he anointed with prepared oil according to the Mosaic fashion. He knew nothing of a Sabbath day, nor was he at all obedient to any of the commands later given to the whole Jewish nation through Moses. Instead, he lived directly according to the Gospel of Christ. Nevertheless, Moses says he was a priest of the Most High God and greater than Abraham; indeed, he is introduced as the one who blessed Abraham. Such a man also was Noah: a righteous man in his generation, whom the God of the universe preserved to keep alive the seed of the human race during the destruction of the flood when all others on earth were perishing. He knew nothing of Jewish customs, neither regarding physical circumcision nor the other things ordained by Moses; yet he is proclaimed a righteous man. And before him was Enoch, who is said to have "pleased God" and to have been "translated so that he was not found." <note>A reference to Genesis 5:24; Enoch was taken by God without dying.</note> This man was of the same character as those who came before him: neither circumcised in body nor living under the Mosaic legislation. Instead, he clearly lived in a Christian rather than a Jewish manner <note>original: "χριστιανικῶς ἀλλ' οὐχ ἰουδαϊκῶς" (*christianikōs all’ ouch ioudaïkōs*)</note>. Even Abraham himself did not live according to those later regulations. From an earlier time before the Law, though he was an old man in years, he first underwent the circumcision of the body as a kind of seal for the sake of those who would later be born from him, passing on this sign to be carried by his physical descendants as a mark of their succession. But before he had children and before his circumcision, from the moment he withdrew from the idols, he was the first to demonstrate the theology of the one God of the universe, proving by his virtuous life alone that he lived in a Christian rather than a Jewish manner. Indeed, testimony is given that he kept the charges, commandments, requirements, and laws of God long before the Mosaic ordinance. For the God who spoke to him says to

He uses biblical citations to prove that the Mosaic Covenant at Horeb was a specific, later arrangement not imposed on the ancient ancestors.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument that the lifestyle of the ancient patriarchs was essentially Christian. He is now demonstrating that the "Covenant" mentioned in the Hebrew scriptures as being given to the ancestors was not the Mosaic Law, but a more ancient, spiritual "Gospel" way of life that preceded the Jewish nation.</meta>

-> PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 1 <-

<page-num>11</page-num>

He did not say that a Covenant <note>original: "Διαθήκην" (Diathēkē). While often translated as 'Testament,' Eusebius uses it here to mean a formal agreement or way of life ordained by God.</note> had not been given to their fathers at all—for that would be a false statement. Indeed, a Covenant was given to Abraham and to Isaac, as the sacred records testify. For this reason, Moses added a qualification: he says that "not *this* [specific Mosaic] covenant" was given to their fathers, hinting instead at another one, a better and distinct one, through which they were shown to be beloved of God. For instance, Abraham is witnessed to have achieved the goal of righteousness through his faith in the God of the universe. Moses himself says: "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." <note>Genesis 15:6. This is a central proof-text for Eusebius to show that "righteousness" existed before the Law of Moses.</note> The text clearly demonstrates that it was *after* he achieved righteousness, and *after* the testimony of his piety, that he received the sign of circumcision; thus, these external rituals contributed nothing to his justification in the eyes of God. 

Consider then Joseph, who lived long before the Mosaic era in the Egyptian palaces; he observed the unwritten laws of virtue, but did not live according to the Jewish customs. If you wish, consider even the leader and lawgiver of the Jewish nation himself, Moses. You will find that from his earliest infancy he spent his time with the daughter of the king of Egypt, participating in Egyptian customs as well as his own ancestral traditions. 

And what need is there to speak of the thrice-blessed Job? He was a true man, blameless, righteous, and God-fearing. Who could worthily describe the height of his piety and his righteous actions? Was it achieved by keeping the Mosaic law? Certainly not through the observation of the Sabbath day, or any other Jewish religious regulation. How could it be, since he is acknowledged to be older in time than Moses and his legislation? For while Moses is reckoned as the seventh in generation from Abraham, Job is the fifth—older than the generation of Moses by two generations.

Observe, then, the life of this man: it involved nothing of the Mosaic legislation, yet it was not foreign to our own **Gospel Teaching**. Tell me, does he not recount his own life in his defense to his companions, saying: 
» "For I rescued the poor from the hand of the tyrant, and I helped the orphan who had no helper. 
» The mouth of the widow blessed me, and I had put on righteousness. 
» I clothed myself in judgment like a double-cloak; I was an eye to the blind, 
» and a foot to the lame; I was a father to the weak." 

These very things are, quite simply, the lessons preached to all of us through the **Gospel Teaching**. Furthermore, as one who knew well that it is necessary to "weep with those who weep"—for indeed, "blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh," and "if one member suffers, all members suffer with it" <note>Eusebius is quoting Job 30:25 but framing it through New Testament concepts from Romans 12, Luke 6, and 1 Corinthians 12.</note>—he displayed a love for humanity <term>philanthropia: a love for mankind that mirrors God's own kindness</term> toward those suffering in life, saying: 
» "I wept over every weak person, and I groaned seeing a man in distress." 

Then again, since the **Gospel Teaching** forbids taking pleasure in shameful things, the blessed man says: 
» "If I have walked with mockers, or if my foot has hurried toward deceit... for I have stood in a just balance, 
» and the Lord knows my innocence." 

Furthermore, while the common law for everyone commands, "You shall not commit adultery," and decrees death for adulterers, the law of the **Gospel Teaching** intensifies this, saying: "It was said to the ancients, 'You shall not commit adultery,' but I say to you, do not even desire it in the first place." Consider carefully the man we are discussing [Job], who lived before the Gospel of Christ, and yet guarded himself against looking with unrestrained desire, boasting of this by saying: 
» "If my heart has followed my eye for the wife of another man..." 
And he gives the reason, adding: 
» "For it is a fire of wrath..."

He uses Job's moral conduct as proof that the Christian way of life is actually the original, ancient religion of the patriarchs.</summary>

### PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 1 ###

<page-num>13</page-num>

-> PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 1 <-

After the death of those God-loving ancestors, the people were led away by Egyptian customs into a polytheistic <note>original: "πολύθεον." The belief in many gods.</note> superstition, as I mentioned. They fell away so far that they seemed no different from the Egyptians, becoming identical to them in everything—both in the error of idols and in their other practices. Quite rightly, Moses—pulling them up as if from a depth of evils—turned them away from godless polytheism and led them back to the God who is the Creator of all. He set before them this first step of piety as an introduction, preparing them for more perfect things. 

Then he wrote laws—prohibiting murder, adultery, theft, and false witness—and commanded that they should not be driven by other mad desires, such as having sexual relations with mothers, sisters, or daughters. He recorded these laws without fear, even though such things were then commonly practiced by those outside. Taking them from a wild and beast-like life, he established for the first time on earth a more rational and law-abiding way of life through written scripture, which at that time was not yet revealed to all men, nor even fully to the race of the Jews.

Furthermore, as if speaking to the disobedient, he forbade idolatry and urged them to worship the one God over all with sacrifices and other <term>bodily rituals</term> <note>original: "σωματικωτέροις." This refers to physical, outward religious acts like animal sacrifice, which Eusebius views as a lower or "introductory" form of worship compared to the "spiritual" worship of the Gospel.</note>. He legislated that they perform their religion according to certain secret symbols. In his divine spirit, he wonderfully perceived that this system should not be practiced forever; therefore, he restricted it to one single place, fearing that his laws might be carried out in disorder unless they were confined to one location. 

For this reason, the Temple in Jerusalem became the center of this system, so that even to this day it is not permitted for any of the Hebrews to perform his laws in a foreign land. According to the Law, they cannot offer sacrifices, build an altar, anoint priests or kings, celebrate the festivals and feasts of Moses, perform purifications for defilement, wash away transgressions, offer gifts to God, or carry out any of the priestly duties mandated in the laws. Because of this, they are rightly subject to the curse of Moses, as they try to keep part of the law while neglecting the whole of what was decreed. Indeed, Moses explicitly declared: 

> » Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all the things written in the Law, to perform them. <note>original: "ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς ὃς οὐκ ἐμμένει ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἐγγεγραμμένοις τῷ νόμῳ, τῷ ποιῆσαι αὐτά." A quotation of Deuteronomy 27:26, also cited in Galatians 3:10.</note>

They fell into this situation because Moses had foreseen through the divine Spirit that when the <term>New Covenant</term> <note>original: "καινῆς διαθήκης." This can be translated as New Testament or New Covenant.</note> through Christ was renewed and proclaimed to all nations, his own legislation would become redundant. He intentionally restricted it to one place so that, if they were ever deprived of it and shut out from their own ancestral land, it would no longer be permitted for them to perform his laws in a foreign country. Thus, by necessity, they would have to accept the second covenant proclaimed through Christ. 

Exactly as Moses predicted, at the very time Christ dwelt among us and the teaching of the New Covenant was being offered to the nations, the Romans immediately captured the city in a siege and destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple. Instantly, the entire Mosaic arrangement was dissolved. The things of the Old Covenant were taken away, and the curse pursued those who unlawfully tried to practice the things of Moses out of season, forcing themselves into them. At the same time, the laws of the new and perfected teaching became beneficial. 

For this reason, the Savior and Lord rightly spoke to those who thought God must be worshipped only in Jerusalem, or on certain mountains or designated places: 

> » The hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshippers will worship neither on this mountain, nor in the ancestral Jerusalem. For God is Spirit... <note>original: "ἔρχεται ὥρα... ὅτε οἱ ἀληθινοὶ προσκυνηταὶ προσκυνήσουσιν οὔτε ἐν τῷ ὄρει τούτῳ, οὔτε ἐν ἱεροσολύμῳ τῷ πατρί." A reference to Jesus' conversation with the Samaritan woman in John 4:21-23.</note>

### PROOF OF THE GOSSPL, Book 1 ###

After the death of those God-loving forefathers, the people were led away by Egyptian customs into polytheism <note>The worship of many gods.</note> and, as I said, they fell into such superstition that they seemed no different from the Egyptians. In every way, they became like them—both in the error of idols and in all other worldly pursuits. It was only right, then, that Moses, as if drawing them up from a depth of evils, tried to turn them away from godless polytheism and lead them back to the one God, the Creator of all. He taught them this first step of piety as an introductory education for those who were being prepared for more perfect things. Then he commanded: do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not swear falsely, do not burn with lust for other men, and do not have sexual relations with mothers, sisters, or daughters—things which were then permitted and practiced without fear. Taking them from a wild and beast-like life, he first established on earth a more rational and lawful way of life <note>original: "πολιτείαν," referring to a structured society or citizenship.</note> through written law. Because the heavenly way of life was not yet revealed to all men, nor to the Jews, he prohibited idolatry as something godless. He commanded them to worship the one God over all through more physical sacrifices, legislating that they perform their religious service through secret symbols of his own. Seeing—and through the Divine Spirit, wonderfully perceiving—that he must not allow things to scatter into infinity, he restricted their worship to one single place. He feared that if they were poured out elsewhere, his laws would be lost. And indeed, they could not perform the sacred rites outside; beyond this one place, it was no longer allowed. For this reason, even to this day, it is not lawful for the children of the Hebrews to offer sacrifice according to the Law, nor to raise a temple or altar, nor to anoint priests or kings, nor to celebrate the festivals and feasts according to Moses outside of their captured mother-city <note>Jerusalem.</note>. Outside of it, they are not released from their errors and defilements by such acts; they cannot offer gifts to God, nor approach Him according to the established customs. Because of this, they have naturally fallen under the curse of Moses, attempting to keep some parts of the Law while breaking it as a whole. For Moses clearly declared: 
<margin>»</margin> "Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all the things 
<margin>»</margin> written in the Law, to do them." <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 27:26.</note> They have fallen into all these things because Moses himself, having foreseen through the Divine Spirit that the New Covenant would be renewed through Christ and proclaimed to all nations, knew his own legislation would be set aside. Therefore, he rightly restricted it to one place so that, if they were ever deprived of it and shut out from the sacrifices of their own land, they would no longer be permitted to perform his legal rites in a foreign land. By necessity, they would then have to accept the second covenant proclaimed through Christ for their generation. So, just as Moses foretold, as soon as Christ lived among us and the New Covenant was put forward as a teaching for the nations, the Romans took the city by siege and destroyed Jerusalem and the temple there. Immediately, the entire arrangement of Moses was dissolved, the Old Covenant was abolished, and the weight of the curse fell upon those who unlawfully tried to practice the Mosaic rites out of season, forcing themselves into them. At the same time and in the same place, the laws of the new and complete teaching were introduced. Therefore, the Savior and Lord rightly said to those who thought God must be worshiped only in Jerusalem, or on certain mountains or restricted places:
<margin>»</margin> "The hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshipers 
<margin>»</margin> will worship neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem, but in spirit..." <note>A reference to John 4:21-23.</note>

<margin>»</margin> its parts; wherever it enters, it destroys from the roots. But even if I have made a gift 
<margin>»</margin> to myself, let it be so. And if I have touched bribes with my hands, then let me sow and 
<margin>»</margin> let others eat, and let me be uprooted from the earth." <note>original: "ἄρριζος δὲ γενοίμην" — Job is using a common ancient metaphor of a plant being pulled up by its roots to describe total destruction.</note> To learn how he conducted himself 
<margin>»</margin> even toward his own household, one can see from what he teaches, saying: "If I ever 
<margin>»</margin> disregarded the claim of my manservant or my maidservant when they had a dispute 
<margin>»</margin> against me." And again, he gives his reasoning: "For what 
<margin>»</margin> shall I do if God makes an examination of me? Were they not formed in the 
<margin>»</margin> womb just as I was? We were all created in the same belly." To these things he adds: "I 
<margin>»</margin> did not cause the widow’s eye to waste away. If I have eaten my morsel alone and 
<margin>»</margin> did not share it with the orphan; if I ever saw the naked perishing and did not clothe him." And 
<margin>»</margin> again, continuing further down, he says: "If I placed my trust in a precious stone; if I 
<margin>»</margin> rejoiced when great wealth came to me; if I laid my hand upon things beyond counting." 
<margin>»</margin> And he adds his reasoning once more: "Or do we not see the sun shining and then 
<margin>»</margin> eclipsed, and the moon likewise waning?" <note>Job is arguing that if he worshipped the sun or moon—common idols—he would be denying God.</note> Then again, while the Gospel teaching says, 
<margin>»</margin> "It was said to the ancients: you shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy; but I 
<margin>»</margin> say to you, love your enemies," <note>referring to Matthew 5:43-44</note> the admirable Job, having received this 
<margin>»</margin> same teaching, fulfilled it. For he says: "If I was glad at the downfall of 
<margin>»</margin> my enemy, or if my heart said 'Aha!'—then let my ear hear my own curse." 
<margin>»</margin> And he adds: "No stranger spent the night outside, but my door was open to every comer." 
<margin>»</margin> This is just like the one who said, "I was a stranger and you took me in." <note>A reference to the words of Jesus in Matthew 25:35.</note> And 
<margin>»</margin> listen to what he says regarding unintentional sins: "For if, having sinned 
<margin>»</margin> unintentionally, I hid my sin; for I was not ashamed before a great multitude so as 
<margin>»</margin> not to confess it in his presence. If I allowed the needy to leave my door with an empty 
<margin>»</margin> bosom; and if I did not fear the hand of the Lord; if I did not tear up a debt-bond 
<margin>»</margin> I held against someone and return it without taking anything from the debtor." 

These things, then, and others like them, were the deeds of God-loving men before the time of Moses. For from this one man <note>Job</note> it is proper to judge the lives of the rest—the incomparable prizes of their <term>theosebeia</term> <note>Godly devotion or piety</note>, because of which they were deemed worthy to be called friends of God and prophets. Since they were such men, what further need was there for the commands given through Moses, which were given to the base and the wicked? Therefore, through all these examples, it has been clearly demonstrated that the Word of Christ, in announcing to all nations the most ancient <term>theosebeia</term> of the forefathers, has shown that the **New Covenant** is nothing other than that most ancient "pious way of life" <note>original: "εὐσεβοῦς πολιτείας"</note> from the times before Moses. Thus, it is both **old** and **new** at the same time: oldest because of the evidence we have shown, but new again because, through the long ages in between, it was as if it had been hidden from men, only to come back to life through the teaching of our Savior. Indeed, during that intervening time I mentioned, while it happened to remain hidden from men—when the New Covenant was, so to speak, "resting"—the Law of Moses stepped in as a sort of guardian and steward for infant and immature souls, or like a physician for the whole Jewish nation who were worn down by the terrible "Egyptian disease." <note>A metaphor for the idolatry and polytheism the Israelites practiced while enslaved in Egypt.</note> To the descendants of Abraham who were no longer able to succeed like their fathers, it handed down a secondary and imperfect way of life. For during their long stay among the Egyptians...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument regarding the history of religion. Having previously discussed how the ancient patriarchs lived by a "Gospel-like" virtue before the Law, he now explains why Moses had to introduce a written Law for the Israelites, who had been corrupted by their time in Egypt.</meta>

-># PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 1#<-

<page-num>13</page-num>

The God-beloved ancestors’ descendants, having been led astray by Egyptian-style habits into the **polytheistic superstition** I mentioned, fell into a state where they seemed no different from the Egyptians. They lived exactly like them, both in the error of idols and in their other customs. Appropriately, then, Moses—as if pulling them up from a **depth of evils**—released them from godless polytheism and led them back to the God who is the creator of all. He presented this as the first step of piety, acting as an introductory gateway <note>original: "ἐν εἰσαγωγαῖς ἐπιπροθύρεσί" — Eusebius uses architectural metaphors to describe the Law as a "porch" or "entryway" to a more perfect room.</note> to more perfect things. 

He then commanded them not to murder, not to commit adultery, not to steal, not to swear falsely, and not for males to have sexual relations with males, nor with their own mothers, sisters, or daughters—practices which were then shamelessly permitted among those people. Taking them from a wild and beast-like life, he established for them a more rational and law-abiding society through written code, for the first time on earth. This was at a time when the appearance of Christ had not yet been revealed to all humanity. 

Because they were, in a sense, deaf to higher truths, he forbid **idolatry** and commanded them to worship the one God of all through sacrifices and more physical rituals. He legislated that they should perform their worship using certain secret symbols. However, through the divine Spirit, he knew that this system should not extend forever. Therefore, he restricted it to **one single place**, decreeing that they must not perform their legal rites anywhere else except in one place alone: **Jerusalem**. Outside of this city, it was no longer permitted.

Consequently, even to this day, it is clearly not lawful for any of the Hebrews—now that they have been deprived of their mother-city—to offer sacrifices according to the Law, nor to raise a temple or an altar, nor to anoint priests or kings, nor to carry out the festivals and feasts commanded by Moses, nor to perform purifications from defilement, nor to be absolved of sins, nor to offer gifts to God, nor to be consecrated according to the established laws. 

By this restriction, Moses effectively placed them under a curse. They might try to keep some parts of the Law, but they are lawbreakers regarding the whole system. <margin>»</margin> For Moses expressly declared: <margin>»</margin> **"Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all the things written <margin>»</margin> in the law, to do them."** <note>This is a quotation from Deuteronomy 27:26, a key verse used by early Christian writers to argue that the Jewish Law was impossible to fulfill without the Temple.</note> 

They have fallen into this situation because Moses, through the divine Spirit, foresaw that when the **New Covenant** through Christ was renewed and announced to all nations, his own legislation would become "weak" <note>original: "ἀσθενὴς" — meaning the Law is no longer "strong" or "effective" because its physical requirements can no longer be met.</note>. This is why he confined everything to one place. He knew that if they were ever deprived of that place and shut out from their own land, it would no longer be permitted for them to perform their legal rites in a foreign land. This forces us to accept the **Second Covenant** announced through Christ. 

Just as Moses had foretold these things, Christ arrived in this life, and the New Covenant was put forward and taught to the nations. Immediately, the Romans took the city by siege and destroyed Jerusalem and the temple there. At that moment, the entire Mosaic arrangement was dissolved. The requirements of the Old Covenant were taken away, and the Curse fell upon those who, past the proper time, still cling to the ways of Moses and try to force themselves to follow them. 

The old was dissolved at the same time as the new and perfect teaching of the Law was established. Therefore, the Savior and Lord appropriately spoke to those who thought God must be worshipped only in Jerusalem, or on certain mountains or specific places, saying: <margin>»</margin> **"The hour is coming, and now is, when the true <margin>»</margin> worshippers will worship neither on this mountain, nor in Jerusalem, in the spirit."** <note>A paraphrase of John 4:21-23. Eusebius uses this to show that Christ moved worship from a physical location to a spiritual state.</note>

<summary>Eusebius explains that Moses gave the Law as a temporary measure to lead the Israelites out of Egyptian paganism, intentionally restricting its rites to Jerusalem so that its eventual destruction would force a transition to the New Covenant in Christ.</summary>

--- Page 636 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument from page 13. Having established that the Mosaic Law was an introductory "entryway" for a people corrupted by Egyptian customs, Eusebius now argues that the prophets themselves predicted the end of this localized, ritualistic system and the return to a universal, spiritual worship—the "archetype" of piety practiced by the patriarchs like Abraham.</meta>

-># OF EUSEBIUS #<-

For God is one, and those who worship Him must worship **in spirit and truth**. <note>original: "ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ" — a direct reference to Jesus’s words in John 4:24, which Eusebius uses here to bridge the Old and New Testaments.</note> Having said these things, and not long after **Jerusalem was besieged**, this very sanctuary and the altar within it—along with the Mosaic worship according to Moses's own dismissal—were abolished. Then, the archetypal piety of the God-beloved men who lived before Moses blazed forth and shone upon all people. This theology, promised through that piety to all nations, advanced those who approached it from the previous stage and from the first elementary instruction <term>στοιχειώσεως (stoicheiōseōs): the basic principles or "ABCs" of religious life</term> of the Mosaic worship, toward a **better and more perfect life**. Thus, the way of those blessed and God-beloved men—I mean Abraham and his circle—who did not worship in a restricted, specific place, nor through symbols and types, but as our Savior and Lord says, "in spirit and truth," was made available to all nations through the appearance of our Savior. The prophets of old had also clearly envisioned this.

<margin>”</margin> For instance, He says through the most wise **Zephaniah**: "The Lord will appear against them and 
<margin>”</margin> will utterly destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth, and they shall worship Him, 
<margin>”</margin> each from his own place." <note>original: "σοφονίας" (Sophonias) is the Greek name for the prophet Zephaniah. See Zephaniah 2:11.</note>

And **Malachi** addresses those of the circumcision <note>The Jewish people, referring to the ritual of the Law.</note> and at the same time proclaims these things regarding the nations, saying:

> <margin>”</margin> "I have no pleasure in you,"
> <margin>”</margin> says the Lord Almighty, "and I will not accept a sacrifice from your hands. For 
> <margin>”</margin> from the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name has been glorified among the nations; and 
> <margin>”</margin> in every place incense is offered to my name, and a **pure sacrifice**." <note>Malachi 1:10-11. Eusebius interprets the "pure sacrifice" not as animal blood, but as Christian prayer and virtue.</note>

For what else does it mean to offer incense and sacrifice to God "in every place," other than that it would no longer be in Jerusalem, nor restricted to any one specific location, but in every land? And that among all the nations, they would offer the incense of prayers and that which is called a **pure sacrifice**—not one of blood, but of pious deeds—to the God over all?

> <margin>”</margin> **Isaiah** also cries out: "In that day," he says, "there shall be an 
> <margin>”</margin> altar to the Lord in the land of Egypt, and the Lord shall be known to the Egyptians. And 
> <margin>”</margin> He shall send them a man who shall save them. And the Egyptians shall know the Lord in 
> <margin>”</margin> that day, and they shall perform sacrifices, and vow vows to the Lord, and perform 
> <margin>”</margin> them. They shall be turned to the Lord, and He shall hear them, and shall heal 
> <margin>”</margin> them." <note>Isaiah 19:19-22. Eusebius views the "man" sent to save Egypt as Christ.</note>

Do we then seem to speak at random when we claim a **transfer** or rather a cessation and dissolution of the Law of Moses is being decreed through the voices of the prophets? For Moses legislated for an altar and sacrifices to be established nowhere else on earth except in Judea alone, and within that, in a single city. But the prophecy says that an altar to the Lord shall be set up in the **land of Egypt**, and that the Egyptians themselves will offer sacrifices to the Lord according to the prophecy—no longer sacrificing to their ancestral gods. It says that neither Moses nor any other prophet would be the cause of their knowledge of God, but rather a certain **new and recent man** sent from God. Since the altar is being transferred contrary to what Moses decided, it is absolutely necessary that a change in the Law of Moses also takes place. Furthermore, if the Egyptians sacrifice to the God over all, they will certainly be deemed worthy of a **priesthood**. But if Egyptians are acting as priests, the regulations Moses laid down concerning the Levites and the succession of Aaron are no longer useful or necessary for the Egyptians. It is time, then, for a **new legislation** for the establishment of the thing described. And was this then proclaimed at random—

<meta>catchword: proclaimed—</meta>

<summary>Eusebius uses prophecies from Zephaniah, Malachi, and Isaiah to argue that the localized Mosaic Law was always intended to be replaced by a universal, spiritual worship accessible to all nations, specifically citing the future conversion of Egypt as proof that the Levitical priesthood must end.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument that the ancient prophecies regarding the conversion of the Gentiles—specifically the Egyptians—are being fulfilled in his own time (the early 4th century AD). He contrasts the "bloody" sacrifices of the old Law and paganism with the "rational" worship of the Christian Church.</meta>

-># PROOF OF THE GOSPEL - BOOK 1 #<-

...has [the prophecy] been spoken? Or has He brought a finality to these words? Consider then if today—I mean in our own time—it is not visible to our very eyes: not only the Egyptians, but every race of men that was formerly turned toward idolatry, to whom these things were spoken and for whom they were hinted at through the example of the Egyptians, has now been set free from the error of many gods and demons, and instead calls upon the one God of the prophets. And sacrifice is no longer offered to many lords, but to the only Lord. Following the sacred oracle, there is in this place an altar of **bloodless and rational sacrifices**, <note>original: "ἀναίμων καὶ λογικῶν θυσιῶν" — This refers to the Christian Eucharist, which Eusebius contrasts with the animal sacrifices of the Jewish Temple and pagan rites.</note> and the new mysteries of the **New and Fresh Covenant** have been raised up throughout the whole inhabited world—both in Egypt itself and among the rest of the nations who used to "act like Egyptians" in their superstitious error. Now, in our own day, the faith that shines brightly with the knowledge of the God of the Universe brings with it the indisputable seal of the things previously prophesied.

To see these things being fulfilled in actual deeds, and no longer merely expected by hearsay, you will find no other point in time from which these events took their beginning than the moment of the **Savior’s appearance**. For the works of Him whom the oracle revealed are clear; for it said that the God and Lord of all things would send to the Egyptians **a man who would save them**. <note>original: "ἄνθρωπον ὃς ὤνησ’ αὐτούς" — Likely referencing Isaiah 19:20, where a "savior" is promised to Egypt.</note> The oracles also revealed Him through Moses, through whom He said:

<margin>>></margin> "**A man shall come forth from his seed**,
<margin>>></margin> **and he shall rule over many nations.**" <note>original: Numbers 24:7 in the Septuagint version, which early Christians interpreted as a prophecy of Christ's lineage and universal kingdom.</note>

Among these nations, the Egyptians would surely be counted. But to speak of these things would require a long discourse, which will be more fully rendered at a proper time of leisure. For now, let it be observed that the things proclaimed were never fulfilled at any time until after the appearance of Jesus our Savior. For from that time until now, among all the Egyptians, and among the Persians, Syrians, and Chaldeans—and even among the barbarians at the very ends of the earth, and those nations who were formerly the most savage and beast-like—yes, and even among those who inhabit the islands (for the prophecy deemed even these worthy of mention), that same way of life practiced by **Abraham**, and the most ancient and primordial form of godliness, is now zealously pursued. 

And who would not be struck with wonder at this extraordinary thing? Those who from time immemorial gave venerable honor to stones, wood, and demons—to man-eating beasts, venomous reptiles, all kinds of animals, and loathsome monsters—as well as to fire, earth, and the lifeless elements of the universe, now, after the coming of our Savior, call upon the **Most High God**, the Creator of heaven and earth, the very Lord of the prophets, the God of Abraham and of his ancestors! 

Consider those who just a short time ago were wallowing in marriages with their own mothers and daughters, <note>Eusebius often cites the end of "barbaric" marriage customs as proof of Christian moral influence.</note> in unspeakable corruptions, and in all kinds of murders—men who differed in no way from predatory beasts. Now, through the divine power of our Savior, they have been transformed as if they had become entirely different people. They study the words of virtue and the teachings of self-control, hastening to the public schools of instruction. There they learn the highest philosophy: to no longer look with lustful eyes, to remain pure even in speech, and to no longer commit the lawless acts that were once common to all. And it is not only men, but also women, the poor and the rich, the learned and the unlettered, even children and slaves, in their gatherings in cities and in the countryside, who are educated and learn the true way in which it is fitting to worship the God over all, and to serve Him in every place, according to the prophecy...

<sig>Bb.ii.</sig>

<summary>Eusebius argues that the global spread of Christianity and its high moral standards—replacing "beastly" pagan customs and animal sacrifices with "rational" worship—is the physical proof that the prophecies of the Old Testament have been fulfilled through Jesus.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument that the New Covenant is not a "new" invention in the sense of being untethered from history, but rather a return to the "primitive" and "natural" religion of the patriarchs (like Abraham) who lived before the specific Jewish Law was given by Moses.</meta>

### EUSEBIUS ###

...by the prophecies, and they proclaim it beforehand, each in his own place: that the God over all will be worshipped by both barbarians and Greeks, not by journeying to Jerusalem, nor by being consecrated through blood and sacrifices; but remaining at home and within himself, and in spirit and in truth rendering to Him an immaterial and pure worship. And this was the New Covenant, not according to the old <note>original: "χρῆσθαι" (OCR: χρύσȣσα) — referring to the usage or practice of the old covenant.</note>; but do not think that by "old" is meant the way of life of the God-loving men <note>original: "θεοφιλῶν ἀνδρῶν" — refers to the patriarchs like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob who lived before the Law of Moses was established.</note> [before Moses], but rather that which was legislated by Moses himself for the Jewish nation. As the Word says:

<margin>»</margin> For again it stated that it would replace the old, of which it says the new is taught as being in no way similar, saying:
<margin>»</margin> "A new covenant, not according to the covenant which I made with
<margin>»</margin> their fathers, on the day I took hold of their hand to lead them out of
<margin>»</margin> the land of Egypt."

At least He says it is not according to this one legislated by Moses. For this was the one handed down to the Jews at the time of the exodus from Egypt. Thus the New Covenant might have seemed contrary to the form of godliness of those God-loving men around Abraham, <note>original: "τῶν ἀμφὶ τὸν ἀβραὰμ" — a common Greek idiom meaning "Abraham and his circle" or those who followed his example of faith.</note> if it had not precisely signaled this by saying, "not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers at that time in which I led them out of the land of Egypt."

Therefore, He promised that the New Covenant would not be according to the law of the Exodus or the wandering in the wilderness legislated by Moses, but according to that older, ancient way of life <note>original: "πολιτείαν" — referring here to a religious "constitution" or spiritual way of living as a citizen of God's kingdom.</note> by which those men before Moses were sanctified. For these reasons, then, taking courage, let us no longer divide the choices of those who profess to follow godliness into two groups, but into three: 

1. The first being that of polytheistic idolatry. 
2. The second being those who fell away from the polytheism of the ancients and, having ascended through Moses to the first step of godliness, reached a middle point.
3. And the third being those who have stepped beyond this through the teaching of the Gospel. 

This third group, having taken up a middle nature, no longer follows the Jewish customs from which it stands apart, yet does not fall back into the previous state [of paganism]; nor do those of us who have withdrawn [from paganism] necessarily have to become Jews. But it has become a kind of **middle nation**, <note>original: "μέσον τι ἔθνος" — This is a famous concept in early Christian thought, viewing Christians as a "third race" (tertium genus) distinct from both Jews and pagans.</note> positioned as if upon a very high mountain peak, separated from the others below on either side. 

For it has utterly escaped godless and multifaceted superstition, along with its unrestrained immoralities and disorders; and likewise, it has escaped the incomplete worship of the Jews under Moses, which was appropriate for "infants" <note>original: "νηπίοις" — a reference to Pauline theology where the Mosaic Law is seen as a "tutor" for a people not yet spiritually mature.</note> and the weak. Observe what it says regarding its own law, which is intended not only for Jews but also for Greeks, Barbarians, and all nations under the sun: a law in which the entire race of mortals will find release. 

Indeed, the Law of Moses, beginning from a single race of men and directed solely toward the Jewish people for the sake of the promises made to their God-loving fathers, called them back to the knowledge of the one God, delivering those who obeyed from the bitter slavery of demons. But I proclaim to all men and to the nations throughout the whole world that advanced knowledge of God and godliness which was chosen by those around Abraham and even those older than him who lived before the times of Moses—among whom many from all nations are remembered as having shone brightly in godliness. And again, while the Law of Moses was restricted to a single specific place on earth for those who chose to follow godliness, hurrying from everywhere...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument that the New Covenant is not a "new" invention in the sense of being untethered from history, but rather a return to the "primitive" and "natural" religion of the patriarchs (like Abraham) who lived before the specific Jewish Law was given by Moses.</meta>

### THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 1, 17 ###

...to all people fearlessly, [the teachings] hand down that piety is not to be sought in a corner of the earth, nor in mountains, or in temples perceived by the senses and made by hands, but that each person should worship and adore the God over all from within their own home. And again: the old law commanded the worship of the God over all with sacrifices consisting of slaughtered animals, with incense and fire, and with imitations of immaterial hymns for the purification of the body; but I <note>Eusebius is speaking here in the voice of Christ, paraphrasing the transition from the Old Law to the New.</note>, handing down the sacred rites <note>original: "ὄργια" (orgia). In this context, it refers to spiritual mysteries or religious ceremonies, not the modern sense of the word.</note> of the soul with a most pure and transparent mind, in temperance and a life according to virtue, command to honor the Divine with correct and pious doctrines. 

And again: Moses, since they were not then murderers, advised them not to kill; but I, to those who have been educated in this and have achieved the elder piety <note>This "elder piety" refers to the faith of the patriarchs like Abraham, which Eusebius argues was more spiritually advanced than the later Law given to the Israelites in Egypt.</note>, legislate what is more perfect, commanding that one should not even be held by the passion of anger. And furthermore, Moses gave instructions to adulterers and the licentious not to commit adultery, nor to be wanton, nor to pursue pleasures contrary to nature, bringing death as the punishment for those who transgress; but I do not want my followers even to look at a woman with licentious desire. 

And again, he said, "You shall not swear falsely, but you shall perform your oaths to the Lord"; but I say to you, do not swear at all, but let your word be "yes, yes" and "no, no"; for whatever is more than these is from the evil one. And again, he commanded those who were wronged to defend themselves and return the injury, saying, "An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth"; but I say to you, do not resist the evil person; but whoever slaps you on your right cheek, turn the other to him also. And to him who wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. 

And again, he advised to love one's friend but to hate enemies; but I, through an abundance of love for humanity and patience, legislate for you to love your enemies and to pray for those who persecute you, so that you may become sons of your Father in heaven, because He makes His sun rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust. 

And in addition to these, while he [Moses] adapted himself to the composition of the masses and prescribed things suitable for those governed by their passions—handing down a different form of piety, altered and lower compared to the old—I [Christ] am calling everyone back to the pious and God-loving life of the most ancient men. And above all, he [Moses] promised an earthly land flowing with milk and honey, as if for infants; but I provide the Kingdom of Heaven to those who are able to receive it. 

These and such things the Word of the New Covenant announced to all nations through the teaching of Christ. And these were the things which Christ, the Son of God, commanded His disciples to announce to all nations, saying:

> Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. <note>Matthew 28:19–20</note>

Christianity clearly proposed and revealed these things, handing them over to be kept by all people, Greeks and barbarians <note>In the Greek world, "barbarian" simply referred to anyone who did not speak Greek or belong to Greek culture.</note> alike. And who we are, and what kind of teacher of such words and lessons is our Savior and Lord Himself, Jesus the Christ of God—He who established this new and yet most ancient way of life <note>original: "πολιτείαν" (politeian). This refers to a "way of life," "citizenship," or "civil conduct."</note> throughout the whole world; so that such things are learned, and philosophy <note>For Eusebius, "philosophy" is not just academic study but a disciplined, ethical way of living according to divine truth.</note> is practiced not only by men, but also by women, by the rich and the poor, and by slaves together with their masters. And indeed, the one who introduced and presided over this new legislation is shown to have lived his life according to the Law of Moses; which is itself a most significant fact, that as a legislator of a new way of life, He should leave a memory...

He highlights the universal reach of Christianity, which calls all social classes and nations to a higher moral philosophy.</summary>

<page-num>18</page-num>
<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

...his own Gospel and the covenant would be spoken of, not as though the teachings of Moses were hostile or contrary. For the ritual requirements that are now called "hostile" to Moses—which provide the godless heretics <note>Eusebius is likely referring to Gnostic groups like the Marcionites, who rejected the Old Testament entirely as the work of an inferior god.</note> with a pretext for great blasphemy against the writings of Moses and the prophets, and which give the circumcised [the Jews] a logical reason for their slander against him—were the very reason they plotted his death, viewing him as a transgressor and an apostate from the Law.

->### How Christ, having first fulfilled the requirements of Moses, established the introductions of a fresh and new way of life.<-

But in fact, having lived his entire life according to the Law of Moses, he employed his apostles as the ministers of his own new legislation. In this way, he taught that the Mosaic regulations were not alien or hostile to his own form of godliness. At the same time, he acted as the author and introducer of a new and saving legislation for all humanity. Thus, he did not appear to transgress against the Mosaic decrees, but rather to bring them to their proper conclusion <note>original: "τέλος" (telos), meaning both "end" and "fulfillment" or "goal."</note>, becoming their fulfiller. It was only after this that he exercised his authority to introduce the law according to the Gospel. We should listen to him speaking in this manner:

> <margin>"</margin> "I did not come to destroy the law, but to fulfill it." <note>Matthew 5:17</note> For if he had not been a "transgressor" of the Mosaic law, it would be irrational to say he "loosed" it or acted illegally. If he were naturally a wicked or lawless person, Christ himself would not have been believed. If he were simply destroying the works of Moses, how could he be described as the one heralded by Moses and the prophets? Furthermore, how would he be seen to possess a new legislation? It would have seemed, reasonably enough, that he had come to innovate simply out of lawlessness, fleeing the punishment due for his crimes. But as it stands, he did not loosen any of the things in the Law at all; rather, he became their fulfiller and their "end," as one might say, according to Moses. Since it was no longer possible for the rest of the nations to apply the Mosaic statutes—for the reasons already explained—it was surely necessary, through the love for humanity <term>philanthropy: the benevolent love of God for mankind</term> of the all-good God, to benefit all people. So that they might come to the knowledge of the truth, he legislated what was suitable and fitting for everyone. He would not have begrudged announcing the Mosaic laws to all people through his apostles, were it not for the fact that "the impossible" stood in the way, as the Apostle [Paul] teaches when he says:

> <margin>"</margin> "For what was impossible for the law, in that it was weak, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh..." <note>Romans 8:3</note> and so on. It was surely impossible for all the nations to meet in Jerusalem according to the Law of Moses; it was impossible for a woman from the ends of the inhabited world, shortly after giving birth, to hurry there to complete her purification rites. There are ten thousand other such rules which one could read for oneself at leisure. Since, therefore, these things were not possible even for those who wished to keep them among the nations living far from Judea, our Savior and Lord did not "loose" these things on his own authority, but rather became the fulfiller of the Law. After providing proof to those who saw him that he was indeed the Christ of God—the one testified to by the ancient prophets of the Jews—he then set forth the fitting commands for all nations through his own disciples. This is why we [Christians] do not claim to have received our legislation from the Jewish prophets, as their law cannot be applied to the nations; yet we have gladly accepted the Jewish prophecies because through...

<page-num>19</page-num>
<header>PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK I, 19</header>

...containing the prophecies. Our Savior and Teacher was, with good reason, the fulfiller of the Law of Moses and the prophets who came after him. For since the outcomes were missing from the divinely inspired <term>prophecies</term>—so that the words might reach their completion—it was necessary for him to become the fulfiller of these very things. For example, consider the prophecy spoken through Moses: 

> <margin>»</margin> "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me; you shall listen to him in everything that prophet says to you." <note>original: Deuteronomy 18:15. This was a foundational text for early Christians to prove that Moses himself predicted a successor who would bring new revelation.</note>

He fulfilled what remained of this prophecy by appearing as a second lawgiver after Moses, providing for mankind’s care and piety toward the God of all things. He [Eusebius] notes that Moses did not simply say a prophet would arise, but added the phrase "like me."

> <margin>»</margin> "For the Lord your God," he says, "will raise up for you a prophet like me; you shall listen to him."

What else did this reveal except that someone very similar to him was intended to appear? Since Moses was a lawgiver of piety toward the God over all, it was likely that the one prophesied to be like him would also be born as a lawgiver similar to him. Indeed, among the prophets who lived after Moses, none is testified to have been "like Moses." For they all directed their listeners back to him [Moses]. 

The Scripture itself bears witness that "no prophet has arisen like Moses." <note>original: Deuteronomy 34:10</note>. Therefore, neither Jeremiah, nor Isaiah, nor any other of the prophets could be the one "like him," because not one of them was established as a lawgiver. Since the world was awaiting the prophet and lawgiver like Moses, no one fits this description except Jesus Christ, who brought divine legislation <note>original: θεονομοθεσίαν (theonomothesian)</note> to all the nations and clarified the true meaning of the things under the Law. 

For consider the sayings: 
> <margin>»</margin> "It was said to those of old: 'You shall not commit adultery.' But I say to you: do not even lust."
> <margin>»</margin> And: "It was said to those of old: 'You shall not murder.' But I say to you: do not even be angry." <note>original: Matthew 5:21-28. Eusebius highlights how Christ "fills up" the law by moving from outward actions to inward intentions.</note>
> <margin>»</margin> And the instruction to no longer worship only in Jerusalem, but in every place. And to no longer offer blood-sacrifices, but to worship in spirit and truth. 

All such things contained in his teaching were the commands of an all-wise and sovereign Lawgiver. This is why the listeners were amazed, as the Divine Scripture says:
> <margin>»</margin> "Because he taught them as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees." <note>original: Matthew 7:29</note>

And so, this fulfilled what remained of Moses' prophecy. Likewise, the rest of the prophecies concerning him and the calling of the nations were divinely fulfilled. He became, then, the fulfiller of the Law and the prophets, bringing the predictions about himself to their conclusion. While he brought the former Law to a close with his arrival, he appeared as the leader of a second law—a new law and a new covenant <note>original: καινῆς διαθήκης (kaines diathekes)</note> for all nations. Thus, he became the shared cause and origin of both systems: I mean Judaism and Christianity. 

This is itself a matter of wonder, which the divine prophecy proclaims in this way:
> <margin>»</margin> "Behold, I place in Zion a chosen stone, a cornerstone, precious; and he who believes in him will not be put to shame." <note>original: Isaiah 28:16 / 1 Peter 2:6</note>

Who else could be the "cornerstone" except the one who joins two different walls together? He builds one structure out of two distinct parts, supporting them through his own teaching. By bringing the Law of Moses—which had stretched forward until his time—to its destination, he joined our building (the one according to the Gospel) to it from the other side. For this reason, he is rightly called the cornerstone. It is also said in the Psalms:
> <margin>»</margin> "The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This was from the Lord, and it is marvelous in [our eyes]." <note>original: Psalm 118:22</note>

» "...in our eyes." <note>original: "ὀφθαλμοῖς ἡμῶν" — quoting Psalm 118:23, often used by early Christians to describe the "rejected stone" becoming the cornerstone.</note> Then he clearly explained the message and the plot by the Jewish nation which the prophesied one suffered: that he was rejected by those "building the old wall"—referring to certain scribes and Pharisees, high priests, and the primary leaders among the Jews. Nevertheless, he says that after their dishonor and rejection, he would be established as the **head of the corner**, having been appointed leader of the <term>New Covenant</term> <note>original: kainē diathēkē; refers to the spiritual agreement between God and humanity established through Christ.</note>, following the interpretation already given. 

Therefore, in departing [from old customs], we have not "fallen into Judaism." Even though we accept the Law of Moses, we must also listen to the prophets who followed him; yet, by not living in a Jewish manner but according to the <term>way of life</term> <note>original: politeia; refers to a person's conduct, citizenship, or spiritual "regime."</note> of the godly men who lived before Moses, we commit no error. For in this very thing, we prove Moses and the prophets who came after him were right, by accepting the Christ they announced and obeying his laws. We make his teaching the foundation of what we preach, thus doing what is pleasing to Moses himself. For he predicted that "the Lord God will raise up a prophet like him," and adds, "every soul that does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from its people." 

Immediately, the Jews, because they did not receive the prophet or obey his holy words, suffered and endured destruction, in accordance with the prophecy. For they neither accepted the law of Christ’s **New Covenant**, nor were they able to keep the commands of Moses without breaking the law; for this reason, they fell away from both the piety of Moses and the original foundations. It was no longer possible for them to fulfill the things legislated by Moses, since their city [Jerusalem] was gone and the Mosaic worship—which was permitted to be performed only there—was shut off from them. 

But we, having accepted the one announced by Moses and the other prophets, and making it our straight path to obey him, would be the fulfillers of Moses’ command, in which he said: 
» "You shall listen to him; 
» and every soul that does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from its people." 

To show which things it was necessary to obey, the prophet [Jeremiah] went a little further, as we have heard, regarding the heavenly commands recorded on a monument. These he did not see fit to entrust to stone tablets like Moses, nor to ink and paper, but to purified souls possessing a rational essence, belonging to his disciples. In these souls he inscribed the laws of the **New Covenant**, fulfilling in action the prophecy spoken through **Jeremiah**:

> » "I will make a **New Covenant**, not according to the covenant 
> » I made with their fathers... for this is the covenant I will make with the house 
> » of Israel: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them 
> » on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people."

### How the Christian Way of Life is Divided into Two Manners

One law was written on lifeless tablets; the other he inscribed as the perfect commands of the **New Covenant** upon living minds. His disciples, having been schooled in the law of their Teacher, provided this teaching to the ears of the many. Whatever was commanded by the perfect Teacher for those who had already stepped beyond the external things, they handed down to those able to receive it. But for those whose souls were still subject to passions and in need of healing, adapting... <note>The text ends mid-sentence with the catchword "adapting" (μόζων).</note>

<summary>Eusebius argues that Christians are the true heirs of Moses because they follow the "Prophet" he predicted, whereas the Jewish people lost the ability to practice their law after the destruction of Jerusalem. He introduces the "New Covenant" as a spiritual law written on the heart rather than on stone tablets.</summary>
