<meta>This page continues Eusebius's explanation of how the Christian "way of life" relates to ancient precedents. He has just finished explaining that the Gospel is a restoration of the primitive religion of the patriarchs, who lived before the Law of Moses was established.</meta>

<page-num>21</page-num>
<header>THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 1</header>

...to fit. In condescending to the weakness of the majority, they <note>The "they" refers to the Apostles and early church leaders establishing the faith.</note> handed down some things to be observed through written laws and others through unwritten customs. Thus, two modes of life have been legislated for the Church of Christ. One is **supernatural** and beyond the common human way of life; it accepts neither marriage, nor the procreation of children, nor the possession of property, nor the accumulation of wealth. It is entirely and completely set apart from the common and customary conduct of men, devoted solely to the service of God through an excess of heavenly love. 

Those who pursue this way appear to have died to the mortal life, carrying only their bodies upon the earth while their souls have been transported to heaven in their minds. Like certain gods, they look down upon the life of men, acting as priests for the whole race to the God over all—not with sacrifices of blood, nor with libations and the smell of burnt fat, nor even with smoke and fire, nor indeed with physical <unclear>offerings</unclear> <note>original: ἀναφοραῖς (anaphorais). In this context, it refers to the physical elevation of sacrifices in the temple.</note>, but with the right doctrines of true piety, with a purified disposition of the soul, and furthermore with deeds and words according to virtue. By these, they appease the Divine, performing a sacred service for themselves and their fellow countrymen. Such is the perfect mode of the Christian <term>way of life</term> <note>original: politeia; often used by Eusebius to describe the "spiritual citizenship" or disciplined regime of a Christian.</note>.

The second mode is more humble and more human; it allows for temperate marriage and the procreation of children, for the management of a household, and for providing instructions to those serving in the military for the sake of justice. It also permits attention to commerce and other more public affairs alongside godly living. For these people, specific times for <term>discipline</term> <note>original: askēseōs; spiritual training or exercise, from which we get the word "asceticism."</note>, study, and listening to the divine words have been set aside. A second grade of piety has been assigned to them, providing a benefit appropriate to such a life, so that no one might be without a share in the saving appearance [of Christ]. Thus, the whole race of men—Greeks and barbarians alike—enjoys the benefit of the Gospel teaching.

---

->Why is it that we do not pursue having many children in the same way as the ancients?<-

---

Given these things, one might reasonably ask: if Christians, through the Gospel teaching, accepted the men who were dear to God of old and before Moses—and if we claim their piety and ours are one and the same—why then did they put the greatest effort into marriage and child-rearing, while we neglect this part? And again, they were recorded as appeasing God with animal sacrifices, yet for us, this is forbidden as if it were unholy. These two points alone, having no small weight, might seem to contradict what we have said, suggesting that those of old did not live according to our way of piety.

In response to these points, I offer a solution from the Hebrew oracles: those who were attested for piety around the time of Moses lived when life was just beginning and being established. (Keep in mind) our situation occurs near the end, as things are fading. Therefore, they were eager for the increase of descendants into a <term>multitude of people</term> <note>original: polyanthrōpia; the state of being populous. Eusebius argues that the biblical patriarchs needed large families to populate the earth, a need he believes has passed.</note>, since at that time the human race was increasing, multiplying, and reaching its peak. But for us, this is not a great concern, as things are already fading and coming to an end, reaching the final limit of life...

<summary>Eusebius describes the two-tier system of Christian life—ascetic "perfection" and the "humble" lay life—and begins to explain why Christians no longer prioritize large families or animal sacrifices like the patriarchs did.</summary>

# EUSEBIUS
## THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 1

...at the consummation of life <note>original: συντελείᾳ (synteleia); refers to the completion or end of an age.</note>, just as the Gospel teaching was already knocking at the doors, a new and secondary birth <note>original: παλιγγενεσίας (paliggenesias); regeneration or rebirth into a new era.</note> of another age—one that was on the very verge of appearing—was being proclaimed. This, then, is one explanation; but there might be a second one as follows: 

The men of old pursued a dual and two-fold life. No obstacles of household or children stood in their way, for they were able to fulfill their religious duties toward the Divine along with their wives and children and households, and were in no way dragged away from their commitment to higher things. In our own time, however, countless external duties tend to drag us away into unforeseen cares, distracting us from our zeal for higher things. The word of the Gospel teaching presents this as the reason for the restriction of marriage, saying: 

,, "But this I say, brothers, the time is short. From now on, let even those who have wives be as though they had none, 
,, and those who weep as though they did not weep, and those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice, 
,, and those who buy as though they did not possess, and those who use this world as though they did not 
,, use it to the full. For the fashion of this world is passing away. But I want you to be free from care. 
,, The unmarried man cares for the things of the Lord—how he may please the Lord; but the married man 
,, cares for the things of the world—how he may please his wife, and so he is divided. Both the unmarried 
,, woman and the virgin care for the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in both body and 
,, spirit. But the married woman cares for the things of the world—how she may please her husband. 
,, I say this for your own benefit, not to put a restraint upon you, but for the sake of what is 
,, appropriate and for devoted service to the Lord without distraction." <note>This is a direct quotation of 1 Corinthians 7:29–35.</note>

In these words, he explicitly presents the reason for abstaining from marriage, while also pointing out the "shortness of the time" and the distractions arising from worldly business—none of which the men of old were entangled with.

There might also be a third reason why the God-fearing men of old took great care in the procreation of children. While the rest of mankind was advancing in wickedness, falling into an unusual and rejected animal-like way of life, and sliding into the godless nation of polytheism <note>Eusebius often characterizes the pagan world as "animal-like" (θηριώδη) in contrast to the "philosophic" life of the godly.</note>, only a very few remained who followed the way of life we described earlier. These few withdrew from the life of the masses and from common social interaction with the rest of men. 

Living separately from the other nations and dwelling by themselves, they sought to emulate a philosophic <term>way of life</term> <note>original: politeia; the organized conduct or "citizenship" of a religious community.</note> that was truly God-fearing, and they kept themselves unmixed with other people. Therefore, so that the living spark <note>original: ζωπυρον (zopyron); a glowing ember or spark used to restart a fire.</note> of their own piety might be preserved through their offspring and not fail or perish along with the death of the men themselves, they naturally took thought for the procreation and rearing of children. They intended to be the teachers and guides of their own children, desiring to leave behind successors of their piety and heirs of their own virtue for those who would come after. 

From this instruction of theirs, countless prophets and righteous men have sprung up, as well as our Savior and Lord himself, and his disciples and apostles. If some wicked men also came from them—just as weeds grow up alongside the grain—one should blame the seed <note>The "seed" here refers to the individual's own choices or nature, not the parents' upbringing.</note> and not those who reared them; for we know that even among the Savior’s disciples, some stumbled by their own free will. Thus, the reason for the procreation of children among the God-fearing men of old has been explained, showing that it no longer has a place among us, since after the [coming] of the Savior...

<page-num>23</page-num>
->**THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 1**<-

...the teaching of the sacred covenants. Myriad customs among peoples, both in cities and in the countryside, have been present for us to see with our own eyes from the beginning. The same purpose exists for those coming together for the divine learning of the covenantal teaching. For these people, it is a thing to be cherished, as it provides sufficiently for the teachers and heralds of the word of piety <note>original: θεοσεβείας (theosebeias); meaning "godly devotion" or "religion."</note>, who have been released from all the bonds of this life and its many distracting cares. Especially for these individuals, a dedication to better things is now pursued through leisure <note>original: σχολήν (scholen); here meaning "devoted time" or "spiritual study."</note> and a withdrawal from marriage. They are not occupied with a "godless or irreligious" procreation of children; rather, they have undertaken the care and godly education of not just one or two children, but of a vast multitude all at once, leading them in a disciplined way of life. If anyone were to examine accurately the lives of the men of old—those about whom we are speaking—he would find that they fathered children in the early stages of their lives, but later showed restraint and eventually ceased. For it is written that:

> "Enoch was well-pleasing to God after he fathered Methuselah." The Scripture accurately records that the man in question was well-pleasing to God *after* the birth of his son, and it testifies that he fathered no more children after that. And Noah, a righteous man, after the birth of his children, was the only one saved with his family during the destruction of those on the earth. Although he lived for many years after this, he is never described as having more children. It is also said of Isaac that after becoming the father of twin offspring from one wife, he stopped his marital intercourse at that point. Joseph also, while living among the Egyptians, acted in this way; he became the father of no more than two children, taking only one woman to be their mother. Even Moses himself, and his brother Aaron, are recorded as having fathered children before the divine appearances <note>original: ἐπιφανείας (epiphaneias); refers to God revealing Himself to them.</note>; but after the divine oracles, one can no longer find children born to them. What need is there to speak of Melchizedek? No father, no mother, and no genealogy or succession is recorded for him. Nor is any recorded for Joshua, the successor of Moses, or for many others. 

To those who inquire about the procreation of Abraham and Jacob, we have provided a more useful explanation elsewhere, in which we discussed the polygamy and large families of the God-loving men of old. We would refer any student of the matter to those writings, noting only this: even according to the laws of the New Covenant, the procreation of children is not entirely forbidden. In this matter, the same regulations apply as those for the God-loving men of old. For the Word says that a bishop <note>original: ἐπίσκοπον (episkopon); an overseer or leader in the church.</note> must be "the husband of one wife." Nevertheless, it is fitting for those who are consecrated and occupied in the service of God to abstain from marital intercourse thereafter. As for those who are not deemed worthy of such a high ministry, the Word relaxes its requirements, almost explicitly proclaiming to all: "Marriage is honorable and the bed is undefiled, but God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers." Let these things be said to support our current proposition.

***

### For what reason was it not handed down to us to burn incense and sacrifice earthy things to God in the same way as the men of old?

Regarding the fact that we do not perform animal sacrifices <note>original: ζωοθυτεῖν (zoothytein); to sacrifice living animals.</note>, despite all the God-loving men of old—whom we say we emulate in their religious zeal—having done so, the following explanation is offered from our side...

<meta>The previous page discussed how the early Patriarchs transitioned from domestic life to a state of spiritual devotion, sometimes moving away from marriage to focus on divine things. This page begins a new argument: justifying the ancient practice of animal sacrifice in the Hebrew tradition, contrasting it with Greek philosophical critiques.</meta>

<page-num>24</page-num>
# EUSEBIUS
<meta>catchword: of the purpose</meta>

...the word itself. It is not as some have supposed, for the sacred words of the Hebrews hold the same view regarding the service of the Divine by those men of old who were beloved of God. For some [Greeks] used to say that one ought not to offer any living creature to the highest gods, nor even burn incense to them. Rather, they claimed that for the ether <note>original: αἰθέριον (aitherion); the upper atmosphere or "pure air" where the gods were thought to dwell.</note> and the stars in the heavens, men should grasp with their hands the green grass—a kind of downy growth of fertile nature—and burn expensive leaves and roots in the fire. To later generations, it seemed a far cry from holiness to stain the altars with the slaughter of animals, assuming such a sacrifice was unholy, unjust, and in no way pleasing to God. They argued that the souls of irrational animals differ in no way from the rational souls of humans. For this reason, they even claimed that those who sacrifice animals deserve to be tried for murder, since the same and similar soul permeates both the human being and the irrational animal. Such was the account of the Greeks concerning the ancients. But the account of the Hebrew Scripture is not of this kind.

For it records that the first humans, at the very first establishment of their life, honored the Divine with sacrifices from animals. It says, at any rate:
» "And it came to pass after some days that Cain brought a sacrifice to the Lord from the fruits of the earth.
» And Abel himself also brought of the firstborn of his sheep.
» And God looked upon Abel and upon his gifts.
» But to Cain and his sacrifices He paid no heed." <note>This refers to Genesis 4:3-5.</note>
Furthermore, one should observe how it is said that the one who sacrificed a living creature was more acceptable to God than the one who brought a sacrifice to God from the earth. Then, immediately from the first of the clean ages, and from all the clean birds, Noah offered whole burnt offerings upon the altar, and "the Lord smelled a sweet savor." <note>original: ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας (osmen euodias); a biblical idiom for a pleasing sacrifice.</note> Moreover, Abraham is also recorded as having sacrificed. Consequently, according to the testimony of Holy Scripture, sacrifice through animals was the first of all to be devised by those ancient men beloved of God.

We might say that the reasoning behind this was not accidental, nor prompted by mere human impulse, but was suggested by a divine inspiration <note>original: θείᾳ δ’ ἐπίνοιαν (theia epinoian); a "divine thought" or "insight."</note>. For since those pious men, being living souls themselves and intimately acquainted with God, were illuminated in their souls by the Divine Spirit, they saw that they needed a great service for the cleansing <term>apokatharsin|a ritual purification or purging</term> of mortal transgressions. They felt they ought to offer to God a ransom <term>lytron|a price paid for release or redemption</term> for their own salvation, life, and soul. Then, having nothing better or more precious than their own souls to dedicate, they instead offered for a time the sacrifice through irrational animals, presenting them as substitutes for their own souls <note>original: ἀντίψυχα (antipsycha); literally "soul-for-soul" or "life-for-life."</note>. They believed they committed no fault or injustice in this, because they were taught that the soul of irrational animals is not similar to the rational and intellectual power of humans, and that it is nothing other than their blood, and the vital power within the blood. This vital power they possessed, offering it to God as a soul in place of a soul. Moses himself clarifies this most clearly, saying:
» "The soul of all flesh is its blood.
» And I have given it to you upon the altar, to make atonement for your souls.
» For their blood shall make atonement in place of the soul.
» Therefore I have said to the children of Israel: No soul among you shall eat blood." <note>A citation of Leviticus 17:11-12.</note>

One must pay careful attention to these words: "I have given it to you upon the altar to make atonement for your souls. For the blood shall make atonement in place of the soul." For he clearly says that the blood of the slaughtered animals makes atonement instead of the human soul. This is the very thing that the law concerning sacrifice suggests to the mind of the observer...
of the purpose

<summary>Eusebius defends the biblical practice of animal sacrifice against Greek philosophers who viewed it as "unjust" or "murderous." He argues that the sacrifice of animals was a divinely inspired "soul-for-soul" substitute (ransom) that allowed ancient people to seek atonement for their sins.</summary>

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 1
<header>PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 1</header>

...considering something. Indeed, he <note>Moses, as the giver of the Law.</note> commands everyone who offers a sacrifice to lay their hands upon the head of the victim, and to bring the animal while holding its head, as if offering the victim in place of his own head. He says, at any rate, concerning each sacrifice:

> » He shall bring it before the Lord, and he shall lay his hands upon the head
> » of the gift.

And this practice was observed for every sacrifice; no offering was ever brought without it. Through these rituals, the Word shows that the lives of the animals were offered as a ransom for the souls of the humans <note>original: ἀντίψυχα (antipsychon); literally "life-for-life" or a substitute for a soul.</note>. But he <note>Moses</note> taught that the blood of irrational animals is their soul <note>See Leviticus 17:11: "For the life (soul) of the flesh is in the blood."</note>, and he by no means presents them as participating in a rational and intellectual essence similar to humans. Rather, their constitution is from matter and mud, similar to the sprouts and plants of the earth. In a single word, Moses says again that God said:

> » Let the earth sprout 
> » grass, herb yielding seed, and fruit-bearing tree.

And again, in a similar way:

> » Let the earth bring forth four-footed animals and beasts of the earth according to their kind.

Thus, irrational animals are said to be of the same race, nature, and value as the sprouts and plants of the earth. Therefore, those who sacrifice animals commit no sin. Indeed, it is even said that meat was given to humans to eat just like the vegetables of the field <note>A reference to Genesis 9:3, where God permits Noah to eat meat as he previously ate plants.</note>. As long as the "better" thing—the great, precious, and divinely-befitting sacrifice—was not yet present to humans, it was necessary for them to render to God the lives of animals as ransoms for their own lives and as substitutes for their own nature. This was decreed by the men of old who were beloved of God. Through the Divine Spirit, they had foreknowledge that a solemn, God-beloved, and great holy victim would one day come to humans—one who would be the purification <note>original: καθάρσιον (katharsion); a means of cleansing or expiation.</note> of the entire world. They themselves, being prophets, performed the symbols of this for a time, prefiguring what was to come. 

But when the fulfillment arrived, following the decrees of the prophets, the former things ceased. They were immediately dissolved by the better and true holy service. This "better thing" is Christ, the ransom of God <note>original: θεοῦ λύτρον (theou lytron).</note>, who was foretold as coming to humans from ancient times, and who would be slaughtered as a fresh victim on behalf of the whole human race. Regarding him, Isaiah the prophet says:

> » As a sheep he was led to slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent. And
> » he adds: This man bears our sins and suffers for us, and we considered 
> » him to be in pain, and under a stroke and in affliction. But he was wounded 
> » for our sins, and weakened for our lawlessness. The chastisement of 
> » our peace was upon him. By his bruise we were healed. And the Lord delivered 
> » him up for our sins. For he himself did no sin, nor was guile found 
> » in his mouth.

Jeremiah, another Hebrew prophet, proclaims similar things in the person of Christ, saying:

> I was as an innocent lamb being led 
> to be sacrificed.

John the Baptist seals these prophecies at the appearance of our Savior. Seeing him, and pointing him out to those present as the one who had been prophesied, he proclaimed:

> Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away 
> the sin of the world.

Since, then, according to the testimonies of the prophets, the great and precious thing has been found for Jews and Greeks alike—the purification of the whole world, the ransom for the souls <note>original: ἀντίψυχον (antipsychon).</note> of all men, a victim pure from every stain and sin, the Lamb of God, the God-beloved and holy sheep, the prophesied lamb—through whose divine and mystical teaching all we from the nations [receive] forgiveness...

# EUSEBIUS
<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

...sin. Regarding the former visions <note>original: θεαμάτων (theamaton); here referring to the symbolic rites and prophetic types of the Old Testament</note>, we do not dispute them; which is why even those of the Jews who have believed in Him abandon the most bitter curse of Moses. They rightly perform the memorial <note>original: ὑπόμνησιν (hypomnesin); often used in early Christian texts to refer to the Eucharist or Lord's Supper</note> of His body and blood every day. Having been deemed worthy of a sacrifice and a sacred ministry superior to those of the ancients, we no longer consider it holy to fall back upon those first and **weak elements** <note>A reference to Galatians 4:9, describing the basic religious rituals of the world before Christ</note>, which contain symbols and images but not the truth itself.

It is logical, then, that those of the Jews who have fled to the Christ of God—if they no longer turn back to the command of Moses but live according to the New Covenant—would be outside the curse defined by Moses. This is because the Lamb of God took upon Himself not only the sin of the world, but also the curse attached to the violation of the commands of Moses. Thus, the Lamb of God became both **sin** and a **curse**: **sin** on behalf of the people of the world, and a **curse** on behalf of those bound by the things written in the Law of Moses. Therefore, the Apostle says:

> » Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a
> » curse for us; and Him who knew no sin, He made to be sin
> » for us. <note>A synthesis of Galatians 3:13 and 2 Corinthians 5:21.</note>

For why should He not become the cleansing of the world—He who gave His own life for the sin <note>original: αὐτόψυχον (autopsychon); literally "life-for-life" or "the soul itself" given as a substitute</note>, who indeed was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a spotless lamb to be sacrificed, and all these things on our behalf and because of us?

Hence, the God-fearing men of old, in the absence of these superior things, rightly held fast to the symbols. As our Savior Himself teaches this very thing, saying:

> » Many prophets and righteous men desired to see what you see, 
> » and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. <note>Matthew 13:17.</note>

But we, having received the true things and the patterns of the images through the mysterious "economy" <note>term: economy (oikonomia); in this context, it refers to God's plan for salvation and the incarnation of Christ</note> of Christ, will no longer need the old ways. He alone, being the Word <note>original: Λόγος (Logos)</note> of God, existing beyond the world, and being the High Priest of all intellectual and rational creation, set Himself apart from the herd of humanity as a sheep and a lamb like us in suffering. He took upon Himself the sins of us all and accepted the curse that was specifically ordained in the Law of Moses. As Moses proclaimed:

> » Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. <note>Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13.</note>

This He suffered for us, becoming a curse for us, and He who made Him sin for us. Since He "knew no sin," He made Him "sin for us," laying upon Him all the punishments intended for us—bonds, dishonor, insults, scourgings, and extreme blows—and above all, the death of the curse. After all these things, having offered Himself as a marvelous victim and an exceptional sacrifice to the Father, He brought it up for the salvation of us all, handing down a **memorial** to us to offer continually to God instead of a physical sacrifice.

The marvelous David, among the prophets, foresaw this by the Holy Spirit and proclaimed it, saying:

> » I waited patiently for the Lord; he inclined to me, and heard my 
> » prayer. He brought me up out of a pit of misery, and from the 
> » miry clay. And he set my feet upon a rock, and directed my 
> » steps. And he put a **new song** in my mouth, a hymn to our God. 

And he clarifies what this "new song" happens to be, saying next:

> » Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you 
> » prepared for me. <note>Psalm 40:6 (LXX 39:7). The Greek Septuagint version used by Eusebius says "a body you prepared," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic text says "ears you have opened."</note> Whole burnt offerings and sacrifices 
> » for sin you did not require. Then I said, "Behold, I come." In 
> » the scroll of the book it is written concerning me, to do your 
> » will, O God, I have desired.

And he adds,

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 1

» I proclaimed righteousness in a great assembly. <note>original: "Εὐηγγελισάμην δικαιοσύνην ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ μεγάλῃ"; a quote from Psalm 40:9 (39:10 in the Septuagint), which Eusebius interprets as Christ speaking to the Church.</note> But since the prophetic voice had already signaled the incarnate presence of Christ and the body prepared for Him—which replaced the ancient system of animal sacrifices and whole burnt offerings—He proclaimed this very thing to the same assembly. This was a great mystery announced beforehand by the prophetic voice in the "heading of the book." Since we have received the command to perform the memorial <note>original: μνήμην (mnemen); in a liturgical context, this refers to the "Anamnesis" or memorial sacrifice of the Eucharist.</note> of this sacrifice upon a table through symbols of both His body and His saving blood, according to the ordinances of the New Covenant, we are again taught by the prophet David to say:

» Thou hast prepared a table before me in the presence of those who afflict me. Thou hast anointed my head with oil, and Thy cup cheers me like the best wine. <note>Psalm 23:5 (22:5 LXX). Eusebius sees this as a direct prophecy of the Eucharist (the table and cup) and Confirmation (the oil/chrism).</note>

In these words, he explicitly signifies the mystical chrism <note>term: <term>chrism</term> (χρίσμα); the sacred oil used in Christian initiation, which Eusebius links to the "anointing" mentioned in the Psalm.</note> and the venerable sacrifices of the table of Christ. Through these, we have been taught to offer throughout our entire lives "unbloody and rational" sacrifices, well-pleasing to the God of all, through His High Priest who is above all. The great prophet Isaiah also wonderfully foresaw and proclaimed this very thing by the Divine Spirit. He speaks thus:

» O Lord my God, I will glorify Thee, I will sing praise to Thy name, for Thou hast done wonderful things. <note>Isaiah 25:1.</note>

And as he continues, he clarifies what these "wonderful things" are, saying:

» The Lord of Hosts shall make for all nations. They shall drink<gloss>—they will</gloss> joy, they shall drink<gloss>—they will</gloss> wine, they shall be anointed<gloss>—they will</gloss> with ointment <note>original: μῦρον (myron); scented oil or myrrh.</note> on this mountain. Deliver all these things to the nations; for this counsel is upon all the nations. <note>Isaiah 25:6–7. The glosses <gloss>ται</gloss> in the Greek text complete the future tense verbs "they shall drink" and "they shall be anointed."</note>

Therefore, one must recognize the "wonderful things" of Isaiah: the fragrance of love and the anointing of ointments, promised not to Israel, but to all the nations. From this, logically, because of the anointing with ointment, they were deemed worthy of the name "Christians." <note>A wordplay on "Christos" (Anointed) and "Christians" being those who receive the "Chrism."</note> Furthermore, he prophesies joy to the nations, hinting at the mystery of the New Covenant of Christ, which is now clearly performed among all nations. Again, the prophetic words proclaim these incorporeal and intellectual sacrifices, containing something like this:

» Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High; and call upon Me in the day of affliction, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify Me. <note>Psalm 50:14–15 (49:14–15 LXX).</note>

And again:

» The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice. <note>Psalm 141:2 (140:2 LXX).</note>

And once more:

» A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit. <note>Psalm 51:17 (50:19 LXX).</note>

All these things, which were prophesied from ages past, are now performed in the present time among all nations through the evangelical teaching of our Savior. Truth itself bears witness to the prophetic voice, through which God, having rejected the sacrifices of Moses, prophesies what would happen among us, saying:

» For from the rising of the sun even to its setting, My name has been glorified among the nations; and in every place incense is offered to My name, and a pure sacrifice. <note>Malachi 1:11. This is a central text for early Christians to justify the Eucharist as the "pure sacrifice" of the Gentiles.</note>

We therefore sacrifice to the God of all a sacrifice of praise. We sacrifice the divine, venerable, and sacredly-befitting victim. We sacrifice in a new way according to the New Covenant: the pure sacrifice. For it is said:

» A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit; a broken and humbled heart God will not despise.

And indeed, we burn the prophetic incense, offering to Him in every place the fragrant fruit of an all-virtuous theology, offering it through prayers to Him. Another prophet also teaches this, saying:

» Let my prayer be set forth before Thee as incense. <note>Psalm 141:2.</note>

Therefore, we both sacrifice and offer incense: at one time performing the memorial of the great sacrifice according to...

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 2

->That it was not by chance, nor in vain, that we attended to the prophetic<-
->books of the Hebrews with all diligence.<-

**T**<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'T' featuring ornate foliate designs and a small face or mask within the letterform.</image-desc>he way of true piety, which has been set before all people through the Gospel teaching, along with the way of life in Christ <note>original: χ̅ω̅ (Christo)</note>, was detailed in my previous work. I established there, and I believe I persuaded the reader, that it was not possible—even for those who wished it—for all the nations to live according to the Jewish laws. Now, returning to the present argument from the beginning, let us run through the testimonies from the prophetic voices. I will do this to make a more abundant defense against our accusers from "the Circumcision" <note>original: ἐκ περιτομῆς (ek peritomes); a common New Testament and early Christian term for the Jewish people.</note>. For they used to claim that we have no part in the promises recorded in their scriptures. They argue that the prophets belonged to them, and that Christ <note>original: χ̅ν̅ (Christon)</note>—whom they call a friend, savior, and redeemer—is proclaimed for them alone. They expect the written promises to be fulfilled for themselves, while claiming that we are strangers to these things, being of a foreign race to whom only the worst punishments are announced throughout the prophecies. Therefore, let us make our defense against them from their very own prophetic books. We agree with them that good things were promised by God <note>original: θ̅ω̅ (Theo)</note>, and that the prophets proclaimed His arrival as a redemption for Israel; this is clearly presented throughout all their scripture. However, it is no longer just to allow their claim that the expectation of good things in Christ <note>original: χ̅ω̅ (Christo)</note> is restricted to Israel alone and not also promised to the nations. Instead, we shall show that the divine scriptures themselves bear witness to this.

->How the prophets among them proclaimed in advance the more favorable news<-
->concerning us, the foreign nations.<-

<margin>P</margin> First, then, since they themselves are accustomed to selecting the more favorable passages for their own benefit and reciting them by heart, let us set against them the proofs concerning the nations from those same prophecies. These proofs will demonstrate that there are countless predictions decreeing good things and salvation for all the nations <note>original: ἔθνεσιν (ethnesin); often translated as "Gentiles."</note>. They also state that the things promised to the nations could not be accomplished in any other way except through the presence of Christ <note>original: χ̅υ̅ (Christou)</note> alone. Having established this argument, we might say that the expectation of the Christ of God <note>original: θ̅υ̅ (Theou)</note> fits us no less than it fits them. Next, once the Jews' hope in the promises is shown to have failed, and it is proven that those from the nations who are saved through Christ are in no way inferior to those of the Circumcision, we will further prove the following: that the divine oracles foretell a complete falling away and rejection of the entire Jewish nation at the time of Christ’s presence and the calling of the nations. These oracles decree favorable things for only a small and easily numbered remnant of them, while showing that their city will be captured along with the temple itself, and all their sacred traditions will be destroyed—things which have clearly been demonstrated by actual events. We shall see how, at one and the same time, through the presence of Christ, there is a redemption from evils for...

# EUSEBIUS

...of Israel and the enjoyment of good things, but on the other hand, the sacred words prophesy the deprivation of good things and a falling away from the piety of God. They also testify through oracles to the time of the prophets. For the time being, let us summarize for the present purpose, selecting a few from the countless thousands of prophecies to provide proof for what has been said. Since they <note>The Jewish people, referred to earlier as "those of the Circumcision."</note> put forward the oracles and prophecies against themselves as if they were intended only for them—signifying only what had happened to them in the past—it is time for us to bring forward a counter-argument and set against them the promises concerning the nations, as they are found among their own prophets.

### From Genesis.
### How the nations of the earth will be blessed in the name of Abraham’s calling.

<margin>>></margin> > And the Lord said, "Shall I hide from Abraham my servant what I am doing? 
<margin>>></margin> > For Abraham shall become a great and numerous nation, and in him shall
<margin>>></margin> > all the nations of the earth be blessed."

The oracle says it will not hide a mystery that is concealed and unnoticed by the many, but will reveal it to the one who loves God <note>original: τῷ θεοφιλεῖ (to theophilei); someone dear to or beloved by God.</note>. This was the mystery concerning the absolute blessing of the nations, which was hidden long ago because all the nations before the time of Abraham were held fast by the unspeakable error of superstition. But now, in our time, this has been revealed, when through the Gospel teaching of our Savior, those who worship God in the same manner as Abraham participate in the same blessing as him. And because it is not possible for all the nations to live as citizens under the legislation of Moses <note>The Law of Moses included specific dietary and geographical requirements impossible for global observance.</note>, we have discussed this most fully in the preceding work, so that no one should suppose the argument refers only to the prophecies concerning the Jews. Having established in that work that this blessing—the one promised to Abraham regarding all nations—applies only to those from all nations who come through Christ <note>original: χριστοῦ (Christou)</note>, we will now refer the studious readers back to those points.

### How all the nations of the earth will be blessed in your seed, which was assigned in succession to Isaac. From the same book.

> And the Lord, speaking to Isaac, says among other things:
<margin>>></margin> > "And I will establish my oath which I swore to Abraham your father, and I will multiply your seed as the stars of
<margin>>></margin> > heaven, and I will give to your seed all this land, and in
<margin>>></margin> > your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed."

Our Savior and Lord, Jesus the Christ <note>original: ἰησοῦς ὁ χριστὸς (Iesous ho Christos)</note> of God, was born from the seed of Isaac according to the flesh. In him, all the nations of the earth are blessed, having learned through him of the God of all things, and having ceased from their previous ways, they now bless the men who were beloved by God. Therefore, the nation itself is blessed, enjoying a blessing equal to those who are blessed by them, according to the word of God spoken to Abraham: "Those who bless you are blessed."

### Concerning the many nations, and the congregations of nations that would be established from Jacob, even though only the single nation of the Jews proceeded from him. From the same book.

<margin>>></margin> > multiply into nations, and congregations of nations shall be from you."

According to the obvious meaning, only the nation of the Jews was established from Jacob. How then does the oracle speak in the plural? Since the Christ of God, being born from the seed of Jacob, established many congregations of nations through the teaching of his covenant, it is reasonable that...

At the present moment, there is no time to collect or interpret them all, as the examples already set forth are sufficient to prove the point at hand. Among the prophets, it was a great point of pride for those of the circumcision <note>A common term in early Christian writing for the Jewish people.</note> to boast that they alone of all the nations were preferred by God, and they alone were deemed worthy of the divine promises. My goal is to show that [the prophets] promised nothing better to the Jews themselves than what was promised to the other nations in the divine pledges. Since it has been demonstrated that the nations were indeed deemed worthy of the divine promises, come now, let us also observe the one through whom it is said the nations would attain God’s calling and the divine promises—for it is good to perceive this—namely, the one said to provide these blessings to the nations. And who else is this but the presence of Christ, through whom even those of the circumcision confess their own redemption will be released? It must be shown, therefore, that the expectation of the calling of the nations was none other than the Christ of God himself, appearing as a Savior not only to the Jews, but also to all the nations. For now, I will use the bare testimonies of the prophets without full interpretation, though I intend to interpret each one at length when I have the leisure; for with God's help, I plan to gather all the prophecies concerning the nations and interpret them together.

...your soul will delight in good things, and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, the faithful and holy promises made to David. <note>Isaiah 55:2–3. The "holy things" (Gr. *hosia*) refers to the mercies or divine promises guaranteed to King David.</note> Behold, I have given him as a witness to the nations, a ruler and one who commands the nations. Nations which do not know you shall call upon you, and peoples who do not understand you shall flee to you for refuge, because of the Lord your God, and the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you.

Having observed through these passages how the presence of Christ was foretold as a source of salvation to be proclaimed not only to the Jews, but also to all the nations, let us now bring forward a third point of proof. This will show how, at the time of his appearance, not only were the most favorable things prophesied for the nations, but the opposite was foretold for those "of the circumcision." <term>Circumcision: A common biblical shorthand for the Jewish people, referring to the covenant sign of Abraham.</term> Indeed, the very oracles they possess explicitly predict that a falling away and rejection of the Jewish nation would occur because of their lack of faith in Christ. This resulted in them no longer being left in their previous state, while those better than the ones "of the circumcision" would be deemed worthy. For now, I will use the bare words of the prophets themselves, without providing a full theoretical explanation of each, so that their meaning remains clear, and because time does not permit a completely exhaustive examination.

And so it is with the name of our Savior, Jesus Christ. Simeon also bears witness to this in the Gospel, who, having taken the child into his arms and held him in his hands, prayed:
> "Now, Master, you let your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation <note>original: "τὸ σωτήριόν σου" (to sōtērion sou) — This term refers both to the act of saving and the person of the Savior himself.</note>, which you have prepared in the face of all peoples: a light for revelation to the Gentiles."
This very "salvation" was also indicated by the Psalmist, saying: "The Lord has made known his salvation; he has revealed his righteousness in the sight of the nations." And seeing this salvation, all people shall fall down in worship, saying that the God of the universe has freely granted salvation to everyone. And they shall worship Him—not in the Jerusalem below <note>Referring to the physical city in Palestine, as opposed to a "heavenly" or spiritual Jerusalem.</note> located in Palestine, but each from his own place, including all those in the islands of the nations. 

Then shall be fulfilled the oracle which says that all men shall no longer call upon their ancestral gods, nor upon idols and demons, but upon the name of the Lord, serving him under a single yoke. And from the furthest borders of Ethiopia, they shall bring to Him "rational and bloodless sacrifices" <term>rational and bloodless sacrifices: A common early Christian phrase referring to prayer, praise, and the Eucharist, contrasted with the animal sacrifices of the Old Testament.</term> through the New Covenant of Christ. These sacrifices will be found not in the Jerusalem below, but upon the altar of every place, even unto the stated borders of Ethiopia.

Is it not true that there is one "bed" <note>The Greek "εὐναί" (eunai) here likely refers to a resting place or a union; Eusebius is discussing the shared inheritance of the people of God.</note> of the peoples by which God is named? This surely happens to be the greatest of the divine promises, which was spoken by Him concerning those who are worthy: "I will be their God, and they shall be my people." Previously, Israel was rightly proud, as they were the only people of God; but it was proclaimed that the Lord, having arrived, would grant this same good to the nations <term>nations: "ἔθνη" (ethnē), often translated as "Gentiles" in a biblical context, referring to all non-Jewish peoples.</term>, saying:
> "Behold, I am coming, and I will dwell in your midst. And many nations shall flee to the Lord for refuge, and they shall be His people."
Regarding these people it is fitting to say: "I will say to the 'Not-My-People', 'You are my people'; and he shall say, 'You are the Lord my God.'"

And if Christ is also the "one from the flower" <note>A reference to the "flower" or "shoot" mentioned in Isaiah 11:1.</note> who was prophesied to sprout from the root of Jesse—which even the Hebrews themselves admit, so that no one disputes it—look at how Isaiah spoke concerning the hope of the nations. He spoke not to Israel, but to the Gentiles who would hope in Him, and not to Israel when he said that He was the "expectation of the nations." Therefore, he says He "shall bring forth judgment to the nations," and "He shall become a light to the nations." And again: "In His name shall the nations hope." 

Salvation shall be given not only to the Jews, but to all men even to the end of the earth. Therefore, it was said to Him by the Father who sent Him:
> "I have given you for a covenant of the race; for a light to the nations, to establish the earth, and to inherit the desolate heritages."
He says He is a "testimony to the nations," so that all the nations who had never learned of Christ, upon knowing the "economy" <term>economy: "οἰκονομία" (oikonomia), referring to God’s plan or arrangement for human salvation through Christ’s life and work.</term> concerning Him and the power within Him, might call upon Him; and that the peoples who did not know Him long ago might flee to Him for refuge.

Not to lengthen my discourse—since it is possible to see this from the prophetic words themselves which we have set forth and those we remember from our studies in the Divine Scriptures—anyone who wishes to read the prophetic voices may see for himself, provided he is not "dim-sighted" <note>original: "ἀμβλυωπῆ" (amblyōpē) — someone with dull or weak vision; here used metaphorically for those who cannot see the spiritual truth.</note>. Such a person would not claim that the promises of God were given to the Jews alone, or that we from the nations are strangers to the divine promises. For it has been shown, on the contrary, that many nations shall be perfected by Christ’s...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument in Book 2 of the *Proof of the Gospel*. Having established that the Gospel is intended for all nations, he now addresses a difficult point: why the Jewish people, the original recipients of the promises, seem to have been bypassed. # PROOFS OF THE GOSPEL Book 2

...enjoying [His] presence, but the Jewish multitudes would fall away from the promises made to their ancestors because of their unbelief in their Christ. Only a rare few among them would believe in our Savior and Lord, and through Him, they would attain the promised spiritual redemption. Regarding these people, the wonderful Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul</note> also teaches somewhere, saying: 
» "Isaiah cries out on behalf of Israel: 'Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a **remnant** shall be saved. For He will finish the work and cut it short in righteousness, because a short work will the Lord make upon the earth.' 
» And as Isaiah said before: 'Unless the Lord of **Sabaoth** <note>original: "σαβαὼθ" (Sabaoth) — A Hebrew title for God meaning "of Hosts" or "of Armies."</note> had left us a **seed**, we would have become like Sodom, and been made like Gomorrah.'" 
To these words, after some other remarks, he adds: 
» "I ask then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he pleads with God against Israel? 'Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars; I alone am left, and they are seeking my life.' But what is the divine response to him? 'I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.' So too at the present time there is a **remnant**, chosen by grace." 

Through these words, the Apostle clearly shows that despite the falling away of the entire Jewish nation, he himself and those like him—the Apostles and Evangelists of our Savior, and all those from among the Jews who now believe in Christ—constitute the "seed" named by the prophet in the passage: *Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed.* He explains that this "remnant" mentioned in the other prophecies is what has been preserved "according to the election of grace." 

Regarding this remnant, let us again expand upon the evidence from the prophets to show, through many examples, that God did not promise the salvation foretold through Christ to the Jewish nation indiscriminately, but only to a few and quite rare individuals who have believed in our Savior and Lord—just as the actual events followed the predictions.

-> That the divine promises do not extend to the entire Jewish nation, but only to a few of them. <-
-> From Isaiah. <-

» "Your land is desolate, your cities are burned with fire; foreigners devour your land in your very presence, and it is made desolate, overthrown by foreign peoples. And unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a **seed**, we would have become like Sodom, and been made like Gomorrah." 

In the beginning of his own book, this great and wonderful prophet sets out the entire theme of his prophecy, teaching that it concerns the vision and contemplation of Judea and Jerusalem. Then, he rebukes the entire Jewish nation, first saying: 
» "The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s crib; but Israel does not know me, and the people have not understood me." 
Then, lamenting the whole nation, he adds: 
» "Woe, sinful nation, a people full of sins, an evil **seed**, lawless sons!" 
By employing these rebukes against them at the very start of his book, he pre-teaches the reasons why they no longer...

# EUSEBIUS

<margin>Eusebius, *On the Preparation for the Gospel* <note>The marginal note says "Preparation," but the content is famously from his other work, *The Proof of the Gospel* (Demonstratio Evangelica), Book 2.</note></margin>

...the prophecy directed against them follows, as seen in the subsequent words: » **"Your land is desolate."** At the time he was prophesying, it was not yet desolate. » **"Your cities are burned with fire"**—yet this had not happened either. Nor had foreigners yet seized their land; nevertheless, he says: » **"Foreigners devour your land in your very presence."** <note>original: "τὴν χώραν ὑμῶν ἐνώπιον ὑμῶν ἀλλότριοι κατεσθίουσιν αὐτὴν" — Isaiah 1:7.</note>

And so it continues. If one looks toward the sojourn of our Savior Jesus Christ and the times from then until now, one sees all these things being fulfilled because of the insults <note>Referring to the rejection and crucifixion of Jesus.</note> offered to Him. For the **"Daughter of Zion"**—this was the system of worship performed upon the mountain called Zion—has been abandoned since the arrival of our Savior, like a **"tent in a vineyard"** and like a **"watchman’s hut in a cucumber field,"** or whatever might be even more desolate than these. <note>original: "σκηνὴ ἐν ἀμπελῶνι... ὀπωροφυλάκιον ἐν σικυηράτῳ" — Isaiah 1:8. These metaphors describe total isolation and abandonment.</note> Foreigners devour their land before their very eyes; at times they are drained by taxes and tributes, and at other times the land that once belonged to the Jewish masses has been made the private property of others. Furthermore, their holy and magnificent metropolis has been laid waste, destroyed by foreign nations. Their cities have been burned with fire, and Jerusalem has truly become a "besieged city."

Yet, because the **Company of the Apostles** and those of Hebrew descent who believed in Christ were preserved from among them—like a fertile seed—they reached out across the whole inhabited world to a multitude of men. They filled every city and place and country with their own spiritual seed, so that from them, the "ears of grain" that grew were the established Churches throughout the world in the name of our Savior. Thus, the divine prophet rightly adds to the threats previously pronounced against them:

> **"Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom, and been made like Gomorrah."** <note>original: "σαβαὼθ" (Sabaoth) — A Hebrew title meaning "of Hosts." Isaiah 1:9.</note>

The holy Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> interprets this clearly by bringing it together in the *Letter to the Romans*:

> **"Isaiah cries out on behalf of Israel: 'Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant shall be saved. For He will finish the work and cut it short in righteousness, because a short work will the Lord make upon the earth.' And as Isaiah said before: 'Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom, and been made like Gomorrah.'"** <note>Romans 9:27-29.</note>

To these words he again adds, saying:

> **"I ask then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he pleads with God against Israel? 'Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars; I alone am left, and they are seeking my life.' But what is the divine response to him? 'I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.' So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace."** <note>Romans 11:1-5.</note>

The argument demonstrates that this prophecy does not point to any other time but to the manifestation of our Savior Jesus Christ. After saying, "Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and Gomorrah," the text first calls the Jewish people "the people of Gomorrah" and their leaders "rulers of Sodom." It then introduces the abolition of the worship according to Moses and the New Covenant announced to all men through our Savior—I mean the **"washing of regeneration"**—and a clearly New Law has been introduced. <note>original: "λουτροῦ παλιγγενεσίας" (loutrou palingenesias) — Titus 3:5. A reference to Christian baptism.</note>

<summary>Eusebius argues that Isaiah's prophecies of desolation were fulfilled during the Roman era after the Jews rejected Christ, but that a "remnant" (the Apostles and early Jewish Christians) survived to spread the Gospel globally.</summary>
<keywords>Eusebius, Isaiah 1, Romans 9, Romans 11, Destruction of Jerusalem, Remnant, Seed, New Covenant, Mosaic Law, Washing of Regeneration</keywords>

Having established the desolation of Judea on the previous page, he now interprets the moral failings of the Jewish leaders and transitions to the promise of a "remnant" through a new spiritual covenant.</meta>

<header>THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 2</header>

...is written in the prophecy concerning such matters. It says: » **"Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom; give ear to the law of God, you people of Gomorrah. What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me?"** <note>original: "ἀκούσατε λόγον κυρίου ἄρχοντες σοδόμων... τί μοι πλῆθος τῶν θυσιῶν ὑμῶν;" — Isaiah 1:10-11.</note> and so forth. These things were specific to their way of life under the Law of Moses; yet the passage seeks a different way for the forgiveness of sins—one through the **salvific washing** <note>original: "σωτηρίου λουτροῦ" — a reference to Christian Baptism.</note> and the way of life proclaimed alongside it. He says: » **"Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean; remove the evil from your souls,"** <note>Isaiah 1:16.</note> and so on. He called them **"rulers of Sodom"** and **"people of Gomorrah"** because of the extremity of their wickedness. He himself explained this in the following verses when he said: » **"For your hands are full of blood."** <note>Isaiah 1:15.</note> 

And again, moving further down, he says: » **"They declared their lawlessness as Sodom did, and made it manifest; woe to their soul, because they have devised an evil counsel against themselves, saying: 'Let us bind the righteous man, for he is troublesome to us.'"** <note>original: "δήσωμεν τὸν δίκαιον, ὅτι δύσχρηστος ἡμῖν ἐστίν" — Isaiah 3:9-10. This was a common "proof text" for early Christians to argue the Old Testament predicted the arrest of Jesus.</note> Here he most clearly mentions a conspiracy against the blood of a single **Righteous Man**; this was the conspiracy against our Savior Jesus Christ. Because of this act, the punishments previously charged against them came upon them.

-> From the same Isaiah. <-

» **"In that day God shall shine forth in counsel with glory upon the earth, to exalt and to glorify the remnant of Israel in Zion, and the remnant in Jerusalem. All those written for life in Jerusalem shall be called holy."** <note>Isaiah 4:2-3.</note> What this **"remnant of Israel"** might be, the prophet himself clarified by saying: » **"All those written in Jerusalem and called holy."** Now, as for what day this is—the day in which God will glorify and exalt the remnant of Israel and those who are to be called holy and written for life—this will be clear to you if you go back through the entire narrative of this section. 

At the start, as a preface to the whole book, the prophet saw a vision **"concerning Judea and against Jerusalem."** <note>Isaiah 1:1.</note> After enumerating the many impieties of the Jewish nation throughout their history, and after threatening them and speaking of their downfall and the total desolation of Jerusalem, he brings his observation of them to a close, saying: » **"For they shall be like a terebinth tree"** <note>A <term>terebinth</term> is a Mediterranean tree similar to a pistachio; here it represents fading life.</note> **"that has cast off its leaves, and like a garden that has no water. And their strength shall be like a strand of flax, and their works like sparks of fire; the lawless and the sinners shall be burned together, and there shall be no one to quench it."** <note>Isaiah 1:30-31.</note>

Having completed this prophecy against them, he uses a pause. When he begins a second subject—a second theme with its own preface—he uses these words: » **"The word that came to Isaiah the son of Amoz, the prophet, concerning Judea and concerning Jerusalem."** Or, as **Symmachus** <note><term>Symmachus</term> was a late 2nd-century translator who produced a Greek version of the Old Testament that aimed for elegance and clarity.</note> interpreted it: **"on behalf of Judea and on behalf of Jerusalem."** 

See what a great distinction this is! Regarding the very people for whom he previously prophesied gloomy things, he now changes his tone to speak of more favorable things. However, the sequence of what follows would not allow one to say these favorable things are meant for the Jewish nation or for what is called "Israel"—for it contains absolutely nothing good for them—nor is it truly "on behalf of Judea" or "on behalf of Jerusalem" in a literal sense. On the contrary, the text brings countless rebukes and accusations against Israel, and gloomy threats against Jerusalem. Instead, it prophesies the **salvific calling** of all the nations and the knowledge of the God who is over all. Furthermore, it sets forth the manifestation of a **New Mountain** and the revelation of a **House of God** other than the one in Jerusalem. Thus, he who speaks "concerning Judea and Jerusalem" says: » **"It shall come to pass in the last days..."**

He argues that the "remnant" promised in Isaiah refers to the early Christian community and the establishment of a "New Mountain" (the Church) that replaces the old temple system.</summary>

<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

» **"...days, the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, and the house of God shall be upon the peak of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills; and all the nations shall come to it. And many nations shall go and say: 'Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob.'"** <note>original: "ἡμέραις ἐμφανὲς τὸ ὄρος κυρίου..." — Isaiah 2:2-3. Eusebius sees this "mountain" as the Church or the spiritual kingdom of Christ.</note>

Regarding the **nations** <term>nations: (Greek *ethne*) usually refers to the Gentiles or non-Jewish peoples</term>, he prophesies these things in an absolute sense. But listen to what he adds immediately afterward concerning the **Jews**: 

» **"For he has abandoned his people, the house of the God of Jacob; because their land was filled, as in the beginning, with divinations like that of the foreigners, and many foreign children were born to them. Their land was filled with silver and gold, and there was no end to their treasures."** <note>Isaiah 2:6-7.</note>

And even more follows these words, to which he adds: 

» **"And they bowed down to the works of their own fingers, and man bowed down and was humbled, and I will not let them go. And enter into the rocks, and hide yourselves in the earth from the face of the fear of the Lord, and from the face of his glory, when he rises to shatter the earth."** <note>Isaiah 2:8-10, 19. The "shattering of the earth" is interpreted by Eusebius as a specific historical or spiritual judgment.</note>

Through these words, he clearly teaches that there will be a certain **Resurrection** <note>original: "ἀνάστασίν" — while this word often means the Resurrection of Christ, Eusebius here uses the context of God "rising" to suggest a moment of upheaval or judgment.</note> of the Lord, in which the entire land of the Jewish nation will be shattered. For the entire discourse was about them. It is the same with the following verses, through which he says: 

» **"For the Day of the Lord of Hosts shall be against every insulter and proud man, and against everyone who is high and lofty,"** <note>Isaiah 2:12. "Lord of Hosts" (Kyrios Sabaoth) is a title emphasizing God's command over the heavenly armies.</note>

and the words that follow these. Therefore, on this very day—the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, and of the handing down of the promises and the knowledge of God—on this very day, he says: 

» **"The Lord alone shall be exalted, and they shall hide all handmade idols, carrying them into the caves."** <note>Isaiah 2:17-18.</note>

He is all but declaring the **rejection of idols**, which he says will be brought about by the Jews themselves and by all other men after the **manifestation of our Savior** <note>original: "σωτῆρος ἡμῶν ἐπιφάνειαν" — This refers to the First Coming of Christ and the subsequent spread of Christianity.</note>, as they condemn every form of superstition. For on that day, he says:

» **"A man shall cast away his golden and silver abominations which they made to worship vanities."** <note>Isaiah 2:20.</note>

In general, it is likely that these things apply to all humanity because of the future **calling of the nations**. Yet, turning specifically back to the Jewish nation, he adds the following under a single line of thought: 

» **"For behold, the Sovereign Lord of Hosts will take away from Judea and from Jerusalem the strong man and the strong woman, the strength of bread and the strength of water; the giant and the strong man, the warrior and the judge, the prophet and the diviner, the elder and the captain of fifty, the wonderful counselor, the wise architect, and the intelligent hearer."** <note>Isaiah 3:1-3. This list represents the total collapse of the social and spiritual infrastructure of ancient Judah.</note>

And there is more following this. Then, having paused, it becomes clear that the preceding parts of the prophecy were introduced by the words: 

» **"The word that came from the Lord to Isaiah the son of Amoz concerning Judea and concerning Jerusalem."** <note>Isaiah 2:1.</note>

It turns out that these things were said **against** them rather than **on behalf of** <note>original: "κατ’ αὐτῶν ἢ ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν" — Eusebius is noting a linguistic irony: the prophecy is titled "concerning/for" (hyper) Jerusalem, but the content is a declaration of its downfall.</note> them—unless, perhaps, there is a hidden meaning contained in these words. For how could he predict that the prophecies were "for" Judea and "for" Jerusalem when he was about to take away from them the strong man and woman, the strength of bread and water, and all the things that distinguished them of old? And how can the following be "for" them? It says: 

» **"Because Jerusalem and Judea have fallen, and their tongues are joined with lawlessness, being disobedient toward the Lord."** <note>Isaiah 3:8.</note>

But indeed, at this time, it is necessary for the **mountain of the Lord** to be preached to all the nations, and the **house of God** upon the mountain, toward which all the nations come together, saying: 

» **"Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob."**

### PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 2.

The Word <note>Eusebius often uses "the Word" (Logos) to refer to the divine voice speaking through the Prophets.</note>, having employed these accusations against the Jewish nation and having threatened them with the ultimate ends, joins to all these things the words we set out previously. He teaches that although the entire Jewish nation is destined to fall away from **godly piety**, a certain few will be left among them who will not share in the universal ruin of the wicked. On the contrary, as if set apart from the depraved and the lawless, and having received the purity of **piety**, they will be deemed worthy of being recorded by God; they will be called the holy servants of God. By these, he clearly signifies the **apostles**, disciples, and **evangelists** of our Savior, and all the rest who believed in him at the time when their entire nation fell away. The Word hints at these things, saying: 

<margin>"</margin> "In **that day**"—evidently the day in which all the things previously charged concerning the
<margin>"</margin> calling of the **nations** <term>nations: (Greek *ethne*) the Gentiles or non-Jewish peoples</term> and the falling away of the Jews—"God shall shine
<margin>"</margin> **in counsel with glory** upon the earth, to exalt and glorify the **remnant of Israel**.
<margin>"</margin> It shall be, that those left in **Zion** and the **remnant** left in **Jerusalem**, all those
<margin>"</margin> written unto life in **Jerusalem**, shall be called holy." <note>original: "ἅγιοι κληθήσονται" — Isaiah 4:2–3.</note> 

By these words, he reasonably showed that the beginning of the prophecy was spoken concerning Judea and Jerusalem, yet it refers to the **true Jerusalem** and the Judea that is understood spiritually in a corresponding sense, about which we have spoken previously. And if anyone considers the divine power of our Savior's **apostles** and **evangelists**, through whom **"their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world,"** <note>original: "εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν ἐξῆλθεν ὁ φθόγγος αὐτῶν" — Psalm 19:4, famously quoted in Romans 10:18.</note> he will see that all the churches of Christ, from then until now, have their words and teachings in their mouths. They hold the laws of Christ proclaimed through them in the **New Covenant** <term>New Covenant: (Greek *kaine diatheke*) often translated as New Testament</term>. Such a person will testify that the prophecy was not about anything else when it said clearly that "God will exalt **in counsel and with glory** over all the earth, and will glorify the **remnant of Israel**." And so, "those left in Zion and the remnant in Jerusalem, all those written unto life, shall be called holy." 

Instead of the phrase used by the **Seventy** <term>The Seventy: (Greek *Hebdomēkonta*) the Septuagint, the standard Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</term>, "in counsel with glory," **Aquila** and **Theodotion** <note>Two other 2nd-century translators of the Hebrew Bible into Greek, known for their literalism.</note> harmoniously interpreted it as **"into power and glory,"** representing the **power** given by God to the apostles, and the **glory** they possess with God for this reason, according to the verse: **"The Lord will give a word to those who preach the gospel with great power."** <note>Psalm 68:11.</note>

And this is revealed plainly: 

<margin>"</margin> **"Hear with your ears, and you shall not understand; and see with your eyes, and you shall not**
<margin>"</margin> **perceive. For the heart of this people has grown dull, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and**
<margin>"</margin> **they have closed their eyes, lest they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and**
<margin>"</margin> **return, and I should heal them. And I said: 'How long, Lord?' And he said: 'Until the cities are**
<margin>"</margin> **desolate for lack of inhabitants, and the houses for lack of men, and the land shall be left**
<margin>"</margin> **desolate.' And after these things, God will remove the people far away, and those**
<margin>"</margin> **remaining on the earth shall be multiplied."** <note>Isaiah 6:9–12. This passage is central to the early Christian explanation of why many Jews did not accept Jesus.</note>

See here as well who these **remaining** ones on the earth are; while all the rest of the land is left desolate, they alone are said to be multiplied. These would be the disciples of our Savior, who came from the **Hebrews** to all people. Having been left like a **seed**, they brought forth fruit in great abundance: the churches of the **nations** throughout the whole world. Observe how he says that only these remaining ones shall be multiplied—

<summary>Eusebius interprets Isaiah 4 and 6 to argue that while the majority of the Jewish people were spiritually blinded and judged, a "remnant"—the Apostles and early Jewish Christians—was preserved to spread the Gospel and establish the Church among all nations.</summary>

<page-num>47</page-num>
### PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 2

You should understand these things according to a spiritual interpretation <note>original: "μυστικὴν θεωρίαν"—literally a mystical contemplation or allegorical reading</note> as having been fulfilled by the apostles of our Savior. Each of them, in the churches they established through the power of Christ, gathered two sheep—that is, two orders of sheep—into the flock of Christ: one group still being instructed in the basics <note>original: "στοιχειούμενον"—referring to catechumens or those new to the faith</note>, and the other already enlightened through the washing of baptism <note>original: "λουτροῦ πεφωτισμένον"—'enlightened through the bath,' a standard early Christian term for baptism</note>. And besides these, they gathered one heifer <note>original: "δάμαλιν"—a young cow</note>, representing the ecclesiastical authority of the elders, which provides the divine and rational nourishment for the members as if they were infants, yielding from themselves a fertile harvest of milk and honey—the fruit of the spiritual food they labored to produce.

There is no need to explain how the divine Word usually compares the masses of those less perfect in faith to sheep, as all of Scripture teaches this. However, regarding the more perfect leader who cultivates the many in the church, the holy Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> confirmed how he might compare such a person to a laboring ox when he said:
> "Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Or does he say it altogether for our sake?
> It was written for our sake, because the plowman should plow in hope, and
> the thresher thresh in hope of sharing in the crop." <note>1 Corinthians 9:9–10.</note>

But if anyone should stumble at such figurative language <note>original: "τροπολογίαις"—tropes or metaphors</note>, it is time for them to realize that they cannot even consider the mentions of "bees," or "razors," or "beards," or the "hair of the feet" <note>References to Isaiah 7:18–20</note> according to their literal meaning without falling into absurd and inconsistent myths. If it is necessary to accept these things not as irrational but according to spiritual contemplation, it is clear that we shall also receive the following in the same way:
> "On that day the mountains shall depart, and the hills, and the forests, and
> it shall consume from the soul even to the flesh. And he who flees shall be
> as one who flees from a burning flame. And those who are left of them shall
> be a number, and a small child shall write them down. And it shall come to pass
> on that day, the remnant of Israel shall no longer be added to. And the
> survivors of Jacob shall no longer trust in those who did them wrong, but
> they shall trust in God, the Holy One of Israel, in truth; and the remnant
> of Israel shall return to the Mighty God. For though the number of the children
> of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them shall be saved.
> For He is finishing the word and cutting it short in righteousness, because
> God will perform a shortened word in the whole world." <note>Isaiah 10:18–23.</note>

Even here, the prophecy declared that in the fulfillment of the threats, it says, "he who flees shall be as one who flees from a burning flame." And "those who are left of them shall be a number, and a small child shall write them down." By these words, it suggests the rarity of those who would be guarded from the destruction of the threatened ones, and perhaps the desolation of Jerusalem. It says these survivors "shall be a number"—that is, they are easy to count and easy to remember, being few and easily numbered.

Such were those who believed in our Savior and Lord, compared to the entire multitude of the Jewish nation; they were the ones deemed worthy of being "written down" by Him, as the Word indicates by saying, "and a child shall write them." The prophecy previously taught us who this "child" <note>original: "παιδίον"</note> was when it said: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son" <note>Isaiah 7:14</note>, and "before the child knows how to call his father or mother." Since it says here "a child shall write them," it was reasonably stated in the earlier passages: "and it shall be that those left in Zion and the remnant in Jerusalem shall all be called holy, everyone written for life." Just as in those verses they were called "the remnant" and were "written for life," so here, "the survivors of them shall be a number, and a child shall write them." And the remnant of Israel and the survivors of Jacob "shall no longer," it says, "depend on those who wronged them, but they shall trust in God, the Holy One..."

<summary>Eusebius uses allegorical interpretation to argue that the "remnant" mentioned in Isaiah refers to the small number of Jews who converted to Christianity, while the "Child" who records their names is Christ himself. He justifies this non-literal reading by citing St. Paul’s use of agricultural metaphors for church leadership.</summary>
