### EUSEBIUS OF CAESAREA

Israel. And see if it was not by this very confidence that those of the Jews who came to the Gentiles—those disciples and apostles of our Savior chosen from the falling away of Israel—making no account of the "rulers of this age" <note>original: "ἀρχόντων τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου"—a phrase often used by St. Paul to refer to worldly or spiritual powers opposing God</note>, or the rulers of the people of the circumcision <note>The Jewish leadership</note> who of old wronged them, went out into all the nations preaching the Word of Christ. They did this with confidence toward God, since they had trusted the prophecy regarding the Holy God of Israel in truth. For they did not give themselves to this work in a formal way, nor with hypocrisy, but with intensity and with their whole selves. Not only did they go forth from their own land, but they accomplished what was commanded of them. And this very thing again became the "remnant," so to speak, the "seed" of the falling away of Jacob, trusting in the Mighty God.

Indeed, this remnant was made like the multitude of the nations, like the sand of the sea, but it was not according to the "stars of heaven" that it was deemed worthy of the salvation from God. As the Apostle somewhere testified, saying: "Isaiah cries out concerning Israel, 'Even if the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only the remnant will be saved.'" <note>Romans 9:27, quoting Isaiah 10:22</note> For there were two promises given to Abraham regarding those who would descend from him: that they would be as the stars of heaven and as the sand of the sea. The god-loving ones shine like the heavenly luminaries—such as the ancient prophets and the apostles of our Savior, to whom He testified, saying: "You are the light of the world." <note>Matthew 5:14</note> But the earthly and "crawling" <note>original: "χαμαιπετῶν"—literally 'falling on the ground,' referring to those with worldly or base interests</note> ones are likened to the sand of the earth.

Rightly, then, in these passages, the prophetic word—since the great multitude of the sons of Israel had fallen from their dignity and the high-mindedness of virtue, becoming entirely earth-bound—was cast out like the sand of the sea (at which time only their remnant shall be saved). Regarding this remnant, we have already exercised ourselves much <note>meaning: "discussed this topic at length in previous sections"</note>. He says these things shall happen when the Lord himself, shortening and finishing the word <note>original: "συντέμνων καὶ συντελῶν λόγον"—a reference to Romans 9:28, suggesting the Gospel is a concise summary of God's will compared to the complex Mosaic Law</note>, shall do so through the whole inhabited world, clearly presenting the Gospel preaching. In this Gospel, while all the Mosaic ritual—performed in images, symbols, and physical observances—is abolished, the concise word of the Gospel, spread to all people, established the prophecies in truth.

> "And it shall be in that day, the Root of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the nations; 
> in him the nations shall hope, and his rest shall be honor. And it shall be in that 
> day, the Lord shall again show his hand, to be zealous for and to seek the 
> remaining remnant of his people, whoever is left by the Assyrians, and from Egypt, 
> and from Babylonia, and from Ethiopia, and the Elamites, and from the rising of 
> the sun, and from the islands of the sea. And he shall raise a sign for the nations, 
> and shall gather the dispersed of Judah from the four wings of the earth." 
> <note>Isaiah 11:10-12</note>

As we have often said these things would happen on a "notable day"—that is, at the time of the Lord’s manifestation—bringing together by reason the sequence of the things shown, we have demonstrated that they refer to the presence of God. At this time, though the whole Jewish nation fell away, the divine words show that some few who are left behind—the remnant—will be saved. Look, for instance, at the text at hand; it presents the day, the time signified by it, and the events following it with great precision. For while prophesying the birth of Christ from the seed of David <note>Jesse was the father of King David</note>, and at the same time the condition of the Jews...

He contrasts the two promises to Abraham, identifying the faithful as "stars" and the unbelieving majority as "sand," while arguing that the Gospel is the "shortened word" that fulfills the law.</summary>

But indeed, in addition to what he demonstrated long ago through the prophets, 
» "the hand of the Lord was added," <note>Isaiah 11:11</note> and to these things, through the perceptible fall of the first 
people, he added that which was lacking for certain more pious ones. These were the mysteries of the New 
Covenant <note>original: "καινῆς διαθήκης μυστήρια"</note>, shown through the hand of the Lord to those left behind from the people. 
But he also speaks of the "zealots" as the "remnant left behind of the people." In agreement with this, 
Aquila and Theodotion <note>Famous 2nd-century translators of the Hebrew Bible into Greek</note> say, "which he shall possess," and "what my people have left me," which 
is left behind from the Assyrians and from the rest of the enemy nations. You might see this 
"remnant of the people" as that which he calls a "sign for the nations." Clearly, through them, 
the Lord displays his own sign among all the nations. And he shall gather through 
him "the lost of Israel, and the dispersed of Judah, from the four 
wings of the earth" <note>Isaiah 11:12; commonly translated as "the four corners of the earth"</note> because through Christ the God, through whom the proclamations of his Apostles 
were sent out, he calls those who were saved "the lost" and "those set 
apart from Christ" in the mind of Israel and Judah. It is the custom of Holy Scripture to show the 
true Israel of souls to God. Just as, conversely, for those with a very foul and wicked disposition 
within the body of Israel, it causes them to be called "Sodom and the people of Gomorrah." That 
remnant, therefore, "according to the election of grace," <note>A reference to Romans 11:5</note> and that which is called in the prophecy the 
"remnant left of the people," announced the sign of the Lord to all the nations, 
and having drawn such souls of the nations from every side to the house of the Lord, 
he gathered one people for God, which even now continues to be assembled from the four wings of the earth 
by the power of Christ. These are the very ones from among the lost of the 
Jewish nation who were added as disciples and apostles of our Savior; though they happened to be from 
different tribes, they were deemed worthy of one calling, one grace, and one Holy Spirit. 
They shall cast away all the "jealousy" which the tribes of the Hebrew nation formerly had toward them, 
as the prophecy says. Having been prepared to think the same things and 
with the same mind, they "plunder" and "take captive" the souls of men from everywhere—not only from the 
mainland, but clearly also from the islands—leading them 
» "into the obedience of Christ." <note>2 Corinthians 10:5</note> Following the oracle, we shall say: "And they 
» shall fly in the ships of strangers, plundering the sea together, and those from the 
» rising of the sun." <note>Isaiah 11:14</note> And you shall examine the rest of the prophecy accordingly, 
testing each word for yourself. First, reject the inconsistent and lowly interpretation of the literal 
text; then, understand the "mind of the Spirit" <note>original: "διάνοιαν τοῦ πνεύματος"</note> as the Spirit of 
God himself suggests you perceive it. For our time does not permit 
us to linger longer on these passages, as we are hurried to complete the proposed thesis.

» "And I will command evils upon the whole world, and their sins upon the ungodly, 
» and I will destroy the insolence of the lawless, and I will humble the insolence of the proud, and those 
» who are left behind shall be more precious than unrefined gold, and a man shall be more precious

very clearly presents the "scarcity" of those who will be saved in the time of the destruction of the ungodly, 
so that there is no room for the suspicion that everyone—without distinction—from the circumcision 
(that is, the great nation of the Jews) will obtain the promises of God.

...[afflic]tion. <note>original: "χιαν." This appears to be the end of a word from the previous page, likely "θλίψιν" (affliction).</note>

> And it shall be in that day that the glory of Jacob shall fail, and the rich parts of his glory shall be shaken. And it shall be as if one should gather standing grain, and reap the grain of the ears. And it shall be as if one should gather ears in a firm valley, and a stalk should be left in it. Or as two or three berries of an olive tree are left on the top of a high branch, or four or five are left on their branches. Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: In that day, a man shall trust in his Maker; and his eyes shall look to the Holy One of Israel, and they shall not trust in their altars, nor in the works of their hands which their fingers have made. <note>Isaiah 17:4–8</note>

Through these words, the "glory of Israel" is clearly prophesied to be destroyed, along with all their abundance. It is said that only a few of them, countable like the "few berries" left on a plant mentioned by Isaiah, shall remain. And these would be those from among them who have believed in our Lord. Following what was said about them, it is prophesied that the whole race of men will turn away from the error of idols and come to know the God of Israel.

> Hear, O islands, you who are forsaken and in pain, hear what I have heard from the Lord of Sabaoth; the God of Israel has declared it to us. <note>Isaiah 21:10 (LXX version). "Sabaoth" means "of hosts."</note>

Observe how here, too, he did not call everyone from the <term>circumcision</term> <note>The Jewish people, physically marked by the covenant</note> to this secret hearing, but only those whom he names "forsaken and in pain." Such were those who, according to the <term>Apostle</term> <note>Paul</note>, groan and lament the wickedness of human life.

> The high ones of the earth mourned, and the earth was defiled because of those who dwell in it. For this reason, those who dwell on the earth shall be poor, and few men shall be left. <note>Isaiah 24:4–6</note>

In these verses, after threatening those from the people of the circumcision who were proven guilty of profaning the Law and the Covenant of God with the punishments decreed for them, he prophesies that a few men from among them would be left. These would be what is called by the Apostle "the remnant according to the election of grace." <note>A reference to Romans 11:5</note>

> Deserted cities shall be left, and the houses that are forsaken shall perish. All these things shall be in the earth in the midst of the nations, in the way that if one should glean an olive tree, so shall they glean them. And when the vintage shall cease, these shall cry out with a voice. But those left on the earth shall rejoice together in the glory of the Lord. <note>Isaiah 24:12–14</note>

Here again, only those "left behind" are said to rejoice, while all the rest are handed over to the things foretold.

> The crown of pride shall be trampled underfoot, the hirelings of Ephraim. <note>Ephraim often represents the rebellious northern kingdom of Israel.</note> And the fading flower of the hope of glory on the top of the high mountain shall be like an early fig; he who sees it, before he takes it into his hand, will desire to swallow it. In that day, the Lord shall be the crown of hope, woven of glory for the remnant of His people. For they shall be left in a spirit of judgment. <note>Isaiah 28:3–5</note>

And here, he prophesies that the Lord will be a "crown of hope and glory" for the "remnant of the people"—not for the whole mass of the nation, but only for those signified by the "remnant." He calls the holy ones among the remnant of the people a crown, while naming the others the "crown of pride" and "hirelings of Ephraim."

> "And those who have been left behind in Judea shall strike root downward and produce seed upward; for out of Jerusalem shall go forth those who are saved, and out of Mount Zion. The zeal of the Lord of Sabaoth <note>Sabaoth is a Hebrew title meaning "of hosts" or "of armies."</note> will accomplish these things." <note>Isaiah 37:31–32</note>

He prophesies that those left from the Jewish nation according to the "election of grace" will strike root below and produce seed above, most clearly representing the "election" of our Savior’s apostles and disciples. For these, being the remnant from the <term>circumcision</term> <note>The Jewish people, physically marked by the covenant of Abraham.</note>, cast the roots of their teaching down into the earth, so as to root it firmly throughout the whole world. Conversely, he commanded the seed and the fruit to be carried upward toward the heavenly promises. These same individuals, left from the Jewish nation and saved while the rest perished, are the only ones called "saved." The zeal of the Lord did all this. For to provoke the ungodly of the circumcision to jealousy, the zeal of the Lord chose these men and made it clear to the others: *And I will provoke them to jealousy with those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will anger them.* <note>Deuteronomy 32:21</note>

> "Thus says the Lord: In the same way that a grape-stone is found in the cluster, and they say, 'Do not destroy it, for the Lord's blessing is in it,' so will I do for the sake of him who serves me. For his sake I will not destroy them all; and I will bring forth the seed from Jacob and from Judah, and it shall inherit my holy mountain. And my chosen ones and my servants shall inherit it and dwell there. And there shall be in the thicket <note>original: "δρυμῷ" — often used for a forest or wooded pasture, here symbolizing the nations.</note> a fold for flocks, and the Valley of Achor shall be a place of rest for the herds of my people who have sought me. But you who have forsaken me, and forget my holy mountain, and prepare a table for Fortune, and fill a mixed drink for the Demon—I will deliver you to the sword. You shall all fall in the slaughter, because I called you and you did not obey; you did evil before me and chose what I did not desire." <note>Isaiah 65:8–12</note>

After a short gap in these verses, the Word says again that it will produce a seed from Jacob and fulfill the promise; and that the "chosen" are those who will dwell in the "thicket"—naming the calling of the nations <note>The Gentiles.</note> in this way. In this calling, the "chosen of the Lord" and those who are like <note>original: "δικῶς" — the scribe likely intended "δίκην" (in the manner of/like).</note> the "seed" would be the apostles and disciples of our Savior themselves. All the rest have been abandoned to the aforementioned threats. The Word shows most clearly that God's promises do not reach the whole Jewish nation by chance, but only the named "seed" and those called the "chosen of God," since *many are called, but few are chosen.* The Word then prophesies that a new and fresh name will be given to these people, saying to the ungodly:

> "For your name shall be left as a loathing for my chosen, and the Lord shall destroy you. But to those who serve me, a new name shall be called." <note>Isaiah 65:15</note>

What then would this "new name" be, which was unknown to the ancients, other than the "Christian" name, derived from the title of our Savior Jesus Christ and blessed throughout the whole world?

I will surely receive the remnant of Israel. I will set them together..." <note>Micah 2:12</note>

<page-num>53</page-num>

## PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 2

...their rejection. In harmony with the passages previously set forth from Isaiah, Micah also declares that God will not simply receive everyone, but only those he calls the "remnant" <note>original: *kataleipois*—those left behind or preserved.</note>. For just as in Isaiah the portion taken from them was called a "seed," so now he calls those helped by Him a "drop." This refers to the choir of the Apostles, who are like a "drop" produced from the otherwise seedless Jewish nation. From this drop, all those throughout the inhabited world who have recognized the Christ of God and accepted His teaching have been deemed worthy of the blessed assembly, having been beautified by their redemption from their enemies.

> "And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, though you are few among the thousands of Judah, out of you shall come forth for me one who is to be a ruler in Israel; and his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity. Therefore he shall give them up until the time that she who is in labor has given birth, and the remnant of his brothers shall return." <note>Micah 5:2-3</note>

And after a few words he adds:

> "And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the Gentiles, in the midst of many peoples, like dew falling from the Lord, and like lambs upon the grass, so that no one may gather them, nor any son of man resist. And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the Gentiles, in the midst of many peoples, like a lion among the beasts of the forest, and like a young lion among the flocks of sheep; who, when he passes through, separates and snatches away, and there is no one to deliver. Your hand shall be lifted up over those who afflict you, and all your enemies shall be utterly destroyed." <note>Micah 5:7-9</note>

Nothing could be clearer than these words, which proclaim the very birth of the Savior in Bethlehem, His eternal existence <note>original: *ousiōsin*—substantial being or essence.</note>, the labor of the Virgin, and the calling of His apostles and disciples. They also speak of the proclamation concerning Christ announced through them across the entire world. For while the Word <note>The *Logos*, or the Son of God.</note> reveals a ruler coming forth from Bethlehem whose "goings forth" are "from the days of eternity," and who is to be born of the Holy Virgin, he says that not all those of the <term>circumcision</term> <note>The Jewish people.</note> shall be saved, but only the "remnant" along with them. To these, Jacob shall serve as a "portion," through whom all the nations shall be refreshed like dew. For he says:

> "The remnant of Jacob shall be among the nations like dew falling from the Lord, and like lambs upon the grass."

Instead of this, **Aquila** <note>A 2nd-century translator known for a very literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> rendered it: "and like droplets upon the herb." **Theodotion** <note>Another early translator whose version of Daniel became more popular than the original Greek Septuagint.</note>, however, translated it as: "and like a snow-shower upon the grass." And again: "so that no one may gather them, nor any son of man resist." Theodotion says: "lest a son of man should stumble," that is, one who is not a "son of man" <note>Eusebius is likely playing on the title "Son of Man" as a divine figure versus a mere human.</note>, and who does not place his faith in a mere son of man. And Aquila says: "who will not wait for a man, and will not expect sons of men." By this, it is shown that the entire hope of the Apostles of our Savior was not in a "son of man" <note>A mere human being.</note>, but in their Savior and Lord—that is, the very Word of God. 

Following this, he adds:

> "And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like a lion among the beasts of the forest, and like a young lion among the flocks of sheep; who, when he passes through, separates and snatches away, and there is no one to deliver."

Through these words, I believe the boldness and the fearless nature of the Apostolic preaching is revealed. For like a roaring lion in the forest of the nations, and falling upon the flocks of human sheep, they separated the worthy from the unworthy and brought them under the Word of Christ. To Him, the following words are addressed: "Your hand shall be lifted up over those who afflict you."

...your enemies shall be destroyed. This is something that can be perceived with our very eyes. For one must remember how many of those who oppressed the Word of Christ <note>The "Word of Christ" refers here to the early Christian message and its followers.</note>, and who even now continue to wage war against it, have been removed, while the Word has prevailed and become greater than all. ->From Zephaniah.<-

"For then I will change the tongue of the peoples <note>original: *glōssan* — language or speech; Eusebius sees this as the universal language of faith replacing diverse pagan tongues.</note>, for the sake of the name of the Lord, that all may serve Him under a single yoke. From the ends of the rivers of Ethiopia I will receive those who supplicate me. In the dispersion, they shall bring sacrifices to me. In that day you shall not be put to shame for all your practices in which you acted impiously against me. For then I will take away from you the cheap insults of your pride, and you shall no longer continue to boast upon my holy mountain. And I will leave in you a people gentle and humble. For they shall graze and lie down, and there shall be no one to make them afraid." <note>Zephaniah 3:9-13</note>

In these verses, the Lord has promised to leave behind a gentle and humble people; he clearly means no other than those who have believed in His Christ, as the others gained no benefit. And again, he signifies that help would be given to the remnant of Israel alone, alongside the calling of the rest of the nations, as he indicated in the introductory parts of the prophecy.

Zechariah prophesies these things after the return from Babylon, foretelling the final siege of the people by the Romans. On that occasion, while the whole Jewish nation was delivered up to their enemies, he says that only the "remnant" of the people would be saved, enigmatically referring to the Apostles of our Savior.

>> Thus I will judge you, says the Lord, and I will bring you under my rod, and I will bring you in by the number of my covenant, and I will choose out from among you those who have revolted and the ungodly. But indeed, I have shown that the divine oracles did not simply or indiscriminately promise good things to everyone from the Jewish nation—to the wicked and godly alike—but only to a rare few of them who could be counted by number. These were either those from among them who believed in our Savior and Lord, or those who were justified before His coming. I believe I have sufficiently demonstrated that the divine promises were not fulfilled indiscriminately for all Jews, and that the words of the prophets apply no more to them than to those from the nations <note>The "Gentiles" or non-Jewish peoples.</note> who have accepted the Christ of God. 

How the meaning of the divine promises will be established at the proper time, we shall see. These points have been necessarily collected by me to refute those of the circumcision <note>A common early Christian term for the Jewish people.</note> who arrogantly boast that the Christ would visit them alone and not all of humanity, and also to provide proof of our own reasonable diligence concerning their scriptures. 

Through my previous work, <note>Referring to Book 1 of the *Demonstratio Evangelica*.</note> I have also established the reason why we do not <term>Judaize</term> <note>To "Judaize" meant for Christians to follow the Mosaic Law, such as dietary restrictions and circumcision.</note> even though we delight in their prophetic writings. Furthermore, I have discussed there, as far as was possible, the nature of the life proclaimed through Christ to all the nations, and the antiquity of the character of the Gospel way of life. <note>Eusebius argued that Christianity was not a "new" religion, but a return to the "ancient" religion of the Patriarchs like Abraham, who lived before the Law of Moses.</note> 

Since these matters have been surveyed beforehand, it is finally time to touch upon more secret matters: those concerning the <term>mystic economy</term> <note>original: μυστικῆς οἰκονομίας (*mystikēs oikonomias*). In this context, "Economy" refers to God’s administration or plan for human salvation.</note> regarding our Savior and Lord, Jesus the Christ of God. Through this study, we might learn why He made His appearance to all men *now*, and not before this; and what was the cause for Him not beginning the calling of the nations long ago, but only recently and after a long age; as well as whatever other matters belong to the secret theology concerning Him. 

Therefore, let us now consider the matters regarding His <term>Incarnation</term> <note>original: ἐνανθρωπήσεως (*enanthrōpēseōs*), literally "becoming human."</note>, but first starting from another point of the argument as if addressing unbelievers, while calling upon the Word of God Himself to be our helper.

->The following are contained in the third book of the *Proof of the Gospel* concerning our Savior.<-

1. How the Hebrew prophets proclaimed the Gospel.

3. How we shall be redeemed in response to those who assume an error has occurred <note>This refers to those who doubted the reality or purpose of Christ's human life and incarnation.</note>.

5. That His disciples did not invent stories, but bore witness in truth to the wondrous deeds performed by Him.

7. How the power of divine virtue surrounding Him is perceived by truth-seekers through its very cooperation.

### Preface.

<image-desc>Large ornamental drop cap letter T within a square frame, decorated with architectural elements and scrolling vine motifs.</image-desc>
THE introductory matters for the *Proof of the Gospel* <note>original: *euangelikē apodeixis*</note> having been sufficiently worked through by me, and the character of our Savior’s gospel teaching having been demonstrated, and the reason having been given why we rejected the Jewish laws while still embracing their sacred words—declining to live according to their customs—and furthermore, since the prophetic scriptures among them have been shown to support us, having long ago mentioned the future of our calling through Christ (a calling we claim as our own and not something foreign to us); it is now a good time to enter into the main subject and begin the fulfillment of our promise. What are these matters but the "economy" <term>economy: (Greek: *oikonomia*) refers to God's "management" or "plan" for the world, specifically the way the Divine Word took on human form to interact with humanity.</term> of Jesus, the Christ of God, according to His human nature? This includes the teaching of the Hebrew prophets regarding the theology of His person, and the predictions concerning His appearance among men—which we shall immediately demonstrate apply to Him alone, based on the clear evidence of the results. But first, we must necessarily consider how the prophets anticipated the very memory of the "Gospel" in relation to the Christ.

### PROOF OF THE GOSPEL Book 3. 59

Because it was beneficial for the nations to have sufficient knowledge and piety for their lives, it was fitting that God should foretell through an oracle that He would raise up another prophet from the Jews for the nations—one who would in no way fall short of the same divine arrangement <term>original: *oikonomia* — God's plan for the salvation and management of the world</term> as Moses himself. God spoke this word to him:
> » "I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you, and I will put 
> » my word in his mouth, and he shall speak to them whatever I command him. And 
> » the man who will not listen to his words, whatever that prophet shall speak in 
> » my name, I will take vengeance upon him." <note>Deuteronomy 18:18–19</note>

And Moses himself, interpreting the word of God to the 
> » people, says: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers 
> » like me; you shall listen to him in accordance with everything you asked of 
> » the Lord God at Horeb on the day of the assembly." <note>Deuteronomy 18:15–16</note>

Now then, did the prophets after Moses—say, Isaiah, or Jeremiah, or Ezekiel, or Daniel, or any other of the Twelve <note>The "Twelve" refers to the Minor Prophets of the Old Testament</note>—stand as a lawgiver comparable to Moses? Not at all. Did any of them accomplish deeds similar to those of Moses? One cannot say so. Indeed, each of them, from their own beginning to their end, referred their listeners back to Moses. They would rebuke the people for their transgressions of the Mosaic Law, urging nothing else but the piety established by law under Moses. Moses certainly does not speak of any of these as being "like" him in a specific, definite sense. To whom, then, does the oracle foretell a prophet like Moses shall be, if not specifically to our Savior and Lord, Jesus the Christ? 

We might examine how this was spoken. Moses was the first to lead the Jewish nation. Finding them devoted to the polytheistic error of the Egyptians, he was the first to turn them away from it, forbidding idolatry with inescapable punishments. He was the first to proclaim to them the theology of the "monarchy of God," <note>original: *monarchias* — the concept of a single supreme divine ruler</note> commanding them to worship only the Creator and Maker of all things. Having also introduced a way of life pleasing to God and setting rules for them, he was proven to be the first and only lawgiver of a pious society <note>original: *politeias* — can refer to both a "way of life" and the "civil order" of a community</note>. 

In a manner similar to Moses—and much more excellently—Jesus Christ was heralded to the remaining nations on the grounds of teaching piety, and was the first throughout the entire world under the sun to stop idolatry. He was the first to set before all men the knowledge and piety of God, the King of All, and was proven to be the first introducer and lawgiver of new ways of life and conduct suitable for the God-fearing. Furthermore, the other matters concerning the creation of the world and the immortality of the soul, and whatever other philosophical doctrines Moses first handed down to the Jewish nation—these Jesus Christ was the first to proclaim more worthily of God to the rest of the nations through his disciples. Thus, while Moses was rightly proclaimed the first and only lawgiver of piety for the Jews, Jesus Christ was established for all the nations, according to the prophecy concerning him which said:
> » "Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them; let the nations know that they are 
> » but men." <note>Psalm 9:20 (in the Septuagint numbering)</note>

Again, Moses confirmed the piety established by him through miraculous works and wonders. Likewise, Christ, employing recorded miracles to inspire faith in those who saw them, established the new teachings of his Gospel instruction. Again, Moses transferred the Jewish nation from the bitter slavery under the Egyptians into freedom. And Jesus...

## PROOF OF THE GOSPEL Book 3. 60

Christ called back the <gloss>the</gloss> race of all men into freedom from the impious "Egyptian" idolatry <note>Eusebius uses "Egyptian" metaphorically here to refer to the state of spiritual slavery to demons, mirroring Israel's physical slavery in Egypt.</note> under the evil demons. Again, Moses promised a holy land and a blessed life within it to those who would keep <gloss>the</gloss> law. In the same way, Jesus the Christ says:
> "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth." <note>Matthew 5:5</note>

He was promising a much better land indeed—one that is immaterial <note>original: *aülon* — non-physical or spiritual</note> and beloved of God. This was not the land in Judea, for that land is in no way different from the rest of the world; rather, he promised the heavenly land that belongs to God-loving souls, to those who successfully live <gloss>the</gloss> life announced by him. This he announced even more clearly as the "Kingdom of Heaven" to those he called blessed. 

Furthermore, consider next the sights that were brought about by <gloss>the</gloss> power of our Savior, which was greater than that of Moses, <gloss>and</gloss> those things which <gloss>the</gloss> Moses commanded. For example: Moses fasted for forty consecutive days, as the Scripture bears witness, saying:
> " <gloss>And</gloss> Moses was there before the Lord for forty days and forty nights; he ate no bread <gloss>and</gloss> drank no water." <note>Exodus 34:28</note>

In like manner, Jesus also did this. At least, it is written:
> "And he was led into the wilderness for forty days, being tempted by the devil; and he ate nothing in those days." <note>Luke 4:1-2</note>

And again, Moses provided food for the people in the wilderness. <gloss>And</gloss> the Scripture says:
> "Behold, I give you bread from <gloss>the</gloss> heaven." <note>Exodus 16:4</note>

And a little later:

And our Savior and Lord likewise says to his own disciples:
> "Why do you reason among yourselves, O you of little faith, because you have no bread? Nor the seven loaves of the four thousand, and how many baskets you took up?" <note>Matthew 16:8-10</note>

Again, Moses passed through the middle of the sea <gloss>and</gloss> led <gloss>the</gloss> people. <gloss>And</gloss> the Scripture says:

Likewise, <gloss>and</gloss> <gloss>the</gloss> even more divine sight: Jesus the Christ, by God’s power, walked upon <gloss>the</gloss> sea, and he made Peter walk upon it as well. It is written:

Again, Moses fixed <gloss>the</gloss> sea by a strong south wind. At least the Scripture says:
> "Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the Lord drove back the sea by a strong south wind." 

And it follows: "the waves were frozen in the midst of <gloss>the</gloss> sea." <note>Exodus 15:8</note> In like manner, but in a much greater way, our Savior rebuked the wind and the sea, <gloss>and</gloss> there was a great calm. Again, when Moses was descending from the mountain, his face was seen to be full of glory. It is written:

His garments became white as light. Again, Moses cleansed a leper. For it is written, "and behold, Miriam was leprous, white as snow." Miriam was Moses' sister, struck with leprosy after questioning his authority.</note> In the same way, but with a greater power of authority, the Christ of God—when a leper approached him and said, "If you are willing, you can make me clean"—replied, "I am willing; be cleansed." And his leprosy was cleansed. Again, Moses said the Law had been written by the finger of God. For it is written: "And he gave to Moses, when he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, stone tablets written by the finger of God." <note>Exodus 31:18</note> And in the Book of Exodus, the magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God." <note>Exodus 8:19</note> In the same way, the Christ of God said to the Pharisees: "But if I cast out demons by the finger of God..." <note>Luke 11:20. In the same way, but much better, our Savior sent out twelve apostles to visit all the nations. Again, Moses gave the law saying: "You shall not murder, you shall not steal, you shall not swear falsely." But the Savior, intensifying <gloss>extending</gloss> the law, forbids not only murdering but even being angry. Instead of merely not committing adultery, he advises not even to look at a woman with a lustful <term>unrestrained</term> desire. Instead of not stealing, he commands one to bestow their own possessions upon the needy. And while Moses forbade swearing falsely, the Savior legislates from the beginning not to swear at all. And should you not also extend your reasoning to the proof that Moses and our Savior and Lord performed things that were similar and close to one another? Before these things, it is good to collect these points at your leisure. For they say that no one knew the death of Moses, nor his burial place. In the same way, no one knew our Savior’s transformation into divinity after his return to life. If, then, through all these points no one else is clearly shown, but only our Savior has accomplished things similar to Moses, you must look henceforth to him alone, and to no other, to apply the prophecy of Moses. Through this prophecy, God promised to present one like him, saying: "I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, just like you, and I will put my word in his mouth. And he shall speak to them whatever I command him. And the man who will not listen to his words, whatever that prophet shall speak in my name, I will take vengeance on him." <note>Deuteronomy 18:18-19</note> Moses himself, interpreting the voice of God to the people, said: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers. You shall listen to him in everything, whatever the Lord your God shall say to you."

Eusebius emphasizes that Christ’s rule extends beyond the Jewish people to all people groups.</note>, confessing him as Lord because of his divine power. For he alone is confessed as Lord and Savior by the lips and through the most genuine faith of countless multitudes from all the nations. What then is to hinder us from saying that he is the one who was prophesied?

Furthermore, Moses did not predict these things carelessly, nor did he set the prophecy in an infinite or undefined time. Rather, he very accurately described the outcome of the prophecies within fixed times. Listen to what he prophesies about this:
<margin>"</margin>“A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes for whom it is reserved; and he shall be the expectation of the nations.” <note>Genesis 49:10. This is the "Scepter of Judah" prophecy, traditionally seen as a timeline for the Messiah's arrival.</note> Through these words, he declares that there would be a continuous succession of leaders and rulers from the Jewish nation until the arrival of the one who is expected. When their own rulers failed, then the promised one would be present. 

By “Judah” here, he does not name the specific tribe; rather, since the whole Jewish nation was called by the title of the royal tribe of Judah in later times—just as they are called “Jews” today—he very wonderfully and prophetically named the whole nation after Judah, just as we also address them as Jews. 

Then he says that rulers and leaders would not fail from their nation until the prophesied one arrived. But when this one appeared, the Jewish rule would immediately be dissolved, and he himself would be the "expectation," not of the Jews, but of the nations. You could not apply this to any of the other prophets, but only to our Savior and Lord. For as soon as he appeared among men, the Jewish kingdom was destroyed. Immediately, the succession of their ancestral rulers failed, as did those who led according to their own laws, for Augustus was then the first monarch of the Romans, and Herod—a man of a foreign race—was appointed as their king. <note>Herod the Great was an Idumean, not a Judean, marking the end of native Jewish kingship.</note> While those rulers failed, he who is the "expectation of the nations" throughout the whole world has appeared according to the divine prophecy. Even until now, all those from every nation who have believed in him place their hope in him as their divine expectation. 

These are the things Moses said, and many others like them, concerning the Christ for our proofs. And Isaiah's words are sister to these...

> » and understanding." <note>Isaiah 11:1–2. Jesse was the father of King David; thus the "root of Jesse" signifies the Davidic royal line.</note> And so forth. Then, proceeding in the prophetic manner, he foretells 
the useful transformation—brought about by the Savior's gentle teaching through Christ—of 
the foreign, barbaric, and wild nations, which were once most savage and beastly in their human ways. 
> » He speaks thus: "And the wolf shall feed with the lamb, and the leopard shall rest 
> » with the kid, and the calf and the bull and the lion shall feed together." <note>Isaiah 11:6. Eusebius interprets these animals metaphorically as different types of people or nations being harmonized by the Gospel.</note> And things 
> » similar to these. These things he also interprets clearly through the words that follows, saying: "And there shall be 
> » one arising to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope." <note>Isaiah 11:10.</note>

For clearly, by likening the nations—who acted like wild beasts in their behavior—to irrational livestock and the aforementioned wild animals, he gave them a figurative form. He says that the "one arising from the seed of Jesse" (from whom our Savior and Lord is genealogically descended) is the choice of these nations. Even until now, the nations who believe in him hope in him, in accordance with the prophecy: "And there shall be one arising to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope." And distinguishing this once again by comparing it with the words found in Moses:
> » On the one hand, "There shall be one arising to rule the nations" corresponds to "A man 
> » shall come forth from his seed and shall lord it over many nations." <note>Numbers 24:7.</note> And the phrase "In him 
> » the nations shall hope" corresponds to "He shall be the expectation of the nations." <note>Genesis 49:10.</note> For 
> » though the wording differs, whether it says "In him the nations shall hope" or 
> » "He shall be the expectation of the nations," the meaning is the same.

Again, the passage from Isaiah prophesies these things concerning Christ:
> » "Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul is well-pleased; 
> » he shall bring forth judgment to the nations." And he adds, "Until he sets judgment 
> » upon the earth, and in his name the nations shall hope." <note>Isaiah 42:1, 4.</note>

Now for a second time in these passages, the prophet establishes that the nations hope in Christ—having said above, "In him the nations shall hope," and here, "And in his name the nations shall hope." It was also said to David that indeed one 
> » from the fruit of his body would be raised up. Concerning whom God says next: "He 
> » shall call upon me, 'You are my father'; and I will make him my firstborn." <note>Psalm 89:26–27 (88:27–28 in the Septuagint).</note> And 
> » concerning this one it is said again: "And he shall have dominion from sea to sea, 
> » and from the rivers to the ends of the inhabited world." <note>Psalm 72:8 (71:8 in the Septuagint).</note> And again: "All 
> » the nations shall serve him, and all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him." <note>Psalm 72:11, 17.</note>

And again, a certain specific place for the prophesied birth is foretold by Micah, who says: 
> » "And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, you are few to be among the thousands 
> » of Judah. From you shall come forth for me a leader, who shall shepherd 
> » my people Israel. And his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity." <note>Micah 5:2. This is the classic prophecy identifying Bethlehem as the birthplace of the Messiah.</note>

It is acknowledged by all that Christ was born in Bethlehem, so that even the cave is shown to the locals there and to those who arrive from foreign lands as travelers. <note>The "Cave of the Nativity" in Bethlehem was already a well-known pilgrimage site by Eusebius's time (4th century AD).</note> This place, where the prophecy indicated he would be born, was foretold; and Isaiah presents it even more clearly, albeit through riddles, when he says: 
> » "Lord, who has believed our report? and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? 
> » We have announced it before him as a child, as a root in a thirsty land." <note>Isaiah 53:1–2.</note>

Instead of this, Aquila interpreted it thus:
> » "And he shall come up as a suckling before his face; and as a root from a pathless land." 
> » And Theodotion: "And he shall come up as a suckling before him, and as a root in a thirsty land." <note><term>Aquila and Theodotion</term> were famous 2nd-century translators of the Hebrew Bible into Greek. Eusebius often compares their versions to the Septuagint to clarify the meaning of difficult Hebrew terms.</note>

And through these things, the prophet, remembering the arm of the Lord—whoever this arm of God was...

# EUSEBIUS

discourse. "Before him," he says, "he was brought up like a nursing child and a helpless one, and like a root from a pathless land." <note>Isaiah 53:2. While modern translations often say "tender plant," Eusebius follows a Greek version that emphasizes the infancy and vulnerability of the "nursing child."</note> Now, the "nursing child" and the "one who nurses" clearly point to the birth of Christ. And the "pathless and thirsty land" refers to the Virgin who gave birth to him—one whom no man had approached—from whom this blessed root came forth, being from a "pathless" source: the infant who is nurtured and nursed. 

But these things the prophet hinted at in a veiled manner. The same prophet interprets the meaning more openly elsewhere when he says: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name 'God-with-us.'" <note>Isaiah 7:14.</note> For this is how "Immanuel" is translated. Such things concerning the coming of Christ to humanity were studied long ago among the Hebrews. 

Do they then describe the one prophesied as some famous ruler or tyrant, or perhaps one of those powerful men of great worldly status? One cannot say so, for no such person appeared; rather, they foretold that he would appear in life exactly as he did, falling short in no way from the truth. After Isaiah said, "We have announced before him as a child, as a root in a thirsty land," he immediately adds, saying:

> » "He has no form nor glory. And we saw him, and he had no form nor beauty. 
> » And his form was dishonored and lacking beyond the sons of men. A man 
> » under stripes and knowing how to bear infirmity; for his face is turned away; 
> » he was dishonored and not esteemed. This man bears our sins and suffers 
> » pain for us. And we esteemed him to be in toil, and under stripes, and in 
> » affliction. But he was wounded because of our sins, and he has been 
> » weakened because of our lawlessness. The discipline of our peace was upon 
> » him; by his bruise we were healed. We all like sheep have gone astray. 
> » And the Lord delivered him up for our sins, and he, because of his 
> » affliction, does not open his mouth. Like a sheep he was led to the 
> » slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he does not open 
> » his mouth. Who shall declare his generation? For his life is taken away 
> » from the earth." <note>Isaiah 53:2–8. This is the "Song of the Suffering Servant," which early Christians universally applied to the Passion of Jesus.</note> And so forth.

Through these words, he signifies that Christ, though himself existing apart from all wrongdoing, would take upon himself the sins on behalf of humanity. Therefore, he will suffer for our falls and feel pain for us, but not for himself. And if he is "wounded" by blasphemous words, this too will be the work of our sins; for he has been weakened because of our sins so that we—once he has taken up our transgressions and the wounds of our own wickedness—might be healed by his "bruise." For indeed, the sinless one will suffer because of the causes found among men. 

The wonderful prophet, not even shrinking back when the Jews were darkened by his death, explicitly rebukes them, lamenting this directly and saying: "Because of the lawlessness of my people he was led to death." <note>Isaiah 53:8.</note> Then, since immediately and not long after the audacity against Christ, total destruction came upon them when they were besieged by the Romans, he does not overlook this either, but adds: "And I will give the wicked in exchange for his burial, and the rich in exchange for his death." <note>Isaiah 53:9. Eusebius interprets the "wicked" and "rich" as the Jewish leadership and the Roman conquerors involved in the turmoil following the crucifixion.</note> 

It would have been enough to conclude the prophecy with these things, if nothing more were to happen after the death of Christ...

### THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 3, 65

...but saw him. Since he was not yet about to return and live again <note>original: "παλινοσεῖν καὶ ἀναβιοῦν" — a phrase suggesting a literal coming back to life or resurrection.</note> immediately after his death or his burial, the prophet places this next in order, adding:

> <margin>>></margin> "The Lord wills to cleanse him of his wound. If you give an offering for sin, your 
> <margin>>></margin> soul shall see a long-lived seed. And the Lord wills to take away from the pain 
> <margin>>></margin> of his soul, to show him light." <note>Isaiah 53:10-11. Eusebius follows the Septuagint version, which emphasizes the "cleansing" and "light" rather than the "crushing" found in modern translations based on the Hebrew text.</note>

Having said above that he was "under a wound" and "one who knows how to bear infirmity," the prophet says that after his death and burial, the Lord "wills to cleanse him of his wound." And how shall this be? "If you give," he says, "an offering for sin, your soul shall see a long-lived seed." Does this "seeing the long-lived seed of Christ" follow for everyone, or only for those who have confessed and brought their gifts for sins to God? For only the souls of these people shall see the "long-lived seed" of Christ—that is, either his eternal life after death, or his "long-lived" Word <note>original: "Logos"</note> which was sown throughout the whole inhabited world and is destined to endure forever.

Again, after saying, "And we accounted him to be in pain," and mentioning his slaughter and death, the prophet says:

> <margin>>></margin> "And the Lord wills to take away from the pain of his soul, to show him light."

Since, therefore, the Lord, the God of all things, has willed to cleanse him of his wound and to show him light, and having willed it, He will certainly provide what He has willed. For nothing that He wills has failed to come to pass. He willed to cleanse him and show him light; therefore, He did these things. Having cleansed him, He showed him light. And since He willed it, and by willing it He took away the pain of his soul and showed him light, the prophet logically connects the next part, saying:

> <margin>>></margin> "Because of this, he himself shall inherit many, and he shall divide the 
> <margin>>></margin> spoils of the strong." <note>Isaiah 53:12.</note>

Then, finally, he mentions the inheritance of Christ in harmony with the second Psalm, through which the Word <note>The "Logos" or divine voice speaking through the scripture.</note>—after naming the conspiracy of those who plotted against him in the passage:

> <margin>>></margin> "The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers were gathered together 
> <margin>>></margin> against the Lord and against his Christ" 

—immediately adds:

> <margin>>></margin> "The Lord said to me: You are my son, today I have begotten you. Ask of me, 
> <margin>>></margin> and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the 
> <margin>>></margin> earth for your possession." <note>Psalm 2:2, 7-8.</note>

The prophet Isaiah here refers to these same nations when he says, "Because of this, he himself shall inherit many," and adds, "and he shall divide the spoils of the strong." For he rescued the subject souls from the opposing powers <note>Refers to demons or spiritual forces of darkness that Eusebius believed ruled the pagan nations.</note> that of old ruled the nations, and distributed them like "spoils" to his own disciples. This is why Isaiah says of him:

> <margin>>></margin> "And they shall rejoice before you in the manner of those who divide 
> <margin>>></margin> spoils." <note>Isaiah 9:3.</note>

And the Psalmist says:

> <margin>>></margin> "The Lord will give a word to those who preach the gospel with great power. 
> <margin>>></margin> The King of the powers of the beloved [shall grant them] to divide the 
> <margin>>></margin> spoils for the beauty of the house." <note>Psalm 68:11-12 (LXX 67:12-13).</note>

It is reasonable, therefore, that here also it says concerning Christ, "Because of this, he himself shall inherit many, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong." And for what reason does this happen? He teaches this next, saying:

> <margin>>></margin> "Because his soul was delivered unto death, and he was numbered 
> <margin>>></margin> among the lawless, and he himself bore the sins of many, and because 
> <margin>>></margin> of their sins he was delivered." <note>Isaiah 53:12.</note>

For in return for these things, the Father rewards him for his obedience and his endurance, and has granted him the things set forth. For he became obedient to the Father even unto death. Therefore "he shall inherit many"—not before, but only after "his soul was delivered unto death" and "he was numbered among the lawless" would this happen. For because of these things, it is said he shall inherit...

# EUSEBIUS

<meta>catchword: to us</meta>

...was thought by many, and "he should divide the spoils of the strong." I think it is beyond doubt that the **resurrection from the dead of the Savior** <note>original: "ἀνάστασιν τοῦ σωτῆρος" — *anastasis* (resurrection) of the *Soter* (Savior).</note> is being proclaimed through these words. For how else is it possible to conceive of one who was "led like a sheep to the slaughter," handed over to death because of the "lawlessness of the Jewish people," and after that lawlessness was "accounted with the lawless" and "delivered to burial"—and then to see him "ruling as Lord," and "light being seen from him," and "inheriting many things," while "spoils are distributed to his own"? 

And in another way, concerning his **return to life after death**, David says somewhere, prophesying in the person of Christ: 
> <margin>></margin> "You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you let your Holy One see 
> <margin>></margin> corruption." <note>Psalm 16:10. Eusebius uses this to prove that Christ's body would not decay in the grave.</note>
And again: 
> <margin>></margin> "Lord, you brought up my soul from Hades; you saved me 
> <margin>></margin> from those going down into the pit." <note>Psalm 30:3.</note>
And again: 
> <margin>></margin> "The one who lifts me up from the gates of 
death, that I may declare all your praises." <note>Psalm 9:13–14.</note>

I believe that no one, even among the most narrow-minded, can look these facts in the face and deny them. Furthermore, the conclusion of Isaiah’s prophecy proclaims the good news to the soul that was formerly "barren and deserted by God," or rather, it proclaims the **Church from the nations** <note>original: "ἐκκλησίαν ἐξ ἐθνῶν" — referring to the global community of non-Jewish believers.</note>, following the vision already described. Since Christ endured all things for her sake, it is natural that after the prophecies concerning him, the prophet adds:

> <margin>></margin> "Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and shout, you who are 
> <margin>></margin> not in labor. For the children of the desolate are more numerous than those 
> <margin>></margin> of her who has a husband. For the Lord said: Enlarge the place of your 
> <margin>></margin> tent and your curtains; fix them, do not spare. Lengthen your ropes 
> <margin>></margin> and strengthen your stakes; spread out further to the right and to 
> <margin>></margin> the left, and your offspring shall inherit the nations." <note>Isaiah 54:1–3. In early Christian thought, the "barren woman" was a symbol for the Gentile world which had no relationship with God before Christ, but then became more fruitful than Israel (the woman "with a husband").</note>

Here, the Word proclaims the good news of the **Church from the nations** spread throughout the whole **inhabited world** <term>oikoumene (οἰκουμένη): the civilized world, often referring to the Roman Empire, but used here to mean the global reach of the Church.</term>, stretching from the rising of the sun to its setting, making this very clear through the phrase, "and your offspring shall inherit the nations." While these points require more detailed work, let these brief remarks suffice for us at present. However, you may be able to collect these same points at your leisure regarding the subject at hand. 

The entire treatise of the *Proof of the Gospel* will, in due time, hand down and interpret each point. For now, regarding the voices and prophecies of the prophets concerning his **appearance in the flesh**, and how they spoke to all men of the coming good things, the things already said are sufficient. They foretold the arrival of a certain Prophet and a Lawgiver of piety similar to Moses; they prophesied his family, his tribe, the place from which he would come, the time at which he would arrive, his birth, his death, his return to life, and his rule over all nations.

All these things have been established, and will be established even more through what follows, as having been fulfilled solely by our Savior and Lord. These things from the **sacred oracles** <note>original: "ἱερῶν λογίων" — referring to the Holy Scriptures.</note> will stand firm for those who believe in them. But for those who disbelieve the prophetic writings, let us meet them with a specific approach, making our inquiry for a time as if concerning a **common man** <note>original: "ἀνδρὸς κοινοῦ" — Eusebius shifts tactics: he will now argue that even if one views Jesus only as a human, his deeds are so superior that they prove a divine nature.</note> similar to others. Thus, when he appears far better by an incomparable excellence and superior to all those who have ever been famous among men, we may then, in due time, take up the facts concerning his **divine nature**, demonstrating from clear evidence that his powers were not, after all, of human nature. Following these things, we will also discuss his **theology** <note>original: "θεολογίας" — here meaning the study or doctrine of Christ's divinity.</note> as far as is possible for us...

He then transitions to a new rhetorical strategy: proving Jesus's divinity by first examining his life as a "common man" to show his incomparable superiority over all other historical figures.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from page 66, Eusebius concludes his messianic interpretation of the "Suffering Servant" in Isaiah 53, transitioning from the scriptural proofs of Christ’s resurrection to a logical defense against those who accuse Jesus of being a mere magician or a deceptive charlatan.</meta>

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL Book 3, 67

...what we promised we would do, we shall now perform. Since most of the unbelievers even to this day never cease calling him a **sorcerer** <note>original: "γόητα" — *goēta*, a term implying one who uses illicit magic or "low" sorcery to trick people.</note> and a **deceiver** <note>original: "πλάνον" — *planon*, a wanderer or charlatan who leads the masses astray.</note>, and heap upon him countless other daily blasphemies, let us come forward and answer them. We shall offer our proofs not from our own resources, but from his own words and the very teaching that he handed down.

## Against those who suppose the Christ of God to have been a deceiver.

<margin>3</margin> I would ask them: has any other such "deceiver" ever been recorded in history who became a teacher of such gentleness and moderation, of self-control and every other virtue for those he "deceived"? Is it right to call by such names one who did not even permit his followers to look upon women with lustful desire? Is he a deceiver who taught his students to practice the highest form of **detachment** <note>original: "ἀπάθειαν" — *apatheia*, a philosophical state of being undisturbed by passions.</note>, to share their possessions with those in need, and to always be persuaded toward philanthropy and social cooperation? Is he a deceiver who draws people away from the noisy, crowded, and turbulent habits of the world, teaching them instead to embrace only the leisure found in the **divine oracles** <note>The scriptures.</note>? He who turns people away from every lie and commands them to honor the truth above all things? He who forbids even the taking of an oath, let alone a false one—for he said: 
» "Let your **Yes** be **Yes**, and your **No** be **No**"? <note>Matthew 5:37.</note>
» How could such a one be justly named a deceiver? Why must I 
say more now? From what has been said previously, it is clear what kind of way of life was sown by him. From this, any lover of truth would confess that he was not a deceiver, but someone truly divine—an introducer of a truly divine piety, not of common or worldly philosophy. He alone renewed the tradition of the ancient, God-loving **Hebrews**, which had somehow perished from among men, and he demonstrated it not to a small few, but spread it across the entire world through his own writings <note>The Gospels.</note> regarding the present subject. Through him, for the first time, those under the stars—men across the whole inhabited world—were shown the God-loving way of life of those thousands around **Abraham**, a way of life now emulated not only by our own people but also by **barbarians** <note>Non-Greeks.</note>. But such are the more moral aspects of his teaching. Let us then consider whether the "deceiver" was ever convicted regarding the most essential of his doctrines. Was it not recorded that he himself was devoted to the one King and God, the Creator of heaven and earth and the whole universe, and that he led his students to Him? Even to this day, the words of his teaching lead every mind—even the unrefined—upward to the highest God, transcending all visible nature. Is he then a "deceiver" because he does not allow for the worship of many gods, but leads us away from that to the highest and only true theology? On this point there is a witness, a friend to their own arguments <note>Eusebius is likely referring to the philosopher Porphyry, an opponent of Christianity who nevertheless respected the antiquity of the Hebrews.</note>, who spoke not long ago concerning the God-loving Hebrews, as has been shown before in the *Preparation for the Gospel*. From these sources, even the children of the modern philosophers have greatly benefited, and they pride themselves on these doctrines. Indeed, the most learned among them, relying on the oracles of their own gods, mention the Hebrews in this way:

> » The **Chaldeans** alone obtained wisdom, and the **Hebrews** as well, 
> » Worshiping in purity the **self-begotten King**, God. 

He named these same people "Chaldeans" because of Abraham, since he was a Chaldean by race.

# EUSEBIUS

<margin>
Eusebius
on the

...as has been recorded. If, then, the ancient children of the Hebrews—who are most highly attested for their wisdom regarding the **divine oracles** <note>The Hebrew Scriptures/Old Testament.</note>—attributed their worship solely to the one Creator God of all, what more is needed than to acknowledge this man [Jesus] as the wonderful teacher of true piety? He brought forward and spread to all mankind, by an invisible and divine power, the things known of old only to the God-beloved Hebrews. He did this so that no longer, as in ancient times, did only a few easily numbered individuals hold right opinions about God; instead, ten thousand multitudes of **barbarians** <note>A term used by Greeks to describe non-Greeks; here it refers to all the nations of the Roman Empire and beyond.</note> (who were once most savage), as well as learned and distinguished men, have been educated to practice piety in the same way as the ancient prophets and righteous men, solely through his power. 

But let us consider the third point: he did not use weapons, nor did he command that the Divine be honored with cattle sacrifices or the slaughter of animal victims, nor with blood and fire, nor with vapors rising from the earth. He considered these things lowly, earthy, and foreign to an immortal nature. He judged that the most pleasing and sweet sacrifice to God is the fulfillment of his own commandments. Through these, people are purified in body and soul, and are adorned with clear light and pious doctrines. By these means, he taught them to imitate and resemble God, saying precisely: "Be perfect, just as your Father is perfect" <note>Matthew 5:48.</note>. If indeed these things were accepted as true, let it not be displeasing to their own teachers [the pagan philosophers] who, as is likely, have drawn even more abundantly from us, since they came after the teaching delivered to us by our Savior, as they have acknowledged in writing:

## That nothing of the earth should be offered as incense or sacrifice to the God over all; from Porphyry’s "On Abstinence from Animal Food."

> To the God over all, as a certain wise man said, we should neither sacrifice nor name anything perceptible to the senses. For there is nothing material that is not immediately "impure" to the Immaterial. Therefore, even the spoken word is not appropriate for him, nor even the inner word when it is defiled by a passion of the soul. But through pure silence and pure thoughts about him, we shall worship him. We must therefore be joined and made like him, offering our own conduct as a holy sacrifice to God. This same conduct is both a hymn and our salvation in the state of **virtuous detachment** <note>original: "ἀπαθείᾳ" — *apatheia*, a philosophical state of being undisturbed by passions or suffering.</note> of the soul. This sacrifice is perfected through the contemplation of God.

## More on the same subject, from the theology of Apollonius of Tyana.

> In this way, then, one might best provide proper care for the Divine, and obtain his favor and kindness beyond any other man: if to God—whom we call the One, separate from all, after whom the others must be recognized—one sacrifices nothing at all, nor kindles fire, nor names him by any sensible thing. For he needs nothing, not even from those "better" than we are <note>Likely referring to the lesser gods or daemons.</note>; nor is there anything the earth produces, or any plant it grows, or any animal it feeds, or even the air, that does not have some stain. One should always use toward him only the **better word** <note>original: "κρείττονι λόγῳ" — referring to the silent, rational prayer of the mind.</note>, I mean the one that does not go through the mouth, but asks for good things from the most beautiful of beings through the most beautiful part of ourselves. This is the **intellect** <note>original: "νοῦς" — *nous*, the highest faculty of the human mind capable of direct spiritual perception.</note>, which requires no physical organ. If then these things...

<meta>The previous page concluded with Eusebius arguing that Jesus was a teacher of true piety who empowered even the "barbarous" nations to live like the ancient Hebrew prophets. ### THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 3, PAGE 69

...as is confessed by the worthy philosophers and theologians who came before us. How then could he be a deceiver, he who delivered to his disciples the ability to perform not only through words, but through deeds that far surpassed words? Through these deeds, they serve the Divine through the living **Right Reason** <note>original: "orthon logon" — here referring to the Logos, or the rational principle of God personified in Christ.</note>. Regarding how and with what reasoning the ancient Hebrews are recorded to have offered sacrifices, we have already dealt with this in the first book of the present work, and we shall be satisfied with those explanations.

Now, in addition to what we have examined, we have come to know through the teachings of Christ that the world is mortal, and that the heaven itself—the sun, the moon, and the stars—are the works of God. We have learned that one must not worship these things, but rather their Creator. We must consider whether we have been "deceived" in being taught to think in this manner. Indeed, the children of the Hebrews (to whom this reasoning belongs) and the most illustrious of the philosophers would agree with these same points, declaring that the heaven, the sun, moon, stars, and the entire universe were brought into being by the Maker of all things. Furthermore, they taught us to expect a "consummation" and a transformation of this universe into something better, following the Hebrew Scriptures in this regard.

Moreover, even **Plato** <note>Eusebius frequently cites Plato's *Timaeus* to show that Greek philosophy at its best agrees with "Hebrew" (Christian) truth.</note> recognized that the heaven, sun, moon, and other stars are of a dissolvable and perishable nature—even if he says they will not actually be dissolved because the One who bound them together does not wish it. Thus, they exist by His will, not by their own nature. 

Jesus taught us to believe that the soul is immortal, in no way similar to that of **irrational animals** <note>original: "alogois zōois" — creatures lacking the 'logos' or rational faculty.</note>, but bearing the images of the powers of God. By educating every "foreigner" and common person to think this way, has he not made those who follow his teachings throughout the whole inhabited world already wiser than those "with raised eyebrows" <note>A common idiom for arrogant or elitist philosophers.</note>? These men declared that the human soul differs in its essence not at all from a gnat, a maggot, or a fly—or even from a snake, a viper, a bear, a leopard, or a pig. They claimed that their own souls, the souls of most "wise" philosophers, differ in no way in their nature and essence from the souls of these beasts.

By continually reminding us of divine courts of justice, and that judgment is no mere "opinion" but a reality, he described inescapable punishments and penalties for the impious, while promising the pious **eternal life** <note>original: "aiōniou zōēs"</note>, the kingdom of heaven, and a blessed existence with God. He did this so they would not wander, but would rather be encouraged to strive for virtue because of the rewards expected by the pious, and to turn away from all wickedness because of the punishments hanging over the ungodly.

Among these doctrines, we have also received the same teaching that there are certain powers after the Supreme God—incorporeal in nature, intellectual, rational, and full of all virtue—who dance around the King of All. Many of these have been sent down even to men under the single saving **economy** <note>original: "oikonomias" — the plan or administration of God for human salvation.</note> of the Father. We were taught to recognize these according to the measure of their worth, while ascribing worshipful honor to the King of All, God, alone.

Furthermore, we have come to know from him that certain hostile powers, enemies to the human race, fly about the air near the earth and dwell with the wicked—powers of demons and evil spirits. He teaches against their leaders, whom men have previously followed. Even though these spirits snatch away for themselves the titles and honors of "gods," because of this "war against God" and their godlessness, they must be turned away from, as we have demonstrated through many proofs in our **Preparation** <note>A reference to Eusebius's companion work, the *Praeparatio Evangelica* (Preparation for the Gospel).</note>.

<summary>Eusebius argues that Jesus’s teachings on the finite nature of the universe and the immortality of the soul align with the best of Greek philosophy (Plato) and Hebrew tradition. He contrasts the Christian view of the rational human soul with the "arrogant" philosophers who equate human souls with those of insects and wild animals.</summary>

# EUSEBIUS

<margin>67.</margin>
These are the sorts of things found in the doctrinal teachings of our Savior, being the holy instructions of men of old who were beloved by God and prophets. If, then, these teachings are venerable, if they are beneficial, if they are philosophical, if they are full of virtue, who would not reasonably label the teacher of these things as truly being the **Son of God**? But let these matters be examined for the time being as they relate to the common nature of humanity, standing as they do as proof of his venerable and life-profiting teaching. Come now, let us also consider his more divine works.

->**Concerning the more divine works of Christ himself.**<-

<margin>37.</margin>
And indeed, let us consider how many images—having been made not for the sake of sensory pastimes—he became the creator of through wondrous works. At one time, he cleansed those with **leprosy** in their bodies by divine power; at another, by the command of his **word** <note>original: "logou" — referring both to his speech and his status as the Divine Word.</note>, he drove out demons from men. At other times, he freely granted healing to those suffering from all kinds of incurable diseases. Once, he said to the **paralytic**, "Arise, take up your bed and walk," and he did what was commanded. At another time, he granted the faculty of sight to the blind. And once, a woman with a **hemorrhage** <note>original: "haimorroousa" — a woman suffering from a chronic discharge of blood.</note>, who had been worn down by her affliction for a long period of years, saw the vast crowds surrounding him. Since they did not allow her to approach and fall at his knees to beg for deliverance from her suffering, she merely touched the very edge of his garment. She was immediately made whole; by taking hold of the hem, she at once took hold of the cure for her ills. She was healthy in an instant, carrying away a supreme example of our Savior’s divine power.

There was also a certain **royal official** <note>original: "basilikos aner" — likely an officer in the service of King Herod.</note> who, falling down before Jesus, immediately received his son back in good health. And another man—though he was a **ruler of the synagogue** <note>original: "archisynagogos"</note> of the Jews—received back his daughter who was already dead. What need is there to mention how another man, already four days dead, was raised by the power of Jesus? Or how he completed a journey across the sea as if upon dry land while his disciples sailed beneath him? And how, when they were tossed by a storm, he rebuked the sea, the waves, and the winds, and how everything—as if silenced by a master’s voice—instantly became still?

When five thousand men followed him, along with a vast multitude of women and children, he satisfied them to the point of fullness from only five loaves of bread. So much was left over that it was enough to fill twelve baskets. Would this not strike one with amazement and reasonably call forth an inquiry into his unutterable power?

Lest my discourse stretch to a great length at present, let his **death** be set above all these things, for it was not like the common death of other men. For he was not destroyed by disease, nor strangled by a noose, nor—in the very end—were his legs cut by iron like other criminals. He underwent no violent end from the human passions that usually kill; rather, he gave up his body to those plotting against him of his own will. He was suspended from the earth, and then, having cried out with a loud voice upon the wood and entrusted his **spirit** to the Father, saying in these very words: "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit," he was thus released. He himself, by his own power, departed from the bonds of the body more easily than...

## PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 3, SECTION 7

[...seen] by his acquaintances, and having been delivered to a proper burial, on the third day he again received life, which he who had previously departed had voluntarily laid down. And he showed himself again in the flesh, in that same body as he was before, to his own disciples. With them, after conversing briefly and spending some time together, he set out on his journey to the heavens—into the ethereal realm and towards the fire <note>referring to the ancient cosmological view of the highest heavens as a place of pure, divine fire</note>—under their very eyes. These are the proofs of the divinity within him. These things we ourselves have wondered at with a sober mind, and we have accepted them with a tested and examined judgment. They have been examined and tested by us through other clear works of revealing words <note>original: "pragmateiōn" — likely referring to Eusebius's other apologetic writings</note>, through which our Lord himself even now is accustomed to reveal small glimpses of his power to those whom he judges worthy. -> Against those who disbelieve the narrative of our Savior's miraculous deeds. <-

<margin>60</margin>
If they should say that our Savior did nothing wonderful from the beginning, nor anything miraculous as his acquaintances testified, let us see if their argument will be persuasive, since they cannot provide the reason why the disciples became his followers and why he was recognized as their teacher. For a teacher promises the instruction of some subject, and disciples, desiring learning, offer and entrust themselves to that teaching. What cause, then, can be given for the disciples' time spent with the Savior and their tireless devotion to him? Of what subjects did they enroll as his students? This is clear, for they surely brought out to others what they had learned from him. And the precept of philosophy which he laid down for them, saying: 
<margin>*</margin> "Do not acquire gold or silver in your belts, nor a pouch

Entrusting themselves to the providence that governs all things, they were to worry about nothing regarding their needs. He also handed down to them things superior to those commanded to the Jews by Moses. For while Moses, as if legislating for those prone to homicide, commanded "do not murder"; and similarly "do not commit adultery" for the most lustful and downward-tending; and again "do not steal" for those most like slaves; it was necessary for the disciples not to be satisfied with these things nor to attend only to the letter of the laws. Rather, he urged them from the center of their soul to cut off the sprouts of vice from the depths of their mind, as if from the roots. He taught them to try to control anger and every shameful desire, or rather, not even to be angry due to an extreme state of passionlessness <note>term: "apatheia" — in Christian and Stoic philosophy, this refers to a state of being unmoved by sinful passions</note> of the soul, nor to look at a woman with unbridled desire. Neither were they to steal, but on the contrary, to give even their own possessions to those in need...
