->words.<- But they were not even to pride themselves on not defrauding others; rather, they were to pride themselves on being defrauded and being led to the slaughter, having chosen to bear such things without remembering the wrong done to them. And why must I gather all the things that he taught and they learned? He taught them to have peace with all others, and to hold to the truth so firmly that they had no need of oaths <note>original: "horkia" — Jesus’s teaching in Matthew 5:34-37 against swearing oaths, advocating for simple "Yes" or "No"</note>, for they were far from committing perjury. He required their character to be so trustworthy that it appeared more faithful than any oath, even unto death; and by this they were distinguished, using truth in their speech. How then is it reasonable to suspect that those who were accustomed to being hearers—and who were already teachers to others, claiming to be disciples of these same things—could have invented the things they testified about their teacher through their actions? Is it plausible to think that they all agreed to lie with one voice, being twelve in number among the elect, and seventy among the rest? It is said that he sent these others out two by two before his face, into every place and region where he himself was about to go. No reason can be found to disbelieve such a great multitude of men who embraced a pious and solemn life, and who disregarded their own private interests above all else—choosing a life of poverty instead of their dearest ones (I mean wives, children, and their ancestral families)—and who carried out their testimony concerning their teacher with one accord, as if they had brought it forth from a single mouth to all mankind. 

This, then, would be the Lord and the Word of the light of truth. But let us also consider the opposite case. For suppose there were a teacher and disciples; and if, as a hypothesis in an argument, the teacher taught none of the things we mentioned before, but the opposite: namely, to break the law, to be impious, to be unjust, to be greedy, to defraud, and whatever other evil might be said. Suppose he urged them to strive to hide all these things, and to conceal their character most shamefully under the pretext of solemn teaching and a public promise of piety. And let us say the disciples followed these things, and things even more wicked than these, because of the "self-taught" nature of vice <note>original: "autodidaktos" — the idea that evil requires no teacher, but is inherent to a corrupt nature</note>. And let them praise their teacher with great, manufactured words, sparing no lying speech; let them describe all these wonders and fabricated miracles so that they themselves might be admired and considered blessed, having been deemed worthy to become disciples of such a man. 

Come then, let us see if it is possible for such a conspiracy to hold together among men of this sort. "Evil is friend to evil," as they say <note>a common Greek proverb, famously cited by Aristotle and Plato</note>, but not to the good. How then, in a multitude of so many men, did this "agreement of the wicked" arise? How did they maintain a unanimous testimony among themselves in all things? How did they maintain this harmony even unto death? One might say that if they were following a sorcerer who made such promises, they themselves were no less sorcerers than their leader. Did they not then know the end that the teacher brought upon himself, or the kind of death he experienced? Why then, even after that most shameful end of his, did they persist—theologizing about him among the dead and choosing to suffer the same things? Who would ever choose such an obvious punishment for no reason? Perhaps he had enticed them while he was still alive and living with them, leading them astray through deception, as one might say. But why is it that after his death—and much more then than before—they honored him when he was dead? For how could he speak to mortals then? And why did they once deny him when the plot against him was being seen? Yet, after his departure from men, they gladly chose to die rather than abandon their good testimony concerning him. If they had been conscious of nothing good in their teacher—neither in his life nor in his teaching—then surely...

# THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 3

...not an action, nor a deed worthy of praise; nor indeed had they been benefited by him in any way, except perhaps <margin>not</margin> wandering in wickedness and deceit. How then did they die so readily, bearing witness to the solemn and glorious things <margin>concerning</margin> concerning him, when it was possible for each of them to live a life free of trouble, and to lead a safe existence at their own hearths with their dearest loved ones? If they were truly wandering deceivers and frauds, how could they consider it desirable to die for another? For they, more than anyone else, would have known accurately that he had been—as someone might say—the cause of no good for them, but rather a teacher of every vice.

For a man who possesses reason and virtue might, for the sake of a good achievement, perhaps even irrationally undergo a glorious death. But a man of a wicked character, being a lover of passion and pleasure, pursuing only his own temporary life and the luxuries available to him, would never choose death over life, nor would he endure punishment for the sake of his own family and friends—let alone for those condemned for their worthlessness.

How then did the disciples of the man we are discussing—if he was indeed a deceiver and a sorcerer, and they were not ignorant of his nature but were themselves ensnared in his souls by an even worse scheme—clearly endure every kind of agony and every form of punishment for their testimony about him? Would this not be contrary to the very nature of wicked men?

Furthermore, pay attention to this: even if they were indeed deceivers and frauds, consider that they were uneducated and entirely "commoners" <note>original: "idiōtai" — meaning laypeople or those without formal rhetorical or philosophical training</note>, or rather, that they were even "barbarians" <note>original: "barbaroi" — in this context, someone whose primary language was not Greek, but Aramaic/Syriac</note>, knowing nothing more than the Syrian language. How then did they go out into the whole inhabited world? By what logic did they dare such a folly? By what power did they succeed in the attempt? 

For it is one thing for rustic men to wander about their own land, deceiving and being deceived, and not keeping silent but proclaiming their business in the cities. But to teach the name of Jesus and his miraculous deeds throughout the countrysides and cities—and for some of them to take the Roman Empire itself and the most imperial city <note>Rome</note> as their portion, while others took Tarsus, others Armenia, others the nation of the Persians, and again others the Scythians; and for some to have already reached the very ends of the inhabited world and arrived at the land of the Indians, and for others to have crossed over the ocean to the islands called Britain—these things I no longer believe to be within the power of man, much less within the power of cheap and common men, and least of all within the power of deceivers and sorcerers.

And having experienced a wicked and perverted teacher, and having witnessed the outcome of his end, what words did they use among themselves to manufacture a consensus about him? For with one mouth they all testified to the cleansing of lepers, the casting out of demons, the raising of the dead, the giving of sight to the blind, and ten thousand other healings of the sick performed by him—and above all, his own return to life after death, which they were the first to see. 

If these things had not happened, and had never even been heard of, how did they witness with one mouth that they had occurred during their own times, remaining faithful to their confession even unto death? Unless perhaps <margin>against him</margin> they formed a conspiracy against him and made a pact with one another to manufacture and lie about things that never happened? And what words is it plausible to say they used in making such a pact, if not something like this:

"Friends, let us testify for this man who just yesterday and the day before was a deceiver and a teacher of wandering, whom we saw before our eyes suffering the ultimate punishment of starvation..." <note>The text cuts off here; Eusebius is using irony to show how absurd a conspiracy to lie would have been given the circumstances of the crucifixion.</note>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s hypothetical argument where he adopts the persona of the Apostles to demonstrate the absurdity of the claim that they conspired to invent the miracles and resurrection of Jesus. ### EUSEBIUS

As for the deceiver <note>original: "πλάστῳ" (plasto) – referring here to Jesus in the hypothetical voice of a skeptic</note>, we know him most accurately, having become initiates of his secret rites. While he appeared solemn to the many, and held a higher reputation among the masses than he deserved, he actually brought nothing great or worthy of resurrection—unless one speaks of his deceitful and treacherous character, and his teaching us crooked things, a pride born entirely of deception. 

Come then, let us give each other our right hands and all together agree to spread a consistent lie to all men. Let us say we saw him granting sight to the blind—which none of us ever witnessed—and providing hearing to the deaf—which no one ever heard—and cleansing lepers and raising the dead. To put it briefly, let us insist that the things we neither saw him do nor heard him say are true and actually happened. 

But since his final end was notorious and his death certain, so that it cannot be hidden, let us shamelessly dissolve this fact as well. Let us testify quite impudently that he was with us all after rising from the dead, and that he shared in our usual meals and food. Let us all maintain this shamelessness and unshakability; let our madness last until death. 

For what is so strange about dying for nothing? Why should it grieve us to receive lashes and tortures upon our bodies for the sake of no benefit? If we must experience even prisons, and if dishonor and insults are shown us for no reason, let us already be prepared for this. Let us all lie together in harmony and invent things for no one’s benefit—not for ours, as the deceivers, nor even for his, the one about whom we spread these lies. 

Let us spread this lie not only to our fellow countrymen but, going forth to all men, let us fill the entire inhabited world <term>The "oikoumene," referring to the known Greco-Roman world.</term> with our agreement concerning him. From this point on, let us legislate for all nations, contrary to the age-old opinions held by them concerning their ancestral gods. Let us command the Romans first of all not to worship those whom their forefathers considered gods. 

Let us also persuade Greece, and proclaim this to their wise men; let us not even let the Egyptians go, but let us wage war against their gods too. Let us not even spare the ancestral laws of Moses <note>Eusebius is highlighting the absurdity of the Apostles—who were Jewish—suddenly deciding to overturn their own ancient Law for a lie.</note> but ruin them. Let us set up one thing—the death of our teacher—as something fearsome, and hand down the fame concerning gods to all men that has existed since the beginning, not with words or speeches, but through the power of our crucified teacher. 

Let us go even to the wild tongue of the barbarians and overturn everything among them. Let none of us lack zeal. For the struggle we dare is no small thing, since no ordinary prizes await us, but rather the punishments likely to come from the laws of each nation: specifically bonds, tortures, prisons, fire, sword, crosses, and wild beasts. We must be most eager for these and meet these evils head-on, having our teacher as our example. 

For what could be more beautiful than to become enemies of both gods and men for no reason, and never to enjoy anything pleasant, nor benefit from our dearest ones, nor obtain wealth, nor possess the hope of any good thing at all, but to wander and be struck down in vain and for nothing? This, indeed, is what is truly profitable, and it brings us into direct opposition with all nations, who have held their gods from the beginning...

### THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 3, 75

...to wage war against all things commonly agreed upon. To claim that the one they saw with their own eyes as their teacher is God, and to herald him as the Son of God, for whose sake they are ready to die, despite having learned nothing true or beneficial from him. On this account, he should be hymned even more—if he did you no good at all! We must do everything to glorify his name, endure every insult and punishment, and accept every form of death for the sake of absolutely nothing true. For perhaps truth is an evil thing, and the liar receives praise through evil.

Therefore let us say that he even raised the dead, and cleansed lepers, and drove out demons, and was the author of other miraculous works <note>original: "παραδόξων ἔργων" (paradoxōn ergōn) – deeds contrary to expectation</note>—not because we were conscious of him doing these things, but inventing everything for ourselves, and deceiving whomever we could. Even if no one else is persuaded, we ourselves, who composed these things, have voted for these webs of deceit against ourselves. 

Is this plausible? Is it consistent with the logic of truth that common men and unlearned <term>idiotai <gloss>In this context, the Greek "idiotai" refers to common people or those without professional training, rather than the modern derogatory sense.</gloss></term> could fashion such a conspiracy and then go out and overcome the Roman Empire? Or that human nature—which possesses an inherent love of life—would endure a voluntary death under persecution for the sake of nothing? Or that those who were discipled by our Savior reached such an extreme of madness that, despite seeing nothing miraculous done by him, they collectively fashioned all these stories together, and then, having composed false words about him, were ready to face death for them?

But what do you say? That they never expected to suffer death for their testimony concerning Jesus? And that they proceeded fearlessly to the preaching about him? But it was not likely that men, who had persuaded everyone of everything, would introduce him as a manifest God to Romans, Greeks, and barbarians alike. 

Yet the history concerning them clearly shows that after their teacher's death, certain people arrested them by official order; they first put them in prison, then released them with orders to speak to no one in the name of Jesus. Finding them afterward announcing the things concerning him publicly to the multitude, they seized them and scourged them, rebuking them for their teaching. And Peter, answering them once more, said:

<margin>»</margin> "It is necessary to obey God rather than men." <note>Acts 5:29</note> After this, Stephen was taken away and killed by stoning, having spoken boldly before the Jewish multitude. At that time, no ordinary persecution arose against those who preached the name of Jesus. And again, Herod, the king of the Jews, killed James the brother of John with the sword, and the same man bound Peter in chains, as it is written in the *Acts of the Apostles*. 

And while these men suffered such things, the remaining disciples held unsparingly to Jesus, proclaiming him and his miraculous works even more eagerly to everyone. In addition to these, James the brother of the Lord—whom those living in Jerusalem long ago called "the Just" <note>original: "δίκαιον" (dikaion)</note> because of the excellence of his virtue—when asked by the high priests and teachers of the Jewish nation what opinion he held concerning Christ, and then answering that he was the Son of God, was pelted with stones by them. And Peter was crucified head-downwards in Rome, and Paul was beheaded, and John was exiled to an island. And while they suffered these things, none of the rest abandoned their purpose, but having prayed, they themselves set out for the same fate as those mentioned before...

# EUSEBIUS

...to face divine punishment for their impiety, yet they bore witness with even greater boldness to Jesus and the works he performed. Indeed, if these were lies they had fabricated by common agreement, it would be a wonder how such a large number of people maintained their consistency in these fictions even unto death. Not one of them, fearing the fate of those who went before, abandoned the group or confessed the plot to others, exposing their secret scheme. Even the one who dared to betray him while he was still alive brought justice upon himself by his own hand <note>original: "αὐτοχειρίᾳ" (autocheiria) – by his own hand, referring to the suicide of Judas Iscariot.</note>.

And is it not equally astonishing that common, uneducated men—who knew neither how to speak nor hear anything beyond their native tongue—could even dream of venturing out to journey among all the nations, let alone succeed in what they set out to do? Consider also how remarkable it is that not a single one of them, in any place, ever gave a conflicting account regarding the deeds of Jesus. 

For if in all disputed matters—whether in courts of law or in common arguments—a dispute is settled by the agreement of witnesses, and since it is a law that "every word shall be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses" <note>original: "δύο ἢ τριῶν μαρτύρων συνίστασθαι πᾶν ῥῆμα" – Eusebius quotes the legal standard found in Deuteronomy 19:15.</note>, how could the truth not be established here? There were twelve apostles, seventy disciples, and a vast multitude besides these, all showing a miraculous consistency and bearing witness to the things done by Jesus—and not without effort, but through the endurance of tortures, every kind of outrage, and death. These things were further confirmed by God, who even now and for all time establishes the message they proclaimed.

Let us grant these points for a moment, as an exercise in exploring an impossible position. Suppose someone were to claim the opposite: that Jesus was a teacher of intemperate words, injustice, greed, and every kind of debauchery, and that his disciples, having been taught such things, became the most wicked of men. This would be as absurd as if someone were to look at the laws of Moses—which say, "Do not murder," "Do not commit adultery," "Do not steal," "Do not bear false witness"—and then slander him by claiming he only said these things ironically as a pretense, while in fact urging his followers to murder, commit adultery, and act contrary to his own laws while only pretending to live a solemn life. 

In this way, one could also slander the instructions of the Greek philosophers, their disciplined lives, and all their teachings, by claiming they wrote virtuous things but lived hypocritically. Indeed, one could slander almost all ancient histories in this manner, rejecting the truth within them and accepting the exact opposite of what is stated. But just as no person of sound mind would hesitate to call such a critic "mad," the same applies to the words and teachings of the Savior. If someone tries to distort the truth and assign to him a character opposite to what he taught, they are surely in error. 

However, let this point be granted as a hypothesis, so that the sheer impossibility of the opposing argument may be fully exposed. Having cleared this up, let us return to the truth of the Holy Scriptures and observe the actual character of Jesus's disciples. From the very start, how could they...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s defense of the Apostles’ character. Following the previous page’s argument that a conspiracy of lies would have crumbled under pressure, he now examines the actual lifestyle and moral rigor of the Apostles to show they were motivated by truth and piety, not worldly gain or deception.</meta>

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 3, Ch. 4

...or should we judge them worthy of every possible acceptance? It is admitted they were unlearned men, and "laymen" <note>original: "ἰδιώτας" (idiotas) – in this context, meaning people without formal rhetorical or philosophical training, commoners.</note> in their speech; yet they were pious and had fallen in love with philosophical teaching. They embraced a life of rigorous endurance and toil through fasts, abstinence from wine and meat, and a deep humbling of the body through prayers and supplications to God. This was achieved even earlier through extreme self-control and the purity of both body and soul. How could one not marvel at them, who out of an abundance of philosophy <note>Early Christian writers often used the word "philosophy" to describe the disciplined, ascetic lifestyle of monks and apostles.</note> renounced even their lawful wives, and were neither mastered by natural pleasure nor enslaved by the desire for children and descendants? Indeed, they did not long for mortal things, but reached out for the immortal.

And who would not be struck with amazement at their lack of greed? This can be judged not merely from their lack of food, but from their teacher himself, who forbade the possession of gold and silver, and legislated that one's belongings should not increase even to the point of a second tunic. When one hears these commands, they seem a heavy burden at first. Yet these men proved the word by their deeds. For example, when someone once asked for help near a certain lame man—at a time when people were seeking food due to a lack of laborers—Peter, having nothing to give, confessed that he was free from all possession of gold and silver, saying: "Silver and gold I do not have; but what I have, I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk." <note>original: "ἀργύριον καὶ χρυσίον οὐχ ὑπάρχει μοι..." – Eusebius is quoting the miracle of Peter at the Beautiful Gate from Acts 3:6.</note>

<margin>»</margin>Furthermore, when their teacher announced grim prospects for them, as he did when he said to them: "In the
<margin>»</margin>world you will have tribulation," and again: "You will weep and lament, but the world will re-
<margin>»</margin>joice" <note>Eusebius quotes John 16:33 and 16:20.</note>, is it not clear how they were being led toward the truth and deep discipline? They did not
<margin>»</margin>flee the exercises of the soul, nor did they pursue those things that lead to pleasure. And regarding the teacher: he did not charm them with deception by placing their private interests outside the reality of what was to come. Instead, by prophesying the things that would happen as other and true words, he instilled in them the choice of a way of life according to his standards. 

Such were the predictions regarding the things that would happen to them because of his name—which he foretold most clearly—that they would be brought before governors and reach even unto kings, and would endure various punishments, not for any evil deed or any other reasonable cause, but for this one thing: his name. This is something that can be seen in action even to this day, making one marvel at the prediction. For the confession of the name of "Jesus" usually inflames the anger of the rulers. Even if a person who confesses Christ is found guilty of no evil deed, they punish and torture him just the same because of the name, as if he were more dangerous than all those who commit unholy acts. Yet if they should swear off the title and deny being disciples of Christ, they are immediately set free, even if they are burdened with ten thousand crimes.

And why should I gather further memories to attempt a description of the character of the Apostles of our Savior, when what has been said is enough to prove the point? To these things I will add one more, and then I will move on to the other type of slanderers. The Apostle Matthew did not start his life in a dignified profession, but was one of those occupied with tax collecting and greed <note>original: "τελωνίας" (telonias) – Tax collectors were often despised in the Roman world for corruption and collaboration with the occupying forces.</note>. Not one of the other Evangelists revealed this—neither his fellow-disciple John, nor Luke, nor Mark. But Matthew himself reveals the life he led, and becomes his own accuser...

,, "...on the earth, it shall be bound in the heavens; and whatever you loose on the earth, it shall be loosed
,, in the heavens." <note>original: "ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς... ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς" – referring to Matthew 16:19, the "Keys of the Kingdom" promised to Peter.</note> Although these things were said to Peter by Jesus, Mark
,, mentions none of them, because Peter—as is likely—did not even report these things in his own
,, teachings. But look at what he does say: when Jesus asked him, Peter
,, answered and said, "You are the Christ." And he strictly warned them that they should tell no one about him.
,, These things Peter reasonably thought should be passed over in silence. For this reason, Mark also omitted
,, them, yet he proclaimed the facts regarding Peter’s denial to all people. For he also wept 
,, bitterly over it. Indeed, he wrote that Mark records these things about him: "And as
,, Peter was in the courtyard, one of the servant girls of the high priest came to him, and
,, seeing him warming himself, she looked at him and said, 'You also were with Jesus of Nazareth.'
,, But he denied it, saying, 'I neither know nor understand what you are saying.' And he went out into the
,, gateway, and a rooster crowed. And the servant girl, seeing him again, began to say to those
,, standing by, 'This man is one of them.' But he denied it again. And after a little while, those standing 
,, by said to Peter again, 'Truly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean.' But he began to
,, curse and to swear, 'I do not know this man of whom you speak.' And immediately, for the
,, second time, a rooster crowed." Mark writes these things; and Peter testifies these things about 
,, himself. For it is said that everything in Mark is a record <note>original: "ἀπομνημονεύματα" (apomnēmoneumata) – memoirs or recollections. Early church tradition held that Mark wrote his Gospel based on Peter's preaching.</note> of the discourses of Peter.

So then, those who decline to record things that would seem to bring them good fame, but instead write down for all ages the accusations against themselves—recounting the charges against the very men who were taught by them, which no one else would have known in later times if they had not proclaimed it with their own voice—how could they not be rightly admitted to have been far removed from all self-love and falsehood? Should they not be seen as providing clear and vivid evidence of a character that loves the truth? 

As for those who think that such men fabricated lies or who try to blaspheme them as deceivers, how could they not appear ridiculous? They show themselves to be friends of envy and malice <note>original: "φθόνου καὶ βασκανίας" (phthonou kai baskanias)</note>, but enemies of truth itself. For they take men who were so far from wickedness and so simple in character—as demonstrated by their sincere spirit in their own writings—and they suppose them to be certain crafty and clever sophists who fabricated things that did not happen. They suggest these men sought to please their own teachers by attributing to them things that did not belong to them.

As it seems to me, one must either believe everything said by the disciples of Jesus, or if we must distrust these men alone, we must also distrust all those who have ever lived, whether among the Greeks or the barbarians, who have written down memoirs of the successful deeds performed by certain good men of their times. If it is reasonable to believe others, but only to distrust these men, then is the envy not obvious? 

Or did those who supposedly lied about their Teacher, handing down in their writings things that never happened, also lie about his sufferings? I mean, why would they invent the betrayal of a disciple, the accusation of the slanderers, the mockery and ridicule of the judges, the insults, the blows to his face, the scourging of his back, and the crown of thorns placed upon him for dishonor? Why would they invent the purple robe draped on him in the fashion of a cloak, and finally, that he himself carried the trophy of the cross; that he was nailed to it, his hands and feet pierced, given vinegar to drink, and struck on the cheek...

<summary>Eusebius argues that the Apostles must be telling the truth because they recorded their own shames (like Peter's denial) and the humiliating details of Jesus's crucifixion, which no "liar" seeking fame would ever invent.</summary>

-> ### EVANGELICAL DEMONSTRATION Book 3 <-

[80]

...and being reproached by those who saw him; but surely these things, and all that accompany them, must have been fabricated by these same disciples. Or is it necessary to believe them in these matters as telling the absolute truth, but in the more glorious and solemn matters to disbelieve them? And from where does this inconsistent judgment concerning them arise? For to say that the same men speak the truth in one breath and lie in another is nothing else than to say opposite things about the same people at the same time.

How then is the proof of these things found? For if their purpose was to fabricate, and to adorn their teacher with false words, they would never have written down the reproaches against him, which revealed to those coming after them that he was indeed unrecognized, and was distressed and troubled in his soul, and that they themselves abandoned him and fled. Or they would not have written that the first and most chosen of them, his disciple Peter, without even being tortured, but merely from the threat of a servant-girl, denied him three times.

For even if others were saying these things, those whose only aim was to grant the most solemn honors to their teacher should surely have denied them. But if they appear to be lovers of truth in the gloomy <note>original: "σκυθρωποῖς" (skythropois) – literally 'sour-faced' or 'sullen,' used here to describe the tragic or humiliating parts of the Passion narrative.</note> narratives, they should be considered all the more truthful in the glorious ones. For those who have once chosen to lie ought rather to have avoided the painful details or passed them over in silence; their companions, being unable to speak of things kept secret, would never have known the use of things that did not lead to their own reputation for virtue.

Why did they not lie, and say that the one who betrayed him with a kiss, having dared to show the signal of betrayal, was immediately struck down? Or that the one who dared to strike him—it is likely the enemy's right hand would have withered? Or that the high priest, for cursing him and joining with the slanderers against him, might have been blinded in his sight? Why did they not all lie and say that nothing gloomy truly happened to him? Instead, they could have said he was invisible, mocking their tribunal, and that those plotting against him were led astray by a phantom <note>Eusebius is here mocking the "Docetic" view—a heresy that claimed Jesus only *seemed* to suffer and didn't have a real body.</note>, thinking they were acting against him while he was not actually present.

If they were going to fabricate, would it not have been more solemn to claim that for such a worker of deeds, there was no way for death to touch him? Would they not write that nothing human or mortal happened to him, but that immediately, having awed all things by his power, he made his return to the heavens with our glory? If they had done so, those who believed their other narratives would surely have believed these things as well. But since they did not forge the truth in the repulsive and gloomy parts, how can they not be worthy, in the remaining matters where they testified to his wonders, to be placed beyond all base suspicion?

The testimony of these men concerning our <term>Saviour</term> <note>original: "σωτῆρος" (Soteros) – Savior; the Greek root implies one who rescues or heals.</note> is sufficient. But it is no worse to use, as an additional witness, the Hebrew Josephus, who in the eighteenth book of the *Jewish Antiquities*, in recording the history of the times of Pilate, mentions our <term>Saviour</term> in these words:

---

### Josephus concerning the Christ.

"Now there was about this time Jesus, a wise man, if indeed it be lawful to call him a man.
> For he was a doer of wonderful works, a teacher of men who receive the truth with pleasure. And he drew over to him many of the Jews and many of the Gentiles. He was the Christ. And when Pilate, at the suggestion of the principal men among us, had condemned him to the cross, those that loved him at the first did not cease to do so. For he appeared to them on the third day..."

### EVANGELICAL DEMONSTRATION Book 3. 81

...to live again, the divine prophets having spoken these and ten thousand other things about him. Wherefore, even until now, the race <note>original: "φῦλον" (phylon) – a term early Christians used to describe themselves as a "new race" or "third people" alongside Jews and Greeks.</note> of Christians has not failed from here. If, therefore, it is also testified according to history—that not only the twelve apostles, nor the seventy disciples were precisely [accounted for], but many from the Jewish side and many from the Greek side were brought to him—it would be clear that he possessed something far greater than what is found among the rest of men. For how else could he have brought over more Jews and Greeks, if he had not used certain wonderful and paradoxical works and a strange <note>original: "ξενιζούσῃ" (xenizousē) – meaning foreign, unusual, or startling.</note> teaching? And the writing of the Acts of the Apostles is a witness that there were many myriads <note>A "myriad" is 10,000; Eusebius is emphasizing the massive scale of early Jewish conversion.</note> of Jewish men persuaded that he was the Christ of God, the one announced by the prophets. 

And history also records that there was a very great church of Christ in Jerusalem, composed of Jews, until the times of the siege under Hadrian. <note>Referring to the Bar Kokhba revolt (132–135 AD), after which Jews were banned from Jerusalem by Emperor Hadrian.</note> At any rate, the first bishops who presided over it in succession are said to have been Jews, whose names are remembered by the locals there even until now. So from these things, it can be said that every slander against his disciples is silenced, since both by them and apart from their testimony, ten thousand multitudes of Jews confess that the man among us, Jesus, is the Christ of God, because of the paradoxical works he performed which brought them under his influence. But having said this much to the ranks of those who were formerly unbelieving, come, let us enter upon the second height [of the argument]. This was the claim that Jesus performed his paradoxical deeds in a disciplined manner, but through sorcery <term>goēteia: a term for low-level magic or charlatanism, often contrasted with divine miracles</term> entirely for the deception of those watching, like some wonder-worker or a sorcerer <note>original: "φαρμακέα" (pharmakea) – one who uses potions or spells.</note> trying to amaze those present.

-> ### Against those who suppose the Christ of God to have been a sorcerer. <-

<margin>6</margin> <margin>7</margin> And indeed, these people must be asked first of all: what would they say to the points previously established? Is it possible to suspect that a man who was a teacher of a venerable and all-beneficial way of life, and of worthy and true doctrines such as we have already described, could have been a sorcerer? For if he were some trickster and a sorcerer, a deceiver and a charlatan, how could he have become the cause of such teaching for all the nations—the kind we see with our own eyes and receive with our ears even to this day? What kind of person would choose to bring together things that cannot be kept silent? For a sorcerer would truly be unholy and foul, being enrolled in forbidden and unholy practices, doing everything for the sake of shameful and filthy gain. Was our Savior and Lord, Jesus the Christ of God, liable to any such things?

> From where, or how, could he be, he who said to his own disciples—as has been testified by them—
> "Do not possess gold nor silver in your belts, nor a bag for the road, nor sandals"? <note>Quoting Matthew 10:9–10.</note>

How could they have attributed these things to him as he spoke, and how could they have deigned to record these traditions in their memoirs, if they saw their teacher was making money and pursuing the opposite of what he taught others? Long ago they would have rightfully condemned him and spat upon his words, and departed from his discipleship, if they saw him legislating such venerable things for them while the lawgiver himself followed his own words in no way at all. Again, the sorcerer and truly the deceiver gives himself over to those who lack taste and to the unholy, for the sake of hunting after unholy and unlawful pleasures, so that his magic arts already become clear...

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 81, where Eusebius began refuting pagan claims that Jesus was a mere "charlatan" or "sorcerer" (Greek: goes). He transitions here into a defense of Jesus’s moral character, specifically his temperance and lack of vanity, to prove he was a divine teacher rather than a magician.</meta>

->## EUSEBIUS<-

...by the same wickedness. Our Savior and Lord—it is impossible to say how much he was devoted to **temperance** <note>original: "σωφροσύνην" (sōphrosynēn) – a core Greek virtue involving self-control, moderation, and moral sanity.</note>, since his disciples again bear witness that he exhorted them not even to look upon a woman with unrestrained desire, when he said:

<margin>,,</margin> “It was said to those of old, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’
<margin>,,</margin> But I say to you, that everyone who looks at a woman to lust after her
<margin>,,</margin> has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

And once, when it was necessary for the benefit and salvation of many, he was seen conversing with a **Samaritan woman**; his disciples marveled that he was speaking with a woman, thinking they were seeing something they had never seen before. Thus, the word of our Savior possesses an inherent gravity and austerity regarding temperance; a great proof of this is that teaching of his, through which he taught them to be pure in the depths of their minds, cutting off passionate desires, saying:

<margin>,,</margin> “There are eunuchs who were born that way, and there are eunuchs who
<margin>,,</margin> were made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs
<margin>,,</margin> for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.”

Again, while the **charlatan** <note>original: "γόης" (goēs) – a term for a wandering magician, sorcerer, or fraudulent "miracle-worker."</note> and the enchanter who misleads the people elevates everything and performs wonders to gain empty glory, often using illusions and boasting to the masses that he knows and possesses something more than others—our Savior and Lord, because he was not a seeker of glory, nor a boaster or an illusionist, showed himself to be the opposite. This is clear from how he told those he healed to tell no one, nor to make him known to the many; and from how he sought out time in the mountains and retreats, fleeing the harmful company of cities and crowds. Since his teaching was not subject to the pursuit of ordinary glory, nor money, nor pleasure, what room is left for the suspicion that he was a deceiver and a charlatan? 

Consider these points further: a charlatan, when he shares his wickedness with others, produces men like himself. Why would he not make them charlatans, deceivers, and **sorcerers** <note>original: "φαρμακοὺς" (pharmakous) – practitioners of "pharmakeia," which included spells, potions, and malicious magic.</note> just like himself? Yet has the whole race of Christians ever been caught practicing charlatanry or sorcery as a result of his teaching? It is impossible to say so. On the contrary, they pursue philosophical principles, as has been demonstrated. How then could he, who trained others to be practitioners of a dignified and temperate life and the highest piety, be reasonably thought of as anything other than the greatest philosopher or a teacher of godly men? For surely every teacher is like those he instructs. Therefore, our Savior and Lord must be confessed as a philosopher and truly pious, and far from being a deceiver or charlatan.

If he was such a person, how else could he have attempted his miraculous works, if not by a divine and ineffable power and by the highest piety toward the God of all things, whom he is shown by his own words to have honored and worshiped as a Father? Furthermore, his disciples who were close to him, and their successors in that way of life, stood far removed from any base or evil suspicion. They did not even allow those they cared for to do what many people do—such as using **inscribed metal plates** <note>original: "πετάλων ἐπιγραφαῖς" – small metal foils (often gold or lead) inscribed with magic spells or names of power, worn as amulets.</note>, or wearing **charms** <note>original: "περιάμμασι" – objects tied to the body for magical protection.</note>, or paying attention to those who use incantations for pain, or seeking cures for their ailments through the wonders of roots and herbs or certain irrational superstitions. All these things have been driven out of the teaching of Christ. One can never see a Christian using a **protective spell** <note>original: "ἀπείργματι" – a defensive or warding spell.</note>, nor incantations, nor the inscriptions of meddling metal plates, nor other such things which many people consider harmless to use. Therefore, as the argument shows—

He now moves to a "proof by results," arguing that the moral transformation of Jesus's disciples—specifically their rejection of magic—proves that Jesus himself could not have been a magician.</meta>

### EVANGELICAL PROOF, Book 3

Can we really believe that the disciples of such a teacher were the followers of a **charlatan** and a **deceiver**? <note>original: "γόητος καὶ πλάνου" (goētos kai planou) — "goēs" refers specifically to a fraudulent miracle-worker or sorcerer.</note> While a charlatan might promise wealth, the **temperance** <note>original: "σωφροσύνη" (sōphrosynē) — a central Greek virtue of self-control and moral sanity.</note> of these students provides a massive refutation. Surely, men who are skilled and knowledgeable show themselves to be far better than those ignorant of their craft; for example, in the case of medicine, the students’ success in the field would be witnesses to the teacher’s mastery of the subject. Would not geometricians bear witness to the one who leads them in geometry? And arithmeticians to the one who leads in arithmetic? Likewise, the students would be the greatest witnesses against a man if he were a charlatan, provided they themselves pursued the same practices as their teacher. 

But for all these years, not a single disciple of Jesus has been found to be a charlatan, even though the governors and kings of various times have put our affairs to the test through the precise examination of torture. Indeed, it is clear there was no charlatanry involved, since not a single person was ever caught in any such thing—even when they were completely out of danger and only being forced by their persecutors to offer sacrifice. If, then, none of our people today, nor any of those ancient disciples of Jesus, were ever convicted of sorcery, then neither was their teacher such a man. 

Lest we seem to be speaking without evidence, receive these proofs from written history. The first disciples of Jesus record in the book of their own **Acts** <note>Referring to the "Acts of the Apostles" in the New Testament.</note> events most dear to the nations regarding their teaching: they show that many who were previously accused of sorcery underwent such a total change that they brought their forbidden books into the open and surrendered them to the fire in front of everyone. Listen to how the scripture describes it:

> ” A number of those who practiced magic arts brought their books together
> ” and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them 
> ” and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. <note>This is a quotation of Acts 19:19.</note>

Therefore, the disciples of our Savior put forward such power of words in their discourses to their listeners that they reached the very depths of their souls, touching and stirring the conscience of each person. This led them to no longer keep their secrets hidden, but to bring their private deeds into the light, and by reproaching themselves, they were delivered from their former wickedness. 

Such were those discipled by them: pure and genuine in their dispositions, so that nothing ulcerous or hidden remained within them; instead, they took pride and spoke freely about the change they had undergone from that time forward. Since they committed their magic books to the fire and decreed their total destruction, is it not plain to everyone that they had no further interest in sorcery, and were from that moment pure of any suspicion regarding it? 

If, then, the disciples of our Savior have proven to be such men, how much more so was the teacher? If you wish to judge the leader by his followers, you have even now ten thousand students of Jesus's words. Among them are great multitudes of men who have set themselves in battle array against the natural pleasures of the body, keeping their minds pure from every shameful passion; they have grown old in a life of **continence** <note>original: "ἐγκρατείᾳ" (enkrateia) — self-restraint, especially regarding sexual desire.</note>, providing brilliant evidence of the nourishment they received from his words. And it is not only men who practice this **philosophy** <note>Eusebius often uses "philosophy" to describe the disciplined Christian lifestyle.</note> in his school, but one could also mention the countless tens of thousands of women throughout the whole world who, like priestesses to the God of the universe, have embraced the highest wisdom and heavenly...

# BY EUSEBIUS

...with the same wickedness. But our Savior and Lord—it is impossible to say how much he excelled in **temperance** <note>original: "σωφροσύνη" (sōphrosynē) — This Greek virtue implies a healthy mind and total self-control, particularly regarding physical desires.</note>, since his disciples again testify that he exhorted them not even to look 
<margin>,,</margin> at a woman with a shameful desire, saying: "It was said to the ancients, 'You shall not commit adultery.'
<margin>,,</margin> But I say to you, that everyone who looks at a woman so as to desire her
<margin>,,</margin> has already committed adultery with her in his heart." And once, when he was necessarily speaking with a sinful woman for the benefit and salvation of many, those appointed <note>The disciples.</note> were amazed that he was speaking with a woman, thinking they were seeing something strange, as if it had never happened before. Thus, the word of our Savior established the gravity and rigor of **prudent temperance** through a great demonstration, as did that teaching through which he taught them to cut off passionate cravings from the very depths of the mind, saying: "There are eunuchs who were born that way, and there are eunuchs who 
<margin>,,</margin> were made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs 
<margin>,,</margin> for the sake of the kingdom of heaven." Again, he was no **charlatan** <note>original: "γόης" (goēs) — a derogatory term for a traveling magician or fraudulent miracle-worker.</note> or sorcerer misleading the people, one who buys everything with deceit and cuts coins <note>A metaphor for fraud or forgery.</note>, often acting for the sake of appearance and boasting that he knows and possesses something more than the masses. But our Savior and Lord was neither mad for glory, nor a boaster, nor a performer; for he chose to tell those he healed to tell no one and not to reveal him to the many. Instead of public displays, he pursued retreats and stays in the mountains, fleeing the numerous and often harmful crowds. Therefore, if he did not undertake his teaching for the sake of glory, nor money, nor pleasure, what room is left for the suspicion that he was a deceiver and a charlatan? Consider these things again: how does he pass on the traits of wickedness to others, and what kind of men does he produce? Does he not produce charlatans, deceivers, and **sorcerers** <note>original: "φαρμακούς" (pharmakous) — those who use "pharmaka" (drugs, potions, or spells) for magic.</note> like himself and similar in all things? Has anyone ever found the entire Christian race to be composed of enchanters or sorcerers because of his teaching? It is impossible to say so. On the contrary, he pursued the path of philosophical reason, as has been shown. He, who alongside others became a champion of a dignified and temperate life and the highest **piety** <note>original: "εὐσεβείας" (eusebeias) — the virtue of proper devotion to God.</note>—who could he justly be considered to be, if not the eldest of philosophers or a teacher of pious men? For surely the character of the one who teaches is seen in the life of those being discipled. Therefore, he must be confessed as a philosopher and truly pious—far from being a deceiver and charlatan—our Savior and Lord. If then he were such a man, how else could he have attempted his wonders except by a divine and ineffable power and by the highest piety toward the God of all things? He is shown by the words about him to honor and worship God as Father above all else. Furthermore, his disciples who followed him from the beginning, and those who succeeded them in their way of life, stood far apart from any base or evil suspicion. They did not even permit those they were healing to do what many often attempt: to use **inscribed plates** <note>original: "πετάλων ἐπιγραφαῖς" — metal amulets inscribed with magical names.</note>, or to wear **amulets** <term>periammata (charms worn around the neck or limbs for protection)</term>, or to pay attention to those who promise incantations, or to make themselves healers of diseases through the wonders of roots and herbs or other such spells. All these things have been driven out of the teaching of Christ, and one can never see a Christian using an amulet, or charms, or the meddlesome inscriptions of plates, or other things which the masses consider indifferent to use. # PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 3

...could anyone think that students of such a teacher were the pupils of a **sorcerer** <note>original: "γόης" (goēs) — a common derogatory term in the ancient world for a magician or fraudulent miracle-worker.</note> and a deceiver? In truth, anyone who professes a skill, whether great or small, is defined by the community of their students. Men who are experts in a craft—who perhaps find wealth because of their expertise—show their students to be much better than themselves; thus, in the case of a medical teacher, the students would be witnesses to the teacher's success in the craft. What about geometers? Whom do they name as their leader, or what do they subscribe to as geometry? And arithmeticians, do they not follow an arithmetician? Even **sorcerers** in their groups have their students as the greatest witnesses, for the students pursue the same practices as the teacher.

But not one person has ever been found to be a sorcerer who was a disciple of Jesus, even though the rulers and kings of our own times have subjected our affairs to an accurate examination through the trial of torture. Indeed, it appears that no one was a sorcerer, as they remained safe from every danger, even when one was forced by them to offer sacrifice <note>Early Christians were often executed if they refused to sacrifice to the Roman gods or the Emperor's image.</note>. If no one among those in our own time, nor among those ancient disciples of Jesus, was ever caught in **sorcery**, then surely the teacher himself was not such a person either.

But so that we do not seem to proceed with unwritten arguments, accept the proofs from written history. The first disciples of Jesus are recorded in the *Book of their own Acts* <note>The New Testament Book of Acts.</note> as approaching the Gentiles with their teaching, so that many of those previously accused of sorcery were led to such a total change of heart that they dared to bring their forbidden books into the open and hand them over to the fire in the presence of everyone. Listen to how the Scripture describes it:

> A number of those who practiced **curious arts** <note>original: "περίεργα" (perierga) — a technical term for magic or the occult.</note> brought their books together and burned them before everyone. And they counted the value of them and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver.

Now all these disciples of our Savior applied such power of speech in their conversations with their listeners that they reached the very depths of their souls, striking and overcoming the conscience of each person. The listeners could no longer bear to hide their secrets, but brought them into the light, convicting themselves and ridding themselves of their former wickedness. Such were those discipled by them: pure and genuine in their dispositions, so that nothing ulcerous or hidden remained in them, but they showed and spoke freely of their change from the worse to the better. Those who handed over their **magical books** to the fire and voted for their total destruction—how could it not be obvious to all that they no longer had any interest in sorcery, but were from that moment pure from every suspicion of it?

If, therefore, the disciples of our Savior have proven to be such people, how much more so was the teacher himself? If you wish to judge the teacher's purpose entirely by those known to him, you have thousands of Jesus's disciples even to this day. Among them are great multitudes of men who have set themselves against the natural pleasures of the body, keeping their minds unscarred by any shameful passion. These have grown old in **self-control** <note>original: "ἐγκράτεια" (enkrateia) — an ascetic practice involving strict moral discipline and often celibacy.</note> throughout their whole lives, providing clear evidence of the nourishment they received from his words. And it is not only men who practice this **philosophy** <note>original: "φιλοσοφοῦσιν" — Early Christians often used the term "philosophy" to describe a dedicated, ascetic, and godly way of life rather than just academic study.</note> under him, but one cannot even count how many thousands of women across the whole world, like priestesses to the God of all, have embraced the highest wisdom and heavenly...

Having argued that Jesus’s students were not trained in sorcery, he now contrasts the widespread, practical virtue of the Christian community with the isolated examples of famous Greek philosophers like Democritus and Crates.</meta>

### EUSEBIUS

...seized by a love for wisdom, they <note>Eusebius is referring here to Christian women who chose a life of asceticism.</note> have disregarded the primary duty of bearing children. Instead, having taken all care for the soul, they have dedicated themselves entirely, body and soul, to the Sovereign King and God of all, practicing complete purity and virginity. 

Indeed, our young students sing the praises of a single man, Democritus, who left his own land under the pretext of philosophy, carrying his reputation here and there; perhaps Democritus is everything to them. And Crates is admired by them above all others because, having left his property to his fellow citizens, he boasted that "Crates sets Crates free." <note>Crates of Thebes was a famous Cynic philosopher who famously gave away his wealth to live a life of poverty.</note> 

But the followers of the words of Jesus are myriads <note>original: "μυρίοι" (myrioi) — ten thousand, or more generally, an immense, uncountable number.</note> in number, not just one or two. They have sold their possessions and shared them with the poor and the needy. Of this, they themselves are witnesses, being present among them, and proving the successes of Jesus’s discipleship through actual deeds, not just words. 

What need is there to speak of how many myriads even among the **barbarians** <note>original: "βαρβάρων" (barbaron). To a Greek writer, this term referred to anyone who did not speak Greek or belong to Greco-Roman culture.</note>—not only our own people—through the words of Jesus, have testified that they recognize only one God: the Savior and Creator of this whole universe? They have borne witness to this while turning away from all impiety and the error of polytheism. Even Plato, who was the only one among the ancient philosophers to know Him, admits he did not dare to bring this knowledge to everyone, 

<margin>»</margin> stating explicitly: "To find the Father and Creator of this universe is a great 
<margin>»</margin> task, and having found Him, it is impossible to tell everyone." <note>A famous quote from Plato’s *Timaeus* (28c), often cited by early Christian authors to show that while philosophers glimpsed the truth, they could not make it accessible to the masses.</note> 

But while that matter seemed to him a task difficult to discover—and indeed, it is truly the greatest task—and while it was impossible for him to speak of it to everyone, it was because he did not possess that great power of **piety** <note>original: "εὐσεβείας" (eusebeias) — a central concept for Eusebius, meaning right worship and godly conduct.</note> which the disciples of Jesus possessed. Through the cooperation of their Teacher, it became easy for them to find and know the Father and Creator of all things. Having found Him, they brought this knowledge to every race of men; they revealed it, fulfilled it, and preached it to all. 

Consequently, from their very teaching, even now and up to the present time, among all the nations on earth, there are immense multitudes—not only of men, but also of women and children, of slaves and of peasants. These people are so far from being persuaded by Plato that they recognize the Maker and Creator of this whole universe as the only God; they worship Him alone and speak of God only through Christ. 

These were the achievements of this new and strange **race** <note>original: "γένους" (genous). Early Christians often described themselves as a "third race," distinct from both Greeks and Jews.</note>. These are the "sorceries" of this supposed error. And such were the disciples of Jesus, from whom one must judge what kind of person their Teacher was. 

Come then, let us investigate the argument on this point as well. Do you call Him a **sorcerer**, O stranger, and do you also call Him a terrible magician and a deceiver? Are you then the only one who is sane, and have you alone established the reality of **virtue** <note>term: "ἀρετή" (arete) — moral excellence or "virtue."</note>? Or must we, following this logic, attribute the causes to teachers in every case? 

For if He became the first and only one to attempt this virtue without anyone teaching Him—having learned nothing from others and having gathered nothing from the ancients—how can we not confess Him to be of a **divine nature**? How could He appear as one who is **self-taught** <note>original: "αὐτοδίδακτος" (autodidaktos).</note> and self-learned in such matters of virtue without books, without words, and without teachers? 

Truly, it is impossible to take up the learning of a common trade, or a logical science, or even the first elements of letters without a guide and a teacher, unless one has transcended the common nature of humanity. We know of no one who was ever the first **self-taught** teacher of grammar, nor a rhetorician who had not studied, nor a natural-born physician, nor a carpenter, nor a creator of any other craft. And why mention these small and human things? For consider the one who showed himself the Teacher of true piety and performed such wonders...

Here, he argues that Jesus cannot be dismissed as a mere magician or a student of Egyptian secrets, because no other teacher in history—Greek or barbarian—has ever founded a global "nation" or inspired such sacrificial loyalty in their disciples.</meta>

# THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 3. 85

...having performed miracles during the time He lived among us, and having worked such paradoxical wonders as we have just detailed, it is clear that He did not arise by chance. He did not gather His power from ancient sources, nor was He helped by modern teachers who had done the same. What else then is clear, but that we must testify and confess that He was a truly **divine being**, and that the one described has surpassed all human nature?

But you might say that He associated with deceptive teachers, and that He did not miss the "wisdom" of the Egyptians or the secret traditions said to exist among them; and that by collecting all these things, He became the kind of man our account presents. Why then, I ask, have no others better than Him arisen—either earlier in time or His own teachers—whether in Egypt or anywhere else? Why has the fame of their accusations against Him not reached all men? Or why is their glory not still sung today in a manner similar to ours? 

Who among the magicians <note>original: "γόης" (goēs) — a term used by critics like Celsus to dismiss Jesus as a common sorcerer or charlatan.</note> of all time, whether **barbarian** <note>In this context, non-Greek peoples like the Egyptians or Persians.</note> or Greek, ever became a teacher of such students? Who was the author of such laws and teachings as the power of our Savior has displayed? Who is recorded to have performed so many healings or such paradoxical acts of benevolence as those our Savior is remembered for? 

Whose acquaintances and dear eyewitnesses have shown themselves to be such proofs—tested like iron—of the things they witnessed, as did the disciples of our Savior? They endured every outrage, underwent every form of torture, and finally, through their own blood, they confirmed the testimony they gave about Him. 

Furthermore, let anyone who tries to oppose our argument say: which of the magicians ever even considered establishing a **new nation** in his own name? To not only conceive of this, but to successfully achieve what was intended—how could this not be seen as something beyond all human nature? For He stood against the decrees of kings, the ancient lawgivers, philosophers, poets, and theologians, opposing every law regarding idolatry. He prevailed over these things, which had lasted for a long age, in a way no magician has ever even imagined. 

Our Savior and Lord did not merely imagine it, and then fail to dare the attempt; nor did He attempt it and then fail to achieve it. For with a single word,

> >> and with a single voice He said to His own disciples: "Go and make disciples of
> >> all nations in my name, teaching them to keep all things that I have commanded
> >> you." <note>A direct reference to the "Great Commission" in the Gospel of Matthew 28:19-20.</note>

He followed His word with action. Immediately, in a short time, every race of Greeks and barbarians alike became His disciples. Laws were hastened to all nations, and the ancient superstitions were dissolved. These were laws hostile to demons and enemies of every polytheistic error; laws that brought self-control to Scythians, Persians, and other barbarians, putting an end to every illegal and beast-like way of life. They were laws that overturned the customs that had prevailed among them for ages, announcing a new and true piety. 

What can anyone say about the times of Jesus of old? Has anything similar or close to this been attempted since then, such that one could reasonably say He was helped by others in the arts of sorcery? If no one can say anyone has been like Him—for no one else was worthy of such virtue—then one must confess that a strange and **divine nature** has lived among us, which alone has achieved things never before remembered among men. But...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s defense in Book 3 of the *Proof of the Gospel*. He transitions from discussing the global impact of Jesus’s followers to addressing the specific accusation that Jesus was a "magician" (goēs) who worked wonders through demonic pacts. He argues that the moral character of Jesus’s teaching and the behavior of His followers—who reject demons even unto death—proves such accusations are logically impossible.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

And let these matters conclude here. But we must return again to the same points and ask whether he <note>Referring to the critic or opponent of Christianity, likely Porphyry or Celsus.</note> has ever seen with his eyes or known by report any <term>sorcerers</term> <note>original: "goētas" — a term for a low-level magician or fraudulent trickster.</note> and <term>magicians</term> <note>original: "pharmakeas" — those who use potions, drugs, or incantations.</note> who perform their enchantments without libations, sacrifices, the invocation of demons, or their supervision. Is it possible, then, that anyone could bring such a slander against our Savior, or against His Word, or against those who even now strive to emulate His life? Is it not clear even to a blind man that we, who follow the thoughts of Jesus, practice the exact opposite of these things? We would sooner surrender our souls to death than dare to offer a sacrifice to demons; we would sooner depart from life than endure being enslaved to evil spirits. 

Who does not know how, with the very name of Jesus and the purest prayers, we take pleasure in driving away every work of the demons? For the Word of Jesus and the teaching received from Him has made us all into powerful enemies and foes of the demons—not their friends or associates, and far from being their subjects or subordinates. How could He, who produced such people as us, have been a slave to demons Himself? How could He have offered sacrifices to evil spirits? Or how could He have called upon demons to help Him in His miraculous works, when even to this day every demon and every unclean spirit shudders at the name of Jesus? They withdraw and give way to the power of His name, as if facing a force that punishes and tortures their very nature. Just as long ago, during the time He lived among us, they could not bear His presence; being strangled by it, they cried out:

> "Let us be! What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come to torment us before the time?"

For if He had truly devoted His mind to <term>sorcery</term> <note>original: "goēteia"</note> and had made use of forbidden practices, would it not be obvious that He was unholy in character—polluted, shameful, godless, unjust, and impious? Being such a person, how or from where could He teach others about piety, or self-control, or the knowledge of God, or about the justice and judgment of the God over all? Would it not be more fitting for Him to advocate for the exact opposite of all these things, in accordance with His own wickedness? Would He not deny God, His providence, and His judgment, and mock those who speak of virtue and the immortality of the soul? 

If such things were to be seen in the deeds and words of our Lord and Savior, there would be nothing more to say. But if He is shown to call upon God the Father, the Creator of all, in every act and word; and if He prepared His disciples to be like Him; and if He was Himself self-controlled, a teacher of self-controlled words, a worker and herald of righteousness, truth, and love for humanity, and an introducer of every virtue and piety toward God the King of all—how can one not conclude from this that He performed His miracles not through sorcery, but by an unspeakable and truly divine power? 

But you have been carried away into such empty folly that you do not attend to sober reasoning or the logical sequence of words, nor are you persuaded by reasonable evidence. Perhaps some might suspect we are just saying these things ourselves. But you, at least, listen to your own demons—to the very gods of the oracles! They testify that our way is not sorcery, as you claim, but piety, friendship with God, and an ascent into the heavens. What testimony could be more trustworthy than the confession of these beings found in your own writings, which you composed against us? In his third volume of *The Philosophy from Oracles*, this author has written the following, recording it in this way:

<meta>This page follows the previous discussion where Eusebius refuted the charge that Jesus was a "magician." Here, he presents a "smoking gun" argument: he quotes Porphyry, one of Christianity’s most intellectual pagan critics, who admits that the pagan oracles themselves spoke highly of Jesus’s character and soul, even while the oracles criticized His followers.</meta>

### PROOF OF THE GOSPEL Book 3

Word for word,
How from the very activity itself the power of the divine virtue surrounding him is perceived by those who love the truth.

<margin>Oracles concerning Christ.</margin>
> It might perhaps seem a strange thing, what I am about to say; for the gods have declared Christ to have been most pious and to have become immortal, and they remember him with good words. <note>Eusebius is quoting from Porphyry’s work *On the Philosophy from Oracles*. Porphyry was a famous opponent of Christianity, making his citation of these "pro-Jesus" oracles very effective for Eusebius's argument.</note> And he <note>Porphyry</note> adds further, regarding those who asked whether Christ is a god, he says:
> That the immortal soul proceeds after the body,
> The one honored with wisdom knows. But truly the soul
> Of that man <note>Referring to Jesus.</note> is most preeminent in piety.
> <margin>Most pious</margin>
> Thus he said that he [Jesus] was exceptionally pious, and that his soul, like others who are immortalized after death, was made immortal, and that the Christians worship him [incorrectly]; but when they asked why he was punished, the oracle declared:
> The body indeed is always exposed to weakening torments;
> But the soul of the pious sits in the heavenly plain.
> And he [Porphyry] adds after this oracle:
> He was, therefore, pious, and like the pious, he has passed into the heavens. Therefore, you shall not blaspheme him, but you shall pity the folly of the men [his followers].

These are the words of Porphyry even now. Is he then a deceiver, O man? Even your own familiar words should shame you. You have, therefore, our Savior Jesus the Christ of God, acknowledged even by his [enemies] as neither a <term>sorcerer</term> <note>original: "goēta" — a fraudulent trickster or low-level magician.</note> nor a <term>magician</term> <note>original: "pharmakea" — one who uses illicit potions or spells.</note>, but pious and most just, wise, and an inhabitant of the heavenly vaults. How then could such a man reasonably have become the creator of "miraculous works" except by divine power? For the sacred words themselves testify to this: that the Word and the highest Power dwelt in human form and shape—or rather, in the very flesh and body—and fulfilled the whole <term>divine dispensation</term> <note>original: "oikonomian" — the plan for the salvation of humanity.</note> among men. And you yourself might perceive the divinity of the power surrounding him if you consider who he was by nature, who associated himself with the life of a common, ordinary, and humble man, and used these as ministers for the Word that covers all things. For he conceived what no one ever had: to sow his own laws and strange teaching among all the nations, and to declare himself the teacher of piety toward the one God over all. To do this, he chose to use the most rustic and common of people as servants of his own counsel. One might likely think these things were done most irrationally. For how could those who were not even able to open their mouths [in public] have become teachers of even one man, let alone a gathering of men? How could they have addressed multitudes, being men who were entirely without education? But this was indeed the proof of the counsel within and the divine power working in them. Calling them, he said first: "Come, follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." <note>A reference to Matthew 4:19.</note> Since he had acquired them as followers from then on, having breathed into them divine power, and having filled them with words and courage—and indeed as one who was truly the Word of God and God himself, the creator of such great wonders—he made them hunters of rational and thinking souls. He put the work into effect with the voice that said, "Come, follow me, and I will make you fishers of men," making them both laborers and teachers.

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s defense of the divine nature of Jesus’s mission. After previously using pagan oracles to show that even critics recognized Jesus’s piety, he now pivots to the historical miracle of the "Great Commission"—how a small group of unlearned men managed to spread a new message across the entire known world against all cultural and linguistic odds.</meta>

### EUSEBIUS

...having been wrought for them by piety, [His teaching] was already being sent out into all the nations, after He had appointed heralds of His doctrine. And who would not be astonished and naturally find this miraculous paradox hard to believe? For no one among the famous men of history—neither king, nor lawgiver, nor philosopher, whether Greek or barbarian—is recorded to have ever conceived of such a thing, nor has anything similar even entered their imagination. For it is a great achievement for any man if he can establish his own profession on his own soil alone, or if he is able to make the laws he thinks are good prevail even over his own single nation. 

But He, who conceived of nothing merely human but rather of something heavenly, see if He did not truly utter the voice of God again, saying in these very words to those most humble disciples of His: 
<margin>»</margin> "Go and make disciples of all the nations." <note>Original: *poreuthentes mathēteusate panta ta ethnē*. This is the famous 'Great Commission' from the Gospel of Matthew 28:19.</note> 

And how, the disciples might well have answered their Teacher, will this be possible for us? For how, tell us, shall we preach to Romans? How shall we debate with Egyptians? What language shall we use with Greeks—we who are men raised with only the Syrian <note>Eusebius refers here to Aramaic, the native language of the disciples in Judea/Galilee.</note> tongue? And as for Persians, Armenians, Chaldeans, Scythians, Indians, and whatever other barbarian nations there might be, how shall we persuade them to abandon their ancestral gods and worship the one Creator of all? Trusting in what skill of words shall we go forth to this task? Or how can we have hope for success, daring to legislate against the laws concerning their own gods that have been established for all nations from time immemorial? And by what power shall we achieve this undertaking? 

When the disciples of Jesus would have reasonably said or thought these things, the Teacher solved their difficulties with a single addition. 
<margin>»</margin> He proposed the solution to their doubts by saying they would succeed *in my name*. <note>Eusebius argues that the "Name of Jesus" functioned as a divine tool that bypassed the need for natural eloquence or political power.</note> 
<margin>»</margin> For He did not simply and indefinitely command them to "make disciples of all nations," but added the 
<margin>»</margin> necessary condition: "in His name." Since the power of His name was so great 
<margin>»</margin> that the Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul in Philippians 2:9–10.</note> said, "God bestowed on Him the 
<margin>»</margin> name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven 
<margin>»</margin> and on earth and under the earth." Thus, rightly revealing the virtue of the power hidden from the many 
<margin>»</margin> in His name, He said to His disciples: 
<margin>»</margin> "Go and make disciples of all the nations in my name." Then He also adds 
<margin>»</margin> a very accurate prediction of the future, saying: "For it is necessary that this Gospel be preached in the whole 
<margin>»</margin> world, for a witness to all nations." <note>A reference to Matthew 24:14.</note>

This word was spoken in a corner of the earth at that time, and only those present heard it. How then was His word trustworthy to them, unless they had received proof of the truth in His words from other deeds He performed? For it must be admitted by anyone who reasons that they believed Him when He spoke. Indeed, He gave the command and no one disobeyed; rather, obeying His power, they made disciples of a vast race of men according to what had been announced, being sent from their own land to all the nations. In a short time, one could see the words fulfilled by their deeds. At any rate, the Gospel was preached in a short time in the whole world as a witness to the nations. Both barbarians and Greeks received the writings concerning Jesus in their own characters and native tongues. And who would not reasonably wonder, seeing the manner of the teaching of Jesus's disciples? For did they go into the middle of a city, then stand in the marketplace, and using a louder voice—
