<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s rhetorical challenge regarding the success of the Apostles. He has just asked how uneducated men, speaking only Aramaic, could possibly hope to convert the diverse and sophisticated nations of the world. Here, he explores the logical absurdity of their success unless a divine power was assisting them.</meta>

### PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 3

...they themselves called together those passing by and then began to give public speeches. And what, then, could have been the subject of their oratory? What was it that their listeners were likely to be persuaded by? And how could men give public speeches who were inexperienced in words and shared in no formal education? Yet, they did not speak to the masses all at once, but rather conversed individually with those they encountered. Let us see, then, what kind of arguments they used to persuade their listeners. For their struggle was no small thing, especially since they did not hide the identity of the one who had been condemned to an ignominious death by their own people. 

If they had hidden this fact—if they had refused to confess to everyone the nature and extent of what he suffered at the hands of the Jews, and had instead brought forward only his solemn and glorious deeds, I mean his miracle-working, his wondrous acts, and his philosophical teachings—their task of making listeners agree would still not have been easy. These listeners were hearing foreign ideas and new words for the first time, and the speakers brought no credible testimony to support what they said. Indeed, such a selective story might have seemed more plausible at first. 

But as it was, they proclaimed that the God they represented had come in a human body, yet was nonetheless the Word of God <note>Original: *Theou Logon*. Eusebius uses the philosophical term *Logos* to bridge the gap between Greek philosophy and Christian theology.</note> by nature, and for this reason had performed such miraculous powers as only God could. But then, on the other hand, they claimed he endured insults and dishonors, and finally the most shameful punishment, reserved for the most wicked of criminals, through a public execution. Would the listeners not have naturally spat upon them as men speaking contradictions? Who would be so foolish as to be easily persuaded by people claiming they had seen a man rise from the dead—a man whom the listener had never seen while he was alive, and who had been unable to help himself in his hour of need? 

How could anyone ever be persuaded by those common and lowly men <note>Original: *idiōtais kai eutelesin*. The term *idiōtēs* refers to a private person or a "layman" lacking professional training, while *eutelēs* suggests someone of little social or financial standing.</note> when they spoke? It would seem a mockery to despise the gods of one’s ancestors, and madness to condemn the traditions of all ages, only to trust these men and the proposals put forward by a crucified man. For they claimed this man alone was the beloved and only-begotten Son of the God who is over all. 

I myself, then, examining this account truthfully in my own mind, find no persuasive power in it, nothing solemn or credible—indeed, nothing even probable enough to persuade a single person of that age. Yet, when I look back at the divine power and see how it persuaded ten thousand multitudes, and how a church of countless thousands was established by those very same lowly and rustic disciples of Jesus, I am forced to reconsider. This did not happen in some obscure or hidden places, but in the most prominent cities: I mean in Rome the queen of cities, in Alexandria, in Antioch, throughout all of Egypt and Libya, Europe and Asia, and in villages, countrysides, and among all kinds of nations. Once again, I am forced by necessity to return to the search for the cause. I must admit they could not have succeeded in such a bold venture except by a more divine and superhuman power, and by the cooperation of the one who said to them: 
<margin>»</margin> "Make disciples of all the nations in my name." <note>Matthew 28:19.</note> 
For having said this, he added a promise through which they were to take heart and eagerly give themselves to the task he had announced. For he says to them: 
<margin>»</margin> "And behold, I am with you always, even until the end of the age." <note>Matthew 28:20.</note> 
Moreover, he is said to have breathed a divine spirit into them and to have given them a kind of wonder-working power, saying at one time: 
<margin>»</margin> "Receive the Holy Spirit," <note>John 20:22.</note> 
and at another time: 
<margin>»</margin> "Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons..." <note>Matthew 10:8. The text here breaks off as Eusebius lists the miraculous powers granted to the Apostles.</note>

He concludes that their success across major world cities like Rome and Alexandria proves they were aided by a superhuman, divine power.</summary>

Having previously discussed the apparent impossibility of the Apostles' mission—unlettered men tasked with converting the world—Eusebius now explains how their miraculous deeds and the specific historical timing of the Roman Empire's rise made their success possible.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

<margin>90</margin>
... “Freely you have received, freely give.” <note>Original: *dorean elabete, dorean dote*. This is a direct quote from the Gospel of Matthew 10:8, emphasizing that the Apostles did not charge for their miracles.</note> They themselves were silent about how the Word <note>Original: *Logos*. Eusebius uses this to mean both the Christian message and the divine Person of Christ.</note> prevailed through them, since the Book of Acts <note>Original: *biblos ton praxeon*. Refers to the New Testament Book of Acts.</note> bears witness in harmony with these events. It records how these things were accomplished by them for the glory and through the power of God, in the name of Jesus, amazing both those present and those who watched. For, as is natural, they first struck the observers with awe through their deeds; only then did they find them eager to inquire who it was that had confirmed the miracle by such power and by such a title. Then, while teaching, they found that faith had already outpaced their own instruction. For the people were not persuaded by mere words, but were already won over by the deeds; thus, they found it easy to believe the words. Some even went so far as to offer bull-sacrifices and libations as if the Apostles were already gods, <note>A reference to Acts 14, where the people of Lystra attempted to sacrifice to Paul and Barnabas.</note> because they had employed the voice of God. And so that they might remain close to them, they even considered them to be some kind of divine beings. The demonstration of these paradoxical works struck their very minds with amazement. And since the people were already so disposed, the Apostles preached much concerning Jesus, and were then reasonably believed to be telling the truth. They bore witness to the Christ, whom they proclaimed to them, not with simple or unproven words, but they persuaded through the very power of their actions, showing forth the works of a living being. If they dared to proclaim Him as God and the <term>Child of God</term> <note>Original: *Theou paida*. Can be translated as 'Son' or 'Servant' of God; Eusebius uses it here to denote Christ's divine origin.</note> since His arrival among men, how could I not rather agree with this? For the opposite—to think it unbelievable or impossible—would be the reaction of those who reasonably calculated that the things being done could not be the works of a mortal nature, but of God. Let no one say otherwise. This, then, was the very thing to seek in Him: by what power did those who were the original listeners to the disciples of Jesus believe, and how did they so opportunely persuade both Greeks and <term>barbarians</term> <note>In this context, 'barbarians' simply means those who did not speak Greek or belong to Greco-Roman culture.</note> to be moved by the Word of God concerning Him? And how, in the midst of cities and throughout the countryside, did they establish the teaching of the worship of the one God over all?

Yet who would not wonder, when reflecting and considering within himself, that it was not a human achievement that the majority of the nations of the inhabited world should come under the single rule of the Romans at the same time as the era of God’s appearance? For at the same time as His wondrous arrival among men, the Roman power also reached its peak, when Augustus first became monarch over most of the nations. During his reign, Cleopatra was captured and the succession of the <term>Ptolemies</term> <note>The Greek dynasty that ruled Egypt following the death of Alexander the Great.</note> in Egypt was dissolved. Since that time, and until now, the kingdom of Egypt—which had stood, so to speak, since the very beginning of human history—was destroyed. From that time also, the Jewish nation became subject to the Romans, as did the Syrians, the Cappadocians, the Macedonians, the Bithynians, and the Lycians; to put it briefly, all the rest of the nations now under Roman rule. Who would not admit that this coincided with the teaching of our Savior for a specific purpose? For he would realize that it was not easy for His disciples to undertake journeys to foreign lands while the nations were at odds with one another and had no social intercourse because of the many different <term>national rulers</term>. <note>Original: *ethnarchias*. Small, independent local kingdoms or tribal leaderships that existed before Roman consolidation.</note> But once these were abolished, they accomplished their goal fearlessly and in safety. The God over all provided the way for them, subduing the tempers of the superstitious in every city through the fear of a greater central authority. For consider: if there had been nothing to prevent those excited by the error of <term>polytheism</term> <note>Original: *polytheon*. The worship of many gods.</note> from warring against the teaching of Christ, you would have long ago seen both cities and fields...

<meta>This page continues from page 90, where Eusebius was describing how the miracles of the Apostles amazed onlookers. He now shifts to discuss how the Christian faith survived the "wars" and "civil strifes" of the Roman world, interpreting the survival and growth of the Church as proof of divine intervention rather than human effort.</meta>

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 3

<margin>91</margin>
...[threatened by] civil strifes, persecutions, and wars of no ordinary kind—as would have happened if those devoted to spirits <note>Original: *deisidaimones*. This term literally means "fearers of spirits," used by Eusebius to refer to the practitioners of traditional Greco-Roman religion (pagans) whose "superstition" he contrasts with Christian "piety."</note> had kept the power over them in their own hands. But as it happened, this too was a work of the God over all, who, by a fear greater than that of the highest authority, subdued the enemies of His own Word. <note>Original: *Logos*. In this context, it refers to both the Christian message and the divine Person of Christ.</note> For He willed that it should advance daily and increase into great multitudes of men. 

Again, so that it might not be thought that it endured merely by the permission of the rulers—if ever any of them, seized by wickedness, proposed to wage war against the Word of Christ—God granted them their desire for a time. This was done both for a demonstration of the <term>athletes of piety</term> <note>Original: *athleton*. Early Christians frequently used athletic metaphors to describe martyrs and confessors who "competed" in the arena of faith against persecution.</note> and at the same time to make it manifest to all that the establishment of the Word was not of human counsel, but from the power of God. 

Indeed, who would not wonder at what happened in those times? For it was customary then that the athletes of piety—who were previously unknown and obscure to all men—were deemed worthy of the heavenly kingdoms by God. Meanwhile, the enemies of piety paid the fitting penalties, being driven mad by incurable scourges, or having their whole bodies destroyed by terrible and ruinous diseases, <note>Eusebius likely refers here to the gruesome deaths of persecuting Emperors like Galerius or Maximinus Daia, which he interpreted as divine judgment.</note> so that they were even forced to come to a confession of their impiety against Christ. 

As for all the others who were honored with the <term>name</term> <note>The "name" refers to the title "Christian."</note> and who boasted in their devotion to Christ: some were trained for a short time by trials, while those who were proven genuine and sincere in their purpose received back their own freedom once again. Through them, the saving Word shone forth more brightly every day, prevailing even among its very enemies. 

They rose up not only against visible enemies, but also against the invisible—if indeed there were any dark and evil demons and their rulers in the air around the earth. <note>This reflects the common ancient worldview that the atmosphere was populated by spiritual forces (demons) that influenced human affairs.</note> These also the genuine disciples of Christ drove out through purity of life and through prayers to God, and through His divine name, echoing the miraculous signs that had previously been performed by Him. In this way, they displayed the proofs of His divine power to those capable of seeing. 

But since we have spent enough time on those who were trained in their own season, it is now a good time to touch upon the more mystical theology concerning Him, and to behold the <term>God-Word</term>, <note>Original: *Theon Logon*. Eusebius is transitioning from the historical and external proofs of Christianity to the internal, philosophical nature of Christ as the divine Reason of God.</note> whoever He was, who performed the miracles through the man who appeared.

# GOSPEL PROOF Book 4, 93

## Concerning the mystic economy regarding our Savior and Lord Jesus, the Christ of God.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' with foliage and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc>

**Since** the matters pertaining to the incarnation <note>Original: *enanthropeseos*. This refers to God "becoming human."</note> of our Savior in the writing before this—being the fourth part of the *Gospel Proof* <note>There appears to be a numbering discrepancy in the manuscript or header; while the header marks this as Book 4, the text refers to the previous section as the fourth. Eusebius is likely transitioning from his historical defense to his systematic theology.</note>—have been sufficiently labored by us, it is now time to touch upon more secret discourses, those concerning the more mystical <term>theology</term> <note>Original: *theologias*. In the early Church, "theology" specifically referred to the study of the divine nature of the Word, as opposed to "economy," which referred to His actions in history.</note> regarding Him. Now, the discourse concerning the first and eternal God, the only unbegotten and the Cause of all things, the Ruler and King of all, is common to all men. But the discourse concerning the Christ is peculiar to us and, in another sense, shared with the Hebrews. Regarding Him, they still acknowledge Him in a way similar to us by following their own scriptures, yet in other ways they fall far short. They neither perceive His divinity, nor do they know the reasons for His presence, nor have they tracked the times in which it was foretold He would come among men. For even now they expect Him as one yet to come, whereas we demonstrate that He has already come once. Furthermore, we pray to see His second presence with divine glory, being persuaded by the predictions and teachings of the God-bearing prophets.

Because the discourse regarding Him is two-fold, one part would be "newer," having entered among men only yesterday or the day before; but the other part is older than all time and all ages. For God, being alone good and the source and spring of every good, wished to reveal His treasure to more participants. Through Him <note>Referring to the Son/Word.</note> He brought forth the entire creation of rational beings—certain incorporeal, intellectual, and divine powers, angels and archangels, and immaterial and entirely pure spirits. He also promised that human souls, who stand as leaders of their own nature, would step forward and exercise mastery over the free choice of the good or its opposite. He also prepared the various bodily instruments they would need, suitable for their different ways of life, and assigned to all of them their own lands and places. For those who remained good, He assigned the better places; conversely, He assigned appropriate places for those who turned toward the opposite—places of discipline.

But rather, as God, having looked ahead through His foreknowledge and seeing that all these things would require a Head for their birth within a great body, He thought it necessary to appoint one <term>steward</term> <note>Original: *oikonomon*. A manager or administrator of a household; here, the manager of the universe.</note> of all creation, a Leader and King of the whole. This is the one whom the divine oracles, proclaimed among the Hebrews by their theologians and prophets, initiate us into. From them it is possible to learn that there is indeed one Source of all things—or rather, something even higher than a source, older than the first, more original than the monad, and better than every name. He is unutterable, inexpressible, inconceivable, the Good, the Cause of all, the Creator, the Benefactor, the Provider, the Savior—He Himself being the one and only God, from whom are all things and through whom all things exist. <margin>»</margin> "For in him we live and move and have our being." <note>This is a quotation from the Book of Acts 17:28.</note> For He would not be or exist without His own will. He is the only Source of all piety and existence. <margin>»</margin> For because He wills, He is. And He wills because He happens to be good by nature; and to the good, nothing...

# 94 EUSEBIUS

He is naturally inclined toward good things. Because He wills these things, He is also able to perform them. Therefore, because He both wills and is able simultaneously, He established for Himself—without hindrance or impediment—everything that is beautiful and profitable, whether visible or invisible. He projected His own will and power as a sort of sun and the very essence <term>ousia</term> <note>Original: *ousian*. In this context, it refers to the fundamental substance or "being-ness" of the universe's foundation.</note> of the birth and constitution of all things. Thus, one should no longer say—without reason—that the existence of things that are comes from things that are not. For nothing could ever come from nothing. For how could "nothing" be the cause of "being" for other things? Everything that exists stands forth from the only One who truly Is. This is what He meant when He said, "I am He Who Is" <note>Original: *ego eimi ho on*. This is the Greek Septuagint translation of the divine name in Exodus 3:14.</note>, from whom everything else has received its existence. Because He alone Is, and is Eternally Being, He Himself became the Cause of being for all who obtained existence from Him, by His willing and by His power. He has granted essence, powers, and forms to all things, richly and without grudge, from Himself.

->How we say that He was begotten by God before all creation.<-

And indeed, preceding all things that exist, He brought into being for Himself an offspring <term>gennema</term> <note>Original: *gennema*. This term emphasizes that the Son was "begotten" or "born" from the Father's essence, rather than "made" like a created object.</note>: the Primary Wisdom, which is entirely intellectual, rational, and all-wise—or rather, Mind-itself, Reason-itself, and Wisdom-itself. And if it is permitted for mortals to conceive of Beauty-itself and Goodness-itself, this is that which was first begotten from Him and by Him, and which is set over the creation of things that followed. It is a perfect creation of a perfect Creator, a wise architectural work of a wise Being, a good offspring of a good Father. For whatever things later received life through Him, He was appointed as their leader, guardian, savior, physician, and the pilot who holds the rudders of the creation of the universe. When the divine oracles <note>A common term Eusebius uses for the Holy Scriptures.</note> speak of Him as God, they appropriately declare Him to be a "Begotten God" <note>Original: *theon genneton*. This was a key distinction in early Christian theology to describe the Son's relationship to the Unbegotten Father.</note>, as the only one who bears in Himself the image of the unutterable and inconceivable Divinity. Because of this image, He both is and is called "God," by virtue of His likeness to the First. In this way, they say He serves the will of the Father as a goodness projected forward, so that through a single, all-wise, and living instrument—acting with technical and scientific precision—all things might be directed by Him: bodies and incorporeal things alike, things with souls and things without, rational and irrational, mortal and immortal. Whatever other natures have been or are being woven together, they are all harmonized under one all-wise bond—the very Word <term>Logos</term> and Law of God—being gathered and bound together as if by a single power of the whole, a single living and ensouled Law and Reason existing in all things and pervading through all things.

->That there are not many sons of the God over all, but logically only one God from God is proclaimed to us.<-

Since the Father is one, the Son also must be one, and not many; there is only one perfect Begotten God from God, and not several. For if there were many, there would be "otherness" and difference, and the introduction of something inferior. Therefore, there is one God, the Father of one perfect and only-begotten <term>monogenous</term> Son, and not of many gods. For since the essence of light is one, it is a total necessity that the light generated from it must also be one and perfect. What second offspring of light could one possibly conceive of, other than the single ray that fills and illuminates everything from it? For everything foreign to this ray would be darkness and not light. In this same way, since the Father of all is the highest, unutterable Light, nothing...

...would indeed be a fitting and familiar example for Him, except for this one thing alone: that which can be said of the Son, that He is "the radiance of eternal light, the spotless mirror of the working of God, and the image of His goodness." <note>Original: *apaugasma gar esti phōtos aidiou...* This is a quotation from the Wisdom of Solomon 7:26, a deutero-canonical book often used by early Christian writers to explain the nature of the Logos (the Word/Son).</note> Therefore it is said that He is the "radiance of His glory and the exact representation of His substance." <note>Original: *apaugasma tēs doxēs kai charaktēr tēs hypostaseōs autou*. Quoting Hebrews 1:3. Eusebius is navigating the fine line between the Son being "from" the Father but also a "distinct" individual.</note>

But while the radiance of light is an inseparable beam, the Son exists uniquely <term>hypostasis</term> <note>Original: *hypestēke*. A central term in early theology referring to individual, personal existence. Eusebius is arguing that the Son isn't just a "quality" of God, but a distinct Person.</note> alongside the Father in His own right. And while the beam of light occupies the place of an "activity," the Son is something other than a mere activity; He exists and is substantial in His own right. Furthermore, the beam co-exists with the light as something that completes it—for light could not exist without its radiance—and they exist together in a single unity. But the Father pre-exists the Son, and He exists prior to the Son's generation, in that He alone is "unbegotten." The Father is perfect and primary in Himself as Father, the cause of the Son’s standing, receiving nothing from the Son to complete His own divinity. The Son, however, having come into being from a cause, is second to Him whose Son He is, having received from the Father both His existence and the nature of His being.

Again, the radiance does not shine forth by the "choice" <term>proairesis</term> <note>Original: *proairesin*. Eusebius emphasizes that the Son's existence is a deliberate act of the Father's will, not an accidental or necessary "overflow" of His nature.</note> of the light, but by an inseparable property of its essence. But the Son became the "Image" of the Father according to His thought and choice. For God, because He willed it, became the Father of the Son, and established a "second light," made like Himself in all things. Yet, if it were not for this—one eternal light being the source—how could there be two? He is like an image, yet not a mere radiance, but a Light that preserves the likeness of the Prototype in every way. And how could the radiance of the One be an image, if it were not one and the same essence? This is so that the likeness might be brought forth not only in essence to the First, but also in number; so that from the One eternal light there might be one perfect offspring, and not many different ones. This offspring is the one who obtained the honor of being theologized as a perfect good, alongside the Beginningless and Unbegotten Essence. Therefore, one must believe that there is one Son of one Father.

For from one specific underlying essence of fragrance, one and the same pleasant scent is poured out and distributed to all; one should not confess it to be many and different scents. Thus, regarding the first and only Good, who is God the King of All—perceivable by the mind and intellect—He established this one "living fragrance" (as it were), and it is not lawful to imagine more than one. And if there were to be another perfect likeness of this, it would be either inferior or worse, which we must never admit in our theology of the Son. For He is "a breath of the power of God, and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty." <note>Original: *atmis gar esti tēs tou theou dynameōs...* Quoting Wisdom of Solomon 7:25.</note>

For from a fragrant body—say, a certain ointment, or flowers blooming from the earth—a fragrant breath is perceived, and this scent of spices is poured out from the first underlying source into the surrounding air without limit. It fills the wide air, yet without any loss, decrease, cutting, or division of the original source. For while the source remains in its own place and preserves its identity with itself, the power coming from it is laid bare to us; it is a fragrant thing that has come to us, having its own existence, yet mimicking as much as possible the very nature of that which generated it.

However, these examples are still earthly, mortal, and part of the lower, corruptible nature of the world. The matters of the theology set before us are entirely beyond any example drawn from physical bodies. The Son is perceived by the sharpest intellect as a "begotten Son," not as one who once "was not" and then "came to be" at a later point in time—but before all time...

### Why the coming forth of the Only-begotten Son of God was necessary for the structure of all things.

But it seemed good to the Father, the King of all, that one Only-begotten and beloved Son should stand before the creation of all things. Since He was about to bring forth a single world—like one great body made of many different limbs and parts—it was not appropriate for Him <note>The Father</note> to do everything directly, as if the divinity of the Father were the "head" removed from the body. For "the head of Christ is the Father." <note>Original: *kephalē gar tou Christou ho Patēr*. Therefore, the Father brought the Son forward as an equal to all things, like a single-formed, living, and ensouled <term>instrument</term> <note>Original: *organon empsychon*. Eusebius views the Son as the "Master Tool" or intermediary through which the transcendent Father acts upon the material world.</note> brought forth from every substance and nature. More than that, He is divine, life-giving, and all-wise; the generator of good things, the provider of light, the architect of heaven, the builder of the world, the maker of powers, the provider for spirits, a saving instrument for souls, the growth-giver for bodies, the provider for all things, the governor, the healer, the king, the judge, and the one who announces the Father's piety.

### How we confess that there are myriad good divine powers, but we recognize the divinity of the Son alone as the "Image" of God the Father.

Therefore, among all created things generally, one must marvel at a single divine power, even if that power leads many others. Not only did He establish all things in the beginning, but He has existed and continues to exist forever, and "without Him nothing was made." For just as in our own body, there is much great variety among the parts, yet there is one creative power of the whole; for by the power of God, the same nature produced the head, another the eyes, another the ears, and another the feet. In the same way, a single universal divine power presiding over the entire world would be the same in heaven and...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument that the diverse and complex universe does not require a multitude of gods to explain it. Instead, he uses the analogy of human multi-tasking and artistic creation to show how a single "Word of God" (the Logos) acts as the unifying master-craftsman of all elements and life forms.</meta>

-> ΕΥΑΓΓ. ΑΠΟΔΕΙΞ. <note>Short for *Evangelikē Apodeixis* (The Proof of the Gospel).</note> lib. Δ. πζ 97 <-

...bringing [forth life], being the Creator of the living beings in the air, on the earth, and in the sea; the Creator of the elements <term>elements (stoicheia): the four basic building blocks of the ancient world—fire, water, earth, and air</term> both in their universal forms and their particular parts, and furthermore, the Creator of countless natures, both of souls and of specific physical forms. And there is not one power for fire, another for water, and again another for earth, nor a varied power for air; rather, it is the one and the same Wisdom, the craftswoman of all things, and that very World-Maker Himself, the one spoken of in theology as the <term>Word (Logos): the divine reason or personified agent of God's will</term> of all things, the Creator of God. 

A witness to these things is the harmony <note>Original: *philia* (friendship). Ancient philosophers often described the balance of opposing elements as a "friendship" or "agreement."</note> of the elements that reconciles them through the mixing of their qualities, proving that the nature of the whole is related and brotherly, as the work of a single Architect. For the earth—the heavy element—riding upon the waters and not sinking into the depths despite its weight, but always being carried aloft and not submerging, is a witness to the Word of God and to God's will and power. 

Again, consider the liquid substances: their communion with the dry land shows no solid support, yet they do not suddenly flood everything in a mass, for they are bound by the unutterable power of God, so that all things might again return to that one Word of God. And what of fire? It has a burning and destructive nature, yet it hides within wood and is diffused through all kinds of living bodies, dwelling together with earth, water, and air. Given to all things by reason and measure—providing just as much as is beneficial to each—and forgetting its own [destructive] power, does it not seem again to serve the Word and Power of God? 

To one who sees the alternating movements of day and night, the increases and decreases of seasons and times, the cycles of years and periods of time, the rotations of the stars, the courses of the sun, the phases of the moon, the sympathies and antipathies of all things, and the single world formed out of all these—is this something irrational? Is it permissible to suggest that "chance" or "accident" is the cause of all things? Or rather, should we truly praise the one Word of God, the Wisdom of God, and the Power of God in this universe, instead of many?

For even in a human being, a single soul and a single rational power can be the creator of very many things at once—whether the same person <insert>(undertakes)</insert> to farm, or build ships, or navigate, or build many structures. A single mind and reason in a human can at times receive thousands of sciences: the same person may practice geometry, study astronomy, and pass on the principles of grammar and medicine, whether through learning or manual practice. And yet, no one has ever thought there were many souls in one body, nor did anyone marvel at a person's "many powers" simply because they could take in many subjects of study. 

If someone takes clay, which is formless matter, and then smooths it with their hands into the shape of some animal—modeling a head in one shape, hands and feet in another, eyes in yet another way, and cheeks likewise, sketching out ears, mouth, nostrils, chest, and shoulders through the art of sculpture—must we believe there are just as many makers as there are shapes, limbs, and parts created in that one body? Or should we praise the craftsman of the whole human being, who fashioned the entire thing with one reasoning and one power? 

Why then, proceeding to the universe—which is one, though composed of many parts—must we suppose many creative powers and name many gods? Why not instead confess the one truly divine Power and Wisdom of God, which by a single power and a single virtue sustains and gives life to all things together, providing from itself a varied supply to all? Just as the single and same strike of the sun's light illuminates all at once...

Ii.i.

<summary>Eusebius argues for monotheism by illustrating how the Logos (Word of God) acts as a single unifying architect of the diverse elements and cosmic cycles. He uses analogies of a multi-talented human and a sculptor to show that one creative mind can produce and manage many complex parts.</summary>

...[the sun illuminates] the air, gives light to the eyes, and warmth to the touch; it fattens the earth, makes plants grow, establishes time, leads the stars, orbits the heavens, and brightens the world. In all of this, it makes the power of God evident to everyone, and accomplishes all these things through a single impulse of nature <note>original: *phýseōs*</note>. Similarly, the nature of fire purifies gold but melts lead; it dissolves wax but dries clay; it parches wood. With a single burning power, it achieves all these diverse effects. In this same way, the heavenly Word <term>Word (Logos): the divine reason or personified agent of God's will</term> of God—who is the Craftsman of the sun, the heavens, and the entire universe—shines upon and leaves His mark on all things through His active power. From His own eternal power, He pours light upon the sun, the moon, and the stars. He governs the heavens, having established the angelic realm as a most fitting image of His own greatness, and He sustains it forever. 

The powers beyond the heavens and the world—those immaterial and spiritual beings of intellectual and rational essence—He fills with life, light, wisdom, and every virtue and goodness from His own treasures, all through one and the same creative art. He never ceases to sustain the substances of the elements, holding within Himself all mixtures, blends, forms, shapes, and colors, and thousands of qualities. Whether in animals, plants, souls, or bodies—both rational and irrational—He provides all things to all at once through a single power, varying them according to the need. To all human beings, He grants a mind capable of recognizing and contemplating His own wisdom. By setting a single sovereign authority over all things, He reveals that this one world is the work of a single world-making Word. 

God the Father has established this Only-begotten Son <note>original: *monogenē*</note> as the Craftsman of His will, setting Him above all things, yet also as the Creator of the things below. The Father sits enthroned upon unutterable heights, while through the Son and in the Son, He brings into existence the creative principles <term>principles (logoi): the blueprints or rational structures used to create the world</term> of all things that were to be, casting into Him the seeds <note>Eusebius uses the Stoic concept of "seminal reasons" to explain how the potential for all life is contained within the Divine Word.</note> of the universe’s composition and governance. Do you not see with your own eyes the entire world, which a single heaven encompasses, and the thousands of circling dances and orbits of the stars? Again, there is only one sun, and not many; for if there were more, their light would overlap and hide their individual rays. Just as there is only one Father, there must also be only one Son. If anyone should complain that there are not more, one might as well ask why there are not many suns, many moons, many worlds, and a thousand other things. I would say such a person is mad, attempting to overturn the things of nature that are already right and well-ordered.

### How, through the creation of the whole, the goodness of God invisibly
### appears to God-loving souls.

Just as among visible things there is one sun which illuminates the entire world of the senses, so also among the "intelligible" <term>intelligible (noētois): things perceived by the mind or spirit rather than the physical senses</term> things, there is one Word of God who shines upon the thousands of immortal and incorporeal powers—the intellectual and rational essences—as if they were stars and luminaries. For it is necessary that the Word of God, being one over all things and reaching through all and being in all, should be the Image <note>The "Image of the Father" is a central concept in early Christian theology, describing the relationship between God and Christ.</note> of the Father, so that the creation might be brought to life in His likeness, according to virtue, power, essence, and the number of the "monad" and "unit" <term>monad (monados): the philosophical term for "one" or "unity," often representing the highest principle of reality</term>. Yet, in other ways, this Word is multifaceted and versatile, dealing with the substances of created things that are subject to thousands of varied changes and transformations due to their own inherent weakness, while the supreme power of the Father remains unutterable and infinitely great beyond all things.

<summary>Eusebius argues for the unity of God and the Logos by comparing them to the sun and fire, which produce many effects from a single source. He explains that the Logos serves as the single creative mediator through whom the Father governs both the physical and spiritual realms.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument regarding the necessity of the Logos (the Word) as a mediator. Having previously established the Logos as the Craftsman of the universe, he now explains why a direct encounter between the Infinite Father and finite creation is impossible, using the sun as a primary metaphor. This sets the stage for discussing human free will and the eventual need for divine intervention in human history.</meta>

-> ### PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 4 <-

-> ### Page 99 <-

Because created nature falls short and is unable to participate directly in the unbegotten and uncontained Godhead, it must look upward from below toward the unspeakable, shimmering rays of the eternal light. Therefore, the all-good Father and Savior of all things—lest created nature be entirely deprived of His fellowship and lose the greatest of blessings—interposed the divine, manifold, and all-virtuous power of His **Only-begotten** and **First-born** Son. This power communing most accurately and closely with the Father, enjoying His secret depths, yet gently descending and accommodating itself to those who fall short of the highest peak, allows their weakness to receive the improvement and benefit that comes from a "second" source. 

We might compare this to how we say the rays of the sun descend gently and mildly; otherwise, we would be unable to enjoy the pure power of its light due to the weakness of our bodies. For if, as a hypothetical argument, the all-bright sun itself were to descend from heaven and live among men on earth, nothing on earth would remain unharmed. All things, both living and inanimate, would be destroyed at once by the sudden assault of light. Indeed, the eyes of those who see would be blinded sooner than they could look; the sun would become a cause of harm and destruction rather than benefit to all. This would not be because the sun is such by nature, but because those receiving its surpassing rays are unable to bear them due to their own inherent weakness.

Why then should you hesitate to wonder at similar truths regarding God? No created thing has a share in the communion of the unutterable and inexpressible power and essence of God, except for one alone: the Son, whom the Father Himself established before all other things out of His providence for the whole. He did this so that created nature might not fall away entirely due to its own unfitness and inability, being so far removed from the unbegotten and uncontained essence of the Father. Instead, by enjoying the provision of this "Middle" power, nature might remain, grow, and be nourished. 

This Only-begotten Word <term>Word (Logos): the rational principle and personal agent through which God acts in the world</term> of God never ceases to assist all things. Pervading everything and traveling through all, He provides equally for the salvation of all: the rational and the irrational, the mortal and the immortal, the heavenly and the earthly, the divine and the invisible powers. To put it simply, He cares for everything that has received a share of existence through Him. 

However, He cares far more exceptionally for the intellectual and rational nature, for whose sake He did not even look down upon humanity. Indeed, He cared for it greatly because of the grace of the Word <note>original: *tē tou logou charin*</note>, which brings humanity into a kinship and continuity with Himself—a nature which the Holy Scriptures say was formed "according to His image." This indicates that the Word of God established the entire intellectual and rational nature as His own image at the very beginning of the creation of the universe. For this reason, He appointed man as a ruling and royal animal over all things on earth, making him free and **self-governing** <term>self-governing (autexousion): the capacity for free will and moral choice</term>. He allowed man the inclination toward what is good or toward its opposite. 

But when man did not use this self-governing power rightly, turning away from the straight path to rush in the opposite direction—considering neither God, nor Lord, nor things holy and pious, but instead attempting all manner of wild and unrestrained deeds like irrational beasts—it was necessary for the All-Good King and Most High God of all to act. He did this so that those on earth would not be like leaderless and unguided cattle...

...men, He appointed divine angels as their protectors and caretakers, like certain leaders of herds or shepherds. Over all of these, He set His **Only-begotten** and **First-born Word** <note>original: *logos*</note> as the supreme authority. To this Word, He assigned a special portion: the angels themselves, the archangels, the divine powers, and the immaterial and heavenly spirits. Along with these, from among those on earth, He set apart the "God-loving souls" among men, who are called by the Hebrew names **Jacob** and **Israel**.

-> How the knowledge of the God of all things was revealed to the Hebrews alone in ancient times, <-
-> being made known through the appearance of Christ. <-

The greatest prophet and theologian, **Moses**, initiated the ancient Hebrews into this mystery in secret teachings, saying: "Ask your father and he will show you; your elders and they will tell you."
> When the Most High divided the nations, when He scattered the sons of Adam, He set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God; and the Lord’s portion was His people Jacob, the allotment of His inheritance was Israel. <note>This is a quote from Deuteronomy 32:8–9 in the Septuagint (Greek) version of the Old Testament.</note>

Through these words, Moses names the Highest and Supreme God of all as the "Most High." He then identifies His **Word** <note>original: *logos*</note> as "Lord"—the one whom we bless as second only to the God of all. By the judgment of the Most High God, the Word tells us (in words mysterious to us) that all nations and the sons of men (called "sons of Adam") were assigned to invisible protectors, namely the angels. However, to the leader and king of all, Christ Himself—as the Only-begotten Son—was given the "Jacob" and "Israel" among men. By this, he means the spiritual, discerning, and God-fearing order of people. 

While still struggling and practicing in the exercises of piety, this group is called by the Hebrew name **Jacob** <note>Jacob was traditionally interpreted as "the supplanter" or "wrestler," representing the soul in training.</note>. But when the soul is deemed worthy of victory and the prizes of God, it is proclaimed **Israel** <note>Eusebius uses a common ancient etymology for Israel: *ish ra'ah El*, meaning "a man seeing God."</note>. This description applies to that original forefather of the whole Hebrew nation, his true children and descendants, the patriarchs, the prophets, and all God-loving men. For do not think the "Jewish multitude" is meant here; it refers only to those of old who were perfected in virtue and piety. This Leader and Protector of all, the Word of God, took these people and called them back to the worship of the Father alone—the Most High—the one above all visible things, beyond heaven and all created existence. He gently and mildly called his subjects back, teaching them to worship only the **Unbegotten** and the Most High God, the Creator of all things.

-> How the rest of the nations, while worshipping the luminaries in the sky, were assigned to angels. <-

Those who were the overseers of the other nations—the angels and shepherds—dealt with people who were unable to see the Invisible God or to ascend to such heights due to their own weakness. These leaders directed the people's attention to visible things in the heavens: the sun, the moon, and the stars. These objects are fitting to the visible nature of the universe and are, in a sense, the closest thing to the "vestibule" of the Great King. Through the magnitude and beauty of these created things, the observers might glimpse the Creator through a proportional reflection. 
> "For His invisible attributes," as the divine Apostle says, "namely His eternal power and deity, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made." <note>A quote from Romans 1:20.</note> And again, the great...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument regarding the divine order of the world. Having previously explained how the Logos (the Word) was appointed over the nations and specifically over Israel, Eusebius now addresses why the "visible gods" (the sun, moon, and stars) were permitted for the Gentiles, and introduces the origin of evil through the fall of a rebellious power.</meta>

### THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 4

The great **Moses** initiates us into these mysteries <note>original: *mystagōgei* — a term used for someone who leads an initiate into sacred secrets</note>. For when he encourages those who are the "portion of the Lord" to reach out with a clear mind and a soul purified toward things that are intellectual and bodiless, he restrains them from being overwhelmed by the sight of the things in the heavens. He adds that "the Lord your God assigned these to all the nations." It is necessary to understand why He assigned them. 

Because a deceptive, invisible, and demonic nature exists, fluttering in the air around the earth—a nature unknown and indistinguishable to men—and because there is a great difference between the good spirits and powers (the divine angels) and those that are inferior, it was not unreasonable for those who fell away from the highest piety toward the Universal King to choose the best of the things seen in the heavens. For there was a fear—and a likely one at that—that while seeking God and investigating invisible things, they might, in their lack of understanding of what is true and hidden, fall into the hands of opposing and demonic powers. Therefore, the first and most excellent creations of God among visible things were handed over to those no longer seeking what is greater. From this point, they were guided toward the contemplation of invisible things as if through a mirrored image <note>original: *eikonos esoptrou* — a reference to seeing truth indirectly, as in a reflection</note>.

-> **Concerning the hostile power that opposes God, and its leader,** <-
-> **and how the life of all men was led astray through him.** <-

Such was the state of things. But the affairs of the rival and apostate power—whether we speak of demons or other even worse spirits drifting more or less into wickedness—depended upon the leader of them all, a certain "mighty demon" in his pride. These beings, having wavered in their piety toward God, fell from their proper station. Out of envy for human salvation, this power used various devices of wickedness against all the nations, even plotting against the "Lord’s portion" out of malice toward what is good. The Spirit in the prophet **Isaiah** rebukes this godless and impious reasoning of the "mighty demon" in this way: 
> "For he said: 'In my strength I will act, and in the wisdom of my understanding I will remove the boundaries of the nations, and I will plunder their strength, and I will shake inhabited cities. And I will seize the whole world in my hand like a nest, and I will take them like abandoned eggs; and there will be no one who shall escape me or speak against me.'" 

These are the voices of one who fights against God, boasting in the strength of his wickedness, threatening to snatch away and throw into confusion the boundaries of the nations that were once handed over to the angels by the Most High. He arrogantly claims he will plunder the world and shake the entire human race, moving them from their former orderly state. To hear how he boasted such things about himself, listen to the same prophecy as it speaks of him again: 
> "How has **Lucifer** <note>original: *Heōsphoros* — literally "The Morning Star" or "Light-Bringer"</note>, who rises in the morning, fallen from heaven! He who sent messengers to all the nations is crushed to the earth. But you said in your mind: 'I will ascend into heaven; I will set my throne above the stars of heaven; I will ascend above the clouds; I will be like the Most High.' But now you shall go down into Hades, even to the foundations of the earth." 

Through these words, the account reveals many things at once: first, the madness that is described; then, the fall from better things to worse, which was the result of his pride. After threatening the nations with destruction, he attacked men with swift assaults...

### THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 1

In various parts of the world, while some people were satisfied with merely using the names of the "Primary Creator God" as a protective charm, they did not refrain from blaming human nature for the choice of evil. Consequently, a long and difficult-to-cure disease took hold of humanity across the earth. Different nations were driven into a frenzy by **wicked spirits** <note>original: *ponērōn pneumatōn* — demonic forces believed to influence human behavior</note> and fell into a bottomless pit of vice. Indeed, behaving like raw-flesh-eating and man-eating beasts, some even considered it a good thing to feast upon the flesh of their closest kin. They shamelessly engaged in sexual relations with their own mothers, sisters, and daughters. They committed foul acts of indecency against their own parents, and some even cast out their dead to be devoured by dogs and birds. Why should I even recount for you the so-called "gods"—who were actually nothing but vile demons—and their cruel and monstrous **human sacrifices**, into which they drove the human race to the point of madness?

It was necessary for us to keep these things before our eyes, as we previously prepared in the introduction to this work. Because the entire inhabited world was being tyrannized by these foul and miserable spirits, and since none of the presiding angels <note>original: *ephestōtōn angelōn* — referring to the traditional belief that specific angels were assigned to guard different nations</note> were able to provide a remedy for such evils, it was only right that the **Divine Word** <note>original: *Theos Logos* — the Son of God, the pre-existent Christ</note>, the Savior of the universe, should intervene. Moved by the Father’s supreme love for humanity, and so that His beloved race would not continue to wallow in the depths of godlessness, He began to shine forth brief and faint rays of His own light. He did this through the prophet Moses and the God-fearing men who came before and after him, offering a cure for human evils through a sacred system of laws. This Word immediately speaks to the Hebrew nation through Moses, saying:

> » “According to the practices of the land of Egypt, in which you dwelt, you shall not do; and according to the practices of the land of Canaan, into which I am bringing you, you shall not do; and in their laws you shall not walk. You shall perform my judgments and keep my ordinances. I am the Lord your God.” Then, after forbidding unlawful marriages and every shameful union—both of women with women and of men with men—He adds: “Do not defile yourselves in any of these things. For in all these things the nations were defiled, those whom I am casting out before your face. And the land was defiled, and I have repaid its iniquity, and the land is burdened with those who dwell upon it.” And again He says: “If you enter into the land which the Lord your God gives to you, you shall not learn to do according to the abominations of those nations. There shall not be found among you one who purifies his son or his daughter in fire <note>a reference to child sacrifice to the god Moloch</note>, nor one who practices divination, or observes omens, or practices augury, or a sorcerer, or one who casts spells, or a medium, or a fortune-teller, or one who consults the dead. For everyone who does these things is an abomination to the Lord your God. For because of these abominations, the Lord your God will destroy them from before your face. You shall be perfect before the Lord your God.”

Such were the thousands of other godly teachings and commands that the Divine Word set before them through Moses. He was delivering to them the **introductory elements** <note>original: *stoicheia* — basic principles or "alphabet" of a spiritual life</note> of a life of piety. This was done through symbols and a kind of "shadowy" and physical worship involving bodily circumcision and other similar rites performed on earth. But as time went on, none of the prophets who followed Moses were strong enough to fully cure the evils of life because of the sheer excess of wickedness. Every day, the influence of demonic activity drove men toward even greater crimes, until even the...

While the Hebrew nation alone was preserved from being swept away by the corruption of the godless, the Savior and Physician of the universe <note>original: *sōtēr kai iatros tōn holōn* — a common patristic title for Christ, emphasizing healing over mere legalistic salvation</note> himself finally descends among men. He comes to aid his own angels in the work of human salvation, a gift which his Father had previously promised to grant him,

> as he himself says, teaching in the Psalms: "The Lord said to me, You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession." 

Therefore, no longer only the righteous and God-loving Israel, nor even only his own special portion, but all the nations upon the earth—which were previously allotted to various angels and covered in every kind of impiety—were brought under his own authority. First, he proclaimed to everyone the knowledge and friendship of his Father, acting as an ambassador of peace. He made known the release and forgiveness of sins and countless blessings, which he also clearly preached, saying,

> "Those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." 

And indeed, he appeared first to his own angels, who had previously presided over the nations. They immediately recognized their Helper and Lord with great accuracy; they approached him as brothers and began to serve him,

> just as the holy scripture of the Gospel teaches: "And angels came and ministered to him," and also stating that a multitude of the heavenly host praised God, saying, "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill among men." 

While he received this alliance from these, his own angels, because they were in need of it, he drove away the demons who had long been lurking in human haunts and tyrannizing the inhabitants of the earth, both seen and unseen. He expelled the races of evil and cruel angels, and that terrible avenging spirit <term>avenging spirit: *alastora* — a term for a vengeful or possessing demon</term> who led the forces in Tyre or Gadara <note>A reference to the "Legion" of demons cast out of the Gadarene man into a herd of swine</note> by the great divine power of the Shepherd. These were forced to speak, saying to him:

> "What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?" 

As for their impious acts, he forcefully countered them through what he did and taught. But the entire human race he healed and cared for with the gentle and soothing medicines of his words, and by his actions and encouraging teachings. He delivered them from all kinds of diseases and sufferings, no less of the body than of the soul. He gladly drew in all those who approached him, rescuing them from ancient superstition, the polytheistic error of demons, and a shameful, undisciplined way of life. He shifted and transformed those who associated with him, moving them from debauchery to a sober life, from impiety to piety, from injustice to justice, and indeed from the tyranny of bitter demons to the divine and serene state of true worship. Furthermore, he opened the gates of heavenly life and the teaching of godly living to the nations throughout the whole inhabited world. He descended to such an extent that he did not only offer the right hand of salvation to the sick and those whose souls were gravely ill, but even loosed the bonds of death for those already at its very gates—those half-dead, or entirely lost, and long since buried. For this, he required a working of power even in Hades <note>original: *aidou* — the realm of the dead</note> and as far as the regions there, so that he might be Lord not only of the living, but also of the dead. Thus, while he is present with the Father and governs the providence of the whole universe with divine power—heaven, earth, and the various natures contained within nature—and to the...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s explanation of the Word’s (Logos) role in the cosmos. Having previously discussed the Word’s descent to aid the nations, Eusebius now details the specific titles and functions of the Word as both a heavenly mediator and an earthly savior, leading into the mystery of the Incarnation.</meta>

<page-num>105</page-num>
<header>PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 4</header>

The Word of God, the Wisdom of God, and the Power of God <note>These are the three primary attributes Eusebius uses to describe the pre-existent Christ</note> oversees and cares for the divine and incorporeal essences that exist beyond the heavens. He is celebrated in the divine oracles as Ruler, Leader, and King, and even as God and Lord. While he illuminates the incorporeal and intellectual natures, he is also called the "Sun of Righteousness" and the "True Light." In serving and cooperating with the Father’s decrees, he is known as the Father's Minister and Creator <note>original: *demiurgos* — a craftsman or architect of the universe</note>. Moreover, he alone knows how to worship God in the proper order, standing as a mediator between the Unbegotten God and those created after Him. He has taken up the care of the universe and acts as a consecrated priest to the Father on behalf of all subjects. He alone makes the Father kind and merciful to all, being the Eternal High Priest. He is also addressed as the "Hand of the Father." This is why the Hebrews of old called him "Christ" <note>original: *Christos* — meaning "Anointed One"</note>, performing a symbolic representation of him through their own anointing rituals. Whether he is understood as the Commander of angels—being titled the "Angel of Great Counsel"—or as the Leader of the heavenly armies, he is called the Lord of the high-priestly power. 

But even here on earth, for the sake of us and our rational nature—which is his own image—he reached out with love for humanity through his suffering. Because his care for the "infancy" of our souls resembles the tending of livestock, he is named the "Shepherd of the sheep." And because he promises to heal the passions of our souls, he might rightly be called "Savior" and "Physician." This is indeed what the name of "Jesus" signifies among the Hebrews <note>The name Jesus/Yeshua is derived from the Hebrew root for "to save" or "salvation"</note>. 

Since there was a time when he needed a human instrument <term>organon</term> <note>Eusebius uses this term to describe the physical body of Christ as a tool for the divine Word</note> so that he might reveal himself to men and teach the true word of knowledge and piety regarding the Father, he did not refuse even this lowly place. Entering into our nature, he came among men—a great marvel to all: God manifested through a man. He did not merely walk among us invisibly or without flesh, as in an obscure and hidden way, but was seen by the very eyes of the flesh. He harmonized his presence with human eyes, allowing men to see his miraculous works. Furthermore, he delivered his teachings more clearly through the ears of the body, using a tongue and a voice. He showed himself as a divine narrator and a wondrous thing—the likes of which has never been recorded—appearing at once as a Savior and a benefactor to all. Thus, the God-Word was called the "Son of Man" and was named "Jesus," because he made his passage to us for the sake of the cure and treatment of human souls. For, as noted, "Jesus" is translated among the Hebrews as "Savior." 

He endured our common way of life, in no way being equal to <unclear>us</unclear> in his essence, but simultaneously guarding the Divinity within the Man. For as he proceeded toward his actions among men, he mixed his greatness with the foundation of our nature. He became subject to the same conditions as we are, clothing himself in man after the fashion of a mortal; yet he was no longer a mere man but God, coming into existence through an undefiled maiden who knew no marriage, rather than from a sexual union or corruption.

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s discourse on the Word (Logos). Having established the Word as the mediator and creator, he now transitions to the specific purpose of the Word’s descent into the human condition, focusing on the victory over death and the liberation of souls from Hades.</meta>

<page-num>106</page-num>
<header>BY EUSEBIUS</header>

The Word of God <note>original: *Theos Logos*</note>, visible to many, clearly demonstrated through his works that his actions were fitting and consistent with his divine origins.

-> How the laws of his love for humanity reached even those who had long ago departed to Hades. <-

The circumstances of his departure from among men were also made to serve his purpose. For even unto death, and even to the dead themselves, the laws of his love for humanity <term>philanthropia: God's innate affection and benevolence toward the human race</term> extended their call, so that he might recall the souls of those who had died long ago. He was concerned for all those souls who had been lost since the beginning of time. His intent was to destroy "the one who holds the power of death," as the divine oracles teach. This was another part of his divine plan <term>oikonomia: the "economy" or organized arrangement of God's actions in history, specifically the Incarnation</term> conducted with power. While as a man he yielded his body to the customary burial, he withdrew from it—

> —as God. Indeed, crying out with a loud voice and commending his spirit to the Father, he released himself and withdrew from the body. He did not wait for death to overtake him, for death seemed to hesitate or even shrink back in fear; rather, he pursued death from behind and drove it away. He broke through the eternal gates of those dark recesses and made a way for the dead who were bound there by the seals of death, providing them a return journey toward life. Thus, even while he was dead, he was raised, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose with him, entering into the truly holy "City of Heaven." As it is fittingly said in the divine scriptures: "Death has been swallowed up in strength" <note>original: *katepien o thanatos ischysas* — a reference to Isaiah 25:8 and 1 Corinthians 15:54</note>. And again: "God has wiped away every tear from every face." He himself was the Savior of the universe and our Lord, the victorious Christ of God, as described in the prophetic utterances. He is presented as attacking death and releasing the souls bound there. Through these acts, he offers a hymn of victory, saying these very words: "From the hand of Hades <note>The underworld or realm of the dead</note> I will rescue them, and from death I will redeem them. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?" Now, the "sting" is sin, and the power of sin is the law.

Such was the divine plan <note>original: *oikonomia*</note> he fulfilled even unto death. One could find many more reasons for this than the few I have mentioned if they chose to seek them. For the Word teaches us that he did this, first, so that he might rule over both the dead and the living. Second, so that he might wipe away our sins, being wounded for us and becoming a "curse" on our behalf <note>A reference to the substitutionary nature of Christ's death in Pauline theology</note>. Third, so that he might be offered to the God of all as a victim and a great sacrifice for the sake of the entire world. Fourth, so that he might work a cleansing—through mysterious means—from the multifaceted errors and demonic influences that plague us. Fifth, in addition to these, so that he might present to his friends and disciples the hope of life after death—not merely with words or phrases, but by demonstrating it through actual deeds. By setting this promise before their very eyes, he made them courageous and more eager to proclaim to all nations, including the barbarians, the way of godly living that he had established. Immediately, therefore, he filled those disciples and followers—the chosen apostles whom he had judged best—with his divine power, so that they might teach the entire human race the knowledge of God <term>theognosia: the direct, experiential knowledge of the divine</term> that he had announced, bringing the message of piety to all nations and barbarians alike...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s explanation of the Word’s (Logos) nature during the Incarnation. Having described Christ's descent into Hades on the previous page, he now addresses how the divine Word could inhabit a human body without being defiled or diminished by physical suffering, using the famous analogy of sunlight.</meta>

<page-num>107</page-num>
<header>PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 4</header>

We have set before us as our task the retreat and flight of demons, the removal of multi-faceted error, and the true proclamation of the knowledge of the one and only God over all. This serves as the resolution of those things that previously troubled us—provided they are not brought up again—and offers the only hope of salvation to all, through which the guide for a most wise and most blessed way of life has been established.

---

-> How He remained beyond suffering, unharmed, and incorporeal during the time of His incarnation. <-

Since things are so, the mind should not be troubled when hearing of a body, of passions, and of death concerning the immaterial and incorporeal Word of God <note>original: *theou logon*</note>. For just as the rays of the sun's light are not affected though they fill all things and touch dead and unclean bodies, much more so the incorporeal power of God would neither suffer in its essence nor be harmed, nor ever become worse than itself, by touching a body in an incorporeal manner. For why not? Even apart from the body through which He became man, was He not always and from of old present throughout the whole of the elements and the very matter of bodies? As the Word of God, He is the Creator <term>demiurge: the divine craftsman or architect of the universe</term>, sealing the things within matter with the principles of His own wisdom. He brings life to the soulless and gives shape to the formless and unsightly things of nature, modeling beauties within it and imprinting incorporeal ideas into the qualities of bodies. He moves those things which are by nature soulless and motionless—earth, water, air, and fire—in a most wise and perfectly harmonious motion. He brings order to all things out of disorder, increasing and perfecting them. By His active and rational power, He almost literally pervades all things, passing through all and touching all. Yet, He is certainly not harmed by touching anything, nor is His nature defiled. In this same way, He was present among men—of old in a small number of people who could be counted, appearing only to the beloved prophets and righteous men—but finally to all people now, even to the wicked and ungodly, to both Hebrews and Greeks alike. Through the surpassing kindness and love for humanity of the most blessed Father, He presented Himself as a benefactor and savior, according to the announcement of those who proclaimed this: 

» "Those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are sick." <note>Matthew 9:12</note>
» "I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." <note>Mark 2:17</note>

Thus, the Savior of all called out, saying: "Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." <note>Matthew 11:28</note> He called and healed abundantly through the human instrument <note>original: *organon*; here referring to the physical body as a tool of the divine</note> to which He had joined Himself, just as a musician demonstrates his wisdom through a lyre. To souls suffering in bodies, He—like the best of physicians—offered Himself as a kindred and suitable remedy, a model of a wise, most blessed, and godly life. He taught truths that were not borrowed from others, but came from Himself and from the Father—truths established of old and from the beginning of the ages for those dear to God, and those given as laws to the Hebrews under Moses. Caring no less for bodies than for souls, He prepared the things done through His flesh to be seen by the fleshly eyes of men, and again, through the ears of the flesh, He provided teachings through the tongue of the flesh. He accomplished everything through the human being He had assumed for the sake of those who could not otherwise perceive the nature of His divinity.

<summary>Eusebius argues that the divine Word (Logos) remains untainted by the physical body and suffering, much like sunlight is not defiled by the objects it touches. He describes the Incarnation as a medicinal act where the Word uses a human "instrument" to teach and heal humanity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument that the Word of God (Logos) remains untainted by the physical world. On the previous page, he used the analogy of sunlight to show how the divine can touch the material without becoming "dirty." Here, he extends that logic to the Incarnation, explaining that Christ was simultaneously present in a human body and throughout the entire universe, acting as a source of life that heals and divinizes whatever it touches.</meta>

<page-num>108</page-num>
<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

...of good power. All these things, therefore, for what is useful and beneficial to all of us, the Word of God <note>original: *theou logos*</note>—who in all things loves humanity—having ministered to the Father’s counsels, was again immaterial and incorporeal, just as He was previously with the Father. He did not change His essence, nor was He vanished from His own nature, nor was He bound by the chains of the flesh, nor did He fall away from His divinity. He did not lose the proper power of the Word. Although He made His dwelling here in a human vessel <note>original: *skutos*, literally "skin" or "hide," often used to refer to the body as a temporary container</note>, He was not separated from His riches elsewhere. Even during the time He lived among men, He continued to fill all things; He was with the Father and was in the Father. At that very time, He took care of all things together, both those in heaven and those on earth. He was by no means shut out from His omnipresence as we are, nor was He hindered from performing His accustomed divine works. Instead, He shared His own attributes with the human nature, but did not receive the qualities of the mortal nature in return. He supplied the mortal with divine power, but did not take onto Himself the participation in mortality. Therefore, being incorporeal, He was not defiled by being with a mortal body, nor did He who is beyond suffering experience any change in His essence because of the mortal. For if a lyre were struck—to take an example—or its strings were broken, it is not likely that the musician playing it would suffer. Nor, if the body of a wise man were being punished, would we say that the wisdom within him, or the soul in his body, was being beaten or burned. 

In this way, it is far more irrational to say that the nature or power of the Word suffered any harm from the passions <term>passions: in ancient theology, "passions" refers to things experienced or suffered, like hunger, pain, or emotion</term> of the body. We have the example of light: the sun’s rays, sent down from heaven to earth, are not defiled though they touch clay, filth, and every kind of pollution. The things touched by the rays are indeed enlightened, but the light itself is not defiled. Nor is the sun ever made dirty by mixing with bodies, or turned into mud. If these physical things are not alien to the nature of bodies, then the immaterial and incorporeal Word of God—who happens to be Life-Itself and intellectual Light-Itself <note>original: *autozōē kai autophōs noeron*</note> and whatever else can be conceived—must necessarily lead into life and rational light everything He touches with divine and incorporeal power. Thus, whatever body He touches is immediately sanctified and enlightened; every disease, weakness, and passion gives way. In place of their lack, they receive the fullness of His power. In this way, when the power of the Word touched the dead body for a little while, He raised it to life. Death fled from life, and darkness was dissolved by the light. The corruptible put on incorruption, and the mortal put on immortality.

---
-> How He renewed humanity and provided all of us <-
-> with the hope of eternal goods. <-
---

For what other purpose was there, except that the whole of humanity should be swallowed up by divinity? That the Word of God, being God—just as He was before becoming human—might also divinize the human nature for our hopes? He did this by showing us a great proof: that the human nature is worthy of His eternal life and of communion in His divinity and blessedness, providing for all of us equally a share in the immortality and kingdom that is with Him and from Him.
