# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 4, PAGE 109
<note>original: ΕΥΑΓΓ. ΑΠΟΔΕΙΞ. — The page header marks this as part of Eusebius’s "Demonstratio Evangelica."</note>

**What the name of "Christ" signifies, and how Christ was proclaimed as God, Lord, and High Priest of all things by the prophets among the Hebrews.**

---

<margin>T</margin> The purpose of His arrival among men was to lead back those who had long wandered away from the knowledge of the Father to their own proper home; and to allow the one who is a kinsman and friend, who has been deemed worthy of His own image, to enjoy his own proper life. He intended to reveal this being as a friend and relative to the Father—the very being for whose sake the Word of God <note>original: *theou logos*</note> Himself submitted to become man. In this way, to put it briefly, the various purposes of the "economy" <note>term: *economy* (oikonomia) — the divine plan or "household management" of God for the salvation of humanity</note> of our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ are held within the prophetic word of the Hebrews. As will be shown shortly, the testimonies drawn from them will prove this, confirming the ancient writings by those written more recently, and sealing the Gospel message with the prophetic testimonies. But since these things are so, it is now time to discuss the title itself by which Jesus was called "Christ," and through how many prophecies He was proclaimed by name. First, let us consider what the name "Christ" <note>note: "Christ" comes from the Greek word *Christos*, meaning "Anointed One."</note> intends to show, before we take up the specific collection of prophetic oracles concerning the subject at hand. I believe it is proper first to distinguish the name of Christ and to articulate the concepts surrounding it, so that nothing we seek concerning it may escape us.

It seemed clear to us, and especially remarkable, that Moses was the first of all to legislate that those consecrated to God should be anointed with a prepared myrrh <note>original: *murō skeuastō*</note> of sweet fragrance. He considered incense and the breath of something good to be necessary. For just as a foul smell is dear to the powers of filth and impurity, so conversely, a sweet fragrance is dear to those powers who love what is good. For this reason, he legislated that the priests use blended incense of a pure fragrance every day in the temple, so that the air might always be purified and the foulness vanished, allowing a certain divine emanation to mingle with those who pray. For this very reason, an angelic and most fragrant ointment was composed by the art of the perfumer, so that those who offer public prayers might be anointed with it; and Moses was the first to give the name of "Christ" <note>original: *Christos* — "Anointed"</note> to those who were so anointed. This anointing was handed down not only to the high priests, but also to the prophets and kings after them, for whom it was the custom that they alone should be anointed with this myrrh.

These matters might seem straightforward enough, yet they are far removed from the divine and magnificent mind of the prophet Moses. For that witness, and truly great hierophant <note>term: *hierophant* (hierophantēs) — an ancient Greek term for a priest who interprets sacred mysteries; Eusebius uses it here to describe Moses as an initiate into divine secrets</note>, knowing that all earthly and bodily substance consists only of distinct qualities, would in no way prefer one physical substance over another. He knew that most things are the offspring of a single, ever-shifting matter, which has nothing stable in its nature but is always flowing and hurrying toward its own corruption. He would not choose the sweetness of bodies nor prefer for its own sake the pleasure derived from the senses. For that would be an affection of a soul that has fallen to the earth and toward bodily pleasure. Many who live in effeminate bodies, being entirely passionate and undisciplined, make use of elaborate perfumes and ointments, yet they carry souls filled with every shameful and filthy stench. Conversely, those who are beloved of God breathe in virtue, carrying an aroma far superior to those from the earth—a fragrance given off by temperance <note>original: *sōphrosynē*</note>, justice, and every form of piety. This fragrance of the material body...

He argues that while Moses instituted physical anointing and incense to ward off evil and represent the divine, the true "anointing" is the spiritual fragrance of virtue and piety.</summary>

# EUSEBIUS
<page-num>108</page-num>

<margin>
Eusebius
on the
Preparation
of the Gospel

</margin>

...good powers. All these things, then, for what is useful and beneficial to us all, the Word of God <note>original: *theou logos*</note>—who is entirely a lover of mankind—ministered to the Father's counsels. He remained immaterial and incorporeal, just as He was before with the Father. He neither changed His essence <note>term: *essence* (ousia) — the fundamental nature or "being" of God</note>, nor did He vanish from His own immaterial nature. He was not fettered by the bonds of the flesh, nor did He fall away from His divinity. Neither did He lose the Word's own power. He was not confined only to the place where He made His dwelling in the human vessel <note>The "vessel" refers to the human body of Jesus.</note>, as if He were hidden from the rest of the universe. Rather, even at that time when He lived among men, He filled all things; He was with the Father, and He was in the Father. He took care of all things at once, both in heaven and on earth, and was by no means shut out from the rest of the world by His presence here, as we are. Nor was He hindered from performing divine deeds in His usual way. Instead, He imparted His own gifts to the human nature, but did not receive the weaknesses of the mortal nature in return. He supplied His own power to the mortal, but did not take back any of the mortal's limitations into Himself.

Therefore, the incorporeal One was not defiled by being born in a body, nor did the impassible One <note>term: *impassible* — incapable of suffering or being affected by external pain or change</note> have His essence thickened by the mortal nature. For even if a lyre, should it happen, is broken, or its strings are silenced, it is not expected that the one who was playing it suffers any harm. Nor, if a wise man's body is punished, would we say that the wisdom within him, or the soul in the body, is beaten or burned. 

By this reasoning, we should say even more strongly that the nature or power of the Word suffered nothing from the body. We have the example of light to guide us: the solar rays sent down from heaven to earth are not stained, even though they touch mud, filth, and every kind of defilement. We might say that these things are illuminated by the rays of light, but we would never say the light itself is defiled or becomes "muddy" by mixing with those bodies. These things are not foreign to the nature of the body. But the immaterial and incorporeal Word of God, being Life-itself <note>original: *autozōē*</note> and intellectual Light-itself <note>original: *autophōs noeron*</note> and all the other things previously mentioned—whatever He touches with His incorporeal power must necessarily be made alive and led by His rational light. In this way, whatever body He touches is immediately sanctified and enlightened; every disease, weakness, and pain withdraws from it. It receives a share of His fullness. Thus, even the dead body, when touched by a small portion of the Word’s power, was raised up and brought to life. Death fled from Life, and darkness was dissolved by the Light. The corruptible put on incorruption, and the mortal put on immortality.

->**As He renewed the human being, He provided for all of us the hope of eternal goods.**<-

And what else can be said, except that every human part was swallowed up by the Divinity? The God Word was God again, just as He was before becoming man. He deified the human nature as the first-fruits of our hope. From this, He deems us worthy of eternal life from Himself, and of communion in His divinity and blessedness. He provides this as the greatest proof to all of us alike: that we shall have immortality and a kingdom with Him and through Him.

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of Christ’s titles and nature. While the previous page focused on the Word’s (Logos) relationship with the physical body, this page shifts to an etymological and prophetic study of the name "Christ" (Anointed One), tracing its origins from the laws of Moses to the Hebrew prophets.</meta>

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 2, p. 109
### KIz.i.

<meta>catchword: -shall.</meta>

->What the title of **Christ** is intended to reveal, and how Christ was proclaimed through the Hebrew prophets as God, Lord, and High Priest of the God of the universe.<-

<margin>T</margin> Being the goal of his arrival among men—to lead back to the knowledge of himself those who had long ago fallen away from the knowledge of the Father—and to restore that which is kindred and dear, being deemed worthy of the same image <note>Referring to humanity being made in the image of God.</note>, and to bring back one who had enjoyed his own life. He intended to reveal the Father as a friend and kinsman to this person, for whose sake the Word of God <note>original: *theou logos*</note> himself underwent becoming man. Thus, to put it briefly, the themes concerning our Savior and Lord, Jesus the Christ, involve various aspects of the divine plan <term>economy (oikonomia) — the way God manages or arranges the salvation of humanity</term> according to the words of the Hebrew prophets. As the testimonies from them will show a little later, the ancient writings confirm the newer ones, and the Gospel is sealed by the testimonies of the prophets. 

Since these things are so, it is now time to explain the title itself by which Jesus is called "Christ," and through how many prophecies he was proclaimed by name. First, let us consider what the title of "Christ" <note>original: *Christos*, meaning "Anointed One"</note> is intended to show, before we begin the specific collection of prophetic sayings concerning the promised Seed. I believe it is proper first to take up the name of **Christ** itself and to articulate the concept behind it, so that nothing regarding its investigation escapes us. 

It is clear from the things closest to us that one might say Moses was the first of all to legislate that certain consecrated persons should be poured upon and anointed with a prepared ointment <note>original: *myro*, often translated as myrrh or fragrant oil</note>. He believed that bodies should breathe out a certain fragrance and goodness, since foul odors are dear to the powers of filth and impurity, while fragrance is dear to those who love the good. For this reason, he also legislated that the priests use incense in the temple every day to create an abundance of fragrance, so that as the air was mixed and the foul odor vanished, a certain divine influence might be mingled with those who pray. For this very reason, he also composed a most fragrant anointing oil through the art of the perfumer, so that those who presided over public affairs might be anointed with it. To these anointed ones, Moses was the first to give the name of **Christ** <note>The word "Christ" (Christos) is the Greek translation of the Hebrew "Messiah," both meaning "Anointed."</note>. This anointing was handed down not only to high priests, but also to the prophets and kings who followed them, for whom alone it was lawful to be anointed with this oil. 

These explanations might be the more obvious ones, yet they remain far from the high and noble mind of the prophet. For that wonderful and truly great hierophant <term>hierophant — a priest or teacher of sacred mysteries; here referring to Moses</term>, knowing that all earthy and bodily substance is distinguished only by its qualities, would in no way prefer one over another. He knew that all things are the offspring of a single underlying matter, never standing still, having nothing stable in its nature, but always flowing and hurrying toward its own corruption. Nor if he chose the sweetness of bodies would he prefer that which is breathed in by the senses for its own sake. For such a feeling would belong to a soul that has fallen to the ground and under the pleasure of bodies. Indeed, countless people whose bodies are effeminate, entirely passionate and unrestrained, use elaborate ointments and various luxuries, yet they carry souls full of every shameful and flowing stench. Conversely, those who are dear to God, breathing in virtue, offer a fragrance far better than any earthly spice—one given off by self-control, justice, and all manner of piety. Or perhaps the material body...

...they were not held in any account. Thus, after having thoroughly discussed these things, the prophet [Moses] made no primary concern of perfumes or incenses. Instead, he handed down images of hidden and divine things—as far as was possible—through symbols to those who were only able to learn of divine matters in this way, rather than clearly. And this is exactly what the divine oracle is recorded as having said: 
> "See that you make all things according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain," <note>original: *ora poiēsēs panta kata ton deichthenta soi en tō orei*; quoting Exodus 25:40 regarding the design of the Tabernacle.</note> 
Thus he completed the symbols and archetypes of certain things, which he was accustomed to naming, and he established the law for the anointing through the use of ointment. Yet the high meaning revealed to him in secret—to speak as far as is possible—held this intention: that which alone is good and truly fragrant and precious, the cause of all life, has been gifted to all those who possess the things of piety.

Deep within the Hebrew tradition, the Word <term>Logos — the divine Reason or Word of God</term> understood the cause of all things to be the Most High himself, the King of all and the Creator God. Therefore, the most powerful and unbegotten power of his divinity—the provider of all things truly beautiful—is called the "Divine Spirit." Because of this, it is called the "Christ" <note>meaning "Anointed"</note> by virtue of participating in that Spirit. 

In these matters, understand "oil" to mean mercy, and not a fire that brings grief over past deeds; rather, understand it as the plant that produces the fruit, which is unmixed with any liquid matter, but is an increaser of light, a healer of labors, and a deliverer from exhaustion. It makes the faces of those who use it cheerful, shining with brilliance like light itself, and it makes the appearance of those who use it transparent and bright. This is what the Divine Scripture says: 
> "to make the face cheerful with oil." <note>Psalm 104:15.</note> 

Therefore, the Word uses this symbolic example to describe the most holy power of the Ruler and King of all, God. He calls the one who was first and alone anointed with this whole fragrance, and who partook of the divine and Fatherly fragrance (which is unshared by all others), and who was the only Word begotten from Him—declaring him God from God by the union of his participation with the Unbegotten and Father and Greater One—he calls him the "Christ" and "The Anointed." 

Because of this, the speaking Word cries out in the Psalms to this very Son of the Father as the Anointed One: 
> "Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever; a scepter of uprightness is the scepter of thy kingdom. Thou hast loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows." <note>Psalm 45:6–7 (Septuagint 44:7–8). Eusebius uses this to prove the Son is called "God" and "Anointed" by the Father.</note>

But while the nature of oil is singular and pleasant, that of ointment <term>myron — a complex perfumed oil or unguent</term> signifies the gathering of many things into one. In this way, the first and unbegotten power of God the King is conceived as something simple and uncomposed, unmixed with any other substance; this is compared to the simple name of "oil." 

But insofar as it happens to encompass a vast array of concepts in itself—such as the power of creating, or of kingship, of providence, of judgment, of love for humanity, and of salvation, and of countless other struggles viewed through the intellect—rightly then is this power, which encompasses many good things, likened to "ointment." The divine words have handed down that the true and only High Priest of God used this ointment. For Moses himself, having been deemed worthy to behold divine things in secret, and the rites concerning the first and only Anointed and High Priest of God having been performed before him in his visions of God, he set forth images on earth and established symbols of the things understood in his vision of God. This was so that those deemed worthy might practice with the symbols until they reached the contemplation of the spiritual realities. For he chose a man fit to serve as a priest to God for a time among men on earth, as was fitting...

He named him **Christ** in reference to the contemplation of things perceived by the mind <note>original: *noētois*; referring to the Platonic/theological concept of reality understood by the intellect rather than the physical senses</note>. By declaring him to possess an incorporeal and fragrant anointing superior to other men, he proclaimed clearly and inexpressibly that even the entire nature of the unbegotten <note>original: *agenētos*; referring to God the Father as the uncreated source</note>—and much more the human nature which falls short of the power of the Unbegotten—needs the fragrance of the Higher One. But it is not lawful for anyone to reach that which is highest and first; for this prize was reserved for the **Only-begotten** and **First-born** alone. For those who come after him, it is impossible to enjoy these good things in any other way than through participation in the Second <note>The "Second" refers to the Son or the Logos, who acts as the intermediary between the Father and creation.</note>.

> Therefore, the image of the Spirit in Moses’s writings was a symbol.
> "There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit." <note>Quoting 1 Corinthians 12:4 to explain the diversity of divine graces.</note>

He believed that priests, prophets, and kings ought to strive to participate in this Spirit above all, so that they might be consecrated not by their own power alone, but by the divine Spirit. But let us examine more precisely how these symbols in Moses’s time worked, and how it was possible for people—even while possessed by the divine Spirit—to be called **Christs** through earthly ointment.

In the 104th Psalm <note>Psalm 105 in modern English Bibles.</note>, David recounts the histories of **Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob**. He calls these God-loving ancestors "Christs," even though they lived before the time of Moses, for no other reason than their participation in the divine Spirit which rested upon them. After narrating how they lived as strangers among foreign nations and how they found a savior in God against mortal plots—just as revealed in the books of Moses—he names them both **prophets** and **Christs** together. This was before the Law of Moses had ever appeared among men, and before the preparation of the ritual ointment had been established by law. Listen to what the Psalm says:

> "Remember his marvelous works that he has done,
> his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth,
> O seed of Abraham his servants, you children of Jacob, his chosen ones.
> He is the Lord our God; his judgments are in all the earth.
> He has remembered his covenant forever,
> the word which he commanded to a thousand generations,
> which he made with Abraham, and his oath to Isaac.
> And he confirmed it to Jacob for a statute,
> and to Israel for an everlasting covenant, saying,
> 'To you I will give the land of Canaan, the lot of your inheritance.'
> And they went from nation to nation, and from one kingdom to another people.
> He allowed no man to do them wrong; yes, he rebuked kings for their sakes,
> saying, **'Touch not my anointed ones <note>original: *christōn mou*; literally "my Christs."</note>,**
> **and do my prophets no harm.'**"

These are the words of David. And Moses also records which kings were rebuked, saying: "And the Lord afflicted **Pharaoh** with great plagues, and his house, because of Sarah, Abraham's wife." And again, concerning the King of Gerar, he writes: "God came to **Abimelech** in a dream by night, and said, 'Behold, you are a dead man because of the woman whom you have taken; for she is a man’s wife.'" Proceeding further, he says: "Now therefore, restore the man his wife; for he is a **prophet**, and he shall pray for you."

Do you see how, through these passages, David—or rather the divine Spirit through him—called those ancient God-loving men and prophets **Christs**, even though they were not anointed with earthly ointment? For how could they have been, since Moses established those laws in much later times? 

Listen also to **Isaiah**, who prophesies most clearly concerning the **Christ**, stating that he would be sent by God to mankind as a redeemer and savior, coming to preach release to those whose souls are captive, and recovery of sight to those who are blind in their minds. For the prophet says that he was anointed not with prepared ointment, but with the Father's—

For he says: "The Lord said to my Lord." Furthermore, he knows him as an eternal High Priest, a priest to God the Most High, co-enthroned with the God who is over all, and as his offspring. For the things of God belong to the priest among the Hebrews without a physical anointing. Therefore, he is named **Christ** by them, loving all that is beneath him. Therefore, the priest revealed in the Psalm would also be **Christ**. For how could he be considered a priest if he had not first become **Christ** (anointed)? Furthermore, he is said to be a priest "forever." This could no longer apply to human nature. For a man who struggles through life knows that our race is mortal and fleeting. Therefore, the priest revealed in these passages is superior to man; he has received from God, with the confirmation of an oath, a priesthood that is both a beginning and without end.

...consecrated sacredly to the Most High God. Appropriately, David also, in his prophecy, spoke of him as being "great" and surpassing all nature, inasmuch as he is the priest of the God over all and a sharer of the throne <note>original: *synthronos*; literally "seated on the same throne," implying equal status in divinity</note> with the Unbegotten Power. He is the Lord of both prophet and king, and a priest not in an ordinary sense, but an eternal one from God. 

The divine Apostle <note>Referring to the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews</note> also says this when examining these passages: 
» "Wherein God, willing more abundantly to show unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath: that by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation." 

And again: 
» "For those priests were made without an oath; but this with an oath by him that said unto him: The Lord sware and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek." 
» "And they truly were many priests, because they were not suffered to continue by reason of death: But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood. Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them." 

Through these words, it is established that there exists a certain divine power among real beings, subsisting in the noetic <term>noetic: relating to the intellect or spiritual realm, as opposed to the physical</term> world, who is consecrated to the God of the universe according to the Hebrew oracles <note>original: *Hebraiōn logia*; a common early Christian term for the Old Testament scriptures</note>. This power was not appointed to the God over all by an earthly or human myrrh, but by a certain god-befitting and divine virtue and priestly power. 

Indeed, the one prophesied through the Psalm was surely an eternal priest and likewise the Son of God, as one begotten by the Most High God himself and a sharer of the throne of his kingdom. It has also been shown that the **Christ** spoken of through Isaiah came from among men, having been anointed by the Father himself through the Holy Spirit, and sent as a redeemer for the captivity of mankind. 

Moses also used this name [Christ], establishing images and symbols among men. For a time, he used a prepared ointment <note>original: *skeuastō myrō*</note> instead of the divine Spirit to anoint and smear the high priest among men, calling him both "Christ" <note>In Greek, *Christos* simply means "Anointed One"</note> and "Sanctified" as a reference to the True One. 

As to how these things are so, who could be a more worthy witness for us than the one who, in his own writing, explicitly taught that the one who appeared to him was God and Lord? According to the noetic and heavenly vision granted to him, he established a more corporeal <note>meaning "physical" or "fleshly"</note> worship on earth, which contained an image of noetic and incorporeal things. It is said, at least, that he sketched a certain type <term>type: a prophetic symbol or "shadow" that points toward a later, greater reality</term> of the angels and divine powers in heaven, for the divine oracle said to him: 
» "See that thou make all things according to the pattern <note>original: *typon*</note> showed to thee in the mount." 

Therefore, just as with the sacrificial blood, he also passed over the high priest, anointing him with earthly myrrh. This was so that he might produce a shadowy and symbolic—but not the true—anointed one <note>original: *christon*</note> and high priest, a representation of the heavenly **Christ** and High Priest. 

I believe it has been clearly demonstrated that the true **Christ** was not a man, but a Son of God, honored at the right hand of the Father’s divinity, and far better not only than mortal and human nature, but also than all the combined rational essence <note>referring to the hierarchies of spirits and angels</note>. 

Furthermore, according to what was said just before, the same David in the 44th Psalm <note>Psalm 45 in modern Bibles</note>, using a heading "For the Beloved" and concerning the "change" of those things that have come to be, proclaims one and the same being as both God, King, and Christ, writing thus: 
» "My heart has uttered a good word; I speak of my works to the King; my tongue..."

# EUSEBIUS

> » ...the pen of a ready writer, fairer in beauty than the sons of men. To these things is added: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; a scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You loved righteousness and hated iniquity. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions."

Consider then more carefully how, according to the title of the Psalm, the discourse begins with a prelude "concerning the beloved ones," following an exhortation to the audience for the understanding of what is to be said. He also marks the reason for the arrangement of the discourse, saying, "For the end, concerning those who shall be changed <note>original: *alloiothesomenon*; referring to those undergoing a spiritual transformation or conversion</note> for understanding, concerning the Beloved." Who would you say are these "to be changed" for whom the Psalm is spoken, if not those who are about to be transformed from their former life and manner, and are to be moved and changed through the things of the Beloved? And this was the Beloved of God, concerning whom the Psalm's prelude tells us we need prophetic understanding.

But if anyone should ask who this "Beloved" is, about whom it was prophesied in the Psalm, the text follows immediately in sequence, saying: "My heart has poured forth a good word" <note>original: *logon agathon*; in Greek, *Logos* means both "word" and "reason" or "principle"</note>. One might say that this refers to that very Word who was in the beginning with God, whom the great evangelist John spoke of in his theology: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Indeed, the phrase "My heart has poured forth a good word," if spoken from the person of the Father and God of all, would reveal the only-begotten Word of God as a Son subsisting from the Father. 

Yet this is not by way of an outflowing, or by division, or cutting, or lessening, or anything conceived of in a physical sense. For such thoughts are impious and entirely far removed from the inexpressible study of God <term>theology: here used in its literal sense, "theologia," meaning the study or discourse concerning the divine nature</term>. In our own specific understanding, we must also interpret these things—such as being born "from the womb" of God and "before the morning star"—in a fitting way, receiving not just a conceptual theory, but that which must be accepted as most certain. The statement "My heart has poured forth a good word" occurs according to the mind of the Divine Spirit as it describes these things. Regarding these matters, it is proper to speak of things conceived according to the usual manner for each point of theology concerning him, and that pious saying: "Who shall declare his generation?" <note>A reference to Isaiah 53:8, often used by early Christians to stress the mystery of Christ's eternal origin</note>. Even if the Divine Scriptures customarily use mortal and human voices for us, adding words like "to be born" and using the name "womb," these belong only to the contemplation of the mind and are not at all subject to the laws of public oratory. 

Thus, one might say that "My heart has poured forth a good word" is spoken regarding the constitution and essence of the First Word, since it is not lawful to interpret "heart" or our other human concepts as applying to the God of all in a literal sense. But one might call the Word who was "in the beginning with God" a "good word" because he is the offspring of the All-Good Father. Moving slightly further into the Psalm, we will find that this very one, the Beloved of God who was prophesied, was anointed—not as if by Moses, nor by any human being, but by the Eternal God and Father of all himself. For as the text proceeds, it says: "Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." And indeed, it is testified here that he was anointed by the God over all...

# THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 4

...how else would anyone name him than "Christ" <note>original: *Christos*, meaning "Anointed One"</note>? Therefore, through these passages, we already have two titles for the one being prophesied: "Christ" and "Beloved." These titles refer to one and the same person, showing that he who is the cause of the anointing is also declared to have been anointed by the God of gladness. This teaches us his dignity, which will be clear to someone who looks back a little, or rather, to someone who examines the entire meaning of the passage. For the Psalm speaks, addressing that very Christ and "Beloved of God" who was prophesied (in the words set out a little earlier, in which it was said):

» "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; a scepter of uprightness is the scepter 
» of your kingdom. You loved righteousness and hated iniquity. Therefore 
» God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions."

Consider, therefore, if these words do not clearly address him directly; for "you," it says, "are God," instead of "O God." Your throne exists forever and ever, and a scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. And since you yourself, being God, loved righteousness and hated iniquity, therefore God, your God, has anointed you and established you as Christ <note>the "Anointed One"</note> above all others. The Hebrew scripture is even clearer on these points, which Aquila <note>a 2nd-century scholar famous for his literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, translating with total accuracy, rendered in this way:

» "Your throne, O God, is for an age and further; a scepter of uprightness is the scepter 
» of your kingdom. You loved the righteous and hated the ungodly act. 
» On this account, God, your God, has smeared you with the oil of joy 
» above your associates."

Indeed, this phrase, "God, your God," contains the Hebrew word itself, "O God, your God," so that it may be clear: "You loved the right, O God, and you hated the ungodly act. Therefore, O God, this one who is the highest and greater God of yours anointed you." This shows that both the one being anointed and the one doing the anointing existed long before, both being God, but with the Anointer being uniquely the God of the one being anointed. This would become clear even by noting the Hebrew language itself. For in the first title, which Aquila clearly translated as "Your throne, O God," saying "O God" instead of "the God," the Hebrew contains *Elohim* <note>Hebrew: אֱלֹהִים (*Elohim*). Eusebius notes this is used here in the vocative case, "O God"</note>. And here, similarly, regarding the phrase "Therefore God has anointed you," *Elohim* is used again, which indicated the case used for addressing someone <note>the vocative case</note>. But instead of the direct or nominative form of the name—as it was said, "Therefore God, your God has anointed you"—the Hebrew contains *Eloah* <note>Hebrew: אֱלוֹהַּ (*Eloah*). Eusebius argues this form identifies the Father as the subject/nominative</note> with great precision. While *Elohim* is selected for the vocative case to mean "O God," *Eloah* means "your God" in the nominative. Thus, the interpretation that says, "Therefore God, your God, has anointed you," is perfectly accurate.

Through these words, the discourse addresses him most clearly as God, saying that he has been anointed by God with the oil of gladness, beyond all those who have ever shared the same title as him. In these passages, you clearly have a God being anointed and becoming "Christ," not with a manufactured ointment, nor by humans coming forward for this purpose, nor in a manner similar to other men. He is the same who is the "Beloved of God," his offspring, the eternal priest, and the Child proclaimed as the throne. Who could this be, other than the pre-existent Word of God—the one who was "God with God" in the beginning, and who is spoken of as God throughout the whole of the divinely inspired Scripture? As the discourse proceeds through more examples in the following sections, it will demonstrate this. Having previously considered these points regarding the essence and the title of Christ, let us now take up the proposed subject and see through how many prophetic predictions Christ was proclaimed by name.

# EUSEBIUS

Through many scriptures, Christ is mentioned by name as the one plotted against by kings, rulers, nations, and peoples. He is proclaimed both as the one acting as the oracle of God <note>original: *theou chrēmatizōn*</note> and as the Son of Man, and he was foretold as receiving the nations and the ends of the earth as his inheritance from the Father.

<margin>1</margin>
> Why did the nations rage, and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth stood up, and
> the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ. To these words
> he adds: "But I have been established as king by him upon Zion, his holy
> mountain, proclaiming the commandment of the Lord. The Lord said to me: You are my son, I
> have begotten you today. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance,
> and the ends of the earth for your possession."

Most clearly through these words, the Holy Spirit calls out to Christ. He names him the "Son of God" in accordance with what was said before, and at the same time, he signifies the plotting that would occur against him and foretells the inheritance of the nations that would come through him. These events were shown by the very outcome of things to have been fulfilled undeniably in the works of our Savior, Jesus Christ. For even now, nations and peoples, kings and rulers, do not cease to stand against him and his teaching in the same way. 

But if anyone from the circumcision <note>meaning the Jewish people</note> refers these words only to the one they still expect, it is time for them to admit that their expected "Christ" must also be plotted against, according to this current oracle <note>original: *logion*</note> which says:
> The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord 
> and against his Christ.

This is a point they would not concede, for they expect the coming Christ to be a powerful person, an eternal king and their redeemer. For if that person were to suffer the same things as our Savior, why should one believe or disbelieve in that one any more than in this one? 

But if they are blocked from this interpretation, they might refer the prophecy to David or to one of the kings of the Jewish nation who descended from him. In that case, it must be shown that neither for David nor for any other recorded in Hebrew history was it ever oracularly declared by God that he was "begotten as the Son of God"—according to the prophecy in the Psalm—nor was he ever plotted against by *all* the nations, kings, rulers, and peoples. 

If none of those figures can be shown to fit, and yet all these things are confirmed by facts—that the Christ of God endured these things long ago and even today is still fought against by kings, rulers, nations, and peoples—what is to stop us from seeing him as the one being prophesied? For the oracle says:
> The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord 
> and against his Christ.

To him alone would the subsequent parts of the Psalm also fit, in which it is said:
> The Lord said to me: You are my son, I have begotten you today. Ask of me, and I will give 
> you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession.

Strictly speaking, these things have received their undisputed fulfillment only in him, as the "sound" of his disciples went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world <note>a reference to Psalm 19:4, often used to describe the spread of the Gospel</note>. Therefore, the Word clearly addresses him as "Christ," teaching from his own person that he is the Son of God through the phrase:
> The Lord said to me: You are my son, I have begotten you today.

Similar to these is the passage in Proverbs <note>Proverbs 8:25</note>, again spoken from his person in this way: "Before the mountains were settled, and before all the hills, he be-
<note>the text breaks here; the full word is "begets me"</note>

<summary>Eusebius argues that Psalm 2's prophecy of a "Son of God" who is persecuted by kings yet inherits the nations can only refer to Jesus Christ, refuting alternative Jewish interpretations regarding David or a future Messiah.</summary>

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 9

» me. And that which was spoken to him by the Father in the 109th Psalm: "From the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten you." <note>original: *ek gastros pro heōsphorou gegennēka se*—this refers to Psalm 110:3 in modern Bibles (109 in the Septuagint), often interpreted by early Christians as the eternal generation of the Word.</note> The sacred scriptures prophesy that one and the same person is named both Christ and the Son of God—one who would be plotted against by men, yet would receive the nations as his lot and hold dominion over the ends of the earth. They signal his divine plan <term>dispensation<gloss>oikonomia: the unfolding of God’s plan in human history, particularly through the Incarnation</gloss></term> toward humanity through two proofs: first, by the conspiracy formed against him, and second, by the subsequent submission of the nations to him.

## Psalm 19 <note>Psalm 20 in modern Bibles.</note>

### Christ mentioned by name as receiving his requests from the Father.

"May the Lord fulfill all your requests. Now I know that the Lord has saved his Christ; he will hear him from his holy heaven." Since our current purpose is to present the instances where Christ is announced by name in the prophecies, we have naturally included these words which clearly herald the Christ. The entire Psalm is a prayer sent up from the person of holy men <note>meaning the prophets or the faithful of the Church</note> to the person of Christ. Because he took upon himself every insult for our sake and on our behalf when he became man, we are taught to pray along with him as he makes his own petitions and needs known to the Father for our sake—especially as he defends himself against our enemies, whether they be visible or invisible. Therefore, we say to him using the words of the Psalm: "May the Lord hear you in the day of trouble; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you. May he send you help from the sanctuary, and support you from Zion." Then, since it is proper to him as the Great High Priest to perform spiritual rites <note>original: *pneumatikas hierourgias*</note> on our behalf through hymns of glory and theology, and since like a priest he offered both himself and the human nature he assumed from the earth <note>original: *hon aneilephen apo gēs anthrōpon*</note> as a whole burnt offering to God the Father, we say to him: "May he remember all your sacrifices, and make your burnt offering fat." And since all that he wills is for the salvation and benefit of the world, we naturally cry out to him: "May the Lord give you according to your heart, and fulfill all your counsel." Following this, we acknowledge his resurrection from the dead, saying: "We will exult in your salvation." For what else could the "salvation of Christ" be understood to be, if not his resurrection from the dead? Through this, he raises up all those who have fallen. Thus we say: "And in the name of our God we shall be magnified; may the Lord fulfill all your requests." After all this, we are taught to say: "Now I know that the Lord has saved his Christ." We did not know this long ago, but only when we first understood his salvation and contemplated the power of his resurrection.

## Psalm 27 <note>Psalm 28 in modern Bibles.</note>

### Christ mentioned by name, and having the Father as protector.

"The Lord is the strength of his people, and he is the protector of the salvations of his Christ." This present Psalm also refers to Christ, containing the prayer which he prayed before the time of his Passion. Therefore, at the beginning, the Psalm says: "To you, O Lord, I will cry, my God; do not be silent toward me," and similar words, "lest you be silent and I become like those who go down into the pit." But toward the end, it prophesies his resurrection from the dead, saying: "Blessed be the Lord, for he has heard the voice of my petition. The Lord is my helper and my protector; in him my heart..."

<summary>Eusebius interprets Psalms 19 and 27 (LXX) as prophetic dialogues regarding Christ's human suffering, his role as High Priest, and his ultimate triumph in the Resurrection. He emphasizes that the "salvation" mentioned in these psalms refers specifically to the act of rising from the dead.</summary>

## Psalm 83 <note>Psalm 84 in modern Bibles.</note>

Christ is addressed by name as the one who acknowledges God as his overseer, and the "one day" is the day of 
his resurrection. The "one house" of God is his Church.
O God our protector, behold, and look upon the face of your Christ. For 
> one day in your courts is better than thousands. I chose rather to be cast 
> aside in the house of my God than to dwell in the tents of sinners. Those 
who acknowledge Christ as the Word, Wisdom, true Light, and Life of God,

dead; either because it is the "one and only" day that is truly the Lord's and the "Lord's Day," <note>original: *kyriakēn* — Eusebius identifies the "one day" in the Psalm with Sunday, the day of the Resurrection.</note> they say it is 
better than ten thousand of the common days, or those 
legislated by Moses during feasts, new moons, and Sabbaths, which the divine Apostle teaches are but "shadows" of days, 
not the days themselves. Only this "one" and "Lord's Day" of our Savior 
does not illuminate in a ceremonial type, but has been chosen only in the courts of the Lord. 
And these "courts" are the Churches of Christ throughout the whole inhabited world, 
which happen to be the courts of the one God. In these, the one who knows such things 
loves and chooses to be "cast aside" <note>This refers to the humility of being even a doorkeeper or an outcast within the Church rather than a leader elsewhere.</note>, declaring that dwelling in these is far 
better than dwelling in the "tents of sinners." By this, he signifies the synagogues of the Jews which 
deny the Christ of God, or the gatherings of heterodox heresies, and of the other unbelieving 
nations; the one who chooses the Churches of Christ declares them to be much better than those.

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book IV

» Remember, Lord, the reproach of your servants, which I have borne in my bosom from 
» many nations; with which your enemies, Lord, have reproached—with which they 
» have reproached the exchange of your Christ. <note>original: *antallagma tou christou sou*. This refers to the "recompense" or "substitution" of the Anointed.</note> It is clear that by these words, Christ is mentioned by name, as is the rejection predicted at his passion. If we were to examine the entire Psalm at leisure, we would demonstrate that these words could apply to no one else but our Savior and Lord. He is called "Christ" by name so that it might be revealed either that he is the one, or that the "exchange"—namely, the Church—is what the so-called enemies of Christ have reproached and still reproach to this day. Indeed, every enemy of Christ's teaching is accustomed to reproach us for the sufferings our Savior endured for us, and especially his death and the cross.

-> Psalm 131 <note>Psalm 132 in modern Bibles.</note> <-

-> Christ is named as the one arising from the seed of David, being called the "horn" of David, <-
-> putting his Jewish enemies to shame, and taking up the sanctuary of the Father. <-

The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not reject him: "Of the fruit of 
» your womb I will set upon your throne." Then, moving further down, he says: "There 
» I will cause a horn to spring up for David; I have prepared a lamp for my Christ. 
» His enemies I will clothe with shame, but upon him my sanctuary shall flourish." 
And here the Lord swears concerning the one from the seed of David, whom he indeed calls his "horn." And again, proclaiming Christ by name, he says he has prepared a "lamp" for him—meaning, likely, the prophetic word. Like a forerunner to Christ, this word alone has dawned upon all people throughout the inhabited world, after the fashion of solar light. David himself was also prepared as a lamp for Christ, holding the rank of a lamp before the Sun and the perfect Light. For he says, "I will cause a horn to spring up," indicating the place, and then signifying that Christ would be born. For in the Psalm, David seems to have foreseen the "sleep" <note>A common early Christian metaphor for death or the time before the Incarnation.</note> before the appearance of Christ, saying: "If I shall enter the bed of my mattress, if I shall give sleep to my eyes, and slumber to my eyelids, and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob." The Divine Spirit then reveals the word spoken by the prophets in Bethlehem: "For behold, we heard of it in Ephratha <note>Ephratha is the ancient name for Bethlehem, the birthplace of Jesus.</note>—which is Bethlehem—we found it in the fields of the wood. We will enter into his dwellings; we will worship in the place where his feet stood." It was fitting, then, after these revelations, that he added: "There I will cause a horn to spring up for David; I have prepared a lamp for my Christ." Perhaps the "lamp" also signifies the body assumed in Christ from Bethlehem, according to another interpretation. The divine power dwelt in it like a lamp or a vessel of clay—as if through an earthen vessel—and through this lamp, it radiated flashes of divine and rational light upon all humanity.

# EUSEBIUS

<margin>Eusebius: On the Preparation for the Gospel, Greek and Latin</margin>

"…and treading upon the high places of the earth. The Lord God Almighty is his name." <note>Amos 4:13</note>
"Hear the word of the Lord, which I take up against you, a lamentation. The house of Israel has fallen; she shall no longer rise. The virgin of Israel has stumbled upon her land; there is no one to raise her up." <note>Amos 5:1-2</note>

This is now the seventh time God announces Christ by name to mankind. He is described as "strengthening thunder and creating the spirit," and the message of the Gospel is called "thunder" because it is heard by all men. Similarly, the "spirit" of Christ breathed into the apostles is revealed, through which the prophecy was clearly fulfilled at our Savior’s advent. At this coming, it is prophesied that God will make "dawn and mist together"—dawn for those who perceive the light of salvation and glory, but for those who disbelieved in him, a mist of sorrow that brings no benefit. To these, the Word proclaims the final sentence, adding a lamentation for the Jewish nation because of the fate that overtook them immediately after their impiety against our Savior Jesus Christ. For truly from that time until now, the "house of Israel" has fallen; once and for all, a sentence has been issued by God concerning their fallen house in Jerusalem and their entire community, so that they shall no longer rise, nor is there anyone to raise them up. Indeed, it says, "there is no one to raise her up." Since they did not receive the living Christ of God, he rightly abandoned them and passed over to all the nations. He taught the cause of this downfall through his own weeping, almost offering a defense when he said: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her! How often I wanted to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing! Look, your house is left to you desolate." <note>Matthew 23:37-38</note>

Christ named by the Lord the Father, and saving his own anointed ones.

"You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones. <note>original: *christous*, the plural form of Christ/Anointed.</note> You brought death upon the heads of the lawless." <note>Habakkuk 3:13</note> Aquila <note>A 2nd-century scholar known for a very literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translates this as: "You went forth for the salvation of your people, for the salvation of your people with your Christ." Where Aquila used the singular "with Christ" instead of the plural, he indicates that salvation was worked for the people through the Son of God. # PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 6

<page-num>121</page-num>

...naming <note>The Greek text begins with the suffix of a word, likely "naming" or "proclaiming," continuing from the previous page.</note> the Christ again, as if referring to the Christ himself, of whom the prophetic spirit declared to them that he would be "captured in their corruptions." <note>Lamentations 4:20</note> This was said so that it might be clear that it was those of the circumcision <note>original: "ek peritomēs," referring to the Jewish people</note> who would plot against him. Here the Word maintains a sense of mystery, that the Christ would be "captured" in a hidden manner—a description that would not fit the second coming of Christ. For the prophetic words proclaim that his second coming will be glorious, accompanied by a heavenly kingdom. 

It is likely for this reason that those of the circumcision fell into error; they took the descriptions of his second appearance and applied them to his first arrival, and thus they could not accept the Word. For it is impossible to imagine him as simultaneously glorious and inglorious in the same moment; both honored as a King, and yet "having no form or beauty, but being dishonored and the least among the sons of men"; <note>Isaiah 53:2-3</note> and again, both the Savior and Redeemer of Israel, and yet plotted against by them, "led like a sheep to the slaughter," and "delivered up to death" by those who demanded it. 

Yet for us, as the reality of these events demonstrates, the prophecies concerning Christ are divided into two patterns. It is confessed that the more sorrowful and somber prophecies were fulfilled during his first arrival, while the more glorious and exalted ones are even now expected at his second coming. A clear proof of the first arrival is the "knowledge of God" <note>original: "theognōsia"</note> which has gone out to all the nations through him. The prophetic voices make various mentions of this, as does the present passage, which says:

<margin>»</margin>
> "Of whom we said, In his shadow we shall live among the nations." <note>Lamentations 4:20</note>

### From the First Book of Kingdoms. Christ named by the Lord the Father as being exalted.
<note>The "Books of Kingdoms" in the Greek Septuagint correspond to 1 and 2 Samuel and 1 and 2 Kings in English Bibles. This citation is from 1 Samuel.</note>

<margin>»</margin>

> » ...he shall do the things in my heart and the things in my soul; and I will build him a faithful house, and he shall walk before my Anointed One <note>original: "christou mou"</note> for all days. <note>1 Samuel 2:35</note>

Having threatened the removal and rejection of the one who does not serve according to right reason <note>A reference to the corrupt priesthood of Eli and his sons in the Old Testament</note>, the Divine Word promises to establish another priest from a different lineage. He says this priest will "walk before his Anointed One," or "walk in the presence of his said one," as Aquila <note>A 2nd-century scholar who translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek</note> interpreted it; or as Symmachus <note>An early translator known for his clear, idiomatic Greek</note> records it, he will be "enrolled before his Anointed." 

Who would this be, who approaches the sacred service of the Christ of God <term>the Messiah</term> in a holy manner, if not the "house" of the Church? This house, the God of all things promises to build himself, like a wise architect and builder. He indicates no other house but the Church established in the name of Christ throughout the whole world. There, everyone who is consecrated to God through Christ is said to perform spiritual services—those of the "incense" <note>Metaphorical incense representing prayer and devotion</note> and of the soul—rather than services involving the blood of bulls and goats. These former rituals, which were performed as symbolic patterns <term>types</term> of old, have been set aside by God, as acknowledged through the prophecy of Isaiah. 

In these prophecies, Christ was heralded by name. Since many things regarding the sufferings of Christ are passed over in silence while focusing on his title, it is necessary to run through the famous reports concerning his "anointing" <term>chrisma</term>, so that it might be declared beforehand as being carried out for the "Beloved" <note>A messianic title</note> in a single Psalm. 

First, the Word reminds us of him as a King, and after other things, he introduces the 

> » divinity of Christ: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; a scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You loved righteousness and hated lawlessness. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions." <note>Psalm 45:6-7</note>

For clearly in these verses, as has been said before, the one being described is himself called "God," because he loved righteousness and hated injustice. For this reason, he has been anointed by another greater God, who is his Father, with a better and superior grace than those found in the symbolic rituals—with what is called the "oil of gladness." Now, the one anointed with such an anointing—not by men, nor through men, but by the Ruler God himself—what else could he reasonably be called but "Christ" <note>The word "Christ" literally means "the Anointed One."</note>? Thus, he is shown to be both "God" and "Anointed" at the same time, just as was established previously in the appropriate places. And according to the prophecy of Isaiah:

> » and these things must be remembered again, as he said: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor, to heal the broken-

hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind." <note>Isaiah 61:1</note> We showed in these passages how the priests of old, who approached the service of God from among men, used to anoint the ritual vessel with oil. But the one revealed through prophecy is said to be anointed with "divine power." Our Savior, Jesus, the only true "Christ" of God, applied this whole passage to himself. Standing in the Jewish synagogue, he took the prophecy and, having read the passage, taught that it was fulfilled in himself. It is written:

> » that having read and folded the book and given it back to the attendant, he sat down; and the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. And he began to say to them: "Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing." <note>Luke 4:20-21</note>

In addition to all these, the writings of Moses must also be compared, who, according to the pattern <term>type</term> shown to him, [appointed] his own brother...

### PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 4

-> Ll.ii. <-

Having established his brother Aaron as high priest, following the oracle that spoke to him: 
> » "You shall make all things according to the pattern <term>typos</term> shown to you on the mountain." <note>Exodus 25:40; Hebrews 8:5</note> 

It is clear that by perceiving with the eyes of his mind and through the Divine Spirit the Great High Priest of all things—the true Christ <term>Anointed One</term> of God—he did not merely record an image of the sensory, physical, and symbolic worship. Rather, he honored the one revealed by the title of "Christ" in truth. This is also presented by the divine Apostle when speaking of the things according to the Law of Moses:
> » "Who serve as a copy and shadow <term>skia</term> of heavenly things." <note>Hebrews 8:5</note> 

And again: 
> » "For the Law, having a shadow of the good things to come." <note>Hebrews 10:1</note> 

And again: 
> » "Therefore let no one judge you in food or in drink, or regarding a festival or a new moon or sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come." <note>Colossians 2:16-17</note> 

For if the laws regarding indifferent matters like food, and those legislated concerning festivals and the Sabbath—being shadow-like—contained a sketch of other teachings and mystical realities, you would not be speaking unreasonably to say that the high priest was also intended as a symbol of another High Priest. Thus, he was named "Christ" <note>original: "christon," meaning anointed</note> as a symbol of the other, the only and true Christ. This true one is as much greater and superior as he is recognized by the God of all things, who says: 
> » "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." <note>Psalm 110:1</note> 

And: 
> » "Rule in the midst of your enemies." <note>Psalm 110:2</note> 

And: 
> » "From the womb before the morning star I begot you." <note>Psalm 110:3</note> 

And: 
> » "The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." <note>Psalm 110:4; Melchizedek was a mysterious king-priest who predated the Jewish Law</note>

Through these words, he is clearly revealed as the offspring and Son of God before the morning star, existing before all creation, and appearing as the Eternal High Priest. But the "Christ" of Moses <note>Referring to the anointed priests of the Old Testament</note>, as if in a brief drama, acted out the symbolic pattern for a short time and now lies counted among the mortals, having handed over the truth to the other, the only and true One. 

The true Christ does not hold a secondary rank to those anointed according to Moses, nor does he touch prepared and earthly matter. Nevertheless, the power of his virtue and his name has filled the whole inhabited world, establishing the race of Christians—named after him—among all the nations. The "Christ" of Moses was not even known to have existed among men except through the writings of Moses. 

One was established after the exodus from Egypt, for the sake of the sprinkled sons and purified by sacrifices of blood, anointed with a prepared ointment by the hand of Moses. But the Archetype and the True One, from the beginning and into the infinite age, being entirely and in every way like unto himself, never changing—He is the Christ <term>Anointed</term> forever. He remained so during his stay among men and similarly after it; anointed not by a man, nor through physical matter, but by the God over all with incorporeal divinity. 

And since the "ointment" <note>original: "myron," referring to the holy oil</note> of his name is being examined, the absolute seal of what has been said would be the oracle found in the very wise Solomon, in the Song of Songs, which says: 
> » "Your name is oil poured out." <note>Song of Solomon 1:3; original: "myron ekkenōthen onoma sou"</note> 

For this man, supplied with divine wisdom and deemed worthy of the more secret visions concerning Christ and his Church—mentioning the one as the heavenly Bridegroom and the other as his Bride—seeks to know what the name of the Bridegroom might be. He proclaims as if speaking to him: 
> » "Your name, O Bridegroom, is oil," 

And not simply oil, but "poured out." What true name could be indicative of "oil poured out" other than the name of Christ? For he would truly be, and truly be named, "Christ" <term>Anointed</term> because of the oil poured over him. What kind of oil this was...

...of myths, the use of which the revealed Christ has shown to be rejected, has been handed down to us from the beginning. Since so much has been declared concerning the title of "Christ," come now and let us also examine the name of "Jesus."

## That the name of Jesus was also honored among those of old who were known to God.

<margin>P</margin>irst, once again, Moses himself—employing a different title for the one who would be his own successor—renamed him "Jesus." For it is written: 
>> "These are the names of the men whom Moses sent to spy out the land; and Moses renamed Hoshea <note>original: "Nausē"</note> the son of Nun <note>original: "Nauē"</note>, Jesus <note>original: "Iēsous," the Greek form of Joshua</note>, and he sent them out." <note>Numbers 13:16</note> 

One could not say that the prophet Moses did this without having reflected deeply on the nature of names. Indeed, he had philosophized extensively about the various divine men in his writings who were renamed and the reasons for their change of name. He introduces Abraham as receiving the complete title of "Abraham" from God as a prize for his virtue <note>Abram was renamed Abraham, meaning "father of many," in Genesis 17:5</note>. What this signifies is not the time to explain now. In the same way, he renamed Sarah "Sarah" <note>Sarai was renamed Sarah, meaning "princess," in Genesis 17:15</note>, and spoke of Isaac being named even before his birth. He also recorded how Jacob received the prize of his wrestling match by being crowned with the name "Israel." 

Moses understood a thousand other things regarding the power and nature of names that are beyond human reach, perceiving them through divine wisdom and knowledge. Yet, although no one before him among those of old had ever used the name "Jesus," he was the first—being moved by the Holy Spirit—to call his future successor in the leadership of the people by this name. This successor previously used a different, older name, but Moses renamed him "Jesus." He believed that the name he was called by his ancestors was merely a shared title <note>original: "synōnymian," a common name</note>. For those who spoke by divine oracle called him "Hoshea." But the prophet of God, having been called to change the name, names the man "Jesus" according to the Holy Spirit. 

He did this because he realized that this man would lead the entire people after his own death, and that the legislation established through himself would eventually reach its end and lose its force. Just as Moses himself would reach an end, he saw that no one else, but only Jesus the Christ of God, would lead the people into a different and better way of life <term>politeia</term> <note>meaning a "way of living" or "citizenship"</note> than the former one. Thus Moses, the most wonderful of all prophets, honored the two men chosen from among all the leaders with the two names of our Savior Jesus Christ, as if with royal diadems. These were the two rulers and guides of the people: the High Priest and his own successor. He appropriately assigned the name "Christ" to Aaron, and the name "Jesus" to Hoshea, as the one who would succeed him after his death. In this way, the scripture of Moses himself was adorned with the titles of our Savior Jesus Christ.

Just as Moses' successor, Jesus <note>Joshua</note>, having been so named, was intended to lead the people, it is said that he bore the name of the Christ who would later be revealed.

Give heed to yourself, and listen to him; do not disobey him, for he will not pull back from you. For my name is upon him." <note>Exodus 23:20-21</note>

The Lord himself says: "My name is inscribed upon him," referring to these very things being declared...

> » and you shall take silver and gold, and make crowns, and you shall place them upon the 
> » head of Jesus the son of Josedech the high priest. And you shall say to him: 'Thus says the 
> » Lord Almighty: Behold the man whose name is the Branch; and he shall spring up from 
> » below and shall build the house of the Lord. And he shall receive virtue, and he shall sit and 
> » rule upon his throne. And there shall be a priest at his right hand, and a counsel of peace 
> » shall be between them both.'" <note>Zechariah 3:1-8 and 6:9-13</note>

This Jesus <note>Joshua son of Josedech</note>, who is proclaimed a "great priest" in this passage, seems to me to preserve a very clear image and a vivid symbol of our Savior Jesus Christ, being honored with the same name and having led the return of the people from the Babylonian captivity. For our Savior Jesus Christ is also the one of whom it was said through Isaiah the prophet: "to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind," and to call all those who hunger, and that "to those who mourn in Zion should be given the oil of gladness instead of ashes." <note>Isaiah 61:1-3</note> You have, therefore, already two great high priests: the one called "Christ" <note>the Anointed</note> in the time of Moses <note>Aaron</note>, and the one now under discussion, "Jesus." Through them, the symbols concerning our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ have been brought to light. But while Aaron, the "Christ" of Moses's time, delivered the people from the slavery of the Egyptians and led them to freedom and the service of God on their journey from Egypt, he might preserve the image of the true Lord, who [delivered us] from Egyptian idol...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius's explanation of how Joshua (Jesus) son of Jozadak, the High Priest during the return from the Babylonian exile, serves as a "type" or prophetic model for Jesus Christ. It picks up mid-sentence discussing the redemption of the Gentiles from idolatry.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

...of idolatry <note>original: *eidōlolatreias*</note>, he redeemed all of us from among the nations. The High Priest Jesus <note>Joshua son of Jozadak</note> mentioned in the prophet predicted the return from Babylon to Jerusalem, providing a sample and pattern of Jesus our Savior, whom we hold as a Great High Priest who has passed through the heavens. Through him, we too have been redeemed from the "Babylon" of this present life—a state of confusion and captivity—and have been taught to hasten toward the Heavenly City, the true Jerusalem. It was fitting that this Jesus, who bore the image of the truth within himself, was also "clothed in filthy garments," and that the devil is said to have "stood at his right hand to oppose him." For in truth, our Savior and Lord Jesus, descending into our state of captivity, took upon himself our sins and wiped away our human filth <note>original: *rhypon*</note>. Out of his love for mankind <note>original: *philanthropia*</note>, he endured the pains of the Passion. Therefore Isaiah says:
» "He bears our sins and suffers for us, and we accounted him to be in labor, 
» in stripes, and in affliction. But he was wounded for our sins, and 
» weakened for our lawlessness." <note>Isaiah 53:4–5</note>
And John the Baptist, seeing the Lord, said:
» "Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world." <note>John 1:29</note>
And Paul, writing similarly about him, says:
» "He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that we might 
» become the righteousness of God in him." <note>2 Corinthians 5:21</note>
And:
» "Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law, having 
» become a curse for us." <note>Galatians 3:13</note>
The prophecy revealed all these things through its divine inspiration when it said: "Jesus was clothed in filthy garments." However, he put these aside during his ascent into the heavens—his return from our state of captivity to his own home—and was crowned with the diadem <note>A royal crown or headband.</note> of the Father's divinity. He was clothed in the most radiant robe of the Father's light, a holy miter <note>original: *kidarēn*; a ceremonial headcovering for a high priest.</note>, and was adorned with the rest of the high-priestly ornaments. It is also not difficult to explain the role of the devil, who even now opposes the teaching of Christ and the Church he established throughout the whole world. The devil grieved our Savior by formerly leading an army against him, specifically when Christ was rescuing us from the devil's own captivity. He tempted him first <note>In the wilderness.</note>, and then a second time when he conspired with those who plotted against Christ during the Passion. Having pushed back the devil and all the invisible enemies and foes under him, Christ prepared us—who were once captives—as his own people. Out of us, as if from "living stones," he established the house of God and a godly society <note>original: *politeuma*</note>, so that the prophetic word fittingly applies to him:
» "Behold the man, whose name is the East <note>original: *Anatolē*. In the Greek Old Testament, this word also means 'Branch' or 'Rising Sun.'</note>; and he shall rise up 
» from below him and shall build the house of the Lord. And he shall 
» receive virtue, and shall sit and rule upon his throne." <note>Zechariah 6:12–13</note>
Pay close attention here: so that you may have a spiritual understanding of the Jesus of old <note>Joshua son of Jozadak</note>, the prophet says he bears the image of the true one: "Behold the man, whose name is the East." But later, moving on as if speaking of another who is the "East" itself, the prophet says to the Jesus who was then present: 
» "Hear now, O Jesus the High Priest, you and your neighbors, for they 
» are men who watch for omens <note>original: *teratoskopoi*; often translated as 'men of a sign' or 'symbolic men.'</note>. Behold, I bring my servant, 
» the East." <note>Zechariah 3:8</note>
If, therefore, the word proceeds to speak of another yet to come—one who is more truly named "the East" than the man then living—it follows that the historical Jesus <note>Joshua</note> was an image of the "East" who was to come. Thus, in that image, he was called not only "Jesus" but also "the East."

### PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 4
Ll.iiii.

» ...delivering, if indeed he holds Him as present, for it was said: "Behold, a man whose name is the East <note>Original: *Anatolē*. This refers to Zechariah 6:12. In Greek, *Anatolē* means the rising of the sun or the East, often used as a messianic title</note>." Reasonably, then, for the sake of the image <note>the prophetic type</note>, he was deemed worthy of the title of Savior, and likewise of the name "East." Since indeed the name "Jesus," when translated into the Greek tongue, signifies "Salvation of God." For among the Hebrews, *Yeshua* <note>original: *Isoua*</note> means "salvation," and the son of Nun is called *Yehoshua* <note>original: *Iōsoue*</note> by the same people. Now, *Yehoshua* means "Yahweh’s Salvation" <note>original: *Iaō sōtēria*</note>, that is, "The Salvation of God." Appropriately, then, wherever "God's Salvation" is named in the Hebrew manuscripts, one is convinced it refers to "Jesus" according to the Hebrew language. Having said this much regarding the title of our Savior, we shall take up the discourse again from a new starting point and move on to the more complete prophetic proofs concerning Him.

# EUSEBIUS'S Preface.

<note>The letter E is decorated with floral and foliage patterns in the original woodcut.</note>

Since the discourse <note>original: *logos*; in this context, it refers both to the written argument and the "Word" of God</note> concerning our Savior Jesus Christ appeared as twofold in the previous volume of the *Proof of the Gospel*: the one supernatural and transcendent, according to which we declare His divinity <note>original: *theologoumen*; literally "we theologize," meaning to describe His divine nature</note> as the only-begotten Son of God, or the essential Word of God, the second cause of all things, or an intellectual essence and the incorporeal nature nearest to God, or a divine and all-virtuous power over created things, or the intellectual image of the unbegotten nature; the other is kin to us and more familiar, according to which we again define Him as the Word of God in human form, declaring the Father’s piety <note>original: *eusebeia*</note>, as He was formerly accustomed to do in human likeness to those around Abraham—appearing to those beloved by God as the renowned leader of the nations, revealing Himself among men through a human nature, and foretelling that He would endure suffering as a mortal similar to us. 

It is therefore time for our discourse to proceed in due order to the prophetic testimonies concerning Him that were promised. We shall first examine the things that were fulfilled, and then we shall confirm the theology <note>the study of His divine nature</note> concerning Him in the Gospels through the ancient prophetic testimony. However, it is necessary to first consider what the manner of divine inspiration <note>original: *theolēpsia*; a "seizing" or "grasping" by God</note> was among the Hebrew prophets, before we have been fully instructed in the things they proclaimed.

->What was the manner by which the Hebrew prophets both foretold the<-
->future and illuminated the only true theology?<-

<margin>M</margin> Greeks and barbarians <note>In the ancient world, "barbarian" simply referred to anyone who did not speak Greek</note> alike record that many divinations and oracles have been established throughout the whole earth. They claim these were demonstrated by the providence of the Creator for the use and benefit of mankind, so that there is no difference between the Hebrew prophets and the oracles of the other nations. For they argue that just as God provided for the Hebrews through such prophets, so He must have provided what was beneficial to the rest of the nations through their local oracles. For they say God does not belong to the Jews alone, but to all other men as well; and that He cares for the latter no less than the former, providing for all equally, just as He has bestowed the sun abundantly on everyone, not only the Hebrews. He also provides the annual supply of necessities, a similar physical construction for all, one law of nature for all, and one nature of a rational soul. In the same way, they claim He provides the science of foreknowing the future abundantly to all men—to some through prophetic men, to others through oracles, to others through the flight of birds, or through the inspection of sacrifices, or through the sending of dreams, or through omens, or involuntary twitches, or certain other symbols. For they say these things have been given to men by the providence of God, so that the Hebrew prophets seem to possess nothing more than anyone else. This, then, is their argument. Our response to them will be as follows: for if one’s argument is based on the belief that there are gods, or divine powers, or de- <note>The text cuts off here. The catchword "mons" on the original page indicates the word continues as "demons."</note>
