# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 5
### 129

...[that] good spirits <term>daimones; in Greek thought, these were intermediary spirits, but Eusebius argues they are malevolent "demons"</term> presided over the aforementioned oracles, or those of the birds <note>referring to augury, the practice of interpreting the flight of birds</note>, or the rest of those named, so that we might in turn return thanks to them as benefactors, as if God over all had gifted those things for the benefit of those who used them. But if, by complete proofs and the very admissions of those spirits themselves, they are now shown to be foul demons and not good—causes of all harm and wickedness—how could they possibly be prophets of God? 

The argument has caught them out as foul through the *Gospel Preparation* <note>original: *Euangelikes Paraskeues*; this refers to Eusebius’s previous multi-volume work, "Praeparatio Evangelica," where he critiques pagan religion</note>. This is evident from the human sacrifices <note>original: *anthropothysia*</note> that were once performed for them in every place, city, and country; from the ways they deceived those who questioned them because of their own ignorance of the future; and from the ten thousand lies of which they were convicted. Sometimes they were exposed by obvious facts, and at other times through the ambiguity of their oracles <note>referring to the famously "double-tongued" or cryptic nature of pagan prophecies, like those of the Delphic Oracle</note>, through which they often surrounded those who fled to them for help with countless evils and led them to ruin. 

Furthermore, their race was previously proven to be loathsome and impure, both because they rejoice in shameful and licentious songs performed about them—including hymns and mythical narrations—and because of the unseemly and harmful histories which they themselves confirmed as true. 

The final proof of all is the weak power of their nature, which shows they should no longer be worshiped or consulted as they once were; this change began from the times of the appearance of our Savior **Jesus Christ**. Since the word of His Gospel teaching ran through all nations, from that moment the oracles failed, and the "deaths of demons" are recorded. All these things are clear, along with ten thousand similar points, through which the beings in question were proven to be evil demons in the *Gospel Preparation*. 

If, then, they happen to be such beings, what reason compels us to think that the oracles of demons are the prophecies of the God over all? Or to compare their affairs to the prophets of God? What kind of predictions were they making for those who asked them? Were they not about unseemly, low, and cheap men—boxers, perhaps, or similar people—for whom they required you to perform astounding sacrifices? And what about the "celestial poems" they were thought to produce? This is the heart of the matter. Did they not leave behind an excess of absurdity through some foul error? 

If these "gods" and "good spirits" were the saviors of men, would they command their suppliants and pious refugees to slaughter their own dearest ones as if they were livestock? They proved themselves to be thirsty for human blood beyond the nature of wild beasts—nothing other than blood-drinkers and man-eaters, revealing themselves as enemies rather than friends. 

Or let anyone who wishes say if he has anything noble and worthy of virtue to show from these famous sources—either prophecies or predictions reaching all humanity, or laws or political arrangements by which all men ought to live, or dogmas of philosophy and lessons presented by the gods to lovers of wisdom <note>original: *philosophia*</note>. But no one could say that such a thing ever existed in human life from those celebrated oracles. For if these existed, we humans would not be living under different and conflicting laws while being legislated by gods. If they were gods and were good, how would they not have used the same decrees? Why would they not have given the most temperate and just legislations? 

Who then—be it **Solon** <note>the famous lawgiver of Athens</note> or **Draco** <note>an early Athenian legislator known for his harsh laws</note> or any other of the multitude of human or barbarian legislators—has ever received anything useful or necessary for the common good through these oracles? If however...

# EUSEBIUS OF PAMPHILUS
### PAGE 130

Indeed, someone might say that they are not senseless, those who established laws for each nation of men—if indeed such a being exists, let them say what kind of god it was who, for instance, led the Scythians to embrace cannibalism <note>original: *anthropoboria*; literally "human-eating"</note>, or who legislated the mixing with one’s own mothers and daughters, or who commanded as a good thing the casting of the elderly to the dogs, or who permitted the marrying of sisters and the coupling of males with males? And why do I need to enumerate those things from the laws of the Greeks and barbarians, to prove that they were not gods, but wicked and poisonous demons <term>daimones; here used in the Christian sense of malevolent spirits</term>, those "wonderful" givers of oracles, who cast down the wretched race of men into sins against nature? 

Since not even the famous gods and seers of the Greeks were seen to provide anything beneficial or profitable for the soul to those who consulted them, what has been previously stated is proven. For why did men, leaving behind the brightest benefits <note>original: *hēlious tinas tas autōn ōpheleias*; literally "certain suns of their benefits," a metaphor for obvious or brilliant truths</note> of their own, travel out to barbarian lands, begging for a trade in learning from somewhere abroad, rather than using the gods as their teachers? For if gods or good spirits were speaking to them, sometimes showing their own power through foreknowledge and the display of wonders, and sometimes teaching complete wisdom through the unerring truth of their lessons, why then did the children of philosophers, having been discipled by these—and I mean those who had devised certain concepts from their own doctrines—not form various sects of philosophers out of a long silence? 

But if the majority of men did not pay attention to them, then surely the deception involving those impious beings among the gods must be made evident from the "benefits" provided by those gods. Who, then, are these? For you do not say that those who hold opposing views convict these people of being led astray. But as it seems, the divination of demons reaches only as far as catching a thief, or finding lost items in the darkness, or some such small thing; things which it is not unlikely that those who spend their time always around the earth should have some knowledge of. But they achieved nothing of a good or wise philosophical doctrine, nor did they establish a righteous way of life or law. 

Rather, if one must speak the truth with every breath, these beings must have been the cause and the beginning of all these evils. For they are the ones who—listening to the accounts of adultery and male-to-male sex, of marrying mothers and unlawful unions with sisters, and ten thousand other battles against God, and the enmities and wars of gods against gods, in the songs, hymns, and stories of men and in the secret rites of mysteries—none of them ever appeared to be indignant at what was said, as if such things were fit for the unrestrained and not even for sober men. 

And why should I persist? Except to perceive, from one greatest example, the cruelty and inhumanity, and the truly defiled nature of what is being shown? I mean the practice of human sacrifice <note>original: *anthropothysia*</note>. For that which rejoices not only in the slaughter of irrational animals, but also in the destruction of men—what extreme of cruelty has it not surpassed? These things are well known, having been witnessed in the writings of the Greek philosophers and historians themselves. From these it is clearly shown that they are wicked demons who, through complex machines—sometimes through oracles, sometimes through omens or symbols or sacrifices or similar things—distort the human race. By this it must be declared that their oracular shrines do not belong to the God of all. Therefore, not even...

# THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 5
### PAGE 131

It would be right to compare those <note>The pagan oracles discussed on the previous page.</note> to the prophets of the Hebrews, among whom Moses stood as the first, serving as a priest of sacred mysteries <term>hierophant; a teacher of holy things</term> and a theologian, who first established what is good for human life. First, he published sacred writings containing beneficial and true doctrines about God, the Maker and Creator of all things, and about the **Second Cause** <term>deuteros aitios; Eusebius uses this term to describe the Word or Son of God as the secondary principle of creation after the Father</term> of the rational and intellectual beings that follow Him. He also wrote concerning the origin of the cosmos and the origin of man, as well as the godly history of the ancient Hebrews who were beloved of God. By sketching these men as if they were icons of virtue, he stirred his subjects to a zeal for good men. He also initiated a light of legislation from God, suited to those who lived at that time, and became the natural introducer of the message of godly worship. Beyond all these things, he declared through predictions what would happen to everyone in the times long afterward, as will be mentioned shortly. 

And after him, the prophets who followed him acted in their own proper way; if ever something concerning daily matters was sought, they would indeed foretell this to those who asked. However, the **sum total of their prophecy** was fulfilled for the sake of great things. For they were not deemed worthy of divine inspiration <term>theophoreia; literally "being carried by God"</term> merely for the sake of fortune-telling about daily matters and the present moment alone, nor for small and humble things. Instead, the power of the Divine Spirit within them had taken up a great theme for the knowledge of all humanity. It did not promise a prediction concerning a man with a diseased body, nor about the immediate and painful concerns of this life, nor about something lost, nor simply about neutral and indifferent things—things which neither improve the soul when present, nor cause loss or harm when absent. 

One might see, as I said, that they foretold these things as well, but not as their primary purpose. Rather, in accordance with higher and more perfect goals, they contained a greater theme than what has been mentioned. Indeed, if anyone were to accurately investigate the entire scope of the writings of Moses and those after him, they would find an exhortation and teaching of piety <note>original: *eusebeia*; a central Greek term for proper religious conduct and devotion</note> which draws one up to the God of the universe, the very Creator of all. One would find a knowledge and theology of the highest kind regarding the **Second Cause**, turning one away from all polytheistic error. Furthermore, one would find the memory of the ancient, God-beloved men who excelled through their deeds in the aforementioned piety, and predictions and proclamations—following the pattern of those men's lives—concerning those who would live in later times. These declare the manifestation and presence of the **Son of God**, who is Himself the "Second Lord" and "God" after the Supreme Father, and who is proclaimed as the Teacher of that same piety and the Savior who would appear for the life of men. Through Him, they foretold that the law of godly worship practiced by the ancient, God-beloved Hebrews would be handed over to all nations, Greeks and Barbarians alike. 

These things Moses and the sons of the other prophets proclaimed beforehand, as if with one mouth. And this was the reason for the influence of the Divine Spirit upon men: to teach the knowledge of God to humanity, and the highest theology concerning the Father and the Son; to educate them in the way of true piety; to remember those who succeeded in the past; to reveal the refutation of those who failed through long discourses; and to ordain the presence of the Savior and Teacher for the knowledge of all people, proclaiming beforehand the transmission of the ancient Hebrew worship to all nations through Him. These are the things which have been proclaimed from ages past, in harmony, upon the monuments and in the sacred books of the prophets. And these...

# EUSEBIUS
### PREPARATION FOR THE GOSPEL, PAGE 130

...one might indeed say that these beings are not even clearly known. For if they were the ones who gave laws to each nation of men, then what kind of "god" should we call the one who, for example, commanded **cannibalism** <note>original: "anthropoborian"</note> among the Scythians? Or the one who legislated that men should have relations with their mothers and daughters? Or the one who, as if decreeing something good, commanded that the elderly should be thrown to the dogs? Or the one who permitted men to marry their own sisters and for males to have intercourse with males?

Why must I enumerate the accounts found in the laws of the Greeks and the barbarians <note>In antiquity, "barbarian" simply meant anyone who did not speak Greek, such as Persians, Egyptians, or Scythians.</note>? This serves as a proof that these were not gods, but rather **evil and wandering spirits** <term>daimones; in this context, Eusebius uses the term to mean malicious spiritual entities that masquerade as gods</term>. These spirits, through their "wonderful" oracle-givers, have cast the wretched human race into atrocities that are entirely against nature. 

Even those gods and soothsayers who are celebrated among the Greeks are never shown to have performed anything truly beneficial or useful for the welfare of the soul for those who consulted them. Why else did men—who sought a way of life that would actually benefit them—turn toward foreign lands <note>original: "barbaron chthona"</note>? They went abroad to collect a "merchandise of learning" from elsewhere, rather than using their own gods as teachers. 

Perhaps, if these were "good spirits" delivering oracles, they might have revealed their own power through foreknowledge and other miraculous works. Or, perhaps, they might have taught the truth of their lessons through an unwavering wisdom. But if that were the case, why did the children of the philosophers not become their disciples? Instead, the philosophers chose to follow the inventions of their own private dogmas, which resulted in a long history of disagreement and the formation of various conflicting schools <note>original: "haireseis"; the root of the word "heresy," meaning a choice or a school of thought</note>. 

If the common people did not pay attention to the gods, they would be treated as ungodly. How then was it not necessary for those who approached the gods to receive some unerring benefit from them? Who then are these gods? For even by your own admission, those who hold opposing views are proven to be in error. 

But as it seems, the oracles of these spirits go only as far as catching a thief, or finding lost property in the dark, or some other trivial matter. It is not unlikely that these spirits, who spend their time always hovering around the earth, should know such things. However, it is a fine thing that no philosopher has ever found a single reliable doctrine through them—neither a way of life nor a law established on right reason. 

Rather, if I must speak the truth with a **sacred voice**, everyone has been harmed by these things more than was necessary. These are the very beings who are the subjects of songs, hymns, and stories by men—tales of adultery, pederasty, marriages with mothers, unions between siblings allowed by law, and clear "god-battles," enmities, and wars of gods against gods. When people hear these things in the secret rites of the mysteries <term>teletais; the initiation ceremonies of the pagan mystery cults</term>, no one is ever seen to be indignant. No one says that such things are shameful, or that they are unsuited even to the most undisciplined and immoderate of men.

And why should I persist in this argument, when it is possible to see their cruelty, inhumanity, and true filth from one single, greatest example? I speak of **human sacrifice** <term>anthropothysia; the practice of offering human lives to the gods</term>. For if a being rejoices not only in the slaughter of irrational animals, but also in the destruction of human beings, what extreme of cruelty has it not surpassed? 

As I have said, these things are testified to by the historians and philosophers of every age. From these accounts, it is clearly shown that these are **evil spirits** <term>ponēroi daimones</term> who use complex devices—sometimes through oracles, sometimes through omens, signs, sacrifices, and the like—to lead the human race astray. Because of this, we must declare that their oracles do not come from the God who is over all. Therefore, there is no comparison...

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 5
### PAGE 131

It would be right and proper to compare these <note>referring to the pagan oracles mentioned on the previous page</note> with the prophets of the Hebrews. Among them, the first to become a <term>hierophant</term> <note>A "hierophant" is one who interprets or reveals sacred mysteries to the initiated.</note> and a theologian was Moses, who became the cause of so many good things for human life. 

First, he published a sacred writing containing logical and true doctrines concerning the Maker and Creator of all things—God—and concerning the **Second Cause** <note>original: "deuterou aitiou"; in early Christian philosophy, this term refers to the Word or Son of God, who acts as the mediator between the ultimate Father and the created world</note> of the rational and intellectual beings that come after Him. He also wrote of **cosmogony** <note>the origin of the universe</note> and **anthropogony** <note>the origin of humankind</note>. Furthermore, he recorded the history of the God-loving Hebrews of old, sketching them as if they were images of various virtues, thereby stirring his subjects to emulate these good men. He also provided a divine legislation suitable for those who used it at that time, and he initiated the light of the Word. He planted the introductions to a God-fearing religion. Above all, he spoke forth predictions of things that would happen a long time later, as will be mentioned shortly. 

Such was that man. The prophets who came after him were of the same character. If some daily matter was ever sought after, they might speak of it to those who asked as a side matter <note>original: "parergon"; something secondary to their main work</note>. However, the core of their prophecy was fulfilled in great matters. For they were not granted divine inspiration for the sake of fortune-telling about daily matters or things already passed, nor for small and lowly things. Rather, the illumination of the Divine Spirit within them was revealed as a magnificent theme for the benefit of all mankind. 

They did not offer predictions concerning a man's disease or body, nor concerning the affairs of this temporary and suffering life, nor about something lost, nor generally about any of those middle or indifferent things which neither improve the soul when present nor cause damage or harm when absent. But when they did speak of these things, they did so not as their primary purpose, but as a consequence of higher and more perfect goals, containing a greater theme than those mentioned. 

If anyone were to go through the whole of Moses's writing and accurately research those who came after him, they would find that, for the sake of knowledge and the teaching of piety, he proclaimed the God of all—the Creator of all things—and the highest knowledge of theology regarding the **Second Cause**. He taught the abandonment of all polytheistic error. Then, he provided the narrative of the God-loving men of old and the special memory of the aforementioned piety, along with vocal predictions—given during their lives—concerning those who would live in later times. He foretold the manifestation and prophecy of God among men—namely, the **Second Lord** and God after the Supreme Father—who would Himself be called the teacher of that same piety and appear as a **Savior** to human life. Through Him, they predicted to all nations, both **Greeks and barbarians** <note>In this context, "Greeks" refers to the civilized Mediterranean world, and "barbarians" refers to all other foreign nations.</note> alike, that the same form of religion practiced by the God-loving Hebrews of old would be handed down. 

These things Moses, and the "sons of the prophets" <note>A traditional term for the followers or schools of the prophets.</note> who followed him, all proclaimed as if with one voice. This was the reason for the influence of the Divine Spirit upon men: 
*   To teach the knowledge of God to humans.
*   To teach the highest theology concerning the Father and the Son.
*   To train them in the way of true piety.
*   To remember those who lived rightly in the past.
*   To provide a rebuke of those [who do wrong] through long discourses.
*   To prophesy the presence of the Savior and teacher for the benefit of wicked men.
*   To proclaim the distribution of the ancient Hebrew piety to all nations through Him. 

These are the things from ages past, spoken in harmony within the other sacred books of the prophets. These very...

### PAGE 132

These things, which we can see for ourselves being fulfilled even now after a long passage of time, are visible to our own eyes. With one voice, all these prophets—by the Divine Spirit—proclaim to all humanity the light of true piety. They preach the purity of soul and body, and a completely delightful cleansing of the mind. They themselves honored these virtues and set them before their subjects, barring those who approached them from every licentious act. They taught them not to imitate the unlawful practices of the **polytheistic error** <note>The "polytheistic error" refers to the worship of many gods, which Eusebius views as a wandering away from the truth of a single Creator.</note>, as if teaching them to avoid an ancient delusion and every demonic enterprise. They spoke against those once-admired **human sacrifices** <note>Eusebius often cites the cessation of human sacrifice as a proof of the civilizing power of the Gospel and Hebrew prophecy.</note> and those shameful and infamous stories about the gods. Instead, they advised them to attend only to God, the Creator of all things, who acts as the overseer and judge of everything done by humans. Nor did they think it right to be ignorant that the **Christ of God** <note>original: "Christon tou theou"</note> would dwell among men as the Savior of the entire human race, established as a teacher of piety for both **barbarians and Greeks** <note>In the ancient world, "Greeks" referred to the Hellenistic, educated world, while "barbarians" referred to all other nations (non-Greeks).</note> alike.

There is a vast difference between being possessed by the Divine Spirit and the madness produced by demonic activity. On one hand, the evil spirit, being like its own native darkness, wraps the soul in gloom and mist through its indwelling. It fills the soul like mud or a corpse, breathing its influence over the natural reasoning and following whatever is said or done through it—acts that are evil, senseless, and frantic. For this reason, it is fitting that they called "divination" a kind of "madness" <note>Eusebius is making a wordplay on the Greek terms *manteia* (divination) and *mania* (madness), a common philosophical critique of pagan oracles.</note>. 

But the good and sober Spirit, being light-like—or rather, being Light itself—whenever it comes upon a soul, immediately produces within it a day of new and most brilliant light. It makes the soul’s capacity for contemplation much clearer and more transparent than it was before, so that the person is sober and awake, able to see clearly and, above all, to judge the things being prophesied. For this reason, we do not seem to call such people "prophets" <note>original: "prophētas"</note> improperly, because the Divine Spirit **shines forth** <note>original: "prophainein"</note> and **pre-illumines** <note>original: "prophōtizein"</note> within them, revealing not only present things but also a precise knowledge of the future. 

Consider whether this account is not far superior and truer: it claims that the Divine Spirit visits souls that have been purified, with a rational mind that is clear and prepared for the reception of the divine. This is contrasted with those who shut up the "divine" in lifeless matter and crooked recesses, or in the impure souls of men and women, or even in crows, hawks, and irrational birds, or in goats and other animals. Furthermore, they seek it in pools of water, in **liver-readings** <note>term: "hepatoscopia" — the practice of inspecting the livers of sacrificed animals to predict the future.</note>, and in the blood of diseased and hideous beasts, or the bodies of venomous reptiles such as snakes, or even weasels and other such things. Through these means, these "wonderful" people supposed the God over all reveals the foreknowledge of the future! 

How could men who have not perceived the nature of God, nor understood the power of the Divine Spirit, think that it would dwell in lifeless things or irrational animals? It does not even dwell in all rational beings, unless they are virtuous souls—such as the account just now described for us regarding the prophets of the Hebrews. These were deemed worthy of the brightness of the Divine Spirit for the sake of great matters that contribute to the improvement of all humanity throughout the inhabited world. And if at times it followed them—like a shadow—to recognize and foretell present things of a middle or indifferent nature that were unknown...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s exploration of the nature of the Son (the Logos) and his relationship to the Father. He moves from scriptural proofs to a philosophical defense of the Son’s "generation," arguing that it must not be understood in physical or material terms like human birth or the division of matter.</meta>

# EVANGELICAL PROOF, BOOK 5
### PAGE 135

...it is holy to say that the Son has proceeded from the Father. For the Divine is without parts and cannot be divided; it is not cut, not partitioned, not stretched out, nor diminished. It does not contract, nor does it become larger, or worse, or better than before. It has nothing within itself distinct from itself that could then "proceed" out of it. For everything that exists within something else does so either as an "accident" <note>original: "symbebekos." In Greek philosophy, this refers to a property that is not essential to a thing’s nature, such as the color white in a body.</note>—such as the color white in a body—or as one thing existing inside another, like a child carried in the <term>womb</term> <note>original: "gastros." Refers to the belly or womb; Eusebius uses this to contrast physical birth with divine generation.</note>, or as a part within a whole, like a hand or a foot or a finger is a part of a body. If these parts were cut or divided, the whole would be left incomplete and mutilated, like a limb that has been amputated.

But surely, to use such an image to represent the unbegotten nature of the God of the Universe, and the generation of his Only-begotten and Firstborn, would be the height of impiety. Therefore, the Son did not exist unbegottenly within the Father from infinite and eternal ages as a part of him, only to change later and be "emptied out" to exist outside of him. For this would imply a change in [God's] own nature. And there would then be two "unbegotten" things: the one who sent forth and the one who was sent forth. And if the nature was originally "better," would not that which was separated by the <term>sixth</term> <note>original: "ektes." This likely refers to a specific Neoplatonic or Gnostic classification of distances or "emanations" (probolai) that Eusebius is rejecting as too materialistic.</note> degree of distance through this "sending forth" be diminished?

It is impossible to conceive of the Son as being a part or a fraction existing unbegottenly from the beginning, only to later be separated and exist apart from the whole. These ideas are unspeakable and fundamentally impious, belonging to the material nature of bodies but entirely foreign to a nature that is bodiless and immaterial. Therefore, one might reasonably declare here once again:

> Who shall declare his generation? <note>Isaiah 53:8. Eusebius uses this verse to emphasize that the origin of Christ is a divine mystery that transcends human language.</note>

For one might suggest that the Son was brought into being from non-existence, just like the rest of the created order—as if he were produced without danger and simply set in opposition to his Father. However, the generation of the Son is different, for he is produced through a unique divine craftsmanship. Just as the Divine Scripture sometimes calls the Son the "Firstborn of all creation" who proceeded from the Father, saying:

> The Lord **created** me as the beginning of his ways, <note>Proverbs 8:22.</note>

...and at other times says he is the "offspring" of the Father:

> Before all hills he **begets** me. <note>Proverbs 8:25.</note>

In this way, we also might speak soundly. We confess that before all ages he was the Word <note>original: "Logos."</note> of the Creative Power, co-existing within the Father, being the Only-begotten Son of the God of the Universe, and having been begotten as the minister and co-worker of the Father in the substantial creation and ordering of all things. For if the nature of the universe contains things that are clear but yet unspeakable and incomprehensible to us—and there are countless such things, such as those promised to the friends of God,

> things which eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and which have not entered into the heart of man, <note>1 Corinthians 2:9.</note>

...as the holy Apostle says—then how much more, beyond all thought, unspeakable and unnamable, inconceivable and unthinkably deep, must be the generation of the Only-begotten of God? Therefore, having nothing more to say or think about it, we should simply say:

> Who shall declare his generation?

But if anyone, moving beyond this, should dare to compare things that are entirely inconceivable to earthly and physical examples, perhaps he might say that the Son exists from the unbegotten nature of the Father and his ever-shining essence, like an immaterial ray of light coming from infinite ages—or rather, before all ages—existing with and always being with the Father, just as fragrance is to ointment or a ray of light is to light. But examples do not match the reality in every respect, as has been said before. For soulless bodies...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument that the Son is not a mere accidental property of the Father, nor a physical division of His substance. He uses metaphors of light, fragrance, and mirrors to explain how the Son can be a distinct "subsistence" while remaining perfectly unified with and derived from the Father's essence.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS
### PAGE 136

...as an accidental property <note>original: "symbebekos." In Aristotelian logic, an accident is a quality (like color) that depends on a substance to exist.</note> possessed among other qualities. For while a ray of light is innate to the nature of the light and exists substantially alongside it, it cannot exist outside of the source in which it resides. However, the Word <note>original: "Logos."</note> of God exists substantially and subsists in himself; he does not coexist with the Father in an "unbegotten" way <note>Eusebius is careful here to maintain that only the Father is without a beginning/cause.</note>, but as the Only-begotten Son, born from the Father alone before all ages. 

Consider fragrance: it is a certain indefinable, physical quality of an underlying object which, by its own nature, fills the surrounding air apart from its source; yet, it remains physical itself. We must not, therefore, understand the term "substantiation" <term>ousiosis</term> <note>The process by which something is given its essence or "being."</note> regarding the Savior in this physical way. For he was not given substance from the Unbegotten essence through any kind of suffering or division, nor does he coexist with the Father without a beginning—since one is unbegotten and the other is begotten, one is the Father and the other the Son. Everyone would agree that a Father must pre-exist a Son. 

In this way, he is also the "Image of God," once again in a manner that is ineffable and beyond our reasoning. He is a certain living Image of God, subsisting in himself immaterially and incorporeally, unmixed with anything contrary to himself. He is not like an image among us, which has one substance as its base and another as its form; rather, he is entirely "Form" himself, made like the Father in his very essence. Thus, he is the most vital "Fragrance of the Father," again in a way that is ineffable and beyond our reasoning. Indeed, many things could be said about this that are inexpressible by human voices and beyond the reach of mortal logic, if one speaks with strict accuracy.

But as it is pleasing for us to hear, so the divine oracles instruct us. Did not the holy Apostle call himself and those near him "the fragrance of Christ," <note>Referring to 2 Corinthians 2:15.</note> and this even more so through participation in Christ's Spirit? And is the heavenly Bridegroom not called "ointment poured out" in the Song of Songs? <note>Song of Songs 1:3.</note> By his "emptying out," all things—visible and invisible, bodily and incorporeal, rational and irrational—have participated and were somehow deemed worthy to be filled, sharing in the communion of the Divine Word. This world gives back the echo of this divine breath to those whose rational senses are not blinded, so that even bodies that are by nature earthy and corruptible breathe out an immaterial and pure fragrance. Its source is the God of all, who, being the Father of his Only-begotten Word, is himself the First, the Lord, and the "Only-Truly-Good," the parent of Goodness. The Son is secondary, supplied as if from a first and leading substance, he who alone is for us a certain "Fragrance of the Father’s substance." We follow the divine word which teaches us:

<margin> » </margin> "For she <note>Wisdom, identified here with the Son/Logos.</note> is a breath of the power of God, and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty; 
<margin> » </margin> she is a reflection of eternal light, a spotless mirror of the working of God, 
<margin> » </margin> and an image of his goodness." <note>Quoting Wisdom of Solomon 7:25-26.</note>

<margin> » </margin> However one may wish to view these matters, I have set them forth. It is enough to show from these things how impious it is to repeat the claim which we are seeking to resolve. Regarding these inquiries, we have often said: 

<margin> » </margin> "Who shall declare his generation?" <note>Isaiah 53:8.</note>

<margin> » </margin> "No one knows the Father," he says, "except the Son, and he to whom the Father [wills to reveal him]; and 
<margin> » </margin> no one knows the Son except the Father." <note>Matthew 11:27.</note>

Therefore, the theology concerning the Father and the Son is equally unknown to all, except for...

In the second [psalm], he honors him with a royal scepter. In the third, he bears witness to his perfection according to virtue. <margin>»</margin> God over all "hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy partners." 
<margin>»</margin> Thus, this signified anointing was neither common nor earthly, nor was it 
<margin>»</margin> similar to that established by Moses, which was prepared from perishable matter, and with which it was the custom for the ancient Hebrews to anoint priests and kings. <margin>»</margin> anointed ones <note>original: "christon," plural.</note>, and do no evil to my prophets." <note>Psalm 105:15.</note>

If we seek these things accurately, it would be well to apply them to our Savior and Lord, Jesus the Christ of God, tracing back to the detailed accounts of his coming among men. According to this coming, he [overthrew] the hostile and invisible powers of the wretched and destructive demons, both the evil and the unclean...

Having been joined in a pure union and communion with the God-Word, she may be brought forward as the one who receives the appropriate interpretation according to what is necessary. <note>Eusebius is interpreting Psalm 45 (LXX 44), seeing the "Queen" as the Church and the "Father's house" as the pagan traditions the converts abandoned.</note>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s demonstration of Christ’s divinity through the Old Testament. Here, he focuses on Psalm 110 (Psalm 109 in the Septuagint) to explain the relationship between God the Father and God the Son as two distinct persons both addressed as "Lord."</meta>

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 5
### PAGE 139

Indeed, in the Prophet <note>Referring to King David as the author of the Psalms.</note>, the Holy Spirit proclaims a second **Lord** for himself, following after the Lord of all things. For he says: "The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand." The first Lord, as Master of the universe, the Hebrews designated with an unutterable title consisting of four letters <note>original: "tetrassaron stoicheion," referring to the Tetragrammaton (YHWH), the sacred name of God in Hebrew which was not spoken aloud.</note>; but the second they did not name in the same way, but specifically called him **Lord**. Naturally, then, our Savior and Lord himself, Jesus the **Christ** of God, once asked the Pharisees: "What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?" When they replied, "the son of David," he followed up by saying: "How then does David, speaking in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying: 'The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand'?" <note>Matthew 22:42-44, quoting Psalm 110:1.</note> In this, he was nearly interpreting the very wording, showing that not only David proclaims him Lord, but also the Holy Spirit within the Prophet. 

If the prophetic Spirit—whom we rightly believe to be the **Holy Spirit**—confesses him to be Lord, and teaches that he sits upon the same throne as the Father <note>term: "synthronos" — literally 'sharing the same throne,' used to denote equal dignity or rank.</note>, and not just as anyone’s lord but as his own Lord, then how much more would the rational powers that come after the Holy Spirit say this? Indeed, the entire creation, both that which is seen in physical bodies and that which exists in bodiless forms, would rightly demonstrate that he is Lord—the only one who shares the Father's throne, through whom all things were made. For, according to the wonderful Apostle: "In him all things were created, those in the heavens and those on the earth, whether visible or invisible." <note>Colossians 1:16.</note> It is only reasonable that he alone possesses the title of **Lord** by likeness to the Father, since he alone has been revealed as sharing the Father's throne. 

It is therefore obvious that it is not lawful for any created being to obtain the right hand of the almighty power and kingdom, unless perhaps for that one alone who is uniquely described in our theology. Therefore, the supreme Lord over all grants to the one and the same person the status of Father, saying: "Sit at my right hand," and "Before the morning star I have begotten you." <note>Psalm 110:3.</note> With the confirmation of an oath, he granted him the inseparable and inviolable honor of a **priesthood** <note>original: "hierosyne"</note> lasting for an infinite age: "The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind: You are a priest forever." <note>Psalm 110:4.</note> 

Who could this be imagined to be? Certainly not a mortal man, nor even one of an angelic nature; for while such are created by God, this one is a priest forever. He is the one who also spoke to the prophets, saying: "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works; before the ages he established me, in the beginning before the mountains were settled, and before all the hills he begets me." <note>Proverbs 8:22-25, often interpreted by early Christians as the pre-existent Christ (Wisdom) speaking.</note> 

Carefully observe the connection between this present Psalm and the words cited previously. In this one, the supreme God seats the second Lord, who is our Lord, upon his own throne, saying: "Sit at my right hand." In the previous one, the Word declared that he would receive the throne forever and ever, proclaiming him as God in the passage: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever." <note>Psalm 45:6.</note> Again, in the text at hand, it says: "The Lord will send you a **rod** of power out of Zion." In that other text: "The rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom." And further, the present text says: "Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet, and you shall rule in the midst of your enemies." The earlier text says: "Your arrows are sharpened, O Mighty One, in the heart of the King’s enemies." The descriptions of the enemies of the one being revealed in both passages are in perfect harmony. Who, then, can fail to see with their own eyes the **Churches** of our Savior blooming in the middle of cities, villages, and lands throughout the whole inhabited world, and the prayers offered to him...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s analysis of Psalm 110, moving from the identity of the "Lord" to his role as an eternal High Priest. He contrasts the temporary, symbolic priesthood of Aaron with the eternal, universal priesthood of Christ, modeled after the mysterious figure of Melchizedek.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS: PROOF OF THE GOSPEL
### PAGE 140

...to the peoples being ruled, and the vast multitudes of those devoted to him from every side, who are surrounded by enemies—both those seen by men and those invisible—and by foes of Christ’s teaching, one would not wonder at the present oracle addressed directly to the one being prophesied: 

> **"Rule in the midst of your enemies."** <note>Psalm 110:2. Eusebius views the spread of Christianity despite Roman and spiritual opposition as the fulfillment of this "rule."</note>

And since in the preceding chapters, specifically in Psalm 44, it was said that "God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions," <note>Psalm 45:7 in English Bibles (44 in the Septuagint).</note> and since anointing is a ritual specific to the priests among the Hebrews, the text naturally proceeds to proclaim him a priest. It provides further teaching about him, through which it instructs us that he alone, beyond any who have ever lived, is an **eternal priest**—a status impossible to apply to any human nature. The text says he serves as a priest **"according to the order of Melchizedek,"** <note>Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7.</note> specifically to contrast him with the priesthood established by the Law of Moses. 

<margin>»</margin> This contrast is with the priesthood of Aaron, or any of his successors. Each of them, not being a priest previously, later became one through a man-made ointment prepared by human hands. In a sense, they were "shadowy" and "symbolic" **christs** <note>term: "christ" — here used in its literal sense of "anointed one." Eusebius is explaining that while Jewish high priests were "anointed" (christs) with physical oil, Jesus is the true "Anointed One."</note>, and being mortal, they eventually laid down their priesthood. Furthermore, that priesthood served the Jewish people alone, not the other nations. It did not proceed with a divine oath from God, but was honored by the judgment of men—so much so that sometimes a priest was found unworthy of God’s service, as is recorded of Eli. <note>1 Samuel 2:12–36, where the house of Eli is rejected by God.</note> Beyond all this, that ancient priest was chosen only from the tribe of Levi, according to the Mosaic regulation. 

But this Priest [Christ] is of a different lineage, not from the succession of Aaron. He does not serve the Divinity with sacrifices of irrational animals and blood, nor with physical worship. Instead, he is named after Melchizedek—a name which, translated into the Greek tongue, means **"King of Righteousness"**; and then he is "King of Salem," which would mean **"King of Peace."** <note>Hebrews 7:2.</note> He is described as without father, without mother, and without genealogy; having, according to the historical account, neither beginning of days nor end of life. He bears nothing in common with the "type" of the Aaronic priesthood. He was not chosen by men; he was not anointed with prepared oil; he did not belong to a family of priests. 

Most extraordinary of all, he was not even circumcised, yet he blessed Abraham, proving himself to be much greater than him. <note>Abraham, the father of the Hebrews, paid tithes to Melchizedek, implying Melchizedek's superior status.</note> He did not serve the Most High God with animal sacrifices or libations, nor did he perform his service in the Temple at Jerusalem. How could he, since it did not yet exist? 

Reasonably, then, since our Savior the Christ was to have nothing in common with the Aaronic type, he was not shown to be a priest later in life after not being one before. He did not merely *become* a priest; he *is* one. We must pay careful attention to the phrasing: 

> **"You ARE a priest forever."** 

<margin>»</margin> It does not say "You shall be," as if you were not one before; nor "You were once, but now are not." Rather, just as He who said: 
<margin>»</margin> > **"I am He who IS,"** <note>original: "Ego eimi ho On" — the divine name from Exodus 3:14.</note>
so "You **ARE**," and you continue as a priest forever. Since his priesthood did not begin at a point in time, and since Christ was not from a tribe of priests, nor anointed with physical, manufactured oil—and since his priesthood was not to end, nor be limited to the Jews but established for all nations—for all these reasons, the text naturally distinguishes him from the service according to the Aaronic "type," and says he shall be a priest **"according to the order of Melchizedek."** The fulfillment of this oracle is truly marvelous when one considers how our Savior, Jesus the Christ of God, followed the pattern of Melchizedek’s priestly service among men, and continues to perform it even now through his ministers...

<summary>Eusebius explains how Christ fulfills the prophecy of an "eternal priest" according to the order of Melchizedek. He contrasts this with the Aaronic priesthood, which was temporary, physical, and limited to Israel, whereas Christ's priesthood is eternal and universal.</summary>

...for being a priest of the nations by descent, he [Melchizedek] is nowhere seen using bodily sacrifices <note>original: "σωματικαῖς θυσίαις" — referring to animal sacrifices required by the Mosaic Law.</note>, but instead blessed Abraham with wine and bread alone. In exactly the same way, first our Savior and Lord himself, and then all the priests proceeding from him among all the nations, perform the spiritual priestly service according to the ecclesiastical laws. With wine and bread, they symbolize the mysteries of his body and his saving blood. Melchizedek had already envisioned these things through the Divine Spirit and used these images of the future, as the writing of Moses testifies, saying:

<margin>»</margin> he continues, saying: **"And many have become priests, because they were prevented by death**

# BY EUSEBIUS HIMSELF

Just as Isaiah, the greatest of prophets, clearly knows that God is within God, he says—similarly to our own belief—that the Father is glorified in the Son, and the Son in the Father.

<margin>E</margin>
> » "I, the Lord, made the earth and man upon it. I with my hand established the
> » heaven, I commanded all the stars. I raised up a king with righteousness, 
> » and all his ways are straight. He shall build my city, and shall return the 
> » captivity of my people, not with ransoms, nor with gifts, said the Lord of 
> » Sabaoth <note>original: "σαβαώθ" — a Hebrew title meaning 'of Hosts' or 'of Armies'.</note>."

For a time, the God who is the Maker of all things speaks through the prophet about a certain king and savior, foretelling that he would build a "commonwealth of piety" <note>original: "εὐσεβείας πολίτευμα" — referring to the established Christian community or way of life</note> and would redeem the captivity that befell humanity through demonic error. Following this, the prophetic spirit hints at the subjection of foreign nations which will happen under the one prophesied. It describes how those who are subjected will worship him as God and will pray "in him," because a greater God dwells within him—namely, the Supreme Father and God of all. The wording is as follows:

> » "Thus says the Lord: Egypt has labored, and the merchandise of the 
> » Ethiopians; and the Sabeans, men of great stature, shall pass over to you and 
> » shall be your servants, and shall follow behind you, bound in chains. They 
> » shall worship you and pray in you, because God is in you, and there is no 
> » God except you. For you are God, and we knew it not, O God of Israel, the 
> » Savior. All who oppose him shall be ashamed and turned back, and shall 
> » walk in shame."

This is the prophecy. I do not think anyone could find fault with it, even if they are extremely ignorant, as the text clearly introduces one who is the "Savior of Israel" as God, and yet speaks of another God dwelling *within* him. "They shall worship you," it says, "and pray in you, because God is in you, and there is no God except you. For you are God and we knew it not, O God of Israel, the Savior." 

As for the phrase "we knew it not," it is spoken from the perspective of those who previously did not recognize him. <margin>This phrase is found only in the Septuagint <note>The 'Seventy' (LXX), the standard Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible used by early Christians.</note>,</margin> as the Hebrew text was different. Aquila <note>A 2nd-century translator known for extremely literal, though sometimes awkward, Greek renderings of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, translating it, says: "Truly a strong God hiding himself, the God of Israel saving." Theodotion <note>Another 2nd-century translator whose work was often preferred for its clarity.</note> says: "For this reason, a strong hidden God saving." 

He calls Christ a "hidden God" in a most wonderful way. He clearly teaches the reason why he alone among all beings is called God alongside the First and Unbegotten <note>original: "ἀγεννήτου" — a key theological term for God the Father, meaning he was not created or 'brought into being' by another.</note>: it is because of the Father's dwelling within him. For the Apostle says that in Christ "all the fullness of the Godhead was pleased to dwell." This is what the phrase reveals: "God is in you, and there is no God except you." Instead of "except you," Theodotion wrote "except him," so that it reads: "there is no God except Him"—referring, of course, to the God who is *in* you, because of whom you also happen to be God. 

According to Aquila, it reads: "Except that in you is a strong one, and there is no other besides you; truly a strong God and one hiding himself, a God who saves." And according to Symmachus <note>A translator known for his elegant, idiomatic Greek style.</note>: "Only in you is God, and there is no other, nor does any other God exist; truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel who saves." Through these words, the text clearly presents Christ as God because of God [the Father]. For since it says "God is in you," for this reason you are a "strong and hidden God." 

Therefore, by these accounts, the Unbegotten would be the one and only God, possessing the title in the primary sense. But the second [the Son] has been deemed worthy of the title by participation in true communion, neither existing by himself, nor subsisting apart from the Father who "deifies" <note>original: "θεοποιοῦντος" — literally 'making God', here meaning the source of the Son's divinity</note> him, nor...

# THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 5

...proclaimed as God by the Father, but being entirely his own—living, subsisting, and existing in his own right—because of the Father who is in him. To him alone, existing in the Father, through the Father, and because of the Father, is divinity attributed. Thus, he is both "one" with the Father and "directed toward the one," <note>original: "πρὸς εἷς" — This reflects the phrasing of John 1:1, where the Word is "with" (pros) God, implying a relationship of distinction and orientation.</note> having received his being not from himself, but from the Father. For this reason, we have been taught to honor not just the Father, but also the Son as God—or rather, to honor the God dwelling within him—just as the prophecies which are not bound by physical limitations <note>original: "αἱ μὴ χεῖρας περιέχουσαι προφητείαι" — likely referring to spiritual prophecies that transcend literal or "hand-made" idols.</note> declare. 

For it is as if a king’s portrait were sent abroad; because it bears the very character and likeness of the king, when the portrait is honored, the king himself is honored. The one being honored is one, not two. For there are not "two kings"—the first and true king, and the one depicted in the portrait—but rather there is one king seen in both, not only in thought, but in name and in honor. In this very way, the <term>Only-Begotten Son</term> <note>original: "μονογενὴς υἱὸς" — A title for Christ meaning the unique, one-of-a-kind offspring.</note> is the only "Image" of the invisible God. Rightly then, because he bears the likeness, he is assigned the title of "Image of the invisible God." He is addressed as God by the Father himself, being so by his very nature and essence, possessing from his first moment of existence a natural—not an acquired—image of the Father. 

Therefore, he happens to be God by nature and the Only-Begotten Son simultaneously. This is not like those who are "adopted" from the outside; rather, the dignity of being the Son of God was granted to him through his own excellence. Even if he is sung of as being by nature the Only-Begotten Son and our God, he is not the "First God," <note>Eusebius often uses "First God" to refer specifically to the Father as the uncaused Source, a common distinction in early Greek theology.</note> but the first Only-Begotten Son of God, and because of this, he is God. The whole reason for him being God is that he alone is the Son of God by nature and is called "Only-Begotten." He preserves throughout his being the "living and breathing intelligent Image" of the only God, being made like the Father in all things and bearing the likeness of that very divinity. 

For this reason, because he is the only Son and the only Image of the unbegotten and uncaused God the Father, he is clothed in the powers of the Father's essence according to the pattern of that likeness. Having been perfectly crafted according to that likeness by the Father—who is the most skilled Craftsman, the all-knowing Painter, and the Giver of Life—the divine scriptures rightly proclaim him to be God. He has been deemed worthy of this title by the Father as a living being, having received it as his own unique property. For the one gives, and the other receives. Consequently, that "One" is primarily and uniquely God by nature, not having received it from another; whereas the "Other" is deemed worthy of the second rank, possessing his divinity as something received from the Father, being the Image of God. A single divinity is perceived in both, following the pattern of the prototype. God is one, existing by himself without beginning or birth, but he is seen through the Son as if through a mirror or an image. 

The prophetic word also trains our vision in this, stating that the one revealed is not to be worshiped as God in any other way than because of the Father dwelling in him.

> » "For in you," it says, "they shall pray, because God is in you; and you yourself 
> » are not God, <note>Eusebius is interpreting the Greek Septuagint text here, which can be read as 'and there is no God besides you' or as a distinction of persons.</note> yet you are the Savior of Israel; and for this reason, 
> » you are a strong and hidden God. Since God is in you, there is no other 
> » besides him." 

Instead of the phrase "Egypt has labored," the Hebrew text and all the other translators have rendered it "the labor of Egypt." <note>Eusebius is noting a textual variant between the Septuagint (Greek) and the versions of Aquila, Symmachus, or Theodotion.</note> The meaning of the passage is this: those who will worship and become servants are the "labor of Egypt," the "merchandise of the Ethiopians," and the "Sabeans." By these, I believe, foreign and insignificant nations are meant—all those who in ancient times were worn out by demonic superstition. For the Egyptians were thought to be the most superstitious of all nations, and the first to start the practice of idol-worship...

# EUSEBIUS

Just as Isaiah, the greatest of the prophets, clearly knows that God is in God, he says—similarly to us—that the Father is glorified in the Son, and the Son in the Father.

<margin>E</margin> "I am the Lord who made the earth and man upon it. With my own hand I established the heaven, and I commanded all the stars. I have raised him up as a king with righteousness, and all his ways are straight. He shall build my city, and shall turn back the captivity of my people, not for ransom, nor for gifts, said the Lord of Sabaoth." <note>original: "κύριος σαβαώθ" — Lord of Hosts, a common Hebrew title for God in the Old Testament.</note> For a time, the God who is the Creator of all things speaks through the prophet, foretelling a certain King and Savior who is destined to build the <term>commonwealth of piety</term> <note>original: "εὐσεβείας πολίτευμα" — referring to the community of the faithful or the Church.</note> and to ransom the captivity that befell humanity through demonic deception. Immediately following this, the prophetic Spirit hints at the subjection of foreign nations, who will be made subject to the one mentioned before. It describes how those who are subjected will worship him as God, and how they will make their pleas in him, because a greater God dwells in him—namely, the Father on high and the God of all. The wording is as follows: "Thus says the Lord: Egypt has labored, and the trade of the Ethiopians, and the Sabeans, men of stature, shall pass over to you, and shall be your servants, and they shall follow behind you bound in shackles, and they shall worship you, and in you they shall make prayer, because God is in you, and there is no God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it, the God of Israel, the Savior. All who oppose him shall be put to shame and disgraced, and shall walk in shame." 

This is the prophecy. I do not think there could be any objection—even from someone who is extremely ignorant—when the wording so clearly and evidently introduces a God who is the Savior of Israel, and yet another God within him. It says, "The righteous shall worship you, and in you they shall make prayer, because God is in you, and there is no God besides you. For you are God and we did not know it, the God of Israel, the Savior." Now, the phrase "which we did not know" is spoken from the perspective of those who previously did not recognize him, according to the translation of the <term>Seventy</term>; <note>original: "ἑβδομήκοντα" — The Septuagint, the standard Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> however, the Hebrew text was different. 

<term>Aquila</term>, <note>A 2nd-century scholar who produced a literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> who translated it, says: "Surely then, a strong God who hides himself, the God of Israel, the Savior." And <term>Theodotion</term> <note>Another early Greek translator of the Old Testament.</note> says: "For this reason, a strong hidden God, a Savior." He most wonderfully calls Christ a "hidden God." He clearly teaches the reason why he calls him alone "God" in a true and genuine sense alongside the Father who is unbegotten: it is the dwelling of the Father within him. For in him, as the divine Apostle says, "all the fullness of the deity was pleased to dwell." This is what the passage reveals when it says: "Because God is in you, and there is no God besides you." Instead of "besides you," Theodotion wrote "besides him," so that it reads: "There is no God besides him"—meaning, the God who is within you, because of whom you also happen to be God. 

According to Aquila, it reads: "Unless a strong one is in you, and there is none besides you; surely then, a strong and hidden God, the God who saves." According to <term>Symmachus</term> <note>A translator known for a more idiomatic and elegant Greek style compared to Aquila's literalism.</note> then: "Only in you is God, and there is no other, nor does any other God exist; you are truly a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Savior." Through these words, the Word of God has clearly presented the cause of Christ being God. For because he says "God is in you," for this reason "you are a strong and hidden God." Therefore, by these means, the true and only God would be one, alone possessing the title in the primary sense. But the second, through <term>participation</term> <note>original: "μετουσίᾳ" — The theological idea that the Son shares in the Father's divinity rather than being a second, independent source of it.</note> in the True One, is deemed worthy of the fellowship, being neither a God unto himself, nor subsisting apart from the Father who makes him God...

### THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 5

...spoken of as God in relation to the Father, but being a complete living being, both living and subsisting, because of the Father within him. <note>original: "ζῶν ὢν ἐν πατρὶ" — Eusebius emphasizes that the Son’s life is not independent but flows directly from the Father.</note> (Being alive in the Father, and from him, and being <term>deified</term> <note>original: "θεοποιούμενος" (theopoioumenos) — meaning "made God" or "receiving divinity." Eusebius uses this to show that the Son's divinity is derived from the Father, the ultimate source.</note> through him, both to exist and to be God) he has received this not from himself, but from the Father. Therefore, we are taught to honor the Father and him as God, because of the God dwelling in him, just as the prophecies that do not contain hands <note>This likely refers to non-anthropomorphic prophecies or spiritual visions.</note> suggest. For as the image of a King is honored because it bears his features and likeness—and when the image is honored, the King himself is honored, and the object of honor is one and not two. For there are not two Kings, the first and true one, and the one depicted in the image; rather, there is one who is considered, named, and honored in both. In this same way, the Only-begotten Son, being the only image of the invisible God, is naturally called "image" and "God of the invisible God," because of the one whose likeness he bears. He is deified by the Father himself, being so constituted in his essence that from his very first existence he carries the Father's image as a natural, not an acquired, quality. Therefore, he happens to be both God by nature and the Only-begotten Son, unlike those who are adopted from the outside, where the dignity and the title of "God" are merely acquired attributes.

However, even if he is proclaimed as the Only-begotten Son by nature and as our God, he is not the "First God," but rather the first Only-begotten Son of God, and because of this, he is God. The entire cause of his being God is that he alone is already God by nature and bears the title "Only-begotten," and that he preserves throughout himself the <term>living and intelligent image</term> <note>original: "ἔμψυχον καὶ ζῶσαν νοερὰν εἰκόνα" — A key Platonic and Christian concept describing the Son as more than a static statue; he is a conscious, living reflection of the Divine Mind.</note> of the only God, made similar to the Father in all things, and carrying the likeness of that very divinity. For this reason, since he alone is the Son and the only image of the unbegotten and unoriginated essence of the Father, having his powers perfected according to the specific power of that likeness—worked out to the highest degree of accuracy by the all-skillful and all-knowing Artist and Life-giver, the Father—the divine words rightly proclaim him to be God. He is worthy of this title from the Holy Father, having received it as something he did not possess by his own separate acquisition. For the one gives, and the other receives. Consequently, in a primary sense, that One alone is God who exists by nature and who did not receive it from another. The other is deemed worthy of the second rank, possessing the status of being God because he received it from the Father, as the image of God. A single divinity is conceived in both according to the model, with the one God being the one who exists of himself without beginning or origin, while he is perceived through the Son as through a mirror and an image. For this reason, the spiritual oracle also teaches us, stating that God is not to be worshiped in any other way...

### THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 5

...they were created; he commanded, and they were created <note>original: "αὐτὸς ἐνετείλατο, καὶ ἐκτίσθησαν" — A quote from Psalm 148:5.</note>. For if He himself commanded, who was it that received such a great command to create, if not the Word of God? He is spoken of in various divine terms throughout our current study, and is rightly addressed as the Word of God because the Almighty has placed within him the creative and productive "word" <note>Eusebius is playing on the dual meaning of *Logos* as both "Word" and "Reason/Order."</note> of all things, handing over to him the task of arranging and governing the universe with reason and order. 

One should not suppose that the Word of God is like the word used among men, which consists of syllables and is composed of names and verbs—an articulated and spoken word. For our word has its essence in sounds and syllables and the things signified by them, produced through the tongue, the arteries, the throat, and the mouth. But the Word of the eternal and incorporeal nature is changed in every way from our own experience and is subject to no human passion, sharing only the name "Word" <note>term: "homonymy" — When two things share the same name but have different natures.</note>. We must not attribute to the God of the universe a voice produced by the striking of air, nor verbs, nor syllables, nor a tongue, nor a mouth, nor anything at all human and mortal. 

The human word is a "breath of the soul" <note>original: "ψυχῆς γὰρ αἰθέριον ὁ λόγος" — Literally "an ethereal thing of the soul."</note> which can in no way exist or stand by itself apart from the soul. For the word in humans is, strictly speaking, without substance <term>anousios</term> and without a distinct existence <term>anhypostatos</term>, being entirely a certain movement and activity of the mind. But the Word of God is not like this; he has his own distinct existence <term>hypostasis</term> that is entirely divine and intellectual. He exists in his own right and acts in his own right, being altogether immaterial and incorporeal, and in every way made like the Father as the true and only God by nature. He carries within himself the "reasons" <note>original: "λόγοις" — Here meaning the formative principles or blueprints of creation.</note> of all created things and the immaterial and invisible "ideas" of things seen. Therefore, the divine oracles address him as both "Wisdom" and "God the Word."

Draw near to me and hear these things. I have not spoken in secret from the beginning. When it happened, I was there. And now the Lord, the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit. <note>Isaiah 48:12–16.</note>

Observe carefully even now how the one who says, "I am the first, and I am forever," the one who established the earth and the heaven, clearly confesses that he has been sent "by the Lord, the Lord." In this way, he silently addresses the Father twice as Lord, so that you might have this undisputed testimony for which we are searching. He calls himself "the first" among created things in a pious sense, attributing the beginningless, unbegotten nature and the "essence beyond the first" to the Father. For that which is "first" precedes a greater number in honor and rank; this would not be appropriate to the Father. For the God over all is not the "first" of created beings, since no beginning can even be conceived for Him...

->Psalm 32 <note>Psalm 33 in modern Bibles</note><-

"By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power." And in the 106th Psalm <note>Psalm 107 in modern Bibles</note> it is said, "He sent his word and healed them from their destructions." And again in the 147th: "He who sends his word to the earth, his word runs swiftly." But indeed, the one speaking in the current Psalm says, "By the word of the Lord the heavens were established," which harmonizes with the Gospel when it explicitly says: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This one was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made." <note>A quotation of John 1:1–3</note> The Evangelist rightly names Him "God," since through the preceding points, He is the one now being spoken of in a divine sense: the Word, Wisdom, and Power of God; and Christ as High Priest, King, Lord, God, and the unchanging image <note>original: "εἰκὼν ἀπαράλλακτος"</note> of God. And because He is someone other than the Father, a minister <note>term: "hypourgos" — a subordinate worker or assistant. Eusebius often describes the Son as the Father's agent in creation</note> to the Father, as if creating at the instruction of a superior, he [David] adds next in the present Psalm: "Let all the earth fear the Lord, and let all the inhabitants of the world be moved by him. For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created." For it is obvious that the one who speaks, speaks to another; and the one who commands, commands another besides himself. It is clear that upon the appearance of our Savior, countless multitudes from all the earth—that is, from all the nations—no longer fear demons as before, but feared the Lord Jesus Himself. And all those who inhabit the world were moved <note>or "shaken" in awe</note> at the name of Christ, in accordance with the oracle now speaking: "Let all the earth fear the Lord; let all the inhabitants of the world be moved by him." These things, then, are from the 32nd and 106th Psalms. Consistent with these are other things in the 148th Psalm, which teaches not only about earthly things, but also those in heaven—and in short, that the entire creation came into being by the command of the God of all. It says, then: "Praise the Lord from the heavens, praise him in the highest. Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers. Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all you stars and light, for he spoke, and they were made <note>catchword: "...created"</note>..."

<summary>Eusebius interprets several Psalms to prove that the "Word of God" is a distinct, personally existing divine being who acted as the Father's agent in creating the universe and converting the nations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius's theological exploration of the Logos (the Word). Having previously established that the Word is substantial and personal, he now contrasts the divine Word with human speech and uses the prophecy of Isaiah to demonstrate the existence of a "second Lord" who acts as the Creator and messenger of the Father.</meta>

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 5

...died; *he commanded, and they were created* <note>original: "αὐτὸς ἐνετείλατο, καὶ ἐκτίσθησαν" — a quotation from Psalm 148:5 regarding the creation of the heavens</note>. For if He himself commanded, who else could be so great as to receive a command concerning such vast things, except the **Word of God**? He is the one who is described as divine in various ways throughout our current thesis, and is rightly addressed as the "Word of God" because the Almighty has, through Him, established the creative and productive principles <note>term: "logoi" — here meaning the rational blueprints or laws of creation</note> of all things, handing over to Him the task of managing and governing the universe with reason and order.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For one should not suppose that the Word of God is similar to the word found among men, which consists of syllables and is composed of names and verbs, existing as spoken sound in the air. Our human word possesses its essence in voices and syllables, and the meanings conveyed by them, being brought forth through the tongue, the arteries, the throat, and the mouth. But the richness of the eternal and incorporeal nature, which is entirely different from our own, would admit nothing human; it uses the same name "Word" only by way of an analogy <note>original: "ὁμωνυμίᾳ" — literally "homonymy," suggesting that while the word is the same, the reality is different</note>.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;One must not attribute to the God of the Universe a voice produced by the striking of air, nor verbs, nor syllables, nor a tongue, nor a mouth, nor anything at all that is human and mortal. For such a word belongs to a soul and cannot possibly exist or subsist on its own without a soul. Such is the word in men: it has no substance or personal existence of its own <note>term: "anhypostatos" — lacking a distinct, individual reality</note>, but is entirely dependent on the movements and activity of the mind. But the **Word of God** is not like this; He has His own proper, perfect, and intellectual existence <note>term: "hypostasis" — a distinct personal reality or substance</note>, existing individually and acting individually, being immaterial and incorporeal. In every way, He is likened to the nature of the Unbegotten and Only God, bearing within Himself the patterns <note>original: "ideas" — the archetypal forms or blueprints</note> of all created things, both the incorporeal and invisible forms of things seen. For this reason, the divine oracles address Him as **Wisdom** and as **God the Word**.

<margin>A</margin>
*Listen to me, Jacob and Israel, whom I call. I am the first, and I am forever; my hand founded the earth, and my right hand established the heaven. I will call them, and they shall stand together. And they shall all be gathered together and shall hear; who has announced these things to them? The Lord who loves you has performed your will upon Babylon, and to take away the seed of the Chaldeans. I have spoken, and I have called. I brought him, and I made his way prosperous. Come near to me and hear these things. I have not spoken in secret from the beginning. When it happened, I was there. And now the Lord, the Lord has sent me, and His Spirit.* <note>Isaiah 48:12–16. Eusebius uses this to show the speaker (the Creator) is distinct from the Lord who sent Him.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Observe now how the one who said, *“I am the first, and I am forever,”* the one who established the earth and the heaven, clearly confesses in this way that He has been sent by the **Lord, the Lord**. In this passage, he addresses the Father as "Lord" twice, according to custom, so that you might have this as an indisputable testimony of the matter we are seeking. He says this to indicate that He exists in a godly manner among created things, while attributing the unoriginated, unbegotten, and superior essence of the "First" to the Father. For the term "first" leads a larger number, being ranked first in honor and order; this would not properly fit the Father. For the God over all is not merely the "first" of created things, since no beginning <note>original: "archē" — can mean "start" or "originating principle"</note> can even be imagined for Him...

->From the same [book]<-

How the same Moses most clearly and openly speaks of two Lords in his theology.

<margin>The</margin> sun rose upon the earth, and Lot entered into Segor, and the Lord rained upon Sodom sulfur and fire from the Lord <note>Genesis 19:23-24</note>. Clearly he proclaims a second [Lord], whom he also teaches was entrusted by the Greater to carry out the punishment against the ungodly. But although we openly acknowledge two Lords, we do not apply the same theological terms to both; rather, piously observing the order, we have been taught that the highest Father is both God and Lord, and even the Lord and God of the second [Lord]. We know the Word of God as the second Lord, being Master of those things under him, but no longer in the same way the Master of the Greater; for the Word of God is not the Lord of the Father, nor the God of the Father, but rather his Image, and Word, and Wisdom, and Power; but of the things after him, he is Master, Lord, and God. The Father, however, is both Father and Lord and God of the Son. Hence, our pious theology reasonably traces things back to one Beginning <note>term: "arche" — the single source or principle of divinity</note> and is established in one God.
