# EVANGELICAL PROOF, Book 5

->From the same source.<-

How the same servant <note>Referring to Moses, the traditional author of Genesis</note> shows that the Word of God is designated as a second God and Lord, and records that he was seen and spoke to the ancients in the form and figure of a human being.

> "And the Lord appeared to Abraham, and said to him, 'To your offspring I will give this land.'" <note>Genesis 12:7</note>
> "And again: 'Abraham was ninety-nine years old, and the Lord appeared to Abraham, and said to him, "I am God. Be well-pleasing before me and be blameless, and I will set my covenant between me and you, and I will multiply you greatly."'" <note>Genesis 17:1-2</note>
> "And further: 'God appeared to him by the Oak of Mamre, as he sat at the door of his tent at noon. Looking up with his eyes, he saw, and behold, three men stood above him. And seeing them, he ran to meet them from the door of the tent and bowed down.'" <note>Genesis 18:1-2; original: "δρυῒ τῇ μαμβρῆ" — the Oak of Mamre</note>
> "And immediately after this vision he adds: 'And the Lord said, "Shall I hide from Abraham my servant what I am doing? Since Abraham shall become a great and numerous nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him."'" <note>Genesis 18:17-18</note>
> "In these words he adds, as if speaking of someone else: 'For I have known that he will command his sons and his house after him, and they shall keep the ways of the Lord to do righteousness and judgment, that the Lord may bring upon Abraham what he spoke to him.'" <note>Genesis 18:19</note>
> These things are recorded as being spoken by the Lord who addressed Abraham, clearly acknowledging *another* Lord whom he regards as his own Father and the Creator of all things. Indeed, Abraham, possessing the accurate perception of a prophet regarding the one speaking to him, follows the previous words by pleading:
> "'...and will you destroy the righteous with the ungodly, so that the righteous shall be as the ungodly? If there are fifty righteous in the city, will you destroy them? Will you not spare the whole place for the sake of the fifty righteous? Far be it from you to do this thing, to kill the righteous with the ungodly, so that the righteous is as the ungodly. Far be it from you, the Judge of all the earth—will you not do justice?'" <note>Genesis 18:23-25</note>
> I do not believe it is fitting to say these things were addressed to angels, or to any of those who serve God. For it does not belong to any ordinary being to 'judge all the earth.' Yet, he is not described as an angel; rather, someone greater than an angel—God and Lord—was seen in a human figure alongside two angels in the record.
> Again, one must not think that the 'God over all' <note>The Father</note> is revealed through these events. For it is not a pious thought to say the Divine Essence changes and takes on the shape and form of a man. It remains, then, for us to acknowledge that this is the Word of God himself, who has been treated as Divine in the preceding arguments.
> This is why, even to this day, the place is venerated by the inhabitants of the region as a divine site in honor of those who appeared to Abraham; and the terebinth tree <note>original: "τερέβινθος" — a large, oak-like tree</note> remains there even now. For those who were guests of Abraham are depicted in a painting; two are placed on either side, while the one in the middle is superior, surpassing them in honor. This would be the Lord we have described, our Savior himself, whom even those who do not know him worship, thus confirming the holy oracles. <margin>A</margin> Therefore, he himself, sowing the seeds of piety among humans from that time, took on human form and appearance and revealed himself to the God-loving Abraham, making known to him the will of the Father.

# EUSEBIUS

himself further away from the first, since He [the Father] is the one who first begot and gave him existence, with the Divine Word alone being designated as the first of all things brought into being. <note>original: "πρώτου τῶν θνητῶν" — literally "first of mortals," though Eusebius uses this in a cosmic sense to mean the first being in the order of generated things.</note> When He willed it—as it is said—"He spoke and they were generated, He commanded and they were created." To whom the creation of mortals was commanded has now been clearly demonstrated: to the one who said, "My hand founded the earth, and my right hand established the heaven." <note>Isaiah 48:13</note> The one who was sent by the Greater acknowledges this, saying: "And now the Lord, the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit." <note>Isaiah 48:16; the repetition of "Lord" is used here to distinguish the Sender from the Sent.</note> The God-Word would be the one saying these things, as confirmed by the phrase "by the Word of the Lord the heavens were established" and the comparison with the Psalm. <note>Psalm 33:6</note>

Nevertheless, even if the Word of God is himself given the title of Lord <note>original: "κύριος" (Kyrios)</note> in theology, he does not hesitate to call his highest and greater Father "Lord" twice, using a different name for him. For he says, "The Lord, the Lord has sent me," implying that the God over all is the primary and true Lord of his Only-begotten Word and of all things generated after him. In a secondary sense, the status of Lord and Master is demonstrated to belong to the Word of God through the Father; as a true and Only-begotten <note>term: "Monogenes" — a unique, one-of-a-kind offspring</note> Son, he himself would also piously be designated as Lord in a secondary degree.

### From Genesis

How even the greatest servant of God, Moses, in his account of the creation of the world, knows that the Father and God of all things held counsel with another regarding the creation of human beings. We have previously learned that this "other" is the Divine Word.

"And God said, 'Let us make man according to our image and likeness.'" And again: "And God said, 'It is not good for man to be alone, let us make for him a helper corresponding to him.'" And lest anyone should think these words were spoken to angels, the text immediately clarifies that the one who received the command was not an angel of God, saying: "And God made man; in the image of God he made him." <note>Genesis 1:26-27; 2:18. Eusebius argues that if God were speaking to angels, the text would say man was made in the image of angels, but it specifies the "image of God," implying the Word is the very image of the Father.</note>

### From the same source

How the same Moses most clearly and openly speaks of two Lords.

"The sun rose upon the earth, and Lot entered into Segor, and the Lord rained upon Sodom sulfur and fire from the Lord." <note>Genesis 19:23-24</note> He clearly proclaims a second [Lord], whom he teaches has been commissioned by the Greater to carry out the punishment against the ungodly. But although we openly acknowledge two Lords, we do not apply the same level of divinity to both. Following a pious order, we are taught that the one is the highest Father and Lord God, and the second is Lord and God. 

The Word of God is the second Lord—Master of those under him, but not in the same way over the Greater. For the God-Word is not the Lord of the Father, nor the God of the Father; rather, he is his Image, Word, Wisdom, and Power. But of those things created after him, he is Master, Lord, and God. The Father, however, is the Father, Lord, and God even of the Son. Thus, our pious theology reasonably traces everything back to one Principle <note>term: "Arche" — the source or beginning of all things</note> and consists in one God.

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 5, 147

->From the same source.<-

How the same servant reveals the Word of God, designated as a second God and Lord <note>original: "δεύτερον θεὸν καὶ κύριον" — Eusebius uses "second God" to describe the Word's relationship to the Father, a common concept in early theology before the Council of Nicaea solidified Trinitarian language.</note>, and records that He appeared and spoke to the ancients in the form and figure of a man.

> And the Lord appeared to Abraham, and said to him, "To your seed I will give this land."
> And again: "Abraham was ninety-nine years old, and the Lord appeared to Abraham, and said to him, 'I am your God. Be well-pleasing before me and be blameless, and I will establish my covenant between you and me, and I will multiply you exceedingly.'"
> And further: "And God appeared to him by the Oak of Mamre <note>original: "δρυῒ τῇ μαμβρῆ" — Mamre is a site near Hebron famous for its ancient trees and its association with Abraham.</note>, as he sat at the door of his tent at noon. And lifting up his eyes, he looked, and behold, three men stood over him. And seeing them, he ran to meet them from the door of his tent, and bowed down to the ground."
> And following the vision, it adds: "But the Lord said, 'Shall I hide from Abraham my servant what I am doing? For Abraham shall become a great and numerous nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him.'"
> Upon these things it adds again, as if speaking about another: "For I knew that he would command his sons and his house after him, and they will keep the ways of the Lord, to do righteousness and judgment, so that the Lord may bring upon Abraham what he spoke to him." <note>Eusebius points out that the "Lord" speaking refers to another "Lord" in the third person, suggesting a plurality of persons within the divine name.</note>
> These things the Lord who spoke to Abraham is recorded as saying, clearly acknowledging another Lord—namely his own Father and the Creator of all things.
> Furthermore, Abraham, having an accurate understanding as a prophet of the one speaking to him, next makes a plea following the words set out above, saying: "Do not destroy the righteous with the ungodly, so that the righteous will be as the ungodly. If there are fifty righteous in the city, will you destroy them? Will you not spare the whole place for the sake of the fifty righteous? Far be it from you to do this thing, to kill the righteous with the ungodly, so that the righteous is as the ungodly. Never, O judge of all the earth, will you not execute judgment?" <note>Genesis 18:23-25</note>

I do not think it is fitting to say that these words apply to angels, or to any of the other ministers of God. For it does not belong to just anyone to judge the whole earth. Moreover, the one described above is not called an "angel," but rather someone greater than an angel—God and Lord—who was seen with the angels at the recorded Oak in the form of a man.

On the other hand, one must not think that the God over all <note>meaning God the Father</note> is revealed through these passages. For to say that the Divine changes and is transformed into the shape and form of a man is not pious. It remains, then, that this is the Word of God itself, who was acknowledged through the previous theological proofs. This is why, even to this day, the site is still venerated by the neighbors as a divine place, in honor of those who appeared there to Abraham. Visitors can still see the wonders of the terebinth tree <note>original: "τερεβίνθου" — a species of tree often confused with oak; Eusebius notes it as a local landmark.</note> and a painting of those who were guests of Abraham. They are depicted in the image: two on either side, and the middle one being greater, surpassing the others in honor. This middle figure would be our Lord and Savior Himself, whom even those who do not know Him worship, thus confirming the divine oracles. He it was who, even then, was sowing the seeds of piety among 
<margin>A</margin>men, appearing to the God-loving Abraham in a human-like form, revealing who He was and passing down the knowledge of his Father.

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument from the previous section of Book 5, focusing on theophany—instances where God appears to humans. Eusebius specifically seeks to prove that when the Old Testament mentions "God" appearing in physical form, it refers to the Word (the Logos) acting as a messenger for the Father.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

->From the same source.<-

How the same prophet <note>referring to Moses as the author of Genesis</note> reveals even more clearly in the story of Jacob the one designated as Lord, whom he also calls both God and Angel, addressing Him as the servant of the God over all.

> And he went toward Haran, and he came upon a place, and slept there, for the sun had set. And he took one of the stones, and placed it at his head, and slept in that place, and he had a dream. And behold, a ladder was fixed on the earth, whose top reached to heaven, and the angels of God were ascending and descending upon it. And the Lord stood firmly upon it, and said, "I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac; do not fear. The land on which you sleep, I will give it to you and to your offspring. And your offspring shall be like the sand of the sea, and shall spread out toward the sea and the east, and toward the north and the south; and in you all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed, and in your offspring. And behold, I am with you, guarding you in every way wherever you go, and I will return you to this land, because I will certainly not abandon you until I have done everything I spoke to you." And Jacob arose from his sleep and said, "The Lord is in this place, and I did not know it." And he was afraid, and said, "How fearsome is this place! This is nothing else but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." And Jacob rose early in the morning, and took the stone he had placed at his head, and set it up as a pillar, and poured oil on the top of it. And Jacob called the name of that place 'House of God' <note>original: "οἶκος θεοῦ" — In Hebrew, 'Bethel'.</note>.

You will find that this same person who is called "Lord God" upon the ladder is later referred to as an "Angel of God," in the passage where Jacob speaks to his wives:

> And the Angel of God said to me in a dream, "Jacob!" and I said, "What is it?" And he said... "I have seen all that Laban is doing to you. I am the God who appeared to you in the place of God <note>original: "ἐν τόπῳ θεοῦ" — likely referring to Bethel, the 'Place of God'.</note> where you anointed a pillar to me, and made a vow to me."

Now, consider this: the one who spoke earlier, saying, "I am the Lord God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac," and to whom the God-beloved Jacob raised a pillar—though He is indeed God and Lord (and we must believe Him when He says so)—He is not the God over all, but rather the "second" <note>original: "δεύτερος" — Eusebius uses this term to distinguish the Logos from the Father, the ultimate source. In this early theological framework, the "Second God" is the mediator who communicates with the physical world.</note> to Him, who ministers and announces the Father's will to humanity. This is why Jacob calls Him an "Angel" in this instance. For he says, "The Angel of God spoke to me in a dream, saying, 'I am the God who appeared to you in the place.'" Therefore, the same person is clearly proclaimed through these words as both Angel of the Lord, and God, and Lord.

This figure is also addressed by the prophet Isaiah as the "Angel of Great Counsel" <note>original: "μεγάλης βουλῆς ἄγγελος" — This is the Septuagint translation of Isaiah 9:6. While modern Bibles usually translate the Hebrew as "Wonderful Counselor," the Greek version used by the early Church emphasized his role as a Messenger (Angel) of God's plan.</note>, and simultaneously as God, Ruler, and One in Authority, in the passage where he prophesies His birth among men, saying:

> For a child is born to us, a son is given to us, whose government is upon his shoulder, and his name is called Angel of Great Counsel, Prince of Peace, Mighty God, One in Authority, Father of the Age to Come.

In the same way, you may observe that Jacob beheld the one previously revealed—who is both God and Lord, and indeed likewise called Angel—appearing in the form of a man, just as He appeared to Abraham. This is how the history records it:

> And having risen that night, he took his two wives, and his two female servants, and his eleven children, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok. And he took them and brought them across the stream, and brought over all his possessions. And Jacob was left alone, and a man wrestled with him...

[Page 149]

> » ...a man wrestled with him until the morning. And when he saw that he could not prevail against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh; and the hollow of Jacob’s thigh grew numb as he wrestled with him. And he said to him, "Let me go, for the morning has dawned." But he said, "I will not let you go unless you bless me." And he said to him, "What is your name?" And he said, "Jacob." And he said to him, "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name; for you have prevailed with God, and shall be powerful with men." And Jacob asked him, and said, "Tell me your name." And he said, "Why is it that you ask my name?" And he blessed him there. And Jacob called the name of that place "The Form of God" <note>original: εἶδος Θεοῦ (*Eidos Theou*), usually rendered as Peniel or Phanuel in English Bibles, meaning "Face of God"</note>. "For I have seen God face to face, and my life <note>original: ψυχή (*psyche*), literally "soul"</note> has been preserved." And the sun rose upon him when the "Form of God" passed by.

These things were spoken by Moses, yet "No one shall see my face and live." <note>A reference to Exodus 33:20</note> In these events, however, Jacob saw God—not simply, but 

"face to face." And since it was not his body but his soul that was preserved, he was deemed worthy of the title "Israel," a name that carries its own meaning, since the name "Israel" signifies "one who sees God" <note>Eusebius follows a common ancient etymology: *Ish* (man) *Ra’ah* (sees) *El* (God)</note>. Therefore, he did not see the God who is over all. For He is invisible and immutable, and in no way changes from one form to another, being the highest of all essence. It was, therefore, another being—one whom there is no time now to examine curiously—who revealed the name to Jacob. 

If anyone should suppose this was a certain angel, or one of the divine spirits in heaven who minister to the saints, they are clearly mistaken. This is proven first by the fact that the subject is described in the primary sense as "God" and "Lord." For even if the Divine Scripture explicitly calls Him God and names Him "Lord," honoring Him with the marking of the four characters used by the Hebrews <note>A reference to the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God (YHWH), which Eusebius notes was "unspoken" or "unutterable" among the Jews</note>, the sons of the Hebrews are accustomed to keep silence regarding the unspoken and ineffable title of God. 

This is also clear from how the Word <note>original: ὁ λόγος (*ho logos*)</note> distinguishes between actual angels when it wishes to call them "angels." For instance, when there were ungodly men in Sodom, the God and Lord who spoke to Abraham did not deign to visit them with His providence, 

> » as the Divine Scripture itself says: "The Lord departed as soon as he had finished speaking to Abraham; and the two angels came to Sodom in the evening." <note>Genesis 18:33-19:1</note> 

And even in the case of Jacob, "angels of God met him; and when he saw them, he said, 'This is God's camp.' And he called the name of that place 'Camps' <note>original: παρεμβολαί (*parembolai*), translating the Hebrew *Mahanaim*</note>." Thus, it was called the camps of Mahanaim. But when he speaks to the one with whom he conversed, he calls the name of the place "Form of God," adding, "For I have seen God face to face." 

Furthermore, when an angel appeared to Moses, the Divine Scripture indicates this by saying, "The angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire out of a bush." <note>Exodus 3:2</note> 

But when it reveals the authority of the one speaking, it calls Him "God" and "Lord," and no longer names Him an "angel." Likewise, at the Red Sea, the text clearly distinguishes between the angel and the Lord, through the words: "And the angel of God, who went before the camp of the sons of Israel, removed and went behind them; and the pillar of cloud also removed from before them." <note>Exodus 14:19</note> Just as in the earlier instances the Lord was introduced speaking to the ancients in the form of a man, so here He speaks through 

> » the cloud. And it says in the following: "And it came to pass in the morning watch, that the Lord looked down upon the camp of the Egyptians in a pillar of fire and of cloud." 

Throughout the entire wilderness, God spoke to Moses in the pillar through the cloud, exactly as...

When the account intends to show an angelic nature, it never calls it "God" or "Lord," but names it "Angel" without any concealment. But when it recognizes the one appearing as "Lord" and "God," it clearly uses these very titles. The words of Holy Scripture show plainly that "Lord" and "God" here do not refer to the Ultimate Cause <note>original: τὸν αἴτιον (*ton aition*), the Father as the source of all being</note>, for they call Him the "Angel of God" even while he had previously been named "Lord" and "God" in the story of Jacob. It follows, then, that there is someone who is truly God and Lord among existing things, second only to the King and God of the universe. This would be the Word <note>original: λόγος (*logos*)</note> of God, existing before the ages; he is greater than every angelic nature, but less than the First Cause.

<margin>E</margin> "And God said to Jacob: Arise, go up to the place of Bethel, and dwell there; and make

„ God said to him, "Make an altar to the God who appeared to you." Who this was

<summary>Eusebius argues that the divine figure appearing to Jacob and Moses is the "Logos" or "second God," acting as an intermediary for the invisible Father. He explains that while the Supreme God is the ultimate speaker, He uses the "Angel of the Lord" (the Son) as a visible instrument to communicate with humanity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius's argument from Book 5 of the *Proof of the Gospel*. Having established that the "Angel of God" who appeared to Jacob was actually the pre-existent Word of God (the Logos), he now addresses the manifestation of God to Moses and the Israelites, distinguishing between the Father (the "God over all") and the Son (the Word) who acts as His visible representative.</meta>

[Page 151]

<header>PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 5</header>

...teaching that "I am the one who is," <note>original: ὁ ὤν (*ho on*), a reference to the divine name in Exodus 3:14</note> and that my name is "Lord." To your fathers, I did not only declare this, but I granted them something even greater: for I was seen by them. Now, one might reasonably ask: who was it that was seen by the fathers? For if it was not the God over all—as has already been demonstrated—it would seem that the one being shown as God and the one Lord was the "Angel of God." How then can the one who is beyond all things, being himself the only God over all, say that he was seen by the fathers? This inquiry may be resolved if we attend to the accuracy of the Scripture. For while the translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the standard Greek version of the Old Testament</note> says, "And I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, being their God," <note>original: θεὸς αὐτῶν ὤν (*theos auton on*)</note> Aquila <note>A 2nd-century translator known for extremely literal renderings of the Hebrew into Greek</note> says, "And I appeared to Abraham and to Isaac and to Jacob in God Sufficient." <note>original: ἐν θεῷ ἱκανῷ (*en theo hikano*). This is Aquila's literal translation of the Hebrew *El Shaddai*.</note> Through these words it is clearly presented that the God over all himself, who alone is "the One who is," was not seen through himself. For he did not manifest himself to the fathers as he did to Moses—through an angel or a bush or fire—but rather he spoke while acting "in God Sufficient." Thus, through the Son, the Father was seen even by the fathers, according to what was said by him in the Gospels: "He who has seen me has seen the Father." For in him and through him, the knowledge of the Father was revealed. Therefore, whenever he appeared for the salvation of men, he was seen through a mortal and healing form <note>Eusebius suggests the Word appeared in human-like form to the patriarchs as a "down-payment" or preview of the later Incarnation</note> for those who loved God, pre-establishing for everyone his future salvation among men and giving a fore-pledge of that coming. But when he was to be the punisher of the ungodly and the chastiser of the Egyptians, he no longer appeared "in God Sufficient," but in the goat-skin and dust <note>original: αἰγίῳ καὶ ἀκονίῳ (*aigio kai akonio*); these terms are difficult, possibly referring to symbols of hardship or the rough nature of the wilderness</note> of punishment and in the form of fire. He appeared beforehand as a flame that was just about to consume them, like common and thorny brushwood. Thus, they say that the bush enigmatically signifies the common, harsh, and shameful wickedness of the Egyptians, while the fire signifies the punishing and chastising power that would consume them.

The Lord said to Moses: "Behold, I am coming to you in a pillar of cloud, so that the people may hear me speaking to you, and may believe you forever," and so forth. And furthermore: "Whenever Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would descend and stand at the door of the tent, and he would speak to Moses. And all the people saw the pillar of cloud standing at the door of the tent; and all the people rose up and worshiped, each at the door of his own tent." Now, the people saw the pillar of cloud, but who was it that spoke to Moses? Was it not none other than the one who had previously appeared to the fathers in human form? For it has been demonstrated that this was not the God over all, but was another—the Word of God whom we address as Christ. He was then beheld by Moses himself and the people in a pillar of cloud for the sake of the multitude, because they were not able, like the fathers, to see him in human form. For it belonged only to the perfect to be able to look upon his future incarnate appearance <note>term: ἐπιφάνειαν (*epiphaneian*), an "epiphany" or manifestation</note> among men. Since the whole people were never able to contain this, he reasonably appeared to them then through fire for the sake of fear and awe, and then through a cloud, as...

### That the nature speaking to Moses was not angelic, but something greater than an angel.

### How the same Lord teaches about another Lord.

### From the Ten Commandments <note>original: δεκαλόγου (*dekalogou*), the "Decalogue"</note>.

Regarding the Father, that is, and the God of all things, the "second Lord" <note>The Son or Word of God</note> initiates his servant into the mystery <note>original: μυσταγωγῶν (*mystagogon*), like a priest leading a candidate into sacred rites</note>.
You could find thousands of other similar examples throughout the entire Holy Scripture

Eusebius is demonstrating that the "Lord" who appeared to the patriarchs and Moses is the pre-existent Word of God (the Logos or Son), who acts as a representative of the "God over all" (the Father). [Page 153]

<header>PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 5</header>

Keeping silent about himself, he <note>the Word/Logos</note> calls upon the Lord by name through a repetition, as if he were speaking of that one—his own Father—as the Master of all others. And indeed, in these passages, it is not Moses (as one might suppose) but rather the Lord himself who calls the Father "another Lord." It is he who, while speaking with Moses, says:
> "I will pass before you in my glory, and I will call out in the name of the Lord."
Having said this, the Scripture immediately adds in its narrative:
> "And the Lord descended in a cloud, and stood there with him, and called out in the name of the Lord."
Therefore, it was the Lord himself who, intending to fulfill his promise, descended and stood before the face of Moses, just as the account says. And the Lord himself calls out, saying:
> "The Lord God, compassionate and merciful," and so forth.
Clearly, the Lord is initiating his servant <note>Moses</note> into the mystery <note>original: μυσταγωγῶν (*mystagogon*), like a guide in a religious rite</note> of who he himself is, and into the knowledge of the greater Lord. He says this elsewhere as well when, praying for the people, he mentions the words set before the Lord, showing that it was the Lord who said them:
> "And now, let your hand be exalted, O Lord, just as you spoke, saying: 'The Lord is long-suffering and of great mercy and true, taking away iniquities and injustices and sins, yet he will by no means clear the guilty, but visits the sins of the fathers upon the children, even to the third and fourth generation.'"
Notice, then, the manner in which the Lord himself in these verses calls the Father "long-suffering" and "of great mercy," and adds the word "true." This is in harmony with the words spoken by our one and the same Savior in the Gospels: "That they may know You, the only true God." <note>John 17:3</note> For he very piously calls the Father "the only true God," rendering the appropriate honor to the Unbegotten Nature, of which the divine words teach that he <note>the Son</note> is the image and the offspring.

### From the Book of Numbers.
#### How the divine Scripture teaches that God is visible to Israel, hinting at God the Word <note>original: θεὸν λόγον (*theon logon*)</note>.

<margin>5</margin>In the Book of Numbers, Moses says in prayer: 
> "For you are the Lord in the midst of this people, you, O Lord, who are seen eye to eye." 
In place of this, Aquila <note>a 2nd-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek</note> rendered it: 
> "For you are the Lord in the inward part of this people, you, O Lord, who are seen as an eye among eyes." 
And Symmachus <note>another 2nd-century Greek translator</note> says: 
> "For you are the Lord." 
And in Exodus it is said: 
> "And Moses and Aaron and Nadab and Abihu went up, along with seventy of the elders of Israel, and they saw the place where the God of Israel stood." 
In place of this, Aquila says, "And they saw the God of Israel." But Symmachus says, "And they saw a vision of the God of Israel." 
Now, since "no one has ever seen God," someone might suppose that the present text contradicts that saving word, as if it were suggesting that he who is by nature invisible is actually visible. But if you take these passages to refer to the Word of God—who appeared to the fathers "in many portions and in many ways"—just as we have previously demonstrated, you would no longer seem to fall into contradictions. For Scripture teaches here that the "God of Israel" who was seen is that very same one who appeared to Israel when a man wrestled with him, and who changed his name from Jacob to Israel, saying: 
> "For you have prevailed with God." 
At that time, Jacob, having perceived his divine power, called that place "The Form of God," <note>original: εἶδος θεοῦ (*eidos theou*), Peniel</note> saying: 
> "For I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved." 
We shall demonstrate in due time that this being is none other than the Word of God.

<summary>Eusebius argues that when the Old Testament speaks of the Lord appearing or calling upon another Lord, it refers to the pre-existent Word (the Son) interacting with or speaking about his Father. He reconciles the invisibility of God the Father with the visible appearances of the "God of Israel" by identifying the latter as the Logos.</summary>

# EUSEBIUS

<margin>
Eusebius

->From the [Book of] Joshua son of Nun.<-

Just as God the Word <note>original: *theos logos*</note>, who spoke with Moses, appeared to the ancient patriarchs, he likewise appeared to Joshua, the successor of Moses, in the form of a man. 
<margin>K</margin> And it happened that when he was in Jericho, he looked up and saw a man standing 
<margin>„</margin> opposite him, with a drawn sword in his hand. Joshua approached and 
<margin>„</margin> said to him, "Are you one of us, or one of our adversaries?" And he said to him, "I have 
<margin>„</margin> now come as the commander-in-chief of the host of the Lord." And Joshua fell on his face 
<margin>„</margin> to the ground and said to him, "Master, what do you command your servant?" And 
<margin>„</margin> the commander-in-chief of the Lord said to Joshua, "Loose the sandals from your feet; 
<margin>„</margin> for the place where you stand is holy ground." These very same things were 
<margin>„</margin> also said to Moses at Horeb during his vision at the bush by the Lord, 
<margin>„</margin> as the Scripture reveals: "When the Lord saw that he drew near to see, the 
<margin>„</margin> Lord called to him from the midst of the bush, saying, 'Moses, Moses, do not draw near 
<margin>„</margin> here. Loose the sandals from your feet; for the place where you stand 
<margin>„</margin> is holy ground.'" Therefore, it was one and the same Person who spoke to both of 
them, as is shown by the identical nature of the command. Yet in the first case, he spoke through the commander-in-chief of his power, whereas to Moses he spoke through the angel who appeared. This "host" refers to the heavenly armies, the super-cosmic powers, the invisible spirits, the divine principalities, and the archangels who minister to God, the King and Leader of all, according to what was spoken 
<margin>„</margin> through Daniel: "A thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times 
<margin>„</margin> ten thousand stood before him." Is not the one who is highest of all these, being the "other Word" of God the Word and the Father’s own Wisdom, his very offspring? Rightly, then, is he 
<margin>„</margin> designated in this passage as "commander-in-chief of the Lord’s host," just as he is 
called the "Angel of Great Counsel" <note>A title for the Messiah from the Septuagint version of Isaiah 9:6</note> elsewhere, the Savior of the children, and the eternal and Great High Priest. It has been demonstrated that this same Person is both Lord and God, and the Christ <note>the Anointed One</note> anointed by the Father with the oil of gladness. 

To Abraham, appearing at the oak, he showed himself in the form of a man with a calm and peaceful appearance, prefiguring his future providential coming among men for their salvation. To Jacob, he appeared as a man to an ascetic and a wrestler <note>original: *agoniste*, a competitive athlete</note> who was about to struggle against his enemies. To Moses and the people, he appeared in the form of cloud and fire, presenting himself as both fearsome and veiled. But since Joshua, the successor of Moses, was about to be deployed against enemies—the former inhabitants of the land of Palestine, who were foreign and most impious nations—he fittingly reveals himself with a drawn sword sharpened against the foes. He shows through this vision that it was he himself who, with an invisible sword and divine power, pursued the impious, campaigning and struggling alongside his own people. Therefore, he appropriately proclaimed himself at that time to be the "commander-in-chief of the Lord."

->From [the Book of] Job.<-

> ,, saying: "Hear me, O Lord, that I also may speak. I will question you, and you 
> ,, teach me. I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear before, but now my eye has seen you. 
> ,, Therefore I have despised myself and wasted away. I have considered myself as dust and ashes."

Now, that these preceding words belong to the Lord the Creator <note>original: *kyrios demiourgos*</note> is easy to recognize, not only from what has already been stated but also from what you can see for yourself in the reading. But the passage, "Have you gone to the source of the sea, and walked in the footprints of the abyss?" and "Have the gates of death been opened to you in fear, and did the gatekeepers of Hades cower when they saw you?"—this prophesies the descent into Hades of our Savior, which he would demonstrate at the proper time. We point these things out now to show how it is more fitting for these words to be addressed to the God-Word <note>The Logos, the second person of the Trinity.</note> than to the God of the Universe <note>The Father.</note>. 

Indeed, Job subsequently testifies—just as the patriarchs did—that he has seen with his own eyes this very Lord who spoke to him through the whirlwind, the storm, and the clouds, saying: "Hear me, O Lord, that I also may speak. I will question you, and you teach me. I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear before, but now my eye has seen you. Therefore I have despised myself and wasted away. I have considered myself as dust and ashes." 

For how could a soul clothed in flesh and the eyes of mortals have beheld the Highest God, the one beyond all things, the unchangeable and unbegotten essence <note>original: *ousia*</note>, unless we were to say that here too the God-Word made himself present, condescending from his own greatness? We have proved in various ways that he is "Lord." This can also be learned from the oracles themselves, through which the Lord again speaks to Job about the devil as if describing a dragon <note>original: *drakon*; referring to the Leviathan in Job 40-41</note>, saying: "Have you not given thought that he is prepared for me?" To which Lord is it fitting to think the dragon is subject, if not to the God-Word and our Savior? It was he who, long ago, overthrew the ruler of this age who was besieging the human race, by "loosing the pangs of death." This is what he himself presents when he says:

> ,, "Have you gone to the source of the sea? Have you walked in the footprints of the abyss? 
> ,, Have the gates of death been opened to you in fear, and did the gatekeepers of Hades cower 
> ,, when they saw you?"

These things were reasonably spoken to Job after the great temptation and the struggle he endured, teaching him that he had struggled only in part, while the greater and mightier war and struggle were reserved for the Lord himself at the time of his own passage into death.

> Thus says the Lord Almighty: After the glory, He has sent me to the nations that plundered you. <note>Zechariah 2:8</note> Then he adds shortly after, saying: And you shall know that the Lord Almighty has sent me. <note>Zechariah 2:9</note> If both the one who sends is Lord and is the Lord Almighty, and the one who is sent speaks in the same way, then there are clearly two; for the one sent says: The Lord Almighty has sent me to the nations.

-> The same [prophet] also concerning the calling of the nations. <-

> Rejoice and be glad, O daughter of Zion, for behold, I am coming and I will dwell in your midst, says the Lord. And many nations shall flee to the Lord in that day. For he says, "I myself, the Lord, will come." But at my coming, it will no longer be the ancient Israel, nor even a single nation on earth, but many nations shall flee to the better and great Lord—who is the God of both myself and of all things—upon whom the fleeing nations shall obtain such great benefit as to even be called and become the people of God, and to dwell in the midst of the one called the daughter of Zion. Thus, it is the custom of the Holy Scriptures to call the Church of God on earth a "daughter," as if she were the child of the heavenly Zion. Therefore, the Word <note>original: *logos*</note> who speaks brings these good tidings:

> "Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion, for behold I come and will dwell in your midst."

It is believed that God the Word will dwell in the midst of the Church. For He also promised this when He said:

> "Behold, I am with you all the days, until the end of the age." <note>Matthew 28:20</note>

And:

Whenever the Lord Himself says, "I will come and dwell in your midst," you will then receive a greater knowledge concerning God the Almighty, because I, the Lord, attribute the cause of my mission to men to the Father who sent me. "And you shall know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you." And next, the Lord Himself speaks somehow concerning another Lord and God:

> "And I will strengthen them in the Lord their God, and in His name they shall boast, says the Lord."

But who would those be who boast in the Lord?

--- Page 802 ---
<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s introduction to Book 6 of the *Evangelical Proof*. Having established in the previous books that the "Word of God" is a "Second God" distinct from the Father, he now shifts his focus to the "Dispensation"—the Incarnation—explaining why and how God the Word descended to earth in human form, as predicted by the Hebrew prophets.</meta>

Since it foretells that God was destined to arrive among humans, it is clear that the reference of what is signified should be made abundant. This is especially true since God the Word appeared in the form and figure of a man to those beloved of God around Abraham, manifesting Himself under the name of "Lord" and "God" through these visions granted to mankind. Come then, let us see how the Hebrew oracles <note>original: *logia*; the inspired words of scripture</note> clearly foretell that He would descend to humans—sometimes as "Lord" and sometimes as "God"—and then ascend again, while also explaining the reasons for this descent. 

Note that while some things are not spoken through riddles, others are quite clear. Those things expressed through concealment and riddles were given in a veiled way for the sake of the Jews, because it was not fitting to state such harsh things against them openly. Had the scriptures clearly signaled their future rejection, it is likely they would have destroyed the text altogether. Indeed, tradition holds that they even plotted against the prophets themselves because of the rebukes they leveled against them. In contrast, the clear prophecies contain the unspeakable calling of the Gentiles <note>original: *ethne*; the non-Jewish nations</note>, announcing the promises of good things according to godliness—not just for the Jewish nation, but for all people throughout the whole inhabited world. Such being the case, it is now time to listen to the divine oracles themselves.

# From Psalm 17.
<note>Psalm 18 in English Bibles.</note>
## A declaration of God's arrival among humans and the calling of the nations resulting from this.

> And he bowed the heavens, and came down; and thick darkness was under his feet. And he rode upon cherubim, and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds. And he made darkness his secret place; his tabernacle was round about him. <note>Psalm 18:9-11</note>

I believe that these words briefly describe His descent. To ensure that these excerpts are not chosen in place of more profound theology, consider this: by saying that He "bowed the heaven and came down," the prophet signifies the lowering <note>original: *hypostolen*; a drawing back or reduction</note> of His own glory. This is what the divine Apostle defined when he said: "Who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant." <note>Philippians 2:6-7</note> 

The phrase "he rode upon cherubim and flew," seems to me to hint at His restoration to divine glory, which He achieved while being escorted by angelic and divine powers. I believe this same thing is indicated by the phrase "he flew upon the wings of the winds." Furthermore, saying that "darkness was made his secret place" and "thick darkness was under his feet" serves to represent the hidden and unutterable <term>dispensation<note>original: *oikonomia*; the divine plan for Christ to become human while remaining God.</note></term> through which all these things were accomplished for Him. 

And as for "his tabernacle was round about him," whom is it appropriate to understand this to mean other than His Holy and Catholic Church, whether on earth or in the heavens? Next, as the word reaches the end of the same Psalm, it simultaneously presents the rejection of the former people <note>The Jewish people</note> and foretells the calling of the Gentiles, through the words: "You shall deliver me from the contradictions of the people; you shall appoint me as the head of the nations. A people whom I knew not served me; as soon as they heard me, they obeyed me. Strange children grew old, and they limped away from their paths." <note>Psalm 18:43-45</note> The meaning of these words will be examined at the appropriate time.

# From Psalm 46.
<note>Psalm 47 in English Bibles.</note>
## The ascent of God who had previously descended, and the calling of all nations, who shall recognize Him as the one and only God.

> Clap your hands, all you nations; shout to God with a voice of exultation. For the Lord...

<summary>Eusebius interprets Psalm 17 (18) as a prophecy of Christ's Incarnation, explaining that "bowing the heavens" represents the Word's self-emptying and "darkness" represents the mystery of the divine plan. He argues that veiled prophecies were necessary to prevent the Jews from destroying scriptures that predicted their own rejection in favor of the Gentiles.</summary>

> The Lord Most High is fearsome, a great king over all the earth. He subjected peoples to us, and nations under our feet. He chose our inheritance for himself, the beauty of Jacob which he loved. God went up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet. Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises. For God is king of all the earth; sing praises with understanding. God reigned over the nations; God sits upon his holy throne. The rulers of the peoples gathered together with the God of Abraham, for the mighty ones of the earth belong to God; they were greatly exalted.

And this passage intends to signify another point: the "ascent" of the Lord God described here relates to his prior "descent" <note>Eusebius argues that for God to "ascend," he must have first "descended" to earth in human form.</note>, after which the possession of all the nations is witnessed. Signs of joy and gladness are proclaimed to all the nations regarding the coming knowledge of God, when the Lord himself—the only Most High God and King of all the earth—is confessed. It says he will "subject peoples to us." To whom does "us" refer? Clearly, it refers to those who prophesy these things. They clearly saw this fulfilled when all the nations that believed in Christ became subject to the words of the prophets. These things could also be said from the person of the apostles of our Savior, who might say, "He chose our inheritance for himself." And what should we understand as their "inheritance" <note>original: *klēronomia*</note> other than the calling of the nations given to them? For Christ said before us:

> The Lord said to me, "You are my son, today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession."

This inheritance given to him by the Father, he subjected to his apostles and prophets—meaning that those who believe in him are subjected to their teachings, following the previously mentioned decrees. Having accomplished all these things during his arrival among men, God the Word <note>original: *Theos Logos*; refers to the pre-existent Christ.</note>—about whom we have discussed much—"ascended with a shout." Explaining this, the Apostle <note>Saint Paul, in Ephesians 4:9-10.</note> says: "What does 'he ascended' mean, except that he also first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same one who also ascended far above the heavens." He says he returned "with a shout" <note>original: *alalagmos*; a joyous or triumphant cry.</note> because of the divine praise of the angels escorting him as he went up. They said, "Lift up your gates, O rulers, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of Glory shall enter." You would not be wrong to call the "sound of a trumpet" the preaching of the Gospel <note>original: *euangelikon kērygma*</note>, which has echoed throughout the whole world. Since the trumpet is louder than any musical instrument, the example is appropriately chosen to represent the teaching about Christ announced to all men, which is mightier and louder than all things throughout the ages. Through this, as if through a trumpet, the Holy Spirit cries out to the hearing of all men the following parts of the Psalm, which say:

> Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises.

Because he is no longer King only of the Jewish nation, but he says God is King "of all the earth." "Sing praises with understanding." For it says it is no longer the deceiving demons, nor idols and deceptive spirits, but God himself who has reigned over all the nations. God himself, who "sits upon his holy throne." Previously, the Word of God had been invited to the throne on which the Father sits, saying: "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." Through this...

<vocab>Psalm, Christ, Apostles, Holy Spirit, Gospel, Prophets, inheritance</vocab>

<summary>Eusebius interprets Psalm 47 as a prophecy of Christ's descent to earth, his triumph over demons, and his ascent back to heaven accompanied by angelic praise. He identifies the "trumpet" of the Psalm as the global preaching of the Gospel and the "inheritance" as the conversion of the Gentile nations.</summary>

But the verse, "The rulers of the peoples were gathered together with the God of Abraham," demonstrates even more clearly that the leaders of the Church of Christ from among the Gentiles have been transferred into the portion <note>original: *klēron*, referring to an inheritance or allotted place</note> of the ancient prophets who were friends of God. These points, when considered at leisure, complete the <unclear>form</unclear> of the narrative.

### From Psalm 49.

-> It is said that God will come visibly to men, and will call back <-
-> every race of men to himself. <-

"The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting; out of Zion comes the magnificence of his beauty. God shall come visibly, our God, and shall not keep silence." And after other verses: "Hear, my people, he says, and I will speak to you, O Israel, and I will bear witness to you. I am God, your God. I will not reprove you for your sacrifices; your burnt offerings are continually before me. I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks, for all the beasts of the forest are mine, the cattle on the mountains, and the oxen. I know all the birds of heaven, and the beauty of the field is with me. If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness is mine. Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High, and call upon me in the day of affliction." <note>Eusebius is quoting Psalm 50:1-14 in modern Bibles. The early Church used these verses to argue that God no longer required animal sacrifices.</note> Even here, the divine Scripture clearly prophesies that God will come visibly, revealing none other than the Word of God <note>original: *Logos*</note>. It presents the reason for his presence most clearly, signifying once again the calling of the nations throughout the whole world. For it says, "He called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting." Following his appearance and the calling of the nations, he teaches the rejection of the more physical worship conducted according to the Law of Moses; this worship reached its end after the appearance of the Word of God to all men. For from that time until now, all people throughout the world have been called, and all the nations from the east to the west. The Jewish form of religion has ceased and been abolished in favor of the New Covenant <note>original: *kainē diathēkē*</note> of the Gospel preaching, rather than the Law of Moses, as all men are now commanded to practice true piety. These words could also refer to the second and glorious manifestation of the Savior.

O God our protector, look, and behold the face of your Christ." <note>Psalm 84:7-9 in modern Bibles.</note> Having foretold that the God of gods would be seen, the prophet prays that his manifestation might come quickly, and teaches the place where he shall be seen...

> By the words, "Look upon the face of your Christ" <note>original: *Christou*, meaning "Anointed One"</note>; it is as if he had said more clearly: "Through the presence of your Christ, reveal yourself." For since he who has seen the Son has seen the Father who sent him, it is fitting that through the "face" of Christ, the God of gods who dwells in Christ is promised to be revealed.

### From Psalm 95. <note>Psalm 96 in English Bibles</note>

-> The presence of the Lord on earth, his kingdom over the nations, and a new song <-
-> given not to Israel, but to the nations. <-

> "Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth. Sing to the Lord, bless his name. Proclaim the good news of his salvation from day to day. Declare his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples, for the Lord is great and greatly to be praised; he is to be feared above all gods." And again: "Ascribe to the Lord, O families of the nations." And again: "Say among the nations, 'The Lord has reigned!'" and at the end of all he adds: "Then all the trees of the forest shall rejoice before the face of the Lord, for he is coming to judge the earth. He will judge the world in righteousness, and the peoples in his truth."

Here again, the Lord's coming among men is prophesied, and that a "new song" would be sung at his presence—this being the <term>New Covenant <note>original: *kainē diathēkē*</note></term>—not by the Jewish nation, but by "all the earth." He explicitly mentions not Israel anymore, but "all the nations," since he says the coming Lord will be a King for them. And who could this be but the <term>Word of God <note>original: *Theos Logos*</note></term>? He, being about to judge the world in righteousness and humanity in truth, has deemed all the human races throughout the world equally worthy of his calling and the salvation from God that follows it.

### From Psalm 96. <note>Psalm 98 in English Bibles</note>

-> A new song, the nations' knowledge of the Lord’s righteousness, and he <-
-> himself coming as judge of all. <-

> "Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvelous things." and what follows. "The Lord has made known his salvation; in the sight of all the nations he has revealed his righteousness." And again: "All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God. Shout for joy to the Lord, all the earth." And at the end of all: "The mountains shall rejoice before the face of the Lord, for he is coming, for he has come to judge the earth. He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in equity."

The presence of the Lord is prophesied here as the cause of many blessings for the nations, which are shown to have reached their fulfillment through the appearance of our Savior. From these verses, one might say that the "new song" of the New Covenant is now being sung among all men, through which his wonders have become known and heard by everyone via the writing of the Gospels. Furthermore, the salvation achieved through his resurrection from the dead has been revealed to all the nations, along with the true righteousness. Through this, it has been clearly demonstrated that God is not the God of the Jews only, but also of the <term>Gentiles <note>non-Jewish nations</note></term>. For as the holy Apostle says, there is one God who

> "will justify the circumcised <note>the Jews</note> by faith and the uncircumcised <note>the Gentiles</note> through faith." The phrase "for he is coming to judge the earth" would be an indication of his second presence <note>the Second Coming</note>.

The sacred scripture of the Gospels records that this prophecy reached its fulfillment at the moment when our Savior and Lord, Christ himself, entered into Jerusalem. A great multitude of people and children preceded him, shouting with joy: "> Hosanna to the
> Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the 
> highest!" For instead of the phrase, "O Lord, save now," found in the Psalm, they shouted more exceptionally, as I said; the term is translated as "save now." <note>The Hebrew *Hoshana* (Hosanna) is a plea for salvation meaning "Save, please."</note> And the phrase, "Blessed is 
> he who comes in the name of the Lord," is clarified by the oracle following it, which says, "God is the Lord, and 
> he has appeared to us." Therefore, the "God and Lord" who appeared to us is one and the same: the 
> Word of God. He is "blessed" precisely because he made his visitation to humanity in the name of the Lord—that is, the Father who sent him. Indeed, when rebuking 
> those of the circumcision <note>A common early Christian term for the Jewish people.</note> who did not believe in him, he said to them: "> I have come in 
> my Father's name, and you do not receive me; if another comes in his 
> own name, him you will receive." It is fitting, then, that the Holy Spirit no longer addresses the Jewish people, but all the nations in the opening of the Psalm.

### From Psalm 143 <note>Psalm 144 in English Bibles</note>

-> The Lord descending from heaven for the sake of human salvation, and a song sung <-
-> because of this—namely, that of the New Covenant. <-

"Lord, what is man that you are known to him, or the son of man that you take account of him? 
» Lord, bow your heavens and come down; touch the mountains, and they shall smoke." And 
» further down it says: "O God, I will sing a new song to you." I believe these things pertain to the current subject. For the writer, marveling at the knowledge of the Word of God among men, is utterly amazed by his <term>loving-kindness <note>original: *philanthropia*</note></term>, through which he lowered his divinity, descended and humbled himself, and deemed the human race worthy of his own knowledge. 
» Here he prays, saying, "Lord, bow your heavens and come down." But in the 
» seventeenth Psalm <note>Psalm 18 in English Bibles</note> it is said: "And he bowed the heavens and came down, and thick darkness was 
» under his feet. And he mounted upon cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds." Through these words he prophesies the events of the ascent—the journey from earth back to heaven. As for how you should understand the "descent" and "ascent" of the Word of God—not as movements from place to place, but as the Scripture refers to his <term>providential dealings <note>original: *oikonomias*</note></term> metaphorically in the manner I have described—we shall explain this in its proper place. It was also necessary to mention the New Covenant here, which the presence of Christ was destined to provide for humanity. This is the New Covenant given by Christ to all nations after the Old. This is why 
» the oracle at hand says: "O God, I will sing a new song to you." As for the phrase, "touch the mountains and 
» they shall smoke," I believe it hints at the desolation and vanishing of all idolatry, which among the ancients was especially practiced upon the mountains. Thus even the Jews themselves were rebuked for practicing idolatry upon every high mountain in imitation of the foreign nations.

# From Psalm 106 <note>Psalm 107 in modern English Bibles. Eusebius uses the Septuagint numbering.</note>

The Word of God is sent to humanity for the healing and salvation of souls that have long been worn out by vices.

> <margin>5</margin> <margin>,,</margin> Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the sons of 
> <margin>,,</margin> men. For he shattered bronze gates, and broke iron bars. He 
> <margin>,,</margin> helped them out of their way of lawlessness. For they were humbled because 
> <margin>,,</margin> of their lawless deeds. Their soul loathed every kind of food, and they drew near to the gates of 
> <margin>,,</margin> death. And they cried out to the Lord in their affliction, and he saved them out of 
> <margin>,,</margin> their distresses. He sent his Word, and healed them, and rescued them 
> <margin>,,</margin> from their destructions. And furthermore: let them exalt him; he turned rivers into 
> <margin>,,</margin> a desert, and springs of water into thirsty ground, a fruitful land into saltiness because of the 
> <margin>,,</margin> wickedness of those dwelling in it. He turned the desert into pools of water, and a parched land into 
> <margin>,,</margin> springs of water. And he settled the hungry there, and they established a city for 
> habitation.

And these words clearly name the descent of the Word of God from the heavens, and describe the successes of his providence. At any rate, it says, "He sent his Word, and <margin>,,</margin> healed them." By "Word of God," we clearly mean the one who exists with the Father, the Savior sent to all humanity who were shaken by passions. We have been taught to speak of his divinity <note>original: "θεολογεῖν" (theologein) – to speak of as God</note> through the sacred Gospels. The passage also hints at his descent even unto death for the sake of those who had already arrived there. It reveals the description of his arrival there, showing the redemption and salvation achieved through him. For those who had reached the gates of death, he alone saved them. These he also rescued, healing them from their destructions. He clarified these things in no other way than by saying the "bronze gates" of death were shattered and the "iron bars" were broken. Indeed, following this, he prophesies the state of desertion for those who do not possess his teachings. For he says, "He turned rivers into a desert and springs of water into thirsty ground, a fruitful land into saltiness because of the <margin>,,</margin> wickedness of those dwelling in it." These things have newly come upon the nation of the Jews, regarding the once-celebrated Jerusalem and her glory; while the "fruitfulness of the nations" refers to the holy and God-beloved men living as citizens within her, though they were once looked down upon with pride by those present <note>The "present" rulers or establishment in Jerusalem</note>. For after the coming of Christ, that place became truly unfruitful, waterless, and entirely a desert—and as the prophecy says—"into saltiness because of the wickedness of those dwelling in it." Following this, he prays fervently, witnessing prophetically to the transformation of the once "desert and waterless" place—meaning either every human soul or the Church gathered from the nations—into a state of piety and fruitfulness through the sacred, divine words. He clearly hints at these things when he says, "He turned the desert into pools of water," and so on. To understand these things belongs only to the wise; which is why, according to the promise stated at the end <margin>,,</margin> of the Psalm, it says: "Who is wise and will keep these things?" and so forth.

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s analysis of Messianic prophecies within the Psalms. Having just referenced Psalm 117 (Septuagint numbering), he now explains its fulfillment in the life of Jesus and transitions to discussing Psalms 143 and 147 as further evidence of the Word’s descent to earth.</meta>

<header>PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 6, 165</header>

The sacred scripture of the Gospel records that this reached its fulfillment when our Savior and Lord, the Christ himself, entered into Jerusalem. A great multitude of men and children met him with joy, crying out:
» **“Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!”**
For instead of the phrase “O Lord, save now,” <note>original: "ὦ κύριε σῶσον δή"</note> which is found in the Psalm, they cried out using the more Hebrew expression **“Hosanna”** <note>original: "ὡσὰν ἀνά"</note>; this is interpreted as **“Save now.”** And the phrase **“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord”** clearly refers to the next part of the prophecy which says, **“God is the Lord, and he has appeared to us.”** <note>Psalm 118:26-27 in modern Bibles.</note> Therefore, the “God the Lord” who appeared to us was one and the same as the Word of God. He is called “Blessed” for this reason: because he made his appearance among men in the name of the Lord, his Father who sent him. Indeed, when rebuking those of the circumcision <note>A term Eusebius uses for the Jewish people of that time.</note> who did not believe in him, he said to them:
» **“I have come in my Father’s name, and you do not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive.”** <note>John 5:43</note>
Rightly, then, the Holy Spirit no longer addresses the people of the Jews, but speaks the words at the beginning of the Psalm to all the nations.

---

->**From Psalm 143**<- <note>Psalm 144 in modern Bibles.</note>

The Lord descending from heaven for the sake of the salvation of men, and a song sung because of this—namely, the song of the New Covenant.

**“Lord, what is man, that you have become known to him? Or the son of man, that you take account of him? Lord, bow your heavens and come down; touch the mountains, and they shall smoke.”**
» And further down he adds: **“O God, I will sing a new song to you.”**
These things align with the subject we have before us. For marveling at the knowledge of the Word of God toward men, the Psalmist is overwhelmed with his <term>philanthropy</term> <note>original: "φιλανθρωπία"; the divine love or "friendship" toward the human race.</note>. Through this love, the Word descended from his divinity, and having "made himself small" from his natural greatness, he deemed the human race worthy of his own knowledge.
» In this passage he prays, saying, **“Lord, bow your heavens and come down.”**
» But in the seventeenth Psalm <note>Psalm 18 in modern Bibles.</note> it is said: **“And he bowed the heavens and came down, and darkness was under his feet. And he mounted the Cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds.”**
Through these words, he presents the manner of his ascent and his journey from earth to the heavens. As for how we should understand the “descent” and “ascent” of the Word of God—given that he does not make movements from place to place, but the Scripture calls the manner of his <term>economy</term> <note>original: "οἰκονομία"; the divine plan or arrangement for salvation, specifically the Incarnation.</note> by these names metaphorically—we shall explain this in its proper place. 

It was necessary to mention in these passages the New Covenant <note>original: "καινῆς διαθήκης"</note> as well, which the presence of Christ was destined to provide for men. This is the New Covenant given by Christ to all the nations after the Old. Therefore, the prophecy at hand says:
» **“O God, I will sing a new song to you.”**
I believe the phrase **“Touch the mountains, and they shall smoke”** alludes to the burning and disappearance of all idolatry, which was especially practiced by the ancients upon the mountains. This also serves as a rebuke to the Jews themselves, who imitated the foreign nations by practicing idolatry on every high mountain.

### From the Second Book of Kingdoms <note>Commonly known today as 2 Samuel.</note>

->The Lord descending from heaven, leading nations who previously did not know him, while the nation of the Jews shall be turned away.<-

<margin>K</margin>
> And David spoke to the Lord the words of this song... Then he says next: "And he bowed the heavens and came down; and thick darkness was under his feet. And he mounted upon the cherubim and flew; he was seen upon the wings of the winds. And he made darkness his hiding place." And at the end of the same song, he says: "You shall deliver me from the contradictions of the people. You shall keep me to be the head of the nations. A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me. Foreign sons lied to me." <note>Quoting 2 Samuel 22:10-12, 44-46.</note>

The God who "bowed the heavens and came down" is the one who mounted upon the human nature he assumed <note>original: "ᾧ ἀνείληφεν ἀνθρώπῳ" — referring to the human body/persona Christ took on</note>, whom the Word now calls "cherubim." He made his ascent accompanied by a bodyguard of divine spirits, who are themselves described as "wings of the winds." He hints that these things occurred in darkness and in a corner <note>original: "ἐν παραβύστῳ" — a phrase meaning "in secret" or "obscurity," perhaps referring to the humble nature of Christ's birth or his hidden divinity</note> according to certain secret and hidden reasons, saying, *and he made darkness his hiding place.* The subsequent verses signify the events following Christ’s incarnation <term>enanthropēsis; literally 'inhumanization' or becoming a man</term> and the "contradiction" or opposition of the Jewish people against him, as well as the obedience of the Gentiles to Christ’s teaching. You can find nearly identical words in the seventeenth Psalm <note>Psalm 18 in modern Bibles.</note>, where these manifestations were foretold.

# EUSEBIUS

Present himself, the Word, having gone forth from his own place, was to descend upon the high places of the earth. And what might these be? Literally, they are the mountains of Israel and the hills mentioned in the prophecy, as well as Jerusalem itself and Mount Zion, in which our Savior and Lord spent most of his time. He prophesies that the ruin and destruction of these would occur at the descent of Christ. And it is perfectly clear that after the presence of our Savior and the things accomplished by him, all the aforementioned things were fulfilled and have come to a state of extreme desolation. Furthermore, the leaders of the Jewish nation, the kingdom that formerly stood among them, the priesthood, and the presiding seat of the teachers, were now figuratively <term>tropically<gloss>from the Greek 'tropikos,' meaning a metaphorical or non-literal interpretation</gloss></term> named "mountains"; these are called "high places" at the presence of the Lord from heaven. And who would not admit that this came to pass, seeing that after the times of our Savior Jesus Christ, everything was removed from their midst—not only utterly destroyed but swept away? The valleys still "melting" even now would be Jerusalem itself and Mount Zion, and the whole city as their gathered assembly, which was to be broken and destroyed, "melting like wax before the face of fire" <note>original: "ὡς κηρὸς ἀπὸ προσώπου πυρὸς" — Micah 1:4</note> because of the grief and mourning over their wounds, the desolation of their homes, and their long and many-yeared slavery. Or, clearly, according to the concept of the Word and the divine appearance, He does not dwell in chasms and hollows, nor in low and earth-bound minds, but in those that are exalted and possess high understanding. In this way, then, the Lord himself figuratively "will descend upon the high places of the earth," as was said. And the "mountains very far beneath him" are those very ones, whether taken by 
<margin>»</margin> the Spirit to be tempted by the Devil—for the Devil took him 
<margin>»</margin> to an exceedingly high mountain—and he was "with the wild beasts." <note>A reference to Christ's temptation in the wilderness as described in Matthew 4 and Mark 1:13.</note> Again, in a more figurative sense, the "mountains" would be the idolatry formerly practiced upon the mountains, and the invisible and demonic powers that operated within them, which the teaching of our Savior resisted and overcame in no small way. For the power of these beings, whether wonder-working or seemingly "beneficent," was cast down when their long and ancient dominion over men failed. Likewise, the "valleys melting like wax before the face of fire"
<margin>Λ</margin> would be the immaterial and incorporeal demons, and that which Scripture calls the 
<margin>»</margin> "fire" <note>original: "πῦρ"</note> of their burning malice, saying: "I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what will I if it be already kindled?" <note>Luke 12:49</note> Being burned by this fire, and not being able to bear the torments from the invisible flame, they withdrew from human bodies. And acknowledging the power that constrained and shook them, they cried out, saying: "Ha! What have we to do with you, Jesus of God? <note>original: "ἰησοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ" — Eusebius's text varies slightly from the standard 'Jesus of Nazareth' or 'Son of God'</note> Have you come to torment us before the time? We know who you are: the Holy One of God!" <note>Mark 1:24 / Matthew 8:29</note> It was most fitting that the rulers over these were also cast down, so that they might not hold sway through the corruption of the rest, through which they had cast everyone down into the error of polytheism, and had even plotted against God's ancient people—the ones of the circumcision—leading them away from God and surrounding them with all kinds of impieties. This is why the Lord made his descent from 
<margin>»</margin> heaven. Hence, he says next: "All these things are because of the impiousness of Jacob, 
<margin>»</margin> and for the sin of the house of Israel." <note>Micah 1:5</note> Furthermore, he explains the reason for the descent of the Word from heaven, enumerating the impieties of the people of the circumcision and the destruction that overtook them because of these, and then the [reasons] throughout the whole...

<summary>Eusebius interprets the prophecy of Micah regarding the Lord's descent, arguing that the "mountains" represent both the literal geography of Israel and the figurative heights of Jewish authority and demonic power, all of which were leveled by Christ's coming. He connects the "melting valleys" to the exorcism of demons who fled from the "fire" of Christ's presence.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Eusebius concludes his thought on how the "descent" of the Word led to the "melting" of the metaphorical mountains—the Jewish leadership and institutions—due to their rejection of Christ. # EVANGELICAL PROOF, Book 6
Pp. i.

...calling the whole inhabited world of the nations. For this reason, the Word of God resided among us, coming from the heavens to the earth. Listen to the very words: *All this is because of the ungodliness of the house of Jacob, and because of the sin of the house of Israel. What is the ungodliness of the house of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what is the sin of the house of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem? Therefore, I will make Samaria like a lodge in a field, and like a plantation of a vineyard; and I will drag down her stones into the abyss, and I will uncover her foundations.* <note>original: "θήσομαι σαμάρειαν εἰς ὀπωροφυλάκιον ἀγροῦ..." — quoting Micah 1:5-6</note> Then he adds: *Evils have come down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem, the noise of chariots and horsemen.* And again: *The glory of the daughter of Jerusalem—shave your head and cut your hair for your delicate children; enlarge your widowhood like an eagle, for they have been taken captive from you.* In addition to these: *Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall be like a lodge for guarding fruit, and the mountain of the house shall become a forest grove.* <note>Eusebius is combining Micah 1 and 3:12 to show the complete destruction of the Jewish capital.</note> Since Zion, Jerusalem, and the so-called "mountain of the house" are the very things declared previously, it is because of them that it was said: *and the mountains shall be shaken beneath him, and the valleys shall melt like wax before the face of fire,* <note>original: "ὡς κηρὸς ἀπὸ προσώπου πυρὸς" — Micah 1:4</note> all due to the ungodliness of Jacob. For because of their impieties, and in accordance with their ungodly deeds, it was not long before the mountains and those dwelling in them were besieged. Mount Zion endured fire and extreme desolation, and the mountain of the house of God became like a forest grove. The prophecy indicates that these things would happen to those people at the time of the Lord’s descent from heaven—events which took a clear and visible turn after the presence of our Savior Jesus Christ. Indeed, if anyone wishes to record the history of our own times, we have seen with our own eyes that place—once so famous—being plowed by Roman men with teams of oxen, and Jerusalem herself, as the oracle says, left like a guard's lodge in a garden, standing in a state of total desolation. These things happened for no other reason than their own impieties. Thus, the heavenly Word came forth from his own place.

And for another reason, it was said previously that the Word of God descended from the heavens and stepped upon the "high places of the earth," so that the mountains—meaning those powers that were formerly lifted up and exalted against the knowledge of God—might be shaken beneath him. These are clearly the opposing <term>daemonic powers<gloss>the spiritual forces of evil or pagan deities in Eusebius’s worldview</gloss></term> which, before his presence, had enslaved both the rest of humanity and the Hebrew nation through the crimes of ungodliness and idolatry. Furthermore, the evil spirits called "valleys"—so named because they dwell in dark chasms and within the "dwellings" of human bodies—melted like wax before the face of fire; by the power of the Divine Word, they fled from humanity.

There is yet another reason, besides these, for the Lord’s descent from heaven, which the Word signifies: so that all the nations upon the earth might be driven away from these demons. Once the ruling spirits were overthrown, the nations might find rest from their ancient, harsh, and immovable tyranny, and take up the knowledge of the God who is over all. In some such way, the voices of his prophecy declare these things in order, linked by a single thread of thought: *And it shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, established upon the peaks of the mountains, and it shall be raised up above the hills, and peoples shall hasten to it; and many nations shall go and say: "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob, and they will show us...*

<summary>Eusebius interprets Micah's prophecies of destruction as being fulfilled by the Roman desolation of Jerusalem, which he claims to have witnessed personally. He further allegorizes the "mountains" and "valleys" as demonic powers defeated by Christ to liberate the nations.</summary>
