He also discusses the symbolic identity of "Israel" and begins to address the cryptic "Assyrian" prophecy in Micah 5:5.</summary>

# EVANGELICAL DEMONSTRATION Book 7 #

<header>EVANGELICAL DEMONSTRATION Book 7</header>

-> From Psalm 131. <-
<note>original: "ψαλμοῦ ρλα΄" (Psalm 131). This follows the Septuagint numbering; in most modern Bibles, this is Psalm 132.</note>

When David inquired what might be the place of the birth of the proclaimed God, it was revealed through the Holy Spirit to be Ephrathah, which is Bethlehem.

"Lord, remember David and all his gentleness; how he swore to the Lord and vowed to the God of Jacob: 'I will not enter the shelter of my house, I will not climb upon the bed of my couch; I will not give sleep to my eyes, nor slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.' Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah, we found it in the fields of the wood. We will enter into his tabernacles, we will worship at the place where his feet stood."
And then he adds: "For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your anointed. The Lord swore truth to David and will not reject him: 'Of the fruit of your body I will set upon your throne.'"
And he continues by saying: "There I will make a horn to spring forth for David; I have prepared a lamp for my anointed. His enemies I will clothe with shame, but upon him my holiness shall flourish."
<note>original: Psalm 131:1–7, 10–11, 17–18. Eusebius interprets the "horn" and "lamp" as symbols of Christ’s power and revelation.</note>

The details indicated here harmonize with the present prophecy concerning the arrival in Bethlehem of the God who was proclaimed beforehand. Regarding this, it is as if David himself, being previously ignorant, prays to learn from God, and after praying, he is instructed. Since he received a divine response in the Psalm saying, "Of the fruit of your body I will set upon your throne," and again, "There I will make a horn to spring forth for David; I have prepared a lamp for my anointed," he naturally fell before God, prostrating himself on the ground in supplication. Persisting even more in prayer, he swears to God that he will not enter the shelter of his house, nor give sleep to his eyes or slumber to his eyelids, nor climb upon his bed, but will lie on the ground worshipping and supplicating until he finds a "place for the Lord" and a "tabernacle for the God of Jacob"—that is, until he learns the knowledge of Christ through the Lord’s revelation to him.

Having prayed and desired to know such things, it was not long before he beheld through the Holy Spirit what was to come; for when God has promised His own, He hears them even while they are still speaking. He is indeed heard and granted a divine response that names Bethlehem to him as the place where the Lord and the <term>tabernacle: original "skenoma," a tent or dwelling place, often used metaphorically for the human body of Christ</term> of the God of Jacob would be established. For seeing these things in the Holy Spirit as if they were present, he adds, having heard it: "Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah."

Ephrathah is the same as Bethlehem, as is clear from the book of Genesis, where it is said of Rachel that "she was buried on the road to Ephrathah, which is Bethlehem." 
<note>original: Genesis 35:19. Eusebius uses the Old Testament’s internal consistency to prove the location.</note>
The prophecy concerning this also contained the words: "And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah." 
<note>original: Micah 5:2. Eusebius links the Psalm to the prophecy of Micah discussed on the previous page.</note>
"Behold," he says, "we heard of it," clearly meaning the birth of Christ and the "dwelling" of the God of Jacob. 

What could the "tabernacle of the God of Jacob" be other than the body of Christ, which was born in the region of Bethlehem? In this body, as in a tabernacle, the divinity of the Only-begotten dwelt. It is not called simply "of God," but with the addition "of the God of Jacob," because no one else dwelt in it but the one who appeared to Jacob in the form and likeness of a man...

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 7 #

<header>PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 7</header>

...as an image of the great and true High Priest, the Christ of God, bearing a certain shadowy and symbolic "christ" <note>original: χριστὸν (christon). Eusebius uses the lowercase "christ" to refer to the Old Testament high priests who were "anointed ones," serving as types or shadows of Jesus, the true Anointed One.</note> upon himself. In any case, regarding the high priest, the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible used by early Christians.</note> says:

<margin>" *</margin>
> ...concerning the high priest, "and he shall not profane the sanctuary of his God, because the holy oil, the Christ of his God, is upon him." The Hebrew version, however, contains the word *nezer* <note>original: ναζὲρ (nazer); Hebrew: נֵזֶר, meaning a crown or consecration.</note> for "oil"; while Aquila <note>A 2nd-century translator known for literalism.</note> renders it: "because the separation <note>original: ἀφόρισμα (aphorisma)</note> oil of the anointing of his God is upon him." Symmachus <note>Another early translator known for elegant Greek style.</note> renders it: "because the untouched <note>original: ἄθικτον (athikton)</note> oil of the anointing of his God is upon him." And Theodotion says: "because the *nezer* oil of the Christ from his God is upon him."

Therefore, whether we use *nezer*—which according to the Septuagint means "holy," according to Aquila means "separation," and according to Symmachus means "untouched"—it follows that the name "Nazirite" <note>original: ναζιραῖον (naziraion)</note> signifies either the "holy one," the "separated one," or the "untouched one." Hence, the priests of old, who were anointed with the specially prepared oil called *nezer* by Moses, were called "Nazirites" because of that *nezer*. But our Savior and Lord, who possesses holiness, untouchability, and separation by his very nature, did not require any human anointing. Nevertheless, he received the title of "Nazarene" among men. He did not become a Nazirite because of the oil called *nezer*, but being such by his nature, he was called a Nazarene by men after the town of Nazareth, where he lived in total pleasingness to his parents according to the flesh. For this reason, it is said in the Gospel of Matthew:

<margin>"</margin>
> "And being warned in a dream"—evidently referring to Joseph—"he withdrew into the regions of Galilee. And he came and lived in a city called Nazareth, so that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: 'He shall be called a Nazarene.'"

For it was necessary that he, who was a Nazirite in nature and truth—that is, holy, untouched, and separated from among men—should be called by this title. But since he did not obtain this title from the *nezer* oil, having no need of human anointing, he acquired the name from the place, Nazareth. Having demonstrated these points, it is time to investigate from what lineage and from which Hebrew tribe the Christ of God, the Savior of our souls, was heralded to come forth. Let us set forth the words of the Gospels concerning this, and like harmonious seals, let us apply the prophetic testimonies to them. Now, Matthew genealogizes the Christ according to the flesh as follows:

<margin>"</margin>
> "The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham was the father of Isaac, Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah," and so forth. The Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul.</note> agrees with these words, saying that he was "set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy scriptures, concerning his Son, who was descended from the seed of David according to the flesh."

Let us then see how these things harmonize with the following prophecies.

<header>PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 7</header>

Our Savior and Lord Jesus, the Christ of God, is the only one among all those who have ever reigned from the seed of David who is acknowledged as the "Son of David" throughout the entire world. His throne is naturally confessed as David's throne, for from David truly and by succession comes this kingdom, extending into the **infinite age**. <note>original: ἄπειρον αἰῶνα (apeiron aiona). Eusebius emphasizes that while earthly kingdoms end, the Messianic reign is eternal.</note> Although many have conspired against this kingdom, it demonstrates its reverence through divine power—and even through the recognition of men—remaining invincible, just as the prophecies foretold. If you hear of the "equally-honored God" <note>original: ὁμοτιμότατον θεὸν (homotimotaton theon). This refers to the high dignity of the Son as equal in honor to the Father.</note> in relation to His Holy One, you should understand this as the Son, the Word of God who existed before all ages, His eternal and only-begotten Child. The voices of the prophets cited previously have described His divinity in various ways. Because of this likeness, God His Father, as if toward a beloved one, will glorify the one from the seed of David for the infinite age. This took place when the **Word became flesh** <note>original: ὁ λόγος σὰρξ γενόμενος. A direct reference to John 1:14, the central doctrine of the Incarnation.</note> and assumed and deified <note>original: ἐθεοποίησε (etheopoiese). This is a strong term meaning "made divine," used by early Church Fathers to describe how Christ's human nature was transformed by its union with his divinity.</note> the lineage of David. Therefore, God proclaims Him as a Son, saying: 
» I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a 
» son. And again: I will also make him my firstborn. For through these words, it is clearly stated that the pre-existing Son of God would come from the seed of David, so that the "Son of David" before God and the "Son of God" in the Son of David are one and the same. Through these things, it was clearly prophesied that the **Firstborn of all creation** <note>original: πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως. A title for Christ from Colossians 1:15.</note>—the Son of God Himself—would be called the Son of David. The text of the Gospel seals this account, through the words which say that Gabriel, standing before the Holy Virgin, spoke concerning our Savior: 
» He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give to him 
» the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, 
» and of his kingdom there will be no end. And a little further on in the same Gospel, 
» Zechariah, the father of John, prophesies these things concerning Christ: Blessed be the 
» Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people, and has raised up 
» a **horn of salvation** <note>original: κέρας σωτηρίας (keras soterias). A biblical metaphor for strength and victory.</note> for us in the house of David his servant, as he spoke through the 
» mouth of his holy prophets from of old. That our Savior and Lord Jesus, the Christ of God, and no other man, has received the promised eternal throne in David is sufficiently confirmed by the testimonies cited: both that of Gabriel and that of Zechariah, through which He is most clearly heralded as being from the seed of David. As for the question of why the holy Evangelists record the genealogy of Joseph—even though our Savior was not from him, but from the Holy Spirit and the Holy Virgin—and how the mother of the Lord herself is proved to be from the family and seed of David, you have already heard these matters discussed in the earlier section concerning the "Questions and Solutions on the Genealogy of our Savior." We refer those who are eager to learn to those writings, as the present time urges us toward a different subject.

> "He shall build a house for my name, and I will set up his throne **forever**. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son." <note>original: εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα (eis ton aiona). This phrase literally means "into the age," but in biblical Greek, it functions as "forever" or "eternity."</note> And in the eighty-eighth Psalm <note>Psalm 89 in modern Bibles.</note> concerning the same person, as if speaking of David, these things are said: "He shall call upon me, 'You are my father, my God, and the helper of my salvation,' and I will make him my **firstborn**, high above the kings of the earth. I will keep my mercy for him forever, and my covenant shall be faithful to him." And again: "I have sworn to David my servant, 'I will prepare your seed forever, and I will build your throne to generation and generation.'" And again: "Once I have sworn by my holiness, will I lie to David? His seed shall remain forever, and his throne as the sun before me, and as the moon established forever." And again: "And I will set his seed for age upon age." Similar to these are the words: "The Lord swore truth to David and will not reject him: 'From the fruit of your body I will set [one] upon your throne.'"

Now, Solomon was certainly David's son and the acknowledged successor to the kingdom. In fulfillment of a prayer and through sacred rites, he was the first to build a temple to God; thus, it is reasonable that **those of the circumcision** <note>The Jewish people.</note> might suppose him to be the one prophesied. To them, it is worth considering whether it is possible to apply to Solomon the oracle which says, "and I will set up his throne **forever**," and again, that which God swore with the weight of an oath by His Holy One—that the throne of the one prophesied would be as the sun and as the days of heaven. For if one examines the duration of Solomon’s reign, he would find it was forty years, and no more. Even if one adds together his entire succession, the total period lasted about five hundred years until the end of the line. <note>Eusebius refers to the period from Solomon to the Babylonian Exile.</note> But let it even be granted that some might think the nation of the Jews lasted until the final siege by the Romans. How then can this fit the prophecy, which decrees that his throne should remain **forever**, and as the sun, and as the days of heaven? Moreover, how could the phrase, "I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son," apply to Solomon?

For the explicit history of his life teaches things about him that are foreign to and far removed from divine adoption. Listen to the list of accusations brought against him: "And Solomon was a lover of women, and took many foreign wives—the daughter of Pharaoh, Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Syrians, Hittites, and Amorites—from the nations of whom the Lord God forbade the sons of Israel, saying, 'You shall not go in to them.'" And it adds to this: "And his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as was the heart of David his father, and Solomon went after Astarte, the **abomination** <note>original: βδελύγματος (bdelygmatos). A term used for idols that provoke religious disgust.</note> of the Sidonians, and after their king, the idol of the sons of Ammon; and Solomon did evil before the Lord." And again, it adds: "And the Lord raised up an **adversary** <note>original: Σατὰν (Satan). In the Septuagint, this word is often used in its literal sense as a "prosecutor" or "adversary" (here, Hadad the Edomite) rather than the fallen angel.</note> against Solomon, Hadad the Edomite."

In light of these and similar things, would one dare to describe God as the Father of such a rejected person, or declare him to be the "firstborn son" to God who is over all? And how can these things be said at one time about David himself, and at another about his seed? It is clear that they do not even apply to David, as will be evident when it is pointed out to you. Therefore, we must seek another person who is revealed in these passages—the one who is the **rising up** <note>original: ἀνάστασιν (anastasin). While it means "resurrection," in this prophetic context, Eusebius also means the "raising up" of a new ruler from David's line.</note> from the seed of David. For no other such person has appeared in history, except for—

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 7

Our one Savior and Lord, Jesus the Christ of God, is the only person among all those who ever reigned from the seed of David who is acknowledged as the "Son of David" throughout the whole inhabited world according to his birth in the flesh. In him, even though the physical kingdom was dissolved, the reign extends into the infinite age. Although it has been the target of a thousand plots, it demonstrates its vigor and invincibility through his prophecies, supported by a divine and heavenly power.

If you hear God "swearing by his Holy One," <note>original: ἁγίου (hagiou) - "Holy One." Eusebius interprets this not just as a quality of God, but as a reference to the Second Person of the Trinity.</note> listen as a child of the truth and understand this "Holy One" to be a name for the Word of God—the one who existed before all ages, His holy and only-begotten Son. The voices of the prophets we cited earlier have described his divinity in various ways. It is by this Son that God the Father swears, as if by his Beloved, that He would glorify the one from the seed of David throughout the infinite age. 

This came to pass when the Word became flesh, taking upon himself and deifying the lineage of David. Therefore, he proclaims him as "Son," saying: 

<margin>»</margin> "I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son." 

And again: 

<margin>»</margin> "And I will make him my **firstborn**." 

From these passages, it is clear that the pre-existing Son of God is said to be "from the seed of David," so that the Son of David and the Son of God are one and the same—the Son of God being also the Son of David. Through these words, it is clearly prophesied that the Son of God himself, who existed before all creation, was to be born as the Son of David. 

This whole matter is further sealed in the Gospel scripture, where it says that Gabriel stood before the Holy Virgin and spoke concerning our Savior: 

<margin>»</margin> "He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him 
<margin>»</margin> the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob **forever**, 
<margin>»</margin> and of his kingdom there will be no end." <note>Luke 1:32-33.</note>

Not long after this, in the same Gospel, Zechariah, the father of John, prophesies these things concerning the Christ: 

<margin>»</margin> "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people, and has 
<margin>»</margin> raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant, as he spoke by 
<margin>»</margin> the mouth of his holy prophets from of old." <note>Luke 1:68-70. "Horn of salvation" is a biblical metaphor for a mighty savior.</note>

The previously cited testimonies—both that of Gabriel and that of Zechariah—sufficiently prove that our Savior and Lord, Jesus the Christ of God, and no other man, has received the eternal throne promised to David. Through these witnesses, he is most clearly demonstrated to have been born from David’s seed. 

As for the question of why the sacred Evangelists provide a genealogy for Joseph <note>Matthew 1:1-17 and Luke 3:23-38. Ancient readers often struggled with why the genealogy follows Joseph if Jesus was born of a virgin.</note> even though our Savior was not descended from him but from the Holy Spirit and the Holy Virgin, and how the Mother of the Lord herself is proved to be of the nature and seed of David—we have already dealt with these problems and their solutions in a previous section regarding the character of our Savior. We refer the studious reader to those discussions, as our present time urges us toward a different topic.

<margin>»</margin> "And he shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends
<margin>»</margin> of the inhabited world." And after a short while it says, "His fruit shall be exalted
<margin>»</margin> above Lebanon. His name shall be blessed forever; before the sun his name 
<margin>»</margin> remains, and in him all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed; all the
<margin>»</margin> nations shall call him blessed." <note>These verses are from Psalm 72:8, 16–17. Eusebius uses them to show that the "King" described has a global and eternal reach that no historical Jewish monarch ever possessed.</note> Since the Psalm is inscribed "For Solomon," the first verse of the Psalm might be referred to him, but everything that follows refers to the "Son of Solomon"—not Rehoboam, who reigned over Israel after him, but the Christ of God who came forth from his seed according to the flesh. For it is impossible to apply the things declared in the Psalm to Solomon, nor to his successor, as anyone who is not utterly ignorant of the Divine Scriptures would confess. For how is it possible to take the things mentioned throughout the whole Psalm as referring to Solomon, or to his son Rehoboam? For instance: "He shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the inhabited world." And: "He shall remain as long as the sun, and before the moon for generations of generations." <note>original: πρὸ τῆς σελήνης γενεὰς γενεῶν (pro tēs selēnēs geneas geneōn). This is a classic "Messianic" proof-text used by early Christians to argue for Christ's pre-existence.</note> And whatever other things similar to these are added. Because of these points, the word at the beginning of the Psalm, "O God, give your judgment to the king," <note>Psalm 72:1</note> might be attributed to Solomon himself without much scrutiny; but the following phrase, "and your righteousness to the king’s son," must be applied to the Son of Solomon—not the one who immediately succeeded him as heir to the kingdom. For that man [Rehoboam] presided over only the Jewish nation for a mere seventeen years, and he was someone who made use of his power poorly. It cannot apply to Rehoboam, who merely succeeded to the time of Solomon's reign, but only to the one from the seed of David, who was also called the "Son of Solomon" just as he was called "Son of David." This was our Savior and Lord, Jesus the Christ. For his throne alone—and no other’s who ever lived—remains as long as the sun. And he, unlike any other human, existed before the moon and before the foundation of the world, insofar as he was the Word of God; he alone distilled from heaven like dew <note>A reference to Psalm 72:6: "He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass." Eusebius links the "rain/dew" to the Incarnation.</note> upon all the earth. For it is said that he has reached out to all men, according to what we have explained a little earlier. His righteousness alone lasts until the end of life—which has been called the "passing away of the moon." Clearly, the power of our Savior holds sway and has dominion from the Eastern sea even to the setting sun. Having begun to work from "the river"—that is, from the mystery in Judea, or from the Jordan where he first appeared and began his work of beneficence toward men—his kingdom was extended from there and passed through the whole inhabited world. And "Lebanon" is understood as Jerusalem, as is shown from very many prophecies, because of the sanctuary and the altar that were in her of old, and the things offered there in honor of God like frankincense; <note>The Greek word for Lebanon (Libanos) is the same as the word for frankincense. Eusebius is making a symbolic connection between the mountain and the aromatic offerings of the Temple.</note> but it is prophesied that the "fruit of Christ"—which is the Church from the Gentiles—shall be exalted above Lebanon.

Therefore, if any lover of learning examines the Psalm for himself, he would confess that the things in it belong to our Lord alone. They belong neither to the ancient Solomon, nor to any other of the kings after him who ruled only the single nation of the Jews—not even over more than a few neighboring nations, and certainly over no other land but Judea.

### From Isaiah.
#### Concerning Jesse, and him who shall be born from his seed.

And there shall come forth a rod from the root of Jesse, and a blossom shall come up from that root, and
> " the spirit of God shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit 
> " of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and godliness; the spirit of the fear 
> " of God shall fill him. He shall not judge according to reputation, nor reprove according to 
> " talk, but he shall give judgment for the lowly, and shall reprove the lowly of the earth. 
> " And he shall have his loins girt with righteousness, and his sides wrapped in truth. 
> " And the wolf shall feed with the lamb, and the leopard shall rest with the kid, 
> " and the calf and the lion shall feed together... and there shall be a root of Jesse, 
> " and he who arises to rule the nations <note>The "nations" (ethne) here refers to the Gentiles, or non-Jewish peoples.</note>, in him shall the nations hope, and 
> " his rest shall be honor. <note>Isaiah 11:1–5, 10. Eusebius uses the Septuagint version, which differs slightly from modern translations based on the Hebrew Masoretic text.</note>

The one indicated here as Jesse was the father of David. Just as in the prophecies prior to this one, it was said that the Christ would come from the "fruit and seed of David," and again from the "seed of Solomon," so here—many years after the death of not only David, but also Solomon—it is established that he would come forth from the root of Jesse, and clearly therefore from David. This present passage resolves the views held among the Jews regarding the time of Solomon’s death. Isaiah prophesied these things concerning someone else yet to come, who was destined to appear from the root of Jesse and the seed of David. That these declarations can be traced back to no one other than our Savior Jesus Christ, who was born of the root of David and Jesse, should be clear without any doubt to those who consider 
> " the promise of the prophecy saying: "And there shall be a root of Jesse, and he who 
> " arises to rule the nations, in him shall the nations hope," 

and the actual results demonstrated in the person of our Savior. For he alone, after his resurrection from the dead—on account of which I believe he was called "the one who arises"—ruled not over the Jewish people, but over all the nations. Thus the oracle does not even require an interpretation, as it stands clearly revealed,
> " how it reached its fulfillment in him; and also, "In him shall the nations hope."

As for the things said regarding the taming of animals and wild beasts during his presence, these may be interpreted <term>allegorically</term> <note>Allegory: a method of interpretation where physical descriptions (like wild animals) represent spiritual or moral realities (like fierce human characters).</note> as referring to cruel and savage men, who possessed beast-like characters, but who were transformed by the teaching of Christ from their irrationality and savagery. These things would clearly be understood allegorically because a reader would interpret the "root of Jesse," the "rod," and the "blossom" mentioned in the prophecy as figures of speech, just as one would perceive "righteousness" as a belt for the sides or "truth" as a covering for the loins. For since it is not possible to interpret these things in any other way than through an allegorical delivery, it follows in the same manner that one must also take the descriptions of the cattle and the animals named in those places as figurative.

> » "In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell confidently, and this is the
> » name which the Lord shall call him, *Iosedekeim* <note>original: ἰωσεδεκεὶμ. This is a Greek transliteration of the Hebrew 'Yahweh Tsidkenu,' meaning 'The Lord our Righteousness.'</note> among the prophets. And in that

> » and they shall no longer serve foreign gods, but they shall serve the Lord their God,
> » and I will raise up for them David their king." <note>Jeremiah 23:6 and 30:8-9 (Septuagint numbering).</note>

Not only long after the death of David, but even after the time of Solomon, Jeremiah promises these things concerning the one who is to be raised up from the seed of David as a king. He also calls him the <term>Rising</term> <note>original: ἀνατολή (Anatole). In Greek, this word means both 'Rising' (like the sun) and 'Branch/Sprout.' Eusebius emphasizes the 'Rising' aspect to link it to the Sun of Righteousness.</note>, and not simply so, but the "Righteous Rising," as one who is established from the Sun of Righteousness. We have already discussed this in our proofs concerning the "Second Cause" <note>The 'Second Cause' refers to the Word (Logos) or the Son, as the secondary principle of the Godhead in Eusebius's theology.</note>, in which we demonstrated that the pre-existent Word of God is called by countless titles, including the "Sun of Righteousness," citing the prophecy which says: 
> "But for you who fear me, the Sun of Righteousness shall rise." <note>Malachi 4:2.</note>

Just as he is the Sun of Righteousness, so the Word prophesies in the present passage that He will raise up for David a "Righteous Rising." He addresses this same king as one who understands and executes judgment and righteousness upon the earth. Furthermore, he gives him the same name as the David who died long ago. For having promised above, "I will raise up for David a Righteous Rising," he says at the end of the passage: 
> "And I will raise up for them David their king." 

But for whom? Was it for David? For he said he would raise up the Righteous Rising *for him*. 

In the book of Zechariah, when prophesying about the same person, he likewise calls him the "Rising," saying: 
> » "Behold a man, his name is the Rising, and beneath him righteousness shall rise." <note>Zechariah 6:12.</note>
> » And again: "I will call my servant, the Rising." <note>Zechariah 3:8.</note>

Yet, after the times of Jeremiah, and even after the times of Zechariah, no one of the circumcision <note>A common early Christian term for the Jewish people.</note> appeared who could be called the "Righteous Rising," or a "wise king performing judgment and righteousness upon the earth." 

If anyone should say that these things refer to Joshua, the son of Josedech <note>Jesus (Joshua) son of Jozadak, the High Priest during the rebuilding of the Second Temple (Haggai 1:1).</note>, it must be stated that the description does not fit him. For he was not of the lineage of David, nor did he reign as a king. How could the phrase "I will raise up David as a king for him" apply to him? For he was of the tribe of Levi and of the high-priestly order—a different lineage than David's—and history records that he was never a king. 

Therefore, if no other such person can be found, it is time to acknowledge that the one prophesied through these words is none other than our Savior and Lord, who is also proclaimed in other places as the "Light of the World" and the "Light of the Gentiles." For he would be the one prophesied, and the prediction stands as true. For he alone, being of the seed of David and sharing the name of his forefather according to the inner meaning—since "David" is interpreted as "mighty in hand" <note>A traditional but folk etymology of the name David used by early Church Fathers.</note>—proclaimed judgment and righteousness through his teaching to all those on earth. He alone of all who have ever lived reigned not over a mere part of the inhabited world, but over the entire earth. He alone caused righteousness to rise, in accordance with what is said about him in the Psalm: 
> » "In his days righteousness shall rise, and an abundance of peace." <note>Psalm 72:7.</note>

As for "Judah being saved" and "Israel" in his days, these are all those who have come to the worship of God through him, both from the people of the circumcision—his apostles, disciples, and evangelists—and all those who embrace the "Jew in secret" and the "true Israel" that sees God. For as the Apostle says:
> "He is not a Jew who is one outwardly..." <note>Romans 2:28.</note>

For he says this is the name which the Lord shall call them: <term>Iosedekeim</term> <note>original: ἰωσεδεκείμ. A Greek transliteration of the Hebrew *Yahweh Tsidkenu* ("The Lord our Righteousness"). Eusebius interprets the name etymologically.</note>, which is interpreted as, *the righteous of God*. This name is perhaps distinguished and derived from "Jesus [son of] Iosedek" <note>Referring to Joshua son of Jozadak, the High Priest in the time of Nehemiah and Zechariah, whom Eusebius views as a "type" or foreshadowing of Jesus Christ.</note>, after whom, in the book of Nehemiah, the disciples of Jesus are called. Among the Greeks, they are addressed by a name more familiar to Greek ears, derived from the title of "Christ" <note>i.e., "Christians."</note>; but according to the Hebrew tongue and among the prophets themselves, they are called <term>Iosedekeim</term> after the name of Jesus, as those who have been saved through him. Therefore it is said: *And this is the name which the Lord shall call them, Iosedekeim, among the prophets.* He says this specifically because every tribe is of the same race, for the people of Judah and Israel are one with another; they shall be named *Iosedekeim* after Jesus. And he says they shall be called by this title, not by men, but by God himself, through his prophets. For if you attend carefully to the word, it says: *And this is the name which the Lord shall call them, Iosedekeim, among the prophets.* As I said, the name is translated into the Greek tongue as *the righteous of God*.

Since they were to be called in this way, God promises to shatter the ancient, heavy, and bitter yoke of demons that previously held them, and to burst the bonds of their impieties, so that they no longer serve foreign gods but bear fruit to him alone in a pleasing manner. This harmonizes with the oracle in the second Psalm concerning the prophecy of Christ and the calling of the nations, which says: 
» "Let us break their bonds asunder, and cast away their yoke from us." <note>Psalm 2:3.</note>
I consider this to be related to the passage at hand: *In that day, says the Lord, I will break the yoke from their neck, and I will burst their bonds, and they shall no longer serve foreign gods, but they shall serve the Lord their God.*

Now, it has been previously stated that the Christ of God would be born from the "fruit of the womb of David," and from the "seed of Solomon," and from the "root of Jesse"—which has indeed come to pass. The divine oracles also name him "David" <note>In several prophecies (e.g., Ezekiel 34:23), the coming Messiah is simply called "David."</note> among many other titles; what has been said is sufficient to establish this. Furthermore, that he was said to come from the tribe of Judah requires no further inquiry, since he was of no other tribe than the one declared (for David himself was from it). However, hear also as a further proof the oracle from Moses, which is given in this manner:

# EUSEBIUS

<margin>
Eusebius
on the
Proof
of the
Gospel
</margin>

The matters set before us have been divinely prophesied, signifying that Christ is clearly revealed through them from the beginning. If, for instance, you were to gather together and compare the prophecies set forth previously with the one currently at hand, you would find that he is proclaimed in a similar way according to a common pattern. For one prophecy spoke of the one "rising from the root of Jesse, who shall also rise to rule the nations; in him shall the nations hope" <note>Isaiah 11:10. Eusebius links the "root of Jesse" (the father of King David) directly to Jesus.</note>; another spoke concerning the "son of Solomon" <note>Referring to Psalm 72 (LXX 71), titled "For Solomon." While it describes an earthly king's reign, Eusebius interprets it as a prophecy of Christ's eternal kingdom.</note> who "shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the world," and "in him shall all the nations be blessed." The prophecy currently at hand says similarly, "until he comes to whom it belongs, and he shall be the expectation of the nations" <note>Genesis 49:10. This is the famous "Scepter of Judah" prophecy, often interpreted by early Christians as the arrival of the Messiah marking the end of Jewish self-rule.</note>. 

If, therefore, the predictions concerning the nations harmonize, and if those referring to these nations have been shown to look toward our Savior, there would be nothing to prevent us from seeing the same person in the present prophecy as well—provided that they are acknowledged to prophesy in harmony with one another. This is especially true since, until the times of the appearance of our Savior, the rulers and leaders of the Jewish nation continued in succession from their ancestors; but at the time of his presence, these successions ceased, and simultaneously the "expectation of the nations" brought to fulfillment the prophecy of Jacob. 

Since, then, Christ is revealed here as well, he is clearly shown to be from the tribe of Judah and no other. And when he was revealed as being from David and Solomon, and having come from the root of Jesse, he was shown to be from that same tribe. For everyone belonging to Jesse was descended from David, and everyone belonging to David was descended from Solomon, all being established from the tribe of Judah. Therefore, our Savior and Lord would be that one and the same person, just as the wonderful evangelist Matthew openly acknowledged when he said: 

» "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of 
» Abraham. Abraham was the father of Isaac; and Isaac was the father of Jacob; and 
» Jacob was the father of Judah," <note>Matthew 1:1-2.</note> and so forth. 

But since these matters have received their proper proof, it is time to look also at the dates and times of the fulfillment of what was predicted.

## Preface.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'A' featuring dense floral and leafy scrollwork patterns within a rectangular frame at the start of the primary text block.</image-desc>
Having demonstrated through many proofs how the Word of God humbled himself for the sake of humanity <note>original: "λόγος εἰς ἀνθρώπους ἐξηυτελίζετο" — refers to the Incarnation, where the divine Word took on a lowly human form</note>, and how, from what source, and in what manner his appearance to those on earth was proclaimed in the prophetic voices of the Hebrews—proving that he was that very one, and no other, the pre-existent Son of God—whom we have further learned through other passages to be God and Lord, Commander-in-Chief <note>original: "ἀρχιστράτηγον" — a title Eusebius uses to describe Christ as the leader of the heavenly hosts</note>, and Messenger of Great Counsel <note>original: "μεγάλης βουλῆς ἄγγελον" — a title for the Messiah from the Septuagint translation of Isaiah 9:6</note>, and the High Priest of God, the Christ; we shall now, following the path of our previous discourse, testify again to the **times** of his appearance based on those same prophetic predictions, beginning as follows. The sacred scriptures proclaimed that the following would be clear signs of the times of Christ's presence: among the Hebrews, there were three previously distinguished and prominent honors by which the nation was governed—the first being the **royal**, the second the **prophetic**, and in addition to these, the **high priestly**. The prophets declared that the simultaneous cessation and total destruction of these offices would be signs of Christ's presence.

Further indicators of those same approaching times were the termination of the religious worship according to Moses, the desolation of Jerusalem and the Temple within it, and moreover, the enslavement of the entire Jewish nation to its foes and enemies. Conversely, other signs of these same times would include an abundance of peace, the abolition of the ancient "polyarchy" <term>polyarchy: the ancient system where every nation and city had its own local king or ruler, leading to constant warfare</term> throughout every nation and city, the turning away from polytheistic and demonic idolatry, and the recognition of the piety of the one God who is the Creator of all things.

All these things, which were destined long ago and proclaimed by the oracles during the times of the prophets to happen at the presence of Christ, will now be presented as having reached their fulfillment in accordance with those predictions. As for the reasons why Christ did not appear earlier, but has now become manifest to human life in these latter times after a long and vast age, much has already been said in previous sections; nevertheless, a few words shall be said now in brief. In ancient times, a great drought of folly and impiety overshadowed the souls of men, and a terrible godlessness dominated the whole of human life, so much so that men seemed to differ in no way from wild and untamed beasts. They knew nothing of cities, or citizenship, or laws, or anything noble and beneficial for life; nor did they apply their minds to sciences or arts, and the very concept of virtue and philosophy never even entered their thoughts. They spent their lives in isolation, in mountains, caves, and villages, attacking their neighbors like bandits, procuring the necessities of life from no other source than the oppression of those weaker than themselves. Indeed, they did not even know the God who is over all, nor did they possess true piety. Yet, being stirred by their natural instincts, they did acknowledge that there was some divine power among existing things (which we call "God"), and by a natural teaching they agreed to call this power by a name signifying "savior" and "benefactor." However, because of their condition, they were not yet able to receive the one who is beyond all visible substance...

<meta>catchword: ...to receive.</meta>

<summary>Eusebius introduces Book 8, arguing that the historical timing of Christ's birth was signaled by the end of Jewish kingship and priesthood, the destruction of the Temple, and the rise of universal peace under Rome. He explains that Christ's arrival was delayed until humanity had moved past its "savage" primitive state and was ready for monotheism.</summary>

> "For this reason some of them worshipped and served the creation rather than the Creator; others became vain in their reasonings, and their senseless heart was darkened, so as to change the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds and four-footed animals and creeping things." <note>This is a quotation from Romans 1:21–23, which Eusebius uses to describe the state of humanity before Christ.</note>

Indeed, they set up images of I know not what kind of dead rulers or tyrants of old, and having attached divine honor to these, they proceeded to theologize, celebrating the actions of those people—even their most licentious deeds—as the "achievements of gods." How then could the all-bright and all-revered Word of Christ, which announces the highest philosophy <note>original: "ἄκρον φιλοσοφίαν" — here meaning the highest spiritual and moral way of life</note>, be suited to those wallowing in such a depth of evil? For this reason, divine Justice, the overseer of all things, visited them as if they were a wild and most harmful thicket <note>original: "ὕλῃ" — literally "wood" or "matter," often used philosophically to describe the chaotic or material state that needs ordering</note>. At times, Justice pursued them with floods, and at other times with conflagrations; sometimes she delivered them to wars against one another, to slaughters and sieges, as they were driven to madness in mutual conflict by the very demons whom they considered to be their gods. The result was that the lives of men in those days were impassable to their neighbors, painful, and devoid of community.

Yet, a few individuals—scanty in number given the state of the world—who were the God-loving prophets mentioned in the Hebrew records, were addressed by Justice through oracles or divine manifestations. She welcomed these men and treated them with the laws introduced through Moses, which were both introductory and beneficial for life. But it was only after the legislation announced to these men and the subsequent prophetic teachings had poured out like a fragrance <note>original: "εὐωδίας δίκην" — a common patristic metaphor for the spreading influence of divine truth</note> among all people, and after the minds of the masses had finally been tamed, and civil constitutions and laws were established for many nations, and the name of virtue and philosophy was being shouted among the many—as if they had ceased from their ancient savagery and their wild and cruel way of life had been transformed into something gentler—that at the appropriate time, the heavenly Teacher of perfect and heavenly doctrines and teachings, the Introducer of the true knowledge of God, the God-Word (the Logos), finally revealed himself. 

This occurred at the described time of his incarnation, announcing to all nations, both Greeks and barbarians, the Father’s love for humanity. He simultaneously offered everyone the means of salvation—a salvation that is true and full of the light of piety—and the kingdom of heaven, holding out the promise of eternal life to all. Let this much be said regarding the timing, explaining why Christ, the Word of God, did not shine upon all men long ago. 

But come, let us examine the signs of the times of his arrival in detail, noting first the Gospel voices concerning his birth. Matthew, marking the time of his appearance, records it this way, saying:

> "Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea, in the days of Herod the king." <note>Matthew 2:1</note> And after a little while he says: "But hearing that Archelaus reigns over Judea in place of his father Herod." <note>Matthew 2:22</note>

And Luke sets out the time of his teaching and public manifestation, saying:

> "In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip being tetrarch..." <note>Luke 3:1</note>

<header>### PROOFS OF THE GOSPEL, Book 8</header>
<page-num>229</page-num>

...and the nation itself was led by its own ancestral leaders and laws until Herod, an alien, and Emperor Augustus took rule over them. As long as a ruler from Judah and a leader from his loins <note>original: "ἐκ τῶν μηρῶν αὐτοῦ" — literally 'from his thighs,' a biblical idiom for biological descendants.</note> had not yet failed, the periods of the prophecies were recorded according to the succession of the nation's leaders. Thus, Isaiah prophesied during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, who were kings of Judah. Likewise, Hosea did the same. Amos prophesied in the days of Uzziah, king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel. And Zephaniah in the days of Josiah, son of Amon, king of Judah. Jeremiah acted similarly. 

But when the ruler from Judah and the leader from his loins failed, the one prophesied through Christ—the "expectation of the nations"—was just about to shine upon human life. At that point, kings of Judah no longer functioned, nor leaders of Israel. These roles having failed according to the prophecies and the appointed times, first Augustus and second Tiberius became supreme, under whom a ruler and king of the Jewish nation was proclaimed <note>Referring to Herod the Great and his sons.</note>, along with the Roman procurators and tetrarchs over Judea. Furthermore, Herod, as I have already stated before, was not of Jewish descent; he was the one who was personally entrusted by the Romans with the governance over the Jews. 

Now that these things have been fulfilled for us, it is time to touch upon the interpretation of the prophecy itself: 
> "Judah, your brothers shall praise you." 
Out of all the twelve sons belonging to Jacob, Judah was the fourth, as we have mentioned previously, and he was himself a tribal patriarch of the Hebrew nation. But it should be clear to those who examine the words of Holy Scripture that the things spoken to him by his father did not refer to the man himself. First, Jacob’s voice to his sons says: 
> "And Jacob called his sons and said, 'Gather yourselves together, and I will tell you what shall happen to you in the last days. Assemble and hear, O sons of Jacob; listen to Israel your father.'" <note>Quoting Genesis 49:1-2.</note> 
He clearly promises to prophesy to them the things that would happen to them in times long afterward—as he says, "in the last days." <note>original: "ἐπ’ ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν" — This phrase usually refers to the Messianic era or the end of the current age.</note> In general, the things spoken to Judah could not reasonably be applied to that first man. For when did the brothers of that Judah praise him? For what great achievement would they have done this? Nor did the sons of his father bow down to him. On the contrary, that description would better suit Joseph, for Judah himself is seen bowing down to Joseph along with the rest of the brothers. 

Setting aside the specific words of the prophecy for a moment: history presents no such thing happening to Joseph, much less to Judah. And then: 
> "Couching, you slept as a lion and as a cub," 
would require a much deeper interpretation than the person of Judah allows. Furthermore, what was said afterward: 
> "A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until the things laid up for him come, and he is the expectation of the nations," 
seems to me to hint at the timing of the arrival of the one who was prophesied. For he says "this" shall not happen until "that" occurs. For the rulers and leaders of the Jewish nation would not cease before the "expectation of the nations" arrived, along with the things laid up for the one prophesied. Theodotion <note>A 2nd-century scholar who produced a Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> interpreted these things similarly to the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX).</note>. But Aquila <note>A 2nd-century convert to Judaism who produced a very literal Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> rendered it in this manner: 
> "A scepter shall not be removed from Judah, and a lawgiver from between his feet, until..."

<sig>Vv.i.</sig>
<meta>catchword: until</meta>

<summary>Eusebius argues that the prophecy of Jacob regarding the tribe of Judah refers to the Messiah, not the historical Judah, evidenced by the fact that Jewish self-rule ended precisely when Christ (the "expectation of the nations") appeared during the Roman era.</summary>

Having established that the "ruler from Judah" must fail before the "expectation of the nations" (Christ) arrives, he now addresses a potential counter-argument: if "Judah" refers strictly to the biological tribe, the prophecy would seem historically inaccurate, as many Jewish leaders came from other tribes.</meta>

### THE PROOFS OF THE GOSPEL
<page-num>230</page-num>

<header>E U S E B I U S</header>

<margin>
Eusebius
on the 
*Preparation 
for the 
Gospel*
<note>The margin identifies the author and work, though the content here is specifically from his *Demonstratio Evangelica* or *Proofs of the Gospel*.</note>
</margin>

"...until he comes, to whom belongs the gathering of the nations." Then, when it is said, "a ruler shall not fail from Judah," we must not understand this as referring to Judah himself—that original forefather—any more than the passage "O Judah, your brothers shall praise you," and what follows, should be applied solely to him. For throughout the vast majority of time, the rulers and leaders of the Jewish nation were established from lineages other than that man’s descendants. 

First, Moses himself led the people, and he was not from the tribe of Judah, but from the tribe of Levi. Then came Joshua, who was from the tribe of Ephraim. After him, they were ruled by Deborah, from the tribe of Ephraim, and Barak, from the tribe of Naphtali. After these came Gideon, from the tribe of Manasseh; then Gideon’s son <note>Abimelech</note>, and after him Tola, from the same tribe. Then came Ibzan <note>original: "ἐσεβὼν" (Esebon)</note>, from Bethlehem, and after him Elon, from the tribe of Zebulun; then Abdon <note>original: "λαβδὼν" (Labdon)</note>, from the tribe of Ephraim. And again Samson, from the tribe of Dan. 

Then, during a period of lawlessness, the priest Eli <note>original: "ἡλεὶ" (Helei)</note> led them, who was from the tribe of Levi. All of these served as judges over Israel, yet they were not from the succession of Judah; having been chosen from various tribes, they nonetheless led. Even when the first king was appointed after them, Saul, he was from the tribe of Benjamin. 

How then can the saying, "a ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins" <note>original: "ἐκ τῶν μηρῶν αὐτοῦ" — literally "from his thighs," a Hebrew idiom for biological descendants</note>, be applied—as some might think—only to leaders from the tribe of Judah? For it is clear that from the time of Jacob’s death for nearly a thousand years, leaders were produced not from the tribe of Judah alone, but at different times from different tribes, right up until the time of David. 

And if, after so long a time, David and his successors who reigned over the Jewish nation were indeed from the tribe of Judah, one must realize that they did not even last for five hundred years. Furthermore, they did not rule over the entire nation, but only over three tribes, and not even all of those. For other kings rose up against them from the larger part of the nation, governing the kingdom of all nine tribes. 

After the death of Solomon, the entire nation was divided from Judah; the successors of David reigned in Jerusalem over only three tribes (as I said, and even then not completely) until the captivity in Babylon. During that same period, in the city called Samaria, leaders of the nine tribes who were not from Judah, but from various other tribes, continued to rule. The first of these was Jeroboam, from the tribe of Ephraim, followed by those who came after him. Thus, even in the intervening years from David until the Babylonian captivity, those from the tribe of Judah did not lead the whole nation. 

And what can be said of the period after the return from Babylon? For another five hundred years until the birth of Christ, they continued under an aristocratic form of government <term>aristokratikē</term> <note>A system where power is held by the "best" or highest social class; here, the priestly nobility.</note>, with the high priests of the time leading the nation, none of whom were from the tribe of Judah. 

From all of this, it is evident that the prophetic word—"a ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins"—does not refer to that first man, Judah, nor to his biological descendants alone. This passage can only be sustained if, according to the explanations we set out previously, it refers to the *entire tribe* or nation. Let us understand it this way: from the beginning, starting from the time of Moses, this identity led the whole nation. Indeed, its power was a sovereign authority from the start, as foretold by Jacob. Even now, the land is called "Judea" after that tribe, and the entire body of the people is addressed as "Jews." Therefore, if we understand the saying this way, it is as if it says more clearly: "The leadership of the..."

He highlights that the Davidic line was short-lived and the post-exilic leadership was priestly, reinforcing that the prophecy's fulfillment rests on the end of Jewish self-rule at Christ's birth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument that the name "Judah" in Genesis 49:10 refers not just to the individual patriarch or his biological descendants, but to the entire nation and its political identity. He addresses the historical reality that many Jewish leaders came from other tribes by using a contemporary political analogy.</meta>

### PROOFS OF THE GOSPEL, Book 8
<page-num>232</page-num>

->PROOFS OF THE GOSPEL, Book 8<-

» ...the tribe of Judah leading every nation. And Symmachus <note>Symmachus was a late 2nd-century translator of the Old Testament into Greek; he was known for his clear, idiomatic style.</note> also says, "authority shall not be taken away from Judah." This authoritative and ruling dignity certainly represents the tribe of Judah that was established afterward. Therefore, they say that neither its "scepter"—as Aquila <note>Aquila of Sinope was a 2nd-century translator who produced an extremely literal Greek version of the Hebrew Bible.</note> says, this being a symbol of royal rule—nor its "authority," according to Symmachus, will be taken away "until he comes," it says, "for whom it is reserved, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations." <note>original: "ᾧ ἀπόκειται" (ho apokeitai). This phrase in the Septuagint Greek translation corresponds to the mysterious Hebrew word 'Shiloh' in Genesis 49:10, which Eusebius interprets as a reference to Christ.</note> What is this "expectation" other than that which was anciently promised to Abraham and the patriarchs after him? 

First, then, it is worth marveling how, though there were twelve tribes among the Hebrews, the name of the nation even now is called by no other but Judah alone <note>The word "Jew" (Ioudaios) is derived from "Judah" (Iouda).</note>; this is for no other reason than the oracle of the prophecy, which assigned the ruling dignity to the tribe of Judah. Furthermore, it happened that their ancestral land was called "Judea" for the same reason. For why was the nation not named after the first of the twelve—I mean Reuben <note>original: "ῥουβὶμ" (Roubim)</note>? Even though he was honored by the divine law as the firstborn? And why not from Levi, who preceded Judah both in time and in the honor of the priesthood? And why did it not happen that the whole nation and land were named after Joseph? For long ago, he held power not only over all Egypt, but over his own kin; and his descendants, much later, led nearly nine tribes of the nation for a very long time. It would seem more likely that the whole nation and land would be inscribed with the name of their forefather <note>Referring to Joseph, whose sons Ephraim and Manasseh became dominant tribes in the northern Kingdom of Israel.</note>. And who would not admit that, if things were done without a secret reason, they would have taken their name from Benjamin? For to his tribe belonged the famous royal capital itself <note>Jerusalem</note>, and the most holy temple of God was allotted to it. 

Yet despite these things, the name of the land and the whole nation did not prevail from those others, but from the tribe of Judah alone, in accordance with the prophecy. Thus, because "a ruler shall not fail from Judah," the name has been applied to the whole tribe for us, and this prophecy alone has been truly fulfilled. Since the time of Moses, individual rulers among them did not cease to arise from various tribes, as I said; but as a whole, the tribe of Judah stood at the head of the entire nation. 

Consider the following as an example of what has been said. Just as in the Roman Empire, there are governors and leaders for each nation, and some are commanders of the army, and those supreme over all are the emperors <note>original: "βασιλεῖς" (basileis), literally "kings," but used here for the Roman Emperors.</note>; and not all of them originate from the city of the Romans, nor from the seed of Remus and Romulus, but from countless nations, as is surely obvious. Yet all of them—both the emperors and the rulers and leaders after them—are inscribed with the name of "Romans," and the power is called "the Roman Empire," and it is tied to that name. 

In this way, one must understand the affairs among the Hebrews: one general name, that of the tribe of Judah, was proclaimed over the whole nation, even though the specific leaders and kings were appointed from various tribes; yet as a whole, they were honored with the name of Judah. Therefore, let it be said by the prophet to the whole tribe: » "Judah, your brothers shall praise you." For he knew that this tribe, having been deemed worthy of such a privilege, would be honored by the rest of the tribes. And since it took the lead in wars, and alone led the whole nation in the battle lines against enemies, it is fittingly...

» ...it is said to the tribe, "your hands shall be on the back of your enemies." Then, because of its ruling and royal dignity, it is said, "you are a lion’s cub." The patriarch and prophet together, glorying in the dignity of the tribe, adds: » "From a shoot, my son, you have gone up." And the phrase, "lying down, you slept like a lion, and like a lion’s cub," represents at once a sense of majesty and boldness, an undaunted attitude toward those attacking from the outside, and a fearlessness and contempt for enemies. Being such a person—or rather, the tribe being such—who, he asks, "shall rouse him up?" <note>Eusebius is quoting Genesis 49:9. The "rousing" of the lion is interpreted here as a turning point in history.</note> He hints that someone great and wonderful, threatening and most capable, would be the one to raise the lamentation and change the aforementioned tribe from its ruling dignity. Who this might be, he teaches us in the next part, showing that this is the one who is to be the "expectation of the nations."

The prophecy foretells that this person would not appear to men until a ruler should fail and a leader from the midst of Judah's rule should vanish. And who is this but our Savior and Lord, Jesus Christ? Following this prediction, at the time of his appearance, the rulers and leaders from the Jews themselves failed; for while their nation remained, the royal and ruling dignity of the tribe of Judah, which had existed from ancient times, was struck down. The Jewish nation, along with all others, was delivered into slavery to the Romans, who then held power.

First, then, Herod—who was of a foreign race <note>Herod the Great was an Idumaean. Early Christian historians emphasized his non-Jewish ancestry to prove that the "scepter" had officially departed from the native line of Judah.</note>—was appointed king over their nation by Augustus and the Roman Senate. This Herod was the son of Antipater; and Antipater was from Ascalon, one of those called "temple-slaves" of Apollo. This Antipater married a woman named Cypros, who was of Arabian descent, and fathered Herod. Since, therefore, Herod was the first of such a race to rule, he did away with Hyrcanus <note>Hyrcanus II was the last major Hasmonean ruler (a line of priest-kings). His removal marked the end of native Jewish dynastic rule.</note>, the last of the succession of high priests who had led the nation, in whom the native rule of the Jewish nation ended. Herod himself, as I said, was the first foreigner to be proclaimed King of the Jews.

At the time of Jesus Christ’s birth, the dignity of the tribe of Judah was abolished, the Jewish kingdom came to an end, and the previous prophecy was fulfilled, which said: » "A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until the things laid up for him come." <note>original: "ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ τὰ ἀποκείμενα αὐτῷ" (heos an elthe ta apokeimena auto). This is the Septuagint's rendering of the Hebrew "until Shiloh comes."</note> He says this person will become the expectation not of the Jews alone, but of the nations. 

Therefore, that which was long ago promised to Abraham—the transfer of the Jewish rulers and leaders' authority to the Romans and to the foreigner Herod—is logically noted by the Evangelist Luke. He marks the time when the Jewish rulers failed, recording the beginning of Christ’s teaching as occurring » "in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea." <note>Luke 3:1. This serves as Eusebius's chronological proof that native Jewish autonomy had ended.</note> Matthew also hints at this very thing. For after recording the birth of our Lord and Savior, he adds: » "Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea, in the days of Herod the king, behold, wise men from the East came to Jerusalem, saying: 'Where is he who has been born King of the Jews?'" <note>Matthew 2:1-2.</note> Through these words, he clearly presents the foreign nature of the rule over them...

This hints that the one who would eventually raise up the throne and transfer the revealed tribe from its ruling dignity would be someone great and wonderful, yet more daring and skillful. <note>Eusebius suggests that only a significant figure—the Messiah—could "rouse" or change the long-standing status of Judah.</note>

For those who still remain from that lineage are slaves to the Romans even until now, being numbered among the rest of the subjects of the Jewish nation. # THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL
## Book 8

...beginning, and the calling by God of foreign nations from the east. For at the same time, foreigners held power over the Jews, and foreigners arriving from the east recognized and worshiped the Christ of God, who had been prophesied of old. <note>original: "ἀλλόφυλοι" (allophyloi). Eusebius is referring to the Magi (the "foreigners from the east") and the Roman occupation (the "foreigners holding power"), seeing both as signs that the specific Jewish sovereignty had ended to make way for the Messiah.</note> Through these events, the prophecy of Jacob is clearly shown to have reached its fulfillment, being completed at the final stage of the Jewish nation’s existence. This is exactly what he signaled to his own children when he said, "Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you what shall happen to you in the last days." <note>Quoting Genesis 49:1. Eusebius interprets the "last days" not as the end of the world, but as the end of the Jewish national state.</note> By "last days," we understand the final period of the Jewish nation’s political structure.

What, then, was to happen to them? The vanishing of the rule of Judah, the casting down of their entire nation, the pause and cessation of their leaders, and the dissolution of the royal and governing dignity of that tribe. Conversely, it marks the beginning and kingdom of Christ—ruling not just over Israel, but over all nations; indeed, He Himself is the "expectation of the nations." <note>original: "προσδοκία ἐθνῶν" (prosdokia ethnōn). This is a central theme for Eusebius: that the Messiah's arrival coincides with the Gospel spreading to the non-Jewish world.</note>

Who could deny that these things were so clearly fulfilled at the appearance of our Savior? Previously, the foretold leaders of the Christ—the listeners of the divine scriptures—flourished under their own rulers and governors, boasting their own kings, local officials, and prophets. The tribe of Judah itself was the royal line, prevailing over its enemies and leading the entire nation. But from that time until now, those who were once distinguished among them have been made subjects of the Romans.

The Christ of God has clearly appeared, and since then, the so-called "expectation of the nations" has been proclaimed to all the world. Or let someone say if it is not true that at the appearance of our Savior, the honors of the Jews—their mother city together with the Temple and the sacred rites performed within it—vanished along with their own governors and rulers. Since that time, the objects of hope and the "expectation of the nations" throughout the whole inhabited world have been taken up, precisely when the things "laid up for the Lord" arrived. <note>Eusebius links the destruction of the Temple in 70 AD and the loss of Jewish autonomy to the successful spread of Christianity.</note>

And what are these things, if not those revealed through Judah? "Your brothers shall praise you, your hands shall be on the neck of your enemies. Judah is a lion's whelp; from a young sprout, my son, you have gone up. Having crouched, you slept as a lion, and as a lion’s whelp; who shall rouse him?" <note>Genesis 49:8-9.</note> For these things, according to another level of meaning, are also the things "laid up" for him.

Let us consider these points: we should observe how the divine oracles are accustomed to address the Christ by various names. Sometimes they call Him "Jacob," as in: "Jacob my servant, I will help him; Israel my chosen, my soul has accepted him; He shall bring forth judgment to the nations," and so on. <note>Isaiah 42:1. Eusebius explains that "Jacob" and "Israel" can be titles for the Messiah, not just the patriarch or the nation.</note> It is added there, "until He sets judgment on the earth, and in His name shall the nations hope."

At other times, they name Him "Solomon" and "David." He is called Solomon in Psalm 71, which is inscribed "To Solomon," but clearly contains things concerning the Christ. <note>Psalm 72 in modern numbering. Eusebius views the descriptions of a universal, eternal king in this Psalm as applicable only to Jesus, not the historical King Solomon.</note> For it says: "He shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the inhabited world," and "all nations shall serve Him." Whatever else this Psalm contains can only fit the Christ.

Again, the Christ is addressed as "David" in Psalm 88. <note>Psalm 89 in modern numbering.</note> Since the things said in it would not fit David alone, but only the Christ, such as: "He shall call upon me, 'You are my Father,' and I will make him my firstborn, high above the kings of the earth. I will keep my mercy for him forever." And again, "His seed shall endure forever..."

## Book 8

<meta>catchword: about</meta>

“...and his throne is like the sun before me, and like the moon established forever.” <note>original: "καὶ ὁ θρόνος αὐτοῦ ὡς ὁ ἥλιος... καὶ ὡς ἡ σελήνη." Quoting Psalm 89:36-37 (LXX 88:37-38).</note> Thus, among ten thousand other titles for Christ through which the divine words signify Him, even the name "Judah" can be applied to Him because of the aforementioned reasons, for He has been shown to be strong, having come from the tribe of Judah. For it is perfectly clear, according to the Apostle, that "our Lord and Savior has sprung out of the tribe of Judah." <note>Quoting Hebrews 7:14. Eusebius uses "the Apostle" to refer to Paul, the traditional author of Hebrews.</note> To this Judah, then, the things prophesied apply in their deeper meaning. And what were these things? First, that He should be **praised** by His brothers. Second, that His **hands** should be upon the back of His enemies. Third, that He should be **worshiped** by the sons of His father.

These things reached their fulfillment when, for a time, He was marveled at and praised for His extraordinary powers and the performing of wondrous miracles. He was worshiped by His own disciples and apostles, whom He did not hesitate to call "brothers," saying through the Psalm: “I will declare your name to my brothers, in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise.” <note>Psalm 22:22.</note> He also gave this command to the women with Mary who received the good news of the Resurrection, speaking of the disciples as brothers: “Go,” He said, “tell my brothers that I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.” <note>John 20:17.</note> Thus, at first, His brothers praised Him as a man only because of His extraordinary wonders, supposing Him to be, as was likely, one of the prophets. 

However, when they later saw the miraculous nature of His works, and how He cast down the "enemy and the avenger"—that is, death, the ruler of this age <note>term: "the ruler of this age" (archōn tou aiōnos toutou). A common New Testament and early Christian title for the Devil or the spiritual power of evil.</note>—along with the rest of the invisible and hostile powers, they believed Him to be God (who had undergone these things) and they worshiped Him. 

The hands of our Savior were "upon the back of His enemies" <note>original: "κατὰ νώτου τῶν ἐχθρῶν." The imagery suggests enemies turning their backs in flight.</note> whenever He performed His deeds, His powers, and His wonders for the destruction of demons and evil spirits. Moreover, when He stretched out His hands upon the Cross, His hands were likewise upon the backs of those who fled from His enmity and gave way. This was even more true when, after delivering His spirit to the Father, He descended into the region of the enemies—fleshless and naked, no longer held by a body—existing as Life itself, about to destroy death and their so-called powers. 

It is likely that at first they had supposed Him to be a common man, like the many, and so they surrounded Him as though to attack an ordinary person. But when they recognized a nature stronger than man and more divine, they were overcome and turned their backs to Him. Against them, He released His hands, driving them away as they fled with His divine and sharpened arrows; for this reason it was said: "Your hands are upon the back of your enemies." 

Even if, until this very day, ten thousand enemies of our Savior attempt to wage war against His Church from time to time, He looks down upon them with an invisible hand and divine power, so that it might be said of them also: "Your hands are upon the back of your enemies." And since the victory over the enemies has finally been secured, then was fulfilled the saying: “The sons of your father shall worship you.” This refers clearly to all the angels in heaven, the ministering spirits, and the divine powers, as well as the apostles and evangelists on earth. After these, it includes all those from the nations (the Gentiles) who, through Him, are inscribed to the one and only true Father God—those who, having learned that Christ is the Word of God, confess that they worship Him as God.

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s detailed Christological reading of Genesis 49. Having established that the "Scepter" departed from Judah upon the arrival of Christ, Eusebius now interprets the specific imagery of the lion, the "shoot," and the "sleep" as metaphors for Christ’s royal lineage, His incarnation, His death, and His resurrection.</meta>

### PROOF OF THE GOSPEL Book 8
#### Page 235

...including the prophecy about the tribe itself, Jacob rightly foretells what follows the previous words, saying: 
» "Judah is a lion's whelp; from a shoot, my son, you have gone up. Reclining, you slept as a lion and as a whelp; who shall rouse him?" <note>Genesis 49:9 (LXX). Eusebius interprets the "lion" as a symbol of the royal dignity of the tribe of Judah, from which Christ descended.</note> 

He calls Him a "lion's whelp" because He was born from a royal tribe—the Christ of David according to the flesh. When He says, "From a shoot, my son, you have gone up," He means that He grew from the seed and root of Jacob, who uttered these very words. He was previously the Word of God, but secondly became the Son of Man through the **divine plan** <term>oikonomia: the Greek term for God's providential arrangement of salvation through the Incarnation</term> which He undertook for our sake. 

The phrase "Reclining, you slept as a lion and as a whelp" would also be indicative of His death. It is the custom of Scripture, according to a specific theological perspective, to call the death of many holy people a "sleep." But the question, "Who shall rouse him?" refers in a marvelous way to His resurrection from the dead. For the one asking "Who shall rouse him?" clearly knows that He *will* be raised. This is added in wonder—"Who then is the one who will do this and raise Him up?"—stirring us to seek out who it is that would raise our Lord from the dead after He had accepted death for our sake. 

Who then would this be but the God and Father of all, to whom alone we must attribute the resurrection of our Savior? This is according to the Scripture that says, "Whom the Father raised from the dead." <note>Cf. Galatians 1:1, Acts 2:24.</note> 

Instead of the phrase "Judah is a lion's whelp; from a shoot, my son, you have gone up; reclining, you slept," **Aquila** <note>Aquila of Sinope was a 2nd-century translator known for his extremely literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> says more vividly: 
» "A lion's puppy, Judah; from capture, my son, you have gone up; having bent, you lay down." 

And **Symmachus** <note>Symmachus the Ebionite was another 2nd-century translator who aimed for more idiomatic and elegant Greek.</note> says: 
» "A lion's whelp, Judah; from the taking of prey, my son, you have gone up; crouching, you were established." 

Through these versions, the resurrection from the dead is clearly presented, or rather, the escape of our Savior from Hades as if from a wild beast’s power. To "crouch" and "be established," rather than simply "falling," shows death through the "crouching," but shows that He was not dragged down like the souls of other men through the phrase "He was established." 

All these things were laid up for Christ. They did not reach their final end as long as the Jewish nation stood, and while their rulers, leaders, and those who carefully studied the divine prophecies about Christ flourished among them. But when the things "laid up for Judah" arrived, and the one prophesied appeared on earth—born from the seed and the "shoot" according to the oracles—and after He reclined and slept (or "crouched," according to Symmachus), He was established and raised up, laying His hands upon the back of His invisible and intellectual enemies. 

His brothers and disciples, who at first were ignorant of Him and marveled at Him, later confessed Him to be God and worshiped Him as God. At that time, the things laid up for Him were fulfilled, which is why it was said: "Until the things laid up for him should come." <note>Genesis 49:10.</note> For from that time until now, since the things laid up for Him have reached their goal, the rulers and leaders of the Jewish nation have ceased, and the rulers of the nations have been established over them. Conversely, the nations, having recognized Christ as the Word of God, have claimed Him as their Savior and their expectation. 

After all these things, it is added: 
» "Binding his foal to a vine, and the colt of his donkey to the tendril; he shall wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape. His eyes are cheerful from wine, and his teeth are white as milk." <note>Genesis 49:11-12.</note> 

I believe that through these words, the "foal" riddlingly refers to the chorus of the Apostles and disciples of our Savior. The "vine" to which He tethered the foal...

### From Daniel.

Just as after a period of seventy weeks of years—which total four hundred and ninety years—the Christ, the Child of God, appeared, the prophecies among the Jews and their formerly distinguished priesthood were to be abolished. They themselves were to be captured by successive sieges like a flood, and their holy temple was to suffer ultimate desolation.

> And while I was still speaking and praying and confessing my sins, and

> » until the completion of the time, a completion shall be given to the
