» ...and Israel acted with strength. <note>Numbers 24:18. Eusebius is completing the quote from the previous page.</note> But as for him, he first committed the greatest impiety. Therefore, one shall come out from them who shall rise up. And who is this prophesied Word of God, who also destroyed those being saved out of the city? I believe he is hinting at Jerusalem, from which everyone who used force perished, or perhaps the entire political structure of their nation.

How these matters reached their conclusion at the same time as the shining forth of our Savior among men—when the former idol-worshipping nations transitioned into his inheritance, while the Jewish nation and their metropolis suffered such things as they never had before—is a matter that I believe requires no long explanation. But let this be the conclusion regarding the harmony between the prophetic prediction and the Gospel fulfillment.

Since the star of the "shining forth" refers to the star that appeared, it is worth paying attention. Moses says that all the stars in the firmament were appointed by God "for signs and for seasons." <note>Genesis 1:14.</note> But a certain strange and unusual star—not one of the many familiar ones, but a new and fresh star appearing in life—signified a strange luminary <term>phostēr; a light-bearer or celestial body</term> shining upon the whole world. This was the Christ of God, a great and new star, whose image was symbolically carried by the star that appeared then to the Magi. 

Since throughout the whole of sacred and divinely inspired Scripture, the primary aim of the intellect is to teach in a more "musical" and divine way, <note>By "musical" (mousikōtera), Eusebius likely means "harmonious" or "spiritually attuned."</note> while also examining historical events in their turn, it is fitting that the prophecy at hand was fulfilled literally <note>original: "pros lexin" — according to the word or literally.</note> by the star announced at the birth of our Savior.

Indeed, flashings of strange stars occur for other famous and eminent men, which are called "comets," "beams," "bearded stars," <note>Eusebius uses the terms komētas (comets), dokidas (meteor-like "beams"), and pōgonias (bearded stars), reflecting ancient Greek astronomical terminology.</note> or other such names, appearing occasionally at great events. But what better or greater thing could ever happen in the whole world than the intellectual light <note>original: "noeron phōs" — a light perceived by the mind or spirit, rather than just the eyes.</note> that was made available to all men through the Savior's appearance, bringing the message of piety and the knowledge of God <term>theognosia</term> to rational souls? For this reason, the conspicuous star signaled the great sign, hinting to all that Christ, the God of all, is the great and new luminary shining upon the whole world. 

Furthermore, the prophecy foretells both a man and a star together, through the words: 

> » A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall rise out of Israel. 

By this, it calls the heavenly luminary the "Word of God" <note>The Logos.</note> while naming the same one a "man." In various other places, it calls him the "Rising," "Light," and "Sun of Righteousness," as we have demonstrated in previous sections.

Then there is the possibility that it names him the "Rising" <note>original: "Anatole" — this Greek word means both "East" and "Rising" (like the dawn), a common title for Christ in early Christianity.</note> because he "enlightens every man coming into the world," saying, "a star shall rise out of Jacob." As for the term "man," it foretells that he shall "rise up" <note>original: "anastēsesthai" — also the word for "resurrection."</note> from having fallen, because of the suffering that happened to him. This is similar to what Isaiah says about him: "And there shall be a root of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the nations; in him shall the nations hope." <note>Isaiah 11:10.</note>

It is certainly clear how the light of our Savior, rising from Jacob—that is, from the people of the circumcision—shone forth to all the nations, but not to Jacob itself, from whence it came. This can be understood from many other prophecies that speak directly to Christ, saying: 

> » Behold, I have set you for a covenant of the race, for a light to the nations. <note>Isaiah 42:6.</note>

Not only this, but also from the words of Balaam, through which he says: 

» There shall come out from his seed...

### From Numbers.

->How it was foretold that Christ would come to Egypt, and from there return.<-

> Balaam the son of Beor says, the man who truly sees says, he who hears the oracles of the Mighty One says, who saw a vision of God in sleep, having his eyes uncovered. How beautiful are your houses, O Jacob, and your tents, O Israel! Like shaded valleys, and like a garden by the rivers, and like tents which the Lord pitched, like cedars by the waters. A man shall come forth from his seed, and shall rule over many nations, and the kingdom of Gog shall be exalted, and his kingdom shall be increased. God led him out of Egypt; his glory is like that of a unicorn <note>original: "monokerōs." While modern bibles often say "wild ox," the Greek Septuagint used "unicorn," symbolizing strength and singular power.</note>. He shall eat the nations of his enemies, he shall suck the marrow of their fatness, and with his arrows he shall shoot through the enemy. He couched and rested like a lion, and like a lion's cub; who shall rouse him? Those who bless you are blessed, and those who curse you are cursed.

After the previous prophecy stated that the Lord would come *to* Egypt, it clearly showed the journey of our Savior Jesus Christ, which took place when He went to Egypt with His parents. In these verses, however, the prophecy follows up by describing the return *from* Egypt, which He made with His parents back to the land of Israel, saying similarly: "God led him out of Egypt." Our Savior and Lord, Jesus the Christ of God, is the only one—and no one else—who came from the seed of Israel and the Jewish nation and ruled over many nations. Therefore, it is undeniably confessed that the present prophecy finds its fulfillment in Him, explicitly proclaiming that a certain man would come out of the Jewish nation and rule many nations. Let anyone who wishes say if they can think of any famous person among the Hebrews who ever ruled over many nations. No one could say such a thing ever happened. But in the case of our Savior, even if we ourselves do not say it, the truth itself will cry out and shout aloud, immediately observing how His divine power—through the human vessel He took from the seed of Israel according to the flesh—even now rules over many nations. He, then, is that one and no other, whom the prophecy foretold, during whose time the "kingdom of Gog" <note>In the Septuagint version of this prophecy, "Gog" (a symbolic enemy of God) is mentioned, suggesting Christ's kingdom triumphs over ultimate evil.</note> was exalted as the power of Christ increased. The pattern of the Roman Empire, which was even anticipated in silence by the teaching of Christ alone. The prophet Ezekiel also mentions Gog, naming him "ruler of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal." <note>original: "ἄρχοντα ῥῶς μοσὸχ καὶ θοβὲλ"</note> By "Rosh," he seems to hint at the city of the Romans, since in the Hebrew language "Rosh" signifies both "beginning" and "head." <note>original: "διὰ τοῦ ῥῶς δηλοῦται"</note> By "Meshech," he refers to Media and the nations around it, which are now subjects of the Romans. By "Tubal," he refers to Iberia, <note>Historical Iberia refers to the region of the Caucasus (modern Georgia) or the Spanish peninsula; here it refers to the northern/eastern reaches of the known world.</note> claiming that the Iberians were descended from Tubal and called "Thobelites." It is said that in the absence of these, Gog is assumed as ruler. This points toward the prophesied presence of Christ, whom God led out of Egypt. This occurred when Herod plotted against Him while He was a child; Joseph, having been divinely warned, took the child and His mother and returned to the land of Israel. And "his glory is like a unicorn" <note>original: "δόξα δὲ μονοκέρως αὐτῷ"</note>—this refers to Christ, in whom it pleased God that "all the fullness of the Godhead should dwell," according to the holy Apostle. <note>A reference to Colossians 2:9. The "unicorn" was a symbol of singular, concentrated power.</note> Through Him, as if protected by a horn, He honors God the Father of all; thus He was named "Unicorn" in other scriptures. This same Word <term>Logos; the divine reason or person of Christ</term> of God, with His intellectual and rational arrows, drove away the enemy and the opposing Devil, along with all the invisible and wicked powers around him, through a superior and invincible power. Even now, He rules over many nations; He thins out their passions and the "mind of the flesh," preparing them for the "strange path" or the "struggle of life." Or, as the Man who came forth from Israel, 
<margin>..</margin> he who has mastered many nations, "he lay down," it says, "and rested like a lion." This refers to when He accepted the divine plan <term>oikonomia; the Incarnation and sacrifice of Christ</term>, according to which He rested like a royal and courageous beast. No one was able to displace His strength or His kingdom. And all who confess Christ, honoring the noble character of the Teacher in both word and life, have received a blessing from God, increasing every day and multiplying, 
<margin>..</margin> according to the command, "Increase and multiply, and fill the earth." <note>Genesis 1:28</note> This divine voice is fulfilled in them more truly and in a manner more worthy of God. Conversely, those descended from the seed of those who plotted against Him—who even now see Him with hostility in their councils—have drawn God’s curse upon themselves from that time until now. Because of this, they never cease to see with their own eyes the ultimate desolation and destruction, not only of their kingdom but of their formerly most venerable sanctuary. It is worth paying attention to the prophecy given to Judah by Jacob, which we have previously applied most clearly to our Savior, and to observe the 
<margin>..</margin> agreement between the two. For just as it is said here, "A man shall come forth from his

<margin>..</margin> "And he shall rule many nations," likewise in that prophecy it says, "And he shall be the 
<margin>..</margin> expectation of nations." <note>Genesis 49:10</note> And again, here it says, "He shall eat the nations of his enemies, 
<margin>..</margin> and with his arrows he shall shoot the enemy through." Similarly in that text, "Your hands 
<margin>..</margin> shall be on the back of your enemies" is written. And the phrase "a lion’s whelp, Judah," and 
<margin>..</margin> "lying down you slept like a lion, and like a whelp; who shall rouse him?" which was said in 
<margin>..</margin> that place, seems to me to differ in no way from the present passage which says, "Crouching 
<margin>..</margin> he rested like a lion, and like a whelp; who shall stir him up?" <note>Numbers 24:9</note> These things are reasonably applied to Christ, so that just as from the mouth—

And if anyone should find fault with the retreat of our Savior to Egypt, let him know that 
there was a reason for it. For it was not fitting for Him to submit to Herod's

have done, if He had pursued Herod who was plotting against Him through

common benefits, but did not defend Himself against any of those who did not listen,

silent." <note>Isaiah 53:7</note> How then was it likely that the divine Child should not retreat from the 
malice of Herod, He who is witnessed even as a man to have retreated and avoided the 
wicked, and to have hidden and fled from the praise following His miraculous deeds? 
At any rate, He commanded those healed by Him to tell no one. But if anyone 
refers the prophecy to the people [of Israel], claiming it was spoken concerning the 
people from the seed of Israel, let him attend to the sequence of the passage. It says 
these things shall be after saying, as if to Jerusalem herself:

,, "And indeed you have suffered all these things, because," it says, "Israel was a child, 
,, and I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son." For how is it possible to 
censure the same people for things, and then again to praise them for the same? But in these matters, it is clear he considers this perspective...

But what if someone should ask: why did John preach and baptize in the **wilderness**, rather than in the cities or in Jerusalem itself? I suppose one might say he did this to fulfill the prophecy. But a person wishing to examine the matter more accurately would ask: what did the prophecy intend to signify by "the wilderness" and the events taking place within it? To such a person we would say that this was also a sign of the abandonment of Jerusalem, its altars, and the <term>liturgy</term> <note>original: "λατρείας" (latreias) — the formal sacrificial worship or service performed in the Temple.</note> according to the Law of Moses. It signaled a time when the forgiveness of sins was no longer provided to them through the sacrifices of the Law, but through the purification of God provided in what was formerly "thirsty and desert"—I mean the **Church of the nations**. In this Church, the prophetic voice cries out: "In the wilderness prepare the way of the Lord." This voice raises up souls that were lying deep in the pit of wickedness, while decreeing that the former heights of Jerusalem—her rulers and kings, called "mountains and hills"—should be brought low. When these things are accomplished, he says: "All flesh shall see the salvation of God." It is clear that "all" refers to every soul living in the flesh upon the earth—ourselves, foreigners, and simply all the citizens of the nations. These things are shown to have come to their conclusion in accordance with the prediction.

I also wonder to myself: what was it about John that so amazed the crowds? Why did they marvel at him, believe in his preaching of a **baptism of repentance**, and leave their own homes in the cities from all directions to flock to the desert? This is especially striking since the records do not describe any [miraculous] act of his. It is not recorded that he raised the dead or performed other miracles. What then was it that amazed everyone? Was it perhaps his strange and altered way of life compared to the many? For he did not come from the desert dressed in normal clothing, but was famous for living apart from the common habits of men. He did not enter a village, a city, or a common gathering of men; he did not even partake in common food. It is written that from his childhood he was » in the deserts until the day of his appearance to Israel. 
» Moreover, his clothing was made of camel's hair, and his food was locusts 
» and wild honey. <note>Matthew 3:4 and Luke 1:80.</note> Perhaps, then, seeing a man who was a <term>Nazirite</term> <note>original: "ναζιραῖον" (naziraion) — a person consecrated to God, often characterized by uncut hair and specific abstinences.</note> to God in his hair, showing a face of godly character, dressed in a strange style of garment, appearing suddenly from some hidden desert and retreating back into the desert's obscurity after his preaching—fasting, solitary, and detached from the masses—they were naturally struck with awe. They no longer suspected him to be a mere man; for how could one be a man who had no need for food? Therefore, they supposed him to be that very **messenger** <note>original: "ἄγγελον" (angelon) — can mean "angel" or "messenger." Eusebius plays on this double meaning.</note> revealed through the prophet: "Behold, I send my messenger..."

I also believe that our Savior’s presence at his baptism is revealed through the phrase: "And my people shall see the glory of the Lord, and the majesty of God." <note>Isaiah 35:2.</note> For then the glory of our Savior was seen, when having been baptized he came up from the water, and the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and remaining upon him. #### Concerning the temptations of Christ after his baptism.

->He who dwells in the help of the Most High shall abide in the shelter of the God of heaven. He will say to the Lord: "You are my helper and my refuge; my God is my helper, and I will hope in Him." For He shall rescue me from the snare of the hunters, and from the troubling word. He shall overshadow you with His shoulders, and under His wings you shall hope. His truth shall surround you with a shield; you shall not be afraid of the terror by night, nor of the arrow that flies by day, nor of the thing that walks in darkness, nor of the mishap and the noon-day demon. A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand, but it shall not come near you. Only with your eyes shall you observe, and see the reward of sinners. Because You, O Lord, are my hope, you have made the Most High your refuge. No evils shall come upon you, and no scourge shall come near your dwelling. For He shall give His angels charge concerning you, to guard you in all your ways. In their hands they shall bear you up, lest you dash your foot against a stone. You shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon.<-

Our Savior and Lord, Jesus Christ the Son of God—who is understood in one sense as the subject of this healing—is the one said to be "dwelling in the help of the Most High," abiding in the shelter of God the Father. Having called upon the Savior and the other <note>i.e., the Father</note> as a refuge during the time of His temptation by the devil, He was rescued from the "snares of the opposing powers," here called "hunters." This occurred when, like an ordinary man, He was led into the desert to be tempted by the devil. For forty days and forty nights in the desert, He was tempted by Satan, and behold—as the divinely inspired writer testifies—He was "with the wild beasts." <note>Mark 1:13.</note> What kind of beasts were these? They are the ones mentioned in the Psalm at hand, which speaks of Him who dwells in the help of the Most High...

...saying, "You shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon." <note>Psalm 91:13. Eusebius views these animals as symbols for various types of demonic powers.</note> He says he will be rescued not only from these, but also from a "troubling word." <note>original: "λόγου ταραχώδους," Psalm 91:3</note> And who might this be, other than the one the Tempter puts forward to him according to the Holy Gospel? It is worth considering why such a great Savior of ours was to be tempted. For before he drove out every disease and every infirmity, along with the troubling spirits and the unclean demons that had held sway over everyone on earth for a long age through polytheistic superstition, he did not come forward to these tasks out of obscurity, as if hiding himself. 

Rather, he campaigned against those formerly invisible rulers who were troubling humanity, using the human nature he had taken upon himself. He threw himself into the midst of the devil himself and the evil gang of demons, treading upon the asp and basilisk, and trampling the lion and dragon. He brought down something much worse: thousands and ten-thousands of demonic enemies—the principalities and powers warring from the right and from the left—and even those called the "world-rulers of this darkness" <note>original: "κοσμοκράτορας τοῦ σκότους τούτου," cf. Ephesians 6:12</note> and the spiritual forces of wickedness. 

Having proven all these to have no strength, and finally having driven far away the leader of evils, the devil himself, by the word of his mouth, he passed through and utterly defeated all the power of the adversaries. By offering himself to those who wished to approach and tempt him, and being pursued by no one, <note>Eusebius implies Jesus sought out the confrontation in the desert rather than being forced into it.</note> he thus proceeded toward the salvation of men. Because of this, when the demons saw him, they recognized him from the excellence he had previously shown in the desert, saying to him, "What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God?" <note>Matthew 8:29</note>

So much for these matters. The following parts of the Psalm are addressed to Christ himself, starting from: "Because with his pinions he will overshadow you"—clearly meaning the Most High—"and under his wings you shall hope; his truth shall encircle you with a shield." <note>Psalm 91:4</note> And since he was tempted for forty days and as many nights, what is said concerning those things attacking him by night is: "You shall not be afraid of the terror by night"; and concerning those warring against him by day: "from the arrow that flies by day." And again, concerning the things at night: "from the thing that walks in darkness"; and concerning those in the day: "from the mishap and the noonday demon." <note>original: "δαιμονίου μεσημβρινοῦ," Psalm 91:6. In early Christian thought, the 'noonday demon' was often associated with spiritual weariness or direct midday attacks.</note> 

Then, since evil powers surrounded him while he was being tempted, and some held his right side, but many more were on the left—as the right is naturally stronger—it is appropriately said to him: "A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand, but it shall not come near you." <note>Psalm 91:7</note> The "side" <note>original: "κλίτος"</note> refers here to the left side, but the name "left" was appropriately kept silent because nothing sinister or "left-handed" <note>original: "σκαιὸν" or "ἀριστερὸν." In Greek, these words can mean 'left' but also carry connotations of being unlucky, awkward, or morally wrong.</note> was to be found in him. 

And since a whole ten-thousand, along with a thousand, are said to fall from both his side and his right, it is fittingly said next: "Only with your eyes shall you observe, and see the reward of sinners." And these things shall happen, he says, concerning you, the Christ of God, because: "You, O Lord, who are our hope, have made the Most High your refuge." <note>Psalm 91:8-9</note> Then, having paused, the Prophet says to the Lord himself: "For you, O Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge," accurately distinguishing between one Lord specifically and His Father, the Most High God. Because he [Christ] made Him his refuge as Father and Most High God...

<summary>Eusebius interprets Psalm 91 as a prophecy of Christ's victory over the devil and demonic legions during the Temptation in the wilderness. He argues that this victory was a necessary precursor to Jesus's public ministry of healing and salvation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s detailed Christological commentary on Psalm 91. Having established that the Savior faced demonic temptations in the wilderness, Eusebius now focuses on the divine protection promised to the Messiah and the specific nature of his "dwelling"—his human body.</meta>

<page-num>271</page-num>
<header>THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 9</header>

...as Christ offers up his own life, it is said to him: "No evil shall come to you, and no plague shall draw near to your dwelling. For he shall give his angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways. They shall bear you up in their hands, lest you dash your foot against a stone." <note>Psalm 91:10–12. Eusebius interprets these verses as the Father's promise to the Son during his earthly mission.</note> Pay careful attention to the manner in which this is expressed: "Because you, O Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge." 

The word "Lord" here is represented in the Hebrew by the <term>Tetragrammaton<note>original: "τετραγράμμου ὀνόματος" — the four-letter Hebrew name of God (YHWH).</note></term> (which is unutterable), as the children of the Hebrews say, and which they are accustomed to use for God alone. However, we have previously demonstrated from many scriptures that this title is also applied to the divinity of the Word <note>The "Logos" or the pre-existent Son of God.</note>. Just so, in the Psalm currently in our hands, the text speaks to the person of the Lord himself: "Because you, O Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge." This is almost like saying: "Since you yourself, O Lord—who are the hope of me, the one prophesying these things—recognize that God the Most High is greater than yourself, you have made Him your refuge." 

For this reason, it was said at the beginning of the Psalm concerning the same person: "He who dwells in the help of the Most High shall abide under the shelter of the God of heaven. He shall say to the Lord: 'You are my helper and my refuge; my God, my helper, and I will hope in Him.'" <note>Psalm 91:1–2.</note> Because you, O Lord, have made the Most High your refuge, the Most High himself says: "He shall deliver you from the snare of the hunters, and from a troubling word." In other translations, this is rendered as "through overshadowing." Having such fatherly help from the Most High, you shall not be afraid of the terror by night, nor of any of the things mentioned before, nor of those that follow. 

Because "you, O Lord, have made the Most High your refuge," therefore "no evil shall come to you, and no plague shall draw near to your dwelling." By "plagues," the text refers to the active operations of demons, which in other places are called "assaults." The text says these are not even able to approach the <term>dwelling<note>original: "σκηνώματι" (skēnōma) — literally a tent or tabernacle; here referring to the physical body.</note></term> of Christ—that is, his body. For how could they, when he drove them out of men with only a word? 

Regarding this "dwelling," David once swore to the Lord and vowed to the God of Jacob, saying: "I will not enter the room of my house, I will not go up to the bed of my couch; I will not give sleep to my eyes, nor slumber to my eyelids, nor rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob." <note>Psalm 132:2–5.</note> And for the sake of this dwelling, it was said: "You shall not be afraid of the terror by night," and "He shall deliver you from the snare of the hunters and from a troubling word," and "No evil shall come to you, and no plague shall draw near to your dwelling," along with all the more "human" things said about him. 

<margin>T</margin>
For instance, "He shall give his angels charge over you, to keep you," and "They shall bear you up in their hands, lest you dash your foot against a stone." These things would not be fitting if said to God <note>i.e., God in His pure divine essence.</note>, but they fit his "dwelling," which he took up for our sake when "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us." <note>John 1:14.</note> 

It seems right to me to confirm these statements by setting out the words of the other translators. Among them, **Aquila** spoke thus: "Because you, Lord, are my hope; you have set the Most High as your habitation. Evil shall not be brought to you, and a touch shall not draw near in your shelter. For he shall command his angels to guard you in all your ways." 

**Symmachus**, however, says: "For you, Lord, are my fearlessness; you have made the Most High your dwelling. No evil shall reach you, nor shall a touch draw near to your tent. For he shall command his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways..."

<sig>Zz.iiii.</sig>

<summary>Eusebius interprets Psalm 91 as a dialogue between the Father and the Son, arguing that the "dwelling" protected from demons is the physical body of Christ. He uses alternative Greek translations by Aquila and Symmachus to support his reading of Christ's human and divine nature.</summary>

> » Therefore, by these very words, it is spoken to the Lord as if concerning another greater being: "He shall give his angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways. In their hands they shall bear you up"—clearly meaning you, the Lord—"lest you, the Lord, dash your foot against a stone." <note>Psalm 91:11–12. Eusebius is analyzing how the Psalm distinguishes between the Father who gives the command and the Son who receives protection.</note> Even the devil made use of these words during the temptation of our Savior, when he took him into the holy city, set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him: "If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down from here; for it is written, 'He shall give his angels charge over you, and in their hands they shall bear you up, lest you dash your foot against a stone.'" To whom our Lord answered and said: "It is written, 'You shall not tempt the Lord your God.'" <note>Matthew 4:5–7.</note> Furthermore, since during the temptation he was with the wild beasts—for he was with the devil—though it is not recorded exactly what kind they were,

the prophecy of the Psalm makes this more clear by hinting at the species of the beasts, saying: "You shall tread upon the asp and the <term>basilisk<note>original: "βασιλίσκον" — a mythical serpent king, often used in early Christian writing to symbolize high-ranking demonic powers.</note>," and "you shall trample the lion and the dragon underfoot." It is therefore testified that he would trample underfoot the most dominant of the intellectual "beasts"—the lion and the dragon, the asp and the basilisk—meaning the devil himself and the ruling, wicked powers that are with him. Moreover, to his disciples and apostles who possessed a virtue similar to his own, he himself grants the authority to "tread upon snakes and scorpions," <note>Luke 10:19.</note> not allowing them to be tempted beyond what they are able to bear. For he alone is the one who, by his own power, brings down the powers that set their hands to wickedness, even the very ruler and tyrant of this age.

### Concerning the Galilee of the Gentiles, where our Savior performed most of his wonders, and concerning the calling of his apostles.

<margin>T</margin>
> » "Drink this first, act quickly, O land of Zebulun, land of Naphtali, and the rest who dwell by the seacoast and beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles. The phrase "Drink this first" (original: "Τοῦτο πρῶτον πίε") is a peculiar reading found in some Septuagint Greek manuscripts of Isaiah.</note> "The greatest part of the people whom you brought down in your joy, they shall rejoice before you as those who rejoice in the harvest, and in the manner of those who divide the spoil. Leaving Nazareth, he went and dwelt in Capernaum by the sea, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: "The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, by the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles—the people sitting in darkness saw a great light, and to those sitting in the land and shadow of death, light has dawned." <note>Matthew 4:12–16.</note> From that time Jesus began to preach and to say, "Repent, for the [kingdom of heaven] is at hand."

## From Isaiah
### Concerning the prophetic reading which our Lord himself went through in the synagogue of the Jews.

> **T**he Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to call for the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of recompense.

Our Lord himself acknowledges that this prophecy was fulfilled in himself. When he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, he entered the synagogue on the Sabbath day according to his custom. When he stood up to read, the book of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him. Opening the book, he found the place where it was written:
> The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to send the oppressed away in liberty, to call for the acceptable year of the Lord. And closing the book, he gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on him. And he began to say to them: "Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing." <note>This event is recorded in the Gospel of Luke 4:16–21.</note>

Through this scripture, our Savior and Lord clearly appears to be anointed in a distinct and superior way compared to the priests of old who were anointed in a more physical manner. He was not anointed with "prepared oil" <note>original: "ἐλαίῳ σκευαστῷ" — the physical holy anointing oil described in Exodus 30.</note>, nor by any human being as others were, but he was anointed with the Divine Spirit—the Spirit of God the Father himself. Sharing in the unbegotten Divinity of the Father, he is proclaimed "God" and "Lord" according to the Holy Scriptures.

Furthermore, in accordance with the prophecy at hand, he is introduced by Matthew as "preaching good news to the poor." This occurred when he saw the crowds and went up onto the mountain; when he sat down, his disciples came to him, and opening his mouth, he taught them, saying: 
> Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. <note>Matthew 5:3.</note>

It is also recorded that he provided "recovery of sight to the blind" for many. He did not only grant sight to those whose physical eyes were mutilated, but he was also the cause of intellectual vision and the knowledge of the God of the Universe for those who were previously "blind of soul" <note>original: "ψυχῇ τυφλώττουσιν."</note>. Moreover, to those who were prisoners and captives led away by invisible and demonic powers, and to those bound by chains of evil, he proclaimed "release" and "liberation" from what held them—provided they believed in his proclamation. As those who had been set free, they might run to him as Savior, being persuaded by his commands. The remaining parts of this divine oracle will be examined in due course in the sections concerning the Promise.

God. Indeed, at the end of Deuteronomy it is said, "There has not yet arisen a prophet 
in Israel like Moses." <note>Deuteronomy 34:10.</note> Even if ten thousand prophets have appeared after him, yet 
none were like him. But this whole promise of God pledges that He will raise up one specific person, and not many, 
who is similar to him. It reveals him to be a lawgiver <term>nomothetēs</term> and a teacher of 
piety to men, such as our Savior and Lord Jesus the Christ alone has been 
shown to be—one who is both a lawgiver and a prophet of the God of the universe, and who has become His servant. 
But whereas Moses led a single nation and was shown to be a lawgiver for them 
alone, and not for other nations, the Christ of God, having received the 
promise from the Father—"Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your 
inheritance"—was put forward as a common lawgiver of piety under the Father, not 
only for the Jews but for all of humanity, providing a legislation that is 
capable and fitting for the calling of all the nations. Just as Moses, by his 
power, [gave laws to the people], so Christ through the Evangelists 
arranged laws for the priests of the whole world, legislating with an authority 
greater than that of a mere human, saying: "You have heard that it 
was said to the ancients, 'You shall not murder'; but I say to you not to even be angry without cause," and 
those things following which are contained in his Gospel teachings. Regarding these, 
the Evangelist bears witness, saying that "everyone was amazed at his teaching; 
for he was teaching them as one having authority, and not like their scribes." <note>Matthew 7:28–29.</note> 
We have already gone through the character of our Savior’s teaching 
and legislation at the beginning of this present work, when we briefly summarized 
what Christianity is; we shall refer readers back to those points now. 
Pay attention to the reason why the Lord promises to raise up a 
prophet for them. For when He had commanded Moses 
himself to purify all the people for three days, so that they might become both 
spectators and listeners of the divine manifestation, they were terrified by 
God's grace. Therefore, at the beginning of the vision, they said in fear 
to Moses, "You speak to us, and let not God speak to us, lest we die." 
Reasonably, because of this, the Lord accepts them for their reverence and 
says, "They have spoken rightly in all they have said. I will raise up for them 
a prophet from their midst, from their brothers, like you." 
Therefore, he has taught us the reason why He made a manifestation 
greater than a [standard] prophet for mankind: it was because of the 
weakness of men and their shrinking back from the greater vision. 
Thus you have the reason for the divine declaration concerning the prophesied 
<margin>Π</margin> prophet. Reasonably, then, those of the circumcision <note>The Jewish people.</note> who were 
expecting him asked John the Baptist, saying, "Are you the Prophet?" And 
he said, "No." <note>John 1:21.</note> But John, in confessing the truth, did not deny that he 
was a prophet—for indeed he was—but he was not *the* Prophet...

<summary>Eusebius interprets the prophecy of Deuteronomy 18, arguing that Jesus is the "Prophet like Moses" because he acted as a divine lawgiver for all nations, whereas Moses was only for the Jews. He contrasts the terrifying direct voice of God at Sinai with the accessible teaching of Christ, which was promised in response to human fear.</summary>

...the prophet who was declared by Moses. He also taught that he had been sent before that very prophet. <margin>»</margin> He rebukes them in other places, saying: "Because I came, and there was no man; I

Thus, we who are from the nations <note>the Gentiles</note> have recognized and accepted the one who was

Gospel teaching. In this way, another prophecy was also fulfilled through Him, 
<margin>»</margin> which says: "Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them; let the nations know that 
<margin>»</margin> they are but men." <note>Psalm 9:20 (9:21 in some numbering)</note> But the nation of the 
Jews, by not accepting the one who was prophesied, paid the deserved 
<margin>»</margin> penalty according to the divine prediction which said: "And the man who 
<margin>»</margin> will not listen to all that the prophet shall speak in my name, I will take 
<margin>»</margin> vengeance on him." <note>Deuteronomy 18:19</note> Vengeance has indeed been taken upon that 
people for "all the blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah," 
and above all for the blood of Christ, which they claimed for themselves and even 
against their own children; to this day they still undergo the punishment for the

->Concerning Christ walking on the sea.<-

"He who speaks to the sun, and it does not rise, and seals up the stars; He who stretched out 
<margin>»</margin> the heaven alone, and walks upon the sea as if upon a floor." <note>Job 9:7-8</note> These 
words would fit only the God and Lord of us all, who is the Creator of the universe 
through His Word. Certainly, He alone of all who have ever lived during the times of 
<margin>»</margin> His incarnation, having taken on a human body and form, is said to have 
<margin>»</margin> walked upon the sea—namely, when He compelled His disciples to get 
<margin>»</margin> into a boat and go before Him to the other side, while He dismissed the crowds. 
<margin>»</margin> And after dismissing the crowds, He went up into the mountain by Himself to 
<margin>»</margin> pray. When evening came, He was there alone. But the boat was already in the 
<margin>»</margin> middle of the sea. Seeing Him walking on the sea, they were terrified, saying, 
<margin>»</margin> "It is a ghost!" and they cried out in fear. But immediately He spoke to them, 
<margin>»</margin> saying, "Take heart; it is I; do not be afraid." <note>Matthew 14:22-27</note> Simply put, 
it would not seem worthy of God <note>in a theological sense</note> to interpret these words 
if one were to take this passage as referring only to the Most High God and Father of all. 
For what would be so grand or noteworthy for the God of the universe to be 
said to walk upon the sea? How could a "walk" upon the sea even be 
understood for Him who contains all things?

## From Isaiah.

# Concerning the wonders performed by Him.

<margin>»</margin>"Be strong, you relaxed hands and paralyzed knees; be encouraged, you 
<margin>»</margin>faint-hearted in mind; be strong, do not fear. Behold, our God renders 
<margin>»</margin>judgment, and He will render it; He will come and save us. Then the eyes 
<margin>»</margin>of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear. Then 
<margin>»</margin>the lame man shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute shall be clear." 
<margin>»</margin><note>Isaiah 35:3-6</note> You can find the fulfillments of these things in the Gospels. 
On one hand, there was the time our Savior and Lord was presented with a paralytic 
lying on a bed, whom He restored to health by His word. On the other hand, there 
were the countless blind and demon-possessed, and those suffering from various 
diseases and infirmities, who were delivered from their sufferings by His saving 
power. Moreover, even until now, throughout the whole world, vast multitudes 
bound by various forms of vice and whose souls are filled with ignorance of the 
God over all, are healed and cured by the medicines of His teaching in a 
marvelous way that surpasses all reason. Furthermore, it has already been 
demonstrated by us in the testimonies regarding His divinity that God is 
foretold in these passages as acting in this manner at the appointed time. It 
follows then to recognize that if He is confessed as God, it is because He 
displayed works of divine and truly godly power. For it belongs to God alone—and 
to no one else—to strengthen the paralyzed, to give life to the dead, to provide 
healing to the sick, to open the eyes of the blind, to heal the hearing of the 
deaf, to straighten the lame, and to restore clear speech to those whose tongues 
are tied. All these things were performed by our Savior Jesus Christ, as 
works of God, and...

<meta>The Greek word "memu-" at the bottom is a catchword, the beginning of the word "initiated" or "mystically" (memuēmenos), which will continue on the next page.</meta>

<summary>Eusebius interprets Christ's miracles, such as walking on water and healing the sick, as symbolic victories over spiritual forces of chaos (the "dragon") and fulfillments of Isaiah's prophecies. He argues that such works prove Jesus's divine nature, as only God possesses the power to restore the blind, deaf, and paralyzed.</summary>

### PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 9
<sig>AAa.ii.</sig>
<meta>catchword: throne</meta>

This has indeed been witnessed by the many who heralded Him throughout the entire inhabited world. The unfeigned and true nature of their testimony is proven by the trial of tortures, their persistence even unto death, and the courage they displayed before kings, rulers, governors, and entire nations, bearing witness to the truth of what they preached. To these very men—His evangelists and apostles—we might say the prophetic spirit calls out:

> Strengthen the relaxed hands and the paralyzed knees. For since they transformed their "manual" and practical powers, as well as their steps and their path, away from the long cycles of worship according to the Law of Moses, He rouses them toward the citizenship of the Gospel, saying: "Strengthen the relaxed hands and the paralyzed knees," <note>Isaiah 35:3</note> clearly preparing them for the race of the Gospel.

Be strong also in exhorting others, and urge them forward to take hold of the salvation of the Gospel—you who were formerly faint-hearted <note>original: "oligopsychoi," literally "small-souled" or discouraged</note>. Let no fear of those attacking the Gospel from the outside seize you, but be strong in the face of these things as well, and do not be afraid. For our God and the Word of God <note>term: "Word of God" (Logos) - the divine reason or person of Christ existing before His birth</note>—not some Moses, or a mere neighbor, or anyone like the prophets—shall be shown not only as the maker of these wonders, but as the very cause of your own strength. 

The clearest proof of our Savior's divine power would be the things prophesied of Him, through which He truly healed the lame, the blind, the lepers, and the paralyzed. He did this sometimes by His word, through the scriptures written about Him, and even still now through the divine virtue of His godhead acting throughout the whole inhabited world. Through these works, He demonstrates what kind of person He was even then to those capable of seeing; for after such a long time, the word announced concerning Him remains enduring and unconquered, as truly the Word of God. He has prepared for Himself all those who would be helped, even while others up to the present day continue to war against His teaching. He draws to Himself myriads of multitudes from the entire world, delivering those who approach Him from every sin and from the ancient diseases of the soul. He invites every race of Greeks and barbarians alike to His pious teaching, becoming the cause of countless blessings through the knowledge of the only true God, and leading them toward a healthy and sober life—which is indeed fitting for the promise of a religion belonging to the God of all.

> Then our same God, being the Word of God, says: "He will render judgment, and He will repay; He Himself will come and save us." <note>Isaiah 35:4</note> For according to the Psalm which says, "Give your judgment, O God, to the king," <note>Psalm 72:1</note> and according to the Gospel teaching which says, "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son," <note>John 5:22</note> He has received the authority to judge from the Father. Judging with righteousness, He repaid the people of the circumcision <note>note: a common patristic term for the Jewish people</note> with the penalty for their disobedience and the outrages they dared against Him and His prophets; yet, for all men without exception who were present at His coming, He saved them equally according to justice, opening the ears of their understanding and their eyes. 

Therefore, the Divine Word calls the time of His presence a "time of repayment," saying in other places that He has come to "proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of repayment." <note>Isaiah 61:2</note> And since the time of repayment has come—in which all the blood shed from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah <note>note: reference to Matthew 23:35, summarizing the history of martyred prophets</note> has been vindicated by Him (even the precious blood of Jesus) upon the generation of those who sinned against Him—they have, as a result, suffered their final destruction...

<summary>Eusebius interprets Isaiah 35 as a command for the Apostles to transition from the Mosaic Law to the Gospel. He argues that Christ’s miracles and the global spread of Christianity prove His divinity as the "Word of God" who brings both healing to the faithful and judgment to the disobedient.</summary>

...thron, and the final siege <note>Referring to the Roman siege and destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD, which Eusebius views as divine judgment on the Jewish leadership.</note>. And the judgment against those men brought about such a retribution against them. As the prophecy says: 

> Behold, our God will repay judgment, and he will repay. <note>Isaiah 35:4</note>

### Concerning the signs and wonders which He performed.

> Then those who seal the law so as not to learn <note>The Septuagint Greek text here is somewhat obscure; Eusebius will later compare it to other translations to clarify.</note> will be manifest. And I will say: I will wait for the God who turned away His face from the house of Jacob, and I will be trustful in Him. Behold I, and the children whom God gave to me. And there shall be signs and wonders in Israel from the Lord of Sabaoth <note>term: "Sabaoth" - a Hebrew title for God meaning "of Hosts" or "of Armies."</note>, who dwells on Mount Zion. And if they say to you: "Seek the mediums <note>original: "engastrimythous" - literally "belly-speakers" or ventriloquists, used for those who summoned spirits of the dead.</note>, and those who speak from the ground, those who talk vanities and speak from their bellies," is not a nation to look toward its God? Why do they seek the dead concerning the living? For He gave a law for help. <note>Isaiah 8:16-20</note>

In the Epistle to the Hebrews, the divine Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul, the traditional author of Hebrews.</note> elaborates on the phrase: "Behold, I and the children whom God gave me," speaking about Christ: "Since then the children have shared in blood and flesh, He himself similarly partook of the same things, so that through death He might destroy the one having the power of death." <note>Hebrews 2:13-14</note> In these words, he names the Apostles as His "children," through whom the Lord of Sabaoth, who dwells on Mount Zion, teaches that He will perform signs and wonders in the house of Israel. He says these men themselves will be manifest, sealing our faces with the seal of Christ <note>A reference to the "seal" (sphragis) of baptism or the sign of the cross.</note>, and being trained no longer to learn the Law of Moses, since it no longer stands, and the so-called "house of Jacob" has been abandoned by God. 

What was stated unclearly in the Septuagint <note>The standard Greek translation of the Old Testament used by the early Church.</note> as: "Then those who seal the law so as not to learn will be manifest. And I will say: I will wait for the God who turned away His face from the house of Jacob, and I will be trustful in Him," Symmachus <note>A late 2nd-century translator of the Old Testament into Greek, known for more literal or clearer renderings than the Septuagint.</note> translated more clearly, saying: 

> "Bind up the testimony, seal the law in my teachings. And I will look for the Lord who hides His face from the house of Jacob, and I will wait for Him." 

And Aquila <note>A 2nd-century Jewish proselyte who produced an extremely literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> also translated in this manner: 

> "Bind up the testimony, seal the law among those taught by me. And I will accept the God who hides His face from the house of Jacob, and I will endure Him." 

These things indeed the Apostles of our Savior are taught to do. To which he adds next: "Behold I and the children, whom God gave me. And it shall be for signs and wonders in Israel from..."

### Concerning the lack of ostentation in the miracles Christ performed.
<note>The Greek term "phanetian" refers to a desire for showy display or boasting. Eusebius is arguing that Christ performed miracles with humility rather than for fame.</note>

<margin>I</margin>
> Jacob is my servant, I will uphold him; Israel is my chosen, my soul has accepted him. He will bring forth judgment to the nations. He will not cry out, nor will he cease, nor will his voice be heard outside. A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoking wick he will not quench, but he will bring forth judgment in truth. He will shine forth and will not be crushed, until he has set judgment upon the earth; and in his name the nations will hope. Thus says the Lord God, who made the heaven and established it, who strengthened the earth and the things in it, and who gives breath to the people upon it, and spirit to those who walk on it. I, the Lord God, have called you in righteousness, and I will hold your hand, and I will strengthen you, and I have given you for a covenant of a race, for a light of the nations, to open the eyes of the blind, and to bring out the prisoners from their bonds, and those who sit in darkness from the prison house. <note>Isaiah 42:1-7</note>

The Evangelist <note>Matthew</note>, being mindful of this passage, cited it when the Pharisees went out and took counsel against him, how they might destroy him because he was healing the sick on the Sabbath. For at that time, as he says, Jesus, knowing the conspiracy against him, withdrew from there. And great crowds followed him, and he healed them all, and he warned them that they should not make him known. To these things he adds, saying that all this happened—that is, his withdrawing, his avoiding those who plotted against him, his striving to remain hidden in the wonders he performed, and his charging those who were healed not to talk idly about him—so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying:

> Behold my servant, whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my spirit upon him, and he will proclaim judgment to the nations. He will not wrangle or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets. A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings judgment to victory, and in his name the nations will hope. <note>Matthew 12:18-21, quoting Isaiah 42:1-4</note>

Observe carefully the manner in which Matthew, having said "Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul is well pleased," mentioned neither Jacob nor Israel. For he did not say "Jacob my servant" or "Israel my chosen," but he set it forth indefinitely, saying "Behold my servant" and "my beloved." Hence, since these names do not lie in the Hebrew prophecy, they have been obelized <note>original: "obelistai" — an obelus (—) was a proofreading mark used by ancient scholars like Origen to indicate that words in the Greek Septuagint were not present in the original Hebrew text.</note> in the version of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>...

<summary>Eusebius explains that Christ’s habit of withdrawing from crowds and silencing those he healed was a fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy regarding the Messiah's humility. He also highlights a textual discrepancy where the Gospel of Matthew matches the Hebrew original more closely than the Septuagint by omitting the names "Jacob" and "Israel."</summary>

...and what was omitted by the other translators <note>original: "hermeneutais" — Eusebius is likely referring to the other Greek versions of the Old Testament by Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, which he often compared with the Septuagint.</note> was passed over because it is not found in the Hebrew text. It was reasonable that these things were not mentioned by the later translators, as they were Hebrew and followed the Hebrew scripture in setting out the prophecy. It is not possible for the Jews, as a people of the circumcision, to think that these promises apply to them; they apply only to the Christ of God, as witnessed by the clarity and the outcome of events. For he alone proclaimed the coming judgment to the nations <note>original: "ethnesi" — meaning the non-Jewish world or Gentiles.</note>, having lived his life among men quietly during his stay on earth, and having established judgment upon the earth. And he not only "did not break a bruised reed," but, if one might say so, he bound it up, set it upright, and made it strong; he drew to himself the weak and those who were broken in heart. Just as he did not overlook the weak and the frail who needed his healing, nor did he break them by condemning them when they repented; so also he did not extinguish those who persisted in evils and were "smoldering" <note>original: "typhomenous" — literally "smoking" or "fuming," used here for those consumed by passions.</note> under their passions, preventing them from acting according to their own choice. Nor did he reserve another time for their punishment, so that he might keep the penalty they deserved for the time of the universal judgment. Therefore it is said, "and a smoldering wick he will not quench." And the phrase, "and in his name the nations shall hope," has reached a pure fulfillment. For the Christian nations have hoped in the name of our Savior Jesus Christ alone, being inscribed with his name as children of the piety that was foretold. For if it was prophesied that he was given as a light to none other than the nations, it is through him, following the prediction, that the eyes of the blind—those whose minds were previously blinded—have been opened. And not only these, but also those whose bodies were failing; and those who were previously covered in darkness and ignorance of true piety, bound by the chains of their own sins, have through him been released from sin and deemed worthy of the light of knowledge and the counsel of the Father. For if you examine the text carefully at your leisure, following the explanations given, you would find every single detail declared therein to be accurately fulfilled in our Lord and Savior alone.

"I saw the Lord sitting on a high and lofty throne, and seraphim stood around him." And he said, 'Go, and say to this people: You shall hear indeed, but you shall not understand; and you shall see indeed, but you shall not perceive. <header>EVANGELICAL PROOF. Book 9.</header>

"...lest they should turn, and I should heal them." <note>original: "kai epistrepsōsi, kai iasomai autous" — quoting Isaiah 6:10.</note> Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke of him. And in the Gospel of Matthew, the disciples approached him and said, "Why do you speak to them in parables?" And he answered and said, "To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom, but to them it has not been given. For this reason I speak to them in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not hear, lest they should turn, and I should heal them." Then was fulfilled in them the prophecy of Isaiah which says, "Go and say to this people: You shall indeed hear, but never understand," <note>original: "akoē akousete, kai ou mē sunēte" — quoting Isaiah 6:9.</note> and so on. Having observed some of the things I have mentioned, John adds: "Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke of him," <note>John 12:41</note> implying that the prophet had seen the Christ in the glory of Christ, even that vision of God <term>theoptia</term> <note>A direct vision or manifestation of God.</note> in which he said, "I saw the Lord of Hosts <note>original: "Sabaoth"</note> sitting upon a high and exalted throne," and the rest. 

Who indeed would not be amazed at this prediction, seeing so clearly even now the unbelief of those of the circumcision <note>original: "ek peritomēs" — a common term for the Jewish people.</note> toward Christ? In ancient times, they clearly saw him performing manifest and wonderful works, yet they did not see him with the eyes of the soul or the vision of the mind. Nor was there in them any faculty of intellectual remembrance to understand who it was that performed such great and marvelous wonders and displayed such power among them. But even though they were deemed worthy to receive the proclamations of eternal life and to listen to the voice of divine wisdom, they did not hear with their understanding; thus the prophecy brought its clear fulfillment upon them. And even until now, though they see the immense power of Christ—through which every race of men has abandoned ancient superstitions and been brought under his way of godliness—they do not apply their minds to it. Nor do they consider how this was never achieved by Moses, nor by the prophets after Moses, for their own people alone—that is, the command not to worship idols or follow the error of many gods—yet it has been accomplished for all nations through the sacred and divine power of the Savior. Furthermore, when they encounter the prophetic testimonies concerning him, they indeed "hear with their ears," but they do not understand, for the prophecy at hand is being fulfilled against them in actual fact even to this day.

And if anyone says anything to you, say to him, 'The Lord has need of them.'" And they went and did as he commanded them. These aspects of the prophecy...

<meta>This page continues Eusebius's Ninth Book of the *Evangelical Proof*, where he distinguishes between the two "advents" of Christ. On the previous page, he discussed Isaiah’s prophecy regarding the spiritual blindness of the Jewish people; he now moves to harmonize the seemingly contradictory prophecies of the Messiah’s humble arrival on a donkey (Zechariah) and his glorious arrival on the clouds (Daniel).</meta>

<page-num>284</page-num>
<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

And the conclusion of this matter takes this form: if the prophecy intended to signify his riding upon a donkey—not his very humble and inglorious presence—would it not have also made this clear? Since there is also a second, glorious advent, this too had to be shown more clearly, as the prophet uncovers the vision, saying:

> *I beheld until the thrones were set, and the Ancient of Days sat. Thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. And behold, with the clouds of heaven, one like a son of man coming. And he came to the Ancient of Days, and to him was given the dominion, and the honor and the kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and languages serve him. His authority is an eternal authority, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed.* <note>Daniel 7:9–14</note>

The details of the first arrival were more human and humble; involving irrational animals, it provided a great sign and wonder—namely, that the "Quiet One" was said to be on a horse, or rather, to be seen openly riding a strange beast of burden. For this would be a token of a common and useful human life. But the details of the second and divine arrival are revealed as most brilliant because of his passage upon the clouds of heaven and his eternal kingdom over all the nations. 

If it is right to compare both prophecies with one another and to meet their logic, how could we sustain the prophecies if we expected only a single arrival of Christ? For since both sides agree that they see Christ himself in both prophecies, it is time for them to answer our questions: how is it possible, at one and the same time and during a single arrival, for the same person to be carried upon the clouds of heaven and also to be riding upon a beast of burden and a young colt? For these two things are very far apart from each other. 

By gathering ten thousand such prophecies about Christ, and by setting them side by side and clashing the different things signified, you will most clearly perceive that some contain signs of his first presence, fulfilled during his first appearance <term>epiphaneia</term> <note>original: "epiphaneian" — a manifest appearance or "epiphany."</note>, while others refer to his second and glorious arrival. For the power of our Savior, during his first presence, secretly destroyed the chariots and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war, from the physical Jerusalem and the people called "Ephraim." <note>A reference to Zechariah 9:10.</note> Because of this, from that time until now, their kingdom no longer stands, nor does their preparation and military power that was strong of old in wars. 

It was well done in these passages to name the whole people of the Jews "Ephraim," rather than Joseph or Judah, so as not to slander the more noble names. You would find also in other prophecies that the great nation is named "Ephraim" with much slander and accusation, just as it is here. Certainly, after the return from Babylon, the people were no longer divided as before; so who else could be signified by "Ephraim" but those who inhabit Jerusalem? Their warlike and military power lasted until the Roman times, but the presence of our Savior brought it down by a divine and unutterable power, exactly as in the prophecy. 

This Word <note>original: "ho logos" — referring both to the Scripture and to Christ as the Word.</note> brings good news to the Church from the nations, commanding her not simply to rejoice, but to rejoice exceedingly because of the presence of the Word of God within her. He calls her the daughter of the heavenly Zion, or even the daughter of the former Synagogue. Therefore, he has sent us—those from the nations who have believed in the Christ of God—to be the offspring and children of Christ,

<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s argument from the previous page, where he contrasted the humble first arrival of Christ with the glorious second coming. Here, he focuses on how the "humble" arrival (on a donkey) brought about a historical era of world peace, fulfilling various Old Testament prophecies.</meta>

[of] Christ, and his apostles, who came forth from the Jewish synagogue <note>The Greek term *synagogue* here refers to the Jewish community or "assembly" as a whole.</note> as if from a mother. And the following things were fulfilled at the presence of our Savior. A simple, unalloyed peace has existed among the nations since the time of his arrival, such as never existed before. At the very least, cities no longer war against cities as they did in the past, nor do nations clash with nations. Nor is human life in a state of constant upheaval as it was of old, when Athenians marched against Spartans, Syrians against Phoenicians, Arabs against Palestinians, and Egyptians against their neighbors. 

Instead, from that time onward, with God's help, all things have changed. Truly, a "multitude of peace" <note>A reference to Psalm 72:7.</note> among the nations has existed from then until now, in accordance with the prophecy. Jesus alone, and the word of the Gospel teaching proclaimed through him, has "ruled from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the setting sun, and from the rivers even to the ends of the earth," <note>original: "ἀπὸ θαλάσσης ἕως θαλάσσης... ἕως τὰς διεκϐολὰς τῆς γῆς"</note> just as was foretold in the prophets. Indeed, Zechariah interpreted it this way, saying: 

<margin>“And he shall speak peace to the nations, and his authority shall be from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth.”</margin> <note>Zechariah 9:10</note>

Compare these words with those in the Psalm inscribed "to Solomon," regarding the son of the king—meaning the one expected from the seed of Solomon—about whom the Psalm says: 

<margin>“And he shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the inhabited world.”</margin> <note>Psalm 72:8 (71 in the Septuagint)</note>

The same Psalm also signifies the peace mentioned, stating: 

<margin>“In his days, righteousness shall arise, and a multitude of peace.”</margin> <note>Psalm 72:7</note>

Isaiah also agreed with these points, through which he says: 

<margin>“And they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; and nation shall no longer lift up sword against nation, and they shall not learn to war anymore.”</margin> <note>Isaiah 2:4</note>

Others, such as Micah and many more of the prophets, harmonize with these things. If you pay close attention, as I said, to the timing, you will be able to see how—from the era of Augustus and the dawning of our Savior’s appearance during his reign—the Roman monarchy prevailed. This ended the ancient divisions and the "rule by many" <note>term: polyarchy (πολυαρχία) – a political system where many different leaders or small states hold power, often leading to internal conflict.</note> that had previously divided the nations. From that time, the world began to receive the law of the prophesied peace. It clearly began then, but the prophecy will be most fully completed when "the fullness of the nations" <note>A reference to Romans 11:25.</note> has entered, which was declared by the holy Apostle.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Christ’s dual "arrivals" (advents). Eusebius is contrasting the humble, physical arrival of Jesus in Jerusalem with the cosmic, glorious arrival predicted in the Book of Daniel to explain why both sets of prophecies are valid but refer to different events.</meta>

# EUSEBIUS

...and the pattern of this conclusion would be thus. If he wished to signify his riding on a donkey—that is, his entire humble and inglorious presence <note>The word "presence" here translates the Greek *parousia*, often used to refer to the "Advent" or coming of Christ.</note>—he did so as a fitting arrival. Since there is also a second glorious arrival, these things come to pass and reveal more clearly the "vision" he described:

> “I beheld until thrones were placed, and the **Ancient of Days** <note>A title for God the Father used in the Book of Daniel.</note> sat. A thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. And behold, with the clouds of heaven, one like a **son of man** <note>original: "υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου" (huios anthropou). In Christian tradition, this title from Daniel 7 is identified with Jesus Christ.</note> was coming. And he reached the Ancient of Days, and to him was given the dominion, and the honor, and the kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him. His power is an eternal power, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed.” <note>Daniel 7:9–14</note>

The circumstances of the first arrival are more lowly and humble; among these, a great sign and proof is shown in the statement that he would "sit upon a donkey" and come "riding a beast of burden and a young foal." This serves as evidence of a common and beneficial life among men. But the circumstances of the second and divine arrival are shown most brilliantly through his transport "upon the clouds of heaven" and the eternal kingdom over all the nations. 

If it is right to set both of these prophecies before those of the **circumcision** <note>A common early Christian term for the Jewish people.</note> and offer an argument to them: how shall we reconcile these prophecies if they expect only one single arrival of Christ? Since they admit to seeing Christ himself in both of the cited prophecies, it is time for them to answer our question: how is it possible at one and the same time, and during a single arrival, for him to be "carried on the clouds of heaven" and also to be "riding on a beast of burden and a young foal"? These two descriptions are vastly different from one another. 

By collecting ten thousand such other prophecies about the Christ, and by setting them side-by-side and comparing the different things they signify, you will perceive most clearly that some contain signs of his first presence—fulfilled during his first appearance—while others refer to his second and glorious arrival. 

For by a hidden power, the entry of our Savior during his first presence effectively "destroyed the chariots and the war-horse from the battle line" <note>Referencing Zechariah 9:10.</note> within the physical Jerusalem and among the people called **Ephraim**. Because of this, from that time until now, their independent kingdom ceased to exist, as did their military preparations and armed power which had been strong in ancient times. 

He fitly used the name "Ephraim" as a symbol for the entire Jewish people, rather than "Joseph" or "Judah," so as not to disparage those more venerable names. You would find in other prophecies that the great nation is called "Ephraim" when accompanied by much disparagement and accusation, just as it is here. Certainly, after the return from Babylon, the people were no longer divided into two kingdoms as before; thus, it is likely that "Ephraim" refers to those dwelling in Jerusalem itself. Their military and armed power lasted until Roman times, but our Savior’s presence brought it down through a divine and secret power, exactly as the prophecy said. 

This Word <term>Logos: The "Word" or divine reason of God, identified here as Christ.</term> brings the "good news" to the **Church of the nations**, commanding her not simply to rejoice, but to "rejoice greatly" because of the presence of the Word of God within her. He calls this Church the "daughter of the heavenly Zion," or perhaps calls her out from the "former synagogue." Because of this, all of us from the nations who have believed in the Christ of God are his offspring and children...

Eusebius argues that the transition from many small warring states to one Roman Empire was a divine preparation for the Gospel.</note> of the nations were dissolved. From that time, the fulfillment of the prophesied peace began to move forward. Clearly, it has begun for now, but the prophecy will be most fully completed when the "fullness of the nations" <note>original: "πλήρωμα τῶν ἐθνῶν" (pleroma ton ethnon). A concept from Romans 11:25 regarding the eventual conversion of the world.</note> has come in, which was declared by the holy Apostle.

# EUSEBIUS
### THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 9. 286

...the prophet Jesus, the one from Nazareth of Galilee. Since, therefore, it is said in the preceding Psalm: <note>Psalm 118:25-26</note> "Hosanna," which, when interpreted, means "Save now!" <note>original: ὡσαννά (*hosanna*), from the Hebrew *hoshiah na*</note>; and the Hebrew contains "O Lord, [save] now" <note>original: αἰνὰ ἀδωναὶ (*ana adonai*), a Greek transcription of the Hebrew *anna Adonai*</note> as "Hosanna." It is manifest that "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord" <note>Psalm 118:26</note> takes its power from that same Psalm, and these things are clearly spoken regarding the Christ of God. Reasonably, then, we have taken the rest of the prophecy as referring to him as well. For it was he who was the "Blessed One," who was also named by another prophet as 
<margin>..</margin> "the one who is coming," where it says: "Yet a little while, and he who is coming will come, and will not delay." <note>Habakkuk 2:3, also cited in Hebrews 10:37</note> He has indeed 
<margin>..</margin> come in the name of the Lord God and of his Father. And he himself would be the "Lord God who has appeared to us." <note>Psalm 118:27</note> At any rate, he confesses that he has come in the name of his Father, 
<margin>..</margin> saying to the Jews: "I have come in my Father's name, and you do not 
<margin>..</margin> receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive." <note>John 5:43</note> Therefore, he himself is 
<margin>..</margin> the Lord God who appeared to us, the Blessed One, the one who came in the name of the Lord; he himself was 
<margin>..</margin> also the "stone" which they rejected <note>Psalm 118:22</note>—those who of old were building up the people of the circumcision <note>The Jewish people</note> through the Mosaic teaching. Having been rejected by them, he was established as the "head of another corner," <note>The "cornerstone" connecting two walls</note> that of the Church from the Gentiles. Because he was not seen by all, but only by the prophetic eyes, the Word declares him to be "marvelous," saying: 
<margin>..</margin> "and it is marvelous in our eyes." <note>Psalm 118:23</note> Furthermore, the Word names his appearance as the "day" 
<margin>..</margin> "which the Lord has made," <note>Psalm 118:24</note> since he himself was the "True Light" and the "Sun of 
<margin>..</margin> Righteousness." <note>Malachi 4:2</note> Regarding this day of God, we also ought to say: "This is the day which 
<margin>..</margin> the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it." Having reached the end of these 
<margin>..</margin> concise points, it is time to transition to the prophecies concerning his Passion.

# THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 10
### 287
