->Preface.<-

<image-desc>Large ornamental drop-cap letter M, intricately decorated with scrolling foliate and floral motifs in a square frame.</image-desc>After the prophecies already presented concerning the arrival of the heralded God among men, it is now the proper time to go through the details of his departure from his life among men. We shall observe, once again, what things were foretold from ancient times in the prophetic ages regarding these events. First, I will go through the arguments supporting his death, which is a significant part <note>The Greek text says "small part," perhaps to emphasize that death was merely a transition compared to his eternal nature.</note> of the current subject. However, before we begin the discourse, we must keep in mind what we have often said regarding his divine plan <note>original: οἰκονομία (*oikonomia*). In early Christian writing, this refers to the "economy" or management of God's plan for human salvation, specifically the Incarnation.</note>. Specifically, we must understand that some things are conceived according to his divinity, and others according to his humanity. On one hand, he is introduced as being the Word of God, and the Power of God, and the Wisdom of God, and the Angel of Great Counsel <note>A title for the Messiah from the Septuagint version of Isaiah 9:6.</note>, and the great and eternal High Priest, who performs sacred rites for the sake of the existence and salvation of all created beings, and who reconciles them to the Father.

On the other hand, he is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, and the sheep led to the slaughter. This "sheep" was the human tabernacle <note>original: σκῆνος (*skenos*). A common metaphor in early theology, describing the physical body as a temporary "tent" for the soul or the Divine Word.</note> which he—acting as a High Priest—took from our own herd, like a lamb or a sheep. Having offered the first-fruits of our race as a beautiful sacrifice, he presented it to the Father. Through this human nature, he conversed with the nature of men; for humanity could not have otherwise heard the Word of God and his incorporeal and intellectual power, nor could we have perceived anything greater through our physical eyes. 

Therefore, whenever you see him described in more humble terms in the passages concerning him, understand that you are looking at "the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world," and perceive that "human tabernacle" by means of this underlying concept. For he is the "Lamb who takes away the sin of the world," according to John the Baptist who says: "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." <note>John 1:29</note> And he is the "sheep led to the slaughter," according to the oracle in Isaiah which states: "He was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent." <note>Isaiah 53:7</note> Furthermore, it was said of him as of a lamb: "For the lawlessness of my people he was led to death." <note>Isaiah 53:8</note>

For it was necessary that the Lamb of God, taken up by the Great High Priest, should suffer on behalf of the rest of the lambs—that is, the whole human flock—and be offered as a sacrifice to God. "For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead also comes through a man," as the Apostle says. <note>1 Corinthians 15:21</note> And, "Just as through one trespass condemnation came to all men, so also through one act of righteousness justification of life comes to all men." <note>Romans 5:18</note> 

Hence, he himself taught his own disciples that he was Life and Light and Truth; yet regarding the other aspects of the theology concerning him, he said to those who were uninitiated in his secrets: "Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you?" <note>John 8:40</note> Just as the specific characteristics of his divinity were presented in the preceding sections, in the same way we shall here treat the "Lamb" in terms of his humanity. This section will follow the order of events concerning his Passion, which encompasses both aspects: those according to his Godhood and those according to his manhood. These things having been usefully noted in advance, let us now begin the...

# EVANGELICAL DEMONSTRATION, Book 10.
### 289

<margin>»</margin> "...the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth." <note>original: σάρκας τῶν ὁσίων σου (*sarkas tōn hosiōn sou*). This is a quote from Psalm 79:2 (78:2 in the Septuagint).</note> Now, the first of these—I mean the words from the seventy-third Psalm <note>Modern Psalm 74.</note>—were spoken while David was still reigning, before the Temple had even been constructed by Solomon. Yet they reached their fulfillment not all at once, but rather in parts: first during the Babylonian siege, and second during the Roman war against the Jews. For every one of the things described was fulfilled during both the first and the second destruction of the Temple, having been foreseen and proclaimed in the aforementioned Psalms by **Asaph** <note>Asaph was a Levite and choir leader under David, traditionally credited with several Psalms.</note>. 

However, the second group of prophecies from the seventy-eighth Psalm <note>Modern Psalm 79.</note> was fulfilled during the times of **Antiochus**, the one called **Epiphanes** <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes was a Hellenistic king of the Seleucid Empire (reigned 175–164 BC) who famously persecuted the Jews, leading to the Maccabean Revolt.</note>. Having become King of Syria, he occupied Jerusalem, defiled the Temple, and tore down the altar. Then, by starving the Jews, he destroyed a vast number of their men and women for the sake of their own Law and their ancestral piety, subjecting them to various punishments. Therefore, it was for that time—and for the deeds committed by Antiochus afterward—that Asaph proclaimed the words of the seventy-eighth Psalm. 

The history of the so-called **Maccabees** <note>A series of books detailing the Jewish rebellion against the Seleucids; Eusebius is quoting from 1 Maccabees 7.</note> bears witness to this account, containing exactly what I have said. It records how a "synagogue of scribes" <note>original: συναγωγὴ γραμματέων (*synagogē grammateōn*)</note> sought justice and placed their trust in **Alcimus** <note>original: Ἰακείμον (*Iakeimon*). Alcimus was a Hellenizing High Priest who betrayed his people.</note> and **Bacchides** <note>A Syrian general and governor.</note>. And as it follows in the text: "He swore to them, saying: 'We will not seek to do harm to you or your friends.' And they believed him. Then he seized sixty of their men and killed them in a single day, according to the word that was written: 

<margin>»</margin> 'They have given the dead
<margin>»</margin> bodies of your servants as food for the birds of the heaven, the flesh of your saints to the
<margin>»</margin> beasts of the earth; they have poured out their blood like water round about Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.'"

Since these things were foretold and accomplished in this way, it is not surprising if, in the same manner, the previously cited oracles of the fortieth Psalm <note>Modern Psalm 41.</note> were intended to signify the time of the conspiracy against our Savior. For not all people understood that, though he was the **Word of God**, and **Wisdom**, and **Life**, and **True Light**, and possessed all the wealth of good things, he "became poor" for our sake by taking on flesh. Having been made like mortal men in their nature, he clothed himself in the form of a servant and a poor man. Particularly at the time when he was fulfilling the prophecy of the Psalm, it is fitting that at the beginning of the Psalm, the one who understands these things about him is called "blessed," as he attains the promise written therein. 

From that point on, the text speaks from the person of the "poor and needy" one—that is, our Savior himself, who became poor for us—saying: 

<margin>»</margin> "I said: Lord, have mercy on me." 

That these things in the Psalm are prophesied from the person of the Savior, the Evangelist **John** is a sufficient witness. For he records that when Jesus had taken a towel and girded himself, and washed the feet of his disciples, he said: 

<margin>»</margin> "I know whom I have chosen; but that the Scripture may be fulfilled: 'He who eats 
<margin>»</margin> bread with me has lifted up his heel against me.'" 

And which Scripture did he mean was being fulfilled in these events, if not the very Psalm we have in hand, in which it is said: 

<margin>»</margin> "For even the man of my peace in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, has magnified his 
<margin>»</margin> deceit against me?" 

Thus, he says at the beginning: "I said: Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you"—and so on through the whole Psalm. **Symmachus** <note>An author of one of the Greek translations of the Old Testament used in Origen's Hexapla; he was known for a more literal or idiomatic style.</note> rendered this passage more clearly in this way: 

<margin>»</margin> "While I said: Lord, pity me; heal my soul, even if I have sinned against you, my enemies [spoke evil]..."

# EUSEBIUS
### 290

> “They spoke evil concerning me: ‘When will he die, and his name perish?’ And if one entered to visit me, his heart spoke vanities; he gathered iniquity to himself. Going outside, he spoke in the same way. Together all who hate me whispered against me; against me they devised evils for me. An unlawful word was poured out within them: ‘Will he that sleeps rise up no more?’ <note>original: καὶ πεσὼν οὐκέτι ἀναστήσεται. Literally: 'Having fallen, will he not rise again?' This refers to the plotters' hope that Christ would remain dead after the crucifixion.</note> For even the man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has greatly lifted up his heel against me. <note>This is famously interpreted in the Gospels as a prophecy of Judas Iscariot’s betrayal during the Last Supper.</note> Following this: ‘But you, O Lord, have mercy on me, and raise me up, that I may requite them.’ By this I know that you favored me, because my enemy does not triumph over me. As for me, because of my innocence, you supported me, and established me before you forever. <note>Psalm 41:5-12 in modern numbering.</note> The versions of **Symmachus** and **Aquila** <note>Symmachus and Aquila were 2nd-century scholars who produced Greek translations of the Old Testament that differed slightly from the Septuagint.</note> have the same meaning.”

Now, it is clear to everyone that the saying, “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you,” might seem inconsistent when spoken from the person of our Savior. However, if we observe the version by Symmachus, it does not read quite that way, but rather: “Heal my soul, *even if* I have sinned against you.” 

Yet He says this because He makes our sins His own. Therefore it is said: “And the Lord delivered Him for our sins,” and “He bears our sins.” <note>Isaiah 53:5-6.</note> He became a “curse” for us—the **Lamb of God** who takes away the sin of the world. Though He knew no sin, God made Him to be sin for our sake, offering Him as a <term>Ransom</term> <note>original: ἀντίψυχον (*antipsychon*), literally “a life for a life” or a substitute.</note> for us all, so that we might become the righteousness of God in Him. Since He came in the “likeness of sinful flesh” and condemned sin in the flesh, these words are appropriately spoken. 

Because of His love and deep affection for humanity, He identifies with our sins and says these things. Further down in the same Psalm, He adds: “But because of my innocence, you have supported me.” 

We have clearly defined Him as the Lamb of God. But how does He make our sins His own, and how is He said to “bear our iniquities,” if not for the fact that we are called His **Body**? As the Apostle said: “You are the body of Christ, and members in particular.” <note>1 Corinthians 12:27.</note> Just as when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it, so too when many members (us) are suffering and sinning, He Himself suffers according to the principles of <term>Sympathy</term> <note>original: συμπάθεια (*sympatheia*), meaning “to feel or suffer with another.”</note>. 

Since the Word of God saw fit to take the “form of a servant” and be united with the common human “tent” <note>A common early Christian metaphor for the human body or physical nature.</note> of our Creator, He takes the pains of the suffering members upon Himself. He makes our diseases His own, and He grieves and toils for us all according to the laws of His love for mankind. 

The Lamb of God did not only do these things, but He was also punished and suffered a penalty on our behalf—a penalty He did not owe, but which we owed because of the multitude of our transgressions. Thus, He became the cause of the forgiveness of our sins by accepting death for us. He transferred to Himself the scourging, insults, and dishonor due to us, drawing upon Himself the curse that was attached to us, becoming a “curse” for our sake. 

What else is this but a “life for a life”? Therefore, the oracle speaks from our perspective: “By His stripes we were healed,” and “the Lord delivered Him for our sins.” So, by naturally uniting Himself to us and us to Him, and making our passions His own, He says: “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you.” 

Those who plot against Him—not only men, but also invisible powers—see the extraordinary nature of His strength and His name, through which, a little later, the **Christians**... <note>The sentence continues on the next page.</note>

<meta>catchword: ...ians (νῶν)</meta>

<summary>Eusebius explains how Christ, as the sinless Lamb of God, can claim to have "sinned" in Psalm 41 by identifying with the human race as His "Body." He describes the atonement as a "life for a life" where Christ takes on the punishments due to humanity out of divine sympathy and love.</summary>

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 10
<note>The original Greek header says Book 7 (βιβ. ζ), but this text is traditionally part of Book 10, which focuses on the Passion of Christ.</note>

### 291

...with which he filled the whole world, they thought they could extinguish him, I suppose, if they plotted his death. See then how he refutes them, saying: **"My enemies spoke evil of me: When will he die and his name perish?"** And since they approached him hypocritically to test him and trap him—as the divine Scripture bears witness—and since they were recently concocting accusations against him, he adds: **"And if he entered to see me, his heart spoke in vain; he gathered iniquity for himself. He went outside and spoke together against me."**

Following these words, he now clearly reveals that most impious traitor himself. This happened when Judas had already made agreements with the rulers of the Jews concerning the betrayal of the Teacher. He no longer came to the divine teaching of the disciples with a sincere heart, nor did he attend as a student should, nor did he rest among the Savior’s company as the others did. Instead, he came to spy out the right moment when it would be necessary to attack him.

This very thing is recorded in the written accounts of the Holy Gospel. **Matthew** says: *Then one of the twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said to them, "What will you give me, and I will deliver him to you?" And they set for him thirty pieces of silver. And from then on he sought an opportunity to deliver him.* <note>Matthew 26:14-16</note>

**Mark** says: *And Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve, went to the chief priests to deliver him to them. And when they heard it, they were glad, and promised to give him money. And he sought how he might conveniently deliver him.* <note>Mark 14:10-11</note>

**Luke** writes: *Then Satan entered into Judas surnamed Iscariot, being of the number of the twelve. And he went his way, and communed with the chief priests and captains of the temple, how he might deliver him to them. And they were glad, and agreed to give him money. And he sought an opportunity to deliver him to them in the absence of the multitude.* <note>Luke 22:3-6</note>

Foretelling these very events, the prophecy at hand adds: **"If he entered to see, his heart spoke in vain; he gathered iniquity for himself. He went outside and spoke together. All my enemies whispered against me."** For **Symmachus** <note>Symmachus was a translator of the Old Testament into Greek; Eusebius often compares his version to the standard Septuagint to clarify meanings.</note> renders it this way: "The ally, entering to inspect, his heart spoke vain things; he gathered injustice for himself. Going outside, he spoke against me. All who hate me whispered together against me."

Therefore, while he entered alone as an acquaintance and a disciple visiting a teacher, he was actually scouting and observing, hiding the plot deep within his own heart. But when he went out, he spoke "together" with the many others, betraying the Savior to his enemies. He plotted secretly with the rulers of the Jews, not only about other matters but specifically about the money for which he promised to deliver him—the very thing he whispered about with them.

Therefore the text says: **"He went outside and spoke together. All my enemies whispered against me; against me they devised evil for me. They laid an unlawful word against me."** It seems that the prophecy calls the agreement regarding the silver pieces an "unlawful word," or perhaps it refers to the impious and unlawful thoughts they had against him—believing he would be extinguished and destroyed by death, and would no longer be found among the living. For this is the meaning of: **"Will he that sleeps rise up no more?"** For...

# EUSEBIUS

### 292

» <note>original: λευκότερον ὁ σύμμαχος ἐξέφωνεν εἰπών</note> Symmachus expressed it more clearly, saying: **"And having fallen, will he not rise again?"** And Aquila says: **"And he who lies down, will he not add to his rising?"** These things were spoken generally concerning all those who plotted against him at the time of the Passion. But specifically again concerning the traitor, as one who had been a disciple, he adds next, saying: **"For even the man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has greatly lifted up his heel against me."** Instead of which, Symmachus again says: **"And a man who was at peace with me, in whom I confided, eating my bread with me, was magnified against me."** 

For it would be a most wretched thing—both simple and most evident—that one who shared a common table and the nourishment of the Teacher’s words, having been stained by worse things, should repay his benefactor with the opposite. But since the enemies said these things in their plotting—**"When will he die and his name perish?"**—and they thought that once he had "fallen asleep" <note>A common biblical metaphor for death</note> he would no longer rise, for this reason the Savior himself and our Lord, using this "recantation" against them and asking the Father that he might obtain the resurrection without hindrance, says: **"But you, O Lord, have mercy on me, and raise me up, and I will requite them. By this I know that you have favored me, because my enemy shall not triumph over me."** 

And it is quite clear what kind of recompense the events took after his resurrection from the dead; and not long after, the repayment came upon those who had plotted against him. Just as his enemy was brought to nothing by death while He attained life, so that those who mock might say: **"Where, O Death, is your sting? Where, O Death, is your victory?"** <note>1 Corinthians 15:55</note> 

If anyone reads the histories written by **Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note> regarding the period after the resurrection of our Savior, he will know the misfortunes that overtook the Jewish nation and their rulers, which they naturally fell into, receiving the wages for what they did against him. And all these things were fulfilled in them according to the prophecy. 

But the resurrection of our Savior from the dead proved to everyone how the Father was well-pleased in him, as he himself teaches, saying: **"Have mercy on me and raise me up, and I will requite them. By this I know that you have favored me, because my enemy shall not triumph over me."** To these things he adds: **"But because of my innocence, you have supported me."** 

Notice the great confidence <note>original: παῤῥησίᾳ (parrhēsia) - bold speech or frankness</note> with which he sends up this prayer to God his Father, testifying to his own "innocence," even though he said earlier: **"Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you."** We have already explained how we understand this in part. <note>Eusebius previously argued that Christ speaks of "sin" as the corporate sin of humanity which he took upon himself.</note> Indeed, Symmachus expressed it more clearly, saying: **"Heal my soul, although I have sinned against you."** This could also be said concerning our sins, which our Savior and Lord took upon himself. But the phrase, **"Because of my innocence you have supported me,"** presents the total purity of his nature. Because of this, teaching the stability and unshakeable nature of the life and salvation following his resurrection, he adds: **"And you have established me before you forever."** Or, according to Symmachus: **"And you shall set me before you for eternity."**

Having just discussed Psalm 41, he now transitions to Psalm 55 (54 in the Septuagint), showing how it mirrors the specific details of Judas Iscariot’s relationship with Jesus and his eventual treachery.</meta>

# THE PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 7

### 293

» **...and hear me. I was grieved in my meditation, and I was troubled by the voice of the enemy, and by the oppression of the sinner. Because they brought lawlessness upon me, and in anger they were indignant with me. My heart was troubled within me, and the terror of death fell upon me. Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me.** And so on. To which he adds: **"Drown them, Lord, and divide their tongues, for I have seen lawlessness and strife in the city. Day and night it shall go around upon its walls; lawlessness and toil are in its midst, and injustice; and usury and deceit have not departed from its streets. For if an enemy had reproached me, I would have endured it; and if he who hated me had boasted against me, I would have hidden from him. But you, a man of equal soul, my guide and my acquaintance, who together with me sweetened my food, in the house of God we walked in harmony."** <note>This is a quotation from Psalm 55:2–14 (Septuagint 54). The "man of equal soul" is historically interpreted by the Church Fathers as Judas Iscariot.</note> 

**For if an enemy had reproached me, I would have endured it; and if he who hated me had boasted against me, I would have hidden from him. But you, a man of equal soul, my guide and my acquaintance, who together with me sweetened my food...** 

This is similar to the passage: **"The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has greatly lifted up his heel against me,"** <note>Psalm 41:9</note> which is found in the prophecy concerning Judas. Just as in that passage he was shown to have once been a man of peace—since he was numbered with the full complement of the disciples and himself held the rank of the Apostles—so also in the present passage he is foretold as being **of equal soul** and a **guide** and an **acquaintance**. 

And again, just as it was said of him in the former passage, **"he who ate my bread has greatly lifted up his heel against me,"** in the very same way it is said by the speaker in the present passage: **"who together with me sweetened my food."** For he was indeed one of those deemed worthy of the secret <term>intercourse</term><note>Meaning private, intimate conversation and teaching.</note> with our Savior and his spiritual nourishment. To the crowds outside and the multitudes, he spoke in parables, but to his own disciples alone—among whom Judas was also counted—he explained everything. 

Therefore it is said, **"he who ate my bread has greatly lifted up his heel against me,"** and, **"who together with me sweetened my food."** For instead of the traditional phrasing, **Aquila** <note>An early 2nd-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek.</note> rendered it saying: **"We together sweetened a secret."** And **Symmachus** <note>A late 2nd-century translator known for his more elegant Greek style.</note> says: **"To whom we communicated sweet conversation."** And instead of **"But you, a man of equal soul, my guide, and my acquaintance,"** Symmachus says: **"But you, a man of equal honor to me, and my guide, and my acquaintance."** 

Since, then, he was considered worthy of such things as a most intimate friend of the Savior, the text reasonably says of him: **"For if an enemy had reproached me, I would have endured it,"** and so on. After prophesying these things concerning Judas, the speaker then teaches in advance his own salvation from death and his escape, saying: **"I cried to God, and the Lord saved me. Evening and morning and at noon I will describe it and declare it, and he shall hear my voice. He shall ransom my soul in peace."** 

By this he signifies, as if in a prayer, the time before his death, during which Judas plotted the betrayal against him. At that time, our Lord and Savior—grieving at the ruin and destruction of his acquaintance, and even more at the rejection of the entire Jewish nation, as one suffering with them as his own initiates and as those most dear—calls all his conversation and teaching with them **meditation** <note>original: ἀδολεσχία (adoleschia); while often meaning "meditation," Eusebius plays on its meaning of "fruitless talk" or "idle chatter," implying Christ felt his words had been wasted on them.</note> because it had benefited them nothing, saying: **"I was grieved in my meditation, and I was troubled by the voice of the enemy, and by the oppression of the sinner. Because they turned aside..."**

<sig>BBB.iii.</sig>

<summary>Eusebius interprets Psalm 55 as a prophecy of Judas Iscariot's betrayal, emphasizing the intimacy Judas once shared with Christ as an apostle of "equal honor." He contrasts Christ's private "sweet" teachings with the eventual treachery and the Savior's subsequent prayer for resurrection.</summary>

# EUSEBIUS

### 294

<margin>
Eusebius, *On the Proof of the Gospel* <note>original: "Eusebio de demonstratione euangelica"</note>
</margin>

...Indeed, he says, **they brought lawlessness upon me, which in anger they held against me.** These words can be referred to the rulers of the circumcision <note>A common early Christian term for the Jewish leadership.</note>, those who maliciously and with treacherous intent tried to ambush him. However, they can also be spoken concerning invisible powers <note>Refers to demons or spiritual enemies.</note> warring against him from the outside and working through the agency of men. This seems to me to harmonize with the things spoken by him in the Gospel at the time of his Passion, when he says to his disciples, **"My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even unto death. Stay here and watch with me."** <note>Matthew 26:38</note> And again, **"Now my soul is troubled."** <note>John 12:27</note> Certainly, the things in the Psalm are similar to these, where it is said, **"My heart was troubled within me, and the dread of death fell upon me. Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me."** <note>Psalm 55:4–5</note> Through these words, he signifies the assaults of the opposing powers against him.

For just as in the prophecies there is mention of a **"spirit of fornication"** <note>Hosea 4:12</note> and it is said, **"a spirit of fornication led them astray,"** and a **"spirit of error"** in the wilderness; in the same way, we might say there is a **"spirit of death"** which produces cowardice, just as the **"spirit of might"** and power and courage is active according to God. Thus, one might also speak of a **"spirit of fear and trembling,"** and yet another besides these, a **"spirit of dread and confusion."** These, one might say, are accustomed to assault all those who in a mystery <note>Refers to the sacramental or spiritual participation in Christ's death.</note> accept the death of ungodliness, but they were laid much more heavily upon him who endured death on behalf of all. 

Whether it was a spirit of cowardice and death, or of fear and trembling, or any other such power that had fallen upon him, it certainly did not crush him; for, like a stripped athlete <note>The "naked athlete" (gymnaios athlētēs) was a common metaphor for a martyr or Christ, stripped of worldly ties to fight spiritual battles.</note>, he had already made life the means for the dissolution of death, and life, in turn, cast death far away. Likewise, the spirit that came upon him to produce fear and trembling was renounced and driven far off by the spirit of might and power. For according to Isaiah, the **"Holy Spirit rested upon him, the spirit of wisdom and the spirit of counsel and might."** <note>Isaiah 11:2</note> Wherefore, he also dispersed the spirit of darkness by the power of his own light, since **"the light shone in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it."** <note>John 1:5</note> Another person might find things similar to these in the twenty-first Psalm <note>Psalm 22 in modern Bibles.</note>, where again it is spoken from the same person <note>Meaning Christ, speaking through the prophet.</note>:

> **"Many calves have surrounded me, fat bulls have encompassed me. They opened their mouths against me, like a ravening and roaring lion."** 

And again: 

> **"For many dogs have surrounded me, a congregation of evildoers has encompassed me."** 

And once more: 

> **"Deliver my soul from the sword, and my only-begotten from the hand of the dog. Save me from the lion's mouth, and my lowliness from the horns of the unicorns."** <note>Psalm 22:12, 13, 16, 20–21. "Unicorns" (monokerōtōn) in the Septuagint refers to wild, powerful oxen.</note>

For in these verses, he clearly calls the evil powers "bulls," "calves," "lions," "dogs," and "unicorns." These surrounded and encircled him at the time of his Passion, yet they were not able to achieve anything against him. 

<margin>*</margin>
These interpretations hold if these parts of the Psalm are referred to our Savior and Lord. But if they are referred not to him, but to another person, you must observe again how the details of the passage might be smoothed out. Nevertheless, regarding the mother-city of the Jews—that is, Jerusalem itself—he adds the following immediately after the prophecy against those who plotted against him: **"I have seen lawlessness and strife in the city,"** and the things that follow. What kind of meaning these hold, there is no leisure to describe at present.

<summary>Eusebius interprets the "fear and trembling" of the Psalms as Christ's spiritual struggle against demonic "spirits of dread" during his Passion, comparing these enemies to the predatory animals mentioned in Psalm 22.</summary>

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 6
### 295

->From Psalm 108.<- <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 109. The Greek numbering (Septuagint) usually lags one behind the Hebrew numbering used in most English translations.</note>

Concerning both Judas and the apostle introduced in his place, and concerning the Jewish nation.

> O God, do not pass over my praise in silence, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful have been opened against me. They have spoken against me with a deceitful tongue, and they surrounded me with words of hatred, and they fought against me without cause. In return for my love, they slandered me, but I continued to pray. They repaid me evil for good, and hatred in exchange for my love. Set a sinner over him, and let the accuser <note>original: "διάβολος" (diabolos). While often translated as "the Devil," in this context it refers to an adversary or legal accuser.</note> stand at his right hand. When he is judged, let him come forth condemned, and let his prayer become sin. Let his days be few, and let another take his office. <note>term: "office" (Greek: episkopēn). This word later became the title for a "Bishop," but here refers generally to a position of oversight or leadership.</note>

And these words set forth have reference to the traitor Judas, as the apostle Peter testifies. After the ascension of our Savior, when all the apostles were gathered together along with many other brothers, he stood up in their midst and said:

> Men and brothers, it was necessary for the Scripture to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand through the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. For he was numbered among us and received a share in this ministry. Now this man acquired a field from the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong, he burst open in the middle and all his intestines spilled out. This became known to all who lived in Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language *Akeldama*, which is "Field of Blood." For it is written in the Book of Psalms: **"Let his homestead become desolate, and let there be no one living in it,"** and, **"Let another take his office."** <note>Acts 1:16–20</note>

After Peter said these things, it remained necessary to take another in place of Judas to fill the number of the twelve apostles, so that the prophecy might be fulfilled. When the lot was cast, the lot fell upon Matthias, and he was numbered with the twelve apostles. Since these things were fulfilled in this way, it follows that the "persona" speaking in the Psalm is none other than our Savior. He sent up to the Father the prayer offered by him during the time of his Passion, and through the Holy Spirit, he saw fit to record it, foreseeing only what would happen concerning him. 

He says, therefore: **"O God, do not pass over my praise in silence."** He is asking that the teaching delivered by him to his disciples—the "praise" of the New Covenant—should not be silenced, but should instead remain in the world for all the ages to come. 

The **"mouth of the sinner"** and **"mouth of the deceitful"** could properly be said of Judas, who went to the chief priests and said to them:

> "What are you willing to give me, and I will deliver him to you?" 

And they weighed out for him thirty silver coins. From that time on, he sought an opportunity to betray him. Having plotted such things against him, he was among those reclining with him at the Passover meal. When our Savior himself reclined with the twelve, while they were eating, he said:

> "Truly, truly, I say to you, that one of you will betray me." 

And being deeply grieved, each of them began to say, "Is it I, Lord?" Among them was Judas, who, opening a mouth full of all deceit and irony, answered and said:

> "Is it I, Rabbi?" 

A deceitful mouth, indeed, through which he gave the sign to those plotting against our Savior, say—

For the Gospel says that while the Savior was still speaking to his disciples, “Behold, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great multitude with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and elders of the people.” To whom the Lord also said, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to seize me? And if one is able to observe, see if there does not sit over the nation of the Jews a sinful ruler and leader, to whom they were handed over after their bold crimes against our Savior. Instead of their ancient, domestic, and God-beloved rulers, they are now forced to serve foreigners and idolaters. 

How could one not marvel at the result of this prophecy? For the Word having said, “Let his days be few,” it is clear how short a time passed after their plot against our Savior—the time in which they seemed to prevail—before they endured the final siege and utter destruction. Because of this, “another took their office,” namely the assembly established through Christ. 

You will understand the rest of the Psalm as being fittingly applied to these same people. The following parts, spoken as if concerning the sons of Judas—in which it says, “Let his children be orphans,” and other similar things—might also be referred back to him, as the primary figure of Judas, and after him, to all those who, in a similar way to him, betray the Word of salvation. You should also understand “his wife” and “the sins of his fathers,” and the things said of “his mother,” as referring to the synagogue of the Jews.

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 6 
<note>original: βιβ. ς. Although the header indicates Book 6, the content corresponds to Book 10 of the *Demonstratio Evangelica* in standard editions.</note>
### 297

...of the assembly of the Jewish nation. For I believe it is concerning her that it is said, "and may the sin of her mother not be blotted out." <note>original: "καὶ ἀμβλῦσαι τὰ μητρὸς αὐτῆς μὴ ἐξαλειφθείη" — Eusebius interprets the "mother" in Psalm 109:14 as the Jewish Synagogue or the nation itself.</note> Again, just as in the prophecy before this one, the Savior and our Lord was called **poor and needy**, and we demonstrated this in the passage, "Blessed is the one who considers the poor and needy." <note>Psalm 41:1 (LXX 40:1).</note> I maintain that he is called by these same names in the present Psalm as well. For it says that such-and-such things would befall Judas and those who were zealous for things similar to him, because of the things he dared to do. 

And that these things might happen, he adds: "Because he did not remember to show mercy, but persecuted the **poor and needy** man, and the one pierced in heart, to put him to death. And he loved cursing, and it shall come to him; and he did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him." Following these words, the Speaker <note>Referring to Christ speaking through the prophet David.</note> again calls himself **poor and needy**, saying: "But you, O Lord, Lord, deal mercifully with me for your name’s sake, for your mercy is kind. Deliver me, for I am **poor and needy**." After other matters, he adds to these: "My knees have grown weak from fasting, and my flesh has changed for lack of oil. And I became a reproach to them; they saw me, and they shook their heads." 

These things also reached their fulfillment when those passing by blasphemed him, wagging their heads and saying, "He saved others; himself he cannot save." <note>A reference to Matthew 27:39–42.</note> And since even until now those of the circumcision <note>term: "those of the circumcision" — a common Patristic way of referring to the Jewish people.</note>, drawing upon themselves the curse of their fathers, are accustomed to anathematize <note>term: "anathematize" — to formally curse or denounce.</note> our Savior and Lord with blasphemous and impious words, as well as all those who have believed in him, he adds the following for this reason: "They shall curse, but you will bless. Let those who rise up against me be put to shame, but your servant shall rejoice. Let those who slander me be clothed with shame, and let them be wrapped in their own disgrace as with a double-cloak." 

"But I will give great thanks to the Lord with my mouth, and in the midst of many I will praise him, because he stood at the right hand of the poor man, to save my soul from those who persecute it." It is quite clear how many evils those who even now make curses against him in their own synagogues must struggle with, having been unable to find any breath of relief since those times. Meanwhile, he himself offers praise to the Father in the midst of many nations through his **New Covenant**, possessing the Father as his helper and the one seated at his own right hand. Therefore, he says, "In the midst of many I will praise him, because he stood at the right hand of the poor man." 

He also teaches of his salvation after death, saying, "to save my soul from those who persecute it." Thus, having said above, "he persecuted the **poor and needy** man, and the one pierced in heart, to put him to death," and having clearly shown that he was describing his own death in the prophecy, he again hinted at the salvation after death by saying, "because he stood at the right hand of the poor man, to save my soul from those who persecute it."

And these things reached their fulfillment when, according to **Luke**, Judas went away and conferred with the chief priests, scribes, and captains of the temple, so that he might hand Him over to them; and they were glad, and agreed to give him money. <note>Luke 22:4–5.</note> And according to **Matthew**, it was when he went to the chief priests to hand Him over; they were glad and promised to give him money. » "What are you willing to give me, and I will deliver Him to you? And they set for him **thirty pieces of silver**." <note>Matthew 26:14–15. Eusebius uses "statēras" (staters) here, a common term for silver coins.</note>

These things are therefore in harmony with the phrase, "and they set my wage at thirty pieces of silver," spoken by the Lord in the prophecy. Indeed, the translation of **Aquila** <note>Aquila of Sinope was a 2nd-century scholar who produced an extremely literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible to assist those who found the Septuagint too interpretive.</note> says: "And he weighed out my wage as thirty pieces of silver." To which he adds: "And the Lord said to me, 'Cast them into the furnace, and see if it is genuine, the way I was tested by them.'" Again, the same Aquila says: "And the Lord said to me, 'Cast them into the furnace. Throw them to the potter.' An immense price, at which I was valued by them!" And he threw it so that the Lord himself acknowledged that the price of thirty pieces of silver had been given for him.

The meaning of this passage seems to indicate something like this: "I, the Lord, starting from the very first day, never ceased my kindness toward you of the circumcision <note>term: "the circumcision" (περιτομή) — a common early Christian way to refer to the Jewish people.</note>, providing you with countless examples of my goodness and doing you ten thousand favors. This was not only through the ancient prophets but also through my own presence—whether by encouraging teachings and rational lessons, or by signs, wonders, and other miraculous acts, including healings and cures. But you, who were deemed worthy of such great benefit, 'give me my wage or refuse it,' asking them, as is fitting, for the fruits of piety and a sign of faith in Him."

But they—as was said in the passage from **Hosea** preceding this one—instead of loving me, they slandered me; and evil was returned to me for good, and hatred for my love, when they set the price at thirty pieces of silver, as if they were valuing Him at the price of a slave. <note>Exodus 21:32 sets the compensation for a gored slave at thirty shekels of silver, a connection Eusebius implies here.</note> But since "the fire itself will test what sort of work each one has done," it was fitting that they were ordered "into the furnace," as he adds, "the way I was tested by them." "Furnace" here seems to be a name he gives to the house of the Lord. Since the Lord said...

<header>PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 10</header>

» ...the furnace. According to the **Seventy** <note>original: "τοὺς ἑβδομήκοντα" — the Septuagint, the standard Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, he says: "Cast them into the furnace," and adds, "and I cast them into the house of the Lord, into the furnace." But according to **Aquila**, where the Lord says, "Cast it"—meaning the silver—"to the potter," he adds: "and I cast it in the house of the Lord to the potter." And according to **Symmachus**, where the Lord says, "Cast it into the furnace," he adds, saying: "and I cast it into the house of the Lord, into the furnace." 

» Was this not also fulfilled when **Judas**, the one who betrayed the Lord, seeing that He was condemned, repented and returned the silver pieces to the chief priests and elders, saying: "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood"? But they said to him: "What is that to us? See to it yourself." And throwing the silver pieces into the temple, he departed, and went away and hanged himself. The chief priests, taking the silver, said: "It is not lawful to put them into the **Corban** <note>original: "κορβανᾶν" — the temple treasury where gifts dedicated to God were kept</note>, since it is the price of blood." And after taking counsel, they bought with them the **potter's field** for the burial of strangers. Therefore that field was called the "Field of Blood" to this very day. 

» Then was fulfilled what was spoken through **Jeremiah** the prophet, saying: "And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him on whom a price had been set, whom they of the children of Israel had priced; and they gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord commanded me." <note>Matthew 27:3–10. Eusebius is quoting the Gospel directly here.</note> 

Next, you should consider this: since these words are not found in the prophecy of **Jeremiah**, must we suspect they were cut out of his book by some malicious interference <note>original: "ῥᾳδιουργίαν" — trickery or tampering with the text</note>, or that a scribal error occurred among those who more carelessly produced copies of the holy Gospels, one person making a mistake and writing "Jeremiah" instead of "Zechariah"? For it ought to have been written thus: "Then was fulfilled what was spoken through **Zechariah** the prophet." 

Furthermore, instead of "I cast them into the house of the Lord, into the furnace," the scribe may have erroneously written, "and they gave them for the potter's field." For clearly, through the prophecy, the silver is said to have been cast into the temple of the Lord; and through the Gospel itself, it is cast into the temple. For it says that **Judas**, having thrown the silver pieces into the temple, departed. 

And it is likely that through those silver pieces the temple became profaned, fulfilling the saying: "Behold, your house is left to you desolate." <note>Matthew 23:38.</note> And see whether the "house of the Lord" was called a **furnace** <note>original: "χωνευτήριον" — a smelting-place or refinery</note> for this reason: because in the house of God it happens that souls are reshaped by the fire of divine words, as if in a refinery. Or, in another sense, because the impure are rejected there, being refined and tested as if in a furnace. 

Hence **Aquila**, by saying "I cast the silver in the house of the Lord to the **potter**" <note>original: "πλάστην" — a molder, creator, or potter</note>, clearly teaches that the Divine Word dwells in the house of the Lord like a potter, shaping and renewing the souls of those who approach. However, since the "price of the one priced" among us was changed into that house and made it profane, he naturally adds immediately: "And I cast away the second staff, the **measuring line** <note>original: "σχοίνισμα" — an allotment or portion measured by a cord</note>, to break the covenant between **Judah** and **Israel**." For from that time the multitude of the nation was cast off from the oversight of God which had previously watched over them. 

I believe the "second staff" refers here to the entire useless nation of the Jews. He named them beautifully, saying: "The one I called **Beauty**, and the second I called **Allotment**." And he clearly adds concerning the second, saying: "And I cast away the second staff, the allotment, to break the covenant between Judah..."

<summary>Eusebius addresses the textual discrepancy where Matthew attributes a quote to Jeremiah that actually appears in Zechariah, suggesting a scribal error. He provides an allegorical interpretation of the "potter" and "furnace" in the temple as symbols of the Divine Word shaping souls or the nation being tested.</summary>

### EVANGELICAL PROOF, Book 10

In addition to what has been said, there is a passage in the prophet **Jeremiah** <note>Jeremiah 12:7-9</note> spoken from the person of the Lord, which states:
> I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my heritage; I have given my beloved soul into the hands of her enemies. My heritage has become to me like a lion in the forest; she has raised her voice against me. Is my heritage not like a hyena’s cave to me?

It is reasonable, then, that following these things, he adds: "And I said, I will not shepherd you; let that which is dying die, and let that which is failing fail, and let the rest eat the flesh of their neighbors." After this, he adds: "And I will take my beautiful staff and cast it away." In place of this, **Aquila** <note>a literalist 2nd-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek</note> says: "And I took my staff, **Splendor** <note>original: "εὐπρέπειαν" (*euprepeian*)</note>, and I broke it,"

namely, the **Mosaic worship** <note>the religious system and rituals established by Moses</note>. Therefore, the "first staff," which was mentioned at the beginning of the discourse, is said to be completed and cast away. But when the "price of the Priced One," which was set by those who gave the silver, was cast into the house of the Lord as into a **foundry** <note>original: "χωνευτήριον" (*chōneutērion*) — a place where metals are melted down; a reference to the potter's field or the temple treasury</note>, then the prophecy concerning the "second staff"—called **Measuring Line** <note>original: "σχοίνισμα" (*schoinisma*) — a cord or rope used to mark out land or a portion</note>—follows:
> And what it will suffer is prophesied in the words: "And I cast away the second staff, the Measuring Line, to scatter the covenant between Judah and Israel."

And since the word has clearly shown the rejection of those people through these things, he appropriately says that he will no longer acknowledge the power of the prophecies among them, but rather:
> among the **Chamanaioi** <note>original: "χαμαναίοις" (*chamanaiois*). In the Septuagint version of Zechariah 11:11, this refers to the "Canaanites" or "merchants," interpreted here as the poor or the humble of the flock.</note>, saying: "And the Chamanaioi, the sheep kept for me, shall know that it is the word of the Lord."

And who could these "Chamanaioi" be, if not us? We who were formerly **foreigners** <note>Gentiles</note> and have been gathered from all the previously godless and impious nations to be the "sheep of Christ" who are kept safe? We have been transformed through His grace, and by understanding the events that have been fulfilled, we have received the true knowledge of the word of the Lord. We, the "Chamanaioi," have known the things that were kept silent; but those who boast of being **Israel** and pride themselves on the **seed of Abraham** neither knew nor understood.

And you shall be removed and humbled from the heritage which I gave you, and I will cause you to serve your enemies in a land which you did not know. For this is what I believe is hinted at by the phrase:

### PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 7 <note>The Greek header indicates Book 7 (ζ'), though the previous page's metadata suggested Book 10; Eusebius often revisits these themes across his work.</note>

To what has already been stated, there is added a passage from Jeremiah, spoken in the person of the Lord:
> "I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my heritage, I have given my beloved soul into the hands of her enemies. My heritage has become to me like a lion in the forest; she has raised her voice against me. Is my heritage a hyena's cave to me?" <note>Jeremiah 12:7-9. Appropriately, therefore, following these things he adds: "And I said, I will not shepherd you; let that which is dying die, and let that which is failing fail, and let the rest eat each other's flesh." > "And the Canaanites <note>The Septuagint version Eusebius used read "Canaanites" (*Chananiaioi*) here in Zechariah 11:11, where most modern bibles read "the afflicted of the flock."</note> shall know the sheep kept for me, because it is the word of the Lord."
But who could these "Canaanites" be, if not us? We who were formerly of other tribes and descended from ancient godless and impious nations, yet are now kept as sheep by Him. Through His grace, we have been transformed; understanding what has been accomplished, we have received a true knowledge of the word of the Lord. We, the "Canaanites" who have been saved, have recognized the things revealed; yet those of Israel, who boast and glory in the seed of Abraham, neither knew nor understood them.

...in the midst of Israel. These were the "Measuring Line" and the "Second Staff." The first, named **Beauty**, could be none other than Jerusalem itself, and the worship in the Temple, and the whole Old Covenant. This is presented from the prophecy itself which says: 

> "And I will take my staff, the beautiful one, and cast it away, to scatter my covenant." <note>Zechariah 11:10. Eusebius interprets the staff "Beauty" as the Law and the Covenant itself.</note>

You see how he called the Covenant itself the "First Staff," and the "Second Staff" the "Measuring Line"; nevertheless, he threatens to cast away both staves, having said earlier: 

> "And I will take for myself two staves: the one I called Beauty, and the second I called Measuring Line." <note>Zechariah 11:7. The term "Measuring Line" (*schoinisma*) can also mean a cord, a plot of land, or a union.</note>

In place of which **Aquila** <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek, known for his literalism.</note> says, "I called the one **Splendor** <note>original: *euprepeia*</note>, and the other I called the Measuring Line." And **Symmachus** <note>Another 2nd-century translator who focused on elegant Greek style.</note> says, "I called the one Splendor, and the other I called the Measuring Line." This, then, is the beauty and splendor of the whole nation, which he reasonably named the Divine Law and the Covenant contained within it. For the solemnities of Jerusalem, and the duties of the high-priestly service, and all those things which were formerly carried out among them according to the divine laws and according to the Old Covenant, were a beautiful adornment to those adorned by them. 

The **Measuring Line** refers to the multitude of the nation, as it is often called by Moses when he says: 

> "The Lord’s portion became his people Jacob; the measuring line of his inheritance was Israel." <note>Deuteronomy 32:9. Eusebius uses this to prove that the "Measuring Line" staff represents the physical population of Israel.</note>

But indeed, he signified that the sudden change of these two staves would happen at the indicated times, as both the ancient Old Covenant within it and the former beauty would vanish, and the Measuring Line and the whole nation would be scattered. This occurred since they valued the one who was honored at the price of **thirty pieces of silver**, and thus they suffered the appropriate dishonor for their impiety. He says then: 

> "And I will take my staff, the beautiful one, and cast it away, to scatter my covenant." 

And again: 

> "And I cast away the second staff, the Measuring Line." 

Upon these things the prophecy adds, saying: 

> "And I will remove the three shepherds in one month." <note>Zechariah 11:8.</note>

I think this riddles <note>riddles: *ainittesthai* — to speak in enigmas or allegories</note> the three orders of those who formerly presided over the people of God: **Kings**, **High Priests**, and **Prophets**. For through these three shepherds, all affairs were formerly administered. Because of their perversion, these three shepherds suffered at one time—that of our Savior. For their **King** was a foreigner and lawless, being of another race and not kindred to the nation <note>A reference to Herod the Great, an Idumean, and his successors who ruled at the time of Christ.</note>; and the **High Priest**, having been appointed to the service by promising [payment], came to the honor not according to the succession of the lineage nor according to the lawful decrees; and the **Prophet**, having ceased until John, no longer worked among them, but in his place was some impious false prophet deceiving the people. 

Reasonably, he threatens to strip away at one time the **three anointings** <note>The "three chrismata": kings, priests, and prophets were all anointed roles in Israel.</note> which formerly adorned the whole nation with every beautiful ornament, saying: 

> "And I will remove the three shepherds in one month, and my soul will be burdened with them." 

Instead of which, **Aquila** says: "And my soul was lopped off among them." And **Symmachus**: "And I was discouraged with them." And **Theodotion** <note>A Hellenistic Jewish scholar who revised the Septuagint.</note>: "And my soul was discouraged with them." And teaching the cause of the discouragement, he added: 

> "For indeed their souls roared against me." 

In place of which again, **Aquila** says: "And indeed their soul was embittered in me." And **Symmachus**: "And their soul reached its peak against me." And he says something similar: "For their souls roared against me," according to what...

<meta>catchword: to those who</meta>

# PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 10
<header>PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, Book 10</header>

Who is the speaker? It is recorded in Jeremiah, speaking in the person of the Lord:
» "I have forsaken my house, I have left my heritage; I have given my beloved
» soul into the hands of her enemies. My heritage has become to me like a lion
» in the forest; she has raised her voice against me. Is my heritage like a hyena’s
» cave to me?" <note>Jeremiah 12:7-9. Eusebius uses this to illustrate God’s rejection of the old religious system.</note> It is reasonable, then, that because of these things he adds: "And I said, I will not shepherd you;
» let that which is dying, die; and let that which is failing, fail; and let those
» who remain eat, each one the flesh of his neighbor." After which he adds: "And I will take
» my beautiful staff and cast it away." Instead of which, **Aquila** <note>A 2nd-century translator known for his literal Greek rendering of the Hebrew Bible.</note> says, "And I took," he says, "my
» staff, the **Splendor** <note>original: *euprepeia*</note>, and I cut it asunder," meaning the worship according to
Moses. Therefore, the first staff mentioned at the beginning of the discourse is
said to be broken and cast away. But when the price of the "Priced One," which the
sons of Israel set for him—the silver given—was cast into the house of the Lord, as if into a foundry,
then the things concerning the second staff—which represents all the nations—follow
» as a prophecy of what will happen: "And I cast away the second staff, the
» **Measuring Line** <note>original: *schoinisma*; can also mean "the cord" or "the allotment."</note>, to scatter the covenant between Judah and Israel."
And since the Word has clearly shown through these things the rejection of those people,
it follows that he is no longer recognized by the "prophesied powers," as he says, but
» by the **Canaanites** <note>In the Septuagint version of Zechariah 11:11, "the poor of the flock" is rendered as "the Canaanites." Eusebius interprets this as the Gentiles.</note>, saying: "And the Canaanites, the sheep who are kept
» for me, shall know that it is the word of the Lord." And who would these Canaanites be,
if not us, who were formerly foreigners and from the unbelieving and
impious nations of old, now the sheep kept for Christ? We, who through his grace
have been transformed and, understanding the sacred rites, have received a true 
knowledge of the Word of the Lord; we, the Canaanites, have known and
understood these things. Those of Israel, who boast and pride themselves
on the seed of Abraham, did not know nor understand.

It foretells that their land would suffer things worthy of mourning after its inhabitants [are gone], and that they would no longer be disciplined briefly as before and then restored, but that their affairs would reach a "final end." For it says their end <note>The Greek word *syntēleia* implies a "completion" or "consummation," often used for the end of an age.</note> comes rising like a river, coming upon them all not without a crash—or perhaps he is alluding to the wrath of the Roman Empire, which would roar against them like a river, as they were formerly in a position of height. And indeed, after the wrath from God against them was revealed, he again signifies the events surrounding the Passion itself. He says, "it shall sink like the river of Egypt," by which I think it is shown that the things which of old were sublime and testified to by God—the advantages of the Jewish nation which were, as it were, set on high—shall sink down like the silt and barriers of the faithless nations that flow by like a river, and shall be moved from a height to a low place. Then, following these things, he reveals the very events that happened at the time of the Saving Passion: "In that day," he says, "says the Lord, the sun shall set at midday, and the light shall grow dark upon the earth in the day." These things received a clear fulfillment when our Savior was "lifted up" <note>A double meaning: lifted up on the cross and exalted in glory.</note> and, according to the Evangelist, "from the sixth hour darkness came over all the land until the ninth hour," and about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" <note>original: *ηλεὶ ηλεὶ λαμμᾶ σαβαχθανί* (Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani). » ...a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord, and so on. <note>Amos 8:11. This concludes the quote from the previous page.</note> He says that all these things would one day happen because of their impiety committed against Christ. The outcome of this prophecy was shown to be vivid and clear following their plot against our Savior. Indeed, it was not before that time, but precisely from then until now, that God has turned their feasts into mourning and their songs into lamentation. He has deprived them of their world-renowned metropolis <note>Jerusalem</note> and the holy sanctuary within it. Through the siege conducted by the Roman Emperor Vespasian, He brought about its destruction, so that they can no longer perform their lawful feasts and solemn assemblies there. And what need is there to mention how the famine of hearing the word of the Lord has overtaken them all? This was their recompense for driving out the Word of God <note>original: "ton theou logon"</note> from themselves, denying Him with one voice, and departing from Him.

<margin>»</margin>...having made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were warming themselves. <note>original: "anthrakian pepoiēkotes... ethermainonto" — This refers to John 18:18, where the servants and officers warm themselves during Peter's denial.</note> For them, the events predicted reached such a conclusion in the literal sense. The Hebrew wording is taken from the prophecy at hand. Indeed, the very syllables *Elei lamma sabachthani* <note>original: "Ἠλεὶ λαμμᾶ σαβαχθανί"</note> are contained in the opening of the Psalm. And the remaining parts could only be applied to him, as the following argument will demonstrate. Or, if anyone wishes to transfer these to another person—whether a king, or a prophet, or any of the God-beloved men who ever lived among the Jews—let them show if they are able to apply these descriptions. <margin>,,</margin> "shall turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship

see if it is possible to apply these prophesied things to any ordinary person. 
It is clear you would not find them fitting anyone else except our Savior alone, who would be the 
most faithful and true witness of all, properly referring the voice of the Psalm to himself, 
as the Evangelists have testified. Matthew <note>original: *ho mathētaios*, "the disciple." Eusebius often refers to Matthew this way.</note> through the 
words he set forth; and Mark, through the things he also recorded in this way, saying: "And when the 
sixth hour had come, darkness fell over the whole earth until the ninth hour; and at the ninth hour 
Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, *Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?* which is translated, 
'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?'" <note>original: *hēlei hēlei lamma sabachthani*</note> And some of those standing by

Come then, following these things, let us see how the things declared through the Psalm 
refer back to him. And first, let us consider the phrase in the inscription, "To the end," 
or, according to Aquila <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek.</note>, "To the Victor," or, according to Symmachus <note>A late 2nd-century translator known for his more idiomatic Greek style.</note>, "A song of victory 
concerning the help." These things occur to us: that the saving Passion, as the words of the 
Evangelist established, took place while darkness occurred from the sixth hour until the ninth 
hour, and was completed around the ninth hour, when he also let out the great cry, 
saying the words shown a little earlier, so that his Passion is clearly confessed to have 
happened toward the evening as night was approaching. But the events of the Resurrection 
from the dead—which was the "help" <note>Greek: *antilēpsis*. Eusebius links the title of the Psalm ("concerning the help") to the Resurrection.</note> of the Father helping him, and drawing him to 
himself out of the regions of death, and receiving him—took place around dawn, 
as is again established from the testimony of the Evangelists. Luke says: "But on the first 
day of the week, at early dawn, they came to the tomb, bringing the spices they had prepared," 
meaning the women, and some others with them. "And they found the stone rolled away from 
the tomb; but when they entered, they did not find the body," because of the awakening of 
our Savior from the dead...

# EUSEBIUS

...in the version of the Seventy <note>The "Seventy" refers to the Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> it is even now called by the Hebrew name. Indeed, there are certain other names used among them in the divine oracles, such as **El**, **Shaddai**, and **Iao** <note>original: *iaō*, a Greek transliteration of the four-letter Hebrew name of God, the Tetragrammaton</note>, and **El**, and others similar to these. The Psalm currently at hand [Psalm 22] contains the words *Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani*, which our Lord also used, but he did not use the name **Elohim** <note>original: *elōeim*</note>. Aquila <note>Aquila of Sinope was a 2nd-century translator famous for his extremely literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, at any rate, knowing the difference between the Hebrew titles for God, saw that the name signified by **Elohim** was different from what is now expressed in *Eli, Eli*. 
" He did not think it right, as the other translators did, to say 'O God, my God' in his translation, but rather 'My strong one, my strong one.' More accurately, it is 'My strength, my strength.' So, according to his 
" understanding, the Lamb of God, our Savior, when saying *Eli, Eli* to the 
" Father, was saying: 'My strong one, my strong one, why have you forsaken me?' And perhaps, because 
" his 'Strong One' forsook him, for this reason he was crucified, just as the Apostle says: 'For indeed he was 
" crucified out of weakness, yet he lives by the power of God' [2 Corinthians 13:4], as if he would not have been crucified if the 
" Strong One had not left him. It was fitting for the Lamb of God—the one 
" led like a sheep to the slaughter, and who remained silent like a lamb before its shearer—to 
" attribute his own powers to God, and to consider nothing to be his own except 
" the Father alone. Therefore, calling his Father 'Strong One,' just as in the eighteenth Psalm <note>Psalm 18:1 (17:1 in the LXX).</note>, 
" he names the Father his strength, his might, and his refuge, saying: 'I will 
" love you, O Lord, my strength; the Lord is my firmament, and my refuge, and my deliverer. 
" My God is my helper, and I will hope in him; my protector, the horn of my salvation, 
" and my supporter.' Therefore, his 'Strong One' willed to forsake him, so that 
" he might descend even unto death, even the death of the cross, and be given as a ransom 
" and a substitute <term>Substitute: From the Greek *antipsychon*, meaning "a life for a life."</term> for the whole world, and a purification for the life of us who have believed in him.
" And he, after a sudden silence in the midst of that humble counsel—being in ignorance, if 
" anyone ever was, of the reasons for his being forsaken by the Father—
" humbled himself even more, and embraced death on our behalf with great readiness. 
" He, who was entirely holy and blessed, became a curse for us; not that he knew sin, 
" but so that we might become the righteousness of God in him. And furthermore, 
" having taken up our sins, he was crucified, he who suffered so that we, who were formerly ungodly, 
" might receive mercy, becoming our substitute and ransom. Thus we might reasonably say 
" the prophetic word: 'He himself bears our sins, and he is pained for us; he 
" was wounded for our sins, and was made weak because of our iniquities, 
" so that by his bruise we might be healed.' For the Lord delivered him over to 
" our sins [Isaiah 53:4-6]; clearly, having been delivered by the Father, and made weak, and having 
" taken up our iniquities, he was led like a sheep to the slaughter. The Apostle 
" agrees with these things, saying: 'He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all' [Romans 8:32]. 
" Moving us to search for the cause for which the Father left him, he says: 'Why 
" have you forsaken me?' This was the cause: the redemption of the entire human 
" race, bought with his precious blood from that former harsh slavery, when 
" they were enslaved to invisible masters, to unclean demons, and to evil rulers and spirits. 
" And in another way, the Father forsook him because Christ himself willed 
" that his disposition toward humanity be rendered to God. Therefore, since no one had power over his soul...

<summary>Eusebius interprets Christ's cry on the cross using Aquila’s translation "My Strong One," arguing that the Father's "forsaking" of the Son was a necessary withdrawal of divine power to allow for Christ's sacrificial death and the redemption of humanity.</summary>

» He himself laid it down willingly on behalf of humanity, as he teaches when he says: "No one takes my life from me. » And Symmachus <note>Symmachus was another ancient translator whose version was often clearer and more idiomatic than Aquila’s.</note> says: "The words of my lamentations have stood far off from my salvation." And according to another version called the "Fifth," <note>The "Fifth" (*Quinta*) refers to an anonymous Greek translation of the Old Testament discovered in a jar near Jericho and used by Origen in his scholarship.</note> it is said: "Far from my salvation are the words of my petitions." 
» See then that in none of these others was "transgressions" mentioned; it happens that such changes sometimes occur through a scribal error. One should understand this from the various translations—unless, perhaps, someone might say that even here he said these things because he was making our transgressions his own. <note>Eusebius suggests that if the word "transgressions" is correct, it refers to Christ taking on the sins of humanity, not his own.</note>
» Following these he adds: "My God, I will cry out by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and not for foolishness to me." Instead of which, Symmachus again says: "My God, I will shout by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and there is no silence." 
» In these words, he marvels at the Father as one not hearing him, for the Savior sees this as something strange and paradoxical. For [the Father] reserved his hearing for the proper time for him to be heard. 
» And this was the time of his relief and rising—that is, the time of the resurrection from the dead—at which time, if we may say so in a word, he himself might justly receive the answer: "At an acceptable time I listened to you, and on the day of salvation I helped you. Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation." <note>Eusebius quotes Isaiah 49:8, which was also famously quoted by the Apostle Paul in 2 Corinthians 6:2.</note>
» These things might also be said differently by our Savior, as he was accustomed to being heard by the Father at all times, but now he trusts that he will be heard, as if he were saying more clearly: "Is it not possible, O Father, for me, your only-begotten and beloved Son, not to be heard, as I shout and cry out to you, my own Father?" 
» Indeed, he teaches this very thing in the Gospel according to John regarding Lazarus, when he said, "Take away the stone from the tomb," he lifted up his eyes to heaven and said: "Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me." <note>John 11:41-42. Eusebius uses the miracle of Lazarus to show that Jesus had total confidence in the Father's response.</note>
» If, therefore, [the Father] always hears him, it is not a matter of doubt. Because he knows precisely that he will be heard even now—since it is impossible for him not to be heard—he says questioningly: "My God, I will cry out by day, and will you not hear?" 
» We should place a punctuation mark at "will you not hear?" and understand the opposite of what the question implies. Indeed, he teaches this a little later as he proceeds through the Psalm, saying that [God] "did not despise nor was he disgusted by the petition of the poor man, nor did he turn his face away from me; and when I cried out to him, he heard me." <note>Psalm 22:24. Eusebius argues that the earlier "silence" was only a temporary prelude to the ultimate answer of the Resurrection.</note>
» How then could he safely say, "My God, I will cry out by day, and you will not hear," unless it is according to the interpretation we have given? Or I think he also speaks in riddles, saying: "My God, I will cry out by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and not for foolishness to me." 
» For he says, the phrase "you will hear" is not said "to me for foolishness" <note>original: *eis anoian*, meaning ignorance or lack of understanding.</note>. For I myself know how we said it, being persuaded that it is your nature not only to assist and hear me, but also all your holy ones. 
» For always and through all things you dwell in your holy ones, and you are the praise of the God-loving man called Israel. For because of you, no ordinary praise comes to everyone who trusts in you: "In you our fathers hoped, and hoping, they were rescued from the evils of their oppressors, and to you they cri—"

[...they hoped] and were saved. In you they hoped, and they were not put to shame. Since, then, all the holy ones obtained these things from you—they cried out and were heard, and were not put to shame—how much more will you hear me, your beloved child, as I cry out more than all others and in greater loneliness? 

But even if I speak in wonder, asking: "Shall I cry out and you will not hear?" yet my words do not lead to folly. For I know how I offer my prayer: not exalting myself nor boasting, but as one who is humble in mind. Since I am gentle and humble in heart, I speak humble things about myself in a manner suited to my own gentleness. 

Thus, I even name myself a <term>worm <note>original Greek: "skōlēx"</note></term>. For what could be humbler than a worm? For this reason, I would not even call myself a "man," having descended from my own proper greatness to such a degree of humility that I seem to differ in no way from a worm, on account of being subject to death and the corruption of the body. 

For from what else does a worm arise, if not from the corruption of bodies? Having descended into this state myself, I rightly recognize myself as a worm and not a man. Therefore, I have become a "reproach of men and despised of the people." I would not have been overturned by the judgment of men, nor would I be an object of contempt, had I not reached the state of a worm at the time of my Passion. 

At that time, then, seeing me hanging upon the cross, they sneered and spoke with their lips; they wagged their heads, saying: "He hoped in the Lord, let Him rescue him; let Him save him, since He desires him." 

These things, though spoken secretly through the Psalm, were clearly prophesying about things that would happen a long time afterward. They reached their fulfillment when—according to Matthew—two robbers were crucified with him, one on the right and one on the left. Those passing by blasphemed him, wagging their heads and saying: "You who would destroy the temple and build it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross!" Likewise, the chief priests, mocking him with the elders and scribes, said: "He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he is the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross and we will believe in him. If he trusts in God, let Him rescue him now, if He desires him. For he said, 'I am the Son of God.'"

According to Luke: "The people stood watching, and the rulers sneered at him with them, saying: 'He saved others; let him save himself, if this is the Christ, the chosen one of God.'" 

And according to Mark: "Those passing by blasphemed him, wagging their heads and saying: 'Aha! You who would destroy the temple and build it in three days, save yourself and come down from the cross!' Likewise, the chief priests, mocking him among themselves with the scribes, said: 'He saved others; himself he cannot save. Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe in him.'" 

How do these events differ from those proclaimed beforehand in the Psalm, in the passage: "But I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and despised of the people. All who saw me sneered at me; they spoke with their lips and wagged their heads: 'He hoped in the Lord, let Him rescue him; let Him save him, since He desires him'"? 

And do not wonder if these things were spoken of and fulfilled according to the Passion of our Savior, since even to this day, among all people who have not yet embraced faith in him, he is considered a "reproach of men." For what could be more inglorious or worse than any reproach than to be crucified? But also [he became] an object of contempt...
