[...the] mockery of the people, that is, those of the circumcision; all of them among the nations even now and to this day are accustomed to mock and despise and spit upon him. Whence also, fittingly, the Apostle says: "But we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness." [1 Cor 1:23] The things said next in the Psalm are even now a subject for many regarding the same matter. These things, then, he prayed concerning the circumstances that had overtaken him even then. But knowing that his first binding into the flesh was no less a trial than the calamity of death—namely, his birth from a female and a virgin—he timely mentions his birth in the middle of his words about death, saying to the Father: 

» "For you are he who drew me out of the womb, my hope from 
» my mother’s breasts; upon you I was cast from the matrix; 
» from my mother’s belly you are my God." [Psalm 22:9-10]

He reasonably brings these things to mind as a consolation for his release from his present troubles. For just as, he says, you became my helper when I took on a human body—when from the very womb that carried me, you yourself, my God and Father, acting as a midwife, drew out the flesh prepared for me by the Holy Spirit, extending your own power—lest any snare or plot of the opposing powers and evil spirits, begrudging my passage to humanity, should destroy me. Since even during the conception by her who bore me, you again overshadowed the womb, so that I might remain hidden from the <term>rulers of this age <note>Eusebius refers to the "archons," spiritual or demonic powers who, according to early Christian writers like Ignatius of Antioch, were kept in the dark about the mystery of the Incarnation to ensure the defeat of death.</note></term>. For this reason, the conception of the holy Virgin was by the Holy Spirit. Hence your archangel Gabriel proclaimed a great mystery, saying to Mary: 

» "The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power 
» of the Most High shall overshadow you." [Luke 1:35]

Just as the power of the Most High then overshadowed the one being conceived, so it drew me out from my mother’s womb when I was being born. In this way, I find great consolation that you will much more surely draw me up from death. And hoping in this, I have trusted in you as my own God and Lord and Father; and I have trusted in you not just in the present moment as one receiving hope, but even since I was taking infant nourishment from my mother’s breasts, being managed in the same way as human infants, though I was the <term>Word <note>original Greek: "Logos"—the divine, eternal reason or person of Christ.</note></term> appearing as if incomplete <gloss>if</gloss> someone being <gloss>the</gloss> Word. 

For I was not actually such an incomplete infant, even if I possessed a body like other men; I was not similar to the many in power or essence, but was unbound and free, as the Lamb of God, even while being suckled at that age—I mean, from my mother’s breasts. And no one will think this a great thing if they learn what came even before: 

» "That upon you I was cast from the matrix, 
» and from my mother’s belly you are my God." 

For while I was still being carried inside the chamber of her who bore me, I beheld you, my God; for I remained unconfused and untroubled in such a communion with the flesh—or rather, I was incorporeal even then, and free from all bonds. Thus was I "cast upon you from the matrix," and you were with me from my mother’s womb, such that my power, while still being carried by the holy Virgin, was sensed by my forerunner John, who himself was being carried in the womb of Elizabeth; so that, moved by my divinity, he leaped for joy and was filled with the Holy Spirit. Recalling all these things, then, and always setting my God and my Father before my eyes, it is only fitting that during the present time of the passion which encompasses me—when I have become a voluntary and obedient servant to you, the Father—

» [they] were saved. But if I speak in wonder, saying "I will cry out and you will not hear"? Yet my words do not descend into folly. Since I am "meek and humble of heart," <note>Matthew 11:29</note> I speak humbly about myself in a manner suited to my own meekness. Thus, I even name myself a "worm." For what could be humbler than a worm? Hence, I would not even call myself a man, having descended from my own greatness into such extreme humility that I seem to differ in no way from a worm, on account of reaching the point of death and the corruption of the body. For from what else are worms produced but from the corruption of bodies? Having descended into this state myself, I reasonably recognize myself as a "worm and not a man." <note>Psalm 22:6</note> Therefore, I have also become:

» "A reproach of men and the outcast of the people," <note>Psalm 22:6</note> not by my own will nor by the character of the men I was seen with, nor would I be an "outcast" had I not reached the state of a worm through the season of my suffering. At that time, at any rate, 

» beholding me hung upon the cross, they sneered and spoke with their lips, they wagged their heads saying, "He hoped in the Lord, let Him deliver him, let Him save him, because He desires him." <note>Psalm 22:7-8</note> Now, these things were clearly prophesied through the Psalm as a riddle <term>aporia</term> <note>literally "a difficulty" or "puzzlement," here meaning a prophetic mystery</note> concerning the things that were to happen a long time later; and they reached their fulfillment when, according to Matthew, two thieves were crucified with him, one on the right and one on the left of the Savior, and those passing by blasphemed him, wagging their heads and saying, "Woe to you who would destroy the temple and build it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross!" Similarly, the chief priests mocking him with the elders and scribes said, "He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he is the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him. If he trusts in God, let Him deliver him now, if He desires him. For he said, 'I am the Son of God.'" And according to Luke: "The people stood watching, and the rulers sneered at him with them, saying, 'He saved others; let him save himself, if this is the Christ, the chosen one of God.'" And according to Mark: "And those passing by blasphemed him, wagging their heads and saying, 'Woe to you who would destroy the temple and build it in three days, save yourself and come down from the cross!' Similarly, the chief priests mocking him among themselves with the scribes said, 'He saved others; himself he cannot save. Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe in him.'" For how would these things differ from the words proclaimed beforehand in the Psalm: 

» "But I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and an outcast of the people. All who beheld 
» me sneered at me; they spoke with their lips, they wagged the head: 'He hoped in the Lord, let 
» Him deliver him, let Him save him, because He desires him.'" And do not wonder if these things were both spoken and fulfilled according to the passion of our Savior, since even until now, among all men who have not yet embraced faith in him, he is considered a "reproach of men." For what could be more shameful or worse than any "reproach" than to be crucified? But also [an] out— <note>The word "outcast" (ἐξουδένημα) is interrupted here.</note>

[It] is an example of the people, specifically those of the circumcision; even now and to this day, all among the nations are accustomed to mock, despise, and spit upon them. Hence, quite reasonably, the Apostle [Paul] says:

> ” "But we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles." <note>original: "ἰουδαίοις μὲν σκάνδαλον, ἔθνεσι δὲ μωρίαν" — 1 Corinthians 1:23</note>
> ” And the things said next in the Psalm you can still see even now being repeated by many regarding this same subject.

He prayed these things concerning the circumstances that gripped him at that time. Knowing that his first binding into the flesh—his birth from a woman and a virgin—was no less a hardship than the calamity of death, he appropriately mentions the words of his birth to the Father during his discourse on death:

> ” "For you are the one who drew me out of the womb, my hope from my mother's breasts; 
> ” upon you I was cast from the matrix, from my mother's belly you are my God." <note>original: "σὺ εἶ ὁ ἐκσπάσας με ἐκ γαστρός" — Psalm 22:9-10. Eusebius views the Messiah as the speaker here.</note>

He reasonably recalls these memories for consolation and release from his current troubles. For he says, "Just as you became my helper when I took on a human body—when you yourself, my God and Father, acting alone like a midwife, drew out my flesh which had been prepared by the Holy Spirit from the very womb that carried me, extending your own power, lest any ambush or plot of the opposing powers and evil spirits—who envied my passage into the human world—should occur. Indeed, even before the conception, you again overshadowed the womb, so that I might remain hidden from the 'rulers of this age' <note>Eusebius refers to the "archons," or demonic powers, who according to early Christian thought were kept in ignorance of Christ's true nature to ensure the crucifixion and subsequent defeat of death.</note> regarding the conception of the Holy Virgin by the Holy Spirit." This great mystery your archangel Gabriel revealed, saying to Mary: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you." <note>Luke 1:35</note>

> ” Just as your power as the Most High then overshadowed me during conception and drew me out from my mother's womb at birth,

so too it is a great consolation to me that you might much more draw me up from death. Expecting this, I have trusted in you, my God and Lord and Father; and I have trusted, not starting this hope in you only now, but even when I was receiving infant nourishment from my mother's breasts, being managed in the same economy <term>economy: 'oikonomia', referring here to the divine plan of the Incarnation and its physical realities</term> as human infants, though seemingly imperfect and without speech <term>without speech: 'alogos', meaning literally 'without reason' or 'without word'. Eusebius is playing on the idea that the 'Logos' (Word/Reason) appeared 'alogos' (speechless) as a baby.</term>. For I was not truly like them, even if I had a body similar to humans; I was not similar to the masses in power or essence, but was free and unbound, as your Lamb of God, while being nursed at that age—I mean, from my mother's breasts. And no one will yet consider this a great thing if they should learn what happened even earlier:

> ” "That I was cast upon you from the matrix, and from my mother's belly you are my God."

For while I was still being carried inside the chamber of the one who bore me, I saw you, my God, inasmuch as I remained unconfused and untroubled in such a communion of flesh—or rather, being even then incorporeal and free from all bonds. Thus was I "cast upon you from the matrix," and "from my mother's belly you were my God," such that my power was sensed while I was still being carried by the Holy Virgin, by my forerunner John, who was himself being carried in the womb of Elizabeth; so that, moved by my divinity, he leaped in exultation and was filled with the Holy Spirit. Recalling all these things, and having my God and Father always before my eyes, it is reasonable that during the present time—the season of the passion that surrounds me—when I have become a voluntary and obedient subject to you, the Father...

> ” I have willingly become a worm, and not a man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people. <note>original: "ἐκὼν γέγονα σκώληξ, καὶ οὐκ ἄνθρωπος..." — quoting Psalm 22:6. Eusebius emphasizes that this humiliation was a voluntary choice by the Savior.</note>

And now, when all those who behold my body nailed to the cross consider it a loathsome sight to look upon, they have mocked me, pouring out such great derision and mockery against me that they not only calculate and contemplate impious things about me in their minds, but also fearlessly utter them and speak openly:

> ” Indeed, they spoke with their lips, they wagged their heads, saying: ‘He hoped in the Lord, let Him rescue him.’ <note>original: "ἐλάλησαν γοῦν ἐν χείλεσιν, ἐκίνησαν κεφαλήν..." — Psalm 22:7-8. from my mother's breasts, the one known to me from my mother's belly and recognized as my God—I cry out to Him and to the same Father not to stand far off from me, because trouble is near. For he says that the instrument <note>likely referring to the cross or the physical body as the tool of salvation</note> is barely yet present, and that which is all-consuming is approaching and pressing upon me: the final cloud of the trouble that is about to happen to me. For I do not yet call this current trouble that surrounds me—neither the cross, nor the reproaches of men, nor the mockery, nor indeed the things that happened before the cross, the scourging, the insults, and all that the sons of men did to me—but rather, I see the descent into <term>Hades</term><note>Hades: the realm of the dead. In early Christian theology, Christ’s descent into Hades was a triumphant mission to liberate the righteous souls held there.</note> approaching, and the assaults of the powers that are opposed and hostile to God.

> ” Therefore I say that trouble is near, because there is no one to help. <note>Psalm 22:11</note>

For how could this not be a certain excess and the greatest trouble of all, in which there is no helper? For He leaps down for the salvation of the souls in Hades, who have expected His arrival for long ages; He comes to crush the bronze gates and shatter the iron bars, <note>allusion to Psalm 107:16 and Isaiah 45:2, traditionally associated with the "Harrowing of Hell."</note> and to loosen the bonds of Hades for the prisoners, as is appropriate for each. This is what happened when many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose and entered with Him into the <gloss>truly</gloss> holy city of God. <note>referencing Matthew 27:52-53</note> But the opposing powers were turned back by the evils of men, causing them no small grief and trouble, as they were shut out even from these souls through the excess of His goodness. But for whose sake were all these things said, as if from His own person? They were said of Him who was carried in the womb and born from a mother's belly, whom we claimed was the Lamb of God. For to Him happen the things concerning the Passion, just as the things concerning His birth in the flesh were fitting. For that which is born also dies; but that which dies does not experience death in a way that is unrelated to the previous path of birth. Our Savior and Lord recounts these things, not insofar as He was by nature fleshless and bodiless, nor insofar as He is conceived as the Word of God and God, but insofar as He was able to say in prayer to the Father: "For You are the one who drew me out of the womb, my hope from the breasts

> ” of my mother. Upon You I was cast from the matrix; from my mother’s belly You are my God." Since, therefore, He has come to the Passion, He prays these words to the Father; and He says that so many opposing powers are about to surround Him,

including unclean demons and spiritual forces of wickedness, and above all the worst of the evil ones, the <term>Ruler of this Age</term><note>Ruler of this Age: a title for Satan or the personification of evil power in the world.</note> himself. Because of their malice, it is fitting to name them "evil beasts"—either "wild bulls" or "calves" or "lions" or "dogs." He is about to stand against them all, yet He will perform no good work for them because they receive nothing of my goodness due to their extreme habit of malice; but neither does He find any helper or fellow-worker among those mentioned in the struggle on behalf of the souls in Hades. > ” I would not be speaking unreasonably to say that trouble is near, and that there is no one to help. <note>original: "θλῖψις ἐγγύς, ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν ὁ βοηθῶν" — quoting Psalm 22:11.</note> Now, we do not think it at all wondrous that the wicked and opposing powers <note>Eusebius refers here to demonic forces.</note> do not work with him or help him toward any good end. But the greatest trouble of all—the one pressing upon him most heavily—is that no one, not even those who are worthy, nor any of the divine powers, dares to step into the kingdoms of death or to assist his soul. For this path was reserved for him alone; for him alone the gates of death were set ajar, and the gatekeepers of Hades trembled when they saw him. He, who holds the power over death, stepped down from his royal thrones, recognizing him alone as his own master, and addressed him with soft pleas and supplication, according to what is revealed in Job regarding these matters. <note>Eusebius likely refers to Job 41, interpreted here as the submission of the Leviathan/death to Christ.</note> More than the impious pursuit of the tyrant, the strength of the Noble One prevails, so that no other heavenly being dared to be present with him in those regions, or to cooperate in the salvation of souls. Reasonably, then, he says that trouble is near and there is no helper. Since the only one capable of helping him even there <note>referring to the Father or the divine nature</note> left him, it was so that the brilliance and excellence of his own free will, and his hard-won victory, might be proclaimed to all. And since not even the only one capable of helping him was his helper then, he reasonably said: *Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?* which is: *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?* <note>original: "ἠλὶ ἠλὶ λαμμὰ σαβαχθανί" — Christ's cry from the cross in Aramaic, quoted in Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34.</note> When he was conceived and carried in the womb by the Holy Virgin, the Father’s power was with him, when the Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin and the power of the Most High overshadowed her; and the Father himself drew the one who was becoming man from the womb, as the word prophesied. But when he was stripped for the season of his

passion and for the hour of death, a helper was no longer present with him. I believe him when he testifies to this himself. For that which was spoken by him on the cross, *Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani*, was also prophetically cried out by the Psalm: *Trouble is near, and there is no one to help.* Does this show anything else, except that as a great athlete he was pitted against so many opponents, while God over all acted as the judge and arbiter of the events? He bore these things as one of those struggling in a contest, calling upon his Father and Overseer to be present with him as a favorable judge, especially since there was no other helper for him except the one who alone arbitrates what takes place. Therefore, he says in

> ” prayer: *Do not stand far off from me, for trouble is near, for there is no one to help.* One may see with divine eyes <note>term: "ἐνθέοις ὄμμασιν" — refers to spiritual or prophetic insight rather than physical sight.</note> how, while he was hung upon the scaffold <note>term: "ἰκρίῳ" — literally a wooden platform or frame, here referring to the cross.</note> in his body, the invisible powers from the surrounding air—unseen by humans—gathered like birds of prey and hostile wild beasts around him, nesting near him, expecting that his body would soon be nothing but a corpse. The rulers and authorities of the air <note>A reference to Ephesians 2:2 and 6:12 regarding demonic hierarchies.</note> flocked together from every side—the spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience—as well as the demons that fly about the earth and through the entire inhabited world of men. It is likely that even the beings from the underworld, and the wild and terrifying beasts in Tartarus <note>term: "ταρτάρῳ" — the deepest abyss of the underworld in Greek thought, adopted by Christian writers to describe the prison of fallen angels or the depths of Hades.</note> itself, were there—those of whom Isaiah spoke when addressing the Morning Star who fell from heaven:

> ” Hades below was embittered at meeting you; all the giants were stirred up for you. <note>original: "ὁ ᾅδης κάτωθεν ἐπικράνθη..." — quoting Isaiah 14:9.</note> Beholding all these things surrounding his crucified body and tearing at him, he describes their gathering as...

» saying, "Many calves have surrounded me, fat bulls have beset me. These aforementioned enemies opened their mouths as if they were going to swallow it up, just as they do with the irrational souls of men. Therefore he says, "They opened their mouth against me like a ravening and roaring lion." To which he immediately adds, "I was poured out like water." <note>original: "ὡσεὶ ὕδωρ ἐξεχύθην" — Psalm 22:14.</note> One might say that this was fulfilled physically and according to the historical account when, as the Evangelist John tells us, one of the soldiers pierced the side of the Lamb of God with a spear, and immediately water and blood came out.

Nevertheless, he also seems to indicate the total death of the spiritual nature <note>Eusebius here uses "spiritual nature" to refer to the life-force or the physical vessel's animation being extinguished.</note> through these words: "I was poured out like water, and all my bones were scattered. My heart became like melting wax in the midst of my belly. My strength dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue cleaved to my throat." <note>original: "ἐξηράνθη ὡς ὄστρακον ἡ ἰσχύς μου, καὶ ἡ γλῶσσά μου κεκόλληται τῷ λάρυγγί μου" — Psalm 22:15.</note> For these descriptions signify the state of a dead body. He immediately brings this to a point, saying, "And you have brought me down into the dust of death." He said these things while foreseeing them before they happened, seeing them as if they were already standing near and surrounding him. 

But then, returning to the events that had already occurred to show his readiness for what was to come, he teaches us what kind of plots he endured, saying, "For many dogs have surrounded me, a congregation of evildoers has beset me." <note>original: "ἐκύκλωσάν με κύνες πολλοὶ, συναγωγὴ πονηρευομένων περιέσχον με" — Psalm 22:16.</note> By these "dogs" and the "congregation," he likely means both the Roman soldiers and those of the Circumcision <note>The Jewish leaders and people who opposed him.</note> who rose up against him. For the soldiers of Pilate, taking Jesus into the Praetorium <note>The headquarters of the Roman governor.</note>, gathered the whole cohort against him. Stripping him, they put a scarlet cloak around him, and weaving a crown of thorns, they placed it on his head, and a reed in his hand. Kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" And spitting on him, they took the reed and struck him on the head. And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the cloak, put his own clothes back on him, and led him away to be crucified. 

They were essentially fulfilling in deed the prophecy: "Many dogs have surrounded me, a congregation of evildoers has beset me." But also the words, "They pierced my hands and my feet, I was numbered with all my bones," and further, "They themselves gazed and stared at me; they divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots." <note>original: "διεμερίσαντο τὰ ἱμάτιά μου ἑαυτοῖς, καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν ἱματισμόν μου ἔβαλον κλῆρον" — Psalm 22:18.</note> This was fulfilled again when they fastened his hands and feet to the cross with nails, and when they took his garments and divided them among themselves. 

John records this, saying: "Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments and made four parts, a part for each soldier. And also the tunic; now the tunic was seamless, woven from the top throughout. They said to one another, 'Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be,' so that the Scripture might be fulfilled which says, 'They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.'" These things, then, the soldiers did. And Matthew, following the recorded facts, spoke in this way: "And having crucified him, they divided his garments, casting lots, so that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled: 'They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.' And sitting down, they watched..."

They were the ones who incited the entire multitude to demand his blood, bringing it upon themselves and upon their own children. <note>A reference to Matthew 27:25, "His blood be on us and on our children."</note> Indeed, Isaiah clearly calls them dogs, saying:

<margin>»</margin> "They are all dumb dogs, unable to bark." <note>Isaiah 56:10. Eusebius uses this to contrast the Jewish leaders with faithful "watchdogs."</note> For it was their duty—even if they did not hold the rank of shepherds—to act at least like good dogs, guarding the master's rational flock and the sheep of the house of Israel. They should have barked with understanding, recognizing and wagging their tails for their own Master and his flock, guarding with all vigilance the sheep entrusted to them. They should have barked if anyone from the outside plotted against the flock. Instead, like truly savage dogs with their barking silenced, they turned against the sheep, becoming wild against the Shepherd, so that:

<margin>»</margin> the verse fits them perfectly: "Many dogs have surrounded me, an assembly of evildoers has encircled me." And all those who, down to the present day, conduct themselves in a similar manner to them—by blaspheming and "barking" against the Christ of God—should not be considered separate from those original enemies. Furthermore, those who, like the most impious soldiers of that time, "crucify the Son of God again and put him to open shame," <note>Hebrews 6:6.</note> would not be far from that same condemnation. All those who even now still mutilate the body of Christ—that is, the Church—are handling his hands and feet, and even his bones.

<margin>»</margin> This is true if indeed "we are all one body in Christ, and individually members of one another," <note>Romans 12:5.</note> and if 

<margin>»</margin> "the head cannot say to the feet, 'I have no need of you,'" nor again the eyes to the hands. <note>1 Corinthians 12:21.</note> Thus, in times of persecution, whenever any action is taken against the members of Christ by enemies and foes, one might appropriately apply the verse: "They pierced my hands and my feet; they numbered all my bones." <note>Psalm 22:16-17.</note> "And they themselves observed and stared at me." And when they "divide his garments among themselves and cast lots for his clothing," <note>Psalm 22:18.</note> this occurs when each person, in various ways, tears away and corrupts the "adornment of the Word"—that is, the literal expressions of the Divine Scriptures—or when they seize upon the doctrines concerning Him with distorted teachings, as the godless leaders of heresies are accustomed to do. In response to all this, addressing his prayer to God, the Lord and Father, he continues, saying: "But you, O Lord, do not remove your help far from me." <note>Psalm 22:19.</note> For having been left for a short time for the demonstration of the struggle, and having stripped for death alone without a helper, he knew that help from the Father would indeed come to him, through which the resurrection from the dead would also occur. Rightly then, in this present prayer, he asks 

<margin>»</margin> to find a way out from the battle-line of his opponents. Therefore he says, "But you, O Lord, do not remove your help far from me; give heed to my assistance." Since you have not kept it far from me, 'deliver my soul from the sword, and my only-begotten from the power of the dog.'" <note>Psalm 22:20. <meta>This page continues Eusebius of Caesarea’s commentary on Psalm 22 (Septuagint 21). On the previous page, he identified the "dogs" surrounding Christ as the hostile leaders of the Jews. He now moves to the specific petitions of the Savior for deliverance from these symbolic beasts and the transition to the Resurrection.</meta>

<page-num>316</page-num>
<header>EUSEBIUS</header>

their call, being like a sword, was stretched out against the soul of our Savior; and a certain one, being a dog of death, put forth a death-bearing hand to devour it. For this reason he says: 
» Deliver my soul from the sword, and my only-begotten <note>original: "τὴν μονογενῆ μου" — In the context of the Psalm, this refers to his "only life" or "solitary soul," but Eusebius likely sees a reference to the "Only-Begotten Son."</note> from the hand of the dog. 
» And there is another evil power among the so-called wild beasts, addressed as a **lion**, which has opened wide the gaping and bottomless mouth of death; along with the others who hide away those in Hades, it rushed to swallow his soul as well. For of old, death had grown strong and swallowed many, being none other than the aforementioned lion, whose mouth they opened against our Savior. It is from this mouth that he himself calls upon the Father to be saved, saying: 
» **Save me from the lion's mouth.** 
And there would also be certain other evil and god-opposing powers arrayed against the "Unicorn" of God <note>The Septuagint translates the Hebrew *re'em* (wild ox) as *monokeros* (one-horn/unicorn). Eusebius interprets this title as a symbol of Christ's unique power derived from the Father.</note>, attempting to lead a counter-attack against him. From these also, the Unicorn of God—our Lord himself, who has the Father alone as his "horn"—asks that his humility be rescued, saying: 
» **and my humility from the horns of the unicorns.** 
What "humility" is this, other than that very state in which, though he existed in the form of God, he humbled himself and emptied himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross? <note>A reference to Philippians 2:6-8.</note> But to have descended so far, reaching even to this point—I mean the state of being carried into Hades and the "hand of the dog" mentioned there—from this, it is likely that those who tell stories to children <note>original: "ὁ παῖδας μυθείων" — likely referring to Greek poets like Hesiod or Homer.</note> heard of such a "dog of death" and depicted it as being triple-headed. 

Having come even to the throat of the aforementioned lion, and having subjected his "humility" to the opposing and god-fighting "unicorns," and having brought this to the end of the entire dispensation <term>dispensation: "οἰκονομία" — the divine plan for salvation through the Incarnation</term> of his emptying and humiliation, he then begins at last to obtain help and assistance from the Father: 
» **But you, Lord, do not move your help far from me; look to my assistance.** 
And having said this, it was not long before he obtained a hearing from the Father, who did not stay far away, nor did he delay for even the shortest time. In actual fact, we might almost say to him, "While you were still speaking, I said: behold, I am here." <note>Cf. Isaiah 58:9.</note> And so, exulting in this, having obtained the Father's help in every respect, he henceforth begins the hymn of victory. After the "morning assistance" <note>A reference to the Psalm's superscription "At the morning dawn."</note> he makes this psalm, in which he says: 
» **I will declare your name to my brethren; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise.** 
As a prophet, then, he promises to his own disciples and apostles the good news of joy and exultation, calling them his "brethren." Consistent with this, Matthew also teaches, saying: 
» **And behold, Jesus met them**—clearly referring to Mary Magdalene and her companions—**saying, "Greetings." And they came up and took hold of his feet and worshiped him. Then Jesus said to them, "Do not be afraid; go and tell my brethren to depart for Galilee, and there they will see me."** 
And John, after the resurrection from the dead, also introduces Jesus saying to Mary: 
» **"Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brethren and say to them, 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God.'"** 
As a prophet, therefore, he says that he will declare the name of the Father to his apostles, whom he calls his own "brethren." And after them, in due order and sequence, he will teach the Father to the Church established throughout the whole inhabited world under his name...

<meta>catchword: ...and [κὲν]</meta>

<summary>Eusebius interprets Christ's plea for deliverance from symbolic animals (dogs, lions, and unicorns) as his struggle against the powers of death and Hades. He then transitions to the Resurrection, linking the Psalm's promise to declare God's name to his "brethren" with the Gospel accounts of the risen Christ meeting the women and disciples.</summary>
<keywords>Psalm 22, Christology, Hades, Resurrection, Unicorns, Cerberus, Mary Magdalene, Apostles, Humility, Emptying, Salvation, Lion's Mouth</keywords>

--- Page 989 ---
<meta>This page continues Eusebius of Caesarea’s commentary on Psalm 22 (Septuagint 21). On the previous page, Eusebius discussed the Savior’s plea for deliverance from symbolic enemies: the sword, the dog, the lion, and the horns of the unicorns. Here, he interprets the transition from Christ's suffering and prayer to his triumphant Resurrection and the establishment of the "Great Church" among the Gentiles.</meta>

<page-num>317</page-num>
<header>PROOF OF THE GOSPEL, BOOK 7 <note>original: "βιβ. ζ" — Although the header indicates Book 7, this section of the *Demonstratio Evangelica* is traditionally categorized as Book 10 in modern editions.</header>

And he promises a hymn; for just as if a teacher, distinguished in wisdom, were to deliver discourses in the midst of disciples so that they, having heard him, might obey—in the same way, he says, **"in the midst of the church I will sing a hymn to you,"** <note>Psalm 22:22</note> referring to the church that has learned and heard from him in the proper manner. They no longer serve the demons as before, but only the one, first God, whom he suggests by proclaiming Him. Having announced these things, he quite consistently leads the church and his own brothers to sing hymns to the Father. Therefore he says:
» **"You who fear the Lord, praise him; all you offspring of Jacob, glorify him."**
» And, **"let all the offspring of Israel fear him, for he has not despised nor been disgusted by the prayer of the poor man, nor has he turned his face away from me; and when I cried out to him, he heard me."** <note>Psalm 22:23-24</note>
Through these words, he clearly presented the deliverance from the aforementioned evils. For if God heard him when he cried out, and he had prayed to be rescued from the **sword** (regarding his soul), from the **dog** (regarding his only-begotten <note>original: "τὴν μονογενῆ" — referring to his unique life or soul</note>), and further from the **lion's mouth** and his humility from the **horns of the unicorns**, it follows to understand that he found deliverance from these things. Thus he says that **"God was not disgusted by his prayer, nor did He turn His face away from him, but heard him when he cried out."** Therefore, having been rescued from such great trials and from death, it was possible for his soul to dwell together with his own disciples and brothers, and to hymn the Father in the midst of the church. 

Observe again how he calls himself a **"poor man,"** <term>poor man (ptōchos): A title used in the Psalms to denote one who is humble and utterly dependent on God, which Eusebius applies to Christ in his state of human suffering.</term> in harmony with the previously cited prophecies through which he was named "needy" and "poor." But since he also presented his resurrection through these words, he turns his discourse back to the Father, saying:
» **"From you is my praise in the great church,"** <note>Psalm 22:25</note>
indicating the Church established in his name from among the Gentiles throughout the whole inhabited world. In this Church, the praise of our Savior is sung continually by the will and cooperation of his Father. Therefore he says, **"From you is my praise in the great church."** For this Church is truly "great," not being assembled from a small corner of people. Nor can the Synagogue of the Jews—or the assembly of the Circumcision—be compared to it in terms of the dignity and supernatural nature of its life, or the greatness of its doctrines. The Synagogue is diminished by a total poverty of reason, life, and thought, and by a forgetfulness of glory. 

Then he adds:
» **"I will pay my vows to the Lord in the presence of all those who fear him."** <note>Psalm 22:25</note>
By "those who fear him," he refers to the "great church" mentioned before, to whom he said, **"You who fear the Lord, praise him."** And what kind of "vows" does he say he will pay, other than those he promised? And what did he promise, other than those things through which he said, **"I will declare your name to my brothers, in the midst of the church I will sing a hymn to you"**? For his vows are the promises which he confirmed he would fulfill in the midst of the church. Following these things, he adds:
» **"The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and those who seek the Lord shall praise him; their hearts shall live forever and ever."**
» **"All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him."**
» **"For the kingdom is the Lord's, and he rules over the nations."** <note>Psalm 22:26-28</note>
Through these verses, he very consistently proclaims the successful achievements following his resurrection, which have indeed been fulfilled.

<sig>DDd.iii.</sig>

<summary>Eusebius interprets Psalm 22 as a prophecy of Christ's Resurrection and the subsequent rise of the Christian Church among all nations. He contrasts the "Great Church" of the Gentiles with the Jewish Synagogue, viewing the global spread of Christianity as the fulfillment of the Psalmist's "vows."</summary>
<keywords>Resurrection, Great Church, Gentiles, Synagogue, Poor Man, Psalm 22, Prophecy, Praise, Vows, Universal Mission</keywords>

--- Page 990 ---
<meta>This page continues Eusebius of Caesarea’s commentary on Psalm 22 (Septuagint 21). On the previous page, the author was discussing the Savior’s prayer for deliverance from the "horns of the unicorns." This page transitions to the fulfillment of that prayer through the calling of the Gentiles and the birth of the Church.</meta>

<page-num>138</page-num>
<header>E U S E B I U S</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<sig>DD iii.</sig>

<margin>
Eusebius
on the
*Preparation
for the
Gospel*.
<note>original: "de Præparatione evangelica" — While the margin attributes this to the *Preparation*, the content belongs to Eusebius’s related work, the *Proof of the Gospel* (*Demonstratio Evangelica*).</note>
</margin>

[...the prophecy has been fulfill]ed through the calling of the nations <term>nations: "ethne" (Gentiles)</term> from every side, and through the selection of men from the ends of the inhabited world. The outcomes of these events, when seen with our own eyes, serve as a clear demonstration of everything spoken through the Psalm. Furthermore, we are the **"poor,"** whom the Savior’s life-giving Word has nourished with the **conceptual and rational bread** <note>original: "τῷ νοητῷ καὶ λογικῷ ἄρτῳ" — This refers to spiritual or intellectual nourishment rather than physical bread.</note> for our souls, even though we were destitute from our very infancy, thereby providing us with eternal life. Therefore the Psalm says:
" **"The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and those who seek the Lord shall praise him; their hearts shall live forever and ever."** <note>Psalm 22:26</note>
And the epilogue of the entire prophecy, adding further details, says:
" **"The coming generation shall be announced to the Lord, and they shall announce his righteousness to a people yet to be born, whom the Lord has made."** <note>Psalm 22:30–31</note>
This clearly foretells the people gathered from the nations, and the generation established upon the earth through our Savior Jesus Christ. For who could this people be, who are said to be **"born to God"** after these events—a people who long ago did not exist, nor had any standing among men, but came into being later? What else could this generation be, which did not exist then but was said to be coming, if not this **Church** established throughout the whole world through our Savior? It is the new people from the nations, regarding whom the Holy Spirit spoke out in wonder through Isaiah, saying:
" **"Who has heard such things, and who has seen things thus? Has the earth travailed in a single day, or has a nation been born all at once?"** <note>Isaiah 66:8</note>

These matters, then—as we are hastening toward other subjects—we have run through and discussed in summary for the present time; let us now move on to the remaining parts concerning the manifestation of our Savior.
